Author: Abhinavagupta Commentator: Bhāskara Editor: Pandey, K. C.

Description: An electronic text derived from *Bhāskari*: A Commentary on Abhinavagupta’s *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī*. Edited by K. C. Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, whose body is consciousness.
Now begins the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī*:
First, from the stainless and full [Self], it manifests the "I" [which is free from desire].
And that which he desires through the two branches, in order to subsequently divide his own power (*kalā*),
belongs to him who possesses the states of opening, expansion, closing, and persistence from his own essential nature.
I bow to that non-duality, the entirety of which consists of the supreme Śiva and Śakti. (1)
The Bhāskarī.
Oṃ! The collection of principles (tattva), numbering sixty-six from Śiva down to the Earth, which has ascended into the domain of measurement within the thirty-seventh plane;
In the thirty-eighth step, and again in that same measure, the Lord, the playful one, ever victorious, shines as some supreme being who creates. || 1 ||

When the supreme state (parā) exists as one whose body consists of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action, and is intent upon manifestation, yet in the absence of that [supreme state], at the time of entering into the subsequent state (aparadaśā),
there arises from that the form of Māyā, which is the fourfold manifestation of the inferior state (aparābhāva).
Victorious is this three-formed Goddess, the Blessed Śiva-Śakti. || 2 ||

The All-pervasive One, having first manifested His own sovereignty— which is withdrawn into His essential nature, consists of the power of action (*kṛti*), comprises all objects, and is perceived within Himself as "I"— then, having emitted the flood of objects and grasped them as "this," [He experiences] this once again.
He who worships this [deity] in his heart manifests mastery over it.
Abiding in the pure state that reaches the stage beyond all affliction, he himself, out of compassion, having directly realized this [state],
manifested a twofold descent and brought about for me the manifestation of his dual nature.
Victorious is this Supreme Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, the protector who is easily attained through devotion to the Guru. || 4 ||
I bow to that Lord of the Gods who removes obstacles, to the deity Jñapti, and to the sandals of the Guru; likewise,
to the treasures of knowledge such as Kaulanarottama and others, and to my Guru, whose exertion has initiated this undertaking.
He who was born into the renowned and pure Rājānaka lineage of Kaṇṭhadhaumyāyana—
that twice-born man named Bhāskara composes this commentary on this newly arisen treatise.
Whether she is capable or incapable, O wise ones, this effort is undertaken by me for the sake of diversion; forgive me, for the conduct of the virtuous does not consist of envy or derision. (7)

For here it is heard that from the venerable Somānandanātha— who had the great secret of the instruction made as clear as a fruit in the palm of his hand through the most intense descent of the power of the Blessed Lord, and who had acquired the teaching of the scripture upon its contemplation— [the knowledge was received].

The illustrious Utpaladeva, having reached the pinnacle of perfection, composed the great treatise known as the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, consisting of verses that are like a reflection of the highly esoteric scripture titled *Śivadṛṣṭi* which was composed by his own guru.

Anticipating that the intended meaning [of the *Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya*] might be difficult to comprehend, he composed a commentary (*vṛtti*) titled the *Laghu-pratyabhijñā*, which was devoted solely to that [essential meaning]. Furthermore, for the sake of favoring those of duller intellect even therein, he composed an exposition (*vivṛti*) titled the *Madhya-pratyabhijñā*. And in that [work], for the benefit of all people—

The illustrious Ācārya Abhinavagupta composed an extensive commentary titled the *Bṛhat-pratyabhijñā*. Perceiving that people were incapable of investigating it, he himself composed a concise commentary on the *Pratyabhijñā-kārikā-sūtras*, renowned as the *Vimarśinī*.

But today, having observed that even there [in the previous work] there was difficulty in comprehension, I, Bhāskarakaṇṭha— the son of Śrīmad-Avatārakaṇṭha, who is himself the son of the illustrious Rājānaka Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha— have been impelled by the Blessed Lord, who has entered the intellect of his disciple.
Having performed the labor of plunging into the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā*— a work numbering one hundred and ten thousand verses—
and having heard the traditional instruction inherited from his own father as well as from the venerable Kaulanarottamas, [he composed this].

Having received the instruction in this knowledge, he has set out to provide its exposition; nor should he be made an object of ridicule by the best of scholars on the grounds of alleged unfitness, for even those who have composed works merely for their own amusement or for the instruction of their own children and others lack the authority [to critique such a work].

However, because the qualified practitioner is permeated by reverence, it is impossible for him to act [otherwise]; or, even if he were to act, what loss would there be on that account? Enough of this.
Now, the explanation:
Although he has attained firm establishment in the contemplation of the supreme reality that is his chosen deity, his mind is rendered helpless by the desire to favor those who are to be graced;
thus, the auspicious invocation consisting of the recollection of that [reality] serves as the cause for the completion of this work without obstacle.

From the state of non-manifestation (*parābhāva*), one perceives the level of *paśyantī*; from that, the level of *madhyamā*; and from that, it brings about the domain of *vaikharī* through the absence of appearances (*nirābhāsa*).
Thus, by being overcome with compassion for those to be graced, [the consciousness]—which is otherwise limited by objects such as the body and the subject—[becomes aware of the "I"].
It is a state established by the creative power of consciousness (*bhāva*), and not the nature of pure "I-ness" (*ahaṃ-rūpa*);
for in that [pure state], since it is impossible to impart instruction, its engagement [in such activity] would be illogical.
For this very reason, he is designated by the name Abhinavagupta. That—referring to the body described in the preceding half-verse containing the word "that" (*tat*).

Paramaśiva is the nature of pure light. Śakti is that which always flashes forth as the experiencer of its own such self-nature, whose body is the light of consciousness unconditioned by the ten directions, time, and so forth.
Śambhu’s own nature, the supreme Śākta reality, which is full of incomparable wonder and aesthetic flavor, triumphs in this world as that which is called Spanda.

According to this principle, there is for him such a self-reflection of his own nature as "I am this"; otherwise, like a crystal or similar object, he would fall into insentience when colored by objects. As he will say:
"Even though light is colored by objects, it would be comparable to a crystal or other insentient things [were it not for its own reflective awareness]."

Thus it is said. Although the state of being supreme belongs only to that which has internalized its own powers (*śakti*), nevertheless, that [supreme state] is to be known as belonging to that [consciousness] when it is extracted [from its powers], by virtue of its inherent fitness. Those two [powers], that is to say, having become one in flavor (*samarasībhūya*), constitute the "Self"—that whose nature (*svarūpa*) is such.
Although their unity is eternal and not merely occasional due to some particular cause, nevertheless—

This was stated by superimposing duality upon a single reality for the sake of instructing the disciple. Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is as follows: "That which is supreme" (*paramam*) refers to that which is higher than the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva; and "that which is [supreme]" (*tat*) refers to that whose nature consists of Śiva and Śakti.
Regarding *advaitam*: the state of two is "duality" (*dvitā*); that which arises therein is "dualism" (*dvaitam*). That which is not dualism is "non-duality" (*advaitam*), meaning oneness.

I praise that which is the foundational wall for the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), which takes the form of the thirty-seventh supreme Śiva-principle, and which is the state of aesthetic unification (*samarasībhāva*) that brings bliss to the world— praising it in accordance with the meaning of the root *vad*, "to speak" or "to praise," by making it the object of an eight-limbed prostration.

And I lead [him] to become the object of supreme esteem for all. For in the world, "abhivādana" (salutation) is conventionally established as a gesture of homage (*namaskāra*), since it is performed by uttering the words "I salute you" (*abhivādayāmi*).
Furthermore, "stuti" (praise) is the speaking of excellence; and that very [speaking of excellence], when it reaches an internal state, becomes "parāmarśa" (esteem). In that regard:

The meaning of *namaskāra* (salutation) is the state of being bowed down (*prahvībhāva*), and the recognition of [the Lord's] supreme excellence (*sarvotkarṣaparāmarśa*) is that which bestows upon Him fitness [for such salutation]. For the author himself will later state that one who is bent down in this or that way is indeed a bound soul (*paśu*). By the qualifier "entire" (*nikhila*), the future totality of all things, both insentient and sentient, is indicated.
This state of being composed of that [consciousness] has been described for one who is born [into it], because otherwise the fullness mentioned in the first half of the verse would be impossible.
He fulfills the expectancy for the word "that" with the phrase beginning with "from the non-manifest" (*nirābhāsāt*).
That which was previously mentioned as having such qualifications is non-duality (*advaita*); "from the non-manifest" means from forms such as Śiva, Śakti, and so forth.
"Emerging from appearances" means, in short, being free from conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as Śiva, Śakti, and so forth, due to its oneness.

And since that [oneness] also exists even in the thirty-sixth principle, Śiva-tattva, it is therefore said to be "full. Nevertheless, because manifestation cannot otherwise be accounted for, there is also the exclusion of all appearances through its being in the state of all things (*sarvabhāvena*).

If it is argued that the Śiva-tattva cannot exist [as such] because its nature is that of a pure light oriented toward fullness, then its very state of being without appearance (nirābhāsatva) is untenable. This would be so if the ocean’s state of absolute oneness were destroyed by the emergence of even a single wave. As it has been said:
"That which is empty yet as if non-empty, in which emptiness the world is situated—that emptiness which exists even amidst the flood of creation is the nature of the Supreme Self. Thus it is said.
And here, "fullness" refers to something internal, characterized by the fullness or lack of fullness of the external world once it has been encompassed within.

But it is not worldly, because that [worldly state], due to the possibility of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), lacks the appearance of fullness. He states the qualification "unmeṣa" (expansion) in order to make fullness itself the object of possibility.
By "unmeṣa"—that is, by the manifestation as separate from the Śiva-portion of the portion consisting of power (*śakti*) contained within Himself—there is "prasaraṇam" (emanation).

The movement [of consciousness] consists in its transition through the states of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth; likewise, by means of the "closing" (nimeṣa)—that is, by the re-establishment of the aspect of Śakti within the aspect of Śiva contained within itself—and "abiding" (sthiti), which is remaining in a state of identity within oneself; [the text says "from such"] because they partake of these. As it has been said:

In the Spandaśāstra: We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), by whose opening and closing [of his eyes] the dissolution and emergence of the universe occur.

Thus, it is only a cloth already filled with colors that is capable of displaying those colors, and nothing else. From such a nature—meaning from its own self—which does not follow after others, that is to say, which is unrelated to anything else; [this refers to] the form that serves as the material cause (upādāna).

"Know that family, O Omniscient One, to be devoid of Śiva and Śakti"—according to this principle, from the body which is the form of the Unsurpassed Family (anuttara-kula), "formerly"—that is, previously; although there is no contact with time here, it was nevertheless spoken thus for the sake of disciples who are subject to time. "I"—[refers to] that which is within oneself.
The aspect of power (*śaktibhāga*), which is conjoined with the self-reflexive awareness (*ahaṃvimarśa*), causes [the object] to shine forth; that is, while shining forth by itself—

being of the nature of the light called *Akula* (the Unstruck) which never deviates from Śiva— it impels [the object] therein through its own efficacious activity, for it is impossible for power alone to do so.

For indeed, the power of fire to burn is never observed to be effective in the absence of its essential nature (svarūpa) which is perceivable by the eye; and this is indicated by the use of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Furthermore, it is a marvel that that which is without appearance (*nirābhāsa*) can be the cause of manifestation.
And here, "manifestation" refers to the self-reflection (*svarūpaparāmarśa*) of Śiva, who is known as Light (*prakāśa*), consisting of that alone.
Because it is His power (*śakti*);

otherwise, it would be impossible for the "first vibration" (*ādyaspanda*) to be an object of verbal designation. For vibration is indeed a slight movement, and that, in the case of Śiva, is precisely the self-reflective awareness (*svarūpaparāmarśa*) of "I. As it has been said:
"The slight movement is just this: the self-reflection of one's own nature.

By this, the manifestation of the two principles known as Śiva and Śakti is stated, because the state of being Śiva arises from Paramaśiva himself when he is delimited by the function of being the illuminator; whereas [the state] of Śakti is...
This is indeed clear. In response to the expectation of what it does next, he states the second sentence:

"dviśākhām" (having two branches). Furthermore, immediately after that non-duality (*advaita*), it possesses two branches—because Śiva and Śakti manifest according to their respective natures, it is endowed with those two branches of that nature.

"His own portion" (*nijakalām*)— that is, his own part which is equivalent to the wheel (*ācakram*) consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), both those already arisen and those yet to arise, wherein the division between Śiva and Śakti has emerged. "To divide" (*vibhaṅktum*) means to make it the object of division by way of the thirty-four principles beginning with Sādākhya and ending with Earth (*kṣoṇī*).

He "aspires" (āśāste), which means he brings [the object] into the domain of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). In both instances, the use of the present tense is for the purpose of indicating continuity. It is precisely here that the emergence of the power of will occurs; therefore, because prior to this there exists only the two powers called Consciousness (*cit*) and Bliss (*ānanda*) residing within Śiva and Śakti.
However, since the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) are included within the thirty-four principles (*tattva*), they are not objects of aspiration.

Furthermore, in this context, the reading "nirāśaṃsāt" (from the desireless) is superior to "nirābhāsāt" (from the non-manifest), as it has been adopted by Śrī Jayaratha in his commentary on the *Śrī Tantrāloka*. And therein:
"From the desireless"—this should be construed as "from that which is devoid of longing due to its fullness.

Although in that context it was intended that Śrī Jayadratha’s state of having two branches consists merely of the two-fold reflective awareness of "I" and "this," nevertheless, that does not satisfy our mind. For the term *dviśākhām* (having two branches) is a reference made by means of a compound word functioning as a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Nor is it appropriate for that which is being established [to be the object of a command]. However, since the establishment of the two branches in the form of Śiva and Śakti has already been accomplished in the preceding statement, there is no fault in its restatement in the subsequent statement. If it is argued that there is indeed an injunctive indication here in the phrase "in order to divide one's own power into two branches," [we reply:]...
This is untenable. For here, one's own *kalā* (creative power) is indeed of the nature of the "I" (*ahaṃ-rūpa*); what two-branched division could there be of it?
This is because it exists by itself through the state of "I-ness. Nor is it logical for that very [power] to possess those branches.
Furthermore, at this time, it is only Śiva and Śakti—whose forms consist of the branches of the *kalā* of the unity of Śiva and Śakti—who [exist].
The reflective awareness (parāmarśa) that has been described belongs to the two forms of "I" and "the illuminator," not to the reflective awarenesses of "I" and "this. For here,
it is the reflective awareness of "I" alone— devoid of the awareness of "this"— that is accepted as being the Śakti.
This is because of the context, as this self-reflective awareness (*idamparāmarśa*) arises in the forthcoming state of Sadāśiva.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the power consisting of the 'I'-reflective awareness (*ahamparāmarśa*) may be a branch [of the tree], but how is it appropriate for the Perfect Śiva? To this we say: no.
This is the reflection of the wisdom of Śrī Somānandanātha, who resides like a pearl in the midst of the noble lineage of the venerable Traiyambaka.

This is because, from the perspective of the unity of Śiva and Śakti, each of them individually is incomplete; otherwise, it would be impossible to speak of the supreme reality as being non-different from Śiva. Indeed, there are scriptural injunctions of this kind.
As it has been said in the *Śrībahurūpagarbhastotra*:
Regarding the phrase "to the one who possesses the two extremes": for in that context, the term "two extremes" refers precisely to Śiva and Śakti. Thus, it is said in that very same [text]:
"Obeisance to you, Bhogapāṇi, whose self is worshipped by the lords of yogins."
To him whose form is made radiant by the exertion to shatter duality.

Thus it is said. And in that context, it is more appropriate for the word *bhoga* (enjoyment) to refer to Śiva as a branch (*śākhā*). Now, one might ask: "In that case, why did the venerable Jayaratha provide a different interpretation there? We reply: because it was unsuitable to describe the *śivatattva* (the principle of Śiva) as a branch. One might further ask: "Why do you not interpret it in this way as well?"
A doubt has been raised. True. We have indeed heard these arguments directly from the mouth of our Guru;
thus, relying upon the *Śrībahurūpagarbhastotra*, we proceeded with this bold undertaking. Enough, therefore, of playful disputations with great souls.
And here, I am the son named Abhinava; Paramaśiva is my father, known by the name Narasiṃhagupta;
and Śakti is my mother, known as Vimalā. Because they are visibly the very forms of Śiva and Śakti, the Self [is born] from those two who constitute its material cause.

That which has such a manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpaprādurbhāva*), namely that which pervades all limbs (*nikhila*); *advaita*—meaning a union in the form of non-duality; that is to say, their couple, mounted upon the primordial sacrifice (*ādiyāga*), is implied by the mention of the specific attributes. For it is well known that the parents of the author bore these names.
This is well-known, as it was stated by him himself in the first verse of the *Tantrāloka*: "I bow. To what?

To that which is "from the non-manifest" (*nirābhāsāt*)—at that moment, free from the manifestation of all objects due to the dissolution of the knowable. For this very reason, it is "full" (*pūrṇāt*), having attained satisfaction (*tṛpti*). Indeed, one who is devoid of any further longing is called satisfied. Likewise:
"Unmeṣaṇa" means looking outward; "prasaraṇam" means movement into ineffable states of being;

"nimeṣeṇa" means abiding within one's own self at the time of emission; "sthitiḥ" means resting in one's own essential nature, which is filled with bliss. "From such [a state]" means from that essential nature known as non-duality, which partakes in these [states].

From its own form— namely, the body called Abhinava, which is the object of the limited denotative word "I" (aham)— it "illuminated in the past," meaning it has illuminated; it manifested itself through the process of the secretion of the substances known as *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*.
He taught the scripture known as the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, which is perfectly pure and provides the means for the supreme human goal that requires no other witness.
Having learned this from the illustrious Lakṣmaṇagupta, I, Abhinavagupta, his disciple’s disciple, compose this brief commentary on that Sūtra.

And thereafter, he prays to divide his own portion— his own part in the form of a son— which has become two-branching through union with the bride, so as to make it possessed of divisions in the form of sons, grandsons, and so forth; [he uses] the present tense to indicate immediate proximity to the present.

For the continuity of one's own offspring is indeed exceedingly dear to parents; and by identifying the parents with Śiva and Śakti, it is stated that one has become a Yoginī. Indeed, in the Āgamas, at the time of ascending to the primary sacrifice (ādiyāga), both women and men maintain the conceit of being Śakti.

Furthermore, the conceit of being of the nature of Śiva (*śivabhāvābhimāna*) has been stated as something that must necessarily be performed for the purpose of producing a yoginī, a son, or a disciple who is fit for the instruction of the Śaiva scriptures.
As it has been said:
He who, while in the womb, possesses a body formed by such a union of the *kalikā*, is declared to be born of the Yoginīs; he is himself a devoted vessel of knowledge.
Thus [it is said]. And this matter, though unfit to be spoken because of its extreme secrecy, is as follows:
the Great Mother is the fresh creation resting upon the pure arts (vimalakalā), and the Father is the one whose body is full and whose radiant splendor is hidden within the five faces.
May my heart, which consists of the emission of existence vibrating from the union of those two, and which is the family of the unsurpassed nectar, throb forth!
Thus, this has been established by the author himself in the first verse of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, and it has been clearly explained by Śrī Jayaratha;
therefore, we too have revealed it here by way of mere indication, so that we alone are not subject to censure.

Having thus performed the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) concerning the supreme reality (*paratattva*), which consists of the contemplation of the excellence of total surrender (*prahvībhāva*), he announces the composition of the treatise by means of a sectarian mark (*tilaka*), preceded by an indication of the lineage of his venerable *maṭhikā*-guru, beginning with the words "Śrītraiyambaka," etc. His [the guru’s] disciple—

I, Abhinavagupta, the disciple of [Abhinava]gupta’s disciple, compose this brief—brief in terms of its words—commentary (*vivṛti*), which is an exposition in the form of a sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), upon those aphorisms (*sūtra*) consisting of verses (*kārikā*). Having done what? Having [honored] the venerable...

Lakṣmaṇagupta—[he was] the disciple of Utpaladeva bearing that name, [and thus] his own teacher; having learned from him—that is, having understood, which amounts to having studied. To the inquiry "Whose disciple was he? and "Whose aphorisms [did he study]?", he says: "The venerable Traiyambaka," and so forth. He—referring to the well-known Utpaladeva—who was an Īśvara.

The Supreme Lord is endowed with absolute excellence; that by which He is recognized is the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* (Recognition of the Lord). That which has this as its title is the treatise—the collection of verses (*kārikā*) that provide instruction.

He declared: "Out of compassion for his own follower, [the Lord] rescued him from ruin and brought him to the state of *vaikharī*. What is the scripture? It is that which belongs to the illustrious Tryambaka—the teacher of the Adhyardhamaṭhikā, known as Tryambaka—who is endowed with the powers (*siddhis*) such as *aṇimā*."
The *traiyambaka* (lineage of Tryambaka) is such that it is praised for being endowed with non-dual instruction;
the *vaṃśa* (lineage) is both a succession of disciples and a bamboo staff. For a lineage exists through both knowledge and progeny;
within it, there is a state of being composed of pearls—that is, having the nature of a pearl due to its extreme purity—which constitutes its very existence.
And the established status within the lineage is logical: for all the *maṭhikās* (monastic centers) number three and a half;

of these, two belong to Amardaka and Śrīnātha, one and a half to Tryambaka—of which one is through the son and the other half through the daughter—and [the remaining] belongs to that Śrīsomānandanātha.

"Consciousness"—the science of knowledge known as the *Śivadṛṣṭi*; its "reflection"—because it acts as its representative through having an identical intention. Furthermore, what is it? It is that of which there exists no other witness or perceiver superior (*uttara*)—that is, more excellent—to it.
The human goal—that which is called liberation (*mokṣa*), the purpose of man—is its means, that is, its instrument of accomplishment.

Furthermore, the state of being a witness for none other [than oneself] should be understood as liberation’s nature as Supreme Śiva; for no witness whatsoever can exist for it, since He alone is the witness for all. Moreover, it is perfectly stainless.

By virtue of expressing non-differentiation from the Pure [State], it is free from the impurity known as "differentiation" through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). By the term "Vijñāna," it is indicated that this teaching of knowledge has come down through the tradition (*sampradāya*). For this very reason, regarding those various commentaries composed by certain scholars who have exerted themselves in writing them here and there, whatever was done by whom, from that alone [the truth is to be understood].

If it is enjoined that a commentary must be composed by his disciples or others after they have studied it, then one's own sheer ignorance is being revealed; otherwise, the commentaries composed upon the Āgama scriptures spoken by the venerable Supreme Lord and the Vedas spoken by Brahmā would not be valid. For [a commentary] cannot be [authentic] in the presence of its author.

Someone has studied something; indeed, it is only possible by having properly studied the science of grammar and so forth. Otherwise, however, a person can only bring to the range of memory what little has been learned from the mouth of a teacher. As for one who always looks only toward the face of the teacher, his proficiency [is limited].

Only those with refined sensibility (*sahṛdaya*) are the authority. There certainly exists a dependence upon tradition (*saṃpradāya*) for the instruction of secrets; yet that [tradition] proceeds through whatever person and by whatever means, since otherwise its occurrence would be impossible. Furthermore, even injunctions made by those who act without such [tradition] and are characterized by ignorance lead only to folly. For [the words] of a fool—
Only fools laugh at this, for among the wise, mere equanimity toward such matters is appropriate;

therefore, enough with this flowery display of words that brings only dejection. Now, let it be granted that in this Pratyabhijñā-śāstra, there exists a foundation in Vāgīśvarī in the form of being preceded by a *maṭhikā*—that is, a lineage of gurus.
This [work] is for those who possess devotion to the teacher of the Maṭhikā, because he is an authority;

but as for those Vedāntins here who, devoid of faith in the teacher of the Maṭhikā, seek authorities in the form of the Śruti—what can we say to them? Truly, this [work] is not for them, who are devoid of faith.

Indeed, no discussion at all should be undertaken. For, if this discussion is not carried out with those who have established their firm conviction in the Sadāśiva-tattva— which, having emerged from the stage of Māyā, exists in proximity to the Śiva-tattva that you desire— then [what purpose would it serve]?

This [debate] should be conducted only with the Buddhists and others who abide in the *buddhitattva* situated below *māyā*. But how is it that they have already attained firm realization (*niṣṭhā*) up to the level of the *sadāśivatattva*? Listen, honorable sirs:
for they regard the very reality of Brahman—which is of the nature of existence, the nature of pure consciousness, and tranquil—as their state of ultimate rest.
They say thus, and so the Śruti declares:
"Brahman is Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
Of that very [Brahman] alone there is all-pervasiveness, its being the substratum of all, and its being the witness of all.
And they speak of its state of absolute oneness (*kevalatva*). Thus says the Śruti:
"The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings."
The overseer of all, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities.

Thus, because that very [Brahman] exists as the substratum for the manifestation of the entire world, they declare it to be devoid of internal, external, and other-differentiated distinctions. For so says the Śruti:
"Brahman is one only, without a second; there is not even a trace of multiplicity here."

Thus, that very reality, known as *Sat* (Being), is established as the thirty-fourth principle, the *Sadāśiva-tattva*, because the two principles called Śiva and Śakti reside above it, and the thirty-three principles beginning with Īśvara and ending with Dharaṇī reside below it. For it is indeed *San*— that which is of the nature of Being (*sadrūpa*).

And "Āśiva" means one who is slightly less than Śiva—meaning one who dwells near Śiva—due to having a nature of light devoid of self-reflective awareness (*nirvimarśa*), whereas Śiva has a nature of light whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
And that very state is the nature of tranquil consciousness; for "tranquility" (is as follows):

It is precisely their freedom from the agitation known as *vimarśa* that is desired [by them]. For they suspect that *vimarśa*, due to its nature as conceptualization (*vikalpa*), is itself an agitation. But this is not correct, because [agitation] consists only in an adventitious attribute of a different genus. For the Light (*prakāśa*) has "I" as its own object.
Reflection (*vimarśa*) is indeed its very nature. As he will state:
"They know reflection to be the essential nature of manifestation; otherwise, even if the light is colored by an object, it would be like an insentient thing such as a crystal."

Thus, as for the reflective awareness "I" directed toward an external object, it may indeed be described as being of a different nature due to the coloring by that external object, as adventitious, and even as subject to agitation (*kṣobha*); yet, in ultimate reality, even that is of the very nature of Light (*prakāśa*) according to the Śaiva system. And since nothing can cause agitation in that which is inherently potent, what further need is there to say more?

If it is argued that [the Lord] possesses the power to cause such agitation, we reply: no, for fire, though capable of burning, is not seen to be agitated by that act of burning; thus, they have not even mentioned this because they lack the necessary qualification.
If that is so, then they must be asked: in your view, is there identity between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman?
Either there is a difference, or else; if they speak only of difference, then silence should be maintained.

But if there is identity, then the authority of the Śruti must be invoked by you as well. [Objection: But was it not the authority of those [scriptures] that was questioned here? By them, in that regard—
This Self is Brahman;
it is truth, the conscious Self; that is truth and the Self.

Many such scriptural passages have been cited as authoritative evidence. If that is so, then it must be said that those very same passages are the authority for our recognition (pratyabhijñā) as well; for recognition indeed results in the realization of identity, since it is engaged in establishing the identity between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara). Now, [one might object: "Is recognition a valid means of knowledge?"
If it is argued, "Let it be so; however, regarding the arguments stated therein, the authority of scripture (*śruti*) must be cited," we reply:
where the proof for recognition is established by means of worldly convention alone, what need is there to postulate the authority of scripture?
As he will state:
"The path is new.

However, there is not even the slightest difference in the result by which a contradiction would arise. Now, it might be argued that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), in the form of unifying what appears as falling [into different categories], is not appropriate here. This is incorrect; for the Self indeed...

It is manifest and appearing; however, its state as the Lord, having been forgotten in the interim due to its own autonomy, is recognized as its object through the realization: "I am indeed that Lord. For even the Self, though appearing, certainly undergoes forgetfulness; otherwise, it would be like the maxim, "You are the tenth."
Because the instruction "That thou art" would otherwise be untenable. Furthermore, lordship (*īśvaratva*) is of two kinds: supreme and non-supreme.
Among these, the supreme "I" has the self alone as its object, whereas the non-supreme "I" has a limited subject as its object;
and "this" (*ayam*) has the object of apprehension as its object. As it has been said:
O Lord of All, your unprecedented state of supreme lordship triumphs in that it is devoid of anything to be ruled;
yet your other [state] is likewise such that this world exists.
The world appears in such a way that it does not truly appear.
Thus, that collection of powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth is merely a form of this [part]. As it has been said:
"Therefore, the direct rule is that he is endowed with the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) alone.
Although even for the individual soul (*jīva*), the reflective awareness of "I" exists by virtue of its own predominance, nevertheless, that...

For that which is called "ascertainment" (*viniścaya*) depends on a duality; according to the principle to be stated, it is not of the nature of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), because it is colored by a non-reflection on the identity of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Rather, it is precisely of the nature of non-sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). As for the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*) in its form as sovereignty—

All "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) is, by virtue of its essence being the "I," entirely devoid of any counter-correlative (pratiyogin). As he will state: "That reflective awareness which is the 'I' (ahaṃpratyavamarśa), though its nature is light (prakāśa), has speech as its body;
it is not a conceptual construction (vikalpa)."

Thus [it is said]. Now, an objection: the object of the individual soul (*jīva*) is clearly a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), consisting of the "I-reflection" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*) permeated by its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*); but how is it known that such [a state] exists for Brahman? True. First of all, even you yourselves assert that Brahman takes the form of the individual soul, according to the analogy of a spark of fire; from that [state],...
Because of the statement regarding the manifestation of the individual soul (*jīva*); otherwise, there would be the consequence of duality (*dvaita*). Likewise:

"Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva*), let me manifest names and forms"—thus, even the state of being a living self is said to belong to Brahman alone. And in that case, if [the scripture] were to speak of Brahman’s...

The soul possesses no power of grasping; from where could it come? For we observe that the power to burn a spark is preceded by the power to burn a massed fire. [Objection: But surely that power is manifested here through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body. [Reply: No, for smoke might even arise from water if it were conditioned by fuel. However, if limited existence were produced by limiting adjuncts, [it would follow that the soul's nature is not inherent].

It is said: let it be said. Furthermore, you yourselves must certainly admit the existence of the power of *māyā*. Is that [power] resident in the individual soul (*jīva*) or resident in Brahman? If it is resident in the individual soul, then it is illogical to say that the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman—which was already established prior to that [power]—was created by it. As it has been said:
Indivisible consciousness alone possesses the nature of both substrate and object;
for darkness that is already established, a subsequent [consciousness] is neither its substrate nor its object.
Thus [it is said]. Now, if it were established in Brahman, its purity would be undermined by impossibility.
As it has been stated:
"How could the universe appear if it were devoid of mutual conflict and destruction?"
Therefore, the Vedāntins have resorted to the view that this [world] is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), being exceedingly subtle.
But then, whose is this *māyā*? It belongs to Śiva; however, in that case, he would not possess the nature of Śiva (*śivatā*).
Now, one might object: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), *māyā* does not exist as any entity at all, by which...
There is no room for the objection you have raised; rather, that [ignorance] is indeed postulated because the difference that appears cannot otherwise be accounted for.

If it is asked, "In what form is it then postulated?"—if one says it is in the form of ignorance (ajñāna), then is that ignorance of the nature of a positive entity (bhāva) or of the nature of a negation (abhāva)?
This must be examined. If it were of the nature of the absence of knowledge, then what would be the use of it?

For the absence of a jar or similar objects is never said to be the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of anything. However, in the case of Māyā, its status as the locus of the world is asserted because it has Brahman as its object through the medium of projection (*vikṣepa*). And thus says the Śruti:
"Indra moves in many forms through his *māyās*.

Nor is it logical that pure Brahman should be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of an impure world; if it were logical, then we would welcome that conclusion. Thus, this [objection] amounts to nothing. Now, if it is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), what is the form of that entity?
It must be stated [that it is inexpressible]. If you say, "It is indeed inexpressible," then how was it spoken by you? If you say, "By way of its inexpressibility," then that too is Brahman alone;
for from it words turn back.

Thus, because the scripture declares that Brahman alone is inexpressible (anirvācya). [Objection: Let it be that he is indeed Brahman; what is the harm? [Reply: True. And in this way, even in your own view, it follows that Brahman itself is the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) of the world, since it is Brahman—acting through the agency of *māyā* as the substratum of the world—that serves as the locus of projection (*vikṣepa*).

Since Māyā is accepted as being Brahman itself, it must be stated that Brahman possesses the capacity to be the substratum of the world. Furthermore, it must be stated what the nature of that capacity is. If it is argued that it is identical with its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then what is the point of conceiving it as a "capacity"? For it is not appropriate to say that a thing itself is its own capacity. Moreover, [if it were identical to Brahman], the capacity would be of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).

It is clearly appropriate that [the nature of consciousness] consists solely of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because we observe that the capacity for reflective awareness exists within that aspect which is delimited by the intellect (*buddhi*). Furthermore, you yourselves maintain that the obscuration produced by *māyā* has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its locus and Brahman as its object. As it has been said:
"Indeed, ignorance (avidyā) is considered by those who know reality to have the individual soul (jīva) as its locus and Brahman as its object.

Furthermore, the obscuration of Brahman with respect to the soul is, in effect, an obscuration of the soul itself, because it is the soul alone that attains that state [of Brahman]; otherwise, the consequence would be the emergence of duality. And in that regard, [it applies] to that which is not occupied by the soul-nature of Brahman.

It follows by necessity that there can be no obscuration within one's own portion; that very [portion] is light. And light, without reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is as good as non-existent. As it has been said:
"Because your activity transcends conceptual construction, though you are perceptible, you have been forgotten."
Just as an object standing before one [is perceived] by a mind directed elsewhere.

Thus, that very [consciousness] is the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*). Now, if that is so, is its establishment here achieved through reasoning alone? Let it be; what is the harm? For even reasoning, when it is in conformity with scripture, is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As it has been said:
"Reasoning is the supreme limb of yoga."
Thus it is; and there is also a scriptural passage on this point:
"He thought."
"Omniscient," and so forth. For here, since there is no second [object], vision is intended to have itself as its own object;
and that very [vision] is the reflective awareness of "I. Indeed, the Blessed Lord, whose nature is consciousness, reflects upon Himself precisely as His own power.

It manifests the world through its own nature, just as water manifests itself through the state of waves. However, it lacks the capacity for self-reflection (*parāmarśa*) due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*). For that which is insentient is indeed devoid of reflection upon both itself and other objects.
But surely, even the perception of self and other is possible for it? This is incorrect; [for it is] devoid of reflection.
For perception (*darśana*) is indeed of the nature of reflection; and that is observed even in insentient things such as crystal, as he will say:
"They know the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) to be the very essence of manifestation; otherwise [it would be nothing]."
Even though light is colored by objects, it remains like an insentient substance such as a crystal.

Thus, even the knowledge that encompasses all objects consists here precisely of the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa) and the limited or unlimited reflective awareness of "this-ness" (idantāparāmarśa),
because it exists as knowledge itself, whose nature is self-luminosity. But surely, you yourselves [rely] on your own experience...

He too is consecrated everywhere; that must also be stated here. True. Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the very nature of self-experience, what need is there to speak of its experience? And in that regard, even Brahman is of the nature of experience alone:
"I am Brahman."

Thus, because that oneness is attained through immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), whereas otherwise only mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*)—such as "Brahman exists"—would remain; and since those two do not depend upon experience, their reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) likewise does not depend upon it. Furthermore, by the power of which light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is everything experienced?

There is a dependence on experience for those two; for it is not reasonable to require another lamp for the purpose of seeing a lamp, since that [lamp] is illuminated by that very [lamp]. Now, one might object: "This rule applies to illumination, but the rule regarding reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is what is being questioned. Oh, what a lapse!

Is it logical that there is any difference between *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), which consist respectively of the grasping of an object and the internal verbalization thereof? This he will explain later through hundreds of arguments; therefore, no further effort is required here. [Objection:
"In that case, how do you maintain that the *sadāśiva-tattva* is devoid of *vimarśa*? [Reply: True. For that—
It is conceived as the boundary between the two types of self-reflection (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*): that which is unmixed with "this-ness" (*idantā*) and that which is mixed with it.
For this very reason, it has been described in this way. For if its object were pure self-reflection, there would be the consequence of [the subject] becoming Śiva;
if its object were a self-reflection mixed with "this-ness," there would be the consequence of [the subject] becoming Īśvara and so forth. This applies to those situated below Māyā.

In this work, the author has composed a commentary on these sūtras, which, through its concise treatment of "I-ness" and "this-ness," aims at their essential meaning and provides an investigation thereof.
Therefore, for the sake of those of dull intellect, I shall provide this correct exposition of the meaning of the Sūtra in order to bring about their recognition.

The very question does not arise; for those two [the *ahaṃ* and *idam*] are grounded in the subject-object duality (*grāhya-grāhaka*) that lies below them, whereas here, the discussion concerns the *ahaṃ* and *idam* as they rest upon the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). However, in the investigation of ultimate reality, even Sadāśiva possesses an impurity, insofar as his self-awareness (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*) has not yet attained a state of absolute purity.
Logical consistency indeed exists [in our position]. However, the claim that it is devoid of that [logical consistency] was stated merely for the sake of providing you with consolation.
But even so, the Vedāntins have certainly not attained our desired thirty-eighth principle, which is the nature of Paramaśiva, since they have only attained the Śiva-tattva. True.

The Śiva-tattva alone is our desired goal; however, by describing it as distinct from the Śakti-tattva, it appears as if it were separate from that [Śakti]. Therefore, the thirty-seventh principle, which consists of their identity, is taught. And since that [identity] cannot be expressed in words, at the time of instruction—

Regarding the statement that there are thirty-eight [tattvas]: even if that [thirty-eighth] were also within the scope of instruction, since it would finally rest upon the thirty-seventh *tattva* itself, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, those Vedāntins who possess aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdayatā*) are asked this further question: "In the Veda spoken by Brahmā, by us..."

No investigation into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been undertaken [by you]. How then have you undertaken such an investigation regarding the scriptural tradition (*āgama-śāstra*) spoken by God? Even there, the search for the authority of revelation (*śruti*) is surely nothing but the work of a fool. If it is asked, "By whom was God seen as the author there?", one must say, "By whom was He seen even in the Veda? If it is argued that "He was seen by Sanaka and others," [we reply: so too [in our case].
If it is argued: "Why is this not tolerated even by the teachers of the monasteries (*maṭhikāguru*), since they too have seen [this]?"—[we reply:

"But surely they possess no authority (*prāmāṇya*). [Objection: "How then do they possess it? [Reply: "If you say 'because of acceptance by the great multitude' (*mahājanaparigraha'), then in this case as well, acceptance has indeed been made by Śrī Durvāsas and others. [Objection: "But in that case, it was accepted by many. [Reply: "True."

"Not everyone has the qualification for the great secrets"—let there be enough of this dispute, which is like raising a vetāla at the commencement of a rite for peace (*śāntikarma*). Furthermore, as even a child has said, [this is so] because it is distinct from the primary means; such is the summary of the secret.
Of what kind of object? One that is undifferentiated by place, time, and so forth, and likewise one that is the domain of a single designation. (1)
Now, regarding what was stated— that cognition has a single denotation as its object—

if that single denotation were to apply only to the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), then how could it be said that there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for every manifestation, given that there is indeed a manifestation consisting in the mixing of manifestations?

To quell the doubt concerning the "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa), he speaks in order to define, from the perspective of ultimate reality, that which is the object of knowledge for a means of valid cognition:
"It differs according to preference, according to need, and according to proficiency."
Even a mere appearance becomes a single object when established through synthesis.

Although the object perceived externally as "a jar" appears to be a single entity, it is not merely that much; rather, it also withstands being analyzed into distinct parts— whether through independent analysis, according to one's specific interest, or by relying on what was previously established.
In that regard, he provides the introduction to the third verse in three ways, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu ca*). Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

In the domain of a single designation— that is, in the domain of a single name— when that [name] is uttered, it refers to the external particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the unique essence of the thing distinct from its general form, and not to the general form itself. What has been said?

In response to this inquiry, he says: "with respect to each manifestation" (*pratyābhāsam*). "With respect to each manifestation" means with respect to every individual manifestation in the form of subjects (*dharmin*) and attributes (*dharma*). [The word] "such a doubt"—that is, a doubt of this kind—is [addressed] by the phrase "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthataḥ*), which refers to what was stated previously.

The laxity of the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been indicated. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "according to one's preference" (*yathāruci*).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

He establishes the method for explaining the verse with the words "yadyapi" (although). "Tāvāneva" means "only one. Then, in response to the expectation of how large this [one] is, he states another position with the words "api tu" (but rather). "Pṛthaṅnirbhajyamānatām" means the state of being the object of separate division.

"Assuming many forms" means up to that point. In response to the question "How so?", he begins the justification with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). While providing this justification, he explains the verse with the words "Or independently" (*svatantraṃ vā*).
He explains "according to one's liking" (*yathāruci*) by [the word] "independently" (*svatantram*), and he explains "according to one's desire" (*yathārthitvam*) by [the same].

Regarding the phrase "due to the state of being an object" (*arthitva*), he explains it as "according to linguistic convention" (*yathā-vyutpatti*) by means of "relying on established usage" (*prasiddhi-upajīvanena*).

This means "in relation to what was previously established. In each respective case, when a threefold analysis is performed, the appearances (*ābhāsāḥ*) manifest distinctly; but if this is so, how [is it otherwise]?

What is the one particular characteristic? It is said: although those manifestations appear separately, that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which serves as their vitalizing principle sometimes rests in each individual manifestation; at that time, there is the apprehension of both the higher and lower universals (*sāmānya*).

[The discourse on higher and lower universals—K. Ṣ. Ṣ.]: Furthermore, when at times there arises a reflective awareness (vimarśa) whose essence is a blending [of these]—expressed as "this is thus" here—by establishing a relationship of subordinate and predominant [factors], then that is a single particular (svalakṣaṇa).

The word *api* has a different grammatical function; it refers to that single reality which has been established through the investigation and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of its integration with the three aforementioned modes. Thus, the three modes are presented in the following verse.
"This will indeed be shown" [is stated] in the *Harṣacarita* during the description of the region named Śrīkaṇṭha;

although these three types are present there, they have not been shown here for fear of prolixity. Here, the student asks a question: "But if this is so... He provides the answer: "It is said," thus stating the proposition (*pratijñā*).

"He makes them fruitful" means he makes those appearances—namely, the aforementioned appearances in the form of space and so forth, and not others that exist by virtue of distinctions such as preference—fruitful.
"Vimarśa" (reflective awareness) refers to the reflective awareness: "This is a jar; this is a jar."

"Anuprāṇitabhūtaḥ" means that which bestows existence by way of being the apprehender; "pratyābhāsam" means in every manifestation, where there is a grasping of each one according to its own nature, free from the synthesis of them as primary—this is the meaning. "Tadā" means at that time.

The apprehension of both higher and lower universals— the apprehension of the two types of universals, namely existence (*sattā*) and the form of cowness (*gotva*) and so forth— occurs such that the apprehension of existence through the apprehension of "existent" is entirely distinct [from the apprehension of the specific universal], because there is no synthesis here in the form of "this is existent."
Likewise, in the case of other universals (aparasāmānya), the apprehension of place and time is distinct for each, just as before:

the apprehension of the universal "cowness" in the word "cow," the apprehension of the universal "whiteness" in "white," the apprehension of the universal "moving-ness" in "moving," and the apprehension of the universal "Dittha-ness" in "Dittha"— all these are indeed distinct from one another here.

Because there is no apprehension [of the object] through such a synthesis as "the cow is white, moving, and named Ḍittha. Furthermore, in another sense— that is, by establishing the relation of primary and subordinate (guṇapradhānatā),
which is to say, by bringing about the state of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva)— here, in this place and time, this—
This object is thus endowed with these qualities; "the life-force of conjunction" means the life-force of unification.

Its "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) is its unique nature, because it is impossible for anything else to be the qualificandum (viśeṣya) in that particular place and so forth—this is the intended meaning. The particle *api* has been displaced in the sequence.
Showing that [the result] is accomplished through investigation (*anusandhāna*), he explains it with the words "by means of investigation" (*anusandhānena*).
He explains the constituent part "investigation" (*anusandhāna*) by the word "mixture" (*miśratā*). He establishes the connection of the locative case with the word "therein" (*tatra*). *Ati*—...

In that regard, even when there is only a single thing whose nature is its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) indeed differs without overstepping [the constraints of] inclination (*ruci*)—which is autonomy; purposefulness (*arthitva*)—which is being under the sway of a desire for causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*); and proficiency (*vyutpatti*)—which is reliance upon the linguistic usage of elders. || 3 ||

To demonstrate *how* and *where*, he says: "Just as appearances—such as those of a tall, round, upright person, smoke, or camphor—are differentiated according to the distinctions of place and time. (4)
Furthermore, he provides a restatement because of its difficulty of comprehension, saying: "even in one [even in that one].

Thus, the clear interpretation here is as follows: when even a single object has been established through mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and even though the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is one—is present, it is mixed with attributes such as place and so forth; then, according to one's preference—

According to one's inclination, likewise according to the pursuit of one's own purpose as desired by the seeker, and likewise according to linguistic proficiency and conventional usage, appearances (ābhāsāḥ) differ with respect to that single object; otherwise, [it would not be so] in the case of a single person in the *Harṣacarita*.
Because it is not appropriate to describe the region known as Śrīkaṇṭha as being a concert hall or the like;

and likewise, since it was raised in the introduction that even a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), though distinct with every manifestation, can be the object of a single designation, by means of that [point].

The sense is that it is logical to state that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is unfit to have a conceptual appearance as its object, and to establish that only the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is the object of a means of valid cognition. || 3 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the fourth and fifth verses with the words "Where, how? (kva yathā). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the word "long" (dīrgha).
In the same way, the various appearances—such as the existence of a jar, its substantiality, its golden nature, and its brilliance—which produce distinct effects, are the referents of words. (5)

In this regard, even with respect to a single individual essence of a person (puruṣasvalakṣaṇa), which is well-known as being conscious, one sometimes contemplates its very length— the state of pervading an extended space— which exists even in young people,
and its nature of being without joints or bonds.
Or circularity, which is possible even for stones; or upwardness, consisting of the act of ascending toward the upper direction, which belongs even to a pillar;
or the capacity for independent states such as going and coming.

The state of being a person (*puruṣatva*) is that which is common to other persons as well; for instance, one might act in such a way by means of independent will or by means of a form of inclination (*ruci*),
just as it has been stated.
Regarding this, the commentary— arising from its own natural flow because the mind’s essence consists in non-distraction—
explains the member of the compound "long" (*dīrgha*) with the word "here" (*iha*). [It refers to] the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the person (*puruṣa*).

—In the unique essential nature of the Person (*puruṣa*). Although consciousness is not logically appropriate for a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is nevertheless stated thus by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). "Pervading an extended space" means having the form of pervading a vast area; for that which is long is what pervades an extended space.

In our system, anything that is logically consistent is indeed authoritative; what need is there to mention the authority of this great secret scripture which brings about the supreme good? As it was said by the venerable Vasiṣṭha:
"Words endowed with reason should be accepted even from a child;
the rest should be rejected like straw—even so it was said by the Lotus-born One."

Thus, the long-desired state of being "sensitive to the heart" (*sahṛdayatā*) has been realized by the Vedāntins. But as for that person who, even by this [work], has not attained that state—that self-deceiver—to him one must simply offer salutations; enough of this elaboration.
Whether it be in one of small intellect everywhere, or in some place in one of very great intelligence—
Or rather, it would not be beneficial even elsewhere, but only within its own self.

Now, one might ask: "In these very sūtras, the author first composed a commentary (vṛtti), and subsequently he himself composed a sub-commentary (ṭīkā) upon that; and you have now composed a commentary on that sub-commentary.
Why has this effort been undertaken, which is like grinding what is already ground? In response to this expectation, he says by means of the *vṛtti*:

And so forth; the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Since [this was stated] by the author of the *Pratyabhijñāsūtra*, the venerable Utpaladeva, by means of a *vṛtti*—wherein a *vṛtti* is defined as "abiding in the mere intended meaning" (*tātparya*), and by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a work centered on that [meaning] is called a *vṛtti*—by such a [work], [it is shown that] these sūtras have this [intended meaning] as their purport (*abhiprāya*).

The meaning is as follows: "pravṛttāni" (set forth) means "dṛbdham," which is to say, explained by means of a textual composition (*grantha*). Furthermore, the investigation of that very [work] is the "tātparyavivekaḥ" (discernment of the purport). It is called a *ṭīkā* because "one understands the meaning by means of it" (*ṭīkyate 'vagamyate 'nayārthaḥ*). By that [commentary], [the work] has been composed; however, the intention is not that the true meaning of the aphorisms (*sūtra*) has been fully revealed. Therefore—

For that reason, I, named Abhinavagupta, having made clear and explicit the meaning— the literal sense— of the *sūtras* (the *kārikās* which consist of mere indications), in this manner— by means of the method about to be described— herein, of the *Pratyabhijñā*.

I shall provide an exposition for the sake of discernment—that is, for the purpose of distinguishing—the Lord who is the expressed meaning, appearing as the continuous thread of "I am He" that manifests; this exposition will be directed toward those of dull intellect, meaning those whose minds are incapable of understanding the meaning of the aphorisms through the primary commentary (*vṛtti*), the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), or even the sub-sub-commentary (*taṭṭīkā*). I shall explain it.
I shall not subject it to the state of being an object of further explanation; for this is a form of the root *khyā* preceded by the prefix *vyā* in the *lṛṭ* (future) tense.
Thus, the meaning is that this effort does not amount to the mere grinding of what has already been ground.
This is because this work, titled *Vimarśinī*, [is established] by the very root scripture itself.

Having understood that the ultimate purpose and so forth— which serve as the cause for the uninterrupted engagement of the multitude of disciples— are accomplished without effort, [the author] nevertheless directly presents the determination of the intermediate purpose and the qualified candidate for this work in order to initiate its commentary, stating "everywhere. This refers to the *Pratyabhijñāsūtra* which is about to be composed.

The commentary is named *Vimarśinī*. Regarding the phrase "among those of little intellect"—that is, among all those of dull understanding—by this he has dispelled any pride in his undertaking the composition of this great work. Recalling that the cause of its difficulty resides in the intellect [of the reader], he says: "even for one of very great intelligence. Even for those of very great intelligence...

Having understood its rarity, he says "anywhere" (*kvāpi*). Fearing that even when it is obtained, one might be seized by stinginess, he says "or not" (*na vā*). To the objection, "In that case, is this [teaching] not then useless?", he says "but rather" (*api tu*). But rather...
This is intended to highlight another alternative position; by means of her arising within himself—
through his devotion and immersion—
the author has directly perceived her, whose power is seen within his own self (*aparokṣātmani*).

Desiring to transmit to another that state of identity with the Supreme Lord— whose power has been witnessed— and considering the attainment of that state to be free from obstacles through the prior surrender of one's own self-identity,
[he acts] as a remnant of the contemplation of total devotion to the excellence of the Supreme Lord.
He indicates the purpose [of the teaching] with the intention of bringing about the fitness for identity with the Supreme Lord:

"Toward those equal to one's own self—such as sons and disciples—it should be beneficial," meaning it should perform the benefit known as diversion and awakening. And thus, this benefit is the intermediate fruit.

The one who desires that [liberation] is the intermediate qualified seeker (*avāntarādhikārī*). Because this is a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the text, the connection (*saṃbandha*) and the subject matter (*abhidheya*) are the primary ones, not even the intermediate ones. Although this very same purpose was already stated in the previous verse by the phrase "for the sake of discerning recognition" (*pratyabhijñā-viviktaye*), nevertheless, by means of the words ending in the locative case...
In accordance with the determination of the qualified authority already established, this has been made manifest right here.
Now,
[the nature of] the unimpeded contemplation of the supreme excellence and the state of total surrender toward the object of the venerable *paratattva*—

Aiming toward the commentary on the verses concerning the nature of the *pratyabhijñā* (recognition) and so forth— which constitute the composition of this treatise that possesses the fourfold connection (*catuṣṭaya-anubandha*) for the purpose of concentrating the minds of listeners intent upon the performance of auspicious rites (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) as a cause for the completion of the work he intends to begin— he first [offers] that which is useful for introducing it.

The author provides an introductory transition (*avataraṇikā*) in the form of highlighting that which is to be described there, for the purpose of consoling the minds of his disciples who are filled with haste,
by means of the words beginning with "the author" (*granthakāra*). "The author" (*granthakāra*) refers to one who is the creator of the treatise (*grantha*).

The illustrious Utpaladeva [refers to] that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) which consists of the state of being bowed down— the condition of servitude denoted by the term "servant"— toward the excellence of the Supreme Lord, who is the thirty-seventh principle in the form of Paramaśiva; this excellence being the state of being superior to all other principles, as expressed by the term "Maheśvara."

"Reflection" (*parāmarśana*) occurs through the sequence of description and illustration; its "subsidiary nature" (*śeṣatayā*) means by way of being a constituent part (*aṅgabhāvena*), that is to say, as a qualification (*viśeṣaṇatvena*). The "purpose" (*prayojana*) is the reality that motivates the *Pratyabhijñā* treatise, which is expressed by the words "the totality," and so forth. He "frames" (*āsūtrayati*)—that is, he binds—it within the sentence of connection.

This is clear from its application as a specific qualifier of the state of servitude (*dāsya*). By this, the fact that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is the primary goal (*śeṣin*) is stated by implication; for if the purpose (*prayojana*) were the primary goal, there would be an indication with the dative case.
Here, the third case is used in the sense of "being in such a state. By what cause? It is that identity (*tādātmya*) with the Supreme Lord. That...

The vibration of the mind as "I am indeed thus" is the state in question; the attainment of its fitness—its realization regarding the object—is brought about by the intellect acting as the cause. This means: having formed this cognition.
For it is precisely through this [cognition] that the person possesses the qualification (*adhikāritva*) with respect to the purpose.
Having somehow attained the service of Maheśvara, desiring to benefit even ordinary people, [I shall compose this work] which is the cause for the attainment of all prosperity.
I shall establish that recognition. || 1 ||

Because length is impossible [in that case], it must refer to a state when it is sometimes endowed with such qualities as being long [i.e., "taducitādyavasthāyām" in the commentary C]. Now, one might object: "Let that very length be its essential nature (svarūpa).
To this he says: "yā" (which). And thus, it is not logical for that [length] to be its essential nature.
The state (*bhāva*). He explains the component "vṛtta" as "niḥsandhi.

This refers to the nature of being without joints or bonds—that is, the form of absolute unity—and "ūrdhvatā," which is loftiness; and therein lies that independent state—autonomy—regarding going, coming, and so forth.

That which has such a form is that whose nature is fitness (*yogyatā*). Here, he begins the justification with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). By independent will—that is, by mere desire devoid of any consideration of purpose. Regarding the term "inclination" (*ruci*): one should act in whatever way [the inclination dictates], such as [perceiving] "this is long," and so forth.

The meaning is that one should conduct legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*). Here, he cites the words of the Elder (*vṛddha*): "As it has been said. The meaning here is this: that is what constitutes *rucir* (consent). What is that? It is that which arises from the mind—the heart—because its essence consists in distraction, that is, because its essence consists in agitation; by virtue of that agitation, [it is established].
It arises spontaneously—that is, it arises without depending on a specific purpose.

Or rather, one might differentiate objects that pervade an extensive space by seeking a causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) characterized by concealment; such is the case in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

One who desires to understand, or one who wishes to instruct another, as to what kind of long name is recited by the elders, should make a distinction. Such is the differentiation among appearances therein. However, the single specific characteristic (*ekasvalakṣaṇa*) resides in a single appearance of space.
And because [consciousness] rests in the appearance of time, it is precisely the appearances of space and time that,

by virtue of their proximity to the negation of pervasiveness and eternity— which are the causes of the nature of a universal— bestow the nature of a particular. In this way, like "human-ness" (*puruṣatva*), other [universals] as well...

Even the semblances (ābhāsas) such as "brāhmaṇa" and so forth are to be examined; thus, in this context, there exists a more well-known distinction of semblances, insofar as they serve as the locus for a great many properties common to both the insentient and the sentient. For at times, indeed, a person, under the influence of agitation—
One employs whatever word is at hand regardless of its specific purpose;
and such linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is preceded by a mental appearance (*ābhāsa*), since otherwise its utterance would be impossible.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion [of the section]. [The text speaks of] "objects" (*arthān*)—that is, entities—that extend over a wide space, meaning they are long.
Characterized by concealment—
meaning having the nature of disappearance— desiring it— that is, longing for it— thinking thus,
"This is long," one who is seeking to understand in this way brings about his own understanding by himself.
Desiring to do so—what is it? By the elders—the agents—it is asked:

what kind of thing, called "long" (*dīrgha*), is sung as being of such a nature? Or, on the other hand, desiring to instruct another—that is, wishing to bring about their proficiency—he [proceeds with] the division.

One should perform the analysis [thinking], "This is long. By this, it is indicated that at the very time of producing the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), that convention serves as the cause for its manifestation. He provides the conclusion:
"In this way"—that is, there, in a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a person. [Objection: But in that case, unity would not exist...

In response to the expectation of how this is "proper," he explains the phrase "in the midst of those distinguished by space and time" with the word "one. "From rest" means from the resting of cognition in the form "this is situated here. To the question "Why? he says: "Space," and so forth.

The "proximity of the refutation" (*savidhā vṛtti*) refers to the operation— namely, the destruction— of those two properties, *pervadedness* (*vyāpyatva*) and *eternality* (*nityatva*), which are the causes for the nature of being a universal (*sāmānyarūpatā*), by means of establishing their limitation (*parimitatā*). Among these, the refutation of pervadedness is effected through [the analysis of] space.

The sequence should be understood as follows: by means of time, there is the refutation of permanence. "Specific form" refers to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). He extends this same principle (*nyāya*) to other properties residing in the person by saying "in the same way. "More well-known" means known to a superior degree. Why?

To this inquiry, he states the reason: "because they are insentient" (*jaḍāḥ*). This is common to both the sentient and the insentient—since it applies to sentient beings such as persons (*puruṣa*) and so forth, as well as to non-sentient things such as trees (*taru*) and so forth.
By this illustration, [it is shown that] even in the case of smoke, there is the property of being smoke (*dhūmatva*) and the property of being produced from wood (*cāndanatva*).
The well-known varieties of manifestation, such as those arising from *śrīkhaṇḍa* sandalwood and others [the term *candanatva* is noted in K. ṣ.
ṣ.], are to be distinguished. By means of a well-known example, even in the case of an unfamiliar object such as a jar, there likewise exists a distinction between its various parts of manifestation.

For instance— when one sees a jar while experiencing as it were a breaking of the heart at the thought that "nothing whatsoever exists here," [it is] because of the state of having as its locus those very numerous properties— which exist in common [with other things] and consist of forms such as length and so forth— that is, because of the fact of having them as its basis.

The meaning is "because that is its object. He provides an introduction to explain the portion beginning with "smoke" by means of the phrase "by this": by this illustration—that is, by this example—the nature of smoke (*dhūmatva*), the nature of being produced from sandalwood (*cāndanatva*), and the fact of having arisen from sandalwood are [established].
And [qualities] such as "arising from *śrīkhaṇḍa* white sandalwood" are to be divided— that is,

they are to be made objects of division according to the objects of one's desire and so forth; in that regard, the division occurs in such a manner that one who desires blackness [seeks] "smokiness," while one who desires fragrance [seeks] "being sandalwood," and so on.

It must be established. Furthermore, the well-known nature of difference here—such as that between "smokiness" and "being made of sandalwood"—is evident because it appears clearly as distinct due to being apprehended by different sense organs;
for difference is not more clearly manifest when residing in a single object. This is why the superlative suffix *tarap* is used here.
By relying on two examples, one more well-known and one well-known. || 4 ||

He explains the second verse in order to state the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*), beginning with the word "well-known" (*prasiddha*). That part which is not well-known is the "unestablished part" (*aprasiddhabhāga*);
and its lack of establishment here is due to the fact that the jar manifests only as a single unity.
However, because there is no manifestation (*prākaṭya*) of the distinction between the appearances (*ābhāsa*) residing therein;

even in that case—that is, even regarding that jar—there is a distinction among the portions of appearances, namely those consisting of existence, jar-ness, and so forth. It is precisely this distinction among the portions of appearances...
He demonstrates this with the words "tathā hi" (for thus): undergoing *hṛdbhaṅga*— that is, the breaking of the heart—
he perceives, due to the non-perception of the real object, only the appearance of existence (*sattvābhāsa*) as "this exists," and other appearances.

However, it is not respected even by its name; likewise, for one seeking water, there is the appearance of a jar; for one seeking an object capable of being independently carried or brought, there is the appearance of a substance; for one seeking value and so forth, there is the appearance of gold; and for one seeking attractiveness, there is the appearance of brilliance—and so on, as indicated by the inclusion of "etcetera."

One who desires a more firm state of being should regard it as an appearance of firmness; in this same way, it should also be applied to inclination (*ruci*) and proficiency (*vyutpatti*). Thus, these various appearances (*ābhāsa-bheda*) alone are the reality (*vastu*), because the essence of reality consists in the state of appearing. Furthermore, that which constitutes the very life-force of an appearance...

That reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) too rests upon each individual manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*), because the word— whose nature is internal discourse (*abhijalpa*) and which is renowned as the very life-force of cognition— rests upon each individual manifestation;
for it is precisely in this way that the heart of the person is broken open, [revealing] the manifestation of being (*sattvābhāsa*).

It does not attend to other forms, such as "pot-ness" and so forth, because here the object of desire and the object of cognition is merely the existence of that [substance] itself. Likewise—in the same manner—it is independent with respect to the suitability of the substance for actions such as bringing it [to oneself], etc. (reading *dravyasyānayanādi* based on the manuscript C).
