Thus it has been said. The phrase "is respected" (*ādriyate*) is to be applied everywhere. Regarding the expression "one desiring value and so forth" (*mūlyādyarthī*):

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the making of various ornaments and the like is included. Regarding the term "splendor" (*aujjvalya*): one becomes radiant and pleasing to the heart. He states the object to be understood by the word "and so forth" as "firm" (*dṛḍha*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such [statements] as "one desiring purity through mere water" and "the appearance of fitness for fetching water.
He extends the application of "desire" (*arthitva*) to "inclination" (*ruci*) and "proficiency" (*vyutpatti*) by means of the word "thus" (*evam*). "Thus" means "like desire. In that regard:
Because proficiency exists only at the time of training, and because inclination consists essentially in the distraction of the mind,
the direct application [of the teaching] is shown, since interest alone is primary in all worldly transactions. In that regard,
by means of the application of two well-known and less well-known locations, [the teaching is established] in the middle among those things that are well-known.
It should be understood that even the application [of a means] to its proper place is indeed effortless. He provides a conclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*).

When the question arises as to why this is so, he says: "because of manifestation" (*ābhāsa*). The underlying sense is that an object which has not been made an object of manifestation cannot truly be an object. [An objection: But let this matter belong to manifestation alone.

In response to the inquiry as to whether there is a distinction or not for the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that arises immediately after that [perception], he explains the phrase "the word of sound" with the words "even that which... The term *prāṇabhūta* means "that which constitutes the life-force"; the sense is that without reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), a manifestation (*ābhāsa*) is indeed as good as non-existent.

The phrase "precisely for each manifestation" means that [the word] becomes indeed distinct. To the question "Why?", he says: "of the word. This refers to that which consists of internal discourse (*abhijalpana*)—that is, having the nature of verbalization, meaning having the form of articulate speech (*vyaktavāk*). By this...

The objection regarding the sound of the ocean and so forth is refuted. Since the word is rooted in reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), when establishing the differentiation of individual manifestations, reflective awareness itself is established effortlessly; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

"An existent jar is red," and so forth. Even the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is restricted to each individual manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); for by the manifestation of "existence," there is merely the accomplishment of the avoidance of the heart's breaking [from fear], while therein [occurs] another manifestation...

That dependence exists because, when a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is to be accomplished by means of the appearance of fire, there is a necessity of depending on another fixed (or unfixed) appearance, just as in the case of the appearance of a vessel, since that [appearance of fire] is invariably concomitant with other appearances.
Thus, by whichever aspect...

An object is investigated by this or that [means], because it appears as nothing more than a mere appearance; thus, through such manifestation and reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), there is purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Alternatively, it is stated thus because of the very apprehension of the word-sound (*dhvani*). Having enacted a state of rest, he demonstrates it:

Regarding the word "sat" (being): by the word "etc. (*ādi*), terms such as "substance" (*dravya*) are included, and these are to be construed as qualifiers of "resting" (*viśrānti*). Explaining that even the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) varies according to each manifestation, he comments on the phrase "performing different functions" (*bhinna-artha-kārin*) with the word "object" (*artha*). In that context, [he explains] that through the persistence (*anvaya*) of one thing, [there is the persistence] of another...

The summary is as follows: that which possesses positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) through its own absence, necessarily possesses the capacity to perform that action. Here, the author provides the reason for this by stating "only the appearance" (*sadābhāsa*).
By the suffix *-mātra*, [the author excludes] the purposeful action such as fetching water, which is to be accomplished by appearances such as jars and the like.
[This is] without expectation. Now, its existence is indeed desired by someone for some purpose, such as fetching water;

however, that which is directed toward the Supreme Lord—this prostration characterized by the application of body, speech, and mind to Him alone as their sole object—is the meaning of *namaskāra*. And that...

It is appropriate for an authoritative person to act in such a way, provided they perceive the excellence of one who is worthy of universal homage; otherwise, this is the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) used in the sense of a cause. As for the fact that bowing down is the cause for the unimpeded completion [of the work], that is self-evident.

[This] is to be applied [to the following]. What kind of author is he? One who has "directly perceived"—that is, established through self-awareness—the power within himself; that is, one whose power is the capacity for the attainment of all prosperity. Otherwise, it would be nothing more than mere deception; [he is the author] of that [work].

"By the Supreme Lord"—that is, by the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*)—[he intends] that "state of being composed of That," which is oneness (*ekībhāva*). "To another"—that is, toward people—"desiring to transmit"—meaning desiring to cause [that state], which is naturally radiant in consciousness, to manifest in their minds by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). For otherwise, it would not be the case that he "desires to benefit even ordinary people."

The intended meaning is that one should say this. For service (*upakāra*) is indeed the state of being absorbed in that (*tanmayatā*), which takes the form of servitude (*dāsya*). Furthermore, what is it like?
It is the offering of one's own identity—that is, absorption in the Supreme Lord—which is explicitly stated in such verses as "having attained servitude to the Supreme Lord" and so forth.

"That which precedes it" refers to that [work]. "Without obstacle"—meaning easily—he considers that attainment to be the realization of identity with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) among people; for this very reason, the ellipsis is "performing that [work].
However, since the promise to compose the *Pratyabhijñā* (Recognition) is explicitly stated here, any further discussion on that point would be redundant.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "In some way" (*kathaṃcit*).
Here, the commentary states:
in order to dispel the doubt among the ignorant as to why he does not offer salutations [at the beginning], he is about to explain the verse.

"Māha iha," etc. He is the One—the Supreme Lord. That which has Him as its sole object—that is, that which has Him as its support—is "tadekaviṣayatā" (the state of having Him as its sole object). The application to that—meaning the impelling toward it—is its characteristic;
she whose nature is such is "tādṛśī. "Prahvatā" is the state of being bowed down. The meaning is:

The subject matter [is as follows]. In this regard, the distinction should be understood as follows: prostration consists of bowing with the body in the form of the eight-limbed gesture (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇati*), verbal expression through speech, and being the object of mental reflection. Regarding the phrase "and that": "that" refers to prostration. The word "tathā" (thus) has the sense of the word "tadā" (then), [referring to] the authoritative person—
For one who acts with foresight, [to bow] to anything— whether insentient or sentient— from all [sources]—
without reflecting upon the reasoning [behind it], even though it is of a non-ultimate nature (*aparamārtha-rūpa*)—
is nothing other than falling into the company of worldly people (*sāṃsārika-jana*), that is, among the cattle-like beings of saṃsāra.
As it has been said:
"Stained by the passion for knowledge (*vidyārāga*), they do not find the supreme deity.
For as long as one is being driven by the impure *vidyā*, *rāga*, and *kalā* belonging to Māyā, there is indeed only the state of a bound soul (*paśutva*).
However, in comparison with others, there may also be excellence due to having transcended several temporal paths. As it has been said:

regarding "the one worthy of salutation"—one who is about to be made the object of the threefold salutation—"excellence" means preeminence in all qualities; "otherwise" means in the absence of the perception of such excellence.
"Reasoning" (yukti) refers to the act of offering salutation toward excellence; "one who does not reflect upon it" means one who does not investigate it.

Regarding "the non-ultimate reality"—that is, a particular deity distinct from the Supreme Lord and resembling a bubble on water—for one who is intent on saluting it, that is, engaged in the act of salutation, this is due to ignorance and the greed for what has been lost or gained.
The word "or" (*veti*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. A worldly person—one who, out of greed for wealth and the like, is intent on bowing down before kings and others—shares their status;
that is, he falls into their midst, shares their same security and fate, or, in other words, becomes similar to them. Here, the author corroborates this with scripture, saying "as it has been said."

He restates what has already been said with the words "the Vaiṣṇavas and others. Here, in this context, the meaning is as follows: the word "but" (tu) is intended to highlight the distinction from the Śaivas and other such groups.
Whosoever they may be—the Vaiṣṇavas and others, including the Buddhists and so forth—they are all [liberated] by means of *vidyā*.
By means of the principle of impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyātattva*), which consists of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), and by passion (*rāga*)— that is, the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*)—
in this copulative compound (*dvandva*), they have been "colored" (*rañjitāḥ*), meaning they have been led to attachment toward lower systems of philosophy such as Vaiṣṇava and Buddhist.
[They fail to perceive] the Supreme (*param*), who transcends all principles (*tattva*), the Divine (*deva*) whose nature is play (*krīḍāśīla*), and the Omniscient (*sarvajña*).

It is endowed with the colors of all objects; likewise, by means of that very knowledge which knows all objects, it "shines" (śālate)—that is, its nature is such. This refers, by implication, to the Lord known as the Supreme God in His own essential form. They do not find Him—they do not attain Him as their own chosen deity—because otherwise, there would be no possibility of error regarding the mere appearances of gods. Thus:

The implication is that their state is nothing but that of beasts, like people who serve kings and others for the sake of the next world. Regarding a matter corroborated by scripture, [it is said] in a verse: "Behold, whose unartificial organs are not [useless], O You whose sovereign power remains unimpaired?"
"Even from a lower state, due to delusion, there arises a desire to praise you, O Giver of Boons, setting aside [all else].
Thus it was said by the illustrious Vidyādhipati. And this is found in the Āgamakāṇḍa.
We shall explain this. Therefore, even the reflection upon all excellence must be accepted therein.

Although it states that much when speaking of the cause as the firmly attained power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*), the state dependent on that [power] is as follows: the word "hi" indicates the reason; [it refers to] that which pertains to *māyā*.

On the descent [of the powers], immediately following *māyā*, there exists its effect, which is *aśuddhavidyā*—consisting of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*). By means of that, there is the *rāgakalā*, a portion of attachment; by this, for one who is being led astray—that is, deluded here and there among the appearances of deities—there arises the state of a bound soul (*paśutva*).

One who remains fixed in the worldly state of birth possesses only the nature of a bound animal (*paśubhāva*), because of their lack of knowledge regarding the supreme reality (*paratattva*). To address the potential objection that, in that case, taking refuge in that state would be entirely useless, he says "the others. The "others" are the followers of Baudhāyana and so forth, as well as the worldly people; the "paths" (*adhvan*) are the levels of the categories of reality (*tattvabhūmikā*). Herein...
It corroborates the view of the venerable Vidyādhipati with the words "as it has been said by him.

The connection is with the distant term "as it was stated by the venerable Vidyādhipati. The meaning of this verse is as follows: by means of the "uncreated"—that is, innate—faculties (*karaṇaiḥ*) consisting of your own manifestations, namely, the external and internal organs (*bāhyāntaḥ-karaṇaiḥ*).

Even when there is an appearance otherwise, for one who— by the power of their own nature— perceives and grasps, according to ultimate reality, that unimpaired and complete sovereignty (*vibhūti*) consisting of the thirty-six principles which belongs to You, who indeed— even among those situated in lower systems such as Vaiṣṇavism and the like— is there [who would not be liberated]?

Setting you aside—having abandoned you, O Giver of Boons (*varade*), that is, setting aside one's own chosen particular deity—the desire for praise (*stutispṛhā*) arises. The meaning is: "not [the desire] of anyone at all. The underlying sense is that even those devoted to other deities are, in the ultimate sense, indeed devoted to you alone. As for what [you] yourself...
The Blessed One has said:
"In whatever way people seek refuge in me, in that very same way do I favor them.
And also in the *Śrītantrāloka*:

This very ground of Supreme Śiva, extending to such a degree, comes within the range of one’s own heart; yet herein no personal effort (*puruṣakāra*) of one's own can be effective, since all such effort consists of *māyā* and is like blinding darkness, whereas this is the non-*māyic*, pure light.

Since it is impossible for that [object] to be a means (*upāya*) with respect to its own opposite, nevertheless, that very form of such a nature must be reflected upon through the sequence of manifestation and description, by means of the interweaving of words such as "is victorious" (*jayati*) and so forth, with the desire to reach the state of being the object of the manifestation of one's own self and the other.
For even those who consider anything other than awakening as an object of worship,
when they investigate that [object], they conceive of it as non-different from awakening.

Why? Because [he is] at least inferior—standing on a level of dualistic categories and thus situated in an inferior vision—and because of delusion, meaning from a cognition in the form of perceiving divinity in what merely appears as a god; that is to say, even from erroneous cognition.
The use of the suffix *-ktvā* (in *vibhramya*) is not faulty, as it is based on the fact that the same agent performs both the desire for praise and its subsequent removal.
And thus, the sense is that in the Vaiṣṇava system and others, there is clearly a transcendence of several paths on the part of those situated at the level of kings and so forth.

Although, from the perspective of ultimate reality, even one intent on offering salutation to a king and the like is indeed intent upon Him alone, nevertheless, due to the great distance [of mediation], that [ultimate intent] cannot even be conceived by such a person. Now, this...

Regarding the question of where the "Analysis of the Levels of Reality" (*tattvabhūmikāvibhāga*) was stated, he says: "And this... This refers to the states such as transcendence (*uttīrṇatva*) and so forth, which exist in accordance with the levels of reality. He provides the conclusion with the words: "Therefore... The meaning is: by virtue of bringing about the fitness for salutation. In that regard—namely, in the act of salutation—it is to be accepted.

The meaning is that even what has not been explicitly stated must be implied. Now, one might raise the objection: "In the case of one touched by the most intense descent of power (*tīvratara-śaktipāta*), the excellence of the Supreme Lord is seen to manifest spontaneously; why then is there a need for its forceful acceptance? Anticipating this doubt, he explains that such acceptance must necessarily be performed.

By the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth: "firm" (*dṛḍhaḥ*) means exceedingly intense; "by itself" (*svayameva*) means without even the reflective awareness of a word denoting it; "having brought all principles within herself" (*svāntaḥkṛtasamastatattvā*);
"the ground of Paramaśiva" (*paramaśivabhūmiḥ*) means the realization of Paramaśiva, that is to say, the very nature of Paramaśiva.
"Within the range of the heart"—that is, as something to be known through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). The phrase "but not" is intended to indicate an alternative position.

Here—in the manifestation of the Supreme Lord’s excellence—the "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*), consisting of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the words that denote Him, "carries through"—that is, it prevails—despite [the world's] being composed of *māyā*.

—By means of the manifestation brought about through differentiation, [he perceives it] as having the nature of *māyā*. "His own adversary"—meaning one who has become an enemy; for it is not observed that darkness serves as a means for the accomplishment of light; such is the sense.
Having thus established its irrationality, even with respect to reality (*tattva*),...
He states the necessity of reflecting upon excellence for the sake of a specific purpose with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
Nevertheless, [the object] being of such a kind— endowed with the quality of excellence—
the meaning of "victory" (*jayati*) must be implied within the act of salutation (*namaskāra*), even when the word "victory" is not explicitly uttered.

Since one who stands as a mere bystander and does not humble oneself before such a person endowed with an excellence of such a superior degree can only be of benefit to another through the Supreme Self, the act of salutation— necessarily implied by that very specific excellence— must certainly be internalized; thus, by this reasoning, [the word] "Victory!"—
In the process of any one act of salutation (*namaskāra*), the implication of the other must necessarily be admitted;

for even acts such as bowing (*vandana*), prostrating (*namana*), remembering (*smaraṇa*), and meditating (*pradhyāna*) have, in their ultimate sense, the mere meaning of saluting (*namaskāra*) or "victory" (*jayati*).
That very form—the nature of the Supreme Lord which has been introduced—is indeed this, and nothing else;

for it is impossible for anything other than that to possess supreme excellence by virtue of being created by Him. He expresses the specific quality of that excellence—the state of abiding in the highest plane—because [the term] is conventionally established (*saṃketita*) therein.

"Speaks" means that which is such a word as "victory" (*jaya*) and so forth; by the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), other synonyms are included. By its "pervasion" (*anuvedha*)—that is, by its penetration—meaning, by way of the mental reflection upon its utterance. That which is to be reflected upon is—

It is the object to be made the focus of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). The instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). By what means? By the sequence of *prakhyā* and *upākhyā*.

*Prakhyā* is the internal reflective awareness whose nature is supreme knowledge (*prakṛṣṭajñāna*) and which has the denoted meaning as its object; *upākhyā* is the clear articulation (*uccāra*) situated near that [awareness], residing in the signifier (*vācaka*). It is by the sequence of these two.
The desire to attain the state of being an object for the manifestation of both oneself and the other—taking the form "may I go"—is by means of that [desire].

In this regard, by the primary term (*prakhyā*), there is the state of becoming an object for the manifestation of one's own self; for it is only the self, as it flashes forth within, that is capable of making itself its own object. By the secondary term (*upākhyā*), there is the state of becoming an object for the manifestation of the other.
For even another person perceives as an object of their own cognition the meaning of a word that has been clearly articulated.

He states the result with the word "iti" (thus). "Iti"—for this reason; it must be "implied" (*ākṣepya*)—that is, even though not explicitly stated there, it must be brought within the scope of implication. But then, [is it not so?]
In response to the question, "Why not simply utter the word 'jaya' (victory), which denotes excellence alone?

he says "jaya" and so forth. Regarding the utterance—the pronunciation—of the word "jaya": here, "neutrality" (*taṭasthatva*) should be understood as the failure to perform a salutation (*namaskāra*). It is to be "internalized"—that is, supplied by way of ellipsis (*adhyāhṛtya*).

It is to be applied accordingly; thus, the sense here is that the objection must necessarily be addressed. Having stated the reasoning in this way, he describes the established reality with the words "by this" and so forth.
This alone is the path. Here, moreover, the author has adopted such a method of exposition wherein—

Both of these are indeed explicitly indicated by their own words; this will become clear at the very occasion of explaining the meaning of the terms. Furthermore, explicit indication by its own word is logical because it is beneficial for all people, for it immediately reaches the heart of everyone, whereas that which is implied by the sense reaches only a few.

Because it is impossible to reflect upon the reality of speech as it arises from one's own intuition, and because a manifestation devoid of reflection upon the reality of speech is tantamount to non-manifestation; and this will become clear further on. With this intention, [the author] composes this [work], avoiding association with the conventional bed of words such as "Victory" (jaya) or "Salutation" (namaḥ).
The author follows this path.
Now, is this the way only for the words *jaya* and *namaḥ*, or for all their synonyms? To this he says: "vandanam" (salutation). In that regard:
The two terms *vandana* (salutation) and *namana* (bowing) have the sense of *namaskāra* (reverential salutation), while the other three have the sense of *jaya* (victory).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other synonyms for these are also included. Now, one might object: "Let this be so;
however, not even one of these two is seen in this particular work. In response to this expectation, he says: "This... [and] "furthermore" (*punaḥ*).

The word "viśeṣe" means "in the particular"; "prakramaḥ" means "the sequence that surpasses all others. The meaning of "dvayam" is that there are two purposes: the purpose of victory and the purpose of salutation. "Svaśabdena" means "by its own denotative word"; "parāmṛṣṭam" means "made the object of reflective awareness," that is to say, "stated. The word "eva" is intended to exclude connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).

Regarding the phrase "padārtha" (the meaning of the word): the explanation of the meanings of words—the clarification through the analysis of stems and suffixes—will become manifest on that occasion, at that time; by this, direct verbal exposition is excluded. For in that context, through the explanation of the term "Maheśvara," its state as the most excellent [is established].

It will become manifest. For in the absence of supreme excellence, even the status of an *īśvara* (Lord) is unfit to be predicated, let alone that of a *maheśvara* (Great Lord). Through the explanation of the term "servant" (*dāsa*), however, humility is indicated; for no one gives even a single cowrie shell to one who does not humble themselves. What [is the point]?
This is the discourse on the gift of all things (*sarvadāna*). Now, one might ask: "Did not the author of the treatise himself show a preference for implication (*ākṣepa*) for the sake of brevity?

In response to this expectation, he says: "The word *sva* [is used]. One might further object: "In that case, is it that what is implied by the sense (*arthākṣipta*) is not at all heart-pleasing? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Only a few..."

The meaning is that [the teaching] is intended for only certain individuals who are engaged in the reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of the reality of speech (*vāktattva*) as it arises from their own intuition (*svapratibhā*).

He states the reason for this here: "from their own intuition" (*svapratibhā*). The word "of all" (*sarveṣām*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Their own intuition is the intellect characterized by ever-new manifestations; that which arises through that [intellect] is the reflective awareness of the reality of speech—the reality of speech...

The object is *avamarśa* (reflective awareness), because *parāmarśa* (higher reflective awareness) is impossible for it. By this, it is indicated that those who always look toward the mouth of the Guru are unfit for the cognition of an already established object through implication (*ākṣepa*) and so forth.
Here, whatever whatsoever flashes forth is that very [reality] of the Lord to be described—

It is merely the manifestation of the very self-nature of form; however, within that, the relationship of means and end, as well as the causal relationship, exists as ultimate reality just as it appears, because the manifestation cannot be denied. As Bhaṭṭa Divākaravatsa stated in the Vivekāñjana:

and so forth,
ending with "...it dissolves by the utterance of the curse."
To the inquiry, "Granted that there may be no reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of the essence of speech (*vāktattva*), what of it?", he replies with the words "the essence of speech.
The meaning is that because it is as if non-luminous (*aprakāśakalpa*), it is like the sight of a newborn infant looking at a lamp;
that is to say, it is similar to non-manifestation. This will be explained further on.

Regarding the phrase "the nature of manifestation" in the verse, [the author] concludes the procedure under discussion with the words "by this. "By this" means by that which consists in being accessible to the heart of all;

The sense is that, in the case of a connection with words such as "prasiddha," "jaya," and "namaḥ," there would necessarily be the requirement of an *ākṣepa* (an implied objection or restriction).
Having thus established the possibility of the salutation (*namaskāra*), [the author uses] the word "kathaṃcit" (somehow).

He expands upon the method of explanation here with the words "iha" and so forth. Whatever little [there may be]—whatever it may be—it is the accomplishment of that which is indeed the activity of *sattva*;
for whatever a thing requires for a purpose, that is precisely its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, he says "tatra" (in that case). "Tatra" means in the *sattva*;
"of another appearance"—namely, the appearance of a vessel consisting of the fetching of water and so forth.

The sense is that otherwise, the bringing of the fire would be impossible. To the question "Why?", he says: "By its semblance" (*tadābhāsena*). By that which is "inseparable"—that is, the necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—with the semblance of existence (*sattvābhāsa*), [there is the cognition] of another semblance (*ābhāsāntara*) which is "determined," meaning necessarily present.

Because another manifestation, such as the fetching of water and so forth, is required; the manifestation of the vessel is necessarily required by the manifestation of fire, and thus it is used as an illustration. He concludes the process with the word "evam" (thus): "by means of"—that is, through the gateway of *sattva* and the other qualities.
The meaning is as follows: an object such as a jar (*ghaṭādi*) is "consisting of manifestation alone" (*ābhāsamātrātmaiva*), that is, its very nature is merely manifestation;
for it manifests precisely in that way—as a mere manifestation—by means of its flashing forth (*pratibhāsanāt*) and by means of reflective awareness (*vimarśanāt*). Thus.

There is a change [in the manifestation], a change in the state of being a seeker, and a change in proficiency;
for in the case of mere inclination, such a manifestation is purposeless. How so? In the state of being a seeker, it is because the object is already excessively attained;
in proficiency, it is merely for the sake of training, so that one may become proficient in this matter. Thus.

In all cases, the triad beginning with inclination (*ruci*) should be applied. Among these, *ruci* refers to: (1) the desire for the knowledge or the instruction of a thing even when it serves no purpose; (2) the state of being a seeker (*arthitva*) in all worldly transactions; and (3) proficiency (*vyutpatti*), both at the time of receiving instruction and at the time of imparting instruction. Likewise, those [three]—
The various manifestations, which perform distinct causal functions— that is, they effect different practical purposes— likewise become the locus, or the object,
of sound (dhvani) and of the word (śabda), which is rooted in that [sound], as well as of reflective awareness (vimarśa); for instance,
because it performs the causal function of concealing its own length, it becomes the object of the reflective awareness, "This is long."
Because it is apprehended as "this is long" and because it is an object of verbal expression; thus it should be understood in all cases.
[4.5] Now, one might object: "If the real entity (vastu) consists only of its individual appearances, then a single pot-essence would not be a real entity. Anticipating this, he says:
Furthermore, the restricted causal efficiency of things arises from the difference in their appearances;
for those [things] that appear as non-different through co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), [their efficiency is fixed].

In that form which is a mixture of appearances, there must necessarily be one appearance that, by virtue of its predominance, must be made the locus of repose for the other appearances; it is that [appearance] of theirs.

The subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) is the same; therefore, he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "nanv em" (But surely...). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the word "ābhāsa" (Appearance).

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains first the word "by way of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmādhikaraṇyena*) with the words "of the appearances" (*ābhāsānām*). "Mixed" (*miśram*) means existing in a state of mixture; that is, having the nature of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

To that extent— in that mixed sleep— one should cultivate the state of rest as the locus of repose (*viśrāntipada*), just as the manifestation of a jar and so forth [is subsumed] within the manifestation of a sentient being when there is a desire to cease the breaking of the heart, or just as the manifestation of a jar [is subsumed] when there is a desire to fetch water.
Of the appearances of "existent" (sat) and so forth—

that is, of those appearances distinct from the primary appearance— it is the common locus, a single location, because [the former] is superimposed as a property (*dharma*) upon that very [locus]. This is the explanation of the *taddhita* suffix.

"He acts by means of that" (*karoti tena iti*). "By means of that" (*tena*) refers to that which is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Together with those appearances (*ābhāsas*) which constitute the contents (*ādheya*), there is a relationship (*saṃbandha*) known as the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). He effects the construction of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) by means of that.

The relation that exists between them is *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical coreferentiality); the manifestation characterized by that— namely, the light directed toward the object and its vitalizing principle, which is a certain word-essence (*padātman*)— is what is meant.
The reflective awareness whose essence is non-dual is the one that vitalizes that appearance of grammatical coreferentiality,
because everything necessarily rests within a single manifestation; therefore,
it is the sentence-essence that sustains that appearance of coreferentiality.

Reflection (*vimarśa*) consists in the consideration of the meaning of a sentence— of the form "this jar exists here now"— and for that reason, those which are non-different are characterized— that is, made specific. By this, it is indicated that this third [case] functions as a characterization (*upalakṣaṇa*).

He explains the term "from manifestation" (*pratibhāsāt*) with the phrase "turned toward the object" (*arthonmukhaḥ*). "Turned toward the object" means set upon making the object its domain; by not deviating from luminosity (*prakāśa*), it also effects the apprehension of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). "Thereafter" (*tadanu*) [means] that which animates that [manifestation]. "Tadanuprāṇakaḥ" [is explained as follows]:...

It is that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*, i.e., *vimarśa*) which prevents light from being considered unreal—that is, that whose nature (*ātman*) is not wordless (*napada*); for its nature is non-wordless. In response to the inquiry as to why it is "not wordless," he says: "of that" (*tasya*).
Because of that universal reflective awareness— which consists of words— there is a rule of resting in a single manifestation;
that is, there is a rule of resting in a single manifestation in the form of a sentence-manifestation, for [resting] in the mere intrinsic nature of a word does not suffice.

The sense is that its predominance [is not perceived] because it is submerged within the sentence. Then, in response to the inquiry as to what the nature of that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is, he explains it by way of a conclusion: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
"Therefore"—that is, for that reason—the appearance of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyābhāsa*).

It vitalizes— that is, it nourishes— the previously mentioned appearance of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyābhāsa*), which exists as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*); this [vitalization] pertains to that which is the essence of the sentence—
existing as the refinement of the sentence and consisting of the reflective awareness of the sentence-meaning.

Vimarśa—*parāmarśa* (reflective awareness)—is that which animates it, being distinct from the *parāmarśa* consisting of individual words; that is to say, it is the *parāmarśa* whose nature is the sentence (*vākya*). Having imitated this very *parāmarśa* whose nature is the sentence, he says "here" (*iha*). Here, in this place.

Now—at this time—this, possessing such qualities, is a jar. In that [expression], "here" is the appearance of space; "now" is the appearance of time; "this" is the appearance of qualities; and "jar" is the appearance of a genus.
And here, it is the appearance of the jar alone that is common [to all].
Having attained the state of a single unique particular (*ekasvalakṣaṇatā*), yet not abandoning their own distinct individual natures (*svarūpabheda*), they possess another, specific,
collective (*samuditā*) causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). This occurs despite the difference in their appearances (*ābhāsa*) and reflective awarenesses (*vimarśa*).

Furthermore, another [type] is fixed (*niyata*) and consists solely of each individual [element]. In the Sūtra, by the two terms *ābhāsa* (appearance) and *pratibhāsa* (manifestation), the act of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is also implied; this should be understood. Moreover, the word "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) indicates a distinction and applies to both cases, like the eye of a crow (*kākākṣivat*).

The state of being the locus [is established] because the appearance of the other is established precisely by having that as its substratum. Filling the expectancy of the two words "yaḥ" and "ye," he provides the construction of the ablative case in the phrase "pratibhāsāt," namely:
"tataḥ. "Tataḥ" means: from the manifestation, and from the reflective awareness consisting of the sentence; that is, for the reason of these two.

He explains "of the non-distinct" as "one. Having attained the state of a single particular (ekasvalakṣaṇatā)—the multitude of entities mixed with space and so forth—it "vibrates," that is, it shines. And this [subject] which is about to be described is of the nature of Īśvara.
One's own self (*svātman*) is that manifestation (*prathā*)—that is, the light (*prakāśa*)—which consists of nothing but that;

the meaning is that it is capable of being the object of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "I" alone. Now, one might ask: "Let this be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). "In that regard" means within the midst of the multitude of entities whose nature is to manifest.

But in the case of exclusion (*vyatireka*), it is "according to manifestation"—meaning without overstepping the state of being manifestation, and not by way of its own form belonging to *māyā*. He states the reason for its being real: "because it is manifestation.
This is because it is "un-negatable"—that is, impossible to deny—since that which is manifesting [is such].

The meaning is that no one can deny this; therefore, the relationship of cause and effect, which is manifest, is also ultimately real. By the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*jñāpya-jñāpaka-bhāva*) and others are included. Here, he cites the consensus of the elders (*vṛddha-saṃmati*), saying: "As it has been said."
"In the *Vivekāñjana*," meaning in the treatise bearing that name;
he characterizes the text therein by its beginning and end with the words "and light indeed.
In that context, however, even though there exists a relationship of cause and effect, in some instances...

It shines forth, encompassing infinite powers that are inseparable from the sovereignty characterized by perfect autonomy, and free from the intervention of any other manifestation conceived as an objective entity untouched by the [limited] cycle of existence; yet, it will be established as belonging to the realm of *māyā*.

And this [reality] is divided into hundreds of intermediate distinctions such as the insentient and the sentient; and from that arises this entire manifestation of the relationship between producer and produced, and knower and known, which takes the form of worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*). But where—

The unimpeded self-luminosity of the Lord himself—which consists of the manifestation of his own pure nature, is endowed with the unsurpassed power (*anuttara-śakti*), and is devoid of any intervention by other manifestations of *māyā*—is the very basis; therein, that very Blessed One alone possesses the status of the cause. And this...

The last [type of relationship] is characterized by favor (*anugraha*). To the question, "What follows from that?", he says: "But there... The meaning of "there" is: in the midst of the entire complex of cause and effect. "In some cases" means in worldly matters; "complete" means not broken or obstructed anywhere.

That which is characterized by sovereignty—whose essential nature consists in not looking to another for anything—is Maheśvaratva, the state of being the Great Lord. By that [state], through its inseparable concomitance—that is, by its own pervasion—it is embraced;
thus, the direct rule is that [the Lord] is endowed with that very power of sovereignty.
Thus, according to the *Tantrāloka*, that which is contained within one's own [consciousness] is the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*)—the assembly of powers;
"kissed" by it means touched, that is to say, pervaded by existing as its essence.
Those entities (*bhāva*)—the objects—which have been "perfumed" (*bhāvita*) by them, meaning manifested, constitute that other manifestation (*prathāntara*).

Knowledge is that which appears as its own object distinct from pure luminosity; by this, there is an intervention—namely, the non-manifestation of one’s own self, which is the nature of the Supreme Lord. It "shines forth"—it manifests. Otherwise, if everything everywhere were of the nature of ultimate luminosity, [there would be no distinction such as] "this is the effect of this" or "this is the effect of that."

The meaning is that it is impossible for [the effect] to be a cause because of the lack of logical division. "By way of being produced by Māyā" means by way of being an effect of Māyā, which follows from the fact that the manifestation of difference would otherwise be inexplicable; the remainder of the sentence is "it will be established right here later on. "Inert" (jaḍa) refers to seeds and the like; "sentient" (cetana) refers to persons and the like. Now, [an objection]:

Let this causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) be of such a nature; however, in response to the inquiry as to what other [relationship] exists, he says "But where... and so forth. Pure—meaning untainted by any object to be manifested apart from itself—is that manifestation (*prathā*), which is the appearance (*avabhāsa*) consisting of one's own essential nature (*svātmarūpa*); that which possesses the power of the Absolute (*anuttara-śakti*) is of that very essence.
Adorned with the power of sovereignty that transcends all, it is unrestrained— its flow unbroken—
the fifth specific activity of the Supreme Lord, which brings about the supreme human goal,
since ultimate liberation is dependent upon it. For liberation elsewhere is indeed different.
We shall explain that liberation from only some things, and not from everything, is a mere semblance of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasābhāsa*). Furthermore,
this second type of causal relation is distinct from the well-known causal relations established through worldly positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Not being perceived as a distinct form, its ultimate reality is to be inferred from the occasional existence of a thing [its ultimate reality being inferred from the appearance of the occasional existence of a thing—K.
ṣ. ṣ.], and it possesses the quality of performing what is extremely difficult to accomplish.
"Self-luminosity" (svātmaprakāśaḥ) means luminosity whose very nature is the self, and not external luminosity.

"The basis" (nibandhanam) refers to the cause that produces its own essential nature by existing as its core; the meaning is: "in that," namely, in that relationship of cause and effect. "Of that alone"—of self-luminosity alone—is the causality.

The state of being the cause; the state of being the effect, however, should be understood as the very attainment of the object [of grace]. The last—the "end-birth" (antabhava)—is the fifth, consisting of the fivefold [powers] grounded in the pentad of creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace.

Because it serves to complete the enumeration. In that context, "concealment" (pidhāna) is the dissolution [of the world] even while it remains as mere latent impression (saṃskāramātra). "Grace" (anugraha) is the act of making [the soul] one's own. The rest is quite clear.
Regarding "the supreme human goal"—that is, the ultimate purpose related to the person known as liberation (mokṣa).

"Prāpakaḥ" means that which brings about attainment. And here, it should be understood as consisting precisely in the establishment of servitude (*dāsya*), because that alone is the desired means. He states the reason for this: "because it is based upon that" (*tannibandhanatvāt*).
[This refers to] ultimate liberation (*paramārthamokṣa*), as taught in the Śiva-scriptures, which consists in the establishment of great sovereignty (*mahāsvātantrya*).

Regarding "of great liberation" (*mahāmokṣasya*): indeed, in response to the inquiry as to whether there is any liberation that is not of the ultimate nature (*aparamārthabhūta*), he says "elsewhere" (*anya*). "Elsewhere" means existing in other systems, such as the Buddhist tenets (*bauddhasiddhānta*) and so forth. "From something" means from a principle such as *māyā*, but not even from *śuddhavidyā* and the rest. As it has been said:
"I am undefiled within by passion and the like; I am empty; I am devoid of agency"—through such knowledge, both in brief and in detail, one is liberated from that much [of bondage].

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Let that relation of cause and effect be of such a nature; what follows from that? To this he says: "And that... The compound is analyzed as follows: *laukika* means both "stamped with the form of difference" (and thus established in the world) and "established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For in the world, when there is the presence (*anvaya*) of one thing, there is the presence of another; and when there is the absence (*vyatireka*) of one...
That whose absence [occurs] is established as its effect.
"Not being perceived" means being impossible to grasp due to extreme subtlety. [Objection: If that is so, then how is it known to exist?
To this he says: "occasional" (*kadācitka*). "Occasional" means occurring at some time; that which is the actual existence of a thing—
The existence of ultimate liberation (*paramārthamokṣa*) is to be inferred (*unneya*)—that is, capable of being known—by that [liberation];
it is such that its true nature (*svarūpa*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). The meaning is that it is to be understood solely through its effects (*kārya*).
Although its wondrous state is manifested by the expansion of its characteristics and sovereignty (*lakṣaṇaiśvarya*), [it remains beyond direct perception].

How can this [text], which consists of such forms as "the first limit, devoid of conceptualization, belonging to the time of emptiness" (prathamakoṭisaṃbhāvanāśūnyakālika), "the removal of the obscuration of self-luminosity" (kārasvaprakāśāvaraṇanirākaraṇa), and "difficult to attain even through hundreds of desires" (manorathaśataduṣprāpa)— accompanied by particles that indicate the beginning (ādyotaka-nipāta)— [be explained]?

It has been explained that [liberation] occurs "in some way," and by a certain means—namely, through the propitiation of the feet of the Guru, who is non-different from the Supreme Lord, and which is itself fashioned by the Supreme Lord. As it has been said:
"In the ultimate sense, it is not possible for liberation, which is eternally present as the supreme reality, to be something produced."
Nevertheless, this was stated by way of superimposition for the purpose of removing that misconception.

Even there, the knowledge of its existence pertains only to the object being liberated, not to any other object, because the liberation of anything else does not manifest in relation to another object. As it has been said:
Whether with body or without body, or even in the state of liberation,
how can there be any experience of enjoyment for one who has not tasted the food?

Thus [it is said]. He establishes that this very relationship of cause and effect is the ground for the application of the word "somehow" (*kathañcit*) by stating, "it is extremely difficult to accomplish" (*atidurghaṭa*). And "the performance of what is extremely difficult" consists in the manifestation of the universe—which exists as one's own self—as something differentiated, and furthermore, the manifestation of that which has been manifested as being one's own self.

"Vimarśana" (reflective awareness) is of two kinds; its definition is as follows: it is that which is brought about—accomplished—by the "vijasana" (sportive manifestation) of that sovereignty which is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). It is such that its state is wondrous—that is, it possesses the quality of being marvelous. Thus, it is marvelous by virtue of being the very form of the sportive manifestation of sovereignty.
Up to the point where, by its power, they have attained the state of a single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). [Objection:
"In that case, let them simply be one. To this he says: "And not" (*na ca*).
The construction is "and not abandoning," the sense being that space and the other factors manifest as distinct.

"He makes the sixth yojana of them" means "of the objects. It is not explained [separately] because it is well known. Furthermore, he explains the word *anyā* (others), which expresses the meaning of another word, as follows: "again, others" means distinct for each respective function (*pratyekakāryāya*). [C: distinct for each respective function]. Thus, "distinct."

To this extent, precisely for that reason, it is distinguished; thus, while not restricted to any single instance, it is intended as being accomplished through all manifestations (*ābhāsa*). Consequently, purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) occurs.
He explains that "purposeful action is restricted due to the differentiation of manifestations" by the word "manifestation" (*ābhāsa*).
When there is a distinction between manifestation (*ābhāsa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), another [awareness] is restricted to the form of each individual alone;

thus, each possesses a distinct nature and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). However, in this context, reflective awareness should be understood as consisting solely of the refinement of the word (*pada-saṃskāra*), because it arises from a single manifestation. But is this not so stated in the Sūtra?

Since even the name of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) was not mentioned [in the previous verse], how could its application have been made in the commentary? To this he says: "The manifestation (*ābhāsa*). It is "implied" (*ākṣipta*), meaning it has been brought within the scope of implication by virtue of being the vitalizing principle (*anuprāṇaka*). But surely, it is the same single word [that is used]?
It is observed that in the commentary, one might ask how [the word] is joined twice; to this he says: "The word 'again' (*punaḥ*).

It is to be applied in both cases—in the form of the collective, regulated purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). By means of the plural number, it is stated that even though there is unity, the distinction of individual natures (*svarūpa*) is not abandoned; and therein—
When the appearance of oneness is real as dependent (paratantra), and when there is a distinctness among appearances, then—

by virtue of their acting as colorers for individual manifestations of a common form— there is an ultimate nature of universality; however, in the case of the pure appearance of a jar, when it is apprehended independently.

The nature of being a universal exists merely by way of fitness, not in reality—in both cases. By the word "plural" (bahuvacanena), he expresses the intended meaning of the plural form "of those that are non-different" (abhedinām);
otherwise, it would be more appropriate here to speak of a singular unity.
The application here is as follows: from a manifestation characterized by grammatical coreferentiality— that is,

due to the identity of the manifestation and its reflective awareness— there arises, moreover, another collective causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of non-distinct entities, owing to the difference in their manifestations.

Furthermore, due to the distinction in the reflective awareness of appearances (*ābhāsa-parāmarśa-bheda*), it becomes otherwise restricted; thus, the word "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) is to be applied twice [or thrice, according to the variant reading].
This occurs in that which exists for each individual appearance, having acquired its being through the mutual blending of appearances.

He states that for the two types of universals residing in the particular (svalakṣaṇa), there is existence both directly and by way of mere capacity; "therein" means in the midst of the two universals residing in the particular as it stands within each individual manifestation. When—
In the appearance of unity— in the appearance of unity for each of the locations and so forth,

in such forms as "this is that location" and "that is this location"— there exists the distinctness of the appearances, namely, the appearances in the form of locations and so forth, which remain established individually.

Individual existence (*pratyekabhāva*) means, in other words, the state of being established in its own respective form. When there is manifestation as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), then those individual manifestations which possess a common form— namely, the external, underlying individual entities— are present.
By means of coloring them— that is, by making them qualified by itself— there arises a state of being a universal (*sāmānyarūpatva*) that is ultimate (*pāramārthika*),
which is to say innate (*sahaja*); for a universal exists precisely as residing in substances and so forth, and indeed, the universal is what is called "spatiality" (*deśatva*).

It is observed that [the universal] is entirely dependent upon the substance whose form is the individual (*vyakti*) known as "place" (*deśa*); nor should it be asserted that the individual alone constitutes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
because the latter has its life-force in the conjunction with space and time effected by the cognizer, whereas this [universal] exists externally.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for it to manifest the universal (*sāmānya*). However, in the case of its exclusion (*vyatireka*), the pure [consciousness]— because it does not exist as co-referential with other manifestations (or, according to the variant reading C, because it exists as co-referential with other manifestations)— is unmixed with their distinctions.

Of the appearance of the jar— that is, of the appearance in the form of a jar which exists as the primary factor due to the desire for fetching water and so forth, meaning the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the jar—
in an independent reflective awareness, that is, in a reflective awareness [of it] as a subject by means of the appearance of it as a distinct entity.

"Existing," by mere fitness— that is, by fitness alone, meaning by its suitability for appearing as a future inherent property (*svābhāvikadharman*). This refers to its nature as a universal (*sāmānyarūpatā*).
For every category of object other than substance (*dravya*) has dependence as its essence; likewise,
even that which is the singular nature of a jar is indeed real—
because it is established as such by the power of appearance, reflective awareness, and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Because of its establishment—[K. ṣ. ṣ.]—thus [it is said]. || 6 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) does not arise from a single [manifestation] alone, but rather a collection of causal efficacies arises from a collection of manifestations?
And if these manifestations, though distinct, combine to produce a single causal efficacy, then what is the limit to their number? This objection is refuted as follows.
Just as the lights of separate lamps or the currents of rivers in the ocean have non-contradictory appearances yet perform a single function, so too is the cognition of unity.

It exists [conventionally], but in reality—that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth—it does not exist; that is to say, it does not exist at this time in its manifest form because its nature is sustained by conceptual construction (*yojanā*). This is because only a property residing within a common individual (*samānavyakti*) possesses the status of an ultimate universal (*pāramārthikasāmānya*). Why?
In response to this expectation, he says: "from substance" (*dravyāt*). "Other" (*anya*) means having the nature of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth;
thus, the sense is that since even a universal (*sāmānya*) is other than substance, its dependence is indeed logical.
He concludes his desired point with the result: "in this way" (*evam*). And the essence of the pot—

The phrase "the nature of the jar" (*ghaṭasvarūpam*)—by means of the word "also" (*api*)—indicates that the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-satyatvam*) belongs to the manifestations (*ābhāsānām*) that exist as distinct entities. He states the reason for this here: "because it is a manifestation" (*ābhāsa iti*).
"Manifestation" (*ābhāsaḥ*) refers to the illumination of the jar (*ghaṭaprakāśaḥ*); "reflective awareness" (*vimarśaḥ*) refers to the conscious deliberation upon the jar (*ghaṭaparāmarśaḥ*).

The purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is the fetching of water; by virtue of those [actions], there is such a determination—that is, the establishment of oneness. The word "iti" marks the completion of the commentary on the verse. (6)
Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"from the collection of manifestations"—that is, from the aggregate of manifestations; of those—

The "limit" (*maryādā*) of the manifestations (*ābhāsānām*) refers to the boundary beyond which there is no further measure—that is to say, the point at which their mutual intermingling ceases, such that the intermingling occurs only for certain things and only in certain places. The "objection" (*codyam*) is the student's challenge; he "refutes" it, meaning he provides a resolution (*pratisamādhatte*). [The reading *pratisamādadhate* is found in manuscript C.]
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the word "separately" (*pṛthak*).
Those rays of light belonging to a lamp which proceed separately possess the capacity for extremely subtle observation (*sūkṣmatama-avalokana-sāmarthya*).

—[K. ṣ. ṣ. Those [causes] which possess the characteristic of sustaining [an effect] but have not performed any purposeful activity (arthakriyā), they alone bring about a state of being coalesced within a single existence; there, no collection of purposeful activities exists. And as for the streams fallen into the ocean...
Just as [the waves] perform causal functions through the initiation of increasingly greater waves, so too, the pot— golden, red,
and [perceived] merely upon being seen— is fit for the causal function of bringing water suitable for washing the head of the Śiva-liṅga.

It performs a purposeful action characterized by intense joy; thus, its capacity for purposeful action is indeed established. As for the question, "What is the limit regarding the mixing of appearances?"—to that it is said:
only those appearances which are non-contradictory mix with one another; for instance, the appearance of form [does not mix with others].
It becomes mixed with the appearance of air due to opposition; and that [appearance] too is raised by the power of necessity (niyati-śakti).
Here is the commentary:
He establishes the method for explaining the verse with the words "separately" (*pṛthak*).

The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which effects the bestowal of capacity— the accomplishment of capability— regarding the perception, that is, the vision, of that which is most subtle (*sūkṣmatama*), i.e., extremely subtle.

[She] whose nature is such [as that]; "did not do" means she did not perform; "that very" [action], namely the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) characterized by bestowing the capacity for most subtle perception; "those whose self has become fully developed" means those whose essence has increased through the persistence of the aggregate (*samudāya*).

"Such [things], they perform—that is, they bring about. Having stated one example, he states a second as well with the words 'the ocean. The connection is as follows: the very onset of the exceedingly numerous waves is itself their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); they become such [entities] by performing that [efficiency]."

Having stated two examples, he explains the application to the case at hand with the words "in the same way" (*tadvat*). Just as this jar is suitable for the water that is used for the *mārjana*— the washing— of the top of a Śiva-liṅga,
and it is precisely that [washing] which constitutes its purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), so too is it fit and appropriate for that [action] upon the Śiva-liṅga.

Because bathing is prescribed specifically with a golden jar; "merely upon being seen"—that is, simply by being seen—there is the capacity for a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*), the word "of the aggregate" (*samudāyasya*) being understood as the ellipsis.
Having stated, with an example, that there is a single purposeful action from the aggregate, [he now speaks] of the appearances (*ābhāsānām*).
He states the limit of the extent of their mixture with the words "yat punaḥ" (but that which...). "Sīmā" means a boundary;

that is to say, the limit of the extent. "Yeṣām" means of whichever appearances. He supports the general [statement] with the particular by saying "nahi" (not). This is because of contradiction, since air is devoid of color.
This is the state of being. Now, one might ask: "How can there be a contradiction between the forms of wind and light?
To this, he says: "And that too...
And that too—referring to that single [space] belonging to those various lights of lamps which are separate, [and which exists] in the ocean.

Just as a single cognition of unity is produced by that which is the one entity of the streams, so too, regarding those appearances—such as "jar," "red," "gold," and so forth—which are not mutually contradictory, the connection is this:
a cognition of unity is produced by that which is the single *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) related to them. By means of this cognition of unity—
It is accepted that [these consist of] manifestation, reflective awareness, and causal efficacy. || 7 ||
But if this is so, since the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) comes to rest with each individual appearance,

then the cognition of fire is the means of knowledge only in the appearance of fire, and the cognition of smoke [is the means of knowledge] only in the mere appearance of smoke; likewise, even the manifestation of the causal relation exists only within those respective limits.

And then, there would follow the undesirable consequence of many further disturbances, such as that even the appearance of smoke might deviate from the appearance of fire; in order to dispel (*vyapohitum*) this doubt, he says:
"There is also contradiction, and it is not proper to question the necessity. This is the intended meaning. [The process: *Note: The term *vyapohitum* is used here as a variant for *apohitum*.*
"Having accomplished [the synthesis], he composes the sutra separately"—this is the connection with the phrase "one object.

The word *vastu* (object) in both instances refers to the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic). Therefore, by that *vastu*, the task (*kāryā*)—which is to be accomplished—is the *svalakṣaṇa* animated by its association with place, time, and so forth.
The essential nature [of the object] does not follow after other [cognitions]; this refers to the "relation," with the word "of the verse" being understood as the ellipsis.
Now, one might ask: let the cognition of unity be the effect of the particular (svalakṣaṇa), but how can a single purposeful action (arthakriyā) be known?
To this he says: "by the cognition of unity. This means: by the cognition of unity acting as the agent; thus, this is accepted.

It is apprehended through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as its own cause. Why is this so? Because [the causes] are manifestation (*pratibhāsa*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, it should be construed thus: that which has a single manifestation has a single reflective awareness, and that which has a single causal efficacy has a single effect. This applies to the triad beginning with manifestation.
Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that the cognition of oneness arises. || 7 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the words "nanvevam" (But if this is so). Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"evam" means in the manner described; "pratyābhāsam" means in each individual manifestation (*ābhāsa*).
"In that much alone"—
meaning in the mere appearance of the causal relationship between the appearance of fire and the appearance of smoke—
and "therefore"— meaning for that reason— it would "deviate," because [the two] are cognizable by distinct means of knowledge; this is the intended meaning.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other deviations (*vyabhicāra*) are included. "To exclude" (*apohitum*) means to distance. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "therein" (*tatra*).

In that regard, with respect to fire and so forth which are undifferentiated, their nature as cause and effect, as heat, and as the referent of various words is understood from a single means of valid cognition.

Regarding this— on this view as well that "the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) rests upon every individual manifestation," there is no defect whatsoever; for instance, although the manifestation of fire is indeed indistinct from other manifestations, such as those of space and time, it remains unmixed with them.
Nevertheless, because its nature consists solely of the universal, that very manifestation—

having embraced as many manifestations as are invariably concomitant with it and are determined by the Lord’s power of necessity (niyati-śakti)— attains the state of certainty established by the means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
It descends; and thus, the appearance of fire possesses an intrinsic,
invariable necessity by virtue of the appearance of its being an effect of fuel, the appearance of its being a cause of smoke, and the appearance of its having heat as its essential nature.
Being perceived as having an essential and invariable concomitance—[K.
ṣ. ṣ.]—it is perceived in that very way everywhere and at all times, because of its oneness. Regarding "asvābhā-": here is the commentary (ṭīkā):

Therein, he explains the word *tatra* with the words *pratyābhāsam*. The phrase "nor is there any fault" (*api na kaściddoṣaḥ*) is supplied as a grammatical ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*). When the question arises as to how there is no fault, he begins the justification by explaining the passage starting with *aviśiṣṭe*.
"Thus, for instance" (*tathā hi*). He fulfills the expectation of the phrase "thus, for instance" with the word "undifferentiated" (*aviśiṣṭaḥ*).

"Undifferentiated" means not having attained the status of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇatā*). To the question "Why is it undifferentiated?", he states the reason: "place" (*deśa*). By the word "foremost" (*pramukha*), the inclusion of form (*ākāra*) and so forth is intended.
By way of being unmixed— that is, by way of being non-blended— that very manifestation, namely the manifestation of fire itself,
is inseparable from— and pervaded by— manifestations consisting of the nature of cause and effect and so forth; [it perceives] all those [aspects] produced by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is that it "enters the state of certainty"—that is, it becomes the object of valid cognition—because its nature is such; he states the conclusion with the words "and therefore" (*tataśca*). And therefore—due to that reason—the "appearance as fire" (*vahnyābhāsaḥ*), which is the appearance in the form of fire...

The fact that fire has fuel as its effect should be understood as being caused by its being illuminated by the fuel. "Natural" means derived from its own nature; therefore, it refers to that which possesses an invariable rule (*avyabhicarita-niyama*). "Everywhere" means in all places, and "always"—
In response to the question, "From what is [the word] understood at all times?", he says: "Because of its oneness.
Even that nature which depends upon human conventions and the like—such as being denotable by the word "fire" or being capable of producing the cognition of a jar, and so forth—[is one].

That too is determined from a single direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for that cognizer, this manifestation of fire is experienced as being co-necessary with another manifestation, whether in its artificial or other form, right from the very beginning. It is devoid of any possibility of a first point—beginningless, and having the form of time.

It possesses a form like a mass of clouds; that which veils its own self-luminosity—the power of *māyā* which acts as a veil over the light of the Self—its removal is its dispelling, and regarding that, there are hundreds of desires: "When will this cease?"

"Of such a nature"—by these [qualities], it is difficult to attain; the meaning is that it is impossible to reach without the intense descent of the power (*śaktipāta*) of the Blessed Lord. "Of this kind"—meaning having the form described above, that is to say, consisting of grace (*anugraha*). "How indeed?"—with the indeclinable *katham* (how), accompanied by an indicative particle.
The meaning is that [the object] is "indicated" (nirūpita), which is to say "suggested" (sūcita) by being joined with the word *cit*.

It is said to be a "suggester" (*dyotaka*) because particles (*nipāta*), which are devoted solely to illuminating a meaning established elsewhere, lack denotative power (*vācakatva*). He shows precisely how the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is accompanied by such a suggester: namely, by the word *kathaṃcit*.
"The connection is exceedingly difficult to establish...

[as it is said]. Regarding the word "āsādya" (having attained): it means having caused [the object] to settle (*sādayitvā*) on all sides (*ā*) in its fully perfected form, that is, having brought it to a state of unimpeded fitness for enjoyment by one's own self; by this much, [the object] has become known as something to be known (*vidita-vedyatvena*).
The qualification for composing a treatise for the sake of others has been shown; otherwise, it would be nothing more than mere deception.
Here, "immediacy" (sāmanantarya) is intended in the sense of preceding [the composition]; otherwise, it would be understood as being restricted by place and time.
Since it is already known, what need is there for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard?

Because of its oneness—that fire exists as a single entity across all places and times by way of its universal nature (*sāmānya*). By this, the explanation of the first half [of the verse] is completed.

He says "is non-intrinsic" (*asvābhāvikaḥ*) in order to explain that which is situated in the latter half of the verse beginning with "that very [nature]," standing in conjunction with the former half:
"non-intrinsic" means adventitious (*āgantuka*), by virtue of being established through conventions made by persons; "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) means the essential form of fire.

To the question "In what sense is it non-intrinsic? he says: "By a person. This refers to that convention (*saṃketa*)—in the form of "this is the meaning of this"—which was established by a person, whether the primordial person (*ādipuruṣa*) or an ordinary person (*sāmānyapuruṣa*), and which is the beginning of the linguistic usage of elders and so forth.
"He looks at the face" refers to such a person. In response to the inquiry "What is that nature?", he says:

"For example. Indeed, fire's being denotable by the word 'agni' is established solely through human convention (*puruṣasamaya*), not as something innate (*sahaja*). He explains the object included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*):

"Regarding 'the jar': the meaning is that it possesses the quality of illuminating the jar by way of being a lamp. For even that [quality] is not inherent in fire, but rather is distinct from its essential nature because it is produced by the power of *niyati* (destiny/fate), since it is occasional; whereas the essential nature [and its form] exist always."
"Because of its stability"—that is, because it is eternally present. "And so forth"—meaning of such a form;

by the word "etcetera," the absence of smell, taste, and so on is included. "That too"—even all those non-inherent natures denoted by the word "whatever," [is known] from a single direct perception alone.

[The cognition arises] from perception alone, as the single means of valid knowledge (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). When the question "Why? is asked, he states the reason by means of the sentence beginning with "tasya" (of that). "Of that"—which exists as the apprehender of fire—by its other, non-artificial form, [as opposed to] the artificial one which looks toward the conventions of persons (*puruṣasamaya*).

Those other manifestations which have been observed— namely, the manifestations of existence (*sad-ābhāsa*) and so forth, which are distinct from the manifestation of fire (*vahny-ābhāsa*)— the state of being inseparable from them is the rule of concomitance, which is to say, pervasion (*vyāpti*); by means of that, it becomes fully known— that is, first correctly cognized— and therefore...

That [object] existing in all places and times is thus cognized— it would be cognized as being inseparable from another appearance; so why, after stating an extraordinary (alaukika) object for the sake of attaining a certain degree of the acquisition of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), does he also speak of something worldly (laukika) by means of some [other] [means]?

The particle *eva* is intended to exclude connection with anything else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*). He cites an authoritative scriptural statement (*śāstravākya*) in support of this, saying "as it has been said. The relationship [of the verse] pertains to the Great Lord and the disciple whose devotion has been awakened.
He introduces the word *āsādya* in order to explain it, saying "having attained" (*āsādya*); here follows a word-by-word commentary (*pratyakṣara-vyākhyā*).
"He begins to do" (*kartumārabhate*) means "from all sides" (*ā samantāt*). This is a form derived from the root *sad* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) followed by the suffix *ktvā*.

Although this verbal root has multiple meanings, this explanation is based on the sense of "going" alone. However, its capacity for self-enjoyment, being unrestrained, is implied as the object (*karman*). He states the conclusion with the words "by this much" (*iyatā*). By this much—

By the word "having approached" (*āsādya*), [it means] by virtue of having known what is to be known—that is, having understood the object of knowledge. "For the sake of others" (*parārthe*) means for the benefit of others;

"has been shown" (*darśitaḥ*), with the word "his own" (*svasya*) being the ellipsis. He states the fault of one who proceeds otherwise when that [knowledge] is absent, using the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
"Mere deception" (*pratārakatāmātram*) means being solely intent on the cheating of others. This refers to that which was expressed by the suffix *ktvā*.

He states the intention regarding the prior time with the words "by way of priority" (*paurvakālyena*). "By way of priority" means by virtue of being earlier in time. "Immediate succession" (*sāmanantarya*) means the absence of any intervention between the act of bringing the slave girl and the establishment of the scriptural authority for recognition. "Otherwise" means in the absence of such immediate succession.
This is the meaning. "Upon reaching the gradation" means when the ultimate limit has been reached.

For the attainment of gradation occurs at the end of the gradation; otherwise, what would be the attainment of that which exists in an ever-increasing sequence? And the very end of the gradation is...
The ultimate limit of gradation (*tāratamya-parākāṣṭhā*). How is it "capable of being performed" (*kathaṃ śakyakriyaḥ*)? That is, how can it be accomplished?

By the principle that "O Rāma, this digit of knowledge (*jñāna-kalā*), once born, increases further," it means that it cannot be accomplished by attaining dissolution (*laya*) into the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*). Even though [the body] remains...
To that extent, the persistence of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is indeed logical, for otherwise its fall would necessarily follow;

nevertheless, it was stated in this way for the sake of instructing the disciple. However, when the latent impression is destroyed at the time of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), nothing remains, nor does he possess the capacity for instruction regarding what is to be done.
When the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the collection of impurities belonging to *māyā* have been destroyed, how could instruction by another be possible?

For there exist those presiding over *māyāgarbha*, such as Viṣṇu, Viriñca, and others; and even those who have transcended that [level], who are appointed over *mahāmāyā*, consisting of the *mantras*, their lords (*mantreśas*), and the great lords of those (*mantramaheśvaras*), who are both pure and impure.
Even those who are pure, such as Śrī Sadāśiva and others,

have become lords through the mere droplets of the sovereign power belonging to Him; that Blessed Lord is the ultimate reality of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), whose nature is uninterrupted light and bliss (*anavacchinna-prakāśānanda-rūpa*).

Maheśvara is the Lord of light, bliss, and sovereignty; by the term "servitude" (*dāsya*), he indicates that the means of accomplishing His recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) yields great fruit. A *dāsa* is one to whom everything desired is given by the Master; by the phrase "the state of being such" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*), [this servitude is defined].

The capacity for the sovereignty that is the nature of the Supreme Lord has been described. By the word "of the person" (*janasya*), which refers to anyone who is being born, he shows that there is no restriction here regarding the qualified subject; for whoever experiences this manifestation of their true nature, for that person alone is there the great fruit.

In the case of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), even though duality has dissolved, residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) still persist; furthermore, there remains the capacity for instruction regarding what is to be done.
Thus, the words *saṃskāra*, *pada*, *parapada*, and *śakyapada* are employed [in the verse].
The reading "upon the destruction of impressions" (*saṃskāraprakṣaye*) is merely a scribal error. For those...
