Among the great scholars (*mahāpaṇḍita*s), this very reading alone shines forth as being most excellent; therefore, let there be salutation to them—enough of that. He explains the word "of Maheśvara" with the words "they come into being" (*saṃbhavanti*).
They possess the agency of the action of coming into being; they are the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) within the womb of *māyā*.
Because it is primarily characterized by the differentiation of impure forms; *mahāmāyā* is *śuddhavidyā*.
They are both pure and impure because they are primarily characterized by both difference and non-difference; "by drops" means by fragments.
Having become *īśvarī*s—meaning, while being non-*īśvara*s, they have become *īśvara*s. "Unlimited" (*anavacchinna*)—

That very sovereignty which is the bliss whose nature is light— bliss that is of the form of light— which has been brought to a state of being delimited by an object, and which is of the nature of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that [light] through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
is indeed the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

"Whose nature is the manifestation of light" means one whose innate nature (*sahaja-svabhāva*) is such according to the principle that will be explained hereafter. By this, the reason for the supremacy of this Blessed One is stated. Having attained "servitude"—the state of being a servant—of him, the Supreme Lord.

Thus it stands as the object [of the verb]. The word *iti* is for the purpose of indicating the essential form (*svarūpa*). Of "accomplishment" (*upapādanasya*)—that is, of "bringing about" (*saṃpādanasya*). "The state of having great fruit" (*mahāphalatvam*) means the condition of possessing great fruit. The phrase "with regard to the attainment of servitude" (*dāsyāsādanaṃ prati*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. He states the meaning of the constituent parts of the word *dāsya* (servitude): "it is given" (*dīyate iti*). By this—

By the word *dāsya* ending in a *taddhita* suffix, the sense is that the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of the Supreme Lord alone constitutes everything. This is because manifestation itself is the ultimate fruit, and because that manifestation cannot be obstructed by those things considered to be obstacles; for according to the maxim, "that which has manifested cannot be unmanifested. As it has been said:
By the word "of the people" (*janasya*), he reveals the matter that is to be indicated: "anyone who is being born.
As it has been said:
"O Lord, this great deed of yours consists essentially of the contemplation of you."
From Brahmā down to a worm, who among them would not be qualified for liberation?

Thus, the prohibition regarding the rules for those qualified [to practice] is made here with reference to the division of social classes (*varṇa*); that is, whereas in the Vedāntas only one who has been initiated and belongs to the three higher classes (*traivarṇika*) has the qualification, it is not so here.
"Neither the knower of the four Vedas nor even an outcaste (*śvapaca*) is dear to Me, if he is not My devotee."

"To him it should be given, and from him it should be received"— but not in every case, because by the phrase "one who is previously afflicted by birth and death," detachment (*vairāgya*) will be indicated as the defining characteristic of the qualified candidate (*adhikārin*). However, in the investigation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*):

Even in the Vedāntas, only one endowed with dispassion possesses the qualification [for study]. For even a Brāhmaṇa devoid of that [dispassion], though exerting himself, is indeed equal to a beast; whereas one possessed of it, even a Śūdra or others, is seen to partake in the fruit of hearing those [teachings] however they may be. Enough of this prolixity. He states the reason for this in a verse: "Of whom..."

"Of whomsoever"— whether of a Brāhmaṇa or a Śūdra— this [realization], which consists of recognition, is the manifestation of one's own nature, the flashing forth of one's own self in the form of Maheśvara. It possesses the great fruit, which consists of the attainment of all perfections and the realization of servitude [to the Lord].

It is the most excellent fruit (*śreṣṭhaphala*). Although this is indeed a subordinate fruit in comparison to the attainment of all-encompassing prosperity (*samastasampat*), it is nevertheless of great magnitude when compared to other fruits. Regarding this as well, he states the reason ending in the fifth case (the ablative): "of manifestation alone," and so forth. Now, [an objection]:
If one were to object that its great fruitfulness would not exist if it were obstructed by time,

he says "And of that" (*tasya ca*). And because that [practice] cannot be obstructed— meaning it is impossible to make it the object of obstruction— by those things considered to be obstacles, namely lack of practice (*anabhyāsa*) and so forth.

In this context, he states the reasoning taught by the former masters as the logical ground with the words "for not," etc. The intended meaning of the reason is that otherwise even fire might sometimes become non-fire, because the mere manifestation (*sphuraṇamātra*) alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) due to its being the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
"In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor is there any obstacle;
even a very small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear.
Thus it is said. And by the feet of the Supreme Guru in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"Once the state of Śiva, which resides in all things, has been known through valid means— whether from scripture or the words of a guru— with firm conviction, [one attains liberation]."
There is no purpose whatsoever for either meditation or ritual action;
once gold has been known, what need is there for the reality [of it] to be established through meditation, ritual action, or the like?
"Truthfulness consists in always maintaining a firmness equal toward one's father, mother, and others.

Here he also cites the words of the *Śrī Gītā*: "In this [path], there is no loss of effort," where "loss of effort" means the loss of the undertaking. He also cites the words of Śrī Somānanda, as well as those of the feet of the Supreme Guru.

Thus [it is said]. In the *Śivadṛṣṭi*—that is, in the treatise named *Śivadṛṣṭi* composed by him—the connection with the preceding [text] is "it is stated. To address the expectation of what was stated, he says: "once. Regarding "in the state of Śiva"—that is, in the condition of Śiva established within one's own self. "By means" refers to either the binding of the posture (*āsana-bandha*) or the divine instrument (*divya-karaṇa*).

"By cultivation"—that is, by thorough examination. In response to the question "How is there no need for action?", he says: "At once. "At once" means in a single instance; "when known"—meaning when it has been correctly scrutinized—refers to gold, that is, to kanaka.
By means of such actions as rubbing on a touchstone and so forth, what further "truthfulness"—that is, the state of being genuine gold—is produced? [None.]
The meaning is that [the doubt] does not arise because it has already been resolved in the first [chapter]. By what kind of means, such as practice (*karaṇa*), etc.?

It means by that which is "always"—at all times—"equal" or similar to [the devotion shown toward] fathers, mothers, and so forth, and which possesses "firmness"—that is, stability—when practiced. It has also been stated by the venerable Vasiṣṭha:

"O Rāma, this digit of knowledge, once known, increases further. Thus, by the phrase "of the person"— meaning one afflicted by the incessant cycle of birth and death— it is indicated that [this knowledge] is an object of compassion.

He speaks of the state of being one who must benefit others. The word "api" (even/also), while revealing its non-difference from his own self, excludes any possibility of another purpose within himself that would exceed the fulfillment of the welfare of others by means of his perfection. And the welfare of others indeed constitutes a purpose, for that is the very definition [of such a purpose].

[Because of its connection with that characteristic—K. ṣ. ṣ. For this is not a divine curse that the purpose is solely for one's own sake and not for the sake of others; because even that [self-interest] would lack a motive if it were not connected to that characteristic (i.e., if it did not possess that characteristic). That which is intended primarily as something to be accomplished is precisely what motivates actions.

That which prompts [action] is the purpose (prayojana). For this very reason, even in the doctrine of dualism (bhedavāda), it was established by the Creator of Logic (Gautama) to demonstrate that the purpose behind the Lord’s performance of creation and so forth is solely for the sake of others: "That object aiming at which a person acts is the purpose."
He explains the word *janasya* with the words "uninterrupted" (*anavarata*). [The phrase] "by being an object of compassion" means by being the domain of compassion.

He states the intention of the word *api* found in the verse with the words "the word *api*. "Non-difference from that" means the non-difference of oneself from those things to be utilized; by this, the word *api* is intended to suggest the possibility of an unprecedented meaning.

Thus it has been indicated. Nor should it be said that because this [the self] is non-different from that [the body], that [the body] is also established by this; for even when there is knowledge of their identity, there is an absence of knowledge of its identity with that, and thus the establishment of this [body], even if it persists, is as good as non-existent. Now, one might ask: how can that which is for the sake of another (parārtha) constitute a purpose?

In response to the expectation of what is "proper," he says: "and for the sake of another. Because it possesses that definition—because it is endowed with the definition of a purpose, such as "that object which...

and so forth—it follows that even that [self-interest] is [a purpose]. If it lacks that definition—that is, if it is devoid of the definition of a purpose—[then it is not a purpose]. Now, in response to the expectation of what that definition of a purpose is, he says:

"By way of being something to be accomplished" (*saṃpādyatvena*). "By way of being something to be accomplished"—that is, as something to be achieved (*sādhyatvena*), intended [as an end], and taken as an object of mental reflection (*anusandhāna*). "The motivator" (*prayojaka*) means that which impels. The point is that sometimes even the welfare of others, when intended as something to be accomplished, becomes the motivator for a person. In this regard:

He employs the view of logic as an aid, for this very reason. Regarding "the composition of Nyāya"—that is, the Nyāya-śāstra consisting of a collection of aphorisms—by the Creator (vedhasā), meaning by Akṣapāda.
In response to the question of what was defined therein, he cites the relevant aphorism: "yam... [and so forth].

Thus: by the word "desiring" (*icchan*), [the author] shows, through the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), that the fruit which has become the object of desire is the cause for engagement in action. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), by becoming increasingly expanded in its nature, culminates in the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). The prefix *upa* signifies proximity; therefore, [it refers to] the person...

The fruit here is the bringing about of proximity to the dharma of the Supreme Lord. For this very reason, he says "all. Indeed, upon the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord, all prosperities—which consist of its very outflow—are already accomplished, just as the wealth of jewels is attained upon finding the Rohaṇa mountain.

For one who has forgotten the ultimate reality of their own self, what is gained by anything else? Having made [this] the subject—having brought it within the scope of the discourse, that is to say, having begun with it—the sense is: "just as in the system of logic (tarka) the Lord’s activity toward creation is solely for the sake of others, so too is mine here," thus he says "desiring."

He introduces the word "icchan" (desiring) in order to explain the term *pada*. "Phalasya" means of the fruit, that is, of the benefit (*upakāra*). "Śatrā" means by the suffix *śatṛ*, since it is used even in the sense of cause (*hetu*). To the objection, "What will be accomplished by mere desire alone?", he says: "And the power of desire. For even externally, every action is preceded by desire.

The state [of being]. He explains the word *upakāra* (benefit) as that which stands as the object (*karman*) of the action of desiring, beginning with the words "the prefix *upa*," etc. The meaning of the word *kāra* as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is not mentioned because it is well-known. He states the conclusion with the words "by that," etc. And thus, the identity expressed by the word "servant" (*dāsa*) is the meaning of the term *upakāra*.

For in the commentary on the word *dāsa* (servant), everything is stated as that which is to be given; and in the ultimate sense, everything is of the nature of unity, which is indeed identity with the Supreme Lord. Relying upon this, he introduces the explanation of the word *samasta* (all-inclusive) and says, "Therefore, he says 'all-inclusive'. It is for this very reason—because of the word "benefit" (*upakāra*)—that...

The meaning is the bringing about of proximity to attributes such as the fullness of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara). For that very reason, it means "precisely from that cause. He states the reason for this here: "the state of being the Supreme Lord" (parameśvaratā). These [powers] consist of its outflow—meaning they have the nature of a stream of the state of being the Supreme Lord, or rather, they are its waves. All of them—

All [the powers] have the nature of fullness and so forth. Regarding "attaining the ascent"—that is, attaining the mountain of jewels or attaining Mount Sumeru—one might ask: "Once that has been attained, would there not be no further need for the attainment of anything else? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "one who has been robbed.
"Robbed" means having fallen into forgetfulness through the power of *māyā-śakti*; "one's own self" refers to that which is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*).

And for him whose own self is the Supreme Lord—filled with creative manifestation (*bhāva*)—and who possesses that which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the supreme object, there is nothing else, such as the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā*, that remains to be desired. For even one who has attained that ultimate reality has nothing else left to long for. As it has been said:
By the author himself:
"For those enriched by the fortune of devotion, what else remains to be prayed for?
Or for those impoverished of it, what else remains to be prayed for?"

Thus, by means of this genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the purpose (*prayojana*) is stated; however, by means of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the means (*upāya*) is indicated. "Of the whole"—that is, of that which consists of existence and non-existence, internal and external, such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—"attainment" (*saṃpat*) refers to its perfection, its accomplishment, or the manifestation of its true nature (*tathātva*). Of that [attainment]...

"Right attainment" (*samyag-avāpti*) is the firm establishment of reflective awareness; that very thing is the "cause" (*hetu*) for that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). For this reason, the sense is that even for one who has forgotten a jewel, a longing for a mere cowrie shell is seen when the blue or pleasure appears with extreme clarity. But then, [one might object]: The meaning is as follows: "right attainment" refers to the firm establishment of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); that very attainment is the "cause" for that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). To illustrate: even for a person who has forgotten a precious gem, a desire for a mere cowrie shell is observed when the blue color or pleasure manifests with extreme vividness. Now, if that is so...
Anticipating the objection that "immediately after attaining that, there would surely still be a desire for other acquisitions," he says: "attained" (*labdha*).

"Attained" means by whom that ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is one's own essential nature (*svātmarūpa*), has been attained. Here, the author cites a verse from his own work, saying: "as it has been said. To the question "what was said? he replies: "devotion" (*bhakti*).

Devotion (*bhakti*)—which has as its object one’s own self in the form of the Supreme Lord, and not another deity—by means of this devotion. In response to the inquiry, "How does this meaning emerge from the word 'entire' (*samasta*) and so forth?", he says: "In this manner. By means of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

The cause for the attainment of all perfections (*samasta-sampat-samavāpti*) is [the Lord] in this very form; the purpose (*prayojana*) is the attainment of all perfections. By this, it is stated that this word functions as an adjective for the words *dāsya* (servitude) and *upakāra* (assistance).
Now, one might ask: "Is this the only compound for this word, or is there another? To this, he says:
"By means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound"—the word "means" (*upāyaḥ*) is used, with "of recognition" (*pratyabhijñāyāḥ*) as the ellipsis.

He demonstrates the *bahuvrīhi* itself, which has recognition as its primary referent (*anyapadārtha*), by way of its analysis (*vigraha*), saying "in its totality" (*samasta*). "In that manner"—that is, in the form of blue, pleasure, and so forth—"manifestation" (*prakāśaḥ*) means appearance (*bhānam*).
The meaning is "valid cognition" (*pramā*). By this, it is stated that this term functions as a qualifier for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Now, in response to the inquiry, "How can a valid cognition of blue, pleasure, and so forth, be the cause of recognition?", he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
[This refers to] the valid cognition of those things such as blue and pleasure which appear with extreme clarity.

"By investigation"—that is, by inquiry as to what its root is; for when an investigation into external means of knowledge (*pramā*) is carried out, the attainment of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), who is the root of that [knowledge], is established without effort, just as clay is [attained] by the search for a jar—this is the sense. "He said"—the remainder is that it was Utpaladeva who said this. "Elsewhere"—in another work. Now, [an objection]:
It is taught here that the attainment of the ultimate subject occurs precisely through the investigation of [the question] "What is it that says 'I'? and so forth.
As it is said elsewhere:
"The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of 'this' as something distinct is that repose in one's own essential nature; that reflective awareness is 'I am this.
Likewise, in that same work:
"The resting of the Light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of 'I-ness' (ahambhāva).
And that very resting is said to be [the state of] sovereignty, agency, and primary lordship, due to the cessation of all dependence."
Thus, by this much, the doubt regarding the extreme difficulty of the means has been refuted. As he will state at the end:
"He says 'this'. The reflective awareness "I am that" is the contemplation of the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhantā*). What is that?
It is [the awareness] of "this," which is a fragmented reflection—the valid cognition (*pramā*) whose objects are blue, pleasure, and so forth.

The state of having accomplished one's purpose (*kṛtārthatā*) consists in the completion of what was to be done. This is a resting (*viśrānti*), that is, a dissolution, within one’s own essential nature—the supreme subject. For the subject indeed dissolves blue, pleasure, and so forth into his own self; otherwise, satisfaction would be impossible. And satisfaction itself is the resting of valid cognition (*pramā*) in the subject, who is that very [supreme subject].

There is the attainment of the supreme subject. Having heard this, even those who are helpless under the sway of blue objects, pleasure, and so forth, should not harbor the conceit of having attained the Supreme Self; for they [should remain] solely intent upon the self-reflection "I" among those who are detached from external and internal states, even while maintaining the bodily existence required for necessary worldly activity.
This is because this teaching is established for the purpose of ensuring that one remains firmly rooted in the Self alone.

One must witness for oneself with one's own mind whether one is subject to the helplessness of blue, pleasure, and so forth, or free from such helplessness; otherwise, one would fall into self-deception. Enough of this. He cites another verse here, beginning with "tathā" (likewise): "Likewise..."

The word "and" (*śabda*) signifies conjunction. Regarding "of the light"—that is, of the cognition (*pramā*) of blue, pleasure, and so forth—"due to the cessation of all expectation" means because of indifference toward everything, which consists in the absence of expectation produced by contentment. What is this "rest"? It is "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*), and so forth.

In response to the question, "What is accomplished by this much?", he says: "By this much. "By this much" means by the statement that [this work] is the cause for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) because it brings about the attainment of all perfections. "In the means" means in the means for recognition. For indeed...
"This new path is easily established" (4.3.16).

Regarding the term "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*) of that Maheśvara: it is the knowledge (*jñāna*) directed toward oneself (*pratīpam*), which is illumination (*prakāśa*). As for the word "directed toward" (*pratīpam*): for the manifestation of one's own self is not...

Because it possesses uninterrupted luminosity, that [consciousness] has never before been experienced as such; however, it will be explained that by its own power, it appears as if interrupted and as if conceptualized. Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) consists in the synthesis of a previously manifested form with a currently manifesting form.

The sense is that the search for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding blue, pleasure, and so forth, is difficult to accomplish. Here, the author cites a verse from this work: "That which... At the end—meaning at the conclusion of the Pratyabhijñā Śāstra—the path—that is, the means—not mentioned by the predecessors, because they stated that only internal reflective awareness (*antar-parāmarśa*) is the means.

He explains the term "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*) with the words beginning with "of that" (*tasya*). Although Maheśvara is remote [in time], he is referred to by the word "that" (*tat*) because of his primacy. He explains the portion "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*) with the word "toward" (*prati*). The meaning of the word *prati* is "counter-to" (*pratīpam*), and the word *abhi* signifies "facing toward" (*ābhimukhyam*).

The word *jñā* means "knowledge. Therefore, *pratyabhijñā* (recognition) is the knowledge of something previously known but forgotten in the interim, occurring once again by way of being brought before one's mind, as in the case of "This is that Devadatta. Now, one might ask:
how can recognition be appropriate regarding the Supreme Lord, who was not previously known? To this, [the author] replies:

Thus, he refutes the objection (*pratīpa*) by providing a reason for the word "thus" (*iti*). Here he states the reason: "uninterrupted" (*avicchinna*). Now, one might ask: "If that is so, why then does it appear as if interrupted during the state of ignorance? To this he says:
"But that..."—"that" refers to the self-luminosity (*ātmaprakāśa*). "By its power"—by the power of *māyā* associated with it. By that very [power].
The use of the word "iva" (as if) is because that delimitation which has been performed lacks the status of being a true delimitation due to its unreality.

Having thus explained the meaning of the individual words, he shows those two forms—which are the two forms [C: following the recognition]—that are recognized by imitating the recognition, using the word "bhāta" (shining/appearing). That which shone previously shines today...
That which is the synthesis—the unification—of those two as they appear, that is her essence.

The meaning of the word *prati* is "synthesis" (*anusandhāna*), and this is also the meaning of *pratīpa*; therefore, one should not suspect a contradiction between the preceding and the following. [This refers to] the individual meaning previously stated being repeated...

This exposition should be understood as being motivated by compassion for ignorant people. By way of summary, it refers to the well-established usage of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) both in the world and in the treatises—
a cognition directed toward an object present before one through the synthesis [of past and present], such as "this is that very Caitra."

In the world as well, when one who has been known— whether by such qualities, such a form, or even merely in a general sense— as "this very son" becomes present once again, the cognition at that moment of re-encounter is indeed animated by *pratisaṃdhāna* (reconnection).
It is designated as "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*), as in such expressions as "this person has been recognized by the king," and so forth.
Here too, he shows this with the words "also in the world. The meaning is "ultimately" or "specifically. This is indicated by the phrase "his son," and so on.

It clarifies that knowledge is established in its particularity. Or, by way of its universal nature—by means of this form "this is something"—the word "or" (*vā*) in both alternatives is intended to indicate predominance. "Of what is known" means "previously. Again, [it is said]:

The meaning is "at the present time. By means of recognition (*pratisandhinā*)—that is, by unifying [the past and present] through the thought "this is that"—it was made to "possess life" (*prāṇitam*), i.e., endowed with existence. To the question "In what context does this conventional usage occur?", he says: "toward the king" (*nṛpam*).
"Toward the king" means "in the presence of the king"; he was "made recognized" (*pratyabhijñāpitaḥ*), i.e., informed, by the ministers—this is the ellipsis.

The meaning is as follows: Suppose a man was previously known by the king either specifically—as "this son of such-and-such qualities and such-and-such appearance"—or generally—as "some person"; having been forgotten in the interim, he approaches the king again and is asked by him, "Who is this? In that situation...
The ministers of that king produce in him a recognition of the object as "this is that very one.

Then the king, whose latent impressions have been awakened, recognizes it himself as "this is that very one. In that case, there is the conventional usage "this has been recognized. By the word "and so forth" (*ityādi*), other [examples] are [intended].

This is the inclusion of worldly conventions. Having stated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states the illustrated point (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "here too" (*ihāpi*). The word "too" (*api*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). In the phrase "when [the Self] has become oriented toward," the word "always" (*sarvadā*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis;
for it is not logical that even at the time of fainting, one's own Self should not be oriented toward itself. That orientation toward It—
Because it is impossible to grasp that state without being oriented toward it (tadaunmukhya).

[C: Without that orientation, because it is impossible to grasp that state, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is knowledge through unification by means of its recollection. Through its synthesis—that is, through unification by means of its recollection—it is known; [this] is recognition.

He demonstrates that very point by imitating it with the word "nūnam" (surely). "Nūnam" is used for certainty: "I am indeed that very Lord. However, there is this distinction between the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*): in the illustration, the use of the pronoun "sa" (he) was shown as a conventional usage, because in the world, recognition of a king who is connected to the people is extremely desired.

In the case of the subject under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*), however, the application is indeed devoid of that [example]: when Īśvara— whose nature consists of full power known through one's own established traditions, ancient doctrines, scriptures, and inferences— is present before oneself, knowledge arises through the recognition of Him.

"Surely he is that very Lord, thinking 'I am [He]'; I shall bring this about. "Bringing about" (upapatti) means possibility; I shall accomplish that which is possible through the performance of actions capable of achieving it, by means of the activity of an agent.
For instance: first of all, He is indeed possible, because His manifestation is uninterrupted.
In this context, the demonstration consists merely in the removal of the power of *māyā*, which is considered to be cessation (*nirodha*).

Since the distinction between self and other is absent in the realization of *pratyabhijñā*, the intention of an agent and so forth—which depend upon that distinction—are impossible; thus, the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) occurs. And such is the case here in this verse.

Because the recognition of the relative within oneself is desired; for in common worldly usage, there is indeed the practice of saying "this is that" based on recognition, and in the scriptures as well, there is the practice of saying "I am the Lord" as recognized by the Guru. Therefore, one should not be deluded otherwise.
Having relied merely on the fact that [the two cases] are equally desired, a slight distinction has been made between the example and the thing exemplified;
enough of this. He provides the explanation of the word "upapādayāmi" (I shall establish) with the words "tām" (that).

This is the form of the root *pad* preceded by the prefix *upa* and ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the present tense (*laṭ*). The meaning expressed by the root *pad* preceded by *upa* is stated as "possibility" (*saṃbhava*).
That [recognition]—the word "itself" (*svayam*) is to be supplied as the subject. He expresses the meaning by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*): "one who is capable of that.

In that [context], namely in the case of possibility, there is the performance of what is capable, which is to say, instigation (*preṣaṇa*). By that, I, Utpaladeva, am the instigator; through his activity—that is, by means of that which constitutes the activity—I bring it about.
The meaning is: "I sustain her as she exists by means of my own activity in the form of impelling.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of even a hare's horn being sustained. To the question, "How indeed does she exist?", he says:
"For thus... And its state of uninterrupted manifestation [is established].

It should be understood as having that [Supreme Reality] as its nature and as its object. For the identity of the object and the subject, he himself will explain later. Now, if such a state is possible, then why have you set out [on this path]? To this he says:
"the obstructor" (*nirodhaka*). That which is considered an obstructor—meaning, that which is regarded as acting as a veil—the complete removal of which...

[The meaning is] "making distant. For it is not said that the sun, whose veil of clouds has been removed by the wind, was produced by that [wind]; such is the sense. He states the purpose for using the *parasmaipada* (active voice) with the words "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*).

This is because [the action] is intended for the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), since the primary agent is the one who desires the result. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [he refers to] other [cases of] the *ātmanepada*—

The apprehension of the signs of the words is impossible; that is to say, it is impossible to conceive because of the perception of absolute unity. Regarding the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice), it is applied according to the rule "from the remainder, when denoting the agent":
having somehow attained service to Maheśvara, which is the cause for obtaining all prosperity.
Having somehow attained and brought about that recognition for people as well,
and desiring for them the supreme service consisting of servitude to Maheśvara— which is the cause for attaining all prosperity—
I shall establish that very recognition, which is the cause for the attainment of all prosperity. "Having attained" (āsādya).

Thus, there are two *ṇic* suffixes in the application of the repetition (*āvṛtti*). Furthermore, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) has not placed the burden [of detailed etymological analysis] upon this much of the explanation, because he is engaged in explaining the intended meaning (*tātparya*). As it has been said:
"In [this work], which is occupied solely with the exposition of the concealed indications in the sūtras."
Thus [it is said]. Even the author of the *Ṭīkā*, intent upon explaining merely the *vṛtti*, did not touch upon this;
we, however, have explained it by making a distinction, [thinking]: "Our effort lies precisely in the commentary on the *sūtra*. This applies everywhere.
Such is the sense of the phrase "implied by the word *śeṣa*" (*iti śeṣaśabdākṣipta*). Having thus provided a commentary for every word, [the author proceeds].
He begins to provide the interpretation (*yojanā*) with the words "And thus... Now, one might object:
how is it appropriate for *āsādya* to be a synonym for *prāpayya*? Anticipating this doubt, he says "having reached" (*āsādya*).
The intended meaning is that by means of repetition—that is, by way of recurrence—it is connected to the ritual act known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

The phrase "because both *ṇic*s have been elided by the rule *ṇeraṇau niṭi*" is a statement of reason. Now, one might object: "But such an extensive elaboration (*prapañca*) is not seen in the *Vṛtti* and other commentaries. To this he says: "To this extent" (*iyati*). "Effort" (*bharaḥ*) means exertion. "Concealed" (*saṃvṛtaḥ*) means having a hidden intention (*gūḍhatātparya*).

In such a commentary (*vṛtti*) whose function is merely an expansion—that is, a mere manifestation of the intended meaning—of that which is the instruction given in the Sūtra, [the author] has not even touched upon it; what then can be said of a detailed explanation? The implied sense is that their intellects have not even been engaged here at all. Thus...

"Everywhere" means that this principle applies to all the sūtras. He provides a conclusion with the word "thus. "The sequence of the lineage of gurus" refers to the connection consisting of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) passed down through the succession of gurus.
By this, the fact that this teaching is well-established by the great gurus is established as its very foundation.

This has been indicated. One should not, however, entertain any doubt regarding its lack of acceptability on this account alone, for it is supremely acceptable due to its status as a great secret (*mahārahasya*). Indeed, instructions concerning great secrets have traditionally come down by way of whispered transmission from ear to ear.
Nevertheless, they have been committed to writing by certain compassionate individuals within the scriptures of the great secrets; yet even so, those...
They remain as secrets precisely because even those who know them are seen to show disregard for them. As it has been said:
"That which is well-known and uncontradicted is considered the true speech of the Goddess of Speech.
Thus, by this verse, the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the purpose (*prayojana*), the purpose of that purpose (*tat-prayojana*), and the purpose of that purpose [are established].
The definition of the qualified candidate (*adhikārin*), the sequence of gurus and lineage (*guruparvakrama*), and the connection (*saṃbandha*) have thus been shown. For it is as follows:

that very object, characterized by all forms of perfection, which was previously explained as the cause in merit, demerit, and so forth—the root cause of transmigratory existence—is now recognized through this [treatise].

By way of etymological derivation from the root *kṛ* (to do), "means" (*upāya*) here is determined to be the supramundane path; thus, the path is sovereignty characterized by the capacity to act with extreme ease. (Yogabhāṣya 4.3.16)

By the word "uncontradicted" (*avigītā*), common worldly consensus is here excluded. For this very reason, those who seek the authority of the sacred revelation (*śruti*) here find it to be indeed preeminent. Since the burden has already been taken up previously, we shall not labor over it again. To show how it is demonstrated, he says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*). By the Teacher, the author.

The term *upāya* (means) is expressed by a *bahuvrīhi* compound as "that in which the cause for the attainment of all perfections resides," referring to the means of recognition (*pratyabhijñopāya*) whose nature is the accomplishment of blue, pleasure, and so forth; this is the "subject matter" (*abhidheya*), shown—that is, directly stated—by way of its being the subject matter, in the sense that "this alone is the subject matter here. By what [is it shown]?

Having performed [it] previously— during the state of transmigratory existence— as the cause, that is, the causal basis, for merit, demerit, and so forth, which are the root causes of saṃsāra; he who possesses the characteristics of all prosperity— that is,
whose nature consists of all forms of excellence such as blue, pleasure, and so on— is the object that has been explained immediately hereafter.

Relying upon the *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is explained as a means for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); that very [Self] is recognized. It attains the status of the term "recognition" with respect to people by way of being a means; [this is expressed] by this treatise (*śāstra*), according to the etymological derivation from the instrumental case (*karaṇa*)—that is, by means of the accomplishment of the purpose of the instrument.

For this is precisely the excellence of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*): that by means of it, through the search for valid cognition regarding its object, people recognize as the very means [to liberation] those things—blue, pleasure, and so forth—which are the root cause of transmigratory existence and the causes of merit, demerit, and the like. Whosoever...

That very entity—blue, pleasure, and so forth—which was previously established for me as the cause of merit and demerit, is itself the means to liberation; otherwise, this [teaching] would be entirely purposeless. Thus, by indicating that which will be defined at the conclusion of the scripture, the means has been shown.
[This is] by virtue of being the denotable object. For this very reason,
there will be another verse following the introduction beginning with "tathā hi jaḍabhūtānām" (Chapter 1, Section 1, Verse 4).
The purpose [of this work] is the knowledge of the means for recognition; the purpose of that is recognition itself;
and the purpose of that, in turn, is the manifestation of the singular form of supreme sovereignty characterized by all forms of perfection.
By this very means, the dull-witted do not become deluded, while the wise cross over from saṃsāra.

Thus, by this [verse], it is shown that in the verse the word "that" (tat) refers specifically to the portion "the aggregate of all perfections" (samasta-sampat), and not to Maheśvara. By what kind of teacher? At the end of the treatise—that is, at the end of the *Pratyabhijñā*—by means of the following Āryā-verse portion: "The path is new," and so forth. That which is about to be described...

The characteristic of performing what is exceedingly difficult to accomplish— consisting in the bringing about of things that are hard to achieve, such as the teaching of the causes of liberation like blue, pleasure, and so forth, which serve as new means— is indicated by [the Lord] toward people through His own sovereignty.
By demonstrating that worldly means are the subject matter [of other teachings], he leads them to the scope of this indication.

How so? Why is this? By me, the author, that very excellence—here, in this scripture—is determined to be the means toward the supramundane path, that is, toward liberation. To the inquiry "What is that very thing? he says: "The totality..."

The passage beginning with "ityādi" and ending with "sa eva" [is explained as follows]. The construction up to the word "hetuḥ" is exactly as before. The phrase "samasta" (entirety) is to be construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in both places, like the eye of a crow (*kākākṣivat*), because otherwise there would be the fallacy of an unsuitable connection (*asaṃbandha*). "Ata eva" means "for this reason"—that is, because the means (*upāya*) is the subject matter (*abhidheya*).

It has been shown for that reason, preceded by an introduction— namely, "for it begins with what is expressed by words. Another verse— one other than the verse characterized by the concluding phrase "recognition is demonstrated"— is presented there, as it is the introduction to the statement of the aforementioned means.

The state [of being]. Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—that is, the accomplishment of the recognition of the Supreme Lord with respect to the individual subject, as well as the means [consisting of] blue, pleasure, and so forth. Having taken the meaning of "all prosperity" (*samasta-saṃpat*) to be the nature of blue, pleasure, and so forth, its status as the primary purpose [is established].
Having established the meaning as the manifestation of the non-dual Supreme Lord, it constitutes the second purpose (or third purpose,
according to manuscript C); beyond that, there is nothing else at all, because that is the ultimate fruit of all, even in its most minute part.
As I have stated myself in my hymns:
"O Lord, the ultimate fruit of actions or ritual injunctions is nothing other than absorption into You;
for those who, however, desire fruits here, their state remains that of fools, characterized by endless instability."

Thus [he says]. This he will state with two quarters [of a verse]: "Placing his foot here... (4.3.16). By the word "of the people" (*janasya*), the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*) is indicated. As he will conclude:
Regarding the phrase "entering incessantly" (4.3.16), the expression "somehow" (*kathaṃcit*) refers to the succession of the lineage of gurus. As he will state:
"As it was taught by the great gurus in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise..."
(4 a. 3 ā. 16 ślo) Thus, by means of this summary of all things that are to be recognized [or, as noted in K. ṣ.
ṣ., "by means of this summary of all things that are to be asserted"], this...
The statement consists of the form of the enunciation (*uddeśa*) and the essence of the proposition (*pratijñā*); the middle section, however, defines the reason (*hetu*) and so forth.
To show that this alone is the ultimate purpose, he says: "thereafter" (*tataḥ param*).

"Even by a fraction of a fraction," meaning even by a tiny portion of a tiny portion. Here he cites his own verse with the words "as it has been said. "Ultimately" means that although at first glance there may be other fruits, in the end, through the purification of the mind and so forth, the fruit is indeed absorption in You (tvad-mayatā). "In this"—that is, in this [context].

In the state of being identical with You (*tvannmayatāyām*). "Mūḍhā" indicates delusion through its indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*); alternatively, "mūḍhā" is in the plural, and thus the connection is "those who are deluded. Furthermore, the elision of the *visarga* [in *mūḍhāḥ*] occurs according to the rule *kharpare śari*. He says "this" (*etat*) because the author of the Sūtras will indeed state this. To the question "By whom will it be stated?"—it follows.

He says, "In this regard... The sequence of gurus (*guruparvakrama*) refers to the connection consisting of the tradition of the lineage of gurus, in the form of "this was received by him from that one. He provides the conclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*).
That which is to be recognized (*pratyabhijñātavya*) is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of this scripture, insofar as it is the object of recognition. This...

—It has been explained that the "statement" (*vākya*) consists of the form of the first verse. It is of the nature of a "proposition" (*uddeśa*), because it mentions the subject matter by name alone. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*) are included.
It consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*): namely, the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).
The nature of the five members [of the syllogism]. By this, the status of this treatise as a *parārthānumāna* (inference for the sake of others) is established.
Furthermore, the final verse—"Thus has it been revealed by me" (4.3.16)—is the concluding section (*nigamana*). In this way, this [treatise] consists of five members.

The purpose of the treatise is the instruction of others. The author’s intention—that the very sequence of the Naiyāyikas possesses ultimate reality within the realm of Māyā—is expressed in the verse:
"Action, relation, and generality" (2.2.1).
This will become manifest in the subsequent sections; such, for now, is the purport of the treatise.

Furthermore, a virtuous person who is well-acquainted with worldly lords reveals a subject to a lord as one endowed with the qualities of a servant, and likewise toward a subject... [upapannam – K. ṣ. ṣ. ...toward a lord.

The phrase "recognition of him" (*tasya pratyabhijñā*) has generally been shown by means of a genitive compound to indicate that [the scripture] reveals the Lord as one endowed with the multitude of qualities beginning with those conducive to approach (*abhigāmika*).
Now, in response to the inquiry, "Why is the position of the logicians (*tārkika*), which rests upon duality, resorted to? he says: "the Naiyāyika."

In the "stage of illusion" (*māyāpada*)—that is, in the determination of reality as it is afflicted by the distinctions existing below the level of illusion—the sense is that it follows the maxim: "As is the Yakṣa, so is the offering. Now, one might ask: "How was this known by you? To this he says:
"Because of the connection with action. He provides the conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means "therefore," "to that extent," or "in this regard, for anyone."

The meaning is that there is no misconception. "Of the text"—meaning either of the treatise known as *Pratyabhijñā* or of the form of its opening verse. "The purport" refers to an entity distinct from those established by worldly consensus. He states this by indicating it through a genitive compound expressing generality (*sāmānya-ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

"And a good person (*sujana*)": by the word "good person," there is an exclusion of the wicked person (*durjana*) who would cause opposition in the midst [of the assembly]. "Endowed with the qualities of a dependent"—that is, filled with those qualities such as being service-oriented and so forth. "Qualities conducive to approachability" (*ābhigāmika-guṇa*) refers to qualities consisting of fitness for approaching [the master] and so on.

It is endowed with these; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), qualities such as being a donor are included. He demonstrates the compound itself through its analytical resolution (*vigraha*): "the recognition of him" (*tasya pratyabhijñā*). The meaning of the resolution is: "the recognition of that person regarding the Lord, and the recognition of that Lord regarding the person. Now, [an objection]:
He says "this" (*etat*) because the attainment of the fruit may occur for a person either after hearing the entire Pratyabhijñā-śāstra,

or even at the very moment of hearing the first verse; and at the time of hearing this verse— the first verse— the [fruit] arises for the disciples through the process of the transmission of its meaning.
Until identity with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) itself arises; for instance, upon hearing the word "of the people" (*janasya*), [one realizes]:

"We are afflicted by birth and death, our activities unrestrained, yet He, desiring to benefit us, having attained the state of servitude to Maheśvara, [is the cause for attaining the convergence of all prosperity]."

He establishes that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); and thus, we have indeed attained such a recognition of that [Self]. For it is precisely in this way that the meaning of the scripture is transmitted to the qualified disciple, like a reflection from an original object.

The meaning of the first person becomes the object of the imperative (loṭ), the optative (liṅ), and so forth, and culminates in the meaning of the first person, rather than remaining in a state of detachment;
the "transition" (saṃkramaṇa) of that meaning is its internal vibration as something already accomplished, and the "process" (krama) thereof is as follows.

By that [word], "of the disciples" (*śiṣyāṇām*) is the inclusion of those who possess the qualification (*adhikārin*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it applying even to disciples who lack desire; for only those possessed by the desire for a fruit remain, as it were, as if they have already attained it at the very time of hearing the means to that fruit, and not others. By the word "only so much" (*tāvat*), [it is meant] that for anyone here...

The meaning is that there is no contradiction. To the question "How is this so?", he says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*). That is to say, let it be seen thus: regarding the qualified person—the specific individual possessed of a desire for the fruit—from the hearing of the word "of the people" (*janasya*).

By hearing the word "iti" from people indicating the afflictions of birth and death occurring in the mind; "in this way"—by this manner. Of the meaning of the scripture—the subject matter of the scripture to be explained hereafter.
Like a reflection in a mirror—by the logic of the original object and its reflection. Transference—the manifestation within the mind.

It may be so. Under what condition? When [the suffix] becomes the object of the *loṭ*, *liṅ*, and so forth—that is, when it has become their denotation. When it culminates—that is, comes to rest—in the meaning of the first person (*nāmni*), or in the meaning of the highest person (*asmadi*), this [author] demonstrates.

Because there would otherwise follow the consequence that there is no distinction in the understanding between one who is qualified and one who is unqualified. Whether the sentence "Those desiring health should serve Śivā" or "Serve [her]!
is addressed to a qualified person, the transition to the second stage occurs in the form "We shall serve."

[K. ṣ. ṣ. *Kakṣyā* refers to the transition; the meaning is that we have attained the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) even though it falls within the third stage (*tṛtīyakakṣyā*) alone—that is, within the limit of phenomenal reality (*bhāvikoṭi*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the present tense (*laṭ*) is included. In the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

In the verse beginning with "upapādayāmi," because the first person (*laṭ* [present tense]) manifested in the disciple's intellect as being established [in the sense of "I establish"], there is the use of the suffix *cvī*. The phrase "for the sake of the meaning of the first person" is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the second person, and even for the third person when it occurs in certain usages for the sake of the meaning of the first person.
Because of the finality [of this], as in the very example being observed here—namely, "you should serve" (*sevadhvam*) and "we shall serve" (*sevāmahe*).

Thus—in this manner; how so? We, who are afflicted by birth and death—and for this very reason, *aparyudasta*, meaning those whose mode of existence (*vṛtti*) has not been led into the state of being an object of exclusion—are such [persons] by virtue of being qualified [for this practice].
We have been [so] taken hold of; this is our teacher, who, desiring to do us a favor,
having attained the state of servitude to Maheśvara, establishes that *pratyabhijñā*— the recognition of the Lord— which is the cause for the attainment of all perfections.
He accomplishes it; and for that reason, we have indeed attained such a recognition— which is the cause for the attainment of all perfections—
because the attainment of the means, within the scope of the qualified seeker, is itself the attainment of the goal, and not by way of remaining indifferent.

But—in the case of exclusion (*vyatireke*)—he does not establish this [transference] with regard to the qualified person (*adhikārin*) by remaining indifferent (*tāṭasthyena*). "What have we to do with him?"—thus, because of that indifferent attitude, no transference occurs. He states the reason for this: "the qualified person. Here, he mentions the statement of Āyurveda, which has perceptible results, as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

"Desirous of health" means those endowed with the desire for health; "may they use *śivā*—the *harītakī*" refers to the first-person form of the imperative (*loṭ*), or "may you use it," which is the second-person form; this is the meaning of the sentence, that which is expressed by the collection of words.

In the form "we shall serve"—that is, culminating in the first person plural—there occurs the second stage in the process of transition. This is because the actual employment of the sentence constitutes the first stage. Where?
In the qualified person—that is, in a specific individual possessed of the desire for health. Of what kind?
When one considers prosperity as having been assimilated into one's own self through the entry of its nature— which is not subject to death— then, precisely from that,
by attaining the pride of fullness (*pūrṇatābhimāna*) within the beautiful reflective awareness of expanded consciousness, another person, however,
lacks such qualification (*anadhikāritā*) because they lack this very nature, being characterized by a life-force consisting of mere indifference (*tāṭasthya*).

Let this intermediate matter, which is exceedingly profound, rest for now—thus it is established. By means of this verse, both the propitiation of the Lord and the presentation of the purpose and so forth for those to be trained are accomplished.
[This occurs] precisely in the third stage—that third stage consisting of service to Him—which falls within the realm of the actualized.

He brings to the state of being an object of his own conceit—by the power of the beauty of the reality itself—that perfection of the human goal (puruṣārtha-sampatti) which is to arise in the fourth stage, namely the perfection of health (ārogya-sampatti), which has been fully assimilated and attained. By what means? By that essential nature (svarūpa) which is "unfettered by time"—that is, untouched by time.

One's own essential nature, known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); by entering into that—that is, by means of an immersion established through the power of one's own nature. Furthermore, of what kind? One in whom consciousness has become expanded—having attained pervasion—due to the attainment, that is, the acquisition, of the sense of fullness.

[It refers to one] whose such [intense] reflection is also beautiful; for it is observed that one who is possessed by excessive desire is satisfied at the very moment of attaining the means to the desired object, so there is no contradiction whatsoever. Now, as to what the case is for one who does not become thus, he says: "of another. This refers to a lack of qualification (*anadhikāritā*).

The state of being qualified (*adhikāritā*)—let it be, enough; such is the meaning. Having summarized the established point, he says "it is settled" (*sthitam*). "It is settled" means it is established. The word "of those to be trained" (*vineyānām*), i.e., "of the disciples," indicates the conclusion at the end of the first verse.
We praise that Śiva, who by the mere act of self-reflection brings about within the heart the introductory exposition of the world’s own thread.
Thus, having accomplished the auspicious benediction for the purpose of completing the treatise, [the author] first,

for the sake of the unimpeded completion of the commentary on the first daily lesson within the first investigation titled "The Authority of Knowledge" (*jñānādhikāra*), [praises] Śrī Śiva, who is his own chosen deity.

He praises [Śiva] and indicates the essential purport of the daily ritual (āhnika) with the words "Ananta": "We ever praise that Śiva, whose supreme vibration serves as the introduction for the manifestation of the infinite multitude of existents."
But surely, the proof (*siddhi*) of God must indeed be established. What is this "proof"? It cannot be origination (*utpatti*), because [God] is eternal.

Nor do the authors of proofs for God posit His origination. If it is argued that "proof" means manifestation (*jñapti*), [we reply: for one whose light is unconditioned, there can be no manifestation consisting of that which is produced by the operation of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
It is simply not conducive to spiritual realization (*siddhi*). Now, one might object: "How can it be said that His light is unconditioned?

For when there is the manifestation of blue, pleasure, and so forth (or the manifestation of a jar, pleasure, and so forth), from where does that [unconditioned] manifestation come? Moreover, even when those [objects] are not manifest—as in deep sleep, fainting, and the like—it is all the more so; for even in self-manifestation..."
Or rather, what has occurred regarding the knowers in respect to the Lord, such that there is no utility for the operation of their means of valid cognition? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this regard, the commentary states:"

We praise—that is, we contemplate as the most supreme—that auspicious one: the Supreme Self whose nature is light and who causes all bliss. Which one? That which is infinite—unlimited—and which, in its manifestation, [reveals] the entire mass of entities—the collection of objects submerged within itself.

The supreme vibration (*spandana*) of that [consciousness], which consists of a slight movement from its own essential nature, manifests as "I" within the internal region and as "this" in external appearance. This is the general vibration known as "I.
It serves as an introduction, for they define an introduction (*upodghāta*) as that which leads to the accomplishment of the subject at hand.

Thus: likewise, that which is struck—that is, stamped—right at the beginning, like a coin bearing the name of a king, is the subject matter of the scripture; this is the *upodghāta* (introduction). It acts like that [coin], because the entire future collection of categories exists first within the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*); otherwise, [it would not be possible].
Because it would otherwise follow that there could be no exit [from the cycle of existence]. By this, it is indicated that this is the introductory section (*upodghātāhnika*);
and its status as an introduction should be understood through its illuminating the entire subject matter of the treatise that is about to be expounded.
Having thus performed the auspicious invocation, [the author provides] the introductory transition for the presentation of the first verse.
"Does he not indeed act?

[The author replies: "Who—being non-inert in nature—could effect either a negation or an affirmation regarding the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who is self-established as the knowing subject within his own self from the very beginning? (1)
The commentary on this point is as follows:

"Now" (*nanu*) introduces the question of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). "Must be performed" (*kartavyā*) means it is necessarily to be done; for otherwise, it would be impossible to establish recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as having that [the object] as its domain, as was previously promised.
[The opponent states: "The state [of existence]. Here, the proponent raises a dilemma: "What is this? The word *kim* expresses a question or a censure.

He says "not first" (*na tāvat*) in order to refute the establishment of its nature as arising. [The opponent asks: "In that case, how is it that the proponent speaks of its arising? To this he replies: "Nor even... [The author] anticipates the student's further question.

Regarding the term "cognition" (*jñapti*), he provides the following reply: "unconditioned" (*anavacchinna*). This refers to the Lord (*īśvara*), who is of the nature of eternal light, who shines perpetually by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*), and whose manifestation is unconditioned. [He is] that which is brought about by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The very attainment (*siddhi*) consisting of that manifestation—namely, cognition—which is delimited by the operation of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), becomes entirely useless. For it is not reasonable to require a lamp for the light of the sun; such is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
"One should not reveal the auspicious net of skillful means with a mere jar; how could the thousand-rayed sun be made to shine by such a vessel?
Thus did he of noble vision reflect.
Indeed, the knower of the Self knows Śiva, who is self-luminous.
Thus it is said:
"While Your true nature exists, manifest everywhere and independent of anything else,
those by whom means are elaborated surely do not know You."

Thus [it is said]. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) raises an objection with the word "nanu. The meaning is: how can it be that it is "unconditioned" (*anavacchinna*), for it is not logical that its manifestation should be an unconditioned manifestation? To support this very point, he says "nīla" (blue). Why? Because it does not [occur]; for indeed...

The meaning is that the cognition of blue is itself the cognition of the Lord. To the objection, "In that case, let there be the manifestation of that [Lord] even when blue and so forth are not manifested," he says "tat" (that). The construction is "nitarāṃ kutaḥ" (whence absolutely?), which means "it does not exist to any superior degree. This is said even while granting the state of uninterrupted manifestation.

He states that the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is of no utility with the words "in self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśe*). "Of the cognizers" (*pramātṝṇām*) refers to the cognizers who are the Lord (*īśvara-pramātṛ*). "What has occurred" (*kiṃ vṛttam*) means what has been accomplished. The meaning is: even in that which is self-luminous—that is, even in that which possesses the nature of self-luminosity established by its being an undivided light.
Having raised this doubt by means of a question and answer, he says—meaning "he speaks"—regarding that which is here:
who is the Lord, of what nature is He, and by what kind of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does He exist? [This concerns] the definition of knowledge.

Would one perform a negation characterized by the knowledge that "there is no accomplishment," or would it be the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) who does so? If it is the cognizer, who exactly is he? Is he the insentient body and so forth, or something else denoted by terms such as "Self" (*ātman*)? And is even that [Self] of the nature of self-luminosity or not? If you say it is the insentient body and so forth, then that very thing, with respect to itself—

How could that which is unestablished (*asiddha*) bring about any establishment (*siddhi*) in another? Even the self (*ātman*), if it were not self-luminous (*asvaprakāśa*), would be merely insentient (*jaḍa*), sharing the same fate as that [unestablished thing]. If you say its nature is self-luminous, then in what kind of form does it shine?
If it shines in the form of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) alone, established in itself, then—

Having thus provided the introduction— namely, the differentiation of cognitions and the internal [perception] of those differentiated ones— he presents and explains the first verse, beginning with "In the agent" (*kartari*). Herein is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

He begins to explain the verse through a stylistic turn with the word "iha" (here). "Iha" means in this world, whose establishment is dependent upon the Lord. "Kaḥ" refers to what kind of entity is contained within it; "kīdṛśe" refers to what qualities the Lord possesses.
Throughout this passage, the word "kim" (what) is intended as an interrogative or a rhetorical challenge. [The author] anticipates the student's response.

Regarding the term "the knower" (*pramātā*): the knower refers to the logician (*tārkika*) and others, since for the Sāṃkhya and other schools, the worldly subject is here a matter of indifference. Here, the teacher poses a question to the disciple, [implying] that it is indeed he [who is the knower]. He demonstrates the meaning of the word "what" (*kiṃ*) by analyzing it as "the body and so forth" (*dehādi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
The apprehension of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. "Other than that" means other than the body and so forth, having the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other synonyms are included. He also raises a twofold doubt regarding the second alternative that was suspected, with the words "that too" (*sopi*). "That too" means even that which is other than those [the body, etc.].
From between the two positions, he restates the first position with the words "that very [thing]" (*sa eva*). "That very thing" means the body and so forth;

"unestablished" (*asiddha*) means lacking proof because its establishment depends solely upon the cognizing subject (*buddhi-pramātṛ*). "In another," meaning in the Lord (*īśvara*), who is distinct from itself. Regarding the first mode of the second position, [the author refrains from further detail] because there is much to be said.
Setting aside the second category for the moment, he says "the Self" (ātman).

For that [Self], acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are equal; there would be no attainment of the auspicious not yet attained, nor its maintenance through non-separation. Therefore, by virtue of being the independent and self-luminous Self, it is first...

How could that which shines in such a manner establish or negate a Lord (Īśvara) who is of the nature of an agent and a knower? If it is argued that he is indeed the subject (pramātṛ) existing in such a state, then who else could he be?
[The opponent replies: "But omniscience and omnipotence do not belong to the subject. [The author replies: "Indeed, the referent of the word 'all' (sarva) does not..."
Yoga differentiates the essential natures of the knower and the agent;

*kṣema* is the preservation of that [differentiation]. He who possesses these two is "equal to that" (*tattulya*). Having thus established the first mode according to the second alternative, he begins to explain it by dividing it further according to his own intended meaning.

Regarding the term *svaprakāśa* (self-luminous): he prompts the student toward the grammatical analysis of the meaning of the word *sva* by asking, "By what kind? It "shines"—it flashes forth for itself. From between the two positions implied by the question "By what kind?", he refutes one with the words "If... *Pariniṣṭhitam*—meaning established as abiding solely in its own nature due to its state of quiescence.
"By that very form which is pure consciousness alone"—to this he provides the following resolution: "Then.

Differentiation (*bhedana*) is the appearance of things as distinct from one another by making a division at the time of perceiving an object; non-differentiation (*abhedana*) is the unification [of those objects] at the time of recollection. Otherwise...

Because it would follow that memory is impossible. For at the time of remembering, the rememberer indeed unifies two prior and subsequent cognitions regarding an object such as blue by making them have a single object; that very process is called "recollection. By this, the Vedānta position is refuted, for according to them [the self] is tranquil...

They assert that the self is merely consciousness once it has reached its final perfection. Furthermore, both "quiescence" and "differentiation"—as well as non-differentiation—are undermined by the impossibility [of their coexistence]. Moreover, since they do not admit the coloring of objects [upon consciousness], they are effectively performing their own refutation of the Vijñānavāda.

Enough with these exhortations to the Great-Souled Ones, who take refuge in the supreme state (*tuttama-pada*). Rather, one takes recourse in the second [state] as the means for accomplishing one's own desired goal; "by that" (*tena*) means "because the previously mentioned [position] is not tenable.
"Independent" (*svatantra*) means capable of both differentiating and non-differentiating cognitions. "He" refers to the Self (*ātman*).

And appearing as such—shining forth by way of independent manifestation—[the author], having recognized that the state of being the Lord (īśvaratva) is utterly inappropriate for one devoid of agency and so forth, [selects] from between the two proposed alternatives for the sake of the disciple: "of what kind? [is the answer].
Relying on the second [alternative], he establishes the desired conclusion with the words "the agent" (*kartṛ*). The word "nanu" introduces the response.
"Of such a nature"—meaning having the essential nature of both agent and knower—"for this reason": why should we establish another God when the Lordship belongs to this very Self standing before us?
This is the state of affairs. Here, the author anticipates the student’s objection with the word "nanu" (surely).

Thus, the intention of the questioner is that it is not logical for the Lord to be the creator. To this, he provides the answer: "Certainly not. Even when there is perception of difference, [the Lord's] eternal knowledge, will, and effort have the [created world] as their object.

Because that which is not a cause cannot have any excellence conferred upon it. If it is argued that being an object consists simply in being brought to manifestation, we reply that it is improper for that which is by nature non-luminous to possess such a state—as we shall explain later.
Furthermore, if its nature were luminosity, the object would likewise be entirely submerged within that very luminosity.

If the ultimate reality consists merely in the fact that "the light shines," then what distinction could there be between the omniscient and the non-omniscient? Since even the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be established in this same way—
just as there is no difference in the essential nature of fire whether it exists in a mass of atoms or otherwise— such is the intended meaning of the subsequent statement.

The term "difference" (bheda) relies as its cause upon an entity established in the Nyāya system. By the phrase "not being a cause"—meaning by not having attained the status of a cause through the function of being an objective support (ālambana-kārakatā)—it is implied that no excellence (atiśaya) can be imparted [to it], because it is impossible for it to be eternal otherwise. In this regard:

The objection raised by the disciple, who cannot tolerate the perception of difference, is presented as "prakāśa" (illumination). Thus, the sense is that it is improper to rely on the perception of difference—which is intent upon establishing objects in the form of objective supports and causal factors—as the cause [of manifestation]. This applies to one who has himself accepted the established tenet.

The doubt and objection of the disciple are themselves adopted as the means for accomplishing his own desired goal by [the Teacher] through the phrase "not appearing" (*aprakāśamāna*). "Leading to suchness" (*tathātva*) means leading [the object] into the state of appearing. For even with hundreds of efforts, fire cannot be made not-fire; this is the intended meaning. The remainder...

Relying on the fact that its very nature is luminosity (*prakāśamānatā-svabhāvatva*), he establishes his desired conclusion with the words "it is manifest" (*prakāśamāna*). It is submerged—that is, drowned—within the Light itself, because it appears as non-different from it; the sense is that it is like a spark within a mass of fire. To the objection, "Let it be submerged, so what of it?", he replies with the word "iti. This means: [The full sentence would be: "It is submerged within the Light itself, because it appears as non-different from it; the sense is that it is like a spark within a mass of fire. Let it be submerged, so what of it? [To this he says: 'iti'. The meaning of *iti* here is that the Light, being the self-nature of all things, is not differentiated by those things, just as the ocean is not differentiated by the waves. Therefore, the Light is not dependent on anything else for its manifestation. Consequently, the Light is established as the ultimate reality, and the entire universe is subsumed within it. Thus, the Light is the sole reality, and the universe is nothing other than the Light. This is the intended meaning. The meaning of *iti* here is that the Light, being the self-nature of all things, is not differentiated by those things, just as the ocean is not differentiated by the waves. The meaning of *iti* here is that the Light, being the self-nature of all things, is not differentiated by those things, just as the ocean is not differentiated

For this reason: "light"—a trace of light in the form of an object—"shines," meaning the Great Light (Mahāprakāśa) becomes manifest. When the ultimate reality consists of nothing more than this, what distinction can there be between the omniscient and the non-omniscient? [What is the difference between] this individual soul (jīva), who is non-omniscient, and this Lord (īśvara)?

The distinction "the Omniscient One" does not exist; the intended meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), everything is of the nature of a single manifestation. As it has been said:
"Blue, yellow, pleasure—these are nothing but the manifestation, which is Śiva."
In this very Self, which is the light of supreme non-duality, who else could there be?

Thus [it is said]. Now, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) applies to that which is implied by the sense (*arthākṣipta*), he says: "the means of valid cognition. This means, "like the cognizer" (*pramātṛvat*).
By way of being established or unestablished—induced respectively by insentience (*jaḍatva*) and non-insentience (*ajaḍatva*).

It must be questioned whether [the self] is established or not; the same applies to its establishment. Therefore, having grasped the object intended as the body, it is the very Self that shines forth, appearing without any separation; it shines even for one in deep sleep, otherwise recollection would be impossible.

And because manifestation is eternal, due to the absence of any cause for its interruption, and because it is manifest even in relation to another subject, it is "to be questioned by oneself and others"— that is, it must be made the object of inquiry. And thus, for this [manifestation] as well...

The sense is that if [the accomplishment] were of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), just like the subject (*pramātṛ*), it would necessarily follow that it is nothing other than the Lord (*īśvara*). Now, one might ask: "Once the accomplishment (*siddhi*)—which, as established in the verse, has the nature of flashing forth as distinct [from the subject]—has been grasped, what can we do? To this he says: "In this way" (*evam*).
The sense is that accomplishment, too, is of the nature of light, just like the subject and so forth. The word "also" (*api*)... [indicates this].

This has the sense of a collective summary (samuccaya). By this, the negation mentioned here is included, since even that does not lose its nature as manifestation (prakāśa). However, for that which effects [manifestation], because it consists of direct perception (sākṣātkriyā) and cannot reside in an agent, its identity with the Great Lord whose nature is manifestation is established without effort.
Having understood this, it was not accepted. "Vidadhīta" is the form of the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *vi* in the optative (*liṅ*) mood.

He states the established conclusion with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). "Viṣayābhimatam" means that which is grasped as an object through the worldly conceit of being an object. "Vastu" refers to the entity in the form of blue and so forth, whether external or internal.

"By way of being the body" means by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). By this, it is stated that even in the manifestation of blue, pleasure, and so forth, the manifestation of the Self is established as the result. [Objection: "Let it be so; however, what are we to do about the fact that in states such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and fainting (*mūrchā*), that manifestation is clearly absent? To this he says: "Even deep sleep," etc. Even with respect to deep sleep...
The meaning is: "even in the state of deep sleep. Here he states three reasons, beginning with "otherwise" (*anyathā*).

"Otherwise" means in the absence of the self's own manifestation. The words "of one who has arisen from that" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. For one who has arisen from deep sleep indeed remembers that state, thinking, "I did not know anything"; and memory occurs only regarding what has been previously apprehended.

It is possible [that memory occurs]; and apprehension is not possible without a self. Since that [self] is indeed self-luminous, one who accepts the occurrence of memory during deep sleep must necessarily accept the manifestation of the self as well. Nor should it be said, "Let there be no memory."
Because one's own experience cannot be denied, let alone those who would attempt to deny it; enough said.
He states the second reason with the words "of light" (*prakāśasya*). The particle *ca* is used for conjunction.

Regarding the "cause of separation"—that is, the cause of separation such as space and time—it is not the case that space, time, and so forth, which are established by light, [can separate] that [light].
It is capable of being severed. He states the third [point] as well with the words "another" (*anya*). For one person does not become asleep while another is in deep sleep;
thus, the meaning is that the manifestation of the Self (*ātman*) is perfectly clear in that state.
Now, in response to the expectation—"What does the manifestation among other subjects have to do with another?"—he says "self and other" (*svapara*).
