Thus [it is said]. "Of that which is created by Him" means produced by that Light. As it has been stated:

because the division of the subject (*pramātṛ*), being created by Him, will be described as belonging to *māyā*. And this [Light] is autonomous. His autonomy consists in the differentiation of the non-differentiated, and in the [re-integration] of the differentiated...

We shall explain in many ways that non-differentiation occurs through internal connection. This very thing is His supreme, sovereign, and primary form consisting of bliss—this was previously referred to by the term "the agent" (*kartari*). However, in order to describe that same sovereignty by dividing it, [He is called] "the knower" (*jñātari*).
This was explained later: "O sprout of wisdom,
even when another is established as 'other,' as long as that other has not been made one's own,
it is impossible to act [for their sake], because the Buddha is the ultimate other."
Thus [it is said]. And the sense is this: one who is created by that [Light] is not even capable of interrupting it itself, much less one who belongs to *māyā*.

Even when [the Light] shines forth partially, as in the case of the sky when it has emerged from behind clouds, even a worldly person indeed employs the conventional expression "the sky shines. Now, let this subject (*pramātā*) shine forth; however, he—
In response to the inquiry, "We do not know what kind of [agency] it is that acts," he says, "And this...

[referring to the preceding]. Now, as to the question, "What is the nature of its sovereignty (*svātantrya*)?", he says, "And sovereignty... [referring to the following]. Regarding non-difference (*abheda*):

although there is unity in terms of being consciousness (*saṃvittva*) among the cognitions of blue and so forth, and the cognitions of pleasure and so forth, this is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

"Bhedanam" (differentiation) means appearing as differentiated by means of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of having distinct objects. "Bhedite ca" (and when differentiated) means when it has appeared as differentiated and been fully cognized; "abhedanam" (non-differentiation) means appearing at the time of recollection and at the extraordinary time of liberation as having a single object, which amounts to its being dissolved by granting rest within one's own self.
For various cognitions, having arisen from that very reality even through internal objects, dissolve back into it.

"We shall explain this," the remainder of the sentence being "right here, immediately below. Now, by which word is that freedom (*svātantrya*) expressed here? To this he says: "That very [reality]. By the Teacher, it is that very freedom which is intended to be spoken of.

The remainder [of the commentary] is as follows: To speak—that is, to explain by relying on the sūtra "the independent one is the agent" (Pāṇini 1.4.54)—the word "in the sense of the agent" (kartari) has been employed. When? At the very beginning. Why? Because of this very thing—the supreme sovereignty (pārameśvarya), which is the nature of Maheśvarahood—belonging to this Self. It is primary.
The primary [reality], consisting of bliss—

that is, filled with bliss because otherwise the manifestation of the universe as its effect would be impossible— is the "form," meaning the essential nature (svarūpa). The sense is that it is logical to first mention the principal [element] itself.

To the inquiry, "But since everything is already covered by this alone, for what purpose was it said 'in the knower'?", he replies: "That very [consciousness]... That which was indicated by the term "agent" (kartṛ) is here referred to. He states the reason for this:
"In knowledge..."—that is, because its essential nature consists of the unfolding of knowledge.

For it will be stated that action is indeed the very nature [of consciousness]. Therefore, what is meant by "the agent, the knower" is precisely this: that which is independent in all actions and possesses all powers. And this alone is the state of having consciousness as its own nature (*saṃvitsvabhāvatā*).

However, when it is called "consciousness" (*saṃvit*), because it touches upon the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) through the process of conceptualization (*vikalpyatva*), it is not [the true nature], since it has been produced [as an object].

We shall explain this as "supreme consciousness" (paramārthasaṃvit). Even when designating him as the "agent and knower, the Great Lord" (maheśvara), that same predicament would arise; therefore, in whatever way it is possible to avoid the stain of being reduced to the level of an object of knowledge (prameya), in that very way [one must proceed].

"One must strive as far as possible"—thus the instruction is given using the locative case (*bhūtavibhakti*). For at the time of instruction, that state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) cannot be entirely avoided for him. By the phrase "within oneself," it refers to the form of the nourishment of knowledge, which, in relation to the seed, is of the nature of its own nourishment.

There is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that the tree which produces a thousand such seeds is clearly the primary [cause]. He states the conclusion with the words "by that" (*tena*); the meaning is: "by that"—that is, by the word "thus" (*iti*). "To whatever extent" (*yāvat*) refers to the magnitude of the collection of qualities. He speaks in order to explain the intention behind the use of the locative case:

"And this very [consciousness]" means: "this"—that is, whose nature is autonomy. "By way of being conceptualized" means by way of becoming an object of conceptual thought pertaining to sound and touch; "the state of being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatām*) means the state of being an object of verbal cognition. "Because it has been emitted" means because it is currently being emitted due to having come into contact with the state of being an object of knowledge. Now, [one might object]: "In that case, [how can there be] the nature of agency and subjectivity?"

In response to the inquiry, "Why was not simply an injunction (*vidhi*) of autonomy formulated, rather than resorting to a restatement (*anuvāda*) expressed in the locative case which establishes its status as an object of knowledge (*prameya*)," he says: "And the agent" (*kartā ca*).
Even with such a statement—that is, even when described in this manner as an injunction—this same principle applies.

It has the nature of being touched by the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*); for indeed, that which is touched by words cannot, by any means, transcend the state of being an object of knowledge. As it has been said:
"That which is non-different from its own self-awareness, when it is expressed to another..."
Then, having reached the plane of verbal expression, it appears as if divided.
Thus [it is said]. To the question "What then should be done?", he says "yathā" (as). "Yathā yathā"—in whatever manner;

"prameyabhūmikā"—the stage of the object of knowledge; "yāvadgati"—to the extent of the means; "yatitavyam"—effort must be made by oneself. Although this is not possible even through internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), nevertheless...

This was stated for the purpose of inducing non-conceptuality in the disciples. By means of the locative case (*bhūtavibhakti*)— that is, by the seventh case ending in the form of the suffix *-ṅi*, which denotes an established entity suitable for designation—
and by the phrase "in one's own nature (*svabhāva*), which is an undecaying form," [the text] refutes the insentient self (*jaḍātman*) as conceived by the Vaiśeṣikas and others.

Refutation of the Argument: The phrase "established from the beginning" means that which is characterized by uninterrupted manifestation. Regarding the term "Maheśvara," this very quality of being Maheśvara consists in the ascent of the status of being a knower and an agent through the nature of uninterrupted manifestation. As for the phrase "the non-inert self," [it refers to one] for whom, as in the case of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, [the self] is inert.
May that Self accomplish the goal concerning the Lord; as for others, such as the Sāṃkhya, they maintain its negation.

Even the Sāṃkhya, by asserting that knowledge—which consists in the manifestation of objects—is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), arrives at the conclusion that the Self is in reality insentient (*jaḍa*); and an insentient Self cannot [even] with respect to itself...
One who possesses only a slight fragment of the freedom of difficult-to-attain illumination is powerless to accomplish or negate anything,

being like a stone; nor is this appropriate even for one whose nature is non-inert, for he would thus effect his own realization within himself only if that [object] were manifesting to him as something new.

Previously it did not shine forth; for that very [state] is superior because it does not result in a split in the sentence. The sense is that syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) brings about fullness in poetry. He explains the word "in one's own self" (*svātmani*) with the words "in one's own self."
The sense is that [the Lord] is asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others as such, even though He does not exist for them, due to their own self-conceit;

by the word "etc. (ādi), the Naiyāyikas and others are included. To explain the meaning of the phrase "established from the beginning" (ādisiddhe), he says "ādi"; this has been established immediately prior. He explains the term "Maheśvara" [by saying] "maheśvare".
Thus [it is said]. *Dhārā* means the supreme limit (*parā kāṣṭhā*). In order to state the intended meaning of the term *ajaḍātmā*, he says:

"the one whose self is non-inert" (*ajaḍātmā*). The word *tu* indicates a distinction (*vyatireke*). By this, the analytical etymology (*vigraha*) is illuminated: "he for whom the self (*ātmā*) is non-inert (*ajaḍaḥ*)"—referring to the Vaiśeṣika and others. *Sāṃkhya* refers to the non-theistic school. By the word *ādi* (and so forth),...

The mention of Baudhāyana and others is for this reason: since the Sāṃkhya asserts that the *puruṣa* is conscious, it is impossible for him to be a proponent of an insentient self; what then need be said regarding his denial of God? For by the very admission of consciousness, the admission of God follows. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "The Sāṃkhya too..."

Thus, by the mere statement that knowledge is an attribute of the intellect (*buddhi*), it follows that [the opponent] is a proponent of a non-conscious self (*jaḍātman*); and consequently, the acceptance of God (*īśvara*) established thereby is as non-existent as a hare's horn—this is the sense. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
"In that case, let the non-inert self itself initiate activity here"—to this he says, "And not...
Why is it not appropriate? To this he says, "For thus... "He" refers to the proponent of the non-inert self; "of him" refers to the proponent of the non-inert self;
"he" refers to the self. Then, [if one asks], "Let there simply be manifestation," to this he says, "Not manifestation."

If there were no manifestation, there would be mere insentience (*jaḍatā*). One might object in this way: "If that [object] does not shine forth, then it is insentient; and it has been stated that this [manifestation] is not possible for what is insentient, nor for what is non-insentient.
Therefore, the manifestation of the jar and so forth is nothing other than the manifestation of consciousness itself. It is not...

This [Self] is not some independent, real entity; rather, it is consciousness itself as the Self. Therefore, just like its eternity, there is no operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) upon it, because self-luminosity is also present therein, unlike the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*). || 1 ||

Now, one might object: "If the activity of an agent (*kāraka*) and the activity of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are not possible in the case of God, then what kind of activity is this that was mentioned—namely, 'I cause [you] to recognize'?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Thus [it is said]. To this he gives the reply: "It would be nothing but insentience. The implication is that, in that case, even according to his own view, it would follow that the self is nothing but insentient. Having rejected its establishment (*siddhi*), he also rejects its negation (*niṣedha*) with the words "and the negation. Now, one might ask: "Even so, what of it? To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). And thus means: even when the negation has been performed. For indeed...
The sense is that non-inertness belongs to that which is devoid of its own nature (ātmabhāva). To the question "But what follows from that?", he says "And not...

The word "stated" is to be supplied as referring to what was mentioned immediately prior. Although the position of non-inertness was previously rejected, he takes it up again by considering a remote possibility, saying: "Nor [is it the case] for the non-inert."

Nor is this [existence] appropriate for that which is non-inert; thus it is connected with what follows later. He provides the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). "That" refers to the manifestation of the jar and so forth. "Independent" means possessing existence apart from manifestation.
He states the result with the word "therein" (*tatra*): because the absence of the operation of causal factors applies to all [entities].
Its status as an example is due to its being established; the existence of self-luminosity is the reason for the absence of the operation of a means of valid cognition. || 1 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the second verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"By this"—meaning by the statement "I shall establish that recognition. Which one?
The meaning is: "to whom does it belong? Having thus provided the introduction and presented the second verse, he explains it with the words: "But...
"But when this [world] is seen yet not perceived due to the power of delusion..."
This recognition is demonstrated by the manifestation of one's own power. || 2 ||

That Self, whose nature is the Lord, shines forth; and since He possesses sovereignty therein, there is no form whatsoever in which He does not shine. Therein, He shines even as that which is non-luminous by nature, and also as that which is luminous by nature. Even therein, within the luminous nature, His manifestation occurs entirely as the luminous nature.

Or "part by part" (*bhāgaśaḥ*); that is, in the manifestation part by part, either through the exclusion or non-exclusion of the whole, or through the exclusion or non-exclusion of a portion, or through the fullness of the aforementioned modes. Thus, there are these seven modes. Among them, the first mode is the manifestation of the insentient (*jaḍollāsaḥ*), and the last is the nature of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśivātmā*).
The middling [beings] are the appearances of living beings;
here the commentary states:
in the Sūtra, however, the word "but" (kintu) is for the purpose of indicating an alternative position different from the one just mentioned. Delusion...

He explains the meaning of this with the word "sa" (he). "Saḥ" means one whose nature is that of both agent and knower. "Tāvat" implies that even a child does not dispute this; such is the sense. And "tatra" refers to the state of being the agent of manifestation.
"Iti" means for the reason of sovereignty (*svātantryāt*). "By no form whatsoever" means by every possible mode of being. Not... [the sentence continues].

"It shines," rather, the meaning is "it indeed shines. The sense is that all cognitions are essentially of the same nature as that [consciousness]. He explains the manifestation by dividing it according to its various forms, saying "therein" (*tatra*). "Therein" means "while being present there. "By way of a non-shining nature" means by way of the state of being an object of cognition (*vedyabhāvena*).
By way of its nature as light—that is, by way of being the knower—therein, it is the second [state] by virtue of being light as such.
That very same [light], through partial differentiation from everything, is the third; through non-differentiation, the fourth;
through differentiation from a few [things], the fifth; and through non-differentiation from those, the sixth—which is that very same [light].

Light is manifest by its very nature as light. Regarding the modes that have been mentioned—the sixfold modes—it is the seventh mode through its fullness [of those]. Although the seventh mode is also the third mode, because it encompasses all modes, following the fourfold internal division of light according to its parts:

This statement does not entail contradiction; otherwise, the description of the fullness of the aforementioned modes would be untenable. Thus, it results in exactly three distinctions: manifestation as that which is non-luminous by nature, manifestation as that which is luminous by nature, and manifestation through the fullness of the aforementioned modes.

Through the fivefold nature of manifestation as the essence of light, the seven modes are established. Now, one might ask: "Granted that these modes exist, what follows from that? To this he says: "Therein. This means: "In the midst of those seven modes. The first is: manifestation as the non-manifesting essence.
These manifestations (*bhāsāḥ*) are indeed the Blessed One’s power called *māyā*, which deludes; by its influence,

although the Self is constantly manifesting as the nature of light (*prakāśātmatā*), it remains "unperceived" due to the partiality of non-manifestation— failing to reach a state of being fully assimilated into the heart— and for this very reason...

When [the subject] does not perform the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) that is to be accomplished by the manifestation of fullness, there arises "non-recognition" (*apratyabhijñā*) for the sake of establishing a specific conceit consisting of the manifestation of that fullness;

this means the emergence of insentience (*jaḍollāsa*), which is to say, the expansion of the object of cognition (*vedyajṛmbhaṇa*). This is because even in the grasping of its own nature, it depends upon another. Thus, [the threefold nature of the subject is established].

The state (*bhāva*). The last [category]—as the manifestation whose nature is light, due to the fullness of the aforementioned modes—is the Supreme Śiva-nature (*paramaśivātman*), having the form of Paraśiva consisting of thirty-seven aspects;
for it is precisely that reality (*tattva*) which has internalized the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) that constitutes Paraśiva. The middle [categories]—

In their entirety, there are five [aspects], beginning with Light (*prakāśa*). Among these, the first and the third possess the nature of Śiva, because they consist of pure Light. Furthermore, its status as a limited individual (*jīvatva*) should be understood as being caused solely by the absence of great fullness (*mahāpūrṇatva*), and not by the perception of duality (*bhedadarśitva*).

But for others, this is caused by their vision of difference, non-difference, or both difference and non-difference; and this will become clear of its own accord later on in the *Pramātṛnirṇaya*. Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "That very [Māyā]"; that is to say, that very [power] which has the form of the manifestation as individual souls (*jīvābhāsa*). And although Māyā exists immediately after Śuddhavidyā, [the text continues:]

The state of Śiva (śivapada) is indeed taught in the Āgamas as being even above [the thirty-six principles], because of touch (sparśa). Otherwise, if only the single Paramaśiva were to exist in the ultimate sense, what occasion would there be for discussion regarding the thirty-six principles distinct from him? Enough of this. "By virtue of that" means by virtue of her.

[This occurs] by the power of *māyā*. He explains the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭe*) as "manifestation" (*prakāśa*). For one's own nature is never unseen by anyone; for even if it is imagined in such a way that it is not seen, its being a manifestation of that [nature] is not lost from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Otherwise, [one could not say], "I did not see it."

Because the use of the word "asmad" (we/us) is impossible; the sense is that it is improper to employ a signifier without the manifestation of the signified. He provides an explanation of the word "asmin" (in this): "asmin" [means] by means of a portion—either in the form of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), or by way of his own part, or by way of the part consisting of bliss. For one under the sway of *māyā* does not [perceive] the object of knowledge.

He perceives the Self, which is of the nature of light, as his own essence, or [perceives] it as being of the nature of bliss. By this, he states the implied object with the words "for this very reason. [This refers to] purposeful action consisting of supreme satisfaction. Of that—of the Self—it consists of the manifestation of fullness.

That which was previously explained is now demonstrated. How so? By means of the "manifestation"—that is, the demonstration—of power, which is well known to reside in the Lord and consists of vision and action;
for actions that are to be accomplished through mental conceit cannot be achieved without the fulfillment of that conceit. Thus...
And he shows an illustration: "By those various prayers [offered]... (4.3.17).
This is what is meant: there is no operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) upon the Blessed Lord, nor...
This is not the operation of a means of making known (*jñāpaka*), but rather merely the removal of delusion (*mohāpasāraṇa*);

for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) come to rest at just that much. Indeed, by the statement "this jar is present because it is perceptible," the jar is not being made known.
Because it is manifested through direct perception itself; otherwise, the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*) in the subject (*pakṣa*).
Only delusion (*moha*) is removed. Both that which is this delusion and its removal are merely the unfolding of the Lord himself, and nothing additional—so it has been said.
And it will be stated [later]. || 2 ||
For the sake of accomplishing that particular form of self-identification (*abhimāna*) whose nature is the manifestation of one's own innate fullness—

though in ultimate reality that perfection exists at all times for everyone, since otherwise the manifestation of the limited ego-sense rooted in impurity would be impossible— it nevertheless occurs through the power of the Supreme Lord’s *māyā*.

There is no conceit regarding that [attainment] at all, just as a poor man has no conceit of a treasure situated in his house when he has buried it in secret; therefore, the sense is that only that much is to be accomplished. The commentary on the word "this" (*iyam*) has already been explained. The meaning of "how" (*katham*) is "by what means" (*kena karaṇena*). [The phrase refers to] that which is well-known.

The word "among all people" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding the phrase "of that which consists of vision and action"—meaning of that which has the nature of knowledge and action—by means of its "manifestation," that is, its demonstration; the use of the causative form (*ṇijanta*) implies "by demonstrating [it] in such a way that it exists even in you. This is stated in the Sūtra as well, serving as a logical reason for proof.
"He places [the brick] with the mantra 'abhimāna'. To the question "What is meant by this?", he says "this" (etat).

"In that much alone"—that is, merely in the removal of delusion—"otherwise," meaning in the absence of appearing as a distinct entity. "In the case of"—namely, in the case of the jar—"of the reason"—namely, of the reason "because of being perceptible."

"Merely delusion" means that the object, the jar, is nothing but delusion. Now, one might object: "If both the delusion and its removal are real, then a hearty farewell must be said to the Great Non-duality (mahādvaita) which you have begun to establish. To this, he says: "And this which is... "Merely a manifestation" means merely the play of power (*śakti*).
The sense is that there is nothing whatsoever apart from that. || 2 ||
Now, one might ask: within the mass of manifest entities, whose power is manifested, and toward whom?

First of all, insentient things possess no power consisting of consciousness; nor can their power consist of action, for since action has its life-force in autonomy, it becomes an impossibility when autonomy is absent. And thus:

In expressions such as "the chariot goes," some accept this as a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), yet it is not appropriate to employ a means of conventional discourse for those who are insentient (*jaḍa*). If, on the other hand, both [the metaphor and the primary sense] are intended with respect to the conscious community of living beings (*ajaḍajīvajjanatā*), then the hope that "the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) is the self of everyone" is utterly remote; such is the case.
Anticipating this objection, he examines it:
here he provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here is the commentary:
"Amidst the mass of existents"—that is, among insentient and sentient objects.

"Whose?"—meaning belonging to whom; the word "by you" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "And with reference to whom?"—meaning with reference to what intended object. [The text] itself makes the division: "of the insentient," etc. "First"—meaning initially. "There is not"—referring to insentience.

The sense is that [the self] is indeed devoid of the powers of knowledge and action. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how is there such common usage as 'the chariot moves'? To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). This refers to *upacāra*—that is, a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on a relationship such as similarity (as in "the platforms cry out"), which is employed for a specific purpose.

"Some" refers to logicians and others. "Accepted" means they have admitted it. In the Śaiva system, because knowledge, action, and yoga exist everywhere as the primary reality in the ultimate sense, the term "some" is used; the connection is that [their position] is not appropriate. The underlying intention is that it is impossible for them to be agents of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

"Both"—how is it that for non-inert things, there is this pair consisting of the manifestation of power and the accomplishment of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), wherein the manifestation of power takes the form of [making themselves known] to other non-inert things? The sense is that here, the power of non-inert things is manifested. "Of everything"—of the entire multitude of entities consisting of both the inert and the non-inert.

"Farther removed"—brought to a state even more distant than far. "Hope" (*pratyāśā*)—hope that has been directed toward non-hope. "It conceives what has been impelled"—thinking "this is that. "It determines"—it brings it into the scope of a definitive judgment. Having thus provided this introduction:
Having presented the verse, he provides its commentary, beginning with "For it is thus" (*tathā hi*):
"For indeed, the support of insentient things is that which rests upon the living;
knowledge and action are considered the life-force of living beings. (3)

The phrase "tathā hi" indicates the commencement of a logical argument (*yukti*); its meaning is: "let it be seen indeed. By the word "tathā," the probandum (*sādhya*) is indicated; others say that by "hi" the reason (*hetu*) is indicated, the sense being that the relevant probandum is now introduced as dependent upon the establishment of the reason. By the word "tena" (by that), it refers to that which resides in the intellect; therefore [for this very reason—K. ṣ.].

Alternatively, the meaning of the word "tathā hi" is that all this is logical because it will be described by the text being remembered in the manner that is about to be explained; for here, first of all,
the mass of existent things exists in such a way as it is investigated, since existence takes recourse in manifestation.
Because [consciousness] unfolds by relying on a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is characterized by the animation of light;
regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides the explanation of the word "tathā hi" as follows: "tathā hi" [means] "for instance," which constitutes the logical justification (*yukti*).

The means (*upāya*) consists in the manifestation of power; its "commencement" (*upakrama*)—that is, its initiation—is what [the particle *hi*] illuminates or indicates, because particles have their expressive power precisely in this regard. He also states the conventional denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) of this very [particle] as "let it be seen" (*dṛśyatām*). Thus, the member *tayā* is explained as "let it be seen," while *hi* [is explained as follows].

"But indeed" (*tu kila*) introduces another opinion; "likewise" (*tathā*) expresses that [other] view. The subject under discussion (*prakṛtam*) is the probandum—the object to be established in the form of recognition. He states another alternative with "by that" (*tena*);
"by that" is the explanation of the word "likewise. Precisely because it exists as a mental construct (*buddhiparivartitvena*), [it is] in the intellect...
"By means of vibration alone"—that is, by means of the *grantha*, the collection of verses (*kārikā*) consisting of the *Pratyabhijñā* (Recognition); "since" is the meaning of the word *hi*;
"all," etc., is the remainder of the sentence. To state the meaning of the sentence, he elaborates the method here:
"in the manifest world. It is "reflected upon"—that is, conceptualized. It "exists"—it partakes in being. Here...

He states the reason for this with the words "of existence" (*astitvasya*). "Of existence" means of the being (*sattā*) that has blue as its locus. "Taking refuge in" means relying upon it as the means of proof (*sādhaka*). "Enlivened by manifestation" means having an experienced reality. "The place" refers to the object of manifestation called blue; [the word] "its" refers to that which is related to it.
That is to say, it has that [consciousness] as its object. Now, as for "resembling a living being" (*prāṇitadeśīya*)—meaning "almost like a living being"—the sense is this:
light (*prakāśa*) has reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as its essence, and reflective awareness likewise has light as its essence.
For if an object were not reflected upon, it would be neither blue nor yellow, neither existent nor non-existent; how could such a thing be established when subjected to inquiry?
What would be the answer? Therefore, whatever is examined as being uncontradicted in a certain way and to a certain extent exists in that way and to that extent;

for this very reason, it will be stated that substance, action, relation, and so forth—even though their natures are extended across space, time, and form—exist as ultimate reality through their unity.

By the verse beginning with "The general relation of action" (2.2.1), this entire universe, though vast, becomes both insentient and sentient upon ascending to the state of concise reflective awareness.
This explanation is based on the usage of the term *deśīyaraḥ*. Regarding "vimarśam"—it refers to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "this is blue.

"Āśritya samunmeṣāt" means from its manifestation or flashing forth. The underlying sense is that otherwise, even in a newborn infant who has seen blue, that [innate] existence would manifest. Here, he provides the justification.

"Unexamined" (*avimṛṣṭa*) means: an entity called "blue" that is endowed with substantial existence (*vastu-sattā*). If it were unexamined—that is, if it were not made the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—then that entity, although being blue, would not be blue; likewise, although being existent, it would not be existent. Similarly, it would not be yellow; "yellow" here is an illustration for "non-blue," and even as non-blue, it would not be so.
It exists; likewise, though existing, it does not exist. In short, it is inexpressible—this is the meaning.

Thus, for this reason. To the inquiry "Why?"—that is, when someone raises the objection, "Whence comes this blue? Whence comes this existence?", what answer can that object give such that it might be of such a nature? For example:

The meaning is that it cannot be said that "it exists," nor can it be said that "it does not exist"; rather, one arrives at a state of mere silence. He states the conclusion with the words "by that" (*tena*): by that, meaning because the capacity for deliberation (*vimarśa*) alone belongs to that which exists, for that reason. As he will say:
"That throbbing is the Great Being.

By means of the words "yāvat" and "tāvat," it is indicated that even if, immediately after the sublation [of the previous view], things were not so, there would be no loss whatsoever; and by relying on this very point, the siddhānta (established doctrine) which is about to be stated—

He states "from that very [source]" as the result. By "as one"—that is, by way of the state of non-distinctive reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). To the question "by what will it be spoken?", he says "by action" (*kriyā*).
Thus, it exists in this twofold form. In that regard, even insentient things, when being reflected upon, are not independent.
When these [objects] are investigated, they do not possess any property that rests within their own bodies,

because that would entail the consequence of them being devoid of insentience (jaḍatva)— as expressed in such thoughts as "blue appears to me" or "blue is known by me. Although those things which have become insentient are essentially composed of consciousness (cinmaya), they possess insentience through the power of the Lord called Māyā.

For those things that have been brought [to consciousness], "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) consists in their abiding in a state directed toward the living cognizer (*pramātṛ*); therefore, so-called insentient objects do not exist separately [from him].
As has been stated by the author himself:
This will become clear in the commentary on this verse, so no further effort has been made here.

Now, to the question "What is accomplished by this?", he says: "And therefore... In that context—between the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*)—those things being "deliberated upon" (*vimṛśyamānāḥ*), meaning made objects of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) as to what their nature might be, are "independent" (*svatantrāḥ*).
[The powers] have their existence dependent [on Him]. To the question "Why not?", he says: "having reflected" (*vimṛśya*).
"Being reflected upon" means becoming the object of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). "In His own body" means in His own essential nature;
"rested" means possessed of stability, because reflective awareness is a quality of the subject—this is the sense. If that is so, then He...
If it is asked, "Where does Dharma find its rest?", we reply: "In sentient beings. For this alone is sentience, namely, the capacity for *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). And so he will say:
"They know reflective awareness to be the very nature of manifestation; otherwise [it would be] like a stone."

Thus [it is said]. Having reflected thus in his mind, he states the reason: "because of the absence of insentience" (*jaḍatvābhāva*). Now, if it is asked, "In that case, how is there the establishment of those insentient things? he replies: "My blue. [This means] "Blue appears to me" and "Blue is known by me," [established] respectively as the agent of the act of appearing and as the object of the act of knowing.

Of them—of those who are insentient, even though they possess the nature of consciousness (*cinmaya*) by resorting to the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), that is, even while existing as the very form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)—by the power of the Lord known as *māyā*, which consists of the forgetfulness of one's own self, they have been brought to a state of insentience; that is, having been reduced to the status of objects of knowledge (*vedya*). [The text continues with] "living... (*jīvantaṃ*).
"The cognizer" (*pramātāram*) refers to the non-inert subject, denoted by the word "I" (*asmacchabda*) in its dative and instrumental forms.
"Having resorted to" (*āśritya*) means having depended upon [the cognizer] as the substratum for the two activities known as manifestation and cognition, which have become his own objects.
He provides the explanation of the term "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) with the words "of that" (*tat*); that is, of that cognizer.

Of the cognizer denoted by the word *asmad* (I/We), which is expressed in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) and instrumental (*tṛtīyānta*) cases; "facing toward" means with direct orientation, that is to say, as the object of apprehension (*grāhyatayā*). "Abiding" means the state of attaining one's own essential nature (*svarūpalābha*); the verb "occurs" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied. He states the resulting conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*). Separately, ...

The meaning is "without depending on a perceiver"; they do not exist—that is, they do not obtain their own nature. Here, the author cites the words of the text, saying "as it has been said. He states exactly what was said: "In this way," etc.:
"In this manner, these [objects], though appearing as if non-existent within the Self, truly belong to the Light alone."
"Inert things are only light itself, by means of their own and other natures.
For it is that very [light] which, being its own self, must be described as such when its form shines forth unconditioned by anything else; and it is not...
There is no such thing as an insentient entity that is not permeated by the nature of light;
for the power of insentient things depends precisely upon the aforementioned principle, and it is with reference to this that the word "thus" (evam) is employed. Thus, within the Self—

When one's own insentient form is established through *māyā*, these insentient objects— blue and so forth— which are objects of cognition, are "unreal" (i.e., they are of an unreal nature due to their incapacity for self-reflection);
yet they belong only to the Light, existing only in relation to the Light, precisely at the time they are grasped by it.

This means that they remain dependent on another because they obtain their own nature [only through it]. Therefore, the One—the Absolute—is Light alone; He belongs to Himself, meaning He is self-referential by virtue of being self-luminous, and thus independent, as there is no dependence on another for His own apprehension. As it has been said:
O Lord, even though our separation has vanished, I am not yours, nor are you mine;
for a wave belongs to the ocean, yet the ocean is never a wave.

Thus [it is asked]: of what nature is it? It is characterized by its own self and others—by way of being the knower and by way of being the known—because it exists by itself as every state of being. As it has been said:
"The object of knowledge attains the state of the knower, and the knower attains the nature of pure consciousness."
If it is true that the Self is consciousness itself, then this entire world is composed of you.

Thus [it is said]. He states the reason for the point illustrated by the words "sa eva hi" (for that very [Self]...). "Existing by its own nature" means abiding as its own relation; "unconditioned by another" means not rendered distinct by another existing as the subject (*grāhaka*). Now, one might object: "Let even an insentient thing be just like that. To this he says "na ca" (nor). "Unconditioned by the nature of light" (*bhārūpānupahitam*)—...

"Unrestricted by the subject whose nature is light"—this is what is meant by the phrase "therefore [it is] the fruit. "Irresistible" (*niruttham*) means incapable of being raised up. By this, the first half-verse has been explained.
As for the statement "it is manifested to the insentient"—that much is indeed irresistible; however, those others who are sentient, distinct from the insentient...

— Thus they are well known by these names; yet, regarding them as well, there remains something to be said concerning the void-nature of the body, the vital breaths, and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*). Let us set aside the vision of ultimate reality for a moment;
even from the perspective of the external world, insentient things indeed possess sentience in the form of knowledge and action. For instance:

Trees, for their part, are clearly endowed with that [consciousness]; otherwise, their attraction of sap toward themselves, the spreading of roots in a suitable location, and their growth upward would not be possible. Therefore, the earth, which is the substrate of those trees, must also be conscious; for it is never observed that the limb of an insentient whole is sentient. This is also the case with water.

An action consisting of the downward movement of water is invariably inferred to be preceded by knowledge, because in the absence of such knowledge, that movement would be impossible. Furthermore, it has been stated that consciousness consists precisely of knowledge and action.
Likewise, fire possesses an action characterized by upward flaming, and wind possesses an inherent action characterized by horizontal movement.

"Being of such a nature," their consciousness is also clearly manifest; and since the remaining ether is both minute and delimited by the ear-cavity, its consciousness is most clearly evident—thus, knowledge is indeed inferred everywhere. As for one who considers that [consciousness] there to be merely imagined through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he...

Let water produce smoke by means of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of fuel; what have we to do with discussions concerning that? As for the fact that they do not engage in various discourses everywhere with one another, through their respective objects and subjects—that is the manifestation of their own nature, even though they clearly abide as consciousness.

Because that [object] is not seen by the eye; because it is understood only through the organ of speech. If it is argued that let there then be the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*) alone—let it be so everywhere, for what loss is there to us?
If it is said that those capacities of the sense organs exist by virtue of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) and the pure consciousness (*śuddhacittattva*), that is true, but only in all cases.

By that very [principle], let it be said that everything is either entirely insentient or entirely sentient; what is the use of these conceptual distinctions? However, in the investigation of ultimate reality, [the Lord] forcibly seizes the hearts of people and makes them dance by means of the multitude of phenomena.
You sport about, concealing your own heart with various turns of expression;
as for that dullard who calls you "dull"—
he is himself poorly trained by his conceit of being a man of taste (*sahṛdaya*).
I consider his dull-wittedness to be a subject of praise, because it allows for the possibility of his being equal to you.

According to this principle, since the very nature of all entities is composed of consciousness alone, the doctrine of a single light (*ekaprakāśavāda*) is firmly established everywhere. As for the specific distinction stated by the author of the text, it is based on the degree of clarity or lack of clarity; or else—
This was stated with the view that instruction is ineffective for insentient things; thus, there is no contradiction.

To explain the second half [of the verse], he sets forth the methodological framework with the words "But those which... Here, "body" refers to the gross body, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to the intellect (*buddhi*). These are indeed insentient, not conscious.
Because of the dependence on another for its own apprehension— for indeed, the body is merely insentient— what then can be said even of those [insentient things]? Therefore, that very thing which,
being of the nature of the jar, the body, the vital breath, pleasure, and the absence thereof, appears as something adhered to, is precisely [the Self].

Reality is that which has the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*); and although multiplicity appears in its initial manifestation, that [multiplicity] belongs to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body and so forth, which are insentient objects of cognition. Therefore, that [multiplicity] is not ultimately real because it involves mutual dependence, for the souls indeed participate in differentiation only through their distinction from the insentient.

It is the state of being its own grasper, because that very aspect of consciousness (cidaṃśa) delimited by it is precisely what constitutes [the subject]. This should be understood to apply to the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth as well.
Regarding "of those too"—that is, of the body and so forth which are connected to the non-inert (ajaḍa)—what is meant?
The sense is that even for them, cognition and action are not appropriate. If that is so, then whose power is manifested?
In response to this inquiry, he says: "For this very reason. "Its absence" refers to the absence of jars and other such objects.

"That which is attached"—meaning that which is grounded in [the Self]—shines, that is, it manifests as existing. Now, one might object: if the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of reality, then because there are many such souls, their oneness would be impossible; to this he replies: "And of that..."
"At the outset" means prior to discrimination (*viveka*). "That" refers to the appearance of multiplicity. "Objects of cognition" (*vedyāḥ*) refers to blue and so forth;

"the body and so forth" (*śarīrādayaḥ*) refers to the physical body, vital breaths, and so on; it is precisely because these constitute the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that [this follows]. In the formal argument—"This individual soul (*jīva*) is manifold, because it possesses the nature of a soul"—the presence of the limiting adjuncts such as the objects of cognition is clearly established in relation to that multiplicity.
Because it is pervasive within that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). For wherever there is the state of being an object of cognition and so forth, there necessarily is plurality;
whereas in the case of "livingness" as the probans (*sādhana*), it is not pervasive.
"The one God is hidden in all beings."
Because of the Vedic scripture stating that the hidden [Brahman] is the individual soul (jīva),
and because of the scripture stating, "Having entered by means of this living self (jīva), I shall manifest names and forms. As it has been said:

"A limiting adjunct (upādhi) is that which pervades the probandum (sādhya) but does not pervade the probans (sādhana). He states the conclusion with the words "tataḥ" (therefore). "Tataḥ" means "from the reason of the limiting adjunct. "Apāramārthika" means "unreal" or "not ultimately real. For even in the theory of difference (bhedavāda), the plurality of ether and so forth established by a limiting adjunct is not [ultimately real].

The sense is that [the world] possesses reality. Here too, he states the reason: "because of mutual dependence" (*anyonyāśrayāt*). He demonstrates this very point with the words "for the individual selves" (*jīvā hi*). The word *hi* means "because.

For the individual selves—both sentient and insentient—would undergo differentiation on account of the distinction between individual selves, such as "this is his body" and "this is what is known by him."
However, the distinctions between entities such as blue, yellow, and so forth,
by virtue of being attached to the subject (*pramātṛ*), have ascended to the very ground of non-duality itself; what then is the point of that?
[ṣ. ṣ. Therefore, since this non-difference of living beings has been established, it follows that the cognizer is "living.

Living consists in being the agent of life, and that [agency] consists of knowledge and action; for he who both knows and acts is said to "live. Thus, this cognizer, by virtue of possessing the powers of knowledge and action—
The sentient beings, being differentiated by their insentient counterparts—due to the cause of distinctions such as the body and so forth—become partakers of duality;

that is, they come to possess this body, and they become those for whom these objects are knowable. In this way, they resort to duality, because otherwise they would consist solely of a single, undivided Light. Likewise, the insentient entities—the body and so forth—are [distinguished] from this [subjective] body.

They would have to admit a distinction [between subjects] by saying "this is the object of knowledge for that one"; otherwise, there would be the consequence of one body or the like becoming another body or the like.

Now, it may be argued that for non-inert (ajaḍa) subjects, the plurality resulting from the influence of adventitious adjuncts (upādhi) such as unreal bodies and objects of knowledge is indeed unreal. Let it be so; however, for inert things, [plurality] arises by virtue of their being truly inert.
To show that this indeed must be true, he says "blue" (*nīla*).

The distinctions between entities such as blue, yellow, and so forth—meaning specific entities like blue, yellow, and the rest. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other external objects as well as internal states such as pleasure and the like are included. The ground of differentiation (*bhedabhūmi*)—

"Having ascended"—that is, having resorted to—the level of differentiation, which consists in appearing as blue and other such [objects]. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter (*prameya*). Now, one might object:
"In that case, the desired unity is not established at all. To this, he says: "What is the use of that?"—meaning, what is the use of those [distinctions]?

By ascending the stage of differentiation. What [is gained]? The meaning is that at this time, since only the unity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is the subject under discussion, there is no loss whatsoever by that [unity]. The point is that once the unity of the soul is established, the unity of the insentient (*jaḍa*) is established without effort. He states the conclusion: "Therefore, this... "This" refers to that which has been established immediately prior. The supreme...
He states the conclusion with the words "iti iti. "Iti" means for this reason. "The living subject" (jīvan-pramātā) means that one who is the agent of living is the subject;

the meaning is that [this] has been established. Now, one might ask: what relevance does this have to the two topics at hand, namely knowledge and action? To this he says "jīvanam," etc. And "that" refers to the agency in the act of living.
In response to the question "How so?", he says: "For that which...

[is] to be designated as "Lord" (īśvara), like the Lord well-known from the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and so forth; even in the absence of such traditional renown, sovereignty (aiśvarya) consists precisely in the nature of possessing the power of knowledge and action regarding all objects.

This is established precisely because [the attributes] are invariably concomitant with that [status]. Furthermore, this is due to the apprehension of such pervasion (vyāpti) in the case of imagined lords, such as kings and the like: "Whoever is a knower and an agent to a certain extent is a lord to that extent, just like a king.
This is because for one who is not a lord, the states of being a knower and an agent are inherently contradictory, and yet the Self is present everywhere.
"He is both the knower and the agent"—thus is recognition established.

The implication is that otherwise, even a dead person would possess the state of being alive. Having established the Lordship of the Self through reasoning, he establishes it further by means of inference with the words "tat" (that), because [it is] life.

The meaning is: "from that cause," namely, from the nature of being the agent of knowledge and action. "This cognizer" is the subject (*pakṣa*); "is to be designated as 'Īśvara'" is the probandum (*sādhya*); "because of the possession of the powers of knowledge and action" is the reason (*hetu*);
"like the Īśvara well-known in the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and so forth" is the example (*udāharaṇa*). And in the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and so forth...

The sense is that since Īśvara is well-known as omniscient and the creator of all, the Self (Ātman) should likewise be inferred to be of such a nature. To the objection— namely, how can one who has not heard the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and so forth, achieve an understanding of the Self’s lordship through that analogy— the author replies with the words "in the case of its non-recognition" (*tadaprasiddhau*).

Even when that is not established—that is, even when the Lord as described in the Purāṇas and Āgamas is not well-known—*aiśvarya* means the state of being the Supreme Lord. *Tanmātra* refers to the mere possession of the powers of general cognition and action, and not the [powers] regarding all objects; *anubandha* means union (*yoga*), and he who possesses this is [the subject].

The state of being connected with that alone is its *tattva* (essential nature); therefore, it is established—that it becomes perfected within the self (*ātman*). And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*): this self possesses the power of the activity of knowing all objects, because of its connection with the powers of knowledge and action. Here, one should oneself [understand] the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-vyāpti*).
To demonstrate this, he says: "That too" (*tadapi*). "That too" means even that which is a means to sovereignty through the union of the powers of knowledge and action.
"In a fabricated lord" (*kalpiteśvare*) means in an artificial lord; that is to say, one who is conceived as a worldly lord due to greed and so forth.
Likewise, because of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigrahaṇāt*)—of knowledge and action—...

Because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between yoga and sovereignty is apprehended therein, he states "whoever [is sovereign] to whatever extent" (*yo yāvati*), following the positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*).

He demonstrates the negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) by implication with the words "of one who is not a Lord" (*anīśvarasya*). Whoever is not a Lord to a certain extent is neither a knower nor an agent to that extent, just like an ordinary person. He then provides the application (*upanaya*).

"And the Self. Therefore, the conclusion "the Lord of All" must be made by oneself, because that alone is desired. He states the result with the word "thus": "thus"—for this reason—recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), namely, the recognition: "Surely, I am that very Lord. And here:

Even by means of the mere union of knowledge and action (*jñānakriyāyoga*), one is indeed capable of all knowledge and action; Sadāśiva and Īśvara possess these two capacities naturally when the emergence of differentiation has not yet fully unfolded.
When differentiation has unfolded in a general way, there are *vidyā* and *kalā*; when it has unfolded in a specific way...
Just as in the case of the group of the organs of cognition and action,
sovereignty— which consists in the application of the knowledge and activity regarding objects— will be established by means of the analogy of a spark of fire.

Even though fire exists in the form of a mere spark, it is observed to be fully capable of burning even a great heap of fuel. If it is asked, "In that case, why do we not, by means of that [spark] alone, bring the king—who is also of that nature—within the scope of inference regarding all objects?"—the answer is true: with respect to his own nature, he too is indeed a subject (*pakṣa*).

However, this [body] is used here as an illustration in comparison with the external body; and it is clear that a body cannot properly belong to the state of being the Lord of All, because it is perishable. For this very reason, it was stated immediately following that he is the "imagined Lord" (*kalpiteśvara*);
so, enough of this. It is precisely the powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and action (*kriyā-śakti*) residing in the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrī-parameśvara*) [that are meant].

It says "knowledge" (*jñāna*) to denote the state of Sadāśiva and the others. Since the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratā*) is the very condition of non-duality between Śiva and Śakti, there is no need to describe them as having the nature of knowledge and action. They are "inherent" (*svābhāvikyau*), meaning they do not deviate from the essential nature of the Supreme Lord. "Unmanifested" (*aprarūḍhaḥ*) means existing in the form of a seed.

Because it remains [in its own state], it has not reached the condition of a sprout; these two are characterized by the "unfolding of difference"—the manifestation of difference in the form of "this-ness. The underlying sense is that this is because the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) is predominant. He will state this later:
"Sadāśiva is the internal closing (nimeṣa)."

Thus [it is said]. Although for Īśvara there is equal predominance of both difference and non-difference, according to the maxim of the two pans of a balance held equally, nevertheless, he is mentioned together with Sadāśiva because of their proximity and equal status. Alternatively, Sadāśiva-hood belongs to the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), while Īśvara-hood belongs to the power of action (kriyā-śakti).

Thus, the nature of *vidyā* belongs to the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), while that of *kalā* belongs to action (*kriyā*). Likewise, it should be applied hereafter that the group of cognitive organs (*buddhīndriya-gaṇa*) pertains to knowledge, and the group of active organs (*karmendriya-gaṇa*) pertains to action. Generally, "germination" (*praroha*) is to be understood as being caused by the lack of clear manifestation (*asphuraṇa*). [This applies to] *vidyā*—

The impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*) consists in the state of being a knower of something limited. The word "as it were" (*iva*) is intended to indicate that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), such becoming is impossible; for this very reason, the suffix *lṛṭ* (the periphrastic future) is employed to indicate this impossibility.
By this, it is established that the powers of knowledge and action constitute the nature of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), [belonging] precisely to Sadāśiva and the others.

Because [the Self] has the nature of the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord. Now, one might ask: although in reality every collection of entities is fit for the designation "conscious," why are only the subjects (pramātāraḥ) indicated as "conscious" by the term *jīvatām*?
In response to this doubt, he says: "The insentient (*jaḍāḥ*). The word *ca* has the sense of the particle *tu* ("but"). "And others"—that is, other [entities].

The meaning is "thus. Regarding the phrase "at the outset" (*āpāte*), the meaning is "at the time of instruction. It is not that consciousness—the light abiding as the nature of all things—shines at the outset;
rather, [the notion] is that "inert things are non-living" and "others are living. Thus, while this may shine at the outset, it does not shine at the outset of true consciousness.
"It appears" (bhāti)—but it does not appear at the moment of the emergence of consciousness. "Of those who live" (jīvatām)—thus, only these mobile beings are specifically indicated. || 3 ||
Now, one might raise the objection: "How indeed are knowledge and action established, such that the conventional usage of 'sovereignty' (aiśvarya) can be proven?
To dispel this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, knowledge is self-established; action, however, being dependent upon the body..."
It would be perceived by others as well, and by that means, the knowledge of another would be deluded. || 4 ||

For this reason, by the word "let them live"—that is, by the expression "let them live"—only those that move, namely the subjects (pramātṛs), are indicated; the meaning is that they are thus designated or spoken of by means of consciousness, which consists of knowledge and action. || 3 ||
Now, he says "nanu" (but surely) in order to provide the introduction to the fourth verse.
Here, the commentary states:
"Because"—that is, because of those two, namely knowledge and action, or because of the accomplishment thereof.

The "exercise of sovereignty" refers to the self; this is the ellipsis. It is "established," meaning it is brought to the state of being the object of proof through excellence. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse, beginning with the words "therein, knowledge."
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:

therein, first, it establishes the self-evident nature of cognition with the words "I am. Self-luminous (*svaprakāśaḥ*) means that, unlike [objects] which are objects of illumination, it does not depend on anything else for its own apprehension; such is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśaḥ*) of "I."

The internal reflective awareness "I," which has light as its support and that light as its object, is firmly established therein—like a painting fixed upon a wall. That which is called "knowledge" is the reality known as knowledge; it does not possess an existence separate from that awareness. And thus, like the reflective awareness of "I"...

The meaning is that its self-established nature (*svataḥsiddhatva*), which consists in being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*), is indeed manifest through the reflection upon its object (*arthaparāmarśa*). How so?
[It is evident] in such cognitions as "I know," "it has been known by me," and "it will be known."

This very thing called "knowledge" is established as the self-luminous reflective awareness of "I" (svaprakāśāhaṃparāmarśa). What else could be deliberated upon therein? For if that were not luminous, the entire universe would be plunged into blinding darkness, or perhaps it would not even exist; for even a child...
It experiences precisely the repose within manifestation. As it has been said:

"I know, it has been known by me, and it will be known"—this is the meaning of the phrase "in this manner. In that context, both "I" and "by me" constitute the reflective awareness of the "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*).

The phrase beginning with "I know" (*jānāmi*) is a reflection upon knowledge. The three modes of application are for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion across the three times. Now, in response to the inquiry as to whether there is anything else further to be said here or not, he says: "What is there [further]? regarding the knowledge that is grounded in the reflective awareness of the "I" (*ahaṃvimarśa*), which is self-evident.
The sense is that, since this is well-known even to children, nothing remains to be said regarding its established nature.

He supports what was stated previously with the word "tat" (that): "of that"—namely, of the knowledge grounded in the self-reflection of "I"—in the absence of manifestation, the "entirety of existence" (viśvam), which is the whole range of objective phenomena, becomes "blind darkness" (andhatamasam).
It has the nature of dense darkness; the meaning is that it is impossible to grasp. As it has been said:
"You alone are the one called Light; all others are equal to darkness.
And likewise:
Regarding the fact that the principle of consciousness is self-luminous, what need is there for arguments?
In its absence, the entire universe would be non-luminous due to its insentience.
And so it is said. He states another exception: "That too" (*tad api*).

"That too" means even the blinding darkness (*andhatamasam*); for even in the apprehension of darkness, it is only light that possesses the capacity [to be perceived]. Indeed, one born blind, whose light has not entered through the gateway of the eyes, is unable to perceive even darkness.

Because non-perception alone belongs to that [darkness]; for perception, which is of the nature of absence, is distinct from the nature of the blue form and from the nature of the substance of darkness. He says "even a child" because this is established even for a child. Regarding "in light"—it refers to the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃvimarśa*) and the knowledge residing therein.
And while the light of the "I" remains as the essential core, one experiences rest—that is, one leads it to become an object of experience for others—as in:
"By what, my dear, should one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

Thus it is said. For if that [the self] were denied, what question could there be, and what answer? In that regard, when one says "I know" and "give," it is understood by this that the self has been obtained; otherwise, the use of the word *mama* (to me) would be untenable. Furthermore, the root *vid* belongs to the *cur-ādi* class, and thus its meaning is "it cognizes. In this context—
He also cites scripture as authority in the words, "the knower" (*vijñātāram*).

In that case, the knower is the subject (*pramātā*) established by the cognition of the "I-reflection" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*). Now, O people who act with foresight, for what—toward what fruit—do you seek that knower?

The meaning is that one should know [the Self] as the very place of rest; since any knowledge other than that—whether directed toward it or distinct from it—is useless, one would not even engage in the activity of seeking such knowledge. Likewise, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could one know it? For its realization is attained through that [Self] alone.
Because the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is impossible therein. As it has been said:
"Even those means of valid cognition which extend the life of things—their supreme life-force is that very Supreme Lord."
Thus: "In what manner—by what form—could one know [it]? For that which is formless, knowledge is simply not possible. As it has been said:
"That of which no delusion is found even by those whose internal organs are deluded..."
We praise that Mṛḍa, whose end is difficult to reach even for those who have gone far.

Thus [it is said]. For here, the word *antaḥ* (within) ultimately denotes one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). It means "difficult to traverse" or "difficult to know. Furthermore, by what form could one, while remaining oneself, know that [Self]? Since one abides as that very form oneself, one is not able to know it; for [knowledge] belongs only to that which is distinct [from the object].
The meaning is that it is possible for [the self] to be an object of knowledge. As it has been said:
"If the self were an object of cognition, there would have to be another as its cognizer;
in that case, the self would be something other, namely that which is being measured."
"I know"—by this, even the application of internal impulsion appears, as indicated by the phrase "from qualities such as white, which are utterly insentient.
Thus, the intention of the Śruti is that it is in no way logical for the Knower to be an object. And so, other Śrutis state:
That which is not thought is thought by him; he who thinks it does not know it.
It is known to those who do not perceive it, and unknown to those who perceive it.
Likewise:
"That which is an object of cognition (vedya) is insentient (jaḍa).
Now, one might object that by this [statement], its very negation follows; to this he says: "In its negation" (tannihnave)—that is, in the negation of that [object].
The meaning is that if the cognizer were denied, it would result in the denial of both the questioner and the speaker. As it has been said:
"If one knows 'Brahman is non-existent,' he himself becomes non-existent.
What is intended here is this: there is no need even for the apprehension of a cognizer, for [the Self] is itself the grasper.

Because it is already established. Nor is it logical for that very [consciousness] to grasp itself, as that would entail its becoming something other than itself. Furthermore, if it does not grasp itself, even the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is untenable, because the entire totality is established from that very [consciousness] itself; thus, it cannot logically serve as a means (*upāya*) toward itself.
[Objection: But surely, by way of being grounded in self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), consciousness possesses the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*).
"Let it be self-established; but how can that [self-establishment] also belong to action, which is indicated by the word 'api'?

To this he says: "And there... That is to say, when that [consciousness] exists, even the exertion (*saṃrambha*) appears within the triad beginning with "I know"—this being an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, among the three starting with "I know," the application of effort also shines forth.

The connection with vibration (spanda), which is expressed by the suffixes of the *kṛt* class, also shines— it manifests as self-luminous, like knowledge established in the reflective awareness of "I. By means of this manifestation— [by means of which state— C.]—
the form "I know" is established in the act of knowing through the conceptualization of the division between root and suffix.

"I know" is its essential nature (*svarūpa*). From that which is "extremely inert"—meaning, from that which is exceedingly inert because it is always dependent on another for its own apprehension—such as a quality like whiteness; by depending upon that [quality], the form "I know" attains the state of being its own inherent nature (*svabhāvatām abhyeti*). And that intense impulse is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
The power of action (kriyā-śakti) arises; as it was said by our venerable supreme preceptor, Śrī Somānanda:
"Even at the time of perceiving a jar or other objects, that which cognizes the jar is action."
Thus, that internal power of action (*kriyāśakti*)— like knowledge itself—

is established by itself and self-luminous; yet, through its own power, moving even into the body by way of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), it exists in the form of vibration (*spandana*).

...up to: it attains—that is, reaches—the nature of consciousness (citsvabhāvatām), which is the state of being consciousness (cidrūpatām). This is because, although internal knowledge exists as an object of apprehension (*grāhyatva*) with respect to the subject-form (*pramātṛrūpa*), it assumes the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabhāva*) with respect to external qualities such as whiteness, thereby functioning as the apprehender (*grāhakatva*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: *sa*...

And so it is said: "Vimarśa" (reflective awareness) consists in the determination of an object. And that is "saṃrambha"—the internal vibration (*spanda*) expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), which constitutes the power of action (*kriyāśakti*);
for otherwise, the employment of the verbal suffix would be impossible—this is the intended meaning. Here, he cites a statement from the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, saying: "As it has been said."

Even at the time of perceiving a jar or other objects, that which occurs as "I know the jar" is the action (*kriyā*); however, the intention of the word "also" (*api*) is that it is not only the "I am doing" occurring at the time of the instrument (*karaṇa*) that constitutes the action. He reveals his established position with the words "by that" (*tena*). It is internal—consisting of the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—and not the activity of the body.

—Form (rūpa). Just like cognition (*jñāna*), it means like the cognition whose nature is that of a cognizer established in the self-reflection (*ahaṃparāmarśa*). Now, if this alone is action, then what of the movement (*spanda*) of the body that is directly perceived? To this he says: "That very same"—that is, the internal action itself—by its own power (*svaśaktyā*).
By its own power; "consisting of activity" means having the nature of activity. "In the realm of *māyā*" means in the state of differentiation;
"the object" means the sphere of perception. As it has been said: "Even in the world, that which is indeed the internal vibration [of consciousness] in the form 'I am going'..."
That activity of motion enters into the body, the location, and the senses.
Thus, by this, the explanation of the second sentence is completed. The word *api* (also/even) is intended to include the fact that [the power] was self-established even at a prior time.
Even in the state of *māyā*, it consists of activity (*vyāpāra*)—that is, it consists of activity and expression (*vyāhāra*).

The object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception and so forth, is that [cognition]; and when it is apprehended in association with another body and so on, it makes known its own nature, which consists of cognition (it makes known that which consists of cognition—K. Ṣ.
Ṣ.), and cognition does not appear as "this" (*idantayā*), for "this-ness" is non-cognition, nor is it any other entity.
Whatever appears in one form or another,

that knowledge alone shines forth supremely; and that which shines is precisely the causality of knowledge— which is the causal form— toward the bodily action, which is the effect-form of the notion "I."

He explains what was stated by the third sentence with the words "And that... (*sā ca*). By means of concomitance—that is, as a constant companion—it makes its own nature known; that is, it leads its own essential form to become an object of cognition through the method of logical inference (*tarka*), [concluding] "it must be so. By this, it is also stated that knowledge is established for the other party.

In this context, the case of the pot being made from clay, and the clay being shaped into a pot by itself, should be taken as the illustration. Now, one might object: "By this, a distinction between one's own cognition and another's cognition is established; and if that is so, the desired non-duality (advaita) becomes as impossible as the son of a barren woman."

To this he says "na ca" (and not). "Jñānam" means the form of the cognized object. "Idantayā" means by the cognition "this"; it does not appear as such because it has just been established that it resides solely within the "I. To the question "Why does it not appear? he says "idantā. For—"hi"—because "idantā" is indeed nothing but ignorance (*ajñānatva*).

Because that term [“object,” *viṣaya*] is applied only to things such as jars, which are distinct from cognition. Now, one might object: “But in this case, the cognition itself appears precisely as ‘this’ (*idantayā*);

what can we do about that? To this he says: “And not...”. An object that is other [than cognition] cannot appear as something else—that is, in its own essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*)—if it were otherwise, then for that which appears in the form of silver...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the pure consciousness (*śukta*) would appear [as an object]. Now, if it is argued that "in that case, let that cognition simply not appear," he says:
"that" (*tat*). That cognition is *param*—meaning absolute—and indeed appears. For even if it does not appear in the manner it is imagined, it exists as the witness (*sākṣitayā*).

"Body" (*vapuḥ*) refers to supreme consciousness (*parajñāna*) as well, which is one's own self alone; "otherness" (*paratva*) belongs solely to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body and so forth.

Furthermore, when that [adjunct] is investigated, it is found to be nothing other than the universal subject (*viśvaḥ pramātṛvargaḥ*); in the ultimate sense, there is only one single subject, and he alone exists. As it has been said: [as stated in the *Krama-ṣaṭka*].
"...there is only manifestation by means of its own self and through others.

Therefore, from the Lord Sadāśiva down to even a worm, [consciousness] exists; otherwise, its manifestation would be unestablished. [Objection: But what follows for that [worm] from this constant manifestation? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "And it shines. That which shines becomes the *vapuḥ*—the essential nature—of that cognizer who is denoted by the word "I" (*ahaṃpadavācya*). Thus, for this reason, even the knowledge of another (*parajñāna*)—which is inferred from the purposeful activity of another's body—is also [included].

One’s own self alone becomes [the other], because it always shines within the supreme, and because the manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā*) regarding this object is established otherwise. Now, one might ask: where do we remove the "otherness" (*paratva*) that appears? To this he says: "otherness. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth are included. No.

The sense is that it is indeed logical for there to be a distinction between the two spaces situated within the two jars. Now, in response to the objection that one should simply remove the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which brings about the notion of "otherness," he says: "And that too. The word *yāvat* is used in the sense of restriction; thus, *sa ca* means "and that [adjunct]," and *yāvadvicāritaḥ* means "as soon as it has been examined. In other words, it is precisely upon being examined that [the distinction vanishes].

"Other" means it does not exist as something distinct from the subject whose nature is light. For it is not logical that space should serve as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for space itself, since such an adjunct is observed in the case of things like jars, which are distinct from it.
He states the conclusion with the word "iti": "iti"—for this reason, the entire multitude of subjects (*pramātṛvarga*).

The multitude of subjects, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), is but a single subject. This is because even the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) situated in the midst [of them] flashes forth as that very [subject]. And he alone—that is, the single subject alone—exists;
he exists as the ultimate reality, since the differentiation of subjects is merely constructed by limiting adjuncts.

Because it does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). As for the one who says: "In the doctrine of a single cognizer (*ekapramātṛvāda*), why is it that when one person experiences pleasure and so forth, others are not seen to be likewise possessed of it?"—he is simply seized by the delusion that the body is the self (*dehātmabhrānti*); for where even the body and such are conceived as unreal, how could pleasure and so forth established therein be real?

What indeed is this talk? Or let it be so; even for that [opponent], there is no loss whatsoever from the perspective of reality. Therefore, enough with these webs of words, which are useless regarding a matter obtainable solely through the grace of the Blessed One.
Regarding this, he cites the consensus of the elders, saying "it has been said. And since this has already been explained, we do not labor over it again. By this—

He states the established conclusion with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*).
