As a result, from the knowledge of Sadāśiva down to the knowledge of a worm, there is only one single cognizer; thus, the cognizer possesses omniscience as a result. The same should be said regarding agency. As it was stated by our supreme preceptor in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
The jar knows through my self, and I know through the self of the jar;
I know through the self of Sadāśiva, or he knows through my self.
Śiva himself remains knowing his own self through various states;
by establishing the oneness of these two, the oneness of all other intermediate cognitions also follows, and when there is oneness of cognition, [there is oneness] of those forms as well.

The unity of the knowers (*pramātṛ*) is also established; and thus, omniscience accrues to one and the same [knower]. This means it follows "as a result"—that is, by way of its fruit—and not directly. As it has been said:
"That very consciousness which [resides] in the sun within the sky that adorns the expanse of the firmament..."
That same consciousness resides within the hollow cavity of the earth, even as it does within the hollow of an insect's burrow.

Thus, by this, the [notion of] worldly omniscience is refuted. Now, one might ask: "Let it be that [the Lord] is thus a knower; what is the status of His being an agent? To this he says: "In this way. The sense is that agency is merely a secondary manifestation (*pallava*) [of His nature]. Here, he cites the words of Śrī Somānanda as an illustration: "The jar [is known] through my Self," etc. The jar—
A jar is the object of cognition. "By my own self"—that is, by my own nature as the cognizer—I am the agent with respect to the cognition of my own object; I cognize it.
O Beloved, as long as these [objects] are not cognizers, how could they be objects of cognition?
According to this principle, because [the Self] vibrates through its own being (*madbhāva*) at the time of sensation and desire, I know [the object] as the nature of a jar;
and I also know it by means of the essential form of the jar, which has attained the state of being a knower through the acquisition of its own being as a jar.
This is because, for me too, at the time of perceiving the jar, there is the acquisition of the jar's being; otherwise, perception would not exist.
As it has been said:
"If that which is distinct were the Buddha, why would everything not be the Buddha?
Having thus stated the identity between the limited subject and the object, [the author proceeds].
It tells us that the state of Sadāśiva belongs to both the infinite knower (*aparimitapramātṛ*) and the limited knower (*parimitapramātṛ*). The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*);

the meaning is that the knowledge of Sadāśiva is mine alone, and my knowledge is his alone. Indeed, a distinction between two fires—one existing as a particle (*kaṇabhāva*) and one existing as a mass (*cayabhāva*)—is never tenable.
The sense is that [the cognition] consists merely of a collection of particles (*kaṇa*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other sentences found therein are intended.
By the term "is inferred" (*ūhyate*), he demonstrates that the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is not established for cognition;
otherwise, he would have said "it is inferred" (*anumīyate*).

Thus, those for whom the state of being soiled by the falling dust of the disputations of logicians has not occurred on this path of direct experience, they— knowing themselves to be the Lord by means of this much alone—
submerge the jar, the body, the vital breath, pleasure, and its absence right there [within that experience], and are indeed possessed by the Lord.
Thus it is. Therefore, this is the introduction (*upoddhāta*). *Upa* means "near to oneself";

that by which excellence—characterized by the recognition of the Lord (*īśvarapratyabhijñāna*)—is struck (*hanyate*) and brought to rest (*viśrāmyate*), like a chisel (*ṭaṅka*). This alone is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of this treatise. Furthermore, from that...

[The word] "grahaṇam" [means] apprehension. Having thus established the identity of one's own cognition and that of another, he says "it is inferred" (ūhyate) in order to state the intended meaning of this; the sense is that the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is asserted by everyone for the object of inference (*anumānaviṣaya*), but not for the object of reasoning (*tarkaviṣaya*).
To establish that this chapter possesses the nature of an *upodghāta* (introductory exposition), he says "that" (*tat*), which is illuminated by the benedictory verse of this chapter.

This being so, it has not occurred—that is, it has not been accomplished—on the path of consciousness, namely on the path of knowledge, by means of these four verses alone, which stand as the *upodghāta*. In that very [context]...

"In the very form of the Lord, the Supreme Self" means immersing [themselves] within—that is, perceiving through that very state of being. "Possessed by the Lord" means having attained the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the Lord. By the word "they become," he expresses the very perfection of immersion; otherwise, [it would not be so].

One should say that they would become [so]. By this, the conceit of absorption into the Lord (*īśvara-samāveśābhimāna*) on the part of those who are helpless under the sway of blue, pleasure, and so forth, is refuted. For it is not possible for there to be a submergence into blue, pleasure, and so forth within those [objects]; for when those [objects] are attained, enjoyment occurs as is appropriate, whereas when they are not attained, there is only disregard. And in that regard, it is one's own mind alone...
It must be accepted as a witness [to this], for otherwise the fault of self-deception would follow; enough of this.

By this, he states the established conclusion with the word "tataḥ" (therefore). "Tataḥ" means: because immersion (*samāveśa*), which is the subject matter of all the scriptures, is established by this very [means], therefore—for that reason—is the meaning. Furthermore, another point:

He provides the etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) of the word *upoddhāta* [as follows]: "Upa" means a stone-splitter (*ṭaṅka*), and [the suffix] "-īśvara-pratyabhijñāna-lakṣaṇa" means having the form of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "I am God. Now, one might ask:
how does this constitute an *upoddhāta*? To this he says: "Just this much," namely, within the self (*ātmani*).

This is precisely the resting place of excellence (*utkarṣaviśrāmaṇa*). He states another etymological derivation as well: "in a whisper" (*upāṃśu*). This is the introductory context (*upodghāta*). Having made it "in a whisper," that is, unextended (*avitata*), by means of this [word] *ud*, the delusion regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) belonging to the scripture is struck away or removed; for the root [from which *ud* is derived] has the sense of "going. Alternatively, [it may be explained otherwise].

The meaning of *han* is "knowledge," in the sense that by means of it the object of cognition (*prameya*) is known. However, some say that the meaning of *han* refers specifically to the act of going toward a woman, as in the expression "he goes to a woman. Thus, it is precisely through the firm cultivation of the meaning of these four verses that Supreme Śiva is attained. So it is said.
Thus ends the determination. May there be auspiciousness. 4.

Thus ends the introduction to the Chapter on Knowledge in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāvimarśinī*, composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, who received instruction from the venerable teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta, the disciple of the venerable teacher Utpaladeva.
Thus ends the first daily lesson. || 1 ||

*Avitatam* means "briefly," that is, in summary. *Prameyaviṣayaḥ* means "the object of recognition. He states another meaning for the word *ghāta* because it has the sense of "going" (*gati*), according to the principle that "the sense of going is the sense of knowing. *Prameyam*—that...

"Of such a form as 'I am the Lord'. According to the opinion of some, he says "but some," in order to reject the view that [the root *han*] signifies knowledge (*jñāna*) rather than motion (*gamana*). "But some," however, say that its meaning is "motion"—that is, having motion as its form—and that its scope (*viṣaya*) is exactly this; they state—that is, they explain—that its meaning is "killing" (*hanti*). Thus it is.

Who? "He goes to a woman. In place of "he goes to a woman," one should rather say "he kills a woman"; for they hold that it is not used elsewhere because its expressive meaning is restricted to violence (*hiṃsā*). He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) resulting from this: "Thus, by the four verses. "Due to firmness" means through constant service day and night.

"By means of reflection" (vimarśanena) means that [the object] is attained—that is, it can be brought within the scope of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). The phrase "four verses" is stated with reference to the fact that the first verse has the purpose of performing an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*). Paramaśiva is the thirty-seventh [tattva], having internalized the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) within himself.
Śrī Parameśvara. The word "iti" indicates the conclusion. The term "śiva" denotes auspiciousness and is intended to point toward the supreme reality. Thus, may there be peace (śivam). 4.
Thus ends the first chapter in the section on Knowledge within the *Śrīpratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*, the commentary known as the *Śrībhāskarī*, composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Now begins the second chapter.

We praise that Śiva, by whom the universe, having been manifested through differentiation as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), is led to the conclusion of the final position of non-duality (*abhedottarapakṣa*).
Second Daily Lesson.
Oṃ! Having extracted the non-duality consisting of the prima facie view from the intermediate position of non-duality, we praise Śiva, who possesses the supreme non-dual position at the conclusion.

Oṃ! Now, at the beginning of the commentary on the second chapter of the section on Knowledge (*jñāna*), the author composes an auspicious verse (*maṅgalaśloka*) that indicates the overall intent of the entire chapter, out of a desire for its completion without obstacles, stating: "The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)."
The commentary on this [verse] is as follows:
by Him—namely, by Śrī Paramaśiva, who is denoted by the word *tat* (that) in the second half of the verse;
the universe—the world consisting of the thirty-six *tattvas*; as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣatayā*).

By way of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) which is to be refuted: through differentiation—that is, by means of the differentiation inherent in the grasping of "this-ness" (*idantā*), which is the life-force of manifestation—having brought [the object] into the state of being an object of manifestation; [it is shown that] non-difference alone—that is, the oneness of the life-force of "I-ness" (*ahantā*)—is the final position (*uttarapakṣa*), the position to be established, and that alone is the ultimate conclusion.
That is the end; it is led—that is, attained. We praise that Śiva—we contemplate him as being supreme above all. By this, the world is said to be of the nature of the play (*krīḍā*) of Paraśiva;
for those who are absorbed in play are indeed independent regarding any object whatsoever.

In this context, that which is the nature of ultimate reality becomes most excellently clarified when it is being defined by means of the refutation of the opposing positions that are suspected. As Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa said:
"Salutations to You, O Lord, who, having manifested the delusion of those bewildered by worldly existence, shatter it;
and who, having assumed the non-dual bliss of knowledge, reveal it.
By this auspicious verse, they themselves produce [the delusion] and then destroy it. By means of this benedictory verse, this daily lesson (āhnika) [is commenced].
It has also been indicated that this takes the form of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Having thus accomplished the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*), he says "here" (*iha*) while stating the purport of the daily lesson (*āhnika*) both collectively and individually.
Here the commentary says:

"In this"—in this path of the treatise—"the nature of the ultimate reality" (paramārtharūpa), meaning the form of the supreme subject matter as the intended purport; "being suspected"—commenced to be doubted by opponents.
But they are not capable of coexistence; those which are counter-positions—opposing, destructive, non-ultimate, and adversarial positions—their refutation is the rebuttal, by means of that.
Here, he cites the consensus of the elders, saying "as it has been said": O Lord—

O You whose nature is play consisting of the disparagement of the manifestation of the universe—though You are worthy of being addressed by the word "we" (asmat), yet because You are meditated upon with the word "you" (yuṣmat) through the experience of the excellence of devotion and perceived as distinct from us—to such a You, who exists in the state of becoming (bhave), let there be *namaḥ*: may there be an attitude of prostration performed by us. To what kind of You? To You who exist in the state of becoming (*bhave*).
In this saṃsāra, which consists of passion and aversion, those living beings who are deluded— those who, having forgotten their own true nature,

possess the error of identifying the self with the body and so forth— their delusion, that is, the confusion of the form described above, is manifested and made evident, and then shattered by the descent of the most intense power (*tīvratara-śaktipāta*).
Furthermore, for the sake of Vidāraka, [he reveals] bliss consisting of knowledge—that is, bliss whose nature is the self-luminosity of the Self.

Of what kind? "Free from duality," meaning distinct from the duality consisting of the pleasure derived from sense objects. Having "concealed"—having brought it under the state of being an object through the veil of the power of Māyā—they "reveal" it by removing that veil.

They reveal this. By this, it is illuminated that even the manifestation of an illusion—namely, that an object forgotten in the interim becomes exceedingly joy-giving upon being regained—is itself caused by compassion. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In that regard, here... "Therein" refers to what was previously stated.
When the object exists as being without self and without a Lord—meaning that in the absence of a self there is an absence of a Lord—those [who speak thus] are mistaken.

"Error" refers to the cognitive distortion consisting in the knowledge of the state of being without self and without a Lord; the point is that its manifestation is necessary, otherwise the classification of error would result in being devoid of an objective basis.
The word "nanu" indicates that this group of eleven verses serves as an indicator for both the beginning and the end.
Here, desiring to explain the ultimate reality after first dispelling the various delusions of those who propound a non-self and a non-Lord, he first presents their [views] in these eleven verses.
"Is it not the case that [the author says], '... appearing as a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)...
and so forth, up to '...
by that, even the agent is imagined'?"

Thus ends [the section]. Therein, by means of two verses, the non-existence of the permanent self (*ātman*) is stated through the non-perception of what is observable, directed toward those who maintain a doctrine of a perceptible self. Therein, by means of three verses, it is shown that the connection of memory is established from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); therefore, because it is established otherwise, it is not sufficient for the inference of a self.

This was stated in response to those who maintain that the self is an object of inference. In that regard, the comprehension of the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) through its qualities such as knowledge is expressed by means of a verse;
having spoken of it in its totality, he now describes it also in its distributive form with the words "therein" (*tatra*). "Therein" means among the eleven [faculties].

"Of the permanent" (*dhruvasya*) means of the eternal. Regarding "the perceptible" (*dṛśya*): for that which is perceptible—that is, existing and capable of being seen—the non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), meaning the non-attainment, serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is stated "perceptible" because it is not appropriate to establish the non-existence of a subject (*pakṣa*)—even if it is unapprehended—merely on the basis of its nature being remote (*svarūpaviprakarṣeṇa*).

Regarding those who maintain that the self is perceived—namely the Śaivas, for they indeed assert that the self is eternally perceptible—and regarding those who maintain that the self is inferable—namely the logicians (Tārkikas) and others—he states the function of the seventh and eighth [sūtras]: "The synthesis in the form of memory" (*smṛtyanusaṃdhāna*). This refers to the synthesis which has the nature of memory. Regarding those who maintain that the self is inferable—the logicians and so forth—he states the task of the seventh and eighth [sūtras].
"Thus. He states the function of the ninth [chapter] with the words "then," etc. The connection with the preceding is "by one verse.

The word "iti" marks the completion of the function of the ninth verse. The word "vadatā" (speaking) is connected with what precedes. He states the function of the eleventh [chapter] with the words "by the verse itself. Therein—in the stable Self.
He provides a conclusion with the words "iti iti. Here, *iti* means "thus" (*evam*).

Now, by this [statement], inference has been refuted. Having thus rejected the self (*ātman*), he proceeds to refute sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)—which consists of the connection between the powers of knowledge and action—by means of [an analysis of] knowledge.

It has been demonstrated in two verses that [the notion of action] is either the very nature [of the agent]—as held by other schools—or something distinct from it—as held by the Sāṃkhya school—and thus it is untenable. Following that, in one verse, it is stated that there is no such thing as "action" anywhere at all.
In this regard, he refutes the arguments for its existence and sets forth the counter-arguments against it. Thereafter—
The non-existence of the relationship was established by the verse through the statement of the absence of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*).

Having stated the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding that very point in the verse itself, he concludes his own position: "The self is not permanent, nor does it possess sovereignty characterized by being a knower or an agent."
The summary of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows.

If it is asked, "Since all of this will become clear by itself, why has such an elaborate exposition been made at the very outset? we reply: it is for the purpose of settling the intellect of the student. This is the composition of the commentary on the meaning of the text.

He promises [to proceed] with the word "atha" (now). The meaning is that the subject matter (*artha*)—that which is to be expressed—of the texts, namely those in the form of *kārikās* and *sūtras*, is being explained (*vyākhyāyate*), that is to say, it is being elucidated (*vivriyate*).
Thus, without even a formal introduction, he presents the first and second verses.
He explains with the words "Now, however" (*nanu*). Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:

the meaning of the word *nanu* is expressed as "now, however. It is used in the sense of an objection (*ākṣepa*)—that is, a formal challenge (*abhiyoga*)—and not in the sense of a question (*praśna*).

Because that [position] is untenable here; he clarifies that very point with the word "here" (*iha*). First—meaning initially—he states the reason for its untenability with the words "of the stable" (*sthirasya*). The word "also" (*api*) is used in a conjunctive sense, and "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*) is the ellipsis.
"Because of non-manifestation" (*aprakāśanāt*) means due to the absence of manifestation. He says "for thus" (*tathā hi*) in order to support this very point.

Likewise, "let it be seen" is the intended meaning. "Manifestation of the jar" (ghaṭaprakāśa) is non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpajñāna) having the jar as its object. "Conceptualization" (vikalpa) is conceptual cognition (savikalpajñāna). "Recognition" (pratyabhijñā) is cognition arising from both [perception and memory], such as "this is that. "Recollection" (smṛti) is cognition arising from mental impressions (saṃskāra), such as "that."

*Utprekṣā* (imaginative construction) is the knowledge of possibility (*bhavitavyam*), that is, inferential cognition. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the knowledge of doubt (*saṃśaya*)—in the form "this or that"—is included. They "shine forth" (*prakāśante*), meaning they manifest through self-luminosity.
Although they have a single jar as their object, it is said that they have distinct objects with respect to the imagined difference (*kalpita-bheda*). In that regard:

Thus, therein—within the group of six cognitions—the manifestation of blue is a cognition appearing as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); the remainder is that this is "stated in the Sūtra," and it is connected with the verb "it occurs.
Now, the meaning of the text is explained.

Now, is it not the case that one cognition has the appearance of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), while another—called conceptual construction—is associated with verbal expression and is manifold? And yet, these two are not distinct. (1)
Since no eternal perceiver whatsoever appears here [in this cognition], even this notion of "I" terminates in the body and so forth. (2)

Regarding the term *svalakṣaṇa*, he provides its analysis (*vigraha*) by relying on a *bahuvrīhi* compound, beginning with "its own" (*svam*). To explain the constituent part "its own" (*sva*), he says "other" (*anya*). Fearing that [the meaning] might be difficult to understand, he states another synonym: "its own nature" (*svarūpa*). It is such that it undergoes contraction within its own nature.

The meaning is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*); this is a usage like [the expression] "the head of Rāhu," because the agent of the act of worship and its substratum are one and the same. He explains the word *lakṣaṇa* as "place" (*deśa*). *Lakṣaṇa* means "essential nature" (*svarūpa*), and since that consists precisely of the application of the triad beginning with place as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the mention of "place and so forth" is made; of which—
He explains the word *ābhāsa* (appearance) as a constituent part [of the compound] by saying "illumination" (*prakāśanam*).

Illumination means light—that is, manifestation. "Inward-turned" (*antarmukham*) means situated in a state of facing toward the subject (*pramātṛ*), which serves as the referent for the other member of the compound.
"O you who assume the nature of that which is directed outward"—that is to say, in the form of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) directed toward an external object as "this.

"In knowledge" means in the reality denoted by the term "knowledge. By this, it is stated that the term "particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) functions as an adjective qualifying "knowledge. "That" refers to the non-conceptual [perception] just mentioned.

Non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*), whose nature is luminosity, remains of a single kind—that is, of one form—even when there is a difference in objects, such as the difference between objects like jars and so forth. He states the reason for this: "even though there is diversity in its own nature.
Here too, he provides the reason through a statement: "for in conceptualization (*vikalpa*)," where "expression" (*abhilāpa*) means verbal designation by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

This refers to the recollection of the denotative word (*vācakasmṛti*). Here, "in non-conceptual cognition" (*avikalpake jñāne*) is the context. He provides the justification for the statement "it does not exist" with the words "for indeed not" (*na hi*), the sense being that if it were a property of the blue object itself, it would have no dependence upon mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). To the question "In that case, from where is this [recollection] brought? he replies "from that" (*tataḥ*). "Prior" (*prācyaḥ*) means belonging to the time of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). Now, from that...?
To explain why this is so, he says: "And when [the mind] is unawakened. "Its awakening" means the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

"Arisen from the perception of an object" means: an object (*vastu*) such as a jar which has become the objective domain; its "perception" (*darśana*) is its manifestation (*prakāśa*); "arisen from that" means produced from that. He states the conclusion: "Thus..."

The word "nanu" expresses an objection: here, it is first of all untenable to claim that the Self is of the nature of consciousness and stable, because even that which is stable and self-luminous does not manifest [itself]. For instance, there is the manifestation of a jar, the conceptualization of a jar, and the recognition of a jar.
Cognitions themselves manifest in such forms as the memory of a jar, the conceptualization (utprekṣā) of a jar, and so forth—

cognitions that belong to different times, have different objects, and possess different forms. Among these, the manifestation of blue (*nīlaprakāśa*) is "a cognition appearing as a particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇābhāsaṃ jñānam*), where "its own" (*svam*) means not following after anything else.

In that knowledge which possesses an outward-turned nature yet maintains an inward-turned manifestation— wherein there is the "appearance," that is, the illumination, of that which has "characteristics" consisting of space, time, and form— it is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), being of a single genus even when the objects differ, and remaining so despite the diversity of its own forms.
[It is] of a single nature in its own form, but diverse in its manifestation—because there is no cause for it. For diversity has its cause in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Thus, for this reason, the first sentence has been explained. And so is the syntactical connection (*yojanā*):
Is it not the case that there is a single cognition appearing as the particular (svalakṣaṇa)?
To explain the second statement, he says: "Thereafter" (tataḥ param).
"Thereafter" means from that cognition; "thereafter" [means] another form, a conceptualizing cognition, manifests.

The remainder follows. Here he states the reason with the words "of everything. In that regard, the conceptualization of a jar has its root directly in the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) of it; whereas the conceptualization of a jewel arising from the perception of the luster of a jewel has its root indirectly in the perception of the luster of the jewel, for by means of the luster...

Through that, there is the perception of light; through that, the conceptualization of light; through that, the conceptualization of the jewel. He provides an explanation of the word *para* (other/superior), saying "param" (it is other). In response to the inquiry, "From what does its otherness [arise]?", he says "sāmānye" (in the universal), with the words "yataḥ" (since/from which) being understood as the ellipsis. *Sāmānyalakṣaṇam* means the nature of the universal (*sāmānyasvarūpam*); of that—

The sense is that conceptual cognition (*savikalpajñāna*) is therefore "other" (*para*). Although, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa*) has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, whereas conceptual cognition has as its object specifically the particular (*viśeṣa*) consisting of the association with place and so forth, let this point rest for now. Now, one might ask: why is the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) not the object of this [conceptual cognition]?

To this, he replies: "In regard to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). [This refers to] that which is based on the linguistic usage of elders—such as the usage of elders consisting of commands like "Devadatta, bring the cow"—and that which is instructional—performed by pointing directly to the object, such as "This is a cow."

There is verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), and that does not exist here; for verbal expression is not a property (*dharma*) of the blue object, nor is it perceptible by the eye; therefore, that [expression] must be remembered from what preceded, and there is no memory as long as the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has not been awakened; and the awakening of that [impression] arises from the perception of the object—thus, at the time of perceiving the object, the verbal expression—
There is no memory.

Beyond that is conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-jñāna*), because every conceptualization has its root either directly or indirectly in non-conceptual [perception] (*nirvikalpaka*). Furthermore, "beyond" (*param*) means having a different form.

The universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is its object, because it is impossible to establish— either through extensive conceptual construction or through mere instruction— a conventional linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) for a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is so extremely restricted; and even if it were established, it would be useless, for by means of that [particular], which does not persist [in other instances], [the purpose cannot be achieved].
Furthermore, there is linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). And that is of many varieties, because it exists together with expression—that is, with verbal discourse in the form of sound.

This is because [particulars] cannot be [the object of such discourse], as the sense is that particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are infinite. Now, [one might ask: "Is not the convention [established] in relation to each [individual]?"
To the objection that "we shall indeed do so," he replies: "even of what has been done. To the question "Why is this futile? he says: "by that.

"Not following" means having reached its completion within a single particular (svalakṣaṇa) alone. Again—at the time of grasping another form—because forms are distinct; otherwise, [it would not be so].

The sense is that it is because [the object] cannot be its own nature (*svarūpa*). He explains the word "in many ways" (*bahudhā*) with the words "and that. "And that" means "and the conceptualizing [cognition]. To answer the question "Why is it such?", he explains the reason while explaining the word "with verbal expression" (*sābhilāpam*), starting with "since," the remainder being "by way of the object of memory. Of the verbalization...
He says "and by verbal expression" (*śabdanañ ca*) in order to explain both the essential nature [of cognition] and its manifoldness.
"This" (*idam*) refers to conceptual knowledge (*savikalpajñāna*); "that" (*tat*) refers to recollective knowledge (*smṛtijñāna*);

"this-that" (*tadidam*) refers to recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); "this might be" (*bhaved idam*) refers to reasoning (*tarka*); and "either this or that" (*idaṃ vā idam*) refers to deliberation (*vimarśa*).
Regarding doubt, which is included by the word "etcetera": Now, in the doctrine of the non-duality of sound (śabdādvaitavāda), sound alone is the substantive; as it has been said:
"Brahman is without beginning or end, the imperishable essence of sound."
From which the process of world-creation evolves in the form of objective entities.
[Objection: "Thus [it is said]. How then have you, by speaking of its being a qualifier, caused it to enter into the very nature of cognition?

To this he says: "And that... [He asks again: "Where else [is it]? To this he says: "But rather... "Of conceptualization"—that is, of conceptual cognition. And "this verbalization" consists of: "this," "that," "this-that," "this might be," or "this or that."

Thus, it is divided in many ways. And that [division] does not reside in the object, but rather appears as making the very nature of that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) itself variegated; thus, conceptual construction has many divisions. In this way, the succession of experience and conceptual construction shines forth by virtue of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).

It might be argued that the succession in which this [duality] is situated also appears [as a reality]; but that is not so, because both of these—whether of the nature of conceptualization or its opposite—are not related to any other "someone" who is a seer or an experiencer distinct from them.
This may be the case for the object of sight according to the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*). The reason for this is: "because of that... [referring to the subject].

Because of the seer, for that very reason—due to the nature of consciousness—he states the conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means "for this reason. He provides the summary with the word "evam" (thus); the meaning is that, to that extent, there is no disagreement here. By this, the second sentence has been explained. Likewise...

And this is the interpretation. "Furthermore"—that is, of a different nature from that [non-conceptual cognition], called conceptual—that is, determinate (*savikalpaka*)—cognition becomes manifold. Why? Because it is "associated with verbal expression" (*sābhilāpam*); this is a qualifying term containing a reason.
Here, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) accepts [the objection] by way of reasoning, saying: "It might be so."

He also raises an undesirable consequence with the words "to which it is attached" (*yallagnā*). The meaning is that "to which it is attached" means that in which [object], namely the self, one has reached a state of finality (*niṣṭhā*)—that is, from the arising of the thought "I know.
Refuting this, he explains the third statement with the words "that is not so" (*tan na*). He states the reason for this with the word "since" (*yataḥ*).

"Of a nature other than non-conceptual"—that is, of a nature that is both non-conceptual and conceptual. Regarding the phrase "of one distinct from this," he states the referent of "the seer" as "the experiencer.
He explains the meaning of the genitive case as "related to. He states the exclusion for the word "eternal" as "of the visible object."
Thus [it is said]. "Of the visible" means of the body and so forth, which exist as visible and are impermanent.

This refers to the Sautrāntika school of those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*), and not to the schools that maintain consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*) or emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). He says "here" in order to explain the segment of the sentence beginning with "of that" (*tasya*).

Regarding the term "the cause" (*hetu*): here, since there is an absence of relationship with a permanent seer (*draṣṭṛ*), he explains the very reason by saying "because" (*yataḥ*). For this very reason—namely, because of being a seer—the implication is that the attainment of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) is necessarily required for a seer. Consciousness (*saṃvit*)—
He states the probandum for the admission of its having the nature of consciousness: "self-luminous" (*svaprakāśa*).

The sense is that consciousness, by its very nature, must necessarily be self-luminous; otherwise, it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍa*). He also states the probandum for this: "it follows" (*āpanna*).

Because it possesses self-luminosity by virtue of its nature, it has attained the conditions for being perceived; therefore, "here"—that is, within this pair of cognitions—there is no manifestation. But surely there *is* a manifestation? Thus, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is unestablished. For instance: "I know," "I ascertain," "I remember this."

The persisting form shines forth in the persisting luminosity as "I," which is indeed distinct from the objects of knowledge such as cognition and memory—which are of the nature of the roots *vid* and so on—and from the object of action which is of the nature of "this. Who says that it shines?
For shining (*bhāna*) is non-conceptual, whereas the cognition "I" is a conceptual construction permeated by words.

But even so, what is being conceptualized by this? Is it the continuum of the body, based on cognitions such as "I am thin"? Or is it the continuum of cognition, which has attained—by virtue of its self-luminosity—the fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension?

"Attainment through the means of valid cognition" (*upalabdhipramāṇaprāptiḥ*) refers to that by which such [a thing] is attained; that is to say, it refers to the fitness for attaining its object. This is a usage similar to the term "effect" (*kārya*), as in "the action is the effect. Here, he explains the word "iti" with the words "etad" (this).
Furthermore, since it is not possible to state the non-existence of a subject (*pakṣa*) even if it has not been perceived, he stated "perception" (*upalabdhi*) and so forth.

By this, the third statement is explained; and thus the construction [is as follows]: that pair—the two types of cognition consisting of the non-conceptual (*avikalpa*) and the conceptual (*savikalpa*)—acting as the agent, does not belong to any eternal seer (*nityadraṣṭṛ*) imagined through conceptualization. Why? Because of him, in this context—namely, within the midst of these two cognitions.

"Because it does not appear"—that is, because it is not seen. Here, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) asks: "But surely... Non-perception of the perceptible means the non-attainment of that which has reached the conditions for perception; the remainder is "of the eternal seer. This very point...

He says "tathā hi" (for thus) in order to provide support. Since the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) consists of action (*kriyā*), it is called the "meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyartha*). From the form of the object—that is, from the essential nature of the objective factor (*karmakāraka*). "Following along" (*anuyāyin*) means that the "I" persists throughout all three usages. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) speaks with indignation: "ka... [The text ends here].

"Thus. He himself states the meaning of the word "thus" with the words "it shines. He supports the implied matter with the words "for shining," [explaining it as] non-conceptual—that is, untouched by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) asks again, "But surely... [meaning] by this conceptual cognition permeated by words.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), wishing to state the reply here, explains the fourth statement with the words "the body" (*śarīre*). This is to be construed as "it is differentiated by this. By "this"—that is, by the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśa*). Why? Because of the cognition "I am the body" or "I am happy," etc. [The variant reading *sukhyahamityādipratīteḥ* is supported by K. ṣ. ṣ.]

And the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) refers only to the continuum (*saṃtāna*), not to something additional. This has been stated: "The cognition of 'I' also—by the inclusion of the word 'etcetera,' [it includes] cognition—necessarily determines, that is, conceptualizes, as being of the nature of a continuum; because it is permeated by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting in the capacity to grasp the difference between similar successive states."

Regarding the phrase "the state of successive similar [moments]" (*sadṛśāparāparabhāva*): we have not denied this, because it is included under the expression "that which is called conceptual construction accompanied by verbal designation" (*sābhilāpaṃ vikalpākhyam*). What is meant is this:
even the cognition of "I" is not the Self, since that too has the nature of a conceptual construction and is unstable.

There is no other cognizer of this cognition distinct from the body and so forth; or, even if such a cognizer existed, it would fall within the category of the object of knowledge. Thus, in either case, there is no proof for a self that is distinct from consciousness and its objects.

Or is it the continuum (*santāna*) that is being conceptualized? Why? Because of such cognitions as "I am thin," and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the cognition "I am fat" is included. By this, an answer has been given relying upon the Cārvāka doctrine.
Likewise, by this [the opponent means] either the continuum of cognition (*jñāna-santāna*)—that is, the stream of cognitions colored by the appearance of objects—or [the self].

It is conceptualized. Why? Because of the cognition "I am happy. This is stated because, according to the Buddhist school, pleasure is nothing but consciousness (*vijñāna-mātra*); thus, the answer is given by relying on the Buddhist Idealist (*Vijñānavādin*) view. Or, the word "or" (*vā*) applies to both cases, indicating two alternative options.

This is for the purpose of indicating the predominance of each in its own respective object. Now, an objection might be raised: "But the cognition 'I' (ahaṃ-pratīti) apprehends one who is emaciated or happy, since in instances such as 'I am emaciated,' it is seen to be in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with those two [qualities]. In response to this expectation, he says: "And [the suffix] expressing possession (matvarthīya)."

A suffix prescribed in the sense of possession is called *matvarthīya*, and in the word *kṛśaḥ*, it takes the form of the suffix *matup*. Furthermore, according to the rule "the elision (*lup*) of *matup* is desired after words expressing qualities," its elision occurs; for example, in the case of "a white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), the analysis (*vigraha*) of the word *śukla* is "that which has the quality of whiteness" (*śuklo guṇo 'syāsti*).

In the word *sukhī*, however, the suffix *-in* is used; that [suffix] refers directly [to the possessor]. "Continuum" (*santāna*) means a series consisting either of the body or of cognitions; for in the Buddhist view, the substratum (*guṇin*) whose nature is a continuum is composed solely of qualities (*guṇa*) in the form of a continuum. "Distinct" (*atirikta*) means separate from the continuum. The aforementioned point...

He states this concisely with the words "that very thing. "That very thing" refers to the matter just mentioned. He shows the analysis [of the compound] with the word "body" (*śarīram*); by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he indicates that consciousness (*jñāna*) also rests within the body.
This is what is signified by the particle *api*. Thus, there is no self (*ātman*) distinct from consciousness and the object of consciousness.
Because that which is visible is not perceived—[because of the non-perception of the visible]—thus [it is said]. || 12 ||

In this regard, the proponent of the self (ātmavādin) sets forth an inference: "Now, if memory follows upon the destruction of experience, how could it occur unless the experiencer were eternal? Therefore, the self must be eternal. (3)
He states the meaning of the word "avasyati" as "santāna" (continuum). By way of being a continuum—that is, by means of the state of a continuum.
Because "avaśyam" (necessarily) functions as the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*), it is connected with the preceding term. He provides the reason for this here:
"because [it is] similar. Those other distinct entities (*bhāvabhedāḥ*) which are similar—namely, the specific entities in the form of moments—are what is meant.

The apprehension of those [objects]—namely, the experience belonging to a previous time—by virtue of its power—that is, by its influence—is the latent impression (*vāsanā*), which is the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) known as cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

When there is "being permeated" by that, meaning being made the object of its infusion, the sense is that the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs through the latent impression alone. Thus it is said.

The word "śabdaḥ" indicates the completion of the reason. He explains the term "eṣā" as "eṣeti. It is "nihnutā"—that is, made the object of concealment. In response to the expectation of why it is not concealed, he says "sābhilāpam" (with verbal expression). But what is meant by this?

Regarding this, he says: "This has been stated. He demonstrates exactly what was stated with the words "I" (*aham*). "The cognition of this" means the manifestation of the cognition of "I"; that which has [this] as its object of cognition is [the subject]. Alternatively, there is the reading *pratyeya*, in which case it is simply a compound with the instrumental case. The word "iti" marks the conclusion. To explain the intended meaning of the word "api," he says:

"Nevertheless," thus [it is said]. The Cārvāka, who maintains that the body is the self, and the Buddhist, who maintains that consciousness is the self, each concludes their own position with "thus. "Consciousness" (saṃvit) means cognition; "the object of consciousness" (saṃvedya) means the body;
[the Self] is distinct from these two, meaning its nature is eternal luminosity. Here he states the reason: "of the visible" (dṛśyasya).

Regarding the "visible" (*dṛśya*)—that which is fit to be seen—the non-perception of that [self] occurs; for when something fit to be seen is not perceived, it is then established as being non-existent. By this, the fourth statement is explained.
And thus is the construction: even this cognition of "I" determines the body and so forth.

The meaning is that [the mind] becomes such as it is because it leads [the object] to the state of being an object of conceptualization in the form of a determinative judgment (avasāya), and not because it consists of the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure and eternal luminosity. || 12 ||
He provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "here" (*atra*). Whether the object intended to be remembered remains at the time of recollection or has perished—what does that matter?
There is no dispute among anyone regarding the fact that the experience itself has perished; and it is precisely that...
Memory arises by conforming [to that experience]. For instance—in memory there is neither the manifestation (*prakāśa*) of the object nor its determinative ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*).
On this point, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
The proponent of the self (ātmavādī) refers to the logicians and others. Inference (anumāna) consists of the forms of positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka).

"He raises it" means that he himself arises, or—by means of the activity of an instigator through performing what is capable of that—he impels [the inference] toward it. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse, beginning with "Now" (atha).
The commentary on this says:
In order to state that the destruction of experience is established as indicated by the locative case, he says "iha" (here).
"Iha" means in the world as it appears. "Smartumiṣṭaḥ" means desired to be remembered. But what of that? When she has died, [the world is] immortal—

The point is that because of the observation of the memory, "She who was my mother [then] is my mother [now]," there is nothing [in the object] that arises or perishes by virtue of the object of memory. The word "experience" (anubhava) implies "belonging to a previous time.
He himself explains the word "just so" (tāvat) with the phrase "there is no dispute regarding all [of this]. That very [point]:
"Having destroyed the experience itself," meaning following after its state—that is, keeping it in view;
by this, the explanation of the phrase "conforming to that" is provided. "Memory" means recollection.
"Arises" means it is produced. He supports this very point with the words "for thus. "Manifestation" means apprehension.

"Non-conceptual knowledge" (*nirvikalpajñāna*) refers to that very state. "Determination" (*adhyavasāya*) is the conceptual knowledge (*savikalpajñāna*) that arises immediately after it. Regarding the phrase "nor even": it is like two fingers—meaning, according to the analogy of two fingers, simultaneous manifestation and determination are to be joined [as impossible]. Regarding the phrase "nor even": of that which is qualified by experience...

[The object] is endowed with the qualification of the experience "this is known"; the meaning is by way of the analogy of a person distinguished by a staff, like a staff-bearer. In response to the expectation of how it could not exist, he says:
"everywhere. That is, in all four modes [of cognition], because of the consequence that there would be the cognition "this."

The meaning is that, in the presence of an experience, it is impossible to have the apprehension "that [is it]. Now, one might object: "Let there be no contact with experience here. To this he says: "But rather... "The manifestation of experience" means the recollection of a previous experience. When the question "Why? arises regarding the reason, he states the sentence as the reason.

Regarding the phrase "of the experience" (*anubhavasya*): the word "but" (*tu*) indicates that it is neither [the relation] between the experience and the object like two fingers, nor between the object as qualified by the experience like a staff [and its bearer]; for in those cases, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "this is everywhere. Rather, it is simply the manifestation of the experience itself.

Memory is primary; however, since experience consists in the manifestation of the object, the appearance of the object is inseparable from the manifestation of that experience. Therefore, if the experience were entirely destroyed, how could memory—which is of the nature of its manifestation—be directed toward the object by means of it?

And since all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is seen to be performed by means of that [cognition], this [cognition], being in its own nature non-deniable (*anapahnavanīyā*), remains non-deniable even when the experience (*anubhava*) has perished.

This indicates the distinction between experience and memory; because experience consists in the manifestation of an object—by virtue of being of the nature of an object-manifestation—the appearance of the object, termed "object-manifestation," is inseparable from the manifestation of the experience—that is, it is attained through the manifestation of the experience. Thus.
The word "śabdaḥ" (the word) indicates that this sentence is the reason for the preceding statement. This is what is meant:
whatever is the manifestation of something cannot be manifested without that thing being manifested; for indeed, a blue lotus is never seen without the manifestation of the quality called "blue."
Thus, in a memory associated with the manifestation of an object, the manifestation of the experience itself holds primacy.
Now, one might object: "But that experience has already perished; what is the use of discussing it? To this, he says: "In every way.
"In every way" means both as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). It is of the nature of the manifestation of that [experience].

It has the nature of the manifestation of experience; "by means of that" means by means of experience. To the objection, "Let there be no memory," he says "and by that"; "by that" means by memory itself. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "eva" (only), or it serves to include what was not explicitly mentioned. "Asau" (this) refers to memory; it is "not to be denied."
It cannot be denied; being existent (*satī*), it makes known—meaning it causes one to infer—some indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) reality. As it has been said:
"If you were not omniscient at all times, then [you would not know] the rising of the sun."
By what means could his memory regarding lost objects be otherwise conceived?

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: "Let it be made known; what is the use of that? To this he says: "That very thing. That very thing—the object made known—is the eternal self (*ātman*) who is the experiencer (*anubhāvaka*). He provides two synonyms for the word "experiencer":
"the agent of experience" (*anubhavakartṛ*) and "the one who experiences" (*anubhavitṛ*). Now, is the self [known] by memory alone?
To the question, "Is it established by this alone, or even by something else?", he says: "Just this much. That is to say, mere memory alone. Now, one might object:
at the destruction of an experience (*bhava*), does it not indicate that something remains undestroyed? And that very thing is the agent of experience—the nature of the experiencer;
the self is the experiencer and is eternal. Thus: "The experiencer is eternal."

Just this much—[K. ṣ. ṣ.]—is indeed the very lifeblood of the establishment of the Self (*ātmasiddhi*). However, the Teacher has not revealed that [Self] in its fullness right here; rather, he did so with the intention that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) should not be concluded too hastily, while he still intended to state what remained to be said. "How could it be?"—in that regard, the object (*artha*) is of no consequence, and as for direct experience (*anubhava*), [it is likewise inconclusive].

If it were destroyed, there would be no recollection by any means whatsoever; and in its absence, all conceptual constructions— which depend upon the recollection of conventional words— would also vanish, leaving only a non-conceptual state that is,
alas, like being blind, deaf, and mute.
"The whole world would perish without anyone to cry out for help"—thus [it is said]. || 3 ||
In response to the expectation, "Why was the full burden not placed right here?", he says: "But that...

That is, the reality which constitutes the very life of the establishment of the Self; it was not further unfolded—not made manifest—by the Teacher right here. With what intention? With the following purpose: [he asks] "What is this? [meaning, why was it not done?]

"May the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) not reach completion here"—that is, may it not come to an end. This is said with the intention of expressing something remaining—that is, some residue—because otherwise it would be devoid of a subject matter; such is the sense. [The question] "How might it be? refers to the intended meaning of this.

He says "How could it be? in order to explain this. The meaning is: a jar or the like, previously perceived and now being remembered; "in that"—namely, in the memory—"the experience" refers to the perception at the time of grasping. To the objection, "Let there be no such thing as memory," he replies with the words "In its absence. "Convention" (saṃketa)—

The relationship is that of the signified and the signifier; "word" refers to the signifying word. They are "dependent upon" or "subordinate to" the memory of those two, because they consist of that [memory]—this is the sense. The word *api* (also/even) implies completeness.
To the question, "Let all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) vanish; what of it?", he says: "the non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*), and likewise "and so forth."

The remainder [of the verse] is as follows: "And so, the universe—the entire world—being free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), meaning being endowed with a class of subjects devoid of conceptualization; it is, as it were, like the blind, the deaf, and the mute—that is, like newborn infants who are like the blind even when seeing, and like the deaf even when hearing."

"Even though they possess the organ of speech, it would be filled with people who are as if mute. For this reason— alas, what a pity!— in this case, due to the excess of activity (or rather, the absence of activity), one must conceive of something of that nature.

It is sufficient for the accomplishment of the task, but the self is not so; for first, the object is remembered, and that occurs by means of the manifestation of the experience, yet the experience has perished—as has been stated. If there were some self, what would be the use of it? For one might as well say that even space exists. Now, if it is argued: "No."

If it is argued that this is accomplished by the self alone, yet the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of experience is also useful here—then let that alone suffice; what is the use of this [self]? He demonstrates this very point:
"Even though the self exists, because of the destruction of the vision [of the object], through that [vision] there is no memory of the objects seen."
Now, by what means does memory arise? It occurs at the very same locus where the original experience took place. (4)
"Nirākrandaṃ" means being unable to call out to one another; "avasīdet" means it would perish.
For it is observed that newborn infants, when abandoned for some reason in a desolate place, come to ruin—this is the intended meaning. || 3 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fourth verse with the words "iha" (here).
Here, the commentary states:
"iha" means in this manifest world; "kāryātirekeṇa" means by way of the effect.
Because cause and effect are distinct; "of such a kind" means "a cause of that sort.

Alternatively, there is a reading *kāryavyatikareṇa*. "Is sufficient" (*paryāpnoti*) means "is capable"; thus, "sufficiently" (*paryāptam*) is the meaning. "Self" (*ātman*); the meaning is that the eternal self has been established by you. This very [point].

He supports this with the words "for the object," and so forth. The meaning is: "and that object"—not being remembered directly, but rather by way of the manifestation of the experience; this is how it connects with what preceded. "It has been stated" means immediately prior.
To the objection, "Even so, the self certainly exists," he replies with "if. This means: "by that self which is of no consequence."

In explaining his own position, he states that another matter must also be addressed, namely "this," because there is no difference in their lack of efficacy; this is the underlying sense. He anticipates the objection raised by the proponent of the Siddhānta with the words "Now it might be said. "This" refers to the effect in the form of memory, and "utility" refers to the means of accomplishment. To this, he provides the following answer:
Regarding the word "therein" (tatra): it refers to that very thing—namely, the latent impression (saṃskāra) itself. By this [it is meant]:

in the case of "memory" regarding "objects" that have been "seen," i.e., experienced, the experience whose nature is perception (*dṛg-ātmā*) is the "doorway" for the contact with the objective aspect; and that [experience], although the self exists, is an experience that has perished, for its...
If [the object] is not destroyed, then this very light remains uninterrupted; what, then, would memory do? And who would be its experiencer?
The meaning is that the Self is incapable of such action, for when a task is accomplished by one means, there is no need to postulate a second.
The meaning is "it is logical. He introduces what has been stated by way of a conclusion, [saying] "that very thing" (*tad etat*).

"That very thing"—the matter just mentioned—he "shows," that is, he makes manifest. Having thus provided this introduction, he presents and explains the verse, beginning with "even though" (*saty api*).

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says, intending to explain the portion of the verse ending with "by what" (*kena*), [the word] "in those seen" (*dṛṣṭeṣu*): he explains the term "seen" as "in those experienced" (*anubhūteṣu*). Regarding objects—such as blue and so forth—the memory that arises...

In that [memory], regarding the contact with a portion of the object—meaning, in relation to the contact with the object designated as a "portion of the object"—the experience of the nature of vision (dṛgātmā), which is of the form of vision, namely the prior experience, becomes the door, that is, the means;
for otherwise, the meaning is that its arising would not occur. Now, one might ask: "What follows from that? To this:

He says: "And that. And that experience—the experience which serves as the gateway—has perished even though the Self remains; for it cannot be said that the destruction of one thing is absent simply because another thing persists. This is the sense. [The opponent asks: "But what follows from that? To this he replies: "Of that. "Uninterrupted" means unbroken. *Kā*...

The meaning is that memory (*smṛti*) would not be possible because there is a contradiction between "that" (the established nature of the object) and "this" (the present perception). Furthermore, with the intention of showing that memory would thus be redundant, he says:
"the experiencer of that. The "experiencer of that" means the experiencer of the object; what could such a person do?

The sense is that this [consciousness] is not useful for the manifestation of the object because it is already manifested by experience itself. The construction here is as follows: even though the self exists, memory—which arises with respect to perceived objects such as blue and so forth previously experienced, by way of that [self], i.e., by way of experience—[occurs] due to the destruction of the perception (*dṛṅnāśāt*).
"Due to the cause being the destruction of that which is called experience (*anubhava*), by what [could it arise]? For the sense is that in the absence of a cause, an effect is not tenable.
He says "yatraiva" in order to explain the remaining portion of the verse. *Vṛttaḥ*—[meaning] occurred.

"Previously accomplished" (*pūrvaṃ saṃpannaḥ*); "footstep" (*padam*) means "object" (*viṣaya*). In response to the inquiry whether that [object] is always the object of memory or only at certain times, he provides the qualification:
"only in that very object" (*yatraiva*) where "experience" (*anubhavaḥ*) has occurred, "that alone" (*tadeva*) is the "footstep" (*padam*) of that memory.
It is called *smaryabhāṇam*. The term *tatpada* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; "that" (*sā*) refers to memory (*smṛti*). || 4 ||
Anticipating the objection—"How can there be the conceit of being the subject (*viṣayitva*) on the part of that [cognition] with respect to the object of another cognition?"—he says:
"the remembered" (*smaryamāṇam*). "The remembered" means that which is being made the object of memory; not...
The meaning is "that which is being experienced. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "she whose [nature] is that word.
He explains the word "sā" (she) as "seti" (as "sā"). || 4 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fifth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"of another cognition"—that is, of one consisting of direct experience; "of that"—of memory.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "yato hi.
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains the first half [of the verse] with the words "anubhavena" (by experience). "Svocitaḥ" means appropriate for oneself, and not—
The meaning is "distinct from itself. Now, as to the question "What is done by that impression (saṃskāra)?", he says: "And the impression... "Staying" means remaining;

"it causes to stay" means it impels toward that [state] by means of its own causal activity while it remains there of its own accord. In response to the expectation "Of what?", he says: "Drawn forth..."
And that branch and so forth is drawn; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the bow and other such things are included.
For a bent branch, once released after being drawn, remains in its own place once again in the form of straightness.
To answer the expectation of "whose [branch]? he says: "for a long time" (*ciram*). "For a long time" means starting from a long period ago; [it refers to] that which has been coiled.

Regarding that which is coiled, as well as that which is being uncoiled— that is, expanded— it is observed that when birch bark or similar material has been coiled for a long time, once it is spread out and released, it remains in that very same state due to the force of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
He applies this definition of the aforementioned latent impression to the present case as well with the words "by that."

"Resembling a previous experience"—meaning similar to a prior experience; the sense is that it establishes a state identical to its former form. "It effects a withdrawal" (upasaṃhāraṃ karoti). "Thus" (iti)—for this reason, only that which is the object of experience becomes the object of memory.

The meaning is that it has as its object a mother previously experienced. By this, the elasticity (*sthitisthāpakatva*) of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), which is the cause of memory, is also stated. Although logicians have stated that it takes the form of a mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), for it is from the mental impression of a previous experience that the occurrence of memory arises.
If this were so, what purpose would there be for a permanent self that is like a useless internal tumor?
As it has been stated:
"The cause of memory is mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which resides solely in the self.
Nevertheless, when investigating the ultimate reality, even among the three types of distinctions, the essential nature is simply the state of maintaining stability (*sthitisthāpakatva*).

For even in the case of velocity (*vega*), its capacity to cause stability resides only in the prior action of its own substratum, such as an arrow. In the verse, the phrase "since" (*yataḥ*) indicates that this sentence serves as the reason for the preceding statement.
By this, the first half-verse is explained.

He says "In that case, then" (*evaṃ tarhi*) in order to explain the second half [of the verse]. By this, it is indicated that the first half represents the position of the proponent (*siddhāntipakṣa*). A *gaḍu* is a lump of flesh located on the hump of a hunchback;
for it clearly causes distress. But what of it? The meaning is: "It does nothing at all for oneself. He states the reason for this here:
"Indeed, all" means that it has provided a supporting hand; the sense is that it has given firm support by way of producing the memory that establishes conventional usage. || 5 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). By this, a permanent self has been suspected by resorting to a *pariśeṣa* (residual) inference. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse with the word "tat" (that).

Here the commentary begins to provide an explanation by way of a figurative turn of phrase with the word "iha" (here). "Iha" means in this world; "viśeṣaḥ" means a distinction from the previous state, that is to say, an excellence (*atiśaya*). That—namely, the distinction—would not be eternal.

The sense is that it is not logical for that which is distinct from its prior form—and for that very reason fallen away from its own nature—to possess permanence. Having refuted the first proposed position, the proponent now sets forth the nature of the second to refute it as well, beginning with "atha" (now). Of this—of the self; by that—

"By means of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—what [is gained]? The meaning is that nothing is gained because it would be purposeless. He raises the objection of the Logicians (*tārkika*) with "Now," and states the reply with "In that case. Again—as before—in the Self, which is of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*), on account of experience (*anubhava*), it is not logical for there to be identity between the agent of production and its material cause.
The state [of being]. "Distinguished" (viśiṣṭam) means: because it exists as "that," it is distinct from the experience existing as "this";
it is such that it produces the effect called memory.
For by experience, an impression (saṃskāra) appropriate to itself is produced, and that impression [retains] its former form...

It establishes stability, as in the case of birch bark or similar materials that have been curled for a long time and are now being straightened by pulling on their edges. Therefore, in this case as well, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produces that memory which conforms to the previous experience;
thus, the object of the memory is indeed the very same object as that [previous] experience.

If that is so, then the "internal goitre" (*antargaḍu*)—just as it serves only for great fatigue—likewise, the eternal self (*ātman*) is merely the fruit of the exertion of conceptual construction; what is the use of it? For the entire family of worldly transactions is supported by the hand of conditioned formative forces (*saṃskāra*). || 5 ||

Now, one might object: "The substratum of that very formation (saṃskāra) must be stated; for, being a quality (guṇa), it requires a substratum, and that which is the substratum would be the self (ātman). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because there is no difference in its own nature among those phenomena (dharma) distinct from it..."
If memory were established through mental impressions (saṃskāra), then the rememberer would be merely imagined, like the seer.

In this case, when a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) arises, if there were a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) of the self, then that quality would be non-different [from the self], and thus the self could not be eternal. Alternatively, if there were no such specific quality of it, then [the production of cognition] would occur through a succession, but not directly. For experience (*anubhava*) produces valid cognition (*pramā*) only directly.
But the refinement (saṃskāra) occurs by means of that [object]. "Worthy of refinement" (saṃskārārtha) means fit for the application of a conventional term denoting refinement.

Again, he raises an objection from the perspective of the Siddhāntin with the word "atha" (now/if). "Consisting of refinement" (saṃskārātmā) means having the nature of refinement; and this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the specific quality produced by refinement, since that too [is involved].

Because it is the object of logical reasoning (*nyāya*). He states the answer: "of that" (*tasya*). Then—at that time—what would that impression (*saṃskāra*) be for this self? The meaning is: nothing at all; for it is not tenable for something distinct to possess a relationship. Now, one might object: "Even so, let it still be related. To this he says:
"And as for the relation"— it will be refuted [later], with "right here" being the understood ellipsis.
Since the absence of deviation in the related follows effortlessly from the absence of deviation in the relation, there is a purpose in resorting to this definition.

What then? If it is argued that the distinction of this [recollection] consists in the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) itself, then since that [impression] is not distinct [from the cognition], it follows once again that the cognition is impermanent—namely, that a cognition distinguished by experience arises through a succession [of moments] as the cause of the effect known as specific recollection; such is the extent [of the position].

The meaning is "conditioned" (*saṃskāra*). Now, if there is a distinct attribute whose nature is conditioning, then what does it belong to? Furthermore, a distinct relation will be refuted later. In this same manner, knowledge, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, and demerit are also to be analyzed. This is what is meant by the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) with respect to the self (*ātman*).

He extends this [analysis] to the qualities such as knowledge by saying "in the same way" (*evam*). "In the same way" means, like the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it possesses the specific distinction produced by that [impression]. "To be conceptualized" (*vikalpanīyāḥ*) means they are to be made the objects of a conceptualization consisting of two alternative positions (*pakṣadvaya*).
He now provides the application of the aforementioned elaboration to the subject matter of the present verse as its explicit meaning (*vācyatva*).

"He said this" means: "this"—the matter just mentioned. To the question "By whom was it said?", he replies "Then" (*tataḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of differences" (*bhinneṣu*), which means "in things possessed of difference":
since the position of non-difference leads to the consequence of impermanence, it is rejected from afar in the Sūtra.

As for the phrase "due to the absence of distinction" (*viśeṣābhāvāt*): indeed, a distinct qualifier is not tenable [if there is no distinction], because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
The meaning is that the quality called "blue," being established, serves as the qualifier of the lotus.
It would not "function"—that is, it would not be able to perform its operation. He states the reason for this: "in the form of one who does not remember.
This means "in an unrefined form"—that is, in a form in which no mental impression (*saṃskāra*) has arisen—the original form existing from the beginning.
The "original primordial form" means the form that existed prior to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). He states the conclusion with the words "thus.

"Thus" means for this reason. Now, if this is so, then what are we to do regarding that which is expressed by the word "I" appearing in the thought "I remember"? To this he says: "I. "He too"—that is, the rememberer—also.

The word "and" (*śabda*) serves as a conjunction, connecting the previously mentioned observer. He himself reveals the intended meaning of the word "also" (*api*) with the words "just as" (*yathā*). Just as the observer—the continuum of the body—is [unaffected] even when "distinct properties" (*abhinneṣu dharmeṣu*) are admitted to exist, so too is it [unaffected] within the "essential nature" (*svarūpe*) of the self.

Since there is no distinction [in the self], that self would not be active in memory; for its former nature—consisting of non-recollection and unconditioned form and so forth—has not departed. Thus, "the establishment of memory occurs from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone. Furthermore, he who is the "recollector" in the thought "I remember" is also merely the continuum of the body.
Furthermore, it is the continuum of cognition (*jñānasaṃtāna*) that is determined [as the self], "just like the seer. For it was stated previously:
"This very perception of 'I' also has its basis in the body and so forth" (1.2.2).
Thus, both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), which serve as proofs for the existence of a self (*ātman*), have been refuted.
And a subverting argument has been indicated: if there is a connection with properties (*dharma-yoga*), there is a loss of permanence; otherwise, what is the use of it? As it has been said:
"If it were like leather, it would be impermanent; if it were like itself [i.e., space], it would be equivalent to a non-entity.
What do rain and sun have to do with space? It is in leather that the fruit of those two resides."
For that is indeed its fruit.
Thus [ends the sixth].
The meaning of the word is that just as [the object] is determined, so too is the rememberer. Now, one might ask: "Where is it that the seer is thus determined?

To this he says: "Previously. He provides the conclusion with the word "thus. The subverting argument is: if there is a connection with attributes (*dharma*), there is a loss of permanence; if there is non-difference from the attributes, there is a loss of permanence.

This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: "If there is a connection with attributes (dharma-yoga), how can there not be a loss of eternality? To this, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). "Otherwise"—that is, if the connection with attributes were not the cause for the loss of eternality—then by that [connection with attributes], what [would happen]? Since that [connection] is something to be accomplished [rather than inherent], nothing at all would result from it alone; such is the meaning. Here...

He states the consensus of the elders with the words "like leather" (*carmopamaḥ*). That—namely, the self (*ātman*)—if it were like leather, resembling leather that has acquired specific qualities of softness or hardness due to the conditions of rain or heat, then it would be impermanent, just like leather; this is the implied sense. Furthermore, that self is [described as] similar to itself—
If it were like space, devoid of any distinctions produced by rain or heat, then it would be equivalent to a non-entity—
it would be, like space, as if having no form whatsoever.
Having thus refuted the self, [the author] now proceeds to refute its sovereignty as well.
In order to examine the very nature of the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*), he says:
"If cognition were of the nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*), then why would it not be eternal, like the Self?
On the other hand, if it were insentient (*jaḍa*), how could there be the manifestation of objects for it? (7)
The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) employs this reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgāpādana*) by means of the opponent's own admission, thinking:
"I shall obtain the reversal of the reductio. In that regard, the proponent of the self (*ātmavādī*) asserts the eternity of the self as follows:
"In this context, what is called 'time' functions as a qualifier for that which is characterized by the state of being 'this' (*idaṃbhāva*)."

Relying upon that matter mentioned in the first half [of the verse], he supports it with the words "by rain and sun. Its result consists of the softness and hardness produced by rain and sun; the word "iti" marks the conclusion of what has been stated. || 6 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "ittham" (thus).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"Thus," by means of the refutation of the valid means of proof consisting of perception and inference.
The meaning is: "and by indicating the sublation [of opposing views]. *Aiśvarya* (sovereignty) consists in being the agent of knowledge and action;
*parīkṣitum* means to make it the object of examination. The word *tāvat* is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence; *āha* means "he says" or "he declares.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse, beginning with the words *jñānaṃ ca*.

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "The opponent" (*paraḥ*)— meaning the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), the author— speaks in order to explain the first half [of the verse] by way of a rhetorical device (*bhāṅgyā*), by relying on the position of the established doctrine (*siddhāntimatāśrayaṇena*), namely this [verse].

It stands as something to be stated; the "adducing of a consequence" (prasaṅgāpādana)—that is, the adducing of an undesirable consequence—is brought about, by implication, against the opponent, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin). Why? Because for me—the proponent of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣavādin)—there will be the attainment of the reversal of that consequence, which is the attainment of what is desired.
