Because this [consequence] is desired by one who would otherwise bring about that which is undesirable. And this very thing is an *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (an accepted tenet), because even the position of the proponent of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) is, for that [opponent], a tenet.
To clarify this very point, he says "tatra" (in that case). "Tatra" means: among the two, namely permanence and impermanence. Thus...

Thus, he fulfills this expectation with the word "here" (*iha*). That which is called "time"—the entity known as time—by qualifying that which is characterized by the state of "this-ness," brings about impermanence through that limitation. And because the Self has the nature of consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*), [it is not so limited].

Because there is no manifestation in the form of "this," it lacks the status of being a substantive (*viśeṣya*); for the relationship between qualifier and qualified depends upon a unifying agent (*yojaka*), and in that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), there is no other unifying agent. One who asserts this is questioned as follows: "In that case, cognition (*jñāna*) too must be self-luminous," and the same logic applies there as well; therefore, that too [is self-luminous].
Why is it not eternal? Furthermore, there can be no relationship between two things that are both eternal;

for that relationship is nothing other than the relation of cause and effect. Therefore, the claim that "knowledge is a power of the Self" is untenable. If, on the other hand, knowledge is not self-luminous, then it cannot be luminous even to another.
For this cognition becomes the illumination of the other object by effecting an immersion into its own self-luminous nature;
therefore, if it were devoid of self-luminosity, it could not be the illumination of the object, just like any other distinct entity. || 7 ||

Of the jar and so forth, which are delimited by the state of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*). "The state of being a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatām*) means the condition of being a qualifier; "that"—namely, the jar and so forth, delimited by the state of "this-ness"—"making qualified," that is, rendering the unqualified qualified; "in that"—in time, which constitutes one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*); "from that contraction," meaning from that limitation (*avaccheda*).
It renders [the object] impermanent; for in the usage "this becomes a jar," there is clearly a limitation of the jar—characterized by the state of "this-ness"—by the present time.
That itself is impermanence, because impermanence consists precisely in the limitation produced by time. Now, let it be so; what follows from that?

To this he says: "And of the Self. By the absence of manifestation as "this"—that is, by the mere fact of being the object of the manifestation "I," and by the absence of being an object of the cognition "this"—there is the state of being a substantive (*viśeṣyatva*), which is the state of being qualified by the temporal qualification. To the question "How is it not so?", he says:
Regarding the term "viśeṣaṇa" (qualifier): it is dependent upon the uniter—that is, dependent upon the agent who establishes the relation—and not inherent.
The point is that otherwise, one thing would not be a qualifier with respect to one [thing] while being a qualificand with respect to another;
for this very reason, they describe this as a semblance of a relation (*saṃbandhābhāsa*). To the question, "But what follows from that? he says: "And not..."

Thus [it is said]. Another proponent [offers this] objection: the unifier (*yojaka*) is other than the self which is self-luminous. He—the proponent of the opposing view who maintains the existence of an eternal self—is subjected to interrogation; that is, he is led to the state of being an object of inquiry. He clarifies this very interrogation with the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Knowledge—that is, the power of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

"Jñānaśaktiḥ"—for this reason; "tatrāpi"—even in that case, namely in knowledge; the second occurrence of the word "iti" is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). [Objection: Let it be granted that even that is eternal; to this he says "na ca" (and not). [Objection: Even if this [knowledge] were insentient (*jaḍa*), it could still function as the manifestation of an object—such is the Sāṃkhya position.
He raises an objection: "Or rather, just as the intellect assumes the form of the object, so too does it [assume] the consciousness of the self."

In this world, there is indeed the conventional usage: "I know the object. In that case, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is merely this: the manifestation of the object. That [manifestation] is not the object's own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), because if it were, it would follow that it would be so for everyone, or else it would not be so for anyone at all—[thus rendering everyone either] omniscient or ignorant.
Or else the world would be [mere appearance]. Nor has this form fallen upon the object from elsewhere; for that indeed would be a fault.
Therefore, surely this property exists in another reality (*tattvāntara*); even there, how could there be the manifestation of the object?
Surely, in that other reality, that object exists as a reflection (*pratibimba*).
[The opponent] approaches [this objection].

To the inquiry, "How then could there not be a connection between two eternal things? he says, "the effect. Later on, he himself will establish that the mere relation of cause and effect constitutes a connection; thus, it is [stated] here.

It is not exhausted. To the question "But what follows from that?", he says "thence" (*tataḥ*). "Wasted" (*avasanna*) means destroyed. The construction is "this [is] that" (*iti adaḥ*), because both possess equal importance; this is the intended meaning. By this, the first half-verse has been explained. And thus is the construction: "knowledge" (*jñānam*) and "the power of knowledge" (*jñānaśaktiśca*) are like the Self (*ātmavat*).

If it were its own nature (*svarūpa*), then—that is to say, that cognition—would it be impermanent? The sense is that it is not logical for it to be impermanent; the implication is that the same fault already mentioned would apply there. Alternatively, "like the self"—is it impermanent? Just as the self is not impermanent, so too is this [cognition] not impermanent; such is the meaning.

To explain the second half [of the verse], he states another position with the word "atha" (now). Even for another—that is, even for an object such as a jar distinct from oneself—this [very] cognition would not be a manifestation; it would not be of the nature of light, just like a lamp which is self-luminous only in relation to a cognizer.

The meaning is that because the illumination of a jar is not observed [to be self-illuminating—C. rather, because the illumination of a jar is observed in the case of a lamp which is self-illuminating]. To the question "Why is there no illumination?", he says: "self-illuminating. For (hi)—because cognition (bodha), that is, knowledge, [is not the illuminator] of another, such as a jar.
It is a distinct principle that is self-luminous;
because of the predominance of *sattva*,
it is capable of receiving reflections, yet because it is veiled by *tamas*, [it does not manifest].

It is turned away from the reflection of everything; because of the removal of *rajas* and *tamas* in one part, it grasps only a partial reflection, and that very thing is called the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*). And this is the grasping of the reflection of objects (or the reception of the reflection).

"Whatever form"—that is, one's own essential nature (*nijasvarūpa*)—in that, "entrance" means penetration; performing or effecting this, the manifestation of even another thing, such as a jar, occurs.

For a jar that has been entered by light, it is through that light that even the lamp itself possesses the very same state of being manifest. He provides the conclusion with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*). This [is the meaning].
—Cognition, like other entities—that is, like objects such as pots which are distinct from cognition. || 7 ||
He provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the words "jaḍopyasau" (even though he is insentient).
Here, the commentary says:
"Even though he is insentient"—that is, even though he is accepted as being of an insentient nature due to the occurrence of the defect of impermanence—"he" (asau)—

"Awakening" (bodhaḥ); this is the Sāṃkhya doctrine, because the doctrine of the Logicians (Tārkika) has been refuted—this is the intended meaning. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "Now, of the object" (athārthasya).
Here is the commentary (ṭīkā):

He explains the portion of the verse ending with "caitanyam" by saying "iha" (here). The meaning is that, for the time being, there is no disagreement on this point by anyone. Regarding the word "tatra" (there): in that context—that is, in that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—this alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). What is this "this much"? It is "the manifestation of the object. [This refers to] knowledge.

The meaning is: "because its essence is mere luminosity. "That" refers to the knowledge denoted by the words "I know this" within that aforementioned ultimate worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). He states the reason for this with the word "all": because otherwise there would be the contingency of [that object] being known [only to one], for blue is not blue only with respect to a single person; such is the sense.
He states another reason according to the alternative view with the words "not anyone. The intended meaning is that this follows the same logical principle (*samānanyāyatvāt*).
[An objection: "But what follows from that? To this he replies: "Thus"—that is, for this reason;

one should understand the sequence such that, if the first position is adopted, [the opponent is] omniscient, and if the second position is adopted, [he is] ignorant. [An objection: "But regarding this matter..."
Lest it be thought that its innate form does not exist but rather that it must be adventitious, he says "nor even" (nāpi).
This—what is called knowledge—is its function; having set aside its prior designation, it is a transformation like curd and so forth.
It consists of a specific transformation characterized by a distinct nature. Thus, "the cognition" maintains "the form of the object.
"Form" means its own nature (*svarūpa*). This very [form] is that which was just mentioned. For [there is no distinction] between the adventitious and the innate.
The meaning is that the two intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) have distinct effects. If one asks, "What then is the effect?", he says:

"That [is] surely... This *dharma*—the *dharma* called knowledge—transfers, that is, adheres, by way of being a reflection (*pratibimbabhāvena*); the instrumental case here denotes the manner of being (*itthambhāve*). Now, [an objection]:...

To the question "What does that *tattva* do?", he says: "That. "That" refers to what was just mentioned; it is "fit for"—that is, suitable for—the "grasping"—the apprehension—of the reflection. This is because of the predominance of *sattva*, which means, by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), its purity. [Objection: If that is so, then why is it not [perceived] in that [mirror]?
Because it reflects even that which is remote in terms of space, time, and so forth, he says: "by darkness" (*tamasā*).

By "darkness"—that is, by the quality of *tamas*—because of being "covered," meaning veiled, [is] "everything," that is, the entire range of objects, both those remote in space, time, and so on, and those not remote.
"By way of reflection"—that is, through the grasping of a reflection; "turned away"—meaning diverted. Now, one might ask:

how then does it grasp that which is not separated by space, time, and so forth? To this he says: "by rajas. By "rajas"—that is, by the quality of *rajas*—through "removal"—that is, through the warding off [of obstacles]—specifically by the quality of *rajas* itself.
This was stated because it has the nature of active manifestation (*pravṛtti*). "Only something"—that is, that which is not too distant;

just as a mirror, though free from breath-fog, receives only a certain reflection, so it is with this—such is the application of the analogy, which should be understood by oneself. Now, one might object: "But surely that [reflection] is a different reality (*tattvāntara*) produced in such a way."
To the question, "What then is its name?", he says: "That very [intellect]. For in the Sāṃkhya system, the intellect (*buddhi*) alone is the agent of cognition. As it has been said:
"How could an object, when transferred to the clear intellect, become an object of awareness?"

"Without that" means: if one asks, "In that case, what is knowledge? he says, "The object. Knowledge is the grasping of the reflection of the object—that is, the apprehension of the reflection, which amounts to its very form. Of this [knowledge], namely, of the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*).
The form of activity—meaning the form of functioning, that is to say, the form of transformation—comes into being.

By this, it is shown that the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the attainment of cognition, consists of the qualities of *sattva* and so forth in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion. [Sukhaduḥkhamohatayā – K. ṣ.]

Because it is an object of enjoyment, it is insentient (*jaḍa*) and, like a mirror, lacks self-luminosity (*aprakāśa*). Furthermore, it is not logically tenable for that which is an object of enjoyment and lacks luminosity to possess a nature consisting of luminosity in the form of subjectivity (*bhoktṛtā*), which is its opposite; therefore, there must be a subject (*bhoktṛ*) distinct from it. And that luminosity has precisely this much as its essential nature.

For how could another nature, which is non-luminous by form and is an object of enjoyment, be conceived as being the very nature of the enjoyer? And if that [enjoyer] exists solely as a nature of pure luminosity, then the identity of intellect (*buddhi*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) asserted by the logicians is refuted. What, then, is knowledge like?

The former refers to that which belongs to a prior time; the designation—that is, the name such as "milk"—is concealed by the transformation into curds and so forth. In the state of curds, the name "milk" simply does not remain. Furthermore, there is a specific transformation distinct from that [prior state], such as the form of an earring and the like.

The meaning is that it is a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*), and its nature is such that by virtue of it, logicians employ the very term "intellect" (*buddhi*) for it. He provides a conclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*).
[The intellect] "sustains," the ellipsis being "as a reflection. Now, if it sustains [objects], then what of this [intellect]?

To show that non-inertness itself follows from this, he says: "And this... The meaning is: "among the *prakṛti* and the rest," that is, "this much"—even the two principles ending with the intellect (*buddhi*)—by way of being of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, that is, by being endowed with the three *guṇas* existing in a state of equilibrium. [By way of equilibrium...]

Because it is characterized by being endowed with the three qualities (guṇatraya) [C], it is insentient due to its state of being an object of enjoyment—that is, because it falls into the condition of being an object of enjoyment. Even though it possesses the capacity for grasping (*grāhakatva*) in relation to other things, it is dependent upon another for its own apprehension. The word "only" (*iyat*) is intended to exclude the possibility that the remaining group of principles (*tattvagaṇa*) might be non-insentient. He states the conclusion with the words "thus" (*iti*). "Thus" means "for this reason."

For that reason, like a mirror, it would be non-luminous—that is, its nature would be distinct from light. [Objection: In that case, would it not follow that the universe becomes blind and mute? To this he says: "And yet... (*na ca*).
"Following logic" (*yukty-anupātī*) means conforming to reason; that is to say, following reasoning. By that which is different from that—

By the method of reasoning (*tarka*), the Sāṃkhyas establish that there must be an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*)—called *puruṣa* and the agent of experience—who is distinct from the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the non-luminous (*aprakāśa*). This proof is intended to demonstrate the instability of certainty regarding the conscious principle (*cetana*). And that [enjoyer] is one whose nature consists solely of this much: being an enjoyer.

This much is its essential nature; as for another essential nature—a different nature consisting of insentience and non-luminosity—it might be conceived, that is, it could be imagined. And that [nature] would be both luminous and an enjoyer, precisely by virtue of having luminosity alone as its essential nature.

If the manifestation of the universe were without external means (*bāhyasādhana*), then the universe would manifest all at once; even the manifestation of a jar would be the manifestation of a cloth, and thus the universe would become confused. And that [manifestation] arises from the object—that is, from the reflection of the object.

Otherwise, how could there be a manifestation of an object from the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), which is its support, given that there would be no connection? Therefore, it is the intellect alone that, due to its transparency, receives even the reflection of the light [of consciousness]. From that—

The conventional usage that "the object shines" is established through the transference—extending down to objects such as blue—which is reflected into the *buddhitattva* (the principle of intellect) once it has been entered by the penetration of Light (*prakāśa*). This occurs by virtue of the power of the reflection of Light being received [by the intellect]. Thus, although cognition is insentient because it is not distinct from the insentient *buddhitattva*, [it nevertheless appears as sentient].

The sense is: "or the reflection of consciousness. Now, [one might ask]: "Let it shine forth; what of it? To this he says: "the jar," because otherwise simultaneous occurrence would be impossible—this is the sense. Now, [one might ask]: "What follows from that too? To this he says: "thus. "The universe" means the world.
It would become confused—it would fall into the state of confusion—and consequently, the conventional usage of "cloth" would apply even to a jar;
this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Let that enjoyer himself, having assumed the state of the object and so forth, become the light [of manifestation].
To this, he says: "And he..."—that is, the enjoyer also, from the reflection of the object—that is, from cognition.

"From that support"—meaning from the support for the reflection of the object—"other"—meaning having a distinct nature—because it is conscious; this is the sense. "Due to the lack of connection"—due to the absence of a relationship. He states the conclusion:
"Therefore. "Because of clarity"—due to the purity produced by the predominance of *sattva*.

"Reflection of light" (*prakāśapratibimba*) means the reflection of the enjoyer whose nature is light; by the word "also" (*api*), there is a conjunction with the reflection of objects already mentioned. Now, one might ask: even if it grasps that [reflection], what of it?
To this he says: "from that" (*tataḥ*). From that—that is, because it also grasps the reflection of light—from that.

The meaning is "for this reason. That *buddhi-tattva*—which is the *mahat-tattva*—is one by which the penetration of light has been attained; that is, it has been reached through the majesty of the reflection-grasping of the *puruṣa*, who is light. For whatever is reflected in something becomes possessed by that thing; such is the nature of the *buddhi-tattva*.

In that regard, it refers to that [consciousness] in which there occurs a "transference"— that is, the manifestation of a reflection— of such an object as blue and so forth, wherein the reflection has been infused; [it refers to] that [consciousness] in which the object such as blue is reflected within the buddhi-tattva (the principle of intellect) which is self-sustained and has come down through a lineage.

This means "of that which is joined with a reflection. The object—namely, an entity such as blue—shines forth within the penetration of light, that is, within the reflection of light that has entered into the intellect (*buddhi*), and not within an external light that serves as the original object (*bimba*). This is because the principle of the intellect alone does not shine by itself, owing to its insentience (*jaḍatva*).
Nor does it belong to the Puruṣa, because of his state of indifference (*udāsīnatva*). [The opponent claims:
"The manifestation of the object occurs through conjunction (*yoga*).
This itself is first of all improper—that the Puruṣa, whose nature is light (*prakāśātmā*), should cast a reflection upon the intellect (*buddhi*).

It is projected because a reflection is observed to transfer into a clear object of similar quality in relation to its source-image, like the reflection of the form of a jar in a lustrous mirror; furthermore,
there is an extreme disparity between the self and the intellect, and the intellect is not pure in relation to the self.

"Let this be for now"—this he indicates by the word "atha. However, he shows that even by means of the theory of reflection (pratibimbavāda), nothing would be resolved: "In that case, it [the reflection] would be insentient; if it were insentient, there would be no manifestation of the object. (8)

If, upon the conjunction with the reflection of consciousness, that reflection itself were not primarily of the nature of light, then nothing would be accomplished by it; for a mirror, even when reflecting a mass of fire, does not burn what is to be burned. Or, if [the reflection] is indeed primarily of the nature of light...
That reflection;

he concludes that Sāṃkhya doctrine with the words "tadevam" (thus, therefore). From the conjunction—that is, the connection—of that reflection of the *cit* (the experiencer) which has been transferred into the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), it is perceived.

The point is that there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the fact that iron performs the function of fire through conjunction with fire; by this, the first half-verse is explained. And thus is the construction: now, in response to the question—just as cognition assumes the external object—
It perceives [objects] as reflections; likewise, it sustains within itself the consciousness—the essential nature of sentience—of the Self, the enjoyer.
Thus, the sense is that even though it is insentient, its illumination of objects is entirely logical.
Now he states the subject matter indicated by the word "this" (etad) with the words "this very [thing]" (etadeva).
He says "which" (yat) in order to fulfill the expectancy of the word "this. He states the reason for its being inappropriate with the words "equal" (samāna).
The latter half [of the verse] is deficient in the word "consciousness" (caitanya).

While about to provide an explanation, he first states the intention [of the author] with the words "But" (*kiṃtu*). By the word "but," which is implied by the sense of the context, the nature of being a rebuttal is indicated; that is, it has been "rebutted"—meaning it has become the object of a rebuttal. To the question "By what does he show this?", he says: "The non-inert" (*ajaḍā*). Having set forth the second half of the verse, he explains it with the words: "Consciousness" (*caitanya*).

In that case, since it is non-different from the intellect (*buddhi*), the intellect itself would become the primary form of light. For this [distinction] has been imagined by those who are afraid of the superimposition of contradictory attributes. That [Self], however, again unfolds its own blazing radiance; and consequently, that very intellect would be composed of consciousness (*cinmayī*), so what is the use of a Puruṣa? Thus...

By way of the reflection of the object, it consists of the object—thus the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*) also follows. To the question, "Whence does this [reflection] possess that form?", the answer must be stated: "From a succession of prior causes. If that very [reflection] is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), [then what is the difference?].

As before, there would be the consequence of [the self] being eternal; and if even that which has the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) were not eternal, then there would be no eternal self whatsoever, of which cognition—namely, the reflection of the self’s consciousness—could be a reflection. To the question, "What would [the world] not have accomplished? he says: "Indeed not."
Thus it has been said:
"The property of consciousness is false in the intellect. To refute the second position, he says: "Now," etc.; that is, the reflection.
The word "śabdaḥ" (the sound/word) marks the completion of the subject matter. [Objection: Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "yataḥ" (because).

"From the superimposition of contradictory attributes"—meaning, from the attainment of consciousness in the insentient intellect—this refers to the proof of reflection. "That very same thing"—namely, the superimposition of contradictory attributes—is "blazing intensely."

It blazes exceedingly. [Objection: But let it yawn; what of it? To this he says, "And therefore... What is the use of a person? Since the primary illumination is admitted to reside in the intellect (*buddhi*), the postulation of that [person] is entirely useless and purposeless—this is the sense. He states another defect as well with the words, "In this way..."—namely, that which consists of objects (*arthamayī*).

"Having the form of the object" (*artharūpā*); because it is the subject under discussion, there is no mention of "cognition" (*buddhi*). This refers to the Vijñānavāda—the adoption of the Buddhist doctrine of the Vijñānavādins. For they too maintain that cognition, which is inherently formless, acquires a form through the object. [The author] establishes its very nature as Vijñānavāda by asking: "Why? Regarding this—
The meaning of "here" in the question is: "the state of having that form"—that is, the state of having the form of the object—from the preceding causal succession;
that is to say, from the series of previously established causes consisting of the forms of objects; [this] must necessarily be stated.

It must be said that this is because there is no other answer; such is the sense. Furthermore, this answer is to be understood as belonging specifically to the Vijñānavādins. He also states the third fault mentioned immediately above with the word "evam" (if this were so):
if it is the case that it is that very same cognition (*buddhi*), then...

The cognition "there must be a capacity" is merely knowledge itself; for the accomplishment of worldly transaction regarding objects is achieved by that much—namely, by the awareness whose nature is the manifestation of an object and that which consists of conceptualization, memory, and so forth.
Thus, there is the attainment of the contrapositive of the reductio (*prasaṅgaviparyayalābha*). And [this] knowledge...
This is the purport of the two verses beginning with "If [it were] of the nature of consciousness" (citsvarūpaṃ cet). || 8 ||

Having thus examined knowledge, he examines action: Action, too, is simply the arising of an object such as the body in various locations and so forth; it is nothing else, because no other [action] is observed.

In this context, regarding that which falls within the scope of appearance— namely, movement in the form of vibration such as "he goes," "he moves," "he falls," and so forth— it exists in an external location immediately following the essential nature of Devadatta when he was situated in the house.

The sense is that this applies by the same logic even to the *buddhi-tattva*, which is accepted as being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). In response to the question "What kind of Self is it?", he says: "Of whom" (*yasya*).
[And] "knowledge" (*jñāna*) means the name "knowledge"; for it is not logical for there to be a power (*śakti*) in the absence of the possessor of that power (*śaktimat*).

The meaning is as follows: he states the established conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). The sense is that there is only pure consciousness (*jñāna-mātra*), and not an eternal self (*ātman*) existing as its agent. To the question, "How is it logical that it is only that [consciousness]? he replies with the words "yorthaḥ" (whatever object...).
"Bodha" is non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); "vikalpa" is conceptual knowledge (*savikalpa-jñāna*).

He states that the intention of the two verses just mentioned is established, saying "iti" (thus). "Iti" means "for this reason"; "prasaṅgaviparyayalābhaḥ" means having the form of obtaining the reversal of the reductio ad absurdum;
"tātparyam" means the intended meaning. || 8 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the ninth verse with the words "Thus" (*evam*).
Here the commentary says:
"He examines" (*parīkṣate*) means he makes it the object of examination; the sense is that [the latter] is a mere offshoot of the former.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it: "Action," etc.
Here, the commentary explains the entire body of the verse up to the words "not from another's vision" with the word "here."
The term *pratibhāsagocaram* means that which has become the object of appearance; that is to say, within that appearance,
only the nature of Devadatta himself is perceived, and nothing whatsoever beyond his own nature.

We perceive another action [in the case of the former]. However, in the sentence "Devadatta stands for a day," there appears the nature of Devadatta as characterized by the time of dawn, and then his nature as embraced by the time of the first watch, and so forth;
whereas in "the milk transforms," there appears the form of the sweet substance and the form of the sour substance.

"Fluid form," "solid form," and so forth—in this way, it is the entity itself that appears through its specific location, its specific time, and its specific form. Furthermore, recognition occurs there due to similarity, even though the body, hair, nails, and so on are distinct. However, when there is a difference in place and form, a difference in time is necessarily present.

Even when there is a difference in place and time, because the place is nothing other than the essential nature (svarūpa) itself, and because there is a difference in the essential nature when there is a difference in time, we perceive—that is, we know—the Devadatta-nature as distinct from the place; that is, as distinct from the place. Having demonstrated action as conditioned by place, he demonstrates it as conditioned by time with the words "Devadatta," etc. By the word "etc. (ādi),...

The apprehension of that very nature [of the object] as embraced by the time of midday and so forth demonstrates the action as being conditioned by form (*ākāra*), as in the case of "milk" and "curd"—that is, sweetness and fluidity in the case of milk, and acidity and solidity in the case of curd.
This is to be applied; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the capacity for grasping or not grasping the essence and so forth is included. Thus it appears.

The connection: he summarizes the point already stated with the words "Thus. "Bhāva eva" means precisely within the momentary entity (*padārtha-kṣaṇa*) consisting of Devadatta’s body, milk, and so forth. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such as 'this is that' observed? To this he replies: "Through similarity. Recognition is the cognition: "This is that Devadatta."
Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) takes such forms as these. Regarding the phrase "in the case of nails, etc.": by the word "etc.

(*ādi*), things such as the flame of a lamp are included; for although the flame of a lamp is indeed different at every moment, it is recognized as "this is that very same one" due to its similarity. [Objection: But how can there be a single entity in the form of Devadatta’s body?

Since you claim that an entity is differentiated by differences of space and time, such that it becomes the object of recognition—which has similarity as its life-force and cause—he says "deśākāra" (space and form).
The word "tu" (but) is used in the sense of "in reality"; "deśākārānyatve" means when there is a difference between space and form—that is, when space and form are distinct.

Just as a difference in time is necessarily inevitable— for Devadatta’s simultaneous presence both inside and outside his house is impossible, nor is it possible for milk and the like to exist simultaneously in the state of curd and so forth— so too, when there is a difference in place and time, a difference in form (ākāra) necessarily follows as a matter of course.

Because it relies on a distinction created by qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), and since a distinction created by qualifiers is observed between a blue lotus and a white lotus, there is no contradiction whatsoever; for when there is a difference in form (*ākāra*), that difference is indeed very clear, so there is no inconsistency here.
As for the non-mention [of spatial distinction], it is because a difference in location necessarily follows from a difference in time and form.
The meaning is this: although space and time ultimately resolve into nothing but form (*ākāra*), nevertheless, from a gross perspective, there is a distinction;
thus they are spoken of as distinct by the Buddhists. In this way, it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

In some cases there is action; however, because that [action] is absent, it cannot be postulated through inference preceded by it, nor even through the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of the effect—since the effect consists of the subsequent moment of reaching the village and so forth, as well as the form and other qualities of the objects in that place. Thus, [action] is not established by either perception or inference.
The non-perception of that [difference]—this expresses the absence of a means of valid cognition (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) for it.
He also states the subverting proof (*bādhaka*):

"Even if there is difference [of substance], there is no difference in form" (or the reading "even if there is difference, there is no difference in form"). Now, [one might object]: "But what of space and time?"

Since [the object] is included within the form (*ākāra*) due to the non-deviation of its forms, and since all [aspects] are implied even by a single form through its sovereign power—even by the mere spatial dimension (*deśa*) consisting of that form alone—why is the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) employed for the purpose of grasping the temporal form?
To this he says: "of the very nature" (*svarūpasyaiva*). That is, of the very nature—that is, of the very body (*mūrti*).

Because there is a difference of place and a difference of essential nature due to the difference in time, although spatial location, time, and form ultimately resolve into— and find their rest within— form alone, nevertheless, from the perspective of gross observation— that is, from the perspective of superficial appearance— there is a distinction; for this reason, by the Buddhists—

These are spoken of as distinct by the disputants who rest upon the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*). The resolution of form within form should be understood as being like "the head of Rāhu. And here, the nature of form is stated precisely because of the manifestation of space; however, since time is formless, its distinction from this [space] is as follows.

He provides the conclusion with the words "Thus," meaning that since the nature of being an aspect (ākāratva) has been established through the non-deviation of its specific distinctions, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. [The phrase] "preceded by that" means preceded by perception (pratyakṣa). Now, one might object: [how can there be] the postulation of that [perception] based on the effect of an action, such as reaching a village?

To the [objection] "We shall do so," he says: "And the effect. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), rice and so forth are included. Regarding "in that place": by the word "etcetera," time is included. That—namely, the action—is "to be postulated" (*kalpyā*), meaning it is capable of being postulated.
To clarify the meaning of the word "because of non-perception" (*adṛṣṭeḥ*), he says: "In this way. By the teacher, the agent, in this way—
By the phrase "due to the non-perception of that [action]" found in the sūtra— referring to the manner just described—

it is stated that there is an absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhakapramāṇa*), meaning the absence of a proving means of knowledge by way of perception and inference (*pratyakṣānumānabhāvena*).
... nor is that [cognition] single, and it is not appropriate for a single [cognition] to be successive. (9)

In this regard, the state of having a prior and posterior form belongs to moments (*kṣaṇa*) through their synthesis by a conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*), but not within the thing-in-itself (*svātman*), for that is merely the bare reality (*vastumātra*). Therefore, the state of being sequential—that is, the state of succession (*kramarūpatā*)—is the characteristic of action (*kriyā*) as it is animated by conceptualization; it is not the characteristic of the real entity (*vastu*).

"It touches something"—[K. ṣ. ṣ. "it does not touch any object for even a moment"; for here the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of "in such a state" (*itthaṃbhāve*). By this, the section ending with "because of non-perception" (*adṛṣṭeḥ*) has been explained.
And thus is the construction: even action is the agent of the object, such as the body; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), [other objects are included].

The term "milk and so forth" refers to the objects of actions such as transformation; by that [action], there occurs in substances such as milk and the body another manifestation produced by those specific qualities—namely, their being born in those particular places and times—and this is not something new. Why? Because it is not observed [otherwise].

"Because it is not perceived through either perception or inference"—this is the introduction to the portion of the verse beginning with "na sā" (it is not). He provides the introduction with the word "bādhaka" (the subverting proof). "Bādhaka" means a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that destroys an action; the particle "api" (also) functions as a conjunction (*samuccaye*). Having thus provided the introduction:

Having introduced the fragment of the verse beginning with "na sā," he explains it: "na sā" [means] "not that. In this context—"tatra"—referring to that action (*kriyā*), "the state of being prior and posterior" (*pūrvāpararūpatā*) refers to the sequence of moments (*pūrvāparībhāva*).
This is because of the synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) of the moments of action by means of a conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*).
By means of a synthesis accomplished through conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), there is a certain—some—moment;

"mere thing" (*vastumātra*) refers to the essential nature of the thing itself, untouched by temporal priority or posteriority; "that" refers to the collection of its respective moments existing as a continuum. In the Buddhist view, time itself does not exist; what then can be said [of its divisions]?

The meaning is that [this applies] to the priority and posteriority produced by those [moments]. He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). [The phrase] "animated by conceptual construction" (*vikalpaprāṇitam*) means determined by conceptual construction (*vikalpādhyavasitam*);
since moments do not enter into one another's essential nature, how could there be a single action? For sequence exists through differentiation.

Since pervasion is absent in what is non-different, and unity is the opposite of difference, how could it be said that "it is both successive and one"? If it is argued that it is "one" because it resides in a single substratum, even there no substratum other than those moments is perceived; for it is only the moments themselves occurring in a continuous series that appear. Furthermore:

How could the substratum, permeated by such moments of action that differ in place, time, and form, be one? For this very reason, the recognition that arises on account of similarity—such as "This is Devadatta; he is the very same person who reached the village"—is not capable of establishing a real identity. 9.

He states a synonym for the state of being sequential (*pūrvāparībhūtatva*) as "the nature of succession" (*kramarūpatā*). "A certain moment"—that is, some moment of action—is "real" (*vastu*), because in the Buddhist view, only moments are real, whereas the continuum (*santati*) is conceptual (*vaikalpika*); [the action] does not touch it, for indeed...

The sense is that a mutual relationship between two conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that are not ultimately real is logical, because otherwise it would follow that even a double moon possesses the nature of being a [single] moon. To the question "How does it not touch [the other]?", he says: "For those...
— *svarūpāviṣṭāḥ* means "possessing a connection with their own nature," because each exists only at its own respective time.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be momentary (*kṣaṇika*). He states the conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means: for this reason, [the series] is one, in the form of a continuum of moments. Having rejected its oneness, he says "for sequence" (*kramo hi*) in order to reject its succession as well by means of that same [rejection], through a cumulative argument. Because of the absence of that—that is, because of the absence of sequence—it is not [so].

The sense is that, indeed, in the absence of the pervader, the existence of the pervaded is untenable. With the word "of one" (*ekasya*), the state of having a single substratum (*ekāśrayatva*) has been indicated; in order to reject this, he says "Now" (*atha*). To refute the unity produced by having a single substratum, he states the following reply.

Regarding the word "tatra" (therein): "distinct from those moments" means distinct from those specific moments. To the question "How is it not perceived?", he says: "The moments themselves. "Existing as a continuum" means having an uninterrupted state. By the word "eva" (itself/only), [he excludes] the nature of action which consists of a succession of moments.

The exclusion of the solar light (*bhānavyāvṛttiḥ*). "By those" refers to the distinct places, times, and forms; that is to say, by those having such natures. "Pervaded" (*āviṣṭaḥ*) means made the object of pervasion. "Substratum" (*āśrayaḥ*) refers to the form of Devadatta’s body and so forth.

He states the conclusion with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). "Real" (*vāstavam*) means existing in the ultimate sense (*paramārthabhūtam*); "sufficient" (*alam*) means capable (*samartham*).
The application of the analogy, "like hair, nails, and so forth," should be made by oneself; thus [ends the section]. || 9 ||

Having thus examined both knowledge and action, [the author] first states the absence of any means of valid cognition regarding that relationship which, when present, connects those two and enables them to accomplish the sovereignty consisting of omniscience and omnipotence:
[The text continues: "To destroy that connection, he first declares the lack of any means of valid cognition concerning it..."
It is observed that when this or that [cause] is present, this or that [effect] comes to be;
there is no other relation than that of cause and effect.
When there is a lump of clay, there is a mound; when that exists, there is a funeral bier, and so on up to a jar.

Thus, only the moments of becoming (*bhāva-kṣaṇa*) are perceived; nothing further appears through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor even through inference (*anumāna*). This should be stated as being just like [the case of] action (*kriyā*). This applies everywhere, including in the relationship between container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) and so forth.
Now he provides the introduction to the tenth verse with the word "evam" (thus).
Here the commentary says: "te" refers to knowledge and action; "dhvaṃsayitum" means to reject; "tadviṣayam" refers to that which has them as its object.

This concerns the subject of relationship; first, regarding these two, the construction is: "in which relationship existing... Having provided this introduction, he presents and explains the verse with the words "tatra" (therein).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

*Stūpaka*: the specific form of arrangement first produced by a potter from a lump of clay taken for the purpose of making a jar; *śivika*: a specific form of arrangement in the shape of a raised object. What is a *śivika* like? It is as follows: as long as it is a jar, it remains in the state of being a jar.

The meaning is "that which persists. Now, one might ask: "Let it be that the three types of arrangements take the form of a stūpa and so forth; what follows from that? To this he says: "In this way. "In this way" means by this manner. "The moments of existence themselves"—meaning the moments of entities in the form of a stūpa and so forth—the word "only" (eva) excludes [anything else], as will be explained by himself.
He says, "not more. "More" means something additional, something that exists as a cause for the jar;
this is precisely the path—after the momentary perception of the separate forms of the bowl and the jujube fruit...
"The arising of a specific jar and jujube fruit that are essentially inseparable"— this very state,
when designated by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) as having a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority in relation to another state,
is called "the causal relationship" (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Nor [is this relationship] distinct from the self (*ātman*) in relation to cognition and action.

There is no relationship of cause and effect with the Self, because it is not an effect of that [cause], and because cognition is an effect of its own causal complex (sāmagrī), and because action is non-existent; thus, there is no connection between cognition and action from which the states of being a knower and an agent could arise. || 10 ||

Thus—this point is to be stated just as in the case of action; the meaning is that just as it was said in the *Kriyānirṇaya*—"there is no action whatsoever that is perceptible, and therefore neither is there any [action] established by inference preceded by perception"—so too must it be stated here.
Now, is this principle applicable only to the relation of cause and effect, or everywhere? To this he says: "everywhere."
*Panthāḥ* means a path, a track, or a way. He demonstrates this very point by saying "in a distinct form.
"Consisting of no interval" means having a connected form. Now, one might ask:
"In that case, how is the well-known relationship of cause and effect established? To this he says: "And this very... This very thing is the state of being (*bhāva*).
The meaning is that the very object, such as a lump of clay, [exists] together with another entity—
namely, another object such as a jar— in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior,
because the clay is prior and the jar is posterior.
[Objection: "But surely this same relationship may exist between the self and its agency and knowership.

To this, he says: "And not... [The reason is] because it is an effect of its own causal complex—that is, because it is an effect of its own specific causal complex consisting of light, the sense organs, and so forth. "Yataḥ" means "because."
This is due to the connection between knowledge and action.

This is the summarized meaning here: when this or that moment of existence (bhāvakṣaṇa) in the form of a lump of clay or the like exists, then this or that moment of existence in the form of a stūpa or the like exists—thus indeed.

Only this much is perceived; nothing else—that is, no other thing in the form of cause and effect distinct from this—is perceived. Now, one might object: "Let there be some other relation besides the relation of cause and effect. To this he says: "There is no other," meaning that there is no relation other than the relation of cause and effect.
The meaning is that this is because it is illogical. || 10 ||
Having thus refuted the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he examines the sublation of the relation by way of both the general and the particular:
"Because that which resides in two [terms] possesses multiple forms, and because that which is already established is independent of anything else."
And because dependence on another and so forth would be illogical, by that [reasoning] even the agent is merely imagined. || 11 ||

First, regarding connection (*saṃbandha*): its general definition is that it consists of a mutual reaching, wherein a single [factor] remains as the locus of the reaching for two things that possess such reaching. And how is this so? For it is not possible for that which has deposited the entire essence of its body in one place to rest in another, because that would entail a difference in its essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*).
By this [same reasoning], conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and other relations based upon them, which have been assigned the burden of being immune to sublation,

should be understood [as untenable]. Furthermore, regarding that relation characterized by dependence (*pāratantrya*) which is conventionally designated among sentient beings through such conceptual construction and among insentient things as well— therein...
He provides the introduction to the eleventh verse with the word "evam" (thus).
Here, the commentary states:
*pramāṇam* means that which establishes; *bādhakam* means that which subverts or destroys, i.e., a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

The universal is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and the particular is the specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*); "by means of these two" means by way of these two doors. He "examines," which means he leads [the object] into the state of being an object of determination. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "dviṣṭhasya."
The commentary on this is as follows:
"To begin with" means that there is no disagreement here.
Regarding the objects that possess contact—namely, those in the form of a bowl and a jujube fruit, and those in the form of threads and a cloth—which possess mutual cohesion:

"Single" (*eka*) means having a single form (*ekarūpa*), which is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because the subject under discussion is relation; and the meaning is: how is it that this universal characteristic is not possible here? "In one" (*ekatra*) means in a single object, such as a bowl or the like, or in the form of threads and the like. He thus explains the word "multiple" (*aneka*) found in the sūtra.

Regarding the term *svarūpa* (essential nature): "rooted in that" means rooted in conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*); "others" refers to relations such as the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth; "the burden" refers to a state.
Having described it by way of the general, he describes it also by way of the particular with the words "that which... and so on, through the conceptualization thereof.

—By the conceptualization of consciousness, [the self] consists of dependence—that is, it takes the form of mutual dependence. In that regard—within that relationship—the conscious [self], being already established, cannot possess dependence precisely because it is already established;
for it is not logical for that which is established to be dependent, as that would entail its becoming unestablished. This is the intended meaning.

That which is already established possesses no dependence, precisely because it is established; for that which is not yet established, it is even less so, since that which lacks its own essential nature cannot possess the properties of another. The same should be said regarding dependence. Furthermore, how can two forms be joined? For the identity of two distinct things is impossible; or if they were one, what would "joining" mean? Therefore:

Just as the object "knower" is a conceptual construction based on its relation to knowledge and is not a real entity, so too the "agent" is a mere mental construct based on its relation to action—this is the summary of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Thus all is auspicious. (11) [Total from beginning: 16]

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Prima Facie View," in the *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the illustrious teacher Abhinavagupta, within the section on Knowledge (*Jñānādhikāra*). 2.
"Of that which is unestablished"—meaning of that which is insentient; "even more so," meaning it does not exist to a greater degree.
"Thus"—meaning like that which possesses dependence—in "expectation," that is, in the relationship consisting of expectation, which is included by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the Sūtra.
Having thus explained the impossibility of the nature of the relationship as stated in the Sūtra, [the author proceeds].

He states the impossibility of the object through his own reasoning with the words "and two. "And two" refers to the forms of the bowl and the jujube fruit, or the forms of the threads and the cloth; he provides the reason for this with the word "of the two. To the objection that they might therefore simply be one, he replies with "or in the case of oneness. Who [is there]? The meaning is: no one at all. This refers to what was stated in the ablative case.

It should be understood that the three reasons [stated] in the preceding verse serve as the grounds for proving the non-existence of a connection. The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) combines the previously established refutation of being a knower with the immediately proven refutation of being an agent by way of demonstrating the impossibility of a connection. As for the word "by that" (*tena*):

Therefore, the word *tasmāt* (therefore) serves as the explanation for what stands in the Sūtra; it does not mean that [the object] does not exist as a reality (*vastu*)—that is, as an ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
By this, it is indicated that the word standing in the Sūtra also functions as an indicator of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
He concludes the object of knowledge (*prameya*) with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means "in this way"; [it refers to] the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Buddhists and others.

The meaning is: a summary of that which constitutes the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), that is, its exposition in a concise form. The word *iti* marks the conclusion; the word *śiva* denotes auspiciousness and is intended to indicate the supreme reality (*paratattva*). Thus, all is auspicious (*śivam*). 11.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Jñānādhikāra of the *Śrībhāskari*, the commentary on the *Śrīpratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Now begins the third chapter.
We praise that Śiva, whose nature is unceasing awakening, without whom not even all philosophical views could exist.
Now begins the third chapter.
Oṃ! There is nothing whatsoever suitable for the five [senses] externally that exists without Him, the Lord;
we praise that Śiva, the primordial root of all cognitions, within our hearts.

Now, at the beginning of the commentary on the third chapter of the section on Knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*), he composes an auspicious verse (*maṅgalaśloka*)— which indicates the overall intent of the entire chapter and is devoted to bowing before his chosen deity— in order to ensure its completion without obstacles, with the words "vinā yena" (without whom).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "By which"—meaning by that which will be described in the second half [of the verse] as the material cause (*upādāna*); "without" (*vinā*);
"all" (*samastāḥ*); the word "also" (*api*) indicates completeness; [referring to] all internal and external entities consisting of blue, pleasure, and so forth.

Objects and views— limited cognitions— would not exist as any thing at all, just as pots and the like cannot exist without clay. We [know] Him as the Unset (anastamita), because He exists as the witness even of one's own mind, however it may be imagined.
Regarding this prima facie argument, in order to refute the claim that "the accomplishment [of memory] arises from latent impressions alone," [the author says]:
"It is true... [and so forth].
This refers to the seven verses beginning with "ityādi" and ending with "jñānasmṛtyapohanaśaktimān. In the second [chapter], there is the refutation of objections regarding action and relation.
This will be discussed in the section on action (*kriyādhikāra*). As for that which others regard as distinct knowledge—
according to the views of the followers of Kaṇāda, Sāṃkhya, and others—
the awakening which is pure knowledge free from the coloring of objects (*viṣayoparāga*), that alone is one's own self (*svam*).

We praise— that is, we contemplate by way of praise for the sake of attaining our desired goal— that certain ineffable reality called the Supreme Self (*paramātman*): that which does not follow after others, whose nature is stability, and which is auspicious (*śiva*), meaning it is of the nature of light and endowed with the quality that serves as the ground for applying the word "auspicious" due to its capacity to produce bliss.
By this, it is indicated that there is praise of a certain internal reality which is the treasury of all consciousness;
and thus it has been stated elsewhere by this very [author]:
"This [reality], which consists of an expansive and throbbing wheel of various phenomena characterized by mutual differentiation..."

Victorious is Śambhu, the destroyer of inauspiciousness, that treasure-house of the lights of consciousness, who, through a portion of the cultivation of oneness, attains non-dual continuity and thus becomes the object [of experience].

Thus, it is indicated that in this chapter (*āhnika*), the proof is established for the creation of knowledge beginning with memory— which stands as the counter-position (*uttarapakṣa*)— by way of its essential nature and its status as the cause of connection. Having thus performed the auspicious invocation, [the author proceeds] with this chapter both in its entirety and in its parts.
He first provides a statement of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) for the purpose of reassuring the disciples with the words "In this...
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"In this"—that is, in the seven verses spoken in the immediately preceding chapter—[the word] "occurs" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

[This concerns] the connection. Now, one might ask: why is that refutation of action and connection not itself criticized, such that the particle *eva* (only) is established as "that very [connection]"? To this he says, "In the case of action. One might further object: let it be so; however, as for what was done by means of the seventh and eighth verses, relying upon the Śākyan doctrine...

In the *Kāṇāda-śāstra* (Vaiśeṣika) and the *Sāṃkhya-śāstra*, that which is intended by the author of the present work—namely, that which is distinct from the self (*ātman*)—has been refuted; therefore, that constitutes yet another refutation.
In this regard, by means of two verses, [the author establishes] cognition as being of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

It has been shown that even though memory arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the experience [of the original object] does not manifest [within it]. Then, having refuted the objection regarding the erroneous nature of memory by means of two verses, [the author], by way of a further consequence, [addresses] all determinate cognitions (*adhyavasāya*) with the third verse.

The suspicion that [the cognition] is erroneous has been quelled. Then, having stated with one verse that "if memory were impossible even when a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) exists, there would be the cessation of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)," it was stated with another verse that its possibility is established in our own position—this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Now, the meaning of the text itself is being examined.
Since separate cognition has already been refuted, it must necessarily be rejected; with this requirement in mind, he says "yattu" (as for that which...).

By the "other"—namely, the Śākya—the word "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. This refers to another critique by the author, Utpaladeva, [directed] toward those who are capable of providing a rebuttal because [the position] is desired.

The meaning is "distinct from the defects"; the intention is that even in the venerable Śiva-system, since knowledge is a power (*śakti*) of the Self, it lacks distinctness from it. Having thus stated the overall purport of this chapter (*āhnika*), which consists of seven verses, he explains it also in detail, beginning with the word "therein" (*tatra*). Therein—

Within these seven verses, there is the non-manifestation in memory— that is, the absence of illumination by memory— of both *jñāna*, which exists in a general sense as the entire range of cognitions, and *anubhava*, which exists in a specific sense as the cognition known as direct experience. By the third [verse],...
With respect to the two preceding verses, the sense is that it is by the fifth;

having spoken by means of the [fifth] verse, the meaning is "by the sixth. Its justification—the justification for conventional usage—was stated by the [seventh] verse; this is the purport of the seven verses.
This means that the intention [of the author] is [to explain] each part individually. He promises to determine the meaning of the treatise with the words "the treatise. [Objection:
True; however, memory-knowledge, though produced from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience and residing within the self, does not perceive the original [first] experience. (1)

By the word "true" (*satyam*), it is shown that from within the opponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*), much must first be accepted by me; whereas that which cannot be accepted is refuted—this is indicated by the word "but" (*kiṃtu*), which expresses a distinction. Here, in this Smṛti, there is no manifestation of the mere object.

That which requires justification would be established through [mere] mental construction (*saṃskāra*) alone; however, without the illumination of experience, he introduces and explains the first verse—without even providing an introductory transition—in the form "that" (*tat*). He says: "True."
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:

"The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) speaks in order to state the intended meaning of the word 'truth' (*satyam*) found in the sūtra. Regarding the phrase "the multitude of things," this refers to the category of entities beginning with the refutation of knowledge distinct [from the Self]. As for the word "shown" (*darśitam*), it refers to this [same category].

The intention is that the word *pada* denotes acceptance (*aṅgīkāra*). [Objection: In that case, since everything must be accepted, the inclusion of the word "much" (*bahu*) is indeed useless; to this he says, "But as for that which... By this, the intended meaning of "but" (*kintu*) has been stated.
He states the literal meaning of "but" as "distinction" (*viśeṣa*). This distinction refers to [the view] from the previous position.
The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). He begins to explain "the knowledge of memory" and so forth with the word "here" (*iha*).

"Here" means in this treatise on recognition (*pratyabhijñā-śāstra*), [this point] is to be established. Then, in response to the inquiry "What is it that is to be established here?", he reveals the object to be established through a sentence, as it requires much to be said.
"But" (kintu) serves to indicate an alternative position from the view that maintains the illumination of the object alone.
He states the matter implied by "but": "experience" (anubhava). Without the illumination of experience...

The sense is: how could [recollection] exist without the awareness of a prior experience? Since it possesses an object only by virtue of having that very [prior object] as its object, it would not be tenable [otherwise]. To the objection that "let it not be so," he says:
"And how..."—by means of that recollection, which takes the form "that," there is practical activity (*vyavahāra*), that is, through desire (*kāṅkṣā*).
The linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding objects is being performed; why should it not be so? To this he says: "experience" (*anubhava*).

Of this—that is, of the entity which is the object of linguistic usage—after that, meaning after the ascertainment of its being a means to pleasure, and after a long period of time, there is "appropriation" (*upādāna*), that is, grasping; the remainder of the sense is "of that very same entity. In this regard:

And in the interim, mindfulness must necessarily be relied upon; for in the absence of the recollection that something is a means to happiness, no one would undertake the acquisition of that thing. [Objection: But surely even the awareness of a previous experience occurs there through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone, just like the final effect, which is the act of acquisition?

How could there be memory, and how, without it, could there be worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) driven by desire? For it is through experience that the capacity of this [object] to be a means to pleasure is determined, and from that follows its acquisition (*upādāna*). In this regard, all that has arisen from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a prior experience. Even though that cognition was not produced by the object [itself], [it nevertheless arises].

"Nevertheless, it has that as its object"—but this does not amount to anything, because within self-abiding, self-luminous knowledge, the prior experience does not shine forth in the same way that an object [is said to] shine. || 1 ||
To address this, he says "tatra" (in that case). "Previous experience" refers to the ascertainment of something being a means to pleasure;

from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that—namely, the impression of its being a means to pleasure—the entire range of effects arises up to and including the act of appropriation (*upādāna*). The point is that even the recollection of the previous experience itself does not arise.
Now, one might ask: what is the object of that memory-cognition? To this he says, "Even though...

The meaning is that it is not present before [the senses], because its object is the previous experience. It has that as its object—namely, the previously experienced object—because that which is being experienced cannot be denied. This is the sense.

The word "śabdaḥ" (the verbal testimony) [is used] to indicate the completion of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Now, one might object: "In that case, by this very fact, its capacity to manifest a prior experience would already have been established. To this, he says: "na ca" (and not). The meaning is: by this much—by its having an object through that which has an object as its own object—not anything at all has been accomplished. How so?

In response to the question "What [is it]?", he states the reason: "The Self" (ātman). Because it is established in the Self—meaning intent upon its own self-luminosity—it follows that in the knowledge of self-luminosity, namely in the knowledge of memory, there is no manifestation (*asphuraṇa*) of the prior, i.e., the initial [perceptual] experience;
and in this matter, one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*) is the witness. This is the intended meaning. || 1 ||
Now, one might object: "Since memory is produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), why should it not also take the prior experience itself as its object?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Vision is self-luminous and cannot be known by another, just as the vision of form [is not known by another]."
If, however, flavor were produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), then because it would be equal to them, there would be no cognition of it. || 2 ||

"Vision" (*dṛk*) is knowledge; and it is distinguished from the insentient by its nature as a single, self-luminous form, for the insentient must be described as being separate from light. Therefore, vision is "self-manifesting," where manifestation (*ābhāsa*) means the state of being luminous.

Now he provides the introduction to the second verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). Here the commentary says: "Because it is born of mental impressions"—that is, because it is produced from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience; "the former" (prācyam)—
First: having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it, beginning with the word "dṛk" (vision). Here, the commentary states:
he explains the word "dṛk" found in the sūtra as "jñānam" (knowledge). And that—namely, knowledge—...

"From the insentient"—that is, from the insentient object known as the "knowable. He establishes this very point even through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*) with the words "for the insentient...

It must be "stated"—meaning it is fit to be spoken. He states the conclusion with the words "therefore... He explains the term *svābhāsāḥ* (self-manifestations) with the word "manifestation" (*ābhāsa*). He explains the constituent part "manifestation" (*ābhāsa*) with the word "light" (*prakāśa*).

"Manifestness" (prakāśamānatā) is the state of being the agent that illumines external correlates; he explains the component "own" (sva) as "form" (rūpa). "Non-deviating" (avyabhicāri) means not following after anything else; by this, its essential nature, called "the illuminator," has been stated. And here, "own" refers to the manifestation (ābhāsa) which constitutes its very nature.

The analysis of the compound *svābhāsā* (self-luminous) should be performed by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* with grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in: "that of which there is self-appearance. Now, resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* with non-coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇya*), he also describes its form known as "self-illuminating" (*svaprakāśaka*) with the words: "and of itself" (*svasya ca*). Of itself—

It is that whose form—its own nature—is the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) of the Self known as "Vision" (*dṛk*). Here, however, there is a double application of the word *sva* through *tantra* (elliptical compounding): [the first] meaning "one's own," and [the second] meaning "whose manifestation is one's own" (*svasyābhāsaḥ*). Alternatively, the word *sva* is elided after the single term *svarūpam*.
If, however, one relies on the formal aspect (rūpa), there would be the undesirable consequence of [the word] being masculine.
It is that whose own form is non-deviating; and it is that whose form is the manifestation of itself.
Even when an external object exists, the manifestation as transferred to that body is not the true form of cognition.

It must be so; for the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition is said to consist precisely in the manifestation of its own nature, which is characterized by the illumination of another. Now, one might object: "That cognition of experience will appear in memory as being self-manifesting itself. To this he says: "Not by another" (*nānyena vedyā*). [This applies] to another [cognition].
If the vision were to appear [as an object], then it would not be self-manifesting; for this indeed is the definition of that which is self-luminous:
if it were to manifest by itself, then surely the vision, even if it were to appear as such, would still be self-manifesting in relation to another.

Because its insentience (jaḍatva), which arises through the power of the external coloring (uparāga) brought about by the majesty of external objects, is indeed difficult to avoid, he says "even though" (saty api). The intention of the word "even" (api) is that in the investigation of ultimate reality (paramārtha), the external does not exist at all. "Transferred to its body" means attached to the nature of the external.

That is to say, it is colored by that [object]. "Illumination" means *prakāśa*. Furthermore, what is its essential nature? To this he says: "Supreme" (*para*). Its nature consists of supreme illumination—that is, the illumination, the very light, of its own innate (*nija*) form, which is the nature of external manifestation; it is precisely that, and not anything else therein.

[The opponent claims] agency; however, if that were the case, it would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*). The remainder [of the statement] is that the so-called self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition is its very nature (*svarūpa*). It is said—that is, it is explained. And thus, the sense is that external contact is to be kept at a great distance. This explains the meaning of the word "eva" (only/itself) in the phrase "not to be known by another" (*nānyena vedyā*).

He provides an explanation with the words "nanu" (surely). Regarding "smaraṇe"—that is, within the scope of memory—the form "bhāsiṣyate" is used in the sense of the object acting as its own agent (*karmakartṛ*). By this, the introduction to the phrase "by another" (*anyena*) has been made. To this, he states the answer with "no," saying "he says. When the expectation arises as to by whom he says this, he presents and explains the statement: "not by another" (*nānyena*).

This has been explained by a literal commentary due to its clarity. To the question "Why are they not objects of cognition? he says: "In another [state]. To the question "Why is that [consciousness] not self-manifesting? he says: "This very [is the definition]. The definition of that which is self-luminous—that is, self-manifesting—is its unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*). By this, [the point of] "it is not cognizable elsewhere" [is established].

It has been indicated that "not elsewhere" (*nānyatra*) is a synonym for "manifestation" (*bhāsyā*). To the question, "What [is required] for that which is self-luminous—i.e., self-manifesting? he says: "by itself" (*svayam*). First, since it is "by itself"—that is, because of its lack of relation—how can the locative case "in another" (*paratra*), which is animated by relation, be logically consistent?

And likewise, by means of the cognition of form, the "vision" regarding taste—the cognition whose object is taste—is not cognized; for in that case, taste would effectively be grasped by the eye itself. Now, if the experience does not manifest in memory, what then could have been accomplished by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), since the cognition of form [would not be present]?

[The cognition] is born from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the knowledge of the taste; how then can this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) arise? Therefore, it is the mental impression alone that would be capable of destroying the faults you have imputed. This is not so, because [the subsequent cognition] has arisen from an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) that has been conditioned by that very mental impression.

Since its nature is luminosity, it has no need for another light; rather, it shines by itself, through itself, and for itself, and not through a means of knowledge distinct from itself for a knower distinct from itself. In that case, because there is no connection with another—due to the absence of a relation—the [cognition], whose very life is relation...

It is rooted in a relationship; otherwise, how could the seventh case-ending (*saptamī-vibhakti*), expressed by the suffix *tra* following the word *para*, be consistent? This is because there would be no object [for the relationship].
Furthermore, it does not stand as a synonym for the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of being explained as the third case in the phrase "by another" (*anyena*).

The meaning is that it "coincides" (saṃgacchate). The sense of the sentence is that the very state of not being an object of the locative case usage in the phrase "elsewhere" (paratra) is the definition of self-luminosity (svaprakāśa). To explain the sentence, "Just as sight [perceives] form, so does it [perceive] taste," he says, "And thus" (tathā ca). The word "thus" (tathā) indicates the comparison expressed by the word "just as" (iva).

The meaning is this: just as the cognition of taste is not perceived by the cognition of form because it is established through its own self-awareness (*svapratīti*), so too the prior experience is not perceived by memory. Now, one might ask: "If it were perceived, what would happen? To this he says: "For in this way," etc.; that is, [it would be perceived] as a result, but not directly, by the cognition of form.

The sense is that once the cognition of taste is apprehended, the apprehension of its object—taste—would necessarily follow as being within the range of the eye, which is the grasper of form. He provides an introduction to explain how there would be "equality with that" if [the cognition] were produced from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the words "nanu" (but). This is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*): by means of the cognition of form...

The undesirable consequence consists in the appearance of a cognition whose object is taste. He concludes the question with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). By you—the respondent—you would be capable of—meaning able to—destroying—that is, annihilating—the defect known as the impossibility of memory which has been alleged.

[This] might be [the case]. He states the answer: "Not so. When the question arises as to why, he says: "For... [The phrase] "by its impression" means by the impression of the initial experience; "from that which has been refined" means from that which has been rendered capable of producing memory.
By this, [it is shown that] in being born of an impression...

Memory is awareness; therefore, let the arrangement of the branches be similar to it, like the previous arrangement, but it is not logical that whatever is produced from a latent impression (saṃskāra) of something must have the nature of experiencing that thing. How, then, is the understanding of similarity achieved? For it is not...

The cognition of experience does not convey similarity, nor does the cognition of memory; for if the two are not mutually cognized, it is impossible to determine a similarity residing in both, and there exists no other entity whose nature consists in the cognition of both. Therefore, following from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), [the subsequent cognition] possesses an object—
