Thus, it is indicated that this is a locative case of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). Alternatively, instead of the reading *saṃskārajatve*, there is the reading *saṃskārajatvam*. From the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—that is, from a cognition similar to that which awakens the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), as it has been said:
"Similarity, perception, reflection, and so forth, are the awakeners of the seed of memory.
For in this context, it is intended that the cognition of something similar [arises] from what is similar; and the seed of memory is indeed the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
"Similar to that" means similar to the previous experience; "the arrangement of branches" means the configuration of the branches.

For a branch that has been fashioned otherwise, when released by the [formative] process (saṃskāra), remains once again in its original configuration; and here, similarity should be understood as being produced by having the same object. He explains "not that movement" with the words "but not. In the reading "by its similarity," the word "but" (tu), although not explicitly stated in the aphorism, is [to be supplied].

It should be supplied [in the compound] by virtue of its logical connection. Taking the analysis (*vigraha*) of *tadgati* as "the cognition (*gati*)—that is, the perception—of that"—namely, of the previous experience—this is the meaning. He states another meaning for this very term: "in similarity.
By analyzing it as "the cognition—that is, the comprehension—of that"—namely, of similarity—this meaning is to be understood. Why not?

To address the point that [the object] is the "goal" (*gati*), he says "for not" (*na hi*). The meaning is that the cognition of experience—the prior cognition whose nature is experience—does not cause [the object] to be known, because it has already been traversed (*gatatvāt*). Furthermore, regarding the claim that the cognition of memory does not [cause it to be known], he states the reason: "mutually" (*parasparam*). This refers to the state of non-cognition, which was established immediately prior.
The meaning is that [the self] enters into the sensation. Now, one might object: "Let someone else perceive the similarity.

To this he says: "of another. Regarding the phrase "due to non-existence," the words "in your view" (*bhavanmate*) are to be supplied as an ellipsis; however, in this [our] view, since the self possesses the nature of perceiving both of those, there is no contradiction whatsoever. He concludes the subject of inquiry with the word "iti" (thus).
"Thus"— for this reason— "only the state of having an object," that is,
"merely the accompaniment by an object" (saviṣayatāmātra) through the object of a previous experience, [belongs] to "this object," namely, the object of memory.
[The author] concludes the object of cognition (*prameya*).

This is the certainty: that which is established by memory is merely the measure [of the object], but it is not an object of direct experience, nor does this object possess the quality of having been made an object of a prior experience. || 2 ||
Now, if in the cognition of memory there were a real manifestation of the experience (*anubhava*), and through that, of its object, then there would be room for what you have said; however,
since memory is of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it does not manifest the experience or its object at all.

It determines [the object], yet this determination is of the nature of an error; so why this insistence? This very point is shown by way of what is being questioned: "Now, even though memory does not have that [object] as its domain, because it determines it as such..."
The state of having a perceived object [arises] through delusion...
Neither that perception nor its object is the object of memory; nevertheless, both are determined by memory through its erroneous nature. "This" refers to the matter just mentioned.

The application here is as follows: "Vision"—that is, cognition—becomes "only its own manifestation," meaning it is self-luminous and is not cognizable by another. Like what? Like vision regarding taste;

the meaning is that just as vision regarding taste is not cognizable by the vision of form, so it is here. However, if it were produced from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it would be identical to that [vision regarding form].
There occurs that cognition, yet there is no comprehension of the prior experience; moreover, there is no comprehension of its similarity either. || 2 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"by way of that"—that is, by means of the manifestation of experience; "of its object"—that is, [the object] which has that [experience] as its domain.

It determines—that is, it delineates—the object of the initial experience, but it does not grasp it. By this, he states the resulting fact: "this is that. Its nature is delusion—it is of the form of delusion—because delusion consists of conceptual construction (vikalpa); such is the sense. This very thing—referring to the matter just mentioned—

"By being suspected"—that is, by being an object of doubt; the meaning here is that this very matter is what the verse suspects. Having thus provided the introduction (*avataraṇikā*), he presents the verse and explains it. Now, [the word] "atha":
here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
Regarding that perception: the prior experience does not become the object of memory;
nor does its object—the object of the prior experience—become the object of memory. If this is so, then how does memory function with respect to it?
He refutes this as follows: "This is inconsistent. (3)
Regarding this, the author states the proof by means of a verse: "First of all, how can it be memory? And how can there be the establishment of an object from an error?
Why is dependence on the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience even required? (4)
The non-deprivation, that is, the non-subtraction, of an object previously experienced— that is, manifested through experience—
and its manifestation in exactly that same way, is the essential nature of memory; for if it were not manifested in such a way, that very nature would utterly collapse.

Therefore, he says "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). It is "determined"—that is, it is brought to the state of being an object of determination; the word "by memory" (*smṛtyā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. He states the reason for this with the word "error" (*bhrama*).
He provides the introduction to the sentence "this very [thing]" (*tad etat*) by using the word "this" (*etat*). That which has been made the subject of the introduction—
He introduces the statement with "This very [point]," which is explained by the word itself (nigadavyākhyāta). || 3 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fourth verse with the words "atra" (here).
Regarding this, the commentary states: "atra" refers to the matter of inconsistency; "kārikayā" means by the verse; and "upapattim" means the logical justification.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it: "The very nature of memory" (*smṛtitva*).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains the word "of what was experienced" (*anubhūtasya*) by itself as "experience" (*anubhava*). [And] of the object—

Regarding the phrase "non-deprivation" (*apramoṣa*) of [the cognition of] a jar and so forth, he explains it himself with the words "non-removal" (*anapahāra*). He states another synonym for this very term with the words "in that very way" (*tathaiva*). "Manifestation in that very way" means shining forth in accordance with a previous experience; that is to say, the manifestation as "that," for if there were only the grasping of "this," [it would not be memory].
The apprehension is indeed new. One's own form—its intrinsic nature;

that is, one's own form—in the absence of its manifestation in such a way, that is, when there is a flash of "this" in the form of a loss [of the original identity], it would fall apart most completely—it would fall apart to the highest degree. But in error, there is the manifestation as "this."

It is necessarily so, for otherwise it would be impossible for it to be an error; therefore, the idea is that it is not logical for an error to be a memory. By this [argument], how could there even be the status of memory in an error?
Furthermore, in an error, either a non-existent thing or the form of the self appears, but the object is not apprehended by it.

Because that [object] is not manifested, the object is not established by it at all; for establishment consists in manifestation. Therefore, how can there be linguistic usage regarding an object through memory and verbal expression? And if that [object] is not manifested, nothing is accomplished by its being produced from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

For that similarity is relied upon in order to be apprehended; yet there is not even the slightest similarity between experience— which consists in the manifestation of an object— and the error called memory, since the latter does not touch the object in any way whatsoever.
The preceding portion has been explained up to this point. Now, for the explanation of the remainder of the first half [of the verse], [the author says] "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*).

In the case of error—that is, in delusion (*bhrama*), according to the position of those who maintain the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti-vāda*)—it is the Self alone that appears. As it has been said:
"That which is the reality of the object of knowledge within appears as if it were outside."

Thus [it is said]. But by that memory, the object—the external object—is not accepted—that is, it is not grasped—because of its non-manifestation, because of its lack of appearance. He states the conclusion with the word "iti": for this reason, by that memory, it is not established—that is, it is not rendered possessed of stability; [this is] establishment.

The establishment of the meaning. By this, it is indicated that in this sentence the word *bhrānteḥ* found in the sūtra should be construed as having the ablative case-ending. He states the second meaning of this very sentence with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*).
And therefore—from memory which consists of error, there is practical activity (*vyavahāra*) by means of desire.
Conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is preceded by desire—that is to say, it is an act of appropriation. How could this be?
For it is never observed that what is established through error becomes the object of conventional usage, because such a thing is not experienced;
this is the intended meaning. By this [it is shown] that the term *arthasthiti* found in the Sūtra means "the conventional usage regarding an object" (*arthavyavahāra*).

This has been indicated. He explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "na ca" (nor...). Regarding "non-manifestation of that"—that is, the non-apprehension of the object—he asks, "How is it not effective? and answers with "tat" (that). "That" refers to being born of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*);
"similarity" refers to similarity with a previous experience; [all this applies to] that which does not touch the object in any way.

If its erroneous nature is admitted, then it has not attained even the slightest contact with the object. By this [admission], it is indeed established that since the experience and its object are determined by that [cognition], there is a similarity between the experience and the memory through that [determined] aspect; and for the establishment of that [similarity], the inclusion of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is necessary.

What is meant by "is determined" (*adhyavasīyate*)? If it means "is manifested" (*prakāśyate*), then there is no error; if it means "is not manifested," then once again the object has not been touched by this [cognition] at all, and thus even the claim of "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is merely a verbal赘疣 (*śabda-gaḍu*). To demonstrate this, he says:
It has been indicated that even a slight contact with sense objects certainly exists within memory. As it has been said:
"Memory is also of two kinds: that which corresponds to reality and that which does not correspond to reality. (4)

Now he provides the introduction to the fifth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). Here the commentary says: "experience" means that which belongs to a prior time; "its object" means the object of experience.

By that memory, which is being conceptualized as an error, [the object] is determined—that is, delineated. Therefore, for the sake of that determination (*adhyavasāya*), and for the sake of establishing similarity (*sādṛśya*). To provide an answer to this, he poses the question: "It is determined"? What is the meaning of "it is determined"?

Having raised the alternative that [the object] has the nature of being manifested, he states the defect with the words "it is manifested. The underlying sense is that it is not logical for that which is the object of manifestation to be an illusion. Having also raised the alternative that it does not have the nature of being manifested, he states the defect with the words "it is not manifested. This is because, by means of this recollection (*smṛti*), there is indeed contact with the act of manifestation itself.

The sense is that determination (*adhyavasāya*), however, is from the very outset restricted to mere verbal expression (*ullekha-mātra*). Thus—*iti*—for this reason, "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is merely a verbal赘疣 (*śabda-gaḍu*), meaning it is utterly useless;
for it is unfit for practical transaction (*vyavahāra*), since one of the two [terms] is insentient (*jaḍa*).

"Because of the determination of memory [arising] from what is imagined as an error regarding the object. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it: "In the case of being an error... That is to say:
"And if the determination were an error, the persistence of the object would not result from an insentient [source]."
Therefore, since there is no lack of insentience [in the Self], there is no persistence of objects based on its own self-referential manifestation.

In this context, whether it be memory or another type of erroneous cognition (*bhrāntibodha*), there is no error in the aspect of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanāṃśa*) as it manifests, because there is no contradiction therein. However, the form of the object (*svākāra*) which is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) therein is erroneous in that respect, because it is erroneously [perceived] as having its own form when it actually lacks such a form, being instead the nature of the external object (*arthatayā*). That...
"The portion characterized by the object is not touched by memory, nor otherwise, nor by error"— regarding this,
the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains the first half [of the verse] with the word "here" (*iha*). "Of memory" (*smṛteḥ*) means of that which is being conceptualized as memory.

Or [of] another—that is, of a delusive cognition (*bhrāntibodha*) which cannot be conceived as being of the nature of memory—in its aspect of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanāṃśe*), that is, in its self-luminous portion which cannot be denied its status as cognition; of what kind? Shining forth (*prakāśamāne*) by itself toward itself.

In that which is of the nature of vibration (*sphuraṇaśīla*), there is no state of error; the condition of being erroneous does not exist. He states the reason for this with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

The meaning is that "therein"—in the aspect of self-awareness—there is also the presence of the nature of grasping an object. Now, one might object: "In that case, it would be logical to consider even this [self-awareness] as valid cognition (*pramā*. To this he says: "But as for that which... (*yastu*). But as for that which...
In that context—within an error—it is "determined" (adhyavasīyate), meaning it is delineated; "its own form" (svākāraḥ) means the form of the cognition.
"That"—namely, its own form—is determined "as not being its own form," because for that reason it is not actually its own form.
It is determined "in a contrary manner" (viparītatayā), that is, erroneously. For that [cognition] is not a valid cognition (pramā), but rather an error alone.

He asks, "Whence does its erroneous nature arise? and replies, "By way of being an object" (*arthatayā*). The sense is that it exists by way of being an object (*arthabhāvena*); at the time of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), knowledge itself becomes identical with the form of the object, because otherwise apprehension would be impossible. He states the conclusion: "Thus" (*iti*). "Thus"—for this reason—in that respect.

When the aspect of its own form (*svākārāṃśa*) is being determined (*adhyavasīyamāna*), there is error and not validity (*prāmāṇya*). And what is that aspect—the aspect of its own form which is being determined?
It is "characterized by the object" (*arthalakṣaṇa*), meaning it has attained the nature of the object (*arthasvarūpatā*), by way of memory (*smṛtyā*), that is, through the state of recollection.
Whether through conceptual construction or otherwise, it is not touched by error— because of the construction of something else similar to it; thus, even though it stands before one,
it remains silent, and by this very fact, insentience necessarily accrues to it in that respect, just like the cognition of a jar.
On the cloth [of the painting], an insentient thing can perform no function regarding the object; consequently, the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) concerning the object would be lost.
However, if one considers that aspect of self-awareness which consists of the determination (*avasāya*), or its own form (*svākāra*):
Even if one resorts to the non-inertness of this [memory], even so, since memory is established only insofar as it consists of "non-inertness," its own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),

and its delineation as its own form (*svākāra*), how can there be an establishment of the object from that subsequent determination (*adhyavasāya*) of memory, when [memory] is unable to grasp even the name of the object?
The capacity to bring about the state of being fit for conventional usage? || 5 ||
Because it is not brought into the state of being an object of perception— for this reason, in that regard— that is, with respect to that aspect— this [cognition],

whether of the nature of memory or another kind of error, becomes silent, having entered a state of muteness; for this very reason, there is insentience (*jaḍatva*) in this [cognition], whether it be of the nature of memory or otherwise.
[The error] has arrived there in that respect; when there is an expectation for an illustration as to "whose [error] is it like" and "where," he says "the jar.
[Objection: Let it come from there, so what? To this he says "and not... [Objection: Let it not do so.
To this he says "and therefore... The meaning is that it would be obliterated, i.e., destroyed.
He says "atha" (now) in order to explain the second half [of the verse]. The word "tu" (but/then) indicates an alternative position (*pakṣāntara*).

"Tat" refers to that which was just mentioned, namely "the form of determination" (*avasāyarūpa*); this connects, despite the intervening words, with the term "its own form" (*svākāra*) further on. "Nijam" means belonging to its own nature; and "ullekha" (manifestation) is its own form (*svākāra*).

The form of determination (*avasāya*) is its own internal aspect; thus, within this much—namely, self-awareness which is one's own nature and consists of a mental representation—it is "perfected," meaning it has reached its conclusion. "Memory" refers to memory as it is conceptually constructed as an error.
Therefore, from that—from such a conceptual construction of memory as an error.

From the determination (*adhyavasāya*) which has the form of memory (*smṛti*), there is "establishment" (*vyavasthāpana*)—the act of establishing. Of what kind? It is that which possesses the capacity for the accomplishment of "practicability" (*vyavahāryatva*)—that is, the suitability for practical activity residing in the object. Only when an object is thus established [does it become so].

It is fit for conventional usage (*vyavahārayogya*). Since no other error is under discussion here, it is not mentioned; let this suffice for now, as this very state belongs to determinate experience (*savikalpa-anubhava*). || 5 ||
Even if a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) exists, memory is not possible in any way; consequently,
all cognitions would be devoid of mutual connection— this which was stated in the five preceding verses is now applied to the present context:
Thus, if cognitions were mutually distinct and lacked mutual awareness, the continuity of human existence— which arises from the synthesis of those cognitions— would perish.

Whatever "condition" (*sthiti*)— that is, whatever worldly practice (*vyavahāra*)— belongs to people, it is dependent upon that "synthesis" (*anusandhāna*) of all cognitions, which consists in the attainment of memory established through the state of having a single object. Thus,
he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "in the latent impression" (*saṃskāre*).
The commentary on this point states:

"It does not hold"—that is, it is not tenable; the sense is that this follows from the reasoning already stated. Anticipating the objection, "Let it not be tenable," he says: "And therefore... [referring to] those things which are devoid of mutual connection.

The meaning is that they are not mutually connected, because memory alone is the cause of connection. "Thus" (iti) means in this manner; "stated" (uktam) means explained with supporting reasoning, by the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin)—this is the ellipsis. By the five verses beginning with "satyam" and ending with "bhrāntitve," [the author speaks] regarding the subject at hand—the proof of the Self which has been commenced.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the word "evam" (thus).
Here, the commentary explains the term "sthitiḥ" (state) as "yā kācana" (whatever [state] there may be), whether pure or impure.

Regarding the term "vyavahāra" (transactional usage): he states the essential nature of *anusandhāna* (synthetic unification) with the word "eka" (one). Its form is that which has as its characteristic the attainment (*prāpti*) of the state of remembrance (*smṛtitā*)—that is, the state of being a memory—which is established through having a single object (*ekaviṣayabhāvena*), meaning by way of sharing the same objective field as the previous experience. In that regard:
In the aforementioned synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*), [the world] is dependent—meaning under its control, or rather, produced from it.

To the question "How is it dependent?", he says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*). "Based on memory" (*smaraṇanibandhana*) means having memory as their effect by way of generating desire; "transactions" (*vyavahāra*) refers to activities such as appropriation and so forth.
In response to the question "Why?", he says: "First.

"First" means that which is the very beginning of them all, by virtue of being the root of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "I"—that is, the reflective awareness (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*) established in such expressions as "I see," which is of that nature...

By that [means], there is a synthesis of the preceding and the following; for in such expressions as "I see," it is observed that one first reflects upon one's own self, and that reflection, in its ultimate result, consists precisely in the unification of two forms of the self characterized by prior and subsequent time. That itself—

Indeed, all worldly transactions are based on memory; for even the very first perceptual cognition is not possible without being sustained by memory, which involves the synthesis of prior and subsequent forms in the thought "I."

Because there would be no resting in the cognizer, it would follow that [the object] is not perceptible. This should be understood to apply likewise to pleasure and so forth. Furthermore, worldly activities such as the impulse toward rejection or acquisition are essentially composed of memory. Thus, that which arises from the "synthetic unification" (*anusandhāna*) of cognitions...
Regarding the "condition of people" (*janasthiti*), when there is the acceptance by others that it is "thus," it is possible that it "would perish"—that is, it perishes.
If one asks why, it is because of "non-continuity" (*anusaṃdhāna*). By what kind of non-continuity? By that which is animated by memory (*smaraṇa*).

Without—that is, in the absence of—a recollection whose object is one's own nature as qualified by another time, which shares the same object as the experience of one's own nature as qualified by a prior time, and which bestows existence [upon that experience], it is not possible—it is not tenable. Why? Because [this occurs] in the knower—the seer.

Because there would be an absence of repose, which leads to the undesirable consequence of [perception] not being direct— since, at first glance, it is only appropriate to say that perception is direct when the act of seeing comes to rest within the cognizing subject denoted by the word "I" through the medium of the eyes, as in "I see. By the word "also," what [is meant] regarding the others, such as inference and so forth?

"Kathayati" means it is illuminated. He extends this very same principle to such cases as "I am happy," even though there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of internal states like happiness, by using the word "evam" (thus). "Mantavyam" means it is to be known.
Now, one might ask: what is the status of linguistic usages (*vyavahāra*) whose forms consist of material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth? To this, he says:

Regarding "abandonment and acquisition": these are indeed of the nature of recollection (*smaraṇamaya*), meaning they have that very form because they are caused by memory; for it is not observed that there is acquisition and so forth regarding what has been forgotten—this is the sense. He applies the stated reasoning to the present context with the word "thus" (*evam*).
"Synthesis" (*anusaṃdhānam*) means a joining together by way of the object. This refers to the word *evam* found in the Sūtra.

He explains it thus: "In the case of the opponent's admission"—that is, by resorting to the Buddhist view, which effectively amounts to not accepting a self—he states the reason by means of a qualification: first of all, cognitions are mutually distinct from one another.

There is the knowledge of direct experience (*anubhavajñāna*), which is distinct from the present cognition regarded as conceptual (*vikalpa*), and distinct from the cognition accepted as memory (*smaraṇa*). These [three] consist merely in the illumination of their own respective objects;
regarding other objects, they are like the dull, the blind, the mute, and the speech-impaired, and they do not possess the nature of illuminating one another. (6)

Thus, there is no synthesis (anusandhāna) consisting of a single identity, either by way of essential nature or by way of being cognized. Nor is there a mutual relationship of object and subject. Furthermore, it is not possible to conceive of a fourth state (turya) that, being based on what is known, could provide the support for synthesis; otherwise, all worldly transactions (vyavahāra) would perish. And yet—
By the mere utterance of the curse you desire, "May they perish," they perish; since they manifest [from that], they should vanish—that is, go to destruction.
He uses the potential mood (*liṅ*) in the sense of possibility, saying "it perishes" (*naśyati*).

He provides the introduction to the phrase "of those mutually distinct" with the word "whence? (kutaḥ). In response to the expectation of what that reason is, he says "mutually" (anyonyam). He demonstrates their very distinctness with the word "other" (anyat).
He explains the sūtra-word "not from one another" (aparaspataḥ) as "these [elements]," namely—
They consist of non-conceptual and conceptual cognition as well as memory; the suffix -mātra is employed here without regard for the manifestation of their own intrinsic nature. || 6 ||
He provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the word "evam" (thus).
Here, the commentary states:
"svarūpataḥ" means by way of its own nature; "vedyataḥ" means by way of the object of knowledge; and "turyam" (the fourth state).

In relation to the triad known as identity with one's own nature (*svarūpaikībhāva*), identity with the object of knowledge (*vedyaikībhāva*), and the subject-object relationship (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*),

there is something else, namely the fourth, which is the cause based on the object of knowledge— the synthesizer that brings about the union of cognitions— and [if it were absent], they would perish, that is, go to destruction. But then, from that...
To the question "Why?", he says: "And not... That is, those conventional usages (*vyavahāra*). To the question "Why do they not perish?", he says: "...because they manifest.
The sense is that it is simply improper to speak of the destruction of that which is manifesting.
Then, what is to be done? To this he says: "Therefore... This—that is, the matter about to be explained—is established.
This follows: one must strive to establish this very point. And he shows that even the establishment of the injunction (*vidhi*) is impossible without the manner we have proposed:
"If the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), who has internalized within himself the infinite forms of the universe, does not [exist]..."
There may be one who possesses a conscious body and the powers of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance]. || 7 ||

No one denies that consciousness first of all shines forth. But if that consciousness rests solely within its own self, how can it be the manifestation of an object? For that [manifestation] would have to be a property of the object itself;
and consequently, the manifestation of the object would be exhausted in that [consciousness] alone.
The meaning is that it must be accepted by force. He states the object required by this word [“this very”] as “etadeva” (this very).
“Udyantavyam” means effort must be made. To the thought, “Therefore we shall simply make effort,” he says “tacca” (and that).
Without that manner which is intended by us—namely, the form of self-justification—[effort is insufficient].
That which is impossible to justify—
having provided such an introductory remark and presented the verse— he explains it with the words "na cet" (if not).
Herein is the commentary (ṭīkā):
They do not deny it—they do not perform a denial. As the Śruti says: "He becomes non-existent; he perceives the non-existent, if he knows [it as such].
By this, the phrase "whose body is consciousness" (cidvapuḥ) has been explained. To the question, "What follows from that luminosity? he says: "But that... (sā tu).

"Resting solely in its own self"—meaning intent solely upon its own self-luminous essential nature—such is consciousness (*saṃvit*). Why is it not the manifestation of the object? To this he says: "For that... For since that manifestation of the object would be a property of the object itself, and not of the nature of independent consciousness.

This is the intended meaning. [The opponent objects: "But let it be exactly so. To this, he says: "And therefore... That is to say, within the self alone (*svātmamātre*), the state of subject and object has dissolved. Therefore, by one who maintains that consciousness is of the nature of the manifestation of an object, the object itself must necessarily be admitted as being included within that very nature. And if that manifestation of the object...

Furthermore, since it is not logical that one thing [the past object] and another [the present consciousness] could be related through memory, it follows that this [consciousness] is indeed one. Because of its unity, the entire mass of objects of knowledge is embraced by it—this must be accepted even by one who does not wish it. Even so, it would manifest at all times as the self of the universe, whether emerging or submerging.

Because it possesses such a nature, and because it is not otherwise, it further grasps within itself another mass of objects— which, though distinct in form, is already firmly established within its own essence— and then, having slipped away from its own nature, it becomes lost to some particular object; for the manifestation of the object rests solely within its own self.
The meaning is that contact with a cognizer is impossible. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how can the relationship between the grasped and the grasper be established? To this he says: "Therefore.
[It is] within the very nature of consciousness—that is, the reality of independent consciousness—[that this occurs].

It is indeed internal to the nature of autonomous consciousness (*svatantra-saṃvid-rūpa*), and not situated outside of it; for if it were [external], it would follow that it is a property of the object (*artha-dharma*), which would result in the impossibility of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva*). This is the intended meaning. Now, is this manifestation of the object one and the same, or is it ever-new in each successive moment? To this, he says: "And that... (*sa ca*).

"Another and another," meaning ever-new. "It is not tenable" because of the impossibility of a synthesizing subject (*anusandhātṛ*)—this is the intended sense (the reading *anusaṃdhātumasaṃbhavāt* is found in manuscript C).
"This" refers to the manifestation of objects; by this, the word *eka* ("one") in the Sūtra has been explained. It has arrived as oneness.

It causes [the subject] to accept the state of being all-encompassing because of its oneness; it must be accepted, for otherwise, due to the difference in objects of knowledge (*vedya*), a difference in that [consciousness] itself would necessarily follow—this is the sense. By this, the term *antaḥkṛta* (contained within) has been explained.
To explain the term *jñāna* (knowledge), he says *evam api* (even so): Even so—
Even while encompassing the entire mass of objects of knowledge,

it would manifest as the universal self— in its entirety— by being "emergent," appearing slightly through its recourse to objects, and "submerged," remaining largely unmanifest due to not resorting to them in their totality; for this is not possible for a single entity.
The sense is that simultaneous manifestation and non-manifestation are logically untenable. He states the reason for this with the word "tathā" (thus):

because of having such a nature—namely, the nature of manifestation—and the meaning is that it is indeed impossible to abandon one's own nature. Nor is it so; the meaning is that this is not experienced. If one asks, "What then should be done? [the response follows].

He says: "Therefore. Another point follows: it results that [the consciousness] manifests some object made its own within itself as something emergent; this is precisely the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
And the nature of consciousness is differentiated by, or permeated with (*saṃbhinna*), this emergent manifestation.

Because it is extroverted and colored by the reflection of that [object], cognition is said to be ever-new. Even so, since these ever-new appearances undergo arising and passing away at every moment, there is precisely that same failure in the continuity of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, regarding a certain appearance previously grasped, that which is the consciousness—

It became extroverted; that which was its introverted nature as the essence of consciousness (citsvarūpa), remaining stable even at another time, perceives its own state of extroversion toward a particular object—this is the intended meaning. "Having a distinct form" means that it exists as an object of knowledge (jñeya)—this is the intended meaning.

"Something indeed" means another [object] with a different form; "from its own nature" means from its own essence, which has internalized the entire mass of knowable objects; "emerged" means manifested;
"arrived" means come forth by force. This very [power], whose form is an emerged manifestation—by this [is characterized] the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
The proof has been established.
Now, one might ask: "If this is the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*), then what is the nature of the cognition of a jar, a cloth, and so forth?
To this he says: "emerged" (*unmagna*). By "emerged manifestations"—that is, by being brought into appearance through the process of objectification.

The nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), though appearing as diverse through manifestations such as the word "jar" and so forth— as if it were differentiated— remains its own innate form; this occurs because of its outward orientation— that is,
by resorting to the state of externalization as "this"— and due to its coloring by the shadow of those [manifestations].
Due to the coloring by appearances and reflections that emerge [from it], there is ever-new knowledge—that is, knowledge in the form of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is ever-new.

This has been stated, and it is observed that even for a single body of water, there is an ever-newness through appearances in the form of waves and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Now, by this...
Thinking that "all worldly transactions might be accomplished by the power of cognition alone," he says: "even so" (*evam api*).

"Even so" means even if the power of cognition consists of ever-new cognitions; the sense is that it is "that very same [power]" as previously described, because the recollection of a prior object would otherwise be impossible. Now, if this is the case, what should be done? To this, he says:

"By that": previously—at the time of experience—when it was grasped or previously grasped, there is "cognition," which consists of experience; of that cognition, which had previously been extroverted as "this," there is the "introverted" state as "I," which is its nature as consciousness (citsvarūpatva), abiding as its very essence.

The state of the nature of consciousness—of what sort? Even at another time—that is, even at the time of recollection—it remains steadfast, existing eternally; it resides within its own self by way of being a latent impression (*saṃskāra*);
that [impression], being ancient, [emerges] as an object from among the mass of knowable things contained within itself, specifically with respect to a particular object.

The power of memory (*smṛti-śakti*). And that which it manifests or remembers as "new" is, in reality, essentially non-different from consciousness (*saṃvid*) because it functions through identity with it; thus, being composed of the universe (*viśvamaya*), it is indeed full. Therefore, nothing at all could be manifested or remembered as "new. This point must also be accepted as following from the flow [of the argument]: namely, that...

That [object] appears as if severed from consciousness, and consciousness [appears severed] from that [object], consciousness from another consciousness, and the object of cognition from another object of cognition. Yet, such separation is not possible in reality;
thus, what is called "separation" is merely an appearance. And this does not, by virtue of its being so [perceived], possess ultimate reality.

When any object of knowledge (*vedya*) is grasped—even though it is not ultimately real—the state of being turned outward (*bahirmukhatva*), which consists in the grasping of it as "this," is reflected upon;
that is, it is brought to the state of being an object of reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) as "that. This is because she (the Power) is capable of doing so therein. This is her [nature].
The power of memory arises; by this, the means for the power of memory is established.
He establishes the power of "removal" (apohana), which bestows life upon the two aforementioned powers, with the words "and that which...

In reality—that is, from the perspective of the ultimate truth—it is together with the one who consists of the universe—that is, she whose form comprises all objects of knowledge internalized within herself.

By way of identity—that is, by having that as its very form—there is the existence or abiding of such [consciousness]; otherwise, it would not be "consisting of the universe" (*viśvamaya*), which is the nature of consciousness, because fullness would be impossible. This is the intended meaning. As for that which has "fallen into the stream"—that is, arrived involuntarily—how could that be [the object] of experience or memory?
Arising is appropriate because those two [the subject and object] and their objects are immersed in consciousness; therefore, he says "yatkila" (as it is well known).
It is "manifested"—it is brought to the state of being an object of manifestation—and this is also an elliptical expression for "it is remembered.
It is "separated"—it is extracted—from that object, and "consciousness" is that which has that as its object.

And from another consciousness— from a consciousness that, while abiding as the unifier of all, appears as something distinct; and from another object of consciousness— the thing which is the object of consciousness—
from another object of consciousness that has not yet attained the status of being an object at that time.

[From] the mass of objects of cognition that has come into the state of being an object—[C]. Now, if this is so, then because even the state of separation remains as something real, there would be a loss of non-duality; to this he says: "And not... [na ca].
It is merely an appearance, nothing more than an appearance. Now, one might ask: "Even so, let it be real nonetheless"; to this he says: "And not... [na ca]. That—

"Cutting off" (*vicchedana*)—by this much, namely by mere manifestation—is the ultimate (*pāramārthika*), that is, the real; for otherwise, this alone would be the supreme reality (*paramārtha*) of everything being emanated. Since this very [manifestation] is called "delimitation" (*pariccheda*) because it cuts off [everything] all around, its capacity to manifest is the power of exclusion (*apohana-śakti*).
All worldly transactions proceed by means of these three powers, and these three powers belong to the Lord alone— that is, the manifestation of Caitra, Maitra, and others,
whose natures consist of being such an experiencer, rememberer, and conceptualizer.
For it is He alone who knows and remembers through each of those various forms.
And he conceptualizes [this], as stated by the Teacher himself:

"Even though the stability of objects is restricted within the individual soul (jīva), which is constrained by the vital breaths and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), it nevertheless remains established in the Supreme Self."

The sense is that this would lead to the consequence of the duality of the moon also being ultimately real. Now, one might object: "Let this principle apply to what is being manifested and to what is being remembered; but what is the case regarding what is being created? To this, he says: "of what is being created. This very thing—namely, manifestation itself—applies everywhere, whether in respect to an object of knowledge or an effect.
The point is that ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is merely manifestation (*avabhāsanamātra*), and thus there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*). Now, one might object:
"In every case, it is proclaimed that manifestation is nothing but delimitation (*pariccheda*); how then can you say this?
To this he says: "Because" (*yataḥ*). Because this very thing—namely, delimitation itself—is [so described] by the learned.
"From cutting around"— because of performing the cutting immediately mentioned, it is called "delimitation" (*pariccheda*);

for that reason, in the manifestation— that is, in the production of the manifestation whose nature has been described— there is "capacity," which is the power of exclusion (*apohana-śakti*), denoted by the term "separation" (*viccheda*).
The power consists of the nature of exclusion (*apohana*).

He explains that this very triad of powers is the cause of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) with the words "by this" (*anena*). "All" (*viśve*) means everyone. Now, one might object: "Even so, the self (*ātman*) you desire is not established"; to this he says: "And that... [referring to] the Blessed One.

The sense is that since power cannot be established without one who possesses power, the nature of the Self as the possessor of power must necessarily be accepted for the reality of the Self endowed with sovereignty. Now, an objection might be raised: "That triad of powers is observed only as residing in Devadatta and others; why do you speak thus? To this, he says: "For... (yat... hi).

Because that very Blessed One, by means of each respective body—his own essential nature—knows, remembers, and conceptualizes; and by what means? By the manifestation of those such as Caitra, Maitra, and others, who are in such a state—that is, who in ultimate reality are of the nature of the Blessed One’s own essence, having the inherent nature of experiencer, rememberer, and conceptualizer.

It occurs. Regarding this, he states the consensus of the Teacher (*ācārya*) with the words "as it has been said. "The stability of objects" (*arthasthiti*) refers to linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) concerning objects; "ceased" (*niruddhā*) means having come to rest; "that" refers to the stability of objects. "And so forth" (*ādi*) and so on.
Furthermore, regarding these powers of cognition and the rest, there is an inconceivable variety of conceptual diversity (*vaicitryavikalpa*).

Its capacity is autonomy (*svātantrya*), which is independent, full, and great sovereignty; this is said in comparison with the sovereignty of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others created by it. Thus, by defining it as "the body of consciousness" (*cidvapuḥ*), the conclusion reached is that it is "the one whose form is the universe" (*viśvarūpa*). And for that very reason:
Because it is distinct from insentient entities that possess a fixed, singular form,
other sentences are grasped by means of this word. By this, the phrase "possessing the powers of knowledge, memory, and exclusion" has been explained.

In order to explain the term *maheśvara*, he states "etāsāñca" (and of these) to describe the great sovereignty (*mahadaiśvaryatva*) of this triad of powers: *vaicitryavikalpa* is the variegated arrangement; its *sāmarthya* is the capacity consisting of the aforementioned triad of powers; and *svātantrya* is the nature of absolute freedom.

"Sovereignty" (*aiśvaryam*) means lordship (*īśvaratā*). Now, one might ask: "In relation to what is his greatness? To this he says: "created by him" (*tannirmita*). By "him"—the aforementioned Blessed One—those such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are "created," meaning manifested;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), Indra and the other gods are included. Their sovereignty is—

The state of being the Lord is according to each [individual]; with reference to that, he provides a summary, saying "Thus it is. "That" means for that reason; "this being so," having established that the body is consciousness (*cidvapuḥ*), by this reason—that is, because the body is consciousness—this much has been reached. What is this much?

"Viśvarūpa" (the Universal Form). The Blessed One is Viśvarūpa—he becomes the essential nature of all things, because in a dream, consciousness alone is seen to possess all forms. And for that very reason—on account of this universal form—they are "perfected," meaning they have reached a final rest in their own essential nature alone; therefore, they are of a single form.

Because they are of an insentient nature, [the Self] has attained supreme sovereignty (*maheśvaryam*), which consists in being endowed with powers such as knowledge, due to its distinctness from them. For if this were not admitted, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that nothing at all would appear; yet it does appear. Therefore, this must necessarily be accepted.

"[This] must necessarily be accepted"—this is the reversal of the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum). "The stability of the world would perish, if it were not so"—this is the connection with the preceding verse. By the word "if" (*cet*), its opposite is indicated. || 7 ||

By virtue of being distinct, that Blessed One attains *aiśvarya*—the sovereignty consisting in the possession of powers such as knowledge; that is, the state of being endowed with the powers of knowledge and so forth. As it has been said:
"If Maheśvara were to remain with a body of a single form..."
The state of being Maheśvara and the state of being the All would have been abandoned by him, just like a jar or other such objects.

Thus, by means of this, he recalls the previously stated *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) and its reversal (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*). "If this is not accepted"—that is, if the nature of consciousness (*cidvapus*) is not admitted—then "this" [the world] would not appear at all, because it would lack a witness (*niḥsākṣikatvāt*); such is the *prasaṅga*.
The sense is: "with respect to the proponent of the prima facie view" (pūrvapakṣavādin). However, this [consciousness] indeed shines forth, because it is witnessed by one's own experience;

therefore, the reversal of the undesirable consequence (prasaṅgaviparyaya) occurs—that this entity called "the body of consciousness" (cidvapuḥ) must necessarily be accepted—this is the sense with respect to the proponent of the final view (uttarapakṣavādin).

He clarifies the connection of this verse with the preceding verse by saying "naśyet" (it would perish). The relationship [between them] is the "yojanā" (synthesis). To clarify the matter indicated by the word "cet" (if), he says "by the word 'cet'. "Its reversal" means the reversal of the maintenance and destruction of the world of beings; thus it is "suggested," for [the meaning of] particles...
Thus, it is auspicious that this is merely a brief indication. From the beginning, [verse] 23.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Impossibility of Other Philosophical Systems," in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, within the section on Knowledge (*Jñānādhikāra*). 3.

Because it is capable [of refutation]. Furthermore, this daily lesson (āhnika) should be understood as being of the nature of the "subsequent position" (uttara-pakṣa), insofar as it takes the form of a resolution to the preceding daily lesson which was established as the "prior position" (pūrva-pakṣa); for the denial of the self constitutes the prior position, and this [lesson] is its resolution.
Because it is the final section. The word "iti" indicates the conclusion. The term "Śiva" denotes auspiciousness and points toward the supreme reality. Thus, all is auspicious. || 7 ||
Thus ends the third chapter of the Jñānādhikāra in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*, a commentary known as the *Śrībhāskarī*, composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Now begins the fourth chapter. We praise Śiva, who, having gathered the collection of jewels of categories within the treasury of his own heart, strings them together continuously with the threads of memory.

Thus, it has been demonstrated according to the sequence of the actual entities that memory is preceded by knowledge, and that the power of exclusion (*apohana*) favors both of them. Now, following the initial approach, memory itself must be examined from the perspective of supporting the reversal of the incidental argument (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*) that was indicated.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

We praise Śiva, who adorns himself with that white *Bhāvamuktāvalī* (The Pearl Necklace of Existence), which he has fashioned by stringing together the aphorisms of the *Smṛti*, and which resides within his own heart.

Now, beginning the explanation of the fourth daily lesson (*anhika*) in the section on Knowledge (*jñāna-adhikāra*), and desiring the completion of that lesson free from obstacles, he composes a benedictory verse (*maṅgala-śloka*) which indicates the purport of the entire lesson and is dedicated to bowing before his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). He does so with the words: "The categories of reality... (*padārtha*).
The commentary on this [verse] is as follows:

We praise that Śiva; of what nature is he? He is a mass of jewels consisting of the very categories of existence—those things existing both externally and internally—which has been gathered within the elephant of his own heart.

[He perceives] that which exists as a mass gathered within the treasury called his own heart, threading it together in a continuous sequence— namely, the thread called *smṛti* (memory)— in the midst of the threads of memory (*smṛtisūtra*),
even though it is dissolved in identity with its own nature, for the sake of worldly transaction.

This means "connecting them in their proper sequence. There is also a suggested meaning (*dhvani*) that even in the case of a treasury, one strings together a collection of jewels existing as a heap with a thread for the purpose of adorning the neck and so forth. Although it might be argued that since things exist as they truly are (*tattvena*), it is improper to speak of them being gathered into a "heap" (*puñjībhāva*), [the author proceeds as follows]:
Nevertheless, this was stated with reference to the subsequent departure [from the house]. By this, it is indicated that he is here defining the power of memory (*smṛti-śakti*).
Having thus accomplished the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*), [he proceeds] with the daily ritual (*ānhika*) both in its entirety and in its parts.
He states his intention thus, for the sake of the student's engagement:
"It is true, but the knowledge of memory... and so forth;
for this is how it was introduced. In that regard, let it be granted that memory might indeed arise from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone.

However, this must be stated: in order to dispel the doubt as to how even one who possesses the power of the Blessed One as accepted by you—that is, one who has become such—could produce this [memory], and for the purpose of determining the true nature of memory, [the author says]: "For he is the perceiver of objects previously experienced... and so forth.
This refers to the eight verses beginning with "ityādi" and ending with "'arthau bhātaḥ pramātari" | Therein, it is stated in one verse that memory is logically established within our own system.
Here the commentary says:

"Favoring both" means it favors both cognition and memory by way of establishing the nature of the object; [it is the favorer] of the "possibility of the reality"—that is, of the ultimate truth—of the thing.
"By means of sequence" (krameṇa) means relying on a sequence, in the sense that the object arises in this very manner.

"In accordance with the procedure" (upakramānusāreṇa)—that is, following the methodological process—it is memory alone, and not the removal of cognition (jñānapohana). This is what was indicated, rather than being explicitly stated; as for the contingency (prasaṅga), it is nothing at all.

An undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpatti) of the form "it would appear [otherwise]"; its reversal (viparyaya)—of the form "but it does appear, therefore this must necessarily be accepted"; the support (samarthana) thereof—its strengthening; by means of the vision (dṛśā) thereof—that is, by way of the perspective (dṛṣṭi), meaning by way of the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa-mārgeṇa)—it is to be discerned (vivecyā).

It must necessarily be investigated. Now, it might be asked: "Since its discrimination (*viveka*) was already performed in the first section (*pūrvāhnika*), what remains to be investigated? To this he says: "True. "Commenced" means begun at the start of the first section. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therein. That is, while that [commencement] has been undertaken, *mā*...
The name [of this work] arose—let it not arise; the sense is that there is only this much indication therein.
To the question, "Was the establishment of your conclusion not accomplished by that?", he says: "This.
In response to the expectation of what is to be said, he says: "Of such a nature" (*tathābhūta*). Of such a nature—

The power—the majesty—of that Supreme Self who is the ultimate reality accepted by you, the Blessed One, endowed with the three powers such as knowledge; [this refers to] this memory; thus [he addresses] the doubt—the doubt of the disciple situated in the form of a question and answer.
The connection is that "it consists of eight verses. Having stated the intention by way of the whole, he explains it also by way of its parts with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
"Therein" means in the midst of the eight verses. "Specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) refers to the nature of an object that does not follow after others.
By the second [verse], it is stated that through experience, memory possesses the capacity to manifest the particular (svalakṣaṇa) that was the object of a prior experience. By the third...
It has been stated that memory is an immersion (*āveśa*) that reaches the point of identity with the experience and its object.
It was established that by the fourth [verse], the manifestation of the experience by memory does not occur through the status of being an object.
By the fifth [verse], it is shown that even the knowledge of a yogi does not take the experience as an object in a state of separation.

By the fourth verse, the very meaning [of the previous statement] has been reinforced. By the sixth, the suspicion that the objectification of experience by memory as a separate entity is merely conceptual has been rendered unreal. By the seventh, through the context of memory, it is shown that even in a mental construction (*vikalpa*), there is an immersion into the identity with the prior experience.

By the eighth [verse], the resting of the object to be remembered, the act of remembering, and the rememberer within the single state of consciousness is stated; and by way of incidental discussion, that of the visible, the seeing, and the seer—this is the intended meaning. Now, the meaning of the verse is explained in sequence.
For he, being one who perceives objects previously experienced, even when existing at a later time, reflects "this is that" and, being independent, is designated as "one who remembers. (1)
The perceiver of an object previously experienced— that inward-turned consciousness—

indeed still exists even now, at the time of recollection; for that which is of the nature of pure consciousness remains as one with the previous experience conditioned by time and with its object— the object of the previous experience— up to the point of complete unification.

*Āveśa*—*samāveśa* (total immersion) culminates in oneness (*ekībhāva*). By the teacher (*ācārya*) who describes—i.e., narrates; there is also a reading *vadatā* (speaking)—even in the case of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), that is, even within conceptual cognition, there is *āveśa*, meaning entry, by way of identity (*aikātmya*), that is, through the state of being one with it. This is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
The meaning that constitutes the intended purport (*tātparya*).
Having introduced the first verse, he explains it with the words "For he" (*sa hi*).
Herein is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

"Previously"—at the time of experience—"the perceiver" (*upalabdhr*), who is "inward-turned," meaning established as the "I," is "cognition" (*bodha*), that is, knowledge; it is not, however, cognition turned outward as "this," which exists as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He explains "from another" (*parataḥ*) by saying "recollection" (*smṛti*). It certainly exists, and it is not the case that its existence therein is non-existent.
Because if it were established by a witness, a contradiction would arise; but if it were not so established, its non-existence would follow. He states the reason for this:
"in pure consciousness alone," because of the impossibility of limitation consisting of specific contractions [of form].

Furthermore, that the object also exists within experience in a state of non-difference is established without effort. However, this much remains to be considered: if there is a reflective awareness of the nature of consciousness within that consciousness—which is not limited by time—and within the entire multitude of entities existing therein, then...

One must exist through this full reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone as "I"; yet, if there is the manifestation of a separate existence through the mode of "this-ness" (*idantā*), even so, there are two possible courses.

That which is produced by Time—that is, by the principle of time (*kālatattva*) consisting of the variety of actions and characterized by distinctions such as the present and so forth—[is the first course].

Contraction (*saṃkoca*) is the act of limiting that consists in being delimited by one's own internal divisions such as the present and so forth; the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*)—the difference in state—that takes that form, is the nature of which is limitation (*avaccheda*), i.e., non-pervasiveness (*avyāpakatā*).

Because of the impossibility of that [limitation], for it is by consciousness alone that there is the limitation of time, which is the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*) consisting in the variety of its activities.
The sense is that [the cognition] is conjoined with it, but not that it belongs to it. Now, one might object: "But that object does not exist at the time of recollection.
To this he says: "of the experience" (*anubhavasya*). By way of non-separation—that is, by identity—it is established without effort;
since it is established merely through the fact that the relationship of apprehended and apprehender would otherwise be inexplicable, there is no requirement for effort here.
[The opponent says: "But then, silence alone would be appropriate. To this he replies: "To this extent," etc.

In "consciousness"—that is, in pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*)—there is the "reflection" (*parāmarśa*), which is a grasping in the form of synthesis, regarding the entire multitude of entities (*bhāvajāta*) everywhere, whether they have become objects or have not become objects, by virtue of their being composed of consciousness (*cinmayatva*).

The "reflection on the nature of consciousness" (cinmayatā-parāmarśa) means, in the ultimate sense, the reflective awareness of one's own state as pure consciousness alone. "By the full"—that is, by that which is filled with all things—for the entire multitude of existing entities rests within the unmeasured I-consciousness (ahantā), which constitutes the primordial vibration. Therefore...
And thus, she is denoted by the *pratyāhāra* (phonetic contraction) consisting of the letters *a* and *ha*, which encompass all phonemes within them;
as it has been said:
"The emanation beginning with the Absolute (*anuttara*) and ending with *ha* is the very nature of the universe."

"Having withdrawn the entire universe"—here, *am* refers exclusively to the suffixal portion, because it is a substitute for the *sup* suffixes; as for the vowel *a* belonging to the base (*prakṛti*), that too is indeed swallowed by the suffix according to the rule *ami pūrvaḥ*. Alternatively, there is again *am* at the end.

The establishment of the Unsurpassed (anuttara), which is considered to be the Bindu; if the sense of "thisness" (idantā) comes to rest in the aspect that syllables are the nature of all things and are the denoters of all— then, by way of the state of Sadāśiva and so forth, characterized as "I am this."

"One should contemplate [this] with the state of Sadāśiva, thinking 'I am this'—[Kṣemarāja]. Now, if that does not take root, then it must exist as a manifestation of "this" alone; and because of the manifestation of something previously unknown, that would be a direct experience (*anubhavana*) and not a memory.
Anticipating this doubt, he says "the independent one" (*svairī*). He impels his own (*svam*), that is, his personal (*ātmīyam*), instrument (*upakaraṇam*).

In his own duties (*svakartavyeṣu*), he is necessarily of that nature and impels himself; he does not, however, depend upon an external impeller for his own duty—thus he is *svairī*, meaning independent.
Because of this independence, he reflects "he" (*sa*); and as for this reflection "he,"...

Such is its nature—that the reflective awareness of one's own essence, which is in every respect untouched by time, is indeed manifestly so; therefore, enough with this extensive discussion of the secret. He states another alternative with the word "atha" (now):
by means of the manifestation as separate entities, that is, by way of appearing as objects of cognition distinct from consciousness.

This is the meaning; the construction is "the reflective awareness" (*parāmarśa*). "Twofold" means having two parts; "way" (*gati*) means mode—meaning, two modes. He states the first mode with the word "I. "Rests" (*viśrāmyati*) means culminates; by that state beginning with Sadāśiva, which exists as "I am this" (*ahamidam*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the states of Īśvara and so forth are included; he will state this as follows: "Īśvara is the external unfolding (*unmeṣa*); Sadāśiva is the internal closing (*nimeṣa*).
Now, he describes the second method with the word "atha" (now). "It does not rise"—that is, it does not find rest; "then" (*tat*) means at that time.
The meaning is that because there is an appearance characterized by unprecedented novelty (*apūrvatā*), the appearance "I" (*aham*) alone is indeed eternal.

He explains the etymological meaning of the word *svairī* with the term *svam*. He states that what is denoted by the component *sva* is "one's own" (*ātmīya*). The "instrument" (*upakaraṇa*) refers to the collection of means consisting of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); [this applies] to one's own duties (*svakartavyeṣu*).
Regarding his own activities in the form of [the agent] who is prone to error, he states another meaning of this very term: "the self" (*ātman*).

He explains the meaning of "composite whole" (*avayavin*) as "independent" (*svatantra*). Now, one might ask: "Let it be independent; what of it? To this he replies: "by that" (*tena*). He reflects—that is, he performs a deliberation—on the thought, "he is the master"; for it is not logical that one who is independent should be dependent on anything else.

The state [of being]. This explanation is given precisely because the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Now, one might ask: what is the nature of that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)? To this he says: "That" (*saḥ*). He fulfills the expectancy for the word "this" (*iyat*) by saying "which" (*yat*), referring to the act of reflecting—namely, *vimarśana*, which is *vimarśa*. In every respect...
It is not merely the non-reflection upon one's own nature as it is not yet fully integrated,

rather, it is that state which, previously at the time of experience, was accompanied by the presence of that specific place, time, and other subjects.
Not separated [from the Self] yet not dissolved into the very state of "I-ness" (ahantā)— rather, remaining just as it was,
veiled by darkness like that which is designated by the term *saṃskāra*— it casts off that veil of darkness; once that has been cast off, it appears there just as before, clearly separated.
[As if separated—K. Ṣ. Ṣ. But surely it would appear as "this" (*idantā*), just as before; it is not so.

At that time, there is merely the reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), which pervades that which is denoted by the word "I" (*ahaṃ-śabda-vācya*); the meaning is simply "not" [the appearance as "this"].

"Reflection through absolute distinction" means reflection as "this. To the question of what its form is, he says "but rather. He himself provides the explanation of the word "prior" as "experience. The sense is that otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of memory regarding that object. By this, it is further indicated that the entire collection of objects, without returning to the domain of memory, dissolves into the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*) itself.
"That"—meaning the object—"is just such"—that is, it remains distinct; the meaning is that it has not been dissolved into the "I-consciousness."
"By *tamas*—that is, by ignorance—it is established in the heart; this is the ellipsis.
