When that obscuring veil has been separated—that is, when it has been rendered distinct from the pure consciousness denoted by the word "I"—it becomes the object of this reflective awareness (*idaṃ-parāmarśa*). Here, the disciple raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).
The sense is that, as before—meaning at the very time of experience—the two remain indistinguishable because there is no difference in their state of being separated.
The Guru provides the rebuttal: "It is not so. Why?
Because that manifestation occurs precisely without setting aside the connection with the body and so forth, which have not been separated from it;
and therefore, there is also the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) at the time of present manifestation and recollection.
Even the reflective awareness of the present moment of manifestation does not close; thus,
by virtue of the predominance of that [present] reflective awareness as its foundation— meaning, by virtue of the predominance of this [present] reflective awareness as its foundation—
the reflective awareness of the prior time is such that it possesses a nature consisting of a contradictory reflective awareness of both the prior and the posterior, namely, "that."

The term *parāmarśa* (reflective awareness) is used. And thus, that very Supreme Lord "remembers. To address the question of what this [awareness] belongs to, he says: "belonging to that time" (*tadānīntana*). For—because of which reason—the reflective awareness "he" is [described as such]; those two [moments of awareness], being distinct in time, are mutually contradictory (*viruddhau*), characterized by opposition due to their difference in time.
The two reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśau*)—those occurring at the time of experience and those occurring at the time of recollection—are its nature (*svabhāva*).

That which has such a nature, being unified as its very essence (*svarūpa*), is described in this way; therefore, the sense is that it appears here precisely through that [nature] by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatā*). Why is it thus? He says "iti" (thus) to indicate that this is indeed its very nature.

Why? Because there is a reflection upon a prior time—a reflection upon the time of experience—and it exists primarily as the foundation for that reflection, namely, by being the substratum for the reflection upon the time of memory;
otherwise, that [experience] would have already passed away. Therefore, this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) possesses the nature of a dual reflection.

Such is the sense. Why is that? He says: "Thus. Why? Because its manifestation—that is, the manifestation of the object being remembered—is separated by the contemporaneous appearance, i.e., by the cognition existing at the time of experience; that which is the connection with the body and so forth has been brought within the scope of conceptual determination (*pariccheda*).

The connection with the object's own intrinsic nature occurs precisely by not disregarding—that is, by depending upon—that [nature]. And likewise, from that—meaning from that manifestation—it remains by taking as its limit the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) at the time of recollection, which consists of the manifestation occurring at the present moment; that is to say, of that object.

Reflection (*parāmarśa*)—the reflection that occurs immediately after experience—does not close, meaning it does not disappear. The expression "reflection with respect to reflection" is used like the phrase "the head of Rāhu," because both [the object and the subject] consist of a single form of reflection. As for the relationship between the limit (*avadhi*) and that which possesses the limit (*avadhimat*), [it is as follows]: *Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.*

This has as its sole purpose the instruction of disciples. Since both manifestation and reflective awareness (parāmarśa) occur in accordance with the nature of an object previously experienced, it is briefly stated that "reflective awareness of a prior time" is primarily based on the reflective awareness of the time of recollection.
Having explained the first three quarters [of the verse], he explains the fourth as well with the word "evam" (thus). He is indeed independent (*svairī*).
Now, one might object: "In that case, does it not follow that he too is a limited subject (*mitapramātṛ*)? To this expectation, the following should be applied as the answer.

The state of being a rememberer (*smartṛtva*)— which is the assumption of the state of a subject of Māyā capable of enduring contact with the temporal moments and other factors appropriate for such reflective awareness—
is composed of both the duality and non-duality of Māyā and Vidyā. Precisely for that reason...

Those versed in the scriptures consider recollection itself—animated by mantras and other factors—to be like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) capable of bestowing all supernatural powers (*siddhi*). And thus it is said:
"Recollection alone, having attained the state of meditation and so forth..."
"The wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) manifests Your glory.

He states the matter indicated by the word "it is pointed out" (*apadiśyate*) with the word "this" (*etat*). The very attainment of the state of a limited subject (*parimitapramātṛbhāva*), which consists of being a rememberer (*smartṛ*), by that Supreme Lord is itself His "being a rememberer" (or, "His being the agent of remembering").
The sense is that [the Self] is not the agent of recollection in an ultimate sense, like a limited subject (parimitapramātṛ).
He states that this very recollection, which exists as the vitalizing force behind external worldly activity, is also the means for attaining the Supreme Self; thus he says, "Māyā. Thus—
For the reason stated previously— that is, because of the grasping of the state of a subject who remembers the dual form within the non-dual reality of consciousness (cittattva)—
there is *māyā*, which is the principle of *māyā-tattva*, and *vidyā*, which is the principle of *śuddhavidyā-tattva*.
Within that which consists of both duality and non-duality, there is duality due to the differentiating nature of *māyā*.

The non-duality of that knowledge consists in its removal [of duality]; "consisting of that" means having that as its nature. Precisely for that reason—by virtue of having both dual and non-dual forms—it is "skillful" regarding the bestowing—that is, the imparting—of all accomplishments (*siddhis*), which are twofold, existing as both external and internal. Regarding that [bestowal], he who is skillful...

"Cintāmaṇi" means its manifestation, that is to say, its likeness. In this regard, the sequence should be understood as follows: by means of the form known as "duality," it is the cause of external accomplishment (*bāhyasiddhi*); by means of "non-duality," it is the cause of internal accomplishment (*antarasiddhi*). Likewise, it is "animated" by mantras and so forth—that is, strengthened by means of their recitation (*uccāra*) and other such practices. In that context:

It should be understood that there is a sequence here: in internal discourse, [the process] is impelled by mantra, whereas in external discourse, it is impelled by means such as the perception of similarity, which are included under the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). The *āgamikas*—those who know the teaching of Śiva—recite His very words, beginning with meditation (*dhyāna*) and the rest.

The state of meditation and so forth—meaning the form consisting of the contemplation of one's chosen deity (*svābhiṣṭadevatā*) and the like; the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), which is in the form of a wish-fulfilling gem by virtue of bestowing everything; and your majesty (*tvadvibhava*)—that is, your greatness. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the sentence. Now, [the opponent] might object: "There is much more to be said here, so that too should be explained. To this, he says:
"Enough" (*alam*) means that it is not the subject at hand; this is the sense. Thus:
"Enough for now. By this compound ending in *tṛn*—namely, *alam-tāvat-anena*—the contact with time is established through effort, by way of the object of experience.

He demonstrates that both [the compound and the sentence] rest upon the same meaning and are firmly established in the cognizer through both difference and non-difference, because of the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) in the *vṛtti*. We shall explain how that [unification] consists of both difference and non-difference. (1)
He states the intended meaning of the compound *pūrvānubhūtārthopalabdhi* with the words "by this" (*anena*).

"By this" refers to that which is contained in the sūtra; "with effort" (*yatnataḥ*) means by the effort consisting of a formal division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) found in the sūtra *dvitīyā śritātīta...*—the word "having been made" (*kṛtena*) being understood as the remainder. [This applies] to the compound ending in *tṛn*.

By the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who has perceived an object previously experienced," [it refers to] a compound ending in the *tṛn* suffix; [this denotes] the contact with time— meaning the contact with the past time expressed by the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), even though [consciousness] is not limited by time— of the experience, that is, of the previous experience, by way of the object, i.e., through the medium of the objective domain (*viṣaya*).

The state of resting in the object—meaning that even while resting in the subject, there is a resting in the object, as in the case of "the blue lotus. The word "experienced" (*anubhūta*) is an attribute of the object; likewise, for both—the experience and the object—in the subject, who constitutes the referent of the final member of the compound.

The teacher—this is the implied subject—demonstrates the resting or repose of the primary perceiver through both difference and non-difference. In that regard, there is contact with time and rest in the object through difference; however, through non-difference, it is because the subsequent member of the compound is predominant.

He states the reason for the two [types] of *tatpuruṣa* in the commentary (*vṛtti*). Regarding "in the *vṛtti*"—that is, in the compound (*samāsa*)—"the attainment of a single meaning by those that have multiple meanings" is *ekārthībhāva*.
Therefore, in a compound, words that existed in mutual distinction become unified. Why is there *ekārthībhāva*?

To address the point regarding the state of being both distinct and non-distinct, he says: "And of that. The meaning is: "And of that"—namely, of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning)—we shall explain later in the *Saṃbandhanirṇaya*.
Such is the construction here. For (*hi*)—because—that [cognition] which perceives the object previously experienced [continues to do so] even subsequently.

For this very reason, it is pointed out—that is, stated—that he remembers while reflecting "this is that"; why? Because he is *svairī*—independent; for indeed, nothing is difficult for one who is independent. || 1 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the second verse with the words "etadeva" (this very same).

There are other verses in order to establish this very principle of memory (*smṛti-tattva*). In that regard, if someone were to say: "In this context, memory is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and by it no object is revealed, because it does not touch upon the object..."

For these are conceptual constructions; and that experience by which the object was brought to manifestation has now become a mere form of renown, and even that is not manifested by memory—because one cognition cannot be experienced by another cognition and because it no longer exists—and thus, due to the absence of the object's manifestation, [the thought] "this... [does not arise].
If it is argued that the cognition "I remember" is merely an error, and thus the same consequence [of contradiction] arises once again, then he is told in reply:
"And it illuminates [the object] at its own time, while reflecting upon what was previously illuminated by the object."
The specific characteristic [of the jar] exists either as the mere appearance of the jar or in its entirety. (2)
The commentary on this point says:
"Now, since the justification for *smṛti* has already been accomplished by the preceding verse, what is the purpose of these other verses?
To this he replies: "This very [point]... [He uses the term] "to justify" (*upapādayitum*) in the sense of "by means of reasoning" (*upapattyā*), rather than "by means of production" (*utpattyā*).

To strengthen [the point]—[C. "to strengthen," by means of other verses—that is, another seven verses. Now, one might ask: for what purpose was the second verse composed? To this he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
"In that regard"—that is, within the midst of the other verses—"someone"—anyone such as a Buddhist or others—by means of this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Why not?

Because it is manifested, he says "the object" (artha). Now, one might object: let that very prior experience manifest it again. To this, he says "by which."
The meaning is that he has become a mere body of fame—that is, he has perished. Now, one might object: "Let memory itself manifest that prior experience.

And this has been determined in the passage beginning with "dṛk svabhāsā," because [the experience] does not exist [at the time of recollection].
Because its object is non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). He states the conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means for this reason;
the word "iti" marks the end of the statement of the Buddhists and others. "Tatprati" means toward the Buddhists and others.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it: "And he would manifest... (*bhāsayecca*).
In this case, regarding the conceptualization through memory—at the very time of remembering—the object is determined (*avasīyate*);

otherwise, one would fall into a state resembling sleep or fainting. And thus, as long as there is a determination of the object, it must be accepted by implication that "from the object" (*arthāt*)—namely, that:

That object shines forth; for if that which is to be determined were not shining forth, determination would be as if blind. And this shining forth occurs neither by the rejection of the present time, nor by its acceptance. This...

For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence [of everything] appearing in that very way. Therefore, the time of the past experience must be required as the projector of the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇya*) of the entity previously experienced, within the aspect of the object (*vedyabhāga*) of the manifestation.
The commentary here states:

"In this world," means in this universe; "in a conceptual construction consisting of memory" (*smṛtivikalpa*)—that is, in a conceptualization whose nature is recollection—there is, for the time being, no disagreement. "Object" (*artha*) refers to an object such as a jar previously experienced; it is "ascertained" (*avasīyate*).

It is brought within the scope of verbal expression; otherwise—that is, in the absence of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*)—it is not observed that those who are asleep and so forth possess determinative cognition. This is the intended meaning. To the question "But what follows from this?", he says: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).
He explains the word *arthāt* found in the sūtra as "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*). This is the word *iyat*.

It is intent on implying a further meaning; it fulfills the expectancy for the word "this much" by stating "that which. That [object]—being determined within the conceptual construction of memory—is referred to as "non-manifestation" when there is an absence of manifestation; he states the fault in this case.
Regarding that which is to be determined—that is, the previously experienced object which becomes the object of determination—[it is said: "aprakāśe" (in the absence of manifestation).

"Blind-like" (*andhaprāyaḥ*) means resembling a blind person because of the absence of having the object as its domain; the sense is that its activity occurs only when the object has already been manifested. Now, does that manifestation exist by being accepted at the time of experience, or by being rejected? To this he says: "And the manifestation... [referring to] the time of that moment.

Regarding the time of the experience: in response to the question "Why?", he says "this" (*idam*). For if that [time] were abandoned, then since the time of recollection itself would become the qualifier of the manifestation, there would clearly follow the undesirable consequence of the manifestation appearing as "this. But if it is accepted, then for that which resides therein, even the manifestation as "this" [is accounted for].

The intended meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the object] being accepted [as present]. To the question "What, then, should be done?", he says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

"Therefore"—that is, because this undesirable consequence of the appearance of "this" (*idam*) would follow if one were to either abandon or accept the prior time—for that reason, the time of past experience—the time of the previous experience—of the entity previously experienced...
Regarding a jar or the like, its specific characteristic— that is, its nature which does not follow after anything else— is,
due to the adherence to the manifestation of that [nature],
to be taken as the support within the cognitive portion at the time of the manifestation of the body, vital breath, and so forth of the rememberer.

By virtue of being intent upon the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). For the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of an entity is indeed a mere manifestation (*ābhāsa-mātra*), since the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) occurs with respect to each individual manifestation. That very [nature], through its intermingling with other manifestations—by way of projecting [them] like a lamp, by way of delimiting [them], and within the objective portion, that is, the aspect consisting of the object of memory—is [thus constituted].

*Apekṣaṇīyaḥ*—to be resorted to as a qualifier. By means of what? By means of *tattā*, which is the state of being one who possesses *abhiniveśa*—that is, obstinacy—regarding that manifestation which consists of light, namely the manifestation belonging to the preceding moment; for at the preceding time, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the jar [was thus perceived].

That very [consciousness] which was manifested is what becomes the object of memory here as well; therefore, with respect to the object called "the jar," that same [consciousness] must be required as a temporal qualifier—this is the summary. Now, one might ask: "What is required regarding the subjective portion? To this he says: "of the rememberer" (*smartuḥ*). That which belongs to the rememberer...

The body, vital breath, and so forth—that is to say, one’s own nature (svarūpa), as well as the time of its manifestation and the time of recollection. In the "knowing portion"—that is, in the aspect of the knower—it is to be "resorted to," meaning it is to be adopted as a qualifier.
By means of what? By means of the "reflective awareness portion"—namely, the aspect known as present-time deliberation (adyatanaparāmarśa).

By that very fact of being intent upon [the object]. Since the one who performs the apprehension—the rememberer—exists only at the time of recollection, therefore it is precisely at the time of recollection that he must be accepted as the substratum by way of being a qualification of the knower (*vedaka*). Even though the existence of the knower, due to his eternality, persists at all times, nevertheless...

This was stated with reference to the specific characteristic known as "the state of being an object of reflective awareness" (parāmarśakatva). Now, one might ask: "The essential nature (svarūpa) of the jar is not present here; how can you speak of its being an object of cognition? To this he says: "It is a mere manifestation" (ābhāsamātra).
It is a mere manifestation, and not some gross object existing as an effect of clay.

"Of the entity"—that is, of an object such as a jar. To the question "Why?", he says: "In each manifestation. "In each manifestation" means in every manifestation, that is to say, in all manifestations of the jar, its qualities, and so forth. "Of the means of knowledge"—that is, of the instrument of valid cognition consisting of outward-turned awareness—"due to its operation."

Because of its activity (*pravṛtti*). This is the point: a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) indeed produces only a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*) everywhere; it does not, by becoming a material cause (*upādāna*), bring about the existence of anything. And without its activity, nothing whatsoever attains existence. As it has been said:
Existence is nothing other than being accessible through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the very nature of an entity is merely an appearance produced by valid cognition.
As for the fact that clay and so forth are observed to be material causes (*upādāna*), even that is merely an appearance; enough with this mere appearance!
In the world, by means of subtle observations whose objects consist solely in the appearance of the entities existing within it—[the author says this] because, [an objection might be raised:

"If the very nature of an entity is indeed nothing but its appearance, then the conventional distinction between clarity and lack of clarity would dissolve everywhere, since there is no difference in being merely an appearance. To this, he says:
"Thus, that very [consciousness] becomes manifest like the convergence of a thousand lights;
even in the absence of a mixture with other appearances, it occurs precisely through the interpenetration of the appearance of time."
It brings about the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇya*) of that manifestation, because it will be stated that the power of time alone is the differentiator.

Thus, first of all, the state of being a specific characteristic belongs to the manifestation of a jar through the manifestation of time, which has arisen in conjunction with the previous manifestation of the body.

That very thing—merely an appearance (*ābhāsamātra*)—through the intermingling with other appearances, that is, by being mixed with the appearances of attributes such as having an upward-pointing top and so forth. Now, [one might object]: if it is merely an appearance, then because it is impossible to grasp the appearance of unique attributes (*asādhāraṇadharma*), the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would not be grasped.

To address this, he says: "in another manifestation. By means of the intermingling with the manifestation of time—that is, by the conjunction with manifestations in the form of time such as the present—and of that manifestation, which is merely the manifestation of a jar in its general form, [one attains] its *svālakṣaṇya*, i.e., its state as a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
"He acts"—the word "knower" (*pramātā*) is to be supplied. To the question "Why?", he states the reason: "Because of time.

This is because [time] is a differentiator—that is, a qualifier. There is no disagreement among anyone on this point that a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is established precisely by means of an uncommon differentiator. And the uncommonness of time is...
Because it is clearly mixed with the manifestation of the location and so forth of the jar-manifestation, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

And thus, in the *Kriyādhikāra*, he will explain how the universal attains the state of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) through its conjunction with time and other factors. He provides the conclusion with the word "evam" (thus). This being the case, first of all, of the jar-manifestation—

The state of being a specific individual (svalakṣaṇībhāva) occurs through that temporal manifestation— which has arisen by means of the assistance (sācivya), that is, the cooperation, of the previous bodily manifestation (the manifestation of the body in the form of the jar) belonging to the manifestation delimited by "jar-ness" at the time of its prior experience; this [assistance] amounts to its functioning as a qualifier.

It exists; the sense is that this follows from the logic already stated. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter (*prameya*). He describes the very nature of memory with the words "tāvatyeva": "in that much alone"—that is, in the form of mere appearance (*ābhāsa-mātra*)—it is extremely clear through other appearances, namely, through appearances in the form of other attributes (*dharma-rūpa*).

The meaning is that it is "extremely clear" due to the cause of being mixed [with other appearances]. The word "second" indicates the completion of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Now, one might object: is memory not already extremely clear when it is mixed with other appearances even to that extent?

Even when there is absolute clarity, the state of being contemporaneous with that time does not break, because it does not manifest as common to others (due to its non-manifestation through commonality). However, if it were to manifest as such, it would be merely a creation of the yogi. But in the case of the speech of Brahmā and so forth, [it is not so].
When recollection becomes manifest, there arises the form "this" or "that. In response to the question of what this refers to, he says:
"absolutely," etc. This means that the temporality of the present moment pertains to the object being perceived, while "that" refers to a prior time;
that is to say, it is the grasping of "that. Why? Because of that commonality which [the object shares] with other perceivers.

It is "without manifestation" for that reason; for the meaning is that a jar, being remembered with extreme clarity by one person, cannot be the object of apprehension for another. The intention of the word "api" (even) is to suggest: what need is there to speak of the case when it is not clearly manifested? [Objection: But how is it observed that the memory of a yogi is common to others?
For others also see that which is remembered by a yogi as being present before them; therefore, he says "tathā" (likewise).

"In such an appearance"—that is, in an appearance characterized by commonality—there is only the "manifestation" (*nirmāṇa*) of that object, meaning its actual production, and not mere recollection; the sense is that [the yogi] possesses the power to do so through the influence of yoga.

Nor should one turn away from those who possess great dispassion and great discernment, even if they are currently unable to manifest objects through mere mindfulness— though they are indeed capable of such manifestation—
because the state of being a great yogi consists simply in discernment preceded by dispassion.

Even in the case of magical illusions (*aindrajālika*), the creation of objects is indeed seen through mere recollection; therefore, one should not understand "the state of a yogi" (*yogitva*) by that alone—enough with this elaboration. Now, what is the purpose of conversing and so forth with deities imagined through recollection?

To the objection that this is merely "livelihood" (vārtā), he says: "with Brahman. This means together with that reality of Brahman which has been brought to the state of being directly perceived through the power of the practice of meditation; "in that which begins with speech"—by the word "beginning," other deities are included.
There is the grasping of what is spoken. In that regard, there is only a novel manifestation because it is imagined.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion. When the expectation arises as to why this is so, he says: "here. The word "tu" has the sense of "yataḥ" (because);
thus, "tu" means "because," [referring to] by other means of knowledge such as scripture—that is, by other authorities such as the treatises.
"Anubhūtam" means that through meditation (*dhyāna*), there is a manifestation that has become the very object of experience. In this context, however,
there is a succession of recollections of the essential nature of Brahmā and others, which have been previously experienced through other means of knowledge such as scripture (*āgama*).

This is the means (*abhyupāya*). By the injunction in the form of "he should manifest" (*bhāsayet*), a restriction (*niyama*) is indicated through the mandate (*niyoga*); it does not mean that he does not manifest, but rather that he necessarily manifests. "At its own time" (*svakāle*) refers to the time of recollection. "Reflecting" (*āmṛśan*) expresses the present tense as it pertains to the portion of the knower. "Previously manifested" (*pūrvābhāsitaṃ*)...
The past time that touches the aspect of the object of cognition— namely, "the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) previously illuminated"—

is also brought forward in the case of the appearance of a jar; the recollection of that which is the very nature of Brahmā and so forth is memory (smṛti), whose form is reflective awareness (parāmarśana).

The very succession that belongs to it constitutes the means (*abhyupāya*), and not the previously realized reality of Brahman (*brahmatattva*), because that [Brahman] is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
He begins to provide the construction of the verse according to the stated method with the words "it would illuminate" (*bhāsayet*).

Since *niyoga* (an injunction) is also a specific type of injunction (*vidhi*), it is said to be "in the form of an injunction. As it has been stated: "An injunction (*vidhi*) applies when there is absolute non-attainment; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when there is partial attainment; and an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) is prescribed when there is attainment both therein and elsewhere."

Thus, [the author] clarifies the very definition of *niyoga* as a restriction (*niyama*), stating that it "does not manifest" (*na bhāsayati*). By this, the word "should manifest" (*bhāsayet*) has been explained. He explains the word "at its own time" (*svakāle*) with the word "recollection" (*smaraṇa*).
The sense is that there is an identity between the time of the recollection and the time of the object remembered. He explains the word "reflecting" (*āmṛśan*).

Regarding the word "touching" (*āmṛśan*): it is situated within the portion consisting of the knower—that is, it functions as a qualifier of the subjective aspect of the knower. The meaning is that it has been stated [in this way] because the suffix *śatṛ* is a substitute for the present tense marker *laṭ*. The phrase "in the middle, namely" (*madhye arthāt*) has already been explained at the very beginning; therefore, it is not explained here. That which was previously indicated...

He explains the two words "svalakṣaṇam" by combining them in the relationship of qualifier and qualified, stating "vedyāṃśa" (the aspect of the object of cognition). "Vedyāṃśasparśī" means that which has become a qualifier of the objective portion; "bhūtakālaḥ" refers to the past time denoted by the suffix *kta*.

The connection is that [the object] has been "shown. To explain the phrase "by the mere appearance as a jar," the cause for the isolated [object] to attain its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇya*) has been shown. The word "now" (*atha*) indicates that this alone is the non-deviating form of memory, whereas its clarity arises from an intensity of desire. He states that very point with the words "in its entirety" (*akhilātmanā*).
Thus; the meaning is: by means of a body mixed with all appearances. || 2 ||

Now, one might object: "If the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is thus manifested, it would appear externally as something distinct; for this alone is what constitutes external manifestation—that which is the manifestation of the particular characteristic. To dispel this doubt, he explains as follows:
Furthermore, it is not logical that the object being remembered should appear if there were a difference [between the past experience and the present memory];
therefore, this knower is the unifier of cognitions occurring at different times. (3)

He states the qualification: "of the solitary" (*kevalasya*). "Attainment" (*āpatti*) means reaching; it is the cause of that [attainment]. This is because the capacity for the manifestation of its own specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*) is established immediately following the manifestation of time within the mere manifestation of the jar. He declares that this alone constitutes memory: "only this much."

Thus [it is said]. "This much" means that there is merely the appearance of the object, and its attainment of its own specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*) produced by past time. "Invariable body" means the unique, uncommon nature (*asādhāraṇa-svarūpa*). [Objection: But [this] is produced by the intermingling with other appearances...

To address the question of whether its clarity (*sphuṭatā*) might sometimes occur or not, he says: "due to the intensity of desire" (*arthitā*). Because of the intensity of desire—that is, because it is intensely longed for—even a memory can indeed become intensely longed for at times.
"Clarity" refers to the state of becoming manifest (*sphuṭībhāva*) produced by the intermingling with the appearance of objective properties (*dharmābhāsa*). He says: "he illuminates."

The meaning is that [it is] because it belongs to a different category from the non-manifest category. That very thing—namely, the manifestness just mentioned—is by what means? To this he says: "akhila" (entire). He explains this word as well with "sarva" (all).
"All appearances"—that is, the appearances of attributes—[are manifested] "by its body," which consists of the essential nature of the jar.
The meaning is "by means of the appearance as a jar. "Āmṛśan" means performing a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

The construction of the verse is: "the independent agent (*svairī*), acting as the subject, would manifest the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which was previously manifested as the object. The two instrumental cases [in *ghaṭābhāsena*] are used in the sense of "being in such a state" (*itthaṃbhāve*). || 2 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here, the commentary says:
"evam" means according to the stated method; "bahiḥ" means as a distinction, as "this-ness" (idantayā). He states the reason for this with the word "etad" (this).

The "manifestation of the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇaprakāśana*) means the manifestation—that is, the illumination—of the particular nature (*asādhāraṇasvarūpa*) related to the jar. Having thus provided this introduction, he presents and explains the verse with the words "And not... (*na ca*).

If that object were to appear as something distinct from the cognition of recollection and as having an external form, then that which is "the appearance of the remembered" would not exist at all; it would not be the remembered itself, but rather it would be as if it were being directly experienced (*anubhūyamāna*). Now, [one might object] that in this way, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)...

Regarding manifestation: how is there manifestation of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? Has this not already been stated? It has indeed been stated. But is it not the case that this is not manifestation at the present time, but rather only at a previous time? And at that time, it was indeed manifest externally. Well then, what is it now? We say: it is reflective awareness (*vimarśana*). But surely...
It follows that manifestation (*prakāśana*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) would occur at different times. What of it? [The answer is:
both—here the commentary explains the word "from memory" (*smṛteḥ*) as being in the ablative case, namely, "from recollection" (*smaraṇāt*). Regarding the term "in difference" (*bhede*):

He explains the word *pada* with the word *bhinna*. He provides his own commentary on this word with the word *vahī*, meaning "as this" (*idantayā*). It would "appear"—that is, it would manifest. To the question "What then would that be?", he says:
"being experienced. That—meaning the object of the act of manifestation—is the thing [which is other].
He provides an introductory transition (*avataraṇikā*) to explain the second half [of the verse], beginning with "But surely" (*nanu ca*). It was "stated"—that is, spoken—in the preceding verse.

He states the answer with "this": "this" refers to what was stated in the preceding verse, namely, manifestation (*prakāśana*). To the question "In that case, at what time does it belong?", he says "but rather" (*api tu*). The word "manifestation" is to be connected with what precedes. But surely...?

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And then" (*tadā ca*). "Then" means at the prior time; [the phrase] "it indeed appears" (*avabhāsata eva*), rather than "it does not appear," is expressed in the present tense, and thus there is no contradiction, as it refers to a present state belonging to the prior time. Again, the student asks: "But surely" (*nanu*). "Now" (*idānīm*) means at the time of recollection.

The Guru says, "Reflection" (*vimarśana*). Again, the disciple asks a question with "But surely" (*nanu*). It follows—that is, it has come forth by force. The Guru says, "Then" (*tataḥ*). When the question is posed by the Guru, the disciple gives the answer, "Both" (*ubhayam*). Both—the pair consisting of Light (*prakāśa*) and Reflection (*vimarśa*).

Otherwise, nothing at all would exist, because this world is mutually sustained by one another. Do not say so; for one whose reality consists solely of distinct cognitions, this problem is indeed irremediable. But in our system, even cognitions belonging to different times appear as a unity by not abandoning their own respective times, through the manifestation of oneness.
As long as the autonomous cognizer, by virtue of being inward-turned, reflects upon a certain portion [of reality],

for that long there is the manifestation of the Light as having an external existence at that moment, while the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) remains inward-turned at this present time. This alone is [the state].
To address how nothing at all could exist, he says "mutually" (*anyonya*). Of this—of both—the manifestation becomes manifestation only through reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); as he will state:
"They know reflective awareness to be the very nature of manifestation; otherwise [it would not be so]."
Even when colored by an object, light remains like an insentient substance, such as a crystal.

Thus [it is said]. But reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is indeed clearly the effect of manifestation (*prakāśa*); for it is only immediately after manifestation that the arising of reflective awareness occurs. And whatever necessarily arises immediately after something else is the effect of that [cause].
As it has been said:
"Effectness (*kāryatva*) is the state of being invariably posterior while not being established otherwise.

To this, he provides a resolution as an explanation of the latter half [of the verse], saying "It is not so. When the question "Why? arises, he says "For that which... *Tattvam* means the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); *apratisamādheyam* means...
It is impossible to refute [this]. Now, one might ask: "In your system, what is the reality? To this he says: "asmad" (our).

By means of the appearance of oneness—which remains precisely through the non-abandonment of that [temporal] state, namely, the non-relinquishing of the difference in time as it appears—there is a certain [reality] which constitutes the essence.
By means of the manifestation of oneness with that which is established in relation to the reality of the subject as another form—meaning, by being that very state;

the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of "being in such a manner. He becomes an independent subject (*svatantraḥ*), that is, one endowed with sovereignty over the joining and separating of the cognitions that constitute his own nature; in other words, he is that very subject who—

At the very moment when, by way of inwardness— that is, through being turned inward— one reflects upon that portion of oneself which is the "I" and which is capable of becoming a future memory, performing the reflective awareness "I" due to its self-luminosity— at that very instant, of the Light...

The manifestation at that time of an external existence belonging to a prior experience is a manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā*) occurring at its own time, which provides an opportunity for reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). The state of reflective awareness—
that is, of *parāmarśa*— is an inward-turned state existing at the present time of recollection, consisting of the nature of "I" (*aham*).

Thus, the state of being an experiencer (*veditṛtva*) exceeds mere sensation (*vedanā*). It is the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) consisting in the ability to effect the binding or the unbinding of fetters (*saṃyojana*) among sensations according to one's will;
and this very thing is called "agency" (*kartṛtva*). Indeed, this alone is what is termed agency.

"I experienced the jar"—or "I experienced the jar," or "that jar"—in order to show that this "identity" (*aikya*), which is the synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*), is non-different from the synthesizer, it is shown through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that "that very identity is the knower. Thus: "This is he."

By this statement, which contains an element of wonder— expressed as "this has been made clearly manifest, as if the reality of the subject (pramātṛtattva) were previously covered"— recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) itself is indicated. As the author himself has said:

The word "śabdaḥ" (the sound/word) marks the conclusion of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Now, one might ask: why then does the apprehension "this am I" not occur? True; in this case, there is no such fullness (*puṣṭatā*) of "this-ness" (*idantā*) and "I-ness" (*ahantā*) as would allow for their respective apprehensions to be established as they are in the state of the Lord (*īśvaradaśā*). However, [this is so] for both of them...

There exist two subtle fragments (leśa) that are unfit for grasping objects; these very two, becoming unified, transform through the sense of "that" (tat), and that itself is the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) "he" (sa). It is precisely this reflective awareness regarding those constituent parts that constitutes the state of being a knower and so forth; thus it says, "this very [thing]. This very—

The reflective awareness of "I" directed toward its own portion is indeed the instrument; it is superior to cognition—that is, superior to outward-directed knowledge which consists of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). As it has been said:
"Sovereignty, agency, and even primary lordship."

Thus [it is said]. He states the intended meaning of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the knower of unity and that which resides in the Sūtra with the words "the jar" (*ghaṭam*).

"I experienced the jar" is the detailed reflection (*parāmarśa*), whereas "that is the jar" is the concise one; "unity" (*aikyam*) means the form of unity, and "synthesis" (*anusandhānam*) refers to the action known as synthesis.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in two things having different grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) while being directed toward a single object and possessing the same case-ending; for it is not logical that there should be a difference between an action and the agent of that action—this is the intended meaning.
This very point is also indicated in the *Śivasūtras* by the aphorism "Consciousness is the Self" (*caitanyam ātmā*). This is that...

He states the meaning that is to be indicated by this [verse] with the words "This is he. By the phrase "This is he," through an utterance pregnant with wonder—an utterance in which wonder is internalized because it cannot otherwise be accounted for—recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) itself is indicated. Why? Because otherwise, it would not have been spoken in such a way.
"Like one who is covered"—meaning, although [the self] exists in reality, it is as if non-manifest due to the influence of an obscuration.
As it has been said:
"Thus, that which was defiled by those who deny self-awareness while speaking of it..."
Having rendered those who were mute by means of clear arguments, that reality of the subject (pramātṛtattva) has been made manifest.
Thus [ends verse 3].

Now, if the very prior experience itself is the manifestation consisting in the external appearance of that which is being remembered, then let it simply be said: "that experience is now made an object by remembrance.
What is the point of this extraordinary [claim] regarding identity? To dispel such delusion, he says:
It is logical that even while appearing, there is a non-appearance due to the obstruction of manifestation.
Thus, the clear manifestation of the reality of the subject—the reality of the Self—is accomplished;
and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is precisely the re-actualization of what was forgotten. In this regard:

He states the author’s own words as an illustration with the phrase "as he said. "Turbidified" (kaluṣīkṛtam)—the ellipsis being "by conceptual constructions" (vikalpaiḥ). "Them"—those who deny consciousness. "Manifested" (prakaṭīkṛtam) means that it has been made manifest by generating recognition (pratyabhijñā) for the sake of the subjects (pramātṛ).

Thus, the summary here is as follows: if there were a difference from memory—that is, if there were a difference between the object which is the content of memory and the memory itself—then, given that difference established by the apprehension of "this-ness" (idantā), the manifestation of the remembered object would not be tenable; for that object would be manifest only [as the present], and not [as the past].

The sense is that it is "being remembered"; by that, there arises a unity of cognitions occurring at different times—namely, experiences, memories, and other forms of knowledge—because they share a single time, and because [the distinction of] different times is irrelevant. And thus, even while being manifest, [there is unity].

The existence of the object as something being remembered is established. Now, one might ask: "Even so, since there is no grasper [of the memory], how is this established? To this he says: "the knower" (*veditā*). This very person—the one who connects [the past and present] through the identity [of the self], which has been explained by implication because of the identity between the action and its agent—is the knower; that is, the grasper is precisely the one who grasps the identity.
Anticipating the objection that this would result in the destruction of non-duality (advaitabhanga), it is argued that the employment of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not faulty. || 3 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fourth verse with the words "nanu ca" (but surely).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"having the nature of external manifestation" means having the nature of external illumination.

"This experience" fulfills the expectancy for the word "this much. "Now" means at the time of recollection. It is said "it is produced," because otherwise it would be impossible for that [experience], having already passed away, to have its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; this is the intended meaning. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter (*prameya*). "By way of identity" means by the identity established through the state of being the knower (*veditṛtā*).

By means of the continuous connection of consciousness, which is non-worldly—that is, not established among worldly things—he provides an introduction and, having presented the verse, explains it: "Not at all," etc.
For the prior experience does not indeed appear separately in memory, as the object does.
"I previously experienced [this]"—from such an appearance of the self's ascent [to the state of the subject]. || 4 ||

The example is given by way of both similarity and dissimilarity. Regarding the word "previously": at the time of experience, that object such as a jar appeared as "prior" and as "distinct" through the mode of "this-ness" (*idantā*); however, at the time of recollection, it does not appear in this way—that is, it does not appear as "this prior experience" as something distinct from the cognition of memory. And just as...

Therefore, at the time of recollection, that object does not appear as distinct from its previous nature—that is, from the cognition of recollection—because at the time of recollection there is no external manifestation. For this same reason, even the "previous experience" does not appear as distinct. How, then, do both appear? [They appear as] "I experienced."

Thus it is said. If it is asked, "What is this being stated? [the answer is: the "Self" (ātman) whose very nature is "I"—here, according to the commentary (*ṭīkā*), the term "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is used in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇayā*) as an illustration; the remainder is that this refers to the aphorism (*sūtra*). In that regard:

First, he clarifies the very point of dissimilarity with the word "prāk" (previously). He explains the term "prāk" as "anubhava" (experience). He explains the term "arthavat" (possessing an object) as "yathā" (just as). That the object is prior is established by the object itself [as it is established by the object alone—C]. The term "pṛthak" (separate)...

He explains [the term] by "as this" (*idantayā*). He explains the word "in memory" (*smṛtau*) by "recollection" (*smaraṇe*). By the two preceding words "previous experience" (*pūrvam anubhavanam*), there is the explanation of the two terms "previous" (*pūrvaḥ*) and "experience" (*anubhavaḥ*).
Having clarified the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), he says "and just as" (*yathā ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction; therefore...

Regarding "from memory and knowledge"—since these two require [the word] "previously" (*prāk*), that term is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). He states that the word "previously" functions as a qualifier for the word "object" (*artha*) by saying "prior. He explains the two words "not separately" (*na pṛthak*) by combining them and commenting: "not as distinct. When there is an expectation for a reason, he says "at the time of recollection" (*smṛtikāle*).

Thus: "just as it fulfills the expectancy for the word," meaning "for that very reason," which is to say, "because of the absence of external manifestation. By this, the section ending with "previously" has been explained.
Such is the application of the two examples. For—since—in memory, there is the prior experience.
It does not appear as something separate; how so? "Like an object" (arthavat)—just as an object previously appeared separately, such is not the case with this experience.
The prior and subsequent cognitions have an inward-turned nature; therein, that which is "ascending" is the state of rest. By that [rest],...

Because, by means of that cause, there is the manifestation of the prior consciousness—which is self-luminous—in its own nature; thus, even though the jar was dissolved therein, it appears as self-luminous.
Herein lies the contradiction of two opposing attributes: the appearance and non-appearance belonging to the experience of the object.
One way of formulating this is that [the absence of the probans] constitutes a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) because of its proof.

Now, the second formulation: in memory (*smṛti*), the prior experience does not appear as something separate. How so? "Like the object"—just as the object previously [experienced] does not appear separately in memory, so too the experience itself does not appear. And in this regard:

It is the nature of a corroborative instance based on similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭāntatva*), because a common property in the form of non-existence (*nabhāna*) is established in both cases. Here, the student asks: "How so? Both—namely, the prior experience [and the subsequent recollection]—[are established].

The sense is that it is not logical for the previously mentioned object not to appear here. To provide an answer to this, he introduces the word "anvabhūvam" (I experienced). The meaning is that it appears in this very manner, namely as "anvabhūvam. Here, intending to state the reason while first addressing a potential doubt from the student, he says "aham" and so forth.

He explains these two words with the word "this" (*etat*). He explains the commentary composed by the author of the Sūtras himself—following the reasoning for the word "I experienced" (*anvabhūvam*)—with the phrase "in this manner, 'I'" (*aham ityevam*).
He explains the word "I" (*aham*) as "having such a nature" (*evaṃsvabhāvaḥ*), meaning "having the nature of the referent 'I'."
The word "iti" is intended to indicate the meaning [of the preceding]. He explains the term "ātman" as "prior.
It is that which consists of prior and posterior consciousness and is inward-turned; its nature—that is, its essential form—is such.
By this, the meaning is established in accordance with the verbal root *ata* (to go continuously), for continuous movement is indeed [its characteristic].

Eternity is precisely that state of pervading prior and subsequent time. In that regard, "in that Self" refers to the locus of ascent; he explains it as "rest. He states the meaning of the ablative case as "by that cause," [referring to] the nature of prior consciousness—that is, the nature of prior experience—which is self-luminous.

Of that which exists as self-luminous; the term "of the nature of prior consciousness," together with its qualification, is brought forward by virtue of its well-known status as the agent of the act of manifestation. Now, one might ask: how is it possible for the jar, which is its object, to ascend? To this [it is replied]:

Manifestation as belonging to one's own domain; and "ascension into the self" means the resting of both the experience and the object. According to the maxim that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together," this occurs with respect to the sense of "we" (asmad-artha), which functions as the agent, whether it be the number itself or the possessor of that number implied by it.
The experience is submerged within the object of cognition (*pratyaya*), and through that [experience], the object itself is also [submerged].

He says "of that which is absorbed in it," meaning of that which is attached to that consciousness as its object, for otherwise manifestation would be impossible. "Of the jar" means of the jar that has become the object.

Manifestation as belonging to self-luminosity means manifestation through the process of "ascension" (*āroha*); the sense is that the true nature of the lotus—its whiteness—does not exist anywhere else apart from that [lotus] itself. By this, the term *ārohaṇa* (ascension) is explained as being devoid of the suffix *ṇic*. For it is the very nature of consciousness residing within the Self.

The object also ascends into the self by means of that [consciousness] spontaneously. He explains this very word as having the causative suffix (*ṇic*) with the words "and into the self. "Resting" (*viśramaṇā*) means the act of causing rest.
In response to the expectation of "of what?", he says "of experience. For the subject [the knower] indeed [rests] in that state of the nature of consciousness.

And that object [the jar, etc. ascends into the Self. In this context, it should be understood that the causative suffix *ṇic* is elided according to the rule *ṇeraniṭi*. Now, one might ask: "If that is so, why is there a mention of the object in the expression 'I experienced' (*anvabhūvam*)? In response to this expectation, he says: "The root" (*prakṛti*). Alternatively, [he asks]: "How is it that in 'I experienced,' the object is not specified?"
In response to the inquiry as to how action finds its rest within the self by way of experience, he says: "prakṛti" (nature).
They speak together—that is, having attained a state of oneness, they declare that nature submerges into the meaning of the suffix;
this is according to the maxim: "Thus established, by the principle of the former teachers, [it is] implied by number."
When the substratum (dharmin) is implied by the property (dharma) expressed as the number denoted by the suffix—
either as the substratum itself or as that which is already endowed with the property of number denoted by the suffix—
according to the view of some, the meaning of the suffix is number alone, while the substratum is merely implied by it.

For some, however, it has the sense of an objective case (pratyaya) related to dharma. When [the self] exists as the agent— that is, established as the agent of the action of experiencing— in the referent of "we" (asmadartha), which is the meaning denoted by the word *aham* (I) in the form of the word *asmat*, there occurs the substitution of the first-person suffix *mip* belonging to the aorist (*luṅ*) and other tenses, according to the rule *asmadyuttamaḥ*.

Regarding the object: "experience" (anubhava) is that which has become the primary meaning of the verbal root *bhū* in its successive stages; "submerged" (bruḍita) means having become dissolved (*līnībhūta*). And by means of that—that is, by means of experience—the object as well, namely the jar which is its referent, is also submerged.

But this [object] does not exist in its own independence; for that very reason, the object (the pot, etc. was not mentioned [as the subject] of the action. Furthermore, at the time of experience, the pot and so forth do not ascend to the status of the "I" (asmadartha), because the prior experience does not appear separately from the latter part of the statement [of the object], for the reason stated previously; therefore, there is oneness of consciousness—this is the connection with what precedes.
The structural interpretation (*yojanā*) is as follows: the intended meaning is this—the experience devoid of an object is of the very nature of the self itself. As it has been said:
"When two things are perceived as existing separately, that which is the form [of the subject] is real, while the other is false.
Thus, upon what could anything be superimposed?
Thus, when experience is submerged, the object is necessarily submerged as well. Now, one might ask: "In that case, what is the distinction between experience and the object?

To this he says: "But not..."—the meaning being that the object [is not submerged]. For when it is said, "Bring the white lotus," the qualifying quality of whiteness cannot be brought; such is the sense.

The intended meaning is that the distinction between these two consists precisely in the nature of autonomy (*svātantrya*) and non-autonomy (*asvātantrya*). By relying on this, he states that the non-specification of an object (*karma*) is logical, saying "for that very purpose. The underlying sense is that there is no requirement for effort regarding an entity that is established without effort. Now, [one might ask] regarding such passages as "an experienced object" (*anubhūto 'rthaḥ*), etc.:
The status of experience as a qualifier of the object is indeed observed;

for while it is true that the relationship between qualifier and qualified is purely conceptual, this relationship between qualifier and qualified is fit only for external practical usage, because the external object is primary and cognition is secondary. However, in internal practical usage...
It suffices to say that knowledge alone is primary, while the object is secondary. Now, one might ask:

"In that case, how is there a mention of an object (*karman*) in the expression 'I experience the jar'? In response to this expectation, he says: "The jar and so forth. It does not contradict [the theory], because [the cognition] is grasped through an outward orientation; otherwise, it would be this...

Because the word [is] inappropriate, the application "amuṃ ghaṭam" (this jar) is correct there. Indeed, the word *hi* makes manifest the causal relationship of this verse with respect to the preceding verse; [it does so] by means of the word *yasmāt* (since). "Separately" means as a distinct entity (*idantayā*). "By the preceding" means by the preceding verse; [the latter half] exists independently of the prior word.
This is stated according to the maxim that "designation occurs primarily by means of the predominant factor.

Since the past tense is indicated by the *luṅ* suffix, the word "previously" (*prāk*) is placed out of its natural order; likewise, the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*) indicates the sense of "I" (*asmadartha*). As for "ascending," the root *ruh-* is used both without the causative suffix (*aṇijanta*) and with the causative suffix (*ṇijanta*).
Even when [the root] ends in the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—[K. ṣ. ṣ. || 4 ||

Now, who indeed has said that "experience does not appear separately"? If you say, "It does not appear like a jar," what of it? For even a jar does not appear as a companion to experience (i.e., it does not appear in the form of experience). He states the reason for joining the word "prāk" with the first half of the verse by saying "by the *luṅ*": "by the *luṅ*" means "by the *luṅ* [tense]."

"Because it is indicated by the suffix" means that this is due to the power of the rule *luṅ*. By using the term "in the first person" (*uttama*), he explains that the word "I" (*aham*) also has a displaced position (*bhinnakrama*) through its conjunction;
for since the meaning of "we" (*asmad-artha*) is indicated by the first-person suffix *-mip*, the word "I" (*aham*) likewise has a displaced position.

The sense is that [the word] does not function as the agent of the thought "I have experienced. Now, in response to the question—how can the single word *ārohaṇa* have two meanings, namely "ascending" and "resting"?—he says: "Ārohaṇa... regarding the word *ārohaṇa*.

The analysis [of the term] applies both to the non-causative (*aṇijanta*) and the causative (*ṇijanta*) forms. *Ruhir* is non-causative; the sense is that its root is *ruha* (in the sense of "germination from a seed"), whose primary meaning is "resting. It is also causative; the sense is that its primary meaning is "causing to rest" (*viśramaṇā*). || 4 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fifth verse with the words "nanu" (surely).
Here the commentary says:
"separately"—that is, as an object of the "this-ness" (idantā); the sense is that it is not proper to say "it is not this. It is true that it appears, but...
With the words "it does not shine like a jar," preceded by the teacher's doubt, he states to his teacher the absence of any loss on his part;

the passage from "like a jar" up to "what of it? conveys this. The sense is: "What of it? There is no loss whatsoever. He explains the very absence of loss by resorting to the principle of parity with a jar.
"Even the jar," it is said. "Anubhavasakhyaḥ" means similar to experience—that is, like experience.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason; therefore, why does that jar not shine?
Why does it not appear? It indeed shines by its own nature.

This is the same in both cases. For instance, it is accepted that past, future, and subtle objects become objects of a yogi’s cognition; likewise, another's mind also becomes an object [of cognition] through "the knowledge of another's mind" (Yoga Sūtra 3.19).
In such passages as these, it is *sattva* itself, when transformed by the activity of cognition (*jñāna-vṛtti*), that is expressed by the word "mind" (*citta*). Otherwise,
how could it be stated that the mental modification (*pratyaya*) is the object of *saṃyama*,
and how could the application of an objective support (*ālambana-yoga*) even be suspected?

The meaning is "it shines. The disciple, however, raises an objection: "How so? The teacher, recognizing that non-shining is untenable, explains the meaning differently: "It shines by its own nature. The meaning is that "non-shining" does not mean not shining like a pot; rather, it means shining precisely in its own essential form (*svarūpa*).

"But the disciple superimposes manifestation upon the experience by way of its own nature"—this is what is meant by "but this. That is to say: this, however, is common [to both], because even the experience does not manifest by way of the nature of the jar. He begins to establish this very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*). For thus:

He clarifies the object implied by the word "sound" with the term "past" (*atīta*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), things such as remote objects are included. "Accepted" (*abhyupagata*) means admitted; it is accepted that just as past objects and so forth become objects [of cognition], the mind of another (*paracitta*) likewise becomes an object.

In response to the inquiry, "Where is this accepted? he says, "of the cognition" (*pratyayasya*). This means in such sūtras of Patañjali as, "the knowledge of another's mind arises from [the knowledge of] cognition" (*paracittajñānaṃ pratyayasya*), and so forth. Now, one might object: "In this instance, the knowledge of the mind (*cittasya jñānam*) is stated, not the knowledge of cognition (*jñānasya*"; to which he replies, "therein" (*tatra*).”
In this context— referring to the Patañjali Sūtra just mentioned—

the *sattva* described is the principle of the Great One (*mahat-tattva*) in the form of the intellect (*buddhi*), which has undergone transformation— that is, reached another state— by means of the modification of knowledge (*jñāna-vṛtti*) through the cessation of the modification of ignorance (*ajñāna-vṛtti*). It is not, however, the mind (*manas*) as it is commonly known in the world.
Because it is described by the word "mind" (*manas*) as being established solely in volition (*saṃkalpa*); otherwise— that is,

in the absence of describing it as a modification of cognition (*jñāna-vṛtti*)— the state of being an object of *saṃyama* for cognition, namely for the cognition of another, would mean its fitness to be made the object of the yogi’s focused meditation (*praṇidhāna*).

How could it be said [that the mind is without an object], since that would entail a contradiction? Likewise, there is the connection with an objective support—that is, the relation of the mind to its own respective object; by implication, how could it be said of that mind, "and yet it is not with an objective support"? Therefore, one's own experience is like the experience of another.
Anticipating the objection that "let them be made objects [of perception]," he shows with the words ending in "appear" (*bhānti*) that the example itself is unestablished;
or, even if it were established by way of concession, he shows with the remainder of the verse that it is dissimilar to the point at issue:
"Even for yogins, visual perceptions do not appear within another perception."
Or rather, those [cognitions] shine forth as having self-awareness alone as their sole means of knowledge, even in the status of being objects of cognition.

Regarding this "other view of the yogins"—that specific kind of knowledge which arises from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and has another's mind as its object—"perceptions" (*dṛśaḥ*), meaning apprehensions, do not appear therein. For instance, [this] might be suspected by the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists). To the question "Where [is this stated]? he says "And not," meaning in this sūtra. This...

The point is this: if, in this sūtra, the word "citta" were intended to denote the mind (*manas*) alone, then in another sūtra one would not have raised the doubt regarding the object of focus—namely, the concern that the yogis' knowledge of others might take as its object only that which is connected to the [other's] sense-objects. This was asked in response to an inquiry made in the ear.
"Because it would result in the movement of the hips and back. He provides the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
"Even one's own"—meaning even his personal experience—should be made an object for the ordinary subject;
the sense is that there is no difference in the nature of being an experience. The example is: "by the knowledge of a yogi."

It consists in being made an object of another's knowledge. By the phrase "they shine" (*bhānti*)— that is, by the portion of the verse beginning with the fourth quarter and ending with the word "shine," which is intent on negation— and by "acceptance," meaning in the form of an admission, or by the "remainder," meaning by the portion in the form "even in the state of the object of knowledge" (*meyapade 'pi*).
Or: having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "of the yogins.
Here the commentary says:
he explains the phrase "in another system" found in the sūtra with the word "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). Of cultivation—
That which has its origin—its manifestation—from the cultivation of the self (ātmabhāvanā), and by the word "etc. (ādi), from the [cultivation of] the instruments and so forth;

that which has as its object the mind of another—that is, the object of another's cognition—a particular kind of knowledge—a knowledge endowed with excellence over other cognitions—in that particular kind of knowledge, [there is] the vision.

Thus he explains the term "perceptions" (*upalabdhayaḥ*), meaning "cognitions. He begins the demonstration of their very manifestation with the words "for it is thus" (*tathā hi*). For it is thus that he reveals the object implied by the word, according to the different views of the Buddhists (*saugatānām*).

To that extent, cognition is of a single nature consisting of self-luminosity; if that were to be known by another cognition, then its own essential form—namely, its manifestation as being knowable by nothing else—would not be manifested.
Even for the Sāṃkhyas, apprehension is merely the reflection of the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* itself is beyond the reach of objective cognition.

How could it be known? [That is, how could it be an object of knowledge? Even for the Vaiśeṣikas, how could consciousness—which inheres non-differently in the self and resides in another—be grasped by the mind, which functions within one's own body? For if that mind were to enter into the other's body, then [consciousness] would belong to that very person as "I."
Because it is embodied— that is, because it is manifested as "I"— there is a distinction from the Self.
For the Sugatas— the devotees of the Sugata, meaning the Buddhists— it is of such a nature that its single, unique form is self-luminous, being cognizable by nothing other than itself.

"Manifestation" (prakāśana) means "self-manifestation" (svaprakāśa). The phrase "it would not be so" implies that it would result in a contradiction of its self-luminosity (or, as C reads, a contradiction of its being self-manifesting).
"The reflection of the person" (puruṣacchāyā) refers precisely to the reflection of the person in the intellect (buddhi); this is what constitutes "apprehension" (upalabdhi).

The result, called "illumination," is distinct from the mental modification known as "cognition" (*jñāna*); it is "of an unperceivable nature" (*asaṃvedyaparvā*), meaning its own form is unperceivable. The term "objects of cognition" (*vedyā*) is an adjective qualifying "perception"; the point is that it is not logical for a reflection to be different in character from the original object (*bimba*). This refers to the Vaiśeṣikas—that is, the logicians (*tārkikas*).
"Samavāyi" means existing by way of inherence (*samavāya-vṛtti*) as a quality; "saṃvedana" means cognition (*jñāna*);

"paragata" means inherent in another self. By what [means]? By the mind (*manas*). Of what kind? Existing within the body (*antaḥśarīra-vartin*), that is, internal to the body. Here, one should apply the very absence of omnipresence (*vibhutvābhāva*) of the mind as the logical reason.
Regarding "entering into that body"—that is, entering into another's body—the meaning is that it becomes one's own body by being produced as such through the transformation of that very other body;
the sense is that a body is one's own body only when it is grasped by the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva). Likewise:

Because it is manifested as "I"—since even another's body is illuminated by the "I"—the distinction of the self (nijātmanaḥ), that is, the distinction from the other self, would dissolve; for distinction consists solely in the grasping of "this-ness" (idantā). And thus, there would be the consequence of a fallacy for them.

[The opponent states: "But surely, according to the Vaiśeṣika school, the self is always inferable; thus, by your claim that the self is grasped through the perception 'I' by means of the mind, you have raised the objection that the distinction [between the self and the mind] would vanish. To this, he replies: "Eternal" (*nitya*). "Always inferable" (*nityānumeyatvam*) means being an object of inference at all times by means of such marks as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth.

This would be undermined by the admission that the self is an object of mental perception; however, it is not tenable for the self to be eternally inferable, and it has already been stated that if one cognition were to be known by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā).
Therefore, for the yogin at the time of perceiving another's mind, there is this much manifestation:

"The manifestation of the jar, pleasure, and so forth, is co-existent with the manifestation of this body. In that context, the jar, pleasure, and so forth appear as "this" (idantayā), whereas the manifestation residing within them appears only as "I" (aham).
It shines by virtue of its self-luminosity.

However, due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the manifestation of another's body, speech, and so forth—which have been made objects of cognition—the entity acquires "thisness" (*idantā*) residing therein.
He also states another fault pointed out by the Vaiśeṣikas themselves, beginning with the word "knowledge."

Regarding the phrase "anavasthānādi" (infinite regress, etc.): this refers to infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in the form of one [cognition] being apprehended by another, and that [other] by yet another, and so forth. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), circularity (*cakraka*) and other such fallacies are included.
Having explained the first half [of the verse], the second half ends with the word "bhānti" (they appear).

He provides an introductory commentary to explain [the verse], beginning with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). "Tasmāt" means: because objects of perception do not appear to yogins within other systems of philosophy, and yet it is entirely illogical that they should not appear at all;
for that reason. By the word "iyān" (of this extent), he states the object required by the context, namely "etad" (this). This refers to the manifestation of this body—

The manifestation of the jar, pleasure, and so forth—which has the nature of being accompanied by, that is, having the habit of occurring together with, the manifestation delimited by another body (the subject)—becomes the manifestation in the form of the jar, pleasure, and so forth.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter (*prameya*). To the question, "But what follows from that?", he says: "Therein" (*tatra*). "Therein" means in that [state].

In the knowledge of another's mind (*paracittajñāna*), an external or internal object—whether in the form of a jar, pleasure, or the like (the word "etc. including all external and internal objects)—appears as "this" (*idantayā*), because it is precisely fit for being grasped as "this. However, that which resides within [that other mind]—

However, that manifestation—experience—which has objects such as a jar or pleasure as its content, shines forth precisely as "I" by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatayā*), that is, through the state of self-manifestation, because it possesses such an inherent nature. The implication is that, in effect, there is no dependence on an external illumination at all, since it exists eternally as one's own self (*svātmatvena*). If that is so, then...
To explain how one says, "This is the cognition of another," he says: "made into a cognizer" (*pramātrīkṛta*).

"Made into a cognizer" means that which consists of the body, vital breath, and so forth of another—though previously not of the nature of a cognizer due to a lack of proficiency—is conceived as being a cognizer; the manifestation therein [of that other] is by way of the "this-ness" (*idantā*).

Even while perceiving this supreme knowledge (*parajñāna*) within the sphere of manifestation, the yogi who has not yet dissolved the distinction between self and other conceives of it as such. But the one who has attained excellence, seeing everything as his own self, considers (or sees) the distinction between self and other to be nothing but his own creation; thus, for him, there is no [such duality].

[The object] is manifested by the cognition of a yogin. Or, even if that were the case, it is not equal to the matter at hand (*prakṛta*). For instance, the cognition "this person experiences" is established solely in another;
the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from that—consisting of the rotation of a previously whirled wheel—is what [produces the illusion].
But the yogin, whose distinction between self and other has not dissolved— having attained the state of Īśvara, yet not merely resting in the stage of Sadāśiva and so forth—
[perceives] that "this-ness" (idantā), which is the objectivity directed toward another body and so forth, even within the portion of light that constitutes the subjectivity of the body and so on.

Even regarding the aspect of manifestation delimited by that [object], one conceives it as "this is supreme knowledge"—one knows it through such conceit (*abhimāna*), but the point is that it does not actually exist in that way.
Now, what is the status of the yogi for whom the distinction between self and other has dissolved? To this he says: "attained" (*prāpta*).

The yogi who has attained excellence—that is, one who has reached the highest state through the dissolution of the distinction between self and other—perceives the entire aggregate of all objects of knowledge as his own self by means of the apprehension "I am.
He considers and knows the distinction between self and other to be merely his own creation; and thus, even for him, [that distinction does not exist].

The sense is that the cognition of another's mind appears through a subsequent cognition. Therefore, even upon seeing the knowledge of another's mind accomplished by some deceptive practitioner through a particular application, one should not fixate upon that alone; for the state of being a supreme yogi consists solely in perceiving one's own self everywhere, since that [supreme state] has no external object.
Enough of this. He states the conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means for this reason; such is the meaning of the sentence here.
