As for the meaning of the individual words: *svasaṃvit*—consciousness that constitutes one's own nature; *ekam mānam yāsām tāḥ*—those for which there is only a single means of knowledge, meaning they are self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*); *tāḥ dṛśaḥ*—those perceptions; *bhānti*—they shine forth, they manifest.

He explains the phrase "or even in the case of the object" (*meyapade'pi vā*) with the words "or let it be so" (*bhavatu vā*). The expression "or let it be so" (*bhavatu vā*) is an explanation of "or even" (*api vā*), which indicates an alternative position. The subject under discussion is the object, which consists of the nature of being cognizable by a perception other than itself; this is equivalent to the following:
"The perception of the yogi is equal to the perception known by another. To the question "Why is it not equal?", he says: "For thus...

"Established in another" means delimited by having another as its agent; by this, that manifestation of the yogi occurs in his own experience, but not through the superimposition of the self in the form "I am experiencing."

Regarding the present [self], however—[as stated in the *Ātmāroha* and here in the *Krama-ṣaṭka*]—"I have experienced this" is a resting in the "I"-portion of experience that has not yet touched upon the state of "this-ness. Thus it is rightly said:
since experience does not appear as something separate, there is therefore identity between [experiences] belonging to different times.
"The knower of cognitions," thus [it is said]. || 5 ||

If it is argued that experience does not appear separately in memory due to its resting within the sense of "I-ness," then [we reply]: another reflective awareness is directly perceived as reflecting upon the experience through the "this-ness" (idantā) of the object,
or rather, as manifesting the experience's resting within objects such as a jar, which are appropriate to the state of "this-ness."

This is the explanation of the term *meyapade*: because the other [the object] is an object of knowledge (*meyatvāt*), "in the locus" (*pade*) means within its sphere of perception, that is to say, by way of being established in the other.
As it has been said:
"That which is measured is the other."

Thus: "in experience" means in the experience of another; "by ascending into the Self" means by resting in the Self—that is to say, delimited by having the Self as its agent. "Light" (*prakāśa*) is a gloss for the word "appear" (*bhānti*), because [the term] is applied here as well according to the maxim of the crow's eye (which moves between two sockets). "Here" refers to the present context.
"Free from the state of 'I'-ness that has not been stirred; untouched by the notion of 'this'. He concludes the collection of objects of knowledge with the words "iti" (thus).

Regarding the word "iti," the meaning is "for this reason. In response to the expectation of what was said, he says "yasmāt" (since). The phrase "naivaṃ hyanubhavo bhāti" (for experience does not appear thus) is the remainder of the verse [verse 5].
He provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "yadyahambhāva" (if there were the sense of "I").
Here, the commentary states:
"another reflective awareness"—that is, a reflective awareness other than the reflective awareness "I experienced."

The form [of the cognition] is "this was seen by me. Having realized that the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*) is utterly inappropriate for the experience itself, he states an alternative view with the words "or rather" (*yadi vā*). "Expanding" means bringing about manifestation; "perceived" means experienced.
He refutes the opponent’s intention—namely, the question of why one does not employ linguistic usage even in accordance with that [recollection]—with the following verse:

"Even when it is recollected as 'that which was seen by me is this,' or likewise through differentiation as 'this is that very same thing,' it is simply the description of that [object] by means of the recollection: 'I have seen it. (6)

For the world at large, there is no such awareness; indeed, he does not consider the vision to be anything separate, thinking, "That vision was mine. Even so—[but rather] that memory which occurs even regarding something that has become thus, belonging to someone who considers himself discerning, that...

The exposition follows from memory, just as a word follows its own sequence—by the recurrence of that other reflection; having thus introduced [the objection], he sets it forth and then provides the resolution. Having thus made the introduction and set forth the verse, he explains it.
"It is remembered" (smaryate).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"In this way" (*evam*) means having the form "that vision of mine occurred"; "cognition" (*saṃvedana*) refers to the knowledge of memory (*smṛtijñāna*).

In response to the inquiry "Why does it not exist?", he says: "For that... "That" refers to the world (*loka*). "Distinct" (*pṛthagbhūtām*)—because it is described as being in a relationship [with the subject], it is adorned by the difference indicated by the genitive case; by this, the phrase "through difference" (*bhedataḥ*) is explained.
"Some" (*kāṃcit*) refers to [a cognition] among the collection of cognitions divided into twenty-two types which are about to be described.

The meaning is "even one [moment]. The intention is that he does not think [of them as separate], because everywhere consciousness rests solely within the "I-component" (*ahaṃ-aṃśa*), such as in the form "I experience," and so forth. Following this very perspective established in the Sūtra, he shows it with the words "that" (*sā*). And this impossibility...

This is indicated by the word *api* (even/also) used in the Sūtra, because the word *api* signifies the possibility of that which is otherwise impossible. The two words *iti* and *evam* serve to refer back to the nature of the Seer (*dṛk-svarūpa*). Even if it were possible in some way [for the Seer to be an object], that which you desire is not [the case].

He says "it is established" with the words "even so" (*evam api tu*). By this, the phrase "even in this way" (*ity evam api*) is explained. He explains "that which is remembered" with the words "of such a kind" (*evaṃbhūtam*). He shows the implied agent with the words "of someone," meaning "one who possesses the conceit of being a discerning judge. By this, the first half [of the verse] is [explained].

This has already been explained. And thus is the construction [of the verse]: "Even that which is remembered as 'this vision of mine was seen by someone'—even such [memory] occurs through differentiation.
Having analytically divided the meanings of the base and the suffix—which are themselves conceptual—the act of making [the distinction] is applied elsewhere.

It is merely a demonstration. Even that [demonstration], if it reflects upon the primary cognition according to the previously stated sequence, does not perceive the experience as something separate; for precisely because it conceives of a distinction that is imagined, like "the head of Rāhu. Otherwise, that [cognition] would be like "that jar. It is a vision.

In this case as well, another preceding perception would have to be required. For by the word "that" (tat), the status of being an object of prior experience is attributed either to the jar or to the vision; otherwise, he employs the word "that" in order to explain the second half [of the verse], saying "that. That—

He explains the term "the analysis of words" (*smṛteḥ vyākaraṇam*), which was mentioned in the first half [of the verse], by means of the word "of the word" (*padasya*). Just as in the case of the word "potter" (*kuṃbhakāra*)—that is, just as in the case of the word "potter"—there is the determination of the meanings of the base and the suffix: namely, the determination of the meaning of the suffix *aṇ* (which occurs after a base ending in the root *kṛ*, according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*).

Thus, by means of a general rule (*sāmānyasūtra*), there is an investigation into the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) at certain times; however, this is conceptual (*kālpānika*) and not innate (*sahaja*), for in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), that meaning belongs only to the indivisible word (*akhaṇḍapada*). As it has been said:
"By means of a sūtra possessing both general and specific [features], through the conceptualization of divisions such as *prakṛti* (root) and so forth"— with this,
he explains the member that is the prefix *vi-* as "having divided.
He explains the member that consists of the collection of root and suffix as "in another [word]."
The meaning is that there is merely a presentation, but not a correct awakening.

Why is it merely a presentation? To this he says: "He too... [referring to the phrase] "that was my vision," which stands as the root-perception because otherwise this [subsequent perception] would not arise; thus he says, "he makes known."

The suffix *ṇic* is used in its reflexive sense (*svārtha*), meaning "he knows. "Experience" (*anubhavam*) refers to that experience which was previously stated as being distinct from [the self] in the words "that vision of mine occurred. To the question "What does he know again?", he says: "That" (*tat*). Just as in the expression "the head of Rāhu," where because Rāhu consists of nothing but his head, the distinction indicated by the genitive case is perfectly clear; so it is here.

The meaning is that this [recognition] is likewise conceptual (*kālpanika*). Otherwise—that is, if one does not accept a conceptual distinction—the former experience, which exists as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) from a previous time, would have to depend upon another distinct perception; for that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) would be dependent.
This is the state of affairs. To the question "Why?", he says: "That. [Objection: But even so, what of it?

To this he replies: "It would be simply 'seeing' (dṛk). Consequently, it would follow that "seeing was experienced by me through another act of seeing. If that were also the case, there would be an infinite regress. [Objection: What is the fundamental nature of memory? It is said: "I saw."

Thus [he says]. Now, one might object: "In this case, it is stated that the act of seeing (*darśana*) rests upon the lotus-face of the beloved and so forth, but it does not reside in the self (*ātman*), because the occurrence of the *niṣṭhā* suffix takes place in relation to the object (*karman*). This very person does not even understand his own words.
For an object is that which is reached by the agent through an action; thus, the act of seeing must indeed reside in the agent. And so it is said:

"And therefore, [the agency] resides only in the agent. To the question, "Even if that were so, what of it? he says, "In that case as well. "In that case as well" means even in another perception; "in such a state" means in the state of requiring another perception. He says "nanu" in order to provide a construction for the word "mayā" (by me).

He states the rebuttal with the words "it is said" (*ucyate*). He makes his very thesis fruitful with the words "by me" (*mayā*). This is also an elliptical indication for [the verbs] "I experienced" (*anvabhūvam*) and so forth.
For this very application of the demonstration, which is intent upon establishing repose in the Self, its purpose is the effecting of the differentiation of the vision of the Self (*ātmadarśana*).

The intention is that the usage is "me dṛgāsīt" (I saw). A clear explanation of this has not been provided, and since the application here is indeed obvious, we have not exerted ourselves [to explain it further]. The student asks: "But here... [referring to] that which rests upon the lotus-face of the beloved and so forth.

By means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the word] rests upon the object; why? He says: "in the object" (*karmaṇi*). This is because of the production of the suffix *niṣṭhā*—that is, the production of the suffix *kta*; for the sense is that the suffix primarily has as its domain the locus of rest.
The Teacher replies: "This very one. "This very one" means the grammarian. "He does not perceive"—he does not.

He knows. In response to the expectation of "which speech?", he repeats that sentence, saying: "by the action of the agent" (*kartuḥ kriyayā*). And here, the rule is: "The object (*karman*) is that which the agent most desires to reach (*kartur īpsitatamam*). That which is desired to be reached with excellence is "most desired to be reached" (*īpsitatamam*), and that alone is what is to be attained. However, in this case, [the same does not apply] even to the action of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*).
The state of being directed toward objects such as water-jars and the like belongs to the seer alone, because it is the seer who acquires excellence through the act of seeing.
Indeed, by the sight of a beloved’s face and so forth, no excellence whatsoever is produced in that face;
rather, it belongs only to the seer, Caitra. Now, one might ask: how can the act of seeing (*dṛś*) reside in the agent? To this he says: "And thus," and "they say."
Although the grammarians have stated that for the root *dṛś* (to see) the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), as it has been said:

"The root *dṛś* has its state residing in the agent; the root *ruh* has its action residing in the agent," nevertheless, by the rule *bhavādayo dhātavaḥ*, it is [the state] of the action itself [that is denoted].
With reference to the state of being a "bhāva" (existence/activity) characterized by the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it was stated that only action (*kriyā*) is denoted by a verbal root;

in accordance with that principle, it was also stated here that for the root *dṛś* (to see), the action resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*). However, in ultimate reality, action alone is not the meaning of a verbal root, as in the case of the root *gaḍi* (to speak) in the sense of "a part of the face," where there is no form of action.

They say that the act of seeing is exactly like this in such examples as "the king causes his servants to see" (*darśayate bhṛtyān rājā*). Even by the followers of Jaimini, seeing—which is of the nature of cognition—is said to consist of a creative impulse (*bhāvanā*) that rests solely within the cognizer; the only difference is its manifestation (*prakaṭatā*).

Since even a single part of the face constitutes the meaning of the verbal root, for this very reason even logicians have described "seeing" as a quality (*guṇa*); enough with this elaboration. Furthermore, although the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) is already established by the word "state" (*bhāva*) alone, the separate designation of "action" is intended solely to indicate its predominance in the majority of cases.
One must not be confused otherwise. In response to the expectation of where the example is found, he says: "he shows himself" (*darśayate*).
The king is the agent; he shows himself to his servants, and they see him—this is the meaning. The underlying principle here is [the application of] the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha-*.
Regarding roots whose meanings involve motion (*gati*), cognition (*jñāna*), and so forth, it is prescribed that when they are used with the causal suffix *ṇic*, the agent alone becomes the object;
therefore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for these is established by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* alone. As for the effort undertaken again by the rule *ṇeraṇau*, it is as follows:

By the rule *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*, the *ātmanepada* ending is established only for those actions residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*), but not for those actions residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyā*) as well. Therefore, this [sūtra] is intended so that it may apply to those too.

And thus, in the examples "the cuckoo remembers the thicket" (*smarati vanagulmaṃ kokilaḥ*) and "the thicket itself causes him to remember" (*smārayati vanagulma enaṃ svayameva*), there is no [application of the *ātmanepada*].

The *ātmanepada* [ending] is used because of the exclusion [of the root] by the rule "not when expressing a mental state" (*anādhyāne*). Consequently, the fact that the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyatva*) is confirmed here precisely by the observation of the *ātmanepada* ending in the usage of the causative (*ṇijanta*); otherwise, since the mere phrase "they see the king" (*rājānaṃ paśyanti*) would suffice to establish the desired point, the example of the causative form would be unnecessary.

"It would be useless. [Objection: But if the agent alone is the primary factor here, then since the completion (*niṣṭhā*) arises from that very agent, there ought not to be an instrumental case in *mayā*, because the nominative alone is appropriate when only the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is intended.
[Response: True; however, in this case, the primacy of the agent is merely implied (*ārthika*).

This is because [the result] is attained through the excellence of that very [action]; however, according to the Grammarians (*śābdika*), it belongs to the action alone. For the Grammarian, whose concern is merely the derivation of words through grammar, the suffix is prescribed for that very [action].
But this author has conducted an investigation into the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); in such an investigation, there is no agreement with the Grammarians.

This is indeed appropriate; for this very reason, the attribution of faults to him is made with total indifference, otherwise he would have entered into a debate with you using the very same arguments. Enough of this! But even so, by the followers of Jaimini...
For indeed, what is called "knowability" is the very innate nature of an entity;
for when one says, "I know what was seen by Caitra," what exactly is it that appears here?

Thus, by this view, it has been stated that the act of seeing resides in the object; in response to the inquiry as to how that [residence] is to be precluded, he says: "even by the followers of Jaimini. *Dṛśiḥ*—the act of seeing—is of the nature of *bhāvanā*, that is, it consists of the form of mental realization (*bhāvanā*).

That *bhāvanā*, having been understood either from the verbal root or from the suffix, is a property of the object known as "the state of being seen" (*dṛṣṭatā*); or else it is another consciousness (*saṃvit*) that is not independent. Thus, this [consciousness] is distinct [from the *bhāvanā*]. (K. Ṣ. Ṣ.)

I have stated "by me" (*mayā*) precisely in order to express the state of resting within the subject (*pramātṛ-viśrāntatva*). Therefore, expressions such as "I experienced" (*anvabhūvam aham*) and "it was experienced by me" (*mayānubhūtam*) are merely a variety of linguistic forms; there is no difference in their meaning. Others, however, join the words in a different sequence, [interpreting] "that vision was mine" (*dṛg āsīt sā me*) in this way, and [the phrase] "it was seen by me" (*mayā dṛṣṭam*).
"Recollection" (smaraṇa) refers to the recollection of that which was just mentioned—"I experienced"—as a proper reflective awareness of it; "api" has the sense of "and. || 6 ||

Thus, according to that view, because the object is nothing other than the creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*) itself; "resting in the subject" means that action is not distinct from the agent—this is the sense. "Manifestness" is called "the state of being seen"—it is the manifestness known as "the state of being seen," which is the fruit of the act of seeing, by virtue of which something is said to be "seen."
The meaning is that immediately after the thought "I see," there occurs the conventional usage of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*).
He states another alternative view with the words "anyā" (it is other). "Dependent" (*asvatantrā*) means lacking independence because it is supported by an object.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter (*prameya*). By the phrase "this is something else," this [view]...
He states the lack of utility for the subject at hand. Now, one might ask: "By what is the state of resting in the cognizer (*pramātṛ-viśrāntatva*) known here?

To this he says: "The cognizer. The distinction indicated by a difference in grammatical substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) has just been refuted. He states the conclusion with the words "by that" (*tena*). By that means, i.e., by the aforementioned method; [he refutes] that which has been otherwise constructed by others.

He explains the construction with the words "others, however. Regarding the phrase "by means of a different sequence," the meaning is that he has performed the construction by way of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) even though the two expressions, "vision was mine" (*dṛg āsīt me*) and "it was seen by me" (*mayā dṛṣṭam*), stand separately.

He demonstrates that very point with the word "vision" (*dṛk*). He explains the word "of this" (*asyāḥ*) with the words "the one just mentioned" (*anantaroktā*). [The word] "just mentioned" (*anantaroktā*)...

And the phrase "she experienced" (*anvabhavat*) is her appropriate reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); the meaning is that the word "of her" (*tasyāḥ*) must be construed together with the word "recollection" (*smṛteḥ*). Now, one might ask: since there is no particle *ca* (and) here to express conjunction, how can this construction be made by way of conjunction? To this he says: "the word *api*."

The word "ca" (and) signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*), which constitutes its meaning. Furthermore, in this interpretation, such a laborious construction is not rejected; rather, it is indeed accepted, according to the maxim beginning with "paramatam" (the opinion of another). || 6 ||

Is it not observed that even that which has been seen by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is not remembered as long as it has not been grasped through a resting in a particular reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), just as grass, leaves, and the like seen on a path are not remembered in their specific forms? This is precisely that point.
This must be investigated: at the time of the conceptualization immediately following [the perception], does that vision appear as "this" or not? Having raised this doubt, he says:
"And whatever I see, or whatever I determine as 'this is a jar'..."
She too considers that perception to be inherent in the perceiver.

In this context, whatever kind of vision there is, it must always manifest through that very same [vision] in its own form; and that, at its own time, is a manifestation appropriate to its nature as "I," which is not illuminated by anything else.
Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "nanu dṛṣṭam" (But surely it has been seen).
Here the commentary says: "dṛṣṭam api" means even though it has been perceived; "nirvikalpena" means by non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*).

"Apprehended" (*parāmṛṣṭam*) means determined (*avasitam*). The remainder of the sense is: "of that resting (*viśrānti*) within a particular reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), immediately following which there arises conceptual knowledge (*savikalpajñāna*)," because it is conceptual knowledge alone that possesses the capacity for reflective awareness (*parāmarśaka*).
The construction is: "it is not remembered in its specific form. "That" (*tat*) means "for that reason. "What is this? (*idam kim*)—[this refers to the object].

In response to this inquiry, he says "immediately following" (*samanantara*). The meaning is that at the time of the conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpaka*) which arises immediately after—that is, at the moment of the conceptual cognition (*savikalpajñāna*) occurring right after the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpajñāna*)—the perception would be considered as having been examined even during the reflective recollection (*smṛtiparāmarśa*) that follows that very [non-conceptual] cognition. The word "iti" [marks the end of the thought].

At the conclusion of the inquiry: even though the subject matter has been completed, he refers back to it once more with the words "this very [thing]. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it, beginning with "And that which...
Here is the commentary:
Therein, he explains the matter first indicated by the word "api" (also/even) with the word "iha" (here). "Iha" means in this manifest world;

"darśanam" (vision) follows "anu" (after/according to); "vapuṣā" means by its own form—by such a form, that is the meaning of "tādṛśena vapuṣā"; "tena" means by that vision; [it is said] "it must appear," for otherwise it would be an appearance of something else.
The meaning is that this results from falling into the state of being an error. And that "vision" (darśana) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), not illuminated by anything else;

for this very reason, the investigation into the conceptualized portions of that [vision] as merely "I" does not constitute a factor anywhere. Let it be so—[or rather, let it be, but—] (Note: The final *bhavatu* appears to be a repetition or an editorial insertion; the intended sense is likely a concessive "let it be," followed by a qualification.)

[K. ṣ. ṣ. It is not merely the vocal organ [that functions], but the determinative cognition (*avasāya*) is also of such a nature; this is indicated by the word "also" (*api*). In that case, the object being grasped by the immediately subsequent conceptualization is grasped either through the medium of the reflective awareness of experience, as in: "I see this."

By the words "as being present" (*vartamānatayā*) and "this" (*imam*), the fact that [the object] is the operation of perception is shown through its appearing as perceptible. Or rather, it is referred to in this very way—as "this jar.
Here, by the word "this," its state of appearing as perceptible is expressed. In that regard, in the latter alternative, of the seeing...

"By its own nature, it possesses appropriate manifestation," meaning it possesses appropriate appearance; the sense is that there is nothing further to be said regarding this. However, where something remains to be said, he states that as well:

"The investigation of the aspect of conceptual construction (*vikalpāṃśa*)"—the discernment of a slight trace of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) arising immediately after that [pure perception]—"is an auxiliary (*aṅga*)."

"It is not helpful"—this is the sense, meaning that it does not touch upon the actual object (*arthasparśitvāt*). Or rather, let it be an auxiliary; let it be an auxiliary—this is the meaning. Even the ascertainment—even the aspect consisting of the conceptualization of perception—is of such a nature: it is not illuminated by anything else. [Objection: But this entire elaboration is not seen in the Sūtra.

In response to this expectation, he says: "by the word 'api'. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the Teacher indicates"; the sense is that the word *api* has the purpose of bringing about the possibility of a thing that was previously impossible. Now, if it is asked whether by this very [statement] perception (*darśana*) also comes to have the status of being a locus of "this-ness" (*idantā*), just like its object, he offers two alternatives therein.

Thus, the meaning is: "given that the conceptualizing aspect is an auxiliary factor. By the immediately subsequent conceptualization—that is, by determinate cognition (*savikalpajñāna*). The object, such as a jar, which has become the domain of the perception of the real thing (*vastu*), is being "reflected upon"—that is, it is being made the object of its own [conceptual] operation.

"By way of the reflective awareness of experience"—that is, through the medium of the reflective awareness of perception. To the question "How so?", he says: "I. The sense is that this refers to the present tense, because the suffix *laṭ* is prescribed for the present time.
The instrumental case here denotes the manner of being (*itthambhāve*). He states the referent of the word "this" (*imam*), which is included within this [phrase], as follows: "this."

Thus: "the state of being a perceptual operation" refers to the existence of that operation called perception which consists of the act of seeing; it is shown as "acting like perception"—that is, by way of behaving as if it were perception—because, in the ultimate sense, it cannot truly be perception, and thus it is designated by the suffix *kyac*.

Likewise, in the subsequent cases as well, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of "being thus" (*itthaṃbhāve*). He states the second alternative as well with the words "or in this very way.

Regarding the phrase "by the word *ayam*," the intention is that the word *ayam*, like the word *idam*, is employed in reference to an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣaviṣaye*). Even though [the forms] *imam* and *ayam*—

Since there is no separate reflective awareness at all, what room is there for the suspicion of "this-ness" (*idantā*)? Consequently, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), its reflective awareness here occurs through "I-ness" (*ahantā*); for in the absence of that [I-ness], conceptual thought would exist even for one with eyes closed.
Thus, when there is contact with the object itself, [the cognition] culminates in a most vivid object—[whereas in the absence of such contact, it remains otherwise].

How could there be a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) that culminates in an object that is most clearly manifest? In the first case, however, even the perception (*darśana*), though being reflected upon, is included within the "I-sense" (*asmadartha*), which is the locus of the ego-feeling (*ahambhāva*).

And although this merely indicates that the object itself is directly perceived, nevertheless, due to its proximity, it follows that the cognition which has that object as its content would also incur contact with it; thus, there is nothing contradictory. Regarding that, having recognized that there is much to be said concerning the first alternative, he sets that aside for a moment and first analyzes the second one, beginning with the words "tatra" (in that case). In the latter [alternative]...

Regarding the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form "this is a jar," [the object] does not exist [as such], because there is no word to denote it—this is the meaning. Now, one might ask: "What follows from that? To this he says: "And therefore" (*tataśca*). By way of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), that is, by virtue of being the only remaining possibility; for it is not logical that there should be a total absence of any reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of it—this is the sense. Now, one might say: "Let even that [reflective awareness] not exist. To this [he replies]:

He says: "In the absence of that. In the absence of that—in the absence of the reflective awareness of "I"—there is the presence of conceptualization (vikalpa), that is, the conceptualization of objects, even in one whose eyes are closed; that is, even in a person who has immediately closed his eyes after experiencing an object due to the pleasure or other sensations produced by that object, for even one with closed eyes...
The meaning is: "for this reason," namely, because he becomes capable of forming conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

When there is contact with the object—meaning, of that very conceptual construction—it is "most vivid" (*sphuṭatama*), that is, it culminates in—that is, comes to rest (*viśrānta*)—in that object which is extremely clear through the apprehension of all phenomena; such is the "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*), meaning, of that [conceptual construction].

How could there be [recognition] for one with eyes closed? Since the act of seeing has already occurred prior to the closing of the eyes, it is impossible for that same seeing to occur again; if that very seeing were firmly established within the self, then how could there be a subsequent determination (*adhyavasāya*) accomplished by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the object following that [original perception]? This is the summary.

It is stated that "with eyes closed" because, for one whose eyes have opened, there arises the possibility of perception, and from that perception, there arises the possibility of conceptual determination (*vikalpa-adhyavasāya*). The word "also" (*api*) refers to the occurrence of an object that is otherwise impossible. He now examines even the first position that was established.

Regarding the phrase "in the first": "in the first" means in that form which is "I see"; the sense is that it is "perceived" by means of the word "I see. It is "included within the referent of the pronoun 'we'" (asmadartha)—that is, submerged within the meaning of the word *asmad*, which serves as the meaning of the suffix according to the rule "the base and the suffix [together express the meaning]. For this very reason, it is the locus of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*).

Since it has become the object of the sense of "I," it is therefore grasped as self-luminous alone, resting within the subject— the word *avasātṛ* (the subject) being used here in the locative sense "within the subject. Thus, even conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) does not make known for consciousness the state of being cognizable by another cognition.

*Avasāyaḥ* (ascertainment) means *avasā* (certainty); by saying "integrated" (*samavetam*), he expresses non-separateness. "*Avasātari*" (in the ascertainer) means in the independent, introverted self of consciousness, which is the locus of the "I-sense. "*Darśanam*" (vision/perception) refers to indeterminate experience; this is also an illustration that includes conceptualization, memory, and so forth, as they too belong to cognition.

For this same principle applies when there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) by means of another cognition: "I am conceptualizing," "I am remembering," "it was conceptualized by me," or "it was remembered by me. This is because conceptualization and the rest manifest precisely through their ascension upon the "I" (*ahantā*). Therefore, these [phenomena] such as conceptualization are specific powers (*śakti-viśeṣa*) of the Self.
It has been shown [in the verse] "possessing the powers of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance]" that this is because his body is at rest therein. || 7 ||

When resting in the subject who has become the object of expression— that is, having attained repose— it is for this very reason that it is grasped as self-luminous. For this reason, even conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*)—
even knowledge accompanied by conceptualization— is not something to be known by another cognition (*bodhāntara-bodhyatām*) of the [original] awareness (*bodha*), which is experience (*anubhava*).

It makes known—that is to say, it causes to be cognized by itself—the state of being knowable by a determinate cognition whose nature consists of the other elements [of the object]; and such being the case, what room is there for the suspicion of the apprehension of "this-ness" (*idantā*) therein?
This is the sense. Having thus stated the meaning of the sentence, he also explains the meaning of the word with the term "ascertainment" (*avasāya*). [The word] *avasā*...

The form [of the word *apṛthaktva*] is derived from the root *sī* (to lie down) with the prefix *ava-* and the suffix *aṅ* in the sense of a state; thus, it means non-separateness (*apṛthagbhāva*) or the state of being inseparable (*ayutasiddhatva*).

Regarding the phrase "in the independent one" (*svatantre*), this refers to the agent (*kartṛ*), since the suffix *tṛc* is produced in the sense of an agent. It means that [the Self] is described as the cognizer (*avasātṛ*) merely by virtue of its agency at that moment, while in reality it consists of consciousness—the nature of experience itself. Furthermore...

The word "and" (*śabdaḥ*) signifies a conjunction. To the question, "Why is this the logical principle? he says: "I conceptualize. This means that, from the perspective that both base and suffix are mounted upon the "I-sense" (*ahantā*), [the suffix] rests solely within that "I-sense.

He states that this entity is the cause for the preceding [element] with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). To the question, "Where has this been shown? he says: [it is shown in the following].
He says: "In the word 'jñāna'. The meaning is: if [the object] is not [present] within this word located at the end of the verse, beginning with "kṛtābhāsaḥ" and so forth. || 7 ||
Thus, in order to summarize the fruit of this much that is to be known, he says:
"Even when one thinks, 'This is seen by me,' or 'That has been seen,' the two objects, non-different from the states of grasped and grasper, appear within the cognizer. (8)

The word "tat" (that) signifies the sense of "therefore," indicating here that the previously stated object of knowledge (*prameya*) is being relied upon as a logical reason. Since it has been stated thus— that there is no appearance of memory as distinct from the experience itself, just as there is none from the object— and since the power of memory belongs to the Supreme Lord alone, therefore this is the established truth in this matter.

Thus, it has been stated here that memory encompasses experience (*anubhava*). And experience is twofold, according to the distinction in its reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*): sometimes, preceded by the reflective awareness of one's own self, it reflects upon (*parāmṛśati*) the object to be experienced, wherein its—

Now he provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the words "evam" (thus). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the word "tat" (that). Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

He explains the word *tat* by saying *tasmāt*. He states the matter to be indicated by this very word by saying *pūrvoktasya* (of what was previously stated). "Dependence" (*upajīvanam*) means arising. Here, regarding the meaning of this verse which possesses the nature of a reason, he clearly states that the previously stated meaning serves as its very cause by saying *yataḥ*.
The word "stated" (uktam) implies "previously" as the ellipsis. To the question "What was stated?", he says: "of experience" (anubhavasya).

This means of a prior experience; "just like an object" (arthasyeva), meaning like a prior object, [it is established] by way of distinction from memory—that is, by way of being the object of memory (*smṛti-viṣayatayā*). Therefore, from that, its reality (*tattvam*) has become firmly established—meaning it has attained stability.

The word "paramārthaḥ" (the ultimate reality) marks the conclusion [of the previous section]. In response to the inquiry "What [is it]? he says "iha" (here). He embraces it—he internalizes it—because otherwise it would be impossible for it to be an object within the scope of that [recollection]; this is the sense. Now, one might ask "So what of it? To which he replies: "anubhavaśca" (and the experience). And the experience—the experience embraced by memory.

Therein, he describes the first division with the words "kadācit" (at times). That reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)— of one's own self, which is of the nature of experience— in the form "it is seen," etc., is that by which one subsequently reflects upon the object of experience (*anubhāvya*), such as a jar or the like, which has become the object of experience.

It brings [the object] into the sphere of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); this is stated with reference to the ultimate identity (*pāramārthika-ekatva*) between the subject and experience. To the question "Where does it reflect? he says: "where" (*yatra*).
The underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) is: in one's own self (*svasyātmani*).

The predominance of the junction (*saṃdhi*) consists in the thought "I see," where one sometimes reflects primarily upon that which is to be experienced; or where there is a sudden encounter with an object precisely due to a lack of intention (*anabhisaṃdhi*);
or where there is a particular insistence regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) such as "this. And even in those cases—

There is indeed a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the manifestation, for otherwise there would be no connection with manifestation. Thus, when both are experienced, a memory arises for each that consists of the reflective awareness of both; this constitutes four varieties of memory and two varieties of experience. This is the synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*).

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is also a synthesis (*anusandhāna*) whose nature is repose; its "predominance" (*prādhānya*) refers to the predominance of intention (*abhisandhi-prādhānya*). Now, one might ask: what is the nature of this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)? To this, he says: "by me."

Here too, the previously mentioned principle—that [the action] resides in the agent (*kartṛstha-kriyatva*)—should be applied. He also states the second distinction with the words "sometimes" (*kadācit*). "Only that which is to be experienced"—that is, only objects such as a jar which are the domain of experience, and not even the entity denoted by the word "we" (*asmad-śabda-vācya*). Having divided the two locations implied by the word "where" (*yatra*), [he explains them as follows]:

He says: "Suddenly" (*sahasā*), meaning without desire—that is to say, unexpectedly. For in that state, there occurs clearly, through agitation, a mere apprehension of the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*). Again, asking "where? he says: "toward the purpose" (*arthe*). That is, toward the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by that thing.

A specific intensity of attachment (*āgraha-viśeṣa*): when there is an excess of desire, because the object itself is predominant due to being excessively longed for, there occurs only a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that object. To the question "What is the nature of this reflective awareness?", he says:
"This" (*ayam*). Now, one might ask: "Is there no reflective awareness of the Light (*prakāśa*) here at all? To this he replies: "Even there... (*tatrāpi*).

Thus [it is said]. Even there—in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "this is"—the sense is that it "indeed exists," though it is not being consciously perceived due to its extreme subtlety. When the question "Why? arises, he says: "Otherwise," because of the impossibility of manifestation—that is, because the manifestation of the object would be impossible. As it has been said:
"Even though consciousness is colored by the object, it is like an insentient thing such as a crystal.
In the same way, memory also possesses this twofold nature through its connection with the two kinds of experience.
He states that there is a fourfold division with the word "evam" (thus). "Pratye-kam" means for each individual experience.
"Consisting of the twofold grasping" means having the form of two types of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*): namely, "this is seen" and "that [is it].

Regarding the four [perceptions]: in the experience "I see," there is one [perception] in the form of "it was seen"; in this very context, there is a second in the form of "that [is it]"; and in the experience "this [is it]," there is a third in the form of "it was seen."

The fourth is of the form "he is right here. Two others are of the nature of "this is seen. Thus, all these six varieties are established. That which consists of the union of both [the former two] is included within this very category. And that, due to these divisions, is eightfold.

Because each [of the eight] is divided twofold by the distinction between resting in the prior and the posterior, there are sixteen ways. Thus, these are twenty-two varieties of consciousness. Among them, first, the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is not external to the light (*prakāśa*), because otherwise its manifestation would be impossible; yet it is also external to that [light].
Because it is impossible for there to be any other referent, and because it is not [the case] that "from that very [source], at that very time, that very thing"—

relying on this much, he establishes that even the sixteen-fold recognition is "synthetic integration" (*anusaṃdhāna*). "Synthetic integration" consists in the unification of what has been remembered and what has been experienced.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—that is, *pratyabhijñā*, which consists of the fusion of these two—has the nature of a synthesis between the aforementioned experience and recollection; it occurs precisely within this very sixfold division.
And that recognition, due to the distinction between these [two] experiences and [two] recollections, is eightfold.

It becomes eightfold, because when the fourfold distinction of memory is connected with the two distinctions of experience, an eightfold state clearly arises. Furthermore, that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) becomes sixteenfold; such is the connection [of the text]. For at times...

In recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the primary factor regarding an object is its being delimited by a prior time, or sometimes its being delimited by a later time. One effects the synthesis of these various cognitions into a single unity, thinking, "These are those very same [objects]. To the question, "But what follows from that? he says: "And among them..."—among them.

And among the twenty-two divisions, "the object of apprehension" (grāhya) refers to the objective domain that exists as something to be experienced (*anubhāvya*), remembered (*smaryamāṇa*), or recognized (*pratyabhijñeya*). To the question "Why so?", he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*).
"Otherwise" means in the absence of its being non-distinct from the external. As it has been said:
Furthermore, a Buddha could not participate in conventional discourse through a distinction in his awakening;
for if Buddhahood were something separate [from the world], why would everything not already be awakened?

Thus [it is said]. That [consciousness], consisting of twenty-two cognitions, [is devoid of objects] because of the impossibility of being an object—that is, because of the impossibility of being an objective referent (*viṣayatva*). Now, one might ask: "In that case, let it possess both forms. To this he says: "And not...
Then, what is to be done? To this [he says]:...

Since it is said that "that which is separate here becomes separate," there must certainly be some other entity here whose nature is the imagined light (*prakāśa*), by virtue of which this mass of objects, becoming separate,
attains mutual distinctness; otherwise, for those things that are non-different from the light...
How could there even be a mutual separation between them? This [separation] is merely a portion of the object of cognition (*vedya*);

it is indeed severed, and yet it never abandons its status as an object of cognition, being apprehended by a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that is devoid of separation and appropriate to the light that is itself free from separation—[as stated in the Kṣemarāja commentary: "appropriate to that which is devoid of separation"].
The subject of illusion (*māyāpramātā*) will be discussed in the passage: "In the body, in the intellect... (1.6.4). And he is called the "grasper" (*grāhaka*).
Thus, within his own self—which is like a stainless mirror [or, as Kṣemarāja reads, a pure mirror]—[the object appears].
He said: "Thus, thus. "Thus" means for this reason; "certainly" means with certainty; "imagined" means that which is conceived through the imagination as having the state of a body and so forth;
"that light" refers to the aspect of light delimited by that [body];
"of whom that is the self" refers to the object (artha) existing as an object of knowledge (prameya) in relation to pure light.

Because it is an object of cognition (*vedyatvāt*). For this reason—since this mass of objects is being experienced—he states "otherwise" (*anyathā*) to point out the fault in the absence of such apprehension. [He refers to] "entities non-different from light"—that is, entities contained within the light of consciousness. Now, if one asks what that object is, he says: "this very one" (*so'yam*).

Thus, it is only a portion of the object of knowledge—that is, a single part within the totality of objects of knowledge—because it possesses a uniform nature; it is not, however, of the nature of the subject, since it is merely a semblance of the subject. Likewise, it is indeed "severed," like a jar or other objects, being rendered distinct from the supreme light by the power of *apohana* (exclusion), through the reflective awareness of "I."

This is the connection [of the words]. By what kind of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)? By that which is appropriate for the light (*prakāśa*) that is devoid of separation, because that alone is, in the ultimate sense, the object of the "I" (*aham*). To the question "Where will this be stated?", he says: "In the body. He explains the subjectivity (*grāhakatva*) of this very [light] with the words "and that. And the subject...

It should be understood as having a threefold nature by way of being the experiencer, the rememberer, and the recognizer. He provides the conclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*): that pair [of subject and object] which the Supreme Lord manifests as non-different from His own nature of light is indeed identical [to Him].

The essential meaning is this: that very agency of the Blessed One in respect to knowledge and memory, which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and the power of memory (*smṛti-śakti*), is what is being described.
As for the literal meaning: it refers to that which the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) reflects upon as "it is seen by me" and "this."
That by which one experiences is said to be of the nature of light (*prakāśa*); from that reflective awareness (*āmarśana*), this is characterized:

the two objects—the jar and so forth, and the body and so forth—which possess the natures of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), appear and shine forth within the subject whose nature is pure light as the two things to be known. Thus, [the cognitions] "this is seen" and "that [is seen]" [arise].

That which the cognizer, whose nature is light, grasps—that by virtue of which he is designated as "one who remembers"—is also characterized by this very same [nature]. This is mentioned here incidentally to further solidify the previously stated point that [memory] subsists upon the form of direct experience (*anubhava*). Furthermore, it serves to establish the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*) as well.
But not sequentially; the point is that because the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*) would exist at different times, no connection between them could be established.

In that which is like a stainless sprout—meaning, like a stainless mirror due to its capacity to receive reflections—the pair (*yugalaka*), namely the dyad of the grasped and the grasper, is precisely that.

The intended meaning—the meaning of the sentence—is simply this manifestation. He announces the explanation of the word-meanings with the words "the literal meaning, however" (*akṣarārthas tu*). The connection is: "the subject (*pramātā*) whose nature is light. By which—by which reflective awareness (*amarśana*); from that—from that definition.

"It is perceived"—that is, it is known—that they have been "joined," meaning they have attained a state of connection. Having thus performed the joining in the case of direct experience (*anubhava*), he performs the joining in the case of memory (*smṛti*) with the word "thus" (*evam*). Following the word "is perceived," the entire series of sentences beginning with "the object of perception" (*grāhya*) and ending with "shines forth" (*prakāśate*) should be joined by oneself.

The application of this [principle] to the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is also established by this very [reasoning], because recognition consists merely of the conjunction of experience and memory; and thus, there is no separate mention of recognition in the Sūtra. But why was cognition (*jñāna*) not mentioned at the time of establishing memory?
Since only a slight determination has been made, he says "experience" (anubhava).

This refers to the state of being dependent upon experience—that is, dependence on experience—because of the context (*prasaṅga*), and not because of the order of sequence; here, at the time of establishing memory, its manifestation (*unmīlana*)—

"Expansion" means, in other words, "discrimination. Now, one might ask: "In that case, why was this [power] not established first—given its seniority due to being mentioned first in the phrase 'possessing the powers of knowledge, memory, and removal,' and because it is the life-force of memory?"

It has been made stainless. The suffix *śatṛ* (present participle) is used here in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). The word "also" (*api*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*). The word "object" (*artha*) refers to that which is perceived as a discrete entity. The perceiver is the imagined subject belonging to the realm of *māyā*, whose nature is impure light. Thus all is auspicious. [Total verse count from the beginning: 31].

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Power of Memory," in the first section on Knowledge of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 4.
True; however,

since it is memory alone that is the means of proving the reality of the Self— which is desired as the nature of the synthesizer because its very life consists in synthesis— whereas the power of cognition serves that purpose only through memory, [the objection] remains untenable.
For the sake of consoling the disciple, the support for *smṛti* (memory) alone was established first;

and by way of that context, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) which is useful for it was also revealed—thus everything is entirely faultless. Regarding the word "āmṛśati," he states the meaning of the present participle suffix (*śatṛpratyaya*) found therein as "in the sense of a characteristic mark" (*lakṣaṇe*).

Because it indicates that the primary meaning [of the word *lakṣaṇa*] functions as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatā*) with respect to the manifestation of two objects that are non-distinct in their status as grasped and grasper, for this very reason it was stated immediately thereafter that "it is characterized twice.
He states the meaning of the word *api* as being in the sense of *ca* (and); "in the sense of *ca*" means in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). The word "meaning" (*artha*) [is used here].

He states that the "object" (artha) is that which is denoted by words. "Separated" means rendered distinct from the Light and from the mass of objective entities by the power of exclusion (apohana); that which is thus knowable is what is expressed by words. He describes the "subject" (grāhaka), the ontological entity, as "that which arises from Māyā. What kind of cognizer is this? Its nature is impure light.

One whose own nature has become fragmented by the power of self-obscuration (*svāpohana-śakti*). The word "iti" marks the conclusion; the term "Śiva" denotes auspiciousness and indicates the supreme reality (*paratattva*). Thus, all is auspicious (*iti śivam*). 8.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Section on Knowledge within the *Śrīpratyabhijñāvimarśinī*, a commentary known as the *Bhāskarī*, composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Now begins the fifth chapter. We ever praise that Śiva, who, by means of the lamp of the power of knowledge, illuminates the multitude of existents submerged within the great cave.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Having kindled the lamp called knowledge— which illuminates the vessel situated within the interior of the house of one's own true nature— we praise Śiva, who is self-luminous.

Now, at the beginning of the commentary on the fifth chapter of the section on Knowledge (*jñāna*), he composes a verse beginning with "The Great" (*mahā*) which indicates the purport of the entire chapter, serves as an auspicious invocation, and is intended for the student’s engagement so that the work may be completed without obstacle and for its further propagation.
The commentary on this [verse] is as follows:

We praise that Śiva. Who is he? That Śiva who is *sadā*—that is, eternally (*nityam*), and not merely at some particular time due to the influence of some specific purpose or the like. As it has been said:
Salutations to the Lord, who always delights in creation, who always dwells in the bliss of maintenance, and who is ever satisfied by devouring the three worlds.
Thus: the power of knowledge alone—that very power called knowledge, whose nature has been described and will be described—is the lamp;

by means of that, within the great cave—in the vast cave whose form is one's own essential nature, which is unlimited and difficult to fathom—it is submerged, that is, [it is not outside]. If it were not within...

By the logic stated here in the word *kṛta*, that collection of entities—the aggregate of existents—which has been submerged, becomes manifest through the power of *apohana*; having differentiated it, it appears as something external.
This is the implied meaning (*dhvani*): just as another person illuminates objects situated within a cave by means of a lamp. By this, here—
It is indicated that the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) alone is what must be established.
Thus far, the nature of the power of memory (*smṛtiśakti*) has been explained; now follows the determination of the ultimate reality of the power of knowledge upon which it depends.
Having extensively examined the determination of the power of cognition upon which that [perception] depends,

he explains it through twenty-one verses beginning with "of those appearing as present" and ending with "it appears sequentially. Therein, by means of the first verse, he makes a formal proposition regarding the subject matter.

"Such is the power of cognition. Then, with two verses, he states that light alone is the true nature (*svarūpa*) of objects. Thereafter, with two [verses], he refutes the existence of objects external to light by means of the critique of the *vāsanās* accepted by the Vijñānavādin.

Anticipating that this might be strengthened, he shows with the third [verse] that even if that is not accepted, nothing at all is obstructed. Then, by means of a verse, while demonstrating the reality of the object according to his own system,
he refutes perception as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence of external objects.

Then, with two [verses], he refutes the inferability of the external world as well. Immediately thereafter, with a verse, he demonstrates that objects necessarily exist within the conscious self by virtue of being apprehended through the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Having thus accomplished this auspicious opening, he states the intended meaning of the chapter (*āhnika*) both collectively and individually.
He says "thus. Here, the commentary states:
"'It has been established' means in the preceding section (pūrvāhnika). 'To be relied upon' means to be depended upon."

Having stated in its entirety the determination of the ultimate reality—the innate nature—of that power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), he speaks of it also individually with the words "therein" (*tatra*). "Therein" means within the twenty-one verses; "regarding the reality" means regarding the exposition of the power of knowledge.
He shows the very nature of the proposition with the word "thus" (*evam*). Thereafter— that is, immediately following the proposition—

by means of the refutation of that *vāsanā* (latent impression), which is the mental trace of phenomena, as it has been accepted (*upagatā*) or admitted by the Vijñānavādins— the Buddhists— even in the absence of its acceptance.

Even in the non-acceptance of categories (*padārtha*), it is not obstructed—that is, it is not impeded; the meaning to be established is not contradicted. "The reality of objects" (*arthatattva*) refers to the innate nature of things;
he rejects it as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), meaning that there is no such thing as a means of valid cognition. [He rejects] its being inferable (*anumeyatām*).
The meaning is that the external—the mass of entities existing outside—is accessible through inference.

He declares, in four verses, by means of the investigation into the nature of experience, scripture, and reasoning, that the very life of the light—which is the nature of the subject—consists solely in reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). Immediately thereafter:

The reflective awareness of knowledge itself manifests the object of knowledge as both pure and not having abandoned its nature as the subject; thus, he states the reasoning for its primacy in three verses.
Furthermore, he states in a verse that when there is the single nature of light, the distinction between knowledge, the knower, and so forth [vanishes], and then [he speaks] regarding the knower.

With two verses, he states that even in pure knowledge—whether of the non-conceptual or conceptual form—it is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone that constitutes its vital essence. Then, with a concluding verse, he supports the distinctness of the knower and the known, which was refuted in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is the purport of this chapter (*āhnika*).
The meaning of the verse is now being examined.

Now, it may be argued that memory, conceptual construction, and so forth have their very life in direct experience (*anubhava*); therefore, if objects appear as distinct within that [experience], then it is appropriate that they appear in the same way even in those [subsequent states]. Otherwise, it would not be so.
With the intention that the very experience of that [object], in the form of the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*), must first be investigated, he says:
"by means of the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśātmanā*)"— that is, by means of the essential form of reflective awareness (*parāmarśasvarūpeṇa*), and not in a gross manner—
"the very act of re-cognition (*pratyavamarśa*)," which is indeed reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), [consists of] experience (*anubhava*), scripture (*āgama*), and reasoning (*nyāya*).

And by means of those [explanations], there is the definition of its own nature (*svarūpanirūpaṇā*). "Of that very thing" refers to the reflective awareness of knowledge (*jñānaparāmarśa*) itself; "the reasoning" (*nyāya*) refers to the logical justification. By the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is included by the use of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). He announces the definition of the meaning of the verse with the words "the meaning of the verse."

Anticipating the student's confusion— namely, "Why has memory alone been determined, and why has the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), upon which it depends, not been determined?"— the author provides an introductory transition to reassure him,
beginning with the word "nanu."
Here the commentary states:
"Experience alone" means non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) itself; "therein" means in that experience;

"even in those"—meaning even in recollection, conceptualization, and so forth—"in the same way" means precisely by way of differentiation. "If not" means if the objects were [not differentiated] within the experience.

The meaning is that they do not appear as distinct. "Otherwise" means that, in that case, it would be appropriate for them to appear as non-distinct. He states the conclusion with the word "tat" (that); "tat" means "therefore. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the first verse: "vartamāne" (in the present).
The manifestation of entities appearing as present is possible only for those that already exist internally, by means of an external form. (1)
For those for whom there is an appearance as "this" in the form of a clear manifestation through presentness,

by means of that which is conceived as external— namely, the state of being separate from the subject (pramātṛ) whose body ranges from the illusory void (māyīya-śūnya) up to the individual soul (āṇava-śarīra)— [there arises this perception].
"Then, the manifestation of those things that are differentiated—that is, separated—from the illusory subject (māyā-pramātṛ)";
regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound word found in the sūtra beginning with "vartamāna," stating: "vartamāna" [and so forth].

The analysis [of the compound] is "by way of being present," relying on an indication where the state (*bhāva*) is primary. He states the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) of this [term] as "with clarity. The meaning is: by way of clarity consisting in the apprehension of the appearance of all phenomena, which is produced by its being situated at the forefront. It is precisely this manifestation.

He says "this" (idam) by imitating [the object] in its own form; the phrase "of those" (yeṣāṃ teṣām) is a compound formed from the separated words "yeṣām" and "teṣām. The expression "yad etat" (that which is this) depends on the anticipation of the word "tat" (that) which is to be employed later;
for a sentence joined by the two words "yat" and "tat" becomes clearly manifest in its external form.

Thus he explains the term "imagined" (*kalpita*): "imagined" refers to those things such as the void (*śūnya*) and so forth, which are illusory (*māyīya*), produced by *māyā*, and established through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) because their existence as subject and object would otherwise be untenable; they are characterized by difference as their very life-force (or, according to manuscript C, by difference as their means of proof).
From those cognizers who terminate with the body— but not from the supreme cognizer—

that state of separation which is imagined by them as a difference from themselves; for this reason, [the word] "as an external self" (*bahirātmanā*) in the sūtra indicates the instrumental case in the sense of cause (*hetau tṛtīyā*), and the word "of the divided ones" (*bhinnānām*) is supplied [as an ellipsis] because it is logical.

He explains [the verse] with the words "tataḥ" (then). In place of the reading "bhāvānām" (of entities), the reading "bhinnānām" (of differentiated things) is preferable; for the term "bhāvānām," which stands as the substantive, is established by implication through its very qualification.
[The phrase "antaḥsthitavatām" means] "of those residing within" the ultimate subject, who consists of pure consciousness, [referring to their] identity with him.

The term "is consistent" (ghaṭate) means that it is established by valid cognition (pramāṇa) precisely for those things whose nature has not been abandoned; thus, it is said that the Lord’s power of knowledge is the manifestation of an entity—whose internal consciousness remains undivided—as distinct [from itself] with respect to a conceptualized subject. || 1 ||
It has been stated that this is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); he now demonstrates that valid cognition:

"Alternatively, difference is implied by the very word 'existence' (*bhāva*). That [existence] is manifestation, which—by implication—occurs in the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*), who consists of pure consciousness. The phrase 'of those situated within'..."

He explains [the word] "by that" (*tena*) as follows: "with that"—that is, with the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*) consisting of pure consciousness—there is "identity," meaning non-difference; he explains the word "is established" (*ghaṭate*) as "by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇena*), namely, by the *kevalavyatirekin* inference which is about to be described. This is the resultant [meaning].
He says "by that" (tena) in accordance with the proposition regarding the object (*vastu*). By this, it is shown that this proposition is based on reasoning (*ārthīya*), not scriptural (*śrautī*).
And here the intended meaning is as follows: [it applies] to those things that exist in their own nature from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).

Even regarding those entities that constitute its own limbs and are fit to be grasped as "I," that which appears as "this" through differentiation by the power of *māyā* occurs only with respect to those things that exist as such while remaining as limbs within it,
and not with respect to those that have departed from it; just as a clay pot exists as clay.

The apprehension of the jar occurs precisely while it remains as such; for the jar, having emerged from the clay, does not become anything at all distinct, since it is endowed with existence solely through the existence of the clay.
Thus, its "remaining within" that [clay] is merely its non-difference from it—not its abiding as something contained within it.
For a jar that exists in the state of clay is said to be "within the clay," not because it exists as a support for it;

whereas its existence outside of it constitutes its very difference from it—a wave of water, being distinct from the clay, is said to be "external to the clay. Therefore, the multitude of objects existing within consciousness is indeed of the nature of consciousness itself.

"Abiding within that" means not remaining there as something independent, but rather "abiding outside of that" refers to appearing as a distinct "this-ness" through the power of *māyā* as differentiated from it; it does not mean going out from there and abiding in some other place. Thus, its abiding outside is indeed the effect of *māyā*. As it has been said:
This is darkness, because [it consists in] [the perception of things] as manifest,
even though they are not distinct from one's own self,
and so forth.
Prior to manifestation, the object would be unmanifest, were it not for its nature as light;
moreover, the light cannot be distinct from the self, for that is what constitutes the object's manifestation.

The object is blue and so forth; if its manifestation consists solely in its very nature as blue and so forth, and not in some other, distinct luminous nature transcending the body of the object, then— just as it is called "blue" for everyone because of the possibility of that [nature]— it would be the same in this case.

It does not belong to anyone, nor does it exist as an object in its own right; for that blue cannot reside in another, since it is impossible for it to be established in another, nor can it be neither blue nor non-blue within itself, because its determination is impossible without the favor of manifestation (*prakāśa*). Likewise...

"Even its being manifest"—this is the introduction to the second verse, beginning with the words "by means of a valid cognition" (*pramāṇena*). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse, beginning with the word "previously" (*prāk*).

Because the impossibility of its being established by another arises from the lack of connection with anything else, the wise declare that very [consciousness] to be blue within itself. Why is it not declared to be non-blue? Because of the favor of manifestation—that is, through the support of manifestation—since without it, no determination is possible; for [without manifestation] there can be no determination.
Because it is impossible; for only an object already grasped by light can be established as having a form such as blue and so forth.
Likewise—and in that same manner—it would follow that light either exists for everyone, or for no one at all, or rather, it would exist only within itself; yet even within itself, it might not exist.
The world would be blind.

Now, if this [object], characterized as blue, were produced as something distinct from the group of moments consisting of the sense-faculties, light, and so forth, even so, that same consequence follows; this very same fault applies even in the theory of manifestation (*prakaṭatāvāda*), in every respect.

Even its state of being an object of cognition—just like blue and so forth—is not admitted to have the nature of an external object; likewise, its status as the agent of manifestation would, by implication, belong to this object "blue" either toward all [subjects]—that is, in relation to everyone—or toward none at all, since in reality it could not belong to anyone whatsoever;
rather, it belongs only to itself. Therefore, even from that perspective...

"In the investigation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it would not exist even in its own self"—this refers to "blindness," meaning a state resembling blindness due to the incapacity to grasp objects. This was stated without regard for its being the cause of omniscience.

The underlying intention is as follows: at the time of perception, it is the very nature of the entity—which, through *māyā*, appears as an existent thing—that shines forth to the subject as its own innate, primordial, and pure luminosity.
It becomes manifest because, at that time, when the cognizer has the desire to see that object, he becomes all-pervasive.
As it has been said:
"When, as if by the mere desire to see, he remains pervading all objects..."
Then, what is the use of much speaking? One will understand for oneself.

Thus, as that object becomes pervasive, it is assimilated into one's own self; and the attainment of identification with that object is precisely the attainment of the nature of pure light, because the subject consists clearly of nothing but light. And this [attainment] cannot occur even with great effort without the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*).

It is indeed difficult to comprehend; however, when that [consciousness] exists, it manifests by itself. For this very reason it is said, "one will realize it by oneself. Otherwise, if its manifestation were not the attainment of the nature of the light of that [consciousness], but rather the nature of the object—like the quality of blue—it would not be manifest.
It would indeed be a provider of distinction; otherwise, without the assistance of another illuminator, its apprehension—just like that of the blue object—would not be possible.

He states the ultimate truth in summary with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*). "In every way" means in every manner.

If consciousness— meaning luminosity, in its technical sense as the state of being manifest— is resting upon an object-body (*artha-śarīra*) and not in the form of pure light alone, then [it occurs] in this way: "It manifests to me," that is,
by being attached to a subject, specifically by being related to a subject denoted by the word "I" ending in the genitive case.

The persistence—that is, the continued existence—of the luminosity belonging to the jar, which consists in its status as the agent of illumination, would be difficult to establish; for that which belongs to one thing cannot logically belong to another. Now, one might object: how is it that the cognizer, who exists as the cause [of the jar's manifestation], does not [belong to it]?

To show that he would [otherwise] be a relative [to the object], he says "the knower" (*pramātā*). For—because—at that time, namely at the moment of perception, the knower consists of the senses and so forth; being dependent on perception, he is attentive to the senses and so forth, and thus, while being of that very nature, he is the illuminator of the form of the object.

For the light that has been accepted as resting within the body of the object, there must necessarily be a cause—indeed, it must exist. Of what is it the cause, and like what? It is like the seed is for the sprout. But surely, by that very fact, its relationship to that [sprout] is established; to this he says: "And not... The sprout is produced from the seed.

The sprout—the essence of the sprout, having attained the state of being a sprout—is not always dependent on the seed; for in the performance of its own function, it is devoid of such dependence. In the same way, the Light (prakāśa), having acquired its own existence and resting within the body of the object, [appears] as if distinct.
The meaning is that it does not depend upon itself. He concludes the exposition with the word "tataḥ" (therefore).

"Tataḥ" means from that; "saḥ" refers to the object; at the time of its apprehension, it is "prakāśātmā"—that is, its nature is pure light by way of being the agent of illumination—if this were not the case, then [it would remain] as before.

Thus he explains the word "as before" (*yathā*) [in the phrase] "prior to the arising of knowledge. Just as this manifestation (*prakāśa*) exists prior to the arising of knowledge, so it should also exist at the time of the arising of knowledge. Now, one might object: knowledge is precisely of the nature of the manifestation of an object.

How, then, could there be an equality of the object regardless of whether cognition arises or does not arise? This might be the case if it were logically possible; however, since cognition—which is of the nature of illumination—is distinct from the object, how could it belong to that object? If, first of all, [the claim is] that "the object is illuminated" in this manner...

The meaning is that the nature of cognition would be non-luminous, because there would be no distinction between its being blue and its not being luminous; however, if a distinction exists, then our desired conclusion is established—this is the point. As it has been said:
And the supreme reality of that which is to be known is Śiva, whose nature is light;
for that which is not of the nature of light can possess neither luminosity nor even substantiality.

Thus, this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed of the nature of reasoning (*tarka*). For instance: "If the object were distinct from pure luminosity, then it would be non-luminous. Regarding the statement "smoke would not have existed": [the opponent asks] "In that case, how did the Teacher employ the discourse of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the introduction? The purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekyanumāna*) operates here: "That which has the nature of pure light exists because it is light," since the very object under consideration at the prior time serves as the instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and because a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is impossible, as the entire mass of objects has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*). Enough of this elaboration.

Here, in order to provide an introduction to the third quarter [of the verse], he raises the position of the logicians with the word "nanu" (now, but).
