For that reason, there would be an equality between the arising and non-arising of cognition with respect to the object—such as the object blue.

He accepts this according to the method of *tarka* (reductio) by saying, "It might be so. To the objection, "Well then, let it be so," he says, "If... Anticipating the question, "How is it not tenable? he explains the third quarter [of the verse] with the words "yāvatā" (since). Since—

Because [it exists] as a related entity—that is, by way of being a related thing (saṃbandhibhāvena); the instrumental case here denotes a specific state or manner (itthaṃbhāve). The meaning is: "How could it be? or "In what manner could it be?
Having introduced the manner in that context, he states the acceptance of the desired consequence (iṣṭāpatti):
Thus, it follows that there is indeed no difference between the object and its cognition, because the nature of the object has been stated to be cognition itself.

Furthermore, if light possesses the nature of the object—and since it has been stated that light consists of the very self of the object—the aforementioned refutation applies. Now, as for the claim that "cognition illuminates the object": [this is the case].

If it is argued that cognition produces an object as something manifesting its own nature (*svarūpa*), then the same fault recurs. Furthermore, this detailed analysis of the meanings of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) regarding the distinction between them has already been extensively developed by me in the *Bhedavidāraṇa* (or *Bhedavādavidāraṇa*); therefore, one should seek it there. Consequently:
There is not even the possibility that a distinct manifestation could be related to an object. And this follows from the following reasoning:
"if... Why does it follow? To this he says: "the object. That is, of the nature of the object—the very essence of the object.

"By way of being knowledge" means by way of having the nature of knowledge; "because it has been stated," the ellipsis being "even against one's will. Now, if it is asked, "What follows from that?", he says: "The object. Since light has the object as its own nature—that is, when it consists of the object—the aforementioned defect applies: the defect consisting of blindness regarding the nature of the object was just mentioned immediately prior.

It may be so. Now, he sets forth the position desired by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) with the word "atha" (now). For in the expression "it acts" (*karoti*), the sense is equivalent to "it is manifesting" (*prakāśamānam*) or "the jar manifests" (*ghaṭaḥ prakāśate*); and the fault in that case has already been stated. The meaning is "in the text. "From that very [source]" means from the very act of shattering duality. He concludes the stated point with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Stating the conclusion, he explains the fourth quarter [of the verse] with the words "and that" (*tac ca*); "by reasoning" (*upapattyā*) means by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇena*).
It has been established even against one’s will: what is it? To answer this question, he says:

the nature of the object is its manifestness (*prakāśamānatva*), which is its non-difference from manifestation (*prakāśa*). And if manifestation were one thing in the case of a jar and another in the case of a cloth, then...

This is the summarized meaning here: without being of the nature of light (*prakāśātmatayā*)—

Without attaining the nature of pure light— which is its own innate essence known as "pure illumination" through the state of being manifest— the object would remain unmanifest at the time of its apprehension just as it was before,
during the time of non-apprehension; yet since it does manifest, it is known to be within the Light.
The meaning is that there is an appearance of the very existing entity (*bhāva*) externally as "this-ness" (*idantā*). Now, one might object:

Now, in response to the inquiry: "Is that [light] different for each object, or is it one?"

The third quarter [of the verse] is to be construed by repetition. The meaning is that manifestation (*prakāśa*) would not be distinct; it would be one and the same. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of the existence of living beings, even if one were to admit that cognition, though distinct [from the object], has the nature of manifesting the object.
He states another refutation:
"If the illumination were distinct [from the object] yet non-different [from it], there would be a confusion of the object;
for the object to be illuminated must have the nature of illumination, and that which is not illumination cannot be established. (3)
If the luminosity that is the nature of cognition were indeed something other than the object— and for that very reason distinct from the object— then,

because it consists solely of luminosity within itself, there would be non-difference [between the two]. For instance, in the case of "the manifestation of blue" and "the manifestation of yellow," that which constitutes the blue portion and the yellow portion is not, first of all, [distinct from] the cognition.
Such is the nature of knowledge—[as stated in] K. ṣ. ṣ.]. Likewise, our own verse also says:
"The appearance of things situated within consciousness as if they were external is appropriate."
Therefore, because there is a division within consciousness as if among objects,
a jar situated within clay never abandons its nature as clay;
for that which exists within it is indeed its true essence, and not a difference.
Thus [it is said]. Now he provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "vyatirikte" (in that which is distinct). Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

"Of that which is distinct"—meaning of that which exists as a separate object; "even having accepted"—meaning even having conceded out of skillful argumentation; "another subverting proof"—meaning another subverting proof in the form of confusion (*saṅkara*). Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "bhinne."

From [the word] *sakāśāt*. He explains the word *bhinne* with the word *tarhi*. "In its own self" means in its innate nature called Light (*prakāśa*). He begins the effort to establish non-difference itself with the words *tathā hi*. [Otherwise] its own nature would result in the abandonment of the doctrine of difference. A distinction between blue and yellow must be admitted on account of their distinct manifestations; for how could it be consistent that by the very same manifestation through which blue is apprehended as "blue indeed," yellow is also apprehended?
Is it produced by the blue, produced by the yellow, or does it share the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīka*) as the blue?
The phrase beginning with "K. ṣ. ṣ. means that there is no disagreement on this point by anyone. As for the phrase "because it would entail the abandonment of the doctrine of difference":

the Vaiśeṣikas are indeed committed exclusively to the doctrine of difference; therefore, if they were to admit that cognition and its object possess an identical nature, [it would contradict their own system].

The sense is that there would be a total abandonment of their own desired doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*), and thus they would fall into the error of contradicting their own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). He raises another alternative with the word "atha" (now/if):
"the blue portion and the yellow portion are the objects of cognition"—that is, if this were the case.

This very thing is the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*). It is precisely this that is being investigated here. It must necessarily be accepted—that is, it must be admitted—otherwise its [the object's] establishment would be impossible. How could that which is accepted—namely, that "by that very light, yellow becomes yellow"—be consistent? That is to say, how could it be logical?

The point is that it is impossible for the cognition of blue to be the determiner with respect to yellow, nor for the cognition of yellow to be the determiner with respect to blue. Here, [the author] states "by the blue" (*nīlena*) to show that the twofold division of objects supported by certain Buddhist schools is not tenable: this manifestation is produced by the blue.

Having existed as an object, it is produced; for this very reason, it becomes the manifestation of blue. Being generated by yellow, it therefore becomes the manifestation of yellow. Or—meaning in the alternative case—it possesses the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*) as that [object];
that is, being endowed with the same causal complex as the blue, it becomes the manifestation of blue, and likewise with yellow, and so forth.

This is the intended meaning here: it is logical that all existing entities, having their existence conferred by momentary consciousness, are indeed momentary; and the momentariness of consciousness itself is well-established, since it arises anew with respect to each object at every moment. In this regard:
First, a momentary cognition produced by a sense faculty initiates its own continuum,
as does the momentary object that is its referent; therein, in the second moment of cognition,
the first moment of cognition becomes the material cause (*upādāna*) by virtue of being the initiator, while its referent— the momentary object— [likewise initiates its own continuum].

That which is asserted on the grounds that it is the cause for the manifestation of the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) could only hold true if the difference between blue and yellow were already established; yet that very difference is what remains to be investigated. Now, if this [consciousness] has the form of blue, then if it is due to the power of a reflection, it is untenable because a second original object (*bimba*) does not appear. Alternatively, if there is non-difference, [the same fault follows].

In that case, the doctrine of difference (bhedavāda) is abandoned; likewise, regarding the theory of instrumentality (*karaṇatā*) and so forth, how can a cognition situated on a mountain peak—which is produced by many factors such as blue objects and is intense in one instance and dull in another—become the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for that very same [cognition]? This is clearly evident in the case of the two subsequent [cognitions].

Knowledge and its object exist within a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrīka*), because knowledge is produced by both the object and the cognition, and the object is likewise produced by both the object and the cognition. As for the distinction between their respective material causes (*upādāna*) and auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), it is so slight as to be entirely insignificant. As it has been said:
"For a single fault is submerged when there is a collection of virtues, like the spot on the moon in its rays.

Thus, those very first and second moments of cognition and object, being produced by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), do not deviate from one another; therefore, this moment of cognition is related to this moment of the object, and so forth.

This should be understood to apply to the third [moment] and those following as well; however, for the first two, the establishment of their status is achieved solely through the relationship of produced and producer, so enough of this.
[The opponent objects: "Let it be exactly like that. To this, he says "ityādi" (and so forth). "Sa eva" means the very difference between blue and yellow.
And thus, the sense is that this is not tenable.
Now, he states the Buddhist position regarding formless and formed cognition with the word "atha" (now). "Asau" (this) refers to manifestation itself;
it becomes the form of blue, and for that very reason it becomes the manifestation of blue—this is the meaning. To this as well, he provides a rebuttal.
Regarding the word "tat": if that—namely, the state of having a blue form—occurs by the power of a reflection, then it is untenable because a second object (the original) is not perceived;

for a reflection of the form of a real object cannot be established in the absence of that object, since a reflection is impossible without its source. By this, the Buddhist position of formless consciousness (*nirākāra-vijñāna*) is refuted.

He also refutes the view of the proponents of *sākāra* (the theory that cognition possesses a form) with the word "atha" (*now*). If there is non-difference—that is, since only the form of the cognition exists, there is indeed non-difference between the object and the cognition—then even you have abandoned the doctrine of difference, just like the Buddhist Vijñānavādins; this is the implied meaning.

Now, in order to refute the view of the logicians (*tārkika*) who maintain that there is a superiority of knowledge based on a superiority of means (*upāya*) and a superiority of the objects of cognition (*prameya*), he says: "In the case of the instrument" (*karaṇe*). "Instrument" (*karaṇa*) means a means;

its state [is expressed by the suffix *-tva*]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of such effects as "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*) is intended. "In the discussion of that" (*tasmin vāde*) refers to the discourse concerning that [superiority]. For they [the logicians]...

They speak thus: "Cognitions are of a single nature and are differentiated solely by virtue of their instruments (*karaṇa*); for in some cases a particular instrument applies and not everything everywhere. Or they are differentiated by the object of cognition (*prameya*), for there is not one and the same object of cognition everywhere. To this, he states the refutation: "He who stands on the peak" (*śikharastha*). On the peak—

The meaning is: of such a person who stands upon a mountain peak—that is, a person who perceives everything simultaneously—whatever knowledge [there is], there is no differentiation because it is non-different from the body of light (*prakāśa*). And this being so, even when one or the other [object] is produced in perception...
If a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) were awakened by the perception of just one thing, it would follow that there would be a recollection of everything [else] by the force [of that alone];

thus, there would be great confusion. One might argue: "Let there simply be the object itself; what is the use of this manifestation (*prakāśa*), which only brings about such faults? To this, he replies: "For that which is unmanifest, there is no establishment at all."

It is not anything at all; for if within itself it is blue, or yellow, or nothing whatsoever, then what is it? That which begins with "more abundant blue" is *bahutaranīlādi*; that which is produced by this—whereby the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes "less abundant yellow" and so on—is sharp (*paṭu*) in one instance, namely, in the case of more abundant blue.
Otherwise—in a case where [the object] is drunk in a smaller amount and so forth—how could there be a distinction such that it is "weak"? Why?
Because the nature of light, which stands as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is of a single essence;
for in that regard, there is no distinction in the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which serves as the instrument, as is understood by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).

Regarding the doctrine that excellence in knowledge follows from excellence in the object of knowledge (*prameya*), one should oneself apply the following reasoning: how could the cognition of an object situated far away and an object situated nearby be sharp in one case and dull in the other?
For when the object is nearby, the cognition is sharp, whereas when that very same object is distant, the cognition is dull; this is because the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is one and the same.
It should be joined as a reason by oneself. He states another defect in the theory of instrumentality (*karaṇatāvāda*) with the word "tathā" (so).

And in such a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—that is, in a latent impression conducive to the simultaneous experience of all objects—and when there is the arising from the perception of one [object] among those many things previously experienced therein:

If [memory] were produced by perception alone, there would necessarily follow the consequence of remembering everything—that is, the consequence of remembering all objects experienced therein. For this reason, there would be an excessive confusion (saṅkara) in memory, because [the cause] is over-pervasive (vyāpti) with respect to memory; such is the sense. Therefore...
The sense is that the doctrine of causality and so forth is also not tenable because of this reason. By this, the first half [of the verse] has been explained.
Here, the student asks: "This might be so. This means: "Let this be the case."

In response to the inquiry "What [is it]? he says: "The object itself. By the phrase "by that which brings about defects"—meaning by that which entails defects such as the aforementioned confusion (*saṅkara*) and blindness—this establishes the third quarter of the verse (devoid of the word *artha*) and provides the introduction to the fourth quarter. The answer follows:

In order to explain the meaning of the fourth quarter along with its constituent words, which resides in the preceding quarter, he says: "To this, it is replied. When the question arises as to what is being said, he says: "Of that which is non-luminous. To the question "Why is there no establishment [of its existence]? he says: "In itself.
That is to say, in itself—merely in its own nature untouched by luminosity—if blue were yellow, or...

In the alternative case, nothing—or rather, something non-existent—might be said by someone; this is the ellipsis. What would be faulty [in that]? For this very reason, it has been stated elsewhere by the author himself: "In this way, these [objects], though appearing as if non-existent in the Self, are in reality nothing but the Light itself."
Inert objects exist only as manifestations of light, through their own selves and through the selves of others.

Thus: if that [object] is manifestation, then it becomes the object; and how could this [object] be manifestation? If the very nature of manifestation belongs to the jar, and that same [nature] belongs to the cloth, and so forth, then manifestation is established as the body of the entire universe. || 3 ||

"What would be corrupted?"—what fault would arise? For that blue object, having arisen, would not engage in a dispute, "I am blue," because, being insentient, it is mute; this is the sense. Here he cites the statement of the venerable Utpaladeva with the words "In this way. Since the commentary on this verse has already been provided previously, [it is not repeated here].

Again, an effort is made. Having set aside the third quarter for now, he provides an introduction by way of stating the result, in order to explain that very portion which is fit for exposition here; thus: "tat" (therefore).
"Tat" means: for that reason, if there were light (*prakāśa*), then the object (*artha*) would exist—that is to say, it would be established.

The disciple asks: "And [what is] manifestation? The sense is: how could that manifestation exist, by which the object is established? To state the answer, he explains the third quarter of the verse—omitting the word "object" (*artha*)—with the words "If... Manifestation occurs at that time. When is that? It is when "if," and so forth, occurs.

What is the meaning of this and so forth? That very luminosity which constitutes the body of a jar becomes the body of a cloth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is meant that it becomes the body of everything. This is also the meaning of the statement: "The self-luminous is the object of illumination. When it is the self-luminous...

This is an indication where the abstract state (bhāva) is primary: it is the nature of luminosity (*prakāśātmatā*). By implication, this is the form of luminosity that exists as the ultimate reality within all objects of knowledge;

it is the luminous object itself that becomes manifest, and not a separate light existing as a subject for each individual object, since the latter is merely a partial aspect of that [universal luminosity].

Because it is imagined as the subject (*grāhaka*), [the author] states that the intended object—which, though not explicitly mentioned in the sūtra, follows by implication—is established as the "one whose body is the universe" (*viśvavapuḥ*). The word "iti" is to be supplied; thus, "having the universe as its body" means being composed of all things, and so the Light (*prakāśa*) is established.
Thus, the summary here is as follows: in the *Prakāśa*—that is, in cognition—when it is "distinct" (*bhinne*), meaning distinct from its own object;

and likewise, when it is "non-distinct" (*abhinne*), then the object itself is the illumination (*prakāśa*). Since the word "object" (*viṣayasya*) is used in the singular to denote the genus, the meaning is "of objects" (*viṣayāṇām*).

One must conclude that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consists precisely in this capacity of the single Light to manifest such a manifold variety of forms, including the states of succession and non-succession, as well as the relationship between cause and effect. And this conclusion holds provided that the Light...

Any other cause for manifoldness has been refuted therein. In that case, since the light is itself non-manifold, its gradual manifestation as manifoldness must have a cause consisting of a reflection; and that which is of the same nature as that reflection is the external form, such as blue and so forth. And although that [external object] is indeed inferable, nevertheless—
Confusion (*saṅkara*) means a state of intermixture [C reads *māhārṇatā*], because all objects would be grasped by a single cognition;
and non-manifestation (*aprakāśa*) means that an object devoid of manifestation is not established, since an object becomes manifest only when it is of the nature of manifestation. || 3 ||
Now he provides the introductory commentary for the fourth and fifth verses with the words "of the one alone.
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"Of the one alone," meaning not of many, as they do not exist as distinct entities corresponding to each respective object.

Such are the sequential and non-sequential relations— those existing in the form of cause and effect and so forth— which abide by virtue of being either well-known or unknown in the world; for example,
the causal relation between Maheśvara and liberation, or between a potter and jars and the like.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) and so forth are included. These very [relationships] are manifold—of various kinds—which constitutes their "universal form" (*vaiśvarūpya*), meaning the state of possessing all forms. That which has the capacity for the manifestation of that [universal form] as its nature is such [a capacity]. This much—only this much—has been stated.

It must be brought to a conclusion—that is, it must be allowed to rest, which is to say, it must be determined. It comes to a conclusion—it rests. Thus, in response to the expectation of "how so?", he says "yadi" (if).
"Another cause"—a cause other than itself—is "apākṛtam"—set aside or removed—because otherwise, the consequence of duality would follow.
The state [of being]. In that regard, having understood the "appropriateness" of the non-sequential, it was said "in sequence";

the cause of variety is the "cause of variety," which consists of a reflection—that is, that which bestows a reflection. Of that reflection—the reflected image of the entity that has been transferred—[there is] that which is of the same kind, i.e., similar.

Because the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) are similar, the "external" refers to the external thing that constitutes the original object; the sense is that a reflection is impossible without an original object. [An objection: "In that case, how can you speak of this external object—which exists as something to be inferred—as being perceptible? To this, he says: "And that... (*tacca*). And that—
And as for the external [object], although it is inferable—

because it is determined by perception in the form "this is blue," and because the establishment of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is sustained by such determination— it will nonetheless be designated as "perceptual. This is what was stated by the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin).
He demonstrates [or shows] that another reason (*hetvantara*) is being suspected as having an external form that is being inferred:
"If that various accidental appearance were to cause one to infer an external object..."
For that which is undifferentiated consciousness cannot be the cause of variegated appearances.
Nor can a diverse awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) serve as the cause here; for what would be the basis for the diversity of that very awakening? (5)
In this context, consciousness is indeed non-different; for its ultimate reality is nothing but pure luminosity (*prakāśa*).
If the nature of the blue object were something in addition to luminosity, then, being of a non-luminous nature, it would not manifest.
Although it becomes an object of inference because it is understood through the sign (*liṅga*) known as a reflection (*pratibimba*), nevertheless, this...

"Blue" [is known] through perception— that is, by the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa)— due to determinative ascertainment (adhyavasāya), because the establishment of the means of valid cognition depends upon such ascertainment, and because the very existence of the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, is animated by determinative ascertainment; for whatever is a means of valid cognition with respect to a particular object...
The meaning is that whatever produces a determination (*adhyavasāya*) is established as such in that regard.

"Designatable by perception" (*pratyakṣavyapadeśya*) means fit for the designation "perception"; the intention is that it will come to be known in the world as "perception. "By those who maintain external objects" (*bāhyārthavādibhiḥ*) refers to certain Buddhists.
It has been stated; thus, another reason—a different reason from the one previously described—is presented. Of what nature is it?

It is such that the external form—the essential nature of external objects—is being inferred by it. He demonstrates this by way of being suspected—that is, as the object of suspicion—and he himself entertains that very suspicion.
...up to this point. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it, beginning with the word "tat" (that).

Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) first explains only the second half of the first verse, starting with "iha" (here): "abhinnaḥ" (undivided)— [The rest of the passage continues with the explanation of the verse.]

It is devoid of differentiation. To the question "From what is it non-different?", he says: "Light" (*prakāśa*). "Ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) refers to the innate nature (*sahaja-svarūpa*). He raises the objection of the proponents of cognition with form (*sākāra-jñānavādin*) by saying "light. [They argue that] "more than light" (*prakāśādhika*) means something additional to the nature called light; [this applies] to this consciousness (*bodha*). He provides the rebuttal with "then" (*tarhi*). That—

Now, if its very nature were simply luminosity (*prakāśatva*), how could there be the manifestation of yellow? Furthermore, if its essential nature (*svarūpa*) consisted solely in the successive manifestations of blue, yellow, and so forth, then in states such as deep sleep, there would be no manifestation of the form "I am devoid of the appearance of blue and the rest. Therefore:

Light is indeed light; since there is not even an atom's worth of another form within it, consciousness is non-different. And regarding that non-different [consciousness], the fact that there are diverse manifestations—such as the appearance of blue at one time and the appearance of yellow at another—is not logically possible if there were a single, undifferentiated cause.

The nature of the effect called "blue" is non-luminous; for it is not logical that an insentient blue object possesses luminosity—this is the intended meaning. It would not shine forth—for a palace that is not white does not become white.

The sense is that this is logical. The disciple raises an objection with "Now" (*atha*). The sense is: "Being manifest as blue" (*nīlaprakāśabhāva*) is its very nature (*svarūpa*); therefore, it is not proper to question its own nature.
To this, he states the rebuttal: "Yellow" (*pīta*), etc. The sense is that a transformation of one's own nature is impossible. Again...

He raises an objection with the word "atha" (now/if). "Tasya" refers to that consciousness; its "svarūpam" (essential nature). Again, he provides a rebuttal with the word "nīla" (blue): "devoid of the manifestation of blue and so forth"—meaning, being devoid of the manifestation of blue by virtue of appearing as pure "I"-consciousness—this occurs in states such as sleep, namely in states such as deep sleep and fainting. [Objection: But in those cases...

The appearance of the self (*ātman*) is not even experienced. True; although the appearance of the self exists there, because it is an object of mere luminosity and has not ascended to the level of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it is as if non-existent, yet it is not non-existent in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), since it exists as the witness of ignorance (*ajñāna-sākṣitayā*). Otherwise, one would not have the recollection, "I was not aware of anything."

The sense is that this is because a subsequent memory would be impossible. And thus, the sense is that the appearance of blue and so forth is not its own nature (i.e., the nature of the cognition itself). He provides the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
"Another form" (*rūpāntaram*) means the nature of blue and so forth, which is a different nature; for this reason—

"Undivided" (*abhinna*) means devoid of differentiation. And of that undivided consciousness (*bodha*), "at some time"—that is, at the moment of perceiving blue, and likewise in the case of yellow and so forth—"of such a kind" refers to those manifestations (*ābhāsāḥ*).
"In them"—meaning within those manifestations—the word "of that" (*tasya*) is to be construed with both [the preceding and following terms], like the eye of a crow. Why?

In response to the inquiry as to why [the previous position] is not tenable, he says "in the cause. Regarding "in the cause"—that is, in the cause known as awakening—he explains his own intended meaning in the first half-verse with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
The repetition "each and each" (*sa sa*) is used for emphasis (*vīpsā*).
Because it is impossible [for such a cause to exist], that very form— variegated, blue, yellow,

and so forth— is accidental; having its cause established by unperceived direct perception, it is, by virtue of its fitness (*aucityāt*), the producer of an external object consisting of a reflection within consciousness as its own intrinsic nature.

The proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādī) maintains that [the object], which resembles its own form and consists of a multitude of distinct aspects appearing in succession, is inferred as being entirely separate from cognition. || 4 ||

And this is not merely a matter of conjecture for him; rather, it culminates in certainty. For instance, the reason stated by the Vijñānavādin—that the cause of diversity consists in the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is not tenable. To begin with, [the opponent defines] *vāsanā* as "a formative impression (*saṃskāra*) that generates memory."

Duality. By this, the phrase "that and that" is explained. "Accidental" (ākasmika) means arisen spontaneously from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), due to the impossibility of an objective support (*ālambana*) or a causal agent (*kāraka*). In response to the inquiry "From what cause did it arise spontaneously?", he provides a qualifying attribute containing the reason: "unknown" (*ajñāta*). "External" (*bāhya*)—

The construction should be understood as: "it makes known the external object. In response to the inquiry as to what kind of external [object] it is, he states the qualifiers beginning with "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). In consciousness—that is, in the cognition described as being directed toward apprehension and undivided—the [object] has entered; that is, it appears as a form (*ākāra*), and for that very reason, it consists of a reflection (*pratibimba*).

It is that which brings about its own nature in the form of a reflection. Likewise, by way of propriety—that is, by virtue of being appropriate—it is similar to its own form, namely its own essential nature called "appearance" (*ābhāsa*); for it is not logical that a reflected image should be dissimilar to the original object (*bimba*). Thus, they descend in succession.
That which has as its self those forms whose divisions are more numerous— that is, exceedingly many— is, in other words,

endowed with manifold distinctions like the various manifestations [of consciousness]. Likewise, it leads one to infer— that is, to act as the agent toward an inference— that [the object] is distinct from cognition, which is described as non-different from awareness.
"It impels the cognizer who is engaged [in perception]"—this is how the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādī*) should be understood to conceive [the situation].

By this, it is indicated that the *liṅ* suffix here denotes "conception" (*saṃbhāvanā*), and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule *ṇeraṇau*. By this, the first verse has been explained. || 4 ||

[Objection: "In that case, is this not merely a possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) and not a reality? To this he says: "And not... The fact that this is a possibility is stated here according to his own philosophical system, as indicated by the word "of this" (*asya*). [The term] "ending in certainty" (*niścayaparyavasāyi*) means resting in certainty; that is to say, it is certain. This...

He begins the explanation of the first half of the second verse by saying "tathā hi" (for instance). That which is characterized by the sublation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is well-known; however, in this context, it is the cause of the diversity of experience (*anubhavavaicitrya*).

This remains to be investigated. Or rather, let there be a potency (*śakti*) consisting of the fitness (*yogyatā*) of cognition, which has the nature of the capacity to produce appearances such as blue and so forth; this potency is the *vāsanā*.
Its "awakening" (*prabodha*) is its orientation toward the production of its own effect; from that, the variety of appearances arises within cognitions.

To this we reply: although it may be said that the appearances existing within cognition are not ultimately real and possess only conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisattva*), nevertheless, whatever is their cause must be substantially real (*vastusat*).
It must be accepted that for a non-entity— which is characterized by the absence of all causal capacity—
it is impossible for there to be an essential nature consisting of the power whose life-force is the accomplishment of an effect. This being the case,
if those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which are desired as the causes of manifestation were distinct from consciousness (*bodha*), [then...]

Form (rūpa) is that which exists in the ultimate sense (paramārthasat); therefore, this is merely a variety of the theory of external objects (bāhyārthavāda), disguised by different terminology. Alternatively, if [memory] consists in the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā), it proves its own impossibility; for memory does not [arise] in this context—within this subject matter.

The cause of the diversity of experience—the object that produces the diversity of experience—is that which is to be sought and investigated; thus, the sense is that by discussing one topic, another has inadvertently been introduced. He states an alternative view with the words "or let it be. And of that—of the power—from that—due to that awakening.
Regarding this, he states the rebuttal with the words "even there. He fulfills his initial proposition (*pratijñā*) with the word "here" (*iha*).
The term "non-ultimate reality" (*apāramārthikatva*) is stated as a synonym for "conventional existence" (*saṃvṛtisattva*);

[the object] is indeed "substantially real" (*vastusat*), meaning "ultimately real" (*paramārthasat*), and not merely conventionally real. In response to the expectation of why this is so, he says: "of that which is non-existent" (*avastunaḥ*).

That which possesses the absence of all capacity is "devoid of all capacity" (*sarvasāmarthyavirahī*); the state of being such is "the condition of being devoid of all capacity" (*sarvasāmarthyavirahitā*). That is its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—that is, its unique property (*asādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*).
Of such a thing, that which consists of capacity is "animated"—meaning its existence (*sattā*) is bestowed—by the accomplishment of its effects.
Its nature consists in capacity, because that [nature] is not established. Now, one might ask: "Let it be so; what of it?
To this he says: "In this way. And that form—being concealed by another term—is expressed by the word *vāsanā* (latent impression) rather than by the word *apūrva* (the unseen force). Therefore...

If they are conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*), then causality is untenable in that form. Alternatively, if they possess ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatā*) in whatever form they exist, then by that same form they would have causality; in that case, since that [reality] is mere cognition and is undifferentiated, the differentiation of effects in the form of appearances such as blue and so forth would be unestablished. Thus...

If the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are not diverse, what hope can there be for their awakening to be diverse? Or, even if the latent impressions were distinct, since there exists no diverse cause—such as space, time, or objects—that is distinct from pure consciousness and yet intended to be the awakener, the awakening would remain non-diverse; thus, it is one and the same.

If it were the case that awakening occurs, then the manifold variety of blue and other objects would appear simultaneously. Now, if it is argued that the various cognitions (or other acts of awareness) existing within one's own continuum are the causes of this awakening, that is incorrect; for [the distinctions of] pleasure, pain, blue, yellow, and so forth, as well as spatial directions such as prior and posterior—
It is concealed; thus, the sense is that there would be the consequence of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

He refutes another alternative by first raising an objection with the word "atha. *Saṃv�it-sat* means non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*); *kāraṇatāyā anupapattiḥ* means unfitness (*ayogyatā*) for being a cause.

The meaning is: "because it has been stated immediately prior. He raises another objection with the word "tathā" (so). Regarding these—namely, the latent impressions (*vāsanās*)—the proponent of the inferable object states his acceptance of the consequence with "tattarhi" (then that).
"That" refers to the ultimate form; "mere cognition" (*jñānamātra*) means pure, transcending the nature of the object.

It is light (*prakāśa*), because that alone is the essence of everything; and that [light] consists of consciousness-only (*jñānamātra*), which is the ultimate nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Now, one might object: "Let there be unity in the latent impressions themselves, but let their awakening possess variety;
it is that very variety which serves as the cause for the diversity of external objects. To this, he says: "In this way" (*evam*). [This occurs] regarding that which is not an object (*aviṣaye*).
When [the latent impressions] have become active, a contrary hope is "counter-hope" (*pratyāśā*).

Even while admitting the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he says, "Or let them be," in order to explain with the second half of the second verse that their awakening is indeed devoid of variety. This is because [of their absence].

Thus, the sense is that otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of non-duality (*advaita*). "Awakening" (*prabodha*) means the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); "simultaneously" (*samameva*) means at one and the same time. Here, the Vijñānavādin reveals his own intention with the word "Now" (*atha*). "In one's own continuum" (*svasantāne*)—

"Existing in one's own continuum" (*svasantānavartīni*) means they abide within one's own—namely, one's individual—continuum, which consists of a collection of moments of cognition such as the perception of blue and so forth.
"Other cognitions" (*jñānāntarāṇi*) refers to cognitions other than the cognition called "illumination" (*prakāśa*), which is non-different from it. He also refutes this point.
That is incorrect;

for if the difference in time were of the nature of mere cognition, and if cognition’s ultimate reality consisted solely in its luminosity, then, given the impossibility of any difference in essential nature, it would be so.

Because it is logically untenable for consciousness to lack differentiation. This same mode of non-differentiation applies equally to other internal cognitions that take the form of an external subject and are designated by the term "other mental continua" (*saṃtānāntara*).
There too, [it applies] to the body—intended by others to be thin, fat, and so forth—and to the vital breath, such as inhalation and exhalation, which belong to another.

Regarding pleasure, pain, and other qualities of cognition: if there is no difference from the nature of pure consciousness—which you yourselves admit to be merely a subtle atom—then we do not know what could possibly possess "otherness" (paratva). If it is argued that this belongs to the "awakening" (bodha) residing therein, then if that too is not [established] by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), [it is untenable].

It establishes non-existence itself [of the object] by means of "pleasure" (*sukha*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "pleasure, pain, blue, yellow, and so forth," all external objects are included; and by the word "and so forth" in the phrase "the distinction between those [objects] and space and time," which consist of prior, posterior, and so on, the distinctions such as south and so forth are included. As for the domain of time:
The inclusion of terms such as "long" and "quick" [is for the sake of illustration]. When there is the nature of consciousness-only—

that is, when the nature of reality is consciousness-only because otherwise the non-duality of consciousness would be untenable— and when consciousness has as its ultimate reality nothing but luminosity—
This being the case— that its essential nature consists solely of the manifestation of the supreme (para)—
and this has been stated precisely according to the opponent’s own tenets, for in the Buddhist system, the establishment of an eternal manifestation is nowhere found. Likewise,
since it follows that no differentiation of the intrinsic nature of consciousness is possible, [the opponent’s position collapses].

The meaning is that since it is impossible for there to be a difference in nature between cognitions, it is incorrect to speak of "other cognitions" (*bodhāntara*); and by that same logic, the diversity of the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is also untenable. Now, one might object:
"Other cognitions are simply the cognitions whose nature is that of other subjects (*parapramātṛ*), not those residing within a single subject. Thus...
Anticipating the objection that "the fault you have stated does not follow," he says, "The other [party]...

The manner of non-distinction—that is, the manner of non-difference—is such that even there, because pure consciousness (*bodha*) is one, the difference produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body is of no consequence; this is the intended meaning. In response to the inquiry "In what way is it equal?", he says, "Even there..."

"Believed by others" means that which is believed to belong to another; for in the Buddhist view, since the collection of qualities (*guṇasamūha*) alone constitutes the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), the term "emaciated" is used. Furthermore, the terms "breath" and "quality of cognition" are stated according to the conventions of the logicians (*tārkika*). "Believed by the inferer" means that which is postulated as the agent of inference.

Since his nature is pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), and because there is no difference—meaning that in the absence of differentiation due to being of the nature of pure cognition—we do not know (we realize) whose "otherness" (*paratva*) could there be.

That which is established is indeed non-existent; for even if it were established, if it were by way of being an object of knowledge (*prameya*), it would be nothing but insentient (*jaḍa*). And yet, even so...

Knowledge has a nature consisting solely of cognition, just like the body and so forth; for if its form were merely self-awareness (*svasaṃvinmātra*), it would not be established for another person. Now, one might object: "In one's own self, activity such as speech is seen to be pervaded by the cause consisting of the desire in the form 'I shall speak'; therefore, in Caitra’s body as well, [speech] must be caused by that [desire]."
It must be so. Furthermore, it is ascertained through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) that there is no volition falling within one's own continuum;
therefore, the volition of another is established, and that itself is a different continuum.
Again, he raises an objection with the words "of consciousness" (*bodhasya*). [The phrase] "resting upon that" means delimited by another body and so forth.

To this, he states the following reply: "He too" (*sopi*). "He too"—that consciousness which is fixed upon that [object]—even though it is insentient (*jaḍatve*), its nature is pure knowledge; the sense is that otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*). To the objection that this [consciousness] is not established as an object of cognition (*prameya*), but rather as the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), he says:

Regarding the phrase "self-awareness" (*svasaṃvit*): because that cognition which consists solely of self-awareness is unestablished—since the awareness of one thing cannot have another thing as its object—this is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
"If the Self were an object of knowledge..."
And so forth. He asks "nanu" (surely) in order to state that [the self] is established through inference. "Vyāhārādikriyā" refers to actions such as speech;
by the word "ādi" (etcetera), actions such as movement are included. "Tat" means for that reason; "tayā" means by that visible action of speech and so forth belonging to Caitra’s body.

"Caused by that"—meaning caused by desire; "must necessarily exist"—the remainder of the sense being that it must exist just like my own actions of speech and so forth. Now, one might object: "Let that desire also belong only to the knower"; to this he says, "And not... The word "ascertained" means that there is no doubt whatsoever in this regard. And therefore—from that.
The striving of another (*parasamīhā*) means the desire of another; it "is established" (*siddhyati*), that is, it attains accomplishment (*siddhi*).
That very thing—namely, the striving of another—is indeed established, but not consciousness.
Another continuum (*santānāntara*) refers to the continuum belonging to another person, as just mentioned immediately before. And the strivings [of others] are indeed quite evident.
And its manifold variety is explained by that very [text] here: "In this context, the appearance of the inferrer's discourse is twofold:
at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), it takes the form 'I, whose life-force is uninterrupted, am speaking.'"

Furthermore, at the time of inference, since the apprehension of pervasion is lived through as a separation—namely, "this person speaks"—and the appearance [of the speaker] is one thing while the pervasion is grasped as another, how could this now serve as the logical reason (*hetu*)? Since the reason for the appearance that "he speaks" remains entirely unknown, how could the intended action be inferred from that reason? Moreover, regarding "this person speaks":

How could that manifestation which appears as something divided to another cognizer—whom one regards as an inferential subject—be the effect of the volition of another, which is regarded as the object of inference? For the effect of that [volition] is the manifestation "I speak," which has its life in non-interruption. And [an effect] consisting of non-interruption...

The sense is that it is logical that the effect consists of a [perceived] interruption; thus, the awakening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for grasping such a relationship between cause and effect is known. To introduce a fault even here, he says: "To this it is replied.
He makes the proposition fruitful by saying: "In this world"—that is, in this world, there is the appearance of discourse (*vyāhārābhāsa*).
The manifestation is of the nature of verbal expression, because the entire collection of entities consists of nothing but manifestation.

He explains this very twofold state by analyzing it as "pervasion" (*vyāpti*). Its life-force is uninterrupted—meaning it is inherently free from differentiation due to its resting in the "I. To the question "What is that?", he says: "the I" (*aham*).

"Life characterized by separation"—meaning life based on division, the sense being that manifestation occurs through dependence on another. "Of the other"—of that whose life is non-separation—"pervasion" refers to the relationship of pervader and pervaded existing together with its own inherent intention.
How could "the other"—that which has life characterized by separation—exist "now," at the time of inference?

The meaning is that it would not be so. He states another fault with the words "he speaks" (*vyāharati*). The sense is that [the other's intention] is indeed unknown, for the desire of another is not perceptible to anyone. "From that cause" means from an unknown cause. Again, he states another fault with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*). "In another cognizer" means in one other than the cognizer in the form of the speaker.

To the question "Why should it not be so?", he says: "For of that... [tasyā hi]. Now, one might object: let the effort of another (*parasamīhā*) not be the effect of an appearance consisting of separation; however, the very appearance consisting of separation, which serves as its cause, could indeed be the effect. To this, he says: "of such a kind" (*tathābhūta*). Of that which is of such a kind—
Regarding such a being: from what source does its existence arise? To this he says, "For not... Why is it not established? To this he says, "The other...

Even if it were preceded by the establishment of another, why [is it not possible]? To this he says, "The other... Because there is no means for establishing another cognizer, [due to the absence of a means of apprehension—K. ṣ. ṣ.], for this which exists within one's own self...

It is established by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that this [consciousness], which possesses an uninterrupted manifestation, produces a manifestation of the form "this" regarding another [object] that is manifested as interrupted; for this matter is preceded by the establishment of another,
and the establishment of another cognizer (*pramātṛ*) depends upon such a state of affairs.
Because [the establishment of such an object depends on this], there is a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Nor is there a rule that an uninterrupted [perception] must necessarily be followed by an interrupted one, for there is deviation from such a rule. Furthermore, even if an interrupted appearance were to arise, its production is not certain merely through the mental synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) of that [appearance].

For it would be appropriate to say "even when that exists, because this does not arise" only if there were another thing; however, no such establishment of a second entity exists, because only a single consciousness remains—this is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
Even when another person is established as "other" by others, as long as that other has not been made one's own,
it is impossible to say, "The Buddha is other than this other."
Furthermore, a Buddha could not participate in conventional discourse through a distinction between the Buddha and awakening;
for if Buddhahood were something separate [from the person], why would everything not be considered awakened?
Thus [he says]. He also introduces the fault known as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) here with the words "being such" (*evaṃbhūta*).
"Being such" means that the object which is unestablished—the entity called the "other"—is dependent upon, or contingent on, that;
because of this mutual dependence, there is the establishment of the other through the establishment of the inference, and the establishment of the inference through the establishment of the other.
The proof of another [mental] continuum results in the fallacy known as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Now, one might object:
"Let there be no causal relationship between these two, yet the rule [of their concomitance] must still exist. To this he replies: "And not... The reason is "because of deviation" (*vyabhicārāt*);
the sense is that at times a mere, uninterrupted appearance is observed. Now, one might ask: "But..."
Because a fragmented manifestation arises merely from the subsequent mental synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) of the cognizer, he says "and not" (*na ca*).

From that synthesis—that is, from the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) belonging to the cognizer who is the substratum of the unfragmented manifestation—the production of that [fragmented manifestation], namely the production of the fragmented manifestation, does not occur. To the question "Why is it not restricted? he says:

Regarding the phrase "in its existence": even when that exists—that is, even when there exists an inferring subject who is the locus of uninterrupted manifestation—this [object] of interrupted manifestation does not arise; yet, when that [subject] is absent, it arises. Therefore, let the interrupted manifestation arise elsewhere.

Since that which is produced elsewhere together with such an effort (*samīhā*) has a disconnected appearance, it is not logical to grasp a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) therein; thus, when [the opponent's] proof is unestablished, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself remains unestablished.
Furthermore, if other subjects (*pramātṛ*) are distinct, then the appearances residing within them—

Indeed, there is only difference, according to the principle that "it is non-distinct from ignorance. Consequently, because there would be an absence of resting upon a single manifestation, the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) of cognizers acting together could not exist; thus, the world would consist of mutually uncolored entities, resembling primordial nature (*prakṛti*) seized by the elements.

It would follow [that it is non-existent]. Furthermore, if another cognition being inferred were distinct from the cognition accepted by the inferrer, then that [other cognition] does not exist at all because of its non-arising—that is, due to the absence of its production; for the discourse of another is not necessarily present therein.

The meaning is as follows: "In its existence" means even when the inferrer exists; for the opponent does not speak only in the presence of an inferrer—this is the sense. Now, one might object: "This is known through inference. To this he says: "severed.
Whatever effort—that is, whatever desire the inferrer may have—is irrelevant, because the pervasion itself remains unestablished; what then can be said of the object to be inferred?
[The author] states: "The state [of being].

Even having accepted the existence of other cognizers, he presents two alternatives; then, recognizing that the undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) follows in the case of non-difference, he demonstrates the fault regarding the position of difference.
"And other subjects" means they are distinct; the sense is that they are distinct from one another.

"Residing in them"—that is, residing in other subjects—refers to the manifestations, namely the manifestations of objects. To the question "Why is there indeed a difference? he says: "from cognition," [referring to] the object.

It becomes non-different from knowledge; it becomes of one and the same form as knowledge. Therefore, the sense is that since there is a mutual difference among the subjects (*pramātṛ*) whose nature is knowledge, a difference in objects (*artha*) for each subject is indeed logical. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And therefore... That very object is one.

With respect to one [person], it would have that form; with respect to another, it would not have that form, or perhaps it would be nothing at all. Consequently, even the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding that object would necessarily differ for each cognizer—this is the summary.
Now, [an objection]: let there be no collective linguistic convention; what of it? To this, he says: "mutually... [anyonya].

Thus [it is said]. "Mutually uncolored" means not mutually connected; it would "result"—that is, it would come to pass—and the implication is that the world would become nothing but a mass of madness. He also points out another defect with the words "being inferred": "another cognition" refers to a cognition belonging to another person. What possibility could there be [for such a thing]?
To this he says: "That which...
The word "that which" (*yat*) implies possibility—that is, the possibility that there exists an object of cognition (*prameya*) distinct from consciousness.

Since the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) and other such arguments are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), what [is gained] by [the claim that the object] is not distinct even from the entire mass of objects of cognition, such as blue, yellow, and so forth?
That by which its rest in its own nature is not tolerated constitutes an offense;
therefore, even other subjects are non-existent [for that subject], or if they were existent,
the manifestations contained within all those other subjects would produce a variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— the cause for the variety of manifestations— in each and every one of them.

Even if it were granted that there is no other cause for this restriction (*niyama*), the diversity of blue and other objects would still not be established; for in this way, the various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the causes for their awakening remain unaccounted for. Therefore, it remains a settled conclusion that consciousness is non-different, because it is impossible for it to be the cause of a difference in manifestations that occurs without a [corresponding] cause.

If it is argued by the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) that "an external object is inferred," why [is this so]? The remainder [of the argument] is: the object of cognition (*prameya*) must be distinct from the cognition itself, just like another cognition that has become an object of cognition. [Objection: But surely there is the simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*) of the object of cognition with the cognition?

To the objection that since [the object] is seen in this very way, how is its difference from consciousness logical, he says: "simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambha*). Because of its inconclusiveness—that is, because of its deviation—since in states such as deep sleep, pure consciousness alone is experienced even without an object of cognition (*prameya*); and as for the status of ignorance (*ajñāna*) as an object of cognition in that state, that too is nothing at all.
The meaning is as follows: [the opponent might object], "Let this possibility exist; what is the harm? To this he says, "Blue," etc.
The point is that, just like the cognition which has become an object of knowledge (*prameya*), the object of knowledge such as blue would also necessarily be distinct from the subject (*pramātṛ*);
and that is not desired. He states the conclusion with the words, "Therefore," etc., even while conceding [for the sake of argument] its establishment.

He states the fault with the words "in the case of [their] establishment" (*siddhau*). "In each one of the others" (*ekaikatra paratra*) means in each of the subsequent ones; "they would produce" (*janayeyuḥ*) means they would generate [them].
And thus, the meaning is that the non-awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) could never be possible.
To the question "Why would they produce them?", he says "in the case of restriction" (*niyame*). Now, if it is asked "What is the fault?", he says "even so" (*tathāpi*).

The meaning is that variety (*vaicitrya*) is indeed manifestation in succession; it would not be possible if all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) were awakened at all times. He provides a conclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*). He states the resulting implication with "and therefore" (*tataśca*).
The word "iti" marks the completion of the commentary on the two verses. [This is] in order to effect the connection of the two verses.

He supplies the words "of the agent" and "of the action" by means of the word *yadi*. By the word *yadi*, there is an explanation of the term *cet*; the verse states the matter indicated by the word *cet*. By this, it is indicated that the word *cet* is to be construed as having a displaced position [in the verse].
This is the meaning of the two verses. The word "if" (*cet*) indicates a doubt regarding the meaning of the sentences in the two verses.
By thus presenting it as something being suspected, the firm conviction of the opponent is demonstrated. (5)
Now, however, in order to weaken this assumption, he says:
"This might be so; since practical activity is concluded within those very appearances themselves, what is the use of another external object that is logically untenable? (6)

When the phrase "it might be so" (*syād etat*) is explained as an acceptance of the aforementioned possibility, then what [is the meaning]? In that case, the construction here is as follows: if the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) states the object [of the action] by means of the agent (*kartṛ*), then why [is it said] "that and that," and so forth?
He summarizes the intended meaning of the two verses briefly with the word "evam" (thus).

"Parasaṃbhāvanā" refers to the expectation held by a Buddhist who maintains that external objects are inferable, directed toward a Buddhist who maintains the Vijñānavāda (Cognition-Only) doctrine; it is used in the sense of being something suspected or anticipated.
"By being shown as the object of apprehension"; "shown" [is used here], and the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of "in this manner" (*itthaṃbhāve*). || 5 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "at present" (adhunā).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"enām"—that which was spoken by the proponent of external objects, as expressed in those two verses.

"Believed in" (saṃbhāvitā) means: to loosen—that is, to weaken by means of reasoning (tarka), but not to remove it completely, because that is the specific function of valid cognition (pramāṇa). By the word "so long as" (tāvat), it is indicated that we shall indeed remove this [belief] even by means of valid cognition. Having thus provided the introduction:
Having set forth the verse, he explains it with the words "syādetat.
Here, the *Ṭīkā* provides a twofold explanation of this phrase "syādetat," as previously stated.

When that which was stated in the two immediately preceding verses— the presumption of external objects (*bāhyārthasaṃbhāvanā*)— is accepted, that is, when it is admitted and brought within the scope of explanation,
[it is said] "but" (*kintu*), as indicated by the remainder of the sentence.

It should be explained that by means of the phrase "tu" (but) as a syntactic supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*), another possibility regarding the weakening of that [position] is shown in the following verse. However, if the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is not tolerated, then it should be construed as a single sentence: "This might be so"—that is, this too would be another possibility which is expressed by this verse.
Even by this painful hypothesis of yours, which seeks to establish external objects, nothing at all needs to be accomplished by them;

for practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is established by those appearances alone which you yourself have accepted. Indeed, there is no practical activity with something that is eternally inferable; so what is the use of an external object where there is no means of proof?

The meaning is: having supplied the ellipsis of the sentence as "the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the sublater (*bādhaka*) [are absent], because there is no manifestation even by way of being inferable if there were a difference from manifestation"; "having that as its object of laxity" means having as its object the laxity of the aforementioned possibility—that is to say, it indicates that [laxity].
Regarding "another kind of presumption" (*saṃbhāvanāntaram*): there is another presumption consisting in the impossibility of [the object] being external;

this is shown by the remainder of the verse, beginning with "in the appearances" (*avabhāseṣu*). It should be explained as follows: it is brought to the state of being cognizable through knowledge. However, this is to be understood as being brought [to that state] by virtue of its status as the "remainder" (*śeṣatayā*).
The meaning is that an explanation of this [verse] must be provided. To provide a second explanation of this very [verse], he says, "yadi tu" (but if).

The word "syādetat" (this might be) is to be construed as part of a single syntactical unit; such is the connection. How so? Why [is it asked]? This too may be another possibility; what is this? [It is explained] by means of this verse.

By the remainder of the verse beginning with "in the manifestations" (*avabhāseṣu*), that which is stated is meant to be fulfilled by this verse to satisfy the expectancy of the word "this" (*etad*). He explains the remaining portion of the verse with the words "by this" (*anayā*).
"By this" means by that which consists of inference; "by them" refers to the external [objects]. To the question "Why should it not be done?", he replies with the word "manifestations" (*ābhāsaiḥ*).

"By them"—meaning by those [objects] imagined as reflections of objects. Now, one might object that they do not exist in my view; therefore, he says "by you. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of establishing worldly transaction" (*vyavahārasiddheḥ*): this is based on the principle that "as is the Yakṣa, so is the offering," meaning that worldly transaction, which consists of appearances, is established by means of objects that likewise consist of appearances.

The meaning is that accomplishment (*siddhi*) is logical. Now, in response to the expectation of how practical activity (*vyavahāra*) can still occur even by those [means], he states the second reason with the words "for not" (*na hi*). He states the conclusion with the word "thus" (*iti*). "Thus" means for this reason; what is gained by the external? The meaning is that nothing is gained because it is useless. By what external thing? In which—where.

Externally, there is no means of proof for the practitioner, nor is there any sublation [of the object]—in this way, it becomes primary, that is, principal, because it is the direct sublater. Why is this so?
From the Light (prakāśa).
First, there is the primary [objection]: the impossibility of the existence [of a whole] in its parts; the non-establishment of inherence (*samavāya*);
the conjunction of contradictory properties such as shaking and not shaking, being covered and not covered, being colored and not colored, and the distinction between different spatial directions;
and, if there were a difference [between the whole and its parts], the absence of manifestation even by way of inference.

In order to clarify the fitness for the employment of the word "tāvat," he states that even the secondary obstacles (*gauṇā bādhakāḥ*) are [included] as "additional arguments" (*abhyuccaya*). By "additional argument"—that is, by way of corroboration (*anvācaya*), meaning as a consequence (*prasaṅga*)—there are these obstacles.
For this very reason they are secondary; whereas previously there was a direct external obstacle, these [obstacles] exist only by way of consequence.

Regarding the term "sublating factors" (*bādhakāḥ*): the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "as follows," meaning "I shall demonstrate them. He demonstrates those very sublating factors with the words "of the whole" (*avayavinaḥ*). "Of the whole"—that is, of that which consists of things such as a cloth—the "impossibility," namely the lack of logical consistency in its existence, within its parts, such as the threads, is the sublation of the whole.

For instance, does the whole (avayavin) reside in all its parts or in one? If it resides in all, does it do so in its entirety or individually? If it resides in its entirety, then since the designation "whole" would be established by the parts alone, the postulation of a whole would be redundant; if, however, it resides individually in one [part], [then...]

Since the whole (avayavin) is not fully present [in each part], what else could remain? If the position is that it resides in one [part], then it follows that the others would lack the status of being parts; for a part exists only as dependent upon the whole.
As for the claim that "inherence is unestablished," this refers to the view that the whole resides in its parts by way of inherence (samavāya).

This is well known: by what does inherence (samavāya) abide there, since conjunction (saṃyoga) is impossible? If it is argued that it abides "by means of inherence," then by what would that [second inherence] abide? Thus, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would result. Alternatively, because inherence is merely postulated among those very threads by way of their arrangement (sanniveśa), inherence is not established as an ultimate reality (paramārtha).
Regarding "trembling and non-trembling": when one side of an object, such as a foot, is moved, there is trembling on that side and non-trembling on the other;
this would not be possible if it were a single unity. The same should be understood regarding concealment and non-concealment, and so forth.
"Distinction made by spatial divisions" refers to distinctions such as east, west, and so on; this is the distinction of spatial divisions (*digbhāgabhedah*).
Even in the doctrine that the external world is a collection of atoms, since there is no aggregate other than the collection itself, there are only atoms;

and if these atoms are joined together in immediate proximity, there must necessarily be a distinction of spatial parts (*digbhāgabhedah*). This is because when six atoms are assembled around a central atom in the six directions, [the central atom would have to possess six distinct sides].

If another atom were attached to the very same location where one atom of the middle-sized atom is fixed, then it would be merely a single atom. If, however, one is in one place and the other is in another,
then it must necessarily be [two distinct atoms].

There would be the consequence of the division of parts; thus, being merely a part—and indeed, being ultimately real as a mere part—it follows that this same path applies to it as well, so that nothing remains external in reality.
Nor should it be argued that this is impossible because material objects cannot occupy the same location, given their conjunction.
Because exclusion [of the whole] does not occur due to their being in different locations, [the opponent might argue]:
"Let there be no composite whole; rather, it is the atoms themselves, when aggregated, that become the external object.
To this, he says: "The atom" (*aṇu*). "Of another"—meaning distinct from the atoms—the atoms alone are the external [object].

The construction is: "they come to be. To the question "But what follows from that?", he says: "And those... And those—meaning the atoms—and because they are without interval, that is, because they are in a state of aggregation; "then"—at that time—"the distinction of spatial divisions" (digbhāgabheda)—that is, the occurrence of a division into six parts in the six directions; and the sense is that this is not desired by you. [In the case of] Devanāga: [The text continues: ...in the case of Devanāga—... [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here.]

Regarding the dice in the form of play: one might object that atoms do not exist with a division of spatial directions (*digbhāga*), but rather they touch at the location of a single central atom; therefore, he says "in six.
This includes the inclusion of the intermediate directions (*vidiś*) within the four cardinal ones; thus, at that time—
The sense is that [an atom] would consist of only a single atom, because all others are attached to that very same spot;
and thus, it follows that all objects would become invisible. He states another alternative with the words "atha" (now/if).
To the objection, "Let there be the consequence of a division of parts; what is the harm?", he replies with the word "iti" (thus/therefore). "Iti" means "therefore," [referring to] the parts.
If it were so, then for that part as well—meaning for even that portion—this very same path would apply; that is to say, the division into six directions.
He says "and not" (*na ca*) in order to reject the theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*) propounded by the logicians (*tārkika*).

Regarding "of the material" (mūrtānām): because atoms are accepted as being "material" by virtue of having a limited dimension or possessing action, it is impossible for them to occupy a single location;
that is, their coexistence in one place is untenable, because when conjunction occurs, the fact of occupying distinct locations is not eliminated.

From their exclusion [of other causes], the effect-substance called the dyad (dvyaṇuka), which has the dimension of an atom, is established as residing in them; and from those three, a large effect [the triad] arises. For this is the doctrine of the whole (avayavin), and that has already been refuted. Furthermore, as for what is said regarding the non-pervasive occurrence of conjunction, how could that be [possible] in that which is partless?

Let it be joined. For if this [inherence] inheres in its own substratum, what else remains for it that it would not pervade? Furthermore, this is a supplementary refutation, so we have not exerted great effort here; it has been demonstrated in detail in the *Prajñālaṅkāra*.
By Ācārya Śaṅkaranandana. || 6 ||
Now, it may be argued that a sublater (bādhaka) is indeed incapable of doing anything to an object established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
because by that very firm means of valid cognition, the status of being non-valid is produced for that which is intended as the sublater and is thereby sublated.

Because it is necessarily characterized by being located in different points of space, that which resides therein—meaning, effectively, residing in two atoms—is the dimension of minuteness (aṇu-parimāṇa), possessed of the dimension called "atomic. This first effect-substance, known as a dyad (dvyaṇuka), arises; then, from those three dyads, a large effect-substance [arises].

The visible effect, known as the triad (*tryaṇuka*), comes into being; however, it is not the case that a mere group of six atoms (*paramāṇu*) conjoins, which would lead to the aforementioned logical fault—this is the intended meaning. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). To the question "Why should this not be stated?", he says: "the whole" (*avayavī*). This means "precisely before," that is, immediately [after the preceding discussion].

In order to state the impossibility of conjunction—which brings about the state of dyads and so forth—within the subject of atoms, [the author] rejects its non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) with the words "And that which... Non-pervasive occurrence means co-existence in the same locus with its own absolute absence; this is impossible in the partless atom, which is devoid of constituent parts.
To explain why this is not tenable, he says: "in its own substratum.
In its own substratum—that is, in its own locus consisting of two atoms—this conjunction exists by way of inherence (*samavāya-vṛtti*).
What remains? The meaning is that nothing at all remains, because it has already been occupied by that [conjunction]. And thus:

The intended meaning is that even the existence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not tenable here. Now, one might ask: "Since this [topic] is worthy of expansion, why has no expansion been made? To this he says: "Abhyuccaya" (supplementation). *Bhara* means excellence or preponderance;
"in the Prajñālaṅkāra" refers to the treatise named *Prajñālaṅkāra*. || 6 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). Having raised the objection that the proving evidence has already been shown here— the *kāryahetu* (logical reason based on effect) in the verse beginning with "tattadākasmikābhāsa" (the various accidental appearances)— he says:

For the Lord, who is the very self of consciousness, manifests the multitude of objects existing within him externally by the power of his will, just as a yogi manifests a collection of things without any external material cause.

In this regard, although it is indeed possible that in dreams, memories, mental fantasies, volitions, and the like, the variety of appearances such as blue and so forth manifests even in the absence of any external cause that could provide them, nevertheless, that variety of appearances is characterized by instability.

Because it is not common to all perceivers and because there is the possibility that it arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous experience, one might suspect it to be a non-entity (*avastu*). Regarding this, however, the *Ṭīkā* states: "By the mere will of yogins... [and so forth].

"By that very [means]" means by that very cause of accomplishment (*siddhi*). Now, one might object: "Granted that the subverting factor (*bādhaka*) has been refuted, but what can we do regarding the claim that there is no establishing proof (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "And it has been shown. "The effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*) refers to the reason in the form of an effect, which consists of the nature of a reflection. Having thus provided the introduction:
