Having presented the verse, he explains it: "The conscious self alone," etc.
Here, the commentary [raises an objection]: "But surely, in dreams and the like, the external causal complex consisting of material causes and so forth is clearly evident."

Anticipating the objection that "the establishment of the variety of objects is already well-known even without [external things], so what is the use of the example of the vision of non-established yogis?", he says: "In this world" (iha). "Those causes which provide external [objects]"—that is, those causes which bring about external blue and so forth—in their absence (vyatirekeṇa).

The meaning is "by way of non-existence. "The variety of its manifestations" refers to the variety of manifestations such as blue and so forth, which exist in dreams and the like; it is because of that exclusivity (asādhāraṇya) among all subjects.
For the point is this: the collection of objects situated within one person's dream and so forth is not within the range of another. This might be suspected.
Thus, although a collection of objects is characterized by instability, non-commonality to all subjects, and being produced from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*),

it nonetheless possesses the same security as the waking state’s collection of objects— which is characterized by stability, commonality to all subjects, and not being produced from latent impressions—
because even stability and the like are merely of the nature of manifestation (*ābhāsa*); and there is no [difference] in the manifestation itself.

Although it is established that [the dream state] possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), it was not taken as an example for the disciple while he remained unawakened; rather, in order to bring about his direct realization, it was treated specifically as the example of a yogin, characterized by its extraordinary nature (*atiśaya*). This extraordinary nature—
It is indicated that once [the truth] has been realized, the disciple becomes fully awakened and investigates everything by himself.
The creation of the diverse variety of cities, armies, and so forth is observed; therein, the material cause (*upādāna*) is well-known to be clay, wood, and so on.

A state consisting of the diversity of semen, blood, and so forth is simply not possible; for it cannot be asserted that omnipresent atoms, suddenly congealed by the will of a yogi, will begin to produce an effect. This is stated only to establish that there is no deviation from the causes well-known in the world. And this is not [the case].

It is well known that gross objects such as jars arise from atoms alone; however, this occurs through the mediation of potsherds and the like. Nevertheless, even in that case, there is a dependence upon specific auxiliary causes and the activity of hands, feet, and so forth.

The excellence of the practice of the trainings consists in the conjunction with the dominant conditions of specific place, time, and dharmas; and when this much is relied upon, the yogi, while fashioning a jar,
produces the pot preceded by the gathering of the entire collection of materials well-known to potters.

It would simply be a potter; therefore, when the well-known cause has been transcended, what is the point of considering other material causes such as imperceptible atoms? In that regard, it is the very consciousness of the yogin that possesses such a power—that the multitude of objects, which consists of a variety of appearances, [is produced].

Having thus dispelled the objection raised by such a doubt, he begins to explain the verse by way of stating an alternative position, starting with the words "yat punaḥ" (as for that which...). [The term] "yoginām" refers to those endowed with the eightfold yoga; therein—

Therefore, in that emanation, it consists of manifoldness—meaning it takes the form of manifoldness by virtue of being the cause of manifoldness. Here, he himself raises a doubt on the part of a disciple with the words "for it is not thus. "Combined" means they have come together of their own accord according to the principle of the primordial creation. To the question "Why should this not be doubted?", he says "because," and so forth. This...

"This object" refers to what is well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddha*). By way of the intervention of shards and so forth—meaning that first the shards and such are produced, and subsequently, through their joining, the jar arises—this is the sense.
Nevertheless, even when there is the intervention of shards and so forth, there is the predominance of the property (*dharma-adhipatya*), which serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
For even in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), this is so even for *adharma*; indeed, both *dharma* and *adharma* function only as auxiliary causes (*sahakāritva*).

"In this much"—that is, in this collection of things (*arthajāta*) consisting of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Regarding that [point], when the question arises as to what that [complex] is, he says:
"That which... Now, one might object: has the collection of objects created by a yogi not been seen? With respect to him, what...?

Shall we offer an illustration? True; we say it is an object created by magic (indrajāla), for even that may sometimes perform a causal function. In that case, the yogi too would be nothing but a magician.
This possibility exists—that consciousness itself has accepted its own sovereignty.

Because it possesses the characteristic of non-resistance, and because consciousness— by virtue of a particular volition— never loses its nature as the non-superior Self, it causes this entire collection of entities, though remaining situated within, to appear as "this" external object, projected outward from the limited forms of consciousness belonging to the vital breath, intellect, body, and so forth; such is the case here.

Why is the sovereignty of the conscious self alone not accepted regarding the manifold variety of the appearance of universal forms—a fact established by one's own self-awareness? Why is one distressed by the labor of seeking other causes?
By the word "alone" (eva), he says this: first of all, by every proponent...

What do you say? [What do you say—C. Even regarding this world created by Īśvara, they declare it to be like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*). As it has been said: "The universe is like a magical illusion."

Thus it is said. What need is there to speak of an entity created by a yogi? For this very reason, even yogis are seen to maintain equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward such things; and as for those who do not possess [this power], they are merely like magicians, since equanimity alone constitutes the "Great Yoga" (*mahāyoga*) in all cases—enough of this. Having stated the illustration, he explains the illustrated point in the following manner:

"It exists"— this fulfills the expectancy for the word "that" (*tac-chabda*). From that which is characterized by non-obstruction— meaning from that whose nature is unimpeded— and by the power of a specific volition,
namely the efficacy of the specific volition "let it arise," [it arises] from consciousness, which constitutes its very essence.

Because of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit-tattva*), due to the non-excessiveness of the self—that is, oneness—and because of its non-departure—that is, its non-perishing—the meaning being that it exists as the singular form of consciousness; thus, "remaining within" means existing within itself.
For the point is this: a jar, which is conventionally designated by its state of being "within the clay," is indeed of the very nature of clay.

From that which is considered the subject—the vital breath, intellect, body, and so forth—from what kind [of subject]? That is to say, from one whose nature of consciousness consists of a mere fragment, capable only of grasping its own object, and which is essentially a trace of consciousness; [this occurs] by way of externality—that is, as something separate—and not otherwise.

[The object would exist] as something distinct from the consciousness of another; otherwise, according to the logic already stated, it would follow that the object remains unmanifest, just as before. He states the conclusion with the word "tat" (therefore):
[it follows that] by means of the investigations into other causes—namely, other causes in the form of atoms and so forth—...

By means of the effort involved in those investigations, he states the expressed meaning of the particle *eva* found in the sūtra with the words "by the particle *eva*. In response to the expectation of what that might be, he says:
"the determination of the object, which is the nature of consciousness; for that is undeniable and established from the beginning."

It has been said: "And its very sovereignty, designated by the word 'God' (deva), is its nature as consciousness; so what is the use of this obsession with searching for another cause? For since it is conceived as 'God' because it illuminates in this manner, therefore, what is the point of an external [cause] which is logically untenable?"—this is the connection with the preceding [verse]. || 7 ||

Regarding the word "by all" (*sarveṇa*): why should it not be denied? To this he says "beginning with" (*ādi*). The sense is that it was stated in the verse beginning with "in the agent" (*kartari*). In order to state the denotation of the word "deity" (*deva*), he says "and of that": "and of that"—meaning of that which consists of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*). For a deity is said to be one whose nature is play (*krīḍāśīla*), and play itself is...
[It is] sovereignty. For this very reason, if someone were to ask, "For what purpose did the Lord engage in the creation of phenomena?

his mouth would be sealed by this [very answer]. Indeed, it is not proper to subject one whose nature is play to questioning. However, in the investigation of the ultimate reality, even this [question] may be considered appropriate to state.

It does not penetrate [the truth]. For it is not logical to remove defects from a creator by relying on the similarity between him and an object created by himself; rather, only indeterminability (*anirvācyatā*) is appropriate here. Yet even that is not tenable upon further investigation, because indeterminability itself is situated in that very same [creator]. Thus, in every respect—
One should indeed remain full of wonder. As it has been said:
"Wonder is a stage of yoga.
But surely even wonder finds no place here, since it is associated only with that which is impossible to accomplish; and yet—

For God, nothing is impossible, as that would contradict His very nature as Lord. True; for this very reason, the most skillful Śākta practitioners have found their final rest in Śakti alone. Nor should one raise the objection here that the superimposition of Śakti leads to the fallacy of duality, because two forms are manifested within a single reality. Or let it be so.

The fall into duality occurs because there is room for it even within our desired supreme non-duality; otherwise, there would be the consequence of a mere general non-duality. Let the consequence of a mere general non-duality occur—what loss is there?
Or let there be a loss, since otherwise the state of Great Fullness (mahāpūrṇatva) would be impossible. Even in Great Fullness, there are increase and decrease.
It is indeed within one's own self. What need is there for much? Wherever rest is established, that is its very form;

yet, since reality transcends that, one should not abide anywhere, nor [be fixed] everywhere—enough with this extensive discussion of the supreme secret, which is unfit to be spoken to those lacking intuition, but appropriate for those who possess it.

"In those who have been awakened by the descent of power (śaktipāta) through the vow of Śrī Bhagavatī, [the truth] manifests spontaneously. Regarding this verse, he establishes its connection with the preceding verse by means of the causal force expressed by the word "hi" (for/indeed).
By the phrase "it is so conceived" (*saṃbhāvyate*), it is indicated here that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). || 7 ||
Now, if in this way the inference based on possibility (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*) arises in both respects, then in that case, why—
given the variety of appearances as reflections in cognition through the example of a jar reflected in a mirror—
should we postulate a cause external to consciousness, considered to be "external," which is distinct from the mirror of consciousness itself? Or rather, what [else]?
Might we say that, by means of the example of the yogi, the very sovereignty of consciousness (*saṃvitsvātantrya*) alone is the cause?
Anticipating the objection that this remains a matter of doubt, he speaks as follows in order to dispel the possibility of inferring external objects through two sūtras:

Inference is not accepted [as a means of knowledge] regarding that which has never appeared before; nor is the sense organ [the cause], for the cause of a real object is the appearance itself, such as that of a seed and so forth. (8)
Furthermore, how could an external object ever exist based on a mere appearance? Therefore, its establishment occurs neither through perception nor through inference.

Not only by the arguments set forth in the immediately preceding verse does the external object fail to appear through perception; for perception is precisely this much: it is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness, such that "this blue appears."
Now he provides the introduction to the eighth and ninth verses with the words "nanvevam" (But if this is so). Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"In both ways," that is, according to the manner stated by the proponent of external inference (*bāhyānumeyavādī*).

The meaning is "in the manner stated in the immediately preceding verse. *Saṃbhāvanānumāna* is inference in the form of a logical possibility (*tarka*), not a firm inference; *bāhyābhimata* means regarded as external; *sāṃśayika* means seized by doubt. Thus [ends] the introduction.
Having composed two verses and introduced them, he explains [the first]: "Inference" (*anumāna*).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"He states that the word has a denotation even in the first case, not only in the subsequent one. The following verse is:

Regarding the phrase "for it is the very nature of consciousness," therein, by means of the aforementioned arguments—namely, the methods consisting of the examples of yogis and so forth—it is established that it is not merely the case that [it] does not appear;
rather, he states the reason for this alone with the words "for only this much. And that is the manifestation.

The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that there is nothing further [to be said], namely, that even by means of inference (*anumāna*), this external object is not established. In this regard, inference is simply unable to function; even if it were to function, it would not bring about the establishment of the subject under discussion. This is the intention.

This is demonstrated by two sūtras: therein, inference (*anumāna*) is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and it is well known that all such conceptual construction is rooted in direct experience (*anubhava*). Therefore, regarding that which has never previously appeared in any way and has never before been experienced, there can be no operation of inference or inferential cognition.

The nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not accepted by any proponent at all. Now, let this discussion regarding inference based on what is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) proceed; but what will you say regarding inference from general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*), such as the inference of the sense faculties from the apprehension of objects? It is said in reply: even in that case, it is by means of conceptual construction that that object [is established].
The word "tathā" (thus) indicates the completion of the reason. It fulfills the expectation of the phrase "not only" by means of the word "yāvat" (as far as).
The meaning of the particle "api" (also), which is situated in the phrase "nor even from inference," is "even so."

Having stated the intended meaning of the word "api," he briefly explains the purport of the two verses with the words "tatra" (therein); the meaning is that "even so" refers precisely to the sense of the word "api. "The establishment of the subject at hand"—that is, the establishment of the external world—is "shown" by these two kārikās; the meaning is that it is indicated. [Objection: Let it be shown, then.

To the question "Why?", he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). This means: when such an intention exists; [in that situation] inference (*anumāna*) is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), not non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpadarśana*), because it is merely a cause for determinative judgment (*avasāya*). "All"—meaning of the nature of inference and so forth—is "rooted in experience," that is, rooted in non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*); such is the meaning of "thus" (*iti*).
The word "becomes well-known" (*prasiddham bhavati*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. By that—that is, by the fact that inference is conceptual (*vikalpatvena*).

He explains the term "never before appeared" (*anābhātapūrvam*) as "never before experienced" (*ananubhūtacaram*); [the phrase] "therein" (*tatra*) refers to "that which has never been experienced before. Here, the logician asks: "But surely" (*nanu*)? This is the discussion:
Regarding the discussion on whether [the object] has been previously experienced:

the sense is that this is not tenable because it is possible to grasp a general pervasion (*sāmānyato vyāpti*) therein; as for where that inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam anumānam*) occurs, he says "as follows" (*yathā*), by means of the expression "artha-olapa."

By means of cognition having a jar or similar object as its content; "in the inference of the sense organs"—that is, in the constant inference of the supersensible eyes and so forth. Here he states the resolution: "it is said. Even there—in the case of the inference of the sense organs and so on, which is of the nature of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation)—"that object" refers to the form of the eye and so forth.

The object is touched— that is, it is established that it is inferable as a universal (sāmānya). Furthermore, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not [grasp] an object such as a sense-organ or the like by way of any specific configuration (*saṃniveśaviśeṣa*) or particular nature.
It does not touch [the object] directly; rather, it is by means of this nature—that it is a cause for some perception—that [the relation is established].

And that nature, characterized as causality, is indeed apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, in cases such as "from a seed, a sprout" or "from threads, a cloth," the causal relationship is established by the power of direct perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*).

This much must be determined. And therein, perception possesses validity with respect to each individual appearance, because the cognitive operation characterized by reflective awareness (vimarśa) proceeds toward—and finds its rest in—the object denoted by each individual word;
and it will be stated that the means of knowledge follows that [reflective awareness].
"In the domain of a single designation, the cognition regarding the object is uncontradicted.

This is experienced; "sthitih" means the established state. He shows the meaning stated in general terms through specific instances with the words "and conceptual construction" (*vikalpaśca*). [This occurs] by way of a particular configuration, such as a specific arrangement, that is, by way of its specific nature.

In its specific form (*viśeṣasvarūpeṇa*). To the question "By what form, then, does it touch?", he says "but rather" (*api tu*). It touches by way of this nature—that is, as a cause for the apprehension of something—meaning in its general form (*sāmānyarūpeṇa*); this is to be connected with the preceding [verb] "touches. And that nature is—

And its nature is made an object of contact; that is, characterized by causality—the very essence of causality—meaning it is of the nature of a property (*dharma*). He says "and likewise" (*tathā ca*) in order to explain the illustrative statement "of the seed, etc.
By the power of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), the object therein is to be determined through perception.

He says "there" (tatra). There, between perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), [the former] possesses validity—that is, the status of being a means of knowledge—within every appearance (*pratyābhāsa*). To the question "From what does it derive [this validity]?", he states the reason: "through reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*). [This refers to] that which is characterized by reflective awareness, namely, that which has the nature of conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*).
Because [the word] functions with respect to that which is denoted by each individual term—

that is, with respect to the specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) in the form of the entire collection of properties and the property-possessor expressed by each individual term; however, it does not function with respect to each individual appearance as is the case with non-conceptual perception.

"And because it follows that" means because it follows reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), namely, because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such as perception and so forth, follow it. Now, one might ask: how is it logical for a means of knowledge, which has reflective awareness as its cause, to follow reflective awareness? To this he says: "Thus" (*iti*). To the question "What does 'thus' refer to? and "Where will this be stated?", he says: [the following].

Regarding the term "single designation": it will be established that the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely an appearance (*ābhāsamātra*). Non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), too, being of the nature of the apprehension of something else, rests solely within mere appearance; thus, it is an appearance of a cause.

In the cognition that "the sprout arises from the seed," it is indeed apprehended as devoid of any specific distinction. Whatever conforms to the restriction of something else, being non-different from it, is its effect;
thus, in every jar, the cause—consisting merely of the material such as clay and its possessor—is established.
[From] the appearance [of the object]. || 8 ||

"Thus" means in this verse; for there, he will explain that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object precisely by way of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by itself. Now, [an objection]: it was stated that the operation of the means of valid cognition occurs only with respect to appearances (*ābhāsa*), and not with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*); so how is this established? To this, he says:
"Appearance" (*ābhāsa*) means "mere appearance"—that is, a solitary appearance, rather than a grasping that implies all phenomena; this will be determined in this very verse, which is the meaning.
He states the function of non-apprehension with the words "even non-apprehension. Non-apprehension—
The non-apprehension of cowness in cows is of the nature of the apprehension of something else— that is,
of the nature of the apprehension of horseness and so forth in horses and the like. For the cognizer,
perceiving cowness in cows through direct perception while not apprehending it in horses and the like, determines that cowness resides in all individual cows.
It rests solely in the mere appearance (*ābhāsa*) and does not rest in the "individual" (*vyakti*) as postulated by others; for this very reason,
the "appearance of the cause"— the appearance of being the cause of perception residing in the sense organ—
is "devoid of particulars," meaning it is free from particulars because it is not grasped as being fixed therein, and thus it is apprehended [in its general form].

The ellipsis to be supplied is "by means of perception and non-apprehension. In response to the question "Where?", he provides an example with the words "from a seed" (*bījāt*); the sense is that the causality of a seed with respect to a sprout is indeed manifest.
Here too, having raised the doubt regarding its imperceptibility, [the author] refers to clay and a jar, which are included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the aphorism.

He explains the relationship of cause and effect by means of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the word "yat" (that which). "Niyama" means necessary occurrence; "anuvidhatte" means it depends upon [the other] for the attainment of its own nature. Now, one might ask: where is this pervasion observed? To this he says: "in every jar" (*pratighaṭam*). That is, in all jars.

In the case of jars, there is a cause consisting of clay and so forth—that is, clay, the staff, and so on. From the manifestation—meaning from the flashing forth—of that which possesses merely such [a cause], namely, of that state of possessing merely such [a cause] (the term *tadvattvamātra* being a Bahuvrīhi compound where the abstract suffix emphasizes the state), that is to say, of being endowed with causes such as clay, the staff, and so forth; by this [it is shown].
The first verse has already been explained. || 8 ||

Furthermore, that which is external to the manifestation is of a non-manifest nature; it is a contradiction to say that such a thing manifests. Moreover, in the absence of manifestation, there is no operation of inference, which consists of conceptual construction.
As for that which is external to a village, a house, and so forth, it is not said to be of a non-village or non-house nature individually.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that fences, marshlands, walls, measures of weight (*tulā*), and so forth, would also be external; rather, it is merely something adjacent to them.

Therefore, the expressions "external to the village" and "external to the appearance" are identical only in terms of their verbal form, not in terms of their actual reality. Thus, as for those who claim that the real object does not appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*):
They think that even for them, inferential conceptualization is not established regarding the external object.
[The author] explains the second verse with "nanu" (is it not so?).
To the question, "Is it not the case that you establish everything by means of manifestation alone? he says, "from manifestation. This is contradictory—

[This is] contradictory. Now, in response to the expectation that "let there be no manifestation (ābhāsa); conceptual construction (vikalpa) alone will perform all the work," he explains the second verse with the words "And in the absence of manifestation" (anābhāse ca).
[Furthermore,] in response to the expectation "Do you bring about everything?", he explains the second verse with the words "From manifestation" (ābhāsāt).

"Contradictory" means opposed. [The opponent objects: "But let there be no appearance; conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) itself will perform all the functions. To this, he says: "And in the absence of appearance," etc. The sense is that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) would be impossible.
[The opponent asks: "If the proof of contradiction is based merely on being external, then what of one who is outside the village?"
Lest it be argued that even the collection of objects would thus fall into contradiction, he says "village" (*grāma*).

In relation to the village, the term "enclosures and marshlands" (*vāṭānūpa*) is used; however, in relation to the house, there is the inclusion of walls, scales, and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including other collections of objects found therein. To the question, "What then is that which is being said? he says "but rather" (*api tu*). But...

However, by the wise, that collection of objects situated outside the village is called "near" (*sannikṛṣṭa*), meaning located in the vicinity of the village; the sense is that because it stands right near the village, it is not opposed to the village.
He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Furthermore, it is not logical to assert an identity of things merely on the basis of a similarity of words.

[The opponent says: "But surely the Buddhists have stated that conceptual construction (vikalpa) does not touch upon the real object at all; yet you establish everything by means of that very [construction]. What is this? To this he replies:
"In this way, we have established that even for determinative cognition (adhyavasāya), the object is one that appears as identical [to the external thing]."
Regarding the aphorism, "And if the determination were an error," [the meaning is as follows]:

if an object such as blue were not permeated by that manifestation which consists of inferential conceptualization (*anumāna-vikalpa*), then it would simply not be inferred at all. If, on the other hand, it is indeed permeated, then according to the principle that "otherwise the object would be unmanifest, just as before," it must have the nature of manifestation alone, and not [anything else].

It is external. Therefore, whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is brought forward when the external is to be proven, it instead proves—on the contrary—its very non-externality; thus, it is indeed contradictory.
For this very reason, he says "in any way whatsoever" (*kathaṃcana*), meaning by any manner, whether in the form of perception (*pratyakṣa*) or in the form of inference (*anumāna*).
Appearance is the manifestation of that which is external and non-manifest; it has never not existed.
Therefore, it is established that "the Lord is indeed the very self of consciousness. || 9 ||

"Thus" (iti) means "this being so. [The opponent asks: "But what exists according to your view? To this he replies: "By us" (asmābhiḥ). "Of the determination" (adhyavasāyasya)—that is, of the determination which is the effect of conceptual construction—means "having an appearing object as its domain," which is to say, "having the external object as its domain. In response to the expectation of where this occurs, he says: "In the state of error" (bhrāntitve).

He concludes his own intention with the word "therefore" (*tena*). [This means] by that which has taken on the nature of a conceptualization in the form of inference—that is, having attained the state of being a conceptualization whose form is inference. He states the result with the word "therefore": the meaning is that it is established according to the principle that "an object is unmanifest, as in the previous case. "That" [refers to] precisely what is contradictory.
The meaning is that, therefore, its measurement is indeed contradictory.
And thus, the sense is that at the commencement of a rite for pacification (*śāntikarma*), the raising of a *vetāla* (corpse-spirit) itself constitutes the external means (*bāhyasādhana*).
[Objection: By which word in the Sūtra is this stated? To this he says: "therefore" (*ataḥ*). [Objection: What does it say? To this he says: "in any way whatsoever" (*kathaṃcana*).
He explains this also with the words "by someone" (kenāpi). By means of this, he states that the meaning of the preceding verse is established, using the word "therefore" (tasmāt).
Such is the construction of these two verses here: the wise person [employs] inference regarding what has not been previously perceived.
This is not desired. The sense-faculty (*indriya*) is indeed manifest, with the implication that this occurs through a universal form (*sāmānyena*). Why?

Because of the manifestation of the causal entity, such as the seed and so forth. Furthermore—in the alternative case—there was no manifestation of the external object whatsoever from the manifestation [of the internal]; therefore, this external object cannot be established even by means of inference.
"There is no accomplishment," [he said]. || 9 ||
Now, one might object: "It was stated that what resides within should manifest externally; therefore, that state of residing within must be established.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The manifestation of the multitude of objects residing within the Self belongs to the Lord."
It certainly exists; therefore, we maintain that desire proceeds from it. || 10 ||
Even when appearing as an external form— even when appearing as something external—
the nature of "I-ness" does not fracture;
for internality consists in identity with the subject.
For it will be said [later] that this is always so, because light is the subject (*pramātṛ*), by virtue of being of its nature.
Now, he provides the introduction to the tenth verse with the word "nanu" (but surely).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:

"It must be established"—meaning it must be supported through reasoning; the sense is that this is proven here by means of mere logic (*tarka*) alone. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "of the Master" (*svāminaḥ*).

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) expands upon the method for explaining the verse, beginning with the words "bahīrūpa" (having an external form): even when there is manifestation as something external— that is, even when it appears as an object outside, or in other words, even when it is grasped as "this"— ...

The state of being "I" (ahantārūpatā) is the state of being internal (āntararūpatā). To the question "Why does it not break off?", he says: "by the subject" (pramātrā). "With the subject"—that is, with the Light (prakāśa)—there is identity (aikātmyam); [with the subject—i.e., with the Light; oneness with the subject—C. this is identity with the subject (pramātraikātmyam), and that belongs to entities (bhāvānām).

And there is identity (*aikātmya*) with the subject (*pramātṛ*). To the question "Why?", he says "of light" (*prakāśasya*) in anticipation of the need for a reason. Now, one might ask: even if light is the subject, what does that have to do with the present context? To this he says "by being of its nature" (*tadātmatayā*). By being of its nature—
Furthermore, because that which does not manifest (or, according to Kṣemarāja’s reading, that which manifests) is devoid of reality,
externalization consists precisely in that reflective awareness as "this-ness" (*idantā*) which occurs in place of the appropriate reflective awareness as "I" (*aham*);
and this state of being internal is nothing other than the very act of reflective awareness in the form of "I," which is perfectly suited to consciousness.

And that [reflective awareness] certainly exists here in the case of blue and so forth, and it is not non-existent; for if it were not present, then the reflective awareness denoted by the word "desire"—expressed as "I shall make a jar," which depends upon a subsequent action—would not be constrained by that which is to be desired (the object of desire) if it were not already reflected upon as having the nature of being desired. Therefore...
Why should even that [desire] not be mixed with them?

Because they would be identical in their nature as light and as the subject; for the multitude of entities, which are not manifesting—according to the maxim "the object is as it was before"—do not partake in the agency of manifestation, and thus lack substantiality.

For an object that does not manifest is not truly an object. Now, in response to the objection that "in that case, it would always be non-external," he establishes its externality according to another perspective with the words "but...
There—in that collection of entities—it is precisely that reflective awareness of "this-ness" (idantā), and not something emerging from it.

"Abiding externally. And that—meaning, "conjoined with consciousness," i.e., conjoined with the consciousness of Yoga—is precisely the act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*), and not abiding within any internal location. And that—namely, the reflective awareness "I"—indeed exists. He states what is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*) with the words "but not... In this context:

He states the reasoning that is favorable [to his position] and supportive of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the words "yadi hi" (for if). "If that were not so"—in this way, worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) would become confounded; they would fall into confusion. How so?
In the case of a potter—that is, a wheel-turner engaged in the making of a pot—with respect to a subsequent action.

That which is expressed by the word "desire" (icchā-śabda) means that it has the nature of desire with respect to that [object]. There arises the reflective awareness (parāmarśa): "May I make a jar. This [awareness] is related to the object of desire—that is, the jar which is the objective domain of the desire, and for that very reason, the object of the reflective awareness whose nature is desire.

If it were not restricted—that is, if it were not brought to a state of limitation by way of being an object—then how could even the desire for a cloth (*paṭecchā*) not exist? For desires are specific worldly transactions (*viśeṣā vyavahārāḥ*). Now, in that case as well, the object of desire (*eṣaṇīya*) is produced at that very moment and thus comes into being in such a manner.

In that case, since such emanation is not possible within the conscious self (*cidātman*) without a will, it will be explained in the passage: "For one who desires to remain [in this state], the will itself is the cause. Furthermore, regarding that [will], there arises the dilemma as to whether another will is constrained by an object or not; if it is constrained by an object, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is constrained by an object...

If the self-nature itself were born [as a separate entity], then there would be no desire for a cloth in a jar; or, if one were to argue that even in that case it arises at that very same moment, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, this entire mass of phenomena possesses a body that is perpetually radiant as the "I" within the conscious Self (*cidātman*), by virtue of its nature of sovereignty characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).

By virtue of the state of being the Lord (*svāmibhāva*), consciousness projects this object outward through a manifold body—by means of succession, non-succession, and so forth—preceded by the manifestation of the subject; the phrase "due to the manifestation of the differentiation of subjects" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Now—if, even there—in that very desire for the jar—

At that time—meaning at the moment of desire—that which is to be desired (*eṣaṇīya*) is "created," that is, brought into being; having thus come into existence, it becomes the realized object of desire. Therefore, the production of that jar is not possible within the conscious self (*cidātman*), whose nature is consciousness, without [the exercise of] will (*icchā*). This is the point.

Regarding the statement "for one who wishes to remain [in this state], desire itself is the cause," which will be described— that is, explained— in this verse: even if there is another desire directed toward the object being created,

and when the dilemma arises as to whether that [desire] is constrained by an object or not, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā), because yet another thing to be desired would be required in that case as well.
In that case as well, there would be another desire, and thus the fault known as infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would arise.
Having recognized that [the fault of] self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and so forth are utterly inseparable, one focuses solely on the infinite regress.
By establishing its weakness through reasoning (*tarka*), one then proceeds with the inference here according to the manner of the established conclusion; therefore, [it is said]: "from that."
This— manifesting before one, possessing a body that is perpetually radiant— is *saṃvit*,
the supreme subject-principle whose nature is light; it "externalizes" this— the mass of objects existing as "I"—
by manifesting it as "this," through the power of exclusion (*apohana-śakti*), even though it was previously established in unity.

It means "it illumines. How so? For the limited subjects (*mitapramātṛ*), who are the perceivers (*grāhaka*) and constitute its own parts, there is a manifestation—that is, an appearance as distinct from itself by means of the power of withdrawal (*apohana-śakti*). That [power] in which this occurs first is such that it first illumines the perceivers.
Even there, in certain appearances, [the Lord] unifies the subjects, as spectators are unified in the sight of a woman’s dance;

for their unity exists only so far as that appearance [of the dance] is concerned. However, regarding the portions of the appearances of body, vital breath, intellect, pleasure, and so forth, because the differentiation has not dissolved, there is no absolute unity. For this very reason, there is a rejoining of the subjects at every moment.

—[By means of the variety of joining and separating the cognizer—K. Ṣ. Ṣ.]—the Supreme Lord unfolds the universe through emanation, withdrawal, and so forth, by means of the variety of separation. As it has been said by the Teacher:
"To him for whom creation is an eternal diversion, who always dwells in the bliss of maintenance..."
"Salutations to You, who are eternally satisfied by devouring the three worlds.
Following that, the sense is "the group of objects to be grasped. Even there—in the externalizing process—how is their unification achieved therein?
To this he says: "In that much," meaning in that manifestation, the manifestation of the dance; what [is it]?

Since they are in every respect one with them therein, he says "the body" (*śarīre*). "Moment by moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*) means at every instant; "joining" (*saṃyojanam*) refers to dancing and the like; "separation" (*viyojanam*) refers to [the soul's departure] from the body and so forth; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the intermediate state of persistence is intended, as well as concealment and grace. Herein lies the agreement of the Teacher (*ācārya*).
He shows this by saying "it is said. To the question "What is said?", he replies with "always" (*sadā*). "Stability-bliss" (*sthitisukha*) is the bliss produced by stability;
[the term refers to one] who dwells in that. "Food" (*āhāraḥ*) means swallowing, which is to say, withdrawal (*saṃhāraḥ*).
Now, how can creation and the other [evolutionary stages], which are mutually contradictory and sequential, occur simultaneously and eternally?

Does it possess the capacity for diversion and so forth? Listen: although it is beginningless, with respect to the intellects of disciples seized by time, in the first creation, there is first of all the withdrawal of the desire-to-withdraw (*saṃjihīrṣā*) which had remained during the period of dissolution.

In that very state, there is the persistence of the will to create that has arisen, as well as the manifestation of the mental dispositions (*bhāvanā*) which are its objects and the will for the persistence of what is yet to arise. In the state of persistence, however, there is the withdrawal of the will to create that was established during the act of creation. In that same state, there is also the [withdrawal] of the will for persistence that has arisen.
There is the persistence of the entities that have become its objects; from the desire to withdraw (saṃjihīrṣā), there is creation;

but in the case of withdrawal, there is the destruction of the entities that were the objects of the desire for persistence which was established during the state of persistence, as well as the persistence of the desire to withdraw that arose in that very state.

The creation [of the world] occurs from the desire to emit that which is being brought into being; thus, it is quite evident that this triad of creation and so forth consists of the triad of creation and so forth, and the eternality of pure consciousness (cinmātra) therein should be understood as its state of being the ever-emergent source. As it has been said:
"Gold does not exist without an arrangement [of parts], nor does Brahman exist without creation," and so forth. Śrī Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa also says:
"Unceasingly, again and again, [the Lord] fashions the three worlds with hundreds of conceptualizations..."

"Even while conceptualizing, a certain one remains unborn and victorious, free from conceptualization. Therefore, it is established that the multitude of objects exists within [him]; without him, there would be no object for them.
There is also a suggested meaning (*dhvani*) that even another universal monarch (*cakravartin*) creates enjoyments, places them in his palace, and brings them forth. Or else:
The fact that the supreme subject always finds delight in creation and so forth should be understood as being performed solely by the limited subjects who are his own created portions; for they,
like waves, are always occupied with creation in some respect, with maintenance in another, and with withdrawal in yet another.

Enough with this elaboration regarding the ocean. He says "Bhaṭṭa" in order to corroborate this point with the words of the venerable Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa. The word "stated" (uktam) is to be connected with what precedes.

To the question "What was stated?", he replies with "muhuḥ" (repeatedly). The phrase "muhurmuhuḥ" (again and again) is stated with reference to the medium-level immersion (*madhyamā-āveśa*), for all [immersions]...

By the power of their own nature, cognizing subjects experience at every moment the established immersion in the *madhyamā*, which culminates in the consciousness of vital breath (*prāṇavijñāna*); for although the void is always identical with that [consciousness],
the body— though slightly pervaded by inertia— is likewise touched by extreme inertia.

These two are not grasped here [directly], yet having entered there by means of the door of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the door of the intellect (*buddhi*), they cause the entire mass of objective phenomena (*bhāvarāśi*) to enter therein along with their own selves;
and rising up from there by the power of their own nature, they produce something entirely new. And that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) which occurs regarding those new phenomena—

That [threefold division] is based solely on similarity; it should be understood as being created by the eternal pure consciousness (cinmātra) which constitutes the supreme subject (parapramātṛ), the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of those [states]. This applies both when the internal intention is intended—resulting in the three worlds in the form of waking and so forth—and when the external intention is intended—resulting in the three worlds in the form of the earth and so forth. And that which...

It is a marvel that he who, through hundreds of conceptualizations, incessantly and repeatedly constructs the three worlds, should become free from conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*). The resolution, however, lies in the phrase "through hundreds of conceptualizations": the constructions of the three worlds pertain to limited subjects (*mitapramātṛ*), whereas he is always indeed free from conceptualization, just as...

Even though a sovereign ruler performs all activities pertaining to every country through his own servants by means of his command, he remains entirely free from anxiety while staying within his own domain. Alternatively, even the most subtle act of reflection is merely the strengthening of the very nature of Light; thus, there is no loss [of that nature] even by means of it.

Concluding his own intention, he explains the remainder of the verse beginning with "not without" (*na vinā*) by means of the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*). "Therefore"—this is the sense of the word "iti" which remains [to be supplied]—thus it is established; that is, it becomes proven.
What is this? This entire collection of entities (*bhāvajāta*) abiding within.
Because of the impossibility of reflective awareness (parāmarśa) [i.e., because reflective awareness is impossible]—thus [it is said]. || 10 ||
Now, one might object: "Reflection (parāmarśa) is indeed conceptualization (vikalpa); how then could it exist in the Blessed Lord, whose nature is non-conceptual pure consciousness?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "They know reflection to be the very essence of manifestation; otherwise [it would not be so]."
Even though consciousness is colored by objects, it remains like an insentient substance such as a crystal. || 11 ||

In this context, if both manifestation (*avabhāsa*), which is luminosity (*prakāśa*), and non-manifestation (*anavabhāsa*), which is non-luminosity (*aprakāśa*)— such as a jar and so forth— were to be established within their own selves through mutual exclusion, then a distinction such as "this is non-inert" and "this is inert" would be as difficult to establish as it is between a jar and a cloth. Now, as for manifestation...

If [consciousness] is not insentient because it is related to an object, then even a jar that has perished would have to be non-insentient simply by virtue of having such a relation. Now, if it is argued that it is not merely a relation to itself, but rather that there is an "illumination" (*avabhāsa*) of the object—why is this so? Because without that [illumination], namely, without its internal abiding, reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) would be impossible.

The sense is that because the desire "I shall do" is impossible [without an object], a desire without an object is not logical. By this, the means of valid cognition known as inference has been applied to the path purified by reasoning.
This is the summary here: from the Lord, who is endowed with the sovereignty called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).

From the *cittattva* (the reality of consciousness), which consists of the manifestation [of all things], there is the illumination of the multitude of existents— that is, the entire mass of phenomena— which abide within itself through identity (*tādātmya*). Without that— that is, without their being established within that [consciousness]— there can be no "contemplation of will" (*icchāmarśa*), such as "I shall do."
Reflective awareness in the form of desire does not arise because it lacks an object. || 10 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the eleventh verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). This is clear. Here, the commentary explains the word *avabhāsasya* (of manifestation) as *prakāśasya* (of light).
By way of mutual exclusion— that is, through reciprocal differentiation—
their distinct establishment (viśiṣṭam avasthānam) is difficult to justify (durupapādam), meaning it can only be established with great difficulty.
This is because their specific characteristics (viśeṣāḥ) are established only according to their own respective intrinsic natures (yathāsvam svarūpasiddhau).

If it is luminosity, then it follows that it is luminous by virtue of being the very nature of the object. Furthermore, it is not logically tenable for one thing to be luminous through the nature of another. Now, if the jar, despite having a different nature [from luminosity], is the cause of the manifestation, then the manifestation would also be the cause of the jar; consequently, the jar too would be non-inert (ajaḍa). Or else...
Since a shadow in the form of a reflection is imparted by another existing thing, such as a jar, that light which bears it is said to belong to the jar;
and if, on that account, it is non-inert (*ajaḍa*), then even crystal, water, a mirror, and so forth, being of exactly the same nature, would also be non-inert.

It might be argued: "Even though it is of such a nature, the crystal and other such things are incapable of perceiving that self and that jar and so forth; therefore, they are insentient (*jaḍa*). This very incapacity for such perception is the life-force of non-insentience, consisting in the sovereignty of the internal and external organs. [The reading *antarbahiṣkaraṇasvātantryasvarūpam* is supported by Kṣemarāja’s commentary.]

The meaning is that the manifestation possesses an intrinsic nature characterized by resting within its own self, which does not depend on anything else. He states another alternative with the word "atha": "prakāśa" means manifestness; "saḥ" (that)—
"Manifestation" (*avabhāsa*) means "having arrived," i.e., having come forth by force. To the objection, "Let that very thing be so," he says, "And not...

Here too, he poses a question with "Now then" (*atha*). The "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is the causal factor as the objective support (*ālambana-kāraka*). He provides the answer with "In that case" (*tarhi*); the meaning is that it is the cause of the jar, providing its establishment by way of being a cognizer (*jñāpaka*).

He raises a doubt again with the word "atha" (now). Even though it exists as something other—that is, even though it exists as something distinct by virtue of its insentience—the phrase "of the jar" means "connected to the jar.
And consequently, because of that connection, such a thing—bearing a shadow in the form of a reflection—[arises].

He poses a question with the word "atha" (now). [The objection is: even though [the mirror] perceives such a thing—a reflection of a jar—and even though there is that which provides the reflection, it is not capable; the meaning is that it is incapable.
He provides the answer with the word "tathā" (thus): "such a reflective awareness," which has as its object one's own self as colored by the jar.
And the reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) whose object is the jar is the life-force of non-inertness—that which bestows existence upon consciousness.

It is the "externalization"—the expansion [of the object] as "this-ness" (*idantā*)—of the mass of entities situated within, by way of internal implication (*lakṣaṇā*). That which possesses such a form, namely freedom (*svātantrya*), is its inherent nature.
But nothing whatsoever is adventitious to it;
for when the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) arises— "I am indeed this very self-luminous light"—
one's own self-consciousness alone considers the subject, the object, the means of knowledge, and so forth, to have fulfilled their purpose (*kṛtārtha*), and not anything else.

It requires something additional; for even a crystal or similar object, though it has grasped a reflection, depends upon another subject for its establishment in that state, and is thus insentient (*jaḍa*) due to its lack of reflective awareness (*nirvimarśatva*). In all cases, however, everything in reality comes to rest in the "I-reflection" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*), because its essential nature is that of the subject whose very being consists of reflective awareness.
Non-inertness alone exists at both the prior and posterior limits. As it has been said:

"That which has such a nature—namely, rest as its defining characteristic—is therefore characterized by not looking toward the face of another," which means it is devoid of dependence on anything else for its own apprehension.
The phrase "of the manifestation" (*avabhāsasya*) is a qualification; within this context, it specifies the locus of the qualified.

Regarding the statement "looking toward another's face," he states the reason for this with the word "I" (*aham*). "I am thus of the nature of light"—[meaning, "I am called the light of the 'I'"—C.]—I am thus of the nature of light, by virtue of my own self-luminous nature.

And [it is said] in the *Prakāśa*: "When the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) arises in the form 'I am the agent of manifestation,' for this reason (*hi*), by the subject (*pramātṛ*), his own consciousness alone—that is, consciousness which constitutes his very nature, and not some object distinct from it such as the knower, the known, or the means of knowledge (the word 'etc. includes the act of knowing)—has its purpose fulfilled."

[The object] has fulfilled its purpose; that cognizer considers [the means of knowledge and so forth] to be "excessive"—that is, distinct from the consciousness that constitutes his own nature—and since they have fulfilled their purpose, he does not desire them. Now, one might object: "Let it be the same for the crystal and other such things as well.
To this, he says: "The crystal, etc. [This is not the case], because in its own nature, the crystal lacks the capacity for reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as something distinct [from the object].
Now, if it is argued that if crystal and the like are indeed insentient (*jaḍa*), then duality would result, [the author] says "all" (*sarva*).

In reality—that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)—everywhere there exists the reflective nature (*vimarśātmaka*); by the logic already stated, this is the nature of the subject (*pramātṛsvabhāva*), which is the nature of the supreme subject known as Light (*prakāśa*). Together with that...
That identity— which is oneness because manifestation would otherwise be impossible—

is the reason for the repose within the reflective awareness of "I"; by virtue of that, there is indeed non-inertness at both the prior and subsequent limits— that is, at the time of the desire to grasp and immediately after the grasping.

It is indeed of the nature of light. Although it remains exactly so even in the interim, this was stated thus with regard to the immaturity of the disciple's intellect. To provide the consensus of the elders on this point, he says "as it has been said.
To the question "What has been said?", he replies "this."
"The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of 'this'—which is [otherwise] fragmented—is that repose in one's own essential nature; that reflective awareness is 'I am this'.
However, the intermediate state itself is that in which the preceding and succeeding limits are being reflected upon as "this-ness."
It is established that for the Blessed One, the very discernment that "saṃsāra is the realm of illusion for the deluded" is primary. || 11 ||
He shows that the primacy of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) has been asserted not only by us regarding the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), but also by other scriptures:
"This has already been explained previously, so we shall not labor over it again; thus, there is no loss of non-duality."

The state [of being]. Now, as to what the intermediate state (*madhyāvasthā*) is like, he says: "the intermediate" (*madhyā*). "This-ness" (*idantā*) means having the form of "this-ness. For those who, by knowing that, always perceive everything as having a single form, there is an absence of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) even while they engage in worldly activity like the deluded; therefore, it is said "of the deluded" (*vimūḍhānām*). As it has been said:
One who is awakened should always remain having scrutinized the field of experience with knowledge;
one should unify everything in a single point, and thereafter one is not afflicted by anything else.

Thus, he states the established conclusion in brief: "Vimarśa" (reflective awareness). Vimarśa alone—having as its object both one's own essential nature called the light colored by the jar and the jar which is the coloring agent—is indeed *parāmarśa* (determinative awareness). It is "primary"—that is, principal—because it establishes the luminosity of one's own nature.
The meaning is that it is even more primary than its own essential nature (svarūpa); thus it is established—meaning it becomes proven.

And so, the point is that there is no loss [of its nature] even though the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) resides within pure light (śuddhaprakāśa). Although, in ultimate reality, this has been established solely by way of the light delimited by the state of being the subject (grāhakatva), [it is nonetheless established].

Otherwise, it would be impossible to speak of the coloring by objects, for even the discourse on coloring is itself impossible within the nature of pure luminosity; nevertheless, by means of that [discourse], this is indeed established for it as well,
though it is not stated directly due to its extreme subtlety, and therefore, in the reflective awareness of one's own self alone—
This very same path applies even to pure luminosity; enough with these subtle investigations. || 11 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the twelfth verse with the words "not only" (*na kevalam*).
This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "the Self" (*ātmaiva*).
"The Self alone is consciousness (*caitanya*), the activity of consciousness (*cit-kriyā*), and the agency of consciousness (*citi-kartṛtā*)."
For that reason, he has been described with such intent as being distinct from the insentient. || 12 ||
Since reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is the primary form of the Self, it is with reference to this very cause—

which serves as its purpose— that the Self, though being the substrate (*dharmin*), possessing its own nature, and substantial (*dravyabhūta*), stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "consciousness" (*caitanya*), which denotes a property (*dharma*). (Or, according to Kṣemarāja’s reading, a word denoting the substrate.)
It has been stated that [the Self] is proclaimed by relying [on this]; for it was recited by the Blessed One in the *Śivasūtras*:
"The Self is consciousness" (1-1). Indeed, the term "consciousness" (*caitanya*) is an indicative mark denoting a quality (*dharma*).
The power of consciousness is unchanging...
[isolation belongs to the seer who is thus established]. (Yoga Sūtra 2.25) The seer is pure perception alone... (Yoga Sūtra 2.20)
For even in such passages as these, the Teacher has shown the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the Self with the word "dharma";
here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains the word "ata eva" (for this very reason) by saying "yataḥ" (since); and "vimarśa eva" means "parāmarśa eva" (nothing but reflective awareness).

Of the Self—of the reality of the subject known as manifestation, whose nature is light; "its form" means its own essence; the word "from that" is to be supplied [as the source]. "This"—namely, the state of being the primary form of reflective awareness (vimarśa) belonging to the Self; "in the form of a purpose" means having the nature of a motive by way of being the motivator.

He explains the word *ātman* as "the substratum" (*dharmin*). Its nature as a substratum means that it has the essential form of a substratum by virtue of being the locus of the attribute (*dharma*) called consciousness (*caitanya*). He explains the word *caitanya* as "the attribute" (*dharma*).
He states that what is expressed by the nominative case is "grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is the meaning of the word "stated" (*udita*).
He explains [the point] with the words "it has been stated. In response to the inquiry as to where and by whom this was said, he says, "by the Blessed One. Now, one might ask:

is the Self described here by means of a word denoting dharma, or is it also mentioned elsewhere? To this he replies, "consciousness" (caitanya). As to why this is an indirect indication (upalakṣaṇa), he says, "the power of consciousness" (citiśakti).

The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) is the immutable Self; for that which is seen by it—the vision whose nature is the Self—there is isolation (*kaivalya*), meaning indifference. "The seer is pure vision alone" is the meaning of these three aphorisms. By the word *dharma*, the power of consciousness is meant as being immutable.

By the Infinite One. For that is called a "substance" (*dravya*) wherein the entire range of categories of objects finds its rest, shines forth, and is sought for the sake of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). If that [Infinite] is not contradicted, then this entire collection of principles, elements, beings, and worlds, resting within consciousness, becomes such [a substance]; therefore, it is He alone.

That very [entity], which has as its nature a distinct category (padārthāntara) serving as the substratum for properties such as qualities and actions, and which rests upon that very essence of primary substance (mukhyadravyasvarūpa), is itself substance (dravya). For it is that [essence] which serves as the foundational wall for the repose of the entire mass of infinite attributes.

By the phrase "and so forth," it is meant "by the remainder" (*anantena*), because these three sūtras are situated among the sūtras of Patañjali. Now, one might object: "In that case, it follows that the self (*ātman*) is secondary (*apradhāna*); for a property (*dharma*) that is dependent on another is clearly secondary. To this he says: "For [it is] substance" (*dravyaṃ hi*). Substance is the substratum of qualities (*guṇa*).
This means "the primary reality. In response to the inquiry "What is that?", he says "that which" (yat).
The meaning is that it is not merely a category of objects consisting of qualities, actions, and so forth, as is maintained by the logicians regarding substances.
It "shines"—it manifests like a jar in clay. Then, in response to the inquiry "Of what nature does it become?", he says:
"And it is sought after" means that people seek it for the sake of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—that is, for their respective individual purposes.
Indeed, no one seeks a jar that has not been extracted from its clay for the purpose of fetching water.
Having perceived the student's acceptance of this point, [the author] proceeds by resorting to the maxim: "When the needle has entered, the mallet follows."
Even regarding the principles (*tattva*) and so forth which are considered to be subjects (*dharmin*), he states that "that" refers precisely to their being the nature of the self (*ātma-dharmatva*).

"Elements" (*bhūta*) refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*); "entities" (*bhāva*) refers to derivative material things (*bhautika*). "Properties" (*dharma*) are the dependent, and "substrata" (*āśraya*) are the subjects (*dharmin*). Those [elements and entities] are distinct categories (*padārthāntara*), and their "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is their essential form (*svarūpa*).
"Of whom such [is the nature]" means whose form consists of all subjects and objects (*dharma-dharmin*).

That very consciousness, which is the nature of the object itself— the primary substance by virtue of being the substratum of all, and not a substance in the sense intended by the logicians— she alone...
The meaning is that consciousness alone is substance (*dravya*), while everything else is merely of the nature of a quality (*guṇa*). For this very reason, it was said by the venerable Lord:
"Renouncing all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone."
Thus, here the word *dharma* refers to the entire collection of existent things (*bhāva-jāta*) and not specifically to religious duty such as the Cāturmāsya sacrifice.
Furthermore, by the word "our" (*asmad*), consciousness itself is the *dharma*;
this is because the abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) is produced from the agentive *kṛt* suffix in the word *caitanya*.

Even by that which expresses a relation, [the action] is shown primarily; for it is so because there is a cognition resting upon the relation, and because the relatum, being of the nature of a substance, is expressed by the base (prakṛti),
while the suffix (añ) makes known the related attribute in the form of the act of consciousness.
The extracted portion is indeed recognized as the extracted portion itself. Furthermore,
the agency within consciousness— that is, autonomy consisting of the forms of conjunction, disjunction, synthesis, and so forth—
exists only within the state of pure selfhood (*ātma-mātratā*).

But it is not consciousness delimited by the body. Therefore, the meaning here is as follows: having abandoned the entire collection of existing things and brought them to a state where they are no longer objects of the intellect, take refuge in Me alone—that certain Reality which abides there as the essence, whose nature is pure luminosity and whose form is pure Being.

"Know that [it is the Self] by virtue of its being the bestower of existence even to itself. Furthermore, it should be understood that all sins therein are precisely the collection of objective entities (*bhāvajāta*) which act as a bond; for bondage itself is sin, and not some kind of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Enough with this elaboration. He provides the conclusion with the word "that" (*tat*): "of that"—namely, of consciousness (*saṃvit*).

That very [consciousness]— being of the nature of consciousness itself— from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the suffix *yu*, which is prescribed for the agent according to the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67),
and by means of the suffix *ṣyañ* prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*), [denotes] the relationship— the relation of attribute and substrate.

It has been shown primarily as the very nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpatvena*); for existence (*bhāva*) is indeed nothing other than the essential nature itself. To support this very point, he begins with the words "For it is thus" (*tathā hi*). Of that which rests in the related [terms]—that is, resting in the correlates—and which consists of substance (*dravyarūpa*), namely, the form of the substratum called consciousness (*cetana*).

"By nature"—by the nature of the element called consciousness (*cit*). "In the form of the activity of consciousness" means that activity alone is primarily the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*); this is the intended sense. "Dharma"—namely, the activity of consciousness—"connected"—endowed with a connection to the conscious subject—"making known"—because it is prescribed in the abstract state (*bhāva*) [of the action].

By indicating [the action] through the suffix *ṣyañ*—that is, by the suffix *ṣyañ*—the extracted portion, namely the part consisting of the act of piling (*citikriyā*) which is separated from consciousness (*cetana*), becomes signified—that is, it is made known. As it has been said:
"For when a word is applied to a substance on account of a certain quality belonging to that class, the two suffixes *tva* and *tal* occur in denoting that [quality]."

Thus [it is said]. And here, the two suffixes (tva and tal) indicate that all states and notions are characterized by this. Now, one might ask: "Let that be so; what follows from it? To explain the word *cit*, he says: *citi*. The construction is: "And the activity of consciousness (*citikriyā*) becomes 'I'. When the question arises as to what the nature of this activity of consciousness is, he says: "Agency resides in consciousness" (*citau kartṛtā*).

It is like an insentient thing in its lack of rest, yet it has as its essence an unconditioned luminosity and does not look toward another for its source. Precisely that [consciousness] brings about a distinction from the insentient non-self, which lacks the sovereignty to perform conjunction, disjunction, and so forth. Thus, by virtue of its supremacy and primacy...

Intending to refer to the Self as "consciousness," [the author] states everything from "the Self" up to "not looking toward another" in order to set aside other attributes and to emphasize the attribute of discernment (*vimarśa*). Furthermore, the activity of consciousness arises from the substance called consciousness (*cetanā*).

By means of the suffix *ṣyañ*, the action called "building" (*cityā*) is extracted; and within the conscious principle denoted by the word *cit*—which ends in an agentive suffix and signifies "one who builds"—resides agency.
For it is only the agent of an action who is truly an agent; otherwise, even if possessing capacity, one would possess only a figurative agency and be like an insentient object.

The state of not resting in mere selfhood—meaning the absence of abiding in one's own nature alone according to the logic of insentient matter, which is to say, being a subject both with respect to oneself and with respect to others.
By this, the compound word *cit-kriyā-citikartṛtā* (the agency of the act of consciousness) is explained. For it is indeed the act of consciousness itself [that constitutes this].

"Citikatṛtā" means agency within consciousness; "by its purport" means with the intention that the very activity of consciousness is known as the agency of consciousness. He explains the remainder of the verse beginning with "tena" (by that) with the words "tadeva" (that very thing).
"Tadeva" refers to the agency of consciousness in the form of the "I"; "vailakṣaṇyādāyi" means that which brings about the differentiation of the self.

The sense is that the apprehension of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*) is impossible with respect to those [objects]. Relying upon this, he provides a clear commentary on the *Śivasūtra* and states the concise meaning of this verse, beginning with the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way).
"By way of supremacy" means by being established in this; "having intended" means having placed it in the mind.
In order to subordinate other attributes—
that is, to render other attributes such as permanence secondary— and in order to elevate the attribute of self-reflection— that is, to make the reflective awareness "I" primary.

And here, regarding this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the very life of manifestation, its status as an attribute of the Self has been set aside in order to establish its stability as non-dual, and it is declared to be the very nature of the Self; yet one should not suspect that, on that account, there is in reality any difference between the Self and that [reflective awareness], for all these [distinctions] serve solely the purpose of instructing the disciple.

The processes and the awakening have as their sole object non-duality (advaita); therefore, only that much should be accepted by which the establishment of non-duality is achieved, and not even duality (dvaita) which follows involuntarily; rather, one must simply resort to freedom from it, for the capacity of words to bring about duality is indeed unavoidable.
As it has been said:
"When that which is non-different in self-cognition is expressed to another, then,
having resorted to the domain of verbal expression, it appears as if it were different."

It has been stated that [the term] is "caitanya" (consciousness). The compound is to be understood as having the sense of "the activity of consciousness" (*cit-kriyā*) and "the state of being the agent of consciousness" (*citi-kartṛtā*). For this is the convention in poetry—that there should be a pause at the half-verse (*ardha-yuk*), not in a technical treatise (*śāstra*). Alternatively, "the activity of consciousness" (*cit-kriyā*) and "the state of being the agent of consciousness" (*citi-kartṛtā*) may be taken separately as the Self (*ātman*) has arisen; however, this has not been read anywhere [in the tradition]. || 12 ||
Thus, even from this perspective, when one investigates the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the mind itself is precisely that which introduces duality here;
for this very reason, as long as "I" (*aham*) flashes forth, there occurs only the touch of a limited subjecthood (*paricchinnapramātṛtva*).
Therefore, in this context, one must simply effect composure within the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), which is by its very nature eternally radiant.
As it has been said:
"Alas! We shall declare the secret; O fools, do not wander within the spheres of the womb.
Hold fast to the heart that is exceedingly near, and exert yourselves for its sake."

Thus [it is said]. But even that does not apply there, because it would result in the fallacy of [the Self] being limited by its being something to be resolved through meditative concentration. As it has been said:
"Abandon your efforts of attention! Indeed, where can you possibly apply attention when entering into That Yourself?
For attention is certainly not appropriate toward the Full, nor does the Full ever become incomplete."
The state of truth.

Thus [it is said]. Enough with these ravings regarding the ineffable reality! He explains the compound stated by way of indication in its clarity: "the activity of consciousness" (*citkriyā*). Now, one might ask: how is this compound possible? For nowhere is a connection between the first half and the second half ever observed. To this he replies: "the half," etc.
"Ardhayuk" means "half-union," but it does not mean the union of the first half with the second half (parārdha).

"Pādaviśrānti" means rest or pause at the foot [of the verse]. "Śāstra" refers to works composed by Śiva and others. He states another alternative with the words "yadi vā" (or else). If that is so, let it be exactly thus; why then resort to an unestablished [interpretation]?
To the thought "we shall do so," he says "thus" (*evam*). The meaning is that this very [teaching] has not been heard through the succession of disciples and grand-disciples.
Here is the summary: for this very reason—namely, because manifestation (*avabhāsa*) has the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

By reason of the intent toward the activity of consciousness and the agency of consciousness, the Self is declared to be consciousness; this is stated by Śiva in the aphorism, "Consciousness is the Self. For—because of that cause—he—the Self—is distinct from the insentient, and he indeed becomes so through that consciousness.

Now, an objection may be raised: just as both "illumination" and "non-illumination" reside within its own self, and therefore when "illumination" is mentioned, no distinction from the insentient (jaḍa) has been expressed; in the same way, both "reflective awareness" (vimarśa) and "non-awareness" (avimarśa) reside within its own self—so how, by that [mere mention of awareness], can the distinction between the insentient and the sentient be established?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Consciousness (citi), whose nature is reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa), is the supreme Word (parā vāk) arising from its own inherent savor (svarasa).
This is the primary autonomy (svātantrya); that is the sovereignty (aiśvarya) of the Supreme Self. (13)

In the expression "it intends" (*cetayati*), that which is the act of intending (*citi*)— the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) characterized by the wonder of one's own self— is its essence (*ātmā*), that is, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For instance, a jar does not produce wonder within itself.
For the most part, the primary dharma is designated by way of its own essential nature, just as the mental dharma of volition (saṃkalpa) is designated as "mind" (manas); this is sufficient. 12.
Now he provides the introduction to the thirteenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"both"—that is, the pair—resides within its own self, but not in relation to one another.
Because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), it cannot be the cause of differentiation, since differentiation is the effect of conceptualization;

therefore, both that [conceptual] reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and non-reflective awareness (*avimarśa*) would have to exist within its own self. For this reason, how could even that pair of reflective awarenesses [bring about differentiation]?
