Anticipating the objection that there is a distinction between the insentient and the sentient, and having raised such a doubt, he says: "Consciousness [says]... and so forth.
Here is the commentary:

He provides the etymological explanation of the word *citi* as "it causes to perceive" (*cetayati*). Regarding this term *cetayati*, the *citi* that resides within this analysis is the action called *citi* which is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātuprakṛti*), and not the *citi* denoted by a primary suffix (*kṛtpratyaya*) prescribed for an agent; therefore, it is stated as "the act of perceiving" (*citikriyā*).

He explains the term *pratyavamarśa* (reflective awareness) as "one's own self" (*svātman*). It is characterized by the wonder of one's own self—the nature of the relish of one's own object, namely "I. He explains the term *ātmā* (self) as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). By this, the analysis of the compound for this word is indicated: that whose self is reflective awareness.

To explain how this is its very nature, he says: "For thus. It is not "wondered at"—that is, the "I" is not reflected upon as one's own self; it is not manifested by that [subject] within itself; it is not manifested as something undivided; therefore, it is said to be "not an object of cognition. However, for Caitra, within his own self, there is the thought "I."
Through the conjunction of impetus, exertion, exhilaration, and manifestation, one is struck with wonder; one's own Self is perceived, and it is revealed within the Self alone.

That limitation which consists of the thought "this," by its very nature as such, exists as something distinct [from the Self], appearing as the innumerable manifestations of blue, yellow, pleasure, pain, emptiness, and so forth.

It is illuminated by yoga; therefore, it is said that "it is cognized by Caitra. And thus, even though reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is non-reflective with respect to its own self, the bliss that is its own object is not experienced. He himself provides the explanation for this: "by its own self" (*svātman*).
It is "reflected upon"—that is, it is brought to the state of being an object of reflective awareness; for this very reason, it is not manifested [as an object].

Here, he provides his own explanation with the word "not. It is not manifested as something delimited—that is, it does not become an object of the undelimited manifestation "I," but rather [it appears] as "this."

It exists as an object with a delimited appearance; for that reason, it is said—that is, declared—what? That by that [object], namely the jar, it is not cognized—that is, it does not attain the status of being the agent of the act of consciousness. Now, let this be the case for the category of the insentient; but what is the situation regarding the category of the sentient? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "by Caitra": within one's own self—that is, within one's own object—the "exertion" (saṃrambha-udyoga) which is the "I-sense," namely the effort directed toward the state of being an agent; the "manifestation" (ullāsa) of that very exertion is itself the "splendor" (vibhūti), that is, sovereignty.
Through its connection with that [splendor], it is manifested within one's own self alone, and not even in another subject.
The sense is that it exists as the object of illumination, because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatvāt*).

By way of being distinct from that [object], it is the "I" (*aham*); whereas the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that "this is Caitra," which occurs through a limited determination (*pariccheda*), resides only in that body and so forth—this is the sense. Its emptiness (*tacchūnyatā*)—

The emptiness of blue and so forth; by this, the apprehension of the appearance in deep sleep is illuminated—that one's own self is not experienced as the grasper of blue and so forth, in the form "I am possessed of the cognition of blue and so forth.
Therefore—for that reason—he provides the conclusion with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). This:
In the introduction, the meaning is that it was "doubted. For consciousness (*cit*) is indeed the act of cognizing;

it is the very nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). Thus, the sense is that this reflective awareness possesses the capacity to manifest the distinction of the insentient from its own support, which is non-insentient. In response to the inquiry "How is this so?", he says:
This [claim] that [consciousness] is non-existent with respect to itself is unproven. For reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is all-enduring;

it assimilates the other into itself, assimilates itself into the other, unifies both, and having unified them, renders even that duality subordinate—such is its very nature. And this reflective awareness consists in internal speech (*antar-abhilāpa*).

It has the nature of verbalization (*śabdana*) consisting of internal discourse; and that verbalization, independent of convention (*saṅketa*), is essentially uninterrupted wonder (*camatkāra*), for it is indeed *vimarśa*.
*Vimarśa*—the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) whose form is the activity of consciousness (*citikriyā*)—is self-accomplished, and not [dependent on anything else].

Because it is luminous, it is capable merely of receiving external reflections; for this very reason, it assimilates even that which is other [to itself], as in the case of possession by a spirit (*bhūtāveśa*). For in that state, one experiences such cognitions as "I am a yakṣa residing in such-and-such a banyan tree. To the question of what further occurs, he says: "the self" (*ātmānam*).

The thought is: "I am not Caitra. He unifies both as well—thinking, "That which is the tree-spirit (vaṭayakṣa) is indeed I. Regarding the phrase "the two": the two refer to oneself and the other; the meaning is, "I am neither Caitra nor am I the spirit. As it has been said:
There is no snake in the rope, yet it produces terror leading even to death;
who indeed can determine the immense power of delusion?

Thus, by these two words alone the intended meaning is established; it should be understood that the remaining qualifiers are solely for the purpose of highlighting the extreme wonder of this reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). In this regard, he explains the term "supreme speech" (*parā vāk*) with the words "and reflective awareness. And [it is] reflective awareness.

And reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) is said to have the nature of consciousness (*citirūpa*), and it is internal— that which exists externally in the form of the *madhyamā* [speech], but has not yet ascended to the level of *paśyantī* nor descended into the state of *vaikharī*; whereas in its internal state, it exists as the nature of *parā*, consisting of non-differentiated speech (*anabhilāpātmaka*).

It has the nature of manifest speech (*vyaktavāgrūpa*), not being indistinct like the crowing of a cock or similar sounds; it is that which has the utterance of sound (*śabdanam*) as its inherent nature, because the recollection of sound itself consists of a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) in the form of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). By this, its status as speech (*vāktva*) is established. It is that which is denoted by the term "the Supreme" (*parā*).

It establishes fullness with the words "and that. And that "verbalization" (śabdana)—which is verbalization consisting of the very nature of reflective awareness—is indeed independent of convention (*saṅketa*);
it is devoid of dependence on convention, unlike external speech. Otherwise, [this would not apply] in the case of newborn infants and the like.
There would be no arising of that [state], for even in that [infant] there certainly exists a subtle self-reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "I";

otherwise, the longing for breast milk and so forth for the sake of one's own self would be illogical—this is the sense. Likewise, it is "uninterrupted"—that which has not fallen away from the Supreme Self due to the absence of contact with objectivity (*idantā*).
The marvel (*camatkāraḥ*)—

which is like the internal indication of the head [of the alphabet] and which constitutes the very life of the conventional, illusory words beginning with *a* (such as "this is blue," "I am Caitra," etc.)— is [the state of consciousness].
Because she is the foundational ground for other reflective awarenesses such as "this is blue" or "I am Caitra," and because she is fullness, she is *parā* (the Supreme).
She is called *vāk* (Speech) because she speaks—that is, she expresses—the universe through reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). For this very reason, she is by her own inherent nature...

It is that whose nature consists of the "I" (aham), which is the savoring of its own essential nature; such is the Self. For this very reason, it is inward-turned (*antarmukha*). That which is the indication of an object—namely, the indication of a thing made by nodding the head and so forth—is similar to the manifestation (*prakhyam*) of that [Self]. Even here, a conventional sign (*saṅketa*) certainly exists, yet it is merely of such a limited scope.

In such cases as these, a convention certainly exists within the performance; nevertheless, this was stated with the intention that [the convention] is not manifest. Likewise, the letters beginning with 'A' are the conventional words belonging to Māyā, by virtue of their nature as differentiation.
Words such as "cow" and so forth have as their object the conventions regarding the products of *māyā*; they are those whose life-force consists in the state of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

And these other reflective cognitions (*pratyavamarśa*), such as "I am Caitra," are of the nature of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) concerning external and internal objects, which constitute this play (*līlā*).
Reflection (*pratyavamarśa*), because it serves as their foundation—that is, because it exists as their substratum. As it has been said:
"The vibrations and non-vibrations of the qualities (*guṇas*) and so forth obtain their self-existence by relying upon the universal vibration."

Thus, "because of fullness" means by such fullness; for the word *parā* has fullness as its very meaning. And so, [it contains] the entire expansion of speech consisting of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, all situated within the womb.

This is the meaning. By this, its status as the supreme (*parātva*) is established. He provides an explanation of the word *vāk* through a cumulative construction (*samuccaya*) by means of the term "speaks" (*vakti*).

He explains the word "speaks" as "expresses" (*abhilapati*). [The phrase] "by means of reflective awareness" (*pratyavamarśena*) means by the function of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśavṛttyā*), and not by the function of mere utterance (*uccāravṛttyā*). The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).

He combines this commentary with the previous one. He explains the word *svarasoditā* (arisen from its own essence) with the words *svarasena*. "Own" (*sva*) means that which has become one's own self; "essence" (*rasa*) means the aesthetic flavor (*āsvāda*), and not [produced] by anyone through any effort whatsoever.

By virtue of its nature as consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), arising as the embodiment of repose in its own self, it is always unceasing, eternal, and simply "I" (*aham*). This alone is said to be the supreme sovereignty, power, lordship, and independence of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is not contingent upon anything else. However, the intermediate [sovereignty] belongs to that which takes the form of the object "this" (*idambhāva*).

Even upon the mere awakening of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), which has non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) as its life-breath, there is a resting solely in the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) within the state of *paśyantī* on the plane of Śrī Sadāśiva and the rest; however, the other [state] occurs only when the sense of "this-ness" (*idambhāva*) itself becomes firmly established in the womb of Māyā.

"By its own nature" (svabhāvena) means up to this point. And that [nature] of hers is precisely the state of being consciousness (cidrūpataiva); thus it is said "by way of the state of being consciousness. Of what kind? It is that whose body (vapuḥ) consists of the repose within itself—the resting as "I" (aham). He explains the word "arisen" (uditā) with the word "always" (sadā): she is always unsetting.
The meaning is "ever-arisen," which is to say "shining forth once and for all. As it has been said:
"This Self shines forth once and for all.
He himself provides the explanation of this term as well, saying "eternal" (nityā). It is simply "I" (aham).
The meaning is that it has the nature of manifesting through the absence of eternal egoity (*nityāhaṃtā*). To explain the second half [of the verse], he says "this very" (*etad*).

And this very thing—namely, *pratyavamarśa* (reflective awareness) itself—is used in the neuter gender in view of the word "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*). It belongs to the Supreme Self, whose nature is Light and who is the limitless subject; it does not, however, belong to...

[This refers to] the limited cognizer who is considered the subject (*grāhaka*), because he is the locus of a limited sense of "I-ness" (*ahantā*). He explains the term *aiśvaryapada* as "lordship" (*īśitṛtva*). He states another synonym: "non-other" (*ananya*). The word "is said" (*ucyate*) implies "by the wise" (*paṇḍitaiḥ*). Now, one might object: let there be "supreme-ness" (*parātva*) here, but how can this [power] possess "both supreme and non-supreme-ness" (*parāparātva*)?

To the question "Where is it? he says: "the higher and the lower. For one whose life-force is non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), because of contact with the *māyā*-principle even above [the level of *kalā*], there is "mere awakening"—that is, mere manifestation—but not yet an orientation toward its own effects; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*),...
This refers to the apprehension of Īśvara and the others, as he will state:
"Īśvara is the external unfolding (unmeṣa), Sadāśiva is the internal closing (nimeṣa).
Even though in the state of Īśvara there is an equal predominance of both "I-ness" (ahantā) and "this-ness" (idantā), [it is still distinct].
Because he possesses a preeminence superior even to Brahmā and the other gods, he is described as being on an equal footing with Śrī Sadāśiva.
In response to the inquiry, "Wherein does his state of being 'other' (aparatva) consist?", he says, "The other (apara). [The term] *nirūḍha* means "rested" or "established. Now, one might object:
what then of Śrī Sadāśiva and the others?

Even for Viṣṇu, Viriñca (Brahmā), Indra, and the others who have attained their status, that [status] arises solely from the grace of the Supreme Lord. Thus, in the ultimate sense, bliss, sovereignty, autonomy, and consciousness consist precisely in this independence from anything else. Therefore, what was stated is correct.
...therefore, it is indeed distinct from the insentient.
Thus [ends verse 13].
He demonstrates that this very point has indeed been shown even in the Pradhāna scriptures: "That radiance is the Great Being, undifferentiated by space or time;
as the very essence, it is declared to be the Heart of the Supreme Lord. (14)
Thinking that sovereignty must indeed exist [for them], he says: "But that" (*tattu*). "That" refers to sovereignty;
"of them" refers to Sadāśiva and the others; "born from the grace of the Supreme Lord" means born from the grace of Paraśiva, whose nature is supreme illumination. As it has been said:
"These [beings] have become lords by means of the droplets of that [Lord's] sovereignty.

Alternatively, in response to the inquiry as to how sovereignty and the rest possess a nature that is independent of anything else, he says "supreme and non-supreme" (*parāparam*). He provides a conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means "for this reason."
By means of this support, he states that what has borne fruit must be established as a proven fact, using the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
The sense is that the capacity of reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) to distinguish between the insentient and the sentient is clearly expressed by this verse. || 13 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fourteenth verse with the words "pradhāna" (the primal matter).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"In the scriptures of the Pradhāna—that is, among the proponents of Mahādvaita."
In the principal scriptures such as the *Mālinīvijaya*, having thus provided an introduction and presented the verse, he explains it: "That is radiance (*sphurattā*).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
The word *sā* (she) refers to that which is intent upon the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the nature of consciousness (*cit*).

With this word of clear meaning, he explains the term *sphurattā* (vibrancy) without further commentary, saying "here" (*iha*). Here—in this context—refers to the sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

When it is asked, "Why does a jar exist here, and why does a sky-flower not exist? the speakers reply, "For the jar manifests to me, but the other does not. If this manifestation were simply the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*), [then the question would remain].

The connection with manifestation means that it would manifest for everyone at all times—or else it would not manifest for anyone at all. Therefore, what is the meaning of "it manifests for me"? It means that my own manifestation, my own vibration (*spandana*), has entered into [me]. And vibration is a slight movement; this alone—

And what is this state of having some form of existence, such that even in a world filled with entities, a jar exists—for what reason?—for a specific cause, because it possesses being (*sattā*) and is established through its existence;
whereas why does a sky-flower not exist? Because it too is established through its non-existence.

When it is said, "Because of its well-known status," and someone intent on reaching a definitive conclusion asks, "How so? those who provide the answer give such a reply. Why? Because the pot "manifests to me"—that is, it becomes the agent of manifestation within my cognition; therefore, the sense is that it exists. As for the other—the sky-flower—it does not.

It vibrates; therefore, the sense is that it does not [independently] exist. To the question "But what follows from that?", he says: "That which is this... "That" means for that reason; "this" refers to that which is appearing; "pot-ness" is the very nature consisting of the state of being a pot;
"vibration" is the agency of vibrating; and he provides a synonym for this: "the relation with vibration."
There must be a connection with the act of manifestation, because it is logical that an agent is connected with an action,

otherwise agency would be impossible; consequently, everything would manifest for everyone at all times— for the "pot-ness" of a pot is not perceived by some people alone— or else, in the alternative case, if its nature were admitted to be non-manifesting.

It might not manifest for anyone else because there would be no distinction [between them], yet this is not logical, since that manifestation belongs only to the single one who is permeated by it—this is the sense. Now, if one asks, "What then is to be said here?", he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He states the answer: "My own" (*madīyam*). "My own" means belonging to me, the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).

"Sphuraṇam" (vibration) means an expansion in the form of manifestation; "spandanam" (throbbing) means a slight movement consisting in the taking of an object such as a jar; "āviṣṭam" (entered) means that the meaning becomes thus. Now, if it is asked what is meant by "spandana," he says: "And spandana... He provides the determination of its "slightness" (kiñcitva) with the words: "This very..."
It appears as moving; it appears as moving by virtue of its mobility.
For its nature as light does not differ even in the slightest, yet it seems to differ. Thus, that which is indeed immovable appears as if endowed with various distinct manifestations.
And it shines forth precisely as endowed with the differentiation of appearances. Therefore it has been said:
"Śiva is the Self alone, whose nature is blissful consciousness, flashing forth within all entities;
whose flow of will is unobstructed, and whose powers of vision and action are ever-expanding."
Thus it is said:
"Whether one is extremely angry or exceedingly joyful, or reflecting 'What shall I do?',
or while running— whatever state one enters, therein vibration (spanda) is established" (Svacchandatantra 22).
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that it is perceived through delusion (*bhrama*). Now, one might ask: why should the movement not be real?
To this he says: "in manifestation" (*prakāśa*). It does not exceed [the nature of consciousness]; that is, it does not become endowed with the specific form of movement.
Because it is extremely pure, it is free from all conceptual construction (*kalpa*); otherwise, extreme purity would be impossible.

For that which manifests another as a reflection while itself appearing as if non-existent is said to be "extremely pure. If one does not accept this extreme purity, then its nature as luminosity (*prakāśatva*) is untenable, for luminosity is indeed a supreme manifestation.

It is not possible for that which is impure [to move], because it is shrouded by impurity; nor is it at all logical for something that is "nothing" to possess the nature of movement, as it is quite evident that a gross entity cannot abide within a substance that has transcended all essence. Nevertheless, that which appears as a reflection is indeed "something."

Although it has been established that it is indeed improper for that which is non-existent (asat) to possess even a slight degree of reality, this was stated specifically for those seized by the delusion of its reality; enough with this elaboration. Now, if it does not exceed [the substrate], then it would have no movement whatsoever; therefore, he says: "as if it exceeds."

The inclusion of the word "śabda" (word) serves the purpose of dispelling the doubt that [the manifestation] might be ultimate reality. For this reason, that which is the nature of light shines—remaining indeed immovable—as if endowed with the differentiation of manifestations, and as if accompanied by the differentiation of manifestations known as movement; for such is its inherent nature, and yet it is not so.
The sense is that an inquiry into intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is appropriate.

Here, he cites the consensus of other treatises with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*). "Sphuran" means that it becomes endowed with *sphurattā* (vibrant manifestation). [This is for] the discernment of the principle of Spanda (*spandatattva*).
"For the sake of discerning the nature of vibration, which consists of slight movement... for the purpose of discerning the reality of Spanda" (Spa.
"And: 'The outflows of the vibration of the qualities and so forth...

(Spanda-kārikā 19). Even in the world, despite the presence of various diversities, a person who does not deviate from their own essential nature is called 'profound' and 'possessing vibration' (*spandavat*). And existence is *bhavana*."

The connection is with the phrase "being constantly engaged. In that context, the construction is as follows: in states such as extreme anger and so forth, the vibration (*spanda*) established there becomes a general vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*) which serves as the substratum for specific vibrations.
The "outflows of vibration" (*niṣyanda*) of the qualities and so forth are the streams of vibrations of pleasure and so on, dominated by the three *guṇas*.

The connection is as follows: having attained their own existence by relying upon the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*), they do not become obstacles for the Knower. This [point] should be examined in the *Spandakārikā-ṭīkā*;
here, however, it is merely an illustration of the conventional usage of the name "vibration" (*spandana*) whose essential nature is the throbbing of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Since that alone is useful, the original author has stated only that much; and we have merely provided a brief coordination of the connections. One should not be misled into thinking otherwise—that a thorough determination was not made due to fear of excessive prolixity and because it was not useful for the present subject. This is the sense: if...

If there were no such thing as *pratyavamarśa* (reflective awareness), then in these great secret scriptures, there would be no discourse regarding *sphurattā* (vibrant manifestation)—which is its synonym—nor regarding its essential nature, *spanda* (vibration).
Therefore, he relies even upon worldly convention as a proof for this, saying "in the world. As for those various...

The distinction is as follows: their variety arises through conjunction; they possess vibration due to the onset of slight agitation; and they possess depth because of their immovability. By this, the absence of "vibrancy" (sphurattā) in the reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) whose nature is consciousness (citi) is established. For the vibration of light (prakāśa-spanda) is simply not possible apart from the reflective awareness of its own essential nature.
In its presence, everything other than it is impossible, just as a heap of cotton is impossible in the presence of fire;
as for the act of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), it is conceived as a manifestation of its sovereign power (*aiśvarya-vijṛmbhā*) and does not entail any such incapacity— enough said.

Agency (*kartṛtā*) is independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to all actions. And since that [agency] pervades even such things as a sky-flower, he now explains the word "Great Being" (*mahāsattā*), beginning with the words "And existence" (*sattā ca*). Having first set aside the member-word "great" (*mahat*), which functions as a qualifier, he takes up the member-word "existence" (*sattā*), which functions as the substantive.
He explains [the word] *bhavana* as "becoming. Regarding "becoming"—that is, existence—he explains the status of being the agent as "all" (*sarva*).

This is the intended meaning: in the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), the root *as* is recited as "in becoming" (*bhuvi*); and "becoming" (*bhava*) is simply manifestation, not a new production. As it was said by the venerable Blessed One:
"Existence does not belong to the non-existent.
Therefore, from that verbal root (*dhātu*), there is the *laṭ* suffix in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), and upon that, the *śatṛ* suffix;

that too, by virtue of being treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), refers only to the agent. Then, by the rule "the elision of *a* in the case of *śnau*," there is the elision of the vowel *a*. After that, the *sup* suffix [is added].

It is established that [the entity] is "existent" (sat), and this occurs in the sense of "coming into being" (prādurbhavan). That which is its state of being (bhāva)—its very own nature—by virtue of which it is called "existent," is existence (sattā); for the suffix -tal is used in the sense of "being" (bhāve).
By this suffix, there is extracted from the substratum (dharmin) the bare form of the action of becoming (bhavanakriyā), which establishes agency as something distinct.

Dharma is said to be manifestation (*prādurbhāva*) by way of its result; and it is precisely by depending upon this that all actions (*kriyā*) obtain their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). For in such usages as "he cooks" (*pacati*), the actual meaning in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*) is "he becomes a cooker" (*pacan bhavati*) and so forth, because in the absence of becoming (*bhavana*), the state of being a cooker (*pācakatva*) would be impossible. Therefore, of this...
The agency of all actions is established everywhere for the agent of the act of manifestation;
moreover, the sovereignty of light consists solely in self-reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) and nothing else.
And manifestation is the form of the disclosure of that which is eternally present as light.
Thus it is established that the nature of existence (*sattā*) consists in the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of one's own self.

To exclude the possibility that this [existence] is a reflective awareness in the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), he says "And that" (*sā ca*), in order to make the use of the word "Great" (*mahat*) fruitful. "And that"—meaning existence—pervades even such things as a sky-flower.

Because of its independence in all actions, when it is said "it does not exist," it is understood by implication that "it becomes non-existent"; therefore, this becoming is not limited, like a becoming that rests solely upon an existent entity (*bhāva*). [Objection: But how is it not limited? [Response: True, because it pervades both existence and non-existence. Indeed, apart from existence and non-existence...

Does it exist or not? If it does not, then our desire has borne fruit; for it is not logical that what is non-existent should possess the property of being pervaded (avyāpyatva), and thus by whom has its own state of being pervaded (vyāpyatva) been set aside? As it has been said:
"Just as the sun rises in the sky even without [visible] objects..."
O Blessed One, in the absence of anything to be known, by what means has your arising been brought about?
The "Great One" (mahatī) does not need to be qualified by space and time, because she herself creates them, just as blue and other qualities do.
For that which appears as being of equal status with something else cannot be its qualifier, just as a bracelet [cannot be the qualifier of the hand].
If it were to exist [as a separate entity], then it would be even more so [not a qualifier], since one must admit that existence itself pervades even that. But surely—

In that case, there would be the consequence of duality. Oh, what forgetfulness! Immediately prior, it was shown that the activity of consciousness and its agent are designated as one; here too, that same principle applies. For this very reason, even by the Vedāntins, Brahman’s form is said to be pure existence alone (*sattāmātra*). As for what they [say]...
They say that its inability to withstand critical inquiry is due to something else entirely; for we too describe the Sadāśiva-tattva in such a manner,
and thus there is no room for this objection regarding those who have not yet ascended to the state of Paramaśiva.

He concludes his own intention with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti"—meaning for this reason—this existence (*sattā*) is "great," that is, it is unlimited; therefore, the sense is that she is called "Mahāsattā" (Great Being) in the Sūtra.
He explains the term "unqualified by space and time" (*deśakālāviśeṣiṇī*) with the word "space" (*deśa*); she alone is of the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).

Consciousness itself creates—that is, by way of its nature as reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it causes [the object] to deviate from the nature of the supreme light, which is to say, it manifests it. For emission (*visarga*) in the form of reflective awareness is threefold: gross, subtle, and supreme.
As it has been said:

"Visarga is said to be threefold. Among these, the "supreme" (para) is denoted by the letter *ā*, because its nature is bliss (*ānanda*); it is through this that the Śiva-tattva, in which non-duality is predominant, manifests. And this has been established in the auspicious verse as being "from the Nirābhāsa."
Now, one might ask: how is it logical for that very *śakti-tattva*, whose nature is the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśa*), to be the cause of its own manifestation?
True; here, the statement regarding its being the cause of manifestation has the sole purpose of providing instruction.
In ultimate reality, however, that *tattva* is always and everywhere composed of all things (*sarvamaya*), and not merely in some place by means of something else.
As it has been said:
"Salutations again and again to that illustrious Guru, the ocean of wonder, who dwells entirely within the Reality."

Thus [it is said]. Here, the Guru, having become one with the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), is to be known as Supreme Śiva himself. By the term "the subtle *a*," the manifestation of the collection of principles (*tattva-vrāta*) beginning with Śiva and ending with Śuddhavidyā—which is characterized primarily by both difference and non-difference—is expressed. Furthermore, the gross breath is denoted by the letter *ha*; by that—

The manifestation of the collection of principles beginning with *māyā*, which is characterized primarily by differentiation (*bheda*), occurs. Thus, it is quite evident that space and time belong to this very [power] in their gross form. Now, one might ask: "Let it create; what of it?
To this he says: "Thus" (*iti*). "Thus"—for this reason—it is not to be qualified by those two, namely, space and time.

It exists, for it is not logical that what is created by that [consciousness] should be its qualifier, as in the case of Caitra being created by that [consciousness]. Furthermore, space and time do not appear on the same level as the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because it is impossible for them to be on the same level when they appear as "this-ness" (*idantā*) and it appears as "I-ness" (*ahantā*). Thus, due to the non-contact with space and time...

There is both omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and eternity (*nityatva*); for, through the power of its creative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), it touches all places and times, and thus its pervasiveness and eternity follow from that as well. As it has been said:
"The Great Being (*mahāsattā*), the Great Goddess, is called the life-force of the universe."

Thus [it is said]. That which is the "essence" (*sāra*), meaning the non-trivial form, is precisely this power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*). This is because it would be redundant for that [form], which was previously established as non-distinct from the subject-object duality (*grāhya-grāhaka*), to become its qualifier at a later time.
He states another reason with the word "since" (*yat*): why do these two not appear as being of equal status? To this he says: "of those two... (*tayoḥ*).

Thus: of those two—space and time; of that—of reflective awareness (vimarśa); in its manifestation—its flashing forth as a reflection within the sphere of supreme light; for the supreme subject, while grasping his own self as "I," grasps even that state of "I-ness" solely through its repose within his own self; otherwise, even that...

The point is this: because it would follow that [the cognition] would be an external conceptual construction (*bāhyavikalpa*), whereas space and time are clearly grasped as "this" (*idantayā*). Thus, at the time of their apprehension, there is no apprehension of her (the cognition), and at the time of her apprehension, there is none of them; so what talk can there be of a relationship between qualifier and qualified? By this, its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and eternity (*nityatva*) are established as a consequence.

He says "thus. The sense is that omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is clearly established by the absence of spatial limitation, and eternity (*nityatva*) by the absence of temporal limitation. Now, one might object:
"In that case, just as one place is not [identical to] another place, nor one time [identical to] another time..."
Likewise, O Blessed One, those two are never different from you.
By this reasoning, it follows that this [consciousness] possesses the same status regarding space and time; therefore, he says "entire" (*sakala*).

This is because of its connection with their manifestation—that is, because of its relation to those two as the creator at the very moment of the creation of space and time. Furthermore, the meaning is "even outside of space and time."

The sense is that these two are included within this [third category]; therefore, the intention is that its acquisition (*yoga*) and preservation (*kṣema*) are not equal to theirs. Here, he cites the consensus of the elders (*vṛddhasammati*), beginning with "Mahā-. By the phrase "the livelihood of the universe" (*viśvajīvana*), it is also stated that it is not restricted by place or time, since even those two [the other categories] are included within the universe; and that which is lived by someone...

That [term] is appropriately its qualifier. Having first established "this very" (*saiṣā*), he explains the word "essence" (*sāra*) by saying "the essence. He states what is denoted by the word "essence" as "not insignificant" (*atuccha*).
This [quality] implies the distinction from non-luminosity even regarding that form which consists of luminosity for the sense organs.
"This very [power]" is also established in the *Śrīsāraśāstra*:
"That which is the essence of this world is that supreme power, Mālinī.
By the words "this very," the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of power is demonstrated. And as for what is called the "Heart" (*hṛdaya*):

The locus of establishment (*pratiṣṭhāsthāna*) is not insubstantial; it is not established as a mere entity like a heap of entities, for otherwise it would be impossible for it to bestow essence upon the world. Indeed, the power to bestow essence upon a bow is never observed in the case of a hare's horn.

And as for the statement that the world is insubstantial (*tucchatā*), that is said merely with respect to its status as a world; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), since it has manifested from the Essence (*sāra*), it too is indeed the Essence. "This" refers to that whose nature was just described. Now, one might ask: how can this possess the quality of being the Essence? To this he says: "the object of apprehension. Its form consists of luminosity (*prakāśātmaka*).
The aspect of manifestation exists as the essence, just as the clay-portion exists as the essence of a jar;

and for that too—the form consisting of manifestation which resides within the objects of perception and so forth—there is a distinction, namely a difference from non-manifest entities. That which implies, i.e., brings about, this [distinction] is what is meant by "the illuminator."

The intention of the word "also" (*api*) is that this [argument] implies a distinction not only for that which is illuminated by another, but for all objects and subjects as well. Thus—this has been set forth in the *Śrīsāraśāstra*, that is, the *Mālinīvijaya*, by the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*). Now, if that is so, [how does it differ] from insentient things?

This very distinctness of the grasped and the grasper creates [the appearance of duality], whereas it is logical that the essence belongs to Light alone. Again, forgetfulness has arisen; what can we do? There is no difference whatsoever between this [duality] and Light;
for the sake of comprehension alone, duality is superimposed upon a single reality. But who are those "insentient" ones, from whom...?

It establishes a distinction from those things that serve as counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*). If they are indeed objects of cognition (*grāhya*), must their distinction [from insentient things] also be established? True; with respect to their essential constituent, it is intended here that they possess a distinction from insentient things. As for that nature termed "objectivity" (*grāhyatā*), it—

There is no inconsistency whatsoever in [the view that] it is also the counter-correlate of difference (*bhedapratiyogin*). To the question, "By which statement is this established there?", he says: "That which is the essence" (*yatsāram*). Those devoted to the Trika scriptures [recognize it] as being denoted by the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*) consisting of the traditional sequence of phonemes from *mā* to *pha*.
The conventionalized power of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa-śakti*); for that very [power] sustains the entire universe within itself.
It is "supreme" (*parā*) because its form is the supreme (*parā*), owing to its predominance of great non-duality (*mahādvaita*).
Thus ends the statement from the *Śrīsāraśāstra*. [This concludes] the explanation of the phrase "this very [power]" (*saiṣā*) established in the aphorism.

"It performs power" (*karoti śakti*). The recognition of power (*śaktipratyabhijñāna*) is the recognition of consciousness (*cit*), which consists of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*); it is a form of synthetic recollection (*anusandhāna*) directed toward that which was previously determined according to one's own philosophical system and is now taken up to be determined again according to the method of another system.
This refers to recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). He explains "the heart" as "the foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*).

From the foundation—[it] is liberated; and that, according to the stated principle, is consciousness for insentient things, and even for that [consciousness], its nature consists of light (*prakāśa*).

[The nature of luminosity—K. ṣ. ṣ. For that [luminosity] as well, there is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). This very heart, which consists of supreme mantra and takes the form of reflective awareness, belongs to that [consciousness] which abides and rests in the supreme state of the universe; wherever it may be, this is its heart. [Wherever—that is, K. ṣ. ṣ.]

[6. It is thus designated: for the mantra alone is the heart of everything, the locus of the existence of both oneself and the universe, because it is that which establishes them; for it is through reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone that the determination of the essential nature of both light (*prakāśa*) and entities occurs. In that regard:

The distinction is as follows: by the principle that "the nature of manifestation is the establishment of [general] light through the form of established vibration," there is the establishment of entities through the form of specific vibration. For indeed, the establishment of all entities is experienced by everyone within the very region of the heart; thus, everything is attested by direct experience.
The sense is that, by logical principle, this [Heart] alone is the "Heart" (the core) because it establishes all things.

And that "Heart"—for non-inert entities, which are of the nature of subjects—that which is called the "conscious" is precisely the limited aspect of light that constitutes their essence; and of that too—

Even for consciousness (*cetanasya*), there exists the nature of luminosity (*prakāśātmakatva*), because it has arisen from pure luminosity; and even for that [pure luminosity] which abides as the self of consciousness, there exists the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*). He explains the word "of the Supreme Lord" (*parameṣṭhinaḥ*) in the middle [of the verse] with the word "of the universe" (*viśvasya*); that is to say:

Of the universe, which consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), in the supreme state—the thirty-seventh station in the form of Paramaśiva. He provides a synonym for the word "abiding" by saying "of that which has come to rest. He refers to that [rest] as a whole by using the pronoun "his" (*tasya*). This is indeed of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

It is precisely the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). Because that Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*) has as his essence the pure light which is the essence of the consciousness that constitutes the core of the subject, he is called the "Heart" (*hṛdaya*) in all scriptures, wherever they may be. By this, the meaning of the term *prokta* (proclaimed) is explained. Of what nature is it?
"Consisting of the supreme mantra" means having the nature of the Great Mantra (mahāmantra). As it has been said:
"Mantras devoid of the first and the last [letters] would be like autumn clouds.
This qualifying attribute contains a reason (*hetugarbha*); for it is precisely because they consist of the supreme mantra that [they are so].
The meaning is "the heart.
And the mantra consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and reflective awareness is composed of the power of supreme speech (*parāvāk*). Therefore it has been said:
"Without those [mantras], there would be no word, no object, nor even the movement of consciousness."
Thus it is said.
In that regard, those who have attained [this state] assume the nature of a mother...
But how can this [state] consist of the supreme mantra? True; "mantra" means secret speech, and that—
Reflection (*vimarśa*) alone [is the essence], because it consists of internal verbalization; and that [verbalization] consists of the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*).

Its "supremacy" (*paratva*) arises from its transcendence over other reflective awarenesses that take the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Alternatively, here the word "mantra" indicates by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) the potency of mantra (*mantravīrya*); therefore—

The meaning is that it is the form of the supreme potency of mantra; and the nature of mantra as potency belongs clearly to *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), for a mantra that is not reflected upon is incapable of bestowing any fruit. As it has been said: "Then his mantras, possessing the power of the Omniscient One, become powerful."
They proceed for the sake of their respective functions, like the sense organs of embodied beings.

Thus, here the power of the Omniscient One is intended as the very act of discernment (*vimarśana*) in the form of one's own power (*ātmabala*). And because the sense organs clearly accomplish their respective functions through that power of the Self, they are taken as the objects of comparison;
furthermore, in the systems such as Śaivism, the Great Mantra consists of various types of collections of seed-syllables (*bīja-varṇa*).
There are many conventions (saṅketa), which, due to their extreme secrecy, are simply unfit to be stated by way of explicit imitation;

they must be obtained from one's own respective gurus preceded by great service and then recited (japya). We, however, have merely determined their potency (vīrya) in this context; but in the investigation of the ultimate reality (paramārtha):

The mere attainment of the potency (*vīrya*) of the mantra through recitation (*japa*) and other such practices is the fruit; however, those who have realized the potency of the mantra remain dedicated solely to the recitation of the mantra even during ordinary conversations. As it has been said:
"Conversation is recitation."

Thus [it is said]. As for its realization, however, it consists merely in the state of being intent upon that which is eternally present through simple attention (*avadhāna*), and not in the acquisition of something previously unknown; and this attention is achieved gradually by means of recitation (*japa*) and so forth.
Homage indeed to those for whom realization occurs even without such [gradual] means, having been struck by the most intense descent of the Lord’s power (*śaktipāta*).
As it has been said:

"He for whom [the practice] is not according to logic, nor through recitation, and which is not preceded by the prescribed rule—[even so], he possesses the appearance of Śiva; we bow to that devotee who is endowed with devotion."

Thus it is said: for those who, although performing the recitation (*japa*) every day, do not apply their attention to its potency (*vīrya*), the ritual procedure itself is their only protection—just as for those seeking oil from sand; and for one who has mastered the potency of the mantra, even the simultaneous utterance of all mantras [is possible].
And so forth, in the Āgamas; and likewise by the venerable Bhartṛhari:
"There is no cognition in the world that exists without the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge is perceived as if permeated by speech."
If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness,
then manifestation would not manifest, for it is that [nature] which possesses reflective awareness.
Thus,
this very consciousness of transmigrating beings exists both externally and internally;
for it is observed that upon departing [from the body], one becomes unconscious, like a piece of wood or a wall.
"It certainly occurs"—enough of this digression. Now, one might ask: how can reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), in its nature as mantra, be the "Heart" (*hṛdaya*)? To this he says: "of all.
Of all—that is, of the entire class of sentient beings—for non-sentient things obtain their very nature only by being grounded in this [reflective awareness]. By this alone...

The sense is that because it establishes the existence and non-existence of all things, the small [space] the size of a thumb is called the "heart" (hṛdaya) merely by virtue of being the locus of this [consciousness]. Now, one might ask: "Let the mantra be the heart; what does this have to do with *vimarśa* (reflective awareness)? In response to this expectation, it has been stated: ...even though it was said: [text follows]...

He speaks again of its nature as reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in order to make it perfectly clear, saying "of the nature of reflection" (*vimarśanātmā*). Now, one might ask: what is the form of that reflection? To this he says "the Supreme" (*parā*). That which is the Supreme Speech—the consciousness-form just mentioned—is its power; [the reflective awareness] consists of that, meaning its nature is a specific vibration (*spanda*). And thus:

The sense is that by establishing the status of mantra for the reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) which consists of the particular vibration belonging to the class of subjects, the status of Great Mantra (mahāmantra) for the reflective awareness consisting of universal vibration belonging to the infinite subjects is established effortlessly indeed.

Here he cites scriptural statements with the words "from that very [source]. The connection is as follows: it is stated in such scriptures as "by Śrī Śiva as the agent," and so forth, regarding the "object" (*karman*) and other categories; the meaning is "without those," that is, without the mantras.
The underlying sense is that everything has its life-force (*prāṇa*) in reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). Regarding the phrase "in that regard": the state of being a subject (*mātṛbhāva*)—

The state of being the Mothers (mātṛbhāva), such as Brāhmī and others, whose nature consists of the eight groups [of phonemes] beginning with 'a' and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādi) including other statements—is mentioned. He cites the words of the venerable Bhartṛhari as well, saying "there," and connects this with the phrase "it has been stated.
When the question arises as to what was stated, he recites those sentences partially: "na... [and so on].

"‘He is that’; ‘if it is the nature of speech’; ‘this very [speech]’—by the word ‘etcetera,’ other sentences found therein are included. In all three of these statements, the purpose is precisely to establish that the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) is the self of all; however, for fear of prolixity, it is not [discussed here]."

And so forth. By this, the statement "the wise know" has been established. Even by the Buddhists, who assert that the validity of manifestation depends upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), this point is almost entirely accepted, since conceptual determination consists of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*). || 14 ||

Now, one might ask: "Why is this power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) alone thus consecrated as such within the Supreme Śiva, whose body is adorned by a multitude of innumerable powers? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It has been explained. [This was stated] in the passage: "By relying on this, the wise know the nature of manifestation."

"By this, he effects the fulfillment (*nirvāha*) of this [statement]. "Fulfilled" means rendered free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣīkṛta*), because the agentive portion of the verbal form has been completed; this is the sense. Anticipating the objection, "But how is it fulfilled, since the Buddhists do not accept this meaning?", he says: "by the Buddhists."
"Dependent upon ascertainment" means with reference to ascertainment. As it has been said:

"Manifestation is according to ascertainment. It is "mostly accepted"—that is, accepted for the most part, but not in every respect—because in that [opponent's] view, there is no reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Because it is an error; for even in the case of an error, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is indeed observed with respect to a cognition qualified by that error, such as "this is an error"—so enough of this.

Now, in response to the expectation—"It was stated that the validity belongs to the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*), but not to the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)"—he states the reason: "because it consists of verbal expression" (*abhilāpa*). This is because it has the nature of verbal expression.
Because it has the nature of sound (*śabda*), it follows that even conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) is indeed reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*); this is established.
Even in that view, reflective awareness has manifestation as its very life-force (*prakāśajīvitatva*). The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the commentary on the verse. || 14 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the fifteenth and sixteenth verses with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"The innumerable powers"—that is, the powers in the form of the objects existing within the world.
As it has been said:
"The entire universe is His powers, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is the possessor of those powers.
His body—His essential nature—is adorned, that is, distinguished, by their series—that is, their row.

In such a one—namely, in the supreme Śiva, known as the thirty-seventh principle (*tattva*) which consists of the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti—in this manner—that is, by acting in this way, meaning in a faulty manner—for what reason? From what cause? Is this very power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), whose nature has just been described?

It is precisely the power of self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃpratyavamarśa*) that is consecrated—that is, it is rendered endowed with consecration. For this very reason, it should make itself the object of knowledge while remaining in a state of separation; yet, because of its orientation toward that object of knowledge, its sovereignty is not fragmented. (15)

The Lord, having projected out of His own freedom—which is non-dual in nature—a self that is [in reality] unliberated from that very freedom, engages in worldly transaction by means of volitions such as "I am the Lord" and so forth. (16)

The power of agency (*kartṛtva-śakti*), which is the essence of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), encompasses all powers; and since that [agency] consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it is logical that this alone holds primacy—this is the intended meaning of the reply. As for the literal sense of the words: the Supreme Lord, whose nature is Light (*prakāśa*), [perceives] His own self...

"Appointed" means she is brought to fulfillment; that is to say, she is established in the position of a high official. Having thus provided the introduction and presented two verses, he explains them, beginning with the words "the Self.
Here is the commentary:
Therein, he states the purport of the first two verses with the word "all" (*sarvāḥ*).

"Consisting of sovereignty" (*aiśvaryātmā*) means having the nature of sovereignty (*aiśvaryarūpā*); "she draws in" (*samākṣipati*) means she internalizes; and "that [power] too"—namely, the power of agency (*kartṛtvaśakti*)—"consists of reflective awareness" (*vimarśarūpā*) means its essential nature is that of self-reflective discernment (*pratyavamarśasvarūpā*).

Since the occurrence of the instruments (karaṇas) is preceded by reflective awareness (vimarśa), and even that activity of the body and so forth which is observed therein is likewise preceded by reflective awareness, it is perfectly clear that the power of reflective awareness possesses agency. Thus— for this reason— the primacy belongs to this very power of reflective awareness over all other powers.
This is the primary point. As it is stated in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:

"Therefore, the direct rule is that [the Lord] is joined with the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) alone. Here, the intended meaning is as follows: the word "therefore" (*tena*) refers back to what preceded it, because it is the power of absolute freedom alone [that constitutes the primary cause].

Therefore, the Lord is indeed endowed with the power of sovereignty (*svātantrya-śakti*), because by that very power all other powers are implied; thus, the positive injunction (*vidhi*) becomes manifest in its directness, as it briefly establishes everything. Thus—in this manner—the answer has been stated according to its intended meaning (*tātparya*).

The meaning is that the intended sense (*tātparyārtha*) here is as follows; this is what has been stated. He announces the explanation of the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) with the word "śabda. He demonstrates the very meaning of the word with the word "ayam" (this). He states the meaning of the term "prabhuḥ" (the Lord) as "parameśvaraḥ" (the Supreme Lord). The term "jñātā" (the knower) is a designation where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary focus.

Since it is of a single nature with the knower, that which is even unknowable is made known; this is what is rendered possible by a firm inference based on probability, because no other cause has been shown to be plausible.
That [occurrence] arises precisely from that very cause, namely agency characterized by the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti), since—

For this [Self] perceives itself; therefore, because it is filled with the universe (*viśvanirbharatvāt*), it shines forth as blue and so on. But how can such a possibility even be conceived—that the Self makes itself an object of knowledge? He says: because its nature (*tattva*) is that of having a single form whose essence is the state of being a distinct knower (*pṛthag-jñātṛtva*); therefore, even though it is unknowable—
It is also incompatible with being an object of knowledge; as it has been said:
"If the self were an object of cognition, its cognizer would have to be something other than itself.
In that case, the self would become that which is other, namely, that which is being measured."

Thus [it is said]. He makes it an object of knowledge—that which is unknowable, being itself, through its own power, manifests as an object of knowledge for the sake of the play consisting of the tasting [of its own nature]. "Thus" (iti) means in this way; that which is conceivable—that is, the subject matter of the possibility indicated by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the word *kuryāt* ("he should do") found in the Sūtra—is brought to the state of being an object of such possibility. Why?

Is it possible? No, because of the impossibility—that is, the unfitness—of any other cause, namely the totality of causes such as the material cause (*upādāna*) distinct from itself; this is established by a firm—not, like other reasonings, a weak—presumptive inference (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*) stated in the verse beginning with "syādetat."

Because it has been shown by means of an inference in the form of a possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). It completes the requirement for the word "that" (*yat*) with the words "that" (*tat*). "That" refers to the object denoted by the word "that"; thus he explains the word from the sūtra, "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), as follows:
"for this very reason" means for the reason of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), that is to say, for the reason of independence (*svātantrya*). It exists.
The meaning is that it is established. In response to the inquiry "Why?", he says "yataḥ" (because).

For—*hi*—from which cause, this—the Supreme Self, whose nature is light—*ayam*, in which part of itself (*yataḥ*), contemplates itself—that is, brings itself into the state of being the object of the reflective awareness "I"—*ātmānaṃ parāmṛśati*, therefore—in that part—*tataḥ*.

Because it is filled with the universe—that is, because it is replete with the entire world in the form of both real and unreal entities—and likewise because it shines as blue and so forth, in accordance with the corresponding reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), due to having that as its very nature;
for otherwise, the manifestation of the world in the form of existence and non-existence would be impossible. Nor [is this] of the nature...

It has been stated many times that this inquiry is appropriate. Here, the student asks, "Now... [nanu]. To the question "What is this?", he says, "The Self" [ātmānam]. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the question. He provides the answer with the words "He said" [āha]; the word "the teacher" [guru] is to be supplied as the subject.

An object of knowledge (*jñeya*) that exists as something external to consciousness cannot exist at all; the particle *tu* serves to emphasize this. The logical arguments for this have already been stated. Furthermore, he states an additional argument: if the object of knowledge were distinct [from consciousness], then that orientation (*aunmukhya*) of the Self—which consists of the knower—toward the object of knowledge [would be impossible].

That which is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is seen; it would not be so for this [consciousness] if it were otherwise. Therefore, by its orientation toward an object distinct from itself, a state of dependence—namely, subordination—is brought upon it. And subordination is the opposite of autonomy (*svātantrya*). Autonomy indeed consists in not looking toward another.
[The characteristic of not looking to another's face—K.
Ṣ. Ṣ. In response to the inquiry "What does it say?", he says "separately" (*pṛthak*). He provides the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) of this word as "from the Light" (*prakāśāt*).
He states the meaning of the particle *tu* as being for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*). By this, [the phrase] "abiding separately" (*pṛthaksthiti*) [is established].

It has been indicated that the word *padam* (the word) is to be joined with the second half [of the verse]. According to the maxim that "every sentence implies a restriction," the word *eva* (only/alone), though not explicitly stated in the sūtra, is to be understood; this was stated [previously] in the rule beginning with *prāgivārthaḥ*. In that context—where external objects of knowledge are impossible—the *yuktayaḥ* (reasons/logical arguments) are the primary reasons.
Because it proceeds by means of directly establishing that [point]. Now, one might object: "In that case, remain silent for now. To this, he says:

"as a supplementary argument" (*abhyuccaya*). The sense is that it is called a "supplementary argument"—meaning an argument of secondary addition (*anvācaya*), or rather, a non-primary argument—because it functions as an argument by way of the contingency of refuting independence. He says:

He fulfills the expectation of this [verse] and explains the remainder of the verse beginning with "tadaunmukhyāt" by means of the word "yadi. "Distinct" (vyatirikta) means inherently different; "then" (tat) refers to that time; "of the Self" (ātmanaḥ) refers to the infinite subject whose nature is light. To the question "Why should it not be so?", he replies with the words "by that" (tena).

"Dependence on another" (*anyādhīnatvam*) means being subject to an object of knowledge distinct from oneself; "of this"—that is, of the Self (*ātman*)—"is brought about"—meaning it is forcibly produced. To the question, "What follows from that?", he says: "And there is dependence on another" (*pāratantryam ca*).
To the objection, "In that case, let there simply be no independence," he says: "And indeed, [there is] independence itself" (*svātantryam eva ca*).
"Not looking to another's face" means independence from others regarding one's own establishment. This is the intended meaning:

the self exists precisely as a knower; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of even objects like pots being considered the self. Therefore, the self is established only through the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). And if that [object] were distinct [from the self], then the self's dependence on another would be manifest.

If the self were seized by dependence on another, then the self itself would be the very nature of the non-self; thus, a self that is not oriented toward its own distinct nature would be nothing but the non-self. And since the non-self is insentient, it follows as a logical consequence that it cannot be directed toward the object of knowledge. Therefore, by the reversal of this consequence:
This follows: being independent and oriented toward non-distinction, he makes himself alone the object of knowledge. || 15 ||

And not only is the object of knowledge (jñeya) merely form such as blue and so forth; rather, having fashioned for itself an identity that exists independently and without abandoning its own nature as the agent, it engages in worldly transaction through the means of meditation—

It would not be so. For one's own essence (*sva-tattva*) is the self (*ātman*); and for that which depends on another, at the time it is subject to that other, its own essence is lost because it has become something belonging to another. And when that [essence] is lost, there can be no continuous movement. Indeed, the meaning of the word "self" (*ātman*) is the state of being a continuous mover, and that [state] exists eternally in its own nature (*svarūpa*) by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In that very way, there is only abiding; there is no constant coming from anywhere. For one who has indeed gone there is generally said to be "established there," and thus it is indicated by the suffix -tānta (the abstract suffix). But if the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) were non-different from itself, it would simply be dependent on itself, and that is not [mere] dependence, because that very state is autonomy (*svātantrya*). Now, one might object: "Let there be no such thing as 'selfhood' (*ātmatva*) at all. To this he says:

"Non-self"—it does not become oriented toward that, because it lacks the capacity for it; for water is never seen to possess an orientation toward obtaining grass. This is the intended meaning. [C: The sense is that water is not observed to be characterized by a longing for the acquisition of grass. Now, one might object, "Let it not be so," to which he replies: "Thus..."
"An undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*)"—the sense is that this is indeed undesirable because it contradicts experience. [Objection: "Well then, what should be done?

To this he says: "Therefore. "From the reversal of the undesirable consequence"—that is, from the reason of the reversal of the aforementioned *prasaṅga*, meaning because one perceives the Self's orientation toward the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Because it is non-different" (avyatirikta). || 15 ||

Now, in order to explain the second verse, he shows the connection [of the topics] with the words "na ca" (nor). He fulfills the expectation of the word "not only" (*na kevalam*) with the word "yāvat" (as far as). He explains the term "unreleased from autonomy" (*svātantryāmukta*) as "not abandoned" (*atyakta*). The word "having created" (*nirmāya*) is explained by its own verbal form (*nigadavyākhyātam*). [This is done] by means of volition (*saṅkalpena*).
The meaning is "having himself performed the consecration" (*ātmanā pādya*). He explains the term *vyavahārayet* by means of *vyavahāreṇa*.

By virtue of its status as a primary derivative (*kṛdanta*), he clarifies the meaning of the verbal root together with its prefix—which has become a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—through the word *dhyāne*.
The connection is as follows: even that which is conceivable—that he joins [others] through instruction on worship and so forth—is possible for this very reason.
Now, one might object: "Is it not contradictory to say that he is both endowed with sovereignty (*svātantrya*) and yet creates? To this, he says [in the commentary]:
"In that regard," because of the sovereignty of that whose nature is non-dual and whose single form is consciousness, this is not at all untenable; namely, that...
It is said that in the sphere of *māyā*, that which appears exceedingly difficult to accomplish is precisely that unimpeded sovereignty (*svātantrya*) in its execution;

this very [sovereignty] is then indicated by the word "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*). For this reason, the phrase "by means of this" (*ata eva*) is not redundant, as it refers to the nature of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*). Alternatively, [it may be interpreted as]: "precisely because of this sovereignty."

Because here the conventional usage of meditation and so forth occurs through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is expressed by the third case ending and by the causative form of the root *yuj*;

for the causative suffix arises from the word "usage" (*vyavahāra*) ending in the third case, just as in the expression "he crosses with an elephant" (*hastinā krāmati*). Thus, he joins [the meanings]: [The text continues: *yojayati*—... [he causes to join].

Even in the absence of being an object (*viṣayatva*), it connects as an object by virtue of its independence. He states the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as "it is possible" (*saṃbhāvyate*). He fulfills the expectancy for the word *yat* with "that" (*tat*).
By this, the application of the word *ataḥ* found in the previous sūtra as a reason (*hetu*) has also been made here. The student [should understand] this.

He raises an objection with "nanu" (surely). To state the answer given by the Guru, he says "atra" (here). When the expectation arises as to what was said, he explains the two words from the Sūtra—"of the non-dual self" (*advayātmanaḥ*) and "by its sovereignty" (*svātantryāt*)—which end in the genitive and ablative cases respectively, [beginning with] "saṃvideka" (consciousness alone). It is not that it is not appropriate; rather...

The meaning is that it is indeed appropriate. To the question "Why is it appropriate?", he says: "That which, indeed... In the realm of *māyā*—that is, in the realm of duality—it is "extremely difficult to accomplish," meaning it is exceedingly struck by impossibility. It is "unobstructed," meaning free from resistance;
the word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates a contrast. By the phrase "for this very reason," [the word] "here" (*iti*), which was situated in the previous sūtra, is also to be applied here.
By the word "evam" (thus), it refers to that which has the nature of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*). Its causal form is called the power of reflective awareness;
the meaning is that it is "non-redundant," i.e., it does not become redundant.
Otherwise, since both causes would express autonomy, there would be redundancy.

This is the state of being. He states another opinion with the words "Or rather" (*atha vā*). For this very reason, due to autonomy—that is, by virtue of autonomy whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—is the meaning. He provides the formal construction (*yojanā*) in order to offer an explanation of the phrase "by means of the volitions [beginning with] Īśa and the others."
This should be connected with the two verses. He shows an example for this point:

because this independent creation (or, according to Kṣemarāja’s reading, the creation of an independent form) is not established—as in the case of the creation of blue and so forth—in such passages as "The Lord is the Blessed One, the Self, eternal, omnipresent, and independent."

For indeed, that object of knowledge, that which is to be worshipped, and that which is to be meditated upon appear as non-different from the knower, the worshiper, or the meditator; thus, it is created by them and is not devoid of the Lord (not having the nature of a non-Lord). For if it were so, there would be an equality between the mental constructs and meditations of "Lord" and "non-Lord," and this is not the case.

Thus, because a distinction in results is perceived, it is therefore an illustration; that is, a particular form within the general. In this regard—concerning the sphere of the conventional usage of objects of knowledge fashioned by the volitions of Īśvara and others—it has been said:
And Śiva, whose power is never lost, shines forth as such when touched [by the object],
due to his sovereignty within the mirror of his own pure consciousness during acts of contemplation and the like.

Thus [it is said]. Now, for what purpose does he show this example here? To this he replies: "Blue," because a creation produced by independent agency—the manifestation fashioned by Īśvara and others whose nature is liberated through sovereignty—is not well-known, that is, it lacks renown in the world. But how is this so?
Since it is logical that those such as Īśa who possess independence are created, he says "Īśvara.

By the word "Īśvara," the term "Īśa" is explained; whereas terms such as "Bhagavān" are included by the word "ādi" (and so forth). "Apṛthagbhūtam" means non-different; "tat prameyam" refers to the object of knowledge in the form of Īśa and the others.

The object of knowledge (*prameya*) is "created" (*nirmita*), meaning produced through volition (*saṅkalpa*); the sense is that because the created nature of the object of knowledge is clearly never lost. Now, one might object: "In that case, let its sovereignty (*svātantrya*) be declared precisely by virtue of being created. To this he says: "And not... Why is it not non-divine? To this he says: "For thus... etc. *Ādi*.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), worship and other such acts are included. Now, one might object: "Let there simply be equality [between the two]. To this he says: "And not thus" (*na caivam*). Why is it not thus? To this he says: "Because of the difference in fruit" (*phale*). The meaning is that there is a difference in the fruits—consisting of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*);
for enjoyment results from serving Nīla and others, while liberation results from serving Īśa and others. As for those who...
Purified by the exceedingly powerful energy of the Blessed One, that very thing by which the dull-witted are deluded— even by blue and the like— the wise cross over from saṃsāra.
A solid mass sinks in water, yet that same mass, when fashioned into a vessel, floats.

That the Supreme Lord manifests both of these objects of knowledge—namely, the manifestation of the voidness of autonomy and the manifestation of being endowed with autonomy—as His very own nature, occurs solely by the power of the energy of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); thus, that [power] alone is primary. || 16 ||

Surely, the determination of existence depends on the power of manifestation (*prakāśa*), and that manifestation has reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as its essence; therefore, when there is no difference in reflective awareness, it is proper to say "that is indeed this," as in the volitions "I am God" or "I am the Self. Furthermore, the conceptualization of a created object occurs through the awareness of it as "this" (*idantā*), whereas autonomy consists in the form of the awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*).
If the emanated being lacks that very nature [of the Self], how can there be independence and liberation for it? To resolve this, he says:
"There is no otherness of this Self due to the difference in the reflective awareness of 'I' and so forth."
Because this creation is perceived as "I," it is like the object denoted by a verbal suffix. || 17 ||

The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) refers to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the reference to the Self (*ātman*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and so forth;

and by the inclusion of the term "verbal suffixes" (*tiṅ*), it is seen that they alone are partakers of the fruit of liberation, for their discourse is of an entirely different kind. As it has been said:
"Having enjoyed worldly pleasures and abandoned the wandering through existence, I shall attain the supreme state"—
such a hope here would befit only one possessed of supreme devotion to Śambhu.
Thus, he states the meaning of the two verses in summary by way of conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Both—the form of blue and so forth, as well as the form of Īśvara and so forth—that is, manifestation (*bhāsana*); for this reason (*iti*), that very power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) alone is the primary [reality], because it is sustained by the light (*prakāśa*) which constitutes its essential nature.
The state of being. || 16 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the seventeenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"That very thing" means "that [nature]"; [it refers to the consequence] in the absence of having that nature.

"In the absence of being an object of the self-apprehension (*ahaṃparāmarśa*). "To set aside"—that is, to make it the object of refutation. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it: "Not the 'I-ness' (*nāhantām*)," etc.
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
He states this meaning with the words "in its own form" (*svarūpe*), and not "in its existence" (*bhāve*), because there would be no connection [otherwise].

For the "own form" is the substratum (*dharmin*), whereas "existence" is a property (*dharma*) residing in the own form that serves as the ground for the application of a word; and here, it is the substratum alone that is employed.
The mention of "action" (*karma*) is an indicator for verbal suffixes that express action; it is an indicator for the form of a power (*śakti*) that has not yet become a substance (*asattvabhūta*).
He states what is to be understood by the word "etc. (*ādi*): "the self" (*ātman*). By the word "etc.," [terms such as] "independent" (*svatantra*) and so forth are included.

Regarding the inclusion [of the suffixes]: he states "suffix" (*pratyaya*) to indicate that which is to be grasped by the *tiṅ* suffixes. This does not refer merely to the suffixes *ti*, *p*, *tas*, and so forth, which are included within its own form;
rather, it refers to all suffixes that denote action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) here is itself merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Since particles (*nipāta*) are also included by this [definition], he states that "action" (*karman*) is to be understood through the word "non-substance" (*asattva*). This is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that entity called "power" (*śakti*), which consists of power— that is, that which is not a substance because it cannot support the use of pronouns (*sarvanāma*)— but it does not refer to [the category of action] alone.

This refers primarily to the apprehension of mere action (*kriyā*) which constitutes the denoted meaning.
