That which is expressed by *tiṅ*-suffixes and the like—namely, action and so forth—as well as conjunctions and the like expressed by particles (*nipāta*), do not possess an inherent form that exists externally as their own primary referent and is thus fit for designation by a pronoun; this is because they exist solely in dependence upon another.

For this very reason, the name "nipāta" (particle) for *nipātas* is indeed meaningful; they are called *nipātas* because they "fall down"—that is, they become objects—by way of indicating meanings that reside in another (*paraniṣṭha*).
Furthermore, the actions and factors of action expressed by verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the like are clearly and undeniably situated in another. However, [the case is different for particles].
Since those words denoting that [self] are particles (*nipāta*), they possess no conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) at all; rather, they function solely through etymological derivation (*yoga*).
This is the sense: the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose nature is "I" (*aham*), as well as the infinite varieties such as "Lord," "cognizer," "Self," "Śiva," and so forth.

Regarding *parāmarśa* (reflective awareness): although its differentiation consists in mutual distinctness, nevertheless, for that reason of differentiation, the distinction suspected between this Self—which is of the nature of the creator and consists of the reflective awareness of "I"—and that which is of the nature of the created, such as the locus of the reflective awareness of Īśvara and so forth, is not tenable. For [Īśvara...]
Even this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) rests upon the reality of the nature of the knower and agent, which is characterized by sovereign power (*īśana*);
and this knower-ship and so forth consist in autonomy (*svātantrya*) with respect to cognition and the rest, as these [terms] are indeclinables (*nipāta*) that do not depend on anything else.

As for words such as *vā* and others that denote conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth, their status as indeclinables is due to both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

Although the external, primary form of the factors of action (*kāraka*) does indeed exist, it exists only as the object (*artha*) [of consciousness] and not as a factor of action; for the state of being a factor of action consists solely of a power residing in the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Otherwise, one who already knows the relationship between cause and effect...
A child should not take up sandals and such for the purpose of cutting [grass] and so forth; enough with this elaboration.

Relying on this, he makes a formal proposition regarding the performance of an action: "that. He explains the word *aham* as the *prakṛti* (base) for the sense of egoity (*ahaṃtā*). He states that the suffix *-tal* refers to their own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

"[He states the meaning of that suffix with the words] 'its own nature' (svarūpam) — [C]. Since the word *parāmarśa* is well-known, it is explained through a mere restatement (*nigadavyākhyāna*). He states the object included by the word 'etcetera' as 'the Lord' (*īśvara*). He explains the term 'due to difference' (*bhedāt*) as 'it is improper' (*anyāya*). Of those—of the reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*), their difference is *tadbheda*; from that."

In this context, the reflective awareness of "I" has the creator (*nirmātṛ*) as its object, while the reflective awarenesses of "Lord" (*īśvara*) and so forth have the created (*nirmeya*) as their objects. He explains the meaning of the fifth case [ending] with the word "from the cause" (*hetoḥ*). He explains the two words "of this self" (*asya ātmanaḥ*) by [the term] "the creator. He explains the word "otherness" (*anyatā*) by [the term] "difference" (*bheda*).

The phrase "connected as a remainder" (*śeṣatvena yuktaḥ*) is supplied [from the context]. He explains the second half-verse, which stands here as the reason, with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). Regarding "ruling" (*īśana*): *īśanam* is the action of becoming capable; *śīla* refers to one whose activity is purposeless—[the Lord is] such a one. It refers to that reality (*tattva*) which belongs to the agency consisting of the nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*).
The intended meaning is that action is indeed described as being merely a sprout of knowledge (*jñāna*). Regarding the phrase "it rests" (*viśrāmyati*):
the meaning is that this is because the *kṛt* suffix is produced from the verbal root *īś* in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*). Now, [the opponent asks]: "Let it rest; what follows from that?

To this he replies with the words "in the state of being a knower" (*jñātṛtve*). And by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "being a knower and so forth," both the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) are included.

Regarding "in knowledge and so forth"—that is, in knowledge (*jñāna*) and, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), in the instrument (*karaṇa*); "looking toward the face" (*mukhaprekṣitva*) means being joined with uninterrupted knowledge (*avicchinnajñānayoga*). [The reading *avicchinnajñānādiśaktiyogaḥ* is found in Kṣemarāja’s commentary. And this "uninterruptedness" consists in the resting within the "I-sense" (*asmadartha*) in the form of "I know" and "I act. This belongs to this Lord (*īśvara*).

The very fact that the Self, while being created from [His own] creation, is to be reflected upon as "I" [is the point]. Alternatively, the ablative case in "sṛṣṭeḥ" (from creation) denotes cause; for this Lord creates even within His volitions regarding the Lord and so forth only that which is fit to be referred to as "I. The suffix -kṛtya is used here in the sense of fitness (*arhe*). As, for example:
Sovereignty (svātantrya) arises; the sense is that it arises from the production of a suffix denoting the agent.

And that [sovereignty] consists in not looking toward another face; and that consists in the yoga of uninterrupted knowledge, for the yoga of interrupted knowledge is characterized by its occasional nature.
It is indeed seized by the state of looking toward another, due to its dependence on causes distinct from itself. And that non-interruption—
which consists of resting upon the referent of "I" (asmadartha) as its very foundation in such forms as "I know" and "I act"—
occurs clearly within the referent of "I," the object denoted by the word *ahaṃ*, as the locus for both cognition and its instruments.
"Because it manifests through its state of abiding"—for this reason, he explains the word *asya* (of this) as *īśvarasya* (of the Lord).
He explains the word *sṛṣṭeḥ* (of creation) as *sṛjyamānasya* (of that which is being created). By this, it is indicated that the suffix *ktin* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
"Of that which is being created" means "of that which is being brought into being by [the Lord's] volition."

"Being the object of the reflective awareness 'I' (ahaṃparāmarśanīyatvam)" means precisely being the objective domain of the reflective awareness "I" (ahaṃparāmarśaviṣayatvam); for even in the absence of its being the direct essence, in effect, its status as the essence is not lost. He states another alternative with the words "or [from] creation" (sṛṣṭer iti vā).
He explains the ablative case with the word "since" (yataḥ). In this alternative, the word "creation" (sṛṣṭeḥ) is formed by the suffix *ktin* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

And there is the state of ending in the fifth case (pañcamyantatā). [Objection: From what is the fitness (yogyatā) understood? To this he says: "in the sense of being worthy" (arhe). The *kṛtya* suffix—namely, the *kṛtya* suffix found in the word *mṛśyatayā*—is used here. "Worthy to be grasped as 'I'" is *ahaṃ-mṛśya*; the state of that is *tattā*, and by that [state] is the meaning. However, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. He provides the explanation of the phrase *tiṅvācyaḥ*, which refers to the meaning of the simile, with the words *yathā*. He states the meaning of the suffix *-vat* with the words *yathā*. He states the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) with the words *kriyā*.
By the word *ādi* (and so forth), the inclusion of comparison (*upamā*) and other such elements is intended. Regarding the phrase *yathāsvam*: therein, it is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

"Having as its ultimate reality the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) that is to be determined by the use of verbal suffixes (tiṅ): that which is to be determined—i.e., manifested—by the use of verbal suffixes, that very [awareness] is the ultimate reality (paramārtha) of which [the word]. Even though [the action] is denoted by the verbal root (dhātu), both the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) express the meaning of the suffix together.

The powers of action, agent, conjunction, option, and so forth— whose ultimate reality consists in the reflective awareness determined by the respective employment of verbal suffixes, the third case ending, the particle *ca*, and so on— are brought into the state of being entities when expressed by words such as "cooking," "agent," "conjunction," "option," and the like.

In such primary reflections as "api pacati" or "caitreṇa ca," they find their rest; otherwise, those cognitions would not even exist. According to the principle of *tadvat*, however, the mention of the suffix *tiṅ* alone is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

This is because [words] such as those ending in kṛt and pratyaya are also employed in relation to action (*kriyā*). Likewise, the power of the *kāraka* has as its ultimate reality a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) to be determined through the employment of the third case-ending and so forth; for it is the third case-ending itself that indicates agency (*kartṛtva*) and instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), while by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the fourth case-ending and others are included.

Since those [particles] also indicate the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and so forth, the application [of this principle] is thus to be made everywhere. In the word *vādi*, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes particles such as *iva* which indicate comparison (*upamā*); for even the power of comparison is ultimately nothing but the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) determined by the employment of *iva* and the like, and such powers are of this nature.
These are expressed by such words as "truth," "cooking," "agent," "conjunction," and "option.

For the word *pāka* (cooking), by virtue of being a noun (*ghañ*-affix) formed from a verbal root (*bhāva-vihita*), denotes an action; likewise, [the words] "agent" and so forth denote the grammatical factors (*kāraka*s).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the entire class of words that denote similarity and the like, such as *upamā* (simile).

Apprehension. For this very reason, they are brought to the state of being existent—having been displaced from their non-substantial state as they existed in the form of the innate nature (*sahajasvarūpa*), they are made identical with the substance (*dravya*) which is capable of sustaining the reflection of novel names and concepts, such that one thinks, "this is a transformation. Furthermore, even so...

In a fundamental reflective awareness (*mūlaparāmarśa*) such as "Caitra cooks" or "and by Caitra," these [notions] find their rest; otherwise—in the absence of resting in a fundamental reflective awareness—those very notions, having already been perceived—that is, having already acquired their own nature—would not exist. For when it is said, "cooking is being performed by this," there immediately arises the reflective awareness, "this one is cooking."
Rest arises [in the mind], for indeed no accomplished entity named "cooking" exists anywhere,

because it is impossible for it to be accomplished as something possessing sequential parts; however, since the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-pratyaya*) is conventionally assigned to that very [process], it conveys [the meaning] instantly, and its status as the root [of the action] is established first for that very reason.

This is because it arises from the reflective awareness of an action (*kriyāparāmarśa*). As for its description as something already established (*siddhatayā*), that is intended only for one who is already proficient in the usage; in this regard, one's own intellect alone is the witness, so no further effort is required. Likewise, being an agent (*kārakatva*) and so forth is also to be understood solely through the effect (*kārya*); it does not exist as something already established. For when it is said, "this is an agent," [the status of being an agent is not perceived independently].

Nothing whatsoever is obtained apart from the essential nature of the entity (*vastu*); however, it is known through its effect that this entity possesses the power of agency (*kārakatva-śakti*). Furthermore, the capacity of existence (*sattva*) to be referred to by all pronouns (*sarvanāma-parāmarśa-sahatva*) applies here as well. What is meant is this: "reference" (*parāmarśa*) is a locus of rest, and that—

That which is ultimate is indeed the absolute reality (*pāramārthika*), and that is precisely of the nature of "I. However, the state of resting in the middle is that which characterizes an object, wherein every pronoun is employed.
That object which is intended to be expressed as something to be differentiated is called a "substance" (dravya).

This should be understood according to the consensus of the elders. He establishes the connection in the form of a relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared, [expressed as] "in that manner" (*tadvat*). And thus, the summary is: "like the object expressed by a verbal suffix" (*tiṅvācyakarmavat*), just as [there is] "the object expressed by a verbal suffix" (*tiṅvācyakarmaṇi*).
This is what is meant: just as the reflection "cooking" (*pāka*) [occurs] with respect to the object expressed by a verbal suffix.

The reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form "he cooks" ultimately rests in the subject itself; likewise, when "Lord" (*īśvara*) is uttered, the ultimate rest lies in the reflective awareness of the "I," because lordship—consisting of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*)—is impossible elsewhere.
As for the notion held by the ignorant regarding the Lord, once [the act of] cooking and so forth has been accomplished...

And the ascertainment [of an object] as being distinct from itself is nothing but an error. Here, he himself announces the statement of the underlying principle with the words "this is what is meant. In response to the inquiry "what is meant," he says:
"that which is called reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Regarding the phrase "the place of rest," it refers to the apprehension of the object.

For immediately after reflective awareness (parāmarśa), the person indeed remains silent; and this state of silence is the experience of objective bliss, which is itself rest. Thus, it is clear that reflective awareness has rest as its locus. And that—namely, the locus of rest—is precisely the ultimate (pāryantika), meaning at the final limit (paryante).

Existence alone— not the intermediate [states]— is the ultimate reality, because the intermediate points of rest are, in the highest sense, of the nature of the path; and that ultimate point of rest is precisely of the form "I," meaning it is nothing other than the reflective awareness of "I."
For even one who rests in the pleasure produced by sense objects is, in the ultimate sense, resting in his own Self;
as it has been said:
"In the connection between the visible object and the seer, that which is the supreme spiritual pleasure..."
Thus it is said. As for those who, while still relishing sense objects, merely pretend to find repose in the Supreme Self, they are simply deceiving themselves;

for, being truly at rest in that [Self], they are always happy regardless of any external thing, and even when obtaining pleasure from sense objects by the force of worldly flow, they remain solely intent on turning away from those objects.

Because one determines that happiness resides in the Self alone; whereas he who is happy only at the time of sense-objects is intent on the objects themselves. As for constant happiness, the Self must be made the witness, otherwise the fault of self-deception would arise—so enough with these objections from others. Now, [what of] that which is by nature manifest in the interim?
To the question, "Where shall we remove the reflective awareness of objects? he says: "That which...

The state of resting in the middle is the intermediate place of repose, consisting both of the reflective awareness of the Lord and the reflective awareness of objects such as blue; it is the village—

What contradiction is there in saying that, in the act of going toward a village, the state of standing at the foot of a tree is described as being "created" in relation to that [destination]? By this, it has already been established that even for blue and so forth, despite the intermediate reflective awareness (*madhyaparāmarśa*) such as "this is blue," they ultimately rest only in the "I" during the fundamental reflective awareness (*mūlaparāmarśa*), and thus their nature consists of the Self. Blue.
For even when one says, "I know this," the reality is merely that it is manifest; as it has been said in the passage beginning with "of this 'this'...
However, the deluded person, through the very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of blue and so forth, falsely imagines satisfaction regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and the like.
In his movement toward [the goal], the root of the tree stands as the point of reference—like the base of a tree—for one who intends to go to a village.

Being weary, he stands at the foot of a tree for the sake of rest; it should be understood that the word *mūla* (root/base) denotes *tala* (foot/bottom) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Now, one might ask: how can the middle [state] be said to have been "created" when it is merely a reflection? To this, he says: "in relation to that."

The meaning is that this [the reflective awareness of the Lord] is preceded by that [the reflective awareness of "I"], which serves as the ultimate point of rest for the reflective awareness of "I. Now, one might object: since the reflective awareness of the Lord is more proximate, let it be that the reflective awareness of "I" finds its rest therein.
"What, then, is the status of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of objects such as blue? To this he says: "By this.

By this—namely, by the means of establishing that the reflective awareness of the Lord (*īśvara-parāmarśa*) finds its repose in the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*)—it has been "demonstrated," that is, fully supported, because there is no difference in their being objects of awareness; this is the sense. And since the emphasis has been placed on this point here, [the same applies to other objects].
It is further elaborated: "But how is this logical? To this he says, "Blue.

For—because—"I know this blue," even in the manifestation [of the thought] "I know this blue" (the phrase "I know this blue" and "I manifest" constitutes the full extent of the reality—K. ṣ. ṣ.), this much alone is the reality.
The meaning is that this [consciousness] possesses the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) because, through the gateway of the blue object, there occurs the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*);
otherwise, the employment of the term "I" would be impossible. Regarding this, he cites the consensus of the Teacher (*ācārya*) with the words "this" (*idam*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the remainder of the verse beginning with "of the fragmented reflective awareness" (*vicchinnavimarśasya*) is included; and here...
Since an explanation has already been provided previously, no further effort is made here. Now, one might ask: "How is it then that the deluded do not understand this?

To this he says: "The deluded. Furthermore, if this is so, then why was it stated that independence (svātantrya) is unconditioned only with respect to objects such as the Lord (Īśvara) and the like, and not with respect to [objects] such as blue and so forth? To this [he replies]:

He says, "The fool. Satisfaction produced by causal efficiency and the like is "satisfaction consisting of causal efficiency and the like"; he conceives himself as such, and thus [is] that very person. In ultimate reality, for one who is seized by dependence, even that satisfaction does not reach the hand.

Thus, it has been stated that blue and other such objects are devoid of autonomy. However, even a fool does not believe that there is a completion of cognition or a fulfillment of causal efficacy regarding the self and so forth without their resting in the fundamental reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) which is their root; therefore, it is stated that even in the manifestation of those [objects], autonomy is never abandoned. || 17 ||

If this is so— if the reality is indeed that all reflections upon the universe ultimately rest within the single, pure reflection of "I"— then why is it said that knowledge, memory, and so forth are its powers (*śakti*), and why is there a distinction within knowledge such as doubt, certainty, and the like?
Regarding the doubt as to how there can be a variety of blue and other colors, the author states the resolution:
"It is said that he possesses the conceit that [the object] does not come [into being]. This was stated even regarding "creation"—that is, even in the case of its being produced.

The point is this: since the fruit of this scripture is solely the awakening of the deluded, if the nature of the Blessed One were in every way inexpressible, transcending even that [inexpressibility], or if it were merely well-known, what would be the purpose of being intent upon a web of systematic elaborations?

Thus, the summary here is as follows: For this Supreme Self—the Self that has been contemplated as being of the nature of the Lord (Īśvara) and so forth, by virtue of its being self-luminous—there is no difference, nor any state of otherness, distinct from the differentiation of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) such as "I-ness" (*ahantā*) which is produced by having diverse objects. Why is this? Because of this [Self's] creative power (*sṛṣṭi*).
How is it that the Lord and so forth, who are being created, are perceived as the "I"? [The answer is: "It is expressed by a verbal suffix (tiṅ).
Or rather, [it means] "of this Lord and so forth, which is the cause of creation. || 17 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eighteenth verse with the words "nanvevam" (But if this is so).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"of the reflections upon the universe"—that is, [reflections] such as "this is the Lord," "this is blue," and so forth.

Of all reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*), that which is pure— meaning the reflective awareness that is exceedingly pure because it is untainted by the coloring of objects, being established solely in the essential nature of Light, namely the "I-reflection" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*)— that alone is the *tattva*, the ultimate essential nature; at that time, that [is the reality].
In response to the inquiry "What is this?", he says: "Knowledge" (*jñāna*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the exclusion (*apohana*) is included.

"Of this"—that is, of the light, of knowledge. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: how can the differentiation of knowledge into doubt, certainty, and so forth, as well as the variety of blue and other objects, be called a "power" (*śakti*)?
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it: "Māyā" [etc.].

By the power of Māyā, that very [power] of the All-pervasive Lord, when its object is differentiated cognition, is designated by such names as knowledge (*jñāna*), volition (*saṃkalpa*), and determination (*adhyavasāya*). (18)

That which appears despite being logically untenable is called "māyā"; therefore, the entire range of appearances that is distinct from the Light of Consciousness (*prakāśa*) is *māyā*. In this regard, the sovereignty of the very nature of consciousness (*cit-tattva*) is the power of *māyā* (*māyā-śakti*). By means of this [power], that which is to be experienced (*saṃvedya*) becomes differentiated—both from the subject (*pramātṛ*) and from one another.

That which is to be cognized by the subject— through the group of instruments differentiated by the power of *māyā* from one another and from the object— is itself the "field" (*gocara*), the point of rest;
here, the commentary states:

He explains the term *māyā* as "untenable" (*anupapanna*). "Untenable" means incapable of logical justification; "manifestation" (*avabhāsana*) refers to the appearance of things as distinct entities. He states the resulting nature of *māyā* with the words "and therefore" (*tataśca*). "And therefore" means for that reason; "distinct" (*bhinnam*)—

It exists as the substratum of differentiation; from the "Light"—the counter-correlative known as the Supreme Light—the "totality of manifestations" arises, which is the collection of cognitions whose objects are the various external and internal entities.
He explains the word "power" (*śakti*) with the words "and therein" (*tatra ca*). And therein—while that totality of manifestations, which is the very nature of *māyā*, exists—

Svātantrya (sovereignty) is the capacity for bringing forth manifestations; that is to say, the state of not being dependent on anything else. The mention of the term *māyāpada* (the sphere of illusion), however, serves merely the purpose of conjunction (*yojanā*). He states the meaning of the instrumental case by the word "by that" (*tayā*).
He provides the analysis and explanation of the compound word beginning with "divided" (*bhinna*) through its division into constituent parts.

Regarding the word "divided" (*bhinnam*), he explains the constituent part "the object of cognition" (*saṃvedya*) as "māyā. The connection of the two words "from the subject" (*pramātuḥ*) and "mutually" (*anyonyataḥ*) with the distant term "divided" is as follows:
from what is it divided? From the subject—that is, from the grasper—and mutually; such is the meaning. [The object of cognition...]

Because this [term] is a word requiring a complement (*sāpekṣa-śabda*), there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of "by means of the group of instruments" (*karaṇavargeṇa*) to fulfill that requirement. "By means of the group of instruments" means by the collection of instruments consisting of both external and internal forms; that is to say, through their mediation. "That which is to be cognized" (*saṃvedyam*) refers to the object of cognition, namely, that which is external or internal.

The "multitude of entities" (*bhāvajātam*) refers to both the differentiated objects of cognition and the multitude of entities themselves. By using the single word *tat* (that), the requirement for two instances of the relative pronoun *yat* is fulfilled. He explains the component *gocarāḥ* (objects of perception) as "resting places" (*viśrānti*). This is indeed an instance of metaphorical usage (*lakṣaṇā*), for cows themselves are the objects of perception (*gocara*).

They come to rest. She is that which effects the synthesis of separated words; being such through her own fitness, she is that very consciousness whose nature is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), which takes the form of the supreme word (*parāvāk*), and is called "knowledge," "volition" (*saṃkalpa*), and "determination" (*adhyavasāya*). By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," doubt and memory are also included.

And so forth. To explain: that principle of consciousness (*saṃvit-tattva*) which is constrained by an external sense organ grasping clearly and by an object that is clear is *jñāna* (cognition). That which is [constrained] by the mind (*manas*) and an unclear object is *saṃkalpa* (volition). And that which is [constrained] by the intellect (*buddhi*) and an object that partakes in the very limit of objectivity (*viṣayatva-paryanta-bhāj*) is *adhyavasāya* (ascertainment).

This is the certainty: the distinctness of the object and of the external and internal organs is untenable because they are non-different from its light; thus, it is manifested as the nature of consciousness (*cittattva*). Since there is a resting place in difference—and not in the absence of difference, as in the case of Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and so forth—[it is established].

The word "satī" (being) is to be supplied [as an ellipsis]. He explains the word "saiva" (that very same) as "pratyavamarśa" (reflective awareness). He explains the phrase beginning with "jñāne" (in knowledge) as "jñānam" (knowledge). The word "sarvatra" (everywhere) has the sense of the third case (locative) included within itself; it is intended to imply the nature of the word, because the nature of the word itself constitutes its name.

He explains the word "stated" (*kathitā*) with the words "is said" (*ucyate*). In order to state the objects to be included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he says "etcetera. The ellipsis is that "such things as these are to be understood. By the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of erroneous cognition (*bhramajñāna*) and so forth. He now begins the description of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of cognition and the other categories.
To explain: by "clearly apprehending" (sphuṭagrāhinā) is meant grasping by way of including all phenomena—that is, effecting the apprehension of the object with clarity;

by "clearly" (sphuṭena) is meant having attained clarity through the power of the four types of proximity (sannikarṣa). By "restrained" (niyantritam) is meant brought to the state of being delimited as either a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) or an object of valid cognition (prameya).

The reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) is that whose essential nature is undivided luminosity. Regarding the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*): it means having the form of valid cognition (*pramā*). He states the essential nature of volition (*saṅkalpa*) by [the word] "by the mind" (*manasā*);

he states the essential nature of determination (*adhyavasāya*) by [the word] "by the intellect" (*buddhyā*). [This refers to] the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) residing in an existent entity (*bhāva*).

"By one who resorts to that which is the limit of the state of being an object"—the sense is that beyond that, there is no further state of being an object for any entity. Now, in response to the inquiry as to how it is logical for knowledge and the other [faculties] to be distinct, he says "of the object" in order to determine this. "By the light"—that is, by the supreme light (paraprakāśa).
"From that non-difference which is simultaneous"—the sense is that it "is manifested" by the power of *māyā*. "Thus" (*iti*) means in this manner.

Because, for this reason, there is a resting in difference, and not as in the case of Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including Śakti and the rest—there is a resting of difference in non-difference; therefore—
For that reason, cognition, volition, and so forth are distinct;

therefore, cognition, volition, and so forth are said to be the powers (*śakti*) of that reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), which possesses an undestroyed non-difference from its own essential nature, for one who synthesizes them. Furthermore, doubt and the like are also distinct.
And the variety of blue and other colors—all this remains unimpaired. || 18 ||

But surely, the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) belongs to the powers of consciousness such as volition and memory, which are conceptual in nature. As for that power of experience characterized by direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)—how can reflective awareness apply there? For reflective awareness consists in the association with specific verbal expressions.

[Consisting of the application of distinctions in verbal expression—K. Ṣ. Ṣ. And the application of specific verbal expressions depends upon the recollection of conventions (*saṅketa*). That, in turn, depends upon the awakening of latent predispositions (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, these [predispositions] arise only through the distinction of objects, because it is logical that the distinction between cognitions is based precisely on the distinction of their objects. This is true for cognitions and the rest as well.
"He establishes its nature as power" means: "of that"—namely, of that which consists of supreme light. "Are said to be" means:

because, like *māyā*, they are established through its capacity; this is the intended sense. And "doubt and the rest"—the word "and the rest" includes doubt and so forth—are said to be powers, as is the manifold variety of blue and other objects.

The connection [of the words] is: "and it has been stated that this is power. The meaning is as follows: in this way, everything—meaning the whole—becomes "unbroken," that is, incapable of being divided; for it is accepted by everyone that nothing whatsoever is difficult for Māyā to accomplish. || 18 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the nineteenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
*pratyavamarśātmakatvam* means having the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśasvabhāvatvam*). Of the power of consciousness (*citiśakteḥ*).

Of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*). The power of experience is the power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*); the connection [of the sentence] is: "how can there be the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) in that power? In response to the expectation of why this is so, he says: "For reflective awareness... [referring to] "of specific expressions"—that is, as non-different with respect to each individual object.
The "joining" (*yojanā*) of existing words—that is, their conjunction through memory—is "consisting of that," meaning it has that very nature.

To the question, "What follows from that? he says: "denotation" (*abhilāpa*). It "requires" [memory], for a word whose object is already known cannot be joined [to its referent] without the recollection of the previously grasped convention (*saṅketa*).

The state; and that—namely, the recollection of the convention (*saṅketa*). That too—namely, the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). And such is this vision—that which possesses such vision; the meaning is "similar cognition. At the first moment—at the time of the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) abiding as the very first.

To dispel the confusion of others as to how there can be the application of verbal expression at the very first moment— namely, "such-and-such a perception"— he says: "Otherwise, how could there be reflective awareness even at the moment of direct perception?"
Running and so forth would be possible even without the act of reconnection [to a new body]. || 19 ||
In this context, first of all, there is for consciousness a connection with verbal expression that is identical to its own nature, appearing like the pointing out of a finger and so forth;

otherwise, when the initial linguistic usage of an infant is observed, no acquisition of meaning (vyutpatti) would ever occur. At the time of conceptual cognition—for another, such as a logician (tārkika)—in order to exclude—that is, to distance it from—[the object].
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it:
"Even at the moment of direct realization, [it] exists.
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
He elaborates the method for explaining the verse with the words "here" (*iha*). "Here" means in this manifest world;

"of consciousness" (*caitanyasya*) means of light (*prakāśasya*); "resembling a pointing with a finger" (*aṅgulīnirdeśaprakhyaḥ*) means resembling—that is, similar to—a pointing made with a finger, which is a designation of an object. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the head and so forth are implied].

The inclusion of the term "initial instruction" (*ādinirdeśa*) refers to the application of verbal expression—that is, the application of words—meaning that there is an invariable concomitance with it; the word "exists" is to be understood as the ellipsis. He provides a proof here by way of negative reasoning (*vyatireka*), saying "otherwise":
"otherwise"—that is, for a child who has not yet been trained but is now intent on learning, and not [for one who has already learned].
For the suckling infant, during the first instance of linguistic usage— namely,

when an activity such as "bring the jar" for an elder or a middle-aged person is observed while they have not previously experienced it at that time— the acquisition of meaning (*vyutpatti*) occurs: "this is the meaning of this sentence."

The intention of the word "thus" (*iti*) is as follows: if such proficiency in grasping conventions through the process of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*) does not exist, what need is there to speak of its result, namely linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)? Why would it not exist?
To this he says: "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*). For—since—the child [proceeds] by means of a succession of non-conceptual cognitions (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*).

First of all, by virtue of initial perception, there is an absence of a succession of experiences consisting of the nature of a subject who hears sound through the auditory faculty— a form of cognition devoid of conceptualization (vikalpa) in the form of reflective awareness regarding the object that is the meaning of the word.

For through a succession of non-conceptual cognitions (*nirvikalpakajñānaparaṃparā*), one hears that sound; from that, one perceives the object before oneself; and then again, one perceives the ground as distinct from it. Thus, how is this its meaning, based on the linguistic convention "bring the jar," "take away the jar"?

Thus, this meaning should flash forth in his heart: "This is a jar," "Bring this," "Take this"— for this meaning has its life-force in such conjunction (*yojanā*), and conjunction is indeed conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

He hears that sound—the word uttered by an elder denoting the bringing of a jar. It is said "indirectly" (*paramparayā*) with reference to the possibility of grasping the convention following repeated hearing. "Then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after that. "That object" (*tam artham*) refers to the referent of linguistic usage.
One perceives the object that is the form of the jar because one is situated right there; then one perceives the ground as distinct from it—that region of earth devoid of the jar.
Upon hearing the word "bring" from a middle-aged person, one brings it because it has been brought back toward another location; hence, [the root] *nī* means "to bring."

The point is this: in ordinary linguistic usage, [the meaning] is understood elsewhere because it has been led there; however, in that context, no one demonstrates the connection between word and meaning by pointing specifically to it, saying "this is the meaning of this. Thus—*iti*—for this reason, from *vyavahāra*—that is, from the word being uttered by an elder, which is the signifier.
From the activity of bringing, fetching, and leading performed by a middle-aged or elderly person—[how] would this [object], being an outsider, [occur] to a child?
[The word] "asya" (of this) implies "the child. How could this matter—"iti"—flash forth in his heart? Why [is this so]? Because [he does not know]:
"This is the meaning of this word. The term "asya" is to be construed with both [parts of the sentence], like the eye of a crow.

Alternatively, by the very phrase "this is the meaning," it is understood that "this is the meaning of this. To the question "Why does it not manifest clearly? he says: "The connection" (*yojanā*). For—since—"this is the meaning"—that is, the fact that "this is the meaning of this"—is such that its connection (*itiyojanā*) consists of a connection of this nature, and one whose vital breath (*prāṇa*) possesses such a connection becomes like that. Thus.
What is it? This object—namely "pot"—becomes denotable by the word "pot";

this object becomes denotable by the word "bring" when one says "bring this object"; and this object becomes denotable by the word "take away" when one says "take away this object. In that context, when first hearing the command "Bring the pot," [the cognition is] undivided...

Only the meaning of the sentence as a whole is understood, and not the meaning of each individual word. Furthermore, through the context of the subsequent utterance "Bring the jar," by the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the word "jar" and the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the word "bring," it is understood that this is the meaning of the word "jar": "bring"—[the jar].
[This is] the operation. Now, for the child, there is such [cognition] due to the recollection of a convention experienced in a previous birth;
nevertheless, at the time of the convention, it was stated that "this is the word for 'bringing'," "this is the word for 'leading,'" and so forth, otherwise [it would not occur].

Knowledge of the meaning [of words] at every step would never be possible. Now, one might object that there is indeed a synthesis (*yojanā*) here; to this he says: "And the synthesis... The sense is that it is an operation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because its nature consists in synthesis.
For in the absence of a conceptual construction that effects synthesis, there is no recollection of words at the time of perceiving a jar.

And when that [recollection] has arisen, since the object has already passed away, even the jar has become nothing but a mental construction (*saṃkalpa*); so what could be joined with what? Even the recollection of the word for it is difficult to establish. But how is it difficult to establish?
For the word was heard immediately before, and in the interval there was merely the sight of the jar.

"It is accomplished"—thus, when the perception of a jar arises, it is entirely logical that the recollection of the word "jar" occurs through the latent impression (saṃskāra) awakened by that [perception]. This is true; however, in the linguistic usage "bring the jar," there is only the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence as an undivided whole (akhaṇḍavākyārtha), whereas in the usage "the jar, bring," the meaning pertains to each individual word.

It is known that in that case, the memory of the original word "ghaṭa" itself is indeed joined with its own meaning; however, regarding the joining of individual words within the sense of an indivisible sentence—
where one thinks, "this is the meaning of this sentence"— it is precisely that recollection of the words which we have described as being difficult to establish.
But is that [cognition] not also difficult to establish,

because there is an intervention between the mere observation of the linguistic usage of middle-aged adults and the experience of the indivisible sentence, and because in the usage of middle-aged adults, the experience [of the sentence] triggers the awakening of latent impressions produced by it?
The recollection of the undivided sentence arises effortlessly. True;

that [recollection] is indeed mentioned—namely, by what recollection of the form of a mass of words (*śabdarāśi*), which consists of a series of divided words, is the undivided meaning of the sentence conjoined, such that "this is the meaning of this"? How is that recollection established? For it is not [established]...

The experience of that [object] has arisen for him at this very moment; and in its absence, such an experience would indeed be difficult to establish. Therefore, it is logical that memory remains as the very nature of that power within consciousness. However, in the investigation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even the form "this is the meaning of this memory" does not exist, because of these three words.

Although it is general in relation to the Sanskrit language, it is particular in relation to regional and other languages; thus, it is said to be "like a pointing with a finger. Even a pointing with a finger, when examined, is indeed a particularity; for this very reason, it is described as "resembling" (prakhya). Therefore, this [object] is something internal.

Reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is of the nature of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*), by means of which even an infant first makes a connection on his own; and that power indeed exists even in animals and the like, for even cows and other such creatures certainly recognize objects when pointed out with a finger or the like. As it has been said:
Even children, animals, and those who are cognizers not participating in linguistic conventions, possess this very consciousness, the essence of which is natural, unconditioned refinement.
Relying on various distinct [forms], they attain diverse states of subjectivity;
that word, because it is being reflected upon as an object through the state of "this-ness" (idambhāva),
falls away from difference.
Thus, its presence in stones and other such objects is likewise unavoidable, because they possess consciousness endowed with power;

otherwise, growth and so forth would be impossible. In this regard, within the consciousness of trees, their own hair and so forth serve as witnesses, and within the consciousness of stones, their own collection of bones serves as witnesses.

Enough with the search for causes regarding things that are inherently indefinable; they simply exist as such. For this very reason, it is entirely appropriate when people say that all entities—whether insentient or sentient—are ultimately directed toward the praise of the Blessed One, because praise consists merely in reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and such awareness, by means of consciousness, is omnipresent.

From the proof [of its existence]: the omnipresence of consciousness is indeed twofold—by virtue of being pure Being (*sanmātra*), by virtue of bestowing existence upon all things, and by virtue of being pure Consciousness (*cinmātra*) which makes everything known; otherwise, of what would the multitude of entities within the universe consist, and by whom would they be known?

It may be so. But how is it logical that mere reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) alone should function as a hymn of praise consisting of the reflective awareness of supreme excellence? True; "supreme excellence" is autonomy (*svātantrya*), and that is the state of not looking toward another, which is precisely what constitutes the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*).
It has been established that He alone exists as the essence everywhere, within both the insentient and the sentient;

thus, all are indeed of the very nature of the Blessed Lord. Who, then, could take pleasure in whom? Enough, therefore, with this microscopic scrutiny of the manifold worlds imagined for the sake of instructing the ignorant.
Let us return to the subject at hand. Here the disciple poses a question with the word "atha" (now).

The meaning is that, through the recollection of the convention experienced in a previous birth—that is, in a prior life—such a connection [of meaning] occurs. But what is meant by "previous birth"? Listen:
First of all, that from which this [consciousness] has arisen is its very prior birth, and it exists there in a latent state (*śaktitayā*).

That which is brought forth by it through its own autonomy is called its "belonging to the time of the prior birth," and it is said that it "remembers" that very thing. However, if your intellect is not capable of grasping this, then consider the father.

Know that this was the previous birth of the son; and because that very [karma] which came to him along with his semen is precisely what belongs to the time of his previous birth, it is said that he remembers it, while the new birth is the son himself. And if your intellect is not engaged even in this matter, then [look to] the treatises on memory (*smṛti*).

Since this [consciousness] has come from a previous birth, that alone is its prior birth; and whatever was done by it there, that very thing it remembers here through the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), as well as the new state of existence through which it will again obtain birth. To this, he gives the reply: "Nevertheless" (tathāpi). At the time of convention—
When the time of convention established in a previous birth persists, that word— the reflective word existing today as the cause for application—
[is perceived] through the state of "this-ness" (idantā),
meaning in the form: "this word is the designator of this object," because it is being reflected upon as an objective entity.
When that which is not grasped by the subject shines forth and comes to rest within the body of consciousness (having been made to rest in the body of consciousness),
it becomes the signifier; if that which shines is the very nature of consciousness itself, then it is so.

"Consisting of expression alone" means: just as cognition may have the nature of pleasure even though the object lacks the nature of pleasure, so too, let it be that the object—form and so forth—is not of the nature of expression; nevertheless, consciousness will manifest as having that very nature. In this view, however:

By having become an object, having fallen away from the differentiation [previously] established, and having become separated from both the supreme subject and the subject who is the void, while appearing— that is, manifesting at that time— resting within the body of cognition, i.e., in the subject who is the intellect (*buddhi*), it is the signifier (*vācaka*).

It occurs as follows: having fallen away from the state of Parā and Paśyantī, and having reached the state of Madhyamā, the word—once firmly established in the cognizing subject (pramātṛ) of the intellect—is called "denotative" when it is restricted to its own specific object.
But having fallen away even from that and reached the state of Vaikharī, it resides in the dual subject consisting of the vital breath and the body.

When that [object] has come to rest more fully— that is, when the nature of the cognitive subject (*buddhipramātṛ*), who is the locus of the resting place for the denoter of its cognition, shines forth— meaning it flashes as self-luminous—
then it shines forth as consisting solely of expression, that is, as consisting solely of sound.

Because its nature is that of the resting place for the expressive word (*vācaka*), the meaning is that the infant’s utterance in another birth is established as being entirely natural. The word "iti" marks the completion of the subject matter (*prameya*). [Objection:
Since there is no object in the form of an utterance, how can consciousness be said to be endowed with identity with it?

Since consciousness arises precisely in accordance with its object, otherwise even that [consciousness] would not lose its status as a supreme subject; therefore, he says "as follows": "Knowledge"—that is, consciousness—"shines forth"—it manifests—by virtue of the temporary independence produced by the object, through the emergence of the bliss that constitutes its own essential nature.
Likewise—that is, in that manner—it will manifest as being of that nature, consisting of speech resting within its own self.

It will become an object of manifestation for itself by virtue of its own self-luminosity; here, the *lṛṭ* (future tense) suffix is used in the sense of both the object and the agent (*karmakartari*). In our philosophical system, however, even the object consists of speech.
Thus he says, "But in this system. Here, "in this system" means in the venerable Śaiva doctrine. As it has been said:
"Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the imperishable reality of Sound (śabdatattva);
from it proceeds the evolution of the world through the manifestation of objects."
Since even the object consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it is in reality nothing but consisting of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*);
for even states such as inertia (*staimitya*)— if they were not composed of reflective awareness— then,
because the activity of the subject whose nature is conceptualization (*vikalpa*) would not arise therein, their very existence would be a matter of mere oath-bound truth.
Furthermore, there would be no recollection; for if a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were to arise that determines an object such as a form, what else could it be?

There would be no state called "stagnation" (*staimitya*), which consists in the withdrawal of all thought; thus, even in that state, there is an internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Moreover, entities indeed endure being expressed by the entire range of words, and therein—

The application of fixed words is performed. For instance: the innate reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) present before a child regarding a physical object (*piṇḍa*) consists of "I" as an uninterrupted [awareness] and "this" as an interrupted [awareness].
Now, if everything is indeed composed of verbal expression (*abhilāpamaya*), then how can there be such a thing as "stolidity" (*staimitya*)?

Because this is possible, he says "staimitya" (stagnation). "Consisting of conceptualization"—that is, having the nature of conceptualization—the activity of the subject who is the cognizer of the intellect (*buddhipramātṛ*), which consists of grasping, does not arise [therein].
This is the ultimate truth of an oath; for if someone were to acknowledge its existence only by means of an oath, then [one should address] him...

It exists; otherwise, no one would admit its very existence, for there is a witness, and that witness is one's own self consisting of consciousness—this is the sense. Furthermore, memory is the recollection occurring at a later time for one who has arisen from a state of stupor, in the form: "I was in a state of stupor. Now, if this is so, then...

"In that case as well, let the determination (*adhyavasāya*) be quite clear. To this he says: "regarding form" (*rūpe*). That which has a determination regarding form—that is, a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—is "one who determines form"; the word "in [a state of] inertia" (*staimitye*) is to be supplied, as is the word "if it should arise" (*yadi... tarhi*). What else?

Here, distinct from this accepted determination (*adhyavasāya*), there is that which is called "stagnation" (*staimitya*)— the state consisting of the withdrawal of all thought. The meaning is that there could be nothing [distinct] at all, because the very determination of stagnation is the cause for the establishment of stagnation.

He states the conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means for this reason. Even there—in the state of stillness (*staimitya*)—there exists an internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). By this, he explains that all words have all things as their objects, using the word "sakalena" (by the whole). "Śabdana" means speaking, or the joining [of a word] with its denotative function. Here...

He provides the justification with the words "tathā hi" (for it is thus). "In the preceding individual"— that is, in the individual body of a cow or similar animal that stands before one— "inherent"— meaning natural, and not consisting of the linguistic impression (*saṃskāra*) experienced here [in this life]— "reflection"— which serves as the cause for the application of the first linguistic usage.

The two occurrences of the word "vā" (or) serve to indicate that, in both cases, the primary element is an option (*vikalpa*). Following that—either following the uninterrupted reflective awareness (*avicchinnaparāmarśa*), or indeed immediately after it—the word "cow" (*gauḥ*) is superimposed, whether as "the cow" or simply as "cow"; this too [occurs] through practice (*abhyāsa*).

It becomes composed of the subject (*pramātṛmaya*). Following that, there is the notion "this is white," "this is a bull," and so forth—this is the principle of convention (*saṅketatattva*). Therefore, there is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) within direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*).

The intention of the word "api" (also/even) is as follows: here, direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) is in reality nothing other than the operation of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) culminating in the thought "I see. For even the opponent maintains that conceptualization is the very function of perception; and it is not logical for a function to be distinct from that which possesses it, since [the function] is indeed the very nature of that [perception].
He. Or let it be;

whether following upon a reflective awareness of a break [in the flow], "gaura" is an illustration of words from regional dialects, while "go" is an illustration of words from various scriptural and linguistic traditions. It is "superimposed," as it were.
It is brought to the state of being an object of superimposition, like silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell;

however, in ultimate reality, it is because the internal reflective awareness (*antaraparāmarśa*) itself exists in the form of the cawing of a crow and so forth, and it is that very [awareness] which is colored by specific phonemes. That too—that sound as well—is composed of the subject (*pramātṛmaya*).

Pervaded by the body of consciousness; and following that—on the basis of the two previously mentioned words—"another" is superimposed as "white," and "another" is superimposed as "ox. In this way, the reality of convention (*saṅketatattva*) comes into being; for no word is restricted to any [specific object] in reality. Indeed, in reality...

The sense is that all languages would be of one and the same form. With the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*), he concludes the expressed meaning of the portion of the verse explained up to the word "reflection" (*vimarśa*).
He states the intention of the word "also" (*api*) occurring within this sentence with the words "of the word 'also'."

Realization (*sākṣātkāraḥ*) means direct perception (*pratyakṣīkaraṇam*). To the question "Why does it extend to the operation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?", he says: "For conceptual construction... [and so on]. Of direct perception—that is, of the means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*). As it has been said: "Direct perception is of two kinds: determinate (*savikalpaka*) and indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*)."

Thus [it is said]. "Even another"—that is, even a logician (*tārkika*), but not a Buddhist, because in his view conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

To the question, "What follows from that?", he says, "And not... [referring to *na ca*]. "Possessing that" means possessing the activity. Why is it not different? To this he says, "That... [referring to *tat*]. And therefore, it is quite clear that direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) consists essentially of reflective awareness (*vimarśamayatva*).
This is the state of being (*bhāva*). This, however, is the means of proof from the perspective of the sentence. Here, he raises the Buddhist position:

direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) has the nature of lasting for only a single moment; even in that case, there is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). And this must necessarily be so. Otherwise, how could it be? If that [reflective awareness] were not present, then one who is moving swiftly with a single-pointed intention, [would not perceive the sequence].

If one recites the syllables too hurriedly, or reads the mantra-text too rapidly, one should not proceed, utter, or cause [the mantra] to be recited in such a manner. For instance, in that context, there may arise: the desire for knowledge (*jñāna*), the desire to step forward (*ācikramiṣā*), the act of stepping forward (*ākramaṇa*), the cognition of having stepped upon [the object] (*ākrāntatājñāna*), the pursuit of another purpose, or the desire to abandon [the current state] (*tityakṣā*).

There is the transition to another location; even in that case, how could the attainment of the desired place occur without the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)—in the form of joining and separating (or connecting and disconnecting)—of such states as "the desire to move" and so forth? Thus...

"Or let it be so" regarding rapid grasping, recitation, and so forth. Its nature is that of a single moment—having the character of a single moment colored by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since according to the Buddhist view everything is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Here too, he establishes the existence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Regarding the phrase "tatrāpi" (even there): even there—that is, even in the direct realization whose nature lasts for only a moment. Anticipating the objection that these [factors] are not admitted here, he says "avaśyam" (necessarily). In response to the expectation of how this is so, he explains the remainder of the verse beginning with "katham anyathā" as the answer: "How otherwise? etc.
He explains the two words "how otherwise" (*katham anyathā*) with the word "if" (*yadi*). "That" (*saḥ*) refers to the reflective awareness (*vimarśaḥ*).

He explains the word "recollection" (*pratisandhāna*) with the word "that" (*tat*). "That" (*tat*) means then; by means of "unification"—that is, by means of the synthesis in the form of the first reflective awareness such as "I am running," etc.—it is intended.
—[It is] precisely the desired destination and so forth. Here, he begins to provide a justification with the words "tathā hi" (for instance).

In that place—in the place first made the object of running—there is cognition [in the form]: "I am running from this place"; from that arises the desire to step forward (*ācikramiṣā*), the wish to step upon it; and from that...
Stepping forward (*ākramaṇam*) is the occupation of that place; from that arises the desire to leave (*tityakṣā*), which is the wish to abandon that place;

then follows the mental apprehension of another place (*deśāntarānusandhiḥ*), namely the mental conception of the place that serves as the support for the second step, wherein there is the desire to step (*ācikramiṣā*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), stepping forward and the other stages are included.

And there is the apprehension [of movement] due to the intention toward another location; by such means— as through a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) consisting of joining and separating, which is both indistinct and necessarily to be admitted— how could the attainment of the desired place occur without this reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)?
This much must be understood for every single step. In that regard, there is specifically the application of the sequence of places (*sthāna*), articulators (*karaṇa*), and so forth.

And here, since the very possibility of the web consisting of knowledge, desire, the act of pervasion (*ākramaṇa*), and so on, does not exist, the meaning is that [the aforementioned] would not occur because of that impossibility.

In whatever form that knowledge and so forth reside within him, that very thing is the innate self-reflection (*sahaja-ahaṃ-parāmarśa*); therefore, one should remain intent upon that alone. As it has been said:
"Whether running or reaching whatever state, therein vibration (*spanda*) is established."

Thus it is said. Nor should impossibility be asserted here regarding [the movement of] knowledge and so forth, because the middle term—which consists of the space between two words and is composed of all things—is present here;
and for the awakened, the middle term is indeed most clearly evident in the transition from one knowledge to another.

For those who are perfectly awakened, everything is at all times entirely composed of that [Reality]; however, for those who are unawakened, there is no qualification for this state at all. As it has been said:
"Since the arising of another thought occurs for one who is intent upon a single thought..."
That, however, should be known as the opening of the eyes; one should perceive it for oneself.
Thus; and the venerable Vasiṣṭha, having kept this very point in mind, [said]:
"Of consciousness that has traveled a great distance from one country to another, in an instant..."
That form which is stainless in the center is the form of the Supreme Self.
Thus it has been said. For those who remain in this very state, the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* manifest as obstacles.
As it has been stated:
"From this comes the point (*bindu*), from this the sound (*nāda*), from this the form, and from this the taste."
They set in motion, in no time at all, embodied beings by means of agitation.

Thus. By the term "embodied beings" (dehin), this is indicated: one must first depart from whatever state one happens to be in; otherwise, even for those practicing in the intermediate station (*madhyadhāman*), disturbances will certainly arise in the interim. Enough of this.
He extends this principle to the recitation for grasping [the object] and so forth, which are included by the word "etc. (*ādi*), by saying "in the same way" (*evam*).

By the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of the entire category of actions performed rapidly; the sense is that even in those cases, there is the manifestation of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). As it has been said:
How can this person, while uttering speech, proceed from one phoneme to the next,
unless they first come to rest within you, the pure conscious self?
The subsequent gross conceptual construction is not perceived; therefore, it is precisely because of this that there is rapidity.
Thus, it must be understood that the latent impression (*bhāvanā*) consisting of sound is condensed by a subtle reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).
For the latent impression of sound, when being unfolded through expansion, becomes the gross conceptual construction.

Just as the expansion of the thought "this" results in [cognitions] such as "a jar" or "white," so too does that [expansion] result in [cognitions] such as "that which has the shape of a broad base and belly" or "that which is the locus of a quality conjoined with the universal of whiteness.
According to the reading *dhāvu gati-śuddhau* ("to run means purity of motion"), the root *dhāv* occurs in the sense of rapid motion by virtue of its own inherent power. || 19 ||
Let it be that such a subtle reflection enters the body of Light;
however, as for the phrase "by way of grossness," one must not suspect otherwise: the pure conscious Self is indeed endowed with the pure reflective awareness of "I."

To address the inquiry "How is this so?", he says "tatra" (therein). "Therein" means in the context of rapid apprehension and so forth. "Of the places" refers to the throat and other locations; "of the instruments" refers to their modes such as *spṛṣṭa* (contact) and so on.

"Here" means at the time of rapid apprehension and so forth; and "the future" [nature] refers to that which, having rested from that [process], is characterized by a tendency toward manifestation (*sphuraṇa*). It is not [that which is already manifest].

"It is perceived"—that is, it is experienced. For this reason, by means of that which consists of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the word-sound—which is extremely contracted in the form of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the sound—it must indeed be cultivated; otherwise, immediately after the utterance of a single phoneme...

The sense is that if the cognition of the second phoneme and so forth were impossible, then the recitation of the second phoneme would indeed be improper. "Contracted" (*saṃvartitā*) means first narrowed down by the method of rapid recitation;
"verbal creative contemplation" (*śabdabhāvanā*) is that which exists between the two phonemes and consists of a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) that serves as the cause for their conjunction.
The construction is as follows: "being transformed"—that is, being brought to clarity—the gross conceptualization (*sthūlo vikalpa*) comes into being.

Regarding this, he states an example with the words "as for instance" (*yathā*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), actions and so forth are included. Of that [conceptualization], such as "the jar is white" and so on—he describes the expansion of the term "jar" (*ghaṭa*) with the word "broad" (*pṛthu*); [he then describes] that of "white" (*śukla*).
"Extension is whiteness. Now, one might ask: how is it that *dhāvati* expresses "swift movement"? To this he says:

"*dhāvu* [means] 'movement'. By virtue of its own power—that is, by the power of its own inherent capacity. For verbal roots possess multiple meanings through their own power even without prepositions (*upasarga*s), just as in the case of the root *yu*.

The intention is that [the roots] have the meanings of "mixing" and "not mixing. The reading *dhāvu* in the sense of "motion" and "purity" is the correct one. The word *iti* marks the completion of the commentary on the verse. || 19 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the twentieth verse with the words, "Let it be so.
Here the commentary says:
"In this way"—meaning by the manner you have described—"subtle"—meaning having the nature of pure *ahaṃ* (I-consciousness) alone.
The penetration of the body of light is clearly of the nature of conceptualization; therein, the word appears as something distinct, just like the blue object—as "this is blue.
How could that [word] be non-different from the nature of light? And it is of the very essence of sound.
Regarding this reflection (*vimarśa*), you maintain that even here—in the state of duality which is of the nature of *māyā*—it is non-different from the Light (*prakāśa*).
Anticipating the doubt as to how this is to be understood, he says:
"The determination 'this is a jar' is something that transcends name and form."
The power of the Supreme Lord shines like the Self itself, and not as a separate "this-ness."

By whom was this said? That the gross word "jar" has the nature of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), which is the very life of manifestation. For even that gross word appears as something distinct from its object, just like the object itself. These two—the word and the object, characterized respectively as name and form—are of a single nature, in the form of the identity "this is that."
That power of the Supreme Lord which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—the capacity for determination (*adhyavasāya-śakti*)—is identical with the Self;
it is permeated by the nature of light (*prakāśa-svarūpa*), because without that [reflective awareness], the nature of light does not manifest. However, where...

Regarding the question of how blue and so forth appear, he says "blue. This word, which is of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is placed here; although the word "also" (*api*) appears later in the sequence, it should be construed as "even by you [opponents], this is accepted. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse:
He explains: "This is a jar.
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) expands upon the method for explaining the verse, beginning with the words "By whom is this [known]? and so forth. Again...

In response to the expectation of what was said, he says: "He too. Again, to the question of whose life is illumination, he says: "Those two. Those two—the well-known name and form; "name" being such as "jar," and "form" being its characteristic or essential nature—these two are the word and the object. By virtue of their single form, [he] himself... of this... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a philosophical work, likely concerning Advaita Vedānta. The translation reflects the available portion.)

He provides the explanation of the word with the phrase "so 'yam" (this is that). "Parāmṛśantī" means leading [the object] to the state of being the object of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which consists in the unification of the word and its meaning;
therefore, the sense is that it is logically distinct from those two. *Adhyavasā*—

Determination (*adhyavasāya*) is of the nature of the operation of the intellect; that which occurs is not the gross word "this is a jar," but rather it shines as the unconditioned "I am the Supreme Lord,
O God," and never shines as something delimited by the form of "this-ness" (*idantā*).
If it were to appear as something discrete, it would be established in another, and thus there would have to be a further reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that;

and since the same would apply there as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, because it would never attain a firm foundation, the manifestation of the blue object itself would not occur. Therefore, every reflective awareness [is rooted] in the Light (*prakāśa*).
"Uninterrupted indeed"—this is the determination (*adhyavasā*). It ends in the suffix *aṅ* according to Pāṇini’s rule *ātaścopasarge* (3.3.106), and is thus feminine. || 20 ||

Śakti, although colored by name and form—which are of the nature of *vimarśa*—is in the ultimate sense of the nature of *vimarśa* as "I" alone. Like the Self (*ātman*) and like Light (*prakāśa*), it shines as the unconditioned "I," because that is its very essence; the meaning is that the coloring [by name and form] is ultimately irrelevant. Now, one might object:
"Why does this [determination] not appear as 'this-ness' (*idantayā*)—that is, as the determination 'this is a jar'? Because it appears as something distinct.

To this he says: "As 'this-ness'. Because it is established in another, due to the absence of repose in its own self and because it is grasped as being fixed upon the object; furthermore, by means of another reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) performed for the sake of ascending back into one's own self.

There must be reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because without reflective awareness there is no ascent into one’s own self; and without that ascent into one’s own self, even a fully accomplished determination (*adhyavasā*) is as good as non-existent—this is the sense. Now, one might ask: "Let there be another reflective awareness, so what of it? To this he says: "In that case also" (*tatrāpi*). In that case also—

Within that very act of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there must likewise be another act of reflective awareness; this is the meaning, the sense being that the same logic applies. Thus, due to such an infinite regress—the consequence of the fault of infinite regress—there would be no manifestation of the blue object at all.

The sense is that [the means of knowledge] is exhausted merely by the subject’s act of determination (*adhyavasāna*). He states the established conclusion of his own desired position as being proven with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). "All"—meaning the nature of the "I" and the nature of "blue" and so forth—is essentially the vibration (*spanda*) of the universal and the particular. The word "iti" marks the end of the commentary.

He explains the word *adhyavasā*: "It is *adhyavasā*. The [suffix] *aṅ* is prescribed in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), meaning that because it ends in the feminine suffix *ṭā*, it is feminine in gender. *Adhyavasa* is the form of the root *ṣo* (meaning "to finish") preceded by the two prefixes; this is according to the rule *ādeca...* (Pāṇini 6.1.45).
The letter *a* [is the substitute] for the vowel *o*. || 20 ||

Now, if it is thus the case that the entire complex of cognitions is established solely as "I," then there is no contact with the plane of the object of knowledge (*vedyabhūmi*); and on the plane of the object, there is a connection with space and time, but not in the aspect of the knower (*vedakāṃśa*).
And in the absence of such a connection with space and time, as for this [distinction] of cognitions according to space—

If succession is observed in relation to the factors of the knower and so forth—and in relation to its own parts or other cognitions—how could that be possible? And in the absence of succession, there would in reality be only oneness;
consequently, it would possess those [powers] such as cognition and memory.
Dispelling the doubt as to how that which was stated— namely, "the Supreme Lord"— can be logically sustained, he concludes what was previously said:
"Simply by virtue of conforming to different objects of cognition, space, and time..."
Cognition, memory, determination, and so forth appear as having a temporal sequence. || 21 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the twenty-first verse with the words "nanu evam" (but if it is so).
Here the commentary says: "evam" means when the manner just described is the case; "pratiṣṭhāne" means while there is stability.

To the question "Why does it not exist? he says: "because it is an object of cognition" (*vedya*). The particle *ca* has the sense of *hi* (for/indeed). [The opponent asks: "Let there be no contact with space and time; what of it? To this he replies: "Space... [and so on]. How could it be so in relation to space—or rather, in relation to the factors such as the subject (*pramātṛ*)? For time alone is the cause of succession. It is not [so].
The meaning is "it may be so. [Objection: But let that also not be. To this he says, "sequence" (*krama*). [Objection: Let there be only oneness; what follows from that?
To this he says, "and therefore" (*tataśca*). And therefore—meaning, when oneness exists.

"By means of knowledge, memory, and so forth, the possessor thereof"—that is, the possessor of the powers of knowledge, memory, and exclusion (*apohana*). It has been stated, "not... [the rest of the sentence is omitted].

The meaning is as follows in the verse beginning with "ced antaḥkṛta. "Nirvahet" means "it would attain accomplishment. He concludes; that is to say, he speaks by synthesizing [the points] in one place. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it, beginning with the word "kevalam."

It is true that the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) is indeed without succession; however, regarding those objects of knowledge (*vedya*) which, by virtue of its own power (*svaśakti*), appear as distinct, there exists a spatial dimension (*deśa*)— consisting of distance, proximity, extension, and non-extension— produced by differences in form (*mūrti*), and a temporal dimension produced by differences in action (*kriyā*).
Time, which consists of forms such as slow or rapid action and so forth— relying upon and taking hold of that time merely by way of its shadow (chāyāmātra),
the portions of cognitions, memories, and determinations appear as if they were their own parts, even though they are partless.

And the appearance of succession is produced by the manifested portions [of consciousness], both in relation to one another and in relation to their own parts; for although it is temporal succession alone that clearly appears within cognitions, not spatial succession.

Here, the commentary explains the word "kevalam" (only/alone) with the passage beginning with "satyam" and ending with "kintu. The phrase "by the power of its own capacity" (*svaśaktivaśāt*) is supplied as a necessary ellipsis. This applies to the entire compound expression beginning with "bhinnasaṃvedya" (having a distinct object of cognition).
