He explains the term *vigraha* (division) as "by way of differentiation" (*bhinnatvena*). He explains the word *saṃvedya* (the perceptible) as "the objects of perception" (*vedyāni*). The objects of perception are the objects such as blue and so forth;

the spatial location (*deśa*) produced by their "differentiation of form"—that is, their differentiation of essential nature (*svarūpabheda*)—is indeed nothing other than the mere differentiation of the essential nature of things.

In response to the inquiry as to what kind of place [is intended], he states its qualification as "far. Likewise, regarding the time produced by that specific action—the distinction of movement—as to what kind of time it is, he says "long. He explains the meaning of the term "in accordance with" (anurodhataḥ) as "shadow" (chāyā). Thus, these two are space and time.

"By mere shadow"—that is, by mere appearance, but not in an ultimate sense; "having relied upon," meaning having taken recourse to. By this, it is indicated that the suffix *tasi* is used here with the elision of the gerundive suffix *lyap*. Having explained the first half-verse, he explains the second half-verse, beginning with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*),...
There is the apprehension of parts such as knowledge and the rest. To the question, "How is it possible for parts to be included by the word 'and the rest' (ādi)?

he says: "their own parts" (svāṃśāḥ). The construction is as follows: even though they are partless, they appear as if they had their own parts, like the parts of space due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). And those [parts] which are thus appearing...

The parts were created by them; thus, "created by those appearing parts" is the meaning. He explains that it appears with succession by the word "sakramam. Therein, the explanation is indicated by the phrase "krama... kṛtaḥ" (where *krama* is supplied); and by the word "avabhāsa," the verbal root *bhās* preceded by the prefix *prati* is explained. Now...

Nevertheless, for one who is deluded, the perception of a mountain appears as if extended, while the perception of a jujube fruit appears as if subtle; thus, even spatial succession is shown [to be an appearance].
Therefore, because there is only the semblance of accepting a succession residing in the object of cognition, succession, though appearing, does not [truly exist].
Because that which appears as non-ultimate is in fact the ultimate, it is therefore rightly said that knowledge and the other qualities are the powers (*śakti*) of this Lord;
[they belong] to the All-pervasive One through his power of *māyā*.

By this verse, the diversity of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of cognitions has been shown; by this [present verse], however, it is the diversity of space and time (*deśakāla*) that is indicated—this is the distinction. Thus all is auspicious. 21.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Power of Knowledge," in the first section on Knowledge of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.

Since the word "succession" (*krama*) is a relative term, when the question arises as to what that succession depends upon for its manifestation, he provides this determination—though already established in the Sūtra—by stating "mutually" (*paraspara*). The sense is that cognition and the other factors do not arise at one and the same time; for indeed, cognition does not occur simultaneously [with all others].
It manifests, however, only through the sequence of relying on the aspects of the subject and so forth; the same applies to memory and the rest.

Having kept the student's doubt in mind, he provides another resolution with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). The word "even" (*api*) indicates that the demonstration of spatial sequence is slightly inappropriate. He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tena*).

And the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) of that which appears should be understood through the reasoning stated in the verse beginning with *prāgivārthaḥ*. By relying on this, he establishes the validity of the previously mentioned entity, saying "therefore" (*tataśca*).
With the words "by the power of illusion" (*māyāśaktyā*), he avoids the charge of redundancy with the preceding verse, stating "illusion" (*māyā*).

By this—by this verse—it is the distinction; thus there is this difference. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the chapter (āhnika). "Śivam" is an expression of auspiciousness and indicates a reflection upon the supreme reality (paratattva). Thus, all is auspicious (śivam). || 22 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Jñānādhikāra of the *Śrīpratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*, the commentary known as the *Śrībhāskarī*, composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. May there be auspiciousness for all the worlds.

Now begins the sixth chapter: We praise that Śiva, who, by his own will, uses the axe of their exclusion to cut through those entities— which are essentially non-different from his own self— into various forms.

Thus, the power of memory (*smṛti-śakti*) and the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) have been described. Now, the power of discernment (*apohana-śakti*), which favors both of those, will be explained at length in eleven verses. [The sixth chapter begins: "That reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) which is of the nature of light..."
We praise Śiva, who, by means of the power of exclusion (apoha), causes to arise the various figurines of existence that reside within the pillar of his own nature, as if they were being cast away.

Now, beginning the sixth chapter within the section on Knowledge (Jñānādhikāra), the author composes an auspicious invocation— consisting of the recollection of the chosen deity known as the Supreme Reality— for the sake of completing that work without obstacle;
he does so by means of a verse indicating the intent of the entire chapter, for the purpose of instructing his disciples.
Regarding the phrase "non-difference from one's own self," the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"We [worship] that Śiva— Śiva being the supreme reality whose nature is the light of consciousness."

We praise— that is, by means of praise, we bring into the scope of our reflective inquiry— some well-known internal reality that bestows happiness. Therefore, [we praise] Him who, by His own will— that is,
by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), which is impelled by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), is inferable solely through its effects, and is exceedingly subtle—

By virtue of being one's own essential nature—not by means of worldly volition, which is a property of the mind—the non-difference (abheda) from one's own self, which is of the nature of light; that is to say, the state of abiding in identity with oneself, characterized by the absence of differentiation. By that [non-difference], [the objects] are "dense" (ghana), meaning they form a single mass, like jars and other such things.
"Ending with the 'mṛd' (clay/matter)": [it refers to] entities—objects of experience consisting of the grasped and the grasper, things that are both insentient and sentient.

"Those entities" are what are being excluded; that is to say, it is the power of exclusion (*apohana-śakti*), by which they are manifested through differentiation from themselves and from one another. That very thing is the "chisel"—the instrument for splitting stone—and from that [instrument].

The meaning is "thus. "Cutting"—that is, manifesting through the distinction between itself and others—it produces the various forms, which are the essential natures (*svarūpa*) of those objects and entities;
it does so by making them appear within its own self as reflections. It becomes such [a state] even with respect to time, which is eternal and immediate.

By the passage beginning with "sattāpradatvena" (by virtue of being the bestower of existence) and ending with "sarvasya jīvataḥ" (of every living being), that which exists as its own essential nature—an existence that is exceedingly great—is determined. In that context, by means of the verse, it is indicated that the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*) is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). Then, by the subsequent verse...

It is said that when the self-reflection (*ahaṃpratyavamarśa*) is pure, the operation of exclusion (*apohana*) is impossible; therefore, its occurrence is only possible within one's own perception. Thus, having manifested agency within one's own self, one partakes in it as such. [This is] the instrument for the act of cutting by means of a weapon.

This indicates its status as a cause; by this, it is suggested that the power of exclusion (*apohana*) is determined here. Furthermore, even a great artisan, while carving sections from a crystal stone with a chisel, creates various figurines;
however, by cutting distinct parts with a distinct instrument, he produces only distinct [objects].

Having thus performed the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), the intended meaning of the entire chapter (*āhnika*) is as follows: by cutting his own forms—which are indeed identical to his own self—by means of mere will (*icchāmātra*) as non-different from himself, he acts; thus, the contrast (*vyatireka*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). Having thus accomplished the auspicious rite, [he states] the purport of the entire chapter...
He says "thus" (*evam*) at the very beginning for the sake of stabilizing the disciple's intellect.
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"It has been described"—the meaning is that it was explained by the two preceding chapters (*āhnika*). "Those two"—refers to the two previously mentioned.

She is such [a goddess] who favors both of those—the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and memory (*smṛti*)—as a pair, leading them to the state of being objects of favor by providing them with their respective objects. In response to the question "By what?
[the answer is: "By eleven verses."

He characterizes this group of eleven verses by means of the first and the last with the words "I am. "Is determined" (nirṇīyate) means that it is brought to the state of being an object of certainty after the destruction of opposing views. Having stated the intention in its entirety, he also explains it in detail with the word "therein" (tatra). Therein:

The meaning is: "within the midst of the eleven verses. *Pratyavamarśa* refers to the reflective awareness (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*) residing in pure light. *Avikalpa* means the absence of conceptualization that implies duality. *Viśeṣa* means the distinction from ordinary worldly reflection.

"It is indicated" means it is merely hinted at, but not stated directly. "Thereafter"—that is, immediately following that. "The impossibility of the operation of exclusion," the sense being that it consists in the exclusion of others;
"impossibility" means the absence of occurrence caused by the non-existence of others. In one's own perception...
By one verse; then by two verses, the conceptual nature of the impure reflective awareness "I";
then by one verse, the conceptual nature of even the subsequent synthesis (*anusandhāna*).
Thus, it is precisely of the nature of such synthesis and so forth—[it is precisely of the nature of such synthesized awareness and so forth].

The Supreme Lord’s nature as creator is [explained] by the verse beginning with *parameśvarasya sraṣṭṛtvam*. Thereafter, the existence of the manifestation of objects within the conscious Self (*cidātman*), which is the subject at hand, is concluded by a verse. Then, by a pair of verses, the manifold variety of that very manifestation of objects in experience, recollection, and so forth, is described.
And that statement is employed for the sake of the recognition of one's own self as the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*) which is the subject at hand;
thus [ends] the essential meaning of this chapter (*āhnika*). Now, the meaning of the text itself is being explained.
This has been stated:
"...the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which is the very nature of manifestation.

In this context, reflective awareness is indeed conjoined with a word whose essence is expression; and it is through that conjunction that [it is established] within the Śaiva system, which constitutes one's own philosophical view. The justification for this is as follows:

The operation of exclusion (apohana) is established even within the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃpratyavamarśa). This refers to that which is "impure"—meaning, although in the ultimate sense there is no absence of purity, it is so called because it pertains to a subject such as the body, which is joined with the impurity known as duality; [this applies] even to the synthetic unification (anusandhāna) associated with that.

The synthesis (*yojana*), which is the effect of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), likewise consists precisely of such a form of synthetic contemplation (*anusandhāna*)—that is, it consists precisely of the nature of synthetic contemplation and so forth, which is the very nature of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). Within the conscious self (*cidātman*)—the light that constitutes the nature of Śiva—it is "withdrawn," meaning it is described by way of withdrawal. Of that very [synthesis]...

It is precisely of the withdrawn manifestation of objects that this is said—and "that statement" refers to the statement of their diversity. He effects the conclusion with the words "iti. "Thus" (*iti*) means: such is the purport of the chapter; the meaning is that this is the purport of the entire chapter taken individually. With the word "atha," he promises to explain the meaning of the text.

"It is explained" means that it is brought within the scope of explanation. At the occasion of explaining the verse beginning with "the nature of manifestation," a matter that might have occurred to the mind of the student as a potential doubt— even if not yet raised— is determined by [the author] himself out of his compassionate gaze, providing an introductory transition (avataraṇikā) appropriate to it.
He says "it has been stated" regarding the first verse, even though it is devoid of such an expectation.
Here the commentary [states]:
"produced by its arrangement"—that is, produced by the arrangement of words—even though it is pure, that is, even though it is incapable of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
As it has been said:

"The state of being conceptual (vikalparūpatva) would follow even for the pure Supreme Lord; yet this is not desired, because that [state] is logically possible only in the sphere of transmigratory existence which consists of Māyā. Having raised this doubt, he says:

That reflective awareness which, though its nature is light and consists of speech, is not a conceptual construction; for a conceptual construction is defined as a definitive ascertainment that implies a duality. || 1 ||

That which is the self— the life-force, the essential nature, devoid of interruption, conceived as an internal acceptance, and non-dual— of light, whose form is pure consciousness (*viśuddhasaṃvidrūpa*), and which has not been turbidified by contact with the body and other such things; [this is what is meant].
Because your activity transcends conceptual construction, even direct perception has been forgotten by you,
just as an object standing before one is ignored by a mind longing for something else.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Let him attain even Paramaśiva. To this he says: "And not... Why is it not desired? To this he says: "Of that..."—that is, of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). "In the nature of Māyā"—by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because it has the form of differentiation which is the effect of Māyā; that is, in its own essential nature. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "I am... (*aham*).
Here the commentary explains and analyzes the term *prakāśātmā* [the nature of light] as follows: "Of light" (*prakāśasya*).
"Pure" (*śuddha*) means that which is pure—that is, consciousness (*saṃvit*), the internal reality of consciousness, which is not stained by objects of cognition (*asaṃvedya-arūṣita*).
"Of such a one whose nature is that"—regarding its purity, he states a qualifying attribute containing a reason: "body and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," the vital breaths and other such factors are included; the meaning is: "of one who has not been brought to a state of limitation by the body and so forth."

He explains the word *ātman*—which has been delimited by the body and so forth—as "life. By this, its status as a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound is indicated, as well as its function as an adjective for the term "recognition" (*pratyavamarśa*). He explains the phrase "the recognition of 'I'" (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*) with the word "I" (*aham*). I...

Thus, because he abides in his own self, which is pure and of the nature of light, the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) takes the form of "I" (*aham*); it does not take the form of "this" (*idam*), as that would involve objective entities. "Reflective awareness" (*pratyavamarśa*) means an internalized awareness (*avamarśa*)—a touching by means of subtle expression—in the form of "I. Now, [an objection]:

Of what nature is this? It is the reflective awareness "I," which consists in resting in the sovereignty of not looking toward the faces of others [i.e., *ananyamukhaprekṣitva-svātantrya*]. This is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

He shows the seed of the suspicion that [speech] might be a conceptual construction (vikalpa) with the words "even though its form is speech" (*vāgvapuri api*). By the word "speech" (*vāk*), he refers to that which is distinct from the object-form—the sound grasped by the ear—and which, appearing internally, is an expression consisting of the nature of verbalization (*śabdana*) that enters into the nature of consciousness; it "speaks" (*vakti*) the meaning through its own superimposition (*svādhyāsa*).

By means of the synthesis "this is that" (*so'yam ity abhisaṃdhānena*). If it is the nature of speech, why is it not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? He says: because it does not possess the defining characteristic of conceptual construction;
for conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consists of various imaginings, and the imagination of what is suspected as being manifold is the exclusion of others (*anyavyavacchedana*).
In view of this requirement, he himself states further qualifiers: "devoid of interruption" (*vicchedaśūnya*).

The intended meaning is that, because it is of the very nature of light (*prakāśa*), its form is likewise eternally non-deviating. By this, its arising as something new—like an external tactile sensation—is precluded; likewise, the conceptualization of an internal acceptance [of such arising] is also excluded.

Thus, the term "conceptualization" (*kalpa*) is used because [the self] consists of the acceptance of itself within its own nature, and not because it is equivalent to an external admission. Likewise, it has the form of not looking toward the face of another; that is, the repose in that sovereignty which is the absence of dependence on another in the apprehension of itself—the nature of which is aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*).

"Rest" (viśrāma) means that which has such a form; it is that which fulfills the expectancy for the word "yat. He says "conceptual construction" (vikalpa) to establish that the qualifier "consisting of speech" (vāgvapuḥ) contains a reason. "Seed" (bīja) means the cause. He establishes the non-worldly meaning of the word "speech" (vāk) by saying "object" (viṣaya).
He states the reason for the phrase "shining within" as "consciousness" (*saṃvit*).

In that regard, the meaning is that it rests within the body of that [consciousness], because it is established solely in luminosity—not, as some might think, in non-luminosity. Now, one might object: "In that case, it would not have the nature of speech. To this, he says:

Regarding the term "by means of sounding" (*śabdanena*), he states its synonym as "expression" (*abhilāpaḥ*). By the word "speech" (*vāk*) found in the Sūtra, the meaning is as follows: this speech, which consists of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa-rūpā*), is indeed inferred even in newborn infants by virtue of their desire for the mother's milk; however, that [desire] only becomes fully manifest once it has reached maturity.
Otherwise, because external expansion would be impossible, it must therefore be experienced by oneself internally alone through the instruction of a guru and so forth. As it has been said:
"Alas, we fools speak [otherwise]!"

Thus [it is said]. In the investigation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is only the state of becoming one with that (*tanmayībhāva*) which is established; there is no need for focused attention (*avadhāna*) therein, because such attention would entail duality (*bheda*).
Furthermore, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and manifoldness (*vividhatva*) exist only as long as the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the possibility of non-fire upon fire has not been removed.
O Lord, since it implies both forms— fire and non-fire— it must necessarily be stated regarding that conceptual construction (vikalpa):
"Abandon all attentions.

For this reason as well, even the mention of "attainment" (*siddhi*) in the investigation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is entirely improper there; because everything is always of the nature of that [Reality], only those who are perfectly awakened are truly wise.
Because those who are awakened are fit for mere instruction, while those who are unawakened have no authority even in that regard.
As it has been said:
"This very power, consisting of action, is subject to the will of Śiva."
She who binds, who abides on her own path, and who is known as the bringer about of accomplishment.

Thus [it is said]. Enough of this digression. Here, he provides the etymological derivation (*vyutpādana*) of the word *vāk* as that which "speaks" (*vakti*). Regarding the phrase "by means of superimposition" (*svādhyāsena*): for indeed, the meaning of the word "pot" is determined through the prior superimposition of the word "pot," as in the cognition "this is a pot. This occurs by means of the mental synthesis (*abhisaṃdhāna*) of "that is this. That which...
The meaning is that this object standing before one becomes denotable by the word "jar" through *yojanā* (synthetic unification).

By this, it is stated that in this context, it is the internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) itself—which is the cause for establishing the convention between the signifier and the signified—that is called "speech" (*vāk*), and not the external, gross sound. Here, the student asks: "If... and so forth.
Regarding this, the author states "he said" (*āha*) in order to relate the answer given by the Guru. To the question "What did he say?", he replies with "For not of this" (*na hyasya*).

"Of this" refers to the act of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). When the expectation arises as to "How so?", he begins the justification with "For thus" (*tathā hi*). In that context, he explains the etymological meaning of the word *vikalpa* as "various" (*vividhā*). "Various"—

Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consists of that which has the form of this [object] and that which does not have the form of this [object]. He states the second meaning with the words "and by way of manifoldness" (*vividhatvena ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction;
"by way of manifoldness" means by way of having the form of this and not having the form of this. He explains the meaning of the word *kalpa* as "the other" (*anya*).
"Of the other"—that is, of that which does not have the form of this—"exclusion" (*vyavacchedana*) means, by implication, the turning away from that which has the form of this.

Having thus explained the meaning of the individual members, he states the function of the diversity expressed by the prefix in the words "and this diversity. This should be construed as "in the non-existent" and "in the existent. He anticipates the objection:
"And that must be determined, and that which is not that must be excluded."
And thus, there would indeed be an appearance of two distinct things, such as a jar and a non-jar;
however, there is no manifestation of anything else that is separate from the Light itself. (2)
Because mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is not apprehended, it causes [the object] to manifest within the cognition of the knower.

He states the function of the combination of the prefix and the root with the word "thereby" (*tena*). "Thereby" means for that reason. "In conceptual construction" (*vikalpe*) means in the domain of conceptual construction. And "that" (*tacca*) refers to the object situated in front, between the two objects of the conceptual construction.

It is to be ascertained—that is, it becomes fit for the determination of its existence. And therefore—[and thus] the object that is merely a subject of doubt—is to be excluded—that is, it is to be negated by the thought "it does not exist. This means that it becomes precisely the effect of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). However, in the ultimate sense, it is only the word "conceptual" (*kalpa*) that is intended here.

Its capacity [to denote] consists in its being expressive through the exclusion of what is determined. Alternatively, the word "of the conceptual construction" (*kalpasya*) is to be supplied; and thus the meaning is as follows: for one who stands upon the locus of conceptual construction—that is, for the conceptual construction—there is both that which is to be determined and that which is to be excluded by it, due to the prefix [denoting exclusion] being applied in a single context.
The meaning is: "because of the superimposition of that which is not its true nature. || 1 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the second verse with the words "tathā ca" (and likewise).
Here the commentary states:
"And likewise" means that I shall demonstrate that very point.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "of two distinct [things]":

for when a jar is perceived, in that very place where the jar stands, there is also a non-jar which, by its nature of occupying a location considered suitable, produces cognition and is brought forth by its own causes.

The nature of cloth and so forth is possible; therefore, because the appearance of both the jar and the non-jar is possible, superimposition (samāropa) has scope. When there is the superimposition of a non-jar, there occurs the operation of exclusion (upohana), characterized by negation.
The state of being conceptualized, animated by that [Light], belongs to the certainty "this is a jar," as well as to the optative and the sense of possibility (*liṅ-sambhāvanā*).
Regarding this Light, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:

He explains the verse by way of a stylistic turn with the words "for in the jar" (*ghaṭe hi*). [The phrase] "in the very place of the jar" means precisely regarding the jar; that is to say, "by way of the nature of the jar. The construction is: "even though it is not a jar, it has the nature of a cloth and so forth. What kind of thing is this "not-a-jar"? It is "suitable"—that is, the location which possesses the capacity for its presence, consisting of the manifestation of a cloth or other such object.

*Deśaḥ*: that very intended place; *tasya yad ākramaṇam*: that which is its occupation; one whose character (*śīla*) is such—that is, in the ultimate sense, he is capable of being present in the location of the jar—this is the meaning.
It is "possible" (*saṃbhāvyate*): the sense of possibility is that it might be so, because of the apprehension of the absence of identity [between the jar and the location].
It is brought within the range of perception. At first, a person seeing a mere individual grasps the nature of the entity only as something indistinct. As it has been said:
"A cow, by its own essential nature, is neither a cow nor a non-cow."

Thus, having determined the absence of identity, one applies that conventional designation to it; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the illusion of silver even in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like. If it is argued that this illusion is caused by similarity, [we reply that] since the common property in the form of existence (sattā) exists everywhere, similarity would exist everywhere as well.

This is of little consequence. As for the fact that the linguistic usage of entities occurs immediately and without confusion, that is produced solely by the proficiency of practice; enough of this. Now, [the opponent asks] "What follows from that? To this he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
"Therefore"—that is, because of the possibility of manifestation. "Superimposition" (*samāropa*) means false attribution (*adhyāsa*). [The opponent objects: "But let it be so..."
The superimposition (*samāropa*) has scope; [to the question] "What follows from that?", he says: "of the non-pot" (*aghaṭasya*).
It is characterized by negation—that is, its nature is the act of negating the non-pot; the word "is appropriate" (*yukta*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Now, [the question] "But what follows even from that? is addressed by the word "thus" (*iti*). "Thus"—for this reason—it is "animated by that" (*tadanuprāṇitā*).
The meaning is that its existence is granted through exclusion (*apohana*), because conceptualization (*vikalpa*) consists precisely in a certainty whose primary function is the negation of others.

He states that the denotation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is "in the sense of possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*); by this, the first half-verse is explained. Thus, that which is conceived as being in its place does not, for its part, lack a manifest form.
For attribution occurs only with respect to that which is of equal status; moreover, it has never been observed that what must be performed by the manifest can ever belong to the unmanifest.
Furthermore, its unmanifest nature would be subverted solely through the force of such things as the imposition of attribution; therefore—

There is no manifestation at all of another distinct entity that is equal in status [to the light], which is of the nature of non-light, incapable of enduring the operation of differentiation consisting of exclusion (*apohana*), and similar to that [light]; in the absence of such a thing, what could there be to exclude? Manifestation...

In brief: because it is the subject under discussion, at the time of perceiving a jar, there would be the manifestation—i.e., the appearance—of two distinct things, namely the jar and the non-jar, existing clearly as separate entities;
the meaning is that this occurs because one perceives the absence of identity between them. And thus, for the purpose of excluding what is not that [the jar], here...
The sense is that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indeed logical.

He explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "this which... (*yastvayam*). Regarding the word "of that" (*tasya*), it refers to the Light (*prakāśa*); regarding the word "in its place" (*sthāne*), it means "in its object.
To the question, "Why would it not be of a non-luminous nature? he replies, "equal" (*tulya*). This refers to that which is of an equal rank (*tulyakakṣya*).

"Of one with equal strength," that is to say, of an opponent. "Possibility" (*saṃbhāvanam*) means an incitement toward possibility (*saṃbhavam*). Now, how can there be equality of status between a jar and a non-jar? True;
just as a jar produces the cognition of existence through its connection with *sattā* (existence), [so too does the non-jar produce the cognition of non-existence].

Thus, by this much alone—that even a non-pot [is not perceived]—the state of being on an equal footing consists in the quality of being a rival in this context. Now, one might object that light and darkness would indeed be on an equal footing;
to this he says, "And not," because otherwise it would follow that even darkness could illuminate objects. This is the intended meaning.
Nevertheless, having granted them equal status, he states the defect with the words "saṃbhāvanā" (possibility).

Since "saṃbhāvanā" involves superimposition and so forth—the word "ādi" (and so forth) including exclusion—it would, by the force of that [superimposition], fall apart—that is, perish—according to the maxim "prāgivārtha" (the sense is as before). Thus, for the sake of possibility...
Because by the very act of being grasped, the absence of luminosity would necessarily follow. He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

He explains the two words "of luminosity itself" (*prakāśasyaiva*) with the word "luminosity" (*prakāśa*). He explains the word "of another" (*anyasya*) with the word "non-luminous" (*aprakāśa*). He explains the word "distinct" (*bhedinaḥ*) with the word "that" (*tat*).

"Of that which has an illumination equal to it"—that is, of that which stands on the same level as the Light. Here too he provides an explanation with the word "apohana. For only that which is of an equal status can stand before one as a rival through its difference; thus it is said, "of that which is of equal status. It does not exist—indeed, at the time of grasping the Light...

The sense is that the apprehension of darkness is possible. Regarding its absence—that is, the absence of manifestation—even if one were to admit the possibility of manifestation, he states the defect with the word "prakāśa" (illumination). Even though the state of being as it was before is impossible [in the case of darkness], there is still the very nature of illumination. Nor is there any difference in the essential nature, location, or time of illumination.

By which the second [category] might be excluded from the one. For this reason—because it is so—since there is no duality and thus no possibility of exclusion (apoha), and because of the absence of the nature of conceptual construction (vikalpa), there is only the reflective awareness "I" within pure consciousness, whose essence is self-awareness; it is not a conceptual construction. || 2 ||

But surely, when a jar is seen in its fully established form, how can a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) that depends upon that perception effect the negation of a non-jar? For the name "non-jar" has not been grasped by anyone, and even the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a non-jar—how could it be awakened when a jar is seen? True; it is so.

The Śākyas alone are to be questioned, and not we, because [the argument] follows the reasoning stated by them; this is the meaning. He says "nor" (*na ca*) in order to state that difference (*bheda*) is also impossible:
for if difference were admitted here, it would be undermined by the impossibility of non-manifestation.
It must be stated that it [the object] exists only together with another manifestation; the sense is that a difference residing within the very nature of the manifestation itself is not tenable.

He explains the meaning of the word *hi* by saying "for" (*hi*). Having clarified that this verse serves as a reason for what precedes—indicated by the word *hi*—he states: "because it is thus. From that—that being so—

"Due to the absence of duality"—that is, due to the absence of the pair known as manifestation and non-manifestation; "in the impossibility of exclusion"—that is, in the impossibility of excluding non-manifestation. "I"—this is the self-reflective awareness established as "I," which is indeed the very act of reflective discernment (*pratyavamarśa*).

It is merely the self-reflection (*parāmarśana*) of one's own nature, which is called the manifestation of that very form; it is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), meaning that there is no exclusion of what is not of that form or what is not manifested. This is the summary here:
by implication, at the time of the manifestation’s own apprehension as "this," it is like the manifestation itself—i.e., like the light of manifestation.

Of another distinct entity—that is, of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) whose nature is non-manifestation—there is no appearance when [the object] such as a jar is grasped, just as there is none of a non-jar;
the particle *tu* indicates a contrast (*vyatireka*). Therefore, because of this, conceptualization (*vikalpatva*) does not exist here.
The word *hi* illuminates the logical connection that since this is so, the reality mentioned in the preceding verse is indeed appropriate.
Now he provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"In that which has a determined form"—that is, one whose nature has reached its finality in its own mere appearance.

Regarding that perception—the one which, depending upon the experience of a jar, leads [the mind] to the state of being an object of expectation—[the opponent asks], "Why is it not produced? To this he says: "Not a non-jar" (*aghaṭa*). The point is that a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is awakened precisely by the perception of something similar;
however, a jar is not similar to a non-jar, but rather is entirely distinct from it. The Teacher gives the reply: "True."
Thus, in this way—
by means of this mere [cognition] which possesses the manifestation of both that and non-that, through the exclusion of what is not that,
this conceptual construction "this is a jar" is said to be the determination of that [object]. (3)

Here, the so-called cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is shown to be distinct from the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), independent within acts of cognition, and the agent by virtue of exercising the power of joining, separating, and so forth; and within that cognizer, there is the manifestation of all objects.

It has also been stated that although [the Self] has pure consciousness alone as its body, it exists through a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [object], according to the analogy of a city reflected in a mirror. And thus, during that state of non-conceptualization, the cognizer experiences— that is, resorts to— both the manifestation of that [object], which is the appearance of a jar, and the manifestation of what is not that [object], which is the appearance of a non-jar.

"This jar is of the nature of consciousness" is the manner [of the statement]. The Buddhist—meaning one who does not accept a supreme self (paramātman) consisting of momentary cognition—is to be questioned—that is, he is to be challenged. To the question "Why is he not to be questioned?", he says: "Because..."

"Thus" means "because it is so. Having thus provided this introduction, he presents and explains the verse—beginning with the words *tadatat*—in order to satisfy the expectancy of the word *yataḥ* established therein.
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

"From the means of valid cognition" (pramāṇāt) means from the instrument of valid cognition whose nature will be explained right here. "In cognitions" (pramāsu) refers to the acts of knowing accomplished by the means of valid cognition. The construction is "the independent one is the agent," and the intended meaning is not that he is the causal agent.
"Establishment" (ādhānam) means accomplishment. "By that" means by that which has pure consciousness as its body.
"By way of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*)": that which has its occurrence as one [with it].

The example "mirror" is given in order to dispel the impossibility of existence suggested by the word "also" (*api*). It "exists"—it manifests as distinct from that [the mirror], because it appears in such a manner.

The state [of being]. "It has been said" means "not within," as stated in that context. To the question "But what follows from that?", he says "And thus. He explains and analyzes the compound word *tadatat* by breaking it down as "that" (*tat*). By the word "serves" (*sevate*), it is indicated that the suffix *kvip* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). "To that extent," in this regard, for anyone...

The meaning is that there is no misconception. In that state free from conceptual construction (*avikalpadaśā*), its nature is consciousness; according to the principle "the object is as it was before," it is the very essence of consciousness. The "universe" (*viśva*) is the mass of all existing things; he whose body is this universe is, like consciousness itself, embodied by the universe (*viśvaśarīra*) and is thus complete. Furthermore, there is no worldly transaction whatsoever with it, nor [are there any...]

Regarding conventional transactions (*vyavahāra*): by manifesting the operation of *māyā*, [consciousness] fragments even that which is full; through this, the exclusion (*apohana*) of what is not a jar—such as cloth and so forth—is performed in the form of negation.
It is precisely by relying on that very exclusion that the ascertainment of that jar is expressed as "it is indeed a jar."

For this very reason, since the object consists in the negation of other possible things, this alone constitutes "delimitation" (*pariccheda*), which is like carving by cutting away from all sides; for this reason—since it is so—it is logical that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) implies a pair. Thus, what was stated in the preceding verse—that "therefore it is logical that conceptual construction implies a pair"—is established.
Thus, the two reasons for the two matters mentioned in the preceding verse are stated in sequence by means of these two verses: [K. Ṣ. Ṣ.

because the two reasons for the two matters are stated in sequence, since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone is thus complete, therefore—by means of a jar whose body is the universe—no worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) whatsoever exists.

The meaning is that because [reality] manifests as a mixture, no worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is possible. If one asks, "In that case, how can there be such a transaction by means of it?", he says: "That" (*tat*). "The operation of *māyā*" refers to the activity belonging to the principle of *māyā* (*māyātattva*), which consists of differentiation. "The object" (*bhāva*) refers to the form of a jar; by means of that—

Through the manifestation of the activity of *māyā*, there occurs the exclusion (*apohana*)—that is, the negation—from one's own self, which consists of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), and from the cloth and so forth, which are non-pots contained within it. Of what nature is this? It is of the nature of negation—that is, the act of negating—and of determination, by means of preventing confusion.

This means "establishing [the object] in its own self alone. Now, one might ask: how is negation understood here, since only this much—"this is indeed a jar"—is manifesting there? To this he says: "ghaṭa eva" (it is a jar *alone*). This refers to the sense of the particle "eva," meaning the sense of the word "eva. "Another thing" (*aparavastu*) refers to an entity that is not of the nature of a jar. For [the particle] expresses restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
The sense is that, as a result, it is simply the negation of others. Now, if one asks, "In that case, what is called 'delimitation' (pariccheda)? he says:
"This very [thing]"—that is, *apoha* itself. "Completely" (*paritaḥ*) means on all sides, that is to say, from other subjects of cognition and from one another.
He explains "because of cutting" (*chedanāt*) himself by saying "because of carving" (*takṣaṇāt*), meaning because of appearing through differentiation.

Up to the point where he says "hi" in order to express the intended meaning of the word; here, the word *iti* is intended to refer back to the very form of the word itself. Since—meaning because—the matter stated in this verse exists, therefore—meaning from that—it is logical that there is a "rejection of duality."
The dual-exclusionary nature of conceptual construction, as stated in the second half of the first verse, becomes logically established.
Now, if it is argued that by this [verse] the status of being a reason (*hetutva*) is stated with respect to dual-exclusion, then [what of] the two [reasons] stated in the preceding verse?

Therefore, "I am" is pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); this is the meaning of the great statement (*mahāvākyārtha*) expressed in the three verses. Even by the Śākyas, this activity of the cognizer alone has been stated in the passage: "There is one [activity] called reflective awareness," where the term refers to the subject (*prapattā*).

To the question "What has been established?", he says: "By the former [half]," etc. By the two entities—namely, the two entities expressed by the first and second halves [of the verse]—the two reasons are stated in sequence. Therein, by the first half of the second verse, that which was stated in the first verse—that it is not... [is negated].

The state of being a cause for "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) has been stated; however, regarding the subsequent [cognition], its status as a cause for "reflective awareness" (*pratyavamarśa*) has been stated in that very same context.

Although there is no use of the word "only" (*eva*) immediately after the term "reflective awareness" in that passage, this was stated by relying on the logical principle that every sentence carries an implicit restriction (*sāvadhāraṇa*).
He explains the meaning of this verse, which is interconnected through its structural composition, with the words "yasmād evam" ("because it is thus").

Because the reality implied by these three words exists, for that reason, "aham" (I)—this very reality—is "pure awareness" (*vimarśa*); that is to say, it is nothing other than awareness itself. It is not...

"Conceptual construction" (vikalpa) means that every conceptual construction is mixed with the imagination of duality; thus—in this way—the "meaning of the great sentence" (mahāvākyārtha), which is the meaning of the supreme sentence containing within it a collection of intermediate sentences, is established in these three verses—that is, in the triad of verses. And here is this:

The division: In response to the expectation—"Why is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) not mentioned in the first verse?"—the statement beginning with "for that has been stated" provides the reason. Granted that conceptual construction implies a duality, what does that have to do with the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), which consists solely in the form of reflective awareness?

Regarding the requirement for the negation of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpatā*), there is a statement of two reasons—one pertaining to the first half [of the verse] and one to the second half—by means of a single indicator of reason (*hetudyotaka*). Among these, the reason for the negation of conceptual differentiation is stated by the first half; for where a duality exists, it is precisely there that conceptual differentiation occurs.

Just as in the case of the reflection on a jar, here it is not so; this is by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). However, regarding the state of having a single nature consisting of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) through the second half [of the verse], since the apprehension of duality is possible there, it follows that here there is only the state of reflective awareness itself; this is by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Here too, in the first half, how...?

Since it is necessary to establish that the apprehension of two [entities] is possible here, the third verse provides a justification by way of stating the reason (*hetu*). However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it is clearly the very subject matter mentioned in the first verse that is being proven; thus, the three verses possess a coherent meaning. Now, as for the Śākyas...

Since they do not tolerate this, he says, "even by the Śākyas. Regarding those who say, "This is the activity" and "by [the Buddha] himself," let us leave aside for now the question of how that [activity] could possibly be justified by them. || 3 ||

Now, one might ask: "In this case, why would even the reflective awareness 'I' not be of the nature of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since it involves the exclusion (*apoha*) of its counter-correlate—the jar and so forth—which are non-I by nature?
With this intention, he says: "That which, having abandoned the true essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) through *māyā*, appears as if distinct..."
Whether in the body, in the intellect, or in the vital breath, it is imagined as if in the sky.

The operation called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). By what kind of Śākyas? By those who, in this verse, speak—meaning declare—the words "the one who attains" (*prapattā*) and "himself" (*svayam*). The sense is that by these two words alone, they have stated that this very meaning is an operation of the subject (*pramātṛ-vyāpāratva*). Likewise...
And this is the verse:
"The single cognition, known as reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa), being established in one place,
itself distinguishes between entities that possess that nature and those that do not."

Thus [it is said]. Herein is the meaning: for (hi) — because in a single cognition—that is, in a single moment of cognition—there exists a single operation called "reflective awareness" (*pratyavamarśa*), which is its name, such being the subject under discussion; therefore, for that reason, the cognizer (*pramātā*) perceives entities (*bhāvān*) as having both that nature and a nature other than that.

He himself analyzes the categories (*padārtha*), that is to say, the moments of existence (*bhāvakṣaṇa*) as they abide in their own time; he subjects them to the process of division by means of both what is to be determined (*niśceya*) and what is to be excluded (*apohya*). In this regard, those things possessing that [specific] nature are established by way of being determined, while those not possessing that nature are excluded. And here, by the term "understanding" (*prapatti*),...

Regarding the statement of the knower: by the word "himself" (*svayam*), it is clearly established that the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)—which consists of differentiation—is related to him, and that differentiation itself is reflective awareness;
thus, it is rightly said that [the act] is both "attainment" (*prapatti*) and "himself. Now, one might object: in that case, would this not also apply to the Buddhist (*Śākya*) view?

Since it would follow that [the Buddhist position] is identical to the Śaiva system, he says "that" (saḥ). That—namely, reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)—how could it be "justified" (*samarthya*) by these Buddhists?
The sense is that it cannot be justified because they do not accept the permanence of the subject (*pramātṛ*), which is what would justify it. But [one might object]: nanu...

To the objection that "in that case, the burden [of proof] must be placed here," he says: "Thus, thus. Let this matter rest; the sense is that it is unfit for further elaboration because it is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta*). This is the summary here:
for—since—by means of the manifestation of "that" and "not-that," through the state of having the entire mass of objects internalized within oneself...
For one who relies on the cognition of "pot" and "non-pot," etc., by the cognizer (*mātrā*) alone— due to the exclusion of what is not that (*atadvyapohanāt*),
namely, the exclusion of the non-pot— the determination of that (*tanniścayanam*), i.e., the determination of the pot,
is called a "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) such as "this is a pot" by the learned ones acting as agents; therefore, there is the apprehension of a duality here.
The sense is that it is indeed possible because of the occurrence of the aforementioned thing; "mātrā" is used in the instrumental case (tṛtīyā) with the sense of the agent. || 3 ||
The reflective awareness "I" as the subject arises from the exclusion of others;
it is indeed a conceptual construction (vikalpa) produced by the manifestation of its opposite. (5)

The reflective awareness of "I" is twofold: pure and māyic. Among these, the pure is that which occurs in pure consciousness—non-different from the universe—or in the Self which is transparent yet suffused with the reflection of the universe. The impure, however, occurs in the form of the object of knowledge.

Regarding the body and so forth: in that case, within the pure reflective awareness of "I," no counter-correlative whatsoever exists that could be excluded, even in the case of a jar or other objects.
Now, he provides the introduction to the fourth and fifth verses with the words: "But if this is so... (nanvevam).
The commentary on this point is as follows:

"Of the counter-correlate" (*pratiyoginaḥ*) means with the intention that it is an adversary by virtue of being opposed (*viruddhatvena*); that is to say, it means "with this very intention in mind. (Note: *prati asya vibhūtasya* is a variant reading for *pratiyoginaḥ*.)
Having thus provided the introduction and presented two verses, he explains them. Regarding the phrase "the essence of consciousness" (*cittattva*), the commentary states:
he establishes the methodological framework (*prakriyā*) in order to state the intended meaning of the two verses, beginning with the word "I" (*aham*).

Having divided the two-fold nature, he says "pure" (*śuddha*). Therein, he describes the pure object as "consciousness" (*saṃvit*). By the suffix *-mātra*, the coloring by the object of cognition is excluded. By this, the *śivatattva* (the principle of Śiva) is grasped.
Furthermore, Sadāśiva and the others, who are the objects of both pure and impure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), are also included here through their collective inclusion.

He explains the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) with the words "the shadow of the universe" (*viśvacchāyā*). The "shadow" (*chāyā*)—meaning the reflection—of the "universe" (*viśvasya*), that is, of the mass of objects of knowledge (*vedyarāśi*) capable of being grasped as "this-ness" (*idantā*); by that [reflection], he is "smeared"—that is, slightly colored—[and this occurs] in that "pure self" (*acchātmā*), which is the Self in the form of Śrī Sadāśiva and others. Although for this purpose...

Although it would have been appropriate to discuss even the "pure-impure" (śuddhāśuddha) reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it has not been done here for fear of prolixity; however, he will provide an indication of it as a specific variety of the "pure" (*śuddha*) in the introduction to the following verse. He states the object of the "impure" (*aśuddha*) as "the knowable" (*vedya*); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other such factors are included.
In that context, the phrase "there" (*tatra*) precludes the notion that the pure [consciousness] has the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

"There" means in the midst of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of both the pure and the impure. "Counter-correlative" (*pratiyogī*) refers to that which rivals by virtue of being on an equal footing. "By way of not being a counter-correlative" (*apratiyogitvena*) has the same meaning as "as before" (*prāgiva*).

This is due to the absence of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) resulting from the nature of manifestation as attained through right means (*nyāya*). By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that since the bodies and other subjects (*pramātṛ*) here possess the essence of manifestation, they lack counter-correlativity and thus cannot be excluded; therefore, in the absence of anything to be excluded (*apohya*).

[In the absence of being something to be excluded (apohya) – K. ṣ. ṣ. how could there be the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) therein? However, when it exists as an impure object of knowledge (*vedyarūpa*)—such as the body and so forth—by means of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) from other bodies or from objects like a jar, it is indeed a conceptual construction; this is the meaning of the sentence. As for the literal meaning of the words: the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) is of the nature of pure luminosity (*prakāśamātra*).

Having cast aside even that which exists by way of dismissal, and having rendered secondary the notion "I am indeed the body and so forth" regarding the differentiated body and other such things—due to the conceit "I am the knower with respect to objects of knowledge such as blue"—the reflective awareness "I am gross" and so forth is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and not pure reflective awareness alone. The reason for this is: "the supreme..."

It has been indicated that [it] does not exist. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Thus" (*iti*). This means: "In the absence of an object to be excluded (*āpohya*)," that is, such being the case when there is no object to be excluded. There—in pure luminosity. He establishes that the impure is of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) with the words: "But the impure... [and so on]. Among cognizers (*pramātṛ*), mutually...

Intending to show that [the object] is established as being subject to exclusion (*apohya*), he says "of the body and so forth. With reference to the object of cognition (*prameya*), he says "and of the jar and so forth. "By way of exclusion" means by way of *apoha*. "The meaning of the sentence" refers to the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
He announces the explanation of the word-meanings with the words "the literal meaning."

The word "syllable" (*akṣara*) is employed with the intention of explaining the meaning of even the individual words by way of their constituent parts. The particle *tu* [is used] in the sense of "as for" (*yathā*) and in the sense of distinction (*vyatireka*). He explains the term "consciousness-principle" (*cittattva*) as "mere luminosity" (*prakāśamātra*). In that context, the word *cit* is explained by the phrase "mere luminosity."

By the word *rūpa*, however, [the author] explains the word *tattva* through the term *hitvā* ("having abandoned"), meaning "even though it exists. This abandonment refers to the concealment (*apahastanayā*) produced by *māyā*, which will be described later. "Having rendered subordinate" means having contemplated [it] as a property of the imagined subject (*kalpitapramātṛdharman*), for [the self] is indeed grounded in the body and so forth.

Knowledge is conceived as a quality belonging solely to the body and so forth. "Distinct" means mutually distinct from one another and on an equal footing with objects such as jars; that is to say, they exist as correlates (*pratiyogitayā*).
By the conceit "I alone [am this]"—by such a form of conceit—with regard to the object of cognition (*prameya*) such as blue and so forth.
The meaning is that the knower (*pramātṛ*) exists as a knower. Regarding the phrase "gross" (*sthūla*) and so forth:

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), expressions such as "I am possessed by thirst" are included. Stating the reason for this, he provides the introduction to the fourth quarter of the second verse with the word "here" (*atra*). [This refers to] the second verse.
He explains the fourth quarter [of the verse] with the word "para" (the other). He explains the constituent part "para" as "the second.

He explains the term "pratiyogin" (counter-correlative) as "equal. To establish the status of being a counter-correlative, he establishes their mutual opposition with the words "anyonya" (mutually). Mutual exclusion (*anyonya-parihāra*) means existing through the exclusion of one another.

The second [type of opposition] is that which consists of the appearance— characterized by superimposition— of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) such as the body or a jar, which is of equal status and contradictory due to mutual exclusion;
because of this, that reflective awareness "I" is sustained by the negation of that [counter-correlate].

[Animated by that negation—K. Ṣ. Ṣ. the thought arises: "I am born, I am stout, not thin, and not a jar or the like"; indeed, the very casting aside of the nature of pure light is the cause of the differentiation of the body and so forth. But when that [nature] is cast aside, [there remains] the Supreme Lord.
Because [the Lord] possesses sovereignty with respect to that which consists of error— the non-manifestation of non-duality, which takes the form of the desire to conceal one's own nature—
he explains the component "manifestation" (avabhāsa) as "superimposition" (samāropaṇa).
The meaning is that it is a cognition consisting of the superimposition of one thing upon another.

He provides the analysis of the word *avabhāsa* as ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) with the words "from that" (*tasmāt*). "Sustained by the negation of that which is not it" (*atanniṣedhānuprāṇita*) means raised or brought forth by the negation of that which is not it; this refers to the root *jan*, which takes the suffix *ḍu*.

He states the meaning of this [verse] with the words "born" (*jātaḥ*). By this, its status as a qualification containing a reason (*hetugarbha-viśeṣaṇa*) is indicated. Following this conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*), he shows [the self] with the word "I" (*aham*). This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. Although explained in general terms, the second half of the first verse—beginning with "in the body," "in the intellect," and so on—[is now to be considered].
He establishes the method [of exposition] in order to explain it specifically, beginning with the word "pure" (*śuddha*).
The expression "of that which has the nature of pure light" (*śuddhaprakāśarūpasya*) is a designation emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*);
therefore, the meaning is "of the state of having the nature of pure light. By the very act of casting aside—[that which is] produced by *māyā*—...
It is merely a concealment. Regarding the phrase "of the body and so forth" (*dehādeḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other such factors.

"The cause of differentiation" (*bhedahetuḥ*) means the cause of division. The word "only" (*eva*) implies that there is nothing else. The sense is this: the body and other such things manifest as distinct from the supreme light precisely because of their insentience (*jāḍya*). Now, [an objection]:
To the question of what the cause of that dismissal is, he says: "In its dismissal. The particle *tu* indicates a contrast.
In its dismissal—that is, in the dismissal of the nature of luminosity—the power of *māyā* becomes the cause for the Supreme Lord, the Great Lord endowed with supreme sovereignty.

What is the nature of the power of *māyā*? It is that whose form is the very desire for that which is the concealment of one’s own self—which is of the nature of light—such that it is instead perceived by limited subjects as being a dull body and so forth; it does not exist as something external and primary like the principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth.
The state [of being]. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is of the form of delusion—it does not exist as ultimate reality;
the cause is the power of *māyā*, which fails to manifest non-duality, and the casting aside of the nature of consciousness [is attributed] solely to the body and so forth.

For one who has not abandoned the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedya*), the conceit of being a knower (*pramātṛtābhimāna*) arises precisely because of the lack of logical justification for anything distinct [from that object]. Thus, the Cārvākas, remaining on the level of the conceit of the body, hold that the person (*puruṣa*) is the body characterized by consciousness; they [regard] the body alone [as such].

It consists of absolute independence (*svātantrya*), that is to say, sovereignty. Now, one might ask: why is this called a rejection of pure light? To this he says: "of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpasya*).
By being devoid of justification—that is, by the absence of logical proof—the conceit of being a subject (*pramātṛtvābhimāna*)—namely, "I..."

The conceit "I am the knower" (pramātā) [is the ego]. Although, in ultimate reality, this conceit belongs only to the aspect of light (prakāśāṃśa) as delimited by that [body], it is nevertheless stated thus with reference to the non-manifestation of that [light] caused by [the sense of] difference.
Here, he begins the justification by resorting to different philosophical views, saying "and so," and [describing the conceit] as consisting of the identification with the body.

Regarding the levels— the stages— those who abide on the level of identification with the body are the Cārvākas, or Lokāyatikas; for them, the "body alone"— meaning the physical body composed of the five elements— is, primarily— that is, as the principal thing— the locus of repose, insofar as it is regarded as the nature of the Supreme Self.

To what extent? How so? Why is this so? Because it is characterized by consciousness—that is, the body is endowed with consciousness by virtue of being composed of the five elements whose consciousness has been acquired through the power of conjunction, according to the analogy of the intoxicating power of liquor contained within the earth.
The person (puruṣa) is the self (ātman). And thus says the Śruti: "This very person consists of the essence of food" (annarasamaya).
However, there is no other transmigrating being within this [body], distinct from it, as is asserted by the Mīmāṃsakas and others.
"Kāyī" means "one who possesses a body. Thus, one should exert effort solely for the sake of the body itself;
however, out of fear of the next world, one should not inflict suffering upon the body through asceticism and the like. As it has been said:
"One should live happily as long as life lasts; death is never outside the realm of possibility."
For one who has been reduced to ashes and is at peace, how can there be a return?

Thus they say, and so forth. Indeed, from the statement, "This is the livelihood for those devoid of wisdom and manly effort," it is known that this doctrine was indeed spoken by Bṛhaspati himself; for this same view is found even in the Veda.

Validity is thus observed, and so too is the Śruti: "After death, there is no consciousness. By this, the non-existence of the next world is effectively stated; for if consciousness were impossible for one who has died, [there could be no such statement].
The next world is established [only] in this way, not otherwise; so why do they all say that this doctrine is entirely flawed?
True. First of all, others say that this doctrine arose for the sake of encouraging the conduct of sinners in the Kali age, but that does not convince our minds.

Since this is our firm conviction: worldly people, being devoted solely to external objects useful for the body, even cause the body itself to suffer for the sake of procuring those things, such as by enduring beatings and other hardships for the purpose of acquiring wealth. [Objection: But they endure those hardships only for the sake of the body; [Reply: True. Having brought that wealth—

It is understood that, through worldly renown, they expend their resources on mere objects rather than achieving true enjoyment; thus, even this body of theirs has fallen into oblivion. Consequently, being devoted solely to various material things and nurturing the delusion of self-identity in these very objects by means of excessive possessiveness, they act as follows:

They would understand the body itself, which exists as internal to them, as the Self; and being properly established therein, they gradually enter even further within. Thus, even the Cārvāka system is dedicated solely to the benefit of others, for otherwise it could not be considered a philosophical system (*darśana*) at all. Indeed, all philosophical systems...

They strengthen various stages solely for the sake of helping others; otherwise, it would be improper for those who perceive the supreme state to rest in an intermediate stage. Now, others say that they have not entered that state but are merely stuck at an intermediate level. This is true, insofar as ordinary people [perceive them thus].

That those who have attained [the state] have not yet reached the vision [of the Guru] there is an impossibility. Just as it is not reasonable to say that a king, while building houses and such along the way for the sake of travelers, has rested right there—since his own excellent home remains elsewhere—so it is here as well; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

In that regard, even among the objects of possessiveness (*mamatā*), possessiveness toward one's son is the most intense; for it is heard in the Veda that "the self, indeed, is born as the son," and for the sake of a son, a person will undoubtedly expend wealth and other resources. In this matter:

His engagement in such a manner is due solely to love; otherwise, it would be according to worldly convention. Furthermore, love itself, upon attaining inwardness, takes the form of the Supreme Self because its essential nature is bliss. As it has been said:
"Love alone is the supreme Brahman."

They say that this is primarily due to the conceit of women, children, and the ignorant; even more so for those possessed of discernment (*viveka*), who— on the basis of the production and transformation resulting from cooking (*pākaja*) and other such factors— consider the body to be unstable, and [who realize] that it cannot exist without the presiding presence of the vital force (*prāṇa-śakti*).

Observing the body to be subject to hundreds of transformations, some who are learned in the Upaniṣads consider the vital breath (prāṇa) alone to be the self, as it is that which is capable of experiencing hunger and thirst. Even more than those, others possessing superior discernment [regard] the vital breath as well...

Not perceiving that, because it is impermanent, it is unfit for reconnection, they regard it as the substratum of knowledge, pleasure, and so forth. Furthermore, when the treatises state that affection (*sneha*) is indeed passion (*rāga*), this is only because it functions toward improper objects, not by its very nature. And therefore—

If those possessed of attachment to wealth and the like are indeed utterly deluded, then those possessed of attachment to their sons, while being devoid of attachment to the body, are likewise [deluded]. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this love is nothing but auspiciousness (*śiva*) to the extent that it becomes directed toward an internal object; for the attainment of the supreme culmination of love is itself the state of supreme bliss, and that alone is [the goal].
It is the attainment of the Supreme Self. However, one who is entirely devoid of affection is simply unfit for instruction in this matter.
Furthermore, total absence of affection is impossible anywhere; rather, it is the affection directed solely toward the Supreme Reality that is designated as "non-affection" (asneha).

This same intention should be applied to the position of all other disputants; one need not exert effort again and again, so enough with this elaboration. Let us return to the subject at hand. Therefore, he states the view of the distinguished Cārvāka as "women and children," etc., [meaning] because of such conceit—that is, because of the conceit that the body is the self—even though this is their [position].

Although it does not exist in that way [as a distinct entity], it is nevertheless described as existing by virtue of its established status through its lack of clarity. For this reason, they are more discerning even than those Cārvākas; the implication is that this certainty is not within the scope of women, children, and the like. Regarding "those produced by cooking" (pākajānām):

By the force of that [argument] regarding the production, transformation, and so forth of color and other qualities— whether they arise from the baking of a pot as asserted by logicians or from the baking of individual atoms according to different views—
they understood, perceiving the body to be unstable.

That which is the substratum of the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*)— its internal abiding as the impeller— by means of that, there is the "possession by hundreds of transformations," that is, being seized by hundreds of transformations such as paralysis and so forth. According to the Vedāntins (those who know the Upanishads), this is indicated by implication (*lakṣaṇayā*) as "another inner self consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*).

The Cārvākas, who are devoted to such Vedic statements as these, believe that they alone know [the truth], yet the sense is that this is not possible. "Fitness for synthesis" (*anusandhānayogyatām*) means fitness for the application of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the essence of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). And here, regarding the vital breath...

The followers of Kaṇāda and others declare that the intellect (*buddhi*) itself is the self (*ātman*). Others, however, considering even that [intellect] to be inferior because it becomes an object of cognition during the state of yoga, maintain that the self is a form prior to being cognized— one that is not of any specific nature,
which is devoid of the entire aggregate of objects of cognition, and which, due to its emptiness, is like the sky.

However, that which has the nature of the space of the great elements (mahābhūta) is twofold, distinguished by its grossness and subtlety. Among these, the first variety exists only above the body, while the second exists above the intellect (buddhi).

The instruction regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is situated sometimes immediately after the void and sometimes immediately after the body, does not entail any contradiction between what precedes and what follows. "Intellect alone" means the very principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) in the form of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"Beginning with the followers of Kaṇāda," etc.
By the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), the Naiyāyikas, the Buddhist Vijñānavādins, and others are included; as it has been said by them:
"The self consists of consciousness" (*ātmā vijñānamayaḥ*). Although they assert that the selfhood belongs to that which is endowed with the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*), nevertheless—

This was stated by relying on the non-difference between the action and the agent. He states the view of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) with the words "others, however" (*apare tu*). "Others" refers to the [opposing] authors. "Of that too"—that is, even of the intellect (*buddhi*). "In the state of yoga"—that is, in the condition of a yogi. For the yogi, having entered within, perceives even the intellect just like the body. Because of the absence of an object of cognition (*vedya*), it...

Considering [the other] to be deficient (*nyūnatva*), they call that reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*)—which is, in effect, the Self—“the Full” (*pūrṇa*). Of what nature is it? It is free from whatever aggregate of objects is to be known (*vedya-rāśi*), because it is the knower (*vedaka*) with respect to them; otherwise, its status as a subject would be impossible. And likewise...

Because it is empty, it is equal to the sky and similar to space; however, its nature is not that of the elemental ether (*mahābhūtākāśa*), for the Buddhist proponents of emptiness accept that as being the self (*ātman*). What is that? It is the stage of the unperceivable.
It is "unperceivable," meaning its very nature (*svarūpa*) is such that it is not "anything" (*kiñcid-rūpa*);

because of its extreme subtlety, it cannot be grasped, and because it is beyond limitation, it does not become "nothing. Yet, it does not become a worldly non-existence (*abhāva*), for that would entail the impossibility of its manifestation as the world.
As it has been said:
"That which is called 'the non-empty' is emptiness, and emptiness is said to be non-existence. That is taught to be non-existence wherein all phenomena have come to an end."

Thus it is said: likewise, that which is empty yet as if non-empty is the principle of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*)—[the principle of the subject whose nature is like the ether of the great elements—K. ṣ. ṣ].

The proponents of Brahman, such as the Sāṃkhyas and others, say that [the world] is empty. Yet even in that object of knowledge (*vedya*), there is another emptiness, and in that too another emptiness—thus, as long as there is differentiation, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) does not cease. For this reason, he says "in the imagined" (*kalpite*). It is not [the case that it ceases].
"And because there is no infinite regress by the power of the manifestation of ultimate reality.

This, in this context, is precisely the *śuddhavidyā-tattva* (the principle of Pure Knowledge) within the venerable Śaiva system. For it is here that the Vedāntins and others find their final resting place; their highest excellence is the state of Sadāśiva. [The following] is the elaboration of the phrase "others":
"Who says it is empty?

refers to the proponents of the doctrine of an empty Brahman—the Vedāntins who are established in the reality of Brahman known as pure consciousness devoid of the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti), and the Sāṃkhyas—those devoted to the Sāṃkhya scriptures; by the word "and so forth," the Pātañjalas are included.
In this regard, those who propound Brahman find rest in non-duality (advaita), whereas the Sāṃkhyas and others find it only in duality (dvaita).

Furthermore, the non-duality of the proponents of Brahman is merely a semblance of non-duality (advaitābhāsa), because they describe that which is transcendent of the universe as being everything. For true non-duality is that which constitutes the nature of ultimate reality (paramārtha).

Wherein everything remains exactly as it is, yet appears as a unity, and wherein duality and non-duality are both internalized—let this digression rest here. We shall now follow the main subject. He states the intended meaning of the word "kalpite" (imagined) with the words "tasmin": "even in that"—that is, even in the body and so forth—which is the object of cognition (*vedya*).

Since its state as an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) cannot be removed due to its limited nature, even though it is a knower (*vedaka*) with respect to that which is external to itself, it remains endowed with the quality called "objectivity" (*vedyatva*) with respect to that which is internal to itself. Thus, it does not require another subject ending in "void" (*śūnya*)—that is, another subject whose form is "nothing at all"—as is understood from the context; and for the same logical reason, it likewise does not require another void.

Thus—in this manner, as long as there is differentiation—that is, as long as differentiation caused by the acceptance of a limited knower persists, so long does conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) not cease. Therefore, for that purpose—for the sake of severing conceptual construction—he says, "in the conceptualized" (*kalpite*); the meaning is that this word [is used] for the very purpose of severing conceptual construction. This is precisely for the purpose of severing conceptual construction.
