The sense is that since the manifold expansion of the subject (*pramātṛ-prapañca*) has already been accomplished, there is no further need for conceptualization (*kalpanā*).

By this, it is indicated that the term "in the sky" (*nabhasi*) alone is qualified by "conceptualized" (*kalpite*), and not the body and so forth; for these appear clearly as existing externally to the ignorant person, whereas that [sky] is being conceptualized through a reflection. Now, one might object:
Nevertheless, an infinite regress would indeed result; therefore, he says "and not" (*na ca*). Why is there no infinite regress?

To this he says "in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthe*). This is the intended meaning: since it is light itself that performs the act of grasping by means of the body and so forth, their status as graspers is established solely through its power.
The light belongs to all, yet it does not arise from the body and so forth; rather, the notion that "the body and so forth" constitute the subject (*pramātṛ*) is a mere conceit of identity.
The reality of consciousness (*cittattva*), which consists solely of contraction, is the void (*śūnya*), just as the ground is the absence of a jar.

But the very *cit-tattva* (the principle of consciousness), when permeated by the shadow of the limited object of knowledge (*saṃkoca-aparavedyāṃśa-cchāyā*)— that is, permeated by the shadow of the portion consisting of the non-object of knowledge— is [perceived as] the intellect (*buddhi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the body, and so forth.
These indeed are the stages (*bhūmi*).

And in that regard, because the body and so forth appear clearly to the ignorant person as external, they are merely imagined for the purpose of shattering the conceptual construction of this very single reality of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*). This is because the one to be instructed is, for the time being,
unacquainted with the manifestation of ultimate reality, and because he lacks the qualification for such a discourse on that [ultimate reality] at this stage.

In the place of supreme illumination (*paraprakāśa*), the consecration of this very [consciousness] is bestowed for the sake of the lower person, just as a royal servant is appointed to a royal station. But once established therein, he will certainly come to know that nature of supreme illumination by himself through the attainment of fitness; so enough with further elaboration. By this, the essential point is established:
He says, "So be it. But even so—meaning, that being the case—the body becomes the subject (*pramātā*);

this is merely a matter of conceit (*abhimāna-mātra*) and not an actual reality. Anticipating the student's doubt as to how the sky can logically possess subjectivity, he says, "Contraction" (*saṅkoca*).
"Merely contracted"—meaning merely its own non-expansion, not the attainment of non-existence as its nature—such is the *cit-tattva*, the essential nature of consciousness, which becomes "void.
The sense is that it is like the orb of the earth fallen from the solar disc, such that the light has not yet reached it. In this regard:

He states "the ground" (*bhūtalam*) as a clear illustration. Just as the ground, which is essentially nothing more than a contraction [of space], becomes the absence of a jar—since even logicians describe the ground untouched by a jar as being the "absence of a jar"—[one might ask: "But how is it possible for this [ground] to have the nature of a body and so forth? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "upon contraction" (*saṅkocopari*): upon contraction— meaning on the surface of the aforementioned contraction—

is that *cit-tattva* (the principle of consciousness) which is permeated— that is, pervaded— by the shadow of the objective portion, which is the reflection of imagined external and internal objects of cognition.

The nature of consciousness becomes the intellect (*buddhi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the shadow (*chāyā*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is intended.

That these—the body and the rest—constitute the various stages (*bhūmikā*) is proclaimed in various scriptures; and [the author] explains their different names and so on with the words "these very ones" (*amo eva*). These very ones—the body and the rest—in successive order (*uttarottaram*), that is, step by step.
By attaining nourishment through yoga, for those ascending—

meaning for yogins who ascend higher and higher through each successive stage by bringing each preceding state to the condition of being an object of knowledge— the specific states such as waking and so forth, or "stationed in the body" (piṇḍastha) and so forth, [arise].
And it is stated in the Āgamas, and its dismissal will be explained [as follows]:
"This very principle of consciousness (cittattva), consisting of agency, is intensified by *kalā*;
it exists as a limited quality of the insentient [principles] such as *śūnya*."

For those yogis who have resorted to [the Self] as their own essential nature— namely, persons endowed with the yoga known as the "Discrimination of the Principles of the Sheaths" (kośatattvaviveka)— there are specific stages (bhūmikās). Likewise, in the various scriptures (āgamas), that is, in the diverse teachings of the venerable Śiva, [these are categorized] by way of the waking state and so forth.

They are spoken of—described—by Śrī Śiva as being, on the one hand, the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turya) which are supramundane; and likewise, by way of the stages beginning with *piṇḍastha*—namely, the states of *piṇḍastha*, *padastha*, *rūpastha*, and *rūpātīta*.
Among these, the state of waking belongs to the embodied subject (*dehapramātṛ*) because of the grasping of external objects through the senses; and here, "ascent" (*āroha*) refers to...

This is to be understood in comparison with external impurity. When this very [impurity] reaches a state of being immeasurable (*aparimita*), it constitutes Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) because action (*kriyā*) predominates. For the cognizer who is the intellect (*buddhi-pramātṛ*), it is the state of dreaming, due to the grasping of objects of knowledge in the form of appearances;

when this very [state] reaches a state of being immeasurable, it is the state of Īśvara. For the cognizer who is the vital breath (*prāṇa-pramātṛ*), it is the state of dreamless sleep accompanied by objects of knowledge (*savedyasuṣupti*).

Because it abides in its own limited nature alone, it possesses the quality of being experienced (*savedyatva*), due to the experience of bliss; otherwise, the subsequent reflective awareness, "I slept happily," would be impossible.
However, when it exists in an unlimited state, this very state is the *Sadāśiva-tattva*.

Furthermore, for the subject who perceives emptiness (*śūnyapramātṛ*), there is the state of dreamless sleep (*suṣuptatva*) because he possesses the nature of a limited subject whose form is "nothing at all" (*na kiṃcit*); however, when this [state] becomes unlimited, his very nature is that of Śiva. And therein, once the state of limitation has taken root, the yogi himself gradually...
Gradually, it indeed attains the state of being immeasurable. As it has been said:
"But when one is firmly established in one [point], then by restraining both dissolution and emergence, one attains the status of the enjoyer; thereafter, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel."

Thus [it is said]. For this is the intended meaning here: when the yogi is "established" (*saṃrūḍha*)—that is, firmly situated as the subject—in one limited [entity] such as the body, then he controls even the dissolution and emergence of that very body—which is limited and perceived as a single [object]—by bringing it to the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*), thereby [realizing its] nature as something created by himself.
Knowing [the state of] being well-fashioned (sunirmitatva), he attains the status of an enjoyer— he acquires the capacity for perception even while occupying a limited body and so forth; thereafter,
through the attainment of full nourishment, he becomes the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara).
It would thus consist of the state of being unlimited, wherein the predominance of both difference and non-difference resides in forms such as Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā) and the rest.
Therefore, this remains established: the reflective awareness "I am impure" is nothing but a conceptual construction (vikalpa). || 5 ||
This notion of "I" is twofold, and it is likewise of two kinds;
therein, the states such as waking and so forth are well known. As for the essential nature of the *piṇḍa* and the rest:
the *piṇḍa* is proclaimed to be the power of Kuṇḍalinī, and the *pada* is proclaimed to be the Haṃsa.
Form is said to be the consciousness-drop (cidbindu); beyond form is the supreme Śiva.

This has been determined in such passages as these. And here, "piṇḍa" (the body) refers by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to a specific intestinal coil in the form of a serpent located within the bodily form of the *piṇḍa*; it is the *kuṇḍalinī-śakti*, because the power known as *kuṇḍalinī*—which is the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*)—is contained within that. "Haṃsa" refers to [the mantra] "haṃsa."
Through the utterance of sound, the vital breath [is activated]. As it has been said:
"Twenty-one thousand six hundred times, day and night, the living soul constantly recites this mantra, 'Haṃsa, Haṃsa.'"
Thus, by the word *jīva*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is intended here; and its status as a "foot" (*pada*) is due to its being the substratum of the paths (*adhvan*). As it has been said:
"The path is established in the vital breath.
*Cidbindu*—the point of consciousness—is of the nature of pure awareness (*vijñāna*), and its form consists of droplets of light.

Because it possesses form due to being delimited, "the Supreme Śiva" refers to Anāśrita Śiva; and he is here the Void (*śūnya*), because his state of transcending form is due to his being ungraspable. This was stated without regard for limitation, since Śiva-hood belongs precisely to that which transcends all limited forms; however, in the case of limitation...
"Because [the self] is an empty subject"—enough with this elaboration. Now, one might ask: "What is meant by 'casting aside' (apahastanam)?

To this he says: "And casting aside... Furthermore, one might ask: "Where will this be explained? To this he says: "Shaken forth by *kalā*. The word "iti" marks the end of the verse. Since its commentary will occur in that very place, no effort has been made here.
He summarizes the established point by saying "that": "That"—meaning for that reason—"is established" (*sthitam*).

The "I-reflection" (*aham-avamarśa*), being impure—meaning it is characterized by impurity because its object consists of the body and so forth, which are defiled by the stain known as duality—is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and not the supreme [awareness].
The meaning is that there occurs a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).
Now, he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "dvividho 'pi" (even though it is of two kinds).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:

The phrase "also of two kinds" means that it exists as both pure and impure, thus possessing two modes. The implication is that this being the case, it results in a fourfold nature. In that regard, he first describes the two forms of the pure:

It consists of the nature of mere experience and has the essence of synthesis; it is pure and twofold: as "I" within the Self of Śiva, and as "I-this" within the Self of Sadāśiva. It is also impure, such as "I am gross," or "I who was gross have become thin," and "I am a child, a youth, an old man—that very same I."

The impure [consciousness] is of two kinds. Regarding that, it has been stated that in the case of the pure, the nature of conceptualization is simply non-existent; however, in the case of the impure, which consists of direct experience, the nature of conceptualization has been established. Yet, even in the impure, because non-duality flashes forth by virtue of its being essentially a unifying synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*), there exists a certain degree of non-conceptuality.
To dispel the doubt that there might be delusion in this regard, he says:

"That which is the association of a previous appearance and so forth with an occasional appearance, arising from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), is called conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); and that too occurs when there is a distinct appearance. (Verse 6)

The phrase "in the body" and so forth continues; an occasional manifestation—occurring at some time, with its location, time, and form being indeterminate—is experience (*anubhava*). That which consists of synthesis (*anusandhāna*) is of the nature of conjunction (*yojana*). Even for that which is impure, there is a twofold division.

He says, "I am fat. In this regard—within the midst of the pure and the impure—it has been stated that [this identity] exists even at the moment of direct realization. It has been established—demonstrated immediately following—in the case of non-difference: "I who was fat, I am now thin."

[This refers to] the unity consisting of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth. Of that [unity]—which is seized by doubt—he says "to dispel," meaning to cut away. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "occasional" (*kādācitka*).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides the following:

the group of words beginning with "in the body," "or in the intellect," and "or in the vital breath"—as well as "or in the imagined ether"—is carried over here as well; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the inclusion of] "in the intellect" and so forth is intended.

"Grasping" (grahaṇam) means that it "occurs," i.e., it "continues. He provides the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) and explanation of the compound term "occasional" (*kādācitka*) as a qualifier for the specific object, such as the body and so forth, by saying "occasional" (*kādācitkaḥ*).
Regarding that [body] which consists of its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is that which—by means of a prior appearance—...

Connection (*yojanā*) is the synthesis through the manifestation of bodies such as that of a child, as in the reflective awareness: "I who was a child am now a youth"; by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is also connection with future manifestations yet to come, as in:
"I shall become an old man. All such connection is conceptualization (*kalpanā*), which is nothing but mental construction (*vikalpa*); it is not pure [consciousness].

[This is] the summary reflection (*pratyavamarśa*). Here, the qualification "of the body and so forth" is intended to indicate the reason—namely, that the manifestation of difference (*bhinna-avabhāsitva*) regarding the body and so forth is only occasional even at that time.
He explains this component by saying "occasionally" (*kadācit*). He states what is to be said regarding this as well by saying "fixed" (*niyata*).
"Of the two fixed [factors]" means of those determined by necessity (*niyati*); "whose form" refers to that which has such a nature regarding space and time.

"Manifestation" (*avabhāsa*) means a flashing forth; "of which"—namely, of the subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the body and so forth, whose own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is non-continuous in nature and exists as distinct in each individual instance.

Up to the point where he applies the meaning of the locative case in the word *tatra* ("therein"). The meaning is: "in such [a state] as the body and so forth. He explains the compound *pūrva* and so on with the word *pūrva*. He explains the constituent part *pūrvābhāsa* ("prior appearance") with the word *bāla* ("child"). By the word *ādi* ("and so forth"), the inclusion of the youth-body and other stages is intended. Having thus repeated the construction itself—

"He shows and explains [it] as 'I am'"—to state the object to be grasped by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he says "etcetera. Following the application (*yojanā*), he says "the Elder. Regarding "I shall become"—meaning "I shall become hereafter"—the word "object" (*grāhya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. He explains the word "that" (*sā*) as "application" (*yojanā*). He states the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) as "all" (*sarvā*)."

The word *api* (also/even) signifies totality. He explains the term *kalpanā* (conceptual construction) with the words "conceptual construction. Relying on the logical principle that "every sentence implies a restriction," he employs the word *eva* (only). He himself states what is excluded by the word *eva* with the words "but not" (*na tu*). "Pure" (*śuddha*) means unmixed with conceptual construction; by this—

It is indicated that even conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) possesses the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśatva*). He says "here" (*atra*) in order to explain the compound word "distinct" (*bhinna*) and so forth as a qualification containing a reason (*hetugarbhaviśeṣaṇa*). "Here" means "in the state of being a conceptual construction. "With the intention of [stating] the reason" means for the purpose of indicating the status of being a reason. It is contained within the qualification.

He clarifies the state of being a cause with the words "yataḥ" (since). "As distinct" means by way of exclusion from one another, from their own objects, and from the light of another. "Manifestness" is precisely the state of being a manifestor, and not a vibration as something pervading all things like pure light. At that time—

It is uninterrupted; for if one were to perform the synthesis "I am this" while perceiving that body and so forth as being full in every respect and devoid of limitation, then how could this state be called the level of Sadāśiva, which is the locus of conceptualization? Rather, it is precisely when it is uninterrupted [that this occurs].

That is "synthesis" (*anusaṃdhi*). If it is asked how there can be synthesis even when [the states] are distinct, he says: "due to mental impression" (*saṃskārāt*), which means by virtue of memory arising from the awakening of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) produced by prior experience;
synthesis occurs in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by virtue of its strength or weakness, and in the intellect (*buddhi*) due to the gradations of knowledge, pleasure, and so forth.

In the void (*śūnya*), because of the connection with expansion and non-expansion, this too is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); likewise [it is so] even in the grasping of the state of the subject (*pramātṛ*). The word "even" (*api*) indicates that the logicality of the uninterrupted nature of distinct manifestation [applies] also in the grasping of the state of the object (*prameya*). Now, one might object:
One might argue that since the status of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) cannot otherwise be accounted for, the appearance of difference must indeed be fragmented;

to this he says, "If indeed... The term "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*) is explained as "the state of being devoid of limitation. "Perceiving" refers to the knower who performs the act of seeing; "I am this" means "I myself am the agent of this [act]."

Because it shines as my very own being, one should—meaning one would—perform that; at that time, the state of Sadāśiva, which is the level of the principle called Sādākhya. "As the locus of conceptual construction" means as the substratum of thought-constructs. By whom could it be described?
Since everything is swallowed up within oneself, the meaning is that no one at all would be able to speak of it.
He will state this [later]:
"Sadāśiva is within a blink of an eye.
To the question "Why should it not be said [so]? he replies with the words "yāvatā" (insofar as). That connection—namely, the plane of Sadāśiva—is present here.

The disciple asks: "Even when [the self] is distinct... The sense is that it is not logical for Caitra to have a recollection of being Maitra within himself. The teacher provides the answer, saying: "He says... When there is an expectation as to what he says, he connects the word *saṃskārāt* (from latent impressions) found in the aphorism. This word, *saṃskārāt*,...

"He explains it as 'prior'"—this explanation is based on figurative usage (*upacāra*). Now, one might ask: "Let such an application of meaning apply to the body, but how is it possible in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? To this he says: "In the vital breath.

The underlying connection (*anusandhi*) is that the application of meaning is possible because the vital breath alone is the cause of strength; such is the sense. And that [vital breath] is "I who..."

It should be understood as being of such a nature that "he who was previously weak is now strong. Regarding the phrase "due to the connection with expansion and non-expansion": even when there is a mental synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) of objects such as a jar, thinking "this very jar is gradually becoming expanded while its state as a void-subject remains," this must be considered a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); however—

In these stages of transition (*anusaṃdhāna-bhūmi*), the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) blazes forth with preeminence like a flash of lightning; thus the teachers have accepted that these constitute the primary means for the initial stage of practicing the supreme state (*parapada*). 6.

He becomes Paraśiva; and the sense is that within him, the connection between expansion (*vaitatya*) and intermediate expansion (*avāntaravaitatya*) is indeed possible. Now, one might ask: "How can there be conceptualization (*vikalpatva*) here? To this he says: "This too"—meaning even this synthesis of expansion and non-expansion—even in the case of the recognition of external objects.

He extends [the principle of] conceptualization by saying "in this way. Now, one might ask: "Insofar as conceptualizations concerning the subject such as the body and so forth have, from the perspective of ultimate reality, a single entity as their object, and likewise in the case of the recognition of external objects, how is it appropriate for conceptualization—which has the exclusion of other entities as its very life-breath—to be applicable? In response to this expectation:

He states another alternative with the word "but" (*kintu*). "By way of predominance"—that is, by way of being superior to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—even though there is a manifestation of distinctions between parts such as space and time, because the form manifests as a unity, the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) has emerged from duality but has not yet attained non-duality; it is oriented toward that [non-duality].

Śuddhavidyā, which exists above the Māyātattva—the seed of differentiation—shines like a flash of lightning; the sense is that although the cognition of oneness flashes forth there at that very moment, it is unable to endure for long because the manifestation of the difference of that object from others arises again. And that state...
This is the domain only of the awakened ones who have firmly established the ground of non-duality, not of the unawakened;

for it is not possible for those who have not tasted a piece of sugar to perceive even a fraction of its flavor except through a small amount of sweet substances, and here too, it is only for those who have previously known that flavor.

Because it is capable of clinging to the relish of that [experience], for those who are well-awakened and always endowed with the consciousness of great non-duality (*mahādvaita*) everywhere, there is only indifference (*upekṣā*) toward this; enough of this. On the basis of this, he explains the tradition (*saṃpradāya*) that has come down from the lineage of gurus. "Thus" (*iti*) means: for this reason.

Of these—namely, the yogic unions (*yojanā*) whose objects are the body and so forth as the subject, as well as those whose objects are external things—the "teachers" are those who possess the cultivation of the supreme state, that is, the preeminent station known as Paraśiva;
this cultivation consists in making the perfected state an object of familiar acquaintance, and not a means of attainment. Of that [cultivation]...

"Being the means for the first kalpa" means being the cause for the initial commencement; "they accepted" means they took it upon themselves [to act]. [The thought is: "The supreme state, obtained through various means or by the grace of the Blessed Lord, must be cultivated even during the period of worldly activity (vyutthāna) in precisely such states as these."

Instruction has been imparted by the gurus through tradition to disciples who have attained awakening, but this has not been written extensively in the treatises on ritual procedures (*prakriyā-śāstra*). For, by means of those [treatises], even the deluded, being seized by worldly objects, would abandon the various difficult methods and instead cling to these [procedures] alone, yet they would not attain that [goal].

Furthermore, the body and so forth do not possess the status of being objects of cognition for a preceding subject, such that the object of cognition would not appear in the absence of the subject's manifestation, nor would its manifestation occur without a preceding manifestation,
nor would that [preceding one] occur without the manifestation of another subject— lest there be an infinite regress; rather, there is pure manifestation (*śuddhaprakāśa*).

The intention of the statement "the Gurus" is that they demonstrate that the light of the universe is indeed pure light (*viśuddhaprakāśa*). However, in the ultimate sense, even by resorting to various means and employing diverse methods, nothing whatsoever will be accomplished without the descent of the Lord’s power (*bhagavacchaktipāta*).
In that case, even the process of activity must have that [unmanifested nature] as its effect; enough of this.
Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "na ca" (nor).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"The state of being perceived by preceding subjects belongs to the body and so forth; [this applies] to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the body."

The state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) and the [state of being] the intellect (*buddhi*) in relation to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth, do not exist; the point is that their limitation (*tad-avacchinnatā*) is likewise imagined (*kalpita*). By which—by whatever [means] previously [it was known] as an object of knowledge (*vedyatayā*) in relation to the subject (*pramātṛ*), and by the subject in relation to the Supreme Light (*paraprakāśa*).

In the absence of light—that is, when there is an absence of illumination produced by the cognizing subject consisting of the intellect—of the imagined ether, the object of cognition, known as supreme illumination, does not shine; for that which is not established in itself cannot function toward the establishment of another. And its illumination—that is, the illumination of the cognizing subject consisting of the intellect—[is likewise absent].

Without the prior manifestation—that is, without the manifestation of the subject as vital breath (prāṇapramātṛ)—that too, namely the manifestation of the subject as vital breath, does not occur; and that, in turn, without the manifestation of another subject—that is, without the manifestation of the subject as body (dehapramātṛ)—does not occur. Thus, in this way, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā).

Since even the cognizer of the body would entail the necessity of another cognizer, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) consisting of that [second] one requiring yet another, and that one yet another, and so forth. Nor is there any cognizer beneath the body—like the supreme light above the sky—by virtue of whom such an infinite regress might not occur; this is the sense. And thus:
The sense is that everything would become the absolute sovereignty of total blindness.

To the question "What, then, exists?", he says: "But rather" (*api tu*). The phrase "but rather" indicates a determined alternative position: [it is] pure light alone [that constitutes] the universe—of everything from the sky onwards, including the entire class of subjects existing as both external and internal.

Furthermore, there is the manifestation of the entire class of objects of knowledge—including those residing in space and so forth—because the subjectivity of the prior [subject] does not lose its status as that very subjectivity; for it is not reasonable to say that an effect produced by the space within a house is not produced by the Great Space (the universal ether). This is the intended meaning. Thus, while determining in this manner...

— By virtue of its fitness, that which is the object of ascertainment is shown to be, according to the reasoning stated, eternally inseparable from the powers of emanation and so forth (even the separation from the powers of emanation and so forth, as noted in the KSTS edition), belonging to the Lord; thus he demonstrates:
Thus, even in the realm of empirical transaction, the Lord, entering the body and so forth,
may by His own will manifest externally the multitude of objects that are already shining within.
That which was previously shown regarding the body, the intellect, and so forth, is established in this way; how so?

If, in the sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—the realm of *māyā*—the Lord alone, whose ultimate reality is Light, enters by His will through the power of *māyā*, assuming the nature of the body, vital breath, and so on, with the body and breath as primary, [then that previous teaching is justified].

Manifesting within pure consciousness the multitude of objects that shine in the form of "I," and bringing them forth externally by mere will according to the reasoning previously stated— namely, "always for the amusement of creation"— thus:

Thus, he demonstrates—He makes manifest toward those who are to be graced. Why is this so? Because for the Blessed One—who is endowed with the great power called sovereignty (*svātantrya*) and is the supreme light—there is always an inseparable union with the powers of emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and the rest; and since that has already been shown previously as being of two kinds, it need not be repeated here.
Again, an effort is made. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "tadevam" (thus, therefore).
Herein is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
"Previously"—in the verse beginning with "having abandoned the essence of consciousness through Māyā," this means:
"when the matter about to be explained is present. The word "is established" (*upapadyate*) is supplied as an ellipsis.
Here the disciple asks, "How? meaning, "How is it established? The teacher provides the answer, beginning with "If... (*yadi*)."

He explains the word "in empirical usage" (*vyavahāre*) as "māyā," meaning in the sphere of the *māyā*-principle, which is characterized by differentiation and is fit for empirical usage. In the aphorism, the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth; here, however, the word "etc. includes the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. He explains the word "Lord" (*prabhu*) as "light" (*prakāśa*). Internally...

Thus he explains [the word] "consciousness" (*saṃvit*) as "awareness. He explains [the word] "shining" (*bhāntam*) as "in this manner, 'I'. For when there is internal shining, there is indeed dissolution into the state of "I-ness. As it has been said:
"[The notion] 'I' is distinct..."
It manifests as "this," and therefore this [conclusion] follows; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). The suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

The words *api* and *eva* have been displaced from their original positions; that which has been stated thus far—namely, "that"—is for that reason, "thus arisen" in the form about to be described. What is that? It is that which the Lord [perceives] mutually.

At the time of worldly transaction— such as buying, selling, observing, or explaining— the body, vital breaths, and so forth belonging to Caitra, Maitra, and others enter into a state of unity within that specific transaction (or, according to the variant reading, within that specific manifestation).
It is that which, while existing as nothing other than internalized and with its internal luminosity unabandoned, causes [the object] to appear externally as a single manifestation;
thus, no explanation has been provided for the word *arthaugha*, as it is well known as a term denoting the multitude of objects.

He explains the word "bahiḥ" (externally) as "idam" (this). He provides the commentary on the word "bhāsayet" (should illuminate) as "bhāsayati" (illuminates). "Tataḥ" means for that reason; "etat" refers to the illumination of the multitude of objects. "Anyathā" means in the absence of that immersion; "anavasthā" refers to the infinite regress mentioned in the introduction.

He states the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) with the word "in the sense of cause" (*hetau*). The construction is as follows: because it illuminates the flood of objects, it is known that [it] enters into the body and so forth. The phrase "the two [words] have a different order" means that this is due to their connection with the words "body" (*deha*) and "Lord" (*prabhu*). Furthermore, in order to explain that the optative suffix is used even in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), he says "thus" (*tadevam*).
"Because it effects the clear conjunction of the two words"—this is what was stated immediately prior.
He provides an explanation of that [word] preceded by its introduction with the word "tat" (that), meaning: for that reason, it has arisen in this way;
that is, it is established. Of what nature? Of the form that will be described—by means of the remainder.
[The nature of this] will be described later. The disciple asks, "What is that? meaning, "What is that which has arisen?

To provide the answer here, [the author] explains once again—in brief and preceded by a formal application—the verse that has already been commented upon, beginning with the words "yat" (that which). By the phrase "buying and selling,"...

The apprehension of impure worldly transaction (*malinavyavahāra*) is indicated by [the words] "inspection" (*prekṣā*) and so forth; the apprehension of pure worldly transaction (*śuddhavyavahāra*) is indicated by [the word] "as one" (*ekatayā*), meaning as non-different from oneself (*svābhinnatayā*). This applies to that specific worldly transaction and not to all worldly transactions, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of attaining the Great Duality right here. It is "as one manifestation" (*ekābhāsatayā*), according to its own nature.
The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), meaning that it is not possible for [the object] to appear as a thing such as a jar;
thus, at this time, unity with one particular subject is created, while unity with another subject is withdrawn.

When a state of persistence is established in the mere form of a jar or the like, concealment (*tirobhāva*) is imposed by the closing off of its full essential nature; meanwhile, grace (*anugraha*) is bestowed by granting the fullness of the appearance of unity within that limited manifestation. Therefore, it is not merely...

By the phrase "as the manifestation of all," the fulfillment of the question "What is this that has arisen? through its clear and complete resolution is achieved; and by the word "by that" (*tena*), he explains that [the Lord] performs the fivefold cosmic functions, beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*). "By that" means: by the Lord, who first enters into the body and so forth, and then brings about the manifestation of the multitude of objects.
With that cognizer— that is, with the cognizer consisting of the body and so forth— at this time— that is,
at the moment characterized by the specific immersion (*āveśa*)— oneness is produced, for otherwise that immersion would be impossible; [this occurs] with another cognizer from this [state].
Unity with the subject who was previously made the object of immersion is withdrawn—
because, despite his pervasiveness, he is joined [to that state] merely by the absence of such orientation; likewise,
because of the closing of his full nature, since immersion in that [state] would otherwise be impossible.

Because of the contraction of one's own full nature within that portion, concealment (*tirobhāva*) is imposed—that is, brought about—in that appearance, namely, in the appearance of an object accomplished at that time; for [concealment] consists in the withholding of the fullness of the appearance of unity. Of this appearance of unity—
Grace (*anugraha*) consists in bestowing fullness upon that which is related to the manifestation of identity with the nature of self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśa*);
it is the act of causing [the object] to dissolve into one's own self during the great emanations, the great sustenances, the great dissolutions, and the outbursts of wrath or concealments.

The Lord’s engagement with the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*) persists constantly even during worldly transaction, as in the acts of grace such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the imparting of knowledge (*jñāna*). As it has been said:
"He who always delights in creation and always dwells in the bliss of maintenance..."
Salutation to the Lord, who is eternally satisfied by consuming the three worlds.
Thus:

"Though incessantly conceptualizing the three worlds with hundreds of mental constructions at every moment, there is a certain unique, unborn one who remains free from conceptualization; may he be victorious!"
And so forth. Likewise:
"Form is a favor; it is brought about, for the manifestation of the object dissolves into the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃvimarśa*). As it has been said:
"Of this fragmented reflective awareness, 'I'..."
Thus, the meaning is that this reflective awareness (*ahaṃvimarśa*) is indeed of the very nature of Light (*prakāśa*).
Regarding "in concealments through provocation" (*prakopatirodhāneṣu*): in those concealments which occur through provocation; and regarding "even in worldly transaction" (*vyavahāre'pi*):
even in pure or impure worldly transactions produced by the manifestation of the grasped and the grasper, it does not [cease].

The intention of the word "also" (api) is that [this process] occurs not only in the Great Emanation and so forth. Among those, the nature of emanation and so forth in the Great Emanation and so forth has already been shown previously; furthermore, the fact that emanation and so forth are always present even in the empirical dealings of limited subjects has been briefly determined in that very same place, and here this is the second mode.

Since this has also been clearly determined by the author himself, the phrase "here too" (atrāpi) [which appears as *na tatrāpi* in manuscript C] should be applied here as well; however, we have not provided a detailed elaboration out of fear of prolixity. Regarding the phrase "as it has been said," which expresses the consensus of the elders, he states "always" (*sadā*) in response to the expectation of what was said. This refers to the following verse:

Since the determination of the meaning has already been made previously, no further effort is exerted; rather, that which remains to be said is stated here. In this context, by the very word *āhāra* (appropriation), both concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*) are also included;
therein, in common usage, concealment and grace have been demonstrated here by the author of the treatise.

However, the two [processes] occurring immediately after the triad beginning with the Great Emanation (mahāsṛṣṭi)—namely, the withdrawal of emanation and so forth—should be understood as follows: first, their maintenance within one's own self in the form of latent impressions (saṃskāra), and then their dissolution into one's own self.
These two must indeed be applied there; enough said on this point. Furthermore, another [matter]:
He cites two statements, namely "at every moment" and "sovereignty," and in these two statements as well:
"...when you manifest sovereignty within yourself."
...of manifestation...
And thus it is said. || 7 ||
In this context, the appearance of the non-existence of an internal object is already established; therefore, what is the point of considering another cause?

This is the subject of inquiry (*prameya*) at hand. To prove that, the logical justification (*upapatti*) has been stated: namely, that without it, there would be no reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) consisting of volition (*icchā*). Consequently, as a corollary, the nature of reflective awareness, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and so forth is explained.
Having thus established [the point], he concludes by demonstrating the subject matter at hand in order to steady the minds of his disciples:
"In this way, whether it be in memory or in conceptual construction, both of which are intent upon exclusion (*apohana*)."
Or rather, it is certain that even within cognition, an internal appearance persists. || 8 ||
In both cases, it has been stated that they always perform the acts of creation and so forth; thus, no further elaboration has been made here—enough. || 7 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the words "here" (*iha*).
Here, the commentary says:
"within"—that is, within the full light; "even while remaining," for otherwise...

Because manifestation is impossible according to the principle stated previously in the verse beginning with *prāgivā*, [the author] says "by that" (*tena*) to address the question: "What kind of reasoning (*upapatti*) is this regarding the subject at hand—the matter (*prameya*) to be undertaken and determined? Furthermore, this has been stated in the portion of the verse beginning with "without that, the reflective awareness of desire does not proceed," in order to provide a resolution.

Otherwise, the concentration of that cognition upon this class of objects placed here would not be possible; thus he establishes it—meaning he proves it through reasoning. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse with the word "evam" (thus).
The commentary here states:
"Intending that the word 'evam' (thus) denotes the cause, he provides the explanation: 'prakāśa' (light).
"Prakāśātmā" means having the nature of pure light; this is in reality (*vastutaḥ*), not merely superficially (*āpātataḥ*), for by that [pure light]...

The status of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) belongs to the body and so forth, each in its own way, with respect to its respective object. The word "also" (*api*) illuminates the fact that while the conceit of being a knower resides in the body and so forth, the pure Light possesses an indubitable status as the knower. This is what is required by the word "thus" (*evam*).
The Supreme Lord alone is the nature of light, because even in the state of the conceit of being a limited subject such as the body and so forth, He remains in reality the true subject;
for this reason, the following is established: [He is present] in memory, in conceptual thought whose life is exclusion (*apohana*), and in the knowledge of direct experience.
The internal manifestation remains precisely as it is, resting within the light; there is no doubt about this.

For if the body and so forth were themselves the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*), then the statement that "the jar and so on are within the body, the vital breath, the intellect, or the void" would be meaningless—since the body and so forth do not exist apart from the jar and so on.

But the *Paramārthaprakāśa*, being all-enduring, states the subject matter and then introduces the word "evam" (thus) and explains it. By this [use of] "evam," it is indicated that the explanation of the word "evam" should be understood as "evam sati" (this being so). What is established by this?

In response to this expectation, he explains the verse beginning with "in memory" (*smṛtau*) as follows: by the word "in recollection" (*smaraṇe*), there is the explanation of "in memory" (*smṛtau*); by the phrase "whose life is exclusion" (*apohanajīvite*), there is the explanation of "devoted to exclusion" (*apohanaparāyaṇe*);
and by the words "internal manifestation" (*antarābhāsaḥ*) and "resting in light" (*prakāśaviśrāntaḥ*), there is the explanation of "within" (*antaḥ*).

The term *ābhāsa* (manifestation) is a synonym for *arthābhāsa* (the manifestation of an object); it is not explained [here] because its status as the agent is already well-known. In the same way, in the case of memory and so forth as well, the construction is that the manifestation remains situated within.
Thus, the underlying sense is that everywhere the manifestor (*prakāśa*) alone is the subject (*pramātā*). The word *iti* [marks the end of the explanation].

This [word] is intended to imply all the meanings stated in the preceding sentence. He explains the word "niścitam" (ascertained) with the words "nātra" (not here). He himself provides the justification for this with the words "yadi" (if), "antarghaṭādi" (the jar and so forth being included within), and the application of the maxim "prāgivārthaḥ" (as in the case of *prāg*), meaning that the jar and so forth would be included [within the cognition]. To the question, "Let it be so; what follows from that?", he says "na" (no).

"Something" (kiṃcit). To the question "How is it not something?", he says "A jar, etc. The sense is that no one indeed obtains a jar within the body. Now, if that is so, how could a jar, etc., exist even outside of light? To this he says "In ultimate reality," meaning "all-enduring" because it is endowed with all powers; otherwise...
The non-occurrence of the manifestation of anything whatsoever—thus, "the universe is within that"—this is established without effort. || 8 ||

Now, if the external manifestation of the class of internal appearances exists everywhere, what then is the difference in manifestation in memory and the like? For this difference is certainly experienced, as there is the flashing forth of clarity, lack of clarity, and so on.
Anticipating the objection that [the object] cannot be denied, he says:
"But [this nature] is innate in cognition, which consists of the manifestation of the external;
however, in memory and other such states, it exists in the form of a prior experience. (9)

Now, one might ask: why is such a state not also postulated for the empty subject (*śūnyapramātṛ*)? True; however, if that were so postulated, he would simply be the supreme Light (*paraḥ prakāśaḥ*). Let it be so—what is the harm?
For the subject does not immediately become all-pervasive upon emerging from the state of being a limited intellectual subject (*buddhipramātṛ*).

However, for a moment, that very subject of emptiness necessarily experiences limitation as it persists in a subtle state of residual impression (*saṃskāra*); consequently, when the unlimitedness that is inherently radiant by nature manifests, there arises for him the state of pure luminosity.

Although even here there certainly exists a sequence consisting of the ascent through the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śuddhavidyā, nevertheless, it was stated thus because no such effort is required there; enough of this. "Therein" means within the manifestation of the ultimate reality (paramārtha). || 8 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the ninth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"of the class of internal appearances"—that is, those situated within the Light (*prakāśa*) which are fit to be grasped as the "I-sense" (*ahantā*).

The "external manifestation" of the collection of appearances such as jars and so forth means their appearing as being in an external location—that is to say, their apprehension as "this. Regarding the phrase "in memory and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes volition and the like; the distinction of appearances [arises] from experience, which is the understood remainder of the sentence.
The sense is that there is no difference in their being internal in both cases. Now, [one might object]: "Let there be a distinction between the manifestation (*bhāsa*) and the appearance (*ābhāsa*).

To this he says: "And not... The sense is: it is not that it is not perceived, but rather it is indeed perceived. To the question "How is it perceived?", he says: "Clearly. In that regard, there is the apprehension of "this" by way of including all attributes (*sarvadharma*).

The apprehension of clarity (*sphuṭatā*) is the apprehension of "this" without implying that [otherness]; the apprehension of lack of clarity (*asphuṭatā*) is the apprehension of "that. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse with the words "But... (*kiṃ tu*).
This refers to the internal manifestation (*antaravabhāsa*) of the cognition of experience, namely, "This is blue. [Note: *antarābhāsam* in Kṣemarāja’s commentary.]
For one who manifests externally, the appearance of its own internal inclusion is innate— having arisen from the sovereignty of emission (*nisarga*), and not, like recollection and so forth,
through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by another cognition. This is as it is in recollection, in creative imagination (*utprekṣaṇa*), and in that which follows upon perception.

Furthermore, that internal manifestation of blue and so forth which is to be determined as external in the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*)—and not merely manifested as external—is not its own inherent nature;
rather, it is born from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience. In this context, what is called a "latent impression" is [the capacity] of the experience...
The commentary on this [verse] states:

"Internally manifesting" (antarābhāsam) means appearing as blue while remaining within; that is to say, the appearance of blue that is fit to be grasped as "I. "Externally manifesting" (bahirābhāsayataḥ) means making it shine forth externally.

Mimicking the external manifestation, he says, "This is blue. "The manifestation within itself" means the manifestation of the entity residing within itself. He explains the word *naisargika* (natural) by [the word] *nisṛṣṭeḥ* (from emission);
there too, he states the meaning of the root (*prakṛti*) as "by virtue of autonomy," for *nisarga* is indeed one's own nature (*svabhāva*), and that...
In the ultimate sense, it is nothing other than one's own sovereignty; that is to say, it is one's own innate power (*nijā śakti*) which constitutes its very nature.

He explains the meaning of the suffix *ṭhañ* with the word "arisen" (*āyāta*). Here, he provides a counter-example with the words "but not," referring to the knowledge—meaning the experience—of something else, namely, that which was previously experienced, and the latent impression (*vāsanā*) and so forth produced by that.

"By its power, the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth arrive"—this is the connection with what precedes. By this, the explanation of the first half-verse is completed. Thus is the construction here. The word "that" (*sa*), which stands in the second half-verse, should also be applied here.
However—in the alternative view—"that" refers to the internal manifestation (*antarābhāsa*), [which exists] within the nature of external manifestation.

In non-conceptual experience, which is a cognition whose nature is the grasping of "this-ness" (idantā), [the manifestation] is innate; it is not produced by mental impressions (saṃskāra) as is the case with memory and so forth. Now, he explains the second half [of the verse]: regarding the word "smaraṇe" (in memory), this is the explanation of the term "memory," and the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes the term "utprekṣaṇe" (in imaginative construction).
The meaning is "mentioning" (ullekhana). Regarding the term "in the determination" (adhyavasāye), this refers to conceptual experience;

the object of determination (*adhyavasāya-viṣaya*) is that which is to be determined as being external, and it is to be made one's own—that is, natural. To the question "Furthermore, of what nature is it?", he says:

There is also persistence over a period of time; therefore, because this persisting experience is intermingled with the manifestation of blue and so forth, even memory and the like—which have attained identity with that [experience]—manifest in the same way. For this very reason, the manifestation occurring at the time of memory [is such].

Since [the object] is determined precisely at the time prior to that experience, it is proclaimed that memory and so forth are themselves devoid of an object and grasp what has already been grasped. This very state is what constitutes "indistinctness";
thus, the distinction between appearances (*ābhāsa*) within the group of internal appearances in experience, memory, and so on, is established.

Manifestation externally means clarity through the absence of any intervention by another; however, when there is intervention, there is a lack of clarity because of the absence of immediate presence. || 9 ||

Now, one might object: "Since all cognition other than sensory perception (*aindriyaka*) arises through mediation, does it not follow that everything else is essentially an external appearance? Anticipating this doubt, he states the distinction with the words "but rather" (*api tu*). One might further ask: "In what sense is it said to be 'of the nature of a prior experience' (*pūrvānubhavarūpaḥ*)?"
The meaning is "being born from a mental impression" (*saṃskāra*); therefore, he says "in that regard" (*tatra*).
To establish this, he first states the meaning of the word *saṃskāra*: "What is called a mental impression" (*saṃskāro nāma*).
Even at another time—that is, at a time subsequent to the time of perceiving the object—it is permeated by the appearance of blue and so forth.

At the time of apprehension, it is colored by the object such as blue; having attained identity with that—that is, endowed with identity with that blueness—just like the previous experience. He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*): it is indeed characterized (*kalita*)—that is, qualified—by that which was its prior time, and not otherwise.

The meaning is that it is endowed with presentness (*idānīntanatā*). By this, it is established that recollection has the nature of a prior experience, and that very quality is what constitutes its being produced from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); such is the intended sense. He states that its lack of an object and its status as apprehending what has already been apprehended—which are well-known in the world—are established by relying on this [very point]. Thus, therefore.

The meaning is "due to a cause. He also describes its lack of clarity with the word "this" (*etad*). Now, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of clarity there is, he says "internal manifestation" (*antarābhāsa*). This means "without the intervention of anything else"—that is, without the intervention of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, by way of this same context, [he explains] the lack of clarity.
"It is determined by way of intervention" means "by intervention," that is to say, by what is produced through mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Since the apprehension [of objects] occurs here itself—both by including all phenomena and by not including them—one should not suspect any contradiction between what precedes and what follows. || 9 ||
This [appearance] exists quite naturally within the conceptual construction that moves at its own will,
due to the manifestation of whatever form is intended within the sphere of the intellect.

That conceptual construction— such as a mental kingdom or a volition— which does not depend upon the operation of direct perception and whose essence consists in distraction, moves, arises, and passes away by its own will,
through its own impulsion, independently of any external impulsion, and with autonomy; therein, that which...
The external appearance of blue and so forth consists of internal appearance; this is the introduction to the tenth verse, beginning with "nanu.
Here, the commentary states:

"Everything"—meaning the entire realm of mental construction (*manorājya*), delusive cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*), and so forth. Having thus provided this introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "that is innate" (*sa naisargikaḥ*).
Herein lies the commentary:

He provides the explanation of the word "vikalpe" (in conceptual construction) by means of the word "yaḥ" (who), since the word "tat" (that) is dependent upon the word "yat" (which). [The phrase] "pratyakṣavyāpāram" means the operation of the means of valid cognition that is perception; "anupajīvan" means not depending upon it; and "vyākṣepasāratayā" means by virtue of having nothing more than mental distraction as its essence. "Ādi" (and so forth).

The word "by sound" (*śabdena*) refers to the apprehension of error. He explains the *kṛdanta* compound "acting according to one's own will" (*svairacāriṇi*), which serves as an adjective for "in conceptual construction" (*vikalpe*), by first providing its analysis: "according to one's own will" (*svairam*). He explains "according to one's own will" (*svaira*) as "by one's own impulse" (*svapreraṇa*); for indeed, the kingdom of the mind and so forth arises and dissolves for a person entirely of itself, and not [by external cause].

It does not depend on the instigation of a person, for in this case there is no question at all of another agent. Regarding this as well, he states the synonym "by its own autonomy" (*svātantryeṇa*); and this autonomy is to be understood as belonging only to the kingdom of the mind and so forth, not to a person, otherwise a contradiction would arise. He explains the word "moves" (*carati*) by saying "it arises" (*udeti*), for here "moving" (*caraṇa*) [is synonymous with arising].

It is indeed [a matter of] arising and passing away; however, this was stated without regard for the slight degree of autonomy that exists here for those who have conquered their minds, because what is intended to be discussed here is precisely the mental construction (*manorājya*) of ordinary people and the like.
He states the meaning of the locative case with the word "tatra" (there); "there" means in such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). That...

He states the meaning of this with the word "yaḥ" (who). "External manifestation" (*bahirābhāsa*) means a manifestation as "this-ness" (*idantā*) or "that-ness" (*tattā*). "Consisting of internal manifestation" (*antarābhāsamaya*) means that which, in the ultimate sense, is capable of being grasped as "I" because it is contained within oneself. He fulfills the requirement for the relative pronoun "yaḥ" by saying "saḥ" (he). "Saḥ" (he)—

It is indeed innate; for instance, even though it has never been seen before, that conceptual construction [arises] regarding an elephant— possessing a pair of trunks equipped with a hundred white tusks— which, while situated internally on the plane of the cognizer, appears externally on the plane of the internal organ, which consists of the mirror of the clear intellect.
It illuminates (or causes to appear) only that which is simultaneous with it. || 10 ||

"Appearance" (ābhāsa) means an appearance produced by the mind alone, independent of any external object; it is innate (naisargika), not born of mental impressions (saṃskāra). To address the question of how it is innate, the author begins the justification with "for instance" (tathā hi): "never before perceived."

The meaning is that it has never been seen before; for an elephant possessing the qualities about to be described is never seen. "White" means bright; "endowed with a hundred tusks," and not merely endowed with two teeth;
"joined with a pair of trunks"—that is, a pair—and not joined with only one trunk; "the tusked one" means an elephant.

On the plane of the subject— that is, on the foundation of the supreme light which is the supreme subject, delimited by the cognitive subject— it "abides," meaning it exists in the form of power, for otherwise its emergence would be impossible. Externally.

On the surface of the internal organ—that is, on the wall of the internal organ which exists as "external" in relation to the Light—of what nature is it? It is that very intellect (*dhī*) which is transparent, acting as a mirror—a looking glass by virtue of its suitability for reflecting external objects—and that [intellect] is the self (*ātman*) of which; such is he.

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—in the form of mental desire and so forth—is a conceptual construction that manifests only for that moment, not persisting through other times. And in this context, the subjecthood of the cognitive subject (*buddhi-pramātṛ*) is relative to the apprehension of the external from its own perspective; it is internal with respect to itself.
There is nothing contradictory in the fact that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) functions as the object of perception with respect to the knower who is [identical with] space.

Now, one might object: even such an elephant as has been described is produced solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); for it is not possible that an elephant of this kind should ever manifest in the mind of a newborn infant. Indeed, a person...

In dreams, royal palaces, and the like, one applies through one's own imagination qualifiers seen in one place to another; although those qualifiers exist as distinct entities due to the power of mental formations (*saṃskāra*),

even if they have not been perceived together in one location, they are nonetheless precisely those same qualifiers that were seen here and there in their distinct and separate states, and not otherwise.
To this extent, it is appropriate to say that these [factors] are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is true.

However, this is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), yet it was stated in this way for the sake of those with coarse intellects, for they are indeed not authorized to investigate the ultimate reality. But then, what is that ultimate reality?

If you say that it must be made manifest by its own innate compassion (*anugadayā*), listen: that very thing is the natural reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which was previously shown to exist even in newborn infants and others as the life-force of the desire for mother’s milk and so forth. For desire is...

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself is indeed *yojanā* (synthesis), and *yojanā* is reflective synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*), which is precisely what constitutes reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). For even in the external world, desire directed toward an object consists essentially in the synthesis of its capacity to produce pleasure; for a child as well, desire directed toward an object consists essentially in the synthesis of its capacity to produce pleasure.

Since the apprehension of a real object is not possible, he even identifies his finger or similar object placed upon the lip with the breast, whereby he performs the act of sucking there as well. Therefore, when one investigates the ultimate reality, he does not actually desire breast-milk due to the absence of the cognition of breast-milk; rather, it is merely a state of satisfaction.

Desiring [to know], he wanders here and there; however, the flickering of the gateway of his mouth is indeed natural to him. Through that agitation for the sake of satisfaction, it is known that within his own self there exists a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form of a unification, which abides as the state of power (*śakti*). As for that which belongs to him...

They speak of a connection with a previous birth, which is also, in its ultimate result, that very same thing; for in the investigation of the supreme reality (*paramārtha*), the previous birth of all beings is indeed the luminous principle (*prakāśatattva*) endowed with all powers. Even immobile beings (*sthāvara*), by assuming their own inherent nature, arise from that very source; within them as well, that reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) exists.
It certainly exists; otherwise, it would be impossible for threads to attract their own substance [of color].

Thus, that subtle reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) exists in all cognitions: it resides directly in that experience (*anubhava*), as well as in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows it, and in memory (*smṛti*) whose object is a thing previously experienced.

However, regarding mental constructions (*manorājya*) and the like that arise according to one's own will, the Teacher established that these are produced solely from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) for those who hold the misconception that they are so; yet that is not correct,
for since it has been shown that their existence is logical even in the case of stationary objects (*sthāvara*), what need is there to mention mental constructions and the like?

The conceptualization of its non-existence [is untenable]; for in the investigation of ultimate reality, whatever possesses existence necessarily possesses an innate self-reflection (*pratyavamarśa*), because everything is filled by that very Being which consists solely of non-deviating pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Therefore, even in the case of non-existence during the investigation of ultimate reality, it is by that very [Being] [that all is fulfilled].

Filling (*pūraṇa*) occurs precisely through the state of non-existence (*asattva-bhāva*), because it is by means of this that filling takes place; for indeed, the meaning of the word *bhairava* is precisely the agency of sustaining (*bharaṇa*) all existence and non-existence. As it has been said:
"That very god Bhairava is characterized by the sustaining of the universe."

And from this investigation into the distinctions between manifestations— which arose in the context of establishing the emergence of internal manifestations— the primary purpose intended in this treatise,
namely the recognition of the Lord within one's own self (*svātmani īśvarapratyabhijñāna*), is established according to the principle of a *siddhānta* based on the nature of the subject matter.
He shows that [this] is accomplished without effort:
"Precisely for this reason, because of the manifestation of the appearance of whatever is intended,
knowledge and action are clearly established for every living being."
That is to say, because external objects do not exist exactly as they are intended,
there is a correct representation even of that which has never been experienced.
By this, [it is explained] for all things in the world— whether insentient or sentient, existent or non-existent— ...

The state of being endowed with reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) has been established. And for that which is endowed with reflective awareness, there is fitness even for engaging in discourse; thus, what some say—that all entities are solely intent upon the praise of the Blessed One—is indeed correct. Therefore, in the investigation of ultimate reality, everything is itself that very [Blessed One].

Who could praise whom? Since it is established everywhere that [the Self] consists solely of the reflective awareness of "I" whose nature is absolute freedom, enough with this proliferation of words which only serves to raise objections regarding a reality that is accessible through one's own intuition alone. || 10 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eleventh verse with the words "asmācca" (and from this).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"In the scripture"—that is, in this *Pratyabhijñā* scripture—"intended"—by the author of the work.
It has been taken into account—that purpose—by way of the principle of *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion of a topic).

*Adhikaraṇasiddhānta* is that wherein, by means of one locus, another matter is established; for example, by taking the non-eternality of sound as the locus, its quality-ness is established. By the method (*nīti*) of that [principle], it is meant.
"Accomplished without effort" means accomplished without exertion. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "for this very reason.
Here is the commentary:

He explains "for this very reason" with the words "yadidam" (this which...). "According to one's desire" means in accordance with one's own will, independently of external objects; "of that which has never been experienced" means that which has never at any time become an object of experience.
Furthermore, the manifestation of conceptualization has been demonstrated by this very reason through logical consequence; from this alone, the following is also established:

whatever being there may be, whether a mere insect or Brahmā, as long as it is engaged in the activity of living, its power of knowledge consists in manifestation and its power of action consists in delineation, both of which are innate.

Furthermore, on that ground, there is not even the possibility of subsisting upon a pre-established creation imagined by a separate God (or, as in the K. ṣ. ṣ. manuscript: "imagined by a God distinct [from the self]").

The "depiction" (*ullekhana*) of a white elephant and so forth refers to its mental construction (*manasi kalpana*) and its manifestation (*avabhāsana*)—its appearing vividly before one through the intensification of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). As it has been said:
"Those afflicted by thieves and the like in a dream..."

"They see even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them. [This is said] by way of a digression—that is, in connection with the discernment of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). To the question "But what follows from that?", he says:
"Precisely for this reason. He fulfills the expectation of the word "this" (*idam*) by saying "who," namely: one who is engaged in the activity of living.
"Living"—meaning all that is moving; "of him"—whether of an insect or of Brahmā, meaning of every living being.
"Innate"—natural. Now, one might ask: does it not exist for immobile beings?
True; it certainly exists for them as well, but it is merely indistinct compared to its clarity [in others].
Thus it has been said. To the question, "Even if that is so, what follows from it?", he says: "From that" (*tataḥ*).
From that cause, by the person, on that ground—the ground of the kingdom of the mind wandering at will—his own sovereignty alone, his innate and natural freedom itself, becomes manifest.

That which is to be recognized is the sovereignty pertaining to the Lord; the sense is that one must make the object of recognition the thought, "This very sovereignty of mine is that [sovereignty]," and consequently, the recognition should be performed as "I am indeed this very Lord. Of what nature is one's own sovereignty? It is of the form: "I know and I act."

That which is the sovereignty of knowledge and action—that is, the agency (kartṛtva) in both cognition and activity—is the very definition and essential nature (svarūpa) [of the Self]. Why, then, should it not be recognized as one's own? Why [is this so]? Because on that level, there is no Lord who is distinct—meaning separate from one's own self—who could have projected [the world].

The "pre-established" (pūrvasiddhā) creation is that creation which exists as already established prior to mental constructions and the like, like an external creation; it is one's own sovereignty itself— such as the intended creation of the form of an elephant endowed with qualities like whiteness— which must be clearly recognized.

"He knows and he acts"—this indicates the characteristic of sovereignty (*svātantrya*) regarding knowledge and action. By the use of the singular number, it suggests that all living beings are, in reality, of the nature of the one Lord. May there be auspiciousness! (11) [Total from the beginning: 63]

There is not even the possibility—that is, the mere conjecture—of its subsistence, which is to say its dependence [on something else] by way of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), because it is clearly imagined by itself and has never been perceived externally; the word "even" (*api*) indicates that what need is there to speak of its actual existence? In that [state],...

The two words "on the ground" (*bhūmau*) are to be construed with both [the preceding and following clauses], like the eye of a crow. This instruction is intended only for one who is awakened (*prabuddha*), because an unawakened person lacks the requisite qualification; furthermore, for one who is perfectly awakened (*suprabuddha*) and perceives everything at all times as the Self, such a requirement is impossible. Nor is it [intended] even for those who are not yet awakened.
Having heard this, one should understand that this delusion occurs regarding the kingdom of the mind and the like when they flash forth due to being helpless under the power of *saṅkalpa*.

However, for those who have completely conquered *saṅkalpa* and whose mental kingdoms never flash forth—even by virtue of the body's own nature—[the following applies]: [When it flashes forth by virtue of the body's own nature...]

C. This teaching is established for the sake of those who, though awakened to the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), are currently unable to effect its recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) during their state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). Or, even if they were to do so, what loss would there be for us?
Enough of this. Now, he speaks of the "singular number" (*ekavacana*) in order to explain the intention behind the singular form of the word *jīvataḥ* found here.

Thus [he] indicates—meaning he speaks by way of indication (*sūcanā*) and not directly; the sense is that "indication" occurs here by virtue of the power of the grammatical rule: "the dual and singular endings are used for two and one [respectively].
[Objection: If that is so, then for what purpose has the word *sarva* (all) been established?
This explains it quite clearly: for the unification of distinct things into one by means of the intellect is indeed the ground for the application of all words. True;

this was said specifically with reference to those whose intellects are seized by duality, for upon hearing "he lives," they would understand that this was said concerning some single living being, and it is precisely for them [that this was said].

There is nothing contradictory in this composition of the treatise. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the daily lesson (*āhnika*). The term *śivam* is an expression denoting auspiciousness and is intended to indicate the supreme reality (*paratattva*). Thus, all is auspicious (*śivam*). 11.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Power of Knowledge," in the first section on Knowledge of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 6.
Thus ends the sixth daily lesson in the Section on Knowledge within the *Śrīpratyabhijñāvimarśinī*, the commentary known as the *Bhāskarī*, composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. 6.
Now begins the seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Single Substratum," within the section on Knowledge (*jñāna*).
[It is] because of its being the single substratum for the jewels of infinite powers...
We praise that Śiva, who has attained perfection through the radiant manifestation of manifold moonlight.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
We praise that Śiva, by whose association with a single substratum the multitude of diverse powers clearly attains the capacity to manifest their effects.
Now, in this section on Knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*), for the purpose of completing the commentary without obstacles and for the sake of further progress,

[the author] composes an auspicious invocation in the form of a recollection of reality (*tattvānusmaraṇa*)— beginning with the word "Ananta"— to instruct his disciples, using a verse that indicates the overall purport of the entire section.

We praise—that is, we contemplate by means of praise—that Śiva, who was mentioned in the preceding sentence as being pervaded by sound (*śabda*); Śiva, whose essence is the mass of powers (*śakti*), whose ultimate reality is Light (*prakāśa*), and who is the form of one's own self as the deity; the Śiva-principle which is infinite—that is, undelimited.
Regarding those "power-jewels"— which, by virtue of being supreme entities, are of the nature of jewels,

namely the collection of powers such as primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and so forth— their [existence] is due to their reliance upon a single locus; and that which is this single locus is the unique substratum (*sthāna*) by virtue of possessing power, and it is through reliance upon that [locus] that they exist.

The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of cause (*hetau*). The various manifestations of moonlight—those flashes of light in the form of valid cognitions (*pramā*) and the like that illuminate their respective objects—attain their perfection; for the powers such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth reside within the Supreme Light, and from that alone they derive their strength.

Having obtained [their respective capacities], they illuminate their own objects. Although, according to the principle that "this entire world consists of powers (śakti), while the Great Lord (maheśvara) is the possessor of power (śaktimat)," all entities are indeed of the nature of power, nevertheless, with respect to the present context—
In this context, only the powers such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth are being grasped;

for it is by these very powers of knowledge and the rest that the self is established, and it is precisely that much alone which is intended here as the Lord (*īśvara*) and as that which is to be recognized through *pratyabhijñā*. This is because this scripture has that [recognition] as its sole purpose. By this—
It is indicated here that in this section (anhika), the determination of the single substratum (*ekādhāra*) of the powers such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth is being made.

Thus, by this much, the nature of the powers such as memory (*smṛti*) and so forth has been shown in detail; however, the fact that the nature of the knower (*pramātṛ*) was also revealed here is for the purpose of supporting their very status as powers, for it is not otherwise.

It follows that one's own body (*svatantra*) must be of the nature of power (*śakti*). Now, however, there is a single substratum for those powers; and because he possesses the freedom (*svācchandyayoga*) to join and disjoin those powers and so forth, he is Maheśvara, and not merely a substratum for powers such as burning and cooking like fire and other insentient things (*jaḍasvarūpa*). This is what [is meant].
Both have been introduced [in the passage]:
"If He were not one who has made the infinite universe His inner self...
In this sūtra, that must be determined by expanding upon it; therein, in order to determine the single locus [of both],...
"And this eloquence which is here...
and so forth...
