[such] worldly convention is experienced.
Having thus performed the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), he explains the intent of the entire work both collectively and individually with the word "evam" (thus).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

[Objection: But surely the cognizer also possesses a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*); so how can it be said that "the nature of the powers has been shown"? To this, he says: "But as for what is here... *Unmīlitam* means made manifest, not definitively determined.
[The purpose is] to establish—that is, to prove. When the question "Why? arises, he says: "For indeed..."

Now, to the question "What does he say now?", he replies: "Now" (*adhunā*). Regarding those powers (*śakti*), there is their joining and separating; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the dissolution of them into oneself is included. Through union with the sovereignty—that is, the autonomy (*svātantrya*)—in that regard, both are [attained]: the oneness of that which is the substratum of the powers.

And the state of being Maheśvara has been introduced—meaning presented or stated. In response to the question "Where? he says "na cet" (if not). That pair must be determined—it must necessarily be ascertained;
the sense is that otherwise, the determination of the state of being Maheśvara would be impossible. There—in that [context].
Since the dyad must be determined, there is one substratum— the single locus for the powers of knowledge and so forth,
which is the form of the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the supreme subject. Having thus stated the intention in its entirety, [the author proceeds].

Thus, with fourteen verses, the daily lesson (*āhnika*) is introduced. Among these, by means of one verse, a single substratum (*āśraya*) is proposed in terms of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Following that, by means of two [verses], the reasoning consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is stated: that all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is tenable only when a single substratum exists, and not when it does not exist. Thereafter—

The nature of conventional reality (*vyavahāra*) is established— in brief— by one verse and by eight verses, respectively, through the relationship of cause and effect, through memory, and through the distinction between the true and the false; thereafter, by one verse...
"Every subject matter is concluded"—this is the summary of the meaning of the chapter (*āhnika*).

Now, the meaning of the verse is explained. As for what was stated: "In every living being, cognition and action are established," how is that so? For what other [entity] exists, distinct from cognition and the rest, to which those two belong?

[The two] might [be so]; for, according to the view of the followers of Kaṇāda and others, the substratum [of the universal] has been refuted; thus he says "there" even in the sense of being separate. "There" means in the midst of the fourteen verses.
"By way of its own nature" (svarūpataḥ) means by its mere essential form, not by the implication of all its attributes.

It is introduced—that is, it is stated—by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), which consists of the nature of agreement and difference, through each verse and through eight verses; that is to say, by ten verses. Among these, by one [verse] there is the determination of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), then by another one [verse] the determination of memory (*smṛti*), and by eight [verses]...

The sequence is "the determination of the distinction between the real and the unreal. It is "concluded" (nigamyate), meaning it is brought to the state of being the object of the conclusion. "Thus" concludes the statement regarding the individual [parts]. "Now" introduces the explanation of the meaning of the verse. Regarding that, he provides the introduction to the first verse with the words "as has been said."
The commentary on this point is as follows:
"How so? means that it is not possible. To address the question "Why?", he says "yāvatā" (insofar as).
"Yāvatā" means "because of which reason. "Te" refers to knowledge and action. Now, previously...

Since it has been established that [the Self] is distinct from that [body] as the substratum of qualities such as knowledge, he says "the follower of Kaṇāda" (the Vaiśeṣika). From the perspective of his own system—that is, from the viewpoint of the Śaiva doctrine—he presents—offers, or in other words, describes—that one substratum by way of its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), that is, by its mere essence alone. Thus...
Having provided an introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "And this which... and so forth, beginning with "Then, among distinct phenomena...
and so on; having raised that doubt, he [explains] from the perspective of his own system (*svadarśanadiśā*).
He introduces that one [subject] by way of its essential nature:
"That which is this intuition (pratibhā), colored by the succession of various objects, is the cognizer whose nature is non-successive and infinite consciousness; he is the Great Lord. (1)

Although the manifestation "the jar appears" shines forth as being indeed conjoined with the object, nevertheless, that is not the jar's own intrinsic nature; rather, it is consciousness itself that shines forth in such a way, because it is attached to the subject, as in [the expression] "it appears to me. And thus says the Veda:
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) initiates the process of explaining the fragment of the verse ending with "akramāḥ" by stating:
"it appears [as follows]. "Connected with the object" (*viṣayopaśliṣṭam eva*) means precisely that which is related to the jar and so forth, which serve as the agents (*kartṛ*).
*Pratibhāna*—the nature of the action expressed as "it shines forth" (*pratibhāti*)—*bhāti*, meaning it flashes forth toward the subjects (*pramātṛbhiḥ*).
That *pratibhāna* is the object's own body;
that is to say, its own (i.e., its intrinsic) nature, which is called "the object. To the question "What, then, is that? he says: "But rather... (*api tu*).

It is consciousness alone—the very activity called "consciousness" which resides in the subject and has the jar as its object—that shines forth, i.e., manifests, in that manner, namely, through its connection with the object. He states the reason for this:
"toward me. This is because [the object] is, at first glance, not separate from the subject.

Even regarding the aspect of the jar’s existence as residing within the agent, it appears to me "only as such" from the ultimate perspective (*paramārthataḥ*), because that [aspect] has the subject alone as its foundation. This is the point here: first, the subject initiates an exertion toward the cognition of the jar due to the influence of desire and so forth; otherwise, [it would not occur].

Because the very introduction of the subject of the pot is inappropriate; for if someone asks him about the news regarding that pot, he says to him, "The pot appears"; and when asked again, "To whom does it appear?", he replies, "To me. Indeed, the word *prati* [indicates] the appearance of the pot.

It is the remover of agency from the cognizer and the establisher of his capacity for it; otherwise, one would have to say "it appears to me. However, in the statement "it appears" without the use of the word "to me," the cognizer [perceives] his own self as the foundational wall.

Having forgotten the jar itself, he brings it forth because he is rendered helpless by an excess of desire for it; yet, on that account alone, it is not appropriate to say that agency belongs to the jar itself or that the Self is indifferent,
since an insentient object like a jar cannot possess agency, and because independence belongs everywhere only to the Self.

Because [the Self] possesses the capacity for universal agency—as it has been stated that "the agent is independent"—it follows that in the cognition "the jar appears clearly," the connection with the subject (pramātṛlagnatva), which is indicated by the prefix *prati*, becomes evident. And if there is connection with the subject, external objectivity (*bāhyatā*) is untenable; and if that is untenable, then objecthood itself is indeed untenable.

Thus [it is said]. Here, in order to establish the authority of scripture (*śruti*), he says "and so" (*tathā ca*); he then cites the very Vedic passage itself with "that very [one]" (*tameva*). And this scripture is as follows:
"There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine."
"Whence comes this fire?
Everything shines after Him alone as He shines; by His light all this is illumined.
Herein the meaning is this: "there"—that is, in that Supreme Light, or rather, in its proximity—the sun...

The external light, the sun, is the most excellent; it does not shine—that is, it does not assume the status of an agent with respect to its own manifestation—because it shines by being attached to that which is called Consciousness (cit) through its shining toward it. Indeed, even the sun does not attain establishment like a jar or other objects without a perceiver (pramātṛ); its manifestation occurs only in the presence of that [Consciousness].
But in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it is established in that very [place]; for the placing of a foot upon a stone and the like is, in the ultimate sense, indeed upon the earth.
As it has been said:
"Otherwise, how could the feet of men be placed upon the earth?"
"Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
By the word *śatru* (enemy), there is the state of incessant vibration; by the *karmapravacanīya* [prefix], there is the [state] fashioned by His sovereignty—
The relationship characterized by the nature of the perceived and the perceiver, produced by the act of manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), has been illuminated.
The point is that as for the question "From where does this fire come?", there is no way at all for fire to appear [apart from consciousness].
Furthermore, the non-appearance of objects distinct from Light follows by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*).

It was not perceived as being even more manifest; for although it would have been appropriate to mention the absence of the sun immediately after the lightning, the fact that the absence of the sun is mentioned first is intended to indicate that compared to it, the lightning and so forth nearby are exceedingly insignificant. Otherwise, however, if the superior sun were absent...

What possibility is there for its appearance? And if that possibility does not exist, what negation can there be of it? [Objection: "In that case, how do these things appear? To this he says: "Tameva" (that very one). "Bhāntam" means ever-shining as "I" by virtue of self-luminosity; "anu-tam" means with respect to that Light which is the nature of the supreme subject; "sarvam"—all.

The light produced by the sun and other sources shines; otherwise, such linguistic usages as "I see the sun" would be impossible. As for the usage "it shines," this occurs by virtue of the subject's desire and so forth, serving the purpose of the cognizer who brings that light to the fore; otherwise, it would be unestablished.
This is the intended meaning. He states the conclusion with the words "of that" (*tasya*), with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) understood as the ellipsis.
For this reason, all this—the external collection of lights in the form of the sun and so forth, which is graspable as "this-ness"—shines by its light;
that is, it shines through the light that has that [Supreme Light] as its support and that has this [external world] as its object, being thus distinguished by its sovereignty.

The meaning is that [the Self] assumes, as it were, the status of an agent with respect to the act of shining; the sense is that, just as by the light of the sun and other sources, the entire collection of objects such as pots and so forth [is illuminated]. Here, he himself also provides a brief statement of the intended meaning by means of the suffix *śatṛ*: "by the suffix *śatṛ*," namely, by the suffix *śatṛ* occurring in the word *bhāntam*.

The connection is that "the state of uninterrupted flashing is illuminated"; the underlying intention is that one might otherwise say it "shines otherwise. He states the intended meaning of the word *anu* as "action" (*karma*). By means of the *karmapravacanīya* particle *anu*, which expresses the action of indication (*lakṣaṇakriyā*), the nature of the indication is shown: "Lightning flashes after (or along) the tree" (*vṛkṣamanu dyotate vidyut*).

In this manner, the relationship consisting of the act of definition (*lakṣaṇakriyā*) is indicated; for just as the flashing of lightning is defined by a tree—that is, it is shown to observers—so too the manifestation of the sun and other luminaries is defined for perceivers by the manifestation of the Supreme Subject (*parapramātṛ*). Now, one might object: in that case, the tree is clearly [perceived].
By that [argument], it is indeed established that lightning alone appears externally through the power of the delineation of objects; however,
in this case, the manifestation of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*) is not clear— so how can this definition [apply] by means of that?

If you say this, who is that [self]? If you say it is the body and so forth—oh, what a qualification for giving instruction to others! If you say it is another cognizer (*parapramātṛ*), does he appear to you or not? If he does not appear, how can there be the usage "by me"?
For the manifestation of the word denoting that [self] occurs only immediately after the perception of the object. If he does appear, then [he appears] right now.

Is it always so? If you say "only today," then since the usage "I am [today]" was made only today, the recollection of the past—"Yesterday I ate this"—is not logical. If you say, "It has appeared for today, but beyond this I do not know whether it will appear or not," that is true; however, as for that notion of "I" delimited by another body, what is it?

Is "I" distinct from You or non-distinct? If distinct, then the conceit of being a limited subject embodied in a body remains exactly as it was; therefore, the lack of qualification for instruction remains likewise.
But if non-distinct, then what [is the point] if one does not accept the separation created by form?
Regarding the doubt concerning an interruption caused by space and time, the manifestation of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*) is always indeed most vivid;
and by that very [manifestation], the manifestation of the sun and so forth is indicated. Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of relationship consists of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he states the qualifiers beginning with *tadīya*.

Thus: that which belongs to him—that is, the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) pertaining to the supreme subject—which consists in not looking toward another in any action; by that [sovereignty] is "prepared" (i.e., brought about) the act of manifestation (*nirmāṇakriyā*), and it is produced by that [act], for otherwise sovereignty would be impossible. Likewise, it takes the form of the relationship between the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*).

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it consists of the state of being the object (*vedyatva*) residing in the jar, the state of being the subject (*vedakatva*) residing in the supreme knower (*parapramātṛ*), and the causal form of the relationship between the object and the subject; whereas from the perspective of the immediate appearance (*āpātataḥ*), it consists of the relationship of the object and the subject as established in the jar, the body, and so forth.

Now, if the manifestation of the jar and so forth is indeed the very consciousness of the supreme subject, then that [manifestation] must be of the nature of consciousness itself; for there is no establishment of the jar or other objects apart from that [consciousness].
And since the supreme subject is one, consciousness too must be one; thus, by virtue of that [oneness], the jar and so forth are also one.
Since it follows that there is only oneness, one must offer a handful of sesame seeds to the notion of succession; therefore, he says "only" (*kevalam*).

"Only" means: by the power—that is, by the force—of the "representation" (*ullekhana*) of objects—that is, of the things to be known—which consists in a free reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) for the sake of play, even though they do not exist externally. Externally...
Successive manifestation (*kramāvabhāsa*)— the appearance in succession regarding various distinct objects—

is "established" (*samarthita*) insofar as it is made the object of proof by way of a prima facie argument (*āpātataḥ*), for otherwise the relationship between teacher and disciple and so forth would be untenable.
The intention is that [otherwise] there would follow the impossibility of even composing this treatise.
Relying on the method already stated, he explains and analyzes the compound *tattatpadārtha* as *sa saḥ*. The form of the two words *tat-tat* in the nominative singular is *sa saḥ*.
That which consists of various forms such as succession and simultaneity— namely,

the succession of things (padārtha) fashioned by the power of space and time, which is the nature of the Lord’s sovereignty to be described later— and by which [consciousness] is colored, that is, affected as if it were a reflection; that which...
"Intuition (pratibhā) has been described as consisting solely of a distinct cognition...
and so forth. And this [intuition] is, for everyone, of the nature of self-luminosity, and in the ultimate sense...
Because it manifests as inward-turned and has pure light as its ultimate reality, there is an absence of differentiation; thus, it is "without succession" (*akramā*).
That very [reality] is Maheśvara.
He provides the explanation of these two terms as "succession" (*krama*); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of "far," "near," and so forth is intended.
In what is to be said— that which will be explained in the section on action (*kriyādhikāra*)— which consists in the sovereignty of the Lord (*īśvara-svātantrya*), that is,

the nature of His independent state known as the grasping of the diversity of forms and the diversity of actions belonging to the Supreme Lord; by those two powers of space and time, [the object] is fashioned (*upakalpita*).
It is established by the manifestation of its own limitedness. He explains the word "krama" (sequence) as "deśa" (space).

"Spatial-temporal succession"—that is, an arrangement such as "this one is situated in this place and belongs to this time," and so forth; by that, meaning by the sequence consisting of spatial-temporal succession. The word "rūṣitāḥ" (colored/affected).

He explains [the term] "reflection" (*pratibimba*). "By way of being like a reflection"—that is, by virtue of its similarity to a reflection—the "manifestation" (*pratibhā*) is "colored," meaning it is brought to the state of being an object of coloring, just as crystal and the like are colored by blue and so forth.
To the question "By whom was this said?", he supplies the missing word *uktā* ("said") as a supplement to the sentence. In response to the expectation of "by whom was it said?", he says:

"Kevalam" means "by this verse. He explains "eṣā" (this) with the words "sarvasya" (of all). "Sarvasya" means of the entire class of conscious beings; "of the nature of self-luminosity" means established through one's own self-awareness by virtue of being self-luminous. He explains the word "akrama" (without succession) with the words "paramārthataśca" (and in the ultimate sense).
Although [consciousness] appears to possess succession due to the influence of space and time at first sight, from the perspective of ultimate reality— that is, from the standpoint of truth—

and with the word "ca" (and) carrying the sense of "tu" (but), it is because, in ultimate reality, it flashes forth as being turned inward— meaning as being attached to the subject in the form "I know"—
and thus possesses the fitness for apprehension as "I."
Because its ultimate reality is pure luminosity— having the nature of pure light—

and because there is no differentiation— since differentiation caused by spatial and temporal limitations is impossible— it is "without succession," untouched by the sequence of space and time; for even when colored by blue and other objects, it remains stainless.

That which has as its form that very nature of consciousness— of awareness— which, like crystal and the like, possesses no internal limitation through contact with objects, whether in terms of space, time, or essential nature; for this very reason:
If it is so for the category of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whose nature is consciousness consisting of outward-directed illumination,
that its internal manifestation as "this, this" becomes infinite— consisting, as it were, of infinite conceptual constructions—
then what need is there to mention the case of the exceedingly pure *pratibhā* (intuitive flash), which is untouched by space and time?

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [indicates the end of the previous section]. Now, he explains the portion of the verse beginning with "the infinite form of consciousness" (*anantacidrūpaḥ*) by saying "that very same" (*saiva*).

Since pronouns are capable of assuming the gender of the object they refer to, it is not improper here to employ the feminine gender for the word *tat*, even though it was previously indicated in the aphorism in the masculine gender.

That very thing—*pratibhā* (intuitive insight) as described by its essential nature—is Maheśvara. The particle *eva* (only/very) is intended to exclude the notion that some external, particular deity imagined by the ignorant might be Maheśvara. In response to the inquiry "Of what kind is Maheśvara?", he applies the qualifiers of Maheśvara mentioned in the Sūtra, beginning with "non-existent" (*avidyamāna*).

He explains and analyzes the compound word beginning with *ananta* by stating "non-existent" (*avidyamāna*). He explains the word *anta* (end) as "limitation" (*pariccheda*). That very thing—namely, that consciousness itself—is what is implied by re-forming the analyzed word back into its compound state through the word "that" (*sā*). Of this...

In order to indicate that the term "the cognizer" (*pramātā*) is the cause with respect to the entire word [“samasta-pada”], he says “for this very reason” (*ata eva*). The meaning is: because [the Self] is of manifold forms (*anantarūpa*), for that reason. He explains the qualifier “the cognizer” as “outward-turned” (*bahirmukha*). “Outward-turned” means that which grasps [an object] as "this is a jar," by way of the "this-ness" (*idantā*).

Of that which has as its very nature (*svabhāva*) consciousness in the form of the *bindu*— which, by virtue of being the illuminator, is the light of the Other (*paraprakāśa*)— there is an end (*anta*), meaning the essential core, within the entire class of means of knowledge (*pramāṇavarga*),
with respect to every single manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*) among all infinite objective forms.

Regarding appearances, in the manner of "this is this"—in this way—it is infinite in its conceptualization (*anantakalpa*); although it is ultimately peaceful (*paramārthataḥ śāntatve*), it appears as if infinite to limited subjects. It consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpamaya*), because its existence is obtained through the exclusion of its counter-correlates (*pratiyogivyavaccheda*). Its essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśātmā*).

The nature of sound consists of mental constructs (*saṃskāra*), birth, memory, and objects; it is a collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—the group of cognitions that constitute the result.
Within that collection of means of valid cognition, there is the process of conjunction, disjunction, and repose, which includes:
establishing [objects] as having a single object, making them distinct objects, and [reflecting upon them] with the recognition "I am."
"Upon one's own wall" refers to the act of ascending; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of exclusion (*apohana*) is intended.
A "construct" (*kalpa*) is a mass of cognitions consisting of conceptualization and having the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);
therein, it is fully endowed with manifold forms of sovereignty, such as the joining, separating, and resting [of concepts].

The subject is said to consist of the pure reflective awareness of "I," which includes various states such as rest; therefore, the external manifestation of a jar— the internal conceptualization "this is a jar"— is accepted [as being essentially that same awareness].

Apprehension, and that nature of it—He is full of that sovereignty which is of manifold kinds; nevertheless, He is pure—not mixed with conceptual construction—which is the modification of the reflective awareness "I," meaning His very essence is the subject (*pramātṛ*). This refers again to that aforementioned subject.

"Parāmarśaḥ" means it is spoken; the word "bhaṇyate" (is spoken) is supplied as a remainder [of the sentence]. By this, it is indicated that the word *pramātṛ* (knower) ends in the agentive suffix *tṛc*.
The construction here is as follows: that intuition (*pratibhā*) which was previously stated by the Teacher, who is the agent—this...

The subject (*pramātā*) is Maheśvara—the subject whose nature is that of Maheśvara, which is to say, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is what is being stated; as for the specific application [of this principle], it is already clear and thus no further effort has been made [to explain it]. As it has been said:
"In the waking state, the objects of knowledge such as sound and touch appear distinct due to their diversity."
Therefore, being solitary, it does not differ from that consciousness, as they are of one single form.
Beginning with these words and ending with "this Self is supreme bliss, because it is the object of supreme love," it is likewise stated:
Thus, that supreme bliss is consciousness, and the self (ātman) is likewise of such a nature;
the identity of these two as the Supreme Brahman is taught in the Upaniṣads.

Thus [it is said]. However, let it suffice to note that while in the Vedāntas the pure essence of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) is the Supreme Lord, here it is so even when it is colored [by objective forms].
By this, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) resulting from this: "And therefore," because this reality has been stated in the verse.

For that reason, it becomes thus— this much alone constitutes the full nature of manifestation, that is, of pure manifestation; the sense is that this alone establishes subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*), which consists of supreme manifestation.
The primordial form "I" is the locus of rest for both of those; thus, this much is the full nature of light. || 1 ||
Right here, in order to demonstrate the logical proof, he first states the positive concomitance (anvaya):
"When entities become established within a single cognizer through the various gateways of their respective distinct cognitions, this state of being known (jñāteya) becomes logically possible. (2)

What is this extent? "Outside"—that is, in the external space—"this jar," which is the manifestation of the jar, or the perception of the jar; likewise "inside"—that is, in the space of the heart—the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that has assumed its prior form, having grasped the essential nature of the jar from a previous time, as well as "I. Of both of these—

The place of rest—the locus of dissolution—for the pair consisting of the manifestation of the jar and the conceptualization of the jar; by this, it is illuminated that the very worldly transaction "I see the jar" possesses the quality of being illumined by the full light. And this...
For those who have emerged from the state of being limited subjects such as the body, who have attained the fragrance of supreme illumination,

and who— until the duration of their bodily existence— are capable of touching that supreme illumination during the time of pure worldly transaction which must necessarily be resorted to; [though some manuscripts read "incapable of touching the supreme illumination"— C.]

This was stated specifically for the group of those who are awakened (*prabuddha*), because those who are unawakened— those who are always identified with and immersed in the state of being a subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the body and so forth— and even the "well-awakened" (*suprabuddha*), have no qualification here [in this context]. Furthermore, upon emerging from the state of being a subject consisting of the body and so forth, one's own mind itself [remains] as the witness (*sākṣitayā*).
It must be apprehended; otherwise, the fallacy of self-contradiction would ensue. Enough of this. || 1 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the second verse with the words "atraiva" (right here).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains:
"atraiva" means precisely when intuition (*pratibhā*) is the subject (*pramātṛ*); "upapattim" means the logical justification; "anvayam" means...

The meaning is: "only a *yojana*," that is to say, we shall explain the logical proof clearly immediately after this. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "tattat" (that and that).
As for the statement that "the determinations of objects are grounded in consciousness (*saṃvit*)," that is not of a different nature—

It is established not merely by resting in pure consciousness whose nature is valid cognition (*pramā*), but rather through those various distinct cognitions that are of the nature of ascertainment (*niścaya*) and constitute valid cognition (*pramā*); these are themselves the "faces," the "gateways," the "means," or the "paths.
If these entities—such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—are [perceived] through those faces, which are like the currents of rivers...
Being carried along, they come to rest within that single great ocean of supreme consciousness in the form of the subject, "I";
regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:

He establishes the method for explaining the verse with the words "consciousness" (*saṃvit*). "Established in consciousness" means existing as the foundation of consciousness; "the determinations of objects" refers to the boundaries of states such as blue, pleasure, and so forth; "of a differentiated form" means having a form that differs at every moment; and likewise—

Regarding "having the nature of valid cognition" (*pramātmakam*): it does not succeed by resting—that is, by finding repose—within that mere consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) which is considered by the Buddhists to be the self (*ātman*) and is their "cognition" (*vijñāna*). For at the time of apprehending blue, the apprehension of yellow does not succeed; and at the time of apprehending that [yellow], the apprehension of the former [blue] does not succeed. Moreover, the cognizer (*pramātā*) is distinct in both cases.

The sense is this: who could establish the essential nature of these two as distinct, since that is possible only for a single cognizer situated in one place who grasps both? In response to the expectation of how this is further established, he states another position and provides the construction of the compound word *tattat* with the words "api tu" (but rather).

He explains and analyzes this term with the words "those various [cognitions]. He explains the word *saṃvit* (consciousness) as "ascertainment," meaning they have the form of ascertainment, specifically the form of the ascertainment of blue, pleasure, and so forth; he explains that these very things—namely, consciousnesses themselves—are the "mouth," explaining it as "door. Furthermore, he states two synonyms for this very same term.

"Expedient means (upāya) are the paths (mārga)"—he thus provides the construction with the third case ending (*taiḥ*). "Resembling the current of a river" means similar to the flow of a river; for by them, grass and other things being carried along enter the ocean. Although not explicitly stated in the Sūtra, these are understood as an implied simile (*ārthopamāna*). This is the sense of the word.
He explains [the word] "blue" (*nīla*). Regarding "being carried away" (*uhyamānāḥ*): like grass and so forth in water, they are wandering helplessly;

knowing that for one who is stationary, the state of being established is inappropriate, the word "being carried away" has been supplied as an ellipsis. He explains and analyzes the phrase beginning with "in one" (*ekasmin*) as follows: "among those being carried away."
Having recognized their fitness for entering the ocean by way of the stream, they grasp the ocean;

that is, they rest primarily in the ocean of great consciousness—which is the ocean whose nature is the Great Light—as they become established therein. Therefore, that which consists of their mutual interconnection among them...

This state of being kinsmen (*jñāteya*) is established through logical reasoning; the nature of kinsmen (*jñātīnām bhāvaḥ*) is the ground for the application of that term, namely, that they should know one another.
Furthermore, kinship consists in the mutual bearing of each other's welfare and security (*yogakṣema*), and this is intended with reference to their interconnectedness (*samanvaya*).
This has been shown here in order to demonstrate that there is never, at any time, an inherent coordination among insentient things. || 2 ||

Thus he explains the word *pada* as *prati*. He explains the constituent part *prati* as "facing toward" (*ābhimukhyena*). He explains the verbal root-base ending in the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), namely *tiṣṭhat*, as "they take rest" (*viśrāntiṃ bhajante*).
This analysis is made by relying on the commonality of being a substitute for the *laṭ* [present tense] suffix, as in the case of "I see the jar."

For the jar, by means of the consciousness called "seeing," clearly finds its rest only in the supreme subject denoted by the word "I"; beyond that, it is submerged in the very nature of the "I. As for the fact that it may be seen again at a later time, that is merely the resting therein once more of that which had been previously severed. It is not [a new perception].

There is a contradiction. [The author] explains the phrase "therefore" (*tataḥ*) as follows: by means of the state characterized by the form of "establishing" (*pratitiṣṭhati*), he expresses the state characterized by the form of the "attainment of kinship" (*jñāteya-upapatti*), which constitutes the meaning of the locative case. "Therefore" (*tataḥ*) means: from that cause, which is that state; "in these"—that is, in these states—that "kinship," which is the relationship, "is established. This is the explanation of this [passage].

"It effects by way of rebirth" means that it fits or is appropriate. Regarding the term "kinship" (*jñāteya*), he says "of kinsmen" (*jñātīnām*) in order to derive it in the sense of a state (*bhāva*) or an action (*karman*). He states the meaning of the state expressed by the secondary suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) with the word "that" (*tat*); that is, the ground for the application of the word "that" (*tacchabda-pravṛtti-nimitta*).

The "ground for the application of the word *jñāti*" means that very property (*dharma*) by which the word *jñāti* is employed; this is the sense of "the state" (*bhāva*) here. In response to the inquiry as to what that ground for its application is, he repeats it, saying "mutually" (*parasparam*). The meaning is that the mutual cognition itself is the ground for the application of the word *jñāti*.

The meaning is as follows. Having stated the meaning of the abstract noun (*bhāva*), he states the meaning of the action (*karman*) with the words "and the action" (*karma ca*). The sense is that kinsmen not only know one another, but they also become intent on rendering assistance.
To the question, "But what is there here [in this context]? he replies with "And that" (*tac ca*). "And that"—namely, kinship (*jñāteya*)—is present "here," in this verse.

"It has been shown" means by way of secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for the ultimate point is that since entities are insentient, two primary meanings are not possible. To the question "Why should we not accept the primary meaning itself?", he says "No. This is for the purpose of demonstrating, that is to say, for the purpose of indicating this. || 2 ||

And thus, he expresses this very point by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka): "For objects that occur in a sequence of space and time and which terminate in themselves, this synthesis [of their diversity] is accomplished by a simultaneous manifestation; otherwise, what kind of synthesis could there be? (3)

For insentient objects, their cognitions, their conceptualizations, and their determinations—which do not abandon spatial sequence and temporal sequence and which are self-contained—meaning, established solely in their own nature—what connection could there be? None at all, is the sense; for such is the case.

Conjunction (*samanvaya*) can be accomplished through a simultaneous appearance (*sakṛdābhāsa*), which consists in the mixing of place, time, and form by means of a unifying appearance (*yojanābhāsa*); it cannot be otherwise. For indeed, when the currents have ceased one by one, the grasses, reeds, and other things being carried along by them do not achieve any kind of conjunction.

Regarding the word "go" (*yānti*): with the intention that there is a distinction of place, time, and so forth due to their multiplicity, the word "simultaneously" (*sakṛt*) is employed for the purpose of negating that [multiplicity]. || 3 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "And likewise" (*tathā ca*). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it, beginning with the word "place" (*deśa*).
Herein is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

He explains "of objects" (*arthānām*) as "of insentient things" (*jaḍānām*). "Insentient things" refers to forms such as blue, pleasure, and so forth; "their cognitions" (*tajjñānānām*) refers to the experiences of blue, pleasure, and so forth.

By the term "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*), recollection and other such mental states are also included. Furthermore, their status as objects (*arthatvam*) consists in being illuminated by another.

It should be understood that this is caused solely by the state of being an object of cognition (*prati-vedyatva*). He explains [the phrase] "of those which terminate in themselves" (*svasamāpinām*) as "in their own nature" (*svarūpe*).

When there is the expectation of why this is not so, he says "for since" (*yato hi*). He explains and analyzes the term "single appearance" (*sakṛdābhāsa*) as "place" (*deśa*). By means of the appearance of connection, [there is] non-difference from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*). In that very same way, [there is] difference.

The meaning is "because they are established"; that [connection] can be established. For the meaning is this: connection (*saṃbandha*) is indeed the joining by means of some commonality of blue and other things which exist as distinct through place, time, and form. He elaborates on the phrase "otherwise" with the words "for not," etc. *Samanvaya* means mutual conjunction.
In this regard, having raised the doubt as to what this "concomitance" (samanvaya) is, [the author] first demonstrates the relationship of cause and effect, which is more extensively pervasive:
"Of perceptions and non-perceptions that fall upon their respective distinct parts..."
The establishment of the relationship between cause and effect arises from a single cognizing subject.
In this case, one does not perceive smoke in the fire while it is present; then one perceives the smoke through direct perception.

However, if one does not perceive the fire, one does not perceive the smoke either—thus, from these five instances consisting of two perceptions and three non-perceptions, the causal relationship [is established].

As for what was said—that [the relationship] between smoke and fire is established—how is that so? For when fire is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nothing is inferred by means of smoke; nor is there anything [inferred] regarding fire.
Thus, at the conclusion of the elaboration of words, the word "once" (*sakṛt*) expresses the existence of the word itself.
"By way of multiplicity": by way of multiplicity—that is, through the multiplicity of appearances—there occurs a distinction of place, time, and so forth;

with this intention (*āśaya*), that is, with this underlying purpose (*abhiprāya*, namely the intent to negate that [distinction]), the word "simultaneously" (*sakṛt*) is employed in the Sūtra, with the aim of negating distinctions of place, time, and so forth.
The state of being. || 3 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the fourth verse with the words "tatra" (therein). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "pratyakṣa" (perception).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
"Here"—in this world of conventional experience—"one does not perceive [fire]" because of the absence of contact with moist fuel;
"then"—immediately after the direct perception of fire—due to the addition of moist fuel;
thus, from such a pentad of reasons. This means that the pervasion is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). In that regard:

The meaning is this: as for what has been stated by the logicians (*tārkika*) and others—namely, that in the method of agreement (*anvaya*), there are three [factors]: the perception of fire, the non-perception of smoke, and the perception of smoke;
whereas in the method of difference (*vyatireka*), there are two: the non-perception of fire and the non-perception of smoke—how can that be? That is not established. Why is it not established?

To this he says "Agni": nothing has been set aside—not even a trace of success has been granted. Anticipating the doubt as to why nothing has been set aside, he explains the phrase beginning with "the cause of success" by saying "in that which is characterized as fire.
That is to say, in that which is characterized as fire—in the mere nature of fire itself.

Because it is the cause of the comprehension of that [object] in its aspect distinct from smoke as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and because it rests upon its own nature in its distinct aspect, it does not penetrate other objects and does not enter into the nature of another cognition. *Pāti* signifies "making known," and *pati* is [the agent of that].
The word *viśrānti* (resting) is employed here by means of *tantra* (multiple application). The same should be stated regarding the fourfold [inference] beginning with the non-perception of smoke.

Consequently, these—namely, fire, the absence of smoke, smoke, the absence of fire, and the absence of smoke—are, in part, situated within the domain of the complete relationship between cause and effect; of that—

Because direct perception of fire is the cause of comprehension—that is, the cause of knowledge. He states the second meaning of this very word with the term "sva" (self). The meaning is: because it is the place of rest (*viśrāntatvāt*), that is, because it has been cast down (*pātitvāt*). When the question arises as to why this is so, he provides two reasons in sequence for these two points with the term "para" (other).

Because it does not penetrate the object-domain of another—namely, because it does not penetrate the smoke that is the object-domain of the cognition of smoke—and likewise because there is no entry—that is, no possibility of entry—into the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of that other cognition, which is the cognition of smoke.
Here, the word "ca" (and) indicates sequence rather than conjunction. The word "iti" [marks the end of the respective arguments].

Thus ends the analysis and explanation of the compound word as a whole. Now, one might ask: how can the constituent part *pātinām* possess two meanings—one being its literal sense and the other being its resting upon the state of being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*)? To this, he says: "The root *pāti*. The root *pāti* is the verbal root *patḷ* (to go) with the causative suffix *ṇic*; it signifies "making known" (*jñāpana*).

Since verbs meaning "to go" (gatyarthāḥ) denote "knowledge," and since in that context the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is employed to denote "making known," the root *pat*—this root alone—is expressive of "resting. For when one who is weary comes to rest, he indeed "falls" (*patati*). It is used in its aforementioned form, ending in the agentive suffix *ṇini*.

The meaning is "made the object of application. He extends this very principle to the other fourfold sets as well with the word "thus" (*evam*), the ellipsis being "because they share the same logic. For this very reason, there is the repetition (*vīpsā*) "tat-tat" in the Sūtra.
To explain the second half [of the verse], he establishes the procedure with the words "and therefore" (*tataśca*). And therefore—
For this reason, just as fire, the absence of smoke,

smoke, the absence of fire, and the absence of smoke— these entities, though perceived separately by individual cognizers, do not [in themselves] constitute the causal relationship between smoke and fire.

In the same way, they are made known by a single cognizer; even conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), when it makes known something beyond direct experience, is not itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, when those five objects have been brought to rest within the ocean of a single consciousness by the fivefold stream of perception and non-perception, they then become one.

Since these [entities] are manifested by the subject through its sovereignty as mutually dependent, and not like jars, cloths, and so forth, that single manifestation (sa eva eka ābhāsaḥ) is the manifestation of the relation of cause and effect; thus there is nothing faulty. || 4 ||

These are the entities— the fivefold group of entities that constitute the objects of the two types of direct perception and the three types of non-perception— which, while being objects of cognition for a cognizer distinct [from the subject], have attained the state of being cognized;
yet they do not bring about the causal relationship between smoke and fire, for [the cognizer] does not perceive the fire as apprehended by another.
The meaning is that another [person] perceives smoke as having fire as its cause, or that [fire] is perceived as having smoke as its effect.

Even when there is a single cognizer, the objects of knowledge themselves do not lead to the cognition of that [cognizer], even though they rest within him; thus he says "tathā" (so). Now, one might object: by means of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) alone, [one can know] fires and other things that are objects of knowledge for different cognizers.

"Let there be the apprehension of the relation between cause and effect, for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has no lack of power anywhere, since it functions even with respect to an object that is undermined by impossibility. To this he says: "Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) also... Here, the Buddhist doctrine is adopted for its utility. Now, if that is so, how can the causal relation perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) [be established]?

It is established; therefore, he says "but when" (*yadā tu*). But when those five objects are made to rest within the single ocean of consciousness—just as [the waves] rest in the ocean—by means of the pentad of direct perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), which stands in the place of the current of a river, that is, by the pentad beginning with direct perception, then...

They exist as unified— that is, they are in motion— by means of the subject (*pramātṛ*), who is the support of all and the grasper; through his own independent and unimpeded power of freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) abiding within himself,
they are manifested as mutually joined and interdependent, and not like jars, cloths, and so forth.

They appear as independent; that single manifestation—the manifestation consisting of the union of the two—is the manifestation of the relation of cause and effect, that is, the manifestation in the form of causality.
Thus, there is nothing faulty; the meaning is that it is not afflicted by any defect whatsoever. || 4 ||
[Objection: But surely that which is established through perception and non-perception will be unified by the power of memory.
[Response: It has already been stated in this regard—that memory also does not operate upon an object beyond what was experienced;
and that [memory] too, being of the nature of a continuity of cognition, cannot exist without the presence of a single cognizing subject.
He shows how this would be so:

"In the case of memory, that very self-awareness which is the means of valid cognition regarding its own occurrence is itself the proof for the existence of the prior experience, and nothing else. (5)

In memory, an object previously experienced appears; in that case, this memory is not a new manifestation of the object, but rather its manifestation is precisely that former experience itself, and that experience—
Now he provides the introduction to the fifth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"That which was done"—namely, the perception (*upalambha*) of the pentad beginning with fire—which has been performed, will be unified.

The word "by the knower" (*pramātrā*) is to be supplied [as the agent]. The Guru gives the answer here with the words "it has been said": "here"—meaning in this matter—"previously"—this is to be supplied—"[in the case of] that which is distinct from what was previously experienced"—meaning different from what was experienced before—"that too"—meaning even memory—"of the two cognitions"—meaning of the two knowledges belonging to the time of memory and the time of the original experience—"which... [is the connection].

*Sam anvayaḥ* means conjunction, that is to say, the act of making [two things] have a single object; she whose nature (*rūpa*) is such is *tādṛśī*. This he shows; the meaning is that he demonstrates this very point.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse with the words "In memory" (*smṛtau*).

Here the commentary says: "The experienced" means previously experienced; "the object" refers to a jar or the like; "therein" (tatra) means while that [object] exists; this memory is not a new manifestation of the object, but rather [a manifestation] of this...
That manifestation of the object— which is a manifestation in the form of memory— is indeed the former experience itself, because they share the same object;
since it consists of the nature of knowledge, it lacks the nature of an object of knowledge, and thus it is not cognizable by another cognition, but rather—

It is self-luminous; and if it were non-existent at the time of recollection, how could it be manifest? Or, even if it were so, the manifestation of recollection and the manifestation of the original experience would be two distinct and mutually separate pairs, and thus recollection would never occur. Therefore, this is established as follows: that which is the self-awareness of recollection [is the very nature of consciousness].

That alone is the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of experience; however, no other means of knowledge—neither perception distinct from self-awareness nor inference and so forth—can operate therein. Consequently, it is established that the very self-awareness which persists for that duration as an uninterrupted unity is the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*). As stated elsewhere:
And that prior experience, having become the nature of memory within the experiencer,
does not become cognizable by another cognition because it lacks the nature of an object of knowledge due to its being of the nature of consciousness; for the power of vision is self-luminous.

The sense is: "according to the principle thus stated"; rather, [consciousness] is self-luminous—having the nature of shining by itself toward itself—and that [experience], if it were non-existent at the time of recollection, how could it shine? For the shining of a hare's horn is never observed; such is the sense.

Or let it be so, meaning "let it exist"; nevertheless—even while possessing a novel mode of manifestation—a manifestation in the form of memory (*smṛti-prakāśa*) and a manifestation in the form of direct experience (*anubhava-prakāśa*) would not be mutually distinct, that is, independent of one another. They would not [be so].

The sense is that there is an absence of a unifier (*yojaka*). He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). "Thus" (*evam*) means in this manner; "this" (*etat*) refers to the occurrence of memory. When the expectation arises as to how this is so, he explains the Sūtra in response to it with the words "that which... (*yadeva*). [In the commentary] there are two terms: "in memory" (*smṛtau*) and "self-awareness" (*svasaṃvittiḥ*).

He explains [the term] "recollection" (*smṛti*). In recollection, there is self-awareness—self-awareness that constitutes its own nature, which is "recollection-self-awareness. He states what is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*) with the words "but not" (*na tu*):
that which is distinct from self-awareness—that is, distinct from the awareness that constitutes its own nature. In that regard—in such [recollection].
In the *Smṛti*, it proceeds— that is, it prevails— to the extent that it pervades the duration of time delimited by memory; thus,

it is "pervading for that long," meaning self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is the awareness of both the memory and the experience, up until the point of the awareness that brings about the state of being.

One might object: "Has the proof of the cognizer not already been established previously through memory? Why, then, has this effort been undertaken again, which is like grinding what has already been ground? To this, he says: "Elsewhere," that is, with respect to the experiencer.

The proof of the subject (*pramātṛ*) was previously stated by means of this shadow-like memory, namely that "no other cognizer is possible"; however, the distinction here is that it is now presented through another method, by way of unification with self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). || 5 ||
Now, one might object: "Even regarding an object that transcends direct experience, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) may indeed be valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

for invalidity arises through the force of sublation (*bādha*), and in the absence of sublation, how could that [invalidity] occur? Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies]: "Furthermore, this very relationship between the sublated and the sublator exists for the sake of distinguishing between the real and the unreal."
[K. ṣ. ṣ. He demonstrates in detail that the very lifeblood of all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) cannot be established without the single reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*):
"Even the relationship between the sublated and the sublator [exists] among those things that contradict one another while being grounded in their own self..."
Because all cognitions arise and culminate in a single cognizer. || 6 ||

When one thing exists, another cannot be the rememberer; this is not established through logical possibility (*upapatti*), for it is never observed that one person remembers what was seen by another—this is the sense. By means of this shadow—that is, this formulation—with memory as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the establishment of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) has been stated and explained.

But now—in this verse, however—the establishment of the subject (*pramātṛ*) through recollection is stated by way of a different formulation—that is, by way of another method consisting in the unity of one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is the very essence.
Such is the distinction; and thus, the sense is that there is no suspicion of redundancy.
Thus, the summary here is as follows: that very self-awareness which occurs in memory is the essential self-reflexive awareness;

it serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the manifestation and the maintenance of its own nature—which is called memory—when it arises within itself, and that same self-awareness [serves as the proof] regarding the existence of the prior experience.
The means for the manifestation and retention of prior experience was valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

there was no other [means], such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, because those are incapable in that regard. Thus, the sense is that the establishment of the single cognizer known as self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is proven. || 5 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "nanvanubhava" (But surely, experience...).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"By that which is the differentiation—the act of making a distinction—between the real and the unreal."
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it:
"The sublated and the sublator. This refers to that which must necessarily be established for the sake of the principle that validity [of cognition] exists only in the absence of sublation (*bādhā*).

The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is: how can even that conventional usage of "sublation" (*bādha*) be explained? In this case, no such thing as the sublation of silver by mother-of-pearl is observed;
nor is it logical to say that the cognition of silver is sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl, [considering] with respect to its own object and its own nature.
Because there is no mutual contradiction between two cognitions that are fully established and at rest;
for if this very contradiction were of the nature of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*),
then all cognitions would be contradictory to one another.
Regarding *bādhyabādhaka* (the sublated and the sublator), the commentary (*ṭīkā*) here first states the meaning of the word as "in the absence of sublation" (*bādhābhāve*). For this purpose—

For the sake of the validity of knowledge (*jñānaprāmāṇya*), that which must necessarily be established—meaning it must necessarily be proven—is also how [it is established]: namely, without being grounded in a single cognizer (*ekapramātṛ*). This is the meaning. The word "also" (*api*) has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Having thus explained the meaning of the word "also," he proceeds to explain the verse.

"It performs the process here"—it is not seen; therefore, the sense is that in the Sūtra, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is specified as belonging exclusively to cognitions. "Even this"—the relationship of the sublated and the sublator among cognitions mentioned in the Sūtra—is also "not tenable," meaning it is not logical. Why?

In response to this inquiry, he connects the term *svātmaniṣṭhā* as a qualifier containing a reason (*hetugarbha*), and explains it by first analyzing its grammatical compound (*vigraha*) with the words "in itself" (*svasmin*). He states that the meaning of the constituent part *sva* is "with respect to the object," which means "in one's own object. He then explains the constituent part *ātman* as "in its own nature" (*svarūpe*).

Since the word *ātman* denotes its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), he explains the term *niṣṭhā* as "of the two [states] that have come to rest. By this, the analysis of the compound is shown to be: "those which are established in their own self and are non-contradictory.
The use of the plural number here is indicated as being based on the intention to express the absence of contradiction between the two [states] themselves.

Now he states the second meaning of this very statement with the word "atha" (now/if). "Atha" means: if this contradiction of cognitions consists solely in mutual exclusion—that is, in reciprocal non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)—such that the cognition of mother-of-pearl does not become the cognition of silver; this is the sense. "Tahi" means: in that case, for all...
Because of the contradiction between cognitions— since contradiction is established by the non-deviation from mutual exclusion—

and because the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is the subject under discussion, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is firmly established within the nature of the entity itself.

Since even finality itself cannot be attained, the distinction between the real and the unreal would utterly collapse. Nor, moreover, should this be explained by means of the *tantra* (the system). This is what is meant: if cognition perishes by itself, then what is the use of another cognition? For that [other cognition], being non-existent at that time, cannot [perceive] its object.

"Establishment in one's own self" means a fixed state of abiding; the phrase "is not obtained" is supplied as a supplement to this [statement], meaning that it does not become obtainable. Here, the plural number refers to the primary subject itself. Now, one might ask: how is this meaning appropriate here? To this he says: "not even" (*nañ api*). "In this"—that is, in this context—"by way of *tantra*."

It should be explained by means of a "tantra" (multifunctional) commentary—which, like a lamp, remains present and simultaneously provides assistance for everything—not merely by this fragment of a verse ending with "of the cognitions" alone; rather, the meaning of the word "api" (also) is that even the negative particle (*nañ*) should be extracted by the intellect and explained through the *tantra* method. In that regard, concerning the first part [of the verse]:

It should be explained as "of non-contradictory [factors]," because they are compounded with the word *virodhi* (contradictory). However, in the second sense, having mentally extracted [the meaning] from that, it should be explained as "not of contradictory [factors]. Otherwise, there would be no connection with the supplied word *labhyāḥ* (are obtainable). And thus, the construction here is as follows: of cognitions...

The relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) also arises solely from the reason of being established within a single cognizer—that is, from resting within a single cognizer. When the question "Why? arises, the qualifying phrase "of those things that contradict [their] abiding in their own self" contains the underlying reason. For these cognitions do not rest in their own objects or in their own essential nature alone.

The meaning is that they are, therefore, by nature prone to deviate from other objects and from their own essential nature. Furthermore, it is not logical for things that are not mutually contradictory to stand in a relationship of sublated and sublator;
however, when they rest within a single cognizing subject, such a relationship established by them is indeed logical.
The sense is that the nature of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is thereby acquired.

Furthermore, within this very context of dependence, the word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied; for since those things which are mutually contradictory—possessing a contradiction characterized by the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) and by a nature that is invariably non-deviant—are without distinction [in this regard].
Belonging to all cognitions, there is a transformation of case endings according to the requirements of the sense;

the state of being the sublated and the sublator is established within itself—the determination of the sublated and the sublator according to their respective natures in the form: "this is the sublated" and "this is the sublator."
The word "attainable" (*labhyā*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. That relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) cannot [arise] from that [source].

Rather, it must arise as established within a single cognizer (*ekapramātṛpariniṣṭhita*); for only when it is grounded in a single cognizer is it logical that the relationship of the sublated and the sublator, by virtue of his sovereignty (*svātantrya*), should be established within himself.

The intention is that even the relationship between the sublated and the sublator (bādhyabādhakabhāva) indeed acquires its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). It is possible to provide a summary of the portion of the verse ending with "of the cognitions" (*jñānānām*) as explained: even the cognition "it is not silver" [establishes] its own absence of silver.

If [the cognition] were to take the object as its domain, it would not sublate the cognition of silver. Furthermore, even if one holds the position that it is destroyed by another cognition, since this same process applies to all cognitions, how could it be that only some specific one is sublated? This is so when both the cognition of silver and the cognition of mother-of-pearl [are present].

This is established when [all cognitions] come to rest in a single self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). For instance, even though cognitions come to rest within the single reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*), because they are extremely difficult to comprehend, he promises to state the meaning once more in brief with the words "this. What has been said?

Anticipating the student’s question as to how this can be so, he says "yadi" (if). "Knowledge"—that is, the knowledge of silver—perishes; the point is that it lasts for only a single moment. It is [sublated] by another cognition, such as "this is mother-of-pearl" or "this is not silver," by means of some other cognition. [Objection: Well then, what of this?
Because it effects the removal of the object, he says "for not" (*na hi*). By that—by another cognition—at that time—the moment of the cognition of silver. [Objection:
But let the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl," being restricted solely to the apprehension of the mother-of-pearl itself, not remove its object; it does not [remove] the silver.

Since the cognition "it is not silver" indeed removes [the previous cognition], he says: "not silver. For the cognition "not silver" has as its object precisely the absence of silver, not silver itself; thus, how could there be a removal? This is the sense. Even assuming that there is destruction, he says: "even so" (*athāpi*). In that case as well—that is, even under that alternative—[the following applies].
How could even a single cognition— namely, the cognition of silver— possibly exist [as valid], given that not all cognitions can occur simultaneously?
Since a subsequent cognition necessarily destroys the preceding cognition,
it would follow that all cognitions are sublated, not merely those concerning mother-of-pearl.

The sense is that this applies specifically to the cognition of silver. Having thus provided a brief explanation of the meaning, he explains the remaining portion of the verse beginning with "udiyāt" (when it arises) with the words "yadā tu" (but when). In "svasaṃvedane"—that is, in the subject whose nature is self-awareness—"etat" refers to the relationship of the sublated and the sublator among cognitions.

In response to the inquiry "How so?", he begins the justification with "For it is thus" (*tathā hi*). "That"—namely, repose—is "experienced," that is, it is felt. This refers to the two cognitions which have reached their culmination in both the qualifier and the qualified; while resting—that is, while partaking in the repose in the form "I see."

The sense is that [the two] rest— that is, attain repose— by means of that mutual appearance of connection, which consists in the production of a cognition qualified by itself; for otherwise, the cognition of the relationship between qualifier and qualified would be impossible.

Not through a lack of mutual embrace, but rather through its very variety, does that repose become experienced; for instance, in the cognitions "this is blue" and "this is a lotus," which come to rest in the subject (pramātṛ) by means of the appearance of their mutual coloring.

For one who rests [in this state], there occurs the knowledge "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth" without mutual contact; or the knowledge "this is mother-of-pearl" and "this is not silver," which effects the uprooting of the knowledge "this is silver" by destroying its persistence in the form of the cognitive activity consisting of the valid cognition (*pramā*) of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
thereby establishing itself in the subject (*pramātṛ*).

It partakes [of this]. Thus, in cases such as the relationship between cause and effect, a variety of restings that are impossible within the objective domain (*prameya*) is constructed by the subject (*pramātṛ*) through its own sovereignty; for that very reason, it must be said that this bestows sovereignty upon the act of cognition (*pramā*). In this way, within a single subject, [the state] of a prior cognition...

By "mutual independence" (parasparānapekṣayā), for indeed no mutual dependence whatsoever is observed between a jar and a cloth; this [term] is also connected here with the word "rests" (viśrāmyati). For sometimes, when there is the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the sublation arises as "this is mother-of-pearl," while at other times it is "this is not silver. Or so it is said.

The application of the word is [to the cognition] "silver"; the meaning is that it refers to the cognition manifested with respect to the object that is actually mother-of-pearl. "Uprooting" means destruction. He provides his own explanation of this with the words "tadīya" (belonging to that):

"tadīyā" means that which belongs to the silver, namely the valid cognition consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśātmakapramā*), which is of the nature of *parāmarśa* (synthetic judgment); [the compound means] having that as its form.
The persistence— that is, the subsequent following— of that activity [of error] therein; its destruction— that is, its annihilation— is brought about by, on the contrary,
persisting in an activity consisting of a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose nature is a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) related to the mother-of-pearl, which is the opposite of that [error].

"Performing the establishment"—that is, the repose in the form described. He extends this very principle to the entire range of relations, such as the relation of cause and effect, by means of the word "thus.
"Impossible regarding the object of knowledge"—meaning, initially, it is undermined by its impossibility in the case of insentient objects of knowledge. Therefore...
For this very reason—namely, because of its being a creation—it bestows sovereignty upon this subject—that is, it brings forth his sovereignty. It must necessarily be stated;
by this, it is declared that all relations have their very life-force in the sovereignty of the subject, otherwise [they would appear] merely superficially.
In insentient objects, which in the ultimate sense are of the nature of pure consciousness and remain each in its own abode, what connection can there be? As it has been said:
"The form of entities in their own abode is the truth; anything else is false."

Thus [it is said]. And here there is a requirement for the word *yat* (which) found in the preceding sentence; and so, that form which entities possess in their own home—that is, in their own abode consisting of the state within pure light (*śuddhaprakāśa*)—that is the real, the ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). Whatever else exists, produced by the subject through his own conceptualization, that is false (*mṛṣā*).

And in this regard, although even for the cognizer there is a state of certainty established through the exclusion of truth only within his own home, the conventional usage of the "sublated" and the "sublator" is thus justified; for indeed, like blue and other objects, those [cognizers] as well—
That very Supreme Lord, by virtue of His absolute freedom, causes worldly transactions to appear; therefore, they too are indeed real. || 6 ||
Nevertheless, this is established by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (daṇḍāpūpikā-nyāya) and does not require further effort; thus, enough.

He provides the conclusion with the word "evam" (thus). By the "avoidance" (*parivarjana*)—that is, by the freedom (*svātantrya*) of the subject (*pramātṛ*)—of the "prior cognition," namely the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl which appeared previously.
"By its eradication," [it means] having become the object of certainty;
"the state" refers to the nature of the cognition of mother-of-pearl. "Thus" means for this reason; "established" means proven by logical reasoning (*upapatti*).
Now, one might ask: how is delusive cognition shown here by this? To this he says: "like blue and so forth."

Thus: even those transactions—meaning even those transactions consisting of erroneous cognition (*bhrama-jñāna*) and so forth—he alone [is the agent], namely, he who is considered the creator of true cognition (*satya-jñāna*) and the rest. "From that" (*tat*); for that reason, "even those"—meaning even those transactions consisting of erroneous cognition and so forth. The word "iti" marks the end of the explanation. This...

[The opponent says: "Existence! If the entire multitude of entities, whether considered real or unreal, is perceived as having the nature of light (*prakāśa*), then everything without distinction is indeed ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). But if they are perceived as mere entities (*bhāvatayā*), then everything is indeed ultimately unreal;
so what room is there for the suspicion of unreality regarding erroneous cognition? (6)
Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "here" (*atra*).
Here, anticipating the opinion of another which he intends to refute, he says:
"Just as the cognition of a bare ground is the cognition of the absence of a jar..."
And likewise, the cognition of mother-of-pearl is the knower of the invalidity of the cognition of silver. (7)

In this case, the cognition of mother-of-pearl, by cognizing its own self, understands its own nature as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*)— according to the principle that "it determines that [object]"—
and the exclusion of others is inseparable from that determination; thus, [there is the exclusion] of that which consists in the cognition of what is not mother-of-pearl.

The cognition of the invalidity of the knowledge of silver is said to be precisely that cognition of the validity [of the knowledge] which is non-different from the cognition of the mother-of-pearl; nor is this anything new here— the commentary states:
In this regard—on this subject—the "opinion of others" refers to the Buddhist view.
To the question "For what purpose does he raise this doubt?", he says: "I shall refute," meaning with the intent of refutation.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse, beginning with the word *vivikta*.
Here the commentary says:

"In this world"—that is, in this context—"the cognition of mother-of-pearl" refers to the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl," which has as its object the mother-of-pearl that was previously made the object of the cognition of silver; [it cognizes] its own self...

The nature of the cognition of mother-of-pearl— its own essential form— is brought by consciousness (*saṃvit*) into the state of being an object of self-awareness through its self-luminosity; it is cognized as its own inherent status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatva*), which exists as non-different from its own self, just like the self itself.
Why? Because of the principle that "it delimits that," meaning because of this reason stated by the Buddhists.
And it is "invariably concomitant with the delimitation of that"—that is, it is never found apart from the delimitation of its own nature as that [object].
Exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) means the exclusion of the cognition of silver that does not possess that [shell’s] form. As it has been said:

"It exists as delimited by that [object], and it exists as delimited by the cognition of other [objects]. For this reason, [the exclusion] of that which consists of the cognition of what is not shell...
With respect to the cognition of mother-of-pearl,

the awareness of its being non-means-of-valid-cognition (apramāṇatva-vedana)— that is, the knowledge of its invalidity— is precisely what the learned call the awareness of validity that is non-different from the cognition of the mother-of-pearl.
The cognition of its being a valid means of knowledge is non-different from the cognition of the mother-of-pearl;
indeed, the cognition of one thing is itself the cognition of the absence of another thing,
for the perception of a bare patch of ground is itself the perception of the absence of a jar.

"It is well known that there arises the cognition of the absence of a jar" (K. ṣ. ṣ.). In this way, the very awareness of the invalidity of the cognition of silver is called its sublation; and thus, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is established.
If this is argued, we reply: "Is that [identity] due to the oneness of the cognizer? (7)
In this context, while intending to establish the reality of the conventional usage of non-existence as a corollary,
he first refutes the illustrative example found in the opponent's system: "The fact that the place is not a jar cannot be established merely through the cognition of a bare spot."
But it is not the case that the nature of the jar, though capable of being perceived, is absent here.

This is unprecedented—a novel point being set forth: namely, that for this reason, the cognition of one thing is itself the cognition of the absence of another thing, because the determination of that [thing] is possible only through the exclusion of what it is not (*atadvyavaccheda*). The word "iti" is intended to indicate the conclusion of the illustrative statement.
At the conclusion of the commentary on the second half [of the verse], he explains the first half— which expresses the corroborative example— in order to state that supporting illustration,
saying "pure" (*śuddha*). For— since—
the apprehension of a pure portion of ground is precisely the apprehension of a portion of ground devoid of a jar.

The apprehension of the absence of a jar occurs; however, the apprehension of the absence of a jar does not consist in the apprehension of some independent entity called "absence. In this way, it becomes well-established that the application [of the example] to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*)—which was indicated in the aphorism by the words *yathā* and *tathā*—is as follows here.

This has been established solely by way of the relationship between cause and effect. [Objection: But what follows from this regarding the relationship between the sublated and the sublator? To this he says: "In this way" (*evam*). "The cognition of invalidity" (*apramāṇatvasaṃvedanam*) means precisely the knowledge of invalidity. He states the conclusion: "And therefore" (*ataśca*).
