"In this way" (*evam*) means by this method.

Siddham—meaning "accomplished"; *iti*—meaning "thus"; *cet*—if; *asmābhiḥ*—by us, those who resemble Buddhists; it explains that whatever object is required by the word *cet* (if), even if not explicitly stated in the Sūtra, is [to be understood] as a supplement (*śeṣa*).

In that case, what would happen to the relationship between the sublated (*bādhya*) and the sublator (*bādhaka*) through the identity of the cognizer (*pramātṛaikyena*), even without that [relationship]?
The meaning is that because it is already established, nothing further occurs. || 7 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the words "here" (*atra*).

It is not only the example that was stated; why is this so? If one asks this, it is said: here, in the case of "there is no jar on the ground," non-existence may sometimes be treated as identity (*tādātmyena*), and sometimes as difference (*vyatirekeṇa*)—as in "on this ground."

Regarding the statement "there is no jar": this first type of conventional usage is established through the cognition of the bare ground, wherein visibility is not a factor— namely, that which by its very nature lacks the conditions for apprehension, such as a *piśāca* or the like, or that which lacks a grasper, such as sound and so forth.
Here the commentary says:
"By way of a relevant illustration"—meaning by way of taking it as an example—"the reality," that is, the ultimate truth;
"in the system of others"—namely, in the Buddhist doctrine—having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse.
He explains: "It is not so. Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"He explains 'it is not so' as follows. This is said in order to fulfill the promise (*pratijñā*).

He explains the first half of the verse beginning with *śuddha* by saying "here" (*iha*). "By way of identity" (*tādātmyena*) means through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*); the meaning is: at times, for the purpose of establishing the nature of the ground, when there is the apprehension of the absence of identity. "At times" (*kadācit*) means at the time of apprehending the absence of a jar on the ground.

"By way of distinction"—that is, by way of grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*), the connection with the preceding clause is "the absence is to be treated [as such]. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*), the meaning is "between the two types of linguistic usage. "From the cognition of the pure ground"—that is, from the cognition of the ground devoid of a jar—"the first" [is established].

The nature of which is the absence of identity; "discourse" means the discourse regarding non-existence. In that—namely, in the first case of the discourse regarding the absence of identity—visibility—the state of necessarily being capable of being perceived by the knower of the absence—is not useful—that is, it does not serve any purpose.
For when the true nature of the ground is established, the absence of the identity of everything else— the entire range of perceivable objects such as jars,

or even imperceptible things like *piśāca* spirits— is apprehended without distinction, on the grounds of their being remote in terms of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭatva*) and so forth; however, this is not the case for the absence of relation (*saṃsargābhāva*) in the "here" of the ground according to the [opponent's] own doctrine.

The meaning is that "it does not exist" refers only to such visible things as a jar (*ghaṭa*) and the like, and not to invisible things such as a *piśāca* demon; this is the intended sense. Here, he himself provides the justification with the words "because of perception" (*upalabdhi*). For (*hi*), because perception itself is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

The uncommon property is its attainment— its acquisition, which means its fitness for perception among sentient beings. That [attainment] occurs by the power of its own nature— that is, by virtue of having such an intrinsic nature—
which certain beings, such as *piśācas*, do not possess.

Because the completeness of the causal complex consisting of the auditory organ and so forth is not ascertained there— due to the absence of the cognition of another object associated with that single cognition— this non-existence of that [complex] is also established through identity (*tādātmya*).

[Non-existence is conventionally apprehended—K. ṣ. ṣ. The ground is perceived, but not a *piśāca* (demon), for even if a *piśāca* or the like were present, it would not be perceived because of its such nature; or—in the alternative case—the "apprehender of that" refers to the completeness of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of the auditory organ and so forth, which is the apprehender of sound. In that regard:

At that time of perceiving the pure ground, by that very same cognition— which, through its totalizing function, at another time grasps the counter-correlate of the absence of everything else— that other entity which is a "related thing" (saṃsargin),
meaning that which is being related to it and which becomes its object— [is perceived].

Because of the absence— due to the non-existence or the lack of certainty— of any cognition whatsoever of an object in the form of sound and so forth, which is produced by the vibration of internal vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the like;
for at that time, there is no means of apprehension for that sound and so forth which has not attained the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).

This means that for whatever object there is no fitness for perception; by the two uses of the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the auditory organ and the other sense organs, as well as the inclusion of objects other than sound which are grasped by them. Of that too—of such things as a *piśāca* who is remote by nature, and who is remote from the causal complex of the perceiving instrument.
And because of the word "also" (*api*) [in the original], there is the inclusion of the entire class of things that have reached the conditions for perception;

this absence is apprehended through identity—that is, by way of being of the same nature, which is to say, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In response to the question "Where? he provides an example: "the ground" (*bhūtala*); by this, [he indicates] the ground's...
The state of being the absence of Piśācas and so forth is precisely what is expressed through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). This is the point:
when a person perceives an object, he perceives it as distinct from everything else;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of confusion, and perception as distinct from everything else is, in effect, the result.
The apprehension of the non-existence of everything other than that [object] involves two kinds of "everything else": that which is capable of being perceived and that which is incapable.

Among these, some things are remote by nature (*svabhāva-viprakṛṣṭa*), such as *piśācas* and the like, or atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like; however, some are remote due to the lack of means for apprehension (*grahaṇopāya-viprakṛṣṭa*), namely those things that are currently being perceived—
That which does not attain the status of an object due to the deficiency of the causal complex of the perceiver (*grāhakasāmagrī*) is of two kinds—namely, that which is unfit for perception;

however, that which is fit for perception is of only one kind, because in its case both types of remoteness—the remoteness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviprakarṣa*) and the remoteness of means (*upāyaviprakarṣa*)—are absent, as otherwise it would be impossible for it to be perceived. Thus [it is said].

It is quite clear that from the knowledge of the pure locus—meaning from the knowledge of the locus alone—the non-pot-nature of that locus is established; that is, the absence of all objects such as pots and so forth is established.
As for the word "sound": however, where visibility (*dṛśyatva*) is necessarily required as a qualification, there [it is established] by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
When non-existence is to be expressed, this is not the appropriate means. || 8 ||
If it is asked, "Why?", we reply: "Because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). He demonstrates this very point:
"The ground is eternally distinct [from objects], because all entities abide within their own selves.
Therefore, how could the cognition of that [ground] ever establish the non-existence of something distinct? (Verse 9)

Having thus explained the first half [of the verse], he says "But where... in order to elaborate upon the second half, which concerns the distinction expressed by the word "but" (*vyatirekeṇa*). "But where"—that is, in that second case of the conventional usage of non-existence, namely, the conventional usage of relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*); for non-existence is indeed...

In brief, it is of two kinds: non-existence through identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) and non-existence through relation (*saṃsargābhāva*). "Perceptibility" (*dṛśyatva*) is the qualifier; that is, the qualifier consisting in the fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) is useful, otherwise [the inference would fail] in the case of things like *piśācas*, which, though present there, are remote by nature.

The point is that this would result in sound and other such things— which are remote from the causal complex of a perceiver— also becoming objects of non-existence. In that case— in regard to that non-existence, which is to be treated as an object of linguistic usage (*vyavahāraviṣaya*) by way of exclusion (*vyatirekeṇa*), that is, by way of its difference from the ground in the form of being a locus situated upon the ground— this:
The means consisting in the perception of a mere patch of ground is not a means for apprehending the absence of everything other than that; for by the apprehension of the bare ground alone,
the absence of anything situated there cannot be asserted, since even an invisible entity such as a *piśāca* might still be present there.

The intended meaning is that [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of it becoming an object of the conventional usage of non-existence. The construction here is as follows: "of the nature of a jar" (ghaṭātmanaḥ)—that is, of the essential form of a jar—even though it is "capable of being perceived"—that is, even though it has reached the conditions for perception—there is its "non-existence" here on this ground, due to the cognition of the bare ground.

The meaning of the word "api" (also/even) is this: if [non-existence] were established [in that way], what need would there be for a discussion regarding the establishment of the non-existence of things such as *piśācas* that have met the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*)? For other disputants indeed establish the non-existence of what is fit for perception through the cognition of a bare ground; however, even that is not accepted by us. || 8 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the ninth verse with the words "kutaḥ" (from what?).
Here the commentary says:
"From what? From what cause would the non-existence of the jar-nature not be established?"—if this is asked, [the answer is as follows].

If you say that, we reply: "Because it would lead to an over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgāt*); the sense is that the very fact of over-extension is the reason here. Anticipating the student's question, "Of what nature is this over-extension?", [the author] says, "That very [thing]" (*tameva*). The sense is: "The author of the Sūtras himself will demonstrate it; why then should we strive?"
Even when a jar is present, the ground remains purely [empty]; for entities do not intermingle.

Consequently, even then, there is knowledge of the pure ground; so, even while the jar exists, why is its absence—not as a distinct entity—expressed in the form "there is no jar on this ground," and why is that knowledge [of absence] not admitted?

The cognition of a portion of the ground as being secluded establishes the absence of a distinct jar— meaning its non-existence— only at a certain time, namely in a state characterized by the jar's non-proximity, and not at all times; in what manner [is this so]?
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it, beginning with the word "viviktam" (secluded).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains the word "śaśvat" (always) as "vidyamāne 'pi" (even though it exists); by the force of the word "api" (even), it implies "but [when] not existing."
"Evermore" (*tarām*) means "constantly" (*śaśvat*), that is, eternally; he explains "separate" (*viviktam*) as "pure" (*śuddham*).

"Pure indeed" means "abiding in its own essential nature alone. To the question "Why?", he explains the phrase "because entities are established in their own self" with the words "for not... [they] become mixed.

The meaning is that they become intermingled; the implication is that, in that case, even a cloth would have to be grasped for the purpose of fetching water. And therefore—by that reason—and "even then"—even while the jar remains in its place—the second half [of the verse] is explained by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), supported by the first half.
He explains: "Thus" means for this reason; even though the jar exists, how—in what manner—is its absence not treated as distinct—that is, it is not brought within the scope of linguistic usage?
He states the very distinction [in the form]: "The jar is not here on this ground."

Having stated the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) of the second half [of the verse] by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he states its word-meaning (*padārtha*) by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as "that knowledge," namely, "the knowledge of the bare ground. He explains the word "jātu" (ever/at any time) with "in a certain state indeed," and so forth. He clarifies that very state with "a jar," etc., [meaning] "distinct."
He states the meaning of the word *padasya* as "of the pot" (*ghaṭasya*). He explains the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) and so forth by saying "non-existence" (*abhāvam*).

By the term "establishes" (*sādhayati*), it is indicated that the suffix *-lyuṭ* here is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). He states the exclusion of the word *jātu* (ever) with "but not" (*na tu*); the meaning is: "in what manner could it be? In no manner whatsoever."
Regarding the excessive consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) stated as the reason in the introduction, he indicates it by way of a suggestion with the words "by this" (*etena*).
It follows—meaning it would follow—that by this [reasoning], one might also have to accept that "there is no *piśāca* here on this ground. || 9 ||

Now, one might object: "In that case, how is it that this worldly practice, which is based on the absence of difference, is seen to be uncontradicted only at certain times? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] demonstrates the method for establishing that [absence of difference], which has not been observed by the ancients:
But is a mass of light or a soft touch such as heat not present for a blind man?
In that case, one would have to establish his own cognition as having the nature of a non-pot. (10)

In this context, the conventional view that "the very existence of one thing is the non-existence of another" must not be abandoned; this is the path of common experience. In that regard, whatever has arisen through the logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) of one entity being [treated as] another entity must be reflected upon and understood. Regarding the term *niṣṭhiteḥ*, the rule *nergadanadapata...* [applies].
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs; therefore, the meaning is "by means of abiding in one's own self. || 9 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the tenth verse with the words "nanvevam" (But if this is so).
Here the commentary states:
"vyavahāraḥ" (conventional usage) refers to such forms as "there is no jar on the ground"; "avigītaḥ" (uncontradicted) means unrefuted.
The meaning is "manifest," occurring only in a certain state—namely, the state consisting of the proximity of a jar or similar object;
"the way" refers to the means. The sense is: "how can there even be talk of describing that which is unperceived?
For the ancients have stated that it is only through the perception of a pure surface that non-existence is established, and this is not tenable.
As stated in the reasoning (*yukti*). Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "But... (*kiṃ tu*).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) establishes the method for explaining the verse with the word "here" (*iha*). It is "apparent" (*prātītika*).
The path—that is, the way—is established by common experience; "therein" means on that path which is not to be abandoned.

Regarding "existence and its absence"—that is, existence and non-existence. [Objection: But what follows from that? To this he says: "And therefore," specifically, it is simply another entity (*vastvantaram eva*).
That very relationship of the container and the contained belongs to existence and its absence; therefore,

that other entity distinct from the jar— such as a stone or a mass of light— which appears in visual cognition upon the ground, is itself designated as "the absence of the jar on the ground" or "there is no jar on the ground."

Or, even in cases where there is no operation of the eye, such as when the eyes are closed or in total darkness, one who perceives on the ground a soft, warm, cold, or neither-warm-nor-cold touch— distinct from the hard touch appropriate to a jar—
designates that very [touch] as "the absence of a jar here," because the touch of air is omnipresent.

The meaning of the sentence is "because it is necessarily so. As for the meaning of the individual words: *kiṃ tu* (but rather) is a reflection upon a question regarding one's own intuition (*pratibhā*) for the purpose of introducing one's own view;

[the phrase *pratibhāpraśnaparāmarśaḥ* refers to this reflection on the question of intuition]. He states the answer to the question, "What, then, is logical in this case? as follows: first, there exists the mass of light upon that ground, which is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

The blind person has a tactile sensation such as heat and so forth; this [sensation] tells them that it is a stone or the like. Regarding "visual"—that is, in the cognition produced by the eye, namely in perceptual knowledge—it is that very thing, such as a stone or the like, or indeed a mass of light and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "even where": by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), damage to the eyes and so forth are included; for in the case of a blind person, it is precisely the damage to the eyes that is the cause for the absence of visual activity. "Distinct" (*vivikta*) means separate. "That very thing" refers to touch itself. Now, one might ask: "If touch were not present, what would be the result? To this he says: "the wind."
He promises to explain the categories with the words "But as for the categories. However, he states the meaning intended by the word "own" (*sva*) according to his own view:
"an inquiry based on one's own intuition" means an inquiry produced by one's own intuition; the reflection upon that is "reflection on an inquiry based on one's own intuition."
He repeats the very question, saying "What? The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the repetition of the question.
Regarding that—in that question—anticipating the inquiry "What does he say?", he explains the meaning of the verse as the object [of the verb], using the word *tatra*.
He explains the term *tatra* as "on the ground" (*bhūtale*). "A mass of light" (*ālokacaya*) means a cluster of light.

"Jñeya" means "the perceptible. Although there is touch even in that which is accompanied by sight, it is stated thus because of the absence of dependence upon that [sight] in the case of touch. By this, the section ending with "there exists therein" has been explained. One should establish the cognition of touch itself—that is, the cognition of its own form as distinct from other things such as a jar.

The agent establishes there on that ground that light and so forth possess the nature of "non-pot," which is to say the nature of the absence of a pot; this meaning is thus possible. The suffix *liṅ* is used here according to Pāṇini’s rule *śaki liṅ ca* (3.3.172).
Furthermore, from the hearing of the subtle sound produced by the vibration of the internal vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is the completeness of the auditory organ and the other senses.

While that [absence] is being produced, one who hears that very sound as conjoined with a single cognition negates other sounds, thinking, "There is no other sound here. He explains the remaining portion of the verse, beginning with "tatsūkṣmaśabdābhāvam api" (also the absence of that subtle sound), by means of the word "tasya" (of that). The word "tasya" [is used].

He explains [the term] as "light" (*āloka*). In that context, "light" refers to [the object] in relation to one possessing eyes, whereas for a blind person, it refers to "touch" (*sparśa*); the word "relative" (*sambandhin*) is to be supplied [as the referent]. He explains "one's own cognition" (*svajñāna*) as "another" (*anya*).
By this, it is indicated that "one's own cognition" is a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). "That" (*tat*) refers to the cognition.
He explains "the nature of being a non-pot" as "non-pot," and he states that this too is a synonym for "the absence of a pot.

He states the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as "this is possible. Now, one might ask: how is this the meaning of the optative? To this he replies: "in the sense of possibility" (*śaki*). [Objection:
But surely, when one has ascertained the completeness of the eyes and other factors through the perception of a mass of light, on the ground...
Let it be granted that there is knowledge of the absence of any object visible to the eye that is distinct from the entire mass of light;

however, how could there be knowledge of the absence of sound and so forth in that state? For at that time, since no sound whatsoever is being heard, there is certainly no knowledge of the completeness of the causal complex (sāmagrī) consisting of the auditory organ and other factors that apprehend sound. To this, he says:

Regarding the term "internal": even in the absence of external sound, one who has closed their ears indeed hears the internal sound produced by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is constantly vibrating and known as the *anāhata* (unstruck); thus it is said. By means of a single cognition—that is, by the auditory cognition capable of grasping all sounds—one perceives that which is associated with them.
Being merged. Now, one might object that if [the senses] are too closely attentive, one does not hear even that; therefore, he says "that":
the absence of that most subtle sound—[he who has] that most subtle internal resonance (antarnāda) as his object when the ear is attentive—he perceives.
One whose internal auditory faculty is fixed upon the most subtle inner resonance perceives the absence of taste, smell, and touch;

for even while perceiving the taste of water in the mouth, the scent of the *tripuṭikā* herb, and the tactile sensation of the body, it is precisely through that very act of perception that the absence of [ordinary] taste is to be known, for it is not otherwise.

This is an absolute certainty: that there is no ascertainment of the completeness of the causes of perception without the apprehension of another object capable of being associated with that single cognition;
for [this would apply to] that which is produced by the recent occurrence of the experience of each respective object.
It is experienced, because internal sounds (*antaraśabda*) are divided tenfold. As it has been said:
"The Blessed One, Śambhu, possesses sound that is tenfold, beginning with resonance (*ghoṣa*). For one who is absorbed in *samādhi*, there is the realization of the absence of all internal sounds.
It should be understood that this is produced by the focused attention on the incessantly arising, immeasurable self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*);

its absence, however, is simply struck down by impossibility, so enough of this. He establishes the perception of the absence of rasa and the other [tastes] with the phrase "the water of the teeth. The "rasa of the water of the teeth" refers to the water in the form of saliva situated in the sense organ of taste.

By one who perceives— that is, experiences— the specific flavor (rasaviśeṣa) which is prone to arise through the sight of objects such as sweets and which always exists in a latent state (śaktitayā), and who thereby maintains the integrity of the gustatory faculty (rasanendriya-avaikalya), the absence of flavor— that is, the absence of relish— is what is to be known.
The same should be applied elsewhere as well. Regarding the *tripuṭikā*: it is situated within the nose and is always endowed with fragrance;
as it has been said:
"In this way, fragrance is clearly present within the nose, and taste is manifest in the saliva of the teeth."

Thus: "pertaining to the body" (*kāyīya*) means connected with the body, because the body, being composed of earth, clearly possesses tangibility. Since internal fire (*tejas*) is visible only through the closing of the eyes, it does not serve as a cause for the complete cognition of the eye; therefore, it is not included here. Previously, by means of touch...
In that case, the knowledge of the absence of the jar which serves as the substrate for the blind man was explained;
however, here, the absence of another touch is known through the tactile sensation of the body, so there is no tautology. To the question "But from what [source] does this follow?", he says:
"For indeed" (*na hi*). For—because of which reason—this, namely, the absolute certainty (*ekānta*), occurs. In these cases...

If it is argued that since there is no suspicion of the instrument's destruction at that very moment, the certainty regarding the completeness of its causes does not require its association with a single cognition, we say: no; for one who desires to perceive the absence of this or that object is observed to exert effort and employ the respective sense organs in their respective locations. || 10 ||

Who [is it]? Among those things capable of being conjoined with a single cognition, there can be no certainty regarding the completeness of the causes of perception without the perception of that other object.
This is the intended meaning here: for a person, in the apprehension of the absence [of an object], there must also be the completeness of his own sense faculties.

It must be determined; otherwise, one who asserts the non-existence of that object on the grounds that its perception is absent due to the defect of impaired sense faculties merely becomes an object of ridicule. Furthermore, the knowledge of the completeness of one's own sense faculties does not depend upon the apprehension of every single object perceivable by them, but rather [it is established] even if only some single object among those perceivable by them is apprehended.
By that very [perception], one grasps the entirety [of the objects] and knows, "My sense faculty is indeed functioning well";

consequently, one determines the non-existence of other [objects] not being grasped, thinking, "They do not exist here. In that case, the cognition of all graspable objects—which is the effect of that sense faculty—is a single cognition, and it has those [non-existent objects] as its object.

When there is one object—another object capable of contact—with a cognition of it, there arises through that [cognition] a knowledge of the completeness of the causal complex for apprehension; otherwise, even if an object is not apprehended due to the remoteness of the means, it would not be fit for the linguistic usage of "non-existence," just as a *piśāca* [is not perceived] due to the remoteness of its nature. Enough of this. Herein:

He anticipates the student's objection with the words "not long" (*acira*). That which has recently occurred—meaning that which has just arisen—is the experience of various objects; by that [experience], something is imagined—that is, being conceived as existing—the instrument, namely the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of the totality of the apprehending factors; at that very moment—immediately thereafter—[it ceases].

At the very moment of perceiving an object currently being produced, because there is no possibility of suspecting its destruction—since it is impossible to entertain a doubt regarding its destruction—the certainty of the completeness of its causes arises. Therefore, what is the consequence of [the cause] being connected within a single cognition? The meaning is that nothing follows, because [the cause] has already become manifest.

He states the answer: "No. He provides the reason for this: "of those and those," meaning one who desires to perceive the non-existence of various objects—that is, one desiring to apprehend their respective absences—[observes] the locus of those and those, namely, the sense organs such as the eyes which grasp those respective objects.

While indeed performing the operation [of perception]— that is, while engaging in the act of grasping for the sake of knowing whether [the object] exists or not, rather than leaving it in a state of indifference— the form of the ball and so forth is "perceived," meaning it is seen.
And thus, by means of the cognition of another object that is in contact with the same single cognition...
The meaning is that the knowledge of the completeness of the causal complex of the apprehender is necessarily required. || 10 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eleventh verse with the words: "But surely, in this way...

But surely, in this way, even for an invisible being such as a *piśāca*, the conventional usage of negation would result even through exclusion (*vyatireka*), for that mass of light is just as distinct from a jar as it is from a *piśāca* and the like. This is what [the author] intends.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Just as a *piśāca* might exist within the light even though it is not perceived by sight, being invisible within the interior of the earth, it cannot be denied in every respect. (11)

Although it is established that the mass of light is distinct from a *piśāca* and that there is light which is not of the nature of a *piśāca*, nevertheless, it is impossible to determine definitively that "there is no *piśāca* here," for a jar, indeed, cannot be excluded even when in the midst of a flood of light— [the same applies to] a jar.
[In the absence of a jar—K. ṣ.
ṣ. Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"In this way—even regarding the conventional usage of the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatirekābhāva*) where there is an absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*)."
When it is the perception of another object, and not the perception of a bare patch of ground, that serves as the means of proof, then even if an invisible thing—

meaning something unfit to be seen— is present, the word "even" (*api*) indicates that the negation of a *piśāca* is indeed logical in the conventional usage of the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*). Here...

[This refers to] its being unconnected [to the ground]. "Even by way of exclusion" (*vyatirekeṇāpi*) means even in such a negative linguistic usage (*niṣedhavyavahāra*) characterized by exclusion, as in "it does not exist on the ground. To the question "Why?", he says: "For that... (*sa hi*). "That very thing" (*tad etat*) refers to the matter just mentioned.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it: "The Piśāca.
Here, the commentary says: "The Piśāca may be without light"; this he explains as "light" (āloka).

Even though a mass of light— a collection of light— is distinct from a *piśāca*, he says "even though" (*yadyapi*) in order to make this very point clearer through another synonym. While it is established that light is not of the nature of a *piśāca*, he states the matter indicated by the word "even" (*api*) with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

Thus it is said. Nevertheless, in this case—regarding the ground—to determine or ascertain that "there is no piśāca" there, because a flood of light is projected (or withdrawn) in its vicinity, it follows from this that "there is no jar here"; however, a piśāca is of such a nature that...
Whether existing within the ground or within light, it does not destroy— that is, it does not obstruct— the density of that ground or light; and therefore,
since its presence is possible within the light, how can there be a linguistic usage of negation through exclusion (*vyatireka*)?

In this way, because the existence of taste and so forth within form is possible, they too are not excluded. Even though a non-light entity other than light might be a *piśāca*, nevertheless, it remains invisible within the interior of the ground.
"Impossible" means that it is not possible. To the question "Why?", he says: "For the pot...

For (*hi*)—that is, because—even in the midst of a mass of light—that is, even within a collection of light—the word "even" (*api*) implying also on a patch of ground—it is "inconceivable," meaning impossible to conceive. Why?

In the vicinity of the jar— that is, in that lower region— because it does not allow for the arrival of a mass of light, due to its acting as an obstruction; for an umbrella or similar object held within the light produces shade only over that much space, whereas its presence on the ground is impossible.
It is indeed clearly distinct from the mass of light. And therefore, this is established: what is it?

Here—on the ground—the jar does not exist. But in the case of exclusion (*vyatireka*), there is a *piśāca* (demon) of such a nature—that is, one whose own-being (*svabhāva*) or essential form is like that—which exists within the ground.

Even while existing in the midst of light, it does not destroy— that is, it does not annihilate— the well-known density or compactness of the ground or of the light itself, because its own body is void. Consequently, it is possible to conceive of its existence even in the midst of light, as it is capable of being so conceived.
By way of exclusion—that is, by being located upon the ground—how could there be the conventional usage of negation?
He extends this same principle elsewhere as well with the word "thus" (*evam*). "Of that too"—meaning even of taste and so forth.
Having thus stated the meaning of the sentence, he states the meaning of the individual words along with their syntactical connection, beginning with "even though" (*yadyapi*). Even though...

He provides the explanation of "non-light" (*anāloka*) as "other than light. Nevertheless, it is still conceivable; just as it is conceivable that he exists even within the light, so too it follows that although he is other than that [light], by this [statement].

The meaning of the verse is this: although the *piśāca* has been excluded from the path, it has nevertheless not been excluded in every respect; therefore, how can linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) based on its non-existence proceed therein? || 11 ||
Having thus demonstrated, by way of a reductio ad absurdum, the true nature of the conventional usage regarding non-existence, he applies it to the present case:
"In this manner, the cognition of mother-of-pearl would be of a positive nature for one who knows the silver;
however, it could not be the indicator of the invalidity of the initial cognition of silver. (12)

That *piśāca* is within—that is, in the midst of—the earth; it is inferred that it is invisible, meaning it is not capable of being seen due to its extreme subtlety. By this, the use of the *liṅ* suffix in the sense of inference (*saṃbhāvanā*) is indicated. Just so—in the same manner—it is inferred that he exists even within the light.
Thus, although light is different from that— namely, the *piśāca*—

because it is impossible for one thing to have the nature of another, and thus the *piśāca* is negated by this path— that is, by way of its identity with it— it is nevertheless not negated in every respect.

Because it is a matter for suspicion that [the jar] might exist apart from light— for this reason, how could conventional transactions based on its absence— that is, based on the absence of a *piśāca*— proceed there, on that ground,
by means of which collection of light the absence of the jar is established?

The meaning is that even in the midst of that [reality], they do not function because it is the locus of its manifestation. He provides the conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means "in this way"; such is the meaning of the verse. This is the construction here: just as an invisible piśāca spirit, though lacking light, exists within the interior of the ground.
Even if it exists, it would be unfit to be seen; likewise, it would be so even within the light, because the same logic applies.
"Therefore" is the ellipsis to be supplied. For this reason, it cannot be denied in every respect;
for even if its nature as light is subject to denial, its existence within that [light] cannot be denied. And therefore, of that...
The point is that it is simply impossible to practice the conventional usage of "absence on the ground" as something distinct [from the ground itself]. || 11 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the twelfth verse with the word "evam" (thus).
This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the word "evam.
Just as in the case of "light is the absence of a jar," when the light is apprehended, there is no [apprehension] of the jar previously apprehended.
Something has occurred; likewise, it is possible that there is the cognition of mother-of-pearl, the absence of the cognition of silver,
the awareness of the validity of the cognition of the pot,
the awareness of the absence of the cognition of cloth, and the awareness of the validity of the absence of the cognition of cloth— yet by this much alone, [the object is not established].

The previously arisen cognition of the cloth ceases to be a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), for all this reflection on the nature of that cognition of the jar pertains only to it and not to any other initial cognition; from this, nothing at all has arisen.
In the same way, let the cognitions "this is mother-of-pearl" and "this is not silver" shine forth by their own nature as "I."

And the means of valid cognition [applies] to the absence of silver in the mother-of-pearl, but not to the silver itself; however, by that much, nothing has happened to the previous cognition of silver, so how could the silver that was its object be unreal? || 12 ||

Here the commentary explains the word "evam" (thus) as "yathā" (as). "Nothing has come about"—no contradiction whatsoever has arisen. "The absence of the cognition of silver" means the absence of the cognition of *rajata* (silver); this much—
Only this much is possible—that it can be conceived—but the sublation of the cognition of silver is not possible. He explains this very point again in detail with the words "as follows" (*yathā*).
"Previously arisen" means previously arisen regarding the object that is a jar; [this refers to] the cognition of a cloth.

"The cognition 'this is a cloth'—in response to the inquiry 'Why?', he says: 'For this... [The phrase] "of another cognition" refers to the cognition "this is a cloth" which proceeds in that very same sequence. "Something," meaning "some sublation" (bādha). He provides the conclusion with the word "thus" (evam), having imitated the very act of manifestation.

It shows itself as "I. And this manifestation by its own self is understood to occur precisely through the subject (*pramātṛ*), for knowledge is not something distinct from the subject that could perform the reflective awareness "I";
thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. By that much—by mere luminosity—it is "something," in some way.

"Bādhā" means "not occurred"—that is, it has not come to pass. For this reason, how could that silver—which was made an object [of cognition] as uncontradicted silver—be unreal? The point is that even in the case of an error, its unreality is not tenable without a single cognizer. In the sense of possibility...
The indicative mark (liṅga). || 12 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the thirteenth verse with the words "nanvidam" (but surely this...).
By the phrase "nanvidam," that very place is referred to where the cognition of silver occurred;
it is precisely there that now the cognition "this is not silver" and "this is mother-of-pearl" has arisen as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). That...

Therefore, it is inferred that the previous cognition of silver is invalid (*apramāṇa*); for it is not possible for two cognitions apprehending two contradictory objects to both be valid with respect to a single object. Thus, this is an inferential [cognition].

Anticipating the objection that there might still be the conventional usage of "sublation" (bādha), he says: "Sublation would not occur through inference even because of the non-establishment of the locus (dharmin);
however, sublation established by self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) is logical, as it arises from a single cognizer. (13)
Not only is sublation not established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), but it is also [not established] through inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding this, the *Ṭīkā* says:
"In that very place"—that is, in that mother-of-pearl shell which exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
In the mother-of-pearl shell itself, [the cognition] has become a means of valid knowledge—meaning it exists as a valid cognition—and has arisen—meaning it has been produced.
"That" (tat) refers to that reason; "therefore" (ataḥ) refers to this cause. In response to the expectation of what is inferred, he says "that" (tat).
In response to the expectation of from what it is inferred, he says "for not" (na hi). [He supplies] the word "this" (etat) to complete the syntactic requirement.

"It fulfills the contradictory" means: the two cognitions— namely, the previously arisen cognition "this is silver," which has as its object silver characterized by a nature and capacity that excludes the two [actual] objects, and the cognition that arises immediately thereafter— [fulfill the contradiction].
The cognition "this is mother-of-pearl" occurs in one place—that is, with respect to a single piece of mother-of-pearl. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
He states the resulting conclusion: "Therefore, this... It is established by inference (*ānumānika*: proven through inference). Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows:
the previously arisen cognition "this is silver" regarding mother-of-pearl is not valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because [subsequently] in that very same place...
"Because it produces the cognition that 'this is a contradictory mother-of-pearl shell'.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "the substratum" (*dharmī*).
Herein is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

He explains the first half [of the verse] with the words "not merely. From self-awareness—that is, from direct experience. To the question "Why?", he applies the reason stated in the Sūtra with the words "of the subject" (*dharmiṇaḥ*). By the word "also" (*api*)—

It is not established, because the locus (*dharmin*) is unestablished; by the word "also" (*api*), the reason (*hetu*) and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) are also [meant to be] unestablished—the word "also" is to be understood in both cases.

Here, when the locus is established, the function of inference is the exclusion of the non-connection of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by means of an established reason that recalls the pervasion.

[The delimiting factor of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma-avacchedaka) – K.ṣ.ṣ.]: And here, in the case of the previously mentioned cognition of silver, which is the subject (dharmin), the property to be proven is invalidity; as for that, either the cognition of mother-of-pearl, or the cognition "this is not silver," or the state of being made an object by those cognitions—residing in the object—would be employed as the logical reason (hetu).

And this is not tenable, because at that time there is an absence of the subject (*dharmin*) which is the cognition of the prior silver; nor are the cognition of mother-of-pearl and so forth its properties (*dharmas*);

and the establishment of a probandum does not occur from a property that does not belong to the subject. Therefore, the claim that "that which is being remembered would be the subject" is also incorrect.

Now, if it is being proved that the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) is not the object of the cognition of silver, [this is so] because of the word "also" (*api*), which expresses a conjunction with the cognition of the mother-of-pearl; and because of the reason and the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the remainder of the argument being "because of non-establishment" (*asiddhi*).
This is to be applied to both cases; the meaning is that it should be joined twice, since the subject (*dharmin*) is also unestablished even by means of inference. Why?

In response to the expectation of what "this" refers to, he provides the justification with the word "here. The exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of the non-connection—that is, the lack of relation—of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) [with the subject] means, in short, that the subject possesses that property by virtue of the property to be proven;
this is the function of inference (*anumānavyāpāra*). By way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the meaning is that it is the object of the function of inference.

In "rūpyajñāne" means in the cognition of silver. "Tatra" means in that probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*). "Being made an object by those two cognitions" means being made an object by those specific cognitions; this resides in the object—that is, it resides in the mother-of-pearl. The use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in "hetūkriyeta" expresses a possibility. [Objection: But among the three [factors],...
Thinking that we shall indeed make some [point] into a reason, he says: "And this is not [the case]. Why is it not logical?

To this he says: "At that time. At that time—either at the time of the cognition of the mother-of-pearl or at the time of the cognition that "this is not silver"—there is the aforementioned cognition of silver; of that aforementioned cognition of silver, etc.

By the word "not," there is the apprehension of the cognition "this is not silver" as residing in the object, as well as its being made an object of that [subsequent] cognition. Now, [the opponent might argue: "Let those properties not belong to it; what of it? To this he says: "And not... The meaning is: from a reason that is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*), that is, from a reason that does not reside in the subject (*pakṣāvṛtti*). "[The object] being remembered"—

The sense is that even if the subject (*dharmin*)— that previous cognition of silver which is being made an object of memory— is established, the reason (*hetu*) lacks the property of being a predicate of that subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), because it is non-existent.
He then raises an objection with another form of inference, beginning with "atha."
Regarding the statement "because it is an object": if that [object] exists at the present time, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*);

if, however, it existed previously, then its objectivity is sublated by one's own prior self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Furthermore, by whom has such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) been grasped—that wherever there is another cognition at the present time, there was not another [cognition] previously?

If it is argued that this is established by another inference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). By this, the following objection is refuted: "How could there be two cognitions regarding a single object? For who indeed could know the single-objectness of those two cognitions? For they themselves—

Thus—it is established in this manner; and so there is no proof of the subject (*dharmin*), nor is there the fallacy of the reason (*hetu*) being non-existent in the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*); such is the sense. Now, one might ask: "What is the reason (*hetu*) employed here?
To this he says: "mother-of-pearl" (*śuktikā*). The word "thus" (*iti*) marks the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Here he provides the rebuttal.

Regarding the word "tat": if "tat" refers to the proof that the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) is not the object of the cognition of silver (*rajata-jñāna*), and the ellipsis is "if it is being performed now," then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*), because it is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*). On the other hand, if [it refers to] "previously," then even at that time the mother-of-pearl was not the object of the cognition of silver; thus, regarding that mother-of-pearl...

If the proof for being the object of the cognition of silver is being established, then by means of the instrument of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), there occurs the state of having a sublated object (*bādhyaviṣayatā*). "Having a sublated object" refers to a reason whose probandum is a sublated object;
the state of that is its nature, which is to say, the state of having a sublated object. For in this case, it is indeed self-awareness itself [that serves as the instrument].

The witness [states]: "Previously, the mother-of-pearl was the object of the cognition of silver. Thus, the meaning is that just as in the case of [the inference] "fire is not hot because it is a substance," there is a sublation of the object here as well.
Regarding this, he states another defect with the words "and by whom," since in the Buddhist system a permanent knower is impossible.

It was stated [above] that "by means of another inference. Regarding the term "infinite regress" (*anavasthā*): it refers to a state of endless succession, such as that one inference depending on another, and that other depending on yet another, and so forth. Relying upon this point, he refutes another objection raised by the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) with the words "by this [it is answered]. It has been answered.
[The author] provides the summary: "In one [object]. In response to the inquiry "What is this?", he says "In one.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter to be refuted. In response to the inquiry "How was it refuted?", he says "For who...
regarding those two cognitions: the cognition "this is silver" and the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl."
One should understand that, according to your view, because a single eternal knower is impossible, no one at all would know;
this is the sense. Now, as to why one would not know, he says: "For they...
For it has been stated that they rest within themselves and upon their own objects; thus, there is no sublation even by means of inference, nor...

Even though such an intervention exists, it is perceived here in the act of cognition because it manifests instantaneously through the establishment of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). For this very reason, it is impossible to say: "Let there be no such thing as sublation (*bādhā*)."

Having thus demonstrated the impossibility [of the opponent's position] regarding the other side, he concludes with the statement previously promised— that the relationship of the sublated and the sublator arises from being established within a single cognizer—
by saying: "That [relationship] is logical if it were produced from a single cognizer," for it is that very [cognizer] who...

Likewise, it has already been explained that [the Lord] is the creator within cognition; thus, "he offers an oblation. For this reason, even the objection based on inference does not hold. Having thus refuted inference through reasoning, its [inference's] rejection by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is also established.
He says "and not so. Here, in this conventional usage of the cognition of sublation (*bādhapratītivyavahāra*), there is such an intervention— namely,
an intervention consisting of the apprehension of a reason suitable for inference, the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and so forth.

[The grasping of the reason suitable for inference and the recollection of the pervasion—C] is not cognized—that is, it is not experienced. Why? To this he says: "by itself" (sva). This means by way of being established through self-cognition—that is, by way of being established through the perception whose nature is self-cognition—suddenly.

Without the apprehension of the logical reason (*hetu*), the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and so forth, he states "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) to explain the second half of the verse by asserting the inexpressibility (*anirvācyatva*) of sublation (*bādhā*). "For this very reason" means for the reason that there is an immediate manifestation; in response to the question "What is this?", he says "let it not be."
By this, the explanation of the phrase "but [it is] established by self-awareness" has been provided.

He introduces the commentary on the fourth quarter with the word "evam" (thus). Regarding the "opponent's position"—that is, the Buddhist position—what was "proposed" (*pratijñāta*) means that which was made the subject of a formal proposition (*pratijñā*); he now concludes (*nigamayati*).

It leads [the subject] to the state of being the object of the conclusion (*nigamana*); the statement of the three middle members [of the syllogism] is to be understood by implication alone. Having thus provided the introduction, he explains the fourth quarter [of the verse]. "They are joined" (*yuktāḥ*). The word "iti" marks the completion of the explanation of the fourth quarter. Here, he provides the justification with the words "for that very... (*sa eva hi*). For— (*hi*)—
Because he alone—the cognizer himself—is likewise the creator;

and this being so, if it is argued that "otherwise it would be impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*) for the sake of establishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), then let it be said as much as you wish: now everything is established. || 13 ||

Not only are these functions— causality, recollection, sublation, and linguistic convention— established in a single cognizer as the general transactions constituting the entire course of worldly life,
but even intermediate transactions such as buying and selling, which are characterized by impurity, are likewise so established.
The states of the teacher and the taught, and so forth, are also stainless; they too reside solely within a single cognizing subject (pramātṛ).

For all worldly transactions have their life-force in unification (*samanvaya*). He demonstrates this through the process of synthesis: "Indeed, every transaction has unification as its vital breath" (*vyavahāro hi sarvaḥ samanvayaprāṇaḥ*). Thus he shows it.
Thus, within the all-pervasive [consciousness] which is inlaid with the appearance of objects that are extremely diverse,
worldly activity— whether accompanied by impurity or free from it— is experienced.
"It becomes the sublater because it pervades both the prior and the posterior"— this has already been explained, that is,

it was already stated previously. He says this to show that even the relationship of the sublated and the sublater, which is asserted by proponents [of other systems] on the grounds that otherwise linguistic convention would be impossible, is established only through the admission of a single cognizer.

"And this being the case" (*sthite ca*): this being the case, there is "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*)—that is to say, an incompatibility (*ayogyatā*) without the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*), which establishes that relationship through the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
"It is said" (*ucyate*) refers to the proponents (*vādibhiḥ*). Now, regarding the acceptance of a single cognizer (*ekapramātṛ*), "everything" (*sarvam*)—

The entire collection of connections through memory is established, because the unifier has been accepted; this is the sense. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the commentary on the verse. || 13 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fourteenth verse with the words "not only" (*na kevalam*).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"In all worldly activity (*lokayātrā*), those things which constitute ordinary conventional usage (*sāmānyavyavahāra*)."

They consist of the nature of supreme worldly transaction (*paramavyavahāra*); that is to say, they are those whose foundation lies in a single cognizer (*pramātṛ*), and thus have acquired their existence therein. Their life-force is integration (*samanvaya*); that is, their very vitality is relation.
"In the manner of summary" means by way of summarizing the entire subject matter of the daily manual (*āhnika*).
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the word "ittham" (in this way):

by this method of reasoning consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as stated in the two verses beginning with "tattadvibhinna," and likewise by the manner of illustrating worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) stated in other verses.

This also must be understood: that [consciousness] which is all-pervasive (*vibhu*) and unconditioned by space and time, and therefore exists as non-different from the appearances of blue, pleasure, and so forth— which, though appearing utterly distinct due to the power of *māyā* and animated solely by duality, are like reflections— [is consciousness] which is "inlaid" (i.e., colored) by them without its own nature being altered.
It means that every worldly transaction is experienced as having come to rest; in this context, experience itself is the most firm proof— thus says the commentary (*ṭīkā*).
He explains the word "ittham" (thus) as "tattat" (this and that).

Regarding the phrase "tattadvibhinna" (distinct from this and that), he explains the word "vibhau" (in the all-pervasive) as "deśa" (space) by means of other verses—namely, those beginning with "tattadvibhinna" and so forth—which must be understood as necessary knowledge; he fulfills the expectancy of the word "idam" (this) with the word "yat" (which).

He provides the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) and commentary on the compound word beginning with *atyartha* by means of the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). "For this very reason" means "precisely because of its omnipresence" (*vibhutvāt*). He explains the component "divided" (*bhinnāḥ*) as "māyā. Regarding the two components of the phrase "the manifestation of objects through that which is animated by differentiation"—that is, by those [entities] whose existence is granted solely by [māyā]—he explains them as follows: * **Bhinnena** (by differentiation): This refers to *māyā*. * **Eka-kevalam** (solely/only): This refers to the fact that the existence of all things is granted by that alone. * **Prāṇitaiḥ** (animated): This means those [entities] whose being has been bestowed [upon them]. * **Arthāvabhāsaḥ** (manifestation of objects): This consists of two parts: 1. **Artha** (objects): Refers to the various categories of objects such as the elements (*bhūta*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth. 2. **Avabhāsa** (manifestation): Refers to the appearance of those objects. Thus, the meaning is that the manifestation of objects occurs through that which is animated by the differentiation provided by *māyā*. This is the sense of the term *arthāvabhāsa*. Furthermore, the word *prāṇita* is used here in the sense of "granted existence," just as one says "the life-force (*prāṇa*) has been granted to him. The word *eka* is used in the sense of "exclusive" (*kevala*), as in the expression "one who is exclusively devoted to Śiva" (*śivabhaktaika*). The word *bheda* is used in the sense of "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*), as in the expression "the differentiation of the object" (*arthaviśeṣa*). The word *avabhāsa* is used in the sense of "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*), as in the expression "the appearance of the object" (*arthapratibhāsa*). The word *māyā* is used in the sense of "delusion" (*bhrānti*), as in the expression "the delusion of the object" (*arthabhrānti*). The word *kṛta* is used in the sense of "produced" (*nirmita*), as in the expression "created by Māyā" (*māyākṛta*). The word *sattva* is used in the sense of "existence" (*astitva*), as in the expression "the existence of the object" (*arthasattva*). The word *datta* is used in the sense of "bestowed" (*arpita*), as in the expression "existence bestowed upon the object" (*arthe sattvam arpitam*). The word *sattā* is used in the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), as in the expression "the being of the object" (*arthabhāva*). The word *kevala* is used in the sense of "exclusive," as in the expression "existence granted exclusively by Māyā" (*māyayaiva kevalaṃ dattā sattā*). The word *prāṇita* is used in the sense of "animated," as in the expression "animated by that which is differentiated" (*bhinnena prāṇitaiḥ*). The word *arthāvabhāsa* is used in the sense of "manifestation of objects," as in the expression "the manifestation of objects through that which is animated by differentiation" (*bhinnaprāṇitair arthāvabhāsaḥ*). The word *atyartha* is used in the sense of "excessive," as in the expression "excessive manifestation of objects" (*atyartho 'rthāvabhāsaḥ*). The word *vikalpa* is used in the sense of "conceptual construction," as in the expression "conceptual construction regarding the excessive manifestation of objects" (*atyarthārthāvabhāse vikalpaḥ*). The word *jāla* is used in the sense of "net," as in the expression "the net of conceptual construction regarding the excessive manifestation of objects" (*atyarthārthāvabhāsakalpanājālam*). He explains [the word] "blue. He supplies the qualifier "reflection" (*pratibimba*) because it is logical to assume the relationship of original object and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*). By this, the following is established:

That very state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-daśā*), which consists of the manifestation of the reality of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva-prakhyātmikā*), is the ground of Śiva (*śivabhūmi*). As it has been said: "In the connection [with the object], there is attentiveness.

By those who have been composed through the instructions bestowed by a great guru, obtained via an exceedingly intense descent of the Lord’s power (*śaktipāta*),

and who— following that [instruction]— are intent on focused attention; even in the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), they remain solely devoted to the contemplation of the reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattva*), according to the analogy of a woman attached to her beloved, and not otherwise.

Even while being solely attached to enjoyments, those who have rendered such pride meaningless and are self-deceivers experience it; they experience that every worldly transaction rests within the Supreme Self— by means of which experience, for these very ones who are intent on attentiveness, [that state] which is regarded as the condition of transmigratory existence by ordinary people [is realized].
For those who wander according to their own perspective, that which is regarded as the state of worldly existence (*saṃsārāvasthā*) is the condition of conventional activity (*vyavahāradaśā*);
specifically, it is the state of activities such as eating, performed with laxity because the maintenance of the body is unavoidable. That very state constitutes [the world] for them.

The ground of Śiva (śivabhūmi)— the state of Śiva whose nature is supreme light— becomes the manifestation of the reality of the subject, which consists of the knowledge of the reality of the Supreme Self; even at that time, from the perspective of external vision alone, this occurs because of the attainment of the nature of the supreme subject, which is the root of all worldly transaction.
Because it is the object of worldly convention. As it has been said:
"By that very thing by which the dull-witted are deluded, the wise cross over from saṃsāra;
a lump of iron sinks in water, yet that same iron, fashioned into a vessel, floats."

Thus [it is said]. Herein is the meaning: the "insentient" (jaḍa) is a person who is ignorant of the aforementioned reasoning; by that very same external worldly activity, he becomes deluded—that is, he experiences delusion in the form of joy caused by the attainment of results and in the form of resentment caused by their non-attainment—because he identifies solely with the body.
Because its sole delight lies in the mere worldly activity concerning objects useful for that [practice]. The wise one—

whether established through a guru after first purifying the mind, being marked by a mild descent of power (*manda-śaktipāta*), or established through the scriptures having received the instruction of a true guru, being marked by an intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*).
However, when [the teaching] is self-evident because one has previously attained the great secret scripture through the purification of the mind,
then the person is one who knows the stated reasoning by virtue of having their heart touched by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) of the venerable *Bhagavatīvratarā*.
By that very [person]— externally...
By means of conventional practice, he crosses over from saṃsāra—which consists of passion and hatred—and attains the state of having transcended it;

that is to say, by being intent solely upon the reality of the Supreme Self (paramātmatattva), which is the ultimate ground that connects [all things] and severs their root-connection [to worldly existence], he does not become a partaker of the indignation caused by the failure to obtain its fruits. By means of that [practice],...

Because he has attained the great fruit. For someone who, while making an effort for the sake of a single cowrie, suddenly obtains a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), does not become subject to joy or resentment caused by the gain or loss of that cowrie. By this [it is shown]:

It is illuminated that for a mind intent on the contemplation of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), even the enjoyments being experienced produce only benefit and not harm. Thus, our own verse states:
"Objects of the mind that arrive in a continuous flow are beneficial."
If you are not pierced by the multitude of mental constructs here, they do not affect you;
for water certainly benefits a boat that is without holes,
yet it constantly drowns one that possesses porosity.

Thus [it is said]. Here he provides an illustration with the words "piṇḍitam" (solidified). Solidified—that is, existing in the form of a mass—iron sinks in water; yet that very same iron, when made into a vessel—that is, fashioned into the state of a pot or similar receptacle—floats.
The sense is that this is due to the all-encompassing nature of reasoning (*yukti*).
In this regard, he cites a statement from the *Rahasya-śāstra*: "Vigilance regarding the connection. This verse is as follows:
"The consciousness of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings;
however, for yogins, there is this distinction: vigilance regarding the connection."

Thus [it is said]. Herein is the meaning: for all embodied beings—meaning for all living creatures, whether they possess that knowledge or do not possess it—the "cognition of the grasped and the grasper" (grāhyagrāhakasaṃvittiḥ) refers, by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇayā), to the cognition of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper; or rather, it refers to the relationship between the grasped and the grasper itself.

The reading: "She becomes equal—that is, similar—to them. For even those who possess that knowledge indeed carry out worldly activities for the sake of maintaining the body, as long as the body lasts, without any distinction from the ignorant. [Objection: In that case, does it not follow that they too are merely ordinary people? To this he says: "Of the yogins. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction.

Even in the worldly activity of yogins who are solely intent upon the Supreme Self, there is this distinction: they possess superiority over the ignorant. What is this? It is the attentiveness—namely, the focused attention—that occurs toward the cognizer who unites them, at the very moment of their conjunction, that is, during the joining of the grasped object and the grasping subject.
The point is that even in impure worldly dealings such as buying and selling, their forgetfulness of the Supreme Self does not arise;
thus, their superiority over ordinary people is quite evident.
And this is accomplished effortlessly by those who practice the middle path (*madhyadhāmābhyāsinaḥ*).

Thus: for those who have not recognized the supreme reality of the Self, worldly activity is stained; for others, that very same activity is stainless. May there be auspiciousness. (14) [Total from the beginning: 77]

The eighth daily lesson (āhnika) begins: We praise that Śiva, the Great Lord, who is eternally established for the perfected ones (siddhas) by virtue of the worldly practice proven through self-awareness.
Now begins the eighth chapter:

We praise that Śiva, who is established within the heart as self-evident, through well-known worldly usage which is accomplished solely by means of memory, and who is the very substratum of that memory.

Now, at the beginning of the commentary on the eighth chapter of the *Jñānādhikāra*, for the sake of completing the work without obstacle, an auspicious invocation consisting of the mental recollection of the chosen deity whose nature is the Supreme Reality is performed; though already accomplished mentally, it is stated here for the purpose of instructing the disciples.

He composes a verse— intended to indicate the purport of the entire manual (*sakalāhnika*)— beginning with the words "svasaṃvedane" (in self-awareness). We [interpret] "him"— that is, Śiva, whose nature was described in the preceding sentence governed by the relative pronoun *yat*— as the unlimited nature of light (*aparicchinna-prakāśa-svarūpa*).
We praise that certain Reality which illuminates all existents and bestows the essence.

Which one? That which is Śiva for the Siddhas—meaning those who are well-awakened (suprabuddha), and not merely awakened (prabuddha), since instruction proceeds only for their sake; nor for the unawakened (aprabuddha), because they [lack the capacity] here.
Because there is no authority even in mere talk [regarding this]. "Established by self-awareness" means witnessed by one's own experience;

that "transaction"—whether impure, consisting of buying and selling and so forth, which cannot be abandoned until the end of the body's existence, or pure, consisting of instruction and so forth—by the power of that [transaction]:

By virtue of his inherent capacity, and not merely through the accumulation of practices such as meditation; eternally—meaning always, and not only during some limited period of meditative absorption; Maheśvara—one endowed with the great sovereignty (*maheśvarya*) consisting of knowledge and action; Siddha—the perfected one.

He abides as the self-established nature of his own Self, and does not abide as something to be established externally; for that which is already established remains so even at the time of worldly transaction,
being the unifier rooted in the causes such as memory and connection.

They recognize the inner reality, which is the supreme subject endowed with the powers of knowledge and action, as Maheśvara himself; they do not, however, recognize any external, limited particular deity—such as one adorned with ashes and the like—who is merely imagined for the sake of the worship of the ignorant. That [deity] too...
Having thus explained cognition, recollection, and exclusion, it has been established by this much that linguistic usage is not possible without a single substratum for these [three].
Is this conceptualized entity produced together with the activity of cognition? If not, then it would be like a stone.

It partakes of the designation "deity" (deva) which signifies one whose nature is play; however, if it is endowed with that [nature], then it is the Self itself—so why weary one's own Self with such conceptualization? Furthermore, the doubt regarding whether knowledge and action are limited or unlimited is merely constructed by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and even this adjunct has not been examined here.

It exceeds that; and here, a spark of fire alone should be taken as the illustration, for it does not possess any difference whatsoever from the great fire, since by gradually attaining power, it too becomes the great fire itself—enough said. This is the place of meditative absorption (samādhi) for the perfected ones (siddhas).

It is not mentioned because it does not exist apart from the locus of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); or, even if it were to exist, it would merely be an object of contempt due to its lack of a common point of rest. Although for them even the locus of transaction is an object of contempt, nevertheless, for those who have found rest in meditative absorption (*samādhi*)...

This was said for the sake of those who are awakened but subject to agitation during the time of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), so that they too may become perfectly awakened. If this were said for those who are unawakened, then, by their own very activity,
they would be caught in the pit of worldly transaction (*vyavahāravaṭa*) and fall even further down from there.

They should resort [to it]. But if they enter here by their own inclination alone, let them enter; the injunction itself will provide protection for them—what need is there for our weak efforts at prohibition therein? As it has been said:
"For those who have fallen into the pit, the injunction will provide protection."
Thus,
by this [verse], it is indicated that in this chapter (āhnika) he will indeed undertake the exposition of Maheśvaratva.
Having thus performed the auspicious invocation, [he proceeds] with the purport of the chapter through both its collective and individual aspects.
He performs a detailed examination (*nirūpaṇa*) in this manner.
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
having explained (*vyutpādya*)—that is, having determined (*nirṇīya*)—each of these individually through three chapters (*āhnika*). Of these—

Of cognition, memory, and exclusion, there is a single substratum—the single locus consisting of the nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). "Empirical transaction" (*vyavahāra*) refers to all worldly activity, whether impure or pure.
By this much is meant: by the chapter (āhnika) just mentioned.

If [the infinite] is not made internal (*antaḥkṛta*), then that which was stated there as "one" is established here. By the demonstration of the internal manifestation (*antarābhāsa*), it is also explained that [He] is "one who has made the infinite forms of the universe internal. As it is said in this very [context]: [As it is said in that very [context]—K. ṣ. ṣ.]...
It has been stated that he is "Maheśvara" (the Great Lord); now that sovereignty (*māheśvarya*) consisting of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) must be established.
And that is of two kinds: having knowledge as its object and having action as its object. In this regard, because the Blessed One is both the knower and the agent—even though...
The single, undivided nature of consciousness consists of light (*prakāśa*) and self-awareness (*vimarśa*); nevertheless, for the sake of exposition,
[the author] has not included this within the previous verse— meaning, in this present verse— the word "one" (*eka*) is used.
The statement that the substratum of cognition and so forth is one—that is, the statement "it is one"—is established;

the meaning is that it is supported by the demonstration of a single substratum. Furthermore, by that which is the support—that is, the proof through reasoning—of the internal manifestations (or, as the reading *anantarābhāsānām* suggests, of the uninterrupted manifestations), it is also [established].
This portion of the verse also has its meaning established; that is, it was determined in the passage "prāgivārthaḥ.

In this very context—in the verse beginning with "na cedantaḥkṛtaḥ"—it is stated: "that Maheśvaratva" means the state of being Maheśvara which establishes Maheśvarahood. Of what nature is it? It is of the nature of absolute freedom (svātantrya).
The nature of not looking to another's face—that is to say, the nature of being an agent—is that which must be established;

the meaning is that it must be proven by means of what remains [to be said]. By this, it is indicated that this very verse, consisting of the series of words beginning with "na ced anta-kṛtaḥ," serves as the aphorism for the qualification for knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*).

For that very [nature] has been established as the seed immediately after the refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), and its definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) is being made word by word. Now, one might ask: "In what manner is the sovereignty of Maheśvara, which consists in absolute independence, to be demonstrated? To this he says: "And that" (*tacca*). And that—namely, the sovereignty of Maheśvara.
That which has knowledge as its object is one kind, and that which has action as its object is another;

thus it is of two kinds. In that regard—when such sovereignty exists—for that reason—because of these two modes—the Blessed One (bhagavān), who is endowed with sovereignty, is the supreme subject (parapramātā).

He becomes both the knower and the agent; for the knower is independent in the act of knowing, while the agent is independent in the action that consists of activity. Now, one might object: since sovereignty is well known to be unitary in all respects, how can it be said to have two modes? To this he says: "Even though... It consists of the nature of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
The state of being simultaneously all-encompassing and self-luminous—

this very division is constituted by that; therefore, although the sovereignty whose object is the activity consisting of knowledge takes the form of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), nevertheless, it belongs to the section on knowledge.

This must indeed be determined within the very section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*), because that is its subject matter. And thus, the meaning of the word "knower" (*jñātṛ*) has been fully determined both from the perspective of the verbal root and the suffix:
it consists of the reflective awareness of the nature of vision (*dṛksvarūpa*). For this very reason, it is a single mass with consciousness (*cit*)—extremely dense—and likewise...
