It is indeed one; for it is not logical that there be a difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), such is the intended meaning. It is of the nature of consciousness—that is, it is the nature of the principle of the subject (*pramātṛ*). Nevertheless, for the sake of exposition—for the purpose of awakening the ignorant—there is a division consisting of Śiva and Śakti, as well as [the division] within Śakti consisting of agency (*kartṛtva*) and knowership (*jñātṛtva*); this [division] is constructed from that [unity].
Thus, having attained the state of being the author of the treatise, he has indeed created it himself. As it has been said:

"We perform the conceptualization of the division between Śiva and Śakti within a single reality alone. And it is not appropriate to raise an objection against a thing that has been conceptually established in the interim based on a perceived necessity.

The [author] states the result of this state of affairs with the words "by that" (*tena*). "By that"—meaning, because this division has as its sole purpose the instruction of others—for that reason, it is "of the nature of knowledge" (*jñānātmikā*)—according to the view that the root *jñā* means "to understand"—it is of the form of knowledge; it is "action" (*kriyā*), meaning action consisting of knowledge, which is the "object" (*viṣaya*) of that [division].

Such is that sovereignty—the agency denoted by the *tṛc* suffix—which, although it takes the form of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), is indeed the power of the agent (*kartṛ-śakti*). And since that power is an "agent" (*kāraka*) according to the etymological derivation "that which acts is an agent," it is indeed action itself; nevertheless, that sovereignty—

It is precisely in the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*), and not in the section on action (*kriyādhikāra*) which is yet to be described, that this must be determined—that is, made the object of a definitive conclusion. Why? Because its object is that [knowledge], meaning its object is knowledge; for there is no such rule that a verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes only action, as seen in cases such as *gaḍi* (to swell) in the sense of "a part of the face."

The sense is that we also observe words denoting things distinct from that [action]. For, in the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*), it is knowledge, its object, and its agent that must be determined; however, if even that knowledge is said to be an action because it is the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then it would be more appropriate to discuss it precisely in the section on action (*kriyādhikāra*).

Otherwise, this entire domain [of discourse] would fall into being entirely devoid of objects. Furthermore, if it were accepted that agency (*kartṛtva*) is an action (*kriyātva*) by virtue of being a causal power (*kārakaśakti*), then the doctrine of the non-duality of action (*kriyādvaitavāda*) alone would result, because the world would consist solely of primary and secondary causal factors. For this very reason, it is included within the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*).

Even having extracted the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), it is determined that the qualification for knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*) alone is established; for the qualification for knowledge occurs in the pure [self], as indicated by the opening statement: "in the agent who is a knower" (*jñātari*).
In that context, what is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is—

The consciousness "I" is that which is constricted by the limitation of relying on the distinctions of manifestations that are themselves internally differentiated. In that regard, the very sovereignty over those manifestations becomes the sovereignty pertaining to the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

The demonstration that "knowledge and action [arise] from this" is established at the conclusion; however, in the section on Action (Kriyādhikāra), having extracted from that [conclusion], there is a determination of the principle of Action—which has attained fullness through its states such as time—and its object. For first the subject experiences "I know," and thereafter he acts; therein—
In the word *jānāmi*, the root denotes knowledge (*jñāna*), while the suffix denotes agency (*kartṛtva*);
however, this agency is nothing other than the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). The separate mention [of agency] is for the purpose of instructing those who are ignorant;
as for the agency in the word *karoti*, that is something else entirely, consisting of effort (*puṣṭi*). Enough, then, with these extremely profound matters.
By means of these futile conceptualizations, he states the resultant reality with the words "and thus":

when there is oneness of cognition and action, the meaning of the word *jñātṛ* (the knower)— that is, the meaning of the verbal root *jñā* as derived from the suffix *tṛc*— is [identical] to that of the base (*prakṛti*), which denotes "awakening" (*avabodha*).

And by virtue of the suffix: because of the *tṛc* suffix which denotes the agent of the action performed within one's own internal self; and "in its entirety" means with complete fullness; it becomes "determined," the sense being that this is established by its denoting a single unified mass consisting of both knowledge and action. Now, [the author] asks, "What follows from that? and says, "In that case... when the teacher is present.

By eleven verses beginning with "The agent" (*kartrā*) and ending with "Since pure knowledge and action [reside] therein" (*yataḥ*), that very [agent]—namely, knowledge as the object (*karma*) and the immediate perception of the senses—is brought to the state of being the subject of description. Why? For what reason? That very [agent] is the doer.

Freedom is the domain of the power of knowledge; upon reaching its ultimate limit, it becomes the Great Freedom (mahāsvātantrya), which is the nature of the supreme I-consciousness (parāhaṃtā). As it has been said:
"From that, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara)."

Thus [it is said]. What is that? It is the constraint (*niyantraṇā*) which has as its support those various manifestations (*ābhāsabheda*)—in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth—which are "self-differentiated," meaning they are manifested by that supreme light (*paraprakāśa*) as being distinct from it through its own power of exclusion (*apohana*).
"...because, as stated in the passage beginning with 'The simultaneous direct perception by the senses... and ending with '...since knowledge and action are pure in that [state]...'"

This is elucidated by these eleven verses. Among them, after stating with one verse that "an appearance either depends on another appearance or does not," it is stated in the following verse that "that very appearance is one.
Then, after stating with two verses that "the appearance of causal efficiency is likewise determined by appearance," [the text proceeds].
Regarding the question "In what appearance does that causal efficiency reside?", [the author] explains it again with two verses:

"Resorting to a restricted form" means being contracted by that [causal efficiency]—that is, having undergone contraction—and existing as a knower of that alone; this refers to the self-awareness "I."
The meaning is "the nature of a limited 'I'. For this very reason, there is sovereignty (*svātantrya*) within those appearances;
yet, in its entirety, the nature of sovereignty exists everywhere. This is the summary: because the nature of a limited "I" [is present] in non-pots, pots, and so forth.

C. That very reality, denoted by the word "knowledge" (jñāna), which exists as the knower, when extracted from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body and so forth, and for that very reason having reached the supreme limit, becomes the Great Sovereignty (mahāsvātantrya) whose nature is the supreme I-consciousness (parāhantā) and omniscience (sarvajñatva). Therefore:

That very point is determined by a group of eleven verses characterized by their beginning and end. Having thus stated the intention of the chapter as a whole, he explains it in detail with the words "therein" (*tatra*).
"Therein" means within the group of eleven verses; "dependence on another manifestation" refers to the state of clarity.

The meaning is as follows: "dependent on another manifestation" refers to a manifestation—such as the manifestation of blue—that requires a manifestation distinct from the forms of the manifestations of seeing and so forth;

the word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), or alternatively, it means that in the state of clarity, it does not depend on other manifestations; the word *vā* (or) is also used in the sense of conjunction alone; and the phrase "that manifestation is indeed one" uses the particle *eva* (indeed).
The sequence is broken; by the first verse— this is the meaning—

and by another verse— the second verse— in that very same way— namely, according to the manifestation (ābhāsa)— it is determined by manifestation— that is, determined by manifestations such as blue— and by two verses— the third and fourth— again.

By means of two verses— the fifth and the sixth— it is shown that the manifestation (*ābhāsa*), variegated— that is, diversified— by other manifestations, has its "inner-ness" (*āntaratva*)— its state of being within the Light— as its foundation, meaning its substratum. This inner-ness consists in being contained within the Light.

By means of one verse, [it is shown that] internality is like a wall for appearances variegated by other appearances (or, "like a wall for that which is variegated by other appearances"—Kṣemarāja). Then, by means of a pair of verses, externality is explained both in terms of its essential nature and its divisions. After that—

The summary meaning of this chapter is as follows: by means of one verse, there is a conclusion regarding the single substratum of powers such as knowledge; by means of another verse, while concluding the state of being Maheśvara, there is an introduction to the forthcoming section on action (kriyādhikāra). Now, the meaning of the verses is examined.
Now, if this entire worldly transaction exists solely by being grounded in the Supreme Lord,
then the well-known variety of its states— consisting mostly of clarity and lack of clarity— would be untenable;
for that Blessed One by whom it is indeed vitalized is one alone, and there is no intrinsic nature of the transaction apart from Him.
Anticipating the doubt, "Do we perceive some reality? he says:
by means of the seventh verse; that is to say, by means of the pair of verses, namely the eighth and ninth.
Then—immediately after that—by means of the tenth verse; that is to say, of that which exists as a single unity.
The meaning is "of the conscious self" (*cidātman*). "Summary" (*upasaṃhāra*) means a concise statement by way of including all attributes;

"by another verse," namely the eleventh; "the state of being the Great Lord" (*maheśvaratva*) refers to the nature of the Great Lord residing within the conscious self; "thus" (*iti*) means in this manner. He announces the exposition of the meaning of the verse with the word "now" (*atha*).
Having thus stated the purport of the entire treatise through both its collective and individual aspects,
he provides the introduction to the first and second verses with the words "nanu" (but/now).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:

"Only by being grounded in the Supreme Lord"—that is, only by having the supreme subject, who is the unifier, as its foundation—"then," of "this" empirical transaction, "by whom"—by which subject acting as its foundation—it is "animated," meaning its existence is bestowed. Now, one might object: "In that case, let the empirical transaction be entirely distinct from that [subject]. To this, he says: "And not..."

"Distinct from that" (*tadvyatirekeṇa*). "Distinct from that" means distinct from the supreme subject whose nature is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*); here the instrumental case is used in the sense of "being in such a state. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the two verses beginning with "occurring at that time" (*tātkālika*).
In some cases, appearances depend solely on the immediate presence of the senses;
otherwise, in other instances such as blindness or thick darkness, they do not. (1)
There is no distinction whatsoever in the existence of the manifestation of an object among conceptual constructions that refer to past, present, or future objects. (2)

The connection between these two joined verses is as follows: by this much alone there is a distinction among appearances, but there is no distinction whatsoever within the appearance of the object itself regarding its own nature.
At the very moment that appearance manifests, it exists; that which is beyond the reach of the senses occurs at that very time.

What is called "perceptibility by the external senses" consists of a distinct manifestation (*ābhāsa*) of the form "I see this," which, being dependent upon and mixed with that [manifestation], constitutes those manifestations in which there is the conventional usage of "clarity. The object of the blind person is "blind"— *Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment from a discussion on the nature of perception and manifestation in a philosophical system such as Pratyabhijñā or Trika, likely from Abhinavagupta’s *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikāvṛtti* or a similar work.*
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"In this regard, he first states the implicit connection between the two verses with the words *kevalam* (merely).
By this much, the meaning is: merely by the difference consisting in the dependence on whether [the object] is perceptible to the senses or not."

Of appearances—namely, the appearances of blue and so forth, as well as the appearances of the cognition thereof and so forth—the "difference" (*bheda*) is their mutual distinctness; furthermore, in another sense, there is a difference residing within its own self, meaning an internal difference (*svagatabheda*). "Connection" (*saṃbandha*) refers to an implicit synthesis. Having stated the connection, [he proceeds with] the explanation...
"At the very moment he begins to act" means: at the very time that this appearance—
the appearance of blue and so forth— shines forth, i.e., manifests, at that very time there is what is called "perceptibility by the external senses," namely,
another appearance consisting of the sensory capacity known as perceptibility by the external senses.

Another manifestation occurs which has the form of being both perceptible and imperceptible; what is its nature? It is such that its form is "I see"—that is, it takes the form "I see. These [manifestations] are dependent upon that—that is, they are joined with dependence on other manifestations. He explains this by saying "intermingled with that. In some cases...

"Appearances"—that is, appearances such as blue and so forth—come into being. Having clarified the object indicated by the word "wherever," he says "yatra" (where). "Yatra" means in that context of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
By this, the portion ending with "appearances" has been explained. Now, the verse fragment beginning with "otherwise" (*anyathā*)...

He explains [the term] "blind" as follows: relying on the figurative sense of "thickest darkness," he explains it as "situated in darkness. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the sūtra, the scope includes subjects (*pramātṛ*) situated in darkness caused by disease and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding another type of worldly transaction characterized by lack of clarity, those appearances there are otherwise; for instance, a person born blind possesses no other appearance characterized by direct perception through the external senses,
whereas for one who has become blind or is situated in deep darkness, that [appearance] does not exist at that time, but rather—
It merely recollects the previous state of being perceptible by the external sense organs. || 1 ||

Therefore, one should not entertain the possibility that there is any distinction in the nature of the appearance of an object even when it exists within certain conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). For those conceptual constructions—
whether they refer to a future thing, have a future as their goal, have the present as their goal, or rest upon a past thing— are all of that nature.

This is what is meant: in such instances as "I see this blue," "I conceptualize it," "I imagine it," "I remember it," "I act upon it," or "I speak of it," this appearance of blue is, in its own nature, neither deficient nor excessive. Thus...

The apprehension of the perceiver, such as the eye and so forth, consists of indistinctness—that is, it has the nature of indistinctness. In that conventional activity, which consists of mere conceptualization, [the cognitions] are otherwise, meaning they are devoid of the intermingling of other appearances. He begins the justification for this with the word "tathā" (thus).

"Hi" means: one who has become blind—whose vision is lost due to disease or the like—recalls (*anusandhatte*), that is, remembers, that which was [previously] perceived by the senses at that very time (*tātkālikam*). By this, the first verse has been explained. || 1 ||
Now, he provides the commentary on the second verse in a manner that yields its fruit, beginning with the words "tasmāt" (therefore).
"Tasmāt" means: because difference exists solely due to the absence of that [mixture] which arises from the intermingling of one manifestation with another manifestation;
for that reason. He explains the phrase "sattāyām" (in existence) as "svarūpe" (in its own nature); this is the possibility.

By the phrase "it should not be done," it is indicated that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility; he explains the entire compound word beginning with "bhāvi" as "te hi. Here, he announces his intention to state the summarized meaning with the word "etad. In response to the inquiry, "What is being said? he says: "I see this blue."

The apprehension of non-conceptual experience; the apprehension of conceptual experience as "I am imagining"; the apprehension of erroneous cognition and the like as "I am visualizing"; the apprehension of recollective cognition as "I am remembering";
the apprehension of the activity of the organs of action as "I am acting"; and [the apprehension] as "I am speaking" by way of predominance.
The activity of the organ of speech is mentioned separately;
for even when one says "I see" regarding yellow and other colors, it is thus. Furthermore, when these appearances are joined together or separated by the Lord through His sovereignty, then this—

The conventional usage of "clarity" and so forth— the conventional usage of clarity, lack of clarity, and so on— occurs when there is a blending of the manifestation "I see" with the manifestation of "blue," etc., through the exclusion of other manifestations such as "I imagine."
This is the conventional usage of manifestation. In this way, the diversity of conventional usage across the three times is logically established.
Furthermore, when manifestations are included within the essential nature of the Supreme Lord, there is no exclusion from anything, nor is there any intermingling with anything. || 2 ||

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), all other worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are included. "Blue appearance" (*nīlābhāsa*) refers to the appearance of blue that has become the object of actions such as seeing; "neither deficient nor excessive" (*anyūnādhika*) means neither lacking nor redundant—that is, it is of a single uniform nature. By way of extension (*atideśa*), the same quality of being neither deficient nor excessive applies to the actions of seeing and so forth as well.

He says "thus": "Thus"—just as with blue, even in the case of yellow and so forth, there occurs an appearance in the form of "I see" or "I am seeing"; that too, in its own nature, is neither deficient nor excessive.
This is the connection with what precedes. The appearance of blue is an illustration for the appearances of yellow and the rest.

Because even the manifestations as yellow and so forth are neither deficient nor excessive. The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "I see also" is intended to include the manifestations of actions such as "I will imagine," since those too are neither deficient nor excessive.
Furthermore—in another sense—when those manifestations [arise] through the Lord's sovereignty...
They are conjoined—mixed with one another—and they are disjoined—they appear as distinct. Then, this well-known conventional usage, such as "clarity" or "lack of clarity," occurs.
When the question arises as to how this is so, he says: "blue. [This occurs] through differentiation—that is, through disjunction.

By implication, the conventional usage of "non-clarity" (*asphuṭatā*) occurs through the reversal of this very [clarity]. The word "thus" (*evam*) extends [the distinction between] clarity and non-clarity to all conventional usages. Now, one might object: "If this alone is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), then it results in dualism. To this, he says: "The Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*). Furthermore—meaning, in another alternative view (*pakṣāntara*).

"In being included within the nature of the Supreme Lord" means in being submerged within the nature of consciousness that constitutes the supreme subject. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the statement of the summarized meaning.

Thus, here is the construction of the two verses: In some cases, appearances—namely, the appearances of blue and so forth, as well as the appearances of the cognitions thereof—exist solely in dependence upon the presence or absence of the sense organs;
however, in other cases, such as in utter darkness and the like, they exist otherwise. Furthermore—

Now, one might object: "Let this be possible in the case of blue and other such objects where there is the operation of the external senses; but since that is absent in the case of pleasure and so forth, how can there be variety? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And in the case of pleasure and so forth, as well as in those things which are the causes of pleasure and so forth..."
Even though the light exists, it remains in that state because it has passed away. || 3 ||
But when pleasure and the like are intensely delineated by conceptual thought, their persistence remains exactly as it was, because they are clearly perceived in that very way. (4)

Although the appearance is indeed the same whether it concerns pleasure such as a garland or sandalwood and its cause, or pain such as a snake or a bracelet and its cause— whether past or future— nevertheless, this [distinction] is "past" in one sense;

for while there is no difference in the existence of the manifestation of the object (*arthāvabhāsa*), there is, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a distinction in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) in certain cases.
It exists. In which conceptualizations, and of what kind? It is that which is about to come into being, "becoming. || 2 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the third and fourth verses with the words "nanv etat" (But is this not...).
Here the commentary says:
"etat" refers to this diversity. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the two verses and explains them.
Regarding the phrase "in pleasure and so forth," the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: the word *sukha* (pleasure) is explained by its well-known usage; as for the word *saukhya* and so forth...

He explains [the word] *srak* (garland) as "in its cause"—that is, in the cause of pleasure. By means of the two occurrences of the word *ādi* (and so forth), he states the objects to be grasped, saying "in pain" (*duḥkhe*). He explains the word *atīta* (past) as "having passed away" (*vyatīte*).
This too is explained by the very words used; intending to show that it is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), he says "in the future" (*anāgate*). In the future...

The meaning is "it will come to be. He explains "in the presence of the manifestation" with the words "even though," etc. "That very one" means "only one. The construction is "even though... nevertheless," which is indicated by the word *api*. This refers to the word *atīta* (past) that has already been explained.
In order to explain the fifth reason and to fulfill the expectation of the phrase "even though," he says:

"This is future. Because there is a mixing [of objects] through one manifestation, and because there is a delimitation through another manifestation, therefore—even though those [objects] are present—that cognizer [experiences them] by means of that [manifestation].

There is no persistence in such a manner as it previously was—such that one thinks, "I am now happy" or "I am suffering"—or as one who has acquired the respective collection of causes and conditions. || 3 ||

"Nevertheless" (tathāpi) means: together with another manifestation—that is, a manifestation distinct [from the object]; "because" (yataḥ)—that is, for which reason—there is a "mingling" (vyāmiśraṇā), meaning a state of being mixed, or rather, a conjunction;
that is to say, of the manifestation of the object, [with] the manifestation of "I experience," namely, the manifestation of presentness.
"Vicchedaḥ" means separation; by that [separation], the meaning is "due to both mixing and separation.

He states the sense of the locative absolute (*satisaptamī*) with the words "even when they exist" (*vidyamāneṣv api*). Here, existence should be understood as being produced by memory; whereas in the case of the future, it is produced by mental construction (*manorājya*). "In them" refers to pleasure and so forth.

And regarding "the causes of that," the word "of that knower" (*tasya pramātuḥ*) is to be supplied as a *śeṣa* (elliptical supplement). He explains "stability" (*sthiti*) with the word "by that" (*tena*). By this, it is indicated that here there is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), as in the expression "one who does not eat at a funeral feast" (*aśrāddhabhojī*). He states the object required by the word "thus" (*tathā*) with the word "as" (*yathā*). As that stability...

"How was it previously? "How so? "In what way? [One thinks: "I am happy now," or "I am suffering now"; or likewise, "I am now one who has properly accumulated (*samārjita*) the collection of various causes—the causes of pleasure and pain. And in this regard:

This much has been stated in accordance with the Sūtra; however, this principle should be applied by way of illustration even to the future, as will be explained later: "Just as [one thinks], 'Now I am happy' or 'I am suffering,' or 'I possess the collection of causes and conditions that have been acquired,' so too [one thinks] 'Today it does not exist. By this—
The explanation of the preceding verse is complete.

And thus is the construction: even though objects such as pleasure and the causes of pleasure exist—existing either as objects of memory or as subjects of mental construction—and even though they appear in that manner.

Even when there is the presence of the manifestation of pleasure and the manifestation of its cause—even while they exist in the form of memory or the form of a mental construction—the cognizer does not abide in them as such; why? Because they are past, for that which is past [does not exist].

The pleasure and so forth being remembered, or their cause, appear as such by virtue of being characterized as future; for indeed, a future pleasure or its cause, whether imagined in a daydream or depicted in a painting, does not appear as such. || 3 ||

But when one intensely (bāḍham) delineates those objects through conceptual construction, then— due to entering into the appearance of the causes for designating the repeated and distinguished experience of pleasure and its causes,
and because it consists in the intermingling with other appearances— it does not [occur] in the manner we have described.
Furthermore, it is conceivable that stability occurs through another [means], such as "I am happy" and so forth;
this is appropriate because, at that time,
he then provides the commentary on the second verse, beginning with "But when," by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
By means of a continuous stream of conceptualization (*vikalpa-santati*) in the form of a kingdom of memory, those objects— namely, objects consisting of pleasure and so forth,

as well as the objects that are their causes— are indeed [grasped] with intensity caused by desire and through repetition— that is, by way of recurrence— which is precisely that which characterizes the mental representation of pleasure and its causes.

"Abhidhāna" means that which has a name; the "appearance" (avabhāsa) of its cause is the "penetration" (anupraveśa)—that is, pervasion—by which [the word] exists. For that reason, he explains the word "tathā" (thus) as "tena" (by that). By what we have stated—that is, by what was said in the phrase "tātkālikākṣa"—[it is meant] by the word "sthiti" (state).

In this way, he explains the word "connected" as "one who is happy," with the word "I am" being understood as the ellipsis. By such a manner—as that which exists in the present—it is said to be "manifested" because pleasure and the like are apprehended solely through the activity of the mind. Furthermore, the activity of the external sense organs [is directed] toward the cause of pleasure and the cause of pain.

Although this is indeed the case, it is nevertheless stated thus by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*). By the word "is possible" (*saṃbhāvyam*), it is indicated that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here merely in the sense of possibility. He provides the introductory transition (*avataraṇikā*) for the remainder of the sentence, "because of the clear observation of this," with the words "this is appropriate. Having provided the introductory transition:

He provides an explanation with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). At that time—namely, during the moment of intense contemplation (*gāḍhollekha*)—this refers to that intense contemplation. Now, one might ask: since the mention of the "past" does not exist in the aphorism, how is it that you have provided an explanation for the "future" as well?
In response to this expectation, he says "the past. Otherwise, there would be no determination of that [sequence].
This is the state of being (*bhāva*). By this, the commentary on the second verse has been provided.

And thus is the construction: the word *tu* (but) indicates a distinction (*vyatireka*) from the subject matter mentioned in the preceding verse. By means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—in the form of memory and in the form of mental projection (*manorājya*)—within the continuum of conceptualization, regarding the past...

When future pleasure and so forth are being intensely— meaning in an uninterrupted stream— scratched out [as objects of cognition], then, in that manner— meaning in the manner we have described, namely by way of being unmixed with other appearances— there would be a state of existence, a clear persistence, just like the time of past or future experience; it would indeed come to be so.
Why? Because this [cognition] clearly perceives the manifestation of pleasure and so forth;
it perceives the manifestation of pleasure mixed with a manifestation of clarity. The mention of the past is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of the future. || 4 ||

Now, what has been stated by this much? That external objects such as garlands and the like are the causes of pleasure and so forth, and that pleasures and the like produced from external things are the causes for the conceit "I am happy.
Consequently, in the absence of externality and in the absence of being produced by that [externality], it would not be so [as previously described]. (K. ṣ. ṣ.)

It might be argued: "In that case, those [appearances] do not exist at all; therefore, how can it be said that there is no distinction anywhere regarding the existence of the manifestation of objects, since existence itself is absent?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "The external nature is held to be a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for manifestations of both existence and non-existence."
Therefore, there is no self as the existence of those internal [factors] that are always existent.
That is to say, from the "indication" (*upalakṣaṇa*), which consists of the act of intense delineation; the meaning is "from the cause of perception.

Thus, the intention of these two verses is that the variety of manifestations (*ābhāsa*) here arises precisely through the intermingling with other manifestations, and not by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*). The form *upalakṣaṇa* is derived from the root *lakṣ* preceded by the prefix *upa* and the causative suffix *ṇic*, followed by the suffix *lyuṭ*. || 4 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fifth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).

Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "By this much"—meaning by these two verses. The Guru says what has been stated [in the previous verses] with the words "bāhya" (external) and so forth. Thus it was said.

The word "syāt" (it might be) is the connection [with what follows]. To the question "What is it? he says: "external. Here the student raises an objection with the words "tataśca" (and therefore). "Tataśca" means: for that reason stated above, it would follow that it was not said that "the object does not exist. [The author asks: "But what of it? To this he replies: "And there... And there, [it is as follows].
The meaning is: "given that there is an absence of externality and an absence of being produced from that [the mind]. "Those very things" refers to pleasure and so forth;

the point is that they are not nothing at all, because that which is merely sketched by conceptual construction (vikalpa) is nothing whatsoever. Now, in response to the expectation that "let them at least be something," he again brings forward the previously mentioned fault with the words "and therefore" (*tataśca*).

The word "iti" (thus) is to be construed as the object of the verb "uktam" (said). He states the reason for this: among those appearances of existence and appearances of non-existence—such as "happiness exists here for me," or "suffering does not exist for me"—their so-called externality is not their true nature, nor is it their own essence. It is not [the self].
For that which is "pleasure" appears in the form of an "external" nature; indeed, the very essence of pleasure is pleasure itself,

and it is only when another manifestation called "externality" is projected by the Lord through the power of His absolute freedom, appearing as mixed with that manifestation of pleasure, that it [becomes] such for it.

It attains the state of an adjunct (*upādhi*), that is, the state of a colorer or a qualifier; and consequently, just as the manifestation of a blue lotus undergoes no change in its own nature when the manifestation of "blue" is absent, nor does the manifestation of a person when the manifestation of a "king" is absent, so too it remains unchanged even in the absence of the manifestation of externality.

Thus [it is said]. The sense is that it is not logical to postulate a property (*dharma*) when the substratum (*dharmin*) does not exist. The word "iti" serves to include all the objects being suspected. The meaning is: having raised a doubt, and having brought it to the state of being an object of doubt by means of a question and answer.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it: "bhāva" (existence), etc.
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"appearances of existence" (*bhāvābhāsāḥ*) are appearances of pleasure (*sukhābhāsāḥ*); "appearances of non-existence" (*abhāvābhāsāḥ*) are appearances of the absence of pain (*duḥkhābhāvābhāsāḥ*).

He explains the nominative phrase "bāhyatā" (externality) as "bāhyatvam" (the state of being external), referring to those appearances of existence and non-existence. He explains the word "ātmā" (self) as "svarūpam" (one's own nature). To the question "Why is it not so?", he says "na hi" (for not). "Hi" means because. Regarding the word "sukham" (pleasure)—that is, of the entity called pleasure—...

The essential nature—the Self—shines as "external" by way of its body, that is, in the form of externality. For no one perceives this [pleasure] comfortably as "this is external," but rather as "pleasure. If so, what is this appearing externality? To this he says: "merely" (*kevalam*). "Another manifestation" (*ābhāsāntaram*) means distinct from the manifestation of pleasure.

"Appearance" (*ābhāsa*). By the Lord—the supreme subject—when—at the time of grasping externality—it is manifested—that is, it is brought to the state of being an object of manifestation. That [is] "externality"; of that, namely, of the appearance of pleasure.
He explains the word "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*) as "the quality of coloring. He states another synonym.

Regarding the term "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatva*): he states the resulting conclusion with the words "and therefore" (*tataśca*). "In its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ*) means nothing has occurred—no loss of its essential nature (*svarūpahāni*) has taken place. "Likewise" (*tathā*) means in that same manner. The mention of the beloved and so forth, even though they are not the subject at hand, is intended to include everything that is generally accepted as external; for some subtle observers [perceive] pleasure and the like [as being external].

Thus they maintain their externality. *Mlānatā* means looseness or slackness. By this [it is meant that], up to the point of "the Self," there is no slackness whatsoever in the essential nature of the appearance of pleasure, the appearance of the absence of pain, or the appearance of the beloved; therefore, these remain eternally internal. || 5 ||

In this case, within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which has the nature of the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi-darpaṇa*), appearances such as blue possess internality because they exist within the internal organ; yet they also possess externality in the form of being objects of apprehension (*grāhyatā*), since they appear as distinct from the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). And this externality is merely...
"External perceptibility" has been explained here in both states. He explains the sentence beginning with "existence" (*sattā*) as follows. He explains the word "thence" (*tataḥ*) as follows.
He explains the word "existence" (*sattā*) as "stability. [He explains] the term denoting the reflection of appearance as the substantive...

He explains the word "of them" (*teṣām*) as "of the internal ones" (*āntarāṇām*). The term "of the internal ones" is connected as a qualifier for the word "of the existent ones" (*satām*). Of what kind are these appearances? They are of the internal existent ones, by virtue of their identity with the subject (*pramātṛ-ekyena*).

The meaning is "of those that are present. The construction here is as follows: by the wise, the externality of the appearances of existence and non-existence is accepted as an adventitious attribute—a qualifying property—just as blueness is [the property] of a lotus; by those same wise ones.

Externality is not accepted as the self-nature of the Self. For that reason, those internal appearances of existence and non-existence always possess existence. Consequently, in the absence of externality, there is no absence of their existence; and thus, within that existence, they possess only particularity.
"Existence," thus [it is said]. || 5 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "here" (*iha*).
Herein the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"In the internal organ" (*antaḥ-karaṇe*)—it is called "internal" because it is the means for grasping internal objects such as pleasure, in contrast to [external objects] such as blue.

While [the Self] abides as the instrument—within the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), which is like a mirror due to its nature as the reflective surface of the intellect and its capacity to receive external reflections because of its purity—even the internality of appearances such as blue and so forth—that is, of appearances having the forms of blue, yellow, and so on—exists. Why is this? To this he says:

Regarding the term "internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*): it is so called because of its being (*bhavatvāt*), that is, because of its manifesting (*sphuratvāt*). Likewise, how is there also externality? It is because it appears as distinct from the knower—the knower whose nature is supreme light. Otherwise, it would be impossible for it to appear as "this," on an equal footing with blue and other objects.

"These [objects] certainly perform causal efficacy (arthakriyā), at least insofar as they produce a cognition whose object is themselves. However, regarding that innerness which is characterized by identity with the subject (pramātṛtādātmya), one might ask: why should these not perform some kind of causal efficacy there? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Because they are internal, when there is identity with the cognizer, there is no causal efficiency (arthakriyā) based on their difference; even when they are external, that [efficiency] arises from the difference between distinct appearances.

The word *ca* has the sense of *tu* (but). And "mere externality" (*kevalabāhyatvam*) is external perceptibility—that is, perceptibility by means of the external senses. [Objection: Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "And here...
Even in the two states—that pair of states consisting of externality and internality—these [objects], such as blue and so forth...

"Ultimately"—that is, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), they certainly do perform their own object's causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—namely, the causal efficiency consisting of the cognition of their own object; the sense is that they do not fail to do so, because self-experience (*svānubhava*) serves as the witness here. Furthermore—"that is," in the alternative case (*pakṣāntara*), that which...
Characterized by identity with the subject—that is, having the nature of oneness with the supreme subject—internality occurs.

In that state of internality, why would these [objects], such as the appearance of blue and so forth, not perform some purposeful action? That is to say, how could they not bring it about? This is the intended meaning.

This statement, "it exists, yet it is not seen," contains within it a sense of possibility. By this, one should understand that even the delusion that yogis possess knowledge that is always directed toward all objects and each object individually is likewise dispelled; for such [omniscience] is impossible as long as the body remains a limiting adjunct (upādhi). Indeed, even one capable of burning everything— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument regarding the impossibility of omniscience while under the condition of embodiment.)

The sound *nikaṇa* is seen to be capable of that [manifestation] in its state of resonance. If it is asked, "In that case, what is the difference between yogins and ordinary people?", we say no; for from their perspective, no conceptualization of difference exists at all.
As for such [distinction] appearing from your perspective, it is for them merely of the nature of this knowledge, for it is not [otherwise].
Ordinary people, seized by the delusion of attaining some extraordinary state, find solace here.
If it is asked, "In that case, how can they possess the status of yogis?", the answer is true: for they are established in the pure consciousness that is the nature of all things;
they perceive reality itself within their own self, and through that, they perceive their own self as all-pervasive.
They know [all things], yet being completely satisfied by that, they desire nothing; nor do they reject what comes of its own accord.
As it has been said:
"By those who are peaceful, nothing is grasped, nor is anything even renounced."
They do not know how to give or take; therefore, they remain in a state of peace.

Thus [it is said]. On this point, our own verse is as follows: "It is not appropriate to say that what is accomplished by *citi* is non-conscious (*acit*); for by her it is never accomplished as either non-conscious or conscious, anywhere or at any time."
Whatever is accomplished through the gates is also Consciousness; having realized this within yourself, perform your own actions like a fool.

Thus it is said. Now, one might object: "In that case, do yogis not possess even a trace of omniscience and omnipresence? No, it is not so. For that which has the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is indeed omniscient by virtue of being the witness of all, and it is omnipresent as pure existence (*sanmātra*) by virtue of bestowing existence upon all things. And it is precisely therein that [the yogi] is certain of his own self-nature.
For them, both exist precisely by virtue of the state of internal contact; as it has been said:
"When [the mind] abides pervading all objects, as if out of a desire to see..."
Then, what is the use of much speaking? One will understand it for oneself.

Thus it is said. For here the intended meaning is as follows: at the time of the desire to see (*didṛkṣā*), the kind of pervasion (*vyāpti*) that occurs among the many objects made the object of that desire—which consists merely of a subtle touch—is exactly the same as that which is described as belonging to the yogin with respect to all objects; it is not, however, that [pervasion] which you have in mind, by which he—

For one who is seized by the great heat [of ignorance], you might describe all phenomena existing across space and time so that your desired goal might be accomplished; however, since that is impossible as long as the body remains, and because your desired goal would ultimately not be achieved, that subtle pervasion is [useless] for the deluded.

That which consists merely of momentary satisfaction, flashing for only an instant like a jewel illuminated by lightning, does not become an object [of stable experience]. For those who are awakened, it comes into their very hands even when merely practiced elsewhere; as for those who are perfectly awakened, they are always absorbed in that—what need is there for them to seek it?
Regarding this [consciousness] which lasts for only a moment, it was stated by [the author] himself, "precisely because of its extreme subtlety," and so forth. As it has been said:
"When that which is non-different in self-awareness is expressed as being other..."
Then, resting upon the plane of verbal expression, it appears as if divided.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, there may occasionally arise for yogis who are exceedingly pure appearances of objects remote in space and time through the power of austerity and other means; however, even these occur only in part and not in their entirety, such that your hope might be fulfilled. And these [appearances] occur solely in accordance with the will of the Lord.

They arise not according to your will, because for those who are indifferent to their own purpose, it is impossible to follow your purpose; however, regarding those who do follow it— those who are like magicians—
the reason is that they possess an "inner-ness" (āntaratva) caused by the identity of the subject (*pramātṛaikya*), and on account of that, [the state] of these [beings].
There is no causal efficacy whatsoever for mere appearances; for that causal efficacy occurs only when there is differentiation.

Since this blue appearance is differentiated from the yellow appearance and since it is differentiated from the cognizer, it therefore possesses its own specific, determined, and distinct causal efficacy.
"It would make [the cognition] belong to the cognizer; let there be only obeisance [to you], so enough of this digression. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus," meaning that having considered this doubt of the disciple, he speaks. Such is the introduction (*avataraṇikā*).
Having composed the verse and presented it, he explains it with the words "because of its internal nature" (*āntaratvāt*).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
regarding the phrase "in the unity of the subject" (*pramātraikye*), he explains the two words "because of its internal nature" as being caused by that [unity].
"Caused by that" means caused by the identity of the cognizer (*pramātṛaikya*). By this, it is indicated that this is a locative case of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).

He explains the fifth case ending with the words "for that reason. He explains the word "of these" (*eṣām*) as "of appearances" (*ābhāsānām*). The term "based on difference" (*bhedanibandhanā*) is an adjective for "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*).
He explains [the verse] by way of its containing the reason (*hetugarbha*), [saying] "for that" (*sā hi*). The meaning is: "when there is difference," that is, when difference exists as the cause.
Now, in response to the inquiry, "How does purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) occur when there is difference? he provides the justification with "for that" (*sa hi*).
Because—from which cause—it is differentiated by itself through the Lord’s power of exclusion (*apohana-śakti*).

It assumes the state of having difference as its object; here the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is used in the sense of the agent being also the object of the action. The same applies in what follows. "One should perform" means one should bring about a restricted, self-accomplished causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—that is, an efficiency consisting of the cognition of one's own objects and so forth—which is fixed solely upon itself. The underlying sense is that this occurs precisely through the emergence of the Lord’s power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*). At that time—

In the state of being another subject. Now, one might object: "In that case, entities would never possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), for they would always remain entirely within the subject and never at any time [emerge] due to any cause. This is true; just as entities, even while appearing, always remain within that [subject], so too [is their nature].
Even the purposeful action (arthakriyā) performed by that [object], though appearing as such, is indeed included within it; therefore,
just as there is no suspicion of difference from the objects regarding the body of the cognizer, so too such a suspicion is not at all appropriate regarding the purposeful action performed by them.

And yet, at that time, this distinction does not exist because of the unity of the subject (*pramātṛ*). For that [distinction] is determined by the difference in the manifestation of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*); thus, even while the manifestation of the beloved remains external, it becomes distant when another manifestation characterized by embracing disappears, and it becomes something else entirely when another manifestation characterized by "this" is approached.
Causal efficacy is seen to be contrary to previous delight; therefore, there is an absence of difference in manifestation.

Since internalization is produced by the unity of the subject, for that reason there is no causal efficacy. However, for those for whom even the manifestation of causal efficacy does not appear, that causal efficacy does not appear at all, being equal [to non-existence].

Because it persists as long as the body remains, the manifestation of existence and the manifestation of its causal efficiency are indeed unavoidable. Non-existence, however, is merely the cognition of something else. As it has been said:
"When the manifestation of ultimate reality shines forth, the entire darkness of ignorance perishes."
At that time, even the wise, though possessing stainless vision, do not perceive the manifold proliferation of worldly existence.
Thus it is said. And here, "the state of having pure vision" should be understood as consisting precisely in the manifestation of objective entities (*bhāva*);

for the wise, by virtue of their sharp-sightedness, perceive correctly just like those who are skillful in worldly affairs; otherwise, the consequence would be insentience (*jaḍatva*). As it has been stated:
"For they are ignorant, as if they were clever"—it has been stated that they do not see because their cognition depends on the state of being something else; enough of this elaboration.

By this, everything up to the end of the section on "causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*) has been explained. Now, [one might ask]: if [the object] is external, what is the basis for that [causal efficiency]?

In response to the question "in what way?", he explains the remainder of the verse beginning with "api" (even) by saying "sā hi" (for that). The use of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is intended to explain the meaning of the suffix "-tas" (the ablative/locative sense of "from" or "by means of"). He explains the word "sā" (that) as "arthakriyā" (purposeful action).

Although it would have been appropriate to apply [the argument] here in the phrase "bāhyatve 'pi" (even in the case of externality), he will apply it specifically to the example regarding the "difference in manifestation" (*ābhāsabheda*).

"Fixed" means fixed by the distinction of appearances (*ābhāsa*). In response to the question "How so?", he begins the justification with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Regarding the "characteristic of embracing"—that is, the essential nature of embracing with her—when there is a "separation," meaning when [the embrace] moves far away, this [other appearance] also moves far away. And the phrase "this" refers to another appearance; such is the sense.

When there is the arrival—that is, the attainment—of another semblance such as "the beloved has gone far away," [the resulting cognition] is other: namely, it consists not in the absence of joy, but rather in the form of distress; for this reason, the word *iti* marks the conclusion of the subject matter (*prameya*). Now, one might object: if there is an absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), then both existence and non-existence would simply be non-existent.
Anticipating the Buddhist position that "the two existences are non-existent" (*yātam*—referring to the state of being or the two entities), he says:
"And causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is merely another appearance. Thus, even the capacity for causal efficacy is not the existence of entities, by which...
In the absence of that, there would be non-existence by way of its own nature (or: non-existence as its very own nature). || 6 ||

But surely, at the time when the external manifestation is being pierced through, the internal manifestation is severed due to contradiction; so how can it be said that "the manifestation of internal objects always exists"? He resolves this:
"Since manifestations consist of consciousness, their existence is always only within."
Because they appear through illusion as if external, this [consciousness] is also external.

In this context, even the appearance of externality and its absence regarding manifestations always occur within [consciousness] itself. "Another manifestation" means a manifestation that is distinct from the manifestations of existence and non-existence. For this reason, in the absence of that—that is, in the absence of causal efficacy (arthakriyā)—there is an absence in terms of its own nature.
There is an absence of intrinsic nature in both the appearances of existence and non-existence.
Now, he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "nanu ca" (but surely).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"At the time—on the occasion—of that 'interpenetration' (*vyatibhedana*), which is the act of distinguishing (*viśiṣṭīkaraṇa*) [the object] by means of an external appearance."

"When this external object is grasped as 'this,'" means at that time. "Internal appearance" (*āntarābhāsa*) means the appearance [of the object] as "this internal. "Thus" (*iti*) means for this reason. In response to the expectation of what is being stated, he says: "internal" (*āntara*).
"Of internal things" (*āntarāṇām*) means of objects situated within the cognizer. The word "iti" [indicates the end of the compound].

At the conclusion of the statement, he addresses this suspected point—meaning he leads it to the state of being resolved by demonstrating its irrationality. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it:
"In the state of consisting of consciousness," and so forth.
Here the commentary says:

regarding "of appearances"— that is, of appearances in the form of blue, pleasure, and so forth— it explains "always" as referring to "the appearance of externality and its absence," meaning at the very moment of the appearance of externality.
The meaning is: "at the time of internal manifestation.

Their stability resides in the light of the subject alone, because these [entities] consist of consciousness; otherwise, they would not manifest at all, as has been stated. However, when, by the power of *māyā*—which consists of the sovereignty of manifesting differentiation—...

When their externality is manifested through the appearance of separation (*vicchedanāvabhāsana*), then, depending upon that, this state of those things appearing [as external] exists both externally and internally. This internal manifestation is not opposed to externality; on the contrary, it serves as the very foundation for all manifestations. Therefore...
"How is there a contradiction?"—this is rightly asked regarding the statement that "the existence of internal things is always [present]. || 7 ||

He explains "within" (*antareva*) as "the knower" (*pramātṛ*). The word "only" (*eva*) is connected to both [parts] like the eye of a crow (*kākākṣivat*). When there is the expectation of "why?", he explains with "since" (*yataḥ*).
By the word "since," the causality indicated by the locative case is stated; this is because the word "state" (*sthiti*) is [used] in its explicit sense.
This is a self-explanatory gloss. Although not explicitly stated in the sūtra, he provides the reason by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
The word "stated" (*uktam*) refers to what was said in the passage beginning with "the meaning is like that of *prāgiva*. The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is used for the purpose of indicating the reason.
Having explained the first half [of the verse], he explains the second half with the words "when" (*yadā*). "By separation" (*vicchedena*) means from another cognizer (*parapramātṛ*).
And in its manifestation through differentiation—that is, in the manifestation of blue and so forth—there is sovereignty, which is independence;

she is one who possesses that nature. "Of these"—of the manifestations of blue and so forth—"that"—externality—"having taken recourse to"—having relied upon. He explains the word "asau" (this) as "sthitiḥ" (the state). By the word "api" (also), it is implied that [it exists] internally as well.

Thus it has been said. By this, it is indicated that in the phrase "because of externality" (*bāhyatvāt*), the ablative case is used due to the elision of a verbal suffix (*lyablope*). He states his own intended meaning—which, though not explicitly mentioned in the aphorism—is logically implied—by saying "this is not [the case]. "This" refers to the internal manifestation; how then could there be a contradiction? The point is that the manifestation of clay is not contradictory to the manifestation of a jar. Thus.
For this reason, that which was stated by the Teacher is rightly said. What is it? "Always," [referring to] the internal—namely, those things such as blue and so forth that exist as internal.
Such is the application of the words in the second half of the verse: "[of those] appearing through *māyā* as distinct."
Of these internal appearances such as blue and so forth that are manifesting—by means of *māyā*, that is, by resorting to an externality created by *māyā*—[it is argued:
"But surely, if there is externality, there must be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and that [efficiency] consists in being accessible to the external senses; and yet..."
Anticipating the objection that "that [causal efficiency] is possible for things delineated by conceptual construction; how then could these [constructs] possess causal efficacy?
Yet we observe that even a *piśāca* or similar entity delineated by conceptual construction produces effects such as terror," he says:
"This very delineation within conceptual construction is also external, appearing as something distinct."
Internal proximity consists in identity with the cognizer; externalness, on the other hand, is indeed difference from that.

Even that object—such as a beloved woman or a thief—which is delineated within conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) that consists of a specific form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is also external; it is not merely that which is perceived externally. This is because even that [object] manifests as distinct from the cognizer, as "this," whereas that which rests solely as "I" within the cognizer [is internal].

That is "interiority" (*āntaratva*); "interior" (*antara*) means "near" (*nikaṭa*), and that [nearness] exists in relation to something else; and that which is to be related to is this state (*sthiti*), which can also be "external. The word "also" (*api*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*); like the eye of a crow, the word *māyā* is to be construed with both [the interior and the exterior]. || 7 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"And that"—namely, externality; "that"—namely, the state of being perceivable by the external senses; "of these"—namely, of those [objects] manifested as conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

[This refers to] those who have fallen [into error]. To show that this should not be so, he says: "And it is seen. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), women and others who cause joy and so forth are included. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "In the conceptual construction" (*vikalpe*).
Here the commentary says:

"Of the reflective awareness"—that is, of the reflective awareness existing in a general form—"being delineated" means being brought into the state of being an object of delineation "in a specific form," that is, in the form of a particular reflective awareness; "that too"—meaning that [particular] as well.
Even a beloved woman, a thief, and so forth—because of which reason they manifest—that is, they shine forth.

To the question "In what manner do they shine forth?", he says: "this," meaning as an object of thisness (*idantā*). To the question "Whence does that very internality arise?", he says: "internal. "Near" means proximate;
and "that" (the word *tacca*) refers to the near, with the sense that [internality] exists in relation to it. This is the remainder of the sentence.

"In the absence of another object of dependence" means when there is no other object of dependence distinct from the knower (*pramātṛ*). And "therefore"—for that reason—there is "identity" (*tādātmya*);
everywhere, it is the knower alone who is the object of dependence in the absence of another object of dependence, and consequently, [the object] is proximate within the knower.

Since identity is indeed attained [identity is attained—K. ṣ. ṣ.], that which is distinct from it is necessarily external; thus, it is logical that even the mental representation possesses causal efficiency. || 8 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that jars and the like possess externality due to the activity of potters and others, but what causes that [externality] for that which is the object of the internal organ? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The manifestation of the mental representation, of pleasure, and so forth, occurs by way of an external nature."
Just as, by the will of the Lord, he exists in the form of a supervisor over those things that arise from the eyes and other senses. || 9 ||

The manifestation of blue and other objects reflected within internal conceptual thought as having an external nature— separated from the cognizer— occurs solely by the will of the Lord (Īśvara), who sustains internal appearances and nourishes external creation; just as it is with those things that have become objects of the eyes and other senses.
*Pratyakṣa*—attained unity, attained identity. *Iti*—for this reason. *Tataḥ*—from that cause.
*Tataḥ*—from that knower. *Iti*—for this reason; [the word] *ullekhasya* is used by way of indication (*lakṣaṇayā*).
Of that which is the object of description. || 8 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the ninth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). This is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it, beginning with the word "ullekhasya" (of the delineation).
He explains the word "ullekhasya" as "antaḥ" (within). He explains the word "bhartuḥ" (of the master) as "antaḥ" (within).

Following the root *ḍubhṛñ* in the sense of "sustaining" and "nourishing," two meanings have been established. By the word *icchayā*, it is indicated that the suffix *tasil* is used here in the sense of the third case (*instrumenal*). By this, the commentary up to the word *bhartuḥ* is concluded.
He explains the illustrative phrase beginning with *adhyakṣa* with the words *yathaiva*. [The senses] such as the eyes—

The analysis [of the compound] is indicated as: "those whose domains (bhuvaḥ) are the objects—namely, the eyes and so forth. He explains [the term] "having the nature of direct perception" by the word "pratyakṣa" (direct perception). The manifestation of blue and other [objects] in an external form is what is designated by the word "knowledge" (jñāna) for those [objects]. This is what is meant:

In ultimate reality, what is called the activity of a potter is nothing other than the will of the Lord (Īśvara) itself, extending as far as the vibration of the body manifested by that [will]; it is not some other thing at all. Consequently, by such a will of the Lord, even blue and other objects, though not external to the Light, become the domain of the external senses through conceptual construction.
They appear as external because they possess a fragmented form for the cognizer;

likewise, what difference is there in their being objects of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)? However, those consisting primarily of pleasure and pain, as described by Bharata and others, take the form of the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Thus, there is the implicit supply of the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Anticipating the difficulty of comprehension, he promises to explain it again, saying:

"This is what is meant. In response to the inquiry, "What is meant? he says: "The potter. What kind of will? That which is manifested by him—manifested by the Lord himself through the power of exclusion (*apohana-śakti*). Who is that [potter]?... [text fragment] ...who is manifested.

*Kāyaspanda*—the bodily movement of a potter; she is one whose limit is that [movement]. For it is the very desire pulsating within that manifests as external movement. As it has been said: "Even in the world, that which is indeed the internal pulsation, such as 'I am going'—"
That activity of motion enters into the body, the location, and the senses as well.
Thus. Furthermore—in another sense—that refers to the activity of the potter. [The opponent asks: "Let it be so; what follows from that?

To this he says: "And therefore. And therefore—from that reason—just as by the will of the Lord, even though they do not exist outside of the Light—that is, they have not gone to an external location—[they appear] from the supreme subject.

Blue and so forth— blue, yellow, and the rest— which are ungraspable by the external and internal organs; being objects of the external organs, they exist as distinct from the imagined subject— the subject consisting of the body and so on—
in the form of a severed nature, as externality, that is, as being graspable through the "this-ness" (idantā) and as residing in an external location.
They appear; likewise—in that same way—even blue and other objects, though they have become the domain of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), appear as having a discrete form and as being external.

This is because, from the perspective of another subject, even the internal organ is external; otherwise, the apprehension "this" would be impossible. This is the intended meaning. In the *Bharata* and other texts—

In the *Bharata-śāstra* and other such works, those things described by the terms *vibhāva* and so forth— meaning those described in the form stated by Bharata and others— are for the most part pleasure and pain, yet they are not exclusively of the nature of pleasure and pain alone,
since their forms as laughter and so forth also exist.
Pleasure, detachment, and so forth, which have the internal organ as their sole sphere of experience (*antaḥkaraṇaikagocarāḥ*),
appear as if they were external; for although the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) possesses sovereignty over volitions (*saṅkalpa*), nevertheless,
because it is impossible to subordinate the ultimate reality of consciousness (*cit-paramārthatā*), that [sovereignty] belongs in fact to the Lord (*īśvara*) alone.
As stated by the author himself:

"Although the stability of objects is restricted to the individual soul (jīva) which is constrained by the vital breaths and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), even there, that [stability] ultimately resides in the Supreme Self."
How could there be any constraint upon that [Self] by means of its own vital breath?
[The forms of the permanent and transitory states:
those consisting of the eight permanent states (*sthāyibhāva*) and the thirty-three transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*), such as love (*rati*), detachment (*nirveda*), and so forth.

By means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the eight aesthetic flavors (*rasa*)— which arise from the conjunction with pleasure, detachment, and so forth— become the sole object of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). While they exist as objects perceived exclusively by the internal organ, they appear as external entities, because they have become separated from the supreme perceiver (*parapramātṛ*).
The meaning is that blue and other such objects possess externality because they are apprehended by the two types of instruments (the senses and the internal organ),

whereas pleasure and the like possess it merely through being apprehended by the internal instrument (*antaḥkaraṇa*). However, worldly pleasure and so forth are included under the term "rasa" as established in the *Bharata-śāstra* because they lack such [intense] nourishment (*puṣṭi*).

Even though in that state suffering itself takes the form of pleasure, nevertheless, its manifestation as suffering is likewise unavoidable, just like the pungency of black pepper in a medicinal elixir (*pānaka*). For even when the pungency of black pepper is perceived in the elixir, it enhances the flavor; likewise, suffering, even when manifesting during the conjunction with the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors, [enhances the aesthetic experience].
It produces only aesthetic relish (*svāda*), for otherwise it would not be consistent with being "rasa"; for *rasa* is simply the relish of the combined excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
As it was stated by Bharata:
"The production of *rasa* results from the conjunction of the excitants, the ensuants (*anubhāva*), and the transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*)."

Thus [it is said]. Since the ninth rasa, the Quietistic (śānta), which has detachment (nirveda) as its dominant emotion, is not under discussion here, it would indeed be improper to speak of it as being on an equal footing with the eight rasas relevant to the present context; therefore, one should not suspect otherwise.
Now, you might object: "In the case of volition (saṅkalpa), the independence of the individual soul (jīva) alone is clearly perceived by you."

To the question "How is this said of Īśvara?", he says: "In his volitions. It is precisely for the sake of the *kṣetrajña*—that is, the individual soul (*jīva*) who identifies with the body—to subordinate, meaning to cause to perish, that [Īśvara's] sovereignty;
and this is so in reality, that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). For indeed...

Thus, where there occurs for the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) who is indeed without desire a creation consisting of volitional intent (*saṅkalpa*)—which has as its essence a spontaneous projection—there the activity belongs clearly to the Lord alone. Therefore, the established conclusion is that even in the case of external existence for those things produced by volition, the will of the Supreme Lord alone is the cause. || 9 ||
Now he concludes the previously mentioned unity and sovereignty:
"Without that unity, the worldly course of cognitions would not exist.
Because of the unity of light, there is that oneness; it is established that the subject is one. (10)
He alone, by virtue of his constant state of reflective awareness, is Maheśvara.
For it is from reflective awareness alone that the pure powers of knowledge and action of the Lord arise. || 11 ||
The sense is that it is appropriate to say that the light of a lamp which has gone outside the house is connected with the door of the house;
and likewise, our own verse also says:
"Even though the state of being a knower (pramātṛtva) appears within the collection of the body and so forth..."
Nevertheless, it surely flashes forth through this door from the sky of pure consciousness;
for just as light that shines outside through the doors of a house certainly belongs to the lamp situated within the house.

Thus [it is said]. Here, he cites the agreement of the venerable Utpaladeva with the words "as it has been stated. By the author of the work—the venerable Utpaladeva. When the question arises as to what was stated, he says "although" (*yadyapi*). "The stability of objects" (*arthasthiti*) refers to the conventional usage of cognition and so forth regarding objects; it is "restricted," meaning determined. For indeed...

The existence of objects such as a jar is seen to be independent of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*). That existence of objects—by means of that [existence], namely, by way of the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—is the limitation (*yantraṇā*), that is, the delimitation, of that Supreme Self. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). "Flowing by its own essence" means by its own will.

That distraction which has the nature of spreading—that is its essence. For sometimes the individual soul (jīva) becomes subject to volitional constructs (saṅkalpa) even without its own will. He states the result with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
The established conclusion (rāddhānta) is the final doctrine (siddhānta). || 9 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the tenth and eleventh verses with the words "now" (*adhunā*).

That which has been established by the preceding text— "that"— meaning for that reason— the entire worldly path (*lokapaddhati*), the course of the world, all conventional activity, does not exist without the unity of cognitions (*saṃvidāṃ*) or knowledges.

It could exist, and it does exist; therefore, there is oneness among these. Nor is this difficult to establish, because consciousness (*saṃvit*) is said to be nothing other than the manifestation of the object. It is only through the power of the coloring by the object that the manifestation of blue is one thing and the manifestation of yellow another, appearing as if directed outward; but in the ultimate sense, however—
Because light is devoid of any contraction of space, time, or form, it possesses only oneness;
thus, light alone is internally established, and it is that very light which is called the subject (*pramātā*). This has now been established through logical reasoning. || 10 ||
The commentary here states:
"Unity" means the oneness of consciousness. "Concludes" means he makes it the object of his final summary.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words: "By that unity."

Here the commentary explains the word "that" (*tat*) with the phrase "this which... (*yad etat*). It explains "of cognitions" (*saṃvidām*) as "of knowledges" (*jñānānām*). It explains "the worldly way" (*lokapaddhati*) as follows:

Regarding the phrase "the worldly path," he states "all" as a synonym for this as well. Regarding these cognitions (*saṃvidām*), "difficult to accomplish" means being struck by impossibility. To the question "Why?", he says "since.
If it is then argued that a difference between cognitions has consequently arisen, he says "merely. "By way of extroversion" means "this."

By way of being extroverted. Now, one might ask: "Does it exist as something real? To this he says: "In the ultimate sense" (*paramārthataḥ*). This means because it is devoid of—that is, free from—the limitation or circumscription (*pariccheda*) consisting of space, time, and form. The underlying intention is that it is not logical for the object of delimitation to possess the capacity to delimit with respect to that which delimits it. By this...
The phrase "due to the unity of light" (*prakāśaikyāt*) has already been explained. He explains "that oneness" (*tadekatvam*) as "oneness" (*ekatvam*).
Oneness is the oneness of light. He explains "the knower is one," and so forth, as "he alone indeed.
And "he alone"—that is, light alone—is "established," meaning it has attained its foundation; this is now demonstrated through logical reasoning.
The two words *śaṣatva* and *na* are supplied [from the previous context]. By this, the commentary on the first verse is completed. || 10 ||

Moreover, this nature of His, characterized by luminosity, does not remain devoid of reflective awareness (parāmarśana) regarding the coloring by blue and other objects— unlike a crystal gem— but rather its form is always being reflected upon; thus, the state of having a reflective nature consists in uninterrupted self-awareness, non-referentiality toward anything else, and being a single mass of bliss.

You, [O Ānanda, his very state of absolute homogeneity is his sovereignty—K. Ṣ. Ṣ.]; that indeed is his sovereignty. For that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), whose essence is the sense of "I," constitutes the pure, ultimate knowledge and action of the Lord who consists of play and so forth; the nature of luminosity is knowledge, and it resides in that very [reflective awareness].
Action (*kriyā*) is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose essence is autonomy; and reflective awareness is that which has internalized luminosity (*prakāśa*).

Now, he explains the second verse with the words "And not... (*na ca*). He unfolds the process (*prakriyā*) in order to explain [the phrase] "by virtue of being reflective awareness" (*vimṛśattvena*), beginning with "And not...": "of this"—that is, of luminosity—its own self is called "luminosity."
