One's own self is devoid of reflective awareness—that is, it is not the object of a reflective awareness whose agent is oneself; here he provides a negative example, saying "like that of a crystal gem. Just as the nature of a crystal gem and its coloring by blue and so forth are not the objects of reflective awareness in the form of "I" or "this," so it is with this [self].
The meaning is that it does not exist. Furthermore, in order to explain what kind of nature this self and its coloring by blue and so forth possess, he says "api tu" (but rather).

The meaning is that the self of this light and its coloring by blue and so forth consist of the form of being contemplated; they become endowed with the forms that are the objects of contemplation, namely "I" and "this. Regarding the state of being a contemplator...
He states a synonym with the word "uninterrupted" (*anavacchinna*). He explains "Maheśvara" as "Māheśvaryam" (the state of being Maheśvara).

The meaning is that this very [state] constitutes his Māheśvarya; by means of that alone he becomes Maheśvara. The word "eva" (alone/only) is the explanation of the term "niyatena" (by the fixed/constant). Having explained the first half-verse, [he now explains] the second half-verse...

"He himself explains: 'It is indeed reflective awareness (vimarśa) itself. He himself explains this as "it is indeed reflective awareness. Since even the state of "this-ness" (idaṃbhāva) ultimately rests within the state of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva), it has been stated that [reflective awareness] is essentially the state of "I-ness. "He himself" refers to that which is well-known in the context at hand. "Of the Lord" (devasya).

He explains [the term] as "play and so forth" (*krīḍādi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the desire for victory and other such motives are included. He explains [the term] "pure" (*śuddha*) as "pertaining to the ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikyau*). He provides a separate explanation for knowledge and action:
"knowledge" (*jñāna*). In that very context—[it refers to] knowledge alone.

Thus, reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) itself constitutes knowledge and action in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*); in the supreme state, knowledge and action consist of the reflective awareness of "I" which has attained identity with the sense of "this-ness" (*idantā-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the plane of the Lord Sadāśiva; and in the non-supreme state, within the realm of Māyā.

The distinction here is that [the term] "present" functions with an emphasis on the state of being (*idaṃbhāva*). However, it has been stated that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is knowledge, for without it, this [consciousness] would be insentient; and since that very [awareness] is action (*kriyā*), this constitutes an introduction to the forthcoming chapter on action. May there be auspiciousness. 10 || 11 ||
From the beginning. || 89 ||

The self whose nature is autonomy (*svātantrya*)—whose form is that of being an agent (*kartṛtva*)—is *vimarśa*; this *vimarśa*, denoted by the suffixes *-tṛ* and *-tṛc*, becomes "action" (*kriyā*). The sense is that action consists of the agent, and the suffix *-tṛc* is prescribed in the sense of the agent.
[Objection: If that is so, then since action alone ultimately finds its rest, knowledge would be secondary.

To this he says, "and reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*). This means that [reflective awareness] has internalized luminosity; that is to say, it is the luminosity that constitutes the essence. By this, the very proof is established that the power of reflective awareness is encapsulated by luminosity.

For this very reason, in the venerable *Bahurūpagarbhastotra*, at the beginning and end of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) which denotes the partless reality (*niṣkalatattva*), [the letters *a* and *ha* are placed].

And its abiding in the middle is in the form of power (*śakti*), which consists of the sequence of phonemes beginning with *a*; enough with this unveiling of the secret. Thus—for this reason—*vimarśa* alone, that is, the self-reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), constitutes the supreme state (*parāvasthā*) in the realm of Śiva; for there, even the name of "thisness" (*idantā*) does not exist.

The very nature of those two—knowledge and action—is that reflective awareness of "I-ness" (ahantā) which has entered into a state of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with "this-ness" (idantā). The meaning is that their essential form is "I am this. The state of the Lord (īśvaradaśā) should also be understood as being right here. "While existing"—that is, while present—the connection with the preceding words "knowledge and action" is thus established. In this way.
The distinction—[the distinction] between knowledge and action, this is the ellipsis. He states the established conclusion with the words "in every way.

Of this—of the Light. It has been stated [in the verse] "the nature of manifestation. And that very thing—reflection itself—is action, because it possesses the quality of flashing forth as action once it has reached full development. Thus—from this, he...

"Of that which is about to come into being"—that is, of what follows immediately after this; "he performs the sowing"—meaning he plants it as a seed—because this [treatise] constitutes its sprout. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the chapter (*āhnika*). The term *śiva* indicates auspiciousness and points toward the supreme reality (*paratattva*). Thus, all is auspicious (*iti śivam*).

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Maheśvarahood," in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* composed by the illustrious and preeminent Māheśvara teacher Utpaladeva, accompanied by the commentary named *Vimarśinī* written by the illustrious teacher Abhinavagupta. 8.
The first chapter, on Knowledge, is completed.
Thus [ends the work] by the son of the most venerable Śrī Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha, who dwells within the region of Śrī Kaśmīra.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Jñānādhikāra* of the commentary on the *Śrīpratyabhijñāvimarśinī*, titled *Bhāskarī*, composed by Śrī Bhāskarakaṇṭha, the illustrious son of Vatārakaṇṭha.
And this first reflective inquiry (*vimarśa*), called the *Jñānādhikāra*, is completed.

That power which, by attaining the state of being denotable through the suffix *jñā* (the knower), effects the excellent weaving of the sovereignty of Maheśvara— who is otherwise expressed by the suffix *tṛc* (the agent)— together with the entity that is its object of expression;
and wherein that power, having arisen as the excellent seed of action, clearly becomes nourished.
Indeed, that chapter on knowledge has already been explained here by me according to Bhāskara.
No egoistic conceit should be formed regarding the mind, for Śiva is the agent who resides therein;
if you possess an egoistic conceit through identity with Him, that indeed is auspicious.
Śiva is the agent, Śiva is the observer, and Śiva alone is the reciter;
Śiva is declared to be the expounder—clearly, everything is an offering to Śiva.
Now begins the second chapter of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, titled "The Chapter on Action" (*Kriyādhikāra*).
Vimarśinī reveals her own power, radiant with the essence of its own faculties, within the mirror of its own vast and clear self,
upon the two shores of the objects of knowledge that constitute the portions of the subject.
May the illustrious Lord of Gaurī reveal to us the supreme Truth, that highest river of action which consists of the ground of the dissolution of manifold existences. 1.

Bhāskarī: Oṃ. By means of which [consciousness], through the essence of its own self-reflection (*amarśa*), it is constantly well-watered on its own ground with the thought "I am," as if from its own seed which consists of pure consciousness (*vid*) that has emerged from deep sleep.
I worship here in my heart that Supreme Śiva, in whom differentiation— pervaded by light, blossoming, and bearing the fruit of duality— is rooted as a climbing vine of activity.

Having thus explained the first chapter, titled "The Authority of Knowledge," for the sake of the unimpeded completion and successful progression of the second chapter, titled "The Authority of Action," [the author states that] even though [the practice] has been properly performed within the mind, externally...

For the sake of instructing his disciples, he composes an auspicious verse in the form of a benediction consisting of the recollection of the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), which indicates the essential purport of all [his] works, beginning with the words "vitata" (spread out). He— [the one] renowned as the Self of all— is "Śrīmān" (the Glorious One), [possessing] the Great [I-consciousness] known as the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśa*).

He is endowed with the sovereignty (*āheśvarya*) whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*); therefore, he is the Lord (*pati*) of Gaurī—that is, of this very power which is exceedingly pure—and thus exists as the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), being the form of the sustainer (*bhartṛ*), which is to say, the Light (*prakāśa*) overflowing with reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). He is the supreme nectar (*paramṛta*), known as his own essential nature (*nijasvarūpa*).
May the perfect, true reality manifest itself— that is, may it cause us, the limited subjects whose objects of egoity are finite,
to shine forth in our own essential nature by means of the sublation of the body and so forth, whereby they [the subjects]...
The sense is that they experience their own self as being of that nature and endowed with that sovereignty.

Who is he? He who is the Lord of Gaurī—both pervasive, meaning all-encompassing, and clear, meaning exceedingly pure due to the absence of any stain caused by the multitude of transferred mental states.

One's own self— the innate self known as "light"— is itself a mirror by virtue of its capacity to receive reflections; within that [mirror], one should contemplate the supreme river of action, which is full because it encompasses all objects and consists of the manifestation of the nourishment of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

He reveals the power of the instrument itself as a river; he causes it to manifest externally by way of reflection, for otherwise its appearance would be impossible. What kind of river? One whose own parts are of the nature of the subject—the form of the perceiver.

Those who are of the nature of the Rudras and the Knower of the Field— that is to say, the limited subjects— and the objects of knowledge— that is, the entire range of graspable things which have become their objects— these alone constitute the two banks,
the two shores consisting of the locus and the object; "therein" means in the midst of them.

By the force of its own power—that is, by the water of its own self-reflexive awareness—it becomes radiant, meaning it attains a state of being beautiful; for it is the power of reflective awareness itself that, having attained the state of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), manifests as the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). "I know."

For in the thought "I do," the initial reflection of the "I" first transforms into the state of "I know," and from that, it manifests as the state of being the instrument; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of even a stone or similar object being an instrument. And this is logical, for [it occurs] between the two banks of a river.

The brilliance produced by the water. Furthermore, of what sort is she? She is the ground—the unique locus—of the numerous waves, which are the various modifications (*bhaṅgī*) consisting of time and so forth. And rivers, by their very nature, possess waves.

They indeed exist. And this very [power], being clearly experienced externally, constitutes the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) for those touched by the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*parameśvara-śaktipāta*) through its operation under the sway of passion, hatred, and so forth; but for those touched [or rather, created] by that [power], it leads to the attainment of that [liberation].
They are indeed like steps, because they lead to the attainment of that [ultimate state] by means of seeking its root;
thus, they should not be viewed from a purely general perspective. As it has been said:
"This very power, whose nature is action, belongs to Śiva and resides within the bound soul (paśu)."
She who binds, who abides in her own path, and who, when known, brings about accomplishment.

Thus, because the Supreme Lord manifests as the individualized states of Anuttara and so forth, there arises the power of His nature, whose singular form is differentiated by the *kalās* beginning with the letter *A*.
From that, there emerges the eightfold group consisting of the vowels and the consonant groups (*ka-varga*, etc. manifested from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) which is His very essence.

For whom? For one who, through the gateway of being subject to volition (*saṃkalpa*), has—despite being ultimately the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*)—fallen into the state of being the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*); for this very reason, such a person is like a bound soul (*paśu*), and this very play of self-concealment constitutes his ultimate limit.
As it has been said:
"He who has become an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds,
having his power eclipsed by *kalā*, is known as a *paśu* (bound soul)."

Thus [it is said]. Herein is the meaning: by the wise, He (the Lord) is known as the designator of the Great Kula—called Mahākula—which is the supreme reality consisting of the Kulākulas internalized within Himself. The word "I" (*ahaṃ*) is of the nature of a *pratyāhāra* (comprehensive contraction), having swallowed within itself the entire collection of phonemes and *kalās*. The term "bound soul" (*paśu*) is used here in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇayā*).

It denotes a "bound soul" (paśu); for this very reason, within the cognition of the bound soul, it exists as the form of the word *asman*—which denotes the individual soul (jīva) expressed by the vowel-less letter *ha*—remaining as the letter *ha* [of the word *vatsa-ha*, according to the commentary].
This is understood to be with respect to the deluded; for the deluded have attained their finality in mere grammar alone.
They understand the word "aham" as the very form of the pronoun *asmad* (we), wherein the suffix *su* has been replaced by *am*, and the *a* has been replaced by *ā*,
for the sake of establishing its status as a complete word (*padatva*) according to the rule that [the substitution] proceeds from the [base] *anuttara*.
The form of the *pratyāhāra* "ahaṃ," ending with the suffix *supratyaya*, includes its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and grasps all the intervening phonemes. Being of what nature is it?
It is [the grasper] of the "mass of sounds" (*śabdarāśi*), that is, of the phonemes in the form of words beginning with *a* and ending with *ha* which have been swallowed within itself.

Having attained the state of being an object of enjoyment— that is, subordination or receptivity— by such a group of powers (śaktivarga), namely the wheel of the *mātṛkā* consisting of words and sentences which are identical with the eight groups (*vargāṣṭaka*),
[the subject] exists among those who are devoid of intellectual acuity.
Even though the *vargas* (classes of consonants) and so forth are initiated by phonemes (*varṇa*), they manifest through their being supported by those phonemes;

for in this regard, one observes the certain cognition that "in this *varga* and so forth, there are this many phonemes. When the expectation arises as to "how did [the phoneme] come to be an object of enjoyment?", he provides a qualifying attribute containing the reason: "the *kalā* (limited agency)."

By means of its *kalās*— its own constituent parts, beginning with the letter *a*, which manifest as distinct from [the whole] in those who lack intellectual acuity— he whose sovereignty (*vibhava*), consisting of the form of all phonemes within, is eclipsed, even though he consists of eighty-one *mātrās*.

The meaning is that because it vibrates as having the nature of two-and-a-half *mātrās*, it has attained the state of being the object of enjoyment (*bhogyatā*) for the group of powers (*śakti*) whose form is the *mātṛkā*.
Furthermore, by the wise, he [is perceived] within his own self, which is the nature of full light.
Light, whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), abides as the agent of the self-appropriation (*ahaṃparāmarśa*).

The individual soul (*jīva*), being bound by the fetters known as the conceptual constructions of the bound (*paśu-vikalpa*), is designated by the term "bound" (*paśu*); thus it is remembered. As it has been said:
"Śiva himself has assumed the state of the bound soul (paśu).
Being of what nature? [He is one who possesses] that which arises from the mass of sounds—the form of his own self-reflexive awareness (vimarśa), which constitutes his very essence.

Of the group of powers— consisting of the eight Mātṛkās beginning with Brāhmī— which has manifested from the collection of phonemes in the form of internal words such as "A" and so forth that denote the Unsurpassed (Anuttara) and other levels, and likewise of that [world] commenced by them.

Having reached the state of being an object of enjoyment—the dependence upon another—of both the collection of words and sentences and the collection of limited powers (*kṣudra-śakti*) by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); as to why he has reached that state, he says: "by the *kalās*. By the *kalās*—

[He is one] whose "vibhava"—that is, the sovereignty (aiśvarya) known as the manifestation of the *mātṛkā*—has been "obscured" (*vilupta*), meaning destroyed by the letters beginning with 'A', which are portions of his own self-reflection (*nija-vimarśa*), because they manifest in a fragmented state. This is the sense: [he is] the Supreme Śiva, whose nature is full consciousness (*pūrṇa-cid-rūpa*).
The Supreme Self, by its own will,

having brought forth the letters beginning with 'A'— which are the designators of the Absolute (Anuttara) and so forth— through a mere fragment of its own self-referential awareness resting within itself, [produces] therein the eight groups of consonants by means of their combination.

Having manifested a manifold collection of words and sentences, and having brought about their nature as conceptual constructs through the state of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), he then makes himself dependent upon those conceptualizations and manifests in the form of a bound soul (*paśu*). And this very [point]...

Regarding the motherhood of the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, they abide as his retinue; for conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), because they surround and restrain the living being (*jīva*) whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), constitute his very retinue. Here, the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) signifies only a member of the retinue and does not denote a biological progenitor. However, with respect to the expansion of speech (*vākprapañca*), [it is otherwise].
Let it also be a denoter of "mother" by virtue of being the cause; enough, then, with this excessive discussion of esoteric matters.
Furthermore, he is celebrated by the learned as the substratum of all principles (*tattva*).

The thirty-seventh is Paraśiva; the *paśu* (bound soul) is traditionally taught as being of the nature of the twenty-five *aṇḍa*-tattvas. Although all *tattvas* are indeed of His very form, it is stated thus with reference to their respective domains (*adhikāra*). Being of what nature? Of the group of powers (*śakti-varga*)—

Having attained the state of being an object of enjoyment— meaning the state of being subject to the command— by the aggregate of powers (*śakti-samūha*) situated within their respective principles (*tattva*) according to their own nature, from where did he come? Because of the *kalās*, beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth (*bhūmi*).
By means of its own parts, which abide as the very nature of reality, [the Lord] has his power eclipsed—that is, his fullness is lost.

Of what kind of group of powers? Of that which has arisen from the Mass of Sounds (śabdarāśi)—that is, manifested from Paraśiva in the form of Bhairava, who is the Mass of Sounds. As it has been said:
"In its nature as a single unifying awareness, the mass of sounds is Bhairava.

By this, it is indicated that the power of action (kriyā-śakti) stands here as that which is to be determined. Now, one might ask: "Why was an auspicious invocation not performed previously at the commencement of the section on knowledge (jñāna-adhikāra)? True; however, in that case—
For the sake of the unimpeded completion of the entire treatise, many auspicious acts were indeed performed;

however, knowing that it [the work] was already rendered auspicious by those very acts, no further [formal benediction] was made. For objects such as a water-pot brought for the purpose of plowing and so forth are not themselves considered auspicious substances [independently].

It would have been appropriate to state that [the repetition] is not for the purpose of sowing seeds and so forth occurring immediately thereafter; however, it is performed here again due to the possibility of an interruption. Even though there is no interruption anywhere in this scripture, which is devoted to the determination of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), [it is mentioned here].

Although such a thing is indeed possible, the author has not abandoned his own stylistic convention for the sake of training his disciples; enough of this digression. [Now, that] wherein one finds rest, the wondrous unfolding of play—
We praise that Śiva, who intensely loves the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and reveals it. || 2 ||
Now, another section is commenced in order to determine the nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
Therein, by means of eight verses, [it begins with] "For this very reason... and so forth.
That which is manifested by such [means] as these...
through the application of its support, [it attains] a state consisting of manifold play.
Like a woman devoted to her husband, that ritual action honors him; we praise that Śiva.
Having thus established the auspicious invocation for the sake of the subject matter (*adhikāra*),
he composes a verse beginning with "yatra" which, while also serving as an auspicious invocation to ensure the completion of the first chapter without obstacles, expresses his underlying intention.

We praise that auspicious reality called the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), whose nature and majesty have been described in many ways. Which one? That in whom—the auspicious one—rests his beloved, she who is the power of action (kriyāśakti). In whom? In that Śiva, [she finds] repose.

"Having approached," meaning having remained as non-different [or, according to the C. reading, as different]; "wondrous" (*citram*), meaning both marvelous due to being struck by its impossibility and manifold;
and "the playful manifestation" (*krīḍāvijṛmbhitam*), meaning the sportive display consisting in the form of the creator of time and so forth.

"She is able to show" means she is capable of showing [it] "excessively"; here the potential suffix (*liṅ*) is used because otherwise, due to her insentience, it would be ineffective—this is the sense. And it is appropriate that the beloved displays her sport after finding rest in her husband, but not through a painting; thus, there is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast).

This is the implied meaning (*vyaṅgya*). As for the "unpleasant" [aspect], it is incapable of that [action] there; thus, the word "beloved" (*priyā*) is used. Furthermore, just as in the expression "I know," the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) finds its rest clearly in Śiva—the very nature of the Supreme Self—who is denoted by the word "I," so too in the expression "I act," the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) clearly finds its rest in that same Śiva. This is manifestly clear.

Because [consciousness] manifests precisely by being attached to the subject (*pramātṛ*), it is indicated that the exposition of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is established in this chapter. Having thus accomplished the two auspicious invocations, he announces the discourse on the section concerning action with the word "Now" (*atha*).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

Now—immediately following the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*). By the word "having expanded upon" (*vitatya*), it is indicated that in the section on knowledge, the determination of the nature of action (*kriyā*) was performed in brief. It is "now commenced."
The intention is that [this was stated] by the author of the Sūtras.
By this much [of the argument], it is shown that action is, in the ultimate sense, non-sequential in the Supreme Lord,
due to its association with the manifestation of the sequence of limited, transmigrating subjects.

And it is established that [the limited transmigrating subject] is also sequential (sakrama). For instance, the refutation of the aforementioned prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated by one verse;
then, the distinction between being sequential and non-sequential is made by one verse; and thereafter, by three verses—

The definition of the nature of succession (*krama*). Then, by means of two verses, the distinction between the domains of that which possesses succession and that which is without succession is established; and once this distinction of domains has been made, it is demonstrated by another verse that, in reality, both find their rest in one and the same place—this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the *āhnika*:

he states the overall purport of the *āhnika* in its entirety with the words "therein" (*tatra*). "Therein" means within the section concerning the action that was promised; the word "first" is to be understood as the ellipsis. [He does so] by means of eight verses.
The meaning is "by the one who begins the first chapter.

He indicates the eight verses by means of the first and the last with the words "ata eva" (for this very reason). It is "established"—that is, it is settled through such reasoning. What is it that is established? [It is established] in the Supreme Lord.
In the venerable Lord Śiva, from the perspective of ultimate reality— that is, from the standpoint of truth— action is non-sequential (*akrama*),
because all sequential order produced by space and time that appears is simultaneously contained within Him; and this is indeed observed in those things appearing as having sequence.

When syllables are transferred by means of a seal (mudrikā), they are ultimately without sequence, because they are transferred simultaneously onto a leaf or similar surface. Furthermore, in this case as well, every cause of sequence—
such as spatial location and so forth— shines only within the body of manifestation itself, according to the principle that "the object is as it was before."

Even though [the Absolute] possesses the power to bring about the sequentiality of the entire collection of entities contained within it, it is not able to render that [collection] sequential; for the sequence thus imagined remains invariably included within it, otherwise the Great Non-duality (mahādvaita) would not be established, and if that were not established...
For if the entire body of scripture, which functions by taking that [Brahman] as its object,

were to result in being without an object, and if it were thus objectless, then all other worldly transactions examined through that [scripture] would fail to be properly established; consequently, the world would consist solely of that [monistic] view.

This is the state of being. Thus, that action, through its connection with the sequential manifestation within those limited transmigratory subjects— who consist of a portion of the supreme subject and who abide in the cycle of existence due to their displacement from the state of rest— is also sequential.
It occurs. In response to the inquiry as to how this is established, he begins to explain the intended meaning of the eight verses individually with the words "tathā hi" (for instance).
It was stated—that is, mentioned—at the commencement of the *Jñānādhikāra* (the chapter on knowledge); that is to say, because it was not applicable there.

The "reconciliation" (*pratisamādhāna*) is the refutation of that which is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Following that—immediately thereafter—is the "division of objects" (*viṣayavibhāga*), which means the classification of objects, that is to say, the explanation by way of distinguishing between different objects. Of those two—
Regarding "successive" (*sakrama*) and "non-successive" (*akrama*): this refers to the first chapter (*āhnika*), meaning the first daily lesson.

Now, the meaning of the verse is analyzed and explained. Therein, once the previously mentioned object of knowledge—which is useful for establishing the power of cognition—has been proven, another object of knowledge follows without effort.
Siddham. Thus he demonstrates according to the method of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*: Kārikā:
For this very reason, it has also been stated that action cannot be successive for a single [entity].
The objection beginning with "one" and so forth has been refuted by the establishment of that very oneness. || 1 ||

As for what was said—that cognitions themselves are differentiated by experience, conceptualization, form, and so forth, and that they have no substratum whatsoever; and that memory is established from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*);
and that if cognition were insentient (*jaḍa*), there would be no manifestation of the object, whereas if it were non-insentient (*ajaḍa*)—[then the following applies].

The claim that [memory] is non-different from the reality of the self because it lacks the limitations of space and time has already been refuted, since we have demonstrated at length that experiences and so forth, being distinct, cannot be logically established [as identical]. Furthermore, memory does not arise from latent impressions alone.
Now he promises to explain the meaning of the verse with the word "atha" (now). "Is analyzed" means it is explained by way of division.
Then he provides the introduction to the first verse with the word "tatra" (therein).
Here the commentary says:

"Another object of cognition" refers to another entity to be determined that was not established during the time of establishing the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) because it was not useful there, but which is useful for establishing the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

"By the method of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*—that is, according to the principle of a conclusion established by implication. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "for this very reason.
Herein lies the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

In that regard, he first states the intended meaning of the word "api" (also) with the phrase "yat" (that which). "Uktam" (stated) refers to the determination of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*). "Of them"—meaning of experience (*anubhava*) and the others—"the substratum" (*āśraya*) is the single locus in the nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*). "Pratikṣiptam" means refuted or resolved.
In response to the inquiry "Why?", he says: "Of distinct [entities]. This refers to "impossibility"—that is, the state of being untenable. It has been "stated"—that is, correctly determined.
"Of him"—of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*)—by means of that sovereignty (*svātantrya*), those objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) which are manifested by it, with them...
"Coloration" (uparāga) means being delimited by its own [object]; "by virtue of that" means by its power. This too has been stated: consciousness is indeed non-inert and of an uncontracted nature;
however, by virtue of the coloration of the object of knowledge manifested through its own sovereignty, [of this—K. ṣ. ṣ.]...

Since it has also been shown that there is the appearance of contraction, not only have the objections concerning the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) been refuted by this collection of reasons, but even the criticisms regarding the sphere of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) have been removed by this very same collection of reasons (or "set of causes").

The word "api" [means "even though they have been removed"—this is the meaning of the word *api*—K. Ṣ. Ṣ.]. As for what was stated: "How can a single sequential action be possible when the substratum possesses a unitary nature?", that being so in each respective case...
Thus, that which was stated—
namely, "because that which resides in two [places] possesses multiple forms"—
is also refuted; for, within this much of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), this alone constitutes its lifeblood.
"Of knowledge," "since"—this has already been refuted, as has also been shown; this too has been stated. Therefore, from this collection of causes—that is, for that reason—[from that cause].
Not only have the objections concerning the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) been refuted—

meaning they have been removed— but even the criticisms and objections regarding the sphere of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) have likewise been removed by this very collection of reasons, by relying upon the established conclusion (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*).
"Prevented"—this is for this purpose; that is to say, in order to illuminate precisely this point. The word "api" (even/also) occurs.

Having thus explained the intention of the word "api" as expressing a conjunction (*samuccaya*), he explains the verse with the words "ekā" (one): the meaning is, "given that there is a single nature, given that there is a single form. It has been said:
The meaning is that [this] refers to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) stated in the section on knowledge (*jñāna*). The word "likewise" (*tathā*) signifies conjunction;

its sense is "in the same manner. "Situated here and there" means "in this verse. "And thus" (*iti ca*) means "and in this verse. "It has indeed been rejected" means "it has indeed been refuted"; for this very reason.

The meaning is "from the causal complex. When explaining the intended sense of the word *api*, that which stands as the expressed meaning of the phrase *ata eva* found in the Sūtra should also be applied here. He speaks in order to explain the reason found in the Sūtra, namely, "because even a single [instance] is established."
"How could one thing possess a manifold nature? To this it has been said:

"Just as in the case of a mirror whose nature is consciousness, when various appearances arise without subverting its unity, what contradiction could there possibly be? Therefore, by the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*),...

Even though this single entity, which is the nature of the object, accepts various contradictory particular natures, to that extent those [natures], appearing in a sequential form precisely because of their contradiction,
bring about that one substratum of action; and therefore, this applies even to relations and so forth.
"Rebirth," thus [it is said]. || 1 ||

But is it not the case that succession alone is the very nature of action, and since succession is impossible where there is no reckoning of time? To this objection—the entire preliminary argument—already stated in the section on knowledge: In the entire [section] on knowledge that has been explained:
Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): to the question "How much is this?", he says "One. Now, one might object: "Does not this alone exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*)?

To this he says "In this" (*atra*). And "in this"—that is, regarding this subject—what has been said? To this he says: "Of that whose nature is consciousness" (*citsvabhāvasya*). This refers to the non-sublation of oneness.
Non-subjection to sublation, which is the absence of contradiction regarding oneness;

by that [means], when there is the possibility of diverse appearances—i.e., when there is the possibility of appearances such as blue, yellow, and so forth—there is no contradiction, namely, no contradiction of a single entity possessing multiple natures; the word "iti" (thus) serves to support this oneness.
Thus, at the conclusion of the explanation, he states the resulting reality with the words "therefore":
by the force of recognition— namely, through the power of such recognitions as "I who saw the jar, I am now touching it"— he, though being one, [is established].
The supreme subject is of the nature of light; he is the self of all objects—
that is, the essence of blue, yellow, and so forth— and [he perceives] the differences of his own nature, namely the forms of blue, yellow, and so on,
as being "contradictory" because they exist through mutual exclusion.
The word "virodhayuktān" (endowed with contradictions) indicates the completion of the [logical] fruit. Here too, he states the resulting conclusion with the words "tataśca" (and therefore).

By the word "ādi" (etcetera), the inclusion of *smṛti* (tradition) and so forth is intended. Thus, the construction here is as follows: that which was stated in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) beginning with "yadapi" (even though), that also—by implication.

In that regard, even that [action] which is not integrated because of its lack of utility is likewise rejected for the very reason stated above—that is, due to the aforementioned collection of arguments. Why? Because of the establishment of the single reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattva*), and so forth. What does this mean? A single, sequential action cannot belong to a single [agent]. || 1 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the second verse with the words "nanu ca" (but surely).
Here, the commentary states:
*kramikatvam* means the state of occurring in a sequence.
That is to say, it consists in having parts arranged in a temporal sequence.
Anticipating the objection—"Since this does not exist in the Lord, who is composed of consciousness, how could He possess such [temporality]?"—he says:
"And the sequential nature of worldly action arises from the power of time."
But it does not apply to one who is eternal; she would be like a sovereign [only] if she were a sovereign. || 2 ||
Regarding the moments that precede and follow the thought "he raises his hand" or "he lowers his hand," these possess a sequence;
for those, such as the followers of Kaṇāda, for whom action (*kriyā*) is nothing other than these very moments, that sequential action appears through direct perception itself.

But those who think that there is some such thing which produces the distinction of form perceived directly as it actually is— [which produces the distinction of what is perceived as it actually is— C.]...
The power that has come into the hands [of the agent], which is beyond the senses and consists in the awakening of activity, is eternally inferable;
it is merely its state of being prior and posterior that is inferred. Thus, the sequential nature of worldly action belongs to the power of time.

In the Lord— who is composed of consciousness, whose nature is the capacity for demonstrating the severance of appearances, who is the Supreme Subject endowed with Maheśvarī (sovereignty), and whose essence is Consciousness— belongs that activity of this Lord. Having thus provided the introduction:
Having introduced the verse, he explains it with the words "possessing succession" (*sakramatvam*).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"In that regard, first he establishes its possession of succession by saying 'it projects' (*utkṣipati*). Regarding the preceding and following [sections]:

The moments—meaning moments of action—consisting of upward and downward throwing, possess a sequence; that is, they are characterized by a sequence through being arranged in a temporal order of prior and posterior. "In that case," meaning while such sequentiality exists, the connection is with those [thinkers] such as the followers of Kaṇāda; by the word "etc. (ādi),...

The mention of the Naiyāyikas and others [is for this reason]. "That"—namely, action—"shines forth," because throwing upwards and so forth are objects of perception; this is the intended meaning. As for those who [hold a different view], such as the Mīmāṃsakas and others—this is the sense.
When the question arises as to what they think, the sentence states "tathābhūta" (being such) by way of its object.

That which brings about— that is, produces— the perceptible difference in form (rūpabheda) observed [in Caitra and others], which consists of a distinction in essential nature (svarūpabheda) caused by the specific conjunctions with various locations such as the hands; [this refers to] the operation (vyāpāra), namely the action (karman) of upward throwing and so forth.
That which is the awakening (*udbodha*) has that [awakening] as its form. "The state of being preceded and followed" means having a sequence;
"of the worldly" means belonging to the world; "having a sequence" means being accompanied by succession.
He explains [the phrase] "from the power of time" with the word "time. He also provides an explanation of this.

Regarding the term "appearance" (*ābhāsa*): the differentiation of appearances—namely, the appearances of blue, yellow, and so forth—is accomplished and rendered possible by a particular power of the Supreme Lord. This is the eternal power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) belonging to the Lord, which is non-different from Him and untouched by time.
There is not even the possibility that it possesses movement; for just as movement is impossible for the Lord, so too is it for this [the soul]. For it has been said:
"If the hand were to possess movement, then the action residing within it would likewise be [subject to movement]. (2)
Now, one might object: "Does not time, by assuming a specific state, delimit an entity according to its own form?
In that case, what indeed is this so-called 'time'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"It is the manifestation of that [time] which consists in the differentiation of things from one another by means of producing their own specific qualifications."

The external ground is the objectification by the subject; the capacity therein—meaning its efficacy—is of the nature of that which belongs to the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara), i.e., related to the Supreme Lord.
He explains "it fits" (ghaṭate) as "it is logically consistent" (upapadyate). By this, it is established.
This concludes the commentary on the fragment of the final verse. He explains the fragment beginning with "na tu" by means of the words "yā tu.
He explains "prābhavyāḥ" by "prabhoḥ. Here too, he states a synonym for it with the word "tat.
He explains "sāśvatyāḥ" by "kālena. [She is] untouched by time.

The meaning is that they are devoid of temporal limitation. By the phrase "there is not even the possibility," it is indicated that the *liṅ* suffix is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). He explains "like that of a master" with the word "just as.
"Of this too" refers to the action (*kriyā*) as well. In this regard, he cites the consensus of the elders, saying "for it has been said."

"Attained to that" (*tadgatā*) means "in the hand" (*hastagatā*); that is to say, it would be such, meaning it would possess sequential progression. The word "iti" marks the completion of the explanation. And this very point:
even though consciousness surges forth, because it is devoid of temporal sequence...
And in that very state, she is present as the full reality, consisting of the forms of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and so forth.
An action such as cooking, because it is delimited by time, depends upon a sequence; even if it is considered barren at its final moment, it does not attain the status of being "cooking."
Thus it has been determined by means of these two verses in the Śrī Tantrāloka. || 2 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here, the commentary explains:
"avacchinatti" means "renders as the object of delimitation"; that is to say, when that [delimitation] exists in each respective case. "Kālaḥ" (time)—
Time is the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, or the blooming of various flowers and so forth;
or it is cold and heat—its true nature is essentially that very sequence.

Those appearances which are established as being limited by a specific measure—such as the moon, the sun, and so forth; the *sahakāra*, jasmine, *kuṭaja* trees, and so forth; cold, heat, and so forth;
or the intoxication and dalliance of cuckoos and the like—are themselves time (*kāla*), because [time] is that through which [these things] are not yet fully established.
Movement, recitation, and so forth are brought to completion by them, just as gold is refined by smelters;
and that very specific nature of the sun and other luminaries is, in reality, the entity known by the names "the Other" (Para) and "Time" (Kāla). Having thus provided this introduction:
Having presented the verse, he explains it with the words "Time" (*kālaḥ*). Here,
the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains [the phrase] "the movement of the sun and so forth" by the words "those which," [and] "by way of measure" (*iyattayā*).

"By way of being delimited," "established"—meaning they have reached a state of finality, having attained the status of being whose nature consists solely of this [delimitation]. "Siddhāḥ" means well-known.
He undertakes to demonstrate these manifestations specifically, saying: "For example."

Just as it fulfills the expectancy for the word "such as," [the example] is "the moon. Although the mention of the moon was not explicitly stated in the aphorism, it is included here by implication through the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), according to its suitability. He explains the compound term beginning with "that and that" (*tattat*) as "the mango tree. He explains the phrase "or cold and heat" as follows:
Regarding the phrase "of cold, heat, and so forth," he explains that it is "to be indicated by those" with the word *parabhṛta*.

For the playful intoxication of the cuckoo (*parabhṛta*) and the like is indeed indicated only by cold, heat, and so on. The term *ābhāsāḥ* is to be construed with all the preceding words ending in the genitive case.
He fulfills the expectation of the word "ye" (who) with the word "te" (they). "They alone"—that is, the manifestations (*ābhāsas*) themselves—become time.
To the question "Why?", he says "yataḥ" (since), in order to state the reason even though it was not explicitly mentioned in the aphorism.
"Unestablished" means not having reached finality by way of its own nature; that is, "without limits."

The meaning is as follows: by means of those [factors]—such as the movement of the sun and so forth—it is delimited by a specific measure; that is, it is established by a specific measure. The sense is that it is made to have a boundary, such as: "I shall go after sunrise," or "I shall recite from its rising until its setting," and so on.

With what, like what? Like gold—that is, like gold—with "parivartakas," meaning with pieces of weights in the form of *guñjā* seeds and so forth. He explains the remainder of the verse beginning with "the very sequence" (*krama eva*) with the words "that very [sequence]" (*sa eva*). He explains "that very [sequence]" as "the sun" (*sūrya*), which is a particularity of its own nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).

The differentiation of intrinsic nature consists of movement and so forth. In reality—that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth—there is no other thing called "sequence" apart from this; and sequence itself is time, nothing else whatsoever.
Thus, the particle *eva* (only/itself) should be applied to both the distinct and non-distinct sequences.
Even the simultaneity of two appearances is, in relation to other appearances, nothing but succession; even the cognition of "slow" or "fast" is,
due to the difference in the extent of appearances, merely succession within the diversity of appearances.

K. ṣ. ṣ. ... indeed, the cognition of priority and posteriority also occurs in that very [time] by means of clarity and so forth; thus he explains "in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthataḥ*) as being measured together with the movement of the sun and so forth, which acts as a standard of comparison for each respective [moment]. "Sequence" (*krama*) is the appearance of sequence residing within the entities (*bhāva*).
He states what is excluded by the word "eva" (only) with the words "nānyaḥ" (not another). "Krama" means the entity known as sequence.
Now, one might ask: "Granted that the movement of the sun and so forth possesses the nature of sequence, what follows from that?
In response to this expectation, he provides a second meaning based on the authority of the Tantras as the reason.

"And it is sequence alone that joins [them]. Here, by the word "that" (*sa*), there is a reference to time. Furthermore, he states what is excluded by the particle "alone" (*eva*) as "not another. "Another" means distinct from sequence;
"this" refers to time. Thus, in the first sense, there is a displacement of the word order, while in the second, there is not.

[This refers to] the state of having no difference in sequence. Now, one might object: how is it logical for simultaneity—a specific point in time—to possess sequential character, given that the two are contradictory? To this, he says: "simultaneity.
[This means] of the two appearances—that is, of a pair of appearances occurring simultaneously.
With respect to another manifestation— whether with respect to a previous manifestation of the elements, or with respect to a manifestation yet to be produced—
it describes the nature of succession even within specific temporal distinctions such as "long" or "quick," by means of the word "long."
The cognition of "slow" (*cirakṣiprādi*) is also nothing but sequence; the meaning is that it occurs only with respect to sequence.

In this regard, the distinction is that the cognition of "slow" arises when there is extension (*vitatatva*), while the cognition of "quick" (*kṣipra*) arises when there is non-extension (*avitatatva*). In that very context—that is, only in sequence, which is the object of sequence—it is only when there is clarity (*sphuṭatva*) that there is the conventional usage of "other" (*apara*).
Because we observe the conventional usage "this is another" regarding a birth that has been directly perceived;

however, the usage of "another" [applies] to what is grasped by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) due to its lack of clarity. Here, he states the established fact: "thus. "Thus"—for this reason—with something equal to a maker of a likeness (*pratimāna-vartaka*).
The diversity of the various manifestations of Devadatta’s appearance, which serves as the locus for the "gold," is thus expressed by the phrase "he goes during the day. (3)
Now, one might object: "In that case, let time be nothing other than the very nature of entities;
what then is this 'power of time'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Sequence is based on difference, and difference, too, exists through the presence or absence of manifestation."
But regarding the existence or non-existence of appearances, it is due to the Lord who produces variegated appearances. || 4 ||
In this case, if time were merely a succession of distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), then the four fingers— having distinct intrinsic natures—
would necessarily belong to distinct times; therefore, [this would apply] to the appearance of dawn.

Being measured—that is, made the object of comparison—along with various movements of the sun and so forth by means of [time] equal to a portion of a *pratimāna*; "standing in the place of gold"—meaning similar to gold—it thus fulfills the expectation of the word "thus," namely, "the day. "The day"—[beginning from] sunrise...
[It refers to] the duration from its commencement until its cessation, which is a specific division of time consisting of its movement.
This is also an illustration [that includes] all distinctions of time, such as moments (kṣaṇa) and so forth. The word "iti" marks the completion of the explanation. || 3 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fourth verse with the words "nanu evam" (but if this is so).
Here the commentary states:
"evam" means "given that time consists of the movement of the sun and so forth"; "bhāvānām" (of entities)—

The nature of the sun and other [luminaries] is that which consists of their movement. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it, beginning with the word "krama" (sequence).
Here is the commentary:

He explains the first half [of the verse], preceded by the formal procedure (*prakriyā*), with the word "here" (*iha*). "Here" means in this manifest world; "merely a difference in nature" (*svabhāvabhedamātra*) refers solely to the difference in the inherent nature of the sun and other [celestial bodies] consisting of their perpetual movement and so forth. If it were of the nature of sequence—

Time would be established as having a sequential nature, but there would not be some other transcendental entity manifested by it; thus, the four fingers— the group of four beginning with the index finger— situated on the hand simultaneously through the binding of the joints, are [perceived as] occurring at different times.

It would be characterized by a difference in time through mutual dependence. To the question "Why so?", he says: "Because it has a different nature. That is to say, for this reason, it has a different nature—namely, that which consists of existence, such as a mass of clear light, and non-existence.

The sequence that constitutes time is animated by the presence and absence of the manifestation of difference; it is produced by those two, and it has been demonstrated in detail that the existence and non-existence of these manifestations are not caused by external factors— thus, this very [sequence] is the nature of consciousness itself.

In dreams, mental constructs, and the like, the self assumes various distinct forms through a diversity of appearances; for even when the four fingers are joined together at their joints, they do not become a single nature.
Because the distinction created by shortness, length, and so forth is manifest, whereas the thumb lacks a single joint-bond with them, it is not perceived [as such].
He provides an explanation according to the method resulting from the support of the aforementioned procedure, beginning with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Regarding the two manifestations—the manifestation of red and the manifestation of a mass of clear light—their respective states of existence and non-existence occur in succession.

Existence and non-existence—by these two it is "enlivened," meaning its reality is granted. And thus, the construction here is as follows: "Krama" (sequence) refers to time established as a sequence;

In accordance with one's inclination (*rucyanusāreṇa*), by means of deliberation— that is, by conceptualization (*kalpitena*)— and by means of a single continuous connection (*tadekānusandhānena*),

The underlying intention (*bhāva*) is as follows: otherwise, movement would be a separate action and the day would be a separate solar activity; what comparison, then, could there be between the two?
