Even regarding entities, a temporal sequence is not logical; nor is there, even independently of a cognizer, such things as distance or pastness within their own nature. To establish this, he says:
"hi"—because, of such an appearance—that is, of the appearance of yellowness and so forth in what is blue and so forth.
Non-existence itself is the reality of opposition—the very nature of contradiction. That which appears in a certain place is not opposed there; rather, that which does not appear is what is opposed.
Thus, the meaning is that opposition, whose domain is defined by appearance and non-appearance, is entirely ineffective regarding appearance itself.
To the objection, "Since this is not stated in the Sūtra, how can it be explained?", he says: "This" (etat).

This refers to the entire network of systematic elaborations (*prakriyājāla*) mentioned in the passage beginning with "of that which has a single nature" (*ekasvarūpasya*). In that context, the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) indicates sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). By the word "also" (*api*), there is a conjunction of both what has been stated and what has not been stated.
The distinction should be understood as follows: "manifestation" refers to the indication [of the object] by means of its entire being. || 5 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the sixth and seventh verses with the words "nanu evam" (But [if] it is so).
Here, the commentary states:
"evam" means "this being the case regarding the matter mentioned in the preceding verse"; and "anābhāsaḥ" (without manifestation)—

And [the Self] is devoid of manifestation; from where does its non-manifestation arise? To this he says: "For that..."—referring to space and time. Following the very nature of perception, he says: "non-existence"—showing the three times.
Having shown the sequence of time, he also shows the spatial sequence with the word "in the house. Even for objects, in relation to the subject...
He says "furthermore" (*kiñca*) because the state of being endowed with the sequence of space and time is not logically tenable.

He refutes even the notion that entities possess a sequence of space and time by their own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*) with the words "nor does [it] destroy" (*na ca*). The underlying sense is that it is the cognizer alone who imagines the spatial and temporal qualification of entities. This is as follows:
Immediately thereafter, there would also be a distinction in the manifestation everywhere according to the sequence of time;
the manifestation of the void and so forth, as well as that of the manifesting subject, would not occur simultaneously.
Even the sequence of space appears among objects to the limited self of the cognizer;
however, to the unlimited one, all objects appear as full within his own self by means of his own self, just like his own self.
In all things, whether singular or manifold in form, that which is the sequence of the nature of time—
explained as its source, the basis for their arising—
is the differentiation of manifestation caused by existence and non-existence; this occurs in relation to the void, vital breath, intellect, body, and so forth.
This is possible because that [object], such as the void and so forth, is devoid of light;

for its manifestation is not its own inherent nature, as is the case with blue and other objects, due to its insentience (jaḍatva). Rather, its manifestation is the flashing forth of consciousness (saṃvit-sphuraṇa). When that [flashing forth] does not exist for it—as in the case of the body during sleep—[it is not manifest].
The subject has been stated. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "In all cases.
Here is the commentary:

He explains the word *sarvatra* as "in all" (*sarveṣu*). In that regard, by the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is a single form, while there is multiplicity due to being qualified by place and so forth.
He explains the phrase "not produced by the sequence of time" (*kālakramākaraḥ*) by first analyzing its components, beginning with the word "time" (*kāla*).

He explains the word "source" (*ākara*) as "origination. Regarding the phrase "the basis of origination"—that is, the locus of origination—it has been explained; that is, it has been brought within the scope of explanation, being explained as "the basis of origination. He then explains the term "differentiation of manifestation" (*ābhāsabheda*).

Regarding the term "of the appearance" (*ābhāsasya*): it is "produced by existence and non-existence"—that is, produced by the presence of the dawn and the absence of a distinct mass of light, and so forth; by this, it is indicated that this is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopa*).
Furthermore, he refers back to that analyzed word as a whole by saying "it."
He states the meaning of the optative (*liṅ*) as "it is possible" (*saṃbhāvyate*). Here, the optative is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).

He explains the qualifier "having a fragmented appearance" (*vicchinnabhāsaḥ*) as containing a reason (*hetugarbha*). The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is for the purpose of indicating causality. "Void and so forth" (*śūnyādi*) means having the nature of the Void and so on.
The cognizer (*pramātā*) is that whose nature as the grasper is a fragmented light (*vichinnā bhāḥ*);

he will explain such fragmentation immediately thereafter. When the question "Why? arises, he says "For not... (*na hi*). "Of that" refers to the void (*śūnya*) and so forth. He provides the reason for this as well.
"Because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*). If that is so, how can there be the manifestation of this void and so forth? To this he says:

"Consciousness" (*saṃvit*). Of consciousness—that is, of the internal reality of consciousness—there is "vibration" (*sphuraṇa*), which is a flash of manifestation caused by the immersion into objects projected through its own sovereignty. Of this—
Regarding "the manifestation of the void and so forth":
when one has fallen into the course of transmigratory existence, there is the manifestation of the void, the vital breath, and so on; at that time, their manifestation is severed.
Thus, there exists a temporal sequence determined by the presence or absence of manifestation.

"I was of the form of the appearance of a child's body; now I am of the form of the appearance of a youth's body. And because that subject, due to not being fully immersed in the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva), is for that very reason [incomplete].

Because it possesses an intensified temporal sequence, it also causes a temporal sequence to appear within entities; that which was "I who was a child" manifests as a self-evident flash of consciousness as the subject with respect to the external world, occurring simultaneously with that state. That is the aforementioned form.
"Manifestation"—of this [world], beginning with the void. Now, in response to the inquiry "When does this not exist?", he says "Just as...

in order to show the states where its impossibility occurs. "In sleep"—that is, in deep sleep (*suṣupti*)—[there is no manifestation] of the body—that is, of the one who identifies with the body—for there, the body does not even flash forth as an object of cognition; what then to say of other things?

Regarding the manifestation as the subject (*pramātṛ*), its being "fallen into the course of transmigratory existence" means being included within the course of *saṃsāra* consisting of buying, selling, and so forth (the phrase "consisting of buying, selling, and so forth" is supplied from the commentary [C.];
by the word "and so forth," the cognitional subject [*buddhipramātṛ*] is included). "Of this" refers to the void (*śūnya*) and the others.
He states the conclusion with the words "thus, appearance": "thus" means for this reason. "The sequence of time"—the sequence known as time—is produced by the presence or absence of manifestation.
He demonstrates this very sequence of time by saying "past," and here:

The appearance of a child is non-existent, whereas the appearance of a youth is existent; this also serves as an illustration for the thought, "I shall become old. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the statement of the result. Thus, [it applies] to the limited subject (*parimita-pramātṛ*).

Having established that temporal succession exists [in the world], the author now demonstrates— using the phrase "And that" (sa ca)— that temporal succession exists among objective entities (*bhāva*), even though this was not explicitly stated in the aphorism but was raised as a doubt in the introduction. This is because immersion occurs within the limited sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*) directed toward objects such as the body.

"From the incomplete"—that is, from that which is devoid of fullness, but not from that whose essential nature is complete like the supreme *aham*-reflection (*parāhaṃvimarśa*). "Therefore"—from this immersion into the state of *aham*-being—"one who possesses" a "heightened" (*udrikta*) temporal sequence, meaning one who has an excessive or superior succession of time. Of such a person...

The meaning is: because existence (*bhāva*) is reality (*tattva*), it causes even objects to appear as having temporal succession—it manifests them as being on the same level as itself; that is to say, just as it treats itself as "past," so too does it treat the collection of objects belonging to that [past] time.
He speaks by following the very sequence of time regarding the object of the state [of being] which is on an equal footing with himself,
saying "I who... That which co-exists with it— co-existing with childhood— is explained by this [passage] ending with "of the void, etc."

Even the appearance of a jar has occurred; however, by another mode of expression, the subject whose manifestation is uninterrupted—being of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*) and "shining forth once and for all" (*sakṛdvibhāta*)—does not possess a succession of time within its own self, nor does it have one with respect to the multitude of objects of knowledge (*vedya*). For that [succession] exists only there [in the object].
"It shines forth without distinction. In this way, even spatial succession (*deśakrama*)— belonging to the limited self (*mitātman*), whose nature is circumscribed,
from the void (*śūnya*) up to the body— shines forth within one's own self as "I am standing here," in relation to oneself.

And even regarding objects, that which exists for me through the limitation of conjunction is "near," while the other is "far. However, since all objects shine as one's own self— that is, as the "I-sense"— within the consciousness-principle (saṃvittattva), which is immeasurable and devoid of any limit in its essential nature, they are therefore full.
[The Selfs] have an extent and essential nature that cannot be delimited, because of that [Self].
Now, he explains the portion of the verse beginning with "atha mātuḥ" (now, of the mother) with the words "na tu" (but not),
by means of a verbal formulation rooted in such scriptural passages as "this Self is manifested once for all."
This is the meaning: "shining without interruption" means "shining all at once" (*sakṛdvibhāta*). "The subject" (*pramātā*) refers to the supreme subject (*parapramātā*).

"In his own self"—that is, in his own essential nature which is consciousness—there does not exist "temporal succession," namely, that which is called time; such is the connection [of the words]. For indeed, by him...
The meaning is that [consciousness], having been granted existence, is capable of bringing about the very limitation of that [object].

With reference to that—that is, with reference to the subject (pramātṛ)—why would it not exist within the collection of objects (bhāvajāta), the aggregate of entities such as blue, pleasure, and so forth? To this he says: "In the object of knowledge (vedya). [He explains: "In the collection of entities. Why does it not exist there? Therefore, he says: [the following].

"That indeed is the dissolution. "That" refers to the entire range of objects of knowledge; "therein" means within the supreme subject; the word "iti" (thus) marks the completion of the objects of cognition. || 6 ||

Extending this same principle to the sequence of space (*deśakrama*), he explains the second verse which expresses it with the word "evam" (thus). "Mitātmanaḥ" means of that which has a limited nature. He demonstrates the very appearance of the sequence of space by using the word "iha" (here).

"From its own perspective"—that is, from the perspective of the limited subject (*parimita-pramātṛ*) itself. The phrase "it shines even within objective entities (*bhāveṣu*)" is to be connected with what precedes. He shows that this [subject] also conforms to the spatial sequence belonging to worldly existence (*bhava*) by using the word "yat" (which). This is due to the limitation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-pārimityena*).

"By virtue of having fewer combined conjunctions," whereas "the other"—meaning that which exists by virtue of having a limited number of conjunctions—the word "iti" marks the completion of the explanation of the first half-verse.
Having explained the first half of the second verse, he explains the second half: "unlimited... (amita).

Thus: "of that which is empty of any such limitation (*iyattā*) regarding its own nature" means that external objects (*bhāvāḥ*) are [perceived] by their own self; he explains this as being "by way of the sense of 'I' (*ahaṃbhāvena*). Since they shine forth as his very own self, he is exactly of that nature; this is a simile of conjunction (*samuccayopamā*). As it has been said:

For this [reality] is without before or after; in terms of both form and action, it is entirely full in every respect. Here, in connection with the discussion of action (*kriyā*), the sequence of time (*kālakrama*) is introduced as a topical subject by way of illustration; and following from that, the sequence of space (*deśakrama*) is also introduced.
Since the definition has been established and the illustration was to be stated previously, it was proper to mention the sequence of space at the outset during the discussion on variety;
however, in the conclusion, the sequence of time pertaining to the subject matter itself is mentioned first, followed by—
Regarding the sequential order of the teaching as it arises incidentally. || 6–7 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since the Blessed Lord—the true subject—is eternally present, no action whatsoever exists, because there is an absence of temporal succession, and action depends upon such succession.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Thus, the sense is that otherwise, being unlimited would be impossible. He explains "full" (pūrṇāḥ) as "unlimited" (aparicchinna). Those whose own nature has no limitation in its extent are such;
the word "they become" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He explains "as one's very self" (svātmeva) by way of providing the reason.
Regarding the word *yataḥ*: "one's own self" (*svātmā*) means one’s innate nature; "of that"—meaning of the immeasurable (*amita*);

"in such a state alone"—because it manifests through the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*), it is indeed full. Thus, there is a cumulative simile (*samuccayopamā*). It is clear that the states of the immeasurable are also full, as is the Self.

This is the simile of accumulation (*samuccayopamā*), as in the example: "like a lute being played with its strings untuned. Regarding this, he cites the consensus of the elders, saying: "It has been said... This refers to the immeasurable reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*).

The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the statement of the elder. Here, he says "kriyā" (action) in order to dispel the doubt being raised regarding the contradiction between what precedes and what follows; the sense is that [the apparent inconsistency] is contextual—that is, relevant—because it is caused by the variety of actions. Following from that context:
Because it follows the sequence of time; "proper" means not deviating from logic; the word "iti" marks the completion of the explanation. || 7 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the words "nanu evam" (but if it is so).
Here, the commentary states:
"in the true subject"—that is, in that which constitutes the ultimate subject—and "of her"—that is, of that action.
Thus [ends] the introduction;
however, that power of creative manifestation belongs likewise to the Lord who possesses such knowledge, whereby the distinction between the knower and the knowable is made manifest. (8)
In this context, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the Supreme Lord consists of the unimpeded freedom of His own nature,
which is the nature of uninterrupted self-reflection (*svātmaparāmarśa*).
It will be concluded in another section that "action is indeed desire, whose nature is not directed toward anything else.
Thus, desire alone is the causality, the agency, and the action. Having composed a verse regarding Caitra, Maitra, and others, he explains it with the words "But... (kiṃ tu).

Here, the commentary first states the meaning of the sentence with the word "iha" (here). "Iha" means in this *Pratyabhijñā* treatise; "of the Supreme Lord" refers to Him who is called Light (*prakāśa*).

Of Maheśvara, it is that self-reflection (*svātmaparāmarśa*) which consists of unimpeded sovereignty— having the nature of sovereignty free from obstruction— and which is likewise uninterrupted, never having undergone interruption due to its eternal and invariable character.

The self-reflection "I" (aham), consisting of that [reflection], whose nature is not directed toward another—that is, whose form is not looking toward the face of another—is indeed Will (icchā); it becomes Action (kriyā) through the process of becoming full, by attaining a state where that [Will] is its ultimate limit. Thus, in this way.

In another section—namely, in the subsequent section—it will be concluded by the Teacher; this is the ellipsis. This being so, desire itself constitutes causality, agency, and action. He states this very point again with an illustration, beginning with "Caitra. Internally...

The very internal desire "I am cooking" is itself the action; thus, even though it is connected with many movements such as placing the pot on the fire and so forth, the thought "I am cooking" is not interrupted. That which is the form of the desire "I am cooking" is precisely that which, through its nature as such movement, [is the action]. (K. reads *tathā spandanātmatayā*)

...shines forth; yet, in that [state], there is in reality no sequence whatsoever. Thus, within this light of the Lord, I shine, I pulsate, I whirl, and I reflect within the mind. Now, one might ask: how is it logical for will (*icchā*) to possess the nature of action (*kriyā*)? To this [it is said]:

He begins the justification with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Of this—namely Caitra, Maitra, and so forth—the acts of placing upon the fire and so forth: "placing upon the fire" (*adhiśrayaṇa*) refers to setting the pot on the stove;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the stirring with a ladle and other such actions are included—those which consist of the form of placing upon the fire and so forth.

Even when they are in contact with many more vibrations, the desire "I am cooking" is not interrupted, because through the state of placing [the pot on the fire] and so forth, that very [desire] attains nourishment and fulfillment.
To the question "Why is it not interrupted?", he says: "But... (*yattu*). The word *tu* indicates a reason; that is, *tu* = since.
Likewise, by way of being non-vibratory—that is, by way of the vibration consisting of the act of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth. Now, one might object:
"In that case, there would be no difference whatsoever between will (*icchā*) and action (*kriyā*. To this, he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
"In that regard"—that is, within that will—"in reality" (*tattvataḥ*), meaning from the perspective of ultimate truth, "no sequence whatsoever" exists.

This occurs because there is a manifestation [of consciousness] through the accomplishment of all that is to be accomplished (*karaṇīya*) within this totality; for this very reason, in the *Śrī Spandaśāstra* texts, it is stated that the very desire directed toward the deity is itself the attainment of the deity. As it is said therein:
"This alone is the arising of that object of meditation within the mind of the meditator:
namely, the attainment of identity with it for the practitioner who so desires. And likewise:
This alone is the attainment of the nectar of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into Nirvana, which bestows the true being of Śiva.

And thus: for the awakened one who perceives the subtle, the attainment of the object of his desire consists merely in the will itself, acting through its independence; whereas that which is the acquisition of a fruit is, for those of gross vision, of the nature of agitation (*kṣobha*) because it is seized by dependence on external things.

The essential meaning of the two verses from the *Śrī Spandaśāstra* is as follows: since one lacks the capacity for the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of indifference toward the time of one's desire, the attainment of the fruit is itself the realization of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Yet, because that [attainment] is dependent on destiny (*daiva*), it remains seized by doubt as to whether it will or will not come to pass. As for those who...

Even the deluded, though vainly clinging to that [notion], let their own minds—which are rendered helpless by the sole desire for the attainment of results—be the witnesses in this matter; otherwise, they would fall into the error of self-deception. Enough of this.
Having stated the illustration, he states the subject illustrated with the word "evam" (thus): "Thus, even for the Lord..."
Even for the Supreme Lord, whose nature is light, such reflective awareness consisting of will— which is the reality of the mere "I"—
is devoid of any temporal sequence; and this very point is what is being stated.

"May the sequence of the variety of the knower and the known unfold"— by this sentence (or rather, by this sentence), even here there is no sequence whatsoever; for when, in the form of will, one thinks "I cook," there is the nature of vibration extending as far as the body.

That which has proceeded, colored by the sequence, shines forth as "Īśe"—having manifested the object of sovereignty, I become its agent; as "Bhāse"—preceded by the agency of self-manifestation, I become the agent of the manifestation of that which is to be sovereign; it is exactly thus.
This should also be applied to throbbing (*sphuraṇa*) and vibrating (*ghūrṇana*). I reflect:

"I am the agent of the reflective awareness of 'I' (*aham-parāmarśa*)," prior to which there is the reflective awareness of "this" (*idam-parāmarśa*). Such a reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), which consists of will—that is, whose nature is mere will—is what is intended.

—Cognition is non-deviant by virtue of its being conscious; in that regard, there is no sequence, because the object thereof is established within itself as its own and as its power (*śakti*). A verbal suffix expressing sequence is employed only for the sake of instruction directed toward ordinary people regarding external universals (*sāmānya*).
Otherwise, like an ordinary person, he too would fall into being overwhelmed by agitation;

consequently, the impossibility of his being the creator of the world—which is the substratum for such an extensive manifestation—would follow, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the appearance of the world could not occur. Even though...

Even the statement that it is the will of the Supreme Lord is indeed inappropriate; nevertheless, such is the majesty of this Brahman that its body consists of all forms— by resorting to the principle that "the body is of every form"— within that reality which consists of everything.
This was stated by superimposing logical consistency upon [the Buddha] solely for the purpose of awakening ignorant people through his quality of being all-enduring; thus,
enough with these arguments devised out of the helplessness of compassion for the sake of ignorant folk, which serve only to reveal darkness.

[The author says: "By means of reflections that are like sisters to the imagined garlands of lamps. Now, since in sentences expressing desire (icchā) only the imperative (*loṭ*) and other such moods are observed, why is there a reference here using the present tense (*laṭ*)?
To this he replies: "This very same [thing]. That is to say, this very reality just mentioned, in this manner—
It is stated by means of a sentence. What is it? "The knower" (*pramātṛ*). Now, one might ask:

why was this not stated by that very first sentence; why was a second effort made? True; however, for the sake of indicating continuity toward those who have awakened, the use of the present tense (*laṭ*) alone is appropriate.

However, for those who lack knowledge [of the meaning], the use of the *loṭ* suffix is indeed intended to directly express desire; thus, there is nothing contradictory. Now, one might ask: "In this sentence, is there a sequence [of stages], or is it devoid of such?
To this he says: "That" (*tat*). Here too, it is merely desire itself that is [intended].
The meaning is that because [the mind] is established therein, there is an absence of external movement.

He describes the external movement of the will in both the example and the thing illustrated with the words "but as" (*yathā tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction; for instance, the form of the will is "I cook."
"I cook"— this is the nature of the desire as it stands; having reached a state of vibration that rests within the body and extends to its limits, it becomes sequentially colored—
that is, its parts become arranged in a temporal sequence of before and after.

Likewise, the will of the Blessed One, which culminates in the distinction between the knower and the known, appears as conjoined with that sequence, just as the surface of a mirror reflects the sequence of the flowing current of a wide, rushing river; and here, only—

Just as a mirror lacks such desire, the Supreme Lord possesses it; thus, in both respects, His power of action consists of the capacity to produce action in the form of succession and the union with the coloring of action in the form of succession. This should be stated similarly regarding spatial succession; however, in that case:
The summary meaning is this: while it is called the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) by others, here it is accepted as being precisely the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
As for the literal meaning: "thus" (*tathā*) refers to that which produces spatial succession through a difference in its own nature.

And that differentiation— both among cognizers such as Śūnya and other subjects, and between them and their respective objects, as well as the mutual differentiation among objects such as jars and so forth— is manifested by the Lord, being characterized by the sequence of time produced through the differentiation of actions.
Just as [an object] appears characterized by a sequence, so too the Will of the Lord,
having culminated in the distinction between subject and object, appears as conjoined with that sequence— that is,
colored by the sequence of subject and object— just like the surface of a mirror.

The meaning is that it shines just as it does when closely embraced by the continuous flow of a wide, flowing river. Now, one might object: "In that case, does it not follow that the mirror and the Supreme Lord are merely similar? To this, he says: "And here... And here—

Between the example and the thing exemplified, that "desire" (icchā) demonstrates the sequence by distinguishing the two states. Here, "capacity" (sāmarthya) should be understood as the nature of desire, while "conjunction with coloring" (uparāgayoga) is the grasping of a reflection; the word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter.

He extends this same principle to the sequence of space by saying "in the same way. In that context—namely, in the sequence of space—"of this" refers to the Supreme Lord; "by others" means by those external to this [system]; and "here" refers to the sequence of action, where "she" is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).

Having thus stated the meaning of the sentence, he promises to explain the meaning of the individual words with the words "But the literal meaning" (*akṣarārthas tu*). The word *tu* has the sense of "I shall now show. He shows the literal meaning itself with the word "Thus" (*tathā*). He explains the entire compound beginning with "Thus" as follows:
Regarding "preceded by the analysis" (*vigrahapūrvakam*), he explains the member *tathā* as "in its own nature" (*svarūpe*).

He explains the word "knower" (*vijñātṛ*) as "of the void and so forth" (*śūnyādeḥ*). By means of this [specification], he expresses the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) of the difference as having that [void, etc. as its locus, using the term "mutually" (*anyonyam*). He explains the word "object of knowledge" (*vijñeya*).

"Thus": by means of this very [statement] being the culmination, he expresses the difference as having a substratum (*dharmī*) and a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) through the words "mutually" (*parasparam*) and "of the knower" (*jñātuḥ*). He fulfills the expectancy of the word "who" (*yaḥ*) with the word "he" (*saḥ*).
"He"—that is, the difference—[is related to] the word "of the Lord" (*īśituḥ*), which, by the force of the sense, is to be understood as ending in the instrumental case.
That manifestation is the power of emanation (*nirmāṇa-śakti*) and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) belonging to the Lord as well;

it is not the action of the void (*śūnya*) and so forth alone. And because that wise one perceives incessantly (*anavaratam*) the manifold variety of distinctions consisting of the actions of the knower and the known created by that [power].
For it vibrates in that very place; therefore, its power of action (kriyā-śakti) also arises from that.
Thus, because there is no interruption in manifestation, and in the absence of succession, [it appears] as a gross perception.
Having cited [the verse], he explains it as being by the Blessed One (*bhagavatā*). The term "is illuminated" (*avabhāsyate*) is explained through its verbal root;

this usage is derived from the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Having explained the second half of the verse, he applies it in order to explain the first half, using the word "that which" (*yat*). He fulfills the expectancy of the phrase "that which... that" (*yattat*) with the word "it" (*sā*).

The feminine gender in the word "sā" (she) is dependent on the action-word [kriyā]. Regarding the term "nirmāṇa-śaktiḥ" (the power of manifestation), he explains it as "action" (kriyā). By the word "api" (even/also), there is the inclusion of the Lord—the Supreme Knower—even though, at first glance, [the context might suggest] the void and so forth. From the void and so forth...

[It refers] to the void (śūnya) and so forth, which appear as possessing that [nature] at first glance. Why? In response to the expectation "does it exist even for the Lord?", he explains the word "of the knower" (*viduṣaḥ*) as a qualifier containing a reason, with the words "and because... (*yataśca*). Since the root *vid* is transitive, the word "thus" (*evam*) is taken as its object.
He explains that with the word "tat" (that). The term "uninterrupted" (*avirata*) means that it occurs at all times, and not only occasionally as in the case of [the powers of] Śūnya and so forth;

this word is supplied [to the text] because it is logically required. In response to the expectation of what follows from that, he says "tatraiva" (in that very [place]). For (*hi*), since *tat*—that is, the emanation (*nirmāṇa*)—occurs *tatraiva*—in that very Lord alone.
