The cognition whose object is the reality of a single or multiple action is indeed real; it is not the case that it is real initially like the [vision of] two moons and unreal at a later time.
This is because, among the previously existing actions and so forth, only the action itself has been determined.

He extends this very same logic to the relations and so forth by saying "in the same way. It has been stated that because the intellect is connected to everything, it [extends] up to time (the phrase *kālaparyanteṣu* was used).
Now, one might ask: how can knowledge of extremely profound relations and so forth arise merely through such an extension of the rule? To this [he replies]:
He says, "Uttara"; the remainder [of the sentence] is that the author of the Sūtras will clarify this. || 1 ||

"Is it not so? [he asks]. For any given thing, if both unity and plurality—which are mutually contradictory—were to exist, then this method of uprooting stability would be produced by a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
Anticipating this objection, he says:

"In that regard, there is a single internal reality; that very same [reality], having attained the state of being perceivable by the senses, assumes multiplicity through [differences of] space, time, and nature. (2)

Anticipating the objection that— if one accepts [the doctrine]— the fact that a single thing has multiplicity is a subverting proof, and the fact that multiple things have unity is a subverting proof, such that stability is uprooted by means of these subverting proofs regarding unity and multiplicity— he says "In that regard" (*tatra*) in order to refute it.
Regarding this, the commentary states:
"In the case of an object—namely, the form of Devadatta’s body and so forth... Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "therein, one."

Within those [categories] such as action and so forth, there is that single internal reality which constitutes their means of valid cognition, having an inward-turned nature; that very same [reality], having attained the state of being perceivable by the senses, appears through space as "here" or "there," through time as "now" or "then," and through its own nature as "emaciated," "stout," and so on.

It attains multiplicity. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): this means that while their reality remains established; "therein"—that is, between those two, unity and multiplicity—the application of "unity is thus" and "multiplicity is thus" according to the manner that will be explained. Unity...
When there is no admixture with the appearances of place and so forth, when it is cognizable by the internal organ alone, and when it is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), there is unity;
whereas multiplicity occurs when there is admixture with other appearances and when it is cognizable by both organs.

And in the manifestation of what appears to be distinct from consciousness, there is a clear distinction of objects regarding unity and plurality. For instance, when Caitra is seen moving, the cognition never arises that "this one is not moving."

Just as [the cognition] "this is not silver" arises, so too regarding the double moon, there occurs a subverting cognition (*unmūlanā-buddhi*) such as: "This is not a double moon; because of ophthalmia (*timira*), my eyes are impaired, and thus I perceive it as such.
As for what was said—"How can that which is one become many?"—to that it is replied: here...

How can that which is indeed a cause become a non-cause? Now, if it is argued that "it is so because of the difference in objects," and that this is not contradictory when there is a difference in objects—by whom has this opportunity been granted?
For it is a reality that an action residing in one or many things possesses oneness or multiplicity.

He demonstrates this by means of a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*): here, in the act of going of Caitra, Maitra, and others, when Caitra is seen moving, the cognition "this Caitra does not move" never arises; therefore, [it is established] regarding the moving Caitra.

Because it is qualified by various places, times, and forms, it possesses multiplicity; yet because of the manifestation "this is that very same thing," it possesses unity. Since Caitra, who possesses this nature of both unity and multiplicity, is the substratum, the action related to him is likewise of a unitary and manifold nature. Such is its form.

The cognition of action is not interrupted midway before reaching the destination to be traversed—unlike the cognition of silver [in the case of mother-of-pearl], where the previously arisen cognition of silver regarding the object "mother-of-pearl" is later sublated by the thought "this is not silver. This [cognition of action] is not like that. Furthermore, this is reinforced by another negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*).

He acts; just like the cognition of silver, even regarding the double moon, there is the uprooting of the dual cognition: "This is not a double moon; my eyes are impaired by the power of a visual disorder (timira), and I am merely speaking of a 'double moon'. [The term *dva...ḷanaṃ* refers to the uprooting of duality.]

It is so. Regarding what was asked by you—"How does that which is one become many?"—in response to that question, the manner in which one thing becomes many is explained: why is it that the very same seed, which serves as the cause for a sprout and such, does not also serve as the cause for a jar and such?
Now, it might be argued that "it is so because of the difference in objects (*viṣaya*)," such that the sprout produced from a seed is one thing,
and the jar produced from clay is another; thus,
due to the difference between these two objects consisting of their respective effects, the seed is the cause of the sprout alone, and not [of the jar].

If it is argued that [the distinction] is expressed as "of the jar," then, given the difference characterized as previously stated, by whom was this opportunity or occasion granted to the seed and so forth, such that there is no contradiction between the seed's being a cause with respect to the sprout and its being a non-cause with respect to the jar and other things?
If you argue that "only the sprout, when its seed has been grasped as both cause and non-cause, becomes the cause [of the sprout],
and not the jar"— such being our perception— then in cases such as "it moves," we maintain that it is indeed perception itself [that establishes this].
Why is that which has been established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) not accepted? Furthermore, it cannot be argued here that there is a difference in their objects (*viṣaya-bheda*);
for instance, when there is no commingling with other appearances, it is merely a single appearance.
Precisely because it is devoid of dependence on anything else and is internal (*antaraṅga*), it is internal (*āntara*) and persists.
And because it is cognizable by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is suited only to grasping the mere appearance of such [an object], it is "internal";

and because it does not deviate from its own nature, and because it is capable of expansion through connection with other appearances, it is perceived as "one reality" (*tattvam ekam*). That very [reality] is here [perceived] through the appearance of space.

In the perception of external objects through the senses, [an object] is cognized as "there" by means of the appearance of time (*kālābhāsa*), as "now" or "then," as "lean" or "stout" and so forth by means of the appearance of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvābhāsa*), and as "manifold" due to its mixed character. Likewise, [it is cognized as follows:]
"And [the cognition] of the master who is established in himself...

If it is argued that this is by means of one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*), then even in cases such as "he moves," since Devadatta, while moving, is differentiated by various places, times, and forms, he would be manifold; yet there is the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very same person."

If it is argued that there is unity because of being an object [of cognition], then why is it not accepted that, in reality, our very self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the authority regarding both unity and plurality?
In this regard—concerning unity and plurality—a distinction of objects can indeed be stated. For instance:

When place, time, and so forth are not differentiated by another manifestation— that is, when Caitra and the like are not perceived through another manifestation— it is therefore merely a single manifestation.

Because it consists of a single manifestation alone, there is no possibility of dependence on anything else; thus, it "persists"—meaning it flashes forth without interruption—and is "internal," meaning inward-turned. Being such, it is that which is appropriate for grasping as a mere single manifestation, undifferentiated by space and so forth, within.

And because it is cognizable by the instrument [of knowledge], while not deviating from such an inward-turned essential nature, it is *tattva*—that which constitutes the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Furthermore:
"The outpourings and flows of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth arise from their reliance upon the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*)."

According to the principle thus stated, because it is of the nature of a universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*) and because it is capable of extending itself through its connection with all other manifestations in the form of individual entities, that very reality is perceived as "the one that is woven through everything. It is this alone that constitutes their innermost essence, whether "here" or "there."

Now, through the manifestation of space as "here," through the manifestation of time as "now" or "then," and through the manifestation of nature as "thin," "gross," and so forth, [the object] is mixed; for this very reason, it is perceived as manifold when it is cognizable by the external senses. Furthermore:
According to the principle stated as "of the Lord who resides within the self," the universe itself, being internal, is one;
that very same [universe] is the object of perception by both types of senses for one who revolves within.
Thus, according to the perspective on the reality of the relationship between cause and effect as it will be explained,
there is multiplicity when [an object] is perceivable by the senses due to the mixing of appearances such as place and so forth;
whereas unity occurs when there is no mixing with other appearances, whether in the state of being perceivable solely by the internal organ or in the state of pure consciousness (cinmātratā).

Furthermore, multiplicity [is established] when there is a mixing with another appearance, when there is cognizability by both instruments [of knowledge], and when there is an appearance of being distinct from consciousness; thus, the distinction of objects is clear. And that very [multiplicity] exists in such a manner solely by the power of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), like the relationship between cause and non-cause, or like the relationship between material cause and auxiliary cause. Now...

This [distinction] between "cause" and "non-cause," and so forth, is merely a designation; likewise, here too, "one" and "many" are merely conventional expressions. Even "blue," "yellow," "non-conceptual," and "conceptual"—all of these are merely conventional expressions within the realm of *māyā*.

In this context, "existent" (*sat*) is like a master—unitary and undivided. Such a universe itself is perceivable by both types of sense organs for one who revolves within [it], according to the perspective on the reality of the relationship between cause and effect that will be explained later; thus, regarding the unity and multiplicity of the objective reality once again...

This has been clarified by the passage beginning with "Unity [exists] when there is no admixture with other manifestations," which explains that unity belongs precisely to that which is either mixed or unmixed with the manifestations of space, time, and so forth.

By the passage ending with "viṣayabhedaḥ," the unity and multiplicity of the reality are once again clarified through the distinction of objects. Its being so— its innate unity— is established solely by the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is that very same thing," as in the case of the essence of a seed.

"Like cause and non-cause, like material cause and auxiliary cause. Just as a single entity whose nature is a seed possesses a dual form—consisting of being a cause with respect to a sprout and a non-cause with respect to a jar and so forth—it follows that it has these two aspects: being a cause and being a non-cause.

Furthermore, a single entity whose nature is clay would possess two forms: being the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to a jar, and being a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) with respect to a sprout.
In the same way, for a single entity, [there would be] internally, within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone—

Everything is the same; therefore, the contradiction between unity and multiplicity is not a sublation. This very point is expressed by the word *eva* (only). In that regard, among those [factors] such as action and so forth, that which is the internal reality is one;
that very same [reality], having attained the state of being perceivable by the senses...
The connection is that it "attains multiplicity due to the difference of place and so forth. In that context, "there" (tatra) refers to the state of being real;
or, between those two—namely unity and multiplicity—the construction is either "unity is thus" or "multiplicity is thus. || 2 ||
Because it is an object of cognition, there is unity; because it is delimited by external space, time, and form, there is multiplicity.

Thus, the contradiction between unity and multiplicity is not a subverting factor. Now, the seed is a cause with respect to the sprout, but it is not a cause with respect to a jar and so forth; by the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi),...

"Clay is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the jar, and [water] is the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) of the sprout"— such is merely a conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra*), not an investigation into the actual nature of things (*vastu-svarūpa-parāmarśana*). Therefore, then:

In this realm of illusion (*māyāpada*), although the reality is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), there exists internally the one and externally the many—such as blue and yellow, the non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) and the conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Thus, there are the knower and the knowledge, whether singular or manifold, blue or yellow, non-conceptual or conceptual. [The conceptual...]

"All knowledge of the knower is merely conventional discourse"—this which you have stated and that which we have stated are entirely the same. Regarding the phrase "that very thing," the word "only" (eva) indicates that it is precisely oneness-and-manyness, and that very thing is what is meant by "perceptibility by the senses. It is precisely that.
He explains this with the words "tatra" (therein). Among those aforementioned [categories] such as action and so forth, that which is the internal reality—
that single reality consisting of the *ahaṃkāra* (I-principle) which serves as their substratum—
is precisely that which, having become perceptible by the senses, [appears] through the differentiation of space and so forth.

C.]—The connection is that "it goes to external multiplicity. Regarding the phrase "therein," the construction is either "therein" (referring to) "truth" (*satyatva*), or "staying therein" and so forth; thus, up to this point, the logical sequence (*anvaya*) has been demonstrated. || 2 ||
But if a distinction between objects is thus admitted, then when one thing appears, many do not; and when many appear, one does not.
How, then, could an object possess both a unitary and a manifold nature? For instance, by means of an external sense organ, Caitra—

They say that a variegated object is experienced as supreme, yet the operation of non-conceptual [cognition] born of the external senses does not consist in the mixing of multiple appearances; for, arising by the force of a proximate object, it is devoid of deliberation. Even by means of mental conceptualization, such an object [is perceived].
By what cognition could an object, which is neither touched nor possessed of a single or manifold form, be grasped?
To dispel the delusion of others, he says:
"These [cognitions] have that pair as their objective support; they are mental after-cognitions (*manonuvyavasāyin*)."
It performs the conceptualizations of karma and so forth, consisting of the activity of a mother. || 3 ||

Now, if it is admitted that there is a distinction between unity and plurality due to the difference between internal and external aspects, then at the very moment that object appears as one, it does not appear as many;
and at the very moment that it appears as many, it is that same object which appears as many.
In that case, since there is no manifestation of unity, how could a real entity possess both unity and multiplicity?

The meaning is that when both unity and multiplicity are apprehended in a single conscious reality, because unity and multiplicity cannot coexist simultaneously, it does not possess both unity and multiplicity.
He demonstrates that very point with the words "tathā hi" (for instance): Caitra, as he goes to various different places, is perceived solely by means of the external sense organs;
and yet, within that single body of Caitra—

The function of non-conceptual cognition— which has as its object a mere thing undifferentiated by space, time, and so forth, and which consists in the manifestation of a mere thing— consists in the blending together of the appearances of space, time, and so forth, which serve as causes for [the perception of] multiplicity.

"It does not exist. This refers to the non-conceptual [cognition] that arises by the force of an object suddenly encountered; it would be non-conceptual with respect to that specific qualification of the object—namely, the place, time, and so forth—which exists at the moment of the conceptualization of reality (*bhūtavikalpa*).

Because it lacks analytical investigation (*pratyavicāraka*), and according to the principle that all such conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is rooted in direct experience, even the mental conceptualization that follows upon that [experience] does not touch a real entity— whether singular or manifold— in its true nature.
However, in the case of innate knowledge whose nature consists in appearing as an external object,
that [innate form] exists in the form of a prior experience within acts such as recollection.
According to the principle thus stated, because that [consciousness] possesses an object of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), by what kind of intellect?

That is, by a non-conceptual intellect or by a conceptual intellect (*savikalpaka*)? This refers to the opponent who maintains the doctrine of non-self (*anātmavādin*) and considers the stream of consciousness alone to be reality.
To dispel delusion, he says: "Those two."

It has been established previously that here, within the *Jñānamālā*, the subject—whose nature is self-awareness and who is like an internal thread—is the very life-force; furthermore, it has been determined that he is autonomous (*svatantra*). He is essentially Śiva by nature, yet in the sphere of *māyā*...

The bound soul (*paśu*) is of a contracted nature; therefore, at the occasion of the mind's expansion, there is a clear manifestation on the plane of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). This occurs because, through the emergence of the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, one remains outside of non-conceptual awareness (*avikalpabodha*) within the indeterminate sensory perception (*nirvikalpaka*).

Regarding the phrase "those two": these [cognitions] have as their object those two—namely, the aforementioned pair of unity and plurality—which they take as the basis for entities such as Caitra or a jar; this is indicated by the expression "connection with action."

The mind [is that which] perceives the cognitions of action and so forth— which are indicated by the *grahaṇaka-sūtra* and consist of the operations of the knower and the object of knowledge as the substrata for those actions, and whose very nature is such operation.

[Regarding the word "nanu" (C.): Thus, it is of the nature of a determinate cognition (*vyavasāyātmaka*) that arises immediately after the conceptualization following non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpavikalpānantarabhāvi*). [It is... a certainty (*niścaya*)... [sixfold...
the means for accomplishing its respective function. (C.)

It is the internal organ alone that effects determination; thus, it is the internal organ alone that accomplishes its respective functions consisting of volition (*saṃkalpa*), self-identification (*abhimāna*), and ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*).
Regarding the phrase "here of the garland of knowledge" (*iha jñānamālāyāḥ*): it refers to the garland of knowledge— which consists of experience and so forth,

and which has been described in the three daily lessons concerning the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*)— the term "end" (*antaḥ*) signifies a certain subject (*pramātṛ*) who, by virtue of being the internal form, sustains the aphorisms as if they were a garland and serves as their very life-force.

That "it exists" was established in the first chapter (*āhnika*) through the determination of the single substratum; furthermore, it was resolved in the eighth chapter through the determination of Maheśvara that this cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is independent. And when he becomes one whose impurity of *māyā* has dissolved through the piercing glance of a true Guru, then he—

The one whose nature is pure is the Self that is Śiva; however, within the sphere of Māyā, which consists of the manifestation of "this-ness," even though he is essentially one with Śiva, he is a bound soul (paśu) whose nature is contracted by the thought "I am Caitra" or "I am Maitra," because he has been obscured by that [Māyā].

Of this subject in the form of a limited being (paśu), "of the mind" means of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) in its aforementioned form; "on the occasion of its manifestation" means on the occasion of its full emergence toward its respective functions such as volition (saṃkalpa) and self-conceit (abhimāna); "I am here" means existing at this time.
The phrase "of such a form" refers to the clear manifestation on the level of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

In the sensory non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), there is the activity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of "I am this," which is not yet distinguished by space, time, and so forth. This [awareness] subsequently gives rise to a determinative judgment (*vyavasāya*) consisting of ascertainment.

The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), performing the conceptualizing [cognition] denoted by the term *anuvyavasāya*, brings about these conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the connection with action and so forth. And those conceptual constructions rely upon that pair consisting of unity and plurality; for that which appears within conceptual constructions [is not real].
For it has been stated that it is "non-existent" (*avastusat*); therefore, even at the time of its initial manifestation, this [object] is manifested precisely as being unqualified by space and time,
in the form "I am this," "this is I," and "I am this."

The meaning is that, because of the arising of the state of Sadāśiva-Īśvara [or, as in C., because of the arising of the compassion of Sadāśiva-Īśvara], such sensory perception, being free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), does not perform the connections with actions that consist of the nature of conceptual cognition (vikalpabuddhi).

According to the principle already stated— that even at the moment of direct perception there is reflective awareness (vimarśa)— the operation of reflective awareness belongs to that which does not fall outside such non-conceptual cognition. It is called "subsequent" (anuvyavasāyin) because it occurs subsequently (anu).

Performing— that is, effecting— the determination (*vyavasāya*), which consists of certainty and is denoted by the word "determination" (or "resolute effort"), the mind— meaning the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—
carries out and accomplishes these functions such as the connection with action. Regarding the phrase "having those two as their support," they are...

Conceptual constructions (vikalpas) rely upon that dyad consisting of unity and plurality. Here, in the conceptual construction of memory, the object is first determined (adhyavasīyate); otherwise, there would be the consequence of falling into a state resembling sleep or fainting. And thus, as long as there is a determination of the object—

By implication, it must be accepted on the strength of the context that this object is what is manifested; for if that which is to be determined were not being manifested, determination would be as good as blind.
Indeed, [it is not the case] that what appears in conceptual constructions... [is not the case] in conceptual constructions.

It has been stated that "insight (pratibhāna) exists as real" [C], yet it has also been stated that it "exists as non-substantial. For existence is indeed luminosity—luminosity itself is reality. And there is no [reality] for conceptual construction apart from its nature as luminosity.

It is logical that there is a distinct operation named "superimposition," "endeavor," "conceit," and so forth; therefore, statements such as "they superimpose the external upon the non-external" are devoid of substance,
and this has already been stated.
"And if the determination were erroneous...

[as stated] in this context. Now, the opponent might say: "How could a conceptual construction (vikalpa) touch upon that particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) which is to be illuminated by sensory cognition? This would indeed be so—if the conceptual construction...

It could not be independent; rather, this is an operation of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), and the cognizer consists of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) culminating in the prior experience. And this very thing is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that prior experience, which [persists] even at the time of the operation of conceptualization (*vikalpana*).

It remains without ever abandoning its nature as the essence of prior experience; therefore, according to the principle stated by the venerable Tantravaṭadhānika— that the prior experience extends as far as the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)— the very manifestation of the object [is established].
Reality (*vastutva*) is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). When that reality has not yet been manifested, there arises with respect to it a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as:

"Is this a *guñjā* berry or fire? or "It is a *guñjā* berry," or "It is fire," or "This is mine—[it is] a *guñjā* berry," occurring sequentially through the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*).
An operation other than that which is accomplished by the activity of the syllable *haṃ* is not logical.

Therefore, regarding the statement "from the non-external, the external," and so forth—the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) is used because the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of an entity is its manifestation; thus, within the non-external continuum of cognition (*jñānasantāna*).

The statement that external objects such as blue, though non-existent in themselves, are superimposed [upon consciousness] like silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell, is devoid of objective reality and is not the ultimate truth. And this very thing—"that" and "this"—is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
This is so because the determinative cognition (*avasāya*) is itself an error.
Thus it has been stated there. With reference to what was called "the reflective awareness" (*anuvyavasāyin*), he says:

"How could a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) touch an object that is to be illuminated by non-conceptual valid cognition (*nirvikalpapramāṇa*) and so forth? The opponent might say: "Because their objects are distinct. [The author replies: "It would indeed be so," and so on.

If conceptual thought were independent by itself without a cognizer, then at that time conceptual thought would not be capable of touching upon the object of non-conceptual awareness. However, this being the case, conceptual thought is not independent in its engagement with objects without a cognizer; therefore—
This conceptualization is mental conceptual cognition; it is the very activity of the cognizer.
And this cognizer consists of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) directed inward from a prior experience, such as "this is a jar. Of that—

"This is that very [object]" for the cognizer; in the operation of the non-conceptual [cognition] following upon experience, there is the nature of being the previous experience (or "the state of being the previous experience"),
which consists of the object previously experienced, its location, and its time.
Without abandoning the investigation of space and time, which serve as its qualifiers,
[consciousness], though its nature is manifestation,
is nonetheless an operation of the reality of the subject who has attained identity with the previous experience.
Conceptual construction has that very [object] as its domain; therefore it was said by the Teacher:
"This very impression of a prior experience belongs to the cognizer;
for even at the time of exclusion (*apohana*), that prior experience remains."

Thus, it is established that although the mental faculty (*manas*) alone performs these conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) regarding action and so forth— which have as their objects things that are either one or many— within the context of the primary activity of the cognizer, which consists in the synthesis of unity and plurality, as indicated by the introductory statement (*grahaṇaka-vākya*). Even though this is so...
That which resides [in the subject] is this very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which exists within the cognizer as the nature of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

According to the stated principle, as long as the prior experience— whose essence is the manifestation of its own object— remains present, even recollection and the like, having attained identity with it, manifest in that same way.
The cognitive activity of the subject (*pramātṛ-vyāpāra*), which has attained identity with such a prior experience, is also a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
it concerns only the object of that prior experience. For this very reason, it was stated by the venerable teacher, the illustrious Utpaladeva:
This very latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience belongs to the cognizer;
for even at the time of exclusion (*apohana*), that prior experience remains present.

And so forth. This very thing is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the previous experience belonging to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), namely, that even at the time of exclusion (*apohana*), the previous experience remains present for the cognizer. "Therefore" means:
from that which consists of the activity of the cognizer, with respect to each individual object.

The activity whose nature consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which has as its essence the conjunction of unity and plurality—is what is meant by "consisting of activity" (*vyāpāramayīḥ*). Thus, these are the conceptualizations of action and so forth, which have that very activity as their inherent form (*prakṛtaṃ rūpam*). These are they.
It is established that it is the mind alone that performs the conceptualization of action and so forth, as indicated by the statement regarding the grasping [of objects].

By the third [verse], it is shown that although these [objects] are cognizable through non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-saṃvedana*), their form becomes clearly manifest only at the time of conceptualization (*vikalpaka*).

Even in a non-conceptual [cognition], there is the appearance of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth in the appearance of a mere jar and the like; nevertheless, at that time, the universal and so forth are not clear, because when two related entities arise as a common coloring factor, there is no abandonment of the succession of successive moments.

Since, upon accepting a collection of parts, there is the manifestation in ultimate reality of categories such as the limit and the limited, relation, action, substance, space, and so forth— therefore, universals and the like are of both unitary and manifold forms, apprehended by mental conceptualization.
Thus it is established. And so, conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is the conceptualizing intellect; by its power, let the status of being a conventional truth be asserted.
However, that is merely a particular mode of truth itself; therefore, like the double moon and such, it is not non-truth. (3)

And in this regard, the sequence for entering into consciousness (*saṃvit*) is as follows: although, according to the previously stated principle, even in the non-conceptual state (*nirvikalpa*)— such as in the manifestation of a mere jar qualified by its attributes— there is indeed an appearance of a universal, a relation, and so forth, which belongs solely to the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), nevertheless, at that time, in the state of non-conceptuality...

Nevertheless, universals and the like do not appear with clarity. He demonstrates this very point with the words "nevertheless, universals and the like" (*tathāpi sāmānyādi*). For even though they possess a common coloring factor (*samānoparañjakatve*), potness residing in a jar is that which is interwoven through all jars located in every place.

According to the stated principle that a relation is "resident in two" (*dviṣṭha*), because a relation resides in both [relata], when the two relata— namely the king and the man— arise as in the expression "the king's man," there occurs,
for the moving Caitra, an action consisting of the successive displacement of his bodily parts in front and behind.
When there is no abandonment of the successive stream of moments— [the stream consisting of moments characterized by the sequence of prior and posterior forms and parts,
C]— and when the collection of parts such as the mouth and so forth is accepted for a jar or the like, then from this [collection], this jar [arises].
"A pot is situated in the eastern part; this is the western part. From that, [one understands] "Caitra was born before this Maitra;
this one was born after," through the apprehension of the limit and the limited, and so forth, in sequence, [applying] to everything from generality (sāmānya) up to time (kāla).

It is established that universals (*sāmānya*) and the like— being of both unitary and manifold forms— are graspable by mental conceptualization (*mānasavikalpa*) due to the manifestation of an object over a period of time. And thus, "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*) as described by you— that which is unreal yet appears real— is conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of that": since even conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) consists of conceptual cognitions whose nature is ultimate form, let its status as truth be asserted; for according to your own statement, that conventional existence is merely a mode of the real itself, such as action and so forth, which possess the nature of conventional truth.
It is not unreal, like the double moon and so forth. || 3 ||
In this regard— even when speaking of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*)— this entire expansion, extending from action up to time,
is such that even there, relation alone is the fundamental basis; for instance,
that which appears as one among similar things is a universal (*sāmānya*), and that which constitutes the extension of Devadatta is his action (*kriyā*).

The unity or extension of parts in space is the "whole" (avayavin); taking this as a limit, there arises "direction" (dik), such as "this is thus from that," "this is to the east of that," and so forth; and there arises "time" (vartamānādi), such as "this series of actions of this [entity] exists through concomitance or non-concomitance."

As for time: for as long as the form that follows upon the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) shines forth, everything beyond that is merely relation; thus, even the factors of action (*kārakas*) possess only the nature of relation, though in some cases this relation [is manifested in a specific way].
It tolerates the knot of other designations, just as the relationship of those possessing dewlaps and so forth is designated by the single term "cows";
this is the sequence of descent of consciousness itself, which consists of the power of action.
The meaning is that consciousness, consisting of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), descends and vibrates in the form of action and so forth.
As it has been said:
"For there is no such entity whatsoever which could be conceptualized in this way."
For consciousness alone shines forth in such a way, and this very shining forth is its sovereignty.

In that regard—even in the case of action and so forth—everything, from the root action down to time, is essentially of the nature of a relationship. He demonstrates this very point with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*), and so on.
That which appears as one, as a continuous thread, among the individual instances such as jars,
is the universal "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Furthermore, that extension of Devadatta as he moves— which occurs across space, time, and form— [is likewise a universal].

Since the parts such as the mouth and so forth of a jar rest within the single nature of that one jar, their unity, as well as their extension through the pervasion of the supporting ground, constitutes the "whole" (avayavin). Taking this mountain as a limit, [one says] "this mountain," or "thus, in front."

The directions such as the east belong to this Caitra; this expansion of action exists in concomitance with him, and thus the present time, in the form of "he goes," exists within the expansion of action consisting of going and so forth by means of Devadatta.

When [the action] is not occurring together with Devadatta—[that is, with those existing together with Devadatta—C.]—there is the time of the past, the future, and so forth. Because it resides in Devadatta, whose form is a single substratum, the action, though being one, possesses both a singular and a manifold nature due to its pervasion of various locations. Thus...

Even universals (*sāmānya*) and the like possess both a single and a manifold nature. For instance, in the case of a tree and so forth, once it has followed upon the meaning of the nominal stem in the form of "substance-existence" (*vastu-sattā*), its entire form shines forth, extending as far as the locative case— as in "the tree stands," "it is stood by the tree," and so on.

All of that is simply relation (*saṃbandha*). This relation, in certain instances, tolerates the conventional usage of "universal" (*sāmānya*) and so forth— a knot of various designations— and at such times it is designated by the name "universal" and so on.
In that regard, the conventional usage of "universal" (sāmānya) and so forth is merely a matter of local tolerance;

however, when the knot of other designations is severed, there is only the linguistic expression of "relation. For this very reason, [the measures] such as *diṣṭi*, *prastha*, *pala*, and so on, take the form of weight (*parimāṇa*), measure (*māna*), and height (*unmāna*).
In this regard, whatever is included therein— whether minute or large, number, distinctness, and so forth— all that is merely the manifestation of relation (*saṃbandha*).
Even those who consider universals (*sāmānya*) and the like to be separate entities must likewise admit inherence (*samavāya*) in that case.
They accepted it as their very life-force; and *samavāya* (inherence), being of the nature of a relation, is that which favors certain things, for they say:
"It favors that power called *samavāya*."
The relation [of inherence] favors this [universal];

thus, regarding the relation, he provides an illustration here: just as the relation in the form of "cowness" (gotva), which runs through individual cows such as Kapilā and others that possess dewlaps and so forth, is [expressed as] "cows."
It is capable of being designated as a single entity despite having a manifold nature;

therein—in the capacity to withstand the knot of alternative designations—there occurs the conventional usage of a relation through universals and the like. In the absence of such a knot of designation in the form described above...
The very expression "the relation" (saṃbandhavācoyukti) is used precisely because it is designated as "that relation. For this very reason— namely,

because the factors of action (kārakas) consist of the nature of a relation— the measurement of the field to be measured by means of the *diṣṭi* and the *hasta*, etc., [is determined] by those two preceding measurements.
Relation (*saṃbandha*) is the connection of a mere portion of a field with its eastern and western regions;
it is the connection between a measure and a substance, namely the dimension inherent in that measure-substance.

The connection of weight (*palādi*) and so forth with prior and posterior measures is the connection of the instrument of measurement (*unmāna*) with the object to be measured (*unmeya*), such as gold and so forth, by means of both prior and posterior measurements; thus it consists of the forms of measure (*pramāṇa*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), and weight (*unmāna*). Among these:

Whatever is included within the measure and dimension of direction— namely, minuteness, magnitude, number, separateness, and so forth— all that, which constitutes worldly transaction, is entirely the manifestation of relation itself. Whatever [categories] such as universals and the rest [are considered], their relation...
They also accepted *samavāya* (inherence) as a distinct category, like a jar; and since *samavāya* is essentially a relation, it must be apprehended by means of a relation—
thus, *samavāya* is "that which is sustained by a relation" (*saṃbandhānugrāhya*).
This is the opinion of some (iti keṣāñcinmate). He states that very point: the relation favors that power called inherence (samavāya);
and whatever is a causal factor (kāraka), that too looks toward the action; and that [action] as well [looks toward] time.

She takes refuge in the Lord of Life (the vital breath), and he too, through the medium of activity, brings about a connection with all states of being; thus, this variegated course of worldly existence is entirely dependent upon that connection. As it has been said:
The Teacher himself says:

"I bow to that Śiva, by whose own will the course of worldly existence is accomplished through all objects established by means of the relationship characterized by both difference and non-difference. Therefore:

In order to first determine the nature of relation itself, he says: "Entities, which are distinct appearances residing within their own selves, become the locus of the cognition of relation when they are joined with a unity consisting of mutual interpenetration within a single cognizer. (4)

Thus, he clarifies the very point already stated with the words, "And as for the factor (kāraka)": the coordination of factors has, according to the method to be explained, "the investigation of action" as its object; it looks toward [verbs such as] "he stands" and so forth. That too—namely, the action—[is dependent].
One takes refuge in Time, which is the Lord of the vital breath (prāṇa) of one's own self and the source of the elements;
that Time, too, exists by way of actions such as "staying," being the essence of all entities that serve as the substrata for those actions of staying and so forth.
This manifold course of worldly affairs is dependent upon relation, for it is relation that intensifies [the connection].
As the Teacher himself has said:
"Established by all objects through a relation whose nature is both difference and non-difference..."
I bow to that Śiva, whose conduct in the journey through the world proceeds according to his own will.
Thus, because worldly life (*lokyātrā*), which consists of action, is composed of relations,
he first defines relation itself: entities appearing as kings and so forth,
and entities appearing as persons and so forth, are established in themselves— within their own very selves.
They rest within form, and for that very reason they possess a distinct appearance— meaning their manifestations are mutually differentiated.

When the king and the man, who were previously external and detached, each fully established in his own self, attain unity on the plane of the subject (*pramātṛ*), yet this is not merely a state of oneness between them.

Because it would entail the dissolution of difference, [the relation] is rather of the nature of a conjunction (*śleṣa*) of mutual forms, characterized by simultaneously mounting the swing of the two poles of difference and non-difference as they submerge and emerge; at that time, those two alone become the objective support for the cognition of the relation.

Regarding the expression "the king’s man": for instance, when the king, though previously apprehended by the intellect, is not satisfied by resting within his own self, he then achieves his purpose by entering into a union with another form, the man; and the man likewise does so—it is this very same union of forms that constitutes a single reality.

When both [the subject and the object] attain unity in the form of mutual interpenetration within the single cognizer— the conscious Self who grasps appearances such as "the king's man"— then they are indeed that very [consciousness].
Words become the objective support for the cognition of the relationship.

Regarding the phrase "having the appearance of being solitary": prior to the resting of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) within the subject who grasps both [the object and the self], these two stand externally as bystanders—mutually unconnected and established in their own selves;
for this very reason, they are fully contained within their own self alone.
In the state of resting solely in one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpamātra*),
when those two proceed toward unity on the plane of the subject who grasps both, that unity consists in identity with that subject (*tatpramātṛtādātmyarūpa*); it is not [merely] their mutual union.
It occurs; for in those two—the king and the servant—there would be the consequence of the dissolution of their status as king and servant.
Rather, through the mutual fusion of forms with the king’s servant, there arises simultaneously—that is, all at once—an appearance consisting of both the king and the person submerged and emerging.

When these two proceed toward oneness, characterized by an ascent to the shore of the dual currents of difference and non-difference, then those very two become the objective support for the cognition of the relation, as in "the king's man. He explains that very point as follows: "In the same way..."
Indeed, when the cognizer who previously apprehended the semblance of a king—
though he had grasped him through his intellect— is no longer satisfied by resting in his own self as distinct from the semblance of the man, then he effects a union with a man in another form.
By resorting [to this], he becomes one who has achieved his purpose. Even a man is not satisfied merely by resting in his own self;

by resorting to a union with a king through another form, he becomes one who has achieved his purpose. That union of forms between the king and the man exists as one alone within the conscious self—the subject.

Likewise, having the nature of abiding and being established upon the consciousness previously attained, it rests in absolute freedom— characterized by the non-appearance of separate existence due to the very immersion into that superior consciousness— and thus it shines forth in that very state.

Even though the ultimate reality of the person has been fully attained, there is thus multiplicity externally, whereas internally there is unity through the mutual fusion of forms; such is the nature of the relationship. || 4 ||

Conceptual constructions take as their objective support both the uniformity of universals and substances even when they appear externally, as well as the distinction between individuals and their constituent parts. (5)
"Of the appearance of the genus"—that is, those [cognitions] which grasp the genus as it appears in its manifest form;

"in that way," meaning established in unity in the manner described, such as in the case of "the king's man," being grounded in the previously acquired cognition [of the relation], namely, grounded in the cognition of the king (rājasaṃvitpratiṣṭha). Therefore...

Thus, through the immersion of the cognition of the additional person (*adhikapuruṣa*), the relationship between the king and the man rests in sovereignty, characterized by the non-appearance of their distinctness; therein—
in the independent self consisting of consciousness alone— it manifests.

Even though the ultimate reality of the person has been fully grasped, immediately after the appearance of the king and so forth, there arises the appearance of "cowness," "potness," and so on. || 4 ||
They rely upon the identity—the non-differentiated form—of "cowness," "potness," and so forth, as being external;

yet they also rely upon their difference and multiplicity through the individual instances (vyakti) such as Kapila and others, and through parts such as the face and other limbs. Both their difference and non-difference are external.
The cognitions of the subject's conceptualizing intellects (*pramātṛvikalpabuddhi*) are the apprehenders—that is, the perceivers—of the genus (*jāti*) which exists as a manifest form;
those are the mental constructions (*kalpanā*). They do not only [perceive] the internal unity associated with the relation, nor merely the external...

They take as their object a manifold nature, even extending outward to the multiplicity characterized by the distinction between individual instances; yet they lead that very multiplicity, which exists externally, to the state of being an object of cognition through a unity that is woven through it. For in the manifestation "cows," they appear as distinct entities, and those [individuals] are indeed separate from one another externally.

[6. The individual manifestations appear externally, which accounts for the use of the plural number; and a persisting form appears among them, because there is a continuous reference to the meaning of a single nominal stem. And both of these [features] exist only externally, since they are pointed out with the finger as "these. Thus, even external existence remains established.
Insofar as they are included within the manifestation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-prakāśa*),

it is not only internally, like a relationship, that they take on a single form, but even externally they take on the form of "cowness" (*gotva*) which is pervasive through individual instances such as Kapila and others.

[The cognition] leads even that unity to the status of being an objective referent (*ālambana*). He demonstrates this very point in brief: when there is the appearance of plurality in the form "cows," they are perceived as distinct [entities].

—C. — by which manifestation they appear externally as distinct individuals such as Kapila and others, there is the use of the plural number to indicate their multiplicity, as in "this is a cow, this is a cow. And there is also among these cows a persisting form.
It occurs as follows: when there is a continuous reflection upon the meaning of a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the form of "cowness" (*gotva*), then it has a corresponding form;
thus, both—oneness and manifoldness—are indeed external.

He demonstrates the external form of both through direct perception by means of the phrase "these," which indicates them with a finger; for even mere externality is included within the manifestation of the ultimate reality of one's own prior connection. [Prior connection is the ultimate reality.]

When there is an absence of any light other than that [of consciousness], it is said that "it shines"; in that case, the distinction or non-distinction of objects as external is not a flaw. And this has been stated:
"Insofar as they consist of consciousness, manifestations always abide within."
Because those things appearing through illusion appear as external, this [consciousness] is also external.

In that regard, the refutation of difference and non-difference is as in the case of variegated cognition (*citrasaṃvedana*). By this, the contradiction regarding red and non-red and so forth, even in the case of a substance, has been answered;
internal unity, however, exists everywhere through the medium of relation, just like that [variegation], in the case of what appears as "a jar."
Those conceptual constructions which grasp a composite substance are not only, like [the notion of] a relation,

directed toward both internal and external forms as being one and many; rather, they also take as their object externally a single entity as a seamless whole, and likewise a differentiated entity by way of its various parts characterized as constituent members.
They accept this, for indeed, the jar appears as a single, dense, and seamless entity, manifesting in an expansive form. || 5 ||

In this regard: "as in the perception of a painting" (*citrasaṃvedana*) means that in a painting there is oneness in the form of the bird (*pataṅga*), while difference consists in its having blue and non-blue colored wings, which constitutes its manifoldness (*anekatva*). By this same principle, even in a substance such as a jar, there is one part...

By stating "one is golden, the other is silver," the contradiction between the red and non-red (or similar opposites) is resolved; the meaning is that every object, because it consists of consciousness (*saṃvinmayatvāt*), can sustain the nature of consciousness—that is, the nature of all forms—within itself. This internal distinction of this genus is established through the medium of its relations.
There is also oneness—indeed, there is one—not only externally; "everywhere" means in all entities, and there is also internal unity by way of relation.
"In this manner" means like a universal (jāti). This refers to the composite substance (avayavidravya) appearing as "a jar."

Those conceptualizations—which are discriminative cognitions—that apprehend [an object] internally as having a single object or externally as having multiple objects do not exist; rather, even externally, they have multiple things as their objects.
He demonstrates that for those discriminative cognitions, there is indeed the nature of being both single and multiple even with respect to external objects.

It is of a single form by virtue of having a nature that is without joints or seams, yet it is of manifold forms, being differentiated through the various parts such as the mouth and so forth— [that is, through the parts characterized as the mouth etc., which are the specific locations of the whole characterized as the face etc.— C].

They accept [the existence of] jars and so forth. An entity appearing as a "jar" manifests as a single form consisting of a unique aggregate without joints or seams, and it appears as an extended form through its various parts such as the mouth, which pervade their respective locations. || 5 ||
The coordination of the factors of action (kārakas) has as its object the deliberation regarding the action itself;
the cognition of directions such as "east" and so forth is based on the relation between a limit and that which is limited.

The mutual correspondence observed among the factors of action (*kārakas*), which are the substrates of powers such as agency (*kartṛtva*), and among substances— for instance, the mutual relation between the knower (*mātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*meya*), and the means of knowledge (*māna*)— is caused solely by the reflective awareness of a specific internalized activity consisting of valid cognition (*pramā*); for it is not otherwise.
The intermediate act of valid cognition (*pramāparāmarśa*) belonging to the causal factors—
the substances such as trees, which serve as the substrata for the capacities of the agent and so forth— is expressed as: "Devadatta [cooks] rice in a pot with wood."

The connection between those [factors] consisting of the agent, instrument, locus, and object—which exists in such expressions as "he cooks" (pacati)—has as its domain the reflective awareness of action; it has the reflective awareness of action alone as its cause. Furthermore, the cognition that grasps space and time takes this [connection] as its limit:
"In relation to this, this was born before," and "Therefore, this is his elder brother."

The day is the movement of the sun starting from the mountain of sunrise (udayagiri) up to the mountain of sunset (caramagiri); the night is the movement starting from that mountain of sunset up to the mountain of sunrise.
The cognition of direction and so forth is based on the relation between the limit (avadhi) and that which possesses the limit (avadhimat).

Regarding the phrase "of the factors" (kārakāṇām), this refers to the factors— beginning with the agent (kartṛ) and ending with the locus (adhikaraṇa)— which serve as the substrata for the potencies [of action], such as Caitra, Maitra, and so forth, as well as trees and the like.
The mutual correlation observed among substances— such as "Devadatta [is cooking] with wood in a pot"— is that very correlation;
it is that which is dissolved within the cognizer.

The coordination of the factors of action (*kārakas*) is caused solely by the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of actions such as cooking, which consist of valid cognition; this coordination has the reflective awareness of the action as its object. Regarding this point, he provides an illustration: "just as in the case of the knower, the object, and the means of knowledge.
[This refers to] the knower, Caitra.

Just as there is a mutual coordination between Caitra’s mother, the object of measurement such as a jar, and the knowledge— which consists of an outward-directed manifestation resting upon both of them— in an action characterized by valid cognition such as "he sees."

Similarly here too, apart from the reflective awareness of valid cognition (*pramā-parāmarśa*)— which consists of actions such as seeing and which resides within the cognizer— the direct, intrinsic synthesis of two entities, such as "Devadatta" and "tree," is not an object of reflective awareness; thus, [there is no synthesis] of the factors of action (*kāraka*).

In this context, "concomitance" (samanvaya) is understood as the direct concomitance of the entity, setting aside [the conventional sense of] "cooking" and so forth; here, the meaning of the object is its state of being non-other and its nature as the cause. This also applies to the potencies of the factors of action (kāraka).
That relationship with its own substrata is also caused by the reflection upon action;
since there is a direct relationship between substances and powers on one hand and action on the other,
it is this very Blessed Action that manifests such an extensive range of relationships.

The middle state consists of the reflective awareness of difference preceded by non-difference between two entities that are otherwise perceived externally as distinct, such as "this is prior to that" or "that is distant from this."

And that form which is perceived as resting in non-differentiation is called "direction" (*diś*). For in this case, there is no concern for the specific discernment of particular parts such as the face and so forth; rather, there is the determination of being facing toward or facing away from those [objects], based on conjunction and the [resulting] conjoined state.
And the inclusion of "scarcity of conjunction" (*saṃyogālpatā*) and so forth is useful;

since it has as its sole cause the reflection upon an action (*kriyāparāmarśa*), the meaning of the object here is "the state of being a cause" (*nimittatā*) consisting in the inability to exist elsewhere without that action. This applies to the *kārakas*.

The meaning is that without the activity consisting of the reflective awareness of the subject (*pramātṛ-parāmarśa*), a mutual connection cannot occur by itself. Furthermore, the mutual connection of the powers of the first and other grammatical factors (*kāraka-śakti*) with their own substrates— the substances such as trees— is [likewise impossible without it].
The notion that "the tree stands" arises solely from the reference to actions such as standing; likewise,

"I see the tree," "it is stood by means of the tree," "he gives to the tree," "he falls from the tree," "this belongs to the tree," and "the tree stands"— all these [grammatical usages] pertain to substances (dravya).

And since there is a direct relationship between the powers and their activity, it is this very same Blessed Lady who is the cause of all worldly transaction, beginning from the nominative case-ending up to the locative.
It manifests the relationship that unfolds through the grammatical factors (kārakas), beginning with the nominative and ending with the locative. Having perceived two external objects,
the cognizer [distinguishes them] as external differences, thinking, "This mountain is to the east of this," and "This is to the west."

Because the two entities being perceived by the eyes and other senses rest together within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they are first non-differentiated; subsequently, however, in the external middle— the central sphere—
there arises the mutual differentiation [of one from the other], such as "this is prior to that."
Furthermore, if that which consists of manifestation is again firmly contemplated as resting in non-differentiation,

it is called "direction" (dik) in a general sense. Here— in this general direction— by the phrase "the regard for the discernment of the parts of those two entities as front, back, right, and left," [it is meant].

The occurrence of the divisions of the directions, such as the east and so forth, arises from the determination of being facing toward or turned away from the parts of those [directions]. By this, the occurrence of specific distinctions such as the intermediate directions is established. Furthermore, "conjoined with this mountain" constitutes conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

The "conjunction with the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*) is the relation with a mountain that is itself conjoined with trees and so forth; furthermore, the inclusion of proximity and other such factors between two entities is useful for the consideration of direction (*dik*).
Since the reflection upon time has as its object real entities (*vastu*), when it takes the form of "prior," "subsequent," and so forth,
there is the reflection on birth, duration, diminution, and so on; and when it takes the form of "long" or "short," there is [the expression] "he will cook" (*pakṣyati*) and "he cooks" (*pacati*).

In cases such as "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*), however, one must necessarily rely on that which is possible— whether manifest, or previously manifest— to serve as the means for the linguistic usage of one's own self-awareness and its vital impulse; otherwise, such usage would be impossible.
Is it not the case that this very boundary has been established by the Śarāvatī river? True;
but what could one do who has not seen it? Furthermore, since its establishment is accomplished by means of objects situated to the east, what need is there for it?
Moreover, even in the eastern direction divided by it, [the designation of "east" occurs] in relation to objects contained within it.

The observation that linguistic usage such as "para" (the subsequent) and so forth is seen [in grammar] is of no consequence. But then, how is it that she is praised in the treatises as the differentiator of those [sounds]? As it has been said:
"May that Śarāvatī protect us."

Thus we say: it is by way of the conventional usage of directions such as "east" and so forth; moreover, the conventional usage of objects is indeed more intrinsic than the conventional usage of space. Furthermore, even the first appearance of the sun varies according to the perspective of the slopes of Mount Meru; thus, everyone...

The division of directions has its very life in conceptual construction; thus, even the statement that the directions are one is improper, because it is impossible for a location whose nature is the undivided form of the Blessed One to have a delimited object as its domain.
Enough with this elaboration. And here, the apprehension of "direction" consists in the relative smallness of the conjunctions of conjunctions.

It is employed for the purpose of determining distance and so forth. For instance, when the earth is in conjunction with the body of the observer, that conjunction constitutes a "conjunction with what is conjoined" (saṃyukta-saṃyoga) for Devadatta;
where that [conjunction] is minimal, there is proximity, but where it is great, there is distance.
From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), however, the conjunction of what is already conjoined is merely an interval; this is sufficient.

To determine the cognition of time (*kāladhī*) as included by the word "etc. (*ādi*), he says: "Time" (*kāla*). If the reference to time takes the form of "prior," "posterior," and so forth—that is, if it takes the form of priority (*pūrvatva*)—then...

In the case of its being of the nature of another, by the word "beginning" (ādi) is meant its being of the nature of the middle; "existence from birth" (janmasthiti) refers to existence starting from birth, and regarding that, there is an investigation into its "smallness and so forth"— by the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), the states of "largeness" and "middleness" are included— and this investigation is employed.

It becomes useful [in this context]. Therein, by the reflection on smallness, there is the apprehension of posteriority in the younger; by the reflection on manyness, there is the apprehension of priority in the elder; and by the reflection on middleness, there is the apprehension of mediocrity in the middle-aged. Here, regarding priority and posteriority as conceived by the logicians—

Furthermore, there is indeed identity between "otherness" (*paratva*) and "non-otherness" (*aparatva*); for that which is prior is "other," while that which is subsequent is "not other" because it is different from the prior. Likewise, in the case of forms such as "long" and "quick," the consideration of birth, duration, brevity, and so forth is required. The apprehension of the "middling" [state]. Here too, the sequence is as follows: by way of smallness, there is the apprehension of swiftness; by way of multiplicity, the apprehension of slowness; and by way of being middling, the apprehension of the intermediate state.
Although the apprehension of slowness, swiftness, and so forth may also occur due to the extreme smallness and other factors of the sun's movement, [the primary cause remains as stated].
Nevertheless, out of fear of prolixity (*prapañca*), it has been stated here as being restricted in this very way. However,
in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— as in *pakṣyati*, *pacati*, *apākṣīt*, and so forth—
the future, present, and past [tenses] are included.
Just as there is a reference to another action, such as cooking, and to a specific result, such as boiled rice,

Or rather, it is precisely the nature of relation that must be expressed; this is the summary in all respects: where the manifestation of an object, finding no satisfaction in resting within itself alone, lacks a final establishment in its own nature due to its expectancy for a rest in the reflective awareness of another manifestation.

This is to say: the state of being turned toward grasping.
That alone is his life, which consists of such other activities as those of the sun and so forth.

The meaning is that [the Self] is the life-force of all things. He announces the summary exposition with the words "in every way.

By means of resting in the Self—that is, by resting solely in one's own true nature, which is designated as the "referent of the word"—one attains satisfaction, [which is the state of the Lord's]... Someone might suspect that there is a flaw at its very root.

Having thus described the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which consists in becoming a kinsman through numerous relations that enliven the entire course of worldly existence, [the author now discusses] its stability and utility.

therefore, such a cognition, involving both difference and non-difference, is not an error. (7)

regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "pūrva" (before). Just as after creation, [the process] occurs again and again...

The meaning is that even if an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) occurs during the production of creation, it does not constitute a fault; such is the sense. To the question "Why is it not a fault?", he says: "For indeed" (*na hi*). By which means—that is, by what kind of loss—there would be a destruction of the root (*mūlakṣati*), namely, a destruction of the foundation consisting in the non-establishment of the preceding term without the establishment of the succeeding one. It would become an object of doubt. As it has been said:

Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the word "evam" (thus).
Here, the commentary [explains]:
*bandhurībhāvam* means loftiness (*udbhaṭatām*), consisting of the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

—The form that is the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*); of that [form], which has become the very bond of relationship; these two were previously indicated by the mention in the phrase "by means of stability and utility" (*sthairyopayogābhyām*). Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "in this very way" (*evameva*).

Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) establishes the method for explaining the verse with the word "here" (*iha*). "Here" means in this manifest world; "of entities" (*bhāvānām*) refers to blue and other such objects, as well as pleasure and other such internal states.

The connection with existence (*sattā-sambandha*)—that is, the connection with the highest genus (*parajāti*) called "existence" as accepted by the logicians—is not the case; that is, existence (*sattva*), meaning "being," does not occur. When the question "Why? arises, he says: "Because it is non-pervasive" (*avyāpakatvāt*).
In that regard, its non-pervasiveness is due to the exclusion of existence from universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth.

Because of faults such as futility (*vaiyarthyādi*), there is no purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) since it would be a distinct entity; nor is there the capacity to perform that action, because its constant presence is not observed. For it has been said:
"Even purposeful action is not innate to things..."

Thus, since its capacity to produce effects— which is understood through the method of agreement and difference consisting of perception and non-perception— is itself imperceptible, it follows that even if such a capacity exists, it remains imperceptible; therefore, it does not possess the fitness to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Even in that case, if there were a further recurrence [of existence], it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); for if existence (*sattā*) is admitted in existence itself, then another existence would be required for that, and yet another for that, resulting in an infinite regress. Likewise, if it were admitted in the ultimate particulars (*viśeṣas*), doubt would arise regarding them; and if, in order to eliminate that doubt, one were to pursue yet other particulars...

An infinite regress [would result]. Likewise, if inherence (*samavāya*) is accepted, then in order for it to reside [in its substrata], one would have to postulate another inherence, leading again to an infinite regress. Now, if it is argued that since universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth possess their own individual existence (*sattva*), they are designated as "existent" by that very fact, and thus do not depend on [the universal] "existence" (*sattā*).

This does not entail the aforementioned fault; however, if the conventional usage of "existence" (sattā) regarding the triad of substance and so forth occurs by means of that [universal existence] alone, then its utility there would be redundant. Alternatively, if the conventional usage of "existence" were to occur there even without it, then the consequence would be that "existence" would apply even to a hare's horn. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), non-existence (abhāva) is also included.
In the acceptance of existence (*sattā*), there is the apprehension of the consequence that its own nature would be contradicted;

for non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed the very state of being non-existent (*asattā*). Likewise, regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*): the causal efficiency performed by entities as they abide in their specific determinations does not constitute the existence of those entities.

Why? Because it is a different entity—because it is a distinct thing. For even existence (*sattā*) is a distinct entity, and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is also a distinct entity; likewise, its capacity to act—that is, the performance of causal efficiency—is not existence itself. Why? Because its presence is never observed at all times; for existence indeed [is that which is always present].

An entity would always remain [in its state], and if its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*) were admitted as belonging to that entity, then the entity would always be engaged in causal activity; however, this is not observed. Therefore, the point is that an entity does not possess the nature of causal efficiency. In this regard:

He states the consensus of the elders with the words "for it has been said. *Sahajā* means "inherent" or "constituting its very nature"; the word "iti" marks the conclusion of the author's statement. Here he states another fault with the words "and of that causal efficacy.
"And of that causal efficacy" means "and of the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*)."

"Consisting of perception and non-perception" means those positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) which take the form of perception and non-perception; "of that which is to be understood through them" means of that which is to be reached, that is to say, of that which is capable of being known by means of its existence and non-existence. The meaning is that even though the object serving as the substratum possesses existence (*sattā*), it would follow that it is imperceptible—that is, there would be the consequence of its non-apprehension at that time—and this is not tenable. [Objection: In that case, then, [existence] is merely the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākaraṇayogyatva*).

Let there be an essence (*sattva*) by which the aforementioned logical fault does not follow; for its capacity (*yogyatā*) is indeed always present. To this, he says: "not an object" (*nārtha*). When the question arises as to why this is so, he says: "of that" (*tasya*).
"Of that" refers to the capacity for performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Because it is difficult to determine at the time of deciding between truth and falsehood,
and because all of this fails to manifest, it is equivalent to a human horn.

And if one were to seek another causal efficiency (or, according to the Kashmiri manuscript, another capacity for causal activity), there would be an infinite regress; therefore, the very state of being manifest—
consisting in the undestroyed vibration of the appropriate reflective awareness— is the existence of an entity, and that [existence] is...
Since relations and so forth possess a nature of both difference and non-difference, their reality is indeed beyond doubt; nevertheless, if an opponent were to object:
"In this world..."
At the time of determining truth and untruth— this being an expression emphasizing the state (*bhāva*)— that is,
at the moment of ascertaining what is connected with truthfulness and untruthfulness— it is difficult to discern; that is,
it is impossible to determine, for the determination of truthfulness and untruthfulness depends precisely upon existence and non-existence.
The term *bhāva* means "it exists. He states the consequence of this fault even in its entirety with the words "of all":

As long as it exists, for the triad beginning with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is manifest only because that which possesses existence (*sattā*) is capable of being manifest;
and in the Buddhist system, existence itself consists in the nature of causal efficiency.

The point is that because [the existence of] dependence is impossible due to its not being included within causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and because [the existence of] "being" (*sattā*) is impossible.
Now, one might argue: "To avoid this fault, we shall simply accept another causal efficiency.
To this, he says: "another causal efficiency" (*arthakriyāntara*). This refers to another causal efficiency—that is, a different causal efficiency.

"In seeking"—that is, in pursuing [an object] by accepting it as a real entity (*sattva-bhāvena*) following upon a prior causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Because of this reason, the very state of being manifest—namely, the agency of manifestation alone—is the existence, that is, the essential nature (*svarūpa*), of the entity (*bhāva*) such as blue or pleasure;
for, by means of its capacity to establish [the object], it attains identity with that [object]. Of what kind is it?

"Unuprooted" (anunmūlyamānaḥ) means not being sublated; "appropriate in that manner" (tathocitaḥ) means suitable for that specific mode; "whose activity consists of the vibration of reflective awareness" (vimarśaparispandaḥ) refers to the operation known as conceptual thought (vikalpa).
Otherwise, even the manifestation of silver regarding a mother-of-pearl shell would entail the actual existence of silver.

The sense is: "it may be so. The truth of these [statements] is beyond doubt— that is, free from uncertainty— nevertheless (*tathāpi*),

In the same way, even in that case, it is by means of that very object—which possesses both difference and non-difference through its nature as a relation and so forth—that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) occurs; however, no purposeful action whatsoever ever occurs by means of that which rests solely within its own self. Every worldly transaction consists of that very experience which has been felt as a semblance of pleasure, and it is precisely this that is desired, not anything else that has not been experienced.
