To this he says: "Sukha" [pleasure]. One is "satisfied" (*tuṣyate*)—that is, one becomes contented—by attaining the state of having accomplished what was to be done; and thus...
The point is that even in the conventional usage known as "easy apprehension," the cognition of the relationship certainly arises.

Now, in response to the inquiry, "How can it have both a unitary and manifold nature there? he says, "If... *tat* refers to the pleasure being experienced. *Tadeva* means that very same pleasure previously experienced.
"Because it has already been attained"—the sense is that desire for what has already been attained is not logical. "That very thing" means:

"it is indeed other," and "that very thing becomes that which is not that," while "that which is not that also becomes that"—this is the connection. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the proof regarding the nature of being both one and many.
He extends this same analysis to the *kapittha* tree and others as well with the word "thus" (*evam*).
And here he states the agreement of the Teacher (*ācārya*), saying:
"In the desire for a desired object, one either reflects upon the desired object itself, or [upon] that which produces the desired object."
Nor is the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) desired [as the cause], for heaven too is a desired place of enjoyment for that unseen merit.
And that which was seen perished along with the very act of seeing; thus its reality is questioned.
When examined through its identity with the seer, that [object]... ||

Thus [it is said]. When there is the expectation of what was stated, he says: "The desired. Here is the meaning: when a wise person desires the desired object—namely, at the time of desiring the desired object by resorting to its definition, and at the time of desiring the means to the desired object—the object itself, that which produces the desired, or the means to the desired [is what is intended].
Or, in both cases, the word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of indicating the primacy of both.

One should reflect—that is, it should be brought within the scope of inquiry—whether this [object] previously perceived is logical or whether it is unperceived. An object established through reflection [is determined] by itself.
He states "and not even" because it is established as such: that [heaven] is not even desired, nor is it perceived;

for in reality, heaven would be an unperceived locus of enjoyment—a place where enjoyment has never been experienced—even though it is desired. And this is stated here with reference specifically to the desirability of objects already perceived through direct experience.

The state of being desired regarding objects established by scripture exists here as well. Now, one might object: "In that case, let there be desire only for what is perceived. To this he says: "And what is perceived... The sense is that it has perished, because of its momentariness. Thus, for this reason, there is no state of being sought after.
The sense is that when [the object] has perished, the state of being a seeker is appropriate. Now, if one asks, "What then should be done?", he says:
"by means of the identity with the seer" (*draṣṭraikyena*). Therefore, that is desired by us;
it is "discerned through identity with the seer"—that is, discerned as oneness with the seer—within the seer.

It means that which exists as a mental formation (*saṃskāra*), namely, that which has been examined and deliberated upon. The sense is that every object is grasped solely through the recollection of its previous experience as pleasure or as a means to pleasure.
If it is asked, "In that case, how does initial grasping occur?", we reply: "Through doubt."

If that is so, then there would be no dependence on a relation in that case; this is not so, for doubt, by virtue of resting upon two alternatives, has its very life in synthesis (*yojanā*). Alternatively, there is some internal synthesis previously established which is the means for all worldly transaction, by means of which even in newborn infants, [the cognition] regarding the breast-milk [occurs].

"Conventional usage is observed"—enough, then, with further disclosure of this secret. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the Teacher's statement. The word "ādi" (and so forth) is intended to include other statements found therein. The aforementioned method—

And so forth. Thus, within this [reality] whose nature is manifestation (*ābhāsa*), even another manifestation that is not currently being perceived has entered into it by way of the form of a universal relation; otherwise, no linguistic or practical activity (*vyavahāra*) would be possible in any way. Therefore, if this [reality] is useful for all places, times, conditions, and persons...

"This is conventional discourse"—if conventional discourse is not real, then we do not know the reality of anything else; thus, one should not be deluded by the thought that there is no error here. May there be auspiciousness! 7.

He provides the interpretation of the verse by relying on the established reality, stating "and thus":

"And thus, and thus being so"—that is, when this nature of blue, pleasure, and so forth has arisen in the form of a manifestation within this self-natured manifestation which is appearing; [in that state], even that which is non-perceptible exists, for there is no question at all regarding the perceptible.
This is the intended meaning. Another manifestation (*ābhāsāntara*)—even if not grasped with clarity—is nonetheless entered into as having the nature of a universal relation;
otherwise, in its absence, no worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) could occur in any way whatsoever.

Because it has been stated immediately prior: this worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is beneficial for all places, times, conditions, and persons—that is, it is of service to a person across all locations, times, and states; if this were not true, then we would not find the truth in anything else.
"We know"—for this reason, a person should not be deluded regarding this matter;
no delusion should be produced. Why is it called "delusion"?
This worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is a delusion because it takes the form of delusion, being established through error. [Objection: If that is so, then how...
The author himself has stated elsewhere:
"A snake does not exist in a rope, yet one experiences fear of it until death;
who indeed can determine the immense power of delusion?"

Thus it is said. This is true; this was stated specifically with reference to those who remain below *māyā*. For them, *māyā*—which is of the nature of delusion (*bhrānti*)—must indeed be relied upon. However, those who have attained the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*) situated above that, and for that very reason have emerged from the principle of *māyā*, [perceive] everything...

Because the world is established as mere manifestation (*bhānamātra*), they perceive it as being of the very nature of pure light (*prakāśa*), which is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*); for light is indeed manifestation itself, yet it is devoid of the coloring (*uparāga*) of objects. But [one might object]: "In that case, does it not follow that the coloring of objects is distinct from that [light]? No; it is that very [light].
Because it is impossible for that [consciousness] to be colored by [objects], or rather, let everything remain exactly as it is;

there is no loss whatsoever for those established in the Great Non-duality (mahādvaita). For in the Great Non-duality, since difference exists as reality and non-difference as its non-separateness, there is no state of being a single form of manifestation.

Otherwise, it would result in the undesirable consequence that [the world] is merely an appearance of non-duality; for just as the collection of lines appearing on a leaf is nothing but the leaf itself, so too the collection of entities appearing in the Light is nothing but the Light itself.
In the absence of that [Light], the unmanifested would simply remain unmanifested. As it has been said:
If Maheśvara were to abide with a body of a single form,
he would have abandoned his nature as consciousness in his state of being Maheśvara, just like a jar or other such objects.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Examination of Difference and Non-difference," in the *Kriyādhikāra* (Section on Action) of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* written by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. || 2 ||

For here, by the word *maheśvara*, it is precisely the Light (*prakāśa*) endowed with the sovereignty called *vimarśa* that is expressed; and as for "consciousness-ness" (*saṃvittva*), it is the manifestation [of the Light] through the being of entities.
As for that "reality" which exists from the perspective of the ignorant, that is something else entirely, because it consists merely in the appearance of reality.

They too should not harbor this conceit, thinking, "We perceive reality in phenomena," for they have not even ascended to the plane of delusion; enough said. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the chapter (*āhnika*), and the word *śiva* is an expression of auspiciousness.
And it is intent upon indicating the supreme reality; may there be auspiciousness. || 7 ||

Thus ends the second chapter in the section on Action (Kriyādhikāra) of the *Śrīpratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*, a commentary known as the *Bhāskarī*, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Bhāskarakaṇṭha. || 2 ||
The third chapter in the Section on Action.
The means of knowledge [operate] during the entry into valid cognition through the sequence of the ascension of their own power.
We praise that Śiva, whose face gazes upon the objects of knowledge.
We praise that Śiva, upon whose support the entire collection of means of knowledge strives to touch, by means of the sun-like [consciousness] entering its own power.
Now, at the beginning of the third chapter on Action (*kriyādhikāra*),

for the sake of completing the commentary without obstacles and for the sake of its widespread propagation, [the author] performs externally as well— though it was already performed internally— the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) consisting of the recollection of reality (*tattvānusmaraṇa*), in order to instruct his disciples.
He concludes with a verse that indicates the purport of the entire treatise, beginning with the words "The means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāni*).

We [interpret] "that"— which is renowned as the supporter of the means of knowledge— and "Śiva," who is the very nature of the light of valid cognition (*pramā*), whose form is not delineated by contact with objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and who is named Śiva.
We praise the supreme reality—we lead it to the status of being the object of the highest contemplation.
Which one? The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whose nature will be described in the first verse of this chapter: the instruments of valid knowledge consisting of outward-directed awareness.

Regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—that is, the domain known as the object; regarding the entry of valid cognition (*pramāveśa*)—that is, becoming the domain of the result known as valid cognition; by implication, this means regarding the instrument thereof (the means of knowledge). Of whom—that is, of Śiva—the [senses] become "gazers upon the face"—that is, they look toward His mouth—for indeed, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)...

The internal reality of the knower (*pramātṛtattva*), which is constantly intent on producing valid cognition regarding the object of knowledge, requires [the Self] as its support; otherwise, being insentient, it would be incapable of that function. As it has been said:
Even the means of valid cognition, which extend the very life of all things,
have that same Supreme Lord as their ultimate life-force.

Thus [it is said]. To the inquiry "How so?", he says: "by one's own power" (*svabala*). "Of one's own power" means of the self's power; "of its ascent" means of its support—that is, by way of sequence, meaning gradually.
For at that time, those means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) indeed depend upon the power of the knower (*pramātṛ*), and the knower likewise...

The sense is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he is indeed Śiva; therefore, the very act of ascending by means of his power is for them the beholding of the face of Śiva. As it has been said:
"Like the senses of embodied beings..."

Thus, for here, while the mantras remain engaged in their own respective domains by virtue of their inherent nature, they possess their own power— this being stated in the context of describing the expansion of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
The true nature of the universal and other categories has been established by means of their relations; now, however, the reality of relation itself must be explained as a single, unified whole.
And that, in the ultimate sense, is of only two kinds: the state of being the signified and the signifier, and the state of being the effect and the cause.

In that regard, within the former [section], which serves as the locus for investigating the relationship between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), everything already stated and yet to be stated is dependent upon it— according to the principle that "the establishment of an entity depends on the means of knowledge.
Thus, in proceeding therein, there is an advancement of one's own power by means of the instruments (*karaṇas*) while exercising one's own authority.
It has been made into an illustration; and just as the instruments [of action] are [illustrated by] the means of valid cognition because they are the instruments for producing valid knowledge,
and it is a well-known thing that is made into an illustration, it is thus quite clear that the means of valid cognition,
in the process of generating valid knowledge regarding their objects of comprehension, proceed by means of their own inherent power.

It is the state of being beheld by the face of Śiva. And this is precisely the intended meaning: "For just as an object, though clearly seen with an attentive mind, shines forth even more clearly when cultivated through the exertion of its own power."

This is also intended in the *Śrīspandaśāstra* within this very *kārikā*: for the mind (*cetas*), being of the nature of outward-turned cognition, is indeed a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Manifestation is valid cognition (*pramā*);
the cultivation of the exertion of one's own power is the "assault" of one's own power. By this—
It has been indicated that he will here carry out the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.
Having thus accomplished the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*), he states the purport of the entire chapter both collectively and individually with the word "thus" (*evam*).
Here, the commentary states:

"In connection with the description of the expansion of the power of action— that is, the manifestation characterized by the states of generality and so forth— preceded by [an explanation of] its relationship."

"Predominant in its relation" means that it has been granted existence by that [relation]. "Established" means established through reasoning; "as a single mass" means as a single lump, that is, as being without joints or seams. "To be explained" means to be told. And that—

And the reality of relation (*saṃbandhatattva*). By the phrase "from the perspective of ultimate truth" (*paramārthataḥ*), the conceptual nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the other [relations] is shown. Although logicians and others have stated that only conjunction and inherence (*samavāya*) are innate, nevertheless, in common usage, those two...

This was stated because there is no such utility [in that case]; here, however, since he is establishing that conventional reality alone is true, he demonstrates the division into two types by saying "the object to be made known" (*jñāpya*). Among those two, in the former—
In the sense of the relationship between the known and the knower; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the "measure" (*mātrā*) and so forth is intended;

"previously stated" means what was said before. "Dependent" means subject to. To the question "Why?", he says: "by the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). The word "iti" has the sense of the word "evam" (thus). Now, from that...

Because it is well-known therein, and because it must necessarily be investigated— both for its utility in supporting the subject matter at hand and because it itself constitutes a form of relationship— in order to define the status of the means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth.
"This is such-and-such," and so forth;
by means of this [cognition], the conventional usage of "Lord" (Īśa) and so on is set in motion.
Thus, with seventeen verses, another chapter begins.

Therein, with two verses, the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is established; thereafter, in order to determine the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), [it is shown that] the operation of the means of knowledge pertains to each individual appearance (*pratyābhāsa*), and not—
In order to demonstrate that there is a rule of restriction based on the fact that [cognition] is grounded solely in a reality whose nature is its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
it is stated in ten verses that the determination of appearances occurs through the power of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*);
and as a consequence of that, the nature of false cognition is stated in one verse.

And the establishment of the nature of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is also possible by relying on the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*); this is demonstrated by the verse: "And all this distinction between the means of knowledge, their results, the objects of knowledge, and so forth, exists when there is a knower (*pramātṛ*) whose form has been shown."
Therefore, it is not an object of cognition (*prameya*) such that the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyāpāra*) would be possible even here;
rather, the means of valid cognition here has as its fruit merely the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāramātra*). This is the intended meaning of the three verses.

Regarding what was stated—that cognitions such as those of action and relation are not of the nature of error—it is precisely to determine that point that he first restates the well-known nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*).
To the question "Why?", he says: "And thus. The subject at hand is the matter that has been commenced and which is to be established.

The object to be established, which consists of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), is [discussed] there for its utility. "The establishment of the means of knowledge and so forth" refers to the systematic arrangement of the means of knowledge (*māna*), the objects of knowledge (*meya*), and so on. "Another chapter" (*āhnikāntara*) means another section. "Therein" means within the seventeen verses. "Its nature as a fruit" refers to the nature of that result.

The nature of valid cognition (*pramā*). Thereafter— that is, immediately following that— in every manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*), by means of the rule (*niyama*) regarding the state of being restricted to a single [entity] (*ekaniṣṭhatā*) of that object which consists of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), according to the verse.

The meaning is "by the thirteenth [verse]"; it is "shown by the verse," meaning by the fourteenth. The connection is that [this state] occurs when the subject (*pramātṛ*) exists—one whose nature has been determined in the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*) and whose form has been demonstrated. "Of him" refers to the subject; "here too" means even in the case of the subject; "here" [refers to the present context].
The intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) for this cognizer is the purport of the entire chapter (*āhnika*) taken individually.
Now, he provides the introductory commentary (*avataraṇikā*) for the first and second verses, stating what was said:

Thus: "That by virtue of which an object is established as being clearly and distinctly 'this is such-and-such,' that is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); and it too is a fresh arising of its own manifestation. (1)

Thus, that cognition whose essence is internal reflective awareness (vimarśa) is an uncontradicted valid means of knowledge regarding an object that is the referent of a single designation, even though [the object] is undivided by space, time, and so forth. (2)

By whose power—that is, by whose efficacy—the entity, such as blue or pleasure, is established; that is, it does not overstep its determined limits of manifestation, being defined as "this" by its own nature and as "of such a kind" through its association with qualifiers such as permanence or impermanence; that, in the world, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

That which has been established must be investigated by the discerning one— having thus provided this introduction regarding the true nature of the subject matter, he presents two verses and explains them as follows:
"This is such-and-such."
Regarding this, the commentary explains "by whose power" (*yadvaśāt*) as "of whom" (*yasya*). It explains the component "of whom" as referring to that whose nature is about to be described.

"By implication" (*sāmarthyāt*): by the word "blue," there is a reference to an external object; by the word "pleasure," there is a reference to an internal object; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), all external and internal objects are included. He explains [the phrase] "it is established" (*vyavatiṣṭhate*) as "it is expressed" (*vyācaṣṭe*).

"Niścitām" (ascertained) means that it appears precisely in the form of blue, pleasure, and so forth. He explains the word "idametādṛgityevam," which consists of a collection of parts, by the word "idam.
He explains the part "idam" as "by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*). [He then explains] the part "etādṛk"...
He explains it as "the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*). And those which serve as qualifiers are such properties as permanence, impermanence, and so forth—[according to the commentary:
those properties whose nature consists of permanence, impermanence, and non-permanence]—those properties, or the connection (*yoga*) with them.

The connection is with that [word]. The word "thus" (*evam*) is explained by the third case ending (*tṛtīyāvibhakti*). The word "established" (*sthitam*) is supplied by way of logical fitness (*yogyatayā*). By this, the explanation up to the end of the word "that" (*tat*) has been completed. And thus, the application here is as follows.

It does not first establish itself by its own power, because it is insentient; for how could there then be an appearance such as "blue appears to me" or "to Caitra"? Therefore, it establishes itself through the power of another. But if that other is also insentient, then it is like one blind man taking hold of the hand of another blind man.

Therefore, that self of consciousness is distinct [from the object]; if it were pure and devoid of differentiation, it could not be the cause for the determination of blue alone, since it would be the same with respect to yellow and other colors as well; thus, it is colored by blue.

That by virtue of which an object is established in the world as "this is such-and-such"—namely, as "this" and as "such-and-such"—is established as *pramāṇa*. Here, because it is difficult to understand, he proposes an investigation as a task to be undertaken, saying "and that": "and that" refers to the entity whose nature has been described.
And the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes the nature and attributes [of things];

it is to be investigated—that is, made an object of inquiry—by the investigator, the discerning one. He performs the investigation itself "here," meaning in this manifest world. The word "first" (*tāvat*) implies that there is no disagreement on this point by anyone.

"By its own power"—that is, by the inherent capacity of the thing's own nature—it does not remain fixed; the meaning is that it does not function within a restricted boundary. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of insentience (*jaḍatva*).
For that which is insentient is not capable of establishing its own state by itself; it [requires] sentience alone.
Because of the attainment of its own nature (*svarūpalābha*). He states another reason with the words "mama" (of mine). "Then" means:

if, in reality, the arrangement were to occur solely by the power of one's own self. "Thus"—in this way—"manifestation"—vibration—how could it be? It would not be; such is the meaning. Why so? Because of "mine."
The point is that there would be no manifestation attached to a subject, such as "the blue appears" or "it appears to Caitra.
Even though the manifestation of one thing does not fall within the range of another, nevertheless...
This has been stated according to the requirements of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*):
therefore, each respective object is established through dependence on another; one performs an investigation of that other, and the other [also does so].
"The other"—whether in the form of the ego or in the form of Caitra—if he were insentient (*jaḍa*).
Then, this becomes like a blind man taking the hand of another blind man—a grasping of the hand for support.

Regarding this, he states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). "Therefore"—for that reason—this other one, the conscious self (*saṃvidātmā*), is joined [to the body]; such is the ellipsis. But surely, that is the conscious self itself?

To the question, "Let that be; what follows from it?", he says: "so'pi" (even that). Even that—the self of consciousness—if it is pure, and for that very reason undifferentiated, remains as the subject without distinction across all [objects] such as blue and the rest, then—at that time—it is solely the cause for the determination of the blue itself.

It would not be the apprehender of blue; rather, it would be so even with respect to yellow and other colors, because that self of consciousness (*saṃvidātman*) is established as such—that is, as the determiner—otherwise its purity would be impossible.
Therefore, for that reason, this manifestation (*ābhāsa*) is colored by blue—that is, by the blue existing as an object.

Being a manifestation characterized by the nature of blue light and directed toward blue, it is the establisher of blue; for its very nature as that light is what constitutes its status as an establisher.
And if that light of blue were not distinct [from the object], then it would belong to yellow as well—since it is of the nature of light.
Because there is no distinction in its identity with the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*), that manifestation belongs to the blue which has been differentiated from it.

And if that manifestation—by which the blue is thus rendered capable of appearing as distinct from it—is itself differentiated from the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), then it would indeed be so. (K. ṣ. ṣ.)
Because if it were not distinct from the Great Light, it would follow that there is no distinction between that [light] and blue and so forth;
nor has it been made non-distinct from the Great Light by being colored by a substance— that is, colored by its own [blue] substance— just as [in the case of the light].
"Facing toward blue," and for that very reason, "having the nature of the manifestation of blue"—being of such a form, he is the establisher of blue;
according to the maxim that "every sentence implies a restriction," he becomes the one who establishes *only* blue. To the question "Why so? he says: "That," for—
Because its very nature as illumination is what constitutes its status as the determiner [of objects].

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that... [referring to the cognition]. "Of the non-distinct"—that is, of the blue which is not different from this [cognition]—"it would be so" at that time. By this reasoning, because it is also non-different from yellow and the rest...

This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). When the question "Why? arises, he himself states this very reason: "consisting of light" (*prakāśātmaka*). He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tena*). "That" refers to [the object] existing as an object (*viṣayatayā sthitaḥ*).
Now, one might ask: "Let it be entirely distinct from that; what of it? To this he replies: "And blue... (*nīlaṃ ca*).
"Thus" (*ittham*) means "this being the case. From that—from the manifestation of its own object—there is a manifestation in the form of differentiation;
that which is fit for such a manifestation of differentiation is "fit for the manifestation of differentiation.
He fulfills the expectation of the word "thus" by saying "if. That manifestation as well—

The appearance (*ābhāsa*) whose nature is blue light is "distinguished"—it undergoes differentiation—because otherwise, by that very means, it would attain oneness with this [light] as well; such is the sense.
He himself provides the reason for this here: "mahā" (great). [This refers to] non-differentiation from the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*).

The meaning is that if there were non-difference from the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), then for that—the manifestation as blue (*nīlaprakāśa*)—there would follow the consequence of the absence of distinction (*vyatirekābhāva*), which amounts to the undesirable conclusion (*aniṣṭāpatti*) known as the non-existence of the application of distinction. [Objection: But then...

Since it endures even the slightest [obstruction], it must surely manifest contraction within itself; for that [contraction] is the very life-force of the contraction of both consciousness and objects— the life-force of their mutual contraction.
This [consciousness], whose nature is the negation of objects, is called "void" (*śūnya*); moreover, the very appearance of contraction is the emergence of the subject belonging to *māyā*.
Therefore, in the ultimate sense, the manifestation of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge occurs through a single power of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-śakti*). Consequently—
"Let even the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), which consists of emptiness, intellect, vital breath, and body, be distinct from blue and other objects, so that the aforementioned fault does not follow";
to this he says, "it does not tolerate [such a distinction]," because it would result in the impossibility of its being tolerant. This is the intended meaning. He states the conclusion: "Thus."
"Surely" (nūnam) means "for this reason. "Surely" (nūnam) indicates certainty.

By that Great Light, within its own self-aspect—which is being projected as the object blue—there occurs contraction (*saṃkoca*), which is limitedness and the differentiation from itself and from the blue.

"Nirbhāsanīyaḥ" means that although [the contraction] exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is capable of being manifested by virtue of its own power. To the objection, "Let it be manifested; what of it?", he says: "Of consciousness" (*saṃvidaḥ*). This contraction, which is to be manifested by the wise, is called "the void" (*śūnya*), meaning the void subject (*śūnyapramātṛ*).
In response to the question "Why?", he provides a qualifying attribute containing the reason: "consisting of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Since it has emerged from the Great Light that is filled with all things, and because it lacks any contact with objects due to its being of the nature of "nothing whatsoever," it is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*).
This is the meaning. Furthermore, the emptiness of the negation—the non-existence denoted by the negative particle—is quite evident;
from the perspective of ultimate reality, the term "form" (*rūpa*) is employed precisely because its nature is the non-existence denoted by the negative particle.
Again, of what kind is it? It is that which constitutes the contraction of consciousness as well as of objects such as blue and so forth.

The term "prāṇa" refers to that which effects mutual non-pervasiveness; the meaning is: he whose existence is obtained by that [prāṇa]. He explains the nature of this very [prāṇa] as the subject (grāhaka) with the words "contraction" (saṃkoca).
This means: of the subject belonging to Māyā (māyīyapramātṛ), that is, of the subject distinct from the supreme subject (parapramātṛ).
*Udthānam* means manifestation. By this, he speaks of the fruit-bearing reality; hence, "by one" (*ekayā*).

For this reason, it is not by something existing as separate for each [individual], but by the single power of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-śakti*) residing in the supreme subject, which consists of the nature of agency and knowledge.

By means of the power whose form is emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), acting as the object of emanation, there occurs, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the manifestation of the subject, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge— the subjects consisting of the void (*śūnya*) and so forth,
the various means of knowledge, and the manifold objects of knowledge.
The meaning is that manifestation occurs; that is, everything manifests simultaneously.

Although, according to the principle that "Brahman does not exist apart from creation," everything is indeed always present here, nevertheless, this was stated by way of a conceptual construction for the sake of instructing the disciple. In this regard as well—
He states the conclusion with the words "by that" (*tena*). By that— that is,

from the subject of *māyā* who is contracted by the assumption of limitation consisting in the acceptance of the support of the [external] day, and who consists of an internalized consciousness throughout infinite time— *sa*...

As long as an appearance regarded as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) possesses the nature of being directed toward an object of cognition (prameya), it too— because it is permeated by the appearance of the object's location, time, and form— is likewise of a different form in every moment, [to be produced as having various distinct appearances— K].
It must be created; as it has been said by Abhinavagupta:

"Since the manifestation of the subject and so forth occurs through a single act of creation, for that reason—at whatever time—the forms consisting of the void, the intellect, the vital breath, the body, and so forth (the word 'and so forth' including...)"
The apprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). This is because even those [limited subjects] possess the status of a knower (*pramātṛ*) in the state of being insentient matter (*jaḍa*).
"Of those" refers to the adjuncts (*upādhi*); "their locus" means the taking as one's own, the acceptance, which consists of that contraction; by the grasping of that [contraction].

From the contracted [subject]—that is, from the state of the subject of *māyā* which has established contraction through its own autonomy, which has manifested as distinct from the supreme subject whose nature is the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), and which is based on *māyā* because its very life-breath is duality—from such a subjectivity; of what kind? For an infinite time.
— for an unlimited time, that is to say, at all times; it is "inward-turned"—
meaning that even at the moment of being directed toward the external, because it rests solely upon the reflective awareness of "I" (the thought "I see"), it has only itself as its object.

"Saṃvedana" is the activity known as "reflective awareness" (parāmarśa); from that which has such a nature, "he"—the well-known manifestation (ābhāsa) recognized by the name "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa)—comes into being. To the question "Of what kind?", he says: "being directed toward the object of knowledge" (prameyonmukhatā).

By this it is shown that when the contracted Great Light (mahāprakāśa) is in an inward-turned state as "I," it constitutes subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*); whereas when it is outward-turned as "this," it constitutes the means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*).
At this time, because of the manifestation of the inward-turned state in the form "I see," [subjectivity is established].
It is indicated that the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) is indeed unlimited.
He fulfills the expectation of the word "as far as" (*yāvat*) by saying "at that time" (*tāvat*); *tāvat* means at that very moment.
Likewise (*tathā*), "he too"—even that semblance of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*)—[arises] moment by moment.

"Of various forms"—meaning not of a single form like the inward-turned subject (*pramātṛ*), but "to be created," i.e., that which is to be produced. When asked for the reason why this is so, he says: "of the object of knowledge" (*prameyasya*).
Of the object of knowledge—that is, of the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—there is "the state of being differentiated" by the appearances of place, time, and form.

The state of being that which possesses "being colored" (uparaktatva) is "coloredness" (tattva); because of that, [it means] in every moment, due to its manifesting as something new through distinctions such as place and so forth—this is the sense.
For the point is that it is logical that the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) must indeed be distinct for each object of knowledge (prameya).

In response to the inquiry, "By whom was this said?", [the author], intending to explain the remaining portion of the verse beginning with "svābhāsaḥ," connects the word *abhinavodayaḥ* contained therein as its designator.

Thus, Abhinava says: "It is not stained even by the fading that occurs during a moment's duration; therefore, it is said to be 'ever-newly arising. Even that [newly arising state], if it were not likewise connected to the illusory subject (māyā-pramātṛ), then for me there would be no manifestation of blue."

For whomever [it belongs], there would be no sense of "this is mine" regarding that which appears as yellow; yet this self-awareness exists, which is not contradicted in any case. Thus, that manifestation appearing as one's own—arising ever anew due to its orientation toward ever-new objects of knowledge—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because of this.
It establishes valid cognition (*pramā*). If one asks, "What is that?"—if it is asked whether it is of the nature of the fruit of valid cognition—the author says:
"That very manifestation, whose nature is consciousness, is the measure (*miti*); it is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*). This is the connection [of the words].
Regarding the phrase "as it has been said" (*taduktam*), the meaning is that it has been stated by this very word. [The following is] the explanation of this word.

"He makes [it] new" (*abhinava*). He explains the component "new" (*abhinava*) as "moment" (*kṣaṇa*). By means of the fading that is produced by that momentary staying—which is the "parivāsa"—[the flower is made new]. With the words "by that" (*tena*), he states the resulting meaning. By this, the word *abhi* expresses the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
This has been illuminated. He provides an introduction in order to explain that "that too is its own manifestation," with the words:

"If that too is of such a nature. "That too" refers to that means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whose nature was previously described; "this" refers to this manifestation; "self-awareness" means established by one's own experience; that which...
He fulfills the expectation regarding this with the words "iti" (thus). From the reason that "this exists," it "becomes thus.

When the inquiry arises as to what it is that becomes thus, he explains by analyzing the components [of the term] with the words "svābhāsa" (self-manifestation), namely, "by way of its own nature" (*svatvena*). By way of its own nature—that is, by being the object of the sense of "mine" which rests upon the grasper (*grāhaka*). It...
The syntactical connection (*yojanā*) up to the point "that very thing is the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇam*) has been indicated.

Thus, the construction here is as follows: "That too"—meaning even the means of valid cognition—"is a new arising and likewise possesses its own manifestation. To the inquiry "Why is it a means of valid cognition?", he states the reason by supplying an ellipsis.
"Since [it is] valid cognition (*pramā*). By this, the first verse has been explained.
Now, he provides an introduction to explain the second verse with the words "What is it? [The answer is:
it has the nature of the fruit of the means of valid cognition—that is, its essential form is that of the fruit of the means of valid cognition which functions as the instrument.
If it is asked, "What is the means of valid cognition (pramā)?"—if you have spoken thus, the Teacher says:
anticipating the question "What does he say?", he explains this second verse as the answer, stating "he himself. He explains "he" by saying "he himself. Every sentence...

The use of the word *eva* (only) is based on the logical principle that it carries an exclusive restriction (*sāvadhāraṇam*). By means of the word *eva*, the inclusive sense of the word *tathā* is indicated, [showing that] "it is precisely this which is cognition" (*miti*). He explains "cognition" (*miti*) as "means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇa*). This is the connection [of the words].

[Objection: But in this way, would not mere synonymy be asserted, rather than the state of being a fruit? [Regarding the nature of the fruit—Kṣemarāja’s commentary]: He says: "In that regard, it is a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its nature as light directed toward the external; whereas that which belongs to that very [light]..."

It has been previously established that the inward-turned self consists of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). By its very essence—though contracted by the state of objects—that same consciousness is the fruit. For just as, in the case of one who possesses discernment, heroism and victory reside in a single locus when one thinks, "I, who am a hero, am the victor."

They are established as cause and effect, for [one says]: "Since I am a hero, therefore I am victorious. In the same way, in the second verse, the connection is exactly thus: "Since there is the manifestation of blue, therefore this is blue. [The phrase] "consisting of internal reflective awareness" (antarvimarśātmā) [is used].
He provides an introduction to explain the two words with "nanu evam" (but indeed, in this way).
"Evam" means in this manner; "paryāyatvam" means the state of being synonyms, and not the state of being effects.
For it is logical that an effect must be distinct from its instruments and so forth, just as the act of cutting is distinct from the axe. It is not [the case that they are synonyms].
And that [distinction] does not exist here either, because both have the nature of a single cognition; this is the intended meaning. He states the answer to this with the words "He says" (*āha*).

The word "the author of the Sūtras" (*sūtrakāra*) is to be supplied as the subject. When the question arises as to what he says, he explains these very two terms with the words "external" (*bāhya*), etc. Therein—

Between the two states of being a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and a result (*phala*), that cognition which establishes the object becomes the *pramāṇa* through its outward orientation in the form of manifestation— such as "I see this" and so forth. But (*tu*), by contrast, of that very same [cognition]—

That which is the inward-turned nature of consciousness as self-reflection— the state of being established as "I," the very essence of reflective awareness— was previously demonstrated and established through reasoning in the section on knowledge; by that very nature, by that essential form, it is consciousness itself.
Cognition itself, in the form of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), becomes the result (*phala*). By what nature is it so?

It is solely by being contracted into the state of an object—that is, having attained limitation through the influence of the coloring of the object; otherwise, the consequence would be that [the cognition] were the subject (*pramātṛ*) itself, for cognition is indeed inward-turned.

In the state of being colored by an object, it has the form of valid cognition (*pramā*); when not so colored, it has the form of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). However, in ultimate analysis, the light that has become differentiated from the supreme light is the cognizer by its own nature; when directed toward the external, it is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, when it is oriented toward its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is the means of valid cognition (*pramā*); when it is in the state of being established, it is the object of valid cognition (*prameya*).

He provides an illustration for one thing having the status of both the instrument and the result, saying "just as" (*yathā hi*). The word *yathā hi* indicates that this is an illustration. "Residing in one" (*ekaniṣṭhe*) means having a single person as its object.

He demonstrates the very establishment [of this] with the words "for since" (*yato hi*). He applies it to the case at hand (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "thus" (*evam*). "Subsequent reflection" (*parāmarśaḥ*) means valid cognition (*pramā*); here he cites the consensus of the elders (*vṛddhasammati*), saying "this is subsequent reflection.
Even though there is a single nature [between the two], there exists the relationship of cause and effect, as it has been stated:
"Because it is established through that [cause], due to its dependence upon it...

Furthermore, in this context, the fruit is of the very nature of the operation, and the operation is established as being non-different in form from that which is operating or that which is being made to operate. Thus—

There is non-difference between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*), because the means of knowledge exists by the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and reflective awareness has speech as its very life; and speech operates solely within a single manifestation (*ābhāsa*)— unmixed with other manifestations such as space and time— as in the case of the word "jar."

Regarding the term "red": because the two appearances of space and time—which are inclined toward bestowing their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa)—are not mixed together, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) operates upon the appearance that is being generalized (sāmānyāyamāna), as has been stated.
To the question "By what [means]?", he says: "By the power of that" (tadvaśāt). "By the power of that" means...

The statement regarding the state of being the cause, and the statement regarding the state of being the effect because of its establishment—thus ends the word "iti" (meaning "so it is"). He states another alternative with the words "kiṃ ca" (furthermore). Here—in this path of cognition—from the cognizer who is actively engaged (*vyāpriyamāṇāt*).

From the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as it is being employed, [the object] is indeed of no other form—that is, non-different. He explains [the phrase] "in that which is undivided by space, time, and so forth" with the words "by the power of reflective awareness" (*vimarśabala*). For this reason, the means of valid cognition, by the power of reflective awareness...
It comes to be so; for in the absence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), even an object grasped by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is as if ungrasped.
And this reflective awareness has speech as its very life, because it consists of the recollection of words. Furthermore, speech [is manifested] through forms such as place and time—

It functions within a single, unique manifestation alone— the universal form— which consists of mere appearance and is untouched by other manifestations, namely those characterized by place, time, and form, which are distinct from the manifestation of the mere object itself.

It resorts to manifestation (*pravṛtti*). In response to the inquiry "How so?", he says: "As 'jar'. "As 'jar'" refers to the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of jar-ness; "red" refers to the reflective awareness of its color. From that—from the imparting, that is, the accomplishment, of the state of being a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

In that regard, concerning the two "inclinations" (*pravaṇa*): indeed, it is only that which is delimited by its respective space and time that constitutes its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because that which is not delimited by space and time is a universal (*sāmānya*).
This is due to the non-mixing of these two manifestations of space and time.

Because there is no state of mixture; because, while appearing as a universal—due to the absence of abiding through absolute exclusion from everything—there is an absence of being a universal, yet it stands as if it were a universal; [this applies] to the appearance, whether it be the appearance of a jar or the appearance of redness; [in such cases, it is] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It functions and undergoes occurrence,

but not with respect to space and time which would establish its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because these are objects for the operation of separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, [it would follow that...].
For even this manifestation "this" occurs only as a manifestation of an object situated in front, unmixed with other manifestations;
as has been stated by the venerable Ācārya himself: "[It is] merely the manifestation of that which is situated in front."
Even when an object is present before one, the reflective awareness that "this is fixed" arises solely through the universal of "this-ness" (idantā) common to all entities.
Thus, the object is merely an appearance;

for if it were the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then both that appearance and its substrate would necessarily fall into having that same nature. Indeed, the distinction between objects of cognition follows only from the distinction between the means of cognition.
[This is] the state of being. [Objection: "Let this principle apply to the manifestation 'this is a jar';
however, in the case of the manifestation where one points with a finger saying 'this,' there is clearly the apprehension of the specific individual (svalakṣaṇa).
To this, he says: "Even in the case of 'this'... [referring to] that which is unmixed with other manifestations.

When it is asked, "By whom was this said? regarding that which is devoid of the mixture of space, time, and appearance—being merely the appearance of an entity, merely the appearance of a jar, or merely the appearance of red—the [text] says: "The Teacher. When it is asked, "By what statement was it said? it says: "In the *Niyata*."

This is the meaning here: this reflective awareness as "this" occurs even with regard to a determined object situated in front—that is, even with regard to a limited object such as a jar standing before one. By the word "even," it is indicated that there is no doubt whatsoever regarding indeterminate objects. It is the "this-ness" (idantā) present in all entities that is addressed here in a general sense.

It arises precisely through commonality. This is the point: even when one perceives a determinate object such as a jar standing before one, thinking "this is a person," one does not grasp its specific particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) at all; otherwise, the utterance of words like "this" or "all" would be impossible. However, when [it is perceived] by others...
When the place and time have been grasped by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one then performs the synthesis [of the object] with them, thinking, "This is here, now.

At that very moment, there is the apprehension of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because its unique nature is brought to mind precisely through the influence of that place and time. Thus ends the word.
Upon the completion of the Teacher’s statement, he states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*). "Therefore"— that is, for that reason—
it is "merely appearance," meaning it is simply a general appearance (*sāmānyābhāsa*),
because it exists by its own primacy and thus does not depend on connection with space and so forth.

A particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not a real entity (*vastu*), because it is conceptual in nature, consisting as it does in the mental synthesis of location and so forth. By this, the superficiality of the intellect of those Buddhists who assert that the universal (*sāmānya*) is not a real entity is demonstrated. But then [one might ask]:
To explain how the apprehension of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is established, he says: "But the specific characteristic...
The *svalakṣaṇa* is the essential nature that does not follow after others; [it is the basis] of those appearances—the appearances of place, time, and substance—which possess a commonality...
Another manifestation, which has the form of a manifestation of an object of action (*karaṇya*), is indeed distinct [from the first];

and with respect to that, there is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it will be explained later that among those manifestations involved in the process of synthesis (*miśrīkāra*), a cognition that grasps what has already been grasped is not a means of valid cognition, according to the principle we have stated regarding determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*).

For one who maintains that validity depends on [the object] when the manifestation directed by words comes to rest in a particular appearance, validity must be admitted as residing solely in each individual appearance; so let it be—
what is the use of this intermediate step?

The appearance of non-coexistence (*adhikaraṇyābhāsa*)—that is, the appearance of mixture—is that very form; yet it becomes another appearance, an appearance distinct from the appearance of the object itself. In that case, there exists a separate and distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By this, the position of the logicians (*tārkika*) is refuted, for they [hold that] it belongs to one and the same [object].

They state that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has both the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its objects, and among those, the particular characteristic is superior. The phrase "that which is beyond that" (*tat-param*) establishes the invalidity of the means of valid cognition that apprehends the particular characteristic. "That" (*tat*) refers to the means of valid cognition.

Regarding "in the cases of mixtures"—that is, in those appearances consisting of mixtures—it is merely "grasping what has already been grasped. For first, the triad beginning with the universal (sāmānya) is indeed already grasped by their respective objects of cognition; immediately thereafter, this [subsequent] means of knowledge [operates].
It performs nothing more than a mere conjunction through the relation of qualifier and qualified;
therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because a means of valid cognition must apprehend an object not previously apprehended. As it has been said:
"A means of valid cognition is that which brings about the apprehension of an object not yet apprehended."

Thus [it is said]. Although in this system validity (*prāmāṇya*) indeed exists everywhere once [an object] has appeared, it was stated in this manner for the sake of refuting the Buddhists and others. [An objection: "Is it not appropriate to elaborate upon this matter?
To this he says: "later on" (*agre*). The sense is that it is not expanded upon here.
He demonstrates that the validity of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), which has been refuted by the Buddhists, is established by the words "of determinative cognition" (*adhyavasāyasya*).
According to our stated method— that is, according to our stated way— [this occurs] through the medium of memory, which is animated by verbal expression (*śabda*).

Having attained the state of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), for that determination (*adhyavasāya*)— the effect of conceptualization whose object is the universal— which has been granted existence by means of a word,
there is a resting upon each individual manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*), because it would otherwise be impossible to apprehend [the object].
When [cognition] has reached its final consummation, even that which depends upon it— that is, even that which is joined with dependence on conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*),
and not merely dependence on manifestation— must be stated by the Śaiva who asserts validity; namely,
that such conceptual determination is grounded in every manifestation (*pratyābhāsaniṣṭha*).

But let it be that such validity—belonging to one whose conclusion is reached merely through logical connection (*yojanā*)—must be accepted or admitted; for what follows from this intermediate or irrelevant point? The meaning is: nothing at all.

Now, if reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), does it not then exist even in the case of a double moon? Not so; for that [awareness] persists with its activity unextirpated, following itself through the connection with latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) until the attainment of the intended and well-known purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Being stable, he becomes such; however, if he tolerates further uprooting in the middle,

then this is not such a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), nor was it even previously— because by means of a single inward-turned form, even from the very beginning, that [duality] has been uprooted, and here there is only self-consciousness (*svasaṃvit*).
The witness [consciousness] experiences at that very moment the non-reflective state (*avimarśīkaraṇa*) of a reflection (*vimarśa*) that had previously occurred, namely: "This is not silver.
He says "nanu" in order to explain the word "unsublated" (*abādhitā*). That—[referring to] the reflection—...
He states the answer: "It is not so. When the question arises as to why this is so, he says: "For that... For (*hi*)—because;

*saḥ*—that [reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)]; by connection with latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), that is, by the power of latent impressions; that which is both desired and well-known, namely the attainment (*prāpti*) of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), wherein that occurs at the ultimate limit (*paryante*).

"For that duration" means for as long as [the state lasts]. "Maintaining the self"—that is, following its own nature known as the awareness of the other (paravimarśa)—and for this very reason, "having its function not uprooted," meaning having its function unimpeded, it thus becomes of the nature of cognition (miti). Furthermore, "on the other hand," if in the middle—should it be so—...

"Uprooting"—that is, sublation—if that [object] endures, then this [cognition], namely reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), was not of the nature of valid knowledge (*miti*) even previously. To the question "Why?", he states the reason: "by one.
That is, by that which exists as a unity—meaning, by that which is non-deviating—and by means of an inward-turned form.

— In its own nature, not in the form of "two moons" (meaning, as that which does not deviate from its form, i.e., as non-deviating); "precisely before"— at the very prior time— because of the uprooting— that is, the sublation— of that reflective awareness of two moons, [in the sense that] "the two moons did not exist."

Since the cognition of two moons has already existed previously, its eradication must likewise logically be of that same prior time; this is the purpose of employing the word "eva" (only/already). Now, what is the proof for this? To this he says: "by one's own consciousness. Why is it the witness? To this he says: "that very [consciousness]."
Thus, by the force of the sense, the term *svasaṃvit* (self-awareness) should be treated as ending in the instrumental case;

for by that self-awareness, there occurs the non-objectification (*avimarśīkaraṇa*)— figuratively, the conferring of the form of "this" (*ayamitirūpatā*)— of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that has already occurred, i.e., that which was previously established.

It is perceived—that is, experienced—how? Why? This very object appearing here before us as mother-of-pearl was not silver at that very time—that is, it was not silver previously; nor did it previously exist as silver and only today attain the state of being mother-of-pearl.
And this has been stated in the investigation of sublation (*bādhavicāra*), and it will also be stated in the passage beginning with "the single reflection on silver" (*rajataikavimarśa*);
such being the case, even in the instance of the double moon (*dvicandra*), as long as there is the production of interest in others for the sake of the object—

While one intends to perform the rite for the purpose of seeing a previously unseen object, that initial perception— such as the notion "this is a second moon"— is uprooted by hearing the words of others, leaving one overwhelmed by contempt, ridicule, grief, and the like.

One conceives [this] precisely through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Now, one might ask: "In that case, where one does not seek causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), how can there be the conventional usage of sublation (*bādha*) or non-sublation? Let it be so—what is lost for us? For activity (*pravṛtti*) does not always proceed from valid cognition alone; rather, in some cases, it proceeds otherwise.

It is indeed due to doubt; or rather, it is because of the superiority of the object as a goal, or even because of the gradations of desire, as in the case of agriculture and so forth—[the phrase] "as found in the case of poisoned food" refers back to what was stated previously, thus reminding [the reader]. (Note: *pūrvametaduktassmārayati* is corrected to *pūrvametaduktaṃ smārayati*.)

And it has been said; it will be said—meaning in this verse that is about to be stated, namely "the single reflective awareness of silver. By this, he states the established fact: "this being the case.
"Consistent with causal efficiency" means that which is intended as having the nature of causal efficiency.
"By contempt and derision"— meaning by the contempt and derision caused by others; being "helpless," that is, having fallen under their power,
one "considers oneself being uprooted"— one perceives oneself as being afflicted.

The connection [of the text]. Here the student poses a question: "But if this is so... He seeks—meaning he attains [the answer]. He states the reply: "Let it not be so. [The word] *truṭitam* means destroyed. To the question "Why is it not destroyed?", he says: "For activity... [The student objects: "But surely there is activity by some other means as well? To this...
He asks: "What then? [The answer is: "In some instance"—meaning in some matter that is free from excessive effort and free from expenditure of wealth.

To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the object" (*artha*). Because of the superiority—the excessiveness or extreme ease of accomplishment—of the side of the object (*arthapakṣa*). Here too, the reason is...

He states "in agriculture and so forth" according to the manner of the illustration. For a person indeed engages in agriculture and the like even while uncertain of the attainment of its fruit, because that fruit—such as rice—is also excellent as a means of livelihood. Another reason for engaging with doubt is...

He states [the view] according to another position: "In the case of desire" (*arthitve*). Regarding "desire"—even in the absence of an excess of objects, there is a gradation of expectancy; from that, which reaches its highest limit through states such as delusion. Here too, he states the reason along with an illustration: "poisonous... (*saviṣa*)... [and so on].

Since we observe that people engage in activities such as theft despite being certain of and having witnessed the resulting transgressions, the primary cause for such engagement on the part of the world is simply an excess of desire; and thus,
the world engages.

In some cases, that which has not had its means of cognition uprooted attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); in other cases, it does so otherwise—namely, by becoming an error (*viparyaya*). Thus, from birth, or even for hundreds of births, he has practiced this distinction between the valid and the invalid means of cognition.

Therefore, its nature is like that of a gem, silver, and so forth. Regarding the transgression seen to be certain or probable: in the case of eating poisoned food, the transgression is seen to be certain; likewise in the case of theft and similar acts.

The phrase "the state of having a perceived transgression" should be applied sequentially [to each term]. By the word "etcetera," acts such as harming others are included. In the case of engaging in eating poisoned food—where the transgression is certain—the form of reasoning is: "My death shall certainly not occur."

Doubt indeed persists; and since reasoning (*tarka*) exists in the interval between certainty and doubt, it remains closely proximate to doubt, so there is no contradiction. Having established the position regarding the object (*arthapakṣa*) as being logical, he states that the position regarding the seeker (*arthitvapakṣa*) follows as a consequence: "That" (*tat*). That—
Therefore, for that reason, the excellence of desire (*arthitvātiśaya*)—

that is, the world's [desire]— is the basis, the cause, for its engagement. And that [world], in some cases— that is, in the case of valid cognition (*pramā*)— and in other cases— that is, in the case of non-valid cognition such as the appearance of two moons— is otherwise.
The meaning is that the person, having uprooted the means of valid cognition (*pramiti*), arrives at its opposite—namely, non-validity (*apramāṇatā*).
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter (*prameya*). Here too, he states the result with the word "evam":
this being so, for that reason, the person [is characterized] by mere appearance alone.

But it is not immediately after the great deliberation (*mahāvicāra*) that one perceives—that is, sees—the distinct nature of that [cognition], namely the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*). How? Like a gem or silver;
the meaning is "like crystal and silver. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), rubies and other such things are included.

The word *eva* (indeed) indicates that the perception of its distinctness [from the body] immediately following inquiry is extremely clear. Why is this so? Because by this person—from birth (*ājanma*), meaning starting from birth, or even from hundreds of births (*ājanmaśatebhyaḥ*), meaning starting from previous hundreds of births—[this distinctness is perceived].

The distinction between valid and invalid means of knowledge has been practiced—that is, brought to the state of habituation—so that through acting with certainty in all cases, there may be no lack of validity for him anywhere; such is the intended meaning of the word. By the phrase "or from hundreds of lifetimes," it is meant that...
By speaking according to the mode of conceptual construction, one perceives a loosening of even a previous birth—
whether from hundreds of prior births or even those yet to come— at the very moment of its appearance; for that [birth] exists in reality.

The distinctiveness has been illuminated. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how is it that there is mention of renown in other births in the scriptures? True; in which ones? In the *adhyātma-śāstras* (spiritual treatises)? Indeed, in the *adhyātma-śāstras*.
To this extent, even this present birth is conceived as unreal from the perspective of ultimate truth; what then can be said of another birth?
As for the occasional mention of another birth that is seen even here, it is with reference to a particular state.

Or rather, [the relationship] indeed exists in dependence upon the states of being father, son, and so forth; however, no evidence whatsoever is seen for the claim that this very same *jīva*, having departed from one place, takes up another body in this world. But how is it that no such evidence is seen? [It is found] in the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā* and other texts.

This is because of the observation of such statements as, "Just as one casts off worn-out garments... and so forth. True; even here, the intended meaning concerns precisely the distinction between states.
For instance, by the Blessed Lord himself in that very same place:

Because of such statements as, "Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body," one might object: "But here a difference in states is taken as the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and not established as the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*). True; it is presented as an illustration for those who already possess that knowledge.
This has been indicated; for those who know that [reality] convey meanings to other knowers of it through mere indication alone.
That the state of being born (*janmatva*) is a particular stage (*avasthābheda*) has been determined by us in detail in the *Līlopākhyāna* within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā*.
Alternatively, it is the very happiness regarding the non-death of the Blessed Lord that is intended here.

And thus the intention here is this: just as there is no suffering in the casting off of a garment, so too it is in death. Furthermore, such a statement is indeed appropriate for one who identifies with the body.
For having heard this, out of fear of the next world, he does not engage in activity here or there;

by this, the intention of the Smṛti scriptures has also been essentially stated. For that very reason, the Blessed Lord said here, "of the embodied one" (*dehinaḥ*). That the son is a future birth is clearly stated by the Śruti.
"The son is indeed born as the self," it is said;
thus, the father's status as the prior birth is perfectly clear, just as in the case of a branch of a cane or the like being transposed [to another], from which it was brought, that is the tree.

What fault is there in saying that the tree produced from its branch in a previous birth is the subsequent birth? Furthermore, with respect to the single principle of consciousness (*cittatva*), all births and deaths have one and the same object; thus, even by the birth and death of another living being, [the birth and death of this living being occur].

It is indeed logical that another living being possesses birth, death, and so forth; and since these are produced by differences in causes and the like, when one considers suffering to be limited and bearable,
and is consequently not driven here and there by the great obsession of desire for objects, at that time—

One who fears non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) and, because of a cognition whose validity is certain, proceeds toward what is either unseen or seen, is not deceived; thus, he is called a "deliberate agent" (*prekṣāpūrvakārin*). By him, the nature of worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been restated.

Even when there is knowledge of the general relationship and so forth, one might, out of delusion, harbor doubts regarding its lack of authority; therefore, no effort has been made here through [discussions of] classification, specific definitions, or critical examination,
just as when a water-jar thrown into a well is drawn up once again in its new state.

In that case, with respect to its oneness, even the water contained therein may be said to have dissolved and arisen anew; likewise, although the soul has died, it can certainly be said to have been born again as one with respect to another soul— enough of this attempt to restrain those who are unrestrained!
By breaking through the injunctions and prohibitions of the Vedic rules— which are merely the form of imagined chains—
the great people, being naturally self-restrained, will indeed come to know this ultimate truth. As it has been said:
For those who have realized the Self, sense objects, prohibitions, and even their own inherent nature [are mere constraints];
but for fools, they are like shackles upon thieves.

Thus [it is said]. Now, if there is no cause for the distinction between validity and invalidity in the two types of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then how is it appropriate that they appear even at first glance, despite the proficiency gained through practice?

In response to the inquiry as to why it is only logical for that which has a clearly manifest cause [to be so], he says: "For there exists... He speaks by summarizing the essential point regarding its validity or invalidity, and then says:
"And from that... meaning "capable of being endured," and "in this or that" object of doubt, and "from that."
Because suffering is endurable, one who fears contradiction— that is, one who is afraid of being deceived—

and who is a person acting with foresight, meaning one who acts preceded by reflection, is said to engage in sacrifices and the like, which concern the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) through its indicative function (*lakṣaṇayā*).
It is said that [this] means activity occurs immediately after the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇya-niścaya*).

By relying on this, he establishes the appropriateness of the restatement of the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as it is well-known in the world, using the word "therefore" (*tena*): "therefore"—because by means of a *pramāṇa*, an object...
Only after reaching a definitive conclusion does a person who acts subsequently come to be called one who acts with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārī*);

for that reason, even when there is knowledge of universals and so forth— which are well-known as causes of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)— the author of the Sūtra [speaks] out of delusion (*moha*).
In order to pacify— that is, to remove— the suspicion of invalidity (aprāmāṇya-śaṅkā) produced by the Buddhists under the influence of delusion,
the nature of valid cognition (pramāṇa-svarūpa) is restated here in accordance with common worldly usage.

The world [considers] that which possesses uncontradicted stability, and for that very reason, which effects a result of inquiry through uninterrupted continuity— that which is of the nature of cognition, grounded in the object of cognition,
and resting within the essential nature of the cognizer— is valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And this [applies] in the case of sensory cognition...

There is indeed no dispute regarding the experience of pleasure and so forth, as well as in the cognition of a yogi, because [cognition] rests directly upon the manifestation in its primary form as the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Although this is well-known, it is stated again by way of restatement, for an object that is intensely desired...

The sense is that it is stated again and again as "thus indeed. Now, one might ask: "In that case, why was [the definition of] division and so forth not formulated? To this he says: "For this very reason.
For this very reason—that is, for the reason of restatement (anuvāda) itself—since the intended object is established by the mere restatement of the general definition in common worldly usage.
The sense is that there has been no restatement at all of well-known [categories] such as division and so forth. Now, one might ask:

"How is it that the general definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so on are 'well-known' in the world, such that it is said they are merely restated? In response to this expectation, [the author states] what is well-known in the world:
He states the definition of the general characteristics of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth by the word "that which.
This means that it possesses an unimpeded continuity; the sense is that it cannot tolerate a reversal of its own nature.
"The fruit of deliberation" (*vimarśaphala*) means that the means of valid cognition is the fruit known as deliberation.
By the phrase "culminating in awakening" (*bodhyaniṣṭha*), there is the description of the outward orientation that causes the withdrawal of the cognizer;

the meaning is that [consciousness] "rests in the essential nature of the cognizer," because it has that as its support, otherwise it would be impossible for it to have external objects. And that resting in the cognizer is "I."

In the usage "I see," it is indeed evident; the word "iti" marks the conclusion of the general definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as established in common worldly usage. With the words "And that," he shows the resting of this general definition upon its specific instances.

And that—namely, the aforementioned general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)—[is present] in sensory cognition—that is, in the knowledge produced by the external senses where the verbal expression "I see" occurs—and in the experience of pleasure and so forth—that is, in the knowledge of pleasure etc. produced by the internal sense, the mind. To the question "Why [is this so]?", he says:

"Primarily indeed" means not by way of dependence on perception as inference and the like do, because inference is preceded by perception. "Directly" means not through an intervention such as the knowledge of a mark (*liṅga*) as in the case of inference and so forth. By this—

The application of the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) to the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), as well as its specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) regarding that which is produced by the senses (*aindriyaka*), and so forth, should be understood as already indicated by the qualifying terms themselves. Now, [one might object]:

"By the logicians (*tārkika*), [the cause of perception is said to be] either a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of both cognition and non-cognition, or the sense organ and so forth, which consist of non-cognition."
It was stated that [the causal complex] possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*); how then can it be said here that only consciousness alone [possesses it]? True;

the status of a means of valid cognition attributed to the causal complex is indeed correct, for we have stated that what is included within that complex is itself a means of valid cognition, since otherwise the nature of being a causal complex would be impossible.
However, what has been said regarding the sense organs and so forth is indeed incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that cognition would arise at all times;
for it cannot be said that the sense organ is ever non-proximate to a living being in any moment,
and the excellence (*atiśaya*) of an instrument consists necessarily in the production of the result upon its proximity, and nothing else.
Furthermore, whatever argument is offered to establish its secondary nature (*gauṇatva*) is merely a resort to the straw of *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass.
