For a cognition directed toward the external necessarily produces an external reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and thus it possesses excellence (*sātiśayatva*). As for the doubt raised regarding the non-difference between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), that [refers to] the external—

Inference, however, is the cognition of one manifestation from another manifestation— whether that other manifestation be of the nature of an effect or of the nature of an essential identity; it consists in the determination of a causal relationship between two distinct entities, or the determination of their co-referentiality.

It must be understood that this occurs only by depending upon the power of the Lord’s necessity (*niyati-śakti*), and not otherwise. Therefore, inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only to the extent that necessity is known, whether in terms of space or time.
Scripture (*āgama*), however, consists of words in the form of different names.

[Ṣ. Ṣ. The activity of the Lord, whose nature is consciousness and whose essence is non-discriminative, is indeed internal; it is necessarily precluded by inward-turnedness (antarmukhatva). Enough with this elaboration. This is also the case in inference.

He provides the application of the general definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by stating "inference" (*anumāna*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates its distinction from the means of valid cognition that is perception (*pratyakṣa*). From an effect-form—such as from the form of smoke in the inference of fire;
or from a nature-form—such as from the form of a *śiṃśapā* tree in the inference of a tree.

"In another manifestation"—that is, in the form of fire or in the form of a tree. Now, one might ask: how can there be a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) or identity (*tādātmya*) in that case? To this he says:
"of another entity. That is, of another entity in the form of smoke or in the form of a *śiṃśapā* tree.
"Or with that," meaning together with fire or with a tree;
"the rule of grammatical coreferentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇyaniyama) means the rule of the relation of identity (tādātmyasaṃbandha);
"subsisting upon the power of the Lord's necessity" (īśvaraniyatiśaktyupajīvana).
Because it is regulated by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) connected to the Lord (*īśvara*), it is dependent upon Him. He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tena*).
And thus, for those dwelling in the region of Nārikela-dvīpa, there is no establishment of the inference of fire through smoke.

The meaning is that this applies both to those who have forgotten the pervasion (*vyāpti*) at the time of forgetting, and to those who have not grasped the pervasion at that time. By this, the general definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been applied to the specific means of valid cognition called inference (*anumāna*), as well as its specific definition.

The nature of [perception] as "the apprehension of one manifestation from another manifestation" should be understood as having been stated directly. He applies the general definition to the means of knowledge that is scripture (*āgama*) with the words "as for scripture... The word "but" (*tu*)—
The term "scripture" (āgama) indicates that which is distinct from the two aforementioned means of valid cognition;

it is the entity known as scripture. Of that whose nature is consciousness—that is, whose essential form is consciousness, meaning its nature is light—it is "internal," existing by virtue of being its very nature.
An activity occurs. When the question "Why? arises, he provides a qualifying attribute containing the reason:
"having the form of internal sound. Although it exists through the absence of the external [speech], it attains the state of *paśyantī* and remains in the state of *madhyamā*.
That which exists as the state of *vaikharī* through the medium of the limited subject—
that is, speech or verbalization— has that as its form; for this very reason, it is most firm (*dṛḍhīyastama*), meaning exceedingly stable, [its] own nature...

Even for perception and the other means of knowledge, that which is examined by it remains as it was examined— just as it is, without any deviation from its own nature; this is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), namely, the self-referential recognition "I am."
Therefore, it is one whose self (*ātman*) is characterized by the attainment of its own nature— that is to say, its outward movement—
as it has been said:
"It has come from the mouth of Śiva and gone into the mouth of Girijā."
This is the doctrine held by the illustrious Vāsudeva; therefore, it is proclaimed as the Āgama.

Thus [it is said]. Herein the intention is as follows: that which has come from the mouth of Śiva, who is Light (*prakāśa*), means that it first exists there in the state of *parā* (the supreme level), having attained the state of *paśyantī*; that is to say, it has manifested therein. Likewise...

"In the mouth of Girijā" means that which has entered the mouth of Girijā—that is, the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*)—who has arisen from the Supreme Lord in an unwavering form (or, according to C., in a form devoid of radiance);
the meaning is that it has been grasped by her through the state of the *madhyamā* [vocal register]. Likewise, by Śrī Vāsudeva:

The meaning is that this scripture, the *Āgama*, is proclaimed by the Lord who pervades the entire class of subjects characterized primarily by differentiation; it is indicated by these three syllables alone.

There is no fault here in the absence of *sandhi* (euphonic combination), as this pertains to the state of the Lord (*aiśvara*). By this, [the nature of] what is established in the *Āgama* scriptures [is explained].

The Śrī Devī said; the Śrī Bhairava said, and so forth—this entire collection of applications should be understood as established. For Bhairava is indeed the all-pervading Light (prakāśa), while the Goddess is the reflective power (vimarśa-śakti) whose nature is play. As for the speech, it exists in the form of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī.

It is fourfold: first, its constant abiding within the manifestation of the Śāstra through the state of Parā; second, its shining forth in that very place through the state of Paśyantī when it is oriented toward emergence;
third, its establishment through the state of Madhyamā during reflective awareness (vimarśa); and at that very moment—
That is called "reflected" (*vimṛṣṭa*); thereafter, it exists externally among the authors of the scriptures in the form of *vaikharī*.
And therein, with reference to its primordial emergence, there is the narration of the dialogue between Lord Bhairava and the Goddess. [Objection: In that case, this would apply everywhere.
Let there be a fine for those who know [the truth], but this statement is entirely improper regarding those who do not know it;
for this very reason, compassionate ones have not made this proclamation everywhere. However, since we are engaged in providing an exposition, this matter has indeed been clarified by us. But then—?

Has the revelation of the secret occurred? It has not occurred; for those who are unqualified, there is an absence of faith in this matter, and while it might be possible for those who are qualified, they cannot afford to be unrestrained. For a revelation is merely an attainment in an unsuitable place—enough said.

By means of this elaboration, it is clearly evident that the scripture, which consists of inner sound and form, possesses an internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*), because light has the essential nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It is like the very life-force even of perception and so forth—that is, even of both perception and inference.
It is like life itself, because even those two [inference and verbal testimony] have deliberation as their vital breath, and thus serve as means of proof.

By this, the externalist position is refuted; for in their systems, it is stated that the means of valid cognition consisting of verbal testimony depends upon perception. To the question "Why?", he states the reason by means of the following statement: "Therefore..."

Thus, because by that scripture—whatever has been touched upon, that is, thoroughly examined and stated—is so [as it is], it becomes exactly thus. Here, he cites a mantra for the removal of poison as an example of that which has perceptible results, beginning with "yathā" (just as). The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the mantra.
"Poison kills me, but I am Garuḍa himself"— in that regard,
even the entire mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) which maintains conformity toward such a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose nature is sound, [is likewise included].

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— such as the Vedic doctrines and so forth, or others such as the scriptures of the Buddhists and Jains— produces by means of verbal expression [the cognition]:
"I am one who performs the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice," "I am going to heaven," or "I am initiated."

Thinking, "I am one who shares in non-returning," "I am compassionate and shall go to the state of a Buddha," or "I am capable of enduring intense afflictions and shall attain the state of an Arhat"— in such cases, no misconception arises,
because on the following day he alone is fit for the practice therein, whereas another is not.

Because it lacks the nature of firm conviction, such verbal expression, consisting of mere deliberation, is simply not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). [Objection: But if this were so, that very scripture would be a valid means of knowledge for some and not for others; yet this is not tenable.
"Because valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is impartial"—you do not understand the nature of experiential realization (*pratīti*).

Nevertheless, it is said that "in that case," validity consists in conformity; "in that case" means "when it exists," that is, when it is of such a kind—namely, in the form of the scriptural tradition (*āgama-śāstra*)—conformity is...

[The quality of] conformity. Now, one might ask: "What is this collection of words? To this he says: "The Veda. "Other" means contrary to the Veda. When the question arises as to why [it is so], he says: "For by that," meaning by the Veda and so forth;
the sense is that it has been attained or reached. To the question "Why does it not arise [in him]? he says: "Of one who has confidence in that."

"Of another"—that is, of one who is not confident; the word "that" is to be supplied as the object. The meaning is that it is indeed not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), and not even a means of valid cognition at all.
By this, it is implied that even a mantra for the removal of poison [is effective] only through recitation (*japa*) and so forth preceded by confidence.
The efficacy in producing results has been stated; and thus,
even great people who desire these results through mere recitation are seen to become objects of ridicule.
There is no inconsistency whatsoever in the fact that even those snake-charmers who possess the appearance of ordinary people achieve such perfection of mantras; as it has been said:
"Having seized that power, mantras come to possess the strength of the Omniscient One."
They proceed for the sake of the embodied beings' specific capacities, like the instruments of action.

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the word "that" (tat), there is a reference to the power of the Self (ātma-bala); and that is indeed the firmness of confidence, not the grasping of a self (ātmagraha), because for those endowed with that [power], all sounds are seen as mantra, and thus they are devoid of dependence on [external] mantras. Here, the disciple—

He raises an objection with the words "nanvevam" (But surely, thus). "Evam" means "this being so"; "kañcit" means "some portion of the object of knowledge"—the sense being that this [consequence] would follow. To the question, "Let this be so;
what is the harm?", he replies, "na caitat" (And this is not [the case]). To the question, "Why is it not tenable?", he replies, "because of its impartiality" (*apakṣapātitvāt*).

Thus, the sense is that it is not proper for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be partial. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the question. He states the answer: "You are ignorant of reality. [The phrase] *pratītivṛttasya* means "of the nature of cognition. Now, if that is so—
"You are not being indifferent; what is the meaning of this statement that 'the means of valid cognition is impartial'?

Does it mean that when one person's cognition of blue is of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it causes blue to appear to everyone, or that the cognition of smoke [causes] fire [to appear to all]? You [have stated this] by way of a morning treasure."

And as for the traditional teaching (āgama) in the form of a prophecy from the perfected ones (*siddhādeśa*)— such as "you have attained [the goal]"— is that a valid authority for everyone, or is it something that applies to someone at some time?
Likewise, here too, there is the verbalization (*śabdana*) consisting of firm reflection upon the object in its entirety.
First of all, the means of valid cognition known as scripture (*āgama*) exists for everyone;

in that regard, just as light, the sense faculties, and so forth— which, by resorting to the assistance of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), are devoid of validity and thus invalid— are not [themselves] false, nor...
In response to the expectation that one should maintain silence, which is the very nature of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), he says: "Nevertheless.
"You shall not be neglected" means you shall not be reduced to the state of being an object of indifference, because [the Self] is all-pervasive; this is the sense.

Relying on the answer provided by the disciple, he poses a question back to the disciple himself in order to give a further reply: "Is it impartial? The meaning is as follows: the connection is that the subject matter (*abhidheya*), or the cognition of smoke (*dhūmajñāna*), illuminates fire for everyone; this is the authoritative instruction (*siddhādeśa*) [attained] through austerity (*tapas*) and other means.
The *siddhādeśa* is the command (*ājñā*) issued by those who are perfected (*siddha*) and endowed with supernatural powers (*siddhi*).

Having recognized the inappropriateness [of the previous method] in this context, he states an alternative position through the very mouth of the disciple, beginning with the word "atha" (now). He provides the answer precisely according to the disciple's response; it is the same here as well.

In order to demonstrate that the word *āgama* is etymologically significant, he says "on all sides" (*āsamantāt*). The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "First of all, the verbal communication designated as *āgama* is a means of valid cognition for everyone.
The intention of the word "first of all" (*tāvat*) is that there is no disagreement on this point by anyone.

Now, one might object: "In that case, how is it that this scripture does not produce a valid cognition (*pramā*) characterized by non-firm deliberation for all people, including Śūdras and others, such that there would be no partiality? To this expectation, [the response is: this fault belongs only to those scriptures intended for specific classes of qualified persons (*adhikārin*), and not to this one.

With the intention that [the means of valid cognition] consists of right knowledge directed toward external objects produced by that [scripture], he provides an answer by way of a figurative expression accompanied by an illustration, beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*). In that regard, the meaning is: while the scripture known as *āgama* exists as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [it serves as] an aid to false knowledge—

It serves as an auxiliary cause for the production of false cognition—which is oriented toward external objects and consists of an appearance of valid knowledge—[in relation to] the agent of that cognition;
this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. For indeed, the production of false cognition is not possible without light, the sense organs, and so forth.

This is the intended meaning. "Light, the sense organs, and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," the contact between the sense organ and its object and other such factors are included. "Accompanied by invalidity"—being accompanied by the invalidity of false cognition, it becomes invalid.

This is because it is impaired by defects such as ophthalmia (*kācakāmala*). Yet, for this reason, there is no partiality whatsoever on the part of perception— the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of correct knowledge— and likewise, the very same word "Jyotiṣṭoma" [is applied].
Even though it provides assistance to the semblance of scripture— which, because its nature consists of non-firm discernment, is for that very reason not a valid means of knowledge—
[it does so] with respect to the valid means of knowledge characterized by the word-nature of true scripture, which consists of firm discernment.

Validity residing in the state of being a yogi is not capable of avoiding the faults of partiality or lack of partiality; for every scripture indeed effects an inquiry that is strictly conditioned by specific qualifications, place, time, auxiliary factors, and so forth.
In the case of a valid cognition that directly perceives form, there is no partiality—meaning a state of being biased—toward any particular person as its instrument;
for it functions by virtue of being free from defects such as disease and the like. Thus, that very [cognition]...
The scriptural injunctions regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites function as authoritative means of knowledge for qualified persons such as Brāhmaṇas; however,
for those devoid of qualification— such as Śūdras, women, and others— they do not produce a firm state of reflective discernment.

In that which consists of unstable discernment, and for that very reason is non-authoritative— even when established as authoritative toward Śūdras and others, it is in reality non-authoritative; and for that very reason, it is a semblance of scripture— even though it lacks the status of being a scripture in the ultimate sense.

Even while providing assistance—that is, acting as an aid—to that which appears as such, it is indeed in the Veda alone that the eligibility of Śūdras and others is prescribed; whereas in what are mere semblances of scripture, such as the Smṛtis and other texts distinct from the Veda, no such eligibility is ordained.
That very expression which consists of a firm discernment and takes the form of the true tradition (āgama) is [the true means].

In the utility—that is, the assistance—of that means of valid cognition which possesses such a characteristic or essential nature, it is capable of rejecting the defects of partiality and non-partiality [or, as C. reads: capable of rejecting and employing].

The meaning is that [the distinction] does not exist because of the absence of ultimate reality (pāramārthikatva), which follows from the fault of merely stating a difference in scope (adhikāra). Why does it not exist? To this he says:
"all indeed" (sarva eva). For (hi)—that is, because—every [injunction], whether in the form of a positive prescription (vidhi) or a negative prohibition (niṣedha), [is such].

"Āgama" refers to that which is restricted by those factors such as the qualified person (adhikārin), place, time, and auxiliary conditions; it is "niyata"—meaning strictly determined and not indeterminate—and it "produces" or brings about the "vimarśa," which is the fruit in the form of valid cognition (pramā). And thus, even in the absence of [the usual] qualification...
For those who immerse themselves in the Vedānta and other such scriptures, it results only in self-deception;

for engagement in a scripture should be undertaken only by one for whom that very scripture has prescribed eligibility, whereas for others who engage in it, nothing but the emergence of faults follows— so enough of this elaboration.

In this context, the restriction regarding the qualified person (*adhikāriniyama*) is: "One who desires heaven should sacrifice. The restriction regarding place (*deśaniyama*) is: "One should sacrifice on level ground. The restriction regarding time (*kālaniyama*) is: "One offers [the oblation] when the sun has risen," and "One should perform the twilight worship in the evening and the morning.
Furthermore, the status of being auxiliary factors (*sahakāritva*) must be applied to all of these. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*),...
The mention of substances and so forth is as in the cases: "One offers with milk," or "One should offer with a gruel of *jantīla* seeds.
Alternatively, even a cooperative factor is indeed separately prescribed, just as the wife's status as a cooperative participant in a sacrifice.
It is either of a positive form or of a negative nature. By this, there is established renown; for it is said:
"Therefore, established renown that is indeed uncontradicted is considered the true speech of the Lord.
By that [speech], whatever, whenever, and wherever [something] is apprehended by those free from doubt. (Kāvyālaṅkāra-Ṣaṭka 6)

In this verse, where the words "where" (*yatra*) and "when" (*yadā*) are used, it follows that perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*) are sublaters of inference (*anumāna*). This is because the word *patnī* (wife) is established only through its connection with the venerable Bhartṛyajña. By this, he states the resulting point.
"By that"—this means: from that reason, namely, because there is a restriction regarding the qualified person (*adhikārī*) and so forth.
And thus, this verse is as follows:
"For well-known tradition (*prasiddhi*), when uncontradicted, is considered to be the true word of the Lord."
Wherever and whenever it has been accomplished by her, this must undoubtedly be accepted.

Thus, "uncontradicted" means not opposed to the Vedas; and so, even if something is well-known, it must be rejected if it is contrary to the Vedas. By the term "well-known," the collection of traditional instructions whose author is unknown is understood. This is the divine voice (aiśvarī vāk).

The word "connected with Īśvara" means the word of the *āgama* (scriptural tradition). By that—that is, by the speech of Īśvara—at whom [as an] eligible recipient (*adhikārī*), in which place, and at which time. And thus, the entire *āgama-śāstra* is indeed transmitted through lineage. Accordingly, it is stated here in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
The determination of the venerable teachers of the Maṭhas, who are the authors of established tradition, has indeed already been made;

therefore, enough with subtle scrutiny regarding these secrets. Now, one might ask: do these instructions not exist in the Veda, such that established tradition is taken as a refuge? True, they may not even exist there, for indeed—
The sovereignty of the illustrious Supreme Lord reaches its culmination in this much alone;
or rather, although they do exist, they have not been made explicit by the commentators because of their extreme secrecy,
but have been indicated by the compassionate Great Gurus to their great disciples through oral tradition from ear to ear.
This has been made clear by the teachers of the Maṭhikā. For their intention is as follows:

those who possess the qualification will understand [the system] without effort—such as the author of the Nyāyabhāṣya and others; therefore, once the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is known...
The entire nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is already known; what is the use of specific definitions?

Even for one who states that non-contradiction (*avisamvādakatva*) is its definition, that [non-contradiction] consists in being a bringer [of attainment], being an instigator [of action], and being the indicator of an object that is capable of being attained and is fit for purposeful activity.
One who states the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not address those who do not accept what is considered a means of valid cognition;

for those others, even if they were to be instructed otherwise, they would be unable to receive its touch, just as a lotus leaf situated in water cannot be touched by it. Furthermore, what restriction regarding eligibility could there be for them in that regard?
It is indeed established, so there is no contradiction whatsoever. [Objection: But surely they have established a rule regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*) therein;

in that regard, some are seen to be non-qualified even though they are initiated, while others are qualified even though they have not undergone initiation—what is to be done in such a case? [Reply: True, in that case...

In the first place, when a guru bestows initiation upon those who lack qualification, greed and other such faults are certainly the cause. However, it is indeed observed that sometimes even great gurus act everywhere with a common, worldly perspective; and in that regard, [the fault lies] with their own unqualified disciples.

It is simply a matter of meager fortune, as in the case of those who have reached the Gaṅgā but lack jars and other such necessities. However, for those who are solely intent upon serving their great gurus, some extraordinary excellence necessarily arises. As for those who, though lacking initiation, are nonetheless qualified—[for them...]

This scripture does not touch upon those who, out of fear, lack the qualification for external [practices]. However, when there is an immersion of devotion (*bhaktyāveśa*), great qualification arises. In time, through union with a great guru and initiation, there will be the attainment of the state of great fruit.

However, if that [attainment] is not reached, those who die in the interim will not obtain the supreme fruit. As for those who, through the intensity of their devotion, do not require external authority, some may eventually fall away from their devotion over time, while others, by the grace of the Lord, will certainly become partakers of the fruit.

In every respect, even regarding external matters, one must certainly strive in whatever way possible; however, if that is impossible, one’s interest should lie in other scriptures. "By this" [is meant]: the word "they say" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By this, the application of the general definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been made to scriptural authority (*āgama*). And here:
The specific characteristic consists precisely in being rooted in internal verbalization.
He concludes the statement regarding the specific characteristics as they are well-known in the world with the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*). "Therefore" means:
because the specific characteristics are well-established in the treatises on logic (*tarkaśāstra*), for that reason.

This is the meaning. Regarding the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*)—that is, the general definition of the means of valid cognition—he states the general definition formulated here by the Buddhists: "that which... Of that [means of valid cognition], it has been said:

"A valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory. That which is regarded as a valid means of knowledge is that cognition in which [the object] rests; its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is, by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). It was not explicitly stated because non-contradictoriness and so forth are [the grounds for] purposeful activity.
The object is not the means of valid cognition;
its essential nature has been stated to be resting upon manifestation, and that is sustained by this very definition—it is thereby established; otherwise, it would not be so.
That [activity] consists merely of facial contortions, shaking the head, wringing the fingers, and so forth; enough with this elaboration. || 2 ||

The meaning is: "because it has been established. And that—the very nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is established, that is, proven, by this very [text], namely by what is stated in that *sūtra*. It is fully accomplished, that is, proven.
Otherwise—that is, if there were no establishment even by this definition—it would be considered a means of valid cognition by others.
The sense is that the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that have been formulated are nothing but objects of ridicule.

For in ridicule, indeed, such things as contorting the face are performed; hence the mention of that [ridicule]. With the word "enough" (*alam*), he prohibits further elaboration. By this, it is implied that although there is certainly another expansion (*prapañca*) to be made, it is simply not being done.
This has been indicated. Since the determination of the phrase "within the scope of a single designation" will occur in the subsequent verse, it is not explained here.
Thus, this is the application and the summarized meaning of the second verse herein. That—
The cognition regarded as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is "like that," meaning it is like its state of being a valid means of knowledge;

that is to say, having abandoned the outward orientation that had arisen during the state of being a valid means of knowledge, it has once again attained the nature of inward-turned reflective awareness (*antarvimarśa*).

"Unsublated" (*abādhitā*) means that it is a valid cognition (*pramā*) because it is incapable of being sublated, and it is a cognition (*miti*). Thus, the construction is made by means of the word "and" (*ca*) in a conjunctive sense. [Objection: In that case, does it not follow that it possesses the status of a cognizer (*pramātṛtva*)? For inward-turned awareness (*bodha*) possesses nothing other than the status of a cognizer. To this [it is replied]:

He says: "In regard to an object. This means that "in regard to an object"—that is, within the sphere of objects—that cognition occurs during the state of contraction; and thus, even when turned inward, it does not possess subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*).
This is because, in comparison with the Great Light which constitutes the essence of the subject, it is limited.

The sense is that, in comparison to this, [consciousness] is "unlimited. The nature of the knower (*pramātṛ*), having become extroverted, becomes the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); then, having returned to an introverted state while still possessing the residual coloring (*uparāga*) of the object, it becomes the act of knowledge (*pramā*). Thereafter, in an instant, upon the abandonment of contraction (*saṃkoca*), [it returns to its original state].
This very act of valid cognition (*pramā*) is itself of the nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).

If the cognizer, by virtue of knowing that [cognition], at that very moment reveals his own true nature through the investigation of the root of the cognition—asking "from where has this arisen? and "where has it dissolved?"—then...

Like valid cognition (*pramā*), it itself dissolves into the manifestation of the Other; and that very [dissolution] is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form "I am indeed that Lord. By the two words "and the path of this very means is new," he will explain its status as an unprecedented means.
Because it is distinct from means such as the well-known restraints (yama) and observances (niyama); this is the summary of the secret.
Of what kind of reality? It is that which is undivided by space, time, and so forth, and likewise the object of a single designation. || 1 ||
Now, as for what was stated— that cognition has a single denotation as its object— in that regard:

if a single denotation were to apply only to the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), then how could it be said that there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for every manifestation, given that there is indeed a manifestation consisting in the mixing of manifestations?

To quell the doubt that [the object] is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), he speaks in order to determine what the object of knowledge (*prameya*) of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is from the perspective of ultimate reality:
"It differs according to inclination, according to need, and according to proficiency."
Even the appearance [of an object] is a single entity when established through synthesis.

Although the object perceived externally as "a jar" appears to be a single entity, it is not merely that much; rather, it also withstands being analyzed into distinct parts. This analysis may be independent, or according to a specific purpose, or by relying on what was previously established.
In that regard, he provides the introduction to the third verse in three ways, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu ca*). Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

In the domain of a single designation— that is, in the domain of a single name— when that [name] is uttered, it refers to the external particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the unique nature of the object distinct from its general form, and not to the general form itself. What has been stated?

In response to this inquiry, he says: "with respect to each manifestation" (*pratyābhāsam*). "With respect to each manifestation" means with respect to every individual manifestation in the form of subjects (*dharmin*) and attributes (*dharma*). [The word] "such a doubt" refers to a doubt of this nature. By the phrase "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthataḥ*), [he indicates] that which was previously stated.

The laxity of the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been indicated. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "according to one's preference" (*yathāruci*).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

He establishes the method for explaining the verse with the words "yadyapi" (although). "Tāvāneva" means "only one. Then, in response to the expectation of how much this [one] is, he states another alternative with "api tu" (but rather). "Pṛthaṅnirbhajyamānatām" means the state of being the object of separate division.

This means "the state of having many forms. In response to the question "How so?", he begins the justification with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). While providing this justification, he explains the verse with the words "Or independently" (*svatantraṃ vā*). He explains "according to one's liking" (*yathāruci*) by the word "independently" (*svatantram*), and he explains "according to one's desire" (*yathārthitvam*) by the same.

Regarding the phrase "due to the state of being an object" (*arthitva*), he explains it as "according to conventional usage" (*yathāvyutpatti*) by means of "relying on established usage" (*prasiddhyupajīvanena*).

This means "in dependence upon what was previously established. In each respective case, when the threefold analysis is performed, the appearances manifest as distinct; but if this is so, how [is it otherwise]?

What is the single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? It is said: although those appearances manifest separately, that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which serves as their vitalizing principle sometimes comes to rest in each individual appearance; at that time, there is the grasping of both the higher and lower universals (*parāparasāmānya*).

[Regarding the linguistic usage of higher and lower universals (parāparasāmānya): However, when at times there arises a reflective awareness (vimarśa) whose essence is a blending— expressed as "this is thus" by establishing a relationship of subordinate and predominant qualities— then that [object] is a single particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).

The particle *api* has a distinct function; it refers to that single reality which is established through the investigation (*anusandhāna*) and the reflective awareness of its manifoldness (*miśratāvimarśa*), according to the three modes previously mentioned. And so, the three modes are [set forth] in the following verse.

"It will indeed be shown"—this [point] remains in the *Harṣacarita* during the description of the district named Śrīkaṇṭha, yet these three types have not been displayed here for fear of prolixity. Here the student asks a question: "But if it is so... He provides the answer: "It is said," [referring to] the proposition (*pratijñā*).

"He makes them fruitful" means: he makes those aforementioned appearances—namely, the appearances consisting of space and so forth—fruitful, but not others which exist by virtue of distinctions such as personal preference (*ruci*) and the like.
"Reflection" (*vimarśa*) refers to the reflective awareness: "This is a jar, this is a jar."

"Anuprāṇitabhūtaḥ" means that which bestows existence by way of being the subject (grāhaka). "Pratyābhāsam" means in every manifestation; the meaning is that there is a grasping of each [manifestation] according to its own nature, free from their synthesis, with each being predominant. "Tadā" means at that time.
The apprehension of both higher and lower universals refers to the apprehension of two types of universals, namely *sattā* (existence) and [particulars such as] *gotva* (cowness).

The apprehension of *sattā* through the cognition "this is existent" (*sad iti*) is indeed distinct [from the apprehension of the particular], because it lacks the synthesis (*yojanā*) in the form "this here is existent."
Likewise, in the case of other universals (*sāmānya*), the apprehension of place and time occurs separately, just as before:

the apprehension of the universal "cowness" in the word "cow," the apprehension of the universal "whiteness" in "white," the apprehension of the universal "mobility" in "moving," and the apprehension of the universal "Dittha-ness" in "Dittha"— all these occur here quite separately.

Because there is no apprehension [of the object] through such a synthesis as "the cow is white, moving, and named Ḍittha. Furthermore, in another sense— that is, by establishing the state of subordinate and predominant [factors],
which is to say, by bringing about the relationship of qualifier and qualified— here, in this place and time, this—

This object is thus endowed with these qualities; "the life-force of conjunction" means the life-force of unification; "its own characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) means its unique nature, because it is impossible for anything else to be the qualificand (viśeṣya) in that particular place and so forth—this is the sense. The particle *api* is to be construed out of its natural order (*bhinnakrama*).
Showing that [the result] is established through synthesis (*anusandhāna*), he explains it with the words "by means of synthesis" (*anusandhānena*).
He explains the component "synthesis" (*anusandhāna*) as "mixture" (*miśratā*). He provides the construction of the locative case with the word "therein" (*tatra*). *Ati*—...

Even when there is only a single thing whose nature is its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) necessarily differs, without overstepping [the constraints of] inclination— which is autonomy— desire— which is subjection to the longing for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)— and proficiency— which is reliance upon the linguistic usage of elders. || 3 ||
To demonstrate *how* and *wherein*, he says:
"By means of [attributes] such as being long, round, upright, a person, smoke, or camphor, appearances—which are distinguished by differences of place and time—are differentiated. (4)
Furthermore, he provides a re-interpretation because of its difficulty of comprehension with the words "even in one" (*ekasminn api*).

Thus, the clear interpretation here is as follows: when even a single object has been established through synthetic connection (*anusandhāna*), and even though the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) remains one despite being mixed with attributes such as space and so forth, [the cognition arises] according to one's inclination.

According to one's inclination, likewise according to the pursuit of one's own purpose as desired by the seeker, and likewise according to linguistic proficiency and conventional usage, appearances (ābhāsas) differ with respect to that single object; otherwise, [there would be no difference] in the case of a single person in the *Harṣacarita*.
Because it is impossible to describe the region called Śrīkaṇṭha as being a concert hall or the like;

and likewise, since the possibility that even a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is distinct with every manifestation, could be the object of a single designation was raised in the introduction, [the author proceeds] by means of that.

The sense is that it is logical to state that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is unfit to have a mere appearance as its object, and to establish that only the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is the object of a means of valid cognition. || 3 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the fourth and fifth verses with the words "Where, how? (kva yathā). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the word "long" (dīrgha).
In the same way, the various appearances—such as the existence of a jar, its substantiality, and its brilliance as gold—which produce distinct effects, are the referents of words. (5)
In this context, even with respect to a single individual essence of a person (puruṣa-svalakṣaṇa), which is well-known as being conscious,
one sometimes contemplates its very length— that is, its pervasion over an extensive space— which exists even in young trees,
and its state of having no joints or connections.
Or circularity, which is possible even for stones; or upwardness, consisting of the act of ascending toward the upper direction, which belongs even to a pillar;
or the capacity for independent existence in the form of coming and going and so forth.
That which constitutes manhood is common to other men as well; for instance, one might act in such a way by means of independent will or by means of desire in the form of preference,
as it has been stated.
Regarding this, the commentary— arising from its own natural flow because the mind is characterized by distraction—
explains the member of the compound "long" (*dīrgha*) as "here" (*iha*), referring to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the person.

—In the unique essential nature of the Person (*puruṣa*). Although consciousness is not logically applicable to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is nevertheless stated thus by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). "Pervasion of an extended space" means having the form of pervading a vast region; for that which is long is indeed pervasive across an extended space.

Otherwise, length would be impossible; "sometimes" refers to the state when it is endowed with qualities such as being agreeable to that [perceiver] (or, according to the commentary C, the state of being agreeable to that). Now, one might object: "Let that very length be its essential nature. To this he says: "which... Thus, it is not logical for it to have that as its essential nature.
The state (*bhāva*). He explains the component "occurred" (*vṛtta*) as "without joints" (*niḥsandhi*).

This refers to the nature of being without the binding of joints—that is, the form of absolute unity—and to "verticality," which is loftiness; and regarding that independence, which is the state of autonomy in coming and going and so forth.

That which has such a form is that whose nature is fitness (*yogyatā*). Here he begins the justification with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). By independent will—that is, by mere desire devoid of any consideration of purpose. Regarding the word "inclination" (*ruci*): as long as one might act in this way, [the thought] "this is long," and so forth.
The meaning is that one should conduct legal proceedings. Here, he cites the words of the Vṛddhas, beginning with "as it has been said.

The point here is this: that is what constitutes *ruci* (consent). What is that? It is that which arises from the mind (*cetas*), because the mind has agitation as its essence—that is, because it has distraction as its essence—and by virtue of that distraction.
It arises spontaneously—that is, it arises without depending on a specific purpose.

Or rather, one might differentiate objects that pervade an extensive space by seeking a causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) characterized by concealment; such is the case in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

One who desires to understand, or one who wishes to instruct another, as to what kind of long name is recited by the elders, should make a distinction. Such is the differentiation among the appearances therein; however, the single specific characteristic (*ekasvalakṣaṇa*) resides in a single appearance of space.
And because [consciousness] rests upon the appearance of time, it is precisely the appearances of space and time that,

by virtue of their proximity to the negation of pervasiveness and eternity— which are the causes of the nature of universality— bestow the nature of particularity. In this way, others as well, such as "humanity" (puruṣatva) and so forth, [are to be understood].

Even the appearances of Brahmins and so forth are to be examined; thus, for now, the most well-known distinction of appearances arises here because they serve as the locus for a great many properties common to both the insentient and the sentient—
meaning that sometimes, indeed, a person, under the influence of agitation, [perceives things otherwise].

One employs whatever word is at hand without regard for its specific purpose; and such linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is necessarily preceded by a mental appearance (*ābhāsa*), since otherwise its utterance would be impossible. The word "iti" marks the conclusion [of this section]. [The text speaks of] "objects" (*arthān*)—that is, entities—that extend over a wide space, meaning they are long.
Characterized by concealment (*tirodhilakṣaṇām*)— that is,
having the nature of disappearance— he, desiring it— that is, longing for it—
[perceives] "this is long," thus seeking to acquire knowledge (*vyutpitsamānaḥ*)— thus effecting his own acquisition of knowledge (*vyutpattim*) by himself.
Desiring to act—what is this? By the elders—the agents—it is asked:
what kind of thing, called "long" (*dīrgha*), is being sung? Or, in another sense (*vā pakṣāntare*):
desiring to instruct another—that is, desiring to bring about their proficiency—he [proceeds with] the division.

One should perform the differentiation, thinking "this is long. By this, it is indicated that at the very time of producing linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), [the word] serves as the cause for the manifestation of that convention. He provides the conclusion with the words "thus" (*ityevam*); there—namely, in a single specific individual (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a person. [Objection: But in that case, unity (*ekatva*) would not exist.

In response to the expectation of why this is "appropriate," he explains the phrase "dividing space and time" occurring in the middle [of the verse] with the word "one. "Of repose" means of the repose of cognition in the form "this is situated here. To the question "Why?", he says "space," and so forth.

The "proximity of the operation" (*savighnāvṛtti*) refers to the activity— namely, the destruction— of those two properties, namely *vyāpyatva* (pervadedness) and *nityatva* (eternality), which are the causes for the nature of being a universal (*sāmānyarūpatā*), by means of establishing their limitation (*parimitatā*). Among these, the destruction of *vyāpyatva* is effected through space (*deśa*).

The sequence should be understood as the refutation of permanence by means of time. "Specific form" means the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). He extends this same principle (*nyāya*) to other properties residing in the person by saying "in the same way. "More well-known" means exceedingly well-known. Why?

In response to this inquiry, he states the reason: "because they are insentient" (*jaḍā iti*). This is common to both the sentient and the insentient—since it applies to sentient beings such as persons (*puruṣa*) and so forth, as well as to insentient things such as trees (*taru*) and so forth.
By this illustration, [the same logic applies] even to smoke, regarding its nature as smoke (*dhūmatva*) and its nature as being produced from birch-bark (*cāndanatva*).
The well-known distinctions of manifestation (ābhāsabheda), such as arising from *śrīkhaṇḍa* sandalwood and so forth, are to be analyzed. By means of a well-known example,
even in the case of a jar— which is an unknown portion— there likewise occurs a distinction between parts of manifestation.
For instance— when one perceives a jar while feeling as if one's heart were breaking because "nothing at all exists here," that which has as its locus those very numerous properties—
which exist in common [with other things] and consist of forms such as length and so forth— is the state of being such; it is from that state (tattva) [that the cognition arises].

The meaning is "because it has that as its object. He provides an introduction to explain the portion beginning with "smoke" by means of the phrase "by this": by this illustration—that is, by this example—the nature of smoke (*dhūmatva*), its being produced from wood (*cāndanatva*), and its having arisen from sandalwood (*candanād-utthitatva*) [are established].
And [qualities] such as "arising from śrīkhaṇḍa" or "white sandalwood" are to be distinguished— that is,

they are to be made objects of distinction according to their respective objects of desire and so forth. In that regard, the distinction is made in such a manner that one who desires blackness [seeks] "smokiness," while one who desires fragrance [seeks] "sandalwood-ness," and so on.

It must be established. Furthermore, the well-known nature of difference here—such as that between "smokiness" and "being made of sandalwood"—is evident because it appears clearly as distinct due to being apprehended by different sense organs;
for difference is not more clearly manifest when residing in a single entity. This is why the superlative suffix *tarap* is employed here.
By relying on two examples, one more well-known and one well-known. || 4 ||

He explains the second verse in order to state the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*), beginning with the words "well-known" (*prasiddha*). This part is "unestablished," hence it is called the "unestablished part" (*aprasiddhabhāga*);
and its lack of establishment here is due to the fact that the jar manifests solely as a unity.
However, because there is no manifestation (*prākaṭya*) of the distinction between those appearances,

even in that case— in that jar— the distinction among the portions of appearances, namely those consisting of existence, jar-ness, and so forth, is precisely the distinction between the portions of appearances.
He demonstrates this with the words "for thus": experiencing a "shattering of the heart"— that is, a breaking of the heart— due to not seeing the actual object,
he perceives only the appearance of existence, thinking "this exists," while [failing to perceive] other appearances.

However, it is not respected even by name; thus, one seeking water perceives the appearance of a jar, one seeking an object capable of being independently carried or brought perceives the appearance of a substance, one seeking value and so forth perceives the appearance of gold, and one seeking attractiveness perceives the appearance of brilliance— and so on, as indicated by the inclusion of "etcetera."

One who desires a more firm state of being should see it as a semblance of firmness; in this same way, it should also be applied to inclination (*ruci*) and proficiency (*vyutpatti*). Thus, these various manifestations (*ābhāsa-bheda*) alone are the reality (*vastu*), because the essence of reality consists in its being manifest. Furthermore, that which is the very life-force of manifestation...

That reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) too rests upon every single manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*), because the word— which consists of mental discourse (*abhijalpa*) and is like the very life-force of cognition— rests upon every single manifestation; for indeed, the heart of the person is broken [by it], as is the manifestation of being (*sattvābhāsa*).
It does not attend to other forms, such as "pot-ness" and so forth,

because here the object of desire and the objective domain is merely the existence of that [substance]. Likewise— in the same manner— it is independent with respect to the suitability of the substance for actions such as bringing it [dravyasyānayanādi-C.], having regard for its capacity for such tasks.
Thus it has been stated. The phrase "it is respected" (*ādriyate*) is to be applied everywhere. Regarding the term "one who desires value and so forth" (*mūlyādyarthī*):

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the making of various ornaments and the like is included. Regarding "splendor" (*aujjvalya*): one becomes radiant and pleasing to the heart. He states the object to be understood from the word "and so forth" as "firm" (*dṛḍha*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such things as [the notion] that water alone is sufficient for purification, or the appearance of fitness for drawing water.
With the word "thus" (*evam*), he extends the application of desire and proficiency to the case of purposefulness (*arthitva*). "Thus" means like purposefulness. In that regard:
Because proficiency exists only during the time of training, and because inclination consists essentially in the distraction of the mind,
the direct application [of the method] is shown, since the desire for results is primary in all worldly transactions.
In that regard, by means of the application of two positions— the more well-known and the less well-known— it is established in the middle.
It should be understood that even the application [of an object] to its proper place is effortless. He provides the conclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*).

In response to the expectation "why?", he says "appearance" (*ābhāsa*). The sense is that an object which has not been made an object of appearance cannot truly be an object. [Objection: But let this be the case only for appearance itself.

In response to the inquiry as to whether there is a distinction between that [manifestation] and the conceptualization arising immediately thereafter, he explains the phrase "the word of sound" with the words "even that which... The term *prāṇabhūta* means "that which constitutes the life-force"; the sense is that without reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), a manifestation is merely like something non-existent.
The phrase "precisely as each manifestation" means that [the object] becomes indeed distinct. In response to the question "Why?", he says:
"of the word. This refers to that which consists of internal discourse—that is, having the nature of verbalization, meaning having the form of articulate speech. By this...

The objection regarding [the word] "ocean-sound" and so forth is refuted. Since sound is rooted in reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), when establishing the distinction between various manifestations, reflective awareness itself is established effortlessly; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

"An existent jar is red," and so forth. Even the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is restricted to each individual manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); for by the manifestation of "existence," there is merely the accomplishment of the avoidance of the heart's breaking [from fear], while in that [process], there is no other manifestation.

That dependence exists because, when a specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is to be accomplished through the appearance of fire, there is a necessity of depending on another fixed (or unfixed) appearance, just as in the case of the appearance of a vessel, since that [appearance of fire] is invariably concomitant with other appearances.
Thus, by whichever aspect...

An object is investigated by this or that [means], because it appears as nothing but a mere manifestation; thus, through such appearance and reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), there is purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Alternatively, it is stated thus because of the very grasping of the "sound" (*dhvani*). Having enacted the state of rest itself, he demonstrates it:

Regarding the word "sat" (existent): by the word "etc. (*ādi*), terms such as "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth are included, and these are to be construed as qualifiers of "resting" (*viśrānti*). Explaining that even the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) varies according to each manifestation, he comments on the phrase "performing distinct functions" (*bhinna-artha-kāriṇaḥ*) with the word "object" (*artha*). In that context, [he explains] that by the persistence (*anvaya*) of which...

The summary is as follows: that which possesses positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) through its own absence, necessarily possesses the capacity to perform that action. Here, he provides the reason by stating "only the appearance" (*sadābhāsa*).
By the suffix *-mātra*, [he excludes] the purposeful action such as fetching water, which is to be accomplished by the appearance of a jar and so forth.

[The opponent] objects: "But surely its existence is desired by someone for some purpose, such as fetching water; therefore, the accomplishment of that [purpose] is also the very activity (*arthakriyā*) of that existent.
For whatever a thing requires for a specific purpose, that is indeed its causal efficiency. To this, he replies: "In that case" (*tatra*). That is to say, regarding the existent (*sattve*).
"Of another appearance"—namely, the appearance of a vessel consisting in the fetching of water and so forth.
The implication is that otherwise, the bringing of fire would be impossible. To the question "Why?", he says:
"By that appearance. This refers to the state of being inseparable from the appearance of existence (sattvābhāsa).

Inseparability (*avinābhāva*) exists because of that [dependence], since it requires another manifestation (*ābhāsāntara*)— such as the manifestation of fetching water— which is necessarily present (*niyata*). The manifestation of a vessel is cited as an example, for it is indeed necessarily required by the manifestation of fire.

He concludes the exposition with the word "evam" (thus). Through the "mukha"—that is, by way of the [three] qualities such as *sattva* and so forth—the "object," such as a jar and the like, is "of the nature of mere appearance" (*ābhāsamātrātmaiva*), meaning it consists solely of the form of appearance;
for it manifests "in that very way," that is, precisely as a state of mere appearance, through its "pratibhāsana," which is its flashing forth (*sphuraṇa*).
"From reflection"—that is, from the act of reflecting;
thus it is established by the word "and. In this way, even a single object is [treated] by the author according to the degrees of being more well-known, well-known, or not well-known.
It is defined in three ways: as "long and round," as "smoke," and as "a real entity. || 5 ||

*Siddham* means that this is established. He provides a concluding summary in order to demonstrate the division of the three places by saying "thus" (*evam*). In this regard, it should be understood that the taking [of an object] from a well-known place is done by means of something even more well-known, whereas the taking of an unknown object is done by means of something well-known.
He demonstrates these very three forms with the word "long" (*dīrgha*).
Such is the summary meaning here: long, circular, upright, and human, as well as smoke, incense, and so forth, which exist according to their well-known prevalence.
Appearances in the form of "long" and so forth; likewise, appearances such as smoke that exist as well-known [conventional realities];

and those differentiated by space and time—[that is,] even though they belong to a single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) existing in a specific place and at a specific time, which consists of the differentiation of space and time.

The peaceful ones (*santaḥ*) are differentiated— they appear as distinct entities by virtue of their inclinations (*ruci*) and so forth; likewise— that is, in that same manner, by way of that illustration—
undocumented varieties of appearances (*ābhāsabheda*), such as the reality of a real jar, a substance, or the brilliance of gold, are differentiated.

Through the power of the triad beginning with *ruc* (inclination), they bring about the manifestation of differentiation. Among these, the manifestation of "long" and so forth occurs sometimes through inclination (*ruc*), sometimes through desire (*arthitva*), and sometimes through proficiency (*vyutpatti*). In that regard, when there is inclination toward those manifestations of "long" and so forth, as well as toward manifestations such as smoke;

There is a change [in the manifestation], a change in the state of desire, and a change in proficiency. For in the case of mere inclination (*rucih*), such a manifestation occurs without purpose. How so? ...In the case of desire, because the object is already excessively attained;
in the case of proficiency, it is merely for the sake of training, so that one may become proficient in this matter. Thus.

In all cases, the triad beginning with inclination (*ruci*) should be applied. Among these, *ruci* (inclination) consists of: the desire for the knowledge or description of a thing even when it serves no purpose; the state of being a seeker (*arthitva*) in all worldly transactions; and proficiency (*vyutpatti*) at the time of receiving instruction and at the time of imparting instruction. Likewise, those [others]—
The various manifestations, which produce distinct effects— that is, perform distinct causal functions— likewise become the locus, or object,
of sound and of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) rooted in that sound;
for instance, because it performs the causal function of concealing its own length, it becomes the object of the reflective awareness, "This is long."
Because it is grasped as "this is long" and because it is an object of verbal designation, this [form] is [an appearance]. This should be understood in all cases.

(4.5) Now, one might object: "If the real entity (*vastu*) consists only of its respective appearances (*pratyābhāsa*), then a single pot-essence would not be a real entity. Anticipating this, he says:
Furthermore, the restricted causal efficiency of things arises from the distinction between their appearances;
for those [things] that appear as non-different, there is a common substratum.

In that form which is a mixture of appearances, there must necessarily be one appearance that, by virtue of its predominance, serves as the locus of rest for the other appearances; it is this [appearance] that is their [locus].

The subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) is the same; therefore, he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "nanv em" (But surely...). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the word "ābhāsa" (Appearance).

Here the commentary explains the word "firstly by way of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmādhikaraṇyena*) with the words "of the appearances" (*ābhāsānām*). "Mixed" (*miśram*) means existing in a state of mixture; that is, having the nature of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
To that extent— in that mixed sleep—

the state of rest (viśrāntipada) is to be cultivated as the locus of repose, just as the manifestation of a jar and so forth [subsides] when there is a desire for the cessation of the heart's fragmentation, or just as the manifestation of a jar [subsides] when there is a desire to fetch water.

Regarding the appearances of "existent" (*sat*) and so forth: that is, the appearance which has been made primary, [is superimposed] upon those other appearances distinct from it. They share a common locus—that is, a single location—because [the former] is superimposed as a property (*dharma*) precisely there. [This concludes] the explanation of the *taddhita* suffix.
"By that, he acts"— that is, by means of that which is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*),
there is a relationship with those appearances (*ābhāsas*) which constitute the contained (*ādheya*),
namely the relationship known as the state of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). He effects the construction of the instrumental case by means of that.

The relation that exists among them is *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical coreferentiality); the manifestation characterized by that— namely, the light directed toward the object (*arthaunmukhya*) and that which animates it (the essence of the word)— is what is meant.
The reflective awareness whose essence is not [merely] sequential— because all that [awareness] is necessarily grounded in a single manifestation—
is that which vitalizes the manifestation of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) which constitutes the essence of the sentence.

Reflection (*vimarśa*) consists in the consideration of the meaning of the sentence— of the form "here, now, this jar exists"— and for that reason, those which are non-different [from it] are characterized— that is, made distinct. By this, it is indicated that this is the third type of characterization (*upalakṣaṇa*).

He explains the term *pratibhāsāt* with the phrase *arthonmukhaḥ*. "Facing toward the object" (*arthonmukhaḥ*) means being engaged in making the object its domain; by not deviating from luminosity (*prakāśa*), it also effects the apprehension of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). "Thereafter" (*tadanu*) refers to that which animates it (*tadanuprāṇakaḥ*).

It is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*, i.e., *vimarśa*) that prevents light from being regarded as something unreal; it is "non-word-natured" (*napadātman*), meaning its nature (*ātman*) or form (*rūpa*) is not composed of words. To the question "Why is it non-word-natured?", he says: "Of that" (*tasya*).
Because of that universal reflective awareness— which consists of words— there is a rule of resting in a single manifestation;
that is, there is a rule of resting in a single manifestation consisting of the appearance of a sentence, for [this does not occur] in the mere intrinsic nature of a word.

The sense is that its predominance [is not perceived] because it is submerged within the sentence. Then, in response to the expectation of what the nature of that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is, he explains it by way of a conclusion: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
"Therefore"—that is, for that reason—the appearance of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyābhāsa*).
It vitalizes— i.e., nourishes— the aforementioned semblance of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyābhāsa*) which exists as an indicator; this is that which consists of the sentence,
existing as the refinement of the sentence and having the nature of the reflective awareness of the sentence-meaning.

Vimarśa—reflexive awareness—is that which animates [the preceding], being distinct from the reflexive awareness consisting of individual words; it is, in other words, the reflexive awareness whose essence is the sentence. Having imitated this very reflexive awareness whose essence is the sentence, he says "iha" (here). "Iha" means in this place.

Now—at this time—this, possessing such qualities, is a jar. In that [expression], "here" is the appearance of space; "now" is the appearance of time; "this" is the appearance of qualities; and "jar" is the appearance of genus.
And here, it is the appearance of the jar alone that is common [to all].
Having attained the state of a single unique particular (*ekasvalakṣaṇatā*), yet not abandoning their own distinct natures (*svarūpabheda*), they possess another, specific,
collective causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). This occurs despite the difference between appearance (*ābhāsa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Furthermore, another [type] is fixed (*niyata*) and consists of each one alone. By the two words "appearance" (*ābhāsa*) and "manifestation" (*pratibhāsa*), it should be understood that "reflection" (*vimarśa*) is also implied in the Sūtra. The word "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) indicates a distinction and applies to both [cases], like the eye of a crow.

The state of being the locus [is established] because the appearance of the other is established precisely by having that as its substratum. Filling the expectancy of the two words "yaḥ" and "ye," he provides the construction of the ablative case in the phrase "pratibhāsāt" (from manifestation), namely:
"tataḥ" (from that). "Tataḥ" means: from manifestation, and from the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) consisting of the sentence; these are the reasons.

He explains "of the non-distinct" with the word "one" (*eka*). "Attained to the state of a single particular" (*ekasvalakṣaṇatāṃ prāptāḥ*) means they have reached the condition of being a single particular by virtue of being mixed with [other] locations and so forth. To the objection, "In that case, let them simply be one," he says "and not... (*na ca*). "And they do not abandon... (*nacojjhanta*...).

The intention is that the connection (*yojanā*) [is established] because the country and so forth manifest separately. He provides the genitive construction "of them" (*teṣām*), meaning "of things" (*vastūnām*). It is not explained [separately] because it is well-known. Furthermore, he explains the word *punar* as expressing the sense of the word "other" (*anya*), [saying] "others" (*anyāḥ*).

Furthermore, it is "other," meaning that for each individual effect it is distinct—though not different from the individual effects themselves—and for this very reason it is "specific. Thus, while so combined, it is not restricted to any single instance, but is intended as the means for accomplishing all appearances; such is the nature of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
He explains that "due to the difference in manifestation (*ābhāsa*), there is a restricted causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)," by the word "manifestation" (*ābhāsa*).

When there is a difference in the manifestation and its corresponding reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there occurs another, restricted causal efficiency—each consisting of a single form alone—that is distinct for each individual. However, in this case, the reflective awareness is...
It should be understood that this very form is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word, because it arises from a single manifestation. Now, one might object:

"Since even the name 'reflective awareness' (*vimarśa*) was not mentioned in the Sūtra, how can its application have been made in the commentary? To this, he says: "manifestation" (*ābhāsa*). It is implied—

It has been brought to the state of being the object of implication by virtue of being a life-sustaining factor (*anuprāṇaka*). Now, one might ask: "Since only a single word is seen, how is it joined twice in the commentary? To this, he says: "The word *punaḥ*.
[It applies] in both cases—in the form of the collective, regulated purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
It is to be applied. By means of the plural number, it is stated that even when there is unity, the distinction of essential natures (*svarūpa-bheda*) is not abandoned;

and in that case, when the plurality—which is dependent upon the appearance of unity—is present among the manifestations (*ābhāsa*), then, by virtue of coloring the individual instances with a common form, it becomes ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).
The state of being a universal belongs to the manifestation of the jar only by virtue of its mere fitness for an independent reflective awareness (*svatantra-parāmarśa*), and not in reality—
this applies to both positions. By means of the plural number, he expresses the intended meaning of the plural in the phrase "of those that are non-different" (*abhedinām*).
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that otherwise, unity alone would be untenable here.

The construction here is as follows: from the manifestation characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—due to the cause being the identity of the manifestation and its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—there is the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of non-distinct entities.
Furthermore, another [form] becomes "assembled" (*samuditā*) due to the difference in appearance—that is, due to the difference in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the appearance;
and again, another becomes "restricted" (*niyatā*) due to the difference in the reflective awareness of the appearance.
Thus, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is applied twice [or thrice, according to the variant reading].

The word "there" (*tatra*) indicates that both universals— those existing by virtue of their mere capacity and those existing directly— reside within the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which has acquired its existence through the mutual blending of appearances (*ābhāsa*) as they abide in each respective manifestation. Therein—

Between the two— the particular (svalakṣaṇa) residing in its own manifestation and the universal (sāmānya) residing in its own manifestation— when there is an appearance of unity, that is, when each [element] such as place appears as one,
in the form "this is the place" and "that is the place," [there is the unification] of each of these manifestations consisting of place and so forth.
Of appearances that have become established, "existence" means being present;

"distinctness" means individuality, that is to say, their abiding in their own respective forms. When there is manifestation as a common nature (*dharmatā*), then those individuals which possess a similar form—
The external entities— the manifestations that serve as the substratum— by acting as coloring agents (*uparañjaka*) through their own qualification, bring about the ultimate,
innate nature of universality belonging to the universal.

Because it exists precisely as being grounded in substances and so forth; for the universal called "spatiality" (deśatva) is indeed observed to be dependent upon the substance in the form of the individual (vyakti) known as "space," and it cannot be asserted that the individual itself is the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa), since...
Because it possesses life through the subject’s imposition of space and time, whereas this [object] exists externally;
otherwise, it would be impossible for it to manifest universality. But in the case of the opposite, the pure [subject] does not abide as being in the same locus as the manifestation of another.
Because it exists as having a common locus with the appearance of other things— namely, the appearance of the jar, which is unmixed with those other differences;
that is to say, the appearance of the form of the jar, which exists as primary due to the desire for fetching water and so forth, meaning the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) of the jar.

In the case of an independent reflective awareness (*svatantraparāmarśa*)— that is, when there is a reflective awareness of something as a subject (*dharmin*) through the appearance of it as a distinct entity—
it occurs by way of mere fitness; that is to say, by means of fitness alone, insofar as it is appropriate for the future manifestation [of the object] as its inherent nature (*svābhāvikadharmatā*).
For every category of existence other than substance possesses a universal nature and has dependence as its essence; thus,
even the single nature of a jar is indeed real.
—Because it is established as such by the power of manifestation (*ābhāsa*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). || 6 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) does not arise from a single [manifestation] alone, but rather a collection of causal efficiencies arises from a collection of manifestations?
And if these manifestations, though distinct, mingle in order to perform a single causal efficiency, then what is the limit to their number? This objection is refuted as follows.
Just as the lights of separate lamps [merge] in the ocean, or as the currents [flow together],
so too the cognition of unity has a single effect despite its non-contradictory appearances.

It exists [conventionally], but in reality—that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth—it does not exist; the meaning is that it does not exist at this time in its manifest form because its nature is sustained by conceptual construction (*yojanā*).
This is because only a property residing within a single individual can possess the status of an ultimately real universal (*pāramārthika-sāmānya*). Why?
In response to this inquiry, he says: "from substance" (*dravyāt*). "Other"—meaning having the nature of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth;
and thus, since even a universal (*sāmānya*) is distinct from substance, its dependence is indeed logical—this is the sense.
He concludes with the result of his own intended position: "in this way. And the essence of the pot (*ghaṭātmā*)...

And the phrase "the nature of the jar" (ghaṭasvarūpam), by means of the word "also" (api), indicates that the ultimate reality belongs to the manifestations (ābhāsas) which exist as distinct [from one another]. Here he states the reason: "because it is a manifestation" (ābhāsa iti).
"Manifestation" refers to the light of the jar; "reflective awareness" (vimarśa) refers to the cognitive awareness of the jar.

"Purposeful action" refers to the fetching of water; "by their power" means by virtue of being established in such a way—that is, through the establishment of their unity. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the commentary on the verse. || 6 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"from the collection of manifestations"—that is, from the aggregate of manifestations; of those—

The "limit" (*maryādā*) of the manifestations (*ābhāsānām*), which consists in the exclusion of their external measure—that is to say, the boundary where the mixing of some [manifestations] occurs only in certain instances—is the objection (*codyam*), meaning the student's challenge; he refutes it, that is, he provides a resolution (*pratisamādhatte*). [The reading *pratisamādadhate* is found in manuscript C.]
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the word "separately" (*pṛthak*).
Those rays of light belonging to a lamp which exist separately possess the capacity for extremely subtle observation (*sūkṣmatama-avalokana-sāmarthya*).

—[K. ṣ. ṣ. Those things which possess the characteristic of being a substratum (*dhāna*) but have not performed any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), they render as having their essence coalesced within a single existence; there, no collection of purposeful actions exists. And likewise, the streams that have fallen into the ocean...
