Just as [the various colors] perform causal functions through the initiation of increasingly numerous waves, so too, upon being merely seen, the golden jar— red— is recognized as suitable for the causal function of fetching water appropriate for the cleansing of the top of a Śiva-liṅga.

It performs a purposeful action characterized by intense joy; thus, its capacity for purposeful action is indeed established. As for the question, "What is the limit regarding the mixing of appearances? it is said in response:
only those appearances that are non-contradictory mix with one another; for instance, the appearance of form [does not mix with contradictory appearances].
It becomes mixed with the appearance of air due to their mutual opposition; and that [appearance] too is brought forth by the power of necessity (niyati-śakti).
Regarding this, the commentary states:
He establishes the method for explaining the verse with the words "separately" (*pṛthak*).

The definition is that which consists in the conferring of capacity— the accomplishment of capability— regarding the observation, that is, the vision, of that which is most subtle (*sūkṣmatama*), i.e., extremely subtle.
She whose nature is such—that he did not create;

that very purposeful activity, characterized by the bestowal of the capacity for most subtle perception; those whose self has reached growth through the persistence of the aggregate, being fully integrated.

"Such as these" (*tādṛśyaḥ*) means "they perform" (*vidadhate*), i.e., they bring about. Having stated one example, he states a second as well with the word "ocean" (*sāgara*). The connection is as follows: the very onset of the numerous waves is itself their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); they are "such" insofar as they perform that [efficiency].

Having stated two examples, he states the application (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "in the same way" (*tadvat*). This jar is suitable for the cleansing—that is, the washing—of the head of the Śiva-liṅga; the fetching of the water used therein is itself the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and it is fit and appropriate for that [action] upon the Śiva-liṅga.

Because bathing is prescribed specifically with a golden jar. "As soon as it is seen"—meaning merely upon being seen—the phrase "performing a single purposeful action" (*ekārthakriyākāritvam*) refers to the aggregate (*samudāya*); this is the ellipsis.
Having thus stated, by means of an example, that the aggregate performs a single purposeful action, [the author now speaks] of the appearances (*ābhāsānām*).
He states the limit of this extent of intermingling with the words "that which again" (*yat punaḥ*). "Limit" (*sīmā*) means boundary (*maryādā*);

that is to say, the limit of its extent. "Of which"—that is, of which appearances. He supports the general [statement] with the particular by saying "for not," because of contradiction, [and] because wind is devoid of color.
The state [of being]. Now, one might ask: how can there be a contradiction between the forms of wind and light?
To this, he says: "And that also...
That also—referring to that single [space] belonging to those various lamp-lights which are separate [from one another] in the ocean.

Just as a single cognition of unity is produced by that which is the one entity of the streams, so too, regarding those appearances—such as "jar," "red," "gold," and so forth—which are not mutually contradictory, the connection is this:
a cognition of unity is produced by that which is the single *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) related to them. By means of this cognition of unity—
It is accepted that there is manifestation, reflective awareness, and causal efficacy. || 7 ||
Indeed, in this way, since the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) comes to rest with each individual manifestation,

the cognition of fire is the valid cognition regarding the manifestation of fire, and the cognition of smoke [is the valid cognition] regarding the mere manifestation of smoke; likewise, even the appearance of the causal relationship exists only within that limited scope.
Furthermore, to dispel the doubt that even the appearance of smoke might deviate from the appearance of fire—and thus lead to many other such logical calamities—it is said:
"And there is also contradiction; nor is it proper to question necessity. This is the intended meaning. [The process:]...
"Having accomplished [the synthesis], he applies the sūtra separately"—this is the connection with the phrase "one entity.

The word *vastu* (entity) refers to the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) in both instances. Therefore, by that *vastu*, the effect is to be accomplished; the *svalakṣaṇa* is animated by the application of space, time, and so forth.
The essential nature [of the object] does not follow after other [cognitions]; this refers to the "relation," with the word "of the verse" being understood as the ellipsis.
Now, one might object: let the cognition of unity be the effect of the particular (svalakṣaṇa), but how can a single purposeful action (arthakriyā) be known?
To this he says: "by the cognition of unity. This means: by the cognition of unity acting as the agent; thus, this is accepted.

It is apprehended through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as its own cause. Why so? Because [the causes] are manifestation (*pratibhāsa*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, it should be construed thus: that which has a single manifestation has a single reflective awareness, and that which has a single causal efficiency has a single effect. This applies to the triad beginning with manifestation.
Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that the cognition of oneness arises. || 7 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the words "nanvevam" (But if this is so). Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
*evam*—in the manner described; *pratyābhāsam*—in each individual manifestation.
"In that much alone"—
that is, in the mere appearance of the causal relation between the appearance of fire and the appearance of smoke;
"and from that"— meaning for that reason— it would "deviate," the sense being that this is because they are cognized by distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other fallacies are included. "To exclude" (*apohitum*) means to distance or remove. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*).

In that regard, with respect to fire and so forth which are undifferentiated, their nature as cause and effect, as heat, and as the referent of various words is understood from a single means of valid cognition.

Regarding this: even in this position—that the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) rests upon every individual manifestation (pratyābhāsa)—there is no fault whatsoever. For instance, although the manifestation of fire is indistinct [in itself], it remains unmixed with other manifestations, such as those of space and time.
Nevertheless, because its nature consists solely of universality, that very manifestation,

having assumed as many manifestations as are invariably concomitant with it and are regulated by the Lord’s power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), attains the state of certainty produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It descends; and thus, the appearance of fire possesses an intrinsic,
non-deviating necessity through its appearance as the effect of fuel, its appearance as the cause of smoke, and its appearance as having heat as its own nature.
Being perceived as having an essential and invariable concomitance with everything at all times, it is perceived as such everywhere and always—because of its oneness. Regarding "asvābhā-":
here is the commentary (ṭīkā):

Therein, he explains the word *tatra* with the words *pratyābhāsam*. The phrase "nor is there any fault whatsoever" (*api na kaściddoṣaḥ*) is supplied as a necessary ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*). When the question arises as to how there is no fault, he begins the justification by intending to explain the passage beginning with *aviśiṣṭe*.
"Thus, for instance" (*tathā hi*). He fulfills the expectation of the phrase "thus, for instance" with the word "undifferentiated" (*aviśiṣṭaḥ*).

"Undifferentiated" means not having attained the state of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇatā*). To the question "Why is it undifferentiated?", he states the reason: "place" (*deśa*). By the word "foremost" (*pramukha*), the inclusion of form (*ākāra*) and so forth is intended.
By way of being unmixed— that is, not intermingled— that very manifestation, namely the manifestation of fire itself,
is inseparable— meaning pervaded— by manifestations consisting of the nature of cause and effect and so forth; [it perceives] all of those, produced by the means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

It "enters the state of certainty"—that is, it becomes the object of valid cognition—because its nature is such; this is the intended meaning. He states the conclusion with the words "and therefore" (*tataśca*).
And therefore—from that reason—the "appearance as fire" (*vahnyābhāsa*), which is the appearance in the form of fire...

The fact that fire has fuel as its effect should be understood as being caused by its being manifested by the fuel. "Intrinsic" (*svābhāvika*) means derived from its own nature; therefore, it refers to that which possesses an intrinsic and non-deviating rule (*niyama*). "Everywhere" (*viśvatra*) means in all places, and "always" (*sarvadā*)—
In response to the question, "From what is [the word] understood at all times?", he says: "Because of its oneness.
Even that nature which depends upon human conventions and the like—for example, being denotable by the word "fire" or having the capacity to produce the cognition of a jar, and so forth—[is one].

That too is determined from a single direct perception alone; for that perceiver, by virtue of the fact that this appearance of fire is experienced as being inseparable from another appearance— whether in its artificial or other form— that appearance of fire, existing in all places and times, is experienced in exactly that way.
Regarding the phrase "it is known," what need is there for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard?

Because of its oneness—that fire exists as a single entity across all places and times by way of its universal nature (*sāmānya*). By this, the explanation of the first half [of the verse] is completed.
In order to explain the various terms occurring in the latter half of the verse, which stand in conjunction with the former half, he says: "non-intrinsic" (*asvābhāvika*).
"Non-intrinsic" means adventitious, by virtue of being established through conventions made by persons; "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) means the very essence of fire.

To explain how it is non-intrinsic (*asvābhāvika*), he says: "by a person" (*puruṣeṇa*). A convention (*samaya*)—that is, a linguistic agreement (*saṃketa*) of the form "this is the meaning of this"—is that which is made by a person, whether by the Primordial Person (*ādipuruṣa*) or by an ordinary person (*sāmānyapuruṣa*); it is that which is the beginning (*ādi*) of such things as the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
"He looks at the face" refers to such a person. To the inquiry "What is that intrinsic nature (svabhāva)? he says:

"For example. Indeed, fire's being denotable by the word "fire" is established solely through human convention (puruṣasamaya), not as something innate (sahaja). He explains the object included by the word "etcetera" (ādi):

"Regarding 'the jar': the meaning is that it acts as an illuminator of the jar by way of being a lamp. For even that [power] in fire is not inherent; rather, because it is produced by the power of *niyati* (destiny/limitation), it is distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*), owing to its occasional occurrence, whereas the nature [and form] always..."
Because of its stability—that is, because it exists eternally—and so forth;

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities such as being devoid of odor and taste are included. That too—namely, every non-intrinsic nature (*asvābhāvika-svabhāva*) denoted by the word "whatever"—is [known] from a single direct perception alone.

[It arises] from perception alone as the single means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). When the question "Why? is expected, he states the reason with the phrase "of that" (*tasya*). "Of that"—meaning of that which exists as the apprehender of fire—by its other, non-artificial form, as opposed to the artificial one which looks toward the face of human convention (*puruṣa-samaya*).

Those other appearances which are observed— namely, the appearances such as "existence" (sat) and so forth, which are distinct from the appearance of fire— the invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*) with them, meaning the rule of coexistence (*sāhacarya-niyama*), which is to say pervasion (*vyāpti*); by means of that, it becomes correctly known— that is, first properly cognized— and therefore...

That [object] existing in all places and times is thus cognized—it would be cognized as being inseparable from another appearance; therefore, what is the use of another means of knowledge there? Since it is established by a single means of knowledge alone, the meaning is that nothing further is required. This refers to the phrase "the referent of each respective word."

He shows the subject matter to be indicated by the four components of the compound through the method of analysis (*vigraha*) with the words "of that" (*tasya*). He states the meaning of "of that" (*tasya tasya*) as follows: "of a word being employed according to one's desire by human convention."

This meaning—that this object has a blazing, radiant form—is indicated by the term "appearance" (*ābhāsa*), which suggests that the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) alone is the refuge in all cases. This is what is meant: whatever is artificial or otherwise, the appearance of an entity is inseparable from another appearance. [Inseparability—]

K. ṣ. ṣ. it appears that there, only the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) alone manifests supremely. That form of necessity [the form of the power of necessity—K. ṣ. ṣ. is the time extended between the prior and the posterior, appearing both as the effect of fuel and as the cause of smoke, and as having the nature of heat.
However, the distinction lies in the fact that, after a very short time, there is the appearance of being denotable by words such as "fire" (and so forth). Consequently,
even the appearance of smoke is non-deviant from the appearance of fire, by virtue of depending upon the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*).
There is no error whatsoever.
By the phrase "according to one's desire," he indicates—
suggests— by means of this, namely by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*), that wherever there is necessity created by human agency...

"The stability of words in their own referents—what doubt can there be regarding that? [This occurs] through the regulation of the manifestation and the process of commingling by the ordinance of Īśvara. By this, he states the aforementioned matter in summary with the word "this. To the question, "What is being said? he replies with the words "whatever... and so forth.

Of the appearance of an entity—that is, of the appearance of an object such as the appearance of fire—by way of its being inseparable from it, meaning by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*) or concomitance (*sāhacarya*). "But" (*param*) means exclusively.
He shows the distinction based on the object of necessity with the words "that, however" (*tattu*). The form of necessity (*niyatirūpa*)—

This is the nature of the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*). In that regard, while the state of being an effect of fuel is manifest, it exists at a prior time because the fire was already present; otherwise, the necessity of its being an effect of fuel would be impossible. Likewise, while the state of being a cause of smoke is manifest, it exists at a subsequent time; otherwise—
It would restrict the causality of smoke to each individual instance;

likewise, while the nature of heat is manifesting, it exists at all times throughout the extended duration by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), because fire is invariably hot at all times. Thus...

The distinction is that the manifestation of being denotable by words such as "fire" and so forth occurs only for a short duration; this is because, within the interval of this convention, it lacks beginninglessness due to its being conceptually constructed, otherwise its status as a human creation would be impossible—such is the nature of the distinction. This is the meaning of the phrase "a distinction of this kind exists."

He states his own intention, which has now borne fruit, with the words "tataśca" (and therefore). "By depending on the power of necessity" (*niyatiśaktyupajīvanena*) means "in view of the power of necessity," that is to say, because necessity exists precisely in this manner. "Disruption" (*viplava*) refers to the absence of fixed rule. Demonstrating the syntactical connection (*yojanā*), first...
The nature of being an effect, the nature of being a cause, heat, and the state of being the referent of this or that word—

that is, being denotable by those respective words— and by the inclusion of the term "etcetera," [the states of] being devoid of smell and taste, being conjoined with the upward direction, and being opposed to water: such is the self (ātman).

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in fire and so forth is held to be known from a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that is to say, it is "cognized. The term "non-interruption" (*aviccheda*)—where "interruption" (*cheda*) refers to the cutting off of the sense object—is a convention used in poetry (*kāvyam*), not in a technical treatise (*grantha*); thus, there is no fault even if both terms occur together in the second and third quarters of the verse.

The employment of the term "separate existence" (*pṛthagbhāva*) as a logical reason is intended to indicate a distinction between categories based on whether they depend or do not depend upon another entity, and based on being produced or unproduced. || 8 ||
He shows the analysis (*vigraha*) of the long compound beginning with *kāryakāraṇa* by saying "kārya. To show the object included by the word "ādi," he says "ādi.
"Ityevambhūtaḥ" means "of such a form. He states that which is denoted by the word "ātman": ... [the text continues] ...which is expressed by the word *ātman*.

Regarding the term *svabhāva*: in this system, because the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) is never lost, the word "self" (*ātman*) is employed. Regarding the phrase "in fire and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), all categories of entities (*padārtha*) are included. This is the explanation of the singular number in the expression "from the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāt*).
"He performs [it] from one" means: he provides the explanation of "mataḥ" (thought/considered) as "saṃviditaḥ" (perceived/cognized).

The word "yāvat" is intended to indicate synonymy (*paryāyatva*). This wards off the fault that would arise from the mere juxtaposition of words situated in the preceding and succeeding [parts of the sentence]; the remainder is that there must be no interruption (*avicchedaḥ kāryaḥ*).

"In the treatise" means in a composition of words that expresses a great secret in summary form. "Absence of fault" means the non-existence of defects. Even though the goal is accomplished by a single abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) standing at the end of the compound, [it is necessary to state] that which stands for each individual member.
He states the intention of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) with the word "separately" (*pṛthak*).

The employment of the abstract suffix refers to the usage of the locative case (*talaḥ*); it denotes the distinction of categories (*vargabheda*) of other entities such as time (*samaya*) and so forth.
Thus, the establishment of the nature of an entity is [effected] by that which rests upon the various appearances (*pratyābhāsa*).

It is established by a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding those appearances as well, that mutual inseparability which exists according to their respective natures is [established] by a single form of consciousness through the cognition of those many [objects].

It is determined through its own inward-turned nature as that which vitalizes the series of prior cognitions regarding the manifestations of objects; and that [determination] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) insofar as it consists in the synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) of the mere appearance of unity, whereas with respect to the individual manifestations being synthesized, it is not a valid cognition because it apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).
It is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*); rather, in that case, each [instance] is indeed a prior means of valid cognition.

However, the utility of bodily activity—which is distinct from the mental activity consisting in the establishment of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity—is, insofar as it falls within the scope of a means of valid cognition, [to be understood] accordingly.

For a *varga* (group) is indeed a collection of similar things, and it is only in that case that a single abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is appropriate, not in a collection of dissimilar things; this is the intended meaning. In that regard, the state of being uncreated belongs to the relation of cause and effect and so forth, while the state of being created belongs to the property of being denotable by words and so forth. || 8 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the ninth verse with the word "evam" (thus).
Here, the commentary states:
"evam"—in the manner described in the preceding verse.

The establishment of the intrinsic nature of entities (*bhāvasvabhāvavyavasthāpanam*)— that is, the determination of the specific character of fire and so forth— is performed individually by a single means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which rests upon every manifestation (*ābhāsa*) present within the entity, with respect to each individual appearance (*pratyābhāsam*).
Because the nature of fire as being the effect of fuel and so forth is established by means of each individual valid cognition;

that which is the mutual inseparability— namely, the rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*) among those appearances, such as the appearance of being the effect of fuel and so forth, according to what is appropriate— that [is the point].
It is determined by way of its nature as consciousness—that is, by its essential nature as consciousness.
By what kind of nature as consciousness? It is that which has occurred previously—having been produced before—and which possesses those various cognized appearances as its objects.

The "aggregate of cognitions" (*saṃvedanakalāpa*) is the collection of means of valid knowledge (*pramāsamūha*); that which has as its "vitalizing principle"—that is, that which bestows existence—its inward-turned essential nature (*svarūpa*), meaning its form consisting of all reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). It is of the nature of synthesis (*anusandhāna*).
It consists of the form of connecting with appearances previously grasped, and that— being of the nature of consciousness—

is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only insofar as there is an appearance of identity, because it has the form of connection; however, in the case of difference, regarding those appearances being synthesized, it is not a means of valid cognition because it would be grasping what has already been grasped.

It is not invalid, for those [objects] were previously grasped by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through their own objects; however, they are here being synthesized, since otherwise a grasp as a unity would be impossible. To address the question "How so?", he says "In that case" (*tatra*). The word "but" (*tu*)...

The word *hi* has the sense of "because"; however (*tu*), since in that case—in those appearances—it is only the prior [cognition], belonging to the very time of perception, that constitutes the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). But if this is so, the engagement of the body would be entirely illogical, because purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is accomplished by mere reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) alone, and not by that [prior cognition].
And because it is to be accomplished by the mere activity of the mind, he says "bhāva" (state/being). As for "yathā"— in whatever manner—
he says this in order to show that manner:
But that activity of the seeker, occurring at that very moment, would be directed toward a particular (svalakṣaṇa) distinct from other particulars such as place and so forth.
First of all, external causal efficiency (arthakriyā) belongs to the particular; and since [efficiency] resides in the particular...
The internalization of the manifestation of space and time is indeed an internal factor;

even there, however, nothing whatsoever exists without reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Rather, by means of reflective awareness, [the manifestation] comes to rest within the subject, who is of the single nature of pure consciousness.

Due to the conjunction of place and time, it indeed abandons its specific form through its unity; thus, in all cases, non-duality is the ultimate reality. Nevertheless, that which is the cause of the manifestation of whatever specific form appears is precisely the sovereign freedom of the Supreme Lord.
It is called the power of illusion (māyā-śakti). Having thus provided this introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "sā tu" (but that [power]).
Here is the commentary (ṭīkā):

He establishes the method for explaining the verse with the words "external" (*bāhyā*). The sense is that they are "external" because they are to be accomplished by external objects. To that extent, there is no disagreement from anyone on this point; such is the meaning. [Regarding] "by way of its own characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*)—
Because it is established through the conjunction with appearances such as place,

and because the real entity (*vastu*) has a nature that does not follow after others, and regarding its own specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*)— that is, in the case of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—
it possesses "internalness," meaning it is the uncommon cause. For it is precisely through the conjunction with place and so forth [that this is established].

The universal becomes the particular. And even there—in that very particular—without reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), that is, without the discernment of its specific qualities, nothing whatsoever comes into being;
for it is only when an object is reflected upon that it attains its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). But surely...
To the objection that there might also be a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), he says: "Reflective awareness" (*parāmarśa*).

By way of reflective awareness—that is, through the medium of reflective awareness—of that which has the sole nature of consciousness, meaning whose essential form is exclusively eternal and all-pervasive consciousness, [there is] due to the non-connection with space and time.

Because of the lack of connection with place and so forth, and due to the reason of oneness, that specific form indeed abandons—that is, relinquishes—its specific form; for this reason, non-duality—the absence of duality—exists in the ultimate sense. Nevertheless, that which...

The state of being a specific form shines forth— it manifests as the object of external things; the cause of that, which is the very sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, is called by the wise the power of *māyā*, precisely because it is the cause for the manifestation of objects that are [otherwise] impossible.
Because it is conceived as being illusory (*māyā*). He provides the application [of the definition] to the Sūtra by relying on the aforementioned method, saying "therein" (*tatra*):
for one who desires a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by a particularity, that [desire] regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)...

Regarding that object in its specific form, the activity of speech, mind, and body occurring at that time constitutes "place"; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," there are many other forms of perception pertaining to time, different essential natures, the subsequent reflection upon them, and so forth.
Their perceptions occur when there is a distinct cause for differentiation, and not otherwise.

That activity does not arise from each individual means of knowledge, but rather from the collection of means of knowledge alone. Furthermore, while a "collection" is not tenable for the opponent, it is for us.

When that [perception] consists in resting within self-awareness alone, he explains the term "one who desires" (*arthin*) as follows: one who is "desirous" (*arthī*)—that is, endowed with desire—is one who seeks a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā-viśe�ha*) to be accomplished by means of a particularity (*viśeṣa*), namely, a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, he is possessed of the longing for that.

Thus, up to this point; he establishes the genitive construction as "of that. He explains "in its own characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇe*) as "in that" (*tasmin*). He explains "pertaining to that time" (*tātkālikī*) as "at that time" (*tatkāle*);
the meaning is "occurring at the time of apprehension. He explains "activity" (*pravṛtti*) as "speech" (*vāk*).

Because activity (*pravṛtti*) is of three kinds, it has been stated thus. He explains the entire compound beginning with "deśe" by first analyzing its grammatical resolution (*vigraha*): "in space" (*deśe*). He states the object to be included by the word "etc.
(*ādi*) as "in time" (*kāle*). "In another nature" (*svarūpāntare*) means in that which is distinct from the nature of space and so forth, yet delimited by it.
Regarding the nature of the object itself— that investigation and so forth (*anusandhānādi*) directed toward that very nature of the object;

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of investigations into place and other such factors is intended— in that regard, there are numerous other perceptions (*adhyakṣāntarāṇi*), meaning those other than the perception that grasps identity, which are many due to the multiplicity of their objects.

"Existing" means they are directly perceived, having the nature of both external and mental forms; he explains "in their difference" (*bhinne*) as "in the difference" (*bhede*). By this, it is illuminated that the suffix *kta* here denotes the state of being (*bhāve*), and that the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitte*).
He states this same meaning again in summary with the words "not from each one individually" (*naikaikataḥ*). First...
For indeed, a person here [in this world] first apprehends each individual factor, such as place and so forth, by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), thinking "this is it now";
then, having performed a synthesis (*yojanā*) of all these through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), he employs speech and other faculties therein.
Even though it was previously stated that the apprehension of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) occurs from only a single valid cognition, [the process described above follows].
Nevertheless, this has been stated here with reference to the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as it pertains to the manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*) residing at the root;
thus, one should not suspect a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Alternatively, regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)...
The apprehension is said to arise from a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the engagement (*pravṛtti*) occurs through many perceptions;

thus, there is no suspicion whatsoever of contradiction between what precedes and what follows. For apprehension occurs even at the mere first encounter, while engagement occurs only after the fundamental investigation—enough of this. Now, [an objection]:
In the statement "the self-luminous [consciousness] arises anew," the momentariness of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇas*) has been asserted;

therefore, how could their collection (*samūha*) be possible? To this, he says: "And the state of being a collection..."—for the opponent, the Buddhist, and for us, those established in the venerable Śiva-system, that [collection]...
[The term] *samūhatā* [is used]. If one asks, "Where was this stated?", it is appropriate [to reply] as was said previously:
"If [the object] is not included within... (2.3.7).

Thus, in this context, this very [synthesis] is the application (*yojanā*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it is called the "synthesizing reasoning" (*yojikā yukti*). It is like the reasoning that combines odor, substance, and so forth. The intended meaning is that activity proceeds from the collection of perceptions alone. This applies even to those perceptions regarding place and so forth (*deśādikeṣvapyadhyakṣeṣu*).

Even when there is a conjunction with the appearance of space and so forth (*deśābhāsādiyojanā*), the connection is that it occurs "in that" which is the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) internal to the subject (*pramātṛ*), being non-different from him; or rather, [the connection is] with other perceptions such as space and the like.

Alternatively, the construction may be: "When the particular (svalakṣaṇa) has become manifest as the cause through various appearing forms (ābhāsāntara), there is activity. Here too, following the method of defining the multiplicity of objects of cognition (prameya), the collection of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-samūha) is stated to be the cause by virtue of its conformity to that [object].

The phrase "na cet" (if not) serves to recall the verse explained previously. For in this verse, it was established that there is a single reality consisting of the aggregate of all consciousness, which is the Self; and in that very reality, the existence of the entire collection of means of knowledge is indeed logical—this is the intended meaning. Of this...
He states that the name "reasoning" (*yukti*) belongs precisely to this "totality" (*samūhatā*), saying "this very [is it]. That [totality] is *samūhatā*.

Here he provides an illustration with the word "fragrance" (*gandha*). He expresses the purport of this verse in summary with the word "thus" (*evam*). He offers an alternative interpretation of the compound term "place and so forth" (*deśādika*).

Regarding the phrase "in space and so forth": even when space and the other [objects] are perceptible, and even when there is the association with the appearance of space and so forth, he provides the explanation of the word "within" (*antaḥ*) as "in the subject" (*pramātari*). Since this [subject] is undivided and one, by this [statement] the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
It has been illuminated that the locative case in "svalakṣaṇe" is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). "Saṅgatiḥ" means connection.
He then provides another interpretation with the words "deśādikaiḥ.
To the question, "What is the result of these two explanations? he says, "atrāpi"—that is, even here.
In both commentaries, "by way of following that" means by way of conforming to the multiplicity of objects of cognition (*prameya*);

the sense is that here too, activity proceeds from the collection of perceptions alone. With this, the commentary up to the word "of the seeker" (*arthinaḥ*) is completed. Thus, the application [of the text] here is clear. The word "but" (*tu*)...
From a single means of valid cognition consisting of a collection of fallacious reasons such as "being an effect" and so forth, there arises that which indicates another alternative:
that [agency] belongs to one who perceives the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinct from other perceivers of place and so on; what is that? It is that which...
"The activity of one who seeks [an object] would be immediate.
Now, is the collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) useful only for perceptual activity?
No, he says:
... even by means of inference. || 9 ||

Activity does not proceed solely from perception— based on a collection of means of knowledge consisting of the various distinctions perceived regarding place and so forth— but likewise from inference as well;
[this applies] even when there is merely the appearance of smoke or merely the appearance of fire.
When smoke is non-deviant from the appearance of fire, and when there is the appearance of a mountain,

those other perceptions [that arise], as well as the distinct inference which is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the form "fire is here"— consisting in the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) regarding that which is apprehended beyond [the initial perception]— it is from the collection of these alone that the seeker [attains the goal].
The connection is that [this] activity is momentary. || 9 ||

Thus, the determination of difference and non-difference arises solely from the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); for that very thing is the manifestation of the power of freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord, Śiva-nātha, whose nature is consciousness. Consequently, regarding what is asserted by others concerning distance, proximity, and so forth—
"That there is no difference in meaning"—this too is established as being possible in no other way whatsoever; thus it is demonstrated.
He provides the introduction to the fragment of the verse beginning with "śiṣṭasya api" by saying: "nanu" (but surely).
Thus [it is said]. "In perception itself"—that is to say, in that which is related to perception and occurs immediately after it. To this he provides the answer, saying "No.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the portion of the verse beginning with "even from inference."
He explains this with the words "not merely. The meaning is that it is precisely so:
it is caused solely by the collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of the various distinctions among direct perceptions (*adhyakṣa*) of place and so forth.
To explain this very point in detail, he says "smoke" (*dhūma*). [This refers to] in the mere appearance of smoke—

In the form of the *liṅga* (the mark), which consists of the mere appearance of fire; in the pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is the non-deviation between the appearances of smoke and fire; in the concomitance (*sāhacarya*); in the mountain-appearance, which is the subject (*pakṣa*); and in that which is distinct from those perceived [smoke and so forth], namely, distinct from what was grasped therein.

In the context of "exclusion of non-connection" (*ayogavyavaccheda*)—that is, the exclusion of the lack of connection with fire, meaning "possessing that"—he shows the nature of the exclusion of non-connection by saying "fire. "Separately" means distinct from direct perceptions; "from that collection" means from the collection of the means of valid cognition consisting of perception and inference. Thus.
The connection [is as follows]: the meaning is that the construction of this portion of the verse is thus. || 9 ||
Now he provides the introductory commentary for the tenth and eleventh verses with the word "evam" (thus).

Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "Thus"—by the aforementioned method—"that very thing"—referring to reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) itself—of that which consists of consciousness (*saṃvedanātman*).
Of that which is of the nature of light,
there is the state of being indirect or direct perception of objects through their distance or proximity,
through being external or internal, by defects, or otherwise by the manifestor. (10)
Even for those things whose appearances and shadows are distinct, their unity is not precluded, because they possess a primary appearance known as a single unifying reflective awareness. || 11 ||

If you establish [the nature of things] based on mere appearance, how can there be no difference between an object that is distant and one that is near, given that appearances differ in some way or another—
whether they are complete or incomplete, obscured or unobscured, and so forth? But surely...

Even in reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there is likewise a distinctness for each individual manifestation; this is true. Nevertheless, that which is the supreme reflective awareness is itself this single object, consisting of a unitary reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*).
By means of that [awareness], which is like the very life-force, its manifestation—that is, its unfolding (*prathana*)—occurs everywhere (*ā samantāt*).
Regarding the "primary manifestation"— that is, the manifestation of existence in a single form—
by others, namely the logicians (*tārkika*). Having thus provided this introduction and presented two verses, he explains them starting with the words "distant and near."
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) sets forth the methodological procedure (*prakriyā*) to explain the verse, beginning with the words "pratibhāsa" (manifestation).
By "mere manifestation"— that is, by a luminosity (*prakāśa*) devoid of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— it establishes the order (*vyavasthā*).

The phrase "of the Buddhist who establishes [the distinctions of] blue and so forth" is the ellipsis to be supplied. To the question "Why is there no non-difference?", he states the reason here with the words "of the appearance" (*pratibhāsasya*). In that regard, at a distance it is incomplete, while nearby it is complete; likewise, at a distance it is obscured, while nearby it is unobscured.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the states of being unclear and clear are included. "In whatever way" means by whichever manner whatsoever. Here, the student asks: "But surely... and so forth—in that very same manner.
"Like a reflection" means by way of being the totality and so forth. He states the answer: "It is true. The other—[meaning one whose nature is the supreme universal (parasāmānya)]—asks:
"Of what kind is that universal form? To this he replies: "This is that very same thing.
By that—by the supreme reflective awareness (paravimarśa)—which is "as if enlivened," meaning which produces the state of being real; |||

He provides the explanation of the particle *ā* as "on all sides" (*samantāt*). He explains the verbal root ending in a *kṛt* suffix as *khyā*, [deriving] *khyānam*. He also states a synonym for this as "expansion" (*prathana*). For indeed, manifestation occurs precisely through reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).
The term *bhāva* means "that which shines forth. He explains the phrase "primary manifestation" as follows:

even though it is appropriate to that [single reflective awareness], there exists a single manifestation within the single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*), because manifestation and reflective awareness are inseparable from one another. Therefore...

The oneness of those whose secondary manifestations possess a shadow of appearance that is distinct from their own nature— consisting of both direct perception and indirect cognition in the form of "that which was inferred is the very same thing that was seen"— remains unimpeded due to the primary manifestation.
The connection is as follows: [the unity] appears primarily because it is sustained by a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*).

This is the unity of appearances that seem divided by being external or internal, such as when one thinks, "That very thing which was seen, I now delineate internally as 'I'. This applies to manifestors such as the light of a lamp and so forth.
The unity of things that appear differently due to defects [is expressed as follows]: "That very red lotus which was seen as blue by means of a lamp, I now see as red by the rays of the sun.
Regarding the word "one" (*eka*): it means of the appearance in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*). Now, [one might ask: is the appearance of a single form...
Since this is not experienced here [in the case of the two distinct objects], he says "one" (*eka*). For— because— in the single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*),

which is clearly being experienced as the general reflective awareness that "this is that very object," there occurs a single manifestation (*ekāvabhāsa*) appropriate to— that is, compatible with— that [awareness].
The appearance as a universal certainly exists; why?

Because manifestation (*ābhāsa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) are never dissociated from one another. For reflective awareness does not arise at all without manifestation or its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), nor does manifestation [arise] without reflective awareness.

Regarding the phrase "without [the notion of] the unreal" (*vinā'satkalpa*), he provides the construction for the suffix *-tas* as "from that" (*tasmāt*). He explains "oneness is unobstructed" (*ekatvamanivāritam*) as "oneness" (*ekatvam*). "Unimpeded" (*apratihatam*) means free from resistance; "it abides" (*āste*) means it remains. By this, the connection has been made with the phrase "of objects through distance and proximity" (*dūrāntikatayārthānām*).

The connection here is as follows: although the qualifier "of those whose shadows appear as distinct" (*bhinnāvabhāsacchāyānām*) will be explained later, it is indeed applicable here as well; thus, the construction is: "of those whose shadows appear as distinct due to being distant or near."

Even for objects such as blue and so forth, which appear as distinct and non-primary, their unity remains unimpeded due to a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*)— that is, by virtue of the common reflective awareness "this" which flashes forth through the primary manifestation.

In the same way, the application [of this principle] should be made in what follows as well. He provides the application for the phrase "by means of being imperceptible and perceptible" with the words "that very [object]," meaning that its connection is with the word "unobstructed" (*anivāritam*). He applies the phrase "as external and internal" with the word "external. The word "iti" [marks the end of the application].
Regarding the completion of the construction (*yojanā*): here too, the construction should be performed just as before.

He connects "by the defects of the manifestor" (*vyañjakasya doṣaiḥ*) with "of the manifestors" (*vyañjakānām*). Or he connects "also otherwise" (*anyathāpi vā*) with "by another manner," such as the lack of proficiency of the sense organs (*indriyāpāṭavādinā*).

Or, even for those things whose appearances and shadows differ due to being on one side, facing each other, and so forth, their unity alone is established by the power of the nature of appearance which conforms to the primary reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa). Thus it is settled. (10–11)

[Objection: Surely, let that same object exist as being both distant and non-distant, since it is equally useful in the respect of the *arthakriyā* (purposeful action) determined by the cognizer; but how can this apply to [the distinction between] external and internal, given that the internal is of no use in the *arthakriyā* determined by the cognizer?

Thus, in order to dispel this misconception, he says, "even by another. He clarifies that very other mode with the words, "the sense organ," etc.; by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of distortions caused by disease and so forth is intended.

By "that which is directed toward one side," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes being turned away from the second side. For even by those two [states], a single object appears as if divided; it conforms to the primary reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), and thus it is of such a nature.

The meaning is that by the power of its essential nature as manifestation—the essential nature of primary manifestation—it becomes "established," which is to say, it is endowed with persistence. || 10 || 11 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the twelfth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"dūrādūrādau" (in cases such as distant and near). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of "perceptible" (*parokṣa*) and "immediate" (*adhyakṣatva*).

That is the very same object; the meaning is that it is one and the same object. Why? To this he says: "by the knower" (*pramātṛ*). Because of its utility in that very way—in that portion of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) which has been determined or ascertained by the knower—whether it stands far away, beyond perception, or nearby, within direct perception.

Or, when it is stable, the blue [object] indeed performs a function exactly similar to that of the cognition whose form is its own object; as for the distinction such as dullness and so forth, that is entirely irrelevant.
But as for the distinction between external and internal and so on, how could that very object [be the same]? It is not.
The meaning is that this is logical. To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the internal [fire].
The point is that fire imagined internally cannot be employed for external fire's functional activity, such as the removal of cold.

*bhaṃktum* means to break or to tear apart (or *toṣayitum*, according to C.). Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*).
Even purposeful action is not innate to objects by virtue of the will of God.
For that [nature] is indeed fixed by him; therefore, there can be no other state for it than its non-activity. || 12 ||

In this context, regarding the statement "the state of being cause and effect" (2.3.8), just as the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is included, so too is purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). However, that which is enumerated therein is not the innate essential nature of the object; for its status as an agent of that [action] is due to the following:

It is determined by the will of the Lord (Īśvara) regarding both existence and non-existence; since this [will] is not the [entity's] own nature (svarūpa), one should not suspect a change in the entity's state due to its non-occurrence,
for change would only be possible through a difference in essential nature, and there is no difference in essential nature.

The capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) has been stated and will be stated many times. Furthermore, by the power of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed one and the same, whether in the external or the internal realm. || 12 ||
Here, the commentary explains "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*) with the word "here" (*iha*). "Here" means in this treatise;
specifically, in this context of "the relation of cause and effect," which is contained within the verse beginning with "therein, being undifferentiated," and so forth.

In the series of words, [the phrase] "as its own nature" (*svarūpam iva*) means "like the nature of being an effect" (*kāryatādi-svarūpavat*). He provides the explanation of the word "innate" (*sahajā*) with the word "object" (*artha*). He explains the word "not" (*na*) as "it does not exist" (*na bhavati*).
He explains the passage beginning with "by the will of the Lord" (*īśvarecchayā*) and ending with "for that" (*sā hi*) as the reason for "being caused by that" (*tatkāritvam*).

For this reason— because its agency, namely fire’s agency in the cessation of cold (which is to say, its own causal efficiency), is determined by the will of the Lord, whether in the case of existence (*bhavana*) or non-existence (*abhavana*). As it has been said:

"And here, destiny is the fifth. For "destiny" (*daiva*) indeed refers specifically to a particular will belonging to the Supreme Lord, whose nature is play (*krīḍāśīla*), by virtue of the etymological derivation "this belongs to the god" (*devasyedaṃ*). Indeed, all phenomena are impelled solely by the will of the Lord.
They accomplish their own specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), but not by their mere intrinsic nature alone.

Otherwise, there would never be any fruitlessness in the existence of entities; yet we observe, for instance, that even fire lacks the capacity to ward off cold during a feverish chill. Enough of this. Therefore, etc.
In order to explain the fragment of the verse, he fulfills the expectation of the word "by that" with the word "that which.

"This" refers to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); "of that" means of causal efficiency; and by the word "also," it is implied that this applies even in cases such as distance and proximity. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the commentary on the verse. || 12 ||

Now, if the determination of difference and non-difference among things arises solely from the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), then all talk of delusion has now ceased in the three worlds; for even in the case of mother-of-pearl, it would follow that it is truly silver, because it is being reflected upon as "this is silver. And consequently—

Since sublation is impossible in the absence of error, for what purpose was it stated that "cognition is uncontradicted with respect to the object" (2.3.2)? He dispels the doubt that if there is no deviation [from the truth], no object of exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) can be found for the qualifier "uncontradicted."

Even when there is a single cognition of silver, the status of [the object] as silver does not exist in the mother-of-pearl; because the location of the limiting adjunct is inconsistent. Likewise, in the case of two moons, the sky is otherwise [than it appears]. (13)

"This is silver, stable, common to all subjects, and capable of causal efficiency"— in this [cognition], there is no falsity whatsoever regarding the "this" aspect, the "silver" aspects, or the aspect of their synthesis, due to the power of the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of these manifestations. However, ...
Regarding what will occur at a later time,
he now provides the introduction to the thirteenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
[Objection: "Let the talk of delusion indeed cease; what follows from that? To this he says, "The mother-of-pearl," etc.
It "occurs"—it comes forth by force. When the question "Why? arises, he states the reason with the words "this," etc.
[Objection: "But even so, what of it? To this he says, "And therefore," etc. The sense is that it has been stated previously. Here...
He states the reason with the phrase "vyabhicāra" (inconstancy). "Vyavacchedyam" means that which is to be excluded or set aside;
"nirasyati" means he removes or distances it. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "rajataika" (the one [cognition] as silver).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) sets forth the method for explaining the verse with the words "this" (*idam*). Regarding the portion "this":
in this part, namely "this," [the phrase] "silver and so forth" (*rajatādi*) is used; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the portion consisting of stability and other qualities is included.

Regarding them—the portions such as "this" (*idamaṃśa*) and so forth—in that part which consists of their conjunction, namely the aspect of synthesis through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is not even the slightest trace of falsity; this is the connection [of the words]. For it is indeed light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone...
The meaning is that [these two] establish the true nature of the object. Now, one might ask:
"In that case, what is the difference between this [cognition] and the cognition of real silver? To this he says: "But...
That is, in the alternative view, at a later time—that is, at the time of sublation—whatever [cognition] will arise...
The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— namely, "this is not silver; it is not a stable object, nor is it accessible to other subjects, nor does it perform the desired function"—
is that which is to be reflected upon by that [subsequent] awareness, and it is precisely what was appropriate at the time of the preceding awareness.
That form is not reflected upon at that time of prior reflection, and there must be something to be reflected upon by that reflection.
In response to the inquiry as to what the nature of this reflection is, he says: "This is not [it]."

"Performing the desired function"—that is, performing the function of silver. The word "iti" (thus) is intended to mark the conclusion of the observation that consists of subsequent reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
"That"—meaning that very reflective awareness—becomes "to be reflected upon by reflection," meaning it is to be investigated by means of reflection.

The designation in the neuter gender by way of generality is not improper, for it is said that "the gender of genders is the unmanifest. Indeed, the truth of that cognition is manifest prior to the arising of sublation;
however, after its production, it is appropriate to investigate whether this [is so].

"Is the sublation real or otherwise? Now, one might ask: "How can that [object] become the object of the reflective awareness of that [subsequent awareness]? To this he says: "Since" (*yat*). "Since"—that is, for the reason that by means of that subsequent reflective awareness (*uttara-vimarśa*), at the time of the preceding reflective awareness (*pūrva-vimarśa-kāla*), [the object is determined as such].

That which is appropriate for the time of the preceding reflective awareness— that is, the well-known form suitable for that prior reflective awareness— is not at all reflected upon; it is not determined at all,
because this new reflective awareness arises as something contradictory to the preceding one.

Therefore, deliberation regarding this [subsequent cognition] is indeed appropriate; however, the point is that once a cognition has arisen in conformity with that [prior one], deliberation concerning it would no longer be appropriate.
Now, one might object: "If deliberation does not arise at a later time, then the truth of that prior [cognition] is certainly not contradicted. To this, he says: "And it must be so" (*bhāvyaṃ ca*).
Because that which was not to be doubted has been stated as being subject to doubt, there must necessarily be a subsequent deliberation;

for a mother-of-pearl shell perceived as silver is incapable of performing the function of silver, and thus for one seeking silver who has engaged with it, there must necessarily arise the realization: "This is not [silver]."
The reflective awareness that "this is silver" (and not "this is a distinct piece of silver") must necessarily occur.
As for that which is useless— such as grass and the like, which one would naturally disregard— the very discussion of it is not appropriate here.

At that very time, the subsequent reflective awareness is "this was not silver" (or "this was indeed not silver"), and not a reflection occurring only at this moment— like a flash of lightning that has arisen and vanished— of the form "this is not. Therefore, in its full form...
That which ought to be manifested up to the point of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) does not, for that long, become manifest;

thus, non-manifestation (*akhyāti*), consisting in incomplete manifestation, is itself the essence of error. By virtue of this, indeed, even other forms of manifestation—such as the manifestation of the non-existent, the contrary, or the indescribable—are said to occur.
The statement "tatraiva" establishes that this cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is of the nature of incomplete manifestation (*apūrṇakhyāti*).
For—since—at that time, during that very reflective awareness of silver, [one realizes] later:
"this was not silver"—meaning this silver did not exist, but was merely perceived by me through delusion.

Thus, there arises a subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form "it was known. However, in the case of a flash of lightning—which has arisen and subsided in a single moment, like a streak of lightning—there is no such reflective awareness as "this is not [the same]. Therefore:
For that reason, by means of its full form— extending up to reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), namely "this is silver," which extends up to the reflective awareness of reality,
meaning up to the point of final rest— the object standing before one must be made manifest.

It was necessary for that [object] to be manifested; yet, due to delusion (*bhrānti*), it is not well-known—that is, it does not manifest. For this reason, *akhyāti*—which is ignorance (*ajñāna*)—consists in incomplete manifestation, meaning it takes the form of incomplete knowledge rather than the mere absence of manifestation.

The reality of error (*bhrāntitattva*) is the very nature of error. The point is that if it were of the nature of the non-existence of appearance (*khyātyabhāvarūpatva*), then even the cognition of silver would be untenable; here, the negative particle (*nañ*) is used in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*) and not in the sense of absolute non-existence. Now, other disputants [hold that] in error there is the state of the appearance of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) and so forth.
Because they conduct their discourse [in this way], he says: "by the power of that" (*tadvaśena*).

By the power of that—that is, by the power of incomplete manifestation (*apūrṇakhyāti*)—let those various disputants assert manifestations such as the unreal (*asat*), the contrary (*viparīta*), or the inexpressible (*anirvācya*); what loss is there?
The sense is that, in this case, there is indeed incomplete knowledge (*apūrṇajñāna*), because of the apprehension of the mother-of-pearl as silver.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*) is included. Here, the proponents [of the theory] say:
"But surely even the cognition of real silver is an incomplete manifestation (*apūrṇakhyāti*). To this they reply: "So what of it?"

"From this, one might conclude that all of this is an illusion; fortunately, the vision of the venerable one shall open. For indeed, the entire realm of māyā is an illusion, yet even therein, it is like a dream within a dream."

They describe the nature of the five types of erroneous cognition (*khyāti*) individually. Among them, in the Buddhist doctrine of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), there is the theory of the appearance of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*). For they maintain that what is non-existent appears there as silver.
However, the followers of Bhaṭṭa and others maintain the theory of the appearance of the contrary (*viparītakhyāti*).

For they assert that a person, by the power of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), perceives silver existing in another place and time as being present in a location and time contrary to its actual state; this is the theory of the indeterminable manifestation (*anirvācyakhyāti*) in the Vedānta system, whereas they [the proponents of *anyathākhyāti*] hold otherwise.

They declare that error is indeed indefinable in terms of being either existent or non-existent, because it cannot be non-existent due to its manifestation, nor can it be existent due to the absence of any grasping by the hand.
In the Buddhist Vijñānavāda school, there is the theory of self-manifestation (*ātmakhyāti*), for according to them, it is the self itself that appears in error.
They say that it appears as an external object; as it has been stated:

"That which is the internal reality of the knowable appears as if it were external. However, for one of well-trained intellect, non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) consists in the form of incomplete apprehension (*apūrṇakhyāti*). And this very [non-apprehension]...
These are the desired [conclusions] of the author of the treatise; enough with this elaboration.

Herein, in the midst [of the discussion], the disciple asks: "But surely" (*nanu*). "Incomplete manifestation" (*apūrṇakhyāti*)—it is precisely of the nature of incomplete manifestation, because [it lacks] the knowledge of the state of being the supreme light (*paraprakāśarūpatā*).
The intended meaning is "because of the state of being full manifestation. The Guru also, having become a disciple, asks "then" (*tataḥ*).

The sense is: "If that were so, then what? What fault would there be? The disciple reveals the fault with the word "this" (*idam*). Regarding "therefore" (*ataḥ*): "This [fault] would come"—what is this?

"Everything is an illusion"— the entire range of appearing objects is an illusion according to the analogy of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. The Guru, indicating his acceptance of this position, encourages the disciple by saying, "By good fortune," meaning "by good fortune, O long-lived one, in this state of bliss."

—Your vision—the complete vision—will open up—that is, it will become manifest—because of the removal of the delusion regarding all objects. It is said "it will open up" (*unmīliṣyati*) because of the acceptance of the future tense according to the rules of logic (*tarka*); otherwise, one would have said "it has opened up" (*unmīlitā*).

To explain how this view is so, he says "illusion" (*māyā*). The term "illusion" refers to the differentiation that is the object of illusion. However, above illusion, everything is indeed truly real; let this suffice for now. Now, if that which appears as real...
If the entire collection of objects is then merely an illusion, this other delusion is said to be like a pustule upon a boil;
for even the reflective awareness (vimarśa) appropriate to continuity lacks stability. And therefore, there is no [reality] whatsoever in the separate appearances of "this-ness" and so forth.

As for the element of confusion, the eradication of the persistence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) regarding the aspect of their mixture is performed by the sublater starting from the very moment the reflective awareness arises; thus, it is established that the state of being an error resides precisely there. Although silver and mother-of-pearl may indeed be one...

[Objection: Even so, does there exist an error regarding silver in the mother-of-pearl by means of that cognition? To this he says, "In that case also" (*tatrāpi*). [This refers to] another [cognition] which is well-known as being an error.
[Objection: But is it not indeed appropriate for that which is well-known as an error to have the nature of an error?
To the question, "How is it logical for a cognition of real silver to be an error? he says: "anuvṛtti" (persistence).

"Anuvṛttyucitaḥ" means that which is appropriate for persistence; by the word "api" (also), it is indicated that there is no lack of possibility regarding the instability of what is commonly recognized as an error.

Furthermore, the instability of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that is appropriate for the state of persistence (*anuvṛtti*) should be understood as being caused precisely by its nature as the supreme reflective awareness of the "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*). For ultimately, everything flashes forth for yogins solely as the object of the reflective awareness of the "I"; otherwise, [it would not do so].
Their state is likewise one of ignorance.
As it has been said:
"This is darkness, which [consists in] regarding entities as being manifest."
"Even though [these objects] are not distinct from one's own self, this misconception of them as 'non-self' occurs.
He states his intended conclusion, which has been established by the aforementioned method, with the words "And therefore" (*ataśca*).
"Separately"—that is, in their respective domains; "none whatsoever," meaning not even the slightest. For this [is what is meant by] "this."
The [cognition] has as its object a thing standing foremost by way of reality, whereas the cognition "silver" has as its object the silver being remembered;
otherwise, even for one who has previously seen silver, the error of silver would arise regarding a mother-of-pearl shell.
In this same manner, the reality of stability and so forth should also be applied. Now, in that case, in which part does falsity reside?
Because this occurs, he says: "But in the aspect of unification.

In the aspect of unification—that is, in the part consisting of the establishment [of the object] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as "this very thing is silver endowed with qualities such as stability"—there is the persistence of the prior reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). It is of that [persistence]...

The eradication [of the previous cognition] is effected by the sublater—the subsequent reflective awareness—from the time of the arising of that [subsequent] reflection, meaning from the moment the previous reflection arose;
the sense is that this occurs through the production of a cognition such as, "This was not silver. Thus—for this reason—in that very [place]:
The state of being an error—that is, delusion—occurs precisely at the point of non-discrimination (*melanāṃśa*).
Relying on the aforementioned method, he provides the application [of the term] to the Sūtra with the words "of silver" (*rajatasya*).
There too, he first explains the compound word "even in the single reflective awareness of silver" (*rajataikavimarśe 'pi*).

Regarding the phrase "of silver": the words "together with mother-of-pearl" have been supplied here according to the context. Alternatively, this inclusion is justified by the rule stating that words whose meaning has already been expressed need not be repeated. He explains the word "api" (also/even) as "tathāpi" (nevertheless). The term "in mother-of-pearl" is explained through its very utterance (*nigada-vyākhyāta*). He explains the phrase "the persistence of silver" as follows:
Regarding the phrase "of silver":
that state which was presented as "this is silver" does not exist, because the locus of the mother-of-pearl— which is a limiting adjunct (upādhi)—
colors itself with the reflection of silver by means of the notion "silver is here."
Because of its lack of correspondence (*asaṃvāda*); "correspondence" (*saṃvādana*) is the manifestation through the persistence of correct investigation (*samyagvimarśa*).

Here, the root *vad* refers to the object of manifestation; because of the absence of that [correspondence], for that reason, he shows this by following the state of that cognition—that is, by following the state of erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "it is silver," the word "that" fulfills the expectancy of the word "which. The word "not" is also explained by its own utterance (*nigadavyākhyāta*), meaning "it does not exist. When the question "Why? arises, he explains [the following] in order to apply the reason "because of the non-correspondence with the location of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*") as the logical ground: "Since..."

And so forth. The term "deśa" (place), which functions as an *upādhi*—that is, as a qualifier—is explained by the word "atra" (here). By the phrase "rajatam atra" (silver here), in this manner, [the silver exists] through its own nature (*ātmanā*)—that is, by its own essential form denoted by the word "this" (*idam*), which stands as the substratum (*ādhārabhāvena*).
"Silver-like appearance" (*rajatacchāyām*) means a silver-like arrangement;

"coloring" (*uparañjayan*) means making it possessed of coloration, that is to say, manifesting it as delimited by its own nature being imposed [upon the substrate], for otherwise it would be impossible for it to function as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). "The locus of the mother-of-pearl" (*śuktideśaḥ*) means the locus whose very nature is mother-of-pearl.

The word "tasya" fulfills the expectancy of the word "yaḥ. He explains the word "sam" by saying "samyak," intending to explain [the phrase] "asaṃvādāt" as "of that [place], namely the locus of the mother-of-pearl.
Here too, he states a synonym, saying "vimarśa" (reflective awareness). By the persistence of this reflective awareness—namely, "there is silver here"—[the cognition is said to be "correct"].

By following the process of reflection (*vimarśa*), he explains the word "discourse" (*vāda*) as "manifestation" (*bhāsana*). Manifestation means appearing as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). He explains "dialogue" (*saṃvāda*) by compounding it as "conversing" (*saṃvādana*), [derived] from a noun stem ending in the suffix *ghañ*.
This explanation is based on the verbal root *bhās* ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*. Now, one might ask: how can "shining" (*bhāsana*) be the meaning here?

To this he says: "the root *vad*. The word "since" (*yataḥ*) should be construed here as being logically connected [to the preceding]. Because—on account of which—the root *vad* (the verbal root *vad*)—in this context, regarding the matter of shining—is the intended sense.

It means "to speak," because verbal roots have multiple meanings; this is the intended sense. Alternatively, one may read *kutaḥ* ("from where") in place of *yataḥ* ("since"); in that case, there is no need for any forced interpretation.
This applies to the negative particle (*nañ*) and the ablative case (*pañcamī*), which have been explained both distributively and collectively.
He performs a reflective consideration for the sake of application: "of that. "Of that" refers to the correspondence with the location of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);
"due to its absence" means because of its non-existence.
He clearly states the causality indicated by the ablative case: "because of the cause," since at a later time there is a desire for silver.
The summary of the point is this: once activity has occurred, that nacre does not manifest as the substratum of "silver-ness";

therefore, even though there was previously a single reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of "this is silver" involving both the silver and the nacre, the status of silver does not belong to the nacre. [This concerns] the silver's relation to the nacre.

A single reflective awareness (*ekavimarśa*) is the single reflective awareness of "silver. Indeed, silver is attributed [to the object] through erroneous cognition; let this be so in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver. However, in the cognition of two moons, where there is the appearance of "two moons," no conjunction with anything else—such as with mother-of-pearl—is manifested therein.
"You yourself have stated that there would be sublation (*bādha*) regarding one aspect of the appearance, while there is no sublation regarding the other aspect.

Who says this—that there is no conjunction with anything? For if this were so, how could there be an appearance characterized by its own specific nature (*svālakṣaṇya*) as being restricted to a particular place and time, [given that it must exist] together with that place and time?"

Even there, there exists an appearance of conjunction (*melanābhāsa*), wherein the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) desiring to manifest is obstructed [or determined, according to Kṣemarāja’s commentary].

The analysis of the compound is: "the state of being silver (*rajatasthitih*) exists within the appearance of conjunction, even in the case of the two appearances of duality and the moon. This is the application of the term "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*).

This [definition] was formulated with reference to the final cognition, because at the initial moment that [object] manifests as silver. By this, the explanation up to the words "due to correspondence" (*saṃvādāt*) is completed.
Now, an introductory transition is provided in order to explain the remainder of the verse beginning with "even in the case of a double moon" (*dvicandre 'pi*).
"Does it not act?"—the meaning is that this is the logical principle (*nyāya*). "In the appearance of two moons"—that is, in the form of that appearance.
"As with mother-of-pearl"—meaning together with the mother-of-pearl, as in the case of silver.
"Along with something"—meaning together with something [else], such as duality. "Where"—[refers to where this occurs].
In that conjunction (*melana*), there is the manifestation of one—*ekābhāsa*; [the word "in"] refers to that part which has such a form.

The Guru, providing the answer while establishing the method (*prakriyā*) to explain the portion of the verse, asks "What is this? He fulfills the expectancy of the word "this" by stating "conjunction. Thus.
The word "vā" (or) indicates the conclusion of the sentence. It supports the impossibility of conjunction by saying "for thus" (*evaṃ hi*).

"For" (*hi*) means because; "thus" (*evam*) means when there is no conjunction; "by way of a fixed place and time" (*niyatadeśakālatayā*) means by the established conjunction at a specific place and time, such as "now, here in the sky, there are two moons."

"How could there be an appearance according to its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)?"—the meaning is that it could not, because of the absence of a synthesis (*yojanā*) consisting of a conjoining [of elements]. For it has been stated many times that the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) consists precisely in its being conjoined with space and so forth; this is the intended sense. He states the conclusion with the word "tat" (that): that—

For that reason, even in that case—namely, in the cognition of two moons—there is an appearance of a conjunction with space and time; that is, there is a conjunction [the phrase "melanābhāsaḥ" implies "is there a conjunction?"—C.].
What is the sublater? This is the remainder of the sense. By the sublater as the agent—that which is the conjunction.
Desiring to follow along, while intending to pursue it, the investigation (*vimarśa*) is obstructed;

it is not that "two moons are here in the sky now" is brought within the scope of cessation—meaning, it is struck down. But surely, by this, there is no obstruction whatsoever to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the appearance of two moons?
It is established; for it exists merely as the conjunction of space and time. Therefore, he says:
"in duality. It must be stated—necessarily spoken—because the existence of a limited object abstracted from space and time is not observed; this is the sense. This—

The persistence and reversal of the reflective judgment (*vimarśa*) must be stated. This is what [the author] says: "Even in the case of the moon having two forms—not only in the case of silver [is there a sublation]. "Sky" (*nabhaḥ*) refers to a particular location. "Otherwise" means that which was reflected upon as being occupied by the double moon is not so; this is [indicated] by the sublater (*bādhaka*).
It is rendered such that the persistence of prior reflective awareness has been uprooted.

Thus, manifestation and their fusion are animated by necessity—this alone is the object of knowledge (*prameya*). These very things will be described as the *tattvas* in the scripture; the reality (*vastu*) is the *tattva*, which is the object of knowledge.
—these are the synonyms [synonym: K. ṣ. ṣ.]. Likewise, the appearance of solidity is earth; the appearance of redness is form and fire; the appearance of cohesion is *rajas*;
while the configuration (*saṃniveśa*) is of the nature of *niyati*. For *niyati* is restriction, and that has non-existence as its life-force.
