He says "tad etat" (this very thing) in order to explain the fragment of the aphorism through a concise statement;
"tad etat" refers to the subject matter just mentioned, and "āha" (he says) is the remainder [of the construction], meaning he says it by means of the fragment of the aphorism.
He explains the very fragment of the sūtra in order to render it free of further expectation: "dvirūpe" (in the two-formed). By this, the analysis of the compound is indicated as:
"the moon is of two forms—i.e., a double moon; in that [moon]. He introduces the word "nabhaḥ" (sky) in order to explain it: "nabhaḥ" (sky). [It refers to] a specific location, and not otherwise.
It possesses some form; otherwise, it would be impossible for it to serve as the substratum for the two moons and so forth—this is the intended meaning.
He explains "otherwise" with the words "the double moon": that region of the sky which is occupied by two moons—that is, occupied by two forms of the moon—is what is being considered.

Having been brought to the state of being an object of reflection by a prior reflection, it does not remain obstructed by a second moon; thus, by such a sublater—that is, by a sublater of this kind—it is rendered such that the persistence of the preceding reflection is uprooted. Thus [it is said].

The word "śabdaḥ" (the sound/word) marks the conclusion of the commentary. Thus is the construction (*yojanā*) in this section of the prose-exposition (*vākyakhaṇḍa*). The sense is that even the sky (*nabhaḥ*), acting as the agent, becomes otherwise [unreal] in the case of a double moon, because it contradicts what has been stated; here, following the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the object of cognition (*prameya*) is established for the sake of determination.

He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by way of summary with the word "thus" (*evam*). "Their union" (*tanmelana*) means the union of appearances (*ābhāsa*). "Animated by necessity" (*niyamānuprāṇita*) means established by the constraints imposed by necessity (*niyati*). He says that this is the very essential nature (*tattvabhāva*) of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
"These very [terms]" refers to what will be stated in the *Āgama* section—the *Āgamakāṇḍa*. Now, one might ask:

how can the object of knowledge (*prameya*) be designated by the word "reality" (*tattva*) in the *Āgama*? To this he says: "the thing" (*vastu*). This means they are synonyms—synonymous words. By the example of the jar, [this applies] to everything.
He explains that the entire class of objects of knowledge (*prameyajāta*) consists of all the *tattvas* with the words "and likewise" (*tathā ca*).
"The appearance of solidity" (*kāṭhinyābhāsa*) refers to the appearance in the form of solidity clearly present in a jar.
"Passion" (*rajas*) is the *tattva* of attachment (*rāga*), because attachment consists of the nature of conjoining. "Configuration" (*sanniveśa*) means arrangement.

"Having the nature of necessity" means having the nature of the principle of necessity (*niyati*). Now, one might ask: "In what sense does the arrangement [of things] possess the nature of necessity? To this he says: "Necessity. This refers to the restriction (*niyama*) established by the Supreme Lord;
and that restriction has non-existence as its life-force—that is, its existence is conferred by non-existence.
For it is precisely through the absence of identity that the manifestation of earth appears as manifold— the broad-based, bulbous form—
and the manifestation of difference is Māyā, and upon that, the manifestation of the light of reality.
Let us leave the Śiva-tattva for now; this will be addressed further on.

For the time being, it must be understood that regarding this object of knowledge (prameya), the Lord alone possesses sovereignty over both its differentiation and non-differentiation, and the perception of difference and non-difference in the appearances residing within the jar is likewise His alone.

It has been established that while the means for entering the vision of non-duality in the ultimate sense must be relied upon, this conventional practice is not contrary to the penetration into the nature of the Supreme Lord. || 13 ||
An entity is restricted to its own essential nature; and the manifestation of the non-existence of the appearance of earth, while shining— that is, appearing— through variety (*vaicitryeṇa*),
[consists in] having the form of a broad-based jar.

Such is the configuration fixed as "pot": the clay, abandoning its own previous form, assumes the configuration of the pot; otherwise, there would result a confusion between the pot and the clay, and the appearance of difference—the internal difference residing within the pot—would not occur.

Māyā—the principle of Māyā comes into being; on its back—that is, on the "back of Māyā" which consists of the manifestation of duality—there occurs the manifestation of the light of reality, namely the manifestation consisting of the agency of perception in the form "the jar shines," and this is the Śiva-principle. And here:

Having understood that the application of all the principles (tattvas) must be performed as a task—[having understood that the application is the task—C.]—he says, "let it be. Regarding the word "ahead," this refers to the section on scripture (āgamakāṇḍa);
this is the application of all the principles to every individual object. He states the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "in every way" (sarvathā). Here—
Regarding the form of the jar and so forth as it appears, "differentiation" (bhedana) means the act of differentiating—that is, appearing as differentiated.
For indeed, the determination of difference and non-difference occurs solely by virtue of manifestation (*prakāśa*).
Relying upon this, he shows a new path toward the way of liberation (*mokṣamārga*).

"Existing in the jar": the differentiation existing in the jar—the differentiation consisting of the manifestation of all the principles (tattvas) from the jar down to Māyā—and likewise non-differentiation—the non-differentiation whose nature is the Śiva-principle; the vision of these two is precisely that [and he is precisely that].

Regarding that entry into the vision which is non-dual in its ultimate nature, a means must be fully relied upon— that is, it must be resorted to. However, this is not even conventional usage— that is, conventional usage concerning objects such as jars— [is applicable] to the nature of the Supreme Lord.
Whatever entry there is, it becomes opposed [to that state], because even by means of that [entry],

through the form of seeking its own true nature, one attains the reality of the Supreme Lord, which is the essence of that [nature]. By the word "api" (even/also), [it is meant] by way of the cause for entering the nature of the Supreme Lord effected by meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

The conjunction of these two is illuminated here. The term "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) is employed with reference to the fact that the non-dual appearance determined by the Vedānta and other systems lacks the status of being an object for external worldly transaction. And it is not because of this alone that [the ultimate] is seized by those who are obsessed with the requirements of word-meanings.

This pride should be maintained; for only those who are free from the sense of "mine" regarding objects, and who perceive even the objects encountered in the flow of daily life as being Śiva himself, have the qualification for this practice. And in that state of freedom from possessiveness, one's own mind itself stands as the witness.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of self-contradiction; therefore, enough of this. || 13 ||
Clarifying this very point, he demonstrates that the establishment of all objects of knowledge depends solely upon the Supreme Lord:
"Difference [is established] by means of qualities such as sound, and non-difference by means of genus and so forth."
In this way, cultivation (bhāvanā) is established within a single cognizer. || 14 ||

Of this persisting and receding manifest reality, which form could be said not to be real? For there is no sublation (bādhaka) in either case; for if there were indeed a sublation of one or the other in its true nature, then upon the arising of that [sublation], that very part [would be unreal].

If it were devoid of the capacity for re-emergence, it would dissolve like a flash of lightning; but this is not the case, and for this very reason, the contradiction between difference and non-difference is difficult to resolve.
Thus, he provides the introduction to the fourteenth verse with the words "etadeva" (this very thing).

Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) establishes the method for explaining the verse with the words "here" (*iha*). It continues: "continuously" (*anuvṛtta*) by way of the universal form (*sāmānyākāra*); "excluded" (*vyāvṛtta*) by way of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); "shining" (*cakāsat*).
"Manifesting by its own form"—let it be said; however, the meaning is that it should be called "real" by its entire form. He states the reason for this with the words "in both cases as well.
"In both cases" means in the inclusive part and in the exclusive part. Now, here...
"Let it be a sublater as well"—what is the harm in that? To this he says:

"from the perspective of reality" (*satyataḥ*). "From the perspective of reality" means from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthena*); that is to say, among the two parts—the excluded and the recurring—it is within one of them. "Then" (*tat*) means at that time, upon its arising.
Upon the arising of a sublation (*bādhaka*), that very part—the part which is the object of sublation—is expressed again by means of a verbal application, with reference to its prior emergence.
"It would dissolve like a flash of lightning" (*vidyudvilāyam vilīyeta*) means "it would dissolve just like a flash of lightning. This refers to the object in the sense of comparison (*upamāna*).
And the particle *ca* indicates the suffix *ṇamul*. It is not the case that there is a sublation from the perspective of ultimate reality (*satyataḥ*) in either one; this is the meaning.

Regarding "difference and non-difference": it refers to the difference and non-difference residing in the recurring portion (*anuvṛttabhāga*), which effectively means the difference and non-difference residing in a single entity.
"Difficult to justify"— meaning impossible to establish—

both the self and the other [world], while some maintain that they are indeterminable as being of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), and others assert that they are merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) due to their attachment to appearances (*ābhāsa*).
He is deceived. However, both [subject and object] appear as resting within consciousness due to the sovereignty of consciousness.
For this is established by one's own self-awareness—even for every animal—that:
Even water and fire, when brought to a state of unity by resting within consciousness, are not contradictory; for this very reason it has been said:
"Therefore, according to the intended mental representation... (1.6.11).
By the Vedāntins, "as being ignorance" means, by way of secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*), as being an effect of ignorance;

"indefinability" (*anirvācyatva*) means the state of being indefinable in terms of existence and non-existence. For in the Vedāntic system, both ignorance and its effects are indeed indefinable. By others—the Buddhists—...

"By being attached to appearances"—meaning by resting solely upon appearances; the sense is that because they are conceptual, they lack external existence. "By those who assert" means by those who declare "the state of being conventional" (*saṃvṛtatva*), that is, "establishment through convention" (*saṃvṛtisiddhatva*). "Deceived" means deceived by delusion; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

For it is only the fool who deceives both himself and another; whereas he who deceives another alone is indeed more base than even that. Now, one might ask: what then is the nature of that duality? To this, [it is said]:

He says: "in consciousness" (*saṃvedane*). This means it is "rested in consciousness"—that is, in manifestation (*prakāśa*) and in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is inseparable from it; "rested in consciousness" means determined as being real by that [consciousness].
Now, one might ask: how can consciousness provide a resting place for two contradictory things within itself? To this [he replies]:

He says, "of consciousness. The sense is that there can be no obstruction for something independent from anything whatsoever, because that would entail the loss of its independence. Regarding this sentence as well, he states the reason: "of all.
For since it belongs to all—the entire class of sentient beings—even including animals—...

In the midst of that, even for a most dull-witted beast, this becomes established through its own self-awareness. What is this? Even the "flaming of water"—that pair of water and fire, though renowned as contradictory—becomes non-contradictory when it comes to rest within consciousness, as if it were external.

Because there is an absence of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator between them. He recalls what was stated previously as an illustration here with the words "for that very reason. When the expectation arises as to what was said, he indicates the verse briefly with the words "for this very reason."
In response to the expectation of what was said, he shows a portion of the *kārikā* with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
And for this reason, by means of the qualities (*guṇa*) which function as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that is, by way of being adjuncts [which bring about specific distinctions]—[K. ṣ.].

Furthermore, there is the differentiation of entities by means of intended objects such as sound and so forth, or even by means of sticks and the like; and there is their non-differentiation due to genus, similarity, or the non-apprehension of difference—
this being the manner in which the connection with action has been established from the point where it was stated, "in this way" (2.2.1), onwards.

He is the Blessed One, who dwells as the sole refuge within our hearts, possessing a sovereignty suited for the manifold and innumerable display of diverse functions— such as the conjunction and disjunction of all cognitions and means of knowledge— within a single cognizing subject.
"This is possible only when there is that which is designated by the term *Śiva*, and not otherwise.

Thus, he explains the verse by relying on the aforementioned methodology, beginning with the words "And therefore" (*ataśca*). He explains the word "by qualities" (*guṇaiḥ*) as "in the form of limiting adjuncts" (*upādhirūpaiḥ*). Here too, he provides a further explanation.

"By way of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). The sense is that a quality (*guṇa*) is indeed merely a differentiator. He states the object included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) with the words "also by means of sticks, etc. In the phrase "by means of sound, etc.," the word "etcetera" includes form (*rūpa*) and so forth; whereas in the phrase "by means of sticks, etc.," the word "etcetera" [includes]...

Regarding the mention of "spears and so forth" (*kuntādigrahaṇam*): there is no contradiction whatsoever in taking both "form and so forth" (*rūpādi*) and "spears and so forth" (*kuntādi*) as the referents of the single word *ādi* occurring in the sūtra. He explains [the phrase] "non-difference from genus and so forth" (*jātyādibhirabhinnatā*) by the word "genus" (*jāti*). Here too, he states the objects to be grasped by the word *ādi* with the words "on account of similarity" (*sādṛśyāt*), and so forth.

"Bhāvānām" (of entities) is explained by the words themselves (*nigadavyākhyātam*). He explains the word "ittham" (thus) as "by the aforementioned method. For the word "nirūpitaḥ" (demonstrated), the verb [is] to be supplied (*adhyāhāraḥ*). He fulfills the expectancy of the two occurrences of the relative pronoun "yat" with the word "saḥ" (that). "Saḥ" refers to difference (*bhedaḥ*).

And he explains that there is non-difference "in a single cognizer" by the word *sakala* (the one-with-all). Regarding the phrase "separation and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the granting of repose and other such acts. He says "in the Blessed Lord" because even one who is independent [but not the Lord] is powerless and thus incapable of acting; [this refers to] such an external entity.
Since it is not logical for there to be a state of being an impeller within internal perceptions, he says: "in our own" (*asmadīya*).

This means: in that [perception] which rests—meaning it abides as the essence and as the impeller—with absolute certainty (*ekāntena*) in our heart; "not otherwise. The meaning is that without such [a perception], [the state of being an impeller] is not tenable.
For even difference (*bheda*) attains its establishment only by way of the two factors— the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)—
as in the expression "this is different from that. In that context, there is the locus indicated by the nominative case,
the counter-correlative indicated by the ablative case, and the difference itself established through those two.

If there were no unifying factor— whether consisting of the three cognitions as a single mass or being their essential core— that could link the various distinct cognitions of their respective objects, how could the apprehension of the property of difference be established? For if they were apprehended without distinction, [difference would be impossible].
Since the requirement for a unifier is accomplished without effort, what is the use of establishing it? Furthermore,
since the qualifiers themselves are the differentiators, what is the need for other ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣas*)— such as "this is that atom" and "this is that atom"?

At the time of the formation of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) that subsequently combines— occurring at the time of the production of the jar qualified by this particular place and so forth— that very self which previously joined together is this one who was formerly...
"He embraced this celestial woman in the abode of heaven"— by this much alone,
indeed, for the yogins, the omniscient ones, and so forth,
[the distinction is established] through the ultimate particulars (antyaviśeṣas) in the treatises on logic.

The distinction among eternal substances has already been stated; however, you have now stated that sound and the others are the distinguishers by way of their generality (*sāmānya*). To this he replies: "And they are indeed qualifiers. This is because they are described as distinct from other [substances]—that is, different from sound and so forth—and as distinct from the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*).

The state [of being]. By "final particulars" (antyaiḥ viśeṣaiḥ), the meaning is "by ultimate particulars" (antyaviśeṣaiḥ). Now, one might ask: how could yogins possibly possess a cognition of difference through gross objects such as sound and so forth with respect to extremely subtle things like atoms? To this he says: "This is that. This refers to him.

It becomes an atom (*paramāṇu*). What is it? It is that which is distinguished by this place and so forth—that is, the subsequent, composite, and joined dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) which exists at the time of the origination of that jar delimited by this particular place and time.
At the time of its commencement, it is "conjoined"—that is, joined with another atom.
The word "previously" implies "in relation to the second atom. By this much alone—by the mere quality called conjunction—there [occurs] that of the atom with respect to another atom.
[This is] a conjunction; indeed, it is the self’s conjunction with the celestial nymph, not the body’s conjunction with the celestial nymph. If you object that this is so, it is true;
however, such [distinctions] are not [necessary] in a discussion with logicians who possess only a coarse vision.
This is the occasion for subtle scrutiny; for in the investigation of ultimate reality, when the entire world is of the nature of Śiva,
what distinction can there be between the omniscient and the yogi, what division between eternal and non-eternal substances, or what determination regarding the category of ultimate particularity?

Relying on the maxim "as is the Yakṣa, so is the offering," and out of compassion for his disciples, it is not appropriate for one who is keen on raising objections toward the Great Teachers who have engaged in various activities here and there.

Thus it is. Alternatively, in the context of Great Non-duality (mahādvaita), both the establishment of everything and the negation of everything are entirely possible; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-duality being merely apparent. Enough of this.
Anticipating that much more remains to be said on this matter, he says:

The appearance of difference regarding atoms, the self, and so forth, is established—enough with this digression. Thus, the reality of the object of knowledge, which consists of both difference and non-difference, attains a state free from doubt by resting within the single subject. || 14 ||

Now, if this cognizer is of such a nature, then one should indeed strive to present the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there, rather than the object of cognition (*prameya*), as it has been said: "For effort directed toward the primary [goal] is fruitful. Anticipating this objection, he [reiterates] the very object of cognition that was introduced at the outset.
The Teacher reminds us:
"For indeed, who that is not insentient could effect either a negation or an affirmation? (1.1.2).
This refers to whatever object [is in question] now that the nature of the means of knowledge and the nature of the Supreme Lord have been understood.
And it is worthy of being sustained; for such is valid cognition, and how could it apply to the Blessed One who is of such a nature? To clarify this, he says:
"In that which is comparable to a perfectly level wall for the variegated painting of the world's diversity..."
When there is contact with the absence of the contradictory, [it occurs] in the Lord who exists in the ultimate sense. || 15 ||

The word *alam* means "by way of an irrelevant [topic]. The sense is that here, in this context, only the unity of the subject (*pramātṛaikya*) is the relevant topic. He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) as an accomplished fact, saying: "consisting of both difference and non-difference. In that regard:

The distinction is that it has the form of non-difference by way of its universal aspect (sāmānyabhāva), and the form of difference by way of its particular aspect (svalakṣaṇabhāva). By this, it is indicated that this chapter shares a single subject matter with the preceding chapter. || 14 ||
Now, he provides the introductory commentary for the fifteenth and sixteenth verses with the words:
"nanvevaṃbhūtaḥ" (But [one might ask], being such as this...).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
"By way of elaboration" (*prapañcena*)— [namely, "in this manner"]— he begins the exposition here with the words "tathā hi" (for instance). Whatever thing exists,
whatever was previously asserted, that very same thing is now [to be established] by means of the nature of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

When [the nature of] the object is known, it becomes fit for a conclusion (*nirvāhaṇa*). Why so? Because the Self is non-inert (*ajaḍātman*), and so forth—this is the connection. "The object" (*vastu*) means the object to be determined, that which is fit for a conclusion, capable of being concluded;
that is to say, capable of being summarized. He demonstrates this very conclusion by way of imitation:
"Thus constituted" (*evaṃbhūtam*) means: that which has the aforementioned form, that is to say, characterized by a constant arising of ever-new [cognitions].

"In one thus constituted"—meaning in that which consists of the unity of all knowledge—"let it proceed," which means it would become fit for apprehension. To make this clear—to elucidate—it is said—he speaks.

Having thus provided the introduction and presented two verses, he explains them with the word "viśva" (the universe): "But what new manifestation could serve as a means of knowledge regarding the primordial subject, whose form is always manifest and who partakes in all cognitions? (16)

It has been stated that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the ever-new manifestation directed toward the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which is grounded in the limited subject (*parimitapramātṛ*). In that case, what utility or even possibility could there be for a means of knowledge regarding that which is already established, whose body is light, and whose very nature is pure luminosity? And so it is said:

When the subject (pramātṛ) is already established, the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) bestows upon the object of knowledge (prameya) an unprecedented establishment consisting of reflective awareness (vimarśa), which is included within the light that is conjoined with that subject. But for a subject who is himself unestablished— [rather, one who is primordially established]— what could there be to which an establishment might be conjoined?

For the manifold variety of the universe shines forth within that Supreme Lord, whose nature is pure light, just as a painting appears upon a wall. If indeed blue, yellow, and so forth were perceived as entirely separate from one another,
then, while resting within their own respective selves, they would likewise remain distinct in relation to one another's domain.
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*),
while establishing the method for explaining the verse, recalls the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) previously stated for its utility, beginning with the words "parimita" (limited).

"Bound to a limited subject"—that is, resting in the apprehender; "manifestation"—meaning cognition—as stated in the verse beginning with "this is such-and-such. There—meaning, this being the nature of the means of knowledge—he himself explains [the phrase] "whose body is light" by saying "mere light."
Having recognized the absolute unsuitability of [the object] for utilization, he says "or possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*).

To support this very point, he says "and thus" (*tathā ca*). "Being" (*sati*) means it possesses existence; "attached to that" (*tallagna*) refers to that light which rests in the subject (*pramātṛviśrānta*), and that which is included within it—
"Consisting of that" means consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is to say, having the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*). "Bestows"—that is, confers or produces.

It is said to be "unprecedented" with respect to the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely, the capacity to apprehend an object not yet apprehended. Regarding the phrase "of that which is unestablished": therein also...

The meaning is that, even when the employment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is accepted, [this occurs] for one who lacks prior establishment before the operation of the *pramāṇa*. Where is it fixed? It is fixed somewhere within that which is the locus of rest for all things.

The sense is that if one were to accept [the universe] as the locus of rest for the cognition of its own object, it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and so forth; furthermore, no other locus of rest is perceived. Now, one might object: "Let that [consciousness] also rest in that very place where the universe rests. To this, he says: "In that [place]," regarding the word *viśva*.

Since it stands as that which is to be established, in response to the inquiry "how does it appear?", he says "just as" (yathā); the meaning is: just as a painting appears on a wall, so too [does this]. Now, one might object: let the universe be independent in itself, and thus its establishment may rest therein alone; to this he says: "for if... (yadi hi).

Thus: "separately indeed"—meaning distinct by virtue of its own predominance, and not by way of resting within the subject. He fulfills the expectation of the word "yadi" (if) with the words "tadā" (then). "In them"—that is, in blue, yellow, and so forth—"in that very same way."
Cognitions are like those who are dull-witted, blind, or deaf, being restricted solely to their own respective objects;

and since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise in accordance with them, they are likewise so restricted. Thus, how can there be a realization that "this is variegated"? For [such a realization] would have to occur in a single place, such as a wall surface devoid of depressions, elevations, and the like.

Just as it is logical for there to be a variegated appearance— such as "this woman has a deep navel and elevated breasts"— in that which possesses divisions like depressions and elevations demarcated by lines, so too is the occurrence of differentiation, consisting of manifold variety, possible because [all things] are attached to the single wall of Light. Thus.
He declares its self-luminosity, which never departs from the wall of light that perceives the distinctions between states of being.

In that regard, what need is there for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which is self-luminous? If it is argued that its manifestation did not previously exist, then it would follow that it does not exist at all, because its very nature consists solely in being manifest. Nor...
The notion that "this does not exist" results in a contact with non-existence;

for he alone is real from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because only luminosity (*prakāśa*) exists, and because it is impossible for that which exists to have the nature of non-existence.
Now, it might be argued: his state of being the Lord (*īśvaratā*) is un-...
Just like blue, yellow, and so forth, they are like those who are dull-witted, blind, or deaf; that is,
similar to the dull-witted, blind, and deaf, they are restricted solely to their own objects— that is,
they reach their conclusion merely in the apprehension of the blue, yellow, and other objects that have become their respective domains.

And as for conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)— namely, the conceptualizations of blue, yellow, and so forth that arise immediately after the cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth— which exist in accordance with those [cognitions], obtaining their existence by following after cognition, and which are thus like those who are insentient, blind, or deaf; therefore:
For what reason? How is this realization possible—how, by doing what, could it be so?

Why is this asked? Because this entire universe exists as a variegated painting (*citram*). Furthermore, where is the realization of such a painting appropriate? To this he says: "In one place" (*ekatra*). But the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction.
"Variegated appearance" refers to the cognition of a woman who exists as a painting.

Having stated the illustration, he states the illustrated point with the words "in the same way. "Consisting of variety" means that the diversity which takes the form of the manifold universe—its establishment [is explained].
The capacity for abiding as a manifold manifestation [exists], the word "becomes" being understood as the ellipsis.

By this, the first half of the preceding verse has been explained. Thus—for this reason—the Teacher [states that] the light which consists of the apprehension of entities through their differentiation—
The limited knowledge belongs to that wall—the supreme subject who constitutes the wall;

[the text] declares his self-luminosity, the state of being self-manifesting, by means of the phrase "in the manifest form. He provides an introductory transition in order to explain the words beginning with "contradictory" (*viruddhe*).

Now it is said: "of this"—that is, of the knower; "he himself"—that is, the knower alone—"thus would be"—it would become so. To the question "Why?", he says: "because he is pure light. For it is not possible to say that whatever possesses a certain nature can exist in the absence of that nature.

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. To address the doubt, "But let that [subject] not exist," he explains [the phrase] "in ultimate reality" (*paramārthasati*) with the words "and not... (*na ca*). Of this—the subject (*pramātṛ*) whose nature is light. To address the doubt, "Why? he says, "Because... (*yataḥ hi*). [This means] because light alone is existence (*sattva*), since...
Nor can it be said that it will be measured (pramāsyate) by means of a supreme measure (prakarṣeṇa mitā), because if it did not manifest as the subject (pramātṛtvena),
whose would this effort be? And if it does manifest, then...

The state of being the subject (*pramātṛtā*) itself is sovereignty (*īśvaratā*). Thus it is said: "In the Lord, the subject, whose form is eternally manifest. It is called *vigraha* because it is specifically grasped—that is, its own unique nature (*asādhāraṇa-svarūpa*). For this very reason, it consists of autonomous manifestation (*svatantra-prakāśa*).

The temporal convention that arises through the contact with non-existence—that is, by entering into non-existence (or, as Kṣemarāja reads: "by entering into non-existence where there is no possibility of contact with non-existence")—does not exist here;
thus it is stated in the *Purāṇa*. In that regard, what is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and for what purpose is there a need for a means of knowledge?
Because its nature is to manifest, only that which is luminous (*prakāśa*) exists; it becomes the agent of action, whereas that which is non-luminous does not.

Even though it exists externally, people say "it shines here" with respect to this location. [The opponent might argue: "Let there be the non-existence of that which exists. To this he says: "and of the non-existent. The sense is that these two are contradictory.
He provides an introductory transition in order to apply the three qualifiers—“in the Lord,” “the cognizer,” and “whose form is always manifest”—with the words, "Now it is said.
[The phrase] *pramāsyate* means "will be made an object of valid cognition. In response to the question "Why?", he says, "For... [and] *cakāsyāt*.

It would manifest by virtue of its own self-luminosity. This "effort" (*udyama*)—the exertion consisting in making *īśvaratā* (divine sovereignty) the object of valid cognition—is such that subjectivity itself is *īśvaratā*. And thus, there is no requirement for *īśvaratā* to be made the object of valid cognition, nor...
For the knower is fit for being made the object of a cognition. As it has been said:
"If the self were to become an object of knowledge, there would be another as its knower."
Having thus provided the introduction, he applies the three qualifiers;
"he says this" is the sense, with the word "the author of the aphorisms" (*sūtrakāra*) being the ellipsis.

When the expectation arises as to what he says, he states the three qualifiers by repeating them, beginning with "in the Lord" (*īśvare*). This is because the term *vigraha* (etymological analysis) is difficult to understand.

He explains [the term] by distinguishing it specifically: "specifically" means in the state of being specific, that is to say, as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Relying on this, he explains the word "in the Purāṇa" with the words "for this very reason. Because its nature is independent luminosity (*svatantra-prakāśa*), it shines at all times.
Because it has been stated by this very term, and because its essential nature is that of self-predominant luminosity;
due to the impossibility of contact with non-existence— that is, the absence of contact with antecedent non-existence—
there occurs the conventional designation of time, namely the conventional designation of the time of origination, "here" in this subject.

The meaning is that the "ancient" (purāṇa) is indeed the very counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). He introduces the question "What is the proof? in order to explain it; he provides a threefold application of the word *kiṃ* because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Why? [He asks: "From what? (kutaḥ).

"What is the utility of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there?"— the meaning is that in that case, no means of valid cognition whatsoever is logically tenable. For what is called a "means of valid cognition" consists of a novel manifestation (*navābhāsa-rūpa*) within the cognizer.

A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) becomes such by effecting a repose characterized as valid knowledge (*pramiti*); likewise, the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), whose manifestation is uninterrupted, experiences all acts of valid knowledge within himself in his inward-turned nature.
Therefore, how could there be a new manifestation or a new act of valid knowledge regarding that [Self]?
[Regarding] the manifestation (ābhāsa): where could it find rest?
Therefore, let it be said that the subject is essentially nothing more than the body, the vital breath, the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), and the void;
and even there, if [it rests] in the objective aspect (vedyāṃśa), but by no means in the aspect of consciousness (saṃvid-aṃśa), even in that case—
Thus [he says]. He explains "ninefold manifestation" with the words "because.

The meaning is that the object called "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*)—that is, the entity known as a means of knowledge—is of the nature of a ninefold manifestation, because this has been stated by the phrase "newly arising" (*abhinavodaya*). [He also mentions] "characterized by valid cognition," which means having the form of valid knowledge (*pramā*).

"Rest" (*viśrānti*) means rest in external objects; "uninterrupted manifestation" (*avicchinnābhāsa*) means uninterrupted luminosity; "he partakes" (*bhajate*) means he resorts to [it] as the locus of rest—this is the meaning.
"Therefore" (*tat*): for that reason; "in him" (*tasmin*): in the subject (*pramātṛ*); "new manifestation" (*abhinavābhāsa*).
Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the form of a novel manifestation; the ellipsis is "that which establishes reality.
For it is not logical that a manifestation of something already manifested (*avicchinnābhāsa*) should establish the reality of what is manifested as distinct (*vicchinnābhāsa*).
He states another defect as well: "and its resulting cognition" (*tatpramitiśca*). And its resulting cognition—
And where could valid cognition—produced by the means of knowledge and directed toward objects—come to rest?

For all cognitions produced by the means of knowledge come to rest in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), because that is his very nature; otherwise, in all applications [of cognition], [one would have to say] "I..."

Because the use of the word "I" is inappropriate in expressions such as "I know," the cognition of the self does not find its rest while that [self] is being established by itself; thus, the implication is that the absence of such rest would necessarily follow for it. He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore."

In that which is almost void of the body, the vital breath, and the *puryaṣṭaka*—that is, in that which is nearly empty of the body, the vital breath, and the intellect—the inclusion of the word "almost" (*prāya*) serves to exclude ultimate subjectivity (*pāramārthika-pramātṛtva*). Otherwise, it would be impossible to speak of its being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-viṣayatva*). For the quartet beginning with the body is inherently external.
It is indeed the internal [subject] as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the external object (*prameya*).

And even there— in the body and so forth, within the objective portion (*vedyāṃśe*), that is, in the part consisting of the object of knowledge— if that [body] were indeed the means of knowledge, it could not in any way whatsoever [be so] in the aspect of consciousness (*saṃvid-aṃśe*).

That [cognition] becomes a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in respect to the aspect of the subject (*pramātṛbhāga*); even though the operation of a means of valid knowledge occurs only in respect to the aspect of the object (*prameyabhāga*) regarding external things, and not in respect to the aspect of consciousness (*saṃvidbhāga*) which consists of manifestation, nevertheless, let this matter rest for now as it is not relevant to the present context. Furthermore, in that regard—[namely], in that which pertains to the body and so forth—
Even in the aspect of consciousness,

because it is contracted precisely due to its orientation toward objects, let it be described in relation to its connection with the true subject who is free from contraction, within the manifestation of the ever-new (abhinava).

Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Even by the Buddhist, that [self-awareness] must be accepted as being connected to an imagined cognizer (*pramātṛ*) in the form "this is my cognition"; however, nothing at all is established by a means of valid cognition with respect to the ultimate cognizer (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*). And this has been stated by me alone:
Everyone feels ashamed within themselves at the thought, "I have been made an object of knowledge";
how then could that Great Lord endure being made an object of knowledge?
Thus [ends the section]. 16.
Now, if it is thus the case that the Blessed One is neither a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) nor subject to logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*), for what purpose [is he invoked]?
Precisely because he is oriented toward objects—that is, for the reason that he is contracted, being the object of contraction—in the form of a fresh manifestation (*abhinavābhāsa*). Therefore...

Thus, with respect to that ultimate subject called "Light"— the true subject who is devoid of contraction— it is, by way of its dependence on being attached to Him, and not in an ultimate sense, "self-awareness" (svasaṃvedana),
meaning awareness that constitutes one's own essential nature, which is the means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

"Let it be said: because [the object] is an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) with respect to the supreme consciousness (*para-saṃvit*), which is itself unconditioned despite being conditioned; otherwise, this very [object] would result in being the supreme consciousness itself—this is the intended meaning.
Now, the Vijñānavādin asserts that it rests solely within itself; otherwise...
Because it would be inconsistent with the doctrine of Vijñānavāda, he says "by the Saugata.

That—knowledge whose nature consists of the aspect of consciousness—is "to be accepted" (upetyam), meaning it must be admitted; it is described as "imagined" (kalpitā) with reference to the fact that the Saugatas do not admit an ultimate subject (paramārtha-pramātṛ).
In the ultimate knower—the true knower whose nature is that of Paraśiva—there is "something," that is, anything at all.

As it has been said: "Even the means of knowledge [are nothing] for things... Here, he says "And it is said" (*uktaṃ ca*) in order to provide his own verse as an illustration. To the question "What is said?", he replies with "That which" (*yat*), meaning "because."
For this reason, every single person—that is, all people—feels shame; that is, they assume the state of being the agent of shame.

Why is this so? Because by this [act], I have been made an object of cognition—that is, known—and determined as to what my essence is, up to the point of being weighed. Therefore, for that reason, this...
How could Maheśvara tolerate being made an object of cognition? For one who is not the Lord merely feels shame because he is incapable of resisting being made an object of cognition by force;
the Lord, however, being capable, does not tolerate it even in the slightest degree, since [the object] is of the nature of his own self.
The meaning is that it is simply not logical for the Supreme Lord to be an object of cognition. || 16 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the seventeenth verse: "But if it be so," etc. Here the commentary says:
"In this way"—meaning by the manner already described; "and untenable"—meaning devoid of logical justification—and "inconsistent."
The treatise has that [reality] as its object; for it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since a treatise consists of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).

And in that regard, its ultimate purpose is precisely to consist of the reality of the sixteen categories, beginning with the means of valid cognition. As for that which is criticized by the Buddhists, such as the necessity of five members [in a syllogism], [it is not the ultimate purpose].

That is merely a dogmatic insistence; for when the sixteen categories are investigated, the other person is correctly instructed by means of the text beginning with, "The one to be instructed is properly instructed regarding the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful," and so forth. What [is gained] for the other?

The purpose [of this treatise] is indeed for the sake of another's comprehension, and that comprehension arises from inference for others (*parārthānumāna*); furthermore, the thesis (*pratijñā*) and other members are useful therein. Therefore, in the ultimate sense, the entire treatise—which brings about the complete comprehension of another—is itself inference for others.
That which is distinct from scripture was formulated by Akṣapāda, the creator of logic (*nyāya*).
To this [objection], he says—beginning with "but here too" (1.1.3)—in order to remind us of what was previously stated.
Up to the point where he says: "having that as its object"—meaning that which designates the Blessed One—"that," namely the treatise (*śāstra*), why? [is it not so?]

To show that it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*). It consists of inference for the sake of others—that is, it has the form of inference for the sake of others. In that treatise, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of abundance; [this work] is refuted—that is, rejected—by the followers of Sugata (the Buddhists).

Because, in his view, the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth have already been rejected. "That" refers to the refutation; the meaning is that it is merely dogmatic insistence, merely obstinacy. To the question "Why?", he says:
"In the sixteen [categories]. That which is to be established—the object to be expressed—is what is being established.

It is made known—that is, it is being taught—to another, namely the one being instructed, by means of a treatise (*grantha*), which refers to the collection of sentences accepted by the Buddhists; the word "etc. includes other [such] sentences. Whatever the purpose of that other person—the follower of the Sugata—[may be].

Since that very [reason] applies to us as well, he says "taddhi" (for that). "Tat" refers to that treatise; "sā ca" refers to the cognition produced in the other person being instructed; and "tatra ca" refers to inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter (*prameya*). By this, [the author] also [refutes] the Buddhist position regarding the five-membered syllogism and so forth.

He was made to accept it through reasoning. He states that this has borne fruit with the words "that": for that reason, [it is] distinct from scripture—that is, distinct from the scriptural treatises—because, by virtue of its being the instructor of the great secret, it is even more direct than perception.

Because it is improper to describe [it] as inference on the grounds of its superiority; by the "Creator of the System" (nyāyanirmāṇavedhasā)—that is, by the one equal to Brahmā in the composition of the Nyāya-śāstra, meaning the author of the Nyāya-śāstra;
"iti"—for this reason; "having thus suspected"—that is to say, having raised such a doubt; "here too"—in this very context.
In the verse that is about to be explained, the word "api" (also/even) serves to indicate a conjunction with the preceding verse; for there too, it is for the purpose of reminding— specifically,
to urge those prone to forgetfulness toward mindfulness by way of recollection.
"Previously, no such usage had occurred here except through the power of delusion; now, by the manifestation of [His] power, the conventional usage of 'Īśa' and so forth is set in motion. (17)
In this regard, this alone is the supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord:

namely, the accomplishment of things that are exceedingly difficult to achieve and utterly impossible for those in our condition—those in the specific state of the primitive beast. And for this reason as well:

What could be more difficult than this: that while the Light shines forth in its own undivided nature, there appears the manifestation of the negation of that shining? Therefore, that is the supreme [belonging to the Supreme Lord] of the Supreme Lord.

That very sovereignty which consists in not manifesting in such a way—[rather] manifesting in that way—is what is called "the manifestation of the state of being a bound soul" (paśu-rūpatā), namely, the arousal of the subjective aspect;
this is the meaning of the word "it says," in terms of its actual sense. Having thus provided the introduction:
Having presented the verse, he explains it with the words "apravartita" (not set in motion).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) establishes the methodological process (*prakriyā*) in order to explain the phrase "by the force of delusion" (*mūḍhatāvaśāt*).

Thus: "Supreme" means unsurpassed; those extremely difficult things which were impossible for us—who possess the particular former state of a beast, that is, the specific condition of being a beast in a previous time—to conceive of.

The principles (tattvas) range from Sadāśiva down to the Earth; their "accomplishment" means their manifestation. Now, one might ask: why is the accomplishment of these entities so exceedingly difficult? To this he says, "And for this reason.
He fulfills the requirement of the word "from this" by saying "since. [This occurs] within the nature of Light—that is, within that which is of the form of Light.

In the case of another subject (*parapramātṛ*), whose nature is that of undivided identity— that is, whose essence is light— the manifestation of the negation of that manifestation takes the form "it does not shine.
Such [negation], while being manifest— meaning its very nature is to pulsate— is of this kind.

In the Vedānta texts, independence (*svātantrya*) is treated as being synonymous with obstruction (*pratibandha*). As it has been said: "When an object is fit for the empirical usage of 'it exists' and 'it appears,' the production of its opposite by setting that [usage] aside is called obstruction."
Thus [he says]. He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*): therefore—meaning for that reason—the supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord exists.
What is that? It is that non-manifestation in such a manner—[of] the Supreme Lord—...
And by means of that, there is also the manifestation of the object of perception (*grāhya*). This very thing is called the Lord’s power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*).
As it has been said:
"Māyā is named 'the deluder'..."

Thus, from such sovereignty— which is of the nature of the power of *māyā*— there arises that state of delusion, which is the destruction of full consciousness, [occurring] within one's own self that is filled with the manifestation of the universe, clearly pulsing through the emergence of the vibration of will.

Of fullness, whose self is filled by the universe vividly throbbing through the arising of the vibration of desire; of sovereignty, whose nature consists of powers such as memory and so forth; and of that which possesses the quality of eternal majesty, spontaneously accomplished due to the absence of the limitations of space and time.

Even for that which is manifesting, there occurs through its own being an arousal of the subjective aspect in the form of non-manifestation; and likewise, by means of that— that is, by means of the arousal of the subjective aspect— ...
The manifestation of the object of apprehension occurs; this very [manifestation] is that which has been described as having the nature of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).
Here, he cites the consensus of the elders, saying "as it has been said. "Deluding" means causing delusion;
the word "iti" marks the end of the elders' statement. By relying on the aforementioned method, this—

Intending to explain the term *pada*, he provides a summary with the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way). "From such a state" means from that which consists in the manifestation of the condition of being a bound soul (*paśutā*); "from sovereignty" means by reason of autonomy (*svātantrya*).
He explains the component part "stupefaction" (*mūḍhatā*) with the word "vinaṣṭa" (destroyed). Of this term as well—

Providing the commentary himself, he offers an explanation of the component "pūrṇa" (full) as "svātmani" (in one's own self). [The meaning is: of such a one who exists within his own self; likewise, by the arising of that vibration (*spanda*) which consists of will, all things have become clearly manifest (*sphuritāḥ*).

The "entities" (bhāvāḥ) are the categories of existence; the "fullness" (nirbharatā) is that which consists of their very self, their nature—that is, fullness, the state of being complete. Of what nature?
Of sovereignty (svātantrya), whose essence consists of the powers of memory and so forth.

Of that which consists of the sovereignty (svātantrya) whose nature is the triad of powers beginning with memory—by this, the analysis of the word's components as "consciousness" (cetanatā) is provided. Furthermore, of what kind? Of that which is devoid of limitation by space and time—that is, free from contraction caused by space and time—and which possesses the attributes of all-pervasiveness and eternity, established without effort.

Of such a one who possesses the two qualities known as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and eternity (*nityatā*): therein, due to the absence of spatial limitation, the quality of omnipresence is established without effort; and due to the absence of temporal limitation, the quality of eternity is established without effort—this is the sequence.
It should be understood as follows:
by virtue of— that is, through the power of— the conceit that [the object] is not manifesting,
[the subject] previously did not proceed toward the cognizer whose nature was described in the two preceding verses.

Let people employ that very linguistic usage regarding the Blessed One—such as "He is full," "He is all-pervasive," "He is independent," and "He is eternal"—which is indeed based on the attributes of lordship and so forth already mentioned;
for that which shines as "I" is indeed full, all-pervasive, autonomous, and eternal, and so on. Let the world proceed with such a conventional designation.

By this scripture— which consists of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) aimed at accomplishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which is of the nature of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that reveals the powers of will, knowledge, and action—
the performance of what is conducive to that [recognition] is carried out for those who set forth that transaction.

The word "pravartyate" (is set in motion) contains two *ṇic* suffixes. By the word "kevalam" (merely), it is meant that nothing new is created, nor is something that is not actually manifest made manifest; rather, it refers to the misconception that what is already manifest does not manifest.

Thus he explains even the individual member [of the compound] with the word "yat" (that which). By the term "abhimananam" (the act of conceiving), the non-ultimate reality of the state of not being manifest is indicated.
He provides the construction of the genitive case with the words "tasyāḥ" (of that); "tasyāḥ" means "of that delusion."

He explains "by the power" as "by the capacity. He explains "never previously set in motion" as "previously. "Previously" means in the state of delusion. He explains "the worldly usage of 'Lord' and so forth" as "complete. "By completeness and so forth" means by the state of being complete and so forth. Of what kind [is it]?

In response to the expectation "What is this worldly transaction (vyavahāra)?", he says: "He who indeed... The construction is: "Let them set that very transaction in motion"—that is, let them impel it toward being an object of activity.
He explains the phrase "by the manifestation of power" with the word "by this. "By this" means by that which is being performed.

By the term "prakāśakena" (by the illuminator), which means "by that which produces knowledge," it is indicated that the word *prakāśa* is derived in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). By the phrase "in the form of recognition" (*pratyabhijñārūpeṇa*), it is meant "in the nature of recognition," because it is the means of accomplishing recognition.

The phrase "by that which is called recognition" (pratyabhijñākhyena) means, in effect, that it is by this. He explains "is set in motion" (pravartyate) as "of those who cause [people] to act" (pravartayatām). "Of those who cause [people] to act" means of those people who lead [others] to the state of being an object of activity; "the performance of what is conducive to that" means the performance of actions that lead people to the state of being objects of engagement in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

The performance of what is capable is carried out; that is, it is set in motion—this is the meaning in this grammatical application (*prayoga*). "Two *ṇic* suffixes" means that both *ṇic*s have been elided by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*. In that context, "he impels one who is setting [an action] in motion" refers to one *ṇic*, while "they two set the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) in motion" refers to the other.
The second *ṇic* suffix [in the word *prerayati*] means "impels. He explains the intention of the word "only" (*kevalam*) with the words "but not" (*na tu*).
"In reality" (*tattvataḥ*) means from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*); "not manifesting" (*aprakāśamānam*) means not being the agent of manifestation.
To the question "What is done again? he replies: "Only while manifesting" (*prakāśamāna eva*). But what [is the point]?
To the objection that this removal is purposeless, he says:
"That is removed. For the very removal of that [ignorance] is the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord, which is liberation;
its non-removal is transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). Indeed, both of these have nothing more than mere conceit as their essence.
And both of these are indeed the manifestation of the Blessed One alone. This is what is meant:

just as for one who is terrified and, while his own self is manifesting, thinks "I have been carried away" out of delusion, that delusion is removed [by being told], "Who indeed are you?"—[so too is the case here].
If you say, "He whose clothing is such and whose face is such [is the Lord]," then look—this very thing exists for you!

Thus, by saying this again and again, nothing new has been created; likewise, for the world of ordinary beings, while the Self is manifesting, they simply do not realize, "I am not the Lord," and so forth.

Delusion is dispelled for one who is conceited due to delusion. For he who is endowed with sovereignty over knowledge and action is the Lord (Īśvara), as is well known in the Siddhāntas, Purāṇas, and other texts; and such you are.
Or alternatively, he upon whom something depends is the lord therein, like a king in his own realm; and so it is with you.
"That very withdrawal" means that which consists in the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord (parameśvaratālābha). "This pair" refers to liberation and transmigratory existence.
"This" refers to that which takes the form of liberation and transmigratory existence. Now, what has been stated by this?

Therefore, he says: "This is what is meant. By a person repeatedly declaring, "Of one possessed"—that is, of one who is *bhūtāviṣṭa*—"thus," delusion is dispelled. Why is this so? [He asks: "Who indeed? "O you who are possessed! Indeed—certainly—who are you? "If you... and so forth.
"You say: 'What is it? [I reply: 'He who possesses such clothing, and likewise he who possesses such a face—that very person am I. Then you look at him:
'Do you have such clothing and such a face?'—this is the meaning of the word *iti*."
Upon the completion of the removal of the delusion regarding the elements (*bhauta-moha*), there is an implication of the meaning of the sentence.

"Of this"—meaning of the elemental one—it was "not composed," i.e., not made; the sense is that [it is not made] because the Self is already established. He effects the application of the illustrative example to the subject of the illustration with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). "While it is indeed appearing"—
[The Self] is indeed of the nature of constantly manifesting as the object of the sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*); [it is said that this] is "excluded"—that is, set aside.

To the question "How is it excluded?", he says: "For he who... [and so forth]. Now, one might object: since the Lord’s powers of knowledge and action pertain to all objects, whereas those of the individual soul (*jīva*) pertain only to a limited portion, how can there be identity between the two?

True; just as even an extremely subtle spark of fire is non-different from a great mass of fire by virtue of its capacity to burn, so too the individual soul (jīva) is non-different from the Lord (Īśvara) by virtue of its independence in knowledge and action.
Although such a distinction exists in the illustrative example, it is merely caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Difference in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) is not possible even in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) does not deviate from its true nature; for it is not logical that the very thing [itself] should be its own limiting adjunct. He states another alternative with the words "or else" (*yadi vā*). "Dependent" (*āyatta*) means remaining under control; the construction is "the entire universe is dependent."
The pervasion is this: the designation of "Lordship" (īśvaratā) regarding the entire universe—which is dependent upon the individual soul—is not caused by any other factor;
for whatever indeed appears as attached to something is filled by that, like a treasure-chest with jewels.
"And the universe is attached to you"— this means that whatever appears within something, that [container] is pervasive over that extent,
just as a casket is pervasive among its gems; and within you, whose nature is consciousness,
the entire scripture from the Earth up to Sadāśiva resides.

It is to be known by way of its dependence upon knowledge and action. "Caused by another" means having a cause distinct from dependence. He states yet another mode with the words "yat khalu" (that which indeed).
"Yallagnam" means that in which something is fixed; by that—namely, the *lagna* (ascendant)—it is called "your *lagna*. I...

The meaning is that [he] knows [it] because the knowledge of your attachment has been established. He also describes the fourth mode with the words "of whom. Here, "being within" should be understood as being identical with that [reality], not merely as residing in the middle region. And the dream-world is clearly...

The state of being internal to the dreamer has not been exerted [as a separate category]. This means that [the universe] consists of thirty-five principles (tattvas), beginning from the jar (ghaṭa) and ending with Sadāśiva. The fifth [or sixth, according to the commentary] is the universe as described in the *Prakriyā*. That in which something arises and dissolves while it remains established is [the locus of the universe].

Just as a sprout on the ground pervades both its preceding and succeeding parts, so too does the universe exist within You, whose nature is light. In this manner, even thousands of other attributes established by the scriptures and other authorities may be applied. Thus, when delusion has been dispelled, even though [the world] remains...

When the body and so forth are sustained merely by their own residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), there occurs an identification with them as the self preceded by the misconception that they are not the self; and likewise, while the jar and so forth are manifesting,
there occurs the misconception that they are not the self— just as for one who has realized the true nature of a magician's illusion.

Just as there is no delusion regarding reality for one who perceives a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), so it is for one who has recognized the true nature of the Self. Consequently, when the body—having reached its end through the process of departure—has ceased to exist, there is nothing but the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratā*). This is the cultivation through practice (*abhyāsabhāvanā*).

He explains the manner [in which this is said] with the words "in which. "Pervading the prior and posterior parts" means pervading the initial and final portions. "Others"—meaning those distinct from the aforementioned qualities such as lordship (īśvaratva) and so forth—refer to the followers of the Āgamas and others;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the Vedāntins are included. He provides the conclusion:

"Thus, in this way": when such delusion—that is, the delusion consisting in the lack of mastery over one's own self—has been removed or cast aside, and likewise when [the body and so forth] are maintained merely by the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that previous delusion; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the mind and other faculties are included].

The mention of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth: when the conceit of selfhood (*ātmatābhimāna*) stands preceded by the conceit of non-self (*anātmatābhimāna*), the sequence should be understood as follows: during the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is the conceit of non-self; at the time of emergence (*vyutthāna*), there is the conceit of selfhood due to the necessity of worldly activity. Likewise:
Regarding objects such as a jar— which, from the perspective of ultimate reality,

exist as the very nature of the Self— while the conceit of non-selfhood is manifesting, that is, while they are appearing through the force of conventional usage, [the realization occurs] for one who has recognized the true nature of the Self as being the Lord.
For the yogin whose true nature as the Self has been made the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there remains a specific delusion (*vyāmoha*)—
consisting of the belief in the reality of the body alone as the Self,
and the belief in the reality of non-Self objects such as jars— which persists everywhere.

Delusion does not arise. How so? For example, for one who has known the reality of a magician’s trick—one who has ascertained the secret of the illusion—even while seeing the trick, which is brought within the range of vision by the power of the nature of the mantra, there is no delusion.
The meaning is that the delusion which takes the form of reality does not exist in that way.

Having described liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), he speaks of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*) with the word "then" (*tataḥ*). This refers to "supreme lordship" (*parameśvaratā*) whose limit is reached through "departure," that is, death.
The intended meaning is that this is due to the attainment of all-pervasiveness. As it has been said:
"Becoming the sun, he blazes; becoming Viṣṇu, he protects the three worlds;
becoming Rudra, he destroys; and as the Grandfather (Brahmā), he creates."

However, for one who, by means of the power taught in the Śiva-scriptures, becomes intent upon the immersion into the state of the Supreme Lord within the jar-like body itself, there arises here in this very body a partial manifestation of the attributes of the Supreme Lord; yet, in reality, there is no fullness, because of the very nature of being a body.

Because when the life-force of contraction dissolves, one attains the state of being the universal self as it truly is. However, for one who maintains the conceit of non-establishment even regarding the collection of causes for accomplishing worldly activity— [the author] speaks of "practice" (*abhyāsa*) to describe the supreme limit of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

"By that taught in the Śiva-scripture"—meaning by that declared in the Śiva-śāstra—"having entered into"—that is, having formed a firm resolve (abhiniveśa), which amounts to "by force" (haṭhena). And this resolve should be understood as consisting solely of uninterrupted reflective awareness (parāmarśa). To the question "Why is there not fullness [in such a case]?", he says:
Regarding the phrase "of the state of having a body" (*dehatvasya*): "in its dissolution" (*galane*) means in its destruction, that is to say, in liberation while without a body (*videhamukti*).

This is because one attains the nature of being the self of the entire universe as it truly exists; the meaning is that one achieves the ultimate state of being the self of all. By this, the great difference between liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and liberation without a body is stated.

For liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is indeed the vision of reality accompanied by its aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), whereas liberation after death (*videhamukti*) is dissolution into that reality.
However, without liberation while living, liberation after death is truly difficult to attain. As for that which was said by the Blessed One:
"And even at the time of departure" (prayāṇakāle 'pi ca). That too refers exclusively to the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
For even at the time of departure, there is indeed still life, since death is impossible for one who is already dead. In whatever manner it may be, it is always thus.
One must indeed be established in the supreme reality, for that is beneficial for both worlds.
As it has been said:
"Having enjoyed worldly pleasures and abandoned the wandering of existence, I shall attain the supreme state."
Thus I hope that this may shine forth here as the supreme [teaching] for one who possesses devotion to Śambhu.

Thus, devotion to Śambhu here consists precisely in being established in the supreme reality (*paratattva*), and not in being established in an imagined form. For one who is established in the supreme reality remains established in that supreme reality even while performing whatever actions naturally arise. And by that, for him, both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*)—

Success alone [is the goal]. In that regard, being solely intent on enjoyment is mere delusion, while being solely intent on liberation is undermined by impossibility; therefore, devotion to both is most excellent. In this context, the Smṛti scriptures are the authority for the means of enjoyment, and likewise for the means of liberation.

[This refers to] the commands of the Lord and so forth. Now, some say that liberation occurs spontaneously for all upon the fall of the body; therefore, one should focus solely on worldly enjoyment. True, but it must be determined whether liberation is undesirable or desirable to them. If it is undesirable, then by them—
This very deliberation is not even appropriate; however, if it is desired, then they should be told:

"If what is desired is accomplished quickly, that is indeed more desirable. Therefore, one should exert effort for the sake of liberation and lead it toward increase day by day. But in the investigation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*):
Although both of these [means of knowledge] depend entirely upon the Lord, and thus He alone is the authority in all matters, nevertheless,

one must also employ one's own external and internal organs, which have been granted their respective capacities by the Blessed One himself. As for one who does not employ them, for him there is no [authority] in that regard.

"Since even the Lord's own activity has been obstructed, what means remains? Thus, enough with these successions of digressions regarding ineffable matters; for in whatever belongs to the Lord, even there, delusion must be dispelled by means of conventional linguistic practices alone. But as for him who...

In every way, it does not depart; therein, the state of being deluded arises through the power of the Lord’s energy (*īśvara-śakti*). Yet, because that [delusion] has reached the path of his ears, through the ripening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), the recovery of his true nature will inevitably occur at some point. Thus, in this manner, [there is the recovery of one's true nature] in the agent.

That which is to be done, He causes all beings to do by Himself. Now, if the emergence of the qualities that are portions of the Supreme Lord's sovereignty occurs solely through the power of the cultivation of practice, then what is the use of this worldly activity devoted to the means of realizing the Supreme Reality?
Regarding the phrase "by means of recognition which reveals the new path," he says: "But for whom... The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction.

For that person—meaning one who has established the determination of the supreme reality through practice and so forth—who maintains the conceit of non-establishment regarding the collection of reasons (*hetukalāpa*), that is, the aggregate of reasons used to accomplish worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
By way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), with respect to those great gurus who are established in that [state], there arises the conceit (abhimāna) that "these [others] are unaccomplished";
according to the maxim that "every statement is restrictive," this [conceit] belongs to him alone.

This is not the case for one who is devoid of practice and so forth. Even in that state— namely, as long as the body persists, even within worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) which is to be abandoned— one experiences delusion (*vyāmoha*) through the very means of worldly activity, that is, through the very entities that cause worldly activity, such as memory and the like.

The meaning is that [the opponent] is to be removed—that is, to be destroyed—according to the principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*, so that devotion may arise toward those who engage in pure worldly conduct (*vyavahāra*) and toward the great gurus who perform such acts.
And thus, as for those who say this: "Only for those intent on worldly conduct..."

"The instruction must be carried out by means of worldly conventions (*vyavahāra*)," they say; yet, by those very means, they are like those who have fallen into one pit and are then cast into another pit. Enough, then, with raising such objections from others, which are invariably indicative of malice. Now, if even when addressed in this way he does not listen, then what?

To address this, he says: "of whom. The term "in every way" (*sarvathā*) is used with reference to the removal of some degree of delusion through the power of practice (*abhyāsa*) and so forth; furthermore, even though [the disciple] is capable and engaged in worldly activity, this was said with reference specifically to the great gurus who possess the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Just as, for example, a provincial ruler lacks sovereignty in comparison to a universal monarch (*samrāj*). Now, one might ask:
"In that case, will this [thought] never at any time occur to his mind? To this he says: "Of him also.
The meaning is that even for him, this will certainly occur to his mind in the course of time. Now, what of one for whom this has not yet reached the path of hearing?
What news is there of him who has gone? Truly, his very first departure was struck down by impossibility; even if that were possible, there would be no practice.

In the state of ultimate realization (*mahāniṣṭhatā*), this reality will manifest of its own accord; otherwise, it would follow that what is self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*) could not possibly exist, yet such self-established states are described in the scriptures.
Furthermore, those who provide such instructions are seen even without having studied the scriptures.

That which was stated in the two verses beginning with "mahāguravaḥ kartari" (1.1.2) has been further refined and re-examined by means of the three verses beginning with "viśvavaicitrye"; such is the case, first of all.
Thus, this is the authority; how could it be otherwise regarding the Blessed One who has become such?
Therefore, what was stated at the beginning of the treatise is now established by way of a different formulation—may there be auspiciousness. (17) [Total from the beginning: 120]

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Means of Knowledge, its Fruit, and the Object of Knowledge," in the *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, within the section on Action (*kriyādhikāra*). 3.

Thus, enough with this elaboration. The phrase "it will be" implies here the removal of delusion; the word "iti" marks the conclusion of the subject matter (*prameya*). He provides the summary with the words "tadevam" (thus, therefore).
This means at the beginning of the treatise, at the commencement of the first chapter (*āhnika*) concerning the qualification for knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*).
"Having prepared" (*upaskṛtya*) means having made it endowed with preparation (*upaskāra*), that is to say, "with distinction.
For preparation is the imparting of qualities (*guṇādhāna*), and that itself is the distinction. He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "thus" (*evam*).
"Of such a kind" (*evambhūtam*) means having the nature of ever-new manifestations and being capable of bearing the status of an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*).

"Being thus"—that is, eternal and self-luminous. It has been stated: "Who could effect its accomplishment? This refers to such a reality at the beginning of the treatise; the meaning is: at the commencement of the treatise, regarding the agent. "Thus"—for this reason, now—

At the conclusion of the third chapter on ritual action (*kriyādhikāra*), that very same [subject] has been "carried through"— that is, established— by means of another fortunate occasion, i.e., by a different arrangement;
for all scriptures have as their primary aim the completion of the subject matter introduced at the outset.

The word "bhāvaḥ" [indicates] the end of the commentary on this chapter. The term "śiva" denotes auspiciousness and is intent upon indicating the supreme reality; thus, all is auspicious (śivam). || 17 ||

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Kriyādhikāra* of the commentary on the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtra* titled *Bhāskarī*, composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
It is completed.
Thus [ends] the section on ritual action. Thus, may there be peace.
We praise that Śiva, the agent who, manifesting both existence and non-existence within the stainless mirror of his own self, creates the wondrous relationship between cause and effect.
