We praise that Śiva, who, as the Sun, reflects all objects within the mirror of his own exceedingly pure surface,
and [who likewise manifests] their relationship of cause and effect.

Now, at the beginning of the fourth chapter of the *Kriyādhikāra*, for the sake of completing the commentary without obstacles and for the sake of its successful progression, [the author] offers a benediction characterized by a salutation to the chosen deity whose nature is the Supreme Reality, performed through both body and mind.

With a verse that indicates the essential purport of the entire treatise, he brings [the subject] within the range of speech for the sake of instructing his disciples: "We praise that Śiva"—that is, we praise Śiva, whose nature is the manifestation of all things and whose nature is the agency of all. Which one?

The agent— Śiva, who exists as the agent of all— in his own mirror of consciousness (svātmadarpaṇa), which is called his own essential nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra) and is stainless (nirmala) because it is capable of self-manifestation and because it is receptive to reflections in the form of the manifestation of other things, [perceives] entities (bhāvān).
Illuminating— that is, causing to appear as reflections within the state of the knower— the multitude of principles (tattvas) beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with the Earth,
it then manifests a manifold causal relationship.
And by manifesting the relationship of cause and effect, he becomes the agent;

that is to say, he exists by manifesting the relationship of cause and effect preceded by the relationship of the signified and the signifier as described in the preceding section. By this, in this present section—

It has been indicated that there will be a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). This is a form derived from the root *bhās* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, used with a present participle (*śatṛ*) in grammatical apposition with the nominative case. In that context, entities (*bhāvāḥ*) themselves are the agents of manifestation; however, this [agent] is their [manifestation] therein.

Having established the true nature of the relationship between the signified and the signifier— which arises from the context of a connection consisting primarily of the expansion of the power of action (kriyāśakti)— he now proceeds to establish the true nature of the relationship between cause and effect.

Another chapter begins with twenty-one verses, starting from "And this" (*eṣa ca*) and ending with "Thus, desire itself is the causality, the agency, and the action" (*evamicchaiva hetutā kartṛtā kriyā*). Therein, in one verse, it is introduced that in our own system, the very relationship between agent and object is the relationship between cause and effect. Following that—
With three verses, the causality of the insentient is refuted. Then, with six verses, the causality consisting of agency is established as belonging to the sentient alone.
Subsequently, as a related point, it is stated in three verses that the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) is necessarily required for inference.

Therefore, even the ultimate reality of cause and effect as taught by the Buddhists (the ultimate reality of the causal relation taught by the Buddhists) relies upon our own doctrine; otherwise, it would be nothing at all— thus [it is stated] in three verses.
"Even the causal relationship demonstrated by the Sāṃkhya is not tenable if the agency of the conscious being as stated by us is not accepted"— this is shown by three [verses].
"And even for a conscious being, this is not possible if it lacks sovereignty"— this is shown by two [verses]."
This is the summary of the meaning; the text (or the meaning of the text) is now being explained.

It impels toward manifestation, and this very impulsion is the performance of what is efficacious. Thus, having accomplished the auspicious invocation, the purport of the entire daily lesson is presented both in its totality and in its individual parts.
He says, "it is action.
Regarding this, the commentary states:
the expansion (*sphāra*) of the power of action—that is, its manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), which is to say, its unfolding (*vijṛmbhaṇa*).

"Tatprāyaḥ" means "of that nature," referring to the occasion (*prasaṅga*) of that relationship, and not because it is the subject under discussion (*prastutatva*); this is the intended meaning. "Tattvam" means its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). "Having established" (*prasādhya*) means having thoroughly proven it in the preceding chapter (*pūrvāhnika*). Having thus stated the intention in its entirety, [he now speaks] by way of individual parts.
He says "there" (*tatra*); "there" means within the twenty-one verses, it is introduced or stated—this is the meaning.
The word "thus" (*evam*) is intended to indicate the exclusion of instruments and so forth from being the cause;
"then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after that; "verse" (*śloka*) means by the second, third, and fourth [verses].
"It is refuted" means it is warded off; "necessarily to be relied upon" means necessarily to be depended upon.
"By three verses" means by the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth verses. Then, that ultimate reality of cause and effect as stated by the followers of Sugata [is refuted] by three [verses].
The meaning is "in the forms of the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth. To the question "Why is this not tenable? he says: "If... and "By three...".
Thus, by way of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), [he establishes] the state of being of a single nature with the subject within the Lord.
Having established that which is to be expressed in worldly discourse, he says the following to show that the state of being the agent is also established from that very source without effort:
"And this [Lord], because of his infinite power, manifests these [objects] in such a manner."
By virtue of the absence of desire for existence, this activity of his is that which constitutes his state of being a creator.

The word *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). This very same primordial subject (*pramātā*) causes these very entities (*bhāvān*), which have been previously manifested as manifestations (*ābhāsān*), to manifest again through an uninterrupted continuity (*avicchinnena prabandhena*). How so?

By the power—that is, by the efficacy—of the Will, which is the Lord’s own nature, free from conceptual construction, non-sequential, and sovereign. Where do these entities of His abide? He says: "Because of His infinite power.
For all entities abide as His very power, having His own nature as their essence.
The meaning is: by means of the forms consisting of seventeen, eighteen, and nineteen. "By two" means by means of the forms consisting of twenty and twenty-one.
Now he provides the introduction to the first verse with the word "evam" (thus); this is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "And this.
Here, the commentary explains "this" as "the Ancient One," and explains "these states" as follows:
"Manifested" (*ābhāsita*) means: not only today, but manifested previously as well;

that is to say, they exist as their own nature (*svarūpa*) from beginningless time. They are called "manifestations" (*ābhāsāḥ*) because they shine forth (*ābhāsante*) on all sides (*samantāt*); those [manifestations].

Alternatively, the meaning is that [the light] is of the nature of manifestation because its essence consists solely in manifestation. "It manifests" (*ābhāsayati*) is explained by the very words of the text. He states "by means of the uninterrupted" (*avicchinnenā*) with the intention of referring to its present state;
for the present state clearly aims to illuminate continuity, otherwise one would simply say "it manifests."
He would say: "By the power of will. To explain this, he provides an introductory transition by asking, "How so?

He then explains this term as the answer to that question: "Of the will. Regarding the word "of the Lord" (*īśituḥ*), it refers to the agent of the will; he says "of the non-different" (*abhinnāyāḥ*) with respect to the non-difference between the power and its possessor.
In order to explain the superiority of this worldly desire (*laukikecchā*), he says: "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*).
This means that its nature is non-conceptual, i.e., it is devoid of the coloring (*uparāga*) of anything to be desired.
He provides an introductory transition to explain [the phrase] "because of possessing infinite power" (*anantaśaktitvāt*) by asking: "Where?"—namely, in the universe (*viśve*).
All [these powers] belong to this primordial subject by virtue of being his very nature—that is, by virtue of being his essential being;
for power is indeed the very nature of the possessor of power.
Thus it has been said.

Regarding the passage "of the Lord who abides in the self" (1.5.10): that which is this manifestation and that which is the will, that is action; such is the creative agency (*nirmātṛtva*) of this Blessed One. || 1 ||
An objection might be raised: "Surely a sprout is seen to emerge from a seed, and yet no conscious agent is observed entering into this process; how then can this [doctrine] be stated?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But for that which is insentient, there is no such power of being such that what was non-existent becomes existent;
therefore, the nature of cause and effect consists precisely in the status of agent and object.
An insentient seed does not possess such a capacity that it could produce a sprout that is either non-existent or existent; as it has been said:
And power does not desire separation from the nature of the possessor of power;
there is an eternal identity between these two, just as between fire and its burning capacity.

Thus [it is asked]. To the question "Where was this said?", he replies with the words "of the Lord" (*svāminaḥ*). Here, the meaning is "in this verse. He explains the remainder of the verse, beginning with "this" (*eṣā*), using the words "that which is this" (*yad etat*). By the word "this" (*etad*), there is a reference to both the proximate and the remote [elements]. "That" (*asau*) refers to the object of manifestation, namely, the state of being the creator (*nirmātṛtva*).

The meaning is "having the form of the creator. According to the principle that "every sentence implies restriction," it means that she is not any other gross form consisting of the instruments [of action]. || 1 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the second verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). This is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "jaḍasya" (of the insentient).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
He explains "of the insentient" as "of the seed. He explains "she" as "being thus.
He explains "power" as "capacity. While explaining "existence," he fulfills the expectation of the phrase "being thus" with the word "that which. [It is] "the nature of being existent."

It renders that which is currently perceived as possessing existence. When it is said, "A sprout is born from a seed," this is not the glory of the sprout, because [the sprout] was non-existent [prior to birth]; and how could the glory of "the sprout is born" belong to the seed, since it is distinct from that sprout? Since this is so, therefore the effect—
That which is manifested by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is indeed *karman* (the object);

this is made manifest through its very function, for it is "that by which the agent acts" through the performance of what is conducive to that end—thus, even the instrument (*kāraṇa*) rests upon the conscious agent. Regarding the phrase "of the non-existent and the existent," this refers to that which has the nature of being non-existent yet exists.
This is the meaning. Or rather, the sense "of a non-existent sprout or of an existent seed" is implied here; or likewise, "of an existent or non-existent sprout. || 2 ||
Now, one might ask: "How is it that this power does not belong to the insentient? To this he says:
"That which is non-existent is non-existent; it is not logical for the non-existent to have the nature of existence.
Furthermore, there is no purpose in the existent obtaining existence once again..."
An effect may be considered either existent, non-existent, both, neither, or indescribable;
for according to the Sāṃkhya school, the effect is pre-existent (*satkārya*), while according to others, it is of the nature of the non-existent (*asadrūpa*).

This is with respect to the views of the logicians (*tārkika*). Here he provides the justification with the words "from a seed. By the phrase "because of non-existence," the intended meaning is that even the greatness of a rabbit's horn is never observed anywhere. With this, the explanation of the first half-verse is completed. Now, the second half-verse...

He provides an introductory remark (*avataraṇikā*) in order to explain [the following], beginning with the words "since it is thus" (*yata evam*). "Thus" means that such a power does not belong to an insentient thing (*jaḍa*). "Being manifested" (*bhāsyamānam*) means having been made an object of manifestation.
The suffix *ṇyat* is used in the sense of an action (*kṛtya*); the intended meaning is that it is indicated (*āviṣkṛtam*), as it is prescribed in the passive sense (*karman*).
By this, it is established that the effect possesses the nature of an object (*karman*). The agent (*kartṛ*) is the independent agent;
"by performing what is conducive to that" means by performing what is conducive to that in the form of instigation (*preraṇa*).
"In the agent" refers to the causal agent (*hetukartṛ*); by this, it is indicated that here the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *kṛ* in its causative form (*ṇijanta*). By this...

The fact that the cause possesses the nature of being the instigating agent has been established. Furthermore, the two words "of the non-existent" (asataḥ) and "of the existent" (sataḥ) have already been explained; now he explains them separately according to three modes with the words "of that which is of the nature of the non-existent" (asadrūpasya). "Of the existent" means "of that which is present. The word "or" (vā) signifies an alternative. Herein lies the third mode.
Thus it is joined, and that very same [element] was previously grasped. || 2 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse with the word "yat" (that which).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

"It is possible"—it can be conceived. But surely, even if it possesses both natures, the Vedāntins contradict themselves by their own words when they say "not so" (*na tu*); what is the point of this? If the pot were non-existent, then...

Since its ultimate reality (paramārtha) is precisely its lack of intrinsic form, how could it admit existence, which is contrary to its own nature? For even by a hundred prostrations, blue does not tolerate yellowness within itself. If, on the other hand, the pot were indeed existent, then what else remains?

It is requested [to be explained] by means of the staff, the wheel, and the thread; furthermore, such qualities as manifestation, objecthood, and clarity are also to be considered in terms of their being existent or non-existent in nature.
"Indeed, in that case, let us remain silent"; [the author] says that even this is not tenable: "And yet, it is said...
(Verse 3).
This means that this matter must necessarily be established. || 3 ||
Since the state of being indescribable (*anirvācyatva*)— which consists in having fear as its nature— is conceived here [as the definition],
he says "consisting of both. The sense is that there is a clear contradiction between "consisting of both" and "not consisting of both."

By this—by the position that [the world] is indescribable—he would accept—that is, he would admit—the ultimate reality, which is the true nature [of things]. To the question "Why?", he says: "For indeed," he does not tolerate—that is, he cannot endure—the yellowness, that is, the state of being yellow. "Anything else" refers to an object distinct from existence.

"From the staff, the wheel, and the string"—the meaning is "from such causes as these. Now, one might object: "But here, manifestation (*abhivyakti*) and clarity (*sphuṭatva*), etc., are established by means of the staff and so forth";
to this he says: "manifestation," etc. "[They are] to be considered"—that is, if they are of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*), then...

The proof for that is indeed fruitless; however, if they are of the nature of non-existence, then the proof for them is struck down by impossibility—this is the sense. By this, the commentary up to the word "object" (artha) is completed.
Now, in order to explain the phrase "atha cocyate" (and then it is said), he provides an introductory transition with "nanvevam" (but if this is so).

To this, he states the reply: "naitat" (this is not so). When the expectation arises as to by whom [this was said], he introduces the segment of the verse to be explained: "atha cocyate. Here, by means of the sentence, [it is shown] as a synonym.

"It necessarily states the existence"—that is, for that reason; this is the meaning: the matter known as the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must necessarily be established. For it is on this basis that the relation of cause and effect is spoken of in the world.

The sense is that [this point] must be established. By this, it is indicated that the two words "kāryakāraṇatā" and "loke," which appear in the subsequent verse, should be construed right here. || 3 ||
And thus, he demonstrates how this is logically established: "In the world, the relation of cause and effect belongs to that which revolves within;
its being perceivable by both types of sense organs occurs due to the power of a certain [internal] factor. (4)

Within the heart of the potter, because it is the object of the inner mind, there exists the vibration of the universe— which, even previously, existed as the singular essence of one's own self-consciousness— as it revolves through its manifold nature in the form of both difference and non-difference.
Now he provides the introduction to the fourth verse with the words "tataḥ" (therefore).
Here, the commentary states:
"The sense is this"—this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). "In this way"—by the method that is about to be described.
"It is appropriate"—it is logical. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "the effect," etc.
Herein is the commentary:

Leaving aside the two words "kāryakāraṇatā loke" because they were already applied in the preceding verse, he now explains the compound *antarviparivartinaḥ* and so forth by first providing its analysis (*vigraha*).
He explains the compound *antarviparivartinaḥ* as follows: [he who] revolves within.

Regarding the term "potter" (*kumbhakāra*): there too, he explains the constituent part "inside" (*antaḥ*) by means of the word "potter. Because it is within the range of the mind—that is, because it becomes an object of the mind through the medium of desire—even prior to its creation, that is, even before its manifestation. This is because, as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the word *antar* possesses all genders.

The third sense is that of indicating; the fact that the word *antaḥ* signifies the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidātmatva*) has already been stated previously. He explains the prefix *vi-* as "by way of manifoldness" (*vicitratvena*). The term *viśvasya* is implied as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), for otherwise the qualifier would result in being without a referent.
And that [term] here—[and thus, in this context, it should be connected with "the jar itself" (ghaṭa eva) because of its manifold nature consisting of difference and non-difference;

C.]—must be connected with "the jar itself. By the phrase "consisting of difference and non-difference" and "by way of its manifold nature," the meaning is: by way of a manifoldness whose form is both difference and non-difference. [The term] "of the changing" (parivartinaḥ) [is to be understood].
He explains [the phrase] "of that which is revolving," and here he himself provides the commentary:

"by means of vibration" (*spandanena*). By "vibration"—that is, by means of the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—[he refers to] "that which is throbbing," meaning the multitude of objects appearing in the state of both difference and non-difference. In that regard:

The non-difference [of the object] through its state as a universal—that which is manifested as being perceivable by both the internal and external organs—is precisely this nature of cause and effect. The mention of "both" is illustrative; for whatever [object], to whatever extent...

"Completion" (*pūrṇā*) means the fulfillment of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), that is to say, the completion [of it]. The "creation" (*nirmāṇa*) of pleasure and so forth is simply the bringing about of their being cognizable solely by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). And this is not [the case] with a potter...

This [universe] resides in that which consists primarily of the vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), the intellect (*buddhi*), the void, and the body; for even this [substratum] is insentient. Therefore, consciousness alone manifests the universe within itself due to the variety of its powers. This refers to "that certain [consciousness]" mentioned previously.

The meaning is that its greatness is inconceivable and beyond questioning. Nor should it be said that even the state of being perceivable by both sense-faculties constitutes a difference in nature; for he explains "both" (*ubhaya*) as a compound (*samasta*).
He explains the entire word *pada* with the words "that which" (*yat*). It is "manifested"—it itself becomes the object of manifestation;

the verbal suffix is used in the sense of the reflexive agent (*karmakartari*). By the word "this" (*eṣā*), there is a reference to the meaning of the sentence. That is to say, it is perceptible by both types of sense organs. [This refers to] that which is contained in the verse.
He explains the word "sā" (that) as "the state of being cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇatā*).

The meaning is that it is spoken of as capacity (*sāmarthya*). "The state of being cause and effect" means the causality with respect to an effect—that is, regarding an effect. He states "completion" (*samāpti*) as a synonym for "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*).

This means "the apprehension of its own nature. The underlying sense is that otherwise, there would be no apprehension of that which is known through inference and other means. Now, one might object: since pleasure and the like are not perceivable by both types of sense organs, they cannot be established as effects; to this, he says: "of pleasure and the like. Of what, then? [is it the case?]

He provides an introductory transition to explain the passage beginning with "na ca" and so forth. This very thing—namely, the state of being a cause that is being established—belongs to this as well, even to the potter’s vital breath and the like.
Following the method of stating the result, he explains the passage beginning with "tataḥ" and so forth, [saying] "of that," meaning of any such thing whatsoever.

The explanation of the term "it" (iti) is given by the word "consciousness" (saṃvit). The explanation of the term "from power" (śaktitaḥ) is given by the phrase "due to the variety of powers" (śaktivaicitryāt). By this, it is indicated that the meaning of "from power" is "from the powers. Now, one might object: "Is consciousness not included by the phrase 'of that certain [one]' (tasya kasyāpi)? To this, he says:
Regarding the word "previously": the intended meaning is that the inconceivable and unassailable majesty belongs to consciousness alone.

Now, one might object: "The state of being conceivable through the alternatives of existence or non-existence, which was mentioned regarding the subject of manifestation and so forth, applies equally even to the case of being cognizable by both types of sense organs. To this, he says: "And not..."
The meaning is that it is "thinkable" (*cintya*). To the question "Why is it not expressible? he says:

"Whether existent or non-existent. For this is the ultimate truth here: just as in the reflection of a jar or other objects being produced by a potter within a mirror, it is of the mirror alone [that the reflection appears].

Such is the power of manifestation (*tathābhāsanamahimā*); just as in the perception of a dream, consciousness possesses such a power, yet by that very power, the conceit arises that "this external object is being made manifest in a clear form. Thus, it is through the power of consciousness (*saṃvinmahimnā*).

When a jar is present upon the potter's staff, wheel, and so forth, it is by the power of that very [jar] that the conceit arises: "This was made by me," "This was made by him," "It flashed in my heart," or "It flashed in his heart. In that regard, for the insentient...
Since pride regarding clay and the like is utterly absent, agency is established in the nature of consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "since this [is so]," the word "here" (atra) refers to this subject matter. To the question "What is it?", he says: "Just as... (yathā).

"Within the mirror" means in the middle of the looking-glass; "being produced" means being made at this very moment, and not already produced—the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes such things as being produced by a potter and so forth. Likewise, the power of manifestation—
The greatness of the jar consists in its appearing as being produced by the potter;
[this is] of consciousness—that is, of dream-consciousness. Here too, the apprehension of being produced by a potter is precisely what is intended. But how is that so even there?

The notion that "this jar is being made by the potter" is observed; therefore, he says, "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). Although there is indeed a perception [of the jar] as being produced by the potter, the meaning is "nevertheless. By its power—by the power of the mirror regarding the reflected image.
By the power of consciousness within its own domain—by this potter—it is "made";
the meaning is that it is not I who perceive [it] merely through my own internal delusion. It "shines forth"—it vibrates;
for in the absence of the mirror, neither the jar would appear, nor the potter, nor by him.

Its state of being brought into existence [is as follows]: for here, it is intended that the potter who has made a pot on his back perceives it as a reflection in a mirror standing before him, and not directly;
likewise, in a dream as well, the pot is perceived precisely as being made by the potter.

Apprehension is accepted; therefore, even here, it is the power of dream-consciousness alone that enables this vision—enough with this elaboration. Having stated the two examples, he states the application to the case at hand with the word "evam" (thus): by the majesty of consciousness.
By virtue of the power of consciousness— which is engaged in grasping the potter who is occupied with the making of a jar—
this being established according to the principle that "the state of things is grounded in consciousness," the word expressing conjunction (*ca*) is to be supplied after the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*).

He demonstrates his own conviction with the words "as follows" (*yathā*). Therein—in that act of establishing the status of the jar, which is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvitsvabhāve*), that is, within consciousness itself—it is established, meaning it is defined by its boundaries.
[Objection: But let this be manifested as having the very form of an entity; what is the point?

It has been stated here that [the object] is perceivable by two sense-faculties; by this, its form as being clearly capable of purposeful action (arthakriyā) is expressed—so what contradiction is there? || 4 ||
And by this investigation, it is shown that the nature of action under discussion is also established:
"In this way, this very single action exists as both internal and external succession."
It has been established that a single [entity] alone is capable of sustaining both aspects. || 5 ||

The phrase "this very [one]" refers to that against which the objection—that it is untenable both in terms of its own nature and its locus—is indeed appropriate; such is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
The consciousness of a potter when joining the wheel, the staff, and so forth, is indeed Śiva himself; for what distinction can there be in consciousness?
Therefore, Śiva, whose singular form is the universe, is the agent in the creation of each individual; even the individual soul’s conceit of being an agent is the work of the All-pervasive Lord.

Thus [it is said]. Here the disciple poses a question with the word "nanu" (surely). "Ittham" means "in the manner stated by you. The teacher provides the answer, saying "uktam atra" (it has been stated here). "Here" means "in this regard. To the question "What has been stated?", he replies: "arthakriyākṣamam" (that which is capable of causal efficiency).

"By this," the meaning is "by being cognizable by both types of sense-faculties. The intention is that since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is implied by its being cognizable by both sense-faculties, it is therefore appropriate to designate that very thing [as the object].
What contradiction is there here? The intention is that there is no contradiction here. The construction of the sentence here is as follows: *tasya*...
For some, by virtue of their own capacity, it is established that [the object] revolving within [the mind] is perceivable by both types of sense organs;
that is what constitutes the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*). This relates to the phrase "and it is called 'the relation of cause and effect' in the world. (4)
Now he provides the introduction to the fifth verse with the words "And by this," which is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the word "Thus.
Here is the commentary:
He explains "this very [consciousness]" with the words "of which. This is a refutation— the denial was false—
because it has been established through reasoning, starting from the internal nature of consciousness itself.

Existence, which consists of manifestation, stands as the external limit by virtue of being the domain of the senses; for that very reason, it is established as having succession through its embrace by action, which is of the nature of the object of cognition.
And because of the identity with the single substratum of both agent and object, it is also one. And that single substratum is—
By virtue of its nature as consciousness—through both its transparency and its autonomy—it sustains both the internal and external forms simultaneously. || 5 ||
He performs a further reflection (*parāmarśa*) for the sake of connecting [it] with the action, [saying] "that" (*sā*).

He explains the word "established" (*upapāditā*) by means of the word "by reasoning" (*upapattyā*). By "reasoning"—that is, by logic—she is "established," meaning that while remaining self-abiding, she has been brought into the sphere of being the object of the performance of those [actions] capable of accomplishing it.

He explains the qualification "existing internally and externally" as a reason with the word "since" (*yataḥ*). He explains the term "existence" (*sthiti*) as "consisting of manifestation" (*ābhāsanārūpā*); the ellipsis is to be supplied as "that whose essence is this.
In that regard, the manifestation of the nature of consciousness is "I," whereas for the external [object], it is of the nature of the instruments; such is the sequence.
It is to be known. He explains the phrase "successive" (*sakramā*) by means of this very cause, saying "from that very [source]":

"by the embracing of that which consists of the object of knowledge"—that is, by the externalization of the action (*karman*), which is the effect (*kārya*) whose nature is the object of knowledge. This much is established; thus [the word] is supplied.

The exclusion of ultimate reality has been established, because otherwise the unity that is about to be explained would be untenable. He explains the words "one" (*ekā*) and "of one" (*ekasya*) as referring to the agent and the object. But who is this single substratum consisting of the agent and the object?
In response to the question of "by what [it] attains identity," he explains [the term] as "both" and "that is one.
With regard to the fact that clarity and autonomy are untenable apart from consciousness, it is stated "as being of the nature of consciousness. He explains the word "both" as "within. Therein:
The sequence is as follows: through transparency (*svacchatva*), there is an internal form; through autonomy (*svatantratva*), there is an external form.
Indeed, internality is essence, and that is possible only for the subtle (*sūkṣma*); moreover, the ultimate limit of subtlety is non-measure even within existence (*sattva*). And that—

This is clearly evident through the analogy of the extremely pure crystal mirror of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Furthermore, autonomy (*svatantratva*) is the capacity to act as one wills; and this, even while being internal to all things, consists precisely in the attainment of external manifestation.

Indeed, a sovereign who engages in even an action appropriate for the lowly by his own will is called independent; thus, everything is faultless. "He endures" (sahate) means that he is all-enduring (sarvasaha); this is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
"Such is the majesty of this Brahman that its very body takes on every form."
Thus. The word "iti" marks the completion of the commentary on the verse. || 5 ||

Now, one might object: "Let this be so in the case of a jar and the like; but where, as in the case of the seed and the sprout, no entry of a conscious agent is observed, why is the sprout not the effect of the seed alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That which is within something is its effect externally, in relation to that [interior];
and thus the dual state of being external or internal is described in relation to the subject (pramātṛ).

Therefore, the mother alone is the cause; and while that [cause] remains established as a duality of appearances, the effect remains as one alone, and thus the activity of that single entity is said to have arisen.

Emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is the external manifestation of that which appears internally, precisely without abandoning its internal form. Therefore, whatever object is said to be "internal" in relation to something else is merely a transformation of that very object's internal form.

[The mere reversal of the internal object-form becomes fit for externalization; it becomes that which is to be externally projected, that which is worthy of being projected outside. And as for the nature of consciousness...
Now, he provides the introduction to the sixth and seventh verses: "But surely..."
Thus it is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the two verses, he explains them with the word "bahiḥ. Here is the commentary (ṭīkā):

He establishes the method for explaining the two verses with the word "antaḥ" (within). Regarding "that which appears within"—namely, the jar appearing as clay while in the form of clay—by "not abandoning that form," meaning by not abandoning its internal form; for the jar...

Even when the state of being a jar (*ghaṭabhāva*) occurs, the clay-nature (*mṛttva*) does not indeed abandon [its essence]; it is not by abandoning it that there is an external manifestation—that is, a manifestation as something distinct from the clay, which amounts to the manifestation "this is a jar. This is the creation—the act of making—it comes into being. But if this is so...
In response to the inquiry, "Let that be so; what follows from it?", he provides the interpretation for the first verse with the words "tataśca" (and therefore).

"Tataśca" means "and for that reason. "It has been said" (*ity uktam*) means "it has been stated. "That object" (*tadvastu*) refers to the object called a jar; [it arises] from that very entity whose nature is clay, and not from anything else.

Of someone [it is said]: although the two words "outside" (*bahiḥ*) and "to be done" (*kāryam*) appear separated in the sūtra, he explains them by joining them as *bahiṣkāryam*. Here he states a synonym:
"worthy of being cast out" (*bahiṣkaraṇārham*), using a *kṛtya* suffix in the sense of fitness (*arhe*). Of what kind is that?
"By its internal form"—this is an expression emphasizing the state of being (bhāvapradhāna); that is, by way of its internal nature or essence (*sāratva*).
"Of that which has merely a pervasive existence" (*viśeṣeṇa paritaḥ vṛttimātra*) means of that whose activity (*vartana*) is solely [that].
For the internal form of a jar is indeed just clay. By this, the explanation for the first half-verse is completed.
To the inquiry, "Let it be so; what follows from that?", he explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "and the nature of consciousness" (*saṃvidrūpaṃ ca*).
With respect to the subject (*pramātṛ*), entities manifest internally; precisely with respect to him...
Therefore, it is logical that these [objects] appear as external through that very [consciousness], by means of which their manifestation as something external occurs.
Consequently, the cognizer alone is the cause, and not the insentient object.
Since that cognizer exists as the cause of the twofold manifestation— internal and external—

without which the two manifestations dependent upon him would be impossible, therefore action, whose nature has been established, belongs solely to the single cognizer and not in any way to the insentient.
It becomes the state of being a creator. || 7 ||
"Appearing within"— by the logic stated in the passage "the object is like [the subject] before," because its status as an object of desire would otherwise be untenable—
existences (*bhāvāḥ*), that is, all entities, have the nature of appearing as one with [consciousness]; this is solely in relation to that, namely,
in relation to the nature of pure consciousness alone.

[With respect to the nature of pure consciousness – C. He connects the object mentioned in the first half [of the verse] here as well, by virtue of its fitness. "Thus" means for this reason; by that very subject who exists as an internal form, of these—namely, those things appearing—[he effects the connection].
The manifestation of all entities as external is thus logically established.
Stating the result, he explains the second verse beginning with "tataśca" (and therefore).
He explains "tena" (by that) as "tataśca," and he explains "mātaiva" (the knower alone) as "pramātaiva" (the cognizer alone).

He states what is excluded by the word *eva* (only/just): "not insentient" (*na jaḍaḥ*). He says "in the sense of 'for'" (*hyarthe*) in order to provide the construction for the passage beginning with "and while situated in the two-fold manifestation" (*sacābhāsadvayasthitau*). The word *ca* (and) remains in the phrase "and that" (*sa ca*);
it is in the sense of "for" (*hi*), which is the meaning of the word *hi*. He provides the construction [by saying] "because" (*yasmāt*), and [refers to] "that" (*saḥ*).
"He explains: 'the cognizer' (*pramātā*). The phrase "of the effect" (*kāryasya*) is explained by its very utterance (*nigadavyākhyāta*).

Regarding the phrase "in the state of the two appearances" (*ābhāsadvayasthitau*), he explains it as "internally" (*antaḥ*). He establishes the connection with the locative case as being "by way of being the cause" (*nimittatayā*). By this, it is indicated that this is a locative of cause (*nimittasaptamī*). He explains the word "that" (*tat*) as follows:
Regarding the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*): he explains "of the one alone" (*ekasyaiva*) as "of the cognizer alone" (*pramātureva*).

He states what is excluded by the particle "alone" (*evakāra*) with the words "but not" (*na tu*). He explains "stated" (*uditā*) as "established" (*prasādhita*), meaning "having an established form"—that is, having its essential nature previously established. This refers to the word "action" (*kriyā*).
He explains [the term] "nirmātṛtā" (agency). The word "bhavati" (it occurs) is supplied as the ellipsis. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the explanation of the two verses.
Such is the construction of the two verses here: "that very [power] is to be excluded from that—by itself..."
It becomes fit to appear as an external object of action. Of what? What is that?
[The author] confirms this very point by means of that [relative pronoun]: "yadapekṣayā" (with reference to which).
For this very reason, the Supreme Lord is accepted as the efficient cause even in the case of the sprout;
otherwise, the causality of other factors such as the seed and so forth would not be logically tenable.
Since the creator is thus nothing other than consciousness itself, for this very reason, the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that in regard to the sprout and so forth—
meaning, within whatever [cause] it exists— the wise have described a twofold, dual-natured external and internal state as belonging to the subject alone.

Because there is nothing else apart from that [consciousness]. And thus, the sense is that all entities have the cognizer alone as their cause. Therefore—by reason of that—the cognizer alone, the subject of knowledge alone, is the cause of entities. And (*ca*) because he is one.

The cognizer alone is the cause for the establishment of the two appearances of the effect— the external and the internal— as has been stated as the reason for their external and internal status. Therefore, for that reason, the action previously established belongs to a single cognizer.

Even for the appearance of another cause, as in the case of the appearance in a dream of a jar being fashioned by a potter, the status of the subject (*pramātṛ*) as the cause is not lost; for the point is that a cause which is not apprehended by the subject cannot function as a cause. || 6 || 7 ||

Now, he introduces the eighth verse (the seventh according to manuscript C) by presenting it for explanation without a formal introductory transition, beginning with the words "ata eva" (for this very reason).
Here is the commentary:
He explains "for this very reason" as "since it is thus. "Thus" means in the manner described;

"the creator"—that is, the agent, meaning the cause—this is to be supplied as a complement to the phrase "by the Naiyāyikas and others. By the word "others," the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth are included. "Is accepted" (iṣṭaḥ).
[The opponent says: "Indeed, the Supreme Lord is intended as the cause precisely because He possesses intelligence; for they have accepted His status as the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa)."
It has been stated that, by way of atoms and so forth— which arise through the sequence of action, disjunction, and so on—
and through the series of initiations by their own constituent parts as inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*),
even things other than that Lord (Īśvara), such as seeds, earth, and water, possess causality. True, it has been so stated.

But that [position] is not tenable, because, according to the reasoning already stated, an insentient entity cannot function as a cause; therefore, it is the Lord alone who, through association with the appearances of seed, soil, and water, manifests in the form of a sprout—this much is the ultimate truth here. || 8 ||
[The author], dispelling the opponent's delusion by asking, "What is contradicted if one does not postulate an intelligent cause distinct from the observed seeds and so forth? says:
"It has been explained. By this, the explanation of the first half-verse is completed. Now, the second half-verse:
He provides an introductory commentary for the explanation with the word "nanu" (surely). The particle "tu" indicates a distinction;
by them—the Naiyāyikas and others—of this [Lord]—namely, Īśvara—through the sequence beginning with action, then division, then the cessation of the prior conjunction, and then...

By means of the sequence beginning with the production of the conjunction with the *uttara* [space], that which has arrived as the state of being mediated by atoms and so forth— that is, the state of having atoms as its cause; by the establishment of that [state], those things which constitute the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*)...
By means of that succession of initiations consisting of their own constituent parts— the series beginning with the formation of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth—
and by that which serves as the cause, the causality of other factors as well, such as seeds, earth, water, and so on, is stated to proceed from that Lord; it does not [proceed] from the Lord alone.

The sense is that for an all-pervading entity (*vyāpaka*), actions such as division and so forth are logically untenable. Having thus provided an introduction by way of the question, he explains the second half of the verse by way of the answer, beginning with "True" (*satyam*).
According to the maxim that "every sentence implies a restriction," this should be construed as meaning "it is indeed as stated."
The word *eva* indicates that which is being excluded, namely *sā tu* ("but that"). "That" refers to the status of being the efficient cause (*nimittatā*) of the seed and so forth;
by this, the term *hetutā* (causality) is explained. The word *upapadyate* (is established) is self-explanatory (*nigadavyākhyātam*).
Since it is clear, nothing further is explained. Here he states the reason: *ukta* ("it has been said"). And this...

This was stated without regard for the ultimate sentience inherent in earth and the other elements. It was spoken thus specifically to the disciple who was occupied with the conceptualization of objects. He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) according to the method of the fruit [of the teaching] with the words "tataśca" (and therefore). "By association" means by way of being accompanied—that is, together with them.

"Having come together" means up to that point. "In the form of a sprout"—that is, by way of being the well-known state of a sprout as the effect of seeds and so forth—"this much alone" (iyān)—meaning just this much—is the "ultimate reality" (paramārtha), the truly existent thing. || 8 ||
Now he provides the commentary on the ninth verse, beginning with "nanu.
Here the *ṭīkā* states:
"uparudhyate" means it is obstructed or countered; the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is used in the reflexive-passive sense (*karmakartari*); [it is the obstruction] of another—
For the Buddhist, [this is] an error;
for indeed, this potter produces a jar through the very arrangement of his own sovereign power, by means of the successive refinement of various clays and other materials. (9)

For it is thus: by beginning with an illustration (*nidarśana*), he confirms that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed of this nature—that insentient causes perform their effects only when impelled by a sentient agent; for if clay and other materials were to produce their effects by mere proximity alone, [this would not be the case].

What role does the potter have in this? If it is argued that they produce [the effects] through a succession of palanquins, funeral mounds, and so forth, and that these depend upon the potter, then our point is established:
even in the production of a palanquin, they require the impulsion of a conscious agent.

Inert causes are never capable of producing an effect without the impulsion of a conscious agent; for if they were so, [the world] would be in a state of constant flux—[that is,] breaking apart and perishing. Having thus provided this introductory transition:
Having introduced the verse, he explains it with the words "tathā hi" (for thus).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
he explains [the verse] with "tathā hi. By way of introducing an illustration—

The phrase "by introducing an illustration" means that he confirms [the point] by means of an illustration itself, because it brings about the firmness of the subject illustrated (dārṣṭāntika); this is the intended meaning. He provides the method for explaining the verse with the words "insentient things" (jaḍāḥ), [meaning] those impelled by a conscious agent, such as a potter and so forth.
The effect—such as a jar and so forth. In response to the question "What are those inert things?", he says: "clay and so forth.
Here he provides the justification with the words "yadi hi" (for if). "By mere proximity"—by a proximity devoid of the instigation of a conscious agent. "Vidadhyuḥ"—they would produce. Here—
"In this jar," [the word] *kṛtyam* means "that which is to be done" (the effect). Here, the disciple Śivika raises an objection:

"Those [causes], such as clay and so forth, as well as that [jar], and the series beginning with the cart-pole and ending with the jar—all these depend upon the potter, because they arise prior to the jar. This is the intended meaning.

To the doubt raised, he provides the answer: "It is established" (*siddham*). That which is to be proven (*sādhyam*)—that is, what is intended to be demonstrated—is the fact that in all cases there is an intelligent agent (*cetana-kartṛtva*). He demonstrates this very point with the words "the palanquin," etc.

Regarding the production of a palanquin—that is, in the initial formation of the causal factors (*kāraka*) known as the palanquin—the word "those" refers to clay and the other materials. The word "iti" [marks the end of the example].

This refers to the completion of the observation of what is already accomplished and what is yet to be accomplished. By the word "api" (even/also), the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika-nyāya*) is indicated: if there is a requirement for consciousness in the production of a palanquin whose form is not yet complete from an unfinished jar, then what need is there to mention the requirement for it in the making of a jar?

"It declares that it has borne fruit" means in some place or at some time. He states the contradiction in the case of the opposite with the words "yadi hi" (if indeed). "It would be" means that it would also apply to clay and other such [materials] which are similar in principle; thus, this is an absolute certainty. And therefore, that which is insentient yet performs an action—

That [activity] depends upon consciousness, just as clay and the like do, and likewise a seed and so forth; such is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For the capacity to produce an insentient effect must have a cause because it occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatvāt*), and no other cause for it is possible since none is perceived; therefore, that [cause] is the impulsion of consciousness (*cetanā-preraṇa*).

If it were not to take the impulsion of volition (*cetanā*) as its cause, then the state of being causeless—which is contrary to its pervader [or, contrary to its pervader, the state of having another cause]—would follow;
and that is not tenable, because that same consequence would apply even to clay and other such materials. Thus.

The pervasion is established; therefore, the sense is that it arises from the state of being the deity of the *kumbhaka* (retention) and so forth. He states the desired conclusion succinctly with the words "iti" and "iti.
"Iti" means for this reason; thus, this is the final certainty (*ekānta*) regarding insentient things.

The sense is that there is no doubt whatsoever regarding the dependence on consciousness (*cetanā*). Here, he states the conclusion with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*). That is to say: since it is insentient and yet performs an action, it must therefore depend on consciousness;
this is to be applied by oneself. This is its inherent nature (*svabhāva*); this is what constitutes its nature. It is not... [the sentence is incomplete in the source].

The meaning is that [the existence of] form and so forth is established. In response to the inquiry "How so?", he provides the justification here with the words "because it is insentient. This is because of its occasional occurrence—that is, because it exists only at certain times—and specifically because it occurs only at the time when another sentient being, whose presence is necessary and not otherwise accounted for, is in proximity.
This means "because its nature is that of cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). Now, one might object: "Let that cause be something entirely distinct from consciousness.

To this he says: "And not... [anything else]. Why is it not possible for some other entity—something distinct from consciousness—to be the cause of this production of non-conscious effects? To this he says: "Because of non-perception" (*anupalambhāt*).

The meaning is that it is not logical for that which is unperceived to possess the quality of being established. "Thus"—for this reason—"that"—the state of producing an insentient effect—would result in being "without a cause," that is, devoid of a causal agent, if it were not to take the instigation of a sentient being as its motive. This state of being without a cause...

Of what nature? Contrary to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*). "Contrary to the pervader" means contrary to—that is, characterized by opposition to—the pervader, which consists of dependence upon consciousness; that is to say, it is sublated by it. The sense is that it is not logical for that which lacks a cause to possess dependence. [This is illustrated] by the inference of fire from smoke.

And coldness located in a place of fire is contradictory to its pervader. Now, one might object: "Let there be causelessness here as well, even though it is contradictory to the pervader. To this, he says: "And not... That is, causelessness. Because of the consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that very thing—namely, causelessness—as something undesirable.
Because [it is so]. The sense is that clay and the like are not observed to act independently of a conscious agent.

He states the conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti"—that is, for this reason, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the property of being an insentient effect and the necessity of depending on a conscious agent is established.

In this regard, there is the Lord (Īśvara). This is what is stated: by means of the arrangement which has the nature of the Lord—that is, by that arrangement which is the form of the Lord—whatever refinement there is of the clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth;
namely, the kneading of the clay, the straightness of the staff, and [the whirling] of the wheel...
The phrase "transformation," and so forth, refers to that sequence of undertaking which takes the form of a cart, a funeral mound, and the like;

by means of this, one necessarily produces a jar, and not otherwise—[the optative suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of necessity (*niyoga*)]. Furthermore, if one does not become angry, then in reality even the potter [does not produce it].

He states that the result [of this] has also been achieved here by means of the sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), which is established as the nature of being the independent self of the universe; thus he says, "And therefore" (*ataśca*). In that regard—meaning in the jar—the sense is: because [the Lord] is the impeller of clay and the other materials.
This is the explanation of the verse based on the aforementioned method.

He asserts this very point, saying "it is said. When there is the expectation of "by whom is it said?", he begins to explain the verse with the words "the Lord" (*īśvara*). The term "potter" (*kumbhakāra*) is explained therein by the phrase "the Lord is indeed the maker of the pot" (*kumbhakṛd eva tatreśvaraḥ*); [this is so] because of his sovereignty (*aiśvaryāt*).

He explains [the phrase] "by means of an arrangement" as "by means of the Lord. That which has a form like that of the Lord is "lord-like" (*īśvararūpā*); by that, [meaning] by means of an arrangement—that is, by means of a construction—belonging to the Lord; in other words, "like the Lord. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the inclusion of] the threads and so forth is intended.
The taking up [of the clay]. He demonstrates the very process of refinement (*saṃskāra*) in sequence with the words "of the clay" (*mṛdaḥ*).

"Rubbing" (*mardana*) means the accomplishment of the suitability for forming a lump. "Straightening" (*praguṇatva*) means placing it straight within the hole of the wheel. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the winding of the rope and so forth are included. By that—

That which has its commencement through a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*) is "commenced by that" (*tadārambha*). He shows the nature of the sequence with the word "palanquin" (*śivikā*). He establishes the connection with the instrumental case using the word "by that" (*tena*). He states the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) with the word "necessarily" (*niyogataḥ*); "necessarily" means "as a rule. He states what is excluded by this necessity:
"Not otherwise. Now, one might ask: "In this context, what is the meaning of *niyoga*? To this he says: "In *niyoga*.

By this, its status as an illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntavākyatva*) is confirmed. As for the application to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the skillful [author] will surely do so himself. And thus, the construction here is as follows: *asau*...
Just as a potter, existing as the lord of clay and other materials by virtue of being their impeller,

produces a jar through the specific arrangement of his sovereignty and the sequential processing of those respective clays and so forth— producing it according to a fixed rule— in the same way, the Lord also produces sprouts and other effects.

The application of the analogy should be made by oneself. Furthermore, in this context, the treatment of the subject of proof (the *sādhya*), namely Īśvara, as an object of comparison is done with reference to the scripture (*śāstra*) and thus does not entail any contradiction. Now, if this is so, then in the case of the pot used as the example, [one would expect] only the potter...

In response to the objection that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), agency has been attributed [to something else] and thus God’s status as the creator of all is not tenable, the author provides an introduction to offer a second explanation of this very verse, beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). [The term] *aiśvaryāt* means "from sovereignty," [referring to] God (*īśvara*).
From the perspective of ultimate reality,
by means of the unfolding of its own inherent power— designated as "necessity" (niyati) in relation to the conditioned factors (saṃskāra)—
the jar is produced; otherwise, how could insentient materials such as clay and so forth [produce it]?
Or rather, why should even the threads not heed the potter’s desire to produce a cloth? This very point has been stated by this same Sūtra with the words "tathā hi" (for it is so).
[Objection: But in that case, the potter would have no status as an agent, and thus his agency would collapse.

The establishment of dharma and adharma: if you accept it through both reason and scripture, then it is exactly so. Nevertheless, even in the midst of this entire manifold creation, it is by the Supreme Lord alone that this has been fashioned:
namely, the unwavering conceit of that beast of a potter regarding his false status as the creator.
The pride of being a debtor is like that of a surety. If, however,
this very will of the Lord were such [as it is], they would not follow after Him— that is, they would not pursue Him— due solely to the necessity (niyati) created by the Lord.
The meaning is that even a potter is able to impel clay and other materials toward the making of a jar.
Thus, the construction here is as follows: this potter, impelled by God, would produce the jar solely through the very order established by God, and not independently. By what kind of order?

The meaning is: "by means of the sequence of refinements of that specific clay and so forth," which is to say, by way of the manifestation of the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) as it has been demonstrated. The word *yuktatvena* (as being appropriate) is to be supplied [to the sentence]. Otherwise, that potter would [also] [use] threads for the making of a jar.
The sense is that "one should impel. Now, to the question "For which verse has this commentary been composed?", he says:
"This very [point]. When there is the expectation of "By which sūtra?", he shows the sūtra partially by saying:
"For instance" (*tathā hi*). He provides an introduction in order to offer a third interpretation as well.
"Indeed, in this way"—that is, in the manner described—"[the world] would perish," meaning it would be destroyed.

The sense is that, by assuming the conceit of being the agent of all things, everyone would become merely those who tread upon the wrong path. [This concerns] the established order of dharma and adharma.

The boundary between dharma and adharma. He states the reply with the word "yadi" (if): if you accept—meaning you produce conviction—in both reason (*yukti*) and scripture (*āgama*), then it is exactly so. [Objection: In that case, how is the destruction of the established order of dharma and adharma to be prevented?
In response to this expectation, he explains the verse that has been introduced as the subject matter with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

"Whatever other entire collection of entities exists—that is, the multitude of things distinct from himself—within the creation of that [collection]. When the question arises as to what this is, he says: "that which... (*yat*).

The conceit of being a debtor held by a guarantor due to the death or other circumstances of the primary debtor is not what is intended here, because that [conceit] is of a real nature. [Objection: Well then, when does this conceit perish? To this he says:

"If" [is used] because of the expectation of what kind [it is]. To this he says "mā"—meaning, "this conceit of his has arisen"—in which case he is not an agent at all. This very point has also been stated by the Sūtra itself with the words "tathā hi. For even for a potter, there is [the process] through the sequence of the preparation of clay and so forth.

The deliberation consisting of an inquiry— namely, "Shall I produce a jar, or shall I not produce it?"— which aims at the determination of one side [of the alternative], arises from the various states belonging to the Lord alone,
which consist in the concealment of His own nature and the manifestation of that reality. Thus.
The potential mood (*liṅ*) is used here for the purpose of inquiry. Therefore, in reality, the Lord alone is the agent everywhere, and since I am He, I am not limited.
"Of him"—that is, of the potter—"the conceit" refers to the conceit: "I am the maker of the jar."
"Let it not arise"—let it not emerge. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the Lord's will.
"This one"—the potter; the sense is that the Lord himself, having generated the conceit of agency in subjects, maintains the order of dharma and adharma. But if that is so, then...
If you argue that for those whose pride has dissolved, only the path of going astray remains, oh, what skill!

For when even the path of those whose pride has dissolved goes to oblivion, what talk can there be of going astray? Nevertheless, by the force of their ancient latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), they...
"Action alone, arriving by way of its own momentum and not opposed by place or time, maintains the stability of the body for the time being;
enough with this elaboration. Now, in response to the expectation of where this explanation was made, he says "this very [point]. Thus, the construction here is as follows: *asau*...
Endowed with false pride, the potter— by means of his sovereign disposition, that is,

solely through the will belonging to the Lord— should produce a jar through the sequence of processing various clays and so forth; he should form the conceit of producing a jar, for in the absence of such conceit [the act would not occur].

The sense is that there is an absence of agency. Among these three explanations, in all of them, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes only an injunction (*niyoga*). Now, he provides an introduction in order to set forth the fourth explanation, beginning with the words "Even for a potter...
[The term] *saṃpraśnātmā* means having the nature of a question. But in this case, whose question is it?
To explain the meaning of the word *pada*, he says: "in the sense of inquiry" (*saṃpraśne*). Thus, the construction here is as follows:

"this"—the potter intent upon making a jar—by means of "various," that is, manifold forms, consisting of the concealment of his own nature and the manifestation of reality (*tattva*) [and the concealment of the infinite nature of his own form].

—C.], by way of its state—that is, by its persistence, through the sequence of processing that particular clay and so forth—it would produce a jar; it is certain regarding the production of the jar, meaning it is certain in one respect, as it were.
By this, he indicates that the established entity is to be made the object of focused attention.

"Therefore" means: for that reason, God alone is the agent everywhere, because even the agency of others ultimately rests in Him alone. And "I am He," because of my connection with the agency and other attributes residing in Him; even a spark of fire is endowed with the power of burning.

For the sense is that it is indeed fire; thus, "I am limited"—meaning only with respect to this body—but rather, "I am the agent everywhere. It is established that one must, in every way, fix this firmly within the heart. || 9 ||

It is observed that the sovereignty of this conscious principle alone unfolds everywhere, such that it brings even insentient things into its own nature; however, insentient things lack the capacity to manifest other objects— this is what was stated.
He confirms this by means of an example well-known to all disputants:
even for yogins, by the power of their will, that [effect], such as a jar and so forth, arises even without clay or seed, performing its respective stable purposeful action. (10)
If it is well known here that causes such as clay and so forth are impelled by volition,
and if I am not the agent of the body independent of them, nevertheless, I am the agent in all respects solely through the agency of the Lord.
One should pay attention—attention must be given—to this much alone: that it is from the perspective of reality (*tattvāt*).
As it has been said:
"He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction..."
"He is the most intelligent among men."
Thus—this is established; it becomes endowed with stability. || 9 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the tenth verse with the words "dṛśyate 'sya" (it is seen by him).
Here, the commentary states:
the construction is "of the conscious one alone. "Everywhere" means in all insentient objects.
He brings [them] to the state of his own self—that is, to consciousness whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).

Now, one might object: "Let that consciousness belong to them as their own. To this he says: "But not... He confirms—meaning he makes firm. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it.
Regarding the phrase "of the yogins," the commentary here establishes the method for explaining the verse by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). As it says: "In this case..."
Thus: "as a cause" means by way of being a cause. "Independent of that" means independent of consciousness.
"That" refers to that time;
if, in ultimate reality, the seed and so forth were the producer of the jar and so forth, or of the sprout and so forth.

If that were the cause, then how could the birth of a jar, a sprout, and so forth occur through the mere will of a yogi in the absence of those [causes], since it would follow that they are without a cause— or rather, that those [other causes] are not causes at all?

[Because it would result in the loss of causality—K. ṣ. ṣ. Now, if it is argued that those jars, sprouts, and so forth produced from clay, seeds, and the like are one thing, while those produced by the will of a yogin and so forth are quite another, you are answered even there:
first of all, non-difference exists because there is no difference in their reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); this has already been stated previously.

In that case as well, the yogi indeed possesses unimpeded will; and his will is precisely such that he thinks, "Let there be a jar which is capable of performing a vast range of purposeful actions, just like a pot produced from clay and other materials.
This is what he says: "Of each and every stable [entity], which is connected with subsequent purposeful actions..."

And a jar or similar object arises in a form that is a cause, characterized by habit, and conducive to the performance of its own specific purposeful activity (arthakriyā), which persists over a period of time. As for those who say:
"The production of a jar or the like does not occur without a material cause (upādāna); however, a yogi [produces them] by means of his will from atoms..."

"Seeing, it causes contact"—this means apart from that [the seed], i.e., apart from the clay and the seed. In response to the expectation "why would it not be so?", he states two reasons by way of an alternative: "because of being causeless," and so forth.

Because it would follow that there are no causes— meaning it would follow that things such as pots and sprouts are devoid of causes; or, in the alternative case (vā), because it would follow that those [materials] such as clay and so forth are not causes with respect to pots, sprouts, and the like.

Because it would follow that there is an absence of causality. Here, the student raises an objection with the words "Now, if it is said... He provides the answer with "In that case also... In response to the expectation, "Tell me something else," he says "In that case also. The meaning is: "it is exactly like that," or "it is precisely of such a nature. It is of such a kind (*tādṛk*).

In response to this inquiry, he says: "Let the jar exist. He explains the entire compound phrase beginning with "tattat" as "tasya tasya," and so forth. He explains "tattat" as "tasya tasya" (of each respective thing). He explains "sthirah" (stable/permanent) as "arthakriyāntare" (in another causal efficiency).

"Other causal efficiencies" (*arthakriyāntara*) refers to other causal efficiencies distinct from this [present] one; the meaning is that they are "concomitant with" or "following after" it. He explains the constituent part *sva* (own) as "belonging to oneself. He states that the expressed meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is "instrumentality" (*karaṇe*). He states that the expressed meaning of the suffix *ta* is "cause" (*hetu*).

Thus [it is said]. Here, he introduces the view of the logicians (tārkika) in order to refute it, with the words "as for those who say. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the raised question. They should be addressed as follows: "If indeed [the object] is perceived through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), scripture (āgama), and so forth..."
The causal relationship among yogis does not undergo reversal—this is what wins over your hearts;
so what is the use of grasping at atoms? If it were not so, then the pot would have its shards, and the body its own limbs, each of which would possess its own well-established [independence].

Since even the slightest change, down to the level of grass or sesame seeds, cannot occur without a worldly cause, both types of causes must be relied upon: for a jar, clay, a staff, a wheel, and so forth; and for the body, the union of male and female, and so forth. [All such things must be relied upon—K. ṣ. ṣ.]

It is observed that [the body] remains for a much longer period of time. However, the arising of a jar, a body, or the like immediately after [the dissolution of consciousness], as asserted by the Yogins, is indeed difficult to justify; rather, it is consciousness itself that becomes such and such [an object]. The Blessed One, the Great God of manifold splendor (Bhūribharga), [declares this].

"His absolute sovereignty consists in both following and transcending necessity"—in this view, those who maintain that sovereignty resides in the well-known worldly causal relationship which follows necessity are addressed as follows:
"They are to be refuted," meaning they deviate—that is, they fail. Your...

The connection is that [the pot] "wins over the heart. The point is that the apprehension of atoms is indeed postulated for the sake of demonstrating deviation (*vyabhicāra*) once the proof through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has been established.
"If not" means if it does not win over the heart; the ellipsis is "the shards are the cause. Of these—

Of the potsherds and their constituent parts, "by even a trace"—meaning even by a fragment such as a blade of grass or a grain of sesame—there is "becoming otherwise," which is to say, deviation; this is "to be expected," meaning it must be anticipated. Of what nature is both? It is that which has been observed over a very long period of time through prolonged storage.
That which has such a persistence by means of a cause is "difficult to justify";

the meaning is that it is simply impossible to justify. [The opponent objects: "But even in your view, this matter is equally difficult to justify. To this he replies with the word "conscious" (*cetana*); the word "but" (*tu*) indicates an alternative position, namely, our own position.

Consciousness itself becomes such and such—it manifests as the form of this or that state—and thus this matter is not difficult to establish; for the sense is that nothing is impossible for the Independent One.
Thus the Lord declares the absence of contradiction even from the perspective of the Śaiva school that holds to the gross view.
The Blessed One is endowed with the sovereignty of Maheśvara; he is Bhūribharga, possessing abundant splendor;

he is Mahādeva; he is one who possesses such autonomy (*svātantrya*) regarding both the following and the transgressing of *niyati* (the principle of necessity). In this context—meaning in this view—he is one who follows *niyati*.

[This refers to] those who follow necessity—meaning, in the worldly sense. Independence exists regarding the well-known worldly relationship of cause and effect; however, it does not exist regarding transcendence.

For one who respects the transgression of that [worldly order], there is independence in the supramundane realm, which is well-known among those who resemble yogins; thus it is not [the case otherwise].

There is no contradiction whatsoever; this much [conflict] exists only in the world of conventional experience (*loka*). In ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, that very [consciousness] manifests as the nature of the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) consisting of the fivefold cosmic acts, such as creation, which take the form of both sequential and non-sequential processes.
For the conscious one causes all entities to appear within the mirror of its own self, like reflections.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). As the former teacher said:

"Homage to that wielder of the trident, who is praiseworthy for his creative power (*kalā*), who weaves the variegated world-picture upon a wall-less surface, without any collection of material causes. (Stavacintāmaṇi, verse 9). || 10 ||

Now, if effects are produced— even by transgressing well-known causes— such that they possess functions identical to those specific effects produced by those [known] causes, then the discourse of inference is shattered. For instance:
How can there be the transgression of one thing by another—
that is, the transgression of necessity (niyati)— on the part of one who is "paying heed," meaning one who brings [the object] into the sphere of attention,
namely the yogin? This is well-known among those who are mostly practitioners of yoga.

Since this is generally well-known among yogis, there is therefore autonomy (*svātantrya*) regarding the supramundane relationship of cause and effect; the sense is that, by virtue of the mundane state, it is the Blessed Lord Mahādeva himself who exists [as that cause]. Now, one might ask: "In that case, what is the difference between this position and your own?"

To this he says: "And of such a measure. And of such a measure—the entity described in your own position—is nothing but the world itself, because it consists of differentiated forms. [Objection: Well then, what exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)?
To this he says: "From the perspective of ultimate reality. That alone—the Blessed Lord alone—[is that which] has the nature of both succession and non-succession.

That which is the universe, and its fivefold activity beginning with creation—namely, the fivefold activity consisting of creation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), concealment (*pidhāna*), and grace (*anugraha*)—is His very nature, that is, His essential form; such is He who shines forth. According to their view:
The sense is that [the fivefold activity] is distinct from the Blessed One’s own nature according to [other] views, whereas in our view, it is his very essence.
To the question "In what manner does he manifest?", he provides the reason: "For he is consciousness.
The sense is that it is not logical for there to be a difference between the mirror and its reflection. Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In this context, he cites the words of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa as an illustration, saying: "As he said... (10).
Now he provides the introduction to the eleventh verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"by that which is the transgression of the well-known causes, such as clay and so forth."

From those well-known causes, those specific effects—namely, the various types of effects such as jars and the like—which possess a common occurrence or nature (vṛtta-svarūpa), [are produced]. In response to the inquiry "How are they broken?", he begins the justification with the words "tathā hi" (for instance). "Anyat" refers to clay and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that [the relation] would thus be merely a matter of necessity (*niyama*), those who consider themselves more authoritative have accepted identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) as the grounds for such necessity;
for there can be no entity devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), nor can there be one with a divergent intrinsic nature.

Because there would be a distinction [between the two] due to a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*); and because, if those two intrinsic natures were not present in each respective mode (*paryāyaśas*), it would follow that they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). The same should be stated regarding an effect that is either causeless or has different causes.
Otherwise—how could it be so for other things such as a jar? For all entities...
