The sense is that [the realization] would not occur because it would terminate in one's own self alone. Having raised this doubt—having anticipated such a question from a disciple—the meaning is: "by those who consider themselves more authoritative, but not by those who are more authoritative in the ultimate sense."

"By the Buddhists" means with the intention of refuting [the existence of] yogis. "The cause of restriction" (niyamanidāna) means the cause of limitation; "having accepted" (upagate) means having admitted. In that regard, the cause of restriction for identity is found in the case of "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*. For here—
The distinction characterized by the *śiṃśapā* tree, having "tree" as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), is indeed quite clear.
In cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," the cause for the restriction of that [smoke's] origination is evident;
here too, the origination of the subject "smoke" from the nature of fire is perfectly clear.

In response to the inquiry "How is this so?", he provides a justification with the words "Indeed not" (*na hi*). Regarding that, he says "lacking intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvam*) in reply to the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*); for "indeed" (*hi*)—that is, because an entity cannot be devoid of intrinsic nature, as it would then lack the very status of being an entity. In reply to the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), he says:
Nor is it [the case] "thus": because of difference; the meaning is that it would follow that the very same thing is different from itself.

The implication is that the difference between entities occurs solely through a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). He states the second undesirable consequence as well with the words "successively" (*paryāyaśaḥ*); "successively" means in sequence, of "that"—namely, of the differentiated entity.

In the absence of two intrinsic natures, there would follow the consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); for an entity that is distinct in each moment, upon the abandonment of the prior intrinsic nature and the non-arrival of the subsequent intrinsic nature— [upon the abandonment of the prior intrinsic nature and the non-arrival of the subsequent intrinsic nature]...
Furthermore, by way of non-arrival [C], it would gradually be swallowed up by non-existence; or else,

at the time of the prior nature there would be the absence of the subsequent nature, and at the time of the subsequent nature there would be the absence of the prior nature, and from that, it would follow that it is indeed devoid of intrinsic nature, for it is not so.

In both cases, the determination is based solely on causality. For it is from its own causes that the *śiṃśapā* tree is produced as having a nature that does not deviate from being a tree, and from its own causes that fire is produced as having a nature that generates smoke; thus, this [nature] now transcends [the constraints of] necessity.

If the relationship of cause and effect were [merely] by the will of a yogin, all of this would fall apart. For by the will of a yogin, even a *śiṃśapā* tree could possess the nature of a non-tree. As for smoke, however, the objection is twofold: either the causal complex of fire and so forth produced by the yogin’s will would not generate smoke, or else it would be the yogin’s will itself [that generates it].

Anticipating the objection that there would be no inference such as "smoke without fire," yet such [an inference] does exist in the world, he says: "When the absence of being a magical creation by a yogin has been ascertained by another means of valid cognition..."
The effect, the cause, or the essential nature—each of these arises from origination as its root. || 11 ||

The will of the yogi also produces an effect that is in every respect exactly like that [original], and not— according to the analogy of a scorpion produced from cow dung and so forth— somehow generating a different effect in terms of its taste, potency, and so on; such is the case.
The point is that it is logical for an adventitious [property] to have the nature of its substrate; for existence (*sattā*) is indeed the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

And thus, since whatever is the intrinsic nature of something does not deviate from it, the fact that identity (*tādātmya*) is the cause of necessity has been established. [Now, as for] the fact that origination from that (*tadutpatti*) is the cause of necessity:
Having established the reasoning regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), he extends that same logic to the cause (*hetu*) by saying "in the same way. Therein, it should be applied respectively:

if there were no cause, production would be impossible; if the causes were different, then difference [of the effects] would follow. And thus, whatever is the cause of something does not deviate from it; this applies to production as well.

The fact that restriction is the cause [of order] has been established. To explain how mere origination, as conceived by the logicians (*tārkika*), can be the cause of restriction, he says: "In both cases. *Vyavasthā* refers to a boundary consisting of restriction. In response to the question "How so?", he says: "From their own causes" (*svahetutaḥ*).

He states the conclusion with the words "tat" (that). "This"—referring to the previously mentioned web of processes—"in that which transcends necessity"—meaning that which deviates from the previously stated rules—"would collapse"—it would perish. To the question "Why?", he says: "by the will of the Yogin. For there is no obstruction whatsoever to the will.
The sense is that [the objection] is appropriate. He shows that the objection is indeed twofold with the words "fire, etc.

The connection with the preceding is: "[it] would not produce smoke. [An objection: "But let there be no inference"; to this he says: "And it exists. "That" refers to the inference. Thus is the introduction.
Having composed the verse and introduced it, he explains it with the words "the yogin.
Here, the commentary explains "for this very reason" by saying "the yogin. It is exactly of that nature—
It is exactly similar to that which is produced by external causes; that is to say, it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in precisely the same manner.

By the "principle" (*nyāya*) of those scorpions and so forth that are born from scorpions, cow dung, and the like—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including insects produced from feces, urine, and other such sources—this principle is applied.
For this very reason, for this same cause, an effect such as smoke serves as the logical reason (*hetu*) in the inference of fire and so forth,

or a nature such as *śiṃśapā*-ness serves as the logical reason in the inference of "tree-ness" and so forth— provided that [the relationship] has been established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
The absence of being a yogic emanation is ascertained through worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) and not otherwise.

For this very reason, in inference, factors such as practice in previous lives and worldly consensus must necessarily be relied upon; and that [consensus] is the seed for both scriptural wisdom (*śruta-prajñā*) and inferential wisdom (*anumāna-prajñā*). Thus it is said.
Patañjali has stated that the scope [of the term] is "truth-bearing" (*ṛtambharā*).

In this regard, the sequence should be understood as follows: there is a difference in *rasa* (flavor) in the case of a scorpion born from cow dung, whereas there is a difference in *vīrya* (potency) in the case of one born from a scorpion; for they are not both produced from both the scorpion and the cow dung.

"The two scorpions are similar because their taste (*rasa*) is weak, but their potency (*vīrya*) is extremely strong"—the sense is that the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of those two is not identical. Regarding the word "stated" (*kathita*), he explains it as "smoke and so forth" (*dhūmādi*) in reference to the previous verse; where is the effect (*kārya*) of that?

In response to the inquiry regarding the cause, he explains by supplying a fact not explicitly stated in the Sūtra, saying "in the inference of fire and so forth. In response to the inquiry as to when this occurs, he explains the first half-verse by fulfilling the expectation of the word "thus" (evam), saying "if [it were otherwise]. For it is not otherwise; for in that case, by that [means], it is not [established].
The point is this: although that effect has been produced, it was accomplished merely by the will of the yogi through his power; how, then, can he be its cause?
Relying on this, he says something else well-known from the Patañjala Śāstra: "Therefore..."
"Thus. For this very reason— that worldly renown (*lokaprasiddhi*) is useful in this context—
the venerable Patañjali [states] that in inference (*anumāna*),
such factors as practice in previous lives and worldly renown are [required], as in the case of an infant's inference regarding breast milk.

He stated— that is, he declared in his own treatise— that the practice of previous births, the well-known instance of inferring fire, and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), are necessarily dependent upon, necessarily connected with, and necessarily required.
What is the nature of the perfection resulting from practice in previous births?

It refers to the object of *ṛtambharā* (truth-bearing), meaning it is described in Patañjali’s treatise as being accomplished through *ṛtambharā*. Nor is this designation meaningless, like the term "oil-drinker" (*tailapāyikā*); for it means that which bears (*bibharti*) truth (*ṛtam*).
Because the term *ṛtambharā* (truth-bearing) is etymologically significant, that which is false according to worldly convention lacks the status of being "worldly convention.
This [wisdom] is the speech of the Lord.

Furthermore, other rationalists have postulated the existence of a perception resembling the direct perception of a yogi for the purpose of grasping all things. However, we place no reliance on conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*), for our subject matter is the very nature of God, and that—

It has been stated more than once that [the cognition] is indeed self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), and even when other objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are obstructed, it is not itself obstructed—even when there is an obstruction of the object of knowledge. Now, one might ask: what is the point of this inquiry regarding the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*)? To this he replies: [it is necessary] because of the *śiṃśapā* tree, which does not deviate from the property of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*).

That which is the root cause of origination is what those learned in the unsurpassed scriptures call "Name. To the question of in which sūtra this was stated, he says: "And that"—meaning, it is declared as being established through the state of practice in previous births and so forth.

And *ṛtambharā* (truth-bearing) wisdom is the seed for the wisdoms derived from scripture and inference—that is, for the knowledge based on established renown and the knowledge based on inference. For sometimes even ordinary people, by virtue of the purity of their minds, perceive future events as if they were directly present before them; and that—

Logicians describe intuitive perception (*prātibha-pratyakṣa*) as, for example, when a young girl says, "My brother will come tomorrow. He states the view of other proponents who rely solely on their own fabricated reasoning with the word "others" (*anye*). The term *yauktikāḥ* means those for whom mere reasoning is the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

"Resembling the direct perception of a yogin" means similar to the direct perception of a yogin; "they have postulated its existence" means they have established it through reasoning. To the objection that a rebuttal must be made here, he says: "In the conventional [realm]."

"In the conventional" (*sāṃvyavahārike*) means that which has arisen from correct worldly practice (*samyagvyavahārāt*); "burden" (*bharaḥ*) means the intensity of the desire [to know]. Why? He says: "For the subject at hand" (*prakṛtaṃ hi*). "The subject at hand" (*prakṛtam*) means what is currently under discussion. "Even when there is an obstruction of the objects of knowledge" (*prameyoparodhe 'pi*) means even when the objects of knowledge are being made into cognitive objects; "it is not obstructed" (*na... uparuddhyate*) means it is not hindered by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇena*).

It can be made an object of cognition. No interpretation has been made for the phrase "or its nature" because of its simplicity. He provides an introduction to explain "born from the root of origination" with the word "nanu" (but surely).
Regarding the "reason of essential nature"—that is, in the reason called *svabhāva*—by this [phrase] "unfit for the effect."
The sense is that since a nature dependent on necessity (*niyati*) is not subject to the creative power of a yogi, it cannot be produced by one.

Having provided this introductory transition (*avataraṇikā*), he provides the explanation with the words "he says" (*āha*). The words "the author of the aphorisms" (*sūtrakāra*) are to be supplied as the subject. When the question arises as to what he says, [the author] first analyzes the compound of this term:

He provides an explanation: "In the state of being a tree. To fulfill the requirement for an object of the action of arising, he supplies the agent and says, "in the state of being a tree. He explains the member "root" as "the cause," meaning that which has the form of a seed.

Thus, that very nature arises as being invariably concomitant with those [specific] constituents; and consequently, there is the cognition of color-form and so forth from taste, because they are dependent on a single causal capacity,
just like the inference of the properties of the cause from smoke and the transformation of fuel.

Thus is the principle of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*). Now, it may be objected that while it is observed that scorpions and the like have multiple causes such as insects and cow dung, their differences in taste, potency, and so forth are something else entirely; for those [qualities] are produced by the conjunction with that [specific cause].

"Accompanied by that alone" means following the mere *śiṃśapā* tree, and not following it as something possessing its properties (*tadvat*); this is an explanation of the root *jan* (to be born), which ends in the suffix *ḍa* prescribed for the agent [in the sense of "born from"], according to Pāṇini 3.2.98 (*pañcamyām ajātau*), followed by the word "iti."

At the conclusion of the commentary, the sense is that for this very reason, since even an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not deviate from being an effect, there is scope for this consideration here as well. Therefore, he states something else as the resulting consequence with the words "And thus" (*tataśca*). Since [it is] an intrinsic nature...

It arises as that which is concomitant with its own specific element (tanmātra) from that cause; "from taste" means from the cause known as taste, that which is dependent on the same causal complex as taste—that is, dependent on the same causal complex as taste—meaning it is concomitant with that specific element. But it does not arise from form and so forth, which exist merely as [separate] causes.

Regarding form and touch—their "cognition" (gati) occurs through the inference of properties from a cause; that is, by means of a cause, there is an inference of another property that is invariably concomitant with that [cause] alone. It does not, however, [occur otherwise].

The meaning is that there is an inference of the causes, such as form and so forth, from the effect, which is the flavor (*rasa*). Alternatively, the suffix *tasil* is used in the sense of the genitive case; thus, the meaning is "of the flavor. He provides an illustration for this with the word "smoke":
just as, in the case of fire, there is an inference of the modification of the fuel by means of smoke, through the inference of the properties of the cause.
"It is so"—this is the meaning. Thus, the principle of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is established.

He provides an introduction in order to offer another explanation of the phrase "born from the root of origination" (*utpattimūlaja*), beginning with the word "nanu. [The objection is: "But was not the distinction between taste, potency, and so forth already stated there?"

To this he says: "It is taste. [The phrase] "this is another matter" means that it is not possible to state a difference in the nature of a scorpion based on differences in its taste, potency (*vīrya*), and so forth; such is the sense. He states the conclusion:
therefore, while it might be tolerable for smoke to lack fire, how could it be so for its own nature?

The possibility of error [is as follows]: no authoritative person would ever accept that what is blue could become non-blue by the mere wish of a yogi. It is said in reply: here, indeed, there are two kinds of essential reasons (*svabhāvahetu*): that in which the relationship of cause and effect is internally contained, and its opposite.
"This mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," and "This is impermanent because it is produced.
Regarding these, in the case of the first, its very root is the relation of cause and effect—so what more need be said there?
But the second is now examined: if, first of all, "being produced" means simply being dependent upon a cause...

How could *svabhāva*—namely, the nature of existence delimited by non-existence—be the *svabhāva* of impermanence? This is because there is a difference in appearance (*ābhāsa*). However, if there were no difference in appearance, then upon the establishment of the reason, the probandum would already be established; at most, only conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) would be proven.

"Thus," [it is said]. "It is named Sahya," [meaning] because of its many births; this is the sense. To the question, "Why is there no possibility of error? he says, "For not... Here, he promises to state the answer with the words, "It is said. He makes the promise fruitful with the word, "In this case," [presenting] two reasons.

He demonstrates this in sequence with the words "it possesses fire. In that context—between the two types of reasons—the first is that in which the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is internally inherent, while the other is its opposite. He performs the investigation itself with the words "if. Dependence on a cause means having the acquisition of one's own nature dependent upon a cause.

By non-existence— that is, by the state of being delimited through non-being (*asattā*)— existence (*bhavana*), which has been made the object of such delimitation, is brought to the state of being delimited; this is what is called "having that as its intrinsic nature" (*tatsvabhāvatā*).

—that which is called "of that form" (tadrūpa), namely impermanence, would be the very nature [of the object], because of the difference in manifestation (ābhāsabheda). The point is this: it is not logical for the two manifestations—namely, the state of being dependent on causes and the state of having existence as its nature—to be one and the same. Now, if it is asked how there can be a difference in manifestation, he says: "But if there were non-difference... (abhede tu).

"Because the probandum is already established. This would entail the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), specifically the variety known as the "unestablished probandum" (*sādhyāsiddha*). For it is only a subject that is itself doubted that is appropriate as the locus for an inference, not one that is already established. This is another alternative position stated by the student.

He raises a doubt with the words "yadi param" (if, at most). "Param" means merely; "sādhyate" means it is brought into the scope of the proof by the formulation: "This must be treated as impermanent because it is produced. To the question "How so? he replies:

By the logic that "this is a tree because it possesses treeness," and since worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) consists of cognition and verbal designation and is necessarily an effect, you yourself have admitted the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) in that very context. Therefore, in all cases...
In the case of essential reasons (*svabhāvahetu*), there is merely the establishment of a conventional usage, even without a difference in appearance;
for, because it consists of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), the "fallacious probandum" (*sādhyābhāsa*) therein is not something additional.
This is precisely the situation regarding exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), and this is the very path for universals (*sāmānya*). Therefore:

The appearance of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyābhāsa*) between the appearance as a *śiṃśapā* tree and the appearance as a tree is determined— dependent on the power of necessity (*niyatiśakti*)— by the force of the cause according to the previously stated principle; therefore, this is an essential nature (*svabhāva*).

"Taruh" (the tree) means that it is to be designated as "taruh. By this principle—meaning by this logical rule—he states the answer even regarding the suspected position: "And [it is] linguistic usage," which consists of cognition and designation—that is, in the form of description and narrative, or in the form of cognition.
"And consisting of the form of words" is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Let that linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) be something produced (*kārya*.

To this he says: "And there (*tatra ca*). The construction is: "And there—in that produced [entity] and in that linguistic usage—it is admitted by you as well," for otherwise there would be the consequence of a confusion of linguistic usages; such is the sense. He states the conclusion:

"Therefore" means: among *svabhāvahetus*—that is, among reasons whose nature is identity (*svabhāva*)—without a difference in appearance (*ābhāsabheda*), that is, setting aside a difference in appearance; for as long as there is a difference in appearance, the object would be something distinct [from the cognition]. To the question "Why?", he says: "because it would be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)."

The word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The meaning is: because it consists of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), specifically in the form of the *āśrayāsiddhi* (unestablished locus) which is non-different from the probandum (*sādhya*). To the question "Why does it consist of a fallacious reason?", he says: "non-superior" (*anadhika*). "Non-superior"—

It is neither deficient nor excessive in relation to the reason; that is to say, it is of that very nature. Now, one might ask: what is the status regarding the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), such as "this horse is excluded from non-horses"?
To this he says: "of the exclusions" (*vyāvṛttīnām*). Here too, it is merely the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

The state [of being]. "Path" means a track; in the case of "this is a cow because it is the locus of cowness," the universal (*sāmānya*) functions as a reason based on its own nature (*svabhāvahetu*). He states the conclusion with the words "therefore.
"Niyataḥ" means having attained the status of being the object of a necessary rule (*niyama*); "by the aforementioned method" means by the method previously stated.

The appearance of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyābhāsa*)—that is to say, the appearance of identity (*tādātmyābhāsa*) or the appearance of having a single nature—is brought about by the power of the cause. For a *śiṃśapā* tree that has not arisen from a seed does not have the nature of a tree. Therefore—from that reason—
And this essential nature (svabhāva) is rooted precisely in the relationship between cause and effect; therefore, it should be understood as stated in general terms:
"Every essential nature as a logical reason is born from a root of origination," and "The manifestations themselves are the reality."
This has been established previously. Consequently, when a single *śiṃśapā* tree is being produced,
because other entities possessing branches and so forth are not produced, there is the appearance of a "tree."

It is indeed possible that there is not even the name of a probandum (sādhya) in the form of a universal distinct from the entities such as branches; for that specific "tree-ness" which is of one and the same nature with it is nothing other than "śiṃśapā-ness," and since that is already established, it is not something to be proven.
"This [appearance] depends on a cause"—if this were so, then even in the case of an appearance, there would be no appearance of impermanence.
Likewise, even in the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), there would be an absence of the appearance of momentariness.
Thus, all *svabhāvahetu*s (essential reasons) depend solely upon necessity (*niyati*) and not otherwise; such is the definitive conclusion. || 11 ||
It is rooted precisely in the relationship between cause and effect— that is, it is rooted precisely in the relationship between producer and produced.
For that very reason— for that cause alone— this aforementioned matter is to be understood in its general sense, and not in its specific detail.

In response to the expectation of "by whom was it said?", he presents the words of the aphorism (*sūtra*) that form the subject of the introduction: "born from the root of origination. Thus, the sense is that, just as in the case of smoke and so forth, here too its being produced by a yogi is logical. [This occurs] without a qualified object (*viśeṣya*).
It has been stated that every essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is characterized by the unfitness [of its subject] for qualification.
The analysis of the compound *utpattimūlaja* is as follows: "born from the root," where "root" refers to origination, which is known as the relation between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
This is said even when, by resorting to the position of appearance (*ābhāsa*), there is an exclusion of the means of conventional practice.
In order to ward off the fault of the probandum being non-different [from the reason], he says: "appearances" (*ābhāsāḥ*).

Since the very root of the arising of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is that [appearance], for that reason, when a single *śiṃśapā* tree is being produced, those things possessing branches and so forth—

"Other objects"— namely other trees— because of their non-creation [from that source], there exists a semblance of a tree which has the nature of a universal (*sāmānyātman*), that is, the form of a universal, which is the probandum (*sādhya*) to be established regarding the *śiṃśapā*. That is of a single form— that is, it possesses a single form being produced.

"Distinct" (viśiṣṭa) means having a specific form (viśeṣarūpa). Thus, there is no fault here of identity with the probandum (sādhyābheda), because the general probandum is established by means of a proven qualification; this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, he precludes the identity between impermanence (anityatva) and producedness (kṛtakatva) by the word "cause" (kāraṇa). And so it is:

The intended meaning is that here too there is no identity with the probandum (*sādhyābheda*). By way of an incidental discussion, he wards off this fault elsewhere with the word "thus" (*evam*). [Objection: But if this is so, how can there be a single nature (*ekasvabhāvatva*) here? [Reply: True; it does not exist for one who is in disagreement, but now it is being established, and it is precisely for the sake of proof (*sādhanārtha*) that [it is stated].

Even that which is already established is attributed the status of being "to be proven" (sādhya) for the sake of awakening those who hold contrary views; otherwise, it would result in the fallacy of a pseudo-reason (hetvābhāsa). Enough with this elaboration. He states the conclusion in its resultant form: "iti" (thus). "Iti" means for this reason; "eṣa" refers to this certainty (ekānta).
Who is this? All reasons based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) occur only in dependence upon necessity (*niyati*), and not by the will of a yogin; otherwise, they would not occur.
Indeed, in the doctrine that things are manifestations (*ābhāsa*), would fire not be a non-entity (*avastutva*) if it were not manifest?

Having raised the objection, "In this way, how can smoke be produced by that which has not appeared [as fire], and consequently, how can there be an inference of the cause, namely fire, from that smoke? he says the following to provide a justification:
"It would arise from the repeated appearance of a single fire belonging to each respective cognizer."
Even from a remote superior cause, there arises something new, such as the appearance of smoke.

The meaning is that, from one instance up to the kitchen, by the power of perception and non-perception, there is merely the arising of the appearance of fire and the appearance of smoke, because [the latter] follows upon the former.

This is what is meant: generally, an object arises from its own well-known cause; however, sometimes—by the will of a yogi, or even by the will of a yogi—error occurs. Thus, in the case of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), it refers merely to origination.
The absence of the yogi’s will as a cause must be determined at the time [of the inference], not at the time of accomplishing one's own goal;

thus, there is no impairment whatsoever of the inference. As for the investigation regarding the subject of the yogi, it has already been conducted previously in the verse beginning with "cidātmaiva hi devo 'ntaḥ," so it is not laboriously repeated here. In this verse:

The construction is as follows: for this very reason—since even a yogi produces an effect by mere will—for this cause, when the non-origination of a yogic creation has been ascertained through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it serves as a reason for the effect; that is, it possesses causality with respect to its own cause, and not otherwise.

Likewise, the nature [of the thing] itself serves as the reason (*hetu*). To the question "Why?", he states the reason by means of a qualification: "because of its arising" (*utpatti*). By this, it is determined that the absence of being a magical creation (*nirmāṇa*) by a yogi applies only to that which has arisen [spontaneously], and not to [the case of] proving one's own probandum (*sādhya*).
The darkness has been illuminated. || 11 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the twelfth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here, the commentary [explains]:
"of that which has not appeared"—that is, having become an object outside the scope of manifestation due to being situated on a mountain.
"How so? means that it is not logical because [the cause] is not a producer. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

He establishes the method for explaining the verse with the words "once" (*ekavāram*). By the power of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), [the relationship is established]; therein, in the kitchen (*mahānasa*), there is the perceptibility of the appearance of smoke and the appearance of fire, while in the great lake (*mahāhrada*)...

There is the non-apprehension of those two; the causal relationship has been grasped. In that regard, according to the view of the Vijñānavādins, there is a different appearance for each individual continuum; thus, it is only between their own respective appearances...
The causal relationship is apprehended [within one's own continuum], for the events occurring in another continuum are not experienced; therefore,
at present, there could be no inference from the appearance of smoke belonging to one's own continuum.

The certainty is that [the appearance of fire] resides in another mental continuum belonging to a cognizer, such as a worm or an omniscient being; however, in this system, at the stage of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*),
all those whose existence is possible in that location—

To that extent, there is for them a single cognizer, and this appearance of smoke and appearance of fire are, as in the externalist school, such that their identity with the Supreme Lord has been established by Him— so it has been said. Therefore, by abandoning the distinction between one's own and another's mental continuum (*saṃtāna*), [they become one].

"In every individual continuum"—that is, in all streams of consciousness—for this reason, for the Vijñānavādin, there are the appearances of smoke and fire belonging to his own stream of cognition (svajñānasantānagatayoḥ). [C reads: *sajñātasantānagatayoḥ*].
The causal relationship has been apprehended. He states "but not" (*na tu*) to exclude such a cause;

that is, [the relationship] between two things residing in different continua—meaning, residing in continua distinct from the perceiver. To the question "Why is it not apprehended?", he says "belonging to that" (*tadīya*). [This refers to] the occurrence belonging to that [other continuum].
Because the occurrence in another mental continuum (*santānāntara*) is not cognized— that is, it is not experienced—
for it is not logical that the cognition of one person should become an object for another.
And therefore— from that reason— at this time, namely at the time of inference, from [a mark] residing in one's own continuum...

[The term "inference" is used] because it pertains to the continuum of consciousness of the inferrer. For on a mountain, even worms and other such creatures situated within a forest fire would indeed be endowed with the experience of it; thus, the mention of "worms" is made.
Furthermore, since the knowledge of all-knowing beings necessarily has everything as its object, the mention of "all" is made.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of other creatures dwelling in the mountains. [An objection: But is this not the same even in your own system? To this he says: "But here" (*iha tu*). In this system—that is, in the Śaiva doctrine—those whose existence is possible in that place, namely, in the kitchen area.
"It is one" [is said] because of the acceptance of its existence outside; for an external object is indeed common to all, whereas that which consists of mere consciousness belongs only to the knower.
"As in the external system"—that is, like the system of the logicians—*tāvati* refers to the appearance of smoke located in the kitchen.
And in the case of the appearance of fire, for those perceivers situated in that same place, there is "unity"—that is, oneness;

specifically, the unity consisting of the form of the perceivers of that [object]. For every [perceiver] grasps an external object in common through the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*). He states the conclusion with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*): therefore—
For the reason stated, by abandoning the distinction between one's own and another's mental continuum,
[one considers] in a general sense that the mere appearance of smoke is the effect of the mere appearance of fire— such is the pervasion (vyāpti).

When the mountain has been apprehended, one again infers that "there is the appearance of fire on this mountain," having recalled the pervasion (vyāpti) that whatever appears as smoke on a mountain is indeed due to the appearance of fire. To that extent...

This means that when one has become unified with other subjects regarding a particular manifestation of smoke, one then becomes unified with those other subjects in respect to the general aspect of the manifestation of fire— which includes its imperceptible (parokṣa) component and is distinguished from other particular manifestations.

The word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*) indicates that having grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), whatever appears as smoke—and by the inclusion of the term "etc. (*ādi*), everything up to what appears as a sprout—is apprehended;
[it means] that every mere appearance of smoke [is the effect] of every mere appearance of fire, and not [only specific instances].

That which belongs to one's own continuum becomes an effect only for that which belongs to its own continuum; therefore, when the pervasion— in the form "wherever there is the appearance of smoke, there is the appearance of fire"— has been grasped, having been made the object of apprehension in places such as a kitchen, etc.

Even when [the fire] exists, once again—that is, once more—the appearance of smoke belonging to one's own continuum is inferred from the appearance of fire alone belonging to another's continuum; thus, the person assumes the state of an inferer. By this—

To explain what is meant by this, he says: "in that much" (*tāvati*). That inferer [acts] in that much—only to that extent, and not everywhere; otherwise, there would be the consequence of omniscience—with respect to a specific appearance of smoke—that is, the appearance of smoke located on the mountain—by other cognizers.
Having become one with other cognizers situated in that same place who perceive that smoke— attaining unity through the apprehension of the appearance of smoke—
it is accompanied by that aspect which is of a non-manifest nature, having become non-manifest due to being beyond the senses.

Alternatively, the expression is one where the abstract state (bhāva) is emphasized: [it means] "accompanied by that aspect which consists of being beyond perception," that is to say, "in the imperceptible. Likewise, it is "distinct from those other manifestations which constitute its particularity"—namely, all the manifestations of individual fires that serve as the substrata for the universal.

When [the cognition] has split, that aspect of generality which belongs to the manifestation of fire becomes one with other subjects— that is, it attains unity through the apprehension of the manifestation of fire together with other subjects situated in that same place. Thus.

The meaning is that this is precisely the point; however, it is not as in the view of the Vijñānavādins, where the apprehension of the appearance of fire occurs through the appearance of smoke apprehended by that same [consciousness]. This is the intended sense. He provides the interpretation of the verse by relying on the aforementioned method: "Furthermore" (bhūyaḥ).

He explains the word "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) as "the pervasion. By the phrase "once again," he indicates that the particle *api* has been displaced from its original position. Regarding the expression "smoke-like appearance and so forth" (*dhūmābhāsādi*), he states what is included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) with the words "because of the inclusion of 'and so forth'. It is new.

That manifestation (*ābhāsa*) too is new and unprecedented; it is not, however, "unfresh" in the sense that smoke produced from smoke is [repeated]. And that [manifestation] must arise from the manifestor (*adhipati*), whether from a manifestor of fire or from a manifestor of a seed; it is capable of being produced only from that and not from anything else. The potentiality is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*). And that manifestation resides within those [causes].
Among those cognizers, there is only one; for if there were multiplicity, this [logical relation] would not be tenable—this is the intended meaning.

And because that single dominant factor, the appearance of fire, is the cause of the appearance of smoke, therefore the appearance of smoke is the infallible effect and the logical mark (*liṅga*) of that very appearance of fire.
When it is certain that there is an absence of being produced by a yogin, he is inferred from that effect, because he is imperceptible precisely due to his sovereign power. || 12 ||
Thus he explains with the words "the unprecedented" (*apūrvaḥ*). The sense is that it has arisen from the fire at that very moment.

Like smoke from a firebrand (*dhūmadhvajavat*): just as smoke arises from the smoke produced by a cowherd’s bellows even after the fire has been extinguished, so too is it "not fresh" (*apratyagraḥ*).

"It is long-standing," and "that"—meaning that appearance as smoke—is [due to] the "sovereign" (*adhipati*), which, being a term for a cause, has been explained by its very mention as being easy to understand. He explains "from the imperceptible" (*parokṣāt*) as "from that which is not being cognized. "From the appearance of fire" (*vahnyābhāsāt*) is likewise [to be understood].

This has been explained by the preceding commentary. Here too, he states the object to be understood by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) as "or from a mere semblance of a seed" (*bījābhāsādeva vā*). He explains the word "might be" (*bhavet*) with the words "from that very [source]" (*tata eva*).
"From that very [source]" means from the semblance of fire (*vahnyābhāsādeva*) alone. Having divided [the compound] as *tattat-pramātṛ-eka*, he explains it as follows: "He... (*sa*).
Regarding the phrase "and the appearance," in response to the inquiry, "Why would there not be as many [appearances] as there are objects?
he explains the state of affairs with the words "in the case of multiplicity. The intended meaning is this: "this" refers to this very appearance of fire;
such is the intention, which means "the state of affairs is as follows": [it concerns] the object situated outside.
The intended meaning is that [this] is indeed common to all cognizers (*pramātṛ*). By this, the explanation of this verse is completed.
And thus is the construction: "Furthermore," meaning not only at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Moreover, even at the time of inference, that which is "new"— namely, the appearance of smoke and so forth arising together with fire and the like— is [produced] from the "sovereign," that is, the causal factor, which exists as "indirect" (parokṣa) because it remains unperceived; for during the day, on a mountain, only the appearance of smoke is directly perceived, not [the fire].
"The appearance of fire. Thus, from that respective appearance of the single fire of the subject (*pramātṛ*), it "may come"—that is, it is capable of coming into being.
The latter half of the following verse states: "The effect is the infallible mark (*liṅga*) of this [fire]."

He applies it here as being appropriate; the effect is the mark—that is, the mark in the form of an effect—because it makes known [the cause] by virtue of being a cause. The yogi applies the previously mentioned entity here as well, by way of ellipsis (*śeṣatvena*) through the method of supplying what is left unsaid. "Thus" means for this reason; therefore—

From the appearance of smoke, how is that appearance of fire inferred? To this he says: "Because. Because it (the fire) is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*). For it is only logical that what is beyond the senses is an object of inference. Why is it inferred from its being beyond the senses? To this he says: "Precisely because of its sovereignty (*adhipatitva*)."

The meaning is that this [object] becomes the cause; otherwise, the consequence would be that all imperceptible objects could be inferred by means of that appearance of smoke—this is the intended sense. || 12 ||

Now, one might object: "In that case, would there not also be an inference of the appearance of fire from the appearance of smoke that has emerged after remaining for a long time within the interval of a cowherd's water-clock? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The effect is an unerring mark (*liṅga*) for [the cognition] belonging to another subject."
The appearance of that [object] arises from the appearance of that very [consciousness] itself, while the subsequent [moment] arises from the dominant condition.

That which is other than the present appearance of smoke— namely, another appearance of smoke belonging to a different cognizer— is remote (*parokṣa*) due to its nature as a dominant cause (*adhipati-rūpa*); thus,
how could that which is not a cause [of the present cognition] arise from such an appearance of smoke?
Now he provides the introduction to the thirteenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here, the commentary in the *Gopalaghaṭikā* states: "by cowherds (*gopālaiḥ*) for the purpose of keeping the cows during the cold season."
Having resided for a long time— that is, for a great duration— in a specific *kuṇḍīra* vessel that has been fashioned and is devoid of large openings, it remains there—
meaning it persists even after the fire has been extinguished, precisely because it lacks large openings suitable for escape; from that...

And having emerged from that subtle aperture, [he emerges] from the smoke— that is to say, from the smoke rising out of the mass of smoke being accumulated in one place. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "kāryam."
Regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:

the portion ending with "the mark" (*liṅgam*) has been connected with the preceding verse; here, however, he explains the section beginning with "another" (*anya*). He explains the word "another" (*paraḥ*) by saying "from the new" (*nūtanāt*).
"Other than the fresh"—meaning other than that which has arisen directly from fire; that is to say, "not fresh.

"Precisely from the appearance of smoke"—that is, precisely from the mass of the appearance of smoke situated within the cowherd's water-clock (gopālaghaṭikā) even after the fire has been extinguished, and not from the appearance of fire itself.
[The smoke] belonging to another cognizer— that is, residing in the continuum of a cognizer situated between the cowherd and the water-jar— because they experience this [smoke],
and because it originates from the causal factor in the form of a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
"From a mass of smoke"—
the remaining intention is that the appearance of fire should be inferred. And those who are skilled indeed perceive the distinction.

With the intention that "the mastery of this subject matter, which is useful for the vast majority of inferential worldly transactions, must be achieved through diligent effort," that which was indicated by the word "new" (*nūtana*) has been made clear by means of its exclusion (*vyavacchedya*). || 13 ||

But if it is thus admitted that the appearance of smoke [arises] from the appearance of fire, then how is it that what was stated— that agency belongs to consciousness alone— is so? For instance, this which is observed, that "when the seed exists, the sprout comes to be," is exactly like the case of smoke and fire.
Anticipating the objection, "In what way is [this] a ground for disregard? he says:
"Even that relationship of cause and effect, expressed as 'when this exists, that exists,' is not possible for insentient things that are devoid of mutual dependence. (14)

For this reason, it is the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*), and not the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*). Regarding the phrase "and those who are skilled": with this intention—that is, by means of this intended meaning—they indeed characterize discernment (*viveka*). Why is this so?
[It is said] "of this meaning," and so forth. "Of this meaning" means "of this inference. Of this...
He explains that the sentence indicates the exclusion of new terms by the word "new" (*nūtana*):
that which is indicated by this term is precisely that, and not any other entity;
it is by way of showing what is to be excluded, and not directly.

"Sphuṭīkṛtam" means made manifest or revealed. Thus, the construction here is as follows: "paraḥ" (the other) refers to one different from the new [fire]; "tadābhāsaḥ" (its semblance) refers to the semblance of smoke that has emerged after remaining for a long time within the interval of a cowherd’s water-clock (*gopālaghaṭikā*); [this arises] from another subject (*anyapramātṛgāt*).

[The smoke] exists as an appearance (*ābhāsa*) arising precisely from that sovereign cause— the sovereign who resides within the continuum of the cognizer situated inside Gopālaghaṭikā, meaning [the sovereign] who is the object of that experience;
it arises from that very appearance in the form of a mass of smoke within Gopālaghaṭikā, and not [from anything else].
Because it is merely the appearance of fire and because that appearance has subsided, there is no inference of fire from it. || 13 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fourteenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "How so? means that it is not logical. When the question "Why? arises:
He begins the justification with the words "tathā hi" (for instance). "Anādarāspadam" means the object of disregard.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "asmin" (in this), stating:
first of all, a single entity alone cannot constitute the relation of cause and effect, nor can two entities [do so].

The nature of cause and effect is not such that they exist simultaneously, like a jar and a cloth; nor is it the case that even when they occur sequentially, their order is indeterminate, like the cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth; and even when there is a fixed sequence, it is not the case that the effect exists first and the cause exists at a later time—thus it is.

The opponent’s view is as follows: the cause is that which necessarily precedes, and the effect is that which necessarily follows. In this regard, if priority and posteriority are not something additional to their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then they are merely those two entities themselves—“that” and “that. Or else, there is no meaning at all to the word "and" (*ca*).

Since that too consists of a relationship of dependence, it would indeed be nothing other than "this" and "that. Now, if "priority" (pūrvatā) means being the cause of existence and "posteriority" (paratā) means being the effect of existence, then the seed's existence, which causes the sprout, must ultimately rest in the sprout.
He brings about the inclusion of the sprout within himself;
here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides a methodological introduction (*prakriyā*) in order to explain the verse, beginning with the words "eka eva" (one alone) and "tāvat" (first).
The sense is that there is no disagreement on this point by anyone. Now, one might object: "In that case, let the causal relation simply be two entities. To this he says: "even two entities.
"Simultaneous" means having the nature of arising at the same time. One might then ask: "In that case, [let it be] only that which arises sequentially..."

Let it be so; therefore, he says "sequence" (*krama*). That pair whose sequence is unrestricted is such [a pair]. Now, one might ask: "Let there also be a restricted sequence here; what follows from that? To this he replies: "restricted" (*niyata*). The construction is: "it is not thus. Then, what is there? To this he replies: "restricted. Regarding the word "restricted" (*niyata*) here:

The condition of being established as non-otherwise (*ananyathāsiddhatvam*) must also be applied; otherwise, even the color of the threads would be a cause with respect to the cloth. "Of the other"—that is, of the externalist, such as the logician (*tārkika*). [The opponent asks: "Let this view belong to him; what follows from that? To this he says: "In that case," [referring to] from its own nature (*svarūpāt*).
The meaning is as follows: "otherness" (*paratā*)—that is, posteriority (*paścādbhāvitā*)—arises from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of cause and effect;
it is merely the two entities themselves in the form of cause and effect, and it is not the case that the word "entity" (*bhāva*) is improperly applied here. It is simply the two entities.

He shows [the meaning] by means of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the words "that and that. The word *ca* also signifies a conjunction (*samuccaya*). To the question "Why? he says: "of that" (*tasya*). Of that—namely, of the conjunction—for a conjunction occurs in dependence upon some action, quality, or the like; it is not independent.

Furthermore, as to how the application of those two states (bhāva) might occur, he says: "that, that. He anticipates the student's question with the word "now" (atha). [The term] *prayojikā* means that which brings about another;
[the state] whose existence (*sattā*) is of such a kind. [The term] *prayojyā* means that which is to be brought about; [the state] whose existence is of such a kind.
To the question raised, he provides the answer with the word "tarhi" (then). "Antarbhāva in the sprout" (*aṅkurāntarbhāvaḥ*) means inclusion within the sprout;
that is to say, the state of being of the nature of the sprout. For whatever rests within something becomes of that very nature, just as clay resting within a jar takes on the form of the jar.

[The opponent says: But surely the non-existence of the sprout exists there; therefore, there would be mere agency toward the non-existence of the sprout. That too is nothing, because it depends on something else. The same should be said regarding the existence of that which is to be employed. Thus, it is not [the case].
It must be stated that positions such as the claim that causal relation (*kāryakāraṇatā*) consists merely in existence alone are untenable; rather,

by means of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*) expressing existence, as in "when this exists" (*asmin sati*), there is the state of being the cause of the other's existence, expressed as "this exists" (*idam asti*).

Even that kind of causality consisting in the state of having an existence dependent on another—characterized by the case-ending used for the object being produced—is not tenable; it is not possible through any means of valid cognition among insentient things, for here mutual dependence is the very lifeblood [of causality], and that is impossible for insentient things. || 14 ||

He says: "In the absence of the sprout. This means that mere agency—merely being a causal agent whose own nature is dissolved [in the effect]—is also merely the state of being an instigator; the sense is that even that mere agency cannot exist without an object. When the question "Why? arises, he himself states the reason:

"Another" means because of dependence on another—that is, dependence on the one to be employed (the *prayojya*). This refers to that state of being an employer (*prayoktṛtva*). By the word "thus," he extends the principle stated regarding the employer to the one to be employed as well. When this extension is applied—[provided there is an application]—the existence of the sprout is dependent upon the seed as its employer.

Resting in the seed, it brings about the internalization of the seed within itself; in the absence of the seed, there would be mere subservience, and even that would be nothing at all because it would depend on something else.
Relying on the aforementioned methodology, he provides the application [of this principle] to the aphorism with the word "evam" (thus). This being so:
These and other such positions are not merely untenable; they are indeed untenable. What are these?
They are: the relation of cause and effect as a single entity alone—that is, the solitary entity denoted by that [relation].

"It comes to pass. By this, it is indicated that the word *api* (also/even), situated here in the phrase "sāpi" (that also), serves to indicate sequential order (*anukrama*) and conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Furthermore, to address what else is untenable, he says "yāvat" (as far as/as much as) using the past tense suffix (*bhūtavibhakti*).

He explains that "it is not tenable" means it is not possible according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [specifying] by the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) in the form of a suffix (*ṅi*) which expresses an established entity (*siddha*), and by the verb-ending (*tip*) which expresses that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

In response to the expectation "of whom?", he says "of the insentient" (*jaḍānām*). In response to the expectation "why is it not possible?", he explains the qualification "devoid of mutual dependence" (*apekṣāvihīnānām*) as the reason, [stating] "mutually" (*anyonya*). Here—in this relation of cause and effect—it is not...
"It is possible. The sense is that dependence is not logical for insentient things.
Thus is the construction here: "In this case," meaning while this entity called clay exists in the form of a cause, if it is asked, "How is this so?"—it is said:

For this meaning of the locative case is not postulated even for the state of existence or non-existence in the case of those who are restricted solely to their own self and devoid of synthetic reflection. (15)
Inert things (jaḍa), it is said, are incapable of synthesizing one another's forms;
the state of being a synthesis of one another is pervaded by consciousness (caitanya), which is the opposite of inertia.
Furthermore, synthesis is essentially the nature of consciousness itself, whereas elsewhere it is merely figurative.
Therefore, because it is devoid of such unifying reflection (*anusandhāna*), how could an insentient entity— whose body is contracted by the satisfaction of resting solely within its own self—
give rise to another thing in the form of an effect called a jar? Thus, that which...
The relationship of cause and effect is also not possible for insentient things that lack dependence; "for those lacking dependence" is a qualifying term containing a reason.
By the word "also," it is implied that the definitions of cause and effect propounded by other disputants are likewise [untenable].
It should be understood that they do not arise. || 14 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fifteenth verse with the word "How" (*katham*).
This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "For not" (*na hi*).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
He explains the phrase "of those devoid of synthesis" by saying "the insentient.
"Mutual form" means the essential nature of one another; "to synthesize" means to make the object of synthesis; "incapable" means unable, for indeed [they are not].
The meaning is that a jar is capable of comprehending the nature of a cloth, or that [the cloth] belongs to it.
Furthermore, to address the question of in whose comprehension such power resides, he says "anyonya" (mutual).
"Anyonyānusandhāna" means mutual comprehension; that which has this as its form is [so described].

The state (*bhāva*) of something is its reality (*tattva*). It is "pervaded" (*vyāptam*): for wherever there is synthesis (*anusandhāna*), there is consciousness (*caitanya*); otherwise, it would follow that even a jar could synthesize the object that is a cloth.
To the question "By what is it pervaded?", he says: "synthesis" (*anusandhānam*). [It is] expectation—the nature of expectation.

The word "ca" (and) indeed has the sense of "hi" (for/indeed). [Objection: But how is the common usage "a jar depends upon clay" observed? To this he says "anyatra" (elsewhere): "elsewhere"—that is, in the case of insentient things—"sā"—that dependence—is "upacaritā"—established by metaphorical attribution—just as in the expression "the boy is fire," such is the meaning.
He explains [the phrase] "of those whose sole abiding is in their own self" by means of this support with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The meaning is as follows: the object, such as blue and so forth, has a resting place—its abiding—in its own self alone, that is, in its own essential nature which consists solely of existence; the satisfaction derived from that [resting] is [what is meant by "satisfaction in one's own self,"] as opposed to [satisfaction] elsewhere.
[He is] one whose body is contracted because of the absence of expansion and restlessness; otherwise,
he would expand— that is, he would engage in an intense movement in the form of mental investigation— into another object, that is, an entity distinct from himself.

It would then follow [that it could arise]. And therefore, whether the seed exists while the sprout does not, or conversely, or both exist, or both do not exist; or whether one is designated and the other is non-designated, or both are designated or both are non-designated—even so, [it would follow that it could arise].

The mere meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha) remains unqualified by other attributes such as conjunction and the like; for that entire [meaning], being of the nature of expectation, finds its rest in consciousness. || 15 ||

The sense is that the movement of one who is satisfied is not appropriate. Explaining the latter half [of the verse] while stating its result, he says "tataśca" (and therefore). Therein, he explains the phrase "sadasattāpade" (in the state of existence and non-existence) with "yadi" (if). "Viparyayaḥ" refers to the seed being non-existent and the sprout [being existent].
The substitution of the form "existent" (*sann*) is as follows: "both" refers to the seed and the sprout;
"one" refers to a single entity, either the seed or the sprout; "other" refers to a distinct entity, either the sprout or the seed.
Regarding the term "with a designation" (*sopākhyam*), this is an explanation of the word "existent," for a designation is possible only for that which exists.

"Indefinable" (*nirūpākhya*) is the explanation of the term "non-existence. He explains [the phrase] "the meaning of the locative case" with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). "The mere meaning of the nominal stem" means the mere nature of the entity itself. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other properties are included. This is indicated by the phrase "is not postulated."

"It performs its function and remains unembraced" means that, because it is rooted in dependence (*apekṣā*), it is not touched [by the fault of being a cause]. By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even by way of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth," it is indicated that there is no mention here at all of the property called "causality" (*prayojakatva*), which is the meaning of the locative case. Why?
In response to this inquiry, he says "of that. "Of that" means of that which consists of the aggregate (samuccaya) and so forth.

Thus, here is the summarized meaning: for—since—those who are devoid of synthesis (*anusandhāna*), meaning those who lack the synthesis of one object with another, therefore they remain in their own self alone.
Of such things—that is, of insentient entities like seeds, sprouts, and so forth—even at the stage of existence (sattāpada);

the word "even" (api) implies pervasion; that is, when it is admitted according to different philosophical views that they are either objects of existence or objects of non-existence, "this"—which was mentioned by the words "in this" in the preceding verse—[applies].

The meaning of the locative case is "causality" (*prayojakatva*); it is not postulated—that is, it is not tenable—because that [causality] is rooted in an expectation consisting of a mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and because that [synthesis] is appropriate only for a conscious being.
The meaning of the locative case is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the existence of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅartha*) as well; thus, "being caused to act" (*prayojyatva*) also exists.

"It is simply not applicable to insentient things. Alternatively, in the following verse, he states directly that action, which is denoted by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), is unsuitable for insentient things. (15)
Since dependence is not possible in insentient things,

for this very reason the meaning of the case-endings— which consists of the relation between action and its factors— is logically established as a connection of entities that rests solely upon a single cognizer. (16)

The very meaning of the seventh case-ending, or indeed of any other case-ending, which consists of the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*), is precisely what constitutes the "conjunction" (*samanvaya*) of entities;
there is no other such thing as a dry, abstract conjunction. And if that [conjunction] exists within the independent nature of consciousness as a duality of entities—

It is only when [the mind] comes to rest that this is possible; otherwise, it is not possible in any way. For even when this [reality] is dealt with by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), it cannot be established as being grounded in the actual thing (*vastu*).
Now, he provides the introduction to the sixteenth verse with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).
This is clear. Having introduced the verse, he explains it with the words "for this very reason.
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
he explains "the meaning of the case-ending" as "the locative. Of the other—

Regarding the forms beginning with the second person (*tiṅrūpāyāḥ dvitīyādirūpāyāśca*): he explains the word "action" (*kriyā*) by saying "action. [He explains] "characterized by the relation between action and its factors" (*kriyākārakabhāvalakṣaṇaḥ*) as having the nature of the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāvasvarūpaḥ*). He analyzes the term "integration of states" (*bhāvasamanvayaḥ*) as follows.

Regarding the phrase "of entities" (*bhāvānām*): "dry" means sapless, that is to say, consisting of conjunction and so forth. And that—namely, the aforementioned "concordance" (*samanvaya*)—and the "pair of entities," which are the two things that serve as the substratum for that concordance, "rest in the nature of consciousness"; the meaning is that they become apprehended by the nature of consciousness.

He explains "having the subject alone as its locus" with the word "independent" (*svatantra*). He explains "is appropriate" (*yukta*) with the word "is logically possible" (*upapadyate*). Otherwise—that is, in the absence of repose—by the maxim that "every sentence is restrictive," it follows that it is appropriate only for the subject alone to be the locus.

Thus it has been indicated that [the verse] is to be construed in this way. The phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), which indicates the reason for the preceding verse, has not been explained because it is easily understood. Here, he begins the justification with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*).
Even when being treated as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—that is, even in the absence of a cognizer (*pramātṛ*), however that may be.

That which has become the object of conceptual construction—namely, this conjunction of action and so forth—does not, by virtue of being grounded in a real entity—that is, by virtue of resting upon a real entity—logically hold up; the meaning is that it does not come to rest in a real entity.
Now, since conceptual construction itself lacks grounding in a real entity, how can it [be said to ground anything]?

For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whose very life-force consists in following after a real entity (*vastu*) as it is being conventionally expressed, exists only by way of conforming to experience; and that [conformity] is absent here, because [the construction] does not originate from a real entity (*vastvaprabhavatvena*). Indeed, it is that which conforms to a real entity...

It has been stated that experience and the object are grounded in their own self. Therefore, the emergence of a sprout when there is a seed, and smoke when there is fire—all of this is logical only when they rest within the subject whose nature is autonomous consciousness (svatantracidrūpa-pramātṛ), and not otherwise. || 16 ||

Now, one might object: "If the dependence characterized by the existence of the prompted and the prompter were to occur when the application (*samanvaya*) resides solely within its own self, then what would happen? To this, he says: "in accordance with the reality" (*vastvanusaraṇe*). For—since (*hi*): [the following applies].

"Having its life-force in the pursuit of the object"—meaning it has acquired its existence through the pursuit of the object; that is to say, it pursues the object. "Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) [exists] solely by way of following experience"—that is, merely by way of following experience. Now, even here, by following experience...

To ensure that [the conceptual construction] is grounded in a real entity (*vastu*), he says: "And that" (*sā ca*). "And that"—namely, conformity with experience (*anubhavānusāritā*)—is present here in the case of the conceptual construction associated with action (*kriyāsamanvayavikalpa*). When the question arises as to why this is so, he says: "Because it originates from a real entity" (*vastvaprabhavatvena*).
The meaning is that conformity with experience occurs only in a conceptual construction that is born from a real entity (*vastuja*). But why is this so?
Since there is no conformity with experience here because the cause does not originate from a real entity (*vastu*), he says:
"for [it] conforms to the real entity" (*vastvanusārī hi*). For (*hi*)—because experience conforms to the real entity.

Now, one might object that the real entity certainly exists here; therefore, he says: "and the real entity" (*vastu ca*). And the real entity is the substratum of the pervasive presence (*samanvaya*).

And the object (*vastu*), being restricted to itself—meaning restricted solely to its own nature—is, in effect, incapable of producing an experience of its own object without a cognizer (*pramātṛ*); therefore, the sense is that even though it exists, it is as good as non-existent. He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Thus, the construction of this verse is as follows: because the meaning of the locative case (*saptamy-artha*) is not tenable for insentient entities that are restricted solely to their own nature, for that very reason, that which is called the "relation of action and agent"— namely, what is known as the relation of action and agent— [is not possible].
The meaning of the case endings— consisting of all that is expressed by the nominal and verbal suffixes—

is the connection with the state of being (*bhāva*), which has insentient existence as its locus; this is logical only when it rests solely upon the subject (*pramātṛ*) and finds its final repose in consciousness alone, and not otherwise.
The sense is that an insentient object, when not grasped by a cognizer, is in every respect merely like something non-existent. Thus [ends verse 16].
Now he provides the introduction to the seventeenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
those two, cause and effect, for which there exists an employed [cause] and an employing [effect], [are as follows...]

The state of being (*tattā*) consists in the existence of both the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*); that is its characteristic—that is, its essential nature (*svarūpa*). [If it were] restricted solely to its own self, it would not be tenable; therefore, for those who maintain the identity (*tādātmya*) of cause and effect—

In the view of the Sāṃkhyas, that [agency] indeed exists; so what is the point of supporting the doctrine of an agent whose nature is the manifestation of consciousness? Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Even if cause and effect possess a mutually identical nature..."
For if there were indeed oneness in difference, there would be no mutual distinctness of essential natures.

If the sprout were the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the seed, then the sprout alone would exist and the seed would not exist at all, or else there would be a contradiction— what then would be the cause and what the effect? Alternatively,
if the seed is one thing and the sprout is another, then they cannot have a mutual identity, for [otherwise] there would be both difference and non-difference.
At one time, two [cognitions] regarding the same object are indeed contradictory. || 17 ||

But even so, the seed, appearing as a variety such as the sprout and so forth, is unimpededly recollected by those possessing very long-continued reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) as having a nature that is indeed uninterrupted, like a flowing stream. And thus, when the question "Where has the seed gone? is asked—

People say that there is no dependence whatsoever on the nature of the sprout when each [entity] rests solely within its own self; however, this is not possible, because by being established in identity (*tādātmya*), they lack establishment in their own selves alone—this is the intended meaning. That...

For that reason, by means of the support— that is, the proof— of the doctrine of the agent (*kartṛvāda*), which consists of the manifestation of consciousness and takes the form of the play of consciousness; having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "paraspara" and so forth.
The commentary (*ṭīkā*) on this point is as follows:

"Contrariety" (*viparyaya*) consists in the form: "the seed itself is not the sprout, nor even a part of it. To the question, "Why is there not a state of mutual identity? he says: "For [there exist] difference and non-difference."
"Having a single part as their object" means "pertaining to a single part. || 17 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the eighteenth verse with the words "nanvevamapi" (But even so...).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"By those [means] which shine (*śālate*) through that reflection (*parāmarśa*) which is exceedingly long; but not..."

The meaning is: "by agents who are intent upon the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the seed. "Irrefutable" (*nirbādha*) means free from subsequent sublation (*auttarakālikabādhārahita*). "Is reflected upon" (*pratyavamṛśyate*) means it is brought into the state of being an object of reflective awareness. He demonstrates this very reflection with the words "and thus," [referring to] "the speakers."

The phrase "possessing a very long and continuous reflection upon the qualified object" (or, according to the commentary, "the qualifier") is to be construed as a qualifier (or, according to the commentary, as the qualified object). In response to the expectation of what the speakers say, he states: "Nowhere. That is the seed.

"It exists; this sprout has become a sprout. In the same way, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), having become everything from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the earth, and having expanded until it has attained the nature of an infinite succession of creations and dissolutions—this is the cognition that grasps the expanded.
Anticipating the objection that the conceptualization of cause and effect, driven by an attachment to parts, is essentially a dismemberment of that very entity, he says:
The division of the single self and action following the sequence of time would likewise exist as the very state of agency through such a process of transformation. (18)

In this context, the far-sighted [sage], relying upon recognition (pratyabhijñā) rooted in any one of the means of valid cognition— namely perception, inference, or scripture— [perceives] that very same equilibrium of pleasure, pain, and delusion as assuming an infinite variety of states of disequilibrium.

The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Having stated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "evam. "Evam" means "in that same way. *Pradhāna*—the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*)—[transforms] into everything from *mahad-ādi*—beginning with the principle of the Great One (*mahat-tattva*)—down to *dharāntībhūta*—reaching as far as the state of earth (*dharā-bhāva*).

It has been transformed; likewise, it has become extended—transformed by way of its appropriate expansion. Furthermore, it attains the state of being that very essence—the nature of the infinite succession of creations and dissolutions—which is itself unlimited because it culminates in infinite entities. Thus.

"Thus, 'comprehending the extended'—there arises a cognition that effects the grasping of a single primordial substance (pradhāna) in its extensive form. [Objection: If that is so, then how is it observed that there is a distinct apprehension of the Great Principle (mahat) and the others as causes and so forth? To this, he says: 'part'."

Regarding the "parts"— namely those in the form of the Great One (mahat) and so forth— the obsession (*abhiniveśa*) which consists of grasping them as distinct entities is a form of forceful insistence (*haṭha*); by virtue of that— that is, through its power— there occurs the conceptualization of the state of cause and effect,
the conceptualization of the relation of cause and effect, with respect to the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*) and the rest.

The distinction is that [in the case of primordial matter] there is merely the conceptualization of causality, whereas in the case of the "Great One" (mahat) and the rest, there is the conceptualization of both effect and cause.
What is this conceptualization of causality and effect? It is of that very entity—

It refers precisely to the primary form of the object itself— namely, that which consists essentially of destruction, meaning it takes on another form. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "of the single self."

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides an exposition to explain the phrase "of a single self," beginning with the word "here" (*iha*). "Here" means in this manifest world; "by a far-sighted agent" means by one who does not look merely at the surface appearance.

That which has as its root any one of the means of valid cognition—namely perception, inference, or scripture—such is it; thus, it is established that [the world] has become universal by relying upon recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). In this regard, by the power of recognition...

That which is of a single essence and a single nature—its differentiation, its state of having various distinct forms, is precisely what is called "action" (*kriyā*). This is because it is followed by a sequence characterized by time; for those [forms], being of mutually different natures, do not appear simultaneously, but rather exist in a state of prior and posterior succession.

Action is being discussed. Since action is thus, by that manner—that is, by way of the specific characteristics of the actions of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the rest—there would be agency itself, and not merely a dry state of causality alone; for this reason, "thus" means by those various modes such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth.
For one who enters into action—which is characterized by transformation and consists of a continuous, gradual manifestation—the state of being transformed (*pariṇamattā*) is established;
that is, it is brought to the state of being an object of proof. Why is this so? This [will be explained] further on.

The entire range of manifest objects is none other than the equilibrium of pleasure, pain, and delusion—that is, the state of equality among the three qualities (guṇas)—which is precisely the Pradhāna and nothing else. Of what nature is this? It is of infinite variety—meaning manifold varieties—which constitutes its state of inequality.
