"Diversity" consists of the forms beginning with the Great Principle (mahat); by "having recourse to" or "relying upon" that [diversity], it has "become manifold"—that is, it has evolved into the state of the world. He explains the phrase "of the single Self" by relying on the aforementioned process, saying "therein. "Therein" means when the aforementioned reality exists.
"By the power of recognition"— that is,
by the power of recognition rooted in any one of the means of knowledge such as direct perception—
and "of a single nature," meaning having a single form called *pradhāna*. He establishes the genitive construction with the word "of that" (*tasya*).

He explains the word *vibheda* by explaining the word *bheda*. Here too, he states a synonym: *anyānya*. "She" refers to what was previously established. "Action" (*kriyā*) is explained by its very utterance (*nigadavyākhyāta*). "Is said" (*ucyate*) is supplied as a grammatical ellipsis (*śeṣa*).

He explains the phrase "following the sequence of time" (*kālakramānugā*) as a qualifier containing a reason by means of the word "since" (*yataḥ*). By the expression "by the characteristic of time"—that is, by the very nature of time—he demonstrates the analysis of the compound: "that which has the sequence of time as its follower. In response to the inquiry "How so?", he provides the justification with the words "for they... (*te hi*).

For—because—those [entities] consisting of the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth are each distinct from one another. To the question, "If they do not appear [as such], what of it?", he says: "The prior," and so on. For the process of cooking is clearly a state that exists with a sequential form, consisting of stages such as softening and so forth. This refers to the first half [of the verse].
Having explained the first half [of the verse], he provides an introduction to explain the second half with the words "yataḥ" (since).

He explains "evam" (thus) as "kālakramānugā" (following the sequence of time), and explains "tathā" (likewise) with the word "tena" (by that). The term "pradhānādeḥ" (of primordial matter, etc. is supplied as a complement. He explains the word "evam" as "kriyā" (action).

"Dry" means devoid of agency; the sense is that a *kāraka* (agent/cause) is so called only when it is engaged in action. He provides the construction for explaining "by way of such transformation" with the word "since" (*yataḥ*). Therein, he explains the component "thus" (*tathā*) with the word "by that" (*tena*), etc.

By the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra) and the rest is intended. The term "constantly" (satatam eva) is supplied by implication according to the context. He supplies [the object] "successive" (kramikām) as the agent of the action of transformation;
that is, having the nature of appearing as such—having the nature of flashing forth in the form of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest—as indicated by the phrase "entering" (āviśataḥ).
Having set aside, abandoned, and turned away from a certain form, and having established that which is to be followed and that which is to be brought about,
there is an immersion in a third form being produced.
By that [cognition], acting as the cause, [the existence] of primordial matter (pradhāna) and so forth [is established]. || 18 ||

Now, one might object: "Has it not been established by this much that the *pradhāna* is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the act of transformation? What is the fault here, for its lack of agency is not asserted as being like that of the *puruṣa*?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

The construction is: "of the primary matter (pradhāna) and so forth, which stands at the beginning. Regarding the term *pariṇamattayā*, he explains the constituent part *pari* as "pari. Here too, he provides a synonym for it: "having abandoned" (*tyaktvā*).
The object to be excluded—what is to be abandoned—is "some form"; thus, the construction is "having abandoned some form. This refers to the word *pari*.

He states the second meaning with the words "to be followed" (*anuvartanīyam*). "To be followed" means to be grasped as something already established; "having fixed" (*vyavasthāpya*) means having specifically established it. He explains the component *ṇamattā* with the word "being produced" (*nirvartyamāna*). "Being produced" means from this...

The supreme object to be accomplished is the third form—the form that constitutes the third stage in relation to what is to be excluded and what is to be followed; in that regard, "submissiveness" means the state of being submissive, becoming humble, or [according to C. the act of making humble, by virtue of that state.
"Vibration" (sphuraṇa) is the meaning. He provides the third-case construction with the words "by that" (tayā).
He states the sense of the third case as "cause" (hetu); this third case is used in the sense of cause.
Such is the construction of this verse. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "eva" (only/itself), [referring to] the single self (ekātmanaḥ).

And the differentiation of a single nature, such as *pradhāna* and so forth, by the power of a single recognition—this very differentiation is indeed action. Why? Because it follows a temporal sequence—that is, it consists of a form characterized by priority and posteriority—and the differentiation of a single entity necessarily entails following a temporal sequence.

[The opponent’s] position: This being the case, in that manner—by way of those respective modes characterized by the infusion of activity into the Pradhāna and so forth—the Pradhāna and so forth would themselves be the agent. By virtue of what cause?
By virtue of their undergoing such transformation—that is, by virtue of their transforming into the state of the Mahat and the other evolutes.
The meaning is "by being the cause. Thus [ends verse 18].
Now he provides the introduction to the nineteenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"iyatā"—by this elaboration; "asya"—of this Pradhāna. It is "iṣyate" (desired/accepted).
It is not tenable for the Sāṃkhyas to claim this, because contradiction between difference and non-difference applies only to that which is insentient;
however, it is logical in the case of the single conscious self (cidātman) due to the distinction of appearances.

Thus, that which was stated— that the subject (*dharmin*), whose nature is undifferentiated, possesses the agency of the act of transformation characterized by independence in its conjunction with a continuous flow of diverse attributes (*dharmabheda*)— does not apply to the *pradhāna* or other such [Sāṃkhya] principles.

This is logical because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*); for that which is called "insentient" possesses a determinate nature and falls within the category of the object of cognition (*prameya*). It must be established as distinct due to a difference in form, like blue, yellow, and so forth, yet it is not non-distinct because it possesses a single nature, like [the universal] "blue-ness," but rather it is that very thing itself.
The intrinsic nature must be both different and non-different, because affirmation and negation function simultaneously as agents in a single locus;
thus should the introduction be joined. [The word "kartṛtvena" (as agent) is to be supplied twice—C. Thus is the introduction.
Having composed the verse and presented it, he explains it with the words "na ca.
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides an explanation of the term "evam" as denoting the agent.

Of that which is of undivided form— of the single-natured substratum (dharmī) in the form of the seed— those various properties (dharmabheda), such as the specific properties of the sprout and so forth, which flow forth and circulate constantly, that is to say, without interruption; their "commingling" (saṃbheda)— is as follows:

By that [inherence], that is to say, by its very existence, there is that which is characterized by autonomy—whose nature is autonomy—which is the agency of the act of transformation; that which fulfills the requirement for the word "that" (tat). That is the entity denoted by the word "that."

Regarding the phrase "of the *pradhāna*, etc.": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the *mahat* and so forth is intended. He explains the qualifier "of the insentient" (*jaḍasya*) as being for the purpose of providing a reason, namely, "because of its insentience" (*jaḍatvāt*). The statement "it is not tenable" (*na yuktam*) is explained through the very words used (*nigadavyākhyātam*). As for the word "and" (*ca*), since it serves merely to fill out the meter, no further explanation is provided.
[The distinction] has been made. To the question "How so?", he provides the justification here with the words "for that which is insentient" (*jaḍo hi*).

That which possesses a finalized nature—that is, a delimited essential form—and which is also insentient, must be established as distinct; that is, it is fit to be established through differentiation. [Otherwise,] it would be non-distinct.

It is appropriate [to say] that "it must also be established as such," meaning that it is precisely one and the same; for otherwise there would be a contradiction. If it is argued that "one intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is different while another is not different," then there would consequently be two intrinsic natures belonging to a single intrinsic nature, and this is not tenable.

"Thus, the distinction between difference and non-difference is severed in all things," according to this principle. In this way, for the insentient— which has fallen into the category of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) because its form is entirely delimited by being established as an appearance such as "this"— there is no such differentiation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*).

Unity is established when [the object] has fallen into the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameya*); however, that which does not fall into the state of being an object of knowledge, but rather—by virtue of its nature as consciousness—is of the ultimate nature of light and has consciousness as its sole essence, being transparent, in that [state] the nature of both difference and non-difference is obtained; for this is indeed evident from experience itself.
The body of a clear object such as a mirror, which remains unimpaired in its own nature,

appears as a form differentiated by thousands of shapes such as mountains and elephants; yet it does not do so by concealing its own nature as mother-of-pearl or the single moon, as is the case with silver or a double moon.
It exists by means of the concealment of its own nature (*svarūpatirodhānena*), just as mountains and the like appear in a mirror.

Indeed, when the mirror manifests in such a way, its very nature as a mirror is all the more revealed through the conceit (*abhimāna*) that "this mirror is stainless" and "this mirror is excellent. For the mountain is not [the mirror].
In that case, it would have to move externally, because of the consequence that it would have to abandon its own location;

nor could it be in one place—meaning in a single location—at one time—meaning at a single moment. To the objection, "But surely this might be so; what fault would there be?", he says: "And not... Why is it not tenable? To this he says: "Because of difference... Thus, for a single [entity]...

Regarding the acceptance of two natures, he provides a summary with the word "evam" (thus). "Idam" (this) refers to that which has the appearance of being established—meaning it is an object of a delimited appearance.
"Sarvataḥ" (from all) means from all things other than itself. This concludes the first half [of the verse].

Having explained the first half [of the verse], he explains the second half with the words "as for that which... (*yattu*). Therein—in that [reality] which is of the nature of pure consciousness alone and is transparent—he explains "is joined" (*yujyate*) as "is logically consistent" (*upapadyate*). In response to the inquiry "How is it logically consistent?", he provides a justification by means of an illustration.

"From experience alone" means: for—where *hi* signifies "because"—the body, that is, the essential nature (*vapuḥ*), having become mixed—that is, commingled—through the concealment of its form, i.e., through the non-manifestation of its innate nature;
likewise, as in the case of mountains and so forth in a mirror, [it does not exist] through the concealment of its form. And it does not exist.
This is to be applied [to the case at hand]. To the question "Why does it not exist [there]?", he says: "For of the mirror...

The meaning is that when there is such a manifestation—namely, the manifestation of mountains and so forth—it "unfolds," i.e., becomes clear, and does not undergo concealment. To the question "Why does it unfold?", he says: "Because this is stainless. But [one might object]: what about the external [object]?
Thinking that the mountain itself comes there and stands [there], he says "no. Of this—the mountain—it is certainly not so;
for it is limited, and it would follow that its surface could not simultaneously appear in two places, like the non-appearance of a reflection in a mirror, nor [could it appear] in the middle.
Because there is no possibility of penetration into that which has a dense, hard, and resistant nature;
because it is not seen there afterwards; and because it appears only from a distance; nor do the visual rays, having descended, rebounded, and returned, [perceive] the mountain itself.
They perceive both the original object and its reflection, because both are observed within the appearance of the mirror situated on the side of the mountain. Therefore...
This is the majesty of stainlessness: that there is both the non-differentiation from infinite manifestations and their unity.

Just as for one standing atop a mountain peak, there is the appearance of thousands of objects within a city all within a single cognition, thus the agency of the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) is established, for it is undivided.
Because the penetration of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is possible through the capacity to endure the penetration of differentiation (bheda). || 19 ||
The sense is that its remaining [there] is logical. Regarding "this"—the mirror; "that"—the mountain;
"on the back"—in the region of the back. To the question "Why?", he says "mirror. The sense is that an object situated on the back of a mirror does not appear. "In the middle"—
"In the middle region of the mirror," and "it does not appear"—this is the connection with what precedes.
"Behind" means on the rear part of the mirror; "there" means on that rear part;
"right in front" means precisely on the front part of the mirror; "there" means in that mirror; by that falling [of light], they are "reflected."

"Arising"—for this very reason, "returning," that is, coming back; "visual"—pertaining to the eyes; "rays"—beams of light; "the mountain itself"—the innate mountain itself, and not one existing as a reflection in a mirror. Why not?
To explain how they perceive it, he says "the reflection" (*bimba*).

Regarding the reflection and the reflected image—between the innate mountain and the mountain that has been reflected [as a reflection, according to manuscript C]—it should be understood that this applies specifically to the reflection within the appearance of the mirror situated on the side. For the original object (*bimba*) itself does not [enter the mirror].

It is seen in a mirror located near a mountain, because it is perceived through its own predominance. He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). To the question "What is this?", he replies: "the fusion with infinite manifestations"—that is, the state of being joined with infinite manifestations—and "oneness," that is, unity; such is the meaning of these two.

Now, one might object: "Even though a mirror possesses purity, it lacks consciousness; furthermore, it is observed to manifest as distinct from the reflection. Therefore, how is it appropriate for it to serve as an illustration?
To this, he says: "On the mountain peak... [referring to those situated] upon the mountain peak.

The appearance of thousands of objects located in a city—belonging to a person situated on a mountain peak—is the cognition of those thousands of objects in the city; that is to say, the attainment of their existence.
Such is the construction here. "Thus" refers to the aforementioned agency in the act of transformation.

That agency of the act of transformation, which is required by the word "tat" (that), is not possible for the insentient—namely, for the *pradhāna*. Why? Because of the contradiction between difference and non-difference;
for difference and non-difference are simply untenable in the case of the insentient. However—

But surely, by this much alone, let consciousness itself, in the form of Brahman, assume this manifold diversity of the universe; what is the use of postulating an Īśvara? [What is the use of the conceptualization of an Īśvara?]

Even if the unity of consciousness is real, there can be no action between two things differentiated by their appearances without the reflective awareness of unity characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).
If it is said that the unity of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) is real, whereas this duality arises from the affliction of ignorance (*avidyopaplava*), then one must ask:
whose is this affliction of ignorance? [To whom does this affliction of ignorance belong? It is not [possible to say].

It is consistent—[K. ṣ. ṣ. it is consistent in its distinction; that [distinction] is possible within the single conscious Self (*cidātman*). Why? Because of the difference in manifestations (*ābhāsa*);
the sense is that, due to its extreme purity, it is capable of tolerating a difference in manifestations. Thus [ends verse 19].
Now, the introduction to the twentieth verse begins with "nanv etāvatā" (but surely by this much).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"by this much"—that is, by the aforementioned elaboration—"consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to that which is devoid of reflective awareness (*nirvimarśa*).
The meaning is that it is "light," the very form of Brahman, according to the Vedic revelation: "Brahman is consciousness. "This" refers to that which appears before one.
Having raised the objection— "by the conceptualization of lordship," that is, by the conceptualization of sovereignty in the form of self-reflective awareness (vimarśa)—

and having brought this [objection] forward as the subject of the doubt expressed by the Vedāntins; and having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "vāstave'pi" (even though it is real).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides the method for explaining the verse, beginning with the words "of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpasya*).
"Real" (*vāstavam*) means innate (*sahaja*); furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates an alternative position; "this" (*ayam*)—

It has the nature of appearing as an existent entity; this is said by the Vedāntins because of the affliction caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), which consists in its own nature as an affliction—such is the intended meaning. And thus says the Śruti:

"Brahman is indeed one, without a second"; likewise, "Indra moves in many forms through his māyās. [The author] fulfills the expectation of the word "yadi" (if) with the word "tadā" (then). "Na saṃgacchate" means it is not consistent; it is not tenable.

For how can Brahman, whose nature is solely knowledge (*vidyā*), possess the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*)? Nor is there anything else that exists in reality, such as a living soul (*jīva*) or the like, to which this ignorance might belong. If it is argued that this ignorance is "indefinable" (*anirvācya*), we do not know to whom it belongs as something indefinable; furthermore, it appears in its own form, yet... [it does not exist].

And that it is "inexpressible"—what does this mean? If you say it is because it cannot be established by reasoning (*yukti*), then what indeed is this so-called "reasoning" that overrides direct experience (*saṃvedana*)? Furthermore, what else could constitute the "impossibility" of something that is actually appearing?
If it is argued that Brahman, which is of the nature of pure being, shines forth as non-different [from itself] in non-conceptual [awareness],

whereas this difference arises through the power of conceptualization— then whose activity is this so-called "conceptualization"? If it belongs to Brahman, there can be no connection with ignorance (*avidyā*), nor is there anything else [to which it could belong].

And if it is argued that the non-conceptual is real while the conceptual is unreal, how can such a distinction be made, since there is no difference in their being manifest? Even though difference manifests within Brahman— the pervasive reality of consciousness (*cittattva*), which is of a single nature with pure knowledge— [it is nonetheless unreal].
Of that which has the single form of knowledge; and thus says the Śruti:
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
For it is not logical that light should have the nature of darkness—this is the sense. Of whomsoever...

Of the living soul (*jīva*) and so forth; "inexpressible" (*anirvācyā*) means it is impossible to say that it is dependent upon this [substratum]; the sense is: what is this? It is nothing at all. For whatever appears can indeed be spoken of—this is the point.
"Sublating experience" (*saṃvedatiraskāriṇī*) means causing the denial of direct experience. But surely there is an inconsistency here.
Therefore, he says: "And there is an impossibility. "Other" means contradictory to its appearing nature.

"The nature of existence" means having that alone as its essential nature. "Undivided" means devoid of internal, external, or homogeneous differences. "In the non-conceptual" means in the state of non-discrimination (*nirvikalpa*). "The operation of conceptualization" [is impossible therein].
The activity called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—that is to say, the conjunction with ignorance (*avidyā*)—is what is attained at that time; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
At that time, the conjunction with ignorance is attained, because conceptual construction is of the nature of ignorance. [An objection: "Let it be so for another [entity].
To this, he says: "And not... Why not? Because "another" refers to anything whatsoever distinct from Brahman.

For what reason has this come about? Is it not the case that in non-conceptual [cognition] there is appearance in one way, while in conceptual [cognition] it is otherwise; and thus, is this distinction between the real and the unreal produced by that? To this he says: "of the state of appearing" (*bhāsamānatvasya*). That which is precisely the state of appearing...

If it is argued that [non-duality] is sublated, then non-difference is likewise [sublated], because it is sublated by the manifestation of difference. For sublation is nothing other than the arising of a contrary cognition; moreover, sublation exists only because of its own manifestation and not otherwise. Thus, difference too is [real] as long as it manifests.
What is ignorance? If it is argued that this non-duality is established by disregarding appearances and taking scripture as the sole authority— [i.e.,

having scripture as its only means of valid cognition]— then even scripture is itself essentially characterized by duality and is a real entity [essentially characterized by duality and is not a non-entity].

And as for the division into knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge—this is nothing at all. Therefore, even while accepting the reality of the oneness of consciousness (*cidekatva*), an action characterized by agency—which consists in the immersion into diverse forms—is not possible; [for such action would contradict] the very nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
The meaning is that the characteristic of misapprehension (*parāmarśa-lakṣaṇa*) is the same for real silver as it is for the silver in mother-of-pearl; thus, it is "sublated" (*bādhita*).
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of difference" (*bheda*). But how is the sublation of non-difference logical?

To this he says: "contrary" (*viparīta*). "The arising of a contrary cognition"—that is, the manifestation of knowledge of a contrary object—is itself [the error]; it is not something other than that.
How so? It is not of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*); such is the meaning. That which appears—
Disregarding— that is, setting aside— the manifestation [of reality] through empirical means such as perception and so forth,
one who takes scripture as the authority [realizes]:
"There is no diversity whatsoever here."

This is established by such scriptural authorities as these. Being of the nature of difference—that is, being primarily characterized by difference—it becomes the ultimate reality; that is to say, it attains existence.
As it has been said:
When that which is non-different in self-awareness is expressed to another,
it then appears as if different, having resorted to the domain of verbal expression.

Thus [it is said]. The construction is as follows: the division of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is indeed of the nature of duality and possesses real existence. "This is nothing" means that this entity described in the Vedas and other scriptures is not anything at all.
He explains the verse by relying on the method previously stated.

"Therefore" means that, having extracted the term "cittatva" (the nature of consciousness) from the phrase "of the two distinct appearances," it is expressed by the words "of that. "Of that" means of the *cit-tattva* (the reality of consciousness), which is the substratum of actual unity.
He restates the previously mentioned nature of action with the words "agency" (*kartṛtva*). The definition of agency is as follows:
The nature of agency (*kartṛtvasvarūpa*) is that which is non-different—meaning the form (*rūpa*) or essential nature (*svarūpa*) devoid of any distinction from the agent.
The immersion (*samāveśa*) therein means, by implication, the perfect absorption of that very agent; she is one whose self (*ātman*) is of such a nature.

If there is autonomy, then everything becomes possible; for reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is indeed a desire in the form of the wish to act (*cikīrṣā*), and within that, everything that is to be created exists as non-differentiated. Thus it has been said.
In the passage, "And for the Lord who is established in his own self...
(1.5.10), it is stated that by him the universe—which is his own essential nature—is truly real;
its ultimate reality consists in being the nature of light, and it exists as nothing other than an uninterrupted non-difference from that light.

Maheśvara manifests through differentiation by means of His very nature as ultimate light— this is precisely what is called His sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), characterized by the power to accomplish the most difficult tasks; the phrase "of the two differentiated by manifestation" implies an action.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of a general relationship (*sambandhasāmānya*), which is subsequently divided according to what is appropriate.

He explains that the appearance of the insentient (*jaḍābhāsa*) and the appearance of the sentient (*ajaḍābhāsa*) are distinct through their manifestation; for if the insentient, such as a jar, were not of the nature of an object (*karmarūpa*), the appearance of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) would not be possible—thus he says, "it is not tenable. This refers to the section beginning with *cikīrṣā* and ending with *vinā*.

He explains [the term] "reflective awareness" (*parāmarśa*). The nature of reflective awareness is the nature of *vimarśa*; "all" means the totality of action and so forth. He explains "desire to act" (*cikīrṣā*) as follows: "For reflective awareness... [and so on]. "In that"—namely, in the desire whose form is the desire to act.
That which is to be emanated is the object to be emanated; "by way of non-differentiation" means through a non-dual arrangement.
The sense is that desire indeed arises as consisting of the very object desired. As it has been said:
"This alone is the arising of that object of meditation within the mind of the meditator."
It is the attainment of identity with that [reality] which occurs for the practitioner who so desires.
Thus [it is asked]. Where was this stated? To this he says: "And of the Lord" (*svāminaśca*). This means "in this [verse]," that is, in this *śloka*.
For here, everything residing in the agent has been established by way of [His] will. He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tena*).
Therefore—by that reason—the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), the Supreme Śiva, [is] His own essential nature alone.

—Because its status as an object of desire would otherwise be inexplicable, it exists as nothing other than one's own essential nature; for this very reason, it is of the nature of reality (*satyarūpa*).

Thus, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is precisely this state of being the essence of light. It is that which possesses such an innate form (*sahaja-rūpa*). Likewise, there is non-difference from the uninterrupted light—that is, from the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*).
The meaning is that for one [the Lord] who possesses such [a nature], even when clay attains the state of being a jar, its "clay-ness" (mṛttva) is not destroyed. Such is the universe— the world—

which He manifests through differentiation as something inherently distinct, by means of a differentiation whose ultimate reality is Light— that is, by means of a differentiation whose existence is derived solely from Light.

It illuminates there because it possesses that capacity; nor is an objection appropriate here, for the same consequence would apply even to fire in the burning of what is to be burned. "That very thing" means the illumination of the universe itself;
"of this" refers to Maheśvara. Regarding the phrase "of the two, [one] distinct from the manifestation," he states "action" to explain the meaning of the genitive case.

He demonstrates this very division with the word "appearance" (ābhāsa). He explains the distinction between the insentient and the sentient with the words "the jar and so forth. The genitive case—expressing the form of the agent—indicates their action: for one there is the state of being acted upon, and for the other, the state of being the agent.

It could not exist. Without the reflective awareness of non-difference regarding the class of objects to be created— which takes the form of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*)— how could this single action belong to two things that are distinct by nature?

In the context of the discussion on causality (*kāryakāraṇatā*), the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) have been mentioned; however, the other factors of action (*kāraka*) as well are included within the single agency of the agent from the ultimate perspective (*paramārthataḥ*). Otherwise, if the multitude of factors such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) were distinct, how could that [agency] be non-different? Or rather, if those two [agent and object] are distinct only through appearance (*ābhāsa*), [then their unity remains].
The desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) regarding those two—the insentient and the sentient—consists in the state of being desired for one and the state of being the desirer for the other;

this occurs without the reflective awareness of their unity as their very nature. Alternatively, it is that reflective awareness of "I" and "this," which, though distinct in appearance, rests in a single unity.
"He effects a conjunction of those two" means that he effects a conjunction with action; "action" means he effects a conjunction with action.

By the phrase "it would not exist," he effects a conjunction with "of one. Of "one"—the insentient—there is "the state of being acted upon," which is action in the form of an instrument; of "the other"—the non-insentient—there is "agency."

Action consists in the nature of agency. He connects [the text] with the words "desire to act" (*cikīrṣā*), [meaning]: "without the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of unity characterized by the desire to act. This means: without that which is the reflective awareness of the object to be created as non-different—that is, as non-different from oneself—and [without] that which is one and of a single form, [between] two things that are distinct.

—The sense is that [the reflection] occurs when both the insentient and the sentient are in proximity, because reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is all-encompassing. Now, one might ask: "In this context, only the agent and the object have been discussed;
what then is the status of the other *kārakas*? To this he says: "the effect" (*kārya*). The other *kārakas*—
The instruments and so forth— those which possess such a quality, namely, that they subsequently enter into that single agency residing in the agent by way of being its auxiliaries; otherwise—

In the absence of mutual penetration (*anupraveśa*), [the action] is distinct—meaning it exists in the form of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth, which are separate from the agent and the object—and it is non-different, that is, one. The sense is that when there is penetration into a single locus, it is indeed possible for many [factors] to possess a single action. Otherwise, [one might apply] a different interpretation:

He states another alternative with the words "or else" (*yadi vā*). He explains the term *cikīrṣā* (the desire to act) in two ways with the words "of one" (*ekasya*). "Of one"—that is, of the insentient (*jaḍa*)—there is "the state of being desired," which is the status of being the object of the act of desiring; "of the other"—that is, of the sentient (*cetana*)—there is "the state of being the desirer," which is the agency of the act of desiring. Its nature (*tatsvabhāvam*) is as follows:
"Having such characteristics"—this is the construction (*yojanā*). Furthermore, he provides another construction with the words "or else" (*yadvā*). In one sense, it means:

that which has as its form (*rūpa*) the repose within the single principle of consciousness (*cittattva*). By this, the phrase "of the two distinct from manifestation" (*ābhāsabhinnayoḥ*) is connected with the word "reflection" (*parāmarśa*).
It has been established. Furthermore, he provides another interpretation with the word "appearance" (*ābhāsa*).
By this, [the phrase] "of the two things distinct from appearance" is connected with "in unity," meaning:
"without that [unity], which consists of the desire for form. Thus, there is a single reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the two things distinct from appearance.

Or else, how can there be action without the characteristic of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*)? Thus, the genitive case is used in relation to either action, the desire to act, or reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); and because it is always dependent [on these], a compound is formed. || 20 ||
He summarizes this as follows:
"In this way, for the One who desires to abide as the world consisting of the manifestations of jars, cloths, and so forth, His very will is the cause, His agency, and His action. (21)

Just as there is no causality and no agency for that which is insentient, so too it has been established that there is no such [agency] for a sentient being who is not the Lord (Īśvara). He demonstrates this by summarizing these arguments with the word "evam" (thus).

The word "ṣaṣṭhī" means the genitive case, specifically the genitive dual. Now, if this were the case, a compound would not be possible for the words *cikīrṣā* and *parāmarśa*, as they are dependent [on other factors]; for it has been stated that "that which is dependent is incapable [of forming a compound]," whereas a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*) applies only to those that are capable.

Because this occurs, he says "eternal" (*nitya*). For some [compounds] depend on something else that is non-eternal (*anitya*), such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) when referring to a wealthy king; in this case, a compound of the word *rājan*, which is dependent, with the word *puruṣa* is simply not appropriate. But some are eternally dependent (*nityasāpekṣa*), such as "Devadatta’s... (*devadattasya*).

In the term *gurukulam*, the compounding of the word *guru*— even though it is dependent [on another word]— with the word *kula* is indeed appropriate. Furthermore, since the connection with oneness is also established through the result of the reference itself, it was not mentioned separately.
Thus is the construction of this verse: even though the oneness of consciousness is real, there would be no activity between two things differentiated by appearance. Without what?
Without the reflective awareness of oneness characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). However, that [reflective awareness] certainly exists.

The state [of being]. Or rather, the construction is: "without the reflective awareness of unity characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), there would be no activity between two things that are distinct from their appearances. Or rather, [the question] "between which two?
is answered by the construction: "without the reflective awareness of those two things that are distinct from their appearances. Or else...
The connection is: "without the reflective awareness of the unity of the two [aspects] which are distinct in appearance.
The term "characterized by the desire to act" (*cikīrṣālakṣaṇā*) is an adverbial modifier of the action. || 20 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the twenty-first verse with the words "etat" (this). This is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the word "ittham" (thus).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
He explains the word *ittham* with the word *yathā*. The term *kāraṇatā* is stated with reference to the general sense of causality.
By this very mode of being a cause, this [effect] has arisen.
This has arisen: that very desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) which belongs to one who intends to act in such a way, having reached its external limit, is designated as "action" (*kriyā*).

That alone is agency (*kartṛtā*), and that alone is causality (*hetutva*); there is nothing else whatsoever. Therefore, [in the expression] *ghaṭastiṣṭhati* ("the jar remains"), [it is the jar itself that is the agent].

The meaning is this: that Great Lord, who is Light, remains—He who, by virtue of His sovereignty, accepts existence as the nature of a jar while desiring to abide in that form, and not because He is unable to sustain that form. Indeed, the world consists of the forms of manifestations such as jars, cloths, and so forth.

That which exists as that very Self is thus [described] by each respective [aspect]; "the agency regarding the birth and maintenance of that world" is stated primarily with the intention of specifying [the particularity]. This means: by way of the mode of causality, that is, by way of establishing the state of being a cause. It has arisen—i.e., it is established. This...

In response to the question "What?", he says: "That which... While providing the construction, he fulfills the syntactic expectancy of the word "that" with the phrase "he who indeed...". "Desiring to act in such a way"—meaning desiring to do so—"of him alone"—meaning of that very person desiring to act in such a way—"that desire"—meaning that specific wish.
By this, it is indicated that the word *tathā* (thus) should be construed with the word *icchā* (will).
"Extending to the exterior" means having the nature of the movement of external limbs; and "that very [thing]" means that very action as previously described, and that alone—this is the meaning.

The neuter gender is used in view of its being a cause (*hetutva*). "Other" means distinct from *cikīrṣā*, which is of the nature of desire (*icchā*). Here, there is no contradiction whatsoever, as the word *cikīrṣā* serves both as an explanation of the word *icchā* and as an implication (*ākṣepa*) of the one who desires to act (*cikīrṣu*). Alternatively, [the explanation may be as follows:]...
By virtue of the qualifier *tiṣṭhāsaḥ* ("desiring to abide"), there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of the qualified entity, namely the one desiring to act (*cikīrṣu*).

For it is the Supreme Lord himself, desiring to act, who abides in the form of the effect; thus, the causality and agency of the two words [in the verse] are clearly joined as adverbs of action by the phrase *saiva ca* and so forth.

He provides an introductory commentary in order to explain [the phrase] "desiring to abide in the form of a jar, a cloth, and so forth," beginning with the words "by that" (*tena*). "Desiring to abide" (*tiṣṭhāsuḥ*) means wishing to remain; "abiding" (*sthānam*) means persistence, which is to say, the existence of one's own nature (*svarūpasattā*); "accepting" (*abhyupagacchan*) means acknowledging. The reason for this is as follows:

"Because of its sovereignty" (svātantryāt): for there is no obstruction whatsoever for that which is sovereign, because that would entail the loss of its sovereignty—this is the sense. "That form" (tadrūpam)—this is an expression where the abstract state is primary;
[it means] not being unable to endure the nature of a jar, but rather being disposed to endure it as some kind of thing (kiñcit).

Such is the meaning. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the explanation of the meaning. He provides the analysis and commentary of that which was introduced [in the previous verse], beginning with "the jar" (*ghaṭa*). "By its own nature" (*tadātmanā*) means by its own essential form (*tatsvarūpeṇa*). The word *tathā* (so) is also used here in the middle [of the sentence] by way of ellipsis (*tantra*).
He introduces [the topic] for the purpose of application with the words "In that manner. He provides the explanation of this very point with the words "by this and that," meaning:
he who desires to abide in the form of those various thousands of actions that differentiate the modifications of existence—such as birth, maintenance, and so forth—which pertain to the world.

He is autonomous; the very desire for things to be "thus" in their manifold forms is itself his action—this is the connection. Therefore, the Blessed Maheśvara alone is the creator of the universe; may there be auspiciousness. || 21 ||

Thus ends the section titled "The Determination of the Reality of Cause and Effect" in the *Kriyādhikāra* of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* written by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The Fourth Chapter. 4.
And this second chapter, titled "The Section on Ritual Action," is complete. || 2 ||

The modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*) are the thousandfold actions that take the form of its various manifestations—such as "is born" and so forth—and he who desires to abide in that very form [is the subject]. He states the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) by saying "independent" (*svatantra*). He establishes the connection with the genitive case by saying "of him" (*tasya*). Thus he explains the word "evam."

Regarding the phrase "of various forms," the expression "that very [consciousness]" fulfills the expectancy of the word "which. By stating the result in the words "in the agent who is the knower," he provides the resolution of the first verse with the words "by that. Through this, even the state of being a knower is established without effort, since there is no [state of being] apart from being a knower.
Because agency is impossible. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the chapter (*āhnika*). The term "Śiva" denotes auspiciousness and indicates the supreme reality (*paratattva*).
Such is the construction of this verse. "Ittham" means in the manner already described.

For the Supreme Lord, who is independent, desiring to act, and wishing to abide in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth, his very will—manifesting in such diverse forms—is itself "action" (*kriyā*). What is this action? It consists of both causality and agency; this is the meaning. The word "thus" (*tathā*) is joined twice by way of *tantra* (elliptical repetition). Thus it is said.
May there be auspiciousness. || 21 ||

Thus, in the work titled *Bhāskarī*, composed by Śrī Bhāskarakantha, the son of Śrīmad Avatārakakaṇṭha, who was the son of the venerable Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha— a great Māheśvara established by himself (svataḥsiddha) and a worshipful teacher (ārādhya-pāda) residing within the illustrious region of Kāśmīra.

The fourth chapter in the section on Action within the *Śrīpratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* commentary is concluded. The second investigation, known as the Section on Action, has reached its end. May there be auspiciousness!

She, who— along with the suffix *tala* and its expressed state— brings about the fullness of sovereignty for Maheśvara (who is denoted by the suffix *tṛc*) by attaining the state expressed by the root *kṛ*.
Wherein that Śakti, delighted by the nature of the fully nourished *vidyā*, is clearly manifest—
this very *adhikāra* has today been explained by me here according to the meaning of Bhāskara.
No egoistic conceit should be formed by the mind, for Śiva is the agent who resides herein;
if you possess that sense of identity through oneness with Him, then that indeed is auspicious.
Śiva is the agent, Śiva is the witness, and Śiva alone is the reciter;
Śiva is declared to be the expounder—clearly, everything is an offering unto Śiva.
The First Daily Lesson in the Section on Scripture. *Vimarśinī* (Commentary).

I bow to that essence of the flood of jewels of the contemplation on the reality of Śiva, by attaining which the entire multitude of rivers of the scriptures reaches fulfillment and the state of having accomplished its purpose.
The ocean of the supreme scriptures.
The Bhāskarī commentary on this [verse] states:
"Having emerged from Śiva, who is called pure consciousness and whose body is immeasurable..."

Indeed, the face of that form of Śivā, whose very essence is contemplative touch, has been attained by all the wise; and since it is considered by them to be like the water of the Gaṅgā, ever joined with many streams, I worship this weapon here within my heart. || 1 ||

Now, for the sake of completing this section on scripture (*āgamādhikāra*), which constitutes the third investigation (*vimarśa*), without obstacles and for the sake of its further propagation, [the author performs] a salutation to the scripture of the supreme reality (*paratattva*)— characterized by being expressive of that reality— which, though already performed mentally, is now expressed outwardly for the purpose of instructing the disciples.

He introduces the auspicious benediction with a verse that indicates the purport of the entire work, beginning with the words "yaṃ prāpya" (having attained whom). "I"— namely, the teacher named Abhinavagupta— [attained] the Śāmbhava [state], which is the Supreme Śiva, the nature of the unity of Śiva and Śakti, the locus for the manifestation of all auspiciousness.

The "reality that is related" (*saṃbandhi yat tattvam*) refers to one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), which consists of the thirty-four principles beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Earth, contained within oneself, consisting of great light, and unconditioned by superimposition (*anāropita*).

The "reflections" (*cintāḥ*) upon that— that is, the deliberations (*vicāraṇāni*) concerning it— are themselves the "jewels" (*ratnāni*), meaning gems, because they are exceedingly worthy of being accepted.

That which is their flood— their multitude— is itself the essence of this [work], because other thoughts are like water; therefore, it is supreme (*param*), transcending the great scriptures such as the Vedas,
since they find rest only in the principle called Sādākhya, whereas this work stands above them.
Because contact with it is impossible, I bow to such a one— that ocean of scripture, renowned everywhere,
which has come from the ocean of the Āgamas, having descended from Śrī Śiva to the mouth of Girijā and reached the mind of Śrī Vāsudeva, as established by its etymological definition. I bow to it.

Because it is endowed with the state of being supreme due to its focus on the most excellent of all things, I bring it into the sphere of prostration—that is to say, I lead it to become the object of an eight-limbed salutation. Which one? All those scriptures—those in the form of the Vedas and so forth.
We praise that Śiva, within whom shines the wheel of the principles (tattvas), beginning with the noble Śrīmat Sadāśiva and ending with the Earth.

The scriptures are themselves "rivers"—rivers insofar as their subject matter is limited; the "confluence" is their collection. Having reached that ocean of scripture, whose nature has been described, even after mentioning some slight distinction within it, at the end...
Having briefly stated the non-duality (advaita) that was taught with great intensity, [the text speaks of] "fullness"—

meaning that which consists of the state of being established in a single purpose with That, having the form of union with That— and, likewise, "fulfillment of purpose" (kṛtārthatā), which is the state of having accomplished what was to be accomplished.

He approaches—because beyond this there is nothing further to be accomplished; even while there remains something yet to be accomplished, the accomplishment is achieved solely through the means provided by the ocean of scripture. And just as rivers, having reached the ocean—the source of jewels—attain fullness and the fulfillment of their purpose, so it is from that point onward.

The implicit meaning (*dhvani*) is that [the Supreme] manifests solely through the state of being the full ocean, and possesses effects precisely because it has those effects as its own activity. By this, it is indicated that in this section on the scriptures (*āgamādhikāra*), the author will explain the reality taught in the scriptural treatises (*āgamaśāstra*) as a means of proving what was previously stated.

Since the authority of the scriptural treatises (*āgama-śāstra*) has already been established previously, we have not exerted further effort here. We praise that Śiva, whose essence is within the heart-region and who shines as the wheel of principles (*tattva-cakra*) extending from the venerable Śiva down to the earth, his very form being radiant.

Now, in this section, for the sake of the unimpeded completion of the first chapter, the author performs an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) characterized by the contemplation of the Supreme Reality in the form of his own chosen deity;
although performed within himself, it is done outwardly for the purpose of instructing the disciples.
He concludes with a verse that indicates the purport of the entire treatise, beginning with "The venerable one" (śrīmat):

"We praise that Śiva"—that is, we bring him into the scope of perfect contemplation. Who is he? He who is "venerable" (śrīmān), endowed with sovereignty in comparison to Īśvara and the other [deities].
He who is Sadāśiva is that very one whose commencement is noble (udāra),
such as it is, and whose end is the earth (vasudhā); [this refers to] the wheel (cakra) of the principles (tattva) whose nature will be described hereafter.
The aggregate consists of thirty-four principles (*tattva*s) in number;

that within which—remaining fixed upon the wall of its own essential nature—it shines, meaning it manifests individually in its own form, for otherwise, being devoid of essence, manifestation would be impossible. By this, the determination of the principles (*tattvanirṇaya*) is established here.
It has been indicated that [the universe] will come into being. Now, according to the principle found in other scriptural traditions (*āgamaśāstra*),
"In that Supreme Reality (paratattva), the thirty-six-fold world shines forth," the reality beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth is contained within the thirty-seventh, Supreme Śiva.

The manifestation of the thirty-six-fold [system] has been explained. Here, how is it that the thirty-four principles (tattvas), beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Earth, are included within the Śiva-tattva? True;
this is so in the essential scriptures (*sāra-śāstra*) such as the *Mālinīvijayottara*, which are devoted to supreme non-duality (*paramādvaita*).
It has been stated exactly thus; therein, the nature of knowledge and action has been determined at length through these two sections.
Now, this must be explained: that which is called "action" (kriyā) is characterized by the manifestation of all phenomenal objects.
This was stated immediately after [the previous verse]: "And what are those universal categories (viśve padārthāḥ)?
In this regard, the intended meaning is that they consist solely of appearances characterized as insentient and sentient, up to the level of the Sadāśiva-tattva.

There is no contact with the power whose nature is pure *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), because that [state] consists of the principle of the tranquil Brahman, which is a light devoid of *vimarśa* as maintained by the Vedāntins;
therefore, the power whose nature is *vimarśa* must also be spoken of as the thirty-fifth.
Endowed with that [nature], Śiva too is indeed distinct from Sadāśiva; thus he possesses the status of the thirty-sixth principle.
He himself will explain the essential nature of these two later on.
And although, in reality, there is absolute identity between Śiva and Paramaśiva, nevertheless, this is stated with the intent of defining their specific natures.

The description as *anāśritaśiva* is given because [the principle] is not supported by anything else; the description as *paraśiva* is intended to express its all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*). Indeed, it is not appropriate to conceive of the pervader as being on an equal footing with that which is pervaded, just as it is not appropriate for one who has fashioned seven rings to consider himself equal to the totality of them.

Regarding the statement that gold has eight aspects (*aṣṭamattva*): even if one speaks of the eightfold nature of that minute residue of gold which remains there, there is no fault; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
As for those who also state that it possesses thirty-eight aspects here, that refers to the time when it was being taught to his disciples.
This is said with the intention that [the number] would fall into a state of limitation; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),

even the statement of thirty-seven [factors] is indeed improper here, for it is not logical for the pervader to be delimited by its own pervaded, just as a silkworm inside a cocoon cannot [delimit] the cocoon itself.

"Because it is capable of being measured. However, in the procedural treatises (*prakriyāśāstra*) consisting of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth, the intended aim is merely the description of the essential nature of the principles (*tattva*), and not the exposition of Great Non-duality (*mahādvaita*);
thus, their definitive conclusion is made only up to the level of the Śiva-principle. Therefore, those systems possess nothing but a vision of duality.

However, they serve as indirect means (*paropāya*) toward Mahādvaita; for it has already been determined that the engagement of the scriptures is indeed distinct for the sake of benefiting various types of qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*), so enough with this elaboration. Alternatively, regarding that reality (*tattva*):
It was not mentioned with the intention that there should be no lapse into the status of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*).
Having thus accomplished the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*), he states the overall purport of this daily lesson (*āhnika*) by first explaining the intention of this section.
He also demonstrates the connection with the two preceding sections by means of the word "evam" (thus).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"By the two sections"—that is to say, in the form of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, then...
To the objection that one should simply remain silent, he says: "Now" (*atha*). The sense is that [what follows] is to be stated as a supplement (*śeṣatvena*).

In response to the expectation of what that might be, he says: "Action" (*kriyā*). Of all things—of every category of objects—that which is their manifestation, both by way of being the essence and by way of being the illuminator, externally...

She is that whose characteristic nature is manifestation. "Immediately thereafter"—that is, in the preceding section—"those" refers to those things which have become objects of manifestation. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of what was to be said; [the phrase] "having the form of manifestations" means by virtue of being established as manifestations.

They consist of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Now, one might ask: what are the categories of objects established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and in how many forms are they subsumed? For direct perception does not extend everywhere for the subject who is under the influence of *māyā*. It is the same with inference; for it is not the case that whatever exists [is perceived].
In each respective case, the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*), pervasion (*vyāpti*), and so forth is possible;

however, why should *Āgama*—whose ultimate reality is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Maheśvara, whose nature is undivided light—not perceive [all things]? Therefore, one should determine the nature of categories (*padārtha*) in accordance with that [scriptural authority].

With the intention of making [the reality] heart-warming— meaning that the state of the subject, which transcends that universe, has been attained through the act of making the universe an object of cognition— the Teacher begins the third chapter, the *Āgamādhikāra*, in order to define it.

In this regard, by means of eleven verses beginning with "Thus, the internal and external activity" (*evam antarbahirvṛttiḥ*) and ending with "due to the distinction between grossness and subtlety" (*sthūlasūkṣmatvabhedataḥ*), that which is established by scripture— the sequence starting from Śiva and ending with the Earth— is shown to consist of the nature of each individual manifestation.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the inclusion of form," he says, "for not... [it] "proceeds"—that is, it prevails or becomes capable. Now, one might object: "In that case, we shall grant the consecration of inference here. To this he replies, "inference... The meaning is that it does not proceed in this manner. Here...

He provides a justification, saying "not indeed. Now, one might ask: what then is the capacity of the scripture (*śāstra*), which is of the nature of the means of knowledge consisting of word (*śabda-pramāṇa*), in this regard? To this he says: "But the tradition (*āgama*).
Tradition refers to the scripture composed by Śrī Śiva and others; it is of the nature of unlimited luminosity (*aparicchinna-prakāśātman*).

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Maheśvara, which consists of an undivided light— that is to say, whose essential nature is great light— and which has as its root the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), belonging to Maheśvara, which rests within itself and has itself as its object.
As it has been said:
"It came from the mouth of Śiva and went into the mouth of Girijā.
For here, Śiva is the Light (*prakāśa*) and Girijā is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). What would one not see [in this]?

"Everything has been scrutinized" means "as far as [his] capacity extends. For this reason—following that, namely following the *āgama*—the determination of categories (*padārtha-nirṇaya*) is the determination of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth; and of the universe, which consists of those thirty-six principles.

*Prameyīkaraṇam*—the establishment, by means of verbal expression, of the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*), even though in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) it is not an object of knowledge; that which is obtained through this—namely, that which is established as "acting by way of exclusion from what is other" (*atadvyāvṛttikārī*) and so forth.
Therefore, that which transcends the entire universe—the world—is the state of the subject (*pramātṛpada*); of that...

"Making it reach the heart" (*hṛdayaṅgamīkāraḥ*) means grasping [the teaching] as something to be accepted; that is, with the intention toward that [acceptance], meaning with the expectation that through the vision of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), there will arise by itself the touch of the reality that is not an object of knowledge (*aprameya-vastu*).
Having thus stated the intention regarding the subject matter (*adhikāra*), [the author] states the intention regarding the entire chapter (*āhnika*) in its totality:
He says "there" (tatra); that is to say, within the context of the subject matter (*adhikāra*).
It is established by scripture (*āgama-siddha*), meaning established by the *Pati-śāstra*; that which is treated as common (*sāmānya*) in other philosophical systems (*darśana*), of which—

This entire manifestation of bodies, worlds, and so forth, preceded by a specific array of the appearance of infinite particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*) through the connection of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
follows that which is established by the scripture of the Supreme Lord and understood also through reasoning.
The purport of this chapter is to demonstrate the collection of principles (tattva) individually.

In this regard, while establishing the thematic connection (*adhikāra-saṃgati*) and concluding the refutation of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he speaks in order to reveal the very nature of the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*).
Thus, the activity that functions internally and externally follows the sequence of time;
yet knowledge and action belong solely to the Mother (Śakti), who is inseparable from Him.
"Each one"—that is, the nature of manifestation belonging to each individual *tattva*—is its very essence;

thus, the sense is that it consists of the form of Great Non-duality (*mahādvaita*). For in Great Non-duality, even difference is indeed capable of appearing; otherwise, there would be the consequence of incompleteness. Thus, in another philosophical system:

It is destroyed when [the object] is distinct; that which is conventionally designated as a "universal" (sāmānya) means it has been made an object of conventional usage by way of being a mere appearance of generality. The sense here is that the impossibility of contact with difference results in a state of incompleteness and is undermined by its own internal inconsistency.
That which is the collection of principles (*tattvagrāma*), and likewise that of which [it is said]—
by virtue of its connection with grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that is, through its having a single substratum—
the manifestation of infinite particular characteristics (*anantasvalakṣaṇa*) is itself the specific arrangement (*vyūhaviśeṣa*).

A particular arrangement; such a manifestation—meaning sovereignty—is what belongs to that [entity], as is understood from the context. The implication is that the conventional usage of terms such as "body" and so forth occurs only through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) among the principles (*tattvas*). In that regard, there is a common substratum (*samānam adhikaraṇam*).

With respect to their predominance, among those principles that constitute the superstratum, any one principle is not separate from them. In the phrase "even by reasoning" (*yuktyāpi*), the word *api* (even/also) serves as a conjunction. "Understood" (*avagatam*) means known as existing; "individually" (*pratyekataḥ*).
"Endowed with its own specific nature," [refers to] the "group of principles"—the collection of *tattvas*.
Now, he provides the introduction to the first verse with the words "therein.
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
The "connection with the context" (*adhikārasaṃgati*) refers to the relationship of this present section with the preceding section,
as well as the refutation— that is, the resolution— of the prima facie argument concerning the nature of cause and effect. Having thus provided the introduction:
Having presented the verse, he explains it with the word "evam" (thus):

"Thus" means that since the relationship of cause and effect as described in other philosophical systems is established upon the nature of insentient matter (*jaḍa*) and is therefore in no way tenable, [it must instead be] of the nature of consciousness (*cit*).
Existing thus, both internally and externally, as the supreme reality of light (*prakāśa-paramārtha*) in the form of such manifestation— that is, in the form of that appearance—
it is designated as "action" (*kriyā*), as it projects the succession of time; this belongs to that very subject (*pramātṛ*).
"Because it is the attribute of that whose body is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśaktivapuṣaḥ*); 'that' means therefore inseparable. Thus, knowledge and action are inseparable.
Knowledge is animated by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and reflective awareness itself is indeed action. And not...

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains the word "thus" (*evam*) with the phrase "because" (*yataḥ*). "Stated in other systems of thought" (*paradarśanoktaḥ*) means as proclaimed in philosophical systems other than the Śaiva method (*naya*); "by way of being both internal and external" (*antarbahirātmanā*).
In the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), manifestation is by way of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpeṇa*); that is to say, by way of having the habit of manifesting as "this-ness" (*idantayā*).

By way of such manifestation—that is, by way of the form of manifestation consisting in the relation of cause and effect—by way of its body, that is, by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*), that is this very activity (*kriyā*). The word "iti" marks the conclusion; [it belongs] to the subject (*mātuḥ*) alone.
The commentary ends here.

Thus is the application [of the words] in this context: "evam" means that when the relationship of cause and effect is untenable in the case of insentient objects; "kālakramānugā" means following the sequence in the form of time; and likewise—

The internal and external activity— though in the ultimate sense it consists of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), yet appearing as if distinct from it through its manifestation— is the activity of the subject alone; the meaning is that it belongs to the conscious one alone.
He explains the remaining portion of the verse beginning with "tat" by means of the word "tasmāt.

He explains the term "karma" as "inseparable" (aviyuktam), meaning non-different (abhinnam), and further explains it as "action" (kriyā). He demonstrates the very inseparability of knowledge and action with the words "jñānam" and so forth.

"Enlivened by reflective awareness" (vimarśānuprāṇitam) means having its existence granted by reflective awareness (vimarśadattasattākam). As was stated previously regarding the nature of manifestation: "Thus [it is]... Now, one might ask: "What does this have to do with action? To this he says: "And reflective awareness itself... and so forth.
"For one devoid of the power of knowledge, there is the yoga of action.

Thus, this [reality], whose nature consists of inseparable knowledge and action, is capable— by means of action— of reflecting hundreds of cycles of emanation and withdrawal contained within the entire aggregate of principles.
That which, though appearing as such in instruction, meditative cultivation, and so forth, is in reality non-manifest— even while being non-manifest in form— is said to be the Śiva-principle. || 1 ||

If the Śiva-tattva is of such a nature, then this entire universe is not distinct from it; for even external activity consists essentially in the grossification of reflective awareness—this is the intended meaning. But even so...

Since it has not yet been established that action is of the same nature as knowledge, he says "na ca" (and not). The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the non-separation of knowledge and action. He states the resulting conclusion with the words "tad etat" (this, therefore).
"Tat" means for that reason; "etat" refers to the agent, which is what is meant by the term "Śiva-tattva. This follows from the very sense of the matter.

It should also be understood that the entity called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) is what is referred to as the *śakti-tattva* (the principle of power), because the *śakti-tattva* consists of the nature of pure *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (I-consciousness). What is that? It begins with "this" (*etat*) and ends with "which" (*yat*). Regarding that, he states two qualifiers for the word "which" (*yat*): "unseparated" (*aviyukta*), and [two] for the word "that" (*tat*).

He states two further qualifications with the word "instruction" (*upadeśa*). Although it does not manifest as such in reality, it appears as such in instruction, meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and so forth;
that is to say, its nature is to appear as the object of instruction, the object of cultivation, and so on, because it possesses the capacity for that—this is the intended meaning.

By the phrase "capable of receiving a reflection" (*pratibimbasahiṣṇu*), it is indicated that the nature of Śiva belongs to the *cittattva* (consciousness-principle) which is incomplete yet capable of receiving a reflection,
whereas the nature of Paramaśiva belongs to the *cittattva* which is complete and serves as the substratum for the reflection. Thus, by this [means], that which is called Paramaśiva—
It should be understood that the thirty-seventh principle is called Śiva, the thirty-sixth is called Śakti, and the thirty-fifth principle has also been mentioned. || 1 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the second verse with the words "nanvevam" (but if this is so). Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"of such a nature"—that is, capable of sustaining all reflections, by means of every mode of being.

That is to say, it has the nature of throbbing; therefore—from that Śiva-tattva—nothing else could be a distinct reality, since nothing exists apart from it, being neither deficient nor redundant, and having that very same single form.
Furthermore, when all principles (tattvas) rest within the one consciousness-reality (cittattva), how [could they be separate]?
Could there not be a sequence [of these levels] due to the non-difference of space and time? This is indeed so;
however, because of the predominance of the internal state, the principle called Sādākhya arises first.
But when there is a focus on external existence, the state of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara) follows after that.
Although the Śiva-principle is indeed one alone, nevertheless its very sovereignty displays within itself a differentiation of form, as it were, by means of reflection.
This very variety of form constitutes the succession of space and time; for [the universe] consists of the variety of forms and actions.

That [is the state]. And then, when the manifestation of the intensity of that intermediate state which consists of the nature of knowledge occurs, there is the "Sādākhya" (the nameable), which exists within the "Sadākhya" (the eternally nameable).
As for the rest—that which is distinct from the Śiva-tattva—what could it be? The meaning is: what would it possibly be?
Here he grants his assent with the word "evam" (thus). This means that it is exactly so.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it: "But [it is] internal," etc.
Here is the commentary:

Having concluded the position presented in the introduction with the words "thus it is," he explains the phrase "but" (*kintu*), which indicates an alternative view, with the words "even though it is one" (*yadyapyekam*).
"Belonging to that" (*tadīyam*) means related to the Śiva-tattva; "in its own self" (*svātmani*) means within itself in the form of Śiva.

The differentiation of essential nature—that is, the differentiation of essential nature existing in the form of Sadāśiva and so forth—he shows by way of being a reflection, that is, in the form of a reflection; he makes manifest to the subjects who constitute his own essential nature. To the question "Why?", he says: "The Form" (mūrti). This...

—The sequence of space and time: therein, the division is that the sequence of space consists of the variety of forms (*mūrti*), while the sequence of time consists of the variety of actions (*kriyā*). However, in both cases here, it is only the variety of essential nature (*svarūpa*); for action is not distinct from essential nature—this is the intended meaning.

He provides the application of the verse in a manner that results in a specific explanation of the object stated in general terms, beginning with "tataśca" (and therefore). He explains the word "internal" (*āntara*) and so forth by saying "jñāne" (in knowledge).

It is of the nature of knowledge—that is, of the nature of a cognition characterized by indistinct reflective awareness (*asphuṭaparāmarśa*); otherwise, there would be the consequence of [the self] becoming Śiva [immediately].

When there is the manifestation of the predominance of that state— that is, when it flashes forth as primary by subordinating activity— he explains the term "sādākhya" (the so-called Sadā) with the words "in the state called Sadā. But what is meant by this?
From the moment the manifestation as "Being" (sat) arises, this reality is the denotable object of that which is called "Being," whose verbal form is the word *Sadāśiva*.
It is appropriate to mention it first in the instruction on the sequence of emanation and so forth; that is the principle (*tattva*) known as Sādākhya.
When there is an appearance of predominance in the state of externality, which consists of the power of action,

that is the principle of Īśvara, called by the term "Parameśvara," belonging to the Supreme Lord. And from that [and because of that], it is the appropriate manifestation following the [principle] called Sādākhya.
Because this is so, he says "since" (*yataḥ*). "Being" (*sat*) means manifestation—*sat* is well-known.

Therefore, the sense is that even existence (*sattā*), when previously delimited by its counter-correlative "non-being" (*asat*) in relation to power (*śakti*) and so forth, is not tenable. He explains the term *sādākhyam* by way of another method:

Regarding the phrase "of that which is called 'existent'": previously, the suffix *aṇ* was prescribed by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ* ("that which occurs there"), whereas here it is prescribed by the rule *tasya vācyam* ("that which expresses it"). Therefore, [the term] "sadākhyāyāḥ" [is used].
The analysis of the compound is: "the reality that is to be expressed is called Sādākhya. He explains [the word] "from the beginning" as "emission" (sṛṣṭi).

In that which consists of the teaching and so forth according to the sequence of emission—that is, the descending order—the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes reflective awareness and the rest; however, [it is also understood] by way of the ascending order.

The sense is that the *sadāśivatattva* is indeed the final [tattva]. Regarding the word "appropriate" (*ucitam*), the sense is that knowledge alone is primary by virtue of its position in the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).
Having explained the first half-verse, he explains the second half with the word "that" (*tat*).

The word "that" (*tat*) is supplied as the agent; he provides an explanation of this supplied term with the words "called Sāda. He explains the phrase "external existence" (*bahirbhāva*) and so forth with the words "of external existence. Although the term "supreme lordship" (*parameśvarapada*) is properly applicable only to the Śiva-tattva, nevertheless, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [it is applied here].
The same [analysis] applies here as well: the analysis of the term *pārameśvara* is "that which belongs to the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara-pada-vācya*).

However, in this context, that power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) manifests itself clearly and slightly unfolds even the "this-ness" (*idantā*) that is its own counterpart, whereby there arises the [cognition] "I am this," from which the "I" (*aham*) [emerges].
Let this be primary, while the reflective awareness of "this" (idam) is secondary;

for this alone is the intensification of the power of action known as external existence. The very reflective awareness of "I" (aham) manifests even in the form of the reflective awareness of "this. And it is precisely here that [the nature] of the pure reflective awareness of "I" [is realized].
And the indication of the nature of conceptualization (vikalpa) should be understood. He explains "from another" (*parataḥ*) with the words "and that" (*tacca*).

"And that"—meaning the principle of Īśvara—is "subsequently," that is, after knowledge, appropriate when there is an intensification of action (*kriyodreka*); this is the sense. Here too, it should be connected with the phrase "in the instruction on the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*) and so forth."
In order to explain the word *tattva* as that which remains in the first half [of the verse], this is what is meant:
here, *tattva* is the state of being that (*tasya bhāvas tattvam*).
That which appears as a single, undivided principle, serving as the cause for the grouping together of various distinct categories—that is *tattva*.

Just as mountains, trees, cities, and so forth, as well as rivers, lakes, oceans, and so forth, possess the nature of earth and the nature of water; likewise, regarding that pure group of consciousness known as the Mantramaheśvaras, at their first creation, within us—

The cycle of objective phenomena (*bhāvacakra*), which is primarily dark and merely opened like a painting just begun, is as if to be known solely through the instruments of perception; likewise, during the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*),
it remains in that very same state due to its orientation toward dissolution.

He provides an introductory statement (*avataraṇikā*) in order to express the intended meaning of the verse by way of summary, saying: "This is what is meant. To the question, "What is it that is meant? he says: "In this context" (*iha*). "Of distinct groups" (*bhinnānāṃ vargāṇām*) means of many groups existing in a state of differentiation.

The cause for grouping—namely, being grouped into one—is that quality by which things, though distinct, appear as equal; the sense is that a "group" (*varga*) is indeed a collection of similar things.
It is "one" (*eka*), existing as a unity among many parts, and for that very reason, it is "undivided" (*avibhakta*).
It is free from dispute. Here, he states "for example" (*yathā*) to provide an external, established entity as an illustration.
