The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the explanation of the term *tattva*. He states the resulting conclusion with "and therefore" (*tataśca*); and therefore, since the reality (*tattva*) consists in the grouping of the classes (*varga*), for that reason...

And for this reason, he is called a Mantramaheshvara— a term established by conventional usage (*rūḍha*)— referring to that group of pure consciousness, a collection of cognitions that perceives non-duality;
[this occurs] at the first creation of that [group], which consists in a falling away from the state of Śiva, whose nature is consciousness endowed with reflective awareness (*savimarśa*).
In this new creation, which is of a descending nature, it is mostly dark— that is,
indistinct due to its not yet having emerged— and likewise like a painting that has merely been outlined,
drawn with ink and the like but not yet brought to fullness with ochre and other pigments; such is the painting.
It is like a painting; that which is the wheel of states—the multitude of objects graspable as "this-ness"—shines forth by way of being a reflection, that is, by way of resembling a reflection.
Likewise, furthermore, in dissolution—that is, in dissolution in the form of the process of ascent—[it shines].

Because it is on the verge of dissolution—that is, on the verge of destruction—the wheel of phenomena (*bhāvacakra*), being exactly as it is—consisting mostly of darkness and resembling a painting that has only just been unveiled—shines forth like a reflection. For whom does it shine, and how? For us—
To the subjects of Māyā, it shines within the internal organ alone as if cognizable solely by the internal organ,

appearing almost like a reflection; and that which constitutes the specific nature of consciousness (cid-viśeṣatva) for that group of conscious beings is precisely this manifestation of such a mass of objects in that manner.

That is the Sadāśiva-tattva. However, for the mass of consciousness (caitanyarāśi) consisting of the Mantreśvaras and others, the universe—which has become manifest and resembles the category of objects reached through the path of our external senses—shines as if it were a reflection; and that [universe] belongs to him.

The principle of Īśvara is the manifestation in such a manner. As for the venerable Sadāśiva and the venerable Īśvara, who exist in the form of the object of meditation and worship and so forth, they should be understood as distinct from Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
one must not be deluded by the similarity of their names. As some have said:
Why have even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra not been included among the categories of reality? || 2 ||
Like an object perceivable by the instruments of cognition— for indeed, an object is grasped by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) only in an indistinct manner—

there is, with respect to that aforementioned group of consciousnesses, such a mass of entities— that is to say, regarding the sphere of the multitude of objective existences— a manifestation characterized by being predominantly turbid and so forth. This is what is meant by "manifestation" (prathana).

That specific state of consciousness— which is called "vibration" (sphuraṇa) due to its manifestation in the form of what has been described as predominantly *dhyāmala* (turbid/obscured) and so forth,
and which is a property known as the "state of being a specific consciousness"— is the *sadāśiva-tattva*.
It is the state of having indistinct reflections throughout the entire aggregate of objective phenomena (*bhāvarāśi*).

The intended meaning is that the very perception of [the object] as being almost entirely vanished is the state of Sadāśiva. Furthermore, it should be understood by oneself that the apprehension through the "I-consciousness" (ahantā) consists of the principles of Śiva and Śakti;
and in this context, the subject is Śiva himself, because the supreme I-consciousness (parāhantā) alone is predominant therein.

The state of Paraśiva, however, is always composed of all things; thus, no conceptual distinction whatsoever exists therein. But here, it has been heard from the venerable Gurus that everyone possesses subjectivity in every respect. Now, let it be that this is the state of Sadāśiva; what of the state of Īśvara?
To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "The Lord of Mantras" (mantreśvara). This means:

of the two subjects who consist of the forms of Mantreśvara and so forth, and who abide in the two stages consisting of the principles of Īśvara and Vidyā—namely, those whose forms are Mantreśvara and Mantra—by virtue of being like reflections.

By this, the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) is excluded; for to them, the universe appears as nothing but reality and not as a reflection. The intention is that the very perception [of the universe] as a reflection constitutes the attainment of the principle of Īśvara and the attainment of the principle of Śuddhavidyā. Now, just as...

In response to the inquiry as to why Sadāśiva and others possess the nature of a *tattva* while Viṣṇu and others do not, he says: "But he who... [The phrase] "in the form of the object of worship and so forth" includes the objects of worship and the like by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*); the word "is conceived" (*kalpyate*) is to be supplied. Separately—
It is indeed distinct from both its essence and its form. Now, one might ask: "In whom has this delusion arisen?
To this he says: "As they have said. (2)
In this context, he also shows another set of names for these two principles: "Īśvara is the external unfolding (unmeṣa), and Sadāśiva is the internal closing (nimeṣa);
and there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the cognitions of 'Being' (sat) and 'I-this' (aham-idaṃ). (3)

In the statement, "From whose unfolding (*unmeṣa*) the world arises," it is precisely the *Īśvara-tattva* that is denoted by the word "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*). For the "unfolding" of the universe is its manifestation as something distinct and external, while "closing" (*nimeṣaṇa*) is the production of its non-manifest state and the intensification of its nature as the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*).

The closing of the eyes (*nimeṣa*), characterized as "the internalization of form" (*antārūpatodrecana*), is the *Sadāśiva-tattva*, because it is the dissolution of the world. This vibration (*spanda*) of the Supreme Lord is purified; although He is immovable, it is characterized by the attainment of an internal form that has not yet fully emerged.
Here, the commentary provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "another name," which is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, it presents the verse and explains it.
"Īśvara" (the Lord).
Regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "Why was this stated? To which it replies: "For of the universe... And its "manifestness" (*sphuṭatva*) consists in its externality.

And that [pair of] clarity and externality is a *dvandva* compound in its collective sense. Regarding "the intensification (*udrecana*) of the nature of 'I-ness' (*ahantārūpatā*)"—that is, of internality—the intensification of the nature of 'I-ness': from what does the *Sadāśivatattva* arise? To this he says, "because" (*yataḥ*). *Sadāśiva* himself is the [source] of the world.

"Dissolution" (*pralaya*) occurs beyond that, because of the impossibility of contact with the world; the word "iti" marks the end of the explanation of the first half [of the verse]. He describes the state of pure vibration (*śuddhaspandatva*) in the two principles (*tattva*) of Sadāśiva and Īśvara with the words "this is pure. Even for that which is immovable—

Because he abides in his own essential nature from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even though he is devoid of movement, this vibration (*spanda*)—which consists of the forms of Sadāśiva and Īśvara—belongs to the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), who is the totality of Śiva and Śakti;
it is pure (*śuddha*). Of what nature is it? It is "unemerged" (*aprarūḍhā*), meaning it has not yet reached growth and is indistinct.
This means that because the world manifests as an unmanifested reflection, it has not yet attained solidity;

that transition into another form—that is, the attainment of differentiation—is its characteristic, which is to say its very nature. In response to the inquiry "From what does this vibration (*spanda*) arise?"—
Because it has a manifest form characterized by slight movement;
for, in the ultimate sense, these powers of the Supreme Lord constitute the entire collection of principles (*tattva*), yet one particular power,
embracing many other powers within itself, is to be worshipped because of its proximity.

Just as a jar has its own nature consisting of "jar-ness," which is independent of anything else and rests solely upon its own form, so too does it have a further nature consisting of "existence" (sattā) which depends on something else and is more remote; likewise, the powers of closing and opening (nimeṣa and unmeṣa) are Sadāśiva and Īśvara, and their presiding deities are named accordingly.
Now, he explains the *vidyātattva*, which is the instrument residing in the two presiding deities (or residing in the two presiding goddesses): "That which is the self of light.
He states the reason for this with the word "something" (*kiñcit*); otherwise, appearances such as Sadāśiva and so forth would be impossible.
The meaning has been established in accordance with the root *spadi*, which signifies "to move slightly," even though this is so in the authoritative treatises (*sāraśāstra*).
Although it has been stated that the state of vibration (*spandatva*) belongs to Śakti alone, nevertheless, according to the method taught here in this *Prakriyā-śāstra*,

it is ascribed to Sadāśiva and the others; for in this scripture, the status of being the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-svarūpatva*) belongs only to Śakti and Śiva externally, and not to Paraśiva— enough said on this point.
It establishes that purity is produced by proximity, or else it declares that these two principles are objects of worship for the Supreme Lord.
For—because—these powers belong to the Supreme Lord; which ones are they? Those which...

The "group of principles" (*tattvagrāma*) consists of the collection of principles beginning with Sadāśiva. They are "to be worshipped" (*upāsyāḥ*) because they are fit for worship either due to the non-attainment of impurities (*mala*) or because they swiftly lead to the attainment of the Possessor of Power (*Śaktimat*). For in the search for a real entity, a jar is obtained only after a long time.

The sense is that [this occurs] immediately upon searching for the object endowed with the nature of a jar. He provides the conclusion with the word "evam" (thus). The phrase "of Śiva, the possessor of power" is the ellipsis; "the two presiding deities" refers to the pair of deities existing as the impellers, namely those called Sadāśiva and Īśvara.

This is the meaning. In that regard, the state of being the presiding deity over the *tattvas* of Śiva and Śakti belongs to those two *tattvas* alone, because they themselves are of that nature. Sadāśiva is the presiding deity in the *tattva* of Sadāśiva;
Īśvara is the presiding deity in the *tattva* of Īśvara; both Sadāśiva and Īśvara [are the presiding deities] in the *tattva* of Vidyā; and after that, in the sphere of Māyā...
Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. As it has been said:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
And this is stated according to the order of dissolution (saṃhāra-krama), not according to the order of creation (sṛṣṭi-krama); it is not otherwise.
This is to be suspected.
Now, he provides an introduction in order to explain the second half [of the verse], beginning with "atha" (now).
Its substratum—

Reflection (*vimarśa*), characterized by resting in the self-luminosity of one’s own nature which is not directed toward anything else—expressed as "I am that"—is called *mātraviśramaṇa*. That which is directed toward something else is expressed as "this" (*idam*);
and that [reflection] ultimately rests, in the highest sense, within the state of being solely self-luminous and no longer directed toward anything else.

In that regard, in the first reflective awareness (vimarśa) there is the Śiva-principle; in the second, the state of a Vidyeśvara; but in the middle form, that reflective awareness which—by the maxim of two scales held in perfect equilibrium—is "I am this," belongs to Sadāśivanātha and the venerable Lord Īśvara, whereas the aspect of "this-ness" (idaṃbhāva) [belongs to the latter].
The distinction is made by the degree of turbidity or clarity.

These two [entities] situated within the pair of *tṛ*— namely, the pair of presiding deities situated within the principles (*tattva*) of Sadāśiva and Īśvara— the instrument (*karaṇa*), which is the means of impulsion, and the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*), which is the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*).
Having thus provided the introduction, he explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "of the light" (*prakāśasya*).
He explains the phrase "of the cognitions 'I' and 'this'" (*ahamidamdhiyoḥ*) with the words "of the light.
And he himself explains the phrase "resting solely in the Self" (*ātmamātraviśramaṇam*) with the words "not other" (*ananya*).

"Not turned toward another" means not directed outward; therefore, it is that which has as its characteristic (lakṣaṇa) or essential nature (svarūpa) the repose within the self-luminosity of one's own Self. This fulfills the expectancy of the word "yat" [in the verse] by providing "saḥ. "Saḥ" means that very state of resting.

The masculine gender [of the pronoun] depends on the words to be supplied through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and the context of deliberation (*vimarśa*). Having explained the component "I" (*aham*), he explains the component "this" (*idam*) with the words "But he who... (*yas tu*). "Facing another" means facing the external. Now, if that is so, does it not follow that duality arises? To this he says: "And that... (*sa ca*). [He uses the word] "again" (*punaḥ*).

The meaning is "at the time of ascent. The meaning is that in the middle, it appears as if false. Now, in response to the inquiry, "In that case, what is the distinction between this [state] and the two previously mentioned realities? he provides the division with the words "therein" (*tatra*). Therein, [the forms are]: "I am this," "I am this," and "this am I."

The meaning is: "in the midst of the fourfold reflective awareness. The meaning is: "in the first reflective awareness," namely, in the awareness "I. And this has been stated by superimposing the identity of Śakti and Śiva; in the second [reflective awareness], namely, in the awareness "this," there is the state of Śuddhavidyā characterized as the status of a Vidyeśvara, for the Vidyeśvaras are indeed of the nature of Vidyā.

They exist in this way because they are imagined merely for the purpose of meditation; this is stated with reference to the second [sūtra], "iti," since otherwise a middle [state] would be impossible. In the middle—namely, when the object is known, in the two types of reflective awareness: "I am this" and "this is I. But then, [one might ask]:

Since it follows that Sadāśiva and Īśvara are indeed one and the same, he says: "of the state of 'this' (idaṃbhāva). "Dhyāmalatā" means lack of clarity; the distinction is that in the principle of Sadāśiva there is a lack of clarity regarding the state of "this," whereas in the principle of Īśvara there is no such lack of clarity. Now, if that is so—

It is true that the analogy of the balanced scales (*samadhṛtatulāpuṭanyāya*) is not appropriate regarding the *sadāśivatattva*; this has been stated here for fear of prolixity, otherwise, in the *sadāśivatattva*, the predominance of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) indeed exists—enough of this. Now, if *śuddhavidyā*...

The two cognitions "I" and "this" have separate substrates within the illusory subject— the cognition "I" residing in the grasper and the cognition "this" in the grasped. By negating that [duality], their unification in a single substrate,
which takes the form of a connection, is what constitutes manifestation.

[The Elucidation of the Nature of the Connection – K. ṣ. ṣ. That pure *vidyā* is distinct from impure *vidyā*, which resides in the subject (*pramātṛ*) within *māyā*. In that regard, when there is the thought "I" (aham)...

When that which is the substratum, whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), causes this "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) to manifest within itself, then, because that [object] is not yet clearly defined, there is the state of Sadāśiva, expressed as "I am this" (*ahamidam*). However, when the substratum has become clearly manifest in the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*), it then infuses the reflective awareness of the "I-portion" (*ahamaṃśa*) into it, resulting in the experience "This is I" (*idamaham*).
That is sovereignty; such is the division. || 3 ||

In response to the inquiry, "If there is a state of upheaval (*uddhurībhāva*) even for the left tooth [of the subject], then what is the difference between this and *māyā*?", he explains with the words "these which... (*ye ete*).
He clarifies that they indeed have distinct substrata (*pṛthagadhikaraṇatva*) by saying "I" (*aham*). [This occurs] in the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Regarding that which is considered the subject (*pramātṛ*)—the void (*śūnya*) and so forth—and the object (*grāhya*), the cognizable (*prameya*):
[one might ask], "What indeed exists here in this *śuddhavidyā*-tattva? To this he says: "by its removal" (*tannirāsena*).
This means by the removal—that is, by the casting away during the stage of ascent—of that [subject-object distinction] which constitutes a separate locus.

But in the state of descent (*avarohadaśā*), by its very nature, there is a "conjunction" (*saṃgamana*)— that is, a conjunction characterized by being seized by both difference and non-difference— within a single substratum, namely within pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as the sole support. He himself explains this "conjunction" as being of the nature of a relationship (*saṃbandha*).

"Expansion" (*prathana*) means the conjunction as "I" with respect to the aspect of consciousness (*cidbhāga*), whereas with respect to the state of being an object of cognition (*cetyatā*), it is the conjunction as "this" (*idam*). That [refers to] the reality whose nature has been described. He explains the word *satī* as "pure" (*śuddhā*). The word *vidyā* is self-explanatory. Why?

In response to the expectation of what constitutes "pure," he says "impure. He demonstrates that this *śuddhavidyā-tattva* possesses the nature of Sadāśiva and Īśvara through a distinction of objects, using the word "therein" (*tatra*). "Locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) means that which serves as the substratum for the object; "he causes to arise" (*ullāsayati*) means that it is from this very [locus] that this [object] has emerged.
The reading is either "jānāti" (he knows) or "ullāpayati" (he causes to manifest). He pours forth—he internalizes;

the meaning is that this occurs within the domain of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). In that regard, during the descent (*avaroha*), after the station of Sadāśiva, there is the taking recourse to the station of Īśvara; however, during the ascent (*āroha*),...

Regarding the mention of the state of Sadāśiva immediately after the state of Īśvara: it should be understood that this [instrument] belongs to Sadāśiva and Īśvara, who are both presiding deities, because they lead, respectively, to the two paths characterized by difference and non-difference. || 3 ||

Now, why is this [knowledge] called "pure"? To this he says: "Because for those things that have attained the state of 'this-ness' and have entered the plane of the knowable, their essence is consciousness, due to the perception of them as they truly are. (4)

*Vidyā* is observation, expansion, and feeling; it consists in accordance with reality and conformity to the object. Its purity is its non-erroneousness. This [purity] belongs to those who have reached and accepted the state of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), and therefore, by means of such appropriate [knowledge] as "this is indeed so."

For entities that have arisen through conceptualization (*parāmarśa*) and are being conceptually determined, consciousness alone—whose nature is luminosity—is the essential reality; and this luminosity is not directed toward anything other than itself.
Here, the commentary states:

Now he provides the introduction to the fourth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it. Regarding the phrase "idaṃbhāva" (the state of being this), the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:

Regarding the phrase "firstly, because of observing things as they are," he explains the component "because of observing" through many synonyms, beginning with "expansion. He then provides the application of the term "as they are" here and explains it as "conformity to the actual state of things."
Of that—of this *vidyā* (knowledge); by this it is indicated that the present reference is one where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary meaning.

And thus, the construction here is as follows: "according to the reality"—that is, in accordance with how the object actually exists; that which is the "vision"—the *vidyā*—because of its being such [a vision], this is "Sadvidyā" (True Knowledge); this is the connection with what precedes.
He states that "purity" (*śuddhi*) is a synonym for the word "existent" (*satī*), which is the meaning expressed by the term;

he explains "those who have reached the ground of the knowable" (*vedyabhūmim upetuṣām*) as "having approached" (*upagata*); and here too, he provides a synonym, saying "accepted" (*aṅgīkṛta*). By means of this support...

He explains the phrase "of those endowed with the state of 'this-ness'" (*idaṃbhāvopapannānām*) with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). He states the essential nature of the state of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*) by means of the term "through reflective awareness" (*parāmarśena*). He explains the word "endowed" (*upapannānām*) as "those being reflected upon" (*parāmṛśyamānānām*). The term "of entities" (*bhāvānām*) is explained through its own verbal form (*nigadavyākhyātam*).

He explains [the phrase] "because its essence is consciousness" with the words "consciousness itself. By this, it is stated that here, by way of a particular formulation (*bhaṅgyā*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is what is expressed as the meaning; therefore, because its essence is consciousness, [it is said]: "I"—that is, "I whose nature is reflective awareness. Thus, it is precisely in that which is their ultimate form...
Because of its being fully developed, the nature of "I am this" (or "I") consists of pure awareness. || 4 ||
The two principles are distinguished from the two deities in their form as presiding subjects;
this is demonstrated through the terminology of the scriptures by way of this methodological approach.

The meaning is that [the distinction arises] because [consciousness] has reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as its essence. He states the conclusion with the word "that" (*tat*), because [the distinction] has become fully developed.

The meaning is this: the nature of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "I am this," which pertains to levels such as Sadāśiva, consists of pure cognition; its nature is that of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), because although there is initially a sense of duality, it ultimately rests in non-duality.

And thus, here is the summary: the conventional designation of the principles (tattva) of Śiva and Śakti applies to the two—manifestation (prakāśa) and the pure self-reflection of "I" (ahaṃvimarśa)—which are eternal and of an inseparable nature;
furthermore, because there is an absence of objectivity (vedyatva), subjectivity (pramātṛtva) also resides therein.
The apprehension of both Śiva and his manifestations occurs solely through the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*).

The conventional usage of the category of Sadāśiva-tattva pertains to the sphere of unlimited *ahaṃtā* and *idantā*. Here, however, the group of conscious subjects consists of the Mantramahēśvaras, who arise from the emergence of objectivity (*vedyatā*).
Regarding entities, however, their apprehension occurs through an "I-ness" (ahantā) that is stained by a slight touch of "this-ness" (idantā);
for all this is indeed "I" alone, and there is no such thing as an object called "this," because only the one pure consciousness exists. When those very two—“I-ness” and “this-ness”—are equalized...

This is the functional domain of the Īśvara-tattva. Here, the Mantreśvara is the subject (pramātā), while the apprehension of entities occurs through both "this-ness" (idantā) and "I-ness" (ahantā) according to the analogy of a balanced scale. However, regarding the object as "this" within the sphere of the objective aspect of consciousness (cic-cetya-bhāga), there is the functional domain of the Śuddhavidyā-tattva.

Regarding objects, however, there is a slight apprehension through "this-ness" (idantā) untouched by "I-ness" (ahantā); moreover, even though the manifestation of pure "I-ness" exists, it remains indeed indistinct,
for otherwise one would fall into the level of Māyā-tattva, where indeed the state called Pralayākala exists in the form of the void (śūnya).

The subject (*pramātā*); nor should it be suspected here that "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) stand in a clear state of mutual opposition—which would result in their falling into the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—for both of these are, in this context, equally immeasurable; however, in the realm of *māyā*, it is otherwise for those two.

There is indeed a clear state of mutual opposition between them; however, as for Paraśiva, who is omnipresent, eternal, and consists of all things, he is not the subject under discussion here. || 4 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fifth verse with the words "adhiṣṭhātṛ" (the presiding deity).
Here the commentary says:
"that pair"—meaning the two deities, in the form of Sadāśiva and Īśvara.
By means of the conventional usage of scripture— that is, by means of the conventional usage of the essential treatise—
having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "In this regard" (*atra*).
Herein, the "inferiority" (*aparatva*) of entities arises from their appearing as non-self (*anātmatvena*).
Indeed, that state of "other" and "self" arises from the concealment of otherness by the sense of "I."

"Otherness" (*paratā*)—which is fullness (*pūrṇatva*) and independence—is "I" (*aham*); "non-otherness" (*aparatva*)—which is incompleteness (*apūrṇatva*) and dependence on another—is "this" (*idam*). And within these two principles, all entities [are situated].
The state of being both supreme (*para*) and non-supreme (*apara*) arises from the contact with both aspects of those whose forms range from turbid to pure.
The state established in the nature of the object of knowledge is the essence of the *tattva*s;
that which illuminates it consists of the Mantreśvaras and others.

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains "otherness" (*paratā*) first as "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*). It further states that "ananyā" is a synonym for fullness. It explains "due to being veiled by 'I-ness'" (*ahantayācchādāt*) as "I" (*aham*).

He explains "otherness" (*aparatva*) as "incompleteness" (*apūrṇatva*). Here too, he provides a synonym, saying "dependence on another" (*anyāpekṣitā*). He explains [the phrase] "because it appears as non-self" (*anātmatvena bhāsanāt*) by saying "this" (*idam*). He explains the word "here" (*atra*) as "in the two principles" (*tattvadvaye*).

The meaning is "in the form of Sadāśiva and in the form of Īśvara"; he explains "of entities" (*bhāvānām*) as "of those having soiled and unsoiled forms. In that regard, the distinction is that there is "soiledness" in the state of Sadāśiva and "unsoiledness" in the state of Īśvara.

He explains that [the state] consists of both parts by means of the "higher and lower states" (*parāparadaśābhyām*). The word "of knowledge" (*vidyāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the explanation.
Such is the final meaning established here. In this context—"in these two principles (*tattva*) called Sadāśiva and Īśvara."

Because external and internal entities (*bhāvānām*) manifest as non-self—that is, they manifest as "this" (*idantayā*)—they possess otherness (*aparatvam*). Likewise, because they are veiled by "I-ness"—that is, because they are enveloped as "I" (*ahantvena valanāt*), which amounts to being grasped as "I"—they possess subjectivity (*paratvam*). Indeed (*hi*).

Therefore, in the sense of the word, for this reason, that *sadvidyā* consists of both the supreme (*parā*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*); the meaning is that it takes the form of a collection of both principles (*tattva*).
This is indicated by these two words, "from manifestation" (*bhāsanāt*) and "from concealment" (*chādāt*).

Relying upon the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyabhāva*) of the principles (*tattva*), one effects the division between the subject who presides over the principles (*tattvādhiṣṭhātṛ-pramātṛ*), the limited cognizer (*pramātṛ*), and the *vidyā* residing therein; thus it is said, "it is the object of knowledge. The state established in the condition of being an object of knowledge constitutes the very nature of the principle (*tattvasvarūpa*); indeed, the state of being an object of knowledge is itself the state of being a principle.
That state of consciousness which has as its essence the object cognized by the pure subject, and which is grounded in that [subject],
is pure *vidyā*; it consists in being the presiding authority over that subject (or, more precisely, over the entire class of such subjects).
This is the summary: [the attainment of] the nature of the venerable Lord Sadāśiveśvara. || 5 ||
Thus, according to the view of some, Śuddhavidyā is that which has as its primary function the manifestation of that portion which is the concealer of "I. Others, however,
maintain that it is that which has as its primary function the manifestation of that portion "this" (idam) which is to be concealed.
Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā). Otherwise, by what would this "this-ness" (idam-aṃśa) be manifested?

For Māyā is absent there, or if it were present, there would be the consequence of its further growth (praroha). Therefore, she is called "pure" because she manifests "this-ness" while being unable to tolerate its growth. And from this manifestation...

Regarding the term *vidyā*: because it is precisely due to that [state] that *māyā* has not yet fully emerged, this is taught by the venerable teachers of the *Raurava* and other scriptures as *mahāmāyā*; he states this very point.
"As far as..."—of what nature is it? It is that which is manifested by those such as the *Mantra-īśvaras*.
The pure subjects—whatever object is their object of perception—that is the "essence" (sāra) of which;
that is to say, she is of that nature. Because of extreme proximity, the Mantra-lords (maṃtreśas) are mentioned directly, while by the word "etc. (ādi), the Mantra-maheśvaras are included.

The state of consciousness established in that [object] is the state of knowledge residing in the pure subject; its "presiding over that subject" means its role as the impeller of the Mantreśvaras and others—this is the summary.
Thus, the meaning is that this is the concise sense of the matter. || 5 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the word "evam" (thus).
Here the commentary states:
"śuddhavidyā" (pure knowledge), because the aspect of consciousness has the nature of pure knowledge; this is the intended meaning.

"Predominant in that" means predominant in manifestation; "otherwise" means in the absence of the predominance of manifestation. [The opponent objects: "But surely its manifestation exists even in the state of *māyā*.
To this he says: "of *māyā*. "Therein" refers to the principle of *śuddhavidyā*; for [if it were otherwise], there would be the consequence of its [the *māyīya*] sprouting forth.
Because it would entail the cessation of Māyā, and thus there would be the consequence of duality—this is the intended meaning.

He states the conclusion with the words "for this very reason": [it is] "incapable of sprouting"—meaning it cannot find rest because it is concealed by the ego-sense (ahaṃtā)—because it is like Māyā that has not yet fully developed.
Because it is similar to a loose illusion. This—namely *śuddhavidyā* (pure knowledge)—is that very thing just mentioned. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it:
"the notion of duality," and so forth.

Others hold that the very cognition of difference regarding entities, which arises even for the agent whose nature is consciousness, is called *vidyā*—just as it is for the *Vidyeśvaras*, who act through the power of *māyā*. (6)

When the subject consisting of Māyā, whose nature is that of the void (śūnya) and so forth, has not yet emerged, and when only the pure consciousness (cinmātra) remains as the subject and the agent, then even though all entities are of the singular nature of consciousness, that which is characterized by the manifestation of difference through their appearing as non-conscious (acidrūpa)— [which is actually characterized by non-manifestation— K.ṣ.ṣ.]— occurs.
That Śuddhavidyā is autonomy; it is similar to the power of Māyā insofar as it manifests duality within the objective portion (vedyabhāga).
Yet it is not Māyā itself, because there is no subversion regarding the aspect of pure consciousness (cinmātra) in the subject, by which [the Vidyeśvaras] [attain their state].

The Bhagavats, beginning with Ananta and the others, exist; for they possess the state of "I" (ahambhāva) grasped as pure consciousness alone, yet they perceive an object of knowledge (vedya) that is distinct from themselves, just like the Lord (Īśvara) according to the dualists. Thus, [they differ] from the subject (grāhaka) in its aspect of being of the nature of pure consciousness.
In its ultimate form, Śuddhavidyā possesses the power to destroy the misconception regarding the object of perception for the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras).
The commentary here states:

the construction is "even though it has not emerged. The word *api* (even/though) indicates the suitability for the manifestation of duality when that [consciousness] does emerge. "In entities" (*bhāveṣu*) means in those whose nature is voidness and so forth, or in the forms of the knower and the known.

In all objects, its characteristic is the manifestation of difference—that is, the nature of appearing as distinct from one's own self, which is known as being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Why? Because it is equal to the power of *māyā*; to this he says: "the object of knowledge" (*vedya*). If that is so, then this [power] must be of the very nature of *māyā*; to this he says: "and yet not" (*na ca*).
"Because of the absence of error"—that is, because there is no occurrence of the error known as being of the nature of insentience (*acid-rūpatā*).
He explains "as the Vidyeśvaras" with the words "by which. "Ananta and the others":
by the word "others," Śivottama and the rest are included. "They"—referring to the Vidyeśvaras.
"For the proponents of duality"—that is, for the logicians (*tārkika*) and others. He provides a conclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*).

The construction is: "from a portion of the nature of consciousness. That power which effects the inversion of the object of perception—that is, its transformation into the form of the non-conscious—belongs to the *vidyeśvaras*.
This refers to Ananta and the others; it is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for those subjects who abide within the principle of Śuddhavidyā.
Such is the construction of this verse: [the emergence occurs] from the agent, who is of the nature of consciousness, even though he is the self.

Just as in the case of the power of illusion (māyā-śakti), that cognition of difference among entities which arises for one who possesses a cognition of difference produced by the power of illusion—that is *vidyā*. Thus say others, namely the teachers of the Raurava and other scriptures; this is the sense of the ellipsis. || 6 ||
Others say: the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara is the manifestation of non-manifested duality belonging to the Blessed One, Paramaśiva.
In that state, where duality is not yet clearly defined, there is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) of Īśvara.

It functions as follows: when there is clarity, it is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*); but when duality has become fully developed—despite the subversion of the object (*grāhya*)—it is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) residing in the Vidyeśvaras within the state of pure consciousness as the subject (*grāhaka-cinmātratā*). However, when both forms of subversion—the object and the subject—have become fully developed...
The power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) resides in the bound subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*); however,
even when the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the dual inversion of both the subject and the object have not yet ceased,
that manifestation of the ultimate reality of things is the operation of the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*).
This is shown in the case of subjects such as yogins and jñānins who are not bound (apaśu):
"The power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) is that which manifests that very nature of sovereignty within the state of being a bound soul (*paśubhāva*)."...
Regarding the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*), characterized by the single flavor of error, by being subject to fetters (*pāśya*), by lack of autonomy,
and by the distinction between the seen, the seer, and the act of seeing—
the author provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "in others" (*pare*).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:

Others, who have reached the further shore of the Trika scriptures, [explain it as follows]: "The manifestation of that differentiation which is unrooted"—meaning, due to its looseness, incapable of resting—[occurs] through autonomy.

"Manifestation" (*prakāśanam*); "the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara" (*sadāśiveśvaratā*); "when difference is unmanifest"—that is, when it is turbid; "of Īśvara," namely Śrī Śivabhaṭṭāraka; "when [difference] has taken root"—that is, when it rests in difference; "among the Vidyeśvaras," that is, among the subjects of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). That is to say:

Among the Mantramaheshvaras, it should be understood that there is the power of will (icchā-śakti), and among the Mantreshas, the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). Regarding the two-fold reversal of the grasped and the grasper—which consists in their appearing as if they were insentient—that [reversal] reaches its culmination and rest; and that is the power of illusion (māyā-śakti).

Regarding "of things"— that is, of entities— the manifestation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the flashing forth of the innate nature (*sahajasvarūpa*) known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); when that manifestation occurs, "this very" refers to the object just mentioned.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it:
"His sovereignty," etc.
Herein is the commentary (ṭīkā):—
He explains "in the state of being an animal" (*paśubhāve*) as "having only error" (*viparyāsaika*):

the state, reality, characteristic, or essential nature of one for whom there is a single "flavor" (*rasa*)— namely, that which consists of the knowledge of non-consciousness even within things that are essentially consciousness (*cinmaya*), occurring within "error" (*viparyāse*).

Even though [this] has arisen, that power of the Supreme Lord which illuminates this sovereignty described by the force of the previously stated reasoning— that by virtue of which certain individuals, having relied upon those reasonings and having their hearts filled with confidence therein, become perfected ones— is the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*). This very [power]...
Even though the position seen in the *Ṣaḍardhasāra* and other texts is presented, it wins over the heart of this teacher because [the word] "others" is not mentioned;
and since the *māyātattva* is being defined immediately following this, he says:
Furthermore, there is that which is called Māyā, the cause of concealment. || 7 ||
Regarding that which is such: he provides a second explanation, "in the state of being subject to bondage" (*pāśanīyatve*).

This means "in the state of being bound" (*bandhyatve*); he also states another explanation, "in the state of lacking independence" (*asvatantratve*). Furthermore, he provides yet another explanation for this very term: "the visible" (*dṛśye*).

By implication (*lakṣaṇayā*), this refers to the knowledge of the distinction between the forms of the grasped and the grasper; even though such [knowledge] has arisen, the word "having arisen" (*jāte*) is supplied as the logical subject. Of that—of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)—only some, namely certain individuals who have been seized by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), [attain it]. To the question "Why does it attract [others]?", he says: "Others..."

Regarding the phrase "thus [it is] not stated": the implication is that for those whose opinion is not approved, an indication would have been made by the word "others," but since it was not made here, it is understood that this very position is intended by the Teacher (*ācārya*). By this, the commentary up to the end of the section on "the power of knowledge" (*vidyā-śakti*) is completed.
The application here is as follows: the words "having arisen" (*jāte*) are to be understood as completing the sense [of the sentence], referring to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).

Even though the state of being a bound soul (*paśubhāva*), that is, the condition of a limited animal (*paśutva*), has arisen for the cognizer, the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) is the illuminator of his aforementioned nature of sovereignty (*aiśvaryasvabhāva*), which is the very essence of lordship (*aiśvaryasvarūpa*).
The sense is that [it] "comes to be," but it does not mean that it becomes a manifestor of "this-ness" (idantā).
He provides an introduction in order to explain the phrase "the concealer" and so forth, with the words "of this":
regarding the "immediacy" (ānantarya), which is the state of being immediate (anantaratā) of this—namely, of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā)—in that [state].
By "appropriateness" (aucitya), he means that for the reason of defining the principle of Māyā, he speaks of— that is, describes— that principle of Māyā.

By the word "appropriateness," [he indicates] that even for those established in the principle of Śuddhavidyā, there may occasionally be the state of Māyā— consisting of the subject and object— remaining nearby until the end of their bodily existence.
It is thus illuminated that [the Lord's] abiding indeed occurs.
Furthermore, the power of *māyā*, while sustaining a fully developed conceit of subjectivity (*pramātṛtābhimāna*) within the insentient realm such as the void (*śūnya*),
causes even entities that are essentially consciousness to be perceived through the conceit of duality.
That deluding power (vimohinī) completely conceals and obscures its own true nature. This concealment (tirodhāna) should not be understood as being of the nature of dissolution (vilayana),
since it is enumerated among the five cosmic acts (kṛtyapañcaka) in the scriptures, even in the case of one who has been initiated (dīkṣita).
Even that which consists primarily of the disparagement of the guru, mantras, and so forth, is indeed an obscuration.

Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "tirodhāna" (concealment). He clarifies that concealment consists of the nature of obscuration. The word "māyā" (illusion) is self-explanatory. The word "punaḥ" (again/furthermore) [indicates...]
This indicates the distinction from Śuddhavidyā. "Prarūḍham" means firmly established or resting;

by this, Śuddhavidyā is excluded, for in that state, the conceit of subjectivity (pramātṛtābhimāna) regarding the void and so forth does not manifest as firmly established, but rather flashes forth [only momentarily], such that those situated therein are considered to have contact with Māyā.
The construction is: "even the entities that consist of consciousness. "By way of difference" means as distinct from consciousness (*citaḥ*).
"Essential nature" refers to the ultimate nature called consciousness belonging both to the Self and to the entities.
He explains [the phrase] "causing concealment" by saying "it veils" (*āvṛṇute*), using the prefix *ā*.
The root *vṛñ* explains the term "disappearance" (*tirodhāna*), while the suffix *tiṅ* [indicates] the agent of the root *kṛ*, which ends in a verbal suffix.

To the question "Why?", he says: "deluding" (*vimohinī*). For a magician who causes delusion makes one forget even his own self, as well as his own objects; this is the sense. Now, as for disappearance...

To address whether there exists anything other than the fivefold activity of the Lord, such as creation and so forth, he says: "Concealment" (*tirodhāna*). Its nature is dissolution—its essential character being the destruction of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). To the question of what else exists, he says: "Even for one who has been initiated. This refers to the disparagement of the Guru, the mantra, and so forth.

"Prāyaḥ" means for the most part; "yatra" refers to where—in which obscuration (āvaraṇa)—such [a state] exists. The intention of the word "api" (even) is that if even one who has been initiated (dīkṣita) becomes intent on reviling the Guru, the mantras, and so forth when seized by Māyā, what need is there to mention others? Furthermore, the word "api tu" (but rather) should be placed before the word "dīkṣitasya" (of the initiated).
This is to be applied [in the same way]. || 7 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the words "tirodhānam" (concealment).
Here the commentary says:
"It is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it.
Regarding the word "in division" (bhede):
When division appears as a single essence, when the non-self is perceived through the sense of "I," whether in the void, in the intellect, or in the body, the power of Māyā unfolds. (8)
In deep sleep, at the time of cosmic dissolution, and likewise in the meditative absorption of non-existence (abhāva-samādhi),

that which is void, resembling space, devoid of self-nature, and characterized by the absence of any object of knowledge, is perceived as the "I" through the lens of the self; or [it is so perceived] during inhalation, exhalation, and the like.
"I am exhaling"—thus the *prāṇa* is like the wind;

or, in the case of the desire to eat among stationary and moving beings, or in the blazing of anger and so forth, it is the *prāṇa* itself augmented by fire (*tejas*); [the mind] is like a reservoir of clear water, possessing the reflection of the object of knowledge (*vedya*).

Or rather, the intellect becomes attached [to the notion] "I know" or "I am suffering" during states such as reflection; however, in states such as "I am thin," it is the body alone— which consists primarily of earth— that is so perceived.

Regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) sets aside the phrase "when difference appears as a single flavor" because it is easily understood, and explains the passage beginning with "by means of 'I-ness'" (*ahantayā*) with the words "in deep sleep" (*suṣupte*). Here, the appearance of difference as a single flavor refers to the entire collection of objective phenomena (*bhāvajāta*).

He explains that "in the void" (*śūnye*) refers to the state of being like space; that knowledge itself is the object of knowledge by virtue of its acid-like nature, but not so during dissolution—that is, in the state of swoon—nor in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of non-existence, which is accomplished through the cultivation of the thought "I am not," and which is thus characterized as "in the void. Regarding the phrase "in the non-self" (*anātmani*): [it refers to the same].

He explains [the phrase] "the state of being an object of knowledge" (*vedyabhāva*) as follows: for that which is not the Self (*anātman*) is indeed fit only for the state of being an object of knowledge.

He explains [the phrase] "when perceived as 'I'" (*ahantayā īkṣite*) as "as 'I'. Regarding the word "is perceived" (*vīkṣyate*), the ellipsis is "by the subject" (*pramātrā*); the meaning is that it is experienced by the subject. Otherwise, [one would think], "nothing existed at all."
The meaning is that memory would be impossible. He connects [the phrase] "in the vital breath" with "by way of fitness," as in "while breathing.
"Resembling air" means having the form of air; this is to be connected with the preceding clause, "is perceived as the Self. Regarding the hunger of both stationary and moving beings, that which...

In that [state], there is the blazing of anger and so forth; "strengthened by fire" means brought to nourishment by fire—the connection here is also with what precedes. He joins it to "in the intellect," saying "clear.
It is "like a reservoir of clear water," meaning similar to a pool of limpid water; it "enters into"—that is, becomes absorbed in—[the object].
The subject (*pramātṛ*) is established in the place of the Self; as to when it is so established, he says:
"in states such as reflection" (*cintādyavasthāsu*). Why [is it said] "within"? The sense is that the internal region is indeed the intellect (*buddhi*) itself.
He connects [the phrase] "in the body" with the words "but the body alone," using the word "but" (*eva*) [to emphasize this].
It is the exclusion of the consciousness delimited by that [object].
It shines as the Self in the form of "I. All this—indeed, all this [beginning with the void]—is in reality nothing but the essence of pure consciousness; it appears as insentient only through Māyā.
It has been stated that such a reality, being established as the locus for the persistent attachment to the nature of consciousness as "I," remains nothing but an unpeaceful, insentient state.
The illusory power (*māyā-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord consists in the non-obstruction in accomplishing even the most difficult tasks— indeed, the accomplishment of the most arduous things—
as it is said that "the illusory power unfolds," which he explains by the words "and all indeed."

"But being of such a kind" means being manifested as having the nature of the non-conscious (acid-rūpa); by this it is indicated that if its conscious nature (cid-rūpatā) were known, its status as the Self (ātmatva) would indeed be logical.
It is the locus of the attachment (abhiniveśa) to the nature of consciousness; that is, it has the "I-ness" (ahantā) as its object.

Up to the point where it says "the state of being dull and unpeaceful": the sense is that once the state of dullness (*jaḍabhāva*) has been stilled, it is indeed logical for that [object] to become the object of the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*). For this reason, that thing which is extremely difficult to accomplish—namely, the differentiation of entities whose nature is consciousness—[is undertaken].
In that state where the dull nature is not yet pacified— within the non-form that is its singular differentiation,
such as emptiness and so forth— the process of accomplishing that which consists in making it the object of the "I-sense" (ahantā).
That which is non-obstructive is her form; such is she.

This is shown by the statement "she unfolds" (*vijṛmbhate*), which refers to her being "skilled in accomplishing the impossible. By the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), [it is indicated that] the forms of the objects of knowledge...
This indicates that even things such as one's son, wealth, and wife are objects of the dogmatic attachment to "I-ness," and that such objects are innumerable. || 8 ||
Now, if that which is non-conscious in nature, such as the void (śūnya) and so forth, were the Self, then by being adhered to as the Self, it would indeed become conscious in nature; thus,
it would possess the very qualities of pure sovereignty, such as omniscience and omnipotence.
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"And that cognizer who is [perceived as] empty and so forth when the object of cognition is distinct—being himself an object of cognition, he is enveloped by the pentad beginning with time. (9)

"There might be a connection with sovereignty and dharma for the void (*śūnya*) and so forth, even though it is being clung to as 'I', because it remains an object of cognition (*meyatā*). He states the intended meaning of the word "or" (*vā*) by means of the inclusion of the term "or. "Innumerable" (*asaṃkhyātam*)—

This was not explicitly stated in the Sūtra; the meaning is that because of extreme dullness, a person indeed identifies even external objects as his own self, for otherwise it would be impossible for him to endure suffering for their sake. || 8 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the ninth verse with the words: "But [it might be argued], because of its insentient nature.
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"At that time—namely, during the state of *māyā*. Having thus provided the introduction:
Having presented the verse, he explains it with the words "And he who...
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides an introduction for explaining the verse regarding the matter that was raised as a doubt.

He accepts [the premise] by way of reasoning (*tarka*) for the purpose of demonstrating the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an over-extension (*vyāpaka-āropa*); that is to say, he means that the connection with the attributes of sovereignty (*aiśvarya-dharma-yoga*), which was raised as a doubt in the introduction, would follow. Now, one might ask:
"In that case, let that [sovereignty] belong to him"; to this he replies: "If I... [and so on]. That [subject] is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) such as the Void (*śūnya*) and so forth.

Even while being attached to the notion "I," and even while performing the apprehension of oneself as "I"— despite not actually grasping one's own self— by indicating that one does not abandon the state of being an object of knowledge (*meyatā*), which remains established by its very nature as the status of an object (*meyabhāva*), while being attached to it as "I."

This is a reductio ad absurdum (*vyāpakaprasañjana*): for wherever there is the possession of sovereignty (*aiśvaryayoga*), there must also be the abandonment of objectivity (*meyatāhāna*). Otherwise, the word "I" would lose its status as a cause for the abandonment of objectivity regarding the persistent attachment (*abhiniveśa*) to "I.
If that were the case, even the object of knowledge (*prameya*) would not appear to him as something distinct from [the self], such as blue and so forth.

To the extent that the cognizer who is described as being "void" (śūnya) and so forth is a cognizer with respect to an object of cognition such as blue— which is considered non-different from his own essential nature—
to that same extent he himself is also a cognizer only while being in the state of being an object of cognition.

For this object of knowledge (*meyam*), by virtue of being an object of measurement, is indeed limited; thus, its distinction from other such objects of knowledge is established. However, the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpam*) is not like this, because it is unlimited.

[The text] illuminates this. Now, one might object: "Let it abandon its state of being an object of knowledge" (or, as the variant *C* reads: "Let it certainly abandon its state of being an object of knowledge"). To this, [the author replies]:

He said, "So it is. For—since that being so, namely, when the status of being an object of cognition (*meyatā*) is lost, this subject (*pramātṛ*), such as the void (*śūnya*) and so forth, would not perceive the object of cognition (*prameya*), such as blue and so forth, as something distinct.
To the question "Why would it not appear [as distinct]?", he says: "Insofar as" (*yāvatā*). Insofar as—

For this reason, that cognizer who is described as "void" and so forth— stated in the scriptures— at the very moment when [an object] such as blue, which is intended to be non-different from his own nature, is nevertheless intended to be distinct from himself (due to the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the apprehension of "this-ness" and "I-ness"), [he remains as such].

The subject becomes [the knower] only as long as there is the object— specifically at that very moment and not thereafter— while remaining in the state of being the object itself; that is, while abiding as the object with respect to the internal consciousness-nature, he becomes the subject by receiving the supporting hand of the nature of the grasper.

He becomes endowed with the state of being a knower (*mātṛtva*); like a provincial ruler (*māṇḍalika*) who, by the support of an emperor, acts as a king within his own domain, otherwise he would not act as a knower apart from that which is to be known (*meya*). To the objection, "But how can he, being an object of knowledge, become the knower?", he says: "For [the object]... (hi). Indeed.

Because that which is an object of knowledge (*meyam*), being measured, is limited; as such, it possesses a distinct exclusion (*vyatireka*) from other objects of knowledge (*meyāntara*) that share its same conditions of existence (*svasamānayogakṣema*).

However, that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) does not become so, precisely because it is unlimited; for that [consciousness]— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the distinction between the finite object of knowledge and the infinite subject.]

At the time of grasping the subject (pramātṛ) such as the void (śūnya), one assimilates that void into one's own self; otherwise, like blue or other objects, even that void would appear as something distinct from the void-subject, yet it does not so appear, for in that state,
the void-subject does not appear to the void-subject as blue appears to another subject.
It appears as distinct from the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), because only duality manifests. [Objection:
In that case, why does only the unreal void (*śūnya*) appear, and not the real nature of consciousness? [Reply:
True; at that time, due to its extreme purity, it is colored by the void and so forth for those who are insentient (*jaḍa*).

It shines forth as that very form; however, those who practice in the intermediate channel see nothing there, such as emptiness and so forth—enough of this. Thus it stands: even when emptiness and the rest are grasped through the "I-consciousness" (ahantā), they do not at all lose their status as objects of knowledge (meyatva) with respect to the internal nature of consciousness; otherwise, [the following would occur].

At that very time, the limitedness of the void and so forth— which, like the nature of consciousness itself, appears as the void and other states— and that which constitutes the "I-sense" (ahambhāva) of the void and so forth, is precisely the pentad beginning with Time. For in this way, Time, manifesting succession within the subject, [functions].

Expanding in accordance with that [cognition], it extends even toward the object of knowledge (*prameya*), such as when one thinks, "I who was thin am now fat, and I shall become even fatter," thus regarding the self in the form of the body as if it were something possessing succession.

Reflecting upon that, it reveals the sequence of the elements (bhūta) and so forth even within the object of knowledge (*prameya*) which accompanies it. For this insentient [sequence] beginning with the void (*śūnya*), *vidyā*—
whose nature is the unfolding of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*)— [reveals] the mass of objects reflected upon the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*).
It distinguishes blue, pleasure, and so forth. *Kalā*, consisting of the reinforcement of limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*), brings about the effect, as in: "I know something," "I do something.
And although the state of being "something" (*kiṃcittva*) is equal in this respect, why is it that only this [specific thing]...?

If the void and so forth were to manifest in the form of blue and so on— just as consciousness manifests in the form of the void and so on— it would not so manifest, because the apprehended object and the apprehending subject manifest with a clear distinction; therefore, it is not logical for that which apprehends them to possess sovereignty.
Regarding the phrase "as if of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpasyeva*): he explains that this very immeasurable state, which belongs to subjects such as the void (*śūnya*),
takes on the form of the five principles beginning with Time (*kāla*), and he also explains its limited nature (*parimitatva*).

And "limitedness" (*parimitatvam*) refers to the quality called limitedness, which is caused by appearing as distinct from its own object of measurement; and "the pentad beginning with time" means that following *māyā*, there is a pentad consisting of time (*kāla*), knowledge (*vidyā*), limited agency (*kalā*), attachment (*rāga*), and necessity (*niyati*). This very [point is as follows]:

To establish this, he says "tathā hi" (for thus). Manifesting it as the primary element, [he shows that] within the subject—the subject whose nature is the void (*śūnya*) and so forth—it "proceeds," meaning it carries out its movement, in accordance with that—that is, in accordance with the subject. In accordance with that...

He demonstrates the expansion [of consciousness] by saying "I am. The meaning is that he exists; he manifests the self—the subject—along with its concomitants, namely the objects of cognition such as blue and so forth, making it evident through the forms: "I have known," "I know," and "I shall know."

This is the meaning. Having established the determination of Time (*kāla*), he now establishes the determination of the principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), which is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the aphorism, using the words "of this" (*asya*). He "distinguishes"—that is, he determines—the form of blue, pleasure, and so forth. [He now proceeds with] the determination of the principle of Limited Agency (*kalātattva*).
"It performs [action] through *kalā*. Therein, he shows the essential nature of *vidyā* by saying, "I know something.

He shows the essential nature of *kalā* by saying, "I do something. He shows the essential nature of *rāga* by saying, "and in this portion. "And in this portion" refers to that which consists of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and that which consists of the effect (*kārya*).
Even when there is some slight degree of similarity— meaning a slight degree of objective reality—

the attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) consisting in the notion "this is precisely that slight thing" functions as passion (*rāga*), which, though appearing as if composed of the attribution of qualities (*guṇa-āropaṇamaya*), operates within the subject regarding the body and so forth, as well as upon the objects of knowledge.

Nor is that lack of dispassion (avairāgya) residing solely in the intellect (*buddhi*); for while that [lack of dispassion] might not exist in an old man toward a young woman, passion (*rāga*) certainly does. Furthermore, attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) is observed even among the eight qualities of the intellect. Why, then, is this attachment restricted to this [specific object]? This is the point [to be explained].
"He is constrained by necessity. Thus, interwoven with *kalā*, *vidyā*, *kāla*, *rāga*, and *niyati*,

and having had his entire sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) stripped away by *māyā*, he remains in this state— possessing only that portion which has been assigned to him from within the mass of all those very powers that were once bestowed upon him.

The limited subject appears as follows: "Now I am knowing this little thing, performing this action, attached to this very object; he who is thus, that am I. And these [limited subjects] also possess distinct objects.

That which is resorted to as something desired is indeed an effect or a real entity; that is to say, it becomes something, meaning it is taken as an object by its material cause (*upādāna*). Thus, when such an objection has been raised—meaning, when this has occurred—in this matter, in this context, there is that which consists of attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*).

It is of the nature of attachment; likewise, regarding the superimposition (*āropaṇa*) of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—that is, superimposition even upon what is non-existent—it is as if that [superimposition] abounds in this present context. Thus, *rāga*—the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*)—is active; it performs its function (*vyāpāra*). To the question "Where? he says: "In the body and so forth."

The meaning is "in the object of knowledge and in the knower"; therein, the distinction is that the knower is the locus of the operation by virtue of being its substratum, whereas the object of knowledge is its locus by virtue of being its objective field. Now, one might ask:
how can passion, which consists of non-detachment and is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), reside upon the *aṇu* (the individual soul)?

To this, he says: "For that" (*taddhi*). "That" refers to the lack of dispassion residing in the intellect (*buddhi*); "attachment" (*rāga*) refers to attachment existing within the categories of reality (*tattva*).

The point is that this attachment is the very internal nature (*antaḥsvabhāva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), and not merely the absence of external dispassion. [Objection: In that case, it would be nothing other than a property residing in the intellect.
Lest there be a lack of dispassion, he says "intellect" (buddhi). The meaning is that even there, attachment—which is passion—exists in a gross form.
By this, one should understand for oneself that knowledge (vidyā) is also distinct from the cognition that is an attribute of the intellect. Of necessity...
He shows its essential nature with the words "right here. "Right here" means in this very object intended;
it is "regulated"—that is, it is brought within the scope of a restrictive rule. He provides the conclusion with the words "thus.
"Woven warp and woof" means interlaced or bound; [it is] "extended toward" that entire mass of phonemes.
He is one who possesses even a mere fraction of that mass of supreme sovereignty (*āheśvarya*) consisting of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth.
To the question of how such a person manifests a portion of omniscience from *vidyā* and a portion of omnipotence from *kalā*, he says: "Now" (*idānīm*). By this word "now,"...

By the word "knowing," there is the indication of *vidyā*; by the word "acting," there is the indication of *kalā*; by the word "attached," there is the indication of *rāga*; by the particle "eva" (only/just), there is the indication of *niyati*;
and by the phrase "that I am," there is the indication of the pentad beginning with *kalā* within the subject (*pramātṛ*).

It sometimes happens that, as elsewhere, even one who is attached to something else is made to act otherwise by necessity. And these [powers] shine forth precisely as being attached to the subject; thus they are the very forms of his powers, distinct for each individual subject. However, on occasion—as in the case of watching actors or wrestlers—they appear through the will of the Lord.
They may even become one; for they possess no life of their own whatsoever apart from the will of the Lord—this has been stated repeatedly and will be stated again. || 9 ||
Regarding what was stated— that there is a knower with respect to the object of knowledge (prameya) characterized by exclusion (vyatirekin)— he demonstrates that object of knowledge therein:
"The object of knowledge is twenty-three-fold, consisting of effects and instruments."
Its undivided form is the single Pradhāna, the fundamental cause. || 10 ||

The observation of activity, however, has as its object the cognizable (*prameya*), which is quite evident; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. In this way, he shows the pentad beginning with time (*kāla*) by virtue of having a single object, using the words "of these" (*eṣām*).
He demonstrates that very point with the words "just as" (*yathā*). Now, [one might ask], how is it that of these...?
To [address] the internal nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), he says: "And these... [The word] "of that very one" means of the cognizer alone.
By the phrase "but sometimes," it is indicated that these [objects] are always distinct from every cognizer.
For in the viewing of a play by actors and so forth, even for many [people], there is only a single temporal manifestation.
It is observed. Now, one might ask: "What role does the will of God (īśvarecchā) have in this? To this he says: "Not so" (na hi).
The "life"—meaning the existence—of these, such as time and the rest, [depends on Him].
Thus, the summary here is as follows: that which is "void" (śūnya) and so forth, in relation to that which is distinct by its own nature (vyatirekiṇi svato bhinne).

Regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*), it becomes the knower (*mātā*); being an object of knowledge, it becomes the knower only by becoming the object of measurement with respect to the internal state of consciousness (*cittatva*). Otherwise, being itself unestablished, how could it bring about establishment in another? For this very reason, because it is limited, it is enveloped by the five [factors] beginning with time (*kāla*).
It exists. The meaning is that its very attainment of the state of being an object (*meyabhāva*) constitutes its delimitation by time and so forth.

However, that which is not the subject (*mātṛ*) in the case of a distinct entity does not itself become an object (*meyībhavati*), just like the *cittattva* (the nature of consciousness); for at the time of the manifestation of the void (*śūnya*) and other states, it remains precisely of that [subjective] nature. || 9 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the tenth verse with the words "yad uktam" (as it was said).
This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it as "trayoviṃśatidhā" (in twenty-three ways).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: that which consists of the twenty-threefold forms of effects and instruments, and that which is their fundamental cause— the one called *pradhāna*, whose nature is the non-differentiation of all effects and instruments— all that is the object of knowledge (*meyam*).

For yogis, mantras, their lords (īśvara), and so forth, everything is indeed an object of knowledge (*prameya*), because they possess mastery over the elements (*bhūta*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the instruments (*karaṇa*), and primordial matter (*pradhāna*). Even for those subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*), everything is an object of knowledge by way of inference, scripture, and so on; thus, this much constitutes the objects of knowledge. Time and the rest, however, are also objects of knowledge.

They are attached solely to the cognizer; thus, because they are of the nature of the power of the cognizer (*pramātṛ-śakti*), they are not reckoned here as objects of cognition (*prameya*) at this juncture—namely, in the context of objects of cognition distinct from the *māyā*-cognizer (in the context of the "nature of the context," *prastāva-ātmani*). For in reality, this [subject] here... [here]... is [the case].
This very cognizer is indeed the object of cognition—[K. Ṣ. Ṣ. even the cognizer is indeed an object of cognition;
however, when he is being made into a cognizer, his state of being an object of cognition is concealed, and thus he is spoken of here [in this way]. || 10 ||
Now, having raised the doubt as to what among these twenty-three is the effect (kārya) and what is the instrument (karaṇa), he says:
"And here, the series of external and internal instruments is thirteenfold."
And the category of effects is tenfold, distinguished by the difference between grossness and subtlety. || 11 ||
The instruments are employed prior to the knower; thus, first of all, there are thirteen instruments. Regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
Regarding the phrase "and that which," there is an ellipsis of the word *yuktatvena* (by way of being joined).
Of that—of the object of cognition (*meyam*) consisting of the body and the instruments—the non-differentiation (*avibhāga*) of the body and the instruments is its form;
such is the meaning, namely, that it has an unmanifest form (*avyaktarūpam*). Now, [one might ask: what about time and the other [factors]?
To the question, "If knowability (*prameyatva*) is indeed manifest, what is meant by saying 'only this much'?", he says: "But time and so forth" (*kālādayastu*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), knowledge (*vidyā*) and the rest are included. This refers to the discussion concerning those objects of knowledge (*prameya*) which are distinct from the subject of illusion (*māyāpramātṛ*); they are "reckoned as objects of knowledge."

The structural interpretation (*yojanā*): "Belonging to this"—that is, related to the category of *māyā*; "being made into a subject" (*pramātrīkriyamāṇaḥ*)—meaning being produced as if it were a subject, even though in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) it is not a subject; "here"—at this present occasion. || 10 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eleventh verse with the words "nanv atra" (but surely here).
This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "trayodaśa" (thirteen).
The commentary on this point states:

"The application of the instruments [of cognition] precedes the knower"—the meaning is by this principle. At the outset, the intellect (*buddhi*) consists merely of the general form of determination (*avyavasāya*); it is devoid of the conceit of subject and object.

The ego (ahaṃkāra) is form; the mind (manas), which is the cause of volition and so forth, is the internal organ—thus the internal organ is threefold. The five sense organs, which are useful for the intellect (buddhi) consisting of the determination of sound and other objects, are: the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose.

Thus, there are five organs of action which are useful for action. To explain: there is a pair consisting of relinquishment and grasping—namely, that which pertains to external objects; in this regard, the hands, the anus, and the feet are the instruments.
That very [faculty] by which [action] is performed within the vital breath (prāṇa) is the organ of speech (vāgindriya).
Through the pacification of its agitation, the organ of generation (upastha) is employed for the activity of rest.
Furthermore, the organs of action (karmendriyas), which pervade the entire body, consist of specific forms of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). Therefore—
One whose hand has been severed takes up [objects] with his arms, or indeed with his palm alone; so it is with the others as well.
It is simply because this [organ] is the locus for obtaining those various distinct and complete functions that its substratum is said to consist of five fingers—thus are the instruments [of action].

Thirteen. And although these are effects (*kārya*), they are first [discussed] by way of their uncommon instrumentality (*karaṇatva*). Among them—within the group of thirteen—is *adhyavasāya*, which is the cognition "this" directed toward an object. It is the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding the grasped and the grasper; this...

The conceit (abhimāna) consisting of the form "this is my object of apprehension" and "I am the apprehender here," and not the egoity (ahantā) that arises in the intellect (buddhi) as devoid of a counter-correlate; [the term] "intellectual organs" refers to the sense organs of cognition. To the question of how these are employed in action, he says: "For instance" (tathā hi).

"Thus, this pair" means this twofold action of such a nature; "having external objects" means having external things as its objects; "in that"—in that twofold action; "the instruments" refers to the three instruments.
"This very thing" refers to the aforementioned pair consisting of abandoning and grasping. By which [it occurs] within the internal vital breath...
It is performed—that is to say, by that through which the relinquishing and grasping of the vital breath (prāṇa) situated within the internal region is performed;

this is the organ of speech (vāgindriya), and not speech itself. By this, it is stated that the effort of the vital breath constitutes the organ of speech, through the pacification of its agitation—that is, the agitation of the vital breath.
The organ called the *upastha*—known as the male and female sexual organs—is useful for the act of resting;

for at the time of union, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) naturally subsides, and thus it is said to be "by means of its subsiding. As for the other [organs], such as the feet and so forth, they are useful for movement and the like, even in one whose feet have been severed. Now, if...

If it is asked how there can be a restriction of the locations of the organs of action—such as the hands and so forth—when they pervade the entire body, he says: "only" (*kevalam*). This is because [the hands and other organs] are the locus for the attainment of those specific, manifest, and full functions (*vṛtti*). Of what kind...

For grasping occurs with a hand endowed with five fingers, and not in such a manner by means of the arms and so forth; in this way, it should be applied by oneself in all cases. He provides the conclusion with the word "thus" (evam): "of these"—that is, of the thirteen instruments.

Designation: The gross effects are the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether. Their subtle forms are smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. Among these, ether and the others possess one quality each, with each subsequent element possessing an increasing number of qualities.

Or rather—this is a difference in philosophical view—and thus it has not been analyzed here due to its lack of utility. In that regard, the gross and differentiated is the inferential mark for the undivided; therefore, the discussion began with the gross form.
Herein, it is the very appearances of earth and so forth that, having become intermingled...
The specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of jars and other objects, having been brought near by the organs of action,
perceived by the organs of cognition, and assumed the forms of conceptualized, desired, and ascertained by the internal organ, are then discerned by knowledge (vidyā).
The intended meaning is that those [states] colored by the *kalās* and so forth come to rest in the subject (*pramātṛ*).
This has been determined by me in detail in works such as the *Tantrāloka-sāra*, which primarily treat that subject;
