therefore, it is not elaborated upon here as it would be of no use in this context. May there be auspiciousness! || 11 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Principles" (*tattvanirūpaṇa*), in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, accompanied by the commentary named *Vimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, within the section on Revelation (*āgamādhikāra*). 1.
He explains the passage beginning with "sthūla" (gross) and so forth. "Darśanabhedaḥ" means difference of opinion.
"Vibhaktam" means manifest. "Avibhāgasya" means of the unmanifest; "atra" means within the gross.

This has been explained in detail. Furthermore, this definitive determination of reality (*tattvaniścaya*) has been properly established by me myself in the ninth chapter (*āhnika*) of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*. However, for fear of prolixity and in accordance with the intent of the original author, it has not been done here;
thus, the meaning is that it should be understood from that very source. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the chapter.

Thus ends the first chapter in the section on Revelation (*āgamādhikāra*) within the *Śrīpratyabhijñāvimarśinī*, a commentary known as the *Bhāskarī*, composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
The second chapter in the section on scripture. *Vimarśinī*.
We praise that Śiva, who, though his own nature is indivisible, causes one to traverse the manifold conceptualization of the Mothers within the wheel of the maṇḍala of his own heart.
We praise that Śiva in our hearts, who, though his essence is the singular light of consciousness (bhāskara), appears here as if he were holding within himself a state composed of limited subjects.
Now, for the sake of completing the second chapter of the section on scripture (āgama) without obstacles and for the sake of its widespread propagation,
[the author] performs— though already practiced within himself— the following external act for the instruction of his disciples:

He composes an auspicious verse at the beginning of the work, consisting of a salutation to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and indicating the overall purport of the entire treatise, beginning with the words "akhaṇḍita" (unbroken).
We praise that Śiva. Who is he? That Śiva who is unbroken—just as...

Likewise, even when a refutation is imagined, because [the Self] remains as the witness and the essence, it is in reality free from refutation; its inherent nature (*svabhāva*)—that is, its very form known as "light" (*prakāśa*)—is such that it is inlaid with self-reflection (*vimarśa*). Even while being thus, [it remains unrefuted].
In the wheel of the maṇḍala of one’s own heart— that is, in the wheel of the maṇḍala of one’s own heart which is of the nature of indivisible consciousness—
one should expand (sphārayet) the manifold conceptualization of the Mothers (mātṛkalpanā).
By this, it is indicated that the investigation of the Mothers will take place in this chapter (āhnika).
Having thus performed the auspicious invocation, he explains the intent of the daily practice (*āhnika*) both collectively and individually with the word "thus" (*evam*).
Thus, once the aggregate of principles (*tattvarāśi*) has been determined, that which was mentioned as being included within it is now stated as the primary subject.

In order to determine the reality of the cognizer (*pramātṛtattva*) by means of an extensive investigation, another chapter is introduced with twenty verses beginning with "In that [reality], this is merely the state of being a cognizer" (*tatraitanmātṛtāmātra*) and ending with "the supreme, all-pervading one whose nature is the universe" (*vyāno viśvātmakaḥ paraḥ*). To explain: here, regarding the cognizer...

The recognition of one's own true nature (*svarūpapratyabhijñāna*) is taught in the scripture. For he who knows his own essential nature—both what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted—and enters, without distinction, into his own Self whose supreme object of attainment is the nature of Śiva, becomes liberated even while living. In that regard:

By one verse, the nature of the triad beginning with Brahmā is presented; then, by two verses, the reality of the subject as that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted; then, by seven verses, the nature of the impurity (mala) that serves that [reality], and the differentiation of subjects caused by it; and finally, by two verses, the nature of immersion (samāveśa).

The purport of this chapter is as follows: by means of five verses, [the author] describes the states such as deep sleep belonging to the subject alone; then, by means of three [verses], he determines the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted regarding those states. Now, the meaning of the text itself is being examined.
In that state, while abiding solely as the subject (mātṛtāmātra), Rudra is the presiding deity;
when the expansion of objects of knowledge (prameya) has differentiated, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are established.

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): when this nature of reality— which is established by scripture and supported by reasoning— is thus present, that very form of the subject (*pramātṛtā*) which is enveloped by the pentad beginning with time (*kāla*),
becomes pure in that state wherein the entire collection of objects of knowledge (*prameyajāta*) has been withdrawn.

In that [power] called Saṃhārā, his status as the presiding deity consists in bringing about that state for his own circle of worshippers by inducing them to enter into meditation on that state, and by turning himself toward them.

The one who worships is indeed the venerable Lord Rudra, the Blessed One, by way of being included within this—that is, by way of being included within the aggregate of principles (tattva-rāśi). That which is to be abandoned extends as far as Māyā; that which is to be accepted extends from above Māyā up to Sadāśiva. Thus it is said.

The word "śabdaḥ" (the word) is used in the sense of the completion of the statement of the intended meaning as a whole. He explains it in detail with the words "therein" (*tatra*). "Tadupayogi" means useful for the reality of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*) regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; "malasvarūpam" means having the nature of the impurities, namely the threefold impurity consisting of *āṇava* and the rest; "tatkṛtam" means produced by those three impurities.
Now, having introduced the first verse without a formal introductory commentary (avataraṇikā), he explains it with the words "tatra" (therein).
Here is the commentary (ṭīkā):
He explains the word *tatra* with the passage beginning with *evaṃbhūte* and ending with *sati*.

He explains the phrase *etanmātṛtāmātrasthitau* with the words *yadetad*. That which is the nature of the subject (*pramātṛtārūpam*)—that very nature of the subject, in that [state] called withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
In this state, the entire range of objects of knowledge has been withdrawn; for this very reason, it becomes pure.
The Lord Bhaṭṭāraka himself, assuming the role of the presiding deity within that state—namely, the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka established in Śuddhavidyā—becomes the Blessed Rudra.

Even within the state of māyā, [this occurs] through contact with the essential nature of the subject, which is the light of the middle way (madhyamajyotis), free from the duality of inhalation and exhalation (prāṇāpāna), merit and demerit (dharmādharma), sun and moon, day and night, and so forth.
With his third eye opened— [the light of which is free from the middle state of day and night]—
Brahmā assumes the status of the presiding deity over the manifestation and accomplishment of the expanded, differentiated objects of knowledge (*prameya*),
characterized by the continuous flow of their succession once they have been projected.

In the expansion [of the object], Viṣṇu is the presiding deity; for this very reason, because of the predominance of that which consists of the manifestation "this is blue" in the form of the expansion of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and because of the absence of entry into the state of the subject (*pramātṛ*) as "I," there is no opening of the third eye. It is the deity alone.
*Daivata* means origin, expansion, and lineage. || 1 ||
This means that he attains the state of Rudra. In response to the inquiry as to by what cause he partakes [of this], he says: "by that state" (*taddaśā*).
For, for one who is joined with the absorption (*samāveśa*) of meditation on that state, there is the attainment of that state.

The meaning is that he also effects [their] orientation toward himself. In response to the inquiry "Who is the Lord Rudra?", he says: "He who"—meaning the Lord Rudra—who [is the one] regarding those two, dharma and adharma, which consist of prāṇa and apāna, as well as the sun and the moon.
By the word "day and night" (*dinaniśe*), the inclusion of "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth is intended by the term "and the rest" (*ādi*); that which is free from these—
unstained by contact with either— is the "middle light" (*madhyamajyotiḥ*),
namely the illumination known as the intermediate state (*madhyāvasthā*) which is attained through external and internal *kumbhaka*.
That form is the very nature of the subject— the nature of the subject who, having emerged from the void, has not yet attained the state of Śiva, and whose form is pure consciousness (cinmātra).
Through contact with that— that is, through its mere unfolding— he becomes one whose third eye is opened.
The third eye has appeared: the *prāṇa* of the nature of the subject is the right eye called the Sun; the *apāna* is the left eye in the form of the Moon;
and that which resides between the heart and the limit of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*) is the fire-nature known as the intermediate state.

By means of which they speak of his state as "three-eyed," [it is] the third eye. By this, the four arms of Śrī Viṣṇu are indeed the doubling of his power of action (kriyā-śakti). The four Vedas of Śrī Brahmā are indeed the manifestation of the Vedas having attained the state of articulated speech (vaikharī-bhāva).

The passage beginning with "the state of having four faces" (caturmukhatva) and so forth is to be understood; however, it should not be considered as referring to superhuman powers (atiśaya) that are undermined by impossibility—enough said on this.
He explains the second half [of the verse] with the word "divided" (bhinna). The expansion (prasara) is of two kinds:

The term *vācya* (the denotable) refers to both origination (*utpatti*) and continuity (*santāna*). In that regard, in the case of Brahman, it is origination; for Brahman is the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) over the origination of objects of cognition (*prameya*). In the case of Viṣṇu, it is continuity; for Viṣṇu is the presiding controller who extends the mass of originated objects through a continuous flow (*pravāha*).

Since it has already been stated that the presiding authority belongs to the venerable lords Sadāśiva and Īśvara on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), there are five causes for the fivefold activity (*kṛtyapañcaka*). As it has been said:

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—ultimately, however, all this rests in Śrī Śiva alone; thus, it is said that the performance of the fivefold cosmic acts (pañcakṛtya) belongs to Him alone. || 1 ||
He now defines the division of that which was described as mere subjectivity (mātṛtāmātra), as well as its various designations according to scripture:
"This cognizer (pramātā) is blinded by Māyā, a transmigrating being bound by karma."
One whose sovereignty is made manifest through knowledge and higher powers, and who is a mass of consciousness, is called liberated. || 2 ||
The subject is called the Lord (pati) when [the objects] are entities whose form is his own body;
through Māyā, he becomes the bound soul (paśu), differentiated and defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth. (3)

Blinded and deluded by *māyā*, and for that very reason imagining actions to be the binders of his own self, this subject—the "void" (*śūnya*) and so forth—enveloped by time and other factors, transmigrates; thus, he is a "transmigrator" (*saṃsārī*). For even the body possesses a similarity to one's true nature.

He wanders, as it were, following along through childhood, youth, and so forth; however, the wandering of the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties persists even in another birth. But for one whose sovereignty has been brought to the state of recognition by means of knowledge (*vidyā*)—that is, by the power of manifesting his true nature—for that very reason, even the body and other such things [are likewise recognized].
And even the universe,
being nothing but consciousness— so perceiving it as such— it is therefore pure consciousness alone, dense and devoid of any admixture with that which is not consciousness.

Now, he provides the introduction to the second and third verses with the words "yad etat" (this which...). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the two verses, he explains them with the word "eṣa" (this).

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains "blinded by *māyā*" as "deluded. It explains "bound by karma" as being caused by that very [delusion], using the phrase "for this reason. And it explains "this" as "time and so forth."

He explains [the term] "the knower" (*pramātā*) as "the void, etc. He provides the explanation of "the transmigrating one" (*saṃsārī*) as "one who transmigrates. Now, one might ask: how can there be transmigration for that which is insentient?
To this he says, "even the body," employing the word "as it were" (*iva*) because, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no transmigration.

Even in another birth—that is, even in a subsequent life in the form of a son and so forth—the intellect of the father indeed comes over to the son as the seed; otherwise, it would follow that such [intellectual capacity] would be impossible for a newborn infant and the like. As for its manifestation later on...
It should be understood that this is merely intended to provide a detailed exposition; enough with further revealing the secret.

He explains the entire compound word beginning with "vidyā" as "by means of knowledge" (vidyayā). Sovereignty (aiśvarya) is lordship consisting of the nature of being a knower and an agent; it is the reality to be accomplished through recognition (pratyabhijñā).

He explains by supplying the phrase "for this very reason. Even the universe—the entire collection of external objects of cognition—is of the nature of that [consciousness]; moreover, because he is free from the bond of rebirth, he is liberated even while remaining in the body.
[He] is fit for designation. But when [the soul] has fallen, Śiva is a single compact mass; thus, who is liberated from what?
However, by way of past status and in relation to other subjects, there is the conventional usage that "Śiva is liberated."
And he who is liberated, perceiving all entities as his own limbs, measures them;

thus he is their master (*svāmī*). Furthermore, because he bestows the ultimate reality of their true nature (*svarūpa-paramārtha*), he is their protector (*pālaka*); for this reason, he is taught in the scripture as the Lord (*pati*). [This applies even to] those differentiated by the power of *māyā*.
When one perceives objects as being truly distinct from oneself, then, bound by those very objects which take the form of fetters,

one is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*). For it is precisely due to the mass of objects to be known that this [soul] experiences afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to live (*abhiniveśa*).

Actions consist of merit, demerit, and so forth; by the word "and so forth," the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) consisting of intention are included, as well as the ripening (*vipāka*) consisting of the experience of results—thus, impurity is of infinite varieties, because of being bound by which one is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*). || 3 ||

In the case of the conjunction, it is consciousness alone—that is, the very nature of knowledge. He explains [the term] "mass of consciousness" (*cidghana*) by means of this very cause, saying "for this reason": consciousness itself is dense; it is that whose form is devoid of any mixture with anything else distinct from itself that is of the nature of non-consciousness (*acidrūpa*).

He explains "liberated" with the words "he again. He explains "it is said" with the words "the application of designation. Having spoken of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*), he implies the liberation after death (*videhamuktatā*) which follows immediately thereafter by the force of the context, with the words "but when [the body] has fallen"; that is, when the body has fallen.
The meaning is "being existent. Now, one might ask: if that is so, how can he be designated as "the liberated Śiva"?
To this he says: "having been" (*bhūta*). This means by way of that state which was previously attained (*bhūtapūrvā*).
He explains the second verse with the words: "And he who... From what [is he] conceiving?

In response to this inquiry, he provides the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) of the term "knower" (*pramātā*) as "one who cognizes" (*pramimīte*). He explains that "he"—the knower—is the "lord" (*pati*) of those entities, meaning their "master" (*svāmī*).
He offers a second interpretation of this word as "essential nature" (*svarūpa*); for it is indeed the essential nature itself.

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the innate (*sahaja*) entity; [the text says "because of its transmission" (*tasya samarpaṇāt*)]. Now, one might ask: has this meaning been stated merely by his own intellect? To this he says: "it was taught" (*upadiṣṭaḥ*). Having explained the first half-verse, he explains the second half-verse with the word "illusion" (*māyā*). "Bound" (*pāśitaḥ*) means fettered. Thus—

For this reason, he explains [the state of being] "defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth" with the words "for it is thus. He explains that this [subject], the cognizer, is a "bound soul" (*paśu*) because of having these as its cause, with the word "since. "Since"—that is, from the cause of which defilement—and "because of being bound," meaning because of being fettered. || 3 ||
That which is this very form of the bound soul (*paśu*) is, according to the scriptures, the threefold impurity (*mala*); thus he says:
"The loss of autonomy for consciousness, and the lack of consciousness even regarding autonomy—this twofold *āṇava* impurity arises from the forfeiture of one's own true nature. (4)

Right here, the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is that which is called Māyā, bestowing birth and experience; while Kārma [karma] resides in the agent who lacks awakening. All three of these arise solely through the power of Māyā.

In this context, the essential nature of *cittattva* (consciousness-principle) consists of the forms of the knower and the agent; its "seizure" is what is called the *āṇava* impurity (*mala*), by which this [consciousness] becomes a limited individual (*aṇu*). In that state, the closing up of one's own nature is contraction (*saṃkoca*). Within that [contraction], there exists the characteristic of agency (*kartṛtva*) within the form of pure awareness.

Whether it be the closing up or the inversion of another essential nature which is freedom (*svātantrya*), in both cases *āṇava-mala* is one and the same, consisting in the loss of one's own true nature.
"In this very [state]" means: when the two-fold contraction of one's essential nature has occurred due to the existence of *āṇava-mala*, for one who is divided...

Now he provides the commentary on the fourth and fifth verses, beginning with "yadeva" (that which...). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the two verses, he explains them, beginning with "svātantrya" (sovereignty).

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides the method for explaining the verse, beginning with "here" (*iha*): "here"—in this non-dual teaching of Śiva; "of that"—of sovereignty (*svātantrya*), which consists of being the knower and the agent; "by which"— [The text continues: ...by which [that sovereignty] is established. This is because it is impossible for the nature of agency to belong to something other than consciousness, such as the body, the senses, or the vital breath. For agency is not observed in a jar or similar objects, nor is it possible for it to exist in the body and so forth, since they are insentient (*jaḍa*). Nor can it reside in the mind (*manas*), because the mind is merely an instrument of cognition. Furthermore, the mind cannot be the agent of its own cognition, because it is itself an object of cognition. Therefore, agency must reside in consciousness alone. Thus, the meaning of the verse is that the nature of agency belongs to the Lord, who is consciousness. This is because the nature of agency is nothing other than the power of freedom, and that power is none other than consciousness. By "impurity" (mala), he means the limited subject (pramātṛ) consisting of the void and so forth; "therein" means within that impurity of the individual nature (āṇava-mala).

He provides his own synonym for "closing" (nimīlana), namely "contraction" (saṃkoca), which should be understood as having the form of a limitation by means of limited knowledge (vidyā) and limited agency (kalā). This is based on the aforementioned method.

He explains the verse with the word "tat" (that). "That"—because there is merely a contraction of the nature of the knower and agent, and not a destruction of its essential nature (*svarūpa*); for that reason, while the form of consciousness remains—that is to say, while the state of being a knower remains—the [contraction] characterized as agency—that is, having the form of agency—[occurs].
Of the one whose nature is autonomy— that is,

of that essential nature which is distinct from the state of being a knower— there is a "closing," which is contraction expressed by the word "loss" (*hāni*) in the Sūtra, or else its "reversal," which is expressed by the word "non-awareness" (*abodhatā*) in the Sūtra.
Or else, there is a perversion of awakening; thus, "in both ways" means by these two modes.

Intending to explain the second verse, he explains the two words *atraiva* (right here) contained within it with the phrase *satyāṇavamale* (when the impurity of finiteness exists). [He then explains] *bhinnavedyaprathā* (the manifestation of differentiated objects of knowledge).
He explains [the word] "of the divided" (*bhinnasya*).

That which is expansion is merely designated by the name "pertaining to Māyā" (*māyīya*). Because it is produced by Māyā, the state of "pertaining to Māyā" applies to all three impurities (*mala*) as well. Among these, for the agent who consists of non-awareness...

When there is the manifestation of objects of cognition distinct from the body and so forth, there exists the *kārma* impurity (*mala*) consisting of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), from which arise birth and experience; and since that [birth] has a fixed limit, it is said that karma has as its fruit [the three factors of] caste, lifespan, and experience. (4–5)
"It is mere designation" (*saṃjñāmātra*)—the sense is that it is like [the term] "oil-drinker" (*tailapāyika*) and so forth.
Otherwise, the statement that those three are produced by the power of *māyā* alone would be improper; this is the intended meaning.
Why is it "mere designation"? To this he says: "It is *māyā*," [meaning] "that which bestows birth and experience. (C.)

The sense is "like [the case of] the oil-drinker and so forth. To the question "Why is it merely a designation? he says, "It is *māyā*"; the sense is that otherwise, the statement "those three are by means of the power of *māyā*" would be improper.
He explains the remaining portion, beginning with "bestowing birth and experience," with the word "therein" (*tatra*), and that—
And enjoyment (*bhoga*) has a fixed duration; it remains for as long as the persistence of the *kārmamala* (the impurity of karma).

For this reason, it is said that the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is that which results in the fruit of birth, lifespan, and enjoyment—that is, the fruit consisting of birth, lifespan, and enjoyment. What is meant by this? It means that the fruit consists of birth, lifespan, and enjoyment born of karma.

Thus, the summarized meaning here is as follows: this *āṇavamala* (the atomic impurity) is the impurity that causes the infinite subject to fall into a state of non-manifestation; thus, by way of the loss of its own true nature, it becomes twofold. Why is this so? Because of consciousness, which is pure spirit (*cinmātra*).

The loss of autonomy is one mode, which is the contraction of the state of being a knower; likewise, the lack of awareness regarding autonomy—that is, the conceit of being distinct from pure consciousness—is the second mode. When this twofold impurity of *āṇava-mala* is present, [the following occurs].
The manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is the impurity called *māyā*, which is the *māyīya* (illusory) impurity.
Now, in order to clarify the nature of these impurities by defining their distinct domains, he first states the domain of the [impurity] known as "the loss of the autonomy of consciousness."
Even though they consist of pure consciousness, those who do not possess supreme agency have been created by the Lord as distinct from Himself due to the absence of that agency.
Those for whom pure consciousness alone is the ultimate reality— and not that [consciousness] which, through resting in its own self, takes the form of bliss and supreme sovereignty as "I"—
they have been created by the Supreme Lord in such a way that they are distinct from His own self. In this regard:
The reason is: because of the passing away—that is, the absence—of agency characterized by supreme sovereignty;
whereas the Supreme Lord possesses the nature of consciousness inseparable from supreme sovereignty—this is the intended remainder of the meaning. || 6 ||

It becomes impurity (*mala*). When the agent is characterized by non-awakening—that is, when it possesses a nature distinct from what is to be known—there exists the *kārmamala*. Of what nature is it? It bestows birth and experience; these three [impurities] arise solely through the power of *māyā*. || 5 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "atha eṣām" (now, of these).
This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the word "śuddha" (pure).

Here the commentary explains the phrase "even though its nature is pure awakening" with the words "of those who. This is an explanation of the word *śuddha* (pure) by means of the suffix *mātra*. The ultimate meaning is as follows:

The place of rest is that which is considered to be the Supreme Self. He explains [the phrase] "not the highest agency" with the words "but not. Sovereignty is independence, whose nature is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
He explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "those" (*te*); "those" refers to those belonging to the Sāṃkhya school and others; "by the Master" (*bhartrā*)...
"He explains by means of the Supreme Lord. Likewise, "in that manner" (*tathā*)—this is supplied [to the text] because of its logical necessity (*yuktatvena*).

The construction is: "separate" (*vyatiriktāḥ*) means "created" (*nirmitāḥ*). He provides the construction of "due to the cessation of agency" (*kartṛtātyayāt*) as a reason here, stating "the reason is this. What [is the purpose] for one whose cognition is pure?

In response to the objection that there is no such thing as "supreme lordship," he reveals his intention with the words "of the Supreme Lord. The meaning is that supreme lordship belongs only to consciousness (*bodha*) endowed with the power of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*), namely the "I" (*aham*), and not to the pure consciousness (*śuddhabodha*) postulated by the Sāṃkhya and other schools. || 6 ||
Now, let it be granted that they are distinct from the Supreme Lord on account of this reason;

but how can there be mutual difference among them, given that their identity in space and time— consisting in their nature as consciousness and being established by their omnipresence and eternity— is identical?
He dispels the doubt: "If there is no mutual difference among them, how can they be created [as distinct entities], and why is the plural number used?"—[by stating]:
"Even though they are identical in their characteristic of being consciousness and so forth, they possess mutual differentiation."
Likewise, through the differentiation of the Lord’s will, they are the Vijñānakevalas.

For here, indeed, it has been stated more than once that it is the Supreme Lord alone— whose power is everywhere unimpeded— who, desiring to become thus, becomes thus, and not anyone else exists in the ultimate sense; and therefore:

Although my nature is that of pervasive and eternal consciousness, by means of such a particular will of the Lord (īśvarecchā) as "I appear through differentiation," [there arises] for those who have transcended the states of the subject— from the body up to the void— their state of being consciousness and their eternity—
Even though there is unity within the collection of attributes such as sovereign power (*vibhutva*) and so forth, there is mutual differentiation among them;

and these are described in the scripture as *vijñānakevalas*. Among them, the *vijñānakevala* is conjoined with only impurity (*mala*), and so on—in this context, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to a nature consisting of pure awareness, while "isolated" (*kevala*) means being devoid of sovereignty (*svātantrya*). (7)
Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the words "nanv asmāt" (surely, from this). Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"from this cause"—that is, from the cause of the cessation of agency. Having thus provided the introduction:
Having presented the verse, he explains it with the words "bodhādi.
Here, the commentary states:
"In order to explain the verse, he follows the reasoning previously stated, beginning with 'iha hi'."

Desiring to become thus, wishing to exist thus, one becomes thus—i.e., one becomes the very nature of the object in that very way. Relying on this, he explains the verse with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*). In response to the expectation of where these [verses] were spoken, he says "Therein" (*tatra*). "In such passages as"—meaning in passages beginning with these.
In the collection of statements, he explains the term "those who are liberated through pure consciousness" (*vijñānakevalāḥ*) as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). || 7 ||

Thus, having established that the portion [of the verse] stating "there is a loss of autonomy for consciousness" pertains to the *vijñānākala*, he clarifies the other aspect— namely, "even autonomy is non-consciousness"— by demonstrating its object.
The Pralayākalas, whose nature is ignorance of Śūnya and the other [levels], are the agents;
they possess the karmic impurity (kārma-mala), while their māyīya impurity is considered to be conceptualized.
In the void, because it is insentient and lacks the nature of consciousness— or rather, in the vital breath or the intellect—
those for whom there is agency through the connection with the wonder of "I" are rendered "without parts" (akalāḥ) by dissolution;
that is, they are devoid of the instruments and effects characterized by the principle of *kalā*, yet they remain agents who lack the nature of consciousness.

For they were indeed established in that manner until the time of dissolution; however, in the subsequent period, they become connected precisely with effects and instruments; because for them, there exists not only the *āṇava* impurity of the liberated one, but also the *kārmika* impurity in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and residual traces (*saṃskāra*).
The self whose nature consists of both dharma and adharma certainly exists. If this were so, there would be for these [souls] the manifestation of distinct objects of cognition.
True; however, this occurs in the state of deep sleep when there is an object of cognition (*savedya*), but it does not occur when there is no object of cognition (*apavedya*).
Therefore, the *māyīya* impurity of these [souls] is established as having a determined objective domain through conceptual construction (*vikalpita*). Likewise...

For some rest in portions such as the void (*śūnya*) and are rendered inert by deep sleep, abiding in the state of dreamless sleep (*suṣupta*) where there is no object of knowledge; others, however, are established in the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth,
being joined with the perception of distinct objects of knowledge consisting of the commonality of the remnants of pleasure and pain.
"Those who are dissolved in the state of dreamless sleep with residual impressions...
Now, he provides the introduction to the eighth verse with the word "evam" (thus). This is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse beginning with "śūnye" (in the void).
Here the commentary says:

it explains the matter included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) according to another perspective, namely, "or in the vital breath" (*prāṇe*). This is because of the connection with the wonder of "I"—that is, because of the connection with the savoring of "I."

"Beginning with emptiness" means preceded by the conceit of self. "By dissolution"—that is, by dissolution in the form of a swoon; "until the time of dissolution"—meaning for as long as the period of dissolution lasts;
"thus made"—meaning they were rendered devoid of parts (*akalāḥ*); "at a later time"—that is, after the dissolution—how?
Because they come into being, he says "since" (*yataḥ*). Here the disciple asks: "If it is so...
regarding these *pralayākalas*. He gives the answer: "True.

In the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptapada*), which is accompanied by an object of knowledge called pleasure (*savedya*), there is for them the manifestation of a distinct object of knowledge (*bhinnavedyaprathā*).

The construction is: "Truth exists. Regarding the phrase "by way of having a determined object"—that is, by way of having as its object various forms of things existing in the state of being seeds—he provides the justification here with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*).
However, the nature of being separated from the body and organs consisting of the gross physical form—which constitutes the definition of the *paralayākala* state—is common to all. (8)
Thus, this aspect—that even autonomy (*svātantrya*) is subject to non-awareness—has been clarified;
and incidentally, the domain of the *kārmamala* has been shown, as well as the occasional nature of the *māyāmala*. Now, however, even in the absence of both the *āṇavamala* and the *kārmamala*,...

It is shown that the pure [self] is the object of the impurity called *māyā*: "Even for those cognitions that possess agency, when the *kārmamala* has perished, but while they still experience distinct objects of knowledge, there is the *māyāmala*; and these are the Vidyeśvaras. (1.9)

Those who perceive pure consciousness alone as the Self, and who, through the emergence of wonder, experience it as "I," are therefore both omniscient and omnipotent; they are the Vidyeśvaras. However, that which appears to them as an object of knowledge (*vedya*) and as an effect—namely, their bodies, instruments, worlds, and so forth—[is distinct].
Being indeed differentiated by the perception of the weaver and the cloth—thus there exists for the Vidyeśvaras the conjunction with the impurity called Māyā. || 9 ||
Now, in order to demonstrate the object common to all three impurities simultaneously, he says:
"For all transmigrating beings, including the gods and others, there are three kinds of impurity.
Even among those, the *kārmamala* alone is the primary cause of saṃsāra. (10)

"For all"— meaning for those situated in the state of deep sleep with experience (*savedya-suṣupta*) and for those situated in the state of deep sleep without experience (*apavedya-suṣupta*)— it is "equal"; the sense is that for all of them, because they are thoroughly asleep, there is an absence of identification with the gross body and so forth.

Thus, the summarized meaning here is as follows: in the state of *vyatireka* (separation), the agents who consist of non-cognition of Śūnya and so forth are the *pralayākalas*. For them—the *pralayākalas*—there exists not only [the cognitive impurity], but also the *kārmamala*, namely the impurity called *kārmika* which consists of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). It is not merely [the other two].

The *āṇava* [impurity] consists of the absence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. Even the *māyīya* impurity of those [beings] is considered imagined, because it exists in the form of latent impressions. || 8 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the ninth verse with the words "evam" (thus).
Here, the commentary states:
"pākṣikatvam" means the state of belonging to the position of dreamless deep sleep accompanied by residual awareness (*savedya*).
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "of the cognitions" (*bodhānām*).
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"The Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvarāḥ*)" refers to those established in Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), known as Mantras.
The cognizers. || 9 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the tenth verse with the word "atha" (now). This is clear. Thus, having provided the introduction, [he states]:
"In this regard, first, the Vidyeśvaras and Vijñānākalas are not *bhavins* (beings subject to rebirth)."

Because they have transcended the path ending with Māyā; even the Pralayākalas remain for some time without worldly existence. However, those fourteen [classes of beings], from the gods down to immobile objects, who revolve within the interval of the Māyā-tattva—

[Enumerated as fourteen-fold—K, Ṣ, Ṣ. All those who are subject to existence (*bhavin*) are transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*) as reckoned in the scriptures; and for them, all three impurities (*mala*) exist simultaneously. Now, among these three impurities, which one brings about their transmigration? He says: even there, among those...
Even when all three exist, the stain of karma is primarily the cause for wandering in saṃsāra. Having introduced a verse, he explains it as follows: "Of the gods and so forth."
Regarding this, the commentary says: "Fourteen. As it has been stated:
"The divine [realm] consists of eight varieties, and the animal womb is fivefold."
And the human realm is of one kind; in brief, the creation of beings is thus twofold.
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva,
Śākra, Saumya, Prājāpatya, and Brāhma—
thus it is remembered as being eightfold.
Thus: the divine class is of eight types. The animal womb is fivefold, divided into beasts, wild animals, birds, reptiles, and immobile beings.
Then there are the *vijñānākalas*, the *vijñānakevalas*, and the *bhavins*—that is, those subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*). Furthermore, who are they?

Because there are those who possess existence (*bhavin*), he says "but those who... He poses a question with "surely" (*nanu*), and provides the answer with "he says" (*āha*). "Having come together" (*sannipatya*) means having joined with others;
here he cites a scriptural statement (*āgama-vākya*) as it has been said.
From karma, however, arise bodies, objects, and organs; thus, the very connection between body, organs, and objects— whether present or future—
occurring continuously in an uninterrupted series, is called *saṃsāra* (transmigration).

Although the impurities of *āṇava* and *māyā* are not the direct causes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), nevertheless, in the absence of *kārma* [impurity], those two are devoid of the power to produce the various states such as the body and so forth within the *vijñānākala* and other levels; thus, *kārma* alone is the primary impurity.

The cause of saṃsāra is enumerated in various scriptures; therefore, once its exhaustion has occurred, the placement of steps upon the ladder of non-transmigration has been provided. With this intention, the abandonment of the conceit regarding the bondage of karma is indeed the primary effort to be made.

This is taught in the Sāṃkhya, Purāṇas, Mahābhārata, and other scriptures. Thus, through the three individual divisions, the three dual divisions, and the single triple division of the three impurities (mala), seven types of subjects (pramātṛ) arise. And so it is stated in the scripture:
There are seven [deities], beginning with Śiva and ending with Sakala, who possess power (*śaktimant*).
Now, as to why this state called *saṃsaraṇa* (transmigration) is termed *bhava* (existence), he says "nanu" (now/then).
It is not called "past" (*bhūta*) with reference to the production of new beings. Well then, [why is it so called]?

Since the *āṇava* and *māyīya* [impurities] are thus rendered useless there, he says "the *āṇava*. By this, he states the resulting reality: "for this very reason. Upon their exhaustion—that is, when the *kārmamala* has been destroyed—and having occurred—having been accomplished—the "bonding of the word" (*padabandha*) is the "touching of the word" (*padasparśa*). He provides the conclusion with "thus" (*evam*). Thus:
In the manner described—namely, by means of the seven impurities (malas)—the seven subjects, beginning with Śiva and ending with Sakala, arise—that is, they come into being. How so?
By means of the three impurities through their three respective individual divisions, and by each one alone.
The meaning is: "by the three impurities. Likewise, "by the three dyads"—namely, by the Āṇava and Māyīya;
by the Āṇava and Kārma; and by the Māyīya and Kārma;
that is to say, by these three pairs. Likewise, "by the one triad," which has become unified.

The meaning is: by means of a single triad in the form of the three impurities (*mala*). Among these, the *śivatattva* arises through the *āṇavamala* alone, because it manifests as being devoid of that [impurity] from the outset, when counted as distinct from *śakti*, and because that very [impurity] constitutes the loss of its sovereignty.

Although the emergence of the *śakti-tattva* occurs through a second division of the *āṇava-mala*, consisting in the non-awakening of one's own freedom (*svātantryābodhatā*), nevertheless it is not counted here, because it is not the subject under discussion;
for the current topic is precisely the determination of those who possess power (*śaktimant*). It is counted as distinct from Śiva.
Power (śakti) indeed takes on the state of being like non-awareness; that very [power] is the non-awareness of sovereignty.

Through the individual impurity (āṇavamala) alone, there is the emergence of Śiva; through the impurity of Māyā (māyīyamala) alone, the emergence of the Mantra-Maheśvaras; and through the impurity of Karma (kārmamala) alone, the emergence of the Mantras.

The sequence is as follows: from the *āṇava* and *māyīya* [impurities] arises the emergence of those called *mantras* and *vidyeśas*; from the *āṇava* and *kārmika* [impurities] arises the emergence of the *vijñānākala*s; from the *māyīya* and *kārmika* [impurities] arises the emergence of the *pralayākala*s; and from the triad beginning with the *āṇava* arises the emergence of the *sakala*s.

Regarding this, he cites the traditional scripture (*āgama-śāstra*), stating "and thus it has been said. Even there, there is an infinite variety of types due to internal subdivisions, the distinction between the subordinate and the primary, and the distinctions between option (*vikalpa*), combination (*samuccaya*), and so forth. || 10 ||
And he demonstrates that there are two types of transmigrating beings due to the emergence and disappearance of these three impurities:
"This very principle of consciousness (cittattva), consisting of agency, is empowered by *kalā*."
The measured [object], such as emptiness and so forth, which has the nature of an acid, exists as a quality. || 11 ||
The primacy of agency and consciousness belongs to the conscious self (cidātman).
Knowledge regarding the void and other qualities is characterized by absorption into that [consciousness]. 12.
And this [is what is meant]: that which is the consciousness of the thirty [gods] and other living beings consists of agency;

because the aspect of pure awareness (*saṃvit*) has been submerged due to the predominance of the factor of agency by means of impurity (*mala*), it is the reality of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), namely freedom (*svātantrya*), [which is manifested] through that which is called *kalā*, whose essence is a power of the Supreme Lord.
[It is] strengthened and vitalized by reality (*tattva*), and suppressed and awakened by impurity (*mala*).
[This applies] to everything from the void (*śūnya*) up to the body.
With the word "therein" (*tatra*), he states that even within this group of seven there is multiplicity due to internal subdivisions. The word "iti" [marks the end of the section].

At the conclusion of the commentary on the verse: by this, the pervasion of the *māyātattva* up to the end of the *śivatattva* is shown; otherwise, how could there be any conception of Śiva and the others within a single *tattva*? Furthermore, [this explains] Śiva’s emergence from the *āṇavamala*.

This is to be understood by virtue of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the *kañcuka* of the *āṇavamala*, which reflects upon that [state]. Otherwise, if a single reality were complete in itself, what room would there be for the conceptualization of Śiva and the rest? The same should be understood regarding Sadāśiva and the others. || 10 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the eleventh and twelfth verses with the words "asya ca" (and of this). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "kalodvalitam" (intensified by *kalā*).

Here the commentary explains "and this" with the words "since": for the *bhavins*— that is, those in transmigratory existence— the *cit-tattva* (the principle of consciousness), which consists of agency— that is, whose nature is gross agency— is [obscured] by *mala*, namely, the *kārmamala*.

He explains [the term] *cidrūpasya* (of the nature of consciousness); he explains [the term] *cittattvam* (the principle of consciousness) by means of that which is called *kalā*. Here he states another synonym, namely *malena* (by means of impurity).
He explains [the phrase] *śūnyāderguṇatayā sthitam* (existing as a quality of the void, etc. by means of [the word] *śūnyādeḥ* (of the void, etc.).
He states the meaning of the genitive case:

it belongs to the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*), and it exists as a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*) because it is non-primary, since it is submerged within the portion of the objects of knowledge (*prameya-bhāga*), ranging from the body and so forth— which have attained the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*)— up to the void (*śūnya*).

The object of cognition— namely, "I am he who is fair-complexioned, he who is happy, he who is thirsty, he who is devoid of all forms"— thus flashes forth for transmigrating beings as this very "this-ness" (idantā) which has internalized the sense of "I" (ahambhāva). This [cognition] consists of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
The state of saṃsāra is as follows:

when, by means of that very sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) which is autonomous in nature, one reflects upon attributes such as pervasiveness and eternity within oneself, according to the aforementioned direction of the Guru’s instruction and so forth.
Then, by bringing forth [the universe] from the void and other objects of cognition as if emerging from them,

the state beyond the fourth (turyātītāvasthā) is established; this occurs when the sense of "I" is permeated by the eternal sovereignty consisting of the contemplation of such manifested glory and power.

By means of the *ahaṃbhāva* (the sense of "I") which is indeed inseparable from the qualities such as sovereignty over the eternal manifestation of reality as it truly is (*tathābhūtavibhava*), [one attains] everything from the void (*śūnya*) to the constituent elements of the body (*dehadhātu*) through the application of the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*).

Regarding the term "related" (*sambandhī*): he explains that [the self] is measured by having this as its cause, in the passage beginning with "since" (*yataḥ*) and ending with "the object of knowledge" (*prameyam*). Now, one might ask: how is it logical for the very nature of the knower (*pramātṛ*) to be an object of knowledge?
To this, he says: "He who is fair-skinned" (*yo gauraḥ*). By the word "fair-skinned," [he refers to] the knower of the body.

Apprehension (*parāmarśa*): "He who is happy" is the apprehension of the cognizing subject (*buddhi-pramātṛ*); "he who is thirsty" is the apprehension of the vitalizing subject (*prāṇa-pramātṛ*); "devoid of all forms" is the apprehension of the void-subject (*śūnya-pramātṛ*). For transmigrating beings, it is precisely this "this-ness" (*idantā*) that has internalized the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "it throbs": in the ultimate sense, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "I" (*aham*), and by following the relative pronoun (*yat*) implied by the demonstrative pronoun (*tat*), only that which has the nature of "this-ness" (*idantā*) is grasped. Furthermore, since the emphasis here has already been placed upon the determination of memory (*smṛti-nirṇaya*), [no further elaboration is needed].

Again, it is exerted: this very state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsārāvasthā*), the condition of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāradaśā*), wherein the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) is internalized and there is only "this-ness" (*idantā*).

Among these, the waking state (*jāgradavasthā*) occurs when the body is the primary subject of cognition (*prameya-pradhāna*), and [the dreaming state occurs] when the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is primary.

The sequence should be understood as follows: the state of the dreaming condition occurs during the stage of the intellect as the cognizer (*dhī-pramātṛ*); the state of deep sleep occurs during the stage of the cognizer consisting of vital breath and emptiness (*prāṇa-śūnya-pramātṛ*), which is dominated by the subject (*pramātṛ-pradhāna*).
He provides the introduction for explaining the second verse with the words "But when" (*yadā tu*).

In the Self—the true conscious Self—having emerged, as it were, from the object of knowledge (prameya), which is the state of being a knower (pramātṛtva) only superficially but in reality consists of the nature of the object; at that time, there is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). This is "as if" with respect to the unfitness for emergence from the perspective of ultimate reality.
The mention of the word [is for the sake of] grasping that which is such:
namely, that sovereignty consisting of majesty and so forth—which is eternal—[that is,] that sovereignty whose nature consists of pervasiveness and so on; of that [sovereignty].

By means of that which possesses such a penetration— just as [mercury] pierces copper and other metals through the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*)— even that [object] seems to abandon its status as an object of cognition in this fourth state.
This twofold state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*) is called "immersion" (*samāveśa*) in the scripture.
For in each case, right immersion (*samyag-āveśana*) alone is the primary factor; other instructions are for the sake of achieving that. As it is sung in the *Gītā*:
"Those who, having fixed their minds on Me... (Gītā 12.2).
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, there are such passages as: "In order to cause the mind to enter" (Gītā 12.9), and so forth. And these are indeed the sprouts of complete immersion (samāveśa).

The manifold varieties of ritual action— such as the praise, prostration, worship, meditation, and absorption (samādhi) offered to the Supreme Lord— are animated by the cultivation of the state of total surrender (*prahvībhāva*) toward the well-known portion of the subject consisting of the body and so forth. As it has also been sung:
"Even if you are unable to practice [meditation], be intent on My work" (Gītā 12.10).
But at the fall of the body, the Supreme Lord alone remains the singular essence; thus, who could enter into what, and how? This is what he says: "Furthermore, as for the primacy of agency..."
And the subordinate status of emptiness and so forth is inseparable from that;

by means of that "union"—namely, the application of the perfected elixir such as mercury which brings about the state of gold—it is "pierced," that is, pervaded. For when the grasp of "I-ness" (ahantā) is present everywhere, the body and so forth are likewise grasped in that very same way.
Even that—emptiness and so forth—is as if abandoned, because even there one grasps it as being of the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*);

otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be the object of the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*). Both states—the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*) colored by the touch of identification with the body, and that which is devoid of the touch of such identification—are likewise [to be abandoned].

"The state beyond the fourth" (*turyātītāvasthā*) and "immersion" (*samāveśa*). By the word *samāveśa*, which denotes union with the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), [this is taught] in the *śāstra*—that is, in the spiritual scripture (*adhyātmaśāstra*). Now, since much has been said in the scriptures, he says "correctly" (*samyak*). "There and there"—in those various respective scriptures.
In this regard, he cites the words of the Śrī Gītā scripture as spoken by the Blessed Lord himself, saying:
"As it is sung in the Gītā. To the question, "What is sung? he replies: "Having fixed [the mind] on Me," etc.
"Having fixed" means having joined [the mind]. Now, one might ask: even though there are well-known [topics] such as praise and so forth, why is this said?

Since immersion (*samāveśa*) has been described in this way, he says "immersion" (*samāveśa*). It is that state of contemplation consisting of the submissiveness of those portions of the subject which take the form of the body and so forth—their becoming subordinate and their bending toward the supreme subject. By means of that...

"Anuprāṇitāḥ" means enlivened or illuminated; here too, he cites a verse from the Śrī Gītā regarding "practice" (abhyāse). Now, one might ask: let liberation while living (jīvanmukti) be of two kinds, but what is the nature of disembodied liberation (videhamukti)?
To this he says: "deha... [meaning] at the fall of the body, that is, in the state of disembodied liberation; this very point—
The subject matter has just been stated. Furthermore, when that which is insentient in nature becomes subordinate, there is also a lack of awareness regarding autonomy;
thus, by setting aside the operation of impurity (*mala*), that further aspect of the self belonging to consciousness—
Furthermore, that which is characterized by awakening, though it had been suppressed by impurity,
now possesses primacy due to its emergence; and this very primacy of agency, which is its state of emergence, is precisely what is meant.

Knowledge is so called because it is the antidote to the impurity consisting of ignorance; this very primacy is the defining characteristic of immersion (samāveśa), by virtue of which the Lord, even while remaining in the body, is declared in the scriptures to be "liberated. || 12 ||
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "yat punaḥ" (as for that which...).

"Tannāntarīyakaḥ" means inseparable from the predominance of agency; "guṇabhāvaḥ" means the state of being subordinate; "tasmin" refers to the void and so forth; and "apahastanāt" means because of its suppression or disappearance by the consciousness (*cit*).
—Even though it is "other" (*para*) than pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it is its own part (*ātmabhāga*);
yet that [otherness] is "subordinated" (*nyakkṛta*), meaning set aside, because of the agency belonging to that [consciousness]—namely, the agency of consciousness (*citkartṛtā*).
This very thing is the "primacy" (*mukhyatva*); it is the primacy of the conscious part (*cidbhāga*) that has been stated as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The essential nature (*svarūpa*)—by virtue of which primary state even a person situated in the body, though living—is [liberated].
Such is the summarized meaning of these two verses here.
This *cittattva* (the principle of consciousness)—which has assumed the state of the body and so forth and constitutes the form of all subjects—is the consciousness (*cit*).

The essential nature [of the Self] exists as a quality—that is, it exists as an attribute—of that which is insentient (acidrūpa), inert (jaḍa), such as the body and so forth, and of the fourfold group of subjects beginning with the Void (śūnya). Of what kind is it?
It is "strengthened"—that is, animated—by the *kalā*-principle, which consists in the state of being a limited agent (*akiñcitkartṛtva*).
Therefore, it consists of agency—that is, its very nature is agency. To the question "Why does it exist as a quality? he provides the qualifying term "measured" (*mitam*) as the reason:
for logicians indeed describe knowledge as being merely a quality with respect to the knower. But—

In the case of exclusion (*vyatireka*), the primacy of agency (*kartṛtā*) that occurs in the void (*śūnya*) and so forth exists when there is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*). If it is argued that, because this is a subordinate quality, the state (*daśā*) consisting of immersion (*samāveśa*)— namely the forms of the Fourth (*turya*) and Beyond-the-Fourth (*tadatīta*)— belongs to the Lord (*pati*), then how can the distinction between the states of deep sleep, dreaming, and waking be said to belong to the bound soul (*paśu*) in the scriptures?
Anticipating this objection, he first describes the very nature of deep sleep (suṣupta) in three verses:

"In the void—which is the self of the absence of intellect and the rest, the locus of the 'I'-sense and agency, and which contains only indistinct impressions of form—there is the emptiness of the knowable. (13)
The internal function of the senses, which impels the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, is considered to be that called "life" (*jīvana*);
or else, it is the sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) within the vital breath, consisting of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*).
When one remains in that alone, it is described as the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), comparable to cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*).
It is both knowable and unknowable, and it is associated with or free from the impurity of Māyā.

In this world, the reality of consciousness (cittattva), concealing its own essential nature, manifests as the object of knowledge— whether as the intellect and so forth up to the body, or as jars and the like;
yet this is a single manifestation of its own sovereignty, and not otherwise.

When [this] is known—that is to say, when the primacy of the conscious self (cidātman), which is of the nature of consciousness (bodha), occurs, that is the characteristic of immersion (samāveśa); it is the knowledge whose essential nature is the immersion beyond the fourth (turyātīta) of the fourth state (turya). As it has been said:

"Abandoning all phenomena (*dharmas*), take refuge in me alone. Here, by the word "phenomena," the entire range of subjects and objects—such as emptiness and so forth—is understood; by "me," the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) is meant; and "taking refuge" here refers to *samāveśa* (total immersion).
Thus; enough with this prolixity. || 12 ||

Now, he provides the introduction to the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth verses with the words "nanvevam" (But if this is so). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "śūnye" (In the void).

Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides the procedure for explaining the first verse, beginning with the word "here" (*iha*). "Here"—that is, in this world—it "appears," meaning it manifests. As it has been said:

Victorious is that unborn Supreme Lord, who, though a solid mass of consciousness, has congealed into the form of the world; he is the master skilled in the playful sport of concealing his own nature.

Whether it be actual sequence or difference, even there, sequence and difference appear through [the Lord's] sovereignty. This being the case, when that portion of the essence of consciousness which consists in the veiling of its own nature is not mixed with any subsequent other portion, then...
It comes to rest either because that [object] does not arise, or because it has perished— as in cosmic dissolution—
or because it is disregarded— as in sleep, meditative absorption, or fainting; and in that very state lies the locus of agency, which is the nature of the "I."

When reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)— due to its lack of clarity— is joined with a pure latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that is formless and has not yet reached the state of being an object of cognition, then that very state is one in which even a trace of the reflective awareness "not" (*na iti*) is no longer required; it is the remainder of the reflective awareness "not."

This world-form, [which exists] through a cognition that does not depend on any object to be negated—[this occurs] here, in this very sovereignty. Now, one might ask: "If that is so, how is it that succession or differentiation is perceived among the entities created by that [sovereignty]? To this, he says: "But even there..."

Thus [it is said]. There too, "even so" (evam sati) means "even this being the case. The sense is that for the one independent [Lord], whether it be the manifestation of succession or the manifestation of difference, it is indeed His very sovereignty.
He explains the verse by relying on the aforementioned method, saying: "tadevam" (thus, in this way).

The portion that conceals its own nature— the aspect of self-concealment— is unmixed with other subsequent portions consisting of past and future objects. This is because of their non-arising— that is, because of the non-arising of those subsequent portions.

The phrase "as in the case of dissolution" (pralaye iva) is presented as an illustration here with the intention of showing the descent (*avaroha*), while "due to destruction" (*pradhvaṃsāt*) is intended to show the ascent (*āroha*). Because of disregard for that [descent], and by way of overlooking the subsequent portion, he provides an illustration for that [ascent] with the word "sleep" (*nidrā*). And in that very same context:

At that very time of resting in that void, he explains the word *pada* as "reflection" (*parāmarśa*). He explains the entire phrase beginning with "indistinct" (*asphuṭa*) by [the word] "because of its indistinctness" (*asphuṭatvāt*). He provides the explanation of the suffix *-mātra* by [the word] "pure" (*śuddha*).
He provides an explanation of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) with the word "yuktaḥ" (joined). He explains "in the void" (*śūnye*) with the word "tadā" (then).

"Then" means at that time; the remainder of the sense is that "that very state is called 'the void' by the wise. Of what nature is it? It is "na" alone—that which consists of nothing more than the form of the word "not" (*na*).
A trace of reflective awareness (*parāmarśaleśa*): by that, it is not required—that is, it has not been made an object of requirement as an objective domain;
it is the object of cognitions such as negation—meaning it is the object of cognitions to be negated at a later time;
it is a very clear reflective awareness, with which there is a commingling or connection (*saṃbheda*) for her.

For when there is a reflection upon a negation, a reflection upon the object of that negation is necessarily present; otherwise, what would be its object? However, in this state, such a reflection is not tenable, because it would entail the loss of the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*). Furthermore, even a reflection upon the object of negation is not appropriate here.

The meaning is that this is because, at a later time, there arises the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) that "I was not aware of anything at all. Even though this awareness is clearly intermingled with the objects of the negation— such as cognition and so forth— it is nonetheless [an awareness of non-existence] due to its necessary connection with the object of negation, just like the thought "I am nothing."
Thus, like such a reflective awareness,

that which has its negatable aspect consisting of the accepted general form is therefore called "void" (śūnya), because the objects of knowledge have been reduced to mere residual impressions (saṃskāra).

In such a state, which consists of the absence of everything from cognition up to the body and blue objects, emptiness (*śūnyatva*) is said to exist; for therein the emptiness of knowable objects is their state of non-existence, remaining only as residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). This indeed is what is meant everywhere by "non-existence," and not the total annihilation of existing things in every respect.
Destruction;

even such [a state] necessarily involves a connection with that which is to be negated—due to its connection with that which must necessarily be negated at a subsequent time—just as in the case of the thought "I am nothing. Thus...

Just as there is a negation based on the commonality of form (*rūpasāmānyato niṣedha*), so too is there a general aspect (*sāmānyākāra*) that has been accepted; that [cognition] by which this [aspect], devoid of specific qualities such as intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, is the object of negation—even in the absence of a direct reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of it—is, in effect, endowed with it. Precisely for this reason—on account of this very cause—...
The meaning is that it is the cognition by which the object of knowledge—consisting of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—is reduced to a mere residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāraśeṣīkṛta*);

otherwise, its manifestation later would be impossible. He provides the construction with the locative case in the phrase "in such a state" (*tathāvidhe*), [meaning] in that whose nature is the absence of intellect and so forth [or, according to another reading, in that whose nature is the presence of intellect and so forth].

Thus he explains [the phrase] "of cognition and so forth. In response to the inquiry, "From what is emptiness said to arise?", he explains [it] as "the emptiness of the knowable" by saying "since. There—in that emptiness—he also reveals its nature as non-existence by saying "a residual impression (*saṃskāra*). But [one might object]: "Is this not elsewhere..."
To the question, "What is non-existence like?", he says: "This very [state]" (iyameva).
This very state is the condition of having only residual impressions (*saṃskāraśeṣatā*). "In every respect" (*sarvātmanā*) means without remainder. As it has been said:
"Non-existence does not exist for that which is real."

Thus, the construction of this verse is as follows: because of the absence of the intellect and other faculties within the Self, there is likewise the state of "I-ness" and agency; subsequently, one reflects, "I was not aware of anything."

Because the recollection of the form of memory would otherwise be inexplicable, [it occurs] in that which is joined with the recollection of agency in the form of "I-ness," in which there exists such an indistinct,
formless latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone, and in the void, which is of the nature of deep sleep.

In the state of emptiness (*śūnyapada*), there is the emptiness of the knowable (*jñeyaśūnyatā*)— that is, the absence of the knowable, meaning that the knowable exists merely as a mental construction (*saṃskāra*). It resides inherent (*samaveta*) in that very empty subject (*pramātṛ*).

In the wheel of vital airs (*vāyu-cakra*), which consists of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*, there is a power characterized by impulsion; and that is the internal function of the two groups—the organs of cognition and the organs of action—which are, respectively, the phenomenal manifestations (*prapañca-bhūta*) of *vidyā* and *kalā*. For their external [function] belongs to those two.
The function [of the internal organ] consists of the discernment of sound and so forth, the manifestation of sound, and the striking of the locations [of articulation], and so on.
As it has been said:
"The function of the general instrument [the internal organ] consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 29).

Thus, the "I-ness" (ahantā), which is itself void and supported by the wheel of the senses, is life; therefore, it is that very void which, as the living being (jīva), transmigrates. Or rather, it is the internal, common vitalizing force of the sensory powers themselves, denoted by the word "prāṇa."
That very [consciousness], consisting of the impelling force of the specific vital winds such as *prāṇa* and so forth, resting upon [the body] with the thought "I am this," is life;

at that time, the *prāṇa* itself is the living soul (*jīva*), the transmigrating being, and that alone is the void (*śūnya*). Furthermore, the *prāṇa* is denoted by the term "the city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), which consists of the pentad of *prāṇa* and so forth, along with the group of the organs of perception.
Now he explains the second verse, beginning with the words "tatraiva" (right there). He explains [the word] "samavetāḥ" (united) as follows.
He explains [the pronoun] "sā" (she) as "śūnye" (in the void). He explains [the phrase] "prāṇādiprerikā" (the impeller of breath and so forth) as "prāṇa" (breath).
He explains [the phrase] "akṣāṇāṃ mātṛvṛttiḥ" (the mother-like function of the senses) as "sā ca" (and she). And "sā" refers to Śakti.
"Consisting of conceptual proliferation" means consisting of affliction; "internal function" means internal activity.

Of those two—the group of the sense organs of cognition and the group of the organs of action—therein, the perception of sound and so forth is the function of the sense organs of cognition, while the manifestation of sound, striking the vocal organs, and so forth [is the function of the organs of action].

The sequence should be understood as "the function of the organs of action. He explains [the term] "called life" with the word "thus" (*evam*). "In the void alone is the I-sense"—that is, the I-sense residing in the void subject; for this reason, that living being who transmigrates is the void alone—the void subject itself.

It occurs. Alternatively, he explains the passage beginning with "or" by saying "yadi vā" (or if). "Adhiśayānā" means having resorted to [it]. To the question, "Well then, whose state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) is this?", he says "tadā" (then).
He applies the phrase "consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka*" to both of the two positions, stating "sa eva" (that very same one). "Sa eva" refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Thus it is. Why is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) said to be denoted by the term "puryaṣṭaka" (the eightfold city)? To this he says: "The vital breath and so forth.
It is precisely because it manifests the group of eight beginning with the vital breath that the collection of organs of action and the intellect characterized by determination are manifested by it.
"Others [hold that] the five subtle elements, mind, ego, and intellect [are the constituents]; [thus] mind,
ego, and intellect exist in the form of the emergence of the subtle elements" (Svacchandatantra 4.9).
And saying, "Earth, water, fire... (Gītā 7.4), they speak thus;
so, that which is of a dual nature, namely the *puryaṣṭaka*, exists within that very same pure [consciousness].
The sense is that rest [is found] therein, which constitutes the state of being the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*). Others, however, explain it otherwise; thus he says:
"the pentad of *tanmātras* [is the pentad of breaths, etc.]"—regarding these "others," it is as follows:

The word "they say" (*āhuḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. What is it that they say? "The pentad of the subtle elements alone" (*tanmātrapañcakam*). This group, beginning with these [subtle elements] and ending with the intellect (*buddhi*), constitutes the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*). The sense is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not the manifestor of this [pentad]. Others [say otherwise].

"What are they like?"—thus they speak. "What [is it]?"—"The emergence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). And thus they speak: "What [is it]?"—"The ground (*bhūmi*). As it has been said: "By means of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*), consisting of mind, ego, intellect, and the subtle elements."
"Constricted," and so forth.
Thus is the interpretation of these two verses for the learned:
"of the senses"—that is, of all the faculties—"internal function"—meaning having the nature of an internal operation—and likewise...

That "I-ness" (ahantā), which impels the vital breaths and so forth, is considered to be called "life" (jīvana). Alternatively, the "I-ness" residing in the vital breath is considered to be called "life"; what kind of "I-ness" is it? It is of the nature of the *puryaṣṭaka*;
that is to say, it takes the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*. Thus.

Now he explains the third verse with the word "evam" (thus). He states the object required by the word "tāvat" (first) with the word "yat" (which). It is "of a dual nature"—consisting of the *ahantā* (I-consciousness) residing in both the void (*śūnya*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*). He provides the explanation of the suffix *-mātra* (only/merely) with the word "śuddhe" (in the pure).
Thus [it is said]. He explains the state of stability (*sthiti-pada*) as "rest" (*viśrānti*).

That which, while *ahaṃtā* (the sense of "I") is in deep sleep, is characterized by awakening, is of the nature of being (*bhāva-rūpa*), and is action (*karma*) whose essence is activity—that is the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*). For it is through impurity (*mala*) that the subject is asleep.

By means of a *kalā*, however, one is as if not asleep; whereas here, through immersion (*nimajjana*)—[reading *nimajjanena* according to Kṣemarāja]—one is thoroughly asleep, and its state or action is such that in that void-like deep sleep (*śūnya-sauṣupta*), there is no object of knowledge distinct from anything else. Thus, due to the absence of the impurity of *māyīya-mala*, it is beyond being an object of knowledge (*apavedya*).

However, because pleasure, pain, and so forth produced by touch exist during the deep sleep of the vital breath (*prāṇasuṣupti*), there is the impurity called *māyā*; thus, that [state] is accompanied by objective cognition (*savedya*). In this way, dissolution (*pralaya*) should also be understood as being like the two types of deep sleep—the intense and the non-intense. That, moreover, is...
Deep sleep (*suṣupta*) is characterized by the absence of the destruction or arising of the body and so forth, lasting for a very long time;

whereas [ordinary] sleep is characterized by disregard for the body and so forth, lasting for a short time—this is the distinction. Even therein, there is sleep caused by fatigue, fainting caused by an imbalance of the bodily humors (*dhātu*), and intoxication, madness, and so forth caused by substances.

"Samādhi is that which is produced by autonomy"—such are the internal subdivisions. However, some maintain that the nature of samādhi is twofold: that which is accompanied by an object of experience (*savedya*) and that which is devoid of an object of experience (*apavedya*). || 15 ||
Now, one might object: "In that case, let the state of deep sleep be free from the manifestation of clearly perceived objects;
however, what is the difference between the states of dreaming and waking, both of which involve the appearance of clearly perceived objects?
Anticipating this doubt, he explains the distinction with two verses.

"He performs the seventh yoga; when that exists," he explains [the term] *sauṣupta* as referring both to the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), [saying] "of the I-ness" (*ahantāyāḥ*). The word "of the I-ness" is an ellipsis for the substantive (*viśeṣya*). He explains *sauṣupta* otherwise [as] "by means of impurity" (*malena*). Here...

"In this deep sleep," [meaning] "upon that immersion"—that is, when there is immersion into the *kalātattva* which constitutes the nature of the agent. He explains the second half [of the verse] with the word "therein" (*tatra*). "Therein" means in the midst of the two types of deep sleep.
By this, [he refers to] the "void deep sleep" expressed as "I was not aware of anything at all," and [the other as] "I slept happily."

It has been illuminated that this is "the deep sleep of the vital breath" (*prāṇasuṣupta*). He explains the phrase "abandoned in the middle, resembling dissolution" (*madhye tyaktaṃ pralayopamam*) with the word "profound" (*gāḍha*). Now, one might object: "In that case, does it not follow that there is identity between dissolution and deep sleep? To this he replies: "That is supreme," [meaning] it is non-arising in relation to the descent.

Thus it has been said; "destruction" (pradhvaṃsa) is stated with reference to the ascending [state]. "Neglect" (anādara) is indifference caused by defects such as sleep and so forth. He states the different names even for deep sleep according to the difference in causes with the words "there too" (tatrāpi). "Substance" (dravya) refers to wine and the like. He states the opinion of others with the words "but some," (kecittu).
"Pratipannāḥ" means they have accepted or undertaken [it]. || 15 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the sixteenth and seventeenth verses with the words "nanvevam" (But if this is so). This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "manomātra" (consisting of mind alone).

Even though they lie within the path of the mind alone, because of the delusion that they are objects of the senses, the creation of entities with vivid appearance is considered the state of dreaming. (16)
That creation which, by being within the range of all the senses and existing as something external and stable, is common to all subjects—that is waking. (17)

The external sense organs—the physical bases of the external senses, such as the eyeballs and so forth—are observed to be closed when one is asleep; yet, when they are closed, no activity of grasping external objects is seen in them. Therefore, [the mind] is indeed pure.
