In the mental path (*manomārga*), entities such as form, touch, and so forth, which are capable of appearing with a clear form suitable for apprehension by the senses, are created by the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) and not by the individual soul (*aṇu*); for [the soul] perceives only what is undesirable, and even what is desirable [is perceived] through connection with other places, times, and so on. Therefore:

Precisely because it abides solely within the mind, this creation is not common to other subjects. As for the fact that within it there appears an objectivity of the external senses and a commonality with other subjects—
although it remains exactly so as long as it shines, nevertheless, at a later time, for one who has awakened...

"It is not so"— through this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), that form appears as being without foundation; here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains "mere mind" (*manomātra*) as "the external sense organs."

"Of one who is sleeping"—meaning, of one practicing sleep—"in the pure"—meaning, unpolluted by the contact of the external senses. He explains "of objects" (*bhāvānām*) as "form" (*rūpa*). He explains "clearly manifest" (*spaṣṭāvabhāsāḥ*) as "the senses" (*akṣa*). He explains "creation" (*sṛṣṭiḥ*) as "they are created."

Thus [it is said]. "Not by the minute one"—that is, they are not created by the minute individual soul (*jīva*). Why are they not created? To this he says: "Of only what is undesirable. Sometimes in a dream only something undesirable is seen;
therefore it is known that it is not created by that *jīva*. For it is not logical for anyone to create their own undesirable [experience].
As for the fact that that very same thing is seen by someone due to a particular cause, therein the agency of the Lord (*īśvara*) is indeed manifest.
He states the second reason as well: "even of what is desired. The word "because of being seen" (*darśanāt*) is also connected here.
If the individual soul (*jīva*) were the creator in dreams, then at some time...

The sense is that seeing one's desired object in some particular place would be illogical. By this, he states the established point resulting [from the argument], namely "for this very reason. "This" refers to the dream-form; for it is not logical that what is in another's mind should become an object of perception for someone else. [This occurs] due to delusion (*vibhrama*).

He explains [the phrase] "by way of being an object of the senses" with the words "as for that which... Therein—in that dream—it shines forth; that is to say, it appears as something real. [The phrase] "not so" refers to the reflective awareness maintained during the waking state.

This is erroneous. For the certainty that those other perceivers and their respective sense organs which appear in a dream are non-different from those existing at the time of waking persists; yet at the time of waking, it is not so, and thus the persistence of that certainty is indeed sublated. Therefore, both [the dream and the waking state] are...
It is said to be "erroneous" (*bhrānta*); and "unsteadiness" (*asthairya*) is nothing other than this very state of being erroneous.
Thus, by the fact of not being an object of the senses, its "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatva*) is implied, and by the very fact of error, its "unsteadiness" is likewise implied.

Thus, it was not shown even at the occasion of defining the attribute that is the counter-correlate of waking (*jāgrat-pratiyogin-dharma*). That creation which is of such a nature is the "dream-state" (*svapna-pada*) because it exists for the bound soul (*paśu*) during the time of dreaming; it is the object (*viṣaya*) at the time of dreaming, and thus possesses such an object.

The state of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtva*) for the bound soul (*paśu*) means, in other words, the dream state. The mention of the "senses" (*akṣa*) is an elliptical expression for the ten external sense organs.
By means of the reflective awareness of their unreality, that form—the form of the objects of the dream—is [perceived].
"By way of being rootless"—that is, by way of being sublatable—for this reason, it is "erroneous," established through delusion. As it has been said:
"A dream is unreal in nature when compared to the waking state."
As for the claim that even the waking state is unreal according to the principle that "even the dream is of an unreal nature," that is here rejected as being irrelevant to the present context.

It is appropriate to state this. In response to the inquiry, "In what way is it erroneous? he says, "Those [objects]," referring to the subjects and so forth. And at the time of awakening, "it is not so"—that which was seen by me in a dream does not exist in that manner. Such is the persistence of the certainty.

The persistence of the certainty regarding the dream is as if it were stolen away—that is, it is utterly uprooted. For that reason, both—the other subjects and the sense organs—are said to be "erroneous" (bhrānta) in the dream, established through delusion. Now, one might object: is there not instability [in that case]?
To the question "How so?", he says: "Precisely because it is an error. He provides the conclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*).
That—namely, its uncommonness and instability—is the nature of those properties which exist as opposites—that is, standing in opposition—to the waking state, i.e., the waking condition.

Regarding the properties (*dharma*) whose nature consists of being uncommon (*asādhāraṇatva*) and so forth—the exposition of these was not shown by [the author] himself; that is, it was not stated directly. The sense is that effort is not appropriate for what is already established merely through implication (*ākṣepa*). He explains the term "dream-state" (*svapnapada*).
Regarding the phrase "at the time of sleep," he explains the word *pada* as a constituent part by stating "the object.
Here, he provides another synonym by saying "of such a nature. He explains that the term *akṣa* serves as an indicator for the ten sense-faculties by stating "the mention of *akṣa*."

But where that which is an object of the external senses and common to all subjects shines as ultimate reality—due to its persistence in ascertainment and its being free from sublation—it is precisely from that [persistence] that the stability of the object arises; that is the "creation" of the bound soul (paśu) and his state of waking; it has that [external object] as its domain.

The state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) is the waking state—so much as this. As long as the persistence and stability of the ascertainment (*niścaya*) shines forth, so long is there waking. Within that very interval, however, because the persistence of the ascertainment is uprooted, there is dreaming; for [dreaming] has the nature of mere appearance (*avabhāsa*).

Among objects, even within a long dream, that state wherein another dream occurs is, in relation to that [inner dream], indeed waking; or rather, even what is considered waking should be understood as merely a dream in relation to another waking state, because after a very long interval of time, the continuity of one's certainty is interrupted. || 17 ||
By demonstrating that these three states are to be abandoned, he indicates that the fourth state (*turya*) and those following it are to be adopted;
he explains the second verse with the words "But where... (*yatra tu*), referring to stability in the form of continuity.
The persistence of continuity. Even in the midst of waking, one accomplishes a dream;

"in its midst" means in the midst of waking. And because of the uprooting of the persistence of certainty—by uprooting the certainty regarding objects that were produced and then vanished at that time—it becomes a dream.

Why? Because things have manifestation as their very essence; the point is that things are established exactly according to how they appear. "In which [dream] one establishes the waking state even within a dream" means another dream—a different dream. Now, is there not a waking state for this dream?

If it is clearly existent, how can there be the conventional usage of "dream"? To this he says, "even that which is considered waking. "Considered waking" (*jāgrad-abhimatam*) means what is regarded as waking.
"At another time"—that is, at the moment of awakening from the two dreams. As it was said by the venerable Vasiṣṭha:

If that which is seen for a moment in the waking state were [the same as] a dream, or if a dream were to persist through a different period of time, then that waking state would attain the nature of a dream, and the dream would indeed become the waking state.
Thus [ends the section]. || 17 ||

Now he provides the introduction to the eighteenth verse with the words "āsām" (of these), which is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse with the words "heyā" (to be abandoned):
"This triad [of powers] is to be abandoned because of the predominance of the quality of agency belonging to the vital breath and the other [faculties]."
Because of its connection with the loss or increase of those [qualities], and with pleasure, pain, and so forth. || 18 ||
In that state where this cognizer perceives affliction—such as rejection, appropriation, the desire for them, and effort—that very state appears to him as something to be abandoned (*heya*).
And this [affliction] is produced solely through the variety of his connection with pleasure and pain; furthermore, this occurs within the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep].
For that body of consciousness— which consists of agency characterized by being solely intent upon resting in one's own self and which is a single mass of bliss through that very rest in the self—
when it possesses breath and so forth, [it becomes the individual subject].

When [the vital functions such as] prāṇa and so forth become subordinate within the stages of the body and so on— which consist of the eight voids (śūnyāṣṭaka)— then, once they have become subordinate, the predominance of prāṇa and the rest manifests. And thus, in that consciousness (cidrūpa), to the extent that there is a loss [of its own nature], to that same extent...
The accumulation of suffering occurs in proportion to whatever emergence [of the ego] there may be, while the accumulation of happiness occurs in proportion to its subsidence.

For instance, at the time of hunger, there is suffering due to the predominance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone; whereas upon satiety, because that [breath] has subsided and the "I-sense" (*ahaṃtā*) has become predominant, happiness is logically appropriate. Thus... [sukham | evaṃ - K. ṣ. ṣ. ...thus.
In the case of massaging or non-massaging of one who is fatigued, the predominance or non-predominance of the body must be considered.
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) establishes the method for explaining the verse with the words "wherein," and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).

The mention of "pleasure and so forth" refers to that affliction of this knower; and "this" refers to what was just mentioned—namely, the rejection, acceptance, the desire for them, and so on—in the three states consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. To the question "From what does this arise?", he says: "Since..."

Thus: that which has as its characteristic—that is, its very nature—the absence of orientation toward anything else (ananyaunmukhya), which is the lack of dependence on another, within that repose in one's own self—namely, in the reality of one's own self which is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), consisting of the reflective awareness "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa)—that indeed is it. That.

The body consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), while that which possesses breath and so forth—that is, that which possesses the function called "living"—is the existent (*sat*). [It becomes] a quality (*guṇatām*), meaning it assumes the state of being a subordinate attribute (*guṇabhāva*). Now, one might ask: "What will be achieved by that? To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). And thus means:
when there is the predominance of breath and so forth. "Loss" (*hāni*) means the state of becoming subordinate.

The meaning is the subordination [of the senses] when the state of being the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth is present. To the question "How so?", he provides the justification with the words "For it is thus" (*tathā hi*). "Of that"—meaning of the vital breath; for the subject who is the vital breath, it is "proper"—that is, logical. He extends this [rule] to the subject who is the body with the word "in the same way" (*evam*). At the time of fatigue...
The sequence is such that the body is primary at the time of massage and secondary at other times;
however, for one who knows the reality of immersion (*samāveśa*), there is simply no arising of suffering at those respective times. As it has been said:
"For even one who is weak, by overcoming that [weakness], proceeds to action;
likewise, one who is extremely hungry should conceal his hunger" (Spanda-kārikā 3.8).
Thus, when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth are predominant, agency (*kartṛtā*) exists only in a subordinate state.
The field of exertion is the conjunction with hundreds of varieties of pleasure and pain;
thus, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there exists a predominance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, along with the subordination of agency.
Therefore, that triad alone is to be abandoned. However, through the unfolding of the predominance of agency—

From the state of *turya* (the fourth) onwards, up to the state of *turyātīta* (beyond the fourth), which consists of its stabilization, that which is to be accepted is to be known as a mass of bliss of a single flavor (*ekarasa*). Now, is the predominance of the body and so forth equal for all, or not?

In response to this inquiry, he says: "But he who... Such a person is one who knows the true nature (*tattva*) of the immersion (*samāveśa*) just described. "At that time" means at the time when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other faculties have become predominant due to the influence of hunger and so forth. Then, he cites a statement from the *Śrī Spanda*: "Even though weak..."

He states the third quarter of this very verse as "one should cover. Therein, in the first quarter, at the time when [the state of] exhaustion occurs for one who knows the reality of immersion (*samāveśa*) and is capable of perceiving the innate nature (*sahajasvarūpa*), there is the prevention of the predominance of the body. But by the third [quarter], however—

The prevention of the primacy of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) at the time of hunger has been established by means of a general illustration. Now, intending to apply [this] to the verse by relying on the method already explained, he provides the conclusion with the word “thus” (*evam*). “Thus”—that is, by the aforementioned reasoning, [regarding] the vital breath and so forth.
He explains "on account of predominance" as "in the predominance of the vital breath and so forth. He explains "of agency"— that is, of the "I-ness"— as "in the subordinate state of agency."

He explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "pleasure" (*sukha*). He explains that "this triad is to be abandoned" with the words "waking" (*jāgrat*). That triad refers to the triad consisting of waking and the other states.
By this, he states that the fourth state (*turya*) and that which transcends it (*tadatīta*) are to be accepted, using the words "agency" (*kartṛtā*).

Due to the unfolding of the predominance of agency—that is, due to the manifestation of the predominance of the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhantā*)—there is the state beyond the fourth (*turyātītadaśā*), which consists of the stability of that [consciousness]; "ending with that" means ending with the state beyond the fourth, which consists of its stability. Why is it to be accepted? To this he says: "One. It is of a single flavor (*ekarasa*).

When there is the attainment of that innate nature— which consists of great non-duality and is a mass of bliss— there follows the subsiding of the helplessness that arises from the desire to acquire and the desire to abandon, which concern objects as their domain; that is, the subsiding of the state of being overpowered by the will to grasp and the will to discard.
For in the states of *turya* and *turyātīta*, through the attainment of the innate nature (*sahajasvarūpa*), desires for the acquisition or avoidance of objects do not manifest at all;
because upon attaining one's true nature, the agitation and exhaustion caused by the impulse to acquire or the desire to abandon have been stilled.
This is the intended meaning. || 18 ||

Now, an objection is raised: "Has it not been stated that the predominance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth is the cause of their being abandoned? If that is the case, then since such predominance is absent in the fourth state (*turya*) and beyond, it would be impossible to emerge from the absorption (*samāveśa*) into them. He dispels this doubt with two verses.
The vital breath consists of prāṇa and apāna during each state of sleep and waking;
that which is of the nature of their cessation is called samāna, as in the states of deep sleep and the equinoxes.
Moving through the middle and upwards, it is called udāna; residing in the fourth state (turya), it consists of fire.
It is Vijñānākala, the Lord of Mantras, while vyāna is the supreme, whose nature is the universe.
That which is called "prāṇa" is the state of the one whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpa), consisting of the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) and having the nature of living; that, for its part,
is of the nature of a general vibration, serving as the consciousness of the insentient body, vital breath, and so forth.

Thus, the summarized meaning here is as follows: this triad—the triad beginning with waking—is to be abandoned by the person (*puruṣa*). Why? Because of the predominance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest; likewise, in the expression "the quality of agency" (*kartṛtā-guṇe*), the indication is one where the state (*bhāva*) is predominant, since the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*) is not predominant.

When it exists, that which consists primarily of loss and gain—namely, pleasure, pain, and so forth, in the form of the loss and gain of vital breath (*prāṇa*)—arises from *yoga*, that is, from connection. || 18 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the nineteenth and twentieth verses with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Here the commentary says:
"tadabhāvāt" means due to the absence of the predominance of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth.

In that immersion—consisting of the dissolution of the *cittattva* (the principle of consciousness) and the immersion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth—there would be the impossibility of emergence, meaning there would be an incapacity for emergence;
for emergence consists precisely in being established once again in the vital breath and so forth. Having thus provided this introduction:
Having introduced the verse, he explains it with the words "prāṇa" (vital breath).
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
he explains that "prāṇa" consists of *prāṇa* and *apāna* by saying "prāṇāpāna."
The connection is that the state consisting of life becomes the very nature of life.

That [state], which consists of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, has as its essence the imposition of the sovereignty of "I" (ahaṃ), characterized by the accomplishment of the restraint of the one whose form is consciousness. [It is] "I..."
Being essentially the superimposition of autonomy, that very [consciousness], consisting of the reflective awareness of conceptual thought (*vikalpa-parāmarśa-mayī*),
manifests through the specific forms of inhalation, exhalation, and so forth.

It assumes five forms. Therein, sometimes abandoning something and sometimes falling into something, taking the form of inhalation and exhalation (*praśvāsa-niḥśvāsa*), it sequentially manifests the specific qualities of *prāṇa* and *apāna*. These two specific qualities—
In the waking state, [the movement of the vital breaths] is clearly evident, because they extend from the body to rest upon an external object, and then back into the body;

or because they rest upon internal objects of cognition such as memory, since the presence of the prāṇa and apāna is perfectly manifest there. Even in dream, these two certainly exist; for even while one is dreaming, the prāṇa and apāna persist.

The two natures of exiting and entering are clearly perceived by another; and the state consisting of rejection and acceptance arises from the very self-awareness of the object of knowledge, being essentially the accomplishment of the state of conscious awareness.

Its nature consists in the bringing about of the state of being conscious; for it is indeed through the penetration of consciousness (*cid-āveśa*) that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other elements become conscious. That which is the superimposition (*āropa*) by way of absolute freedom—the imposition [of the sense] "I" upon the vital breath and so forth—is its essence; thus, it consists of the reflective awareness of conceptual thought (*vikalpa-parāmarśa-mayī*).
The construction is as follows: by virtue of projecting duality, it takes the form of conceptualization and the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "I.
That very state—indeed, the very abiding of the nature of consciousness—manifests through the specific forms of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth;
that is, by way of the states of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *udāna*, *samāna*, and *vyāna*—therein, within the midst of these five forms.
That state of the conscious nature, while abandoning even that limited object called the region of the heart,
and being thus of the nature of inhalation and exhalation, sequentially manifests the state of *prāṇa*— the condition of the out-breath— and the state of *apāna*— the condition of the in-breath.

For *prāṇa* is that which causes movement outward, while *apāna* is that which causes entry inward. He explains this very point with the words "each in both sleep and waking": "that" refers to what was previously mentioned;
"the two distinctions"—namely, the two-fold division in the form of *prāṇa* and *apāna*; "to that extent," meaning that there is nothing further here.
The sense is that this is a misconception held by someone. "Having issued forth" means through the nostrils;
having emerged as far as the *dvādaśānta* (the limit twelve finger-breadths beyond the head) via the lower aperture, [it enters] the object—the external air.
Having described the existence of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* during the waking state, he speaks also of the dream state with the words "even in the dream."

By another— that is, by someone else who is awake— due to the perception of what is to be known, namely the experience of the objects present in the dream state, there occurs a state consisting of rejection and acceptance,
whose nature is the abandonment and grasping within the region of the heart.

It is indeed experienced; therefore, in the waking state, vitalization consists of the two specific forms of prāṇa and apāna, and likewise in the dream state. Deep sleep is the dream itself when it becomes fully nourished;
at that time, the subject is in the state of deep sleep (suṣupta), and this is his "deep-sleep stage" (sauṣupta-pada). That [stage] is also of two kinds.
One assumes a specific form known as "the same" (samāna), which pertains to living beings. Even though the movement of prāṇa and apāna is observed during dreamless sleep—
which is accompanied by sensation— nevertheless, there is a state of rest between those two within the abode of the heart, which is devoid of the senses.

In that particular region, that very state is primarily called deep sleep (*suṣupta*). Therein lies the severance and rest of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths for a certain duration; its essence consists of the activity of equalizing the entire range of vital fluids and other elements throughout the upper, lower, and lateral directions. Precisely because of this:
By causing the expansion of the heart-lotus, the *samāna* wind effects the digestion of what has been eaten and drunk;

because it maintains the equilibrium of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* for a certain time—despite their forms as day and night—and because of its interruption [of their flow], it is equal to the time of the equinox (*viṣuvat*). It is so called because it "deserves" (*arhati*) the state of being pervasive (*viṣu*), that is, equalization.
The suffix *vati* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.117 (*tadarham*).

The existence of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* is indeed perceived—that is, it is known—because without the movement of the *prāṇa*, the perception of objects cannot occur. He states the conclusion with the words "by that" (*tena*). [This refers to] the act of breathing (*prāṇana*)—

The state of the one whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*) consists of the form of vital breath (*prāṇana*); it is the same in dream. That is to say—in that manner, in dream, the state of the one whose nature is consciousness consists of the form of vital breath, being composed of the two specific [movements] of *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
He explains the second half [of the verse] with the word "suptam" (asleep). That very thing—namely, deep sleep itself.
"Of him"—meaning, of that cognizer (*pramātṛ*). "That"—refers to the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*);

by this, the explanation of the term *sauṣupte* has been provided. The word *api* signifies totality; [it refers to] that specific form called "the same" (*samāna*), which is "pertaining to the vital breath" (*prāṇīya*).

"Connected with the vital breath" (*prāṇasaṃbandhi*) means accompanied by what is to be felt (*savedya*), as is inferable from the subsequent reflective awareness: "I slept happily. Regarding those two—the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—he explains the word "severance" (*chede*) as "rest" (*viśrāntiḥ*). "For some time" means as long as [the state does not cease].
The meaning is that it exists as a certain form for that duration; "having that as its nature" means having the nature of cutting [or transformation];
"rasa etc."—by the word "etc.," food and so forth are included. "Precisely from that"—meaning precisely from the activity of equalizing—is the digestion of what has been eaten and drunk.
He explains the phrase "as in the equinoxes" by saying "in the day," meaning that [the breath] acts in such a way as to produce a state of exhaustion.
This is because of the equality— due to the balance— of day and night in their forms of heat and cold, and because of the cessation— the resting in the region of the heart.

"Equal to the time of the equinox" means similar to the time known as the *viṣuvat*; for it is there that day and night are indeed equal. He provides an etymological analysis (*vigraha*) based on the verbal root *viṣḷ* (in the sense of "pervasion"), thus forming the word *viṣum*. Furthermore, by resorting to the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "pervasion," he states its synonym.

Regarding "making equal": the suffix *vati* is used for comparison even between things that are not identical, as seen in the usage *udvato nivataḥ*; for this is established by logic (*nyāya*), not merely by explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*). Or rather, it refers to a specific distinction.

It impels incessantly, characterized by the decrease and increase of day and night—thus, in the present participle (*śatṛ*), it is *viṣuvat*. And in that *viṣuvat*, there exists the state of the breath (*prāṇa*) and downward breath (*apāna*) as they are being severed, in the form of their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); for that indeed is the severance, but not in its entirety.

It has been stated more than once that there is no destruction. Consequently, the "equalization" (*samānīkaraṇa*)—which consists in bringing about a similarity in the form of the seeds of both rejection and acquisition—is not possible for that which is all-pervading (*vyāpaka*). Now, in response to the expectation of which sūtra provides the suffix *-vat* here, he says: "That which is worthy of it" (*tadarham*).

The meaning is "by this sūtra. Now, one might object: "In this case, because [the word] is an indeclinable (avyaya), the locative plural ending would not be applicable. To this, he says: "in the sense of a standard of comparison" (upamāne).
The intention is that this is due to usage—that is, because of the observation of these two Vedic usages. Otherwise, in this case...

The intention is that it would not be appropriate for it to end in the singular genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyekavacanāntatva*). [This refers to the rule: *udaḥ neśca upasargācchandasi dhātvarthe* (Pāṇini 6.1.94).

Thus, there is the suffix *vati*; from that, the sixth case singular ending *ṅas*. Now, one might ask: "From what [source] is it established that only the suffix *upamānavati* is indeclinable? To this he says: "For that," meaning "indeclinability," is established by logic (*nyāyasiddham*).
The meaning is that it is established by the rule "a taddhita suffix not taking all case-endings [is called avyaya]. "Vācanika" means technical (paribhāṣika);
[the root] *ṣū* is used in the senses of procreation and sovereignty.
Thus, by resorting to the verbal roots, he performs the analysis as "viśeṣam" (the distinction).

Having explained the prefix *vi*, he demonstrates it clearly by saying "dina" (day). Or (*vā*), in the alternative sense, [it refers to] day and night, as well as their deficiency and excess; this is an expression where the abstract state is predominant, namely "day and night."

And the characteristic of its deficiency or excess is as follows: it impels—that is, it restrains—whatever has such an essential nature. For at the time of the equinox (*viṣuvat*), all time indeed flows away; otherwise, the scriptures (*āgama-śāstra*) would not declare that one must necessarily apply oneself to it as something to be practiced.

The meaning is that this word is established when the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed after the root *ṣū* (to flow) preceded by the prefix *vi*. Now, one might object: "In that case, due to the flowing away of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the state of the *turya* (the fourth) alone would result.
To this he says: "And there..."—referring to that which is being severed, i.e., that which attains rest in the region of the heart.
"Of prāṇa and apāna" is a collective dvandva compound. That very thing—namely, the state of being in the form of latent impressions (saṃskāra)—has been stated thus:
"There is no non-existence of that which exists."

Thus [it is said]. He states the conclusion with the words "And therefore": regarding "rejection and acquisition"—that is, the rejection and acquisition of the heart-region consisting in the stability of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—[this occurs] in deep sleep (*suṣupti*). And within this much, the entire class of bound souls (*paśu*) ending with the *pralayākala* is included.
But when that circulation of the vital breath (prāṇana), causing the left and right paths to become desolate,

flows upward in the form of the middle [channel], then that flow is the dissolution— characterized by the taking up of the essence of non-duality of the entire duality— like [the melting] of congealed ghee.

The function of *udāna* effects [this] starting from the level of the *vijñānākala* up to the end of *sadāśiva*, and that state consists of the *turya* (the fourth). For above *māyā* lie the *vijñānākalas*; thus, from that point onward, the dissolution of duality proceeds. When duality has dissolved, however, [there remains] the reality (*tattva*) consisting of the entire aggregate of objects of knowledge.

The function of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), in the form of pervading the body which consists of the categories of the elements and the worlds— as well as the activities of the body consisting of those same categories— is of the nature of *vyāna*; it is appropriate for Paramaśiva, who is the soul of the universe, and is of the nature of that which transcends the fourth state (*turyātīta*).
The subject (pramātā) is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa), consisting of the forms of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna; thus there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
To the question, "In what [space] do these abide?", he says: "and in this much," by which he means "within."
It is indicated that even the *vijñānākalas* exist here in a subtle manner (*leśataḥ*).

He explains the second verse with the words "But when" (*yadā tu*). "The function of breathing" (*prāṇanāvṛttiḥ*) refers to the state of the one whose nature is consciousness known as "breathing"; "making [it] barren" (*khilībhāvayantī*) means making it subordinate (*nyagbhāvayantī*).

This means they lead [the object] to the state of being an object of equanimity (*upekṣā*). By way of the "middle form"—that is, by way of the nature of the channel called *suṣumṇā*—and "upwards," meaning by way of the upper region because of its supreme excellence. "Dissolution" (*vilāpana*) means causing to merge; of that which has become solid (*āśyānasya*)—
Of that which has become condensed, there occurs the function of *udāna*— the vital activity known as *udāna*.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to where its movement resides, the term "Vijñānākala" is explained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as "Vijñāna," referring to those situated in the middle.

It should be understood that the state of mantras and so forth being objects of the function of *udāna* is established without effort. And that aforementioned function of *udāna*, from that point onward— that is, starting from the *vijñānākala*—
is indicated by the phrase "composed of fire" (*hutabhuṅmaya*) through the simile "like congealed clarified butter."

This has been explained. Clarified butter, having become solidified, is absorbed by the fire itself; moreover, it is well known in the Āgamas that the central channel (madhya-nāḍī) possesses the nature of the fire-channel, while the left and right channels possess the status of the moon-channel and the sun-channel respectively. Thus [is] vyāna.

He explains the fragment of the verse beginning with "vilīne tu": that which consists of the aggregate of all objects of knowledge—the body composed of the categories of principles (tattva), elements (bhūta), and worlds (bhuvana), i.e., having the form of the principles and so forth—its pervasion therein; by means of that form, [the state] appropriate for Paramaśiva [is attained].

The meaning is that she becomes fit for Paramaśiva, whose nature is the unity of Śiva and Śakti; she is of the nature of the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), having the form of the stage beyond the fourth. "Thus" (iti) means for this reason; "grammatical coordination" (sāmānādhikaraṇya) refers to the designation in the aphorism by means of a single nominative case ending.

And he is the *vijñānākala*, and he is the *mantra*—due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—and he is the *īśa* who consists of the forms of Sadāśiva and Īśvara; this is the *udāna*. This is what is meant: even though...

Even in the states of *turya* and *turyātīta*, there exists vitalization (*prāṇanā*), for otherwise neither the state of being alive nor emergence from samādhi would be possible; nevertheless, because these two stages consist primarily of resting in non-duality through the withdrawal of duality— [due to the predominance of resting in non-duality]— they are so designated.

Because the diversity of pleasure, pain, and so forth is incompatible [with it], it is to be accepted precisely as consisting of supreme bliss, whose nature is repose within one's own unitary self. However, in states such as deep sleep, because it exists in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), there is no manifestation of a clear object of cognition; rather, it consists of the non-manifest emergence of objects and the appearance of clear objects of cognition.
Since differentiation exists, there is a variety of pleasure, pain, and so forth; thus, [this world] is precisely that which is to be abandoned.

Therefore, it is rightly said: "This triad is to be abandoned," and so on. Furthermore, for the Blessed One whose body is the universe, his very nature consists of the vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.

By this very [process], through the forms of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna, there is the state of Śiva, which consists of the entire group beginning with the *pralayākala* and *vijñānākala*, characterized by universal movement, arousal, entry, and dissolution— or rather, according to the K.ṣ.ṣ.,
the state of Śiva consisting of the group beginning with the *vijñānākala* up to Sadāśiva. Thus it is also by this.
This has been shown. As it was stated:
"From where [does] the Lord [arise]? By way of having the form of Sadāśiva and Īśvara"—thus it should be connected. This is the *udāna*:
the meaning is that the *vijñānākala* becomes the *mantreśa*, who is the *udāna*. By this—

The analysis of the compound *vijñānākalamaṃtreśaḥ* is based on the assumption of a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) construction. He announces his intention to state the underlying meaning with the words "this is what is meant.
He fulfills the expectation raised by the word "this" (*etad*) with the phrase "even though... [and so forth]. [The term] *prāṇanā* means having the nature of vitalizing or sustaining life.

This refers to the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Otherwise— that is, in the absence of the vital breath— through the withdrawal of differentiation (*bhedopasaṃhāreṇa*), meaning by the dissolution of differentiation,

because [the state] is primarily characterized by resting in non-duality (*abhedaviśrāntipradhānatvāt*), it is indicated that, by virtue of this secondary nature and the influence of the body's own constitution, there may even be a resting in differentiation.

Regarding these two states, namely the Fourth (turya) and that which transcends it (tadatīta): [the author asks] "But how can there be a state of non-acceptance in deep sleep and so forth? To this he says: "in deep sleep and so forth" (suṣuptādau).
That very manifestation of the object of knowledge, which is indistinct due to its nature as a latent impression (saṃskāra), having been made distinct—

"Of one whose form is such that it consists of the manifestation of the object of knowledge. He states another intention with the words "and of the Blessed One": "of the Blessed One"—that is, Paramaśiva—and "and" (*ca*) serves as a conjunction;
"whose body is the universe" (*viśvaśarīrasya*).

For one whose body is the universe consisting of the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, there occurs the very nature of the vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—which is the state of being Śiva for the entire group of beings, including the sakala, pralayākala, and vijñānākala. By the word "etc. (ādi), [the remaining categories are included].
"The universe consists of thirty-six principles; these are the powers of Śambhu, beginning with Prāṇa.
Thus [ends the section], from the beginning [up to verse] 171.

The inclusion of "mantras and so forth" (mantrādi)— this too is indicated, that is, made manifest by suggestion, by this sūtra. Not only is there the mere quality of being to be abandoned or accepted regarding the five states, but also the nature of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and downward breaths (apāna), etc., as consisting of the Sakala and other categories.

The word "also" (api) implies that [these states] have been shown. In this context, the nature of prāṇa and apāna constitutes the state of being a "sakala" (one with parts); the nature of samāna constitutes the state of being a "pralayākala" (one dissolved in dissolution); and the nature of udāna constitutes the state of being the class beginning with the "vijñānākala" (one awakened by knowledge).

The distinction is as follows: the forms of the Vijñānākala, Mantreśvara, Mantra, and Maheśvara correspond to the nature of vyāna, while the nature of śiva corresponds to the state of [the supreme] vyāna. However, in the perspective of dualism (bheda-darśana), it is called *prāṇa* because it exits through the mouth and nose, and it is called *apāna* because it leads the essence downward.
Apāna is so called because it moves downward; from its equalizing function, it is Samāna;
from its upward-leading function, it is Udāna; and from its pervading the umbilical cord of the embryo, it is Vyāna.
Thus, the determination of the pentad beginning with Prāṇa is made solely on the basis of their functions within the body alone. This is the traditional teaching (āgama).

"It accords with what was stated" (*saṃvādayati yathoktam*). The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the scriptural passage and the conclusion of the commentary on the chapter (*āhnika*). The term *śiva* denotes auspiciousness and is intended to indicate the supreme reality (*paratattva*).
Thus, the summary in these two verses is as follows: For both the sleeping and waking states, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the life-force;
it consists individually of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, as is clearly observed. That *prāṇa*, in the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupte*), has the nature of that [waking] cessation.

That which consists of the cutting off of the prāṇa and apāna becomes known as samāna; for at that time, the apāna remains dissolved in the region of the heart for a short duration, while the prāṇa does not rise.
As it has been said:
"When the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the pericardium (purītat), then there is deep sleep (suṣupti).

In what, as it were, does this state of deep sleep occur? "As in the equinoxes (viṣuvat)"—that is, as in the points of the equinox; for even there, for a certain period, there is indeed an equality between day and night, and thus that serves as the point of comparison.
It is grasped. The vital breath known as *udāna* becomes one that moves through the fourth state (*turyaga*). Of what nature is it?

It is "upward-moving" (*madhyeva-ūrdhvaga*)—that is, it goes upward, toward the upper region, specifically through the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*). Likewise, it consists of fire (*hutabhuṅmaya*), having the form of fire, because it resides within the channel of fire.

Likewise, that udāna becomes the Lord of Mantras (mantreśa) who is free from the limited state of consciousness (vijñānākala). The vyāna—the vital breath known as vyāna—becomes the Supreme (para), whose nature is Paraśiva;
for this very reason, it is the soul of the universe (viśvātmaka), meaning its nature is everything, and for this very reason, it possesses the quality of transcending that [universe].
This is to be known. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
In the *Pettā*, within the section on the means of valid knowledge (*āgama*), the second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Reality of the Knower," concludes. || 2 ||
And this third chapter on the scriptures is complete.

Thus, in the commentary on the *Śrīpratyabhijñāvimarśinī*, composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha— the son of the venerable Avatārakaṇṭha, who was the son of the venerable Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha, the worshipful master residing within the illustrious region of Kāśmīra—
The second daily lesson in the section on the scriptures (*āgamādhikāra*) within the work titled *Śrībhāskarī* is completed.
And this third reflection (*vimarśa*) is finished. May there be auspiciousness!
This third chapter, which clearly establishes the thorough discernment of the principles (*tattva*) and has indeed been correctly explained by Bhāskara,
is here completed by me as the section on the intellect (*buddhi*), accompanied by sound reasoning and the names of the traditional authorities (*āgama*).
By virtue of the tradition of the illustrious true guru, and likewise in accordance with the scriptures.
No egoistic conceit should be formed regarding the mind, for Śiva is the agent who resides therein;
if you possess that conceit through identity with Him, let it be, for it is auspicious.
Śiva is the agent, Śiva is the observer, and Śiva alone is the reciter;
Śiva is declared to be the expounder, and it is clear that everything is an offering unto Śiva.
The First Chapter of the *Vimarśinī* Commentary on the Section on the Compendium of Reality (*Tattvasaṃgraha*)
We praise that Śiva who manifests himself to his devotees as possessing the non-dual variety of infinite means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and so forth.
The Sun-like Lord,
who maintains a great unity within the very multiplicity of infinite objects of knowledge and so forth—
He who is both full and yet more than full, whose nature is not any [particular] form, is composed of wonder.
May Śiva protect us.
Now, for the sake of the unimpeded completion of the fourth reflection (*vimarśa*)— which consists of a single day and is titled "The Section on the Compendium of the Meaning of the Scriptures"—
it is thus established through one's own self-awareness, logical reasoning, and scripture:
The very nature of the Self, which is the form of Maheśvara, has been extensively determined through the three sections [of the treatise]; now,

in order to instill that same reality briefly into the intellects of his disciples, he presents a summary of the meaning of the scriptures in eighteen verses, beginning with "The Self alone [is the cause] of all living beings," and so forth.

By means of this single chapter, ending with the words "brought about by the lotus," [the author] has explained [the subject]. Therein, one verse states the ultimate nature; nine verses describe the nature of bondage from the perspective of the reality of the knower and the known; and seven [verses] concern that which consists of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
The essential truth of liberation is shown through a concluding verse—this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Now, the meaning of the text itself is being examined:
"One's own Self alone is the one Great Lord (*maheśvara*) of all living beings."
I am the universal form, "this," expanded by the undivided reflective awareness.

And for the sake of the accumulation [of merit], he composes a benediction in the form of a recollection of the Supreme Reality— which, though already performed within himself, is now set forth externally for the instruction of his disciples—
by means of a verse that indicates the purport of all his works, beginning with the word "Ananta."

We praise that Śiva. Who is he? He is Śiva, who [resides] within the variety—that is, the manifoldness—of the infinite objects of knowledge and the means of knowledge for those devotees whose hearts have been struck by the most intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and who are characterized by worship in the form of spiritual immersion (*samāveśa*).
"Manifestation through diversity" means that very non-duality—the Great Non-duality whose nature is the state of supreme fullness, having internalized within itself both duality and non-duality;
it "shines" by means of that, which is its characteristic. "The Self" refers to that which is of the nature of perfect light.

Its own nature (*svarūpa*) is made manifest—it, being by its very nature self-luminous and thus characterized by the tendency to manifest itself, impels [the subject] toward that [object] through an operative activity consisting in the performance of what is capable [of that manifestation]. This usage is like the expression "the head of Rāhu. For there is nothing whatsoever distinct from itself; rather, [the distinction] is a conceptual differentiation (*vyatireka*) effected through that [medium].
Or rather: for devotees who have attained firm establishment in non-duality indeed perceive the Great Non-duality even while in the state of duality. As it has been said:
"Having enjoyed worldly pleasures and abandoned the delusion of existence, I shall attain the supreme state."
Thus I hope that this may shine forth here as the supreme devotion of one who is devoted to Śambhu.
Thus, having performed the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), he explains the intended meaning of the section consisting of a single day both collectively and individually with the word "thus" (*evam*).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
By means of the logical proof of self-awareness— that is, by the reasoning of one's own experience— one is to "establish" or "transmit" [the teaching].
Then, without a formal introduction, he presents and explains the first verse, beginning with the words "one's own Self indeed."

In this world, insentient things appear as if submerged within consciousness; for the objective reference "this" finds its ultimate rest only in the subjective awareness "I. Consequently, insentient things are devoid of self, while living beings alone are sentient because they possess a self; and of these...

Maheśvara alone is his own self; he is Maheśvara himself and not anyone else. Since he is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*), and there is no difference whatsoever in consciousness by way of space, time, or essential form—let the body, vital breath, and so forth differ as they may—they are merely...
Those belonging to the class of the insentient are indeed immersed in consciousness; thus, because the one conscious Self alone, through its sovereignty,
manifests the manifoldness within itself, it is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) who has internalized the sense of "this-ness" (idantā).

Here the commentary explains "of living beings" (*jantūnām*) with reasoning: "here" (*iha*) means in this manifest world; "immersed in consciousness" (*cetana-nimagnāḥ*) means resting in consciousness by way of perception. Why?
In response to the question "What does it pierce?", he says: "This" (*idam*). "This" means:

in this manner, the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the insentient (*jaḍa*), which has consciousness as its substratum and the insentient as its object. In the reflective awareness of consciousness as "I"—that is, in the form of "I," which has consciousness as its substratum and that [consciousness] as its object.
Regarding the [term] *parāmarśe* (in the reflective awareness), he states the conclusion with the words *tataśca* (and therefore). "Nirātmānaḥ" means "those who are as if soulless";

for this reason, he establishes the genitive construction with the word *teṣām* (of them). And "of them"—that is, of those living beings denoted by the term *jantu*—the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) is their very own self (*svātman*).

By the two applications of the word "only" (*eva*), the absence of absolute difference is indicated: Maheśvara alone is one's own self. He states what is excluded by the two uses of the particle "only" with the words "but not another. When the question "Why? arises, he himself provides the logical connection as the reason and explains the term "one" (*eka*).
"And because of this" means that he is Maheśvara, whose nature is his own self. Now, one might ask:

"Since he is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*), what follows from that? To this he says: "And of consciousness. The word "kāmam" is used in the sense of certainty. "Belonging to the side of the insentient" (*jaḍapakṣyāḥ*) means those which exist on the side of the insentient; [he is] "of universal form" (*viśvarūpaḥ*).

He connects the qualification with the word "as a cause" by means of its independence. "Vaiśvarūpyam" means the state of being the universal form (*viśvarūpatām*). Intending to explain the phrase "I am this," he states the resulting conclusion with the word "therefore. "Antarnītām" means dissolved within one's own self.
Having performed this, he is filled with the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃvimarśa*) consisting of resting in his own Self, which is turned away from all else;
for this very reason, omniscience and omnipotence are not to be achieved by him through effort. For, just as in the case of the objects of the various cognitive and active senses...

Thus, both the state of being a knower and the state of being an agent belong to the one Self alone; likewise, that which is the knowledge and the instrument regarding the multitude of objects—which have as their domain thousands of *rudras* and *kṣetrajñas* standing in the place of the senses—is all located within the single conscious Self.
— Thus [ends the first verse].
Now, one might object: "If this Self is indeed one alone, in the form of Maheśvara, then what is bondage, for the sake of whose liberation this effort is undertaken? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, within the portion of 'this' created by Himself, [the Self appears] as the intellect and so forth, in the form of the subject."
By this [means], that [object] has been brought to the state of being grasped as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 2 ||

In this regard, while Maheśvara abides thus within his own self— that very mirror of one's own self which is the nature of light— the Supreme Lord, by his own sovereignty, first brings about contraction and then projects that "this-portion" (the objective world).

For this very reason—precisely because of the fullness of the *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (the reflective awareness of "I")—both omniscience and omnipotence (*sarvajñatva* and *sarvakartṛtva*) are not to be established through effort for him, the Great Lord who is one's own self (*svātmamaheśvara*).
To the question "Why [are they not to be established by effort]?", he says: "In the manifold..."—that is, in the objects of the various cognitive and active faculties (*buddhi-karmendriya*).
As that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it becomes the object of the various faculties of cognition and action;

[this refers to] the Self—the reality of the self as delimited by the body. Having stated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states the illustrated point (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).
The Rudras are the subjects (*pramātṛ*) who abide above *māyā*. The word "iti" [marks the end of the statement].
At the conclusion of the commentary on the verse. || 1 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the second verse with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the word "tatra" (therein).
Here is the commentary:

Regarding the word *tatra*, he explains it by relying on the locative case of existence (*satsaptamī*) as "thus" (*evam*). Furthermore, by relying on the locative case of locus (*ādhārasaptamī*) through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application), he provides another interpretation as "in that very [place]" (*tasminneva*). He explains the word *anena* as "by that" (*tena*), meaning by its own essential nature (*svātmarūpeṇa*).

He explains [the phrase] "in this portion of his own creation" with the word "by virtue of his sovereignty" (*svātantryāt*). "Preceded by contraction" means having contraction as its prerequisite. Among those [five], that which consists of the intellect (*buddhi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the body is [perceived] through the intellect as "this-ness" (*idantayā*).

This object of knowledge, appearing through a constructed and incomplete sense of "I" (*ahaṃ-bhāva*) as the subject that grasps what is distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties— being incapable of overcoming the state of "this-ness" (*idam-bhāva*)— shines forth.
"I am Devadatta," "I am Caitra"—thus [they think]. || 2 ||
"Let it be so even thus; nevertheless, whose is the bondage? For who else exists apart from the Lord? To resolve this, he says:
"In the midst of that," which he explains as: "in the midst of this portion [of the universe], beginning with..."

The object grasped by the word is described as "prāṇa. It is that which is to be known as "this"—the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa) existing as an object of knowledge with respect to itself. [The phrase] "of that which is distinct from the intellect and so forth" means:
of that object of knowledge, such as blue or pleasure, which is distinct from that intellect and so forth; [it exists] as the subject (grāhakātman).
He explains it as "by way of being the subject" (*grāhakatayā*). Being appropriate as the subject— that is, being fit for the reflective awareness of the sense of "I"—
it is "artificial," meaning non-natural, because of its incapacity, that is, its lack of power, regarding the subjugation of the sense of "this-ness" (*idambhāva*).

Being existent, it shines forth through the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*), that is, through the grasping of "I-ness" (*ahantā*). In response to the question of how it shines forth, he says: "I am Devadatta."
Thus, the clear construction of this verse is as follows: "there being"—that is, while Maheśvara exists as one's own self (*svātman*);
by "this"—meaning by Maheśvara as one's own self; and again, by applying the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*), the word "there" (*tatra*) should be construed with both.
"There"—in the wall that is one's own self in the form of Light (*prakāśa*), within the portion of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāga*) created by himself.

Within this sphere of "thisness" (idaṃbhāga) produced by itself— meaning, within the collection of objects of knowledge created by itself through metaphorical extension— that [intellect and so forth], although it is an object of knowledge with respect to itself, is well known as a knower with respect to external things; such is the intellect and the rest.

As the nature of the subject—that is, as the subjectivity directed toward blue, pleasure, and so forth—it is the locus of the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃkāra-parāmarśa-pada*), meaning it is the site of being the object of the "I"-reflection;

it has been brought [to this state], attained through its own sovereignty. For this very reason, even in the doctrine of a single Lord (*ekeśvara-vāda*), there is [the status of] the bound soul (*baddha*).
The sense is that it is indeed appropriate to exert effort for the sake of liberating the subject, such as the intellect and so forth. || 2 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the third verse with the words "nanvevam" (But if this is so).
This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "sasvarūpa" (possessing its own nature).
That person, consisting of the non-recognition of his own true nature, is considered manifold;
therein, in the state of emanation, there are activity and bliss, and experience consisting of pain and pleasure. (3)
True; from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no bondage whatsoever.
Rather, it is that very [consciousness] which, by virtue of its own unsurpassed sovereignty, manifests itself as contracted; at that time, [it obscures] its own full form.

That very non-cognition—which, despite the manifestation [of objects], consists in a lack of reflective awareness—is presented here as the cause; he whose essence is merely the non-recognition of fullness is called the *puruṣa*.
For this very reason, he is manifold, due to the particularity of each respective body, vital breath, and intellect.
Because of the assumption of contraction (*saṃkoca*). And that person, as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), experiences the connection characterized by enjoyment (*bhoga*).
Now, enjoyment for him consists of the two—action and bliss—which are imagined; imagined action is suffering, for *rajas* is indeed both manifest and unmanifest.
Suffering is said to be of the nature of agitation; goodness (sattva), being of the nature of illumination, is happiness;
whereas darkness (tamas), being of the nature of non-illumination, is a state of rest in the middle, corresponding to dissolution. || 3 ||
Regarding this,

the commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains the phrase "non-comprehension of the essential nature" by saying "it is true. The word "true" (*satyam*) is an expression of acceptance used specifically with reference to the matter raised in the introductory section (*avataraṇikā*).
It has been applied. He [the author] explains that very thing: "He who is of the nature of his own self" refers to the Supreme Lord himself;

it is of the nature of non-reflection (*aparāmarśa*), and not of the nature of the absence of knowledge, because the latter is impossible—this is the intended meaning. He provides an explanation of the suffix *mayaṭ* with the words "that very same," referring to what was under discussion.
That which is presented in abundance is introduced. Having analyzed the compound, he states the meaning as "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*).

He explains "man" (*pumān*) as "the person" (*puruṣaḥ*). In response to the inquiry "how is he manifold?", he himself provides the logical connection by saying "this and that" (*tattat*); [that is,] by way of distinction (*viśeṣeṇa*), through the state of being particularized.

This is the meaning. Space is not perceived because it lacks such contraction. Having explained the first half [of the verse], he establishes the connection (*saṅgati*) in order to explain the second half with the words "And that" (*sa ca*).
"Connection" (*saṃbandhana*) means the linking together with objects. Having established the connection—

He explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "and enjoyment" (*bhogaśca*). He explains that it consists of the nature of pain and pleasure with the word "pain" (*duḥkham*). Now, one might ask: how can action, which denotes volition (*kṛti*), have the form of pain? To this he says: "rajas. *Rajas* is a term denoting activity (*pravṛtti*) whose nature is action.

The quality of rajas, and sattva—the quality known as sattva; by way of this context, he also provides a determination of the quality of tamas: "Tamas" is that which stands in the place of dissolution—meaning it is similar to dissolution—but not dissolution itself, because in that state all qualities are destroyed. || 3 ||
Now, what is excluded and what is included by the phrase "in creation"?
To this he says:
"The knowledge and the action which belong to the Lord regarding entities that are the forms of His own limbs..."
In the third [category], Māyā, those two alone constitute the sattva, rajas, and tamas of the bound soul (paśu).
The light of the three worlds, which is the very nature of the Lord of universal form, as well as the reflective awareness (vimarśa), constitute respectively knowledge and action;
these two exist precisely through the non-abandonment of the reflective awareness of one's own nature.
However, that reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) which occurs even as a differentiation—

though resting ultimately within the self-reflection of one's own nature (*svarūpaparāmarśa*) in the form "I am this"— is the Lord’s power of *māyā*, the ultimate reality of Sadāśiva and Īśvara; these are the three powers residing in the Blessed One.
"Natural and uncreated" (naisargikyo 'sṛṣṭāḥ). Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides the introduction to the fourth verse, beginning with "nanu" (now, however); this is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "svāṅge" (in his own limb).
Here the commentary says:
he explains "of the Lord" (*patyuḥ*) as "of the one whose form is the universe" (*viśvarūpasya*). [This refers to Him] in the forms of His own limbs.
He explains "in entities" as "in their own nature. "Everywhere"—that is, throughout the entire multitude of entities.

He explains "knowledge" as "light" (*prakāśa*). He explains "action" as "reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*). "Those two" refers to light and reflective awareness; the feminine gender is used in view of the word "action" (*kriyā*). "Māyā" [is explained as follows].

He explains [the phrase] "in the two-fold essential nature" as follows: by not abandoning the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the two-fold essential nature— that is, the two-fold primordial nature consisting of light (*prakāśa*) and self-awareness (*vimarśa*)— there occurs a discernment even as distinctness, that is, as a difference from itself.
"Reflection" (*parāmarśanam*)—by the force of the word "also," reflection as non-different [from the object] is also to be understood.

What kind of reflection? "Its own nature" (*svarūpa*); the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) are to be supplied. For this very reason, Sadāśiva and Īśvara are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)—that whose innate nature (*sahajaṃ svarūpam*) is "I am this."

"Of such a kind [is the power] of the Blessed One—the Lord (pati)—and not of the bound soul (paśu); this is the intended meaning. He shows that these three are to be distinguished from the category of "creation" by saying "these.
However, when their true nature is not fully understood, knowledge regarding distinct entities is merely action; it is only [in its pure state] that it is truly knowledge.
Diversity is devoid of both light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); thus, the light of the bound soul (*paśu*) consists,
in sequence, of light, light-and-non-light, and non-light—
characterized respectively by pleasure, pain, and delusion, and possessing the natures of illumination, activity, and restriction.
The qualities that are subject to regulation are sattva, rajas, and tamas. || 4 ||

But if this is so, then just as the powers of knowledge, action, and *māyā* are said to be non-different from the Supreme Lord, it would follow that the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* of the bound soul (*paśu*) are likewise [non-different].
Yet, they are counted as distinct from its male essence (*puṃstva*). How is this to be understood?
It dispels doubt:

the state of being a power belonging to the possessor of power, established through their distinction, is not predicated of these qualities which undergo transformation as instruments and effects. (5)

"Uncreated," the sense is that they exist as their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). He explains the portion of the verse beginning with "those very [things]" by saying "in their essential nature. "In the non-recognition of the essential nature"—that is, when there is a failure to recognize the ultimate essential nature caused by *māyā*. By the term "distinctness" (*bhinnatvam*),...

The term *māyā* is used here by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He clarifies the meaning of the word "pure" (*śuddha*) with the word "light" (*prakāśa*). For the *māyā* of the Lord consists of light and self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), whereas this [māyā] is devoid of those; such is the meaning. He then explains the sequence of the qualities *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Regarding the phrase "in sequence": therein, *sattva* is characterized by pleasure and has the nature of illumination; *rajas* is characterized by pain and has the nature of activity; *tamas* is characterized by delusion and has the nature of restriction—this is the sequence to be understood. Restriction (*niyama*) is non-activity due to dullness. (4)
Now he provides the introduction to the fifth verse with the words, "But surely, in this way...
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"In that same manner they follow," meaning they follow by virtue of being powers (*śakti*). "[They] are counted" means...
The sense is that [the categories] beginning with *prakṛti* are enumerated as distinct from the *puruṣa*.

For *prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and its effects, such as the *mahat* and so forth, consist precisely of *sattva* and the other qualities. Having thus provided this introduction:
Having introduced the verse, he explains it with the words "Difference" (*bheda*).
This would indeed be true if there were no apprehension of difference;
however, this difference—or rather, this conventional usage of difference—is what is being investigated. And in that regard:

The *puruṣa* has the nature of contracted pure consciousness (*saṃkucitacinmātrasvabhāva*). Its capacity for manifesting objects of existence and so forth is not innate, because that would entail its being constantly active; rather, it is produced through connection with something else. And therefore, from that [bondage], the bound soul (*paśu*)...

Since these qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest, exist as distinct from that which is suspected of possessing power (*śaktimat*), it is not said that the powers are "separate" [from it]— rather, they are so described because they serve as its instruments (*upakaraṇatvāt*).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
In the introduction, he states the resolution of the matter that was raised with the words "yadi" (if).

"Apprehension of difference" (*bhedagraha*) means the apprehension of the qualities (*guṇas*) as distinct from the Puruṣa. Intending to explain the verse by way of a stylistic turn, he first declares his intention to investigate this very difference: "This difference, however... (*bhedastvayam*).

Thus [it is said]. It performs precisely the investigation of difference therein, and in that regard: "contracted"—that which has come to a state of contraction by virtue of its own sovereignty; "whose nature is pure consciousness" (cinmātra)—meaning one whose essential form (*svarūpa*) is such; "the person" (*puruṣa*), known as the individual soul (*jīva*), is the "egg. Of this—

For the *puruṣa*, "illumination and so forth"—meaning illumination, manifestation, and the rest—is its innate form (*naisargikaṃ rūpam*), that is to say, its inherent nature (*sahajaṃ svarūpam*). To the question "Why?", he says: "always" (*sarvadā*).
"In connection with that" (*tatprasaṅgāt*) means in connection with the illumination and so forth of objects; for not even for a moment [is it otherwise].

The sense is that it is logical to abandon [the notion of] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, how can there be manifestation and so forth, which have existence as their object, for that [intrinsic nature]? To this he says: "But rather" (*api tu*). "[Produced by connection with another]" means produced by connection with a separate instrument. He states the resulting conclusion in order to provide a formal interpretation of the verse.

And thus: "by way of distinction" means that they exist as distinct entities. "From that"—meaning from that cause—it is connected [to the statement] that sattva and the others are not called powers (*śakti*).
Of what nature are these powers? They are said to be "expressed as non-distinct," meaning they are non-different from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*).
As it has been said:

"The identity of these two is eternal, like that of fire and its power to burn. By this, it is established that these qualities possess the nature of power (*śaktitva*), since they exist as distinct from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*).
The phrase "it is not taught" has already been explained. Now, in response to the inquiry—"It was said 'of the qualities' (guṇānām); how then do these possess the nature of being qualities?"—he says:
"But... [This is] because of their being instruments for the Supreme Lord with respect to external production.
Because it serves as an auxiliary; the meaning is that it is subordinate to that which has arrived [from the higher source]. As it has been said:
"Taking up the clay lump of the egg of power (śakty-aṇḍa), by means of the process of the revolving wheel of the egg of Māyā..."
With the rod of the primordial egg, the Blessed One, the potter, fashioned the vessel of the cosmic egg.
These are called the *guṇas*. Now, why are they said to be distinct from the *puruṣa*? It is said in reply:

here, this group of thirteen instruments (*karaṇa*)—consisting of the transformations of pleasure, pain, and delusion—and the tenfold effects (*kārya*)—likewise consisting of the transformations of pleasure, pain, and delusion—are so described.

It is experienced as having pleasure and so forth as its intrinsic nature; thus, if pleasure, pain, and delusion— which function through identity with the categories of instruments and effects— were to enter into identity with the Puruṣa who pervades them, then the Puruṣa would become composed of the entire creation down to the level of effects and instruments.

And since transformation (*pariṇāma*) is refuted, it follows that the Person (*puruṣa*), by virtue of his power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), is of universal form (*viśvarūpa*). Thus, there is no person who is not indeed the Lord (*īśvara*);
therefore, in an investigation into the true nature of the Person—which consists of non-recognition (*apratyabhijñānamaya*)—the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are indeed distinct.
It remains. || 5 ||

Thus [it is said]. For here, by the word "root" (*mūla*), there is the inclusion of *prakṛti*, whose nature is the state of equilibrium among the qualities such as *sattva*; and since the status of the staff as an instrument (*upakaraṇatva*) is well-known, there is no contradiction. He provides an introduction in order to explain the remaining term, "instrument" (*karaṇa*).
"Is it not so?"—referring to those qualities (*guṇas*). Here, he announces his intention to state the resolution with the words "it is said" (*ucyate*).
To make this announcement fruitful, he provides an introductory transition and explains the word "here" (*iha*), which has been made the subject:
"this"—that is, the tenfold group of effects standing before us, consisting of the subtle elements (*sūkṣmabhūtas*).
The meaning is: the fivefold group beginning with sound, which is the form of the gross elements, and the fivefold group beginning with space.
Regarding "pleasure and so forth" (*sukhādi*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), pain and delusion are included.
Pleasure, pain, and delusion constitute the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) whose nature is pleasure and so forth.
Those whose existence is through identity with the group of instruments and effects are such [entities].

Furthermore, "transformation" refers to the transformation of the three *guṇas* into the form of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth; it is called "defiled" because the state of being that [intellect, etc. is accepted as belonging to the *puruṣa* alone—this is the intended meaning. Thus, for this reason.
For this reason. [Objection: Let this be so; what follows from it? To this he says, "And thus" (*tathā ca*).

And that being the case, no individual soul (*jīva*) or person (*puruṣa*) would exist; rather, everyone would be God alone, because of having the form of the universe—this is the sense. He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Regarding the person who consists of non-recognition— that is, the individual soul (*aṇḍa*) who has not attained the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "I am He" with the Supreme Lord—
when one investigates his true nature, qualities such as *sattva* and the others appear as distinct; otherwise, they would not.
Because that would entail the consequence of [the self] being the Lord (Īśvara). Thus—so it stands—it becomes established. || 5 ||

"But how can knowledge and the rest take the form of *sattva* and so forth with respect to the bound soul (*paśu*)? To this he says: "Existence, bliss, and action belong to the Lord; their absence belongs to the bound soul.
That which consists of both is the passion (*rajas*) of the bound soul, which is suffering, composed of both *sattva* and *tamas*, and characterized by attachment. (6)

In this context, the Lord of the universe is the protector through the act of emanation and so forth, characterized by the manifold appearance of the universe— [that is, the manifold appearance of the universe as it manifests]—
and his essential nature is self-luminous. That which is the existence (*sattā*) of this Lord of the universe is his agency of being (*bhavanakartṛtā*).

That "vibration" (*sphurattā*), previously explained in the passage [Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.14], "That vibration is Great Being," is called the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) when, being of the nature of the wonder consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it is inseparable from the light of consciousness (*prakāśa*).
And because it consists in resting within one's own self through the abandonment of turning away from the Supreme (paraunmukhya), that very state is bliss;
thus, in this way, the Lord possesses this nature solely by virtue of being the conscious Self (cidātmatā). For the bound soul (paśu), however, there is both existence and its absence.
Here the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
Now he provides the introduction to the sixth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). This is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it, beginning with the words "sattā" (existence).
Regarding this,

the commentary explains "of the Lord" as "here": that which has as its very definition the manifold variety of manifestation— that is to say, that whose essence consists solely in the act of manifesting.
By means of the fivefold [acts] beginning with emission— namely, emission (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), destruction (dhvaṃsa), concealment (pidhāna), and grace (anugraha)—
he is the protector (pālayitṛ), that is, the guardian; because he protects, he is called the Lord (pati).

The meaning is "according to this principle. He provides the construction of the genitive case with the words "of that" (*tasya*). He explains the word "existence" (*sattā*) as "becoming" (*bhavana*).

The sense is that the state of being the agent of becoming—that is, the agency of the action of *bhū*—is "existence" (*sattā*), according to the principle that "that which exists (*sat*) is 'being' (*asti*); its state (*bhāva*) is existence (*sattā*). Where has this been explained?

Therefore, he says: "That is *sphurattā* (vibrancy). The word "iti" means "in this verse. He provides the construction for the term "action" (*kriyā*) with the words "that very same" (*saiva*). "That very same" refers to existence itself (*sattaiva*). "Consisting of reflective awareness" (*vimarśātmakaḥ*) means having the form of the reflective awareness "I" (*ahaṃvimarśarūpaḥ*). "The aesthetic wonder" (*camatkāraḥ*) is the savoring of one's own essential nature (*svarūpāsvādaḥ*); that is its form.

"Of which [she is the possessor]"—this refers to her. He also provides a construction for the word "Ānanda" (Bliss) as "being oriented toward the Supreme. "That very [thing]" means existence itself (*sattā*). He provides the conclusion with the words "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*). "This muchness of form" means the nature of existence and bliss (*sattānandarūpatā*). By this, everything up to the end of the section on "the Lord" (*pati*) has been explained. As for the passage beginning with "the absence thereof" (*tadabhāvaḥ*), etc.:

Bliss (*ānanda*) and its absence exist because their respective natures are contracted; therefore, that portion of existence which consists of bliss is *sattva*, whose function is the manifestation of light and happiness,
while its absence is *tamas*, which takes the form of obscuration and delusion— these two are *sattva* and *tamas*.
Although blue and non-blue exist through mutual exclusion like cause and effect (or rather,
like the properties of being an effect and being a cause), nevertheless, they are so in relation to a single substratum (*dharmin*) which is the object of a single reflective awareness.
