It appears through mutual intermingling, according to the principle of the nature of variegated colors produced by the blending of blue and non-blue;

therefore, this dual nature consisting of a mixed essence is the quality of *rajas*. For this very reason, *sattva* and *tamas*, whose natures are respectively luminous and non-luminous, abide here in conjunction.

The nature of suffering (*duḥkhatva*); for pleasure is indeed a single, solid manifestation (*prakāśa*) of a beloved son and so forth, while delusion (*moha*) is a single, solid non-manifestation (*aprakāśa*). That which is somehow manifest, such as in the form of a body afflicted by disease—which is undesirable—and that which is somehow non-manifest, such as...
That very state of suffering consists in being endowed with the undesirable quality of being subject to disease;

and he explains this very point with the words "but for the animal. Its absence—that is, the absence of its existence. To the question "Why? he says "contracted. [Objection: But what follows from that? To this he says "by that."
"Manifestation and blissful function" (*prakāśasukhavṛtti*) means having the nature of manifestation and bliss; "sattva" refers to the quality of *sattva*;
"its absence" (*tadabhāva*) means the absence of the portions consisting of existence and bliss; and "tamas" refers to the quality of *tamas*.
The phrase "like [the relationship of] cause and effect" is connected with the subsequent sentence.

Because the states of being the effect and the cause manifest simultaneously in a single substratum (dharmin), with reference to that substratum which is made the object of a single unifying cognition (*ekaparāmarśa*), there is a "variegated butterfly" (*citrapataṅga*)—
a butterfly endowed with a variegated form— and of its color, which consists of both blue and non-blue, [there is the following]:

By means of logic (*nyāya*). Relying on this, he explains the term "consisting of a duality" with the word "that" (*tat*). He explains "passion" (*rajas*) as the "quality of passion" (*rajoguṇa*). He explains "adhering" (*śleṣi*) as "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and connects it with the phrase "for this very reason. Here—in the quality of passion—by means of "adhesion," that is, by way of association, there is the state of suffering (*duḥkhatva*).

The nature of suffering. It establishes that very state of suffering through the term "dear" (*priya*); [as] the *Prakāśa* states: "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) means being evident by virtue of not being swallowed up. Having established pleasure and delusion, it also establishes the desired suffering for one who acts; "in some way" (*kathañcit*) means by some part.
By the undesirable— that is, the unwanted— the body, being afflicted by disease, indeed longs for death alone;
for manifestation depends upon the body, while non-manifestation is the state of not depending on the body,
as in one whose ailment has departed.

By that [state], there is the possession of auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇadharmayogitā*). That very thing—namely, the nature consisting of both light and non-light—is this very thing: suffering itself.
The ultimate reality of action (*kriyāparamārtha*) consists essentially in the sequence of prior and posterior. In this regard, however, the state of being neither [light nor non-light] is...
It does not exist, because it does not enter into any cognition whatsoever, whether of a conceptualized or non-conceptualized nature.

To explain: first, blue appears in a cognition of a non-conceptualized nature; however, the absence of blue—even though it is a mere nothing—is conceptualized by imagination, since it appears [in thought] as such for the duration of conventional discourse.

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)—let it indeed appear as both blue and non-blue due to the mixing of those two; however, that which is of neither form, if it is not made an object by a non-conceptual cognition of blue, then it would follow the conceptual cognition of "non-blue. Now, [if] that conceptual cognition...
If it were not made an object by non-conceptualized cognition, it would simply be blue; thus, for the bound soul (paśu), there is no fourth quality. The word "api" has the sense of "and":
for the bound soul, that existence is *sattva*, its absence is *tamas*, and that which consists of both is *rajas*. Thus.
The connection. || 6 ||

The ultimate reality of action (*kriyā-paramārtha*) is the innate nature of action. The sense is that because the quality of *rajas* has the form of activity (*pravṛtti*), and because activity is clearly of the nature of action.
[Objection: But let there also be a fourth quality which is of neither nature; to this he says: "not both."

"Because of non-penetration"—that is, because of the absence of transition. "Of that"—referring to that which is of neither form. Here he begins the justification with the words "for thus. By the word "first," there is the rejection of its being ultimately real and unconstructed. "In the intellect"—in the cognition of blue.

"From the mixing of both"—that is, from the cause of the intermingling of blue and non-blue; by the word "name," it is indicated that this appearance is undermined by impossibility. The construction is: "if [it] has not been made an object"; "it pursues" means, the intention being, for the sake of grasping itself. Now, the disciple—
He poses a question with the words "api" (also). Here too, he brings forward a fault with the word "akalpita" (unconstructed).
He explains the meaning of the word "api" with the words "api-śabdaḥ" (the word "api"). The meaning is that it is used in the sense of "ca," for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Having clarified the connection, he shows it with the words "paśoḥ" (of the bound soul). *Sattvam* refers to the quality of *sattva*.
The absence of that is the absence of *sattva*; *tamas* is the quality of *tamas*.

Thus, the application [of the terms] here is clear. The existence (*sattā*) of the Lord—the Supreme Lord—is His own abiding as the nature of radiant vibration; thus there is bliss (*ānanda*), and likewise there is action (*kriyā*).

Because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), even the triad exists as power (*śakti*) and is therefore one; for the bound individual soul (*paśu*), there is its absence—meaning the absence of existence and bliss—and by the word "also" (*api*), its presence as well;
thus, it consists of both, having the nature of the presence and absence of existence and bliss.
That which is well-known as *rajas* is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*). What is *rajas*? It is action;

the meaning is that its ultimate reality is action, by virtue of its being of the nature of activity. Furthermore, what is it? It is suffering—that is, its form is suffering—and likewise, it consists of *sattva* and *tamas*; for this very reason, it is "adhesive," meaning it is characterized by clinging.

Thus, the principle of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*), consisting of the Lord (*pati*) and the bound soul (*paśu*), has been briefly determined. Now, in order to determine the principle of the object (*prameyatattva*),
he says the following to first establish that "this is the principle of the object" with respect to the Lord:
Even those [cognitions] of the Lord which arise from non-conventional reflective awareness of "this-ness" appear variegated, being both mixed and distinct. (7)

It has been stated here that objects are indeed nothing but manifestations (*ābhāsa*). These are sometimes mixed together through a single act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which occurs when they possess a particularized form; at other times, they are reflected upon precisely as unmixed, which occurs when they possess a universal form. Thus, these objects possess both natures.
[Even those who possess both natures—K.

ṣ. ṣ.]—by means of the non-conventional, unconstructed state of "this-ness" (idaṃbhāva), there arises from the very nature of things the state of existence for that which consists of being and bliss, and the absence thereof for that which lacks it.

The state of *tamas* is present equally in both cases; however, while it exists as *śakti* in the Lord (*pati*), in the bound soul (*paśu*) it exists as the quality of *rajas*. Thus, its absence is not applicable here. Although even the absence of existence (*sattā*) is likewise undermined by impossibility, nevertheless, [regarding] the immeasurable...
This was stated with reference to sentient beings.
Now he provides the introduction to the seventh verse with the word "evam" (thus). This is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "ye 'pi" (even those who...).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

He recalls the previously mentioned matter for the sake of explaining the verse with the word "here" (*iha*). And those [appearances]—with the phrase "and sometimes," he reveals the matter intended to be stated by the word "when.
"Specific form" (*viśeṣarūpatā*) means "particularity" (*svalakṣaṇatā*); for therein lie the appearances of space and so forth.

They are indeed mixed. These appearances (*ābhāsas*) are of a dual nature—that is, they possess a mixed and unmixed essence—referring to objects such as blue, pleasure, and so forth. By this, the two terms "mixed" (*vimiśra*) and "distinct" (*vibhinna*) are explained. The word *asāmayika* is a compound.
He explains the word *pada* by means of its etymological analysis (*vigraha*), starting with the phrase "by that which is not conventional" (*asāmayikena*).

By "that which is not conventional"—meaning by that which consists of innate reflective awareness (*sahaja-parāmarśa-rūpa*), resembling the pointing of a finger [and so forth, consisting of innate reflective awareness of differentiation—K. ṣ. ṣ.]—even for the Lord, [objects] are not to be made objects of perception.
From the newborn infant up to the Lord Himself, they appear in that manner as a manifoldness through the mode of the general and the particular; for their "manifoldness" consists in this:
that their state of being mixed and unmixed shines simultaneously, resting within a single I-consciousness.

In the state of the Lord (īśvara), as an inseparable concomitant of the efflorescence of existence (bhāva), there is the void (śūnya)— which consists merely of the meaning of the negative particle uncolored by any object of negation and is characterized by the contraction of consciousness—
shining forth through the very light of consciousness as the negation of the "I" (ahantā).
He causes his teeth to shine with splendors that are not shared by others. || 7 ||

He explains [the word] "by the non-conceptual" (*akalpitena*). He explains the member "this-ness" (*idantā*) as "by the state of being this" (*idaṃbhāvena*). He explains the member "reflection" (*parāmarśa*) as "innate" (*sahaja*).
[Thus, it means] by way of the form of innate reflection, and not...

By means of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) consisting of the recollection of a word made the object of convention; for this very reason, by that which is similar to the pointing out [of an object] with a finger and so forth. He explains the word "of the earth" (*bhuvaḥ*) as "those which are to be made objects of perception. By this, [he excludes] that which is not conventional (*asāmayika*).

The analysis of the compound is indicated as "the objects of the ground of the reflective awareness of 'this-ness'. He explains the intended meaning of the word *api* with the phrase "even of the Lord. By this, it is indicated that the word *api* has been displaced [in the sentence]. Likewise, by this [phrase], it is shown that they are to be made the objects of the non-conventional reflective awareness of "this-ness."

It is indicated that the manifestation of entities through a general reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*), like that of a newborn infant, constitutes the state of Īśvara. He explains [the word] "thus" (*tathā*) by [the word] "by that" (*tena*).
He explains [the phrase] "appearing as variegated" (*citrāvabhāsinaḥ*) by [the word] "as variegated" (*citratayā*). When the question "Why? arises:

He provides the justification with the words "for [it is] variegated. "Resting in a single I-ness" means resting in a single subject. By this, having directly clarified the nature of the state of the Lord (*īśvara*), he states the conclusion. "Thus"—for this reason—it is "void" (*śūnya*).
Due to its proximity, it is precisely the subject of emptiness (*śūnyapramātṛ*) who has entered the state of *māyā*;

in the stage of Īśvara— that is, in the condition of Īśvara— it is the non-temporal "this-ness" (*idantā*), which takes the form of the negation of "I-ness" (*ahantā*)— that is, the form "I am not"— and which resembles a direct pointing with the head.
It causes this state to manifest—that is, it expands it. Of what nature is the void?

It is that which possesses the necessary concomitance—the pervasion—of the manifestation of objects, namely blue, pleasure, and so forth, which are cognizable as distinct from themselves; that manifestation being the non-conceptual flashing forth [of them] as distinct from themselves.

Therefore, [the Self] has the nature of the contraction of consciousness; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its being grasped as "I. Likewise, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), which is non-existence (*abhāva*), is such that its form consists solely of that which is untinged by the object to be negated—that is, devoid of contact with a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)—and not merely in the form of "I am not."

Form (rūpa) is, for this very reason, manifested solely through the light of consciousness—that is, by way of the very existence of the light of consciousness—and not, as in the case of the realm of Māyā, as something manifested through a state of non-existence; rather, it appears to itself by virtue of its own self-luminosity. || 7 ||
Thus, such is the nature of the object of knowledge regarding the Lord (pati) in the form of Īśvara;
but as for the Blessed One Paramaśiva, how could even the discourse on the object of knowledge arise?
For it is precisely the capacity to give rise to the discourse on the object of knowledge that constitutes the state of Sadāśiva-Īśvara in the Blessed One.
Therefore, he now dispels the doubt as to what the nature of the object of cognition is with respect to the bound soul (*paśu*) by means of these three verses:
"But those objects which appear as distinct must be postulated [as belonging] to the inner self (*pratyagātman*)."
[It exists] within the range of memory, imagination, and so forth, under various distinct designations.
His creation is unique and subsists upon the creation of the Lord;
yet, through ignorance, it is perceived as real by that [individual soul] due to the power of the Lord.
By means of the activity of conceptualization— which is of the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), which is immovable in order to obstruct its own repose,
and which takes the form of the diversity of various phonemes— || 10 ||

It highlights the distinction: whereas for the inner self (pratyagātman), objects exist as such in the form of cognizable entities, they do not exist in the manner described for the Lord (īśvara). Those objects whose appearances are differentiated by being either mixed or unmixed are [referred to as] "diverse" (bhinna).
Objects, which consist of both the particular and the universal, are unmixed for each individual inner self—[unmixed self-awareness—K.
Ṣ. Ṣ.]—here the commentary states:
Now he provides the introduction to the eighth, ninth, and tenth verses with the word "evam" (thus).
This is clear. Then, having presented the verse, he explains it with the words "te tu" (but they), where the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:

"It illuminates"—the meaning is that particles (*nipāta*) function as illuminators (*dyotaka*). Now, one might ask: "What is this distinction? To which he replies: "of the inner self" (*pratyagātmanaḥ*). "In this way" (*ittham*) means by the manner that is about to be described.
The word "thus" (*iti*) marks the conclusion of the statement of the distinction. The word *bhinna* is a compound.

He explains [the term] by means of its analysis as "mixed" (*miśra*). In this context, "mixed" refers to those things whose nature is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while "unmixed" refers to those whose nature is the universal (*sāmānya*). He explains the component "appearance" (*avabhāsa*) as "manifestation" (*ābhāsa*), meaning a distinct manifestation.

Having thus formed a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the two members, he provides the explanation: "having the nature of both the particular and the universal. The term "objects" (*arthāḥ*) is explained by its very utterance (*nigadavyākhyāta*). By this, the analytical resolution (*vigraha*) is indicated as: "those objects which have a distinct appearance. [This refers to] the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
Thus he explains the term "per person" (*pratipuruṣam*). He explains the prefix *prati* as a distributive particle:
"to be fashioned" (*prakalpyāḥ*), meaning "to be conceived," refers to that which has the nature of self-awareness and realization, whose essence is the unmixed light of the "I" (*ahaṃprakāśa*).

According to the individual latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of each living being, through various designations such as "this one is dear" or "this one is an enemy," and in accordance with specific mental dispositions,
[the mind] engages in recollection and imagination, employing those respective diverse pleasures, pains, and so forth.

"In the conceptualization of one thing and then another, and in the application of mental constructs (*vikalpa*),"— by this it is meant that for the Lord, objects are made the focus of pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) independently of the nature of mental constructs; whereas for the bound soul (*paśu*), those same objects become established upon a mental construct characterized by the impulse of mutual exclusion (*apohana*).
"Because it is useful for worldly transactions such as rejection and acquisition.

Now, if the object is exactly the same whether it is non-conceptualized or conceptualized, what is the distinction regarding the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) as being either the Lord (*pati*) or the bound soul (*paśu*)? It is said: "Of that... [and so forth].
"Creation performed by the animal (paśu)"—

[as stated in the phrase] "unmixed" (*avyāmiśra*). "Unmixed" means that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which constitutes one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), has not entered into a state of being mixed with anything else through the limitation of objects.

"Consciousness" (*saṃvedana*) is itself "comprehension"—that is, knowledge; that is its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Here too, he provides a synonym by saying "unmixed" (*asaṅkīrṇa*); the meaning is that it consists of the form of the individual self-luminosity (*ahaṃprakāśa*) determined for each person. He explains "to be postulated" (*prakalpyāḥ*) as "to be imagined" (*kalpanīyāḥ*).
In response to the expectation of "by whom," he explains the phrase "distinct for each" with the words "for every living being.

This is stated by supplying the word "appropriately" (*yuktatvena*), meaning: in accordance with—that is, in conformity with—the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) consisting of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) which is produced by one's own individual tendencies (*svavāsanā*) for every living being.
He clarifies these very perceptions [with the words] "this is dear.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what use there is for those perceptions, he himself says something: "meditation" (bhāvanā).
Furthermore, in response to the inquiry as to where those perceptions are employed—

He explains "within the range of memory, imagination, and so forth" with the words "in recollection. He states the object to be included by the word "and so forth" (ādi) with the words "in conceptualization" (saṅkalpane). For when a beloved is remembered, pleasure arises, whereas when an enemy is [remembered], pain arises; this should be applied by oneself. Now, by this—

To the question "What is meant by this?", he says: "This is what is meant. He demonstrates exactly what was said with the words "of the Lord. "Objects of pure reflective awareness" means they are fit to be made objects of the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (idantā), which is like pointing with a finger.
"O you who take delight in the mutual exclusion [of things]— that is, those engaged in the forceful application of distinguishing one thing from another—
because this is necessary for practical discourse (*vyavahāra*). The underlying sense is that otherwise, because of their being conflated, practical discourse would not be possible.
Now he provides the commentary on the second verse, beginning with "nanu" (but surely).
Here, the commentary states:
"In the state of being the Lord and the bound soul"—that is, by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), in the absence of the Lord being an object of cognition.
And in the absence of the state of being an object of knowledge for the individual soul (*paśu*),
there exists [a level] above those objects created by Īśvara; therefore, depending upon that creation of Īśvara, it is unique and restricted to each individual subject (*pratipramātṛ*).
For example, when one thinks, "This is for my heart," that which is created belongs to him alone at that time, not to anyone else. [Objection:
But if even an animal possesses the power of creation, is it then the Lord (Īśvara) himself? [Reply: True, he is indeed the Lord. [Objection:
If this is so, why does the creation not become common [to all]? It would be so, if...

One should fully understand one's own power; for as long as that [power] remains unrecognized by one who is under the sway of another, the activity of conceptualization—the capacity for conceptualizing—arises. Now, by what is it aroused in him?
He says: by the nature of the Supreme Lord’s reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which is characterized as the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*).

Having provided the introduction, he promises to state the resolution in order to explain the verse, saying: "It is said. He shows that the genitive case in the word *tasya* (of that) functions as an agentive genitive by stating:
"performed by the animals" (*paśukartṛkā*). The word *sṛṣṭiḥ* (creation) is explained by its very utterance (*nigadavyākhyātam*). [The word] *uparivartinī* (situated above).
For it is precisely upon the son and others created by the Lord that a person projects qualities such as attractiveness;

this has been established by logical necessity (*arthāt*). Relying on this, he explains [the phrase] "subsisting upon the creation of the Lord" with the words "for this very reason. "Subsisting" means depending upon; otherwise, [it would not be so].

The sense is that it lacks an objective referent (*nirviṣayatvāt*). He explains "unique" (*asādhāraṇī*) by saying "restricted to each individual cognizer" (*pratipramātṛniyatā*). He demonstrates this very restriction with the words "for example" (*tadyathā*). Here, the student asks, "But surely... (*nanu*). The teacher, relying on the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthadṛṣṭi*), [responds].
"He accepts it, saying 'It is true'—that is, the bound soul (paśu). Again, the disciple asks: 'But if this is so'—meaning, such being the case—'why does it not happen?
The implication is that it would be more logical for the creation of the Lord to be common to all. The Guru replies:"
"It might be" (*bhavet*); "might be" means "it could be. To the objection that "then it certainly does exist," he says "if" (*yadi*).

The word "animal" (*paśu*) is to be supplied as the subject; the sense is that [the animal] does not know. Now, in response to the inquiry "How is it that it does not know?", the remaining second half of the verse follows.

He explains the third verse with the words "yāvatā" (to the extent that). "Yāvatā" means for which reason; "sā" refers to that [power] whose nature is emission (*sṛṣṭi*). "Tasya" refers to that bound soul (*paśu*); "vikalpakriyā" means having the form of the activity of conceptualization;
"vikalpanaśaktiḥ" means the power of performing conceptualization. "Udeti" means it arises or is produced. Now, as for that—

"Let it arise," [the author] says, anticipating the question: "Since the power of being dependent on another cannot arise by itself, who causes it to arise? He answers with the word "nanu. He provides the reply with the word "āha.
When the expectation arises as to what he says, he explains [it] with the words "īśaśaktyā" (by the power of the Lord), [expounding it as] "īśvarasya" (of the Lord).
By way of being reflective awareness— that is, through the state of internal, pure reflective awareness—

of that which is characterized as the mass of sounds, whose nature is the collection of phonemes beginning with 'A'. By forming a compound of the word *īśa* with the word *śakti*, [the author] intends to prevent an interruption of his own repose in the middle.
That power which consists of the circle of deities beginning with Brāhmī, whose purpose is the obstruction of the supreme sovereignty characterized by repose in one's own essential nature.

It is variegated by those various diversities of phonemes beginning with *ka*; and because that conceptualizing activity of the bound soul (*paśu*) lacks stability in any single point, it is flickering; thus, it is permeated by the diversity of phonemes such as "this is a friend" or "this is an enemy."

"By means of that activity of conceptualization (*vikalpana-kriyā*), which is characterized by being permeated [by consciousness], there occurs the unique creation of the bound soul (*paśu*), whose very nature is that of the Lord (*īśvara-svabhāva*) itself.
Having thus provided the syntactical connection (*yojanā*), he explains [the word] *svarūpa*. He explains the component *sva* as follows:

Regarding the term *svarūpa*: he explains the fourth case-ending (*caturthī-vibhakti*) as "purpose" (*prayojana*). He explains the word *śakti* as "the [powers] beginning with Brāhmī. That which is characterized by resting in one's own nature (*svarūpa-viśrānti-lakṣaṇaḥ*)—that is, whose very nature is resting in its own form—is the obstruction to supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya-uparodhaḥ*).
That which has as its purpose the taking of refuge in the dharma known as supreme sovereignty—
that wheel of deities beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Śavargī,
consisting of the eight Mātṛkās beginning with Brāhmī— is "composed of that," meaning it has their very nature. [This refers to] each respective phoneme...

He explains the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth) as a qualifier by means of the words "taistaiḥ" (by those various [factors]). With reference to the absence of such variety in the *ava* group—[reading *tādṛgvaicitryābhāvamupekṣya* for *tādṛgvaicitryābhāvamapekṣya*]—it is said to begin with the letter *ka*. For indeed, the variety of the letter *a* arises through the power of its fivefold energy (*śakti*).

"The *k*-group [arises] from the vowel *i*, and the *c*-group from [the vowel *e*], and so forth. By that aforementioned power (*śakti*), there is this activity of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-kriyā*), for conceptual construction consists precisely of phonemes, since its nature is the recollection of sound.
He explains the term "mobile" (*calayā*) as a qualifier, saying "of that" (*tasya*). "Of that"—meaning, because it is the substratum of this [conceptual construction].

Because the limited soul (*paśu*), who is the *aṇu*, remains [in this state], there is an absence of firm establishment—meaning an absence of rest—and thus he is "fickle. As a result of this, the word "this and that" (*tattad*) is applied here as an attribute; by means of that fickle nature, whatever occurs such as "this is a friend" or "this is an enemy," and so forth.

"Varṇavaicitryam" means "interwoven with" or "pervaded by" that [variety of phonemes]. He then refers back to the word containing the aforementioned qualification; and by providing the object for the question "by what? which arose from doubt, he fulfills the expectancy through that act of conceptualization (*vikalpanakriyā*).
He explains the compound *tadātmanaḥ* by first providing its analysis (*vigraha*) as "of that Īśvara.

By this, it is indicated that *tadātmanaḥ* is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "of that [Īśvara], who is the self of the bound soul (*paśu*). The "uncommon creation" is the creation of conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*).
The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Because it is easy to understand, [the example] is:
"A five-faced, four-tusked elephant runs in the sky.
Thus, even in this case of being mixed (*vimiśratā*), there is the creation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

One subsists solely upon those appearances created by the Lord; thus it is said that the entire creation pertaining to bound souls (*pāśavī sṛṣṭiḥ*), which is the creation of mental representations (*pratyayasṛṣṭiḥ*), subsists upon the creation of the Lord. || 10 ||

The phrase "in the form of the vital breath" (*prāṇarūpayā*) has not been explained. He provides the justification for the statement "subsisting upon the creation of the Lord" by means of the word "five" (*pañca*) in the context of mixture—namely, in the application of a new fivefold state to the teeth and so forth, and in the application of the movement of a new space to the elephant; [he applies] those...
"Manifestations"—that is, manifestations in the form of the five teeth and so forth—he "subsists upon," meaning he depends on them;

for all of this has been created by the Lord alone in various places as separate entities, while the individual soul merely performs the act of joining them together according to its own will. If it were not created by the Lord, what [could the soul do]?

The sense is: "With what would one join [it]? Therefore, for this reason, it has been stated that the entire "fettered creation"—namely, the creation of individual souls (*jīva*), the creation of mental cognitions (*pratyaya*), and the creation of conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*)—subsists upon the creation of the Lord (*īśvara*). This is what was said; such is the meaning.
Thus, the summarized meaning of these three verses is as follows: "But" (*tu*) signifies distinction;

regarding the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—the agent who exists as the individual soul (*jīva*) in the form of a bound creature (*paśu*) within each person—"those" [objects] consist of distinct manifestations, which have the nature of both general and particular, and whose essence is manifestation (*ābhāsa*).
Objects such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, which are distinct from one another and from themselves,

when they become the objects of memory, imagination, and the like— that is, when they are apprehended by memory and other such cognitions— are designated by various distinct names corresponding to their respective diversities.

The creation of that inner self (*pratyagātman*)— which is to be conceptualized (*prakalpyāḥ*), meaning thoroughly imagined (*prakarṣeṇa kalpanīyāḥ*), through designations such as "distinct animal-nature" and so forth, as well as "Dittha-ness" and so forth, because it brings about pleasure, pain, and the like by means of specific mental impressions (*bhāvanāviśeṣa*).— is [as follows]:

The creation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which consists of the mental fabrication of designations regarding the reality of objects that appear as distinct, is unique [to each individual]. For what is a friend to one person is not necessarily the same for another. Likewise, it subsists upon the creation of the Lord (*īśa-sṛṣṭi*)—that is, by standing above the Lord’s creation, it depends upon it.

Indeed, it is within the person created by the Lord that the individual soul (jīva) subsequently establishes a state of friendship; now, if the creation pertaining to bound souls (paśu) is of the nature of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), then what would the supreme creation of the Lord do for the bound soul? This is resolved as follows:

But it does not create that body even in its own essential nature; this aforementioned creation of the individual soul (jīva) exists as if real only through ignorance—that is, by existing as something unknown due to its being one's own power (svaśakti), for otherwise it would follow that this [creation] too possesses the status of God. Of that self—of that bound soul (paśu) whose nature is that of God.

Through that which is connected [to consciousness], through the moving one, and likewise through the form belonging to the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—that is, through the accomplishment of the vital breath (*prāṇasiddhi*)—and thus through the activity of conceptualization (*vikalpakriyā*), which is variegated by the diversity of various phonemes, [the world] comes into being.
For it is precisely by means of conceptualization that the individual soul (*jīva*) produces all appearances. But [one might ask] of that bound soul (*paśu*): [how can this be]?
In response to the question "For what reason does that act of conceptualization exist?", he says:
"for the sake of obstructing its own repose. This is to be construed with the phrase "by the power of the Lord" (*īśaśaktyā*).
That power of the Lord—which consists of the vowels and so forth—is for the purpose of resorting to the repose of His own sovereignty.

By that power, which consists of the eightfold group beginning with Brāhmī and is denoted by the eight groups of letters (rūpavarga), she manifests her own power and reveals her own sovereignty. By means of the conceptualization of those forms, she brings under her control the individual soul (jīva) in its form as a bound creature (paśu). As it is said in the Spandaśāstra:
Having become an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds,
and having had his sovereign power eclipsed by *kalā*, he is known as a bound soul (*paśu*).
Thus [it is said]. And since the commentary on this has already been provided under the section on "Action" (*kriyā*), no further effort is made here.

Of what kind is the power of the Lord? It is that which is variegated (*citrayā*) by means of that very variety of phonemic forms—the forms of the letters beginning with *ka*—which is therefore wondrous.

From the *avarṇa*, which denotes Brahmanī, there arises the sevenfold group beginning with the *ka*-group, which takes on diverse forms and denotes the great sovereignty (*māheśvarya*) and other powers. Among these, from the vowel *a* arise the *ka*-group and the letter *ha*.

According to the statement that "the throat is the locus of the letter *a*, the visarga, and [the gutturals]," it is indeed the letter *a* itself which, having attained grossness in the throat, manifests as the *ka*-group,
the letter *ha*, and the visarga. From the letter *i*, the *ca*-group and the letter *ya* [manifest].

Because of the statement that "the palate [is the locus] of the *icuyaśas*," this should be applied accordingly in all cases. As for the production of vowels such as *ā* from consonants such as *a* within the *ava*-group (*avarga*), that need not be counted here due to its subtlety. For instance, the vowel *a*:

It is conventionally designated as the unsurpassed essential nature (*svarūpa*) endowed with the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*). Its manifestation as a formal appearance occurs when the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), which was previously latent within it, becomes manifest.
From that very same [nature], due to its consisting of consciousness, the letter *i* arises when the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) becomes manifest. Of that...
This creation of Īśvara is both common and otherwise, because it appears clearly;
through the abandonment of conceptual construction and one-pointedness, one gradually attains the state of Īśvara. (11)
The divine creation (*aiśvara-sarga*) is twofold: common, such as a jar and so forth, and uncommon, which is designated otherwise (as indicated by Kṣemarāja).
Upon the attainment of the object known as "that which is to be sought" (*eṣaṇīya*), there arises the letter *ī*, which is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) called "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*).

At its manifestation, there is the emergence of the letter *u*. At the manifestation of the gross form of that very same [sound], there is the emergence of the letter *ū*. Following that, there is the letter *ṛ*, which does not produce any phoneme but consists of the kindling of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). Indeed, the letter *ra* is the designator of fire.

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is the letter *i*; their conjunction is the letter *ṛ*. Its intensification is the letter *ṝ*. Likewise, from the power of will arises the letter *ḷ*, which is of the nature of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*). Since the letter *la* denotes "taste" (*rasa*) by virtue of being dental, and "taste" itself is indeed "relish," that very [letter] conjoined with the letter *i* becomes the letter *ḷ*.

The grossness of that [sound] is the letter *lū*. The conjunction of the Absolute (*anuttara*) and Will (*icchā*) is the letter *e*. Again, the conjunction of the Absolute with the subject (*pramātṛ*) is the letter *ai*. The conjunction of the Absolute with Expansion (*unmeṣa*) is the letter *o*. Once more, the conjunction of the Absolute with the subject is the letter *au*.

The attainment of a slight increase in *anuttara* is the *visarjanīya*; the attainment of a slight increase in *unmeṣa* is the *anusvāra*. Up to this point is the subtle creation (*sūkṣma-sṛṣṭi*). And this very [creation] is that whose power is obscured by *kalā*.

This has been stated by this word: for indeed, by the *kalās* beginning with the letter *a*, which bring about differentiation, the sovereign power (*vibhava*) of Śrī Śiva, characterized by oneness, is utterly eclipsed. Beyond this, however, is the gross creation (*sthūlasṛṣṭi*), because it consists of the gross forms of the letters *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ*.

Enough with this elaboration regarding the seven groups beginning with the *ka*-class. The word "tattadvarṇe" (in each respective letter) is to be connected to both [contexts] by means of *tantra* (elliptical repetition). || 10 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the eleventh verse with the words "nanvevam" (But if this is so).
This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "sādhāraṇa" (common).
Here the commentary explains the word *aiśa* as *aiśvara*.
It clarifies its twofold nature by stating "and common" (*sādhāraṇaśca*), for otherwise it would have been designated differently.
By this [statement], "otherwise" refers to the double moon and so forth; and its general characteristic is what is called "clear manifestation.
This very creation, when—by means of the process of abandoning conceptual construction—it is grasped by that non-conceptual [cognition],...

In this way, when the meaning of "A" becomes clearly manifest by relying on one-pointedness, it becomes the locus for the reflective awareness of sovereignty as "I am this," through the method of avoiding the opening and closing of the eyes while maintaining the internal object and the external gaze.
By means of the instruction on avoiding the opening and closing of the eyes— as indicated by Kṣemarāja— gradually,

through the increasing intensity of practice, it strikes down the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) and reveals the state of the Lord (*īśvara*). Furthermore, as for this creation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-sarga*):
Commentary: He connects [the phrase] "because of its clear manifestation" with "and of that.
The sense is: because those two kinds of creation are endowed with clear manifestation.
Having explained the first half-verse, he explains the second half-verse with "so this. So this...

Creation is twofold: divine creation (*aiśa-sarga*). He explains the two words "by means of the gradual abandonment of conceptual construction" (*vikalpahānena krameṇa*) with the word "when" (*yadā*).

"By means of the gradual abandonment of conceptual construction" means by the sequence of abandoning conceptual constructions accomplished through the practice of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth. "In that" refers to the form of divine creation.

"One-pointedness" (*ekāgratvam*) means the state of being one-pointed (*ekāgrabhāvam*). "Having resorted to" (*avalambya*) means having relied upon (*āśritya*). By this, it is indicated that the ablative case in the expression "from one-pointedness" (*aikāgryāt*) is used with the elision of a verbal suffix (*lyablope*). He explains the term "the station of lordship" (*īśvaratāpadam*) as "the station of the reflective awareness of sovereignty in the form 'I am this'."

It becomes a term for the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) related to the Lord. When, in order to fulfill the expectancy of the word "when" (*yadā*), He Himself states something in its resultant form, [He says] "then" (*tadā*).
Then, by way of abandoning both inward focus on the object (*antarlakṣya*) and outward vision (*bahirdṛṣṭi*), as well as the closing and opening of the eyes (*nimeṣonmeṣa*).
With the internal as the object of focus and the gaze directed outward, free from blinking or opening of the eyes—
this indeed is the Śāmbhavī Mudrā, concealed in all the scriptures.

Thus, according to the sequence taught in the *Mahārahasya-śāstra*, by means of the gradation of practice— that is, by attaining the ultimate limit of practice— one strikes down the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*),
which is to say one destroys it, as well as [the limited] lordship, and [awakens] the lordship that exists in the ultimate sense.
It reveals—that is, it makes manifest. As it has been said:
"This very power of Śiva, whose nature is action, resides within the bound soul (paśu);
when it remains on its own path, it is the binder, but when known, it brings about accomplishment."

Thus, the remainder [of the sentence] is that the meaning of "having the internal as the object" (*antarlakṣya*) would be as follows: the person (*puruṣaḥ*) has as his object of attention (*lakṣyam*) the internal reality (*āntaraṃ vastu*) called pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*), which exists as the innermost essence (*sarvāntaḥ-sāratvena*) within.

That which is called "animal" (pāśava) also becomes common [to all] if it is known by the power of the Lord (īśa-śakti) through a reversal of the previously mentioned form— that is, when one has realized identity with that [power]— just like the various ritual options such as nourishment (āpyāyana), malevolent rites (abhicāraṇa), and pacification (śānti).
Of one who has deposited the mantra and whose internal organ (mind) has been purified through meditation. || 11 ||

Such [is he]. Likewise, externally—that is, with respect to any external object grasped through concentration (*dhāraṇā*)—he should be one whose gaze (*dṛṣṭi*) is fixed upon it; furthermore, he should be free from the opening and closing of his eyes, maintaining a steady gaze fixed right there on that object.

This is because, through the very power of one's own nature (*svabhāva*), the destruction of views occurs by attaining non-conceptuality; otherwise, even for one intent on focusing on pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), external conceptual constructions would still manifest by the force of one's own nature. But for the deluded person, this occurs by abandoning the opening and closing [of the eyes].

Even if non-conceptuality is attained, it would be of the nature of insentience; therefore, it is said that "the object of focus is internal. Alternatively, "having the internal as the object" means the cultivation of the state of pure consciousness (*cinmayatā*) everywhere.

"Having the external as the field of vision" means engaging with external objects like an ordinary person. "Freedom from opening and closing [of the eyes]"— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The following is a continuation of the thought based on standard Tantric and Advaitic contexts:* "—refers to the state of being free from the duality of manifestation and withdrawal."
It has been stated that this is the absence of conceptualization and discursive thought regarding those objects; enough with further revealing the secret.
This Śāmbhavī Mudrā—the mudrā consisting of the Śāmbhava means (upāya)—is a specific state that bestows bliss, hidden in all the scriptures by the learned.
By the phrase "it has been stated," the attainment of the state free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpatā) was explained by way of the common creation (*sarga*).

Now, with the phrase "in another way," he explains that its attainment can also occur by way of the uncommon creation, according to an alternative perspective, beginning with "furthermore" (*kiñca*). [This refers to] the fettered state (*pāśava*).
That which is produced by Īśvara as residing within the sacrificial animal, appearing in the form of two moons and so forth—
by means of that which is known through the reversal of the previously mentioned form,
that is, by knowing it through the reversal of the state of *mātṛkā*— I am pure.

"By means of the state of thorough comprehension" (parāmarśabhāvena) means "having known. "Thoroughly comprehended identity" (parijñātaṃ tādātmyam) refers to one for whom there is oneness with the Lord—that is, one's own identity with Him. For such a person, even that creation becomes entirely common, whereby every object imagined by the yogi [becomes manifest].
They experience [the result] beforehand. And here, one should not be deluded by the conceit "I am the Lord," whether expressed in words or performed through action;
for in this context, the firmness of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is required, otherwise they would not apply such firmness to the mantras that produce the illusions of a magician.
And those endowed with innate gnosis (sahajajñāna) should not be confused by this; enough of this prolixity.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "nourishment" (āpyāyana). Nourishment means growth; "abhicāraṇa" means malevolent magic (abhicāra); "śānti" means the rite of pacification (śāntikarma); and by the word "etc. (ādi), [other rites are implied].

The grasping of all objects to be accomplished through mantras and so forth; "of the one for whom the mantra has been deposited" means of the practitioner who has employed the mantra. This was said with reference to those seized by such conceit regarding the mere recitation of the mantra; [it applies] to one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been purified by the mantra. Regarding the mantra:
This means: of one whose mind is engaged in meditative cultivation. || 11 ||

Thus, by the expulsion of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), when one has become assimilated to the non-conceptual form, liberation is shown to be one's own direct realization (*svapratyaya*) characterized by the direct perception of the universal self (*viśvātmaka-sākṣātkāra*). Now, [this is further explained].

He demonstrates that [this state] exists even in the absence of the expulsion of conceptual constructions (vikalpa): "For one who fully understands, 'All this is my own manifestation,' there is the state of the Great Lord (maheśatā), even amidst the proliferation of conceptual constructions, for he is the Self of the universe. (12)
For that which is called the inner self (pratyagātman) is not some other limited being such as "I" who am a bound soul (paśu);
rather, it is that Supreme One alone, who is the single mass of light consisting of the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping, and He is I.
"And I myself [am that]," it is said;
now he provides the introduction to the twelfth verse with the word "evam" (thus).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):
By the expulsion of conceptualization— that is, by the abandonment of conceptual thought— in that state of self-identification, which is oneness in the form of non-conceptuality;
[this is] characterized by the direct realization of the universal Self, namely, the direct realization of Supreme Śiva.

"Consisting of its own nature" means consisting of self-cognition alone—that is, the knowledge of the Self itself—and not the cognition of a separate Supreme Lord. "Even in the absence of the removal of conceptualization"—that is, even in the absence of the abandonment of conceptual thought—"him"—namely, liberation. Having thus provided this introduction:
Having presented the verse, he explains it with the words "All [is] mine.
Here, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) initiates the procedure to explain the portion "of me, the Self of the universe" (*viśvātmano mama*).
"Indeed not. For—because—that which is called the *pratyagātman* (the inner self), namely the individual soul (*paśu*) or *aṇu*, is not some other entity distinct from the Supreme Lord.
Who is that? It is he who is referred to as "I" and "mine" by means of the word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), spoken of as the possessor (*svāmin*).

...up to: furthermore, in response to the inquiry "Who is this 'I'?", he speaks according to another perspective by saying "api tu" (but rather). "Parigrahītau" means those two who have been made the objects of apprehension by standing as witnesses;
"ghana" means dense or compact, [referring to] that light (*prakāśa*) by which the grasped and the grasper are so constituted.

He who is the Supreme—who, even while transcending all, is the reality consisting of everything—that alone am I. Now, one might object: "Become that which you are; but he is not you, because he is the All. To this, he says: "And he" (*sa ca*).
And he—the Supreme—is indeed I, because I abide as "I" everywhere.
But even among immobile beings, there is another [kind]; therefore, the creation of diversity is also my sovereign power characterized by absolute freedom.
When such a realization has become firm, one whose conceptual constructions have not yet been entirely exhausted remains liberated even while living.
He is liberated. As it has been said:
"Even doubt should not be suspected; this state of being free from doubt is manifest. (12)
Indeed, there must be the recognition "I," for otherwise it would be impossible for a tree to draw sap toward itself.

However, in the case of difference, no one else can be "I," because that would result in insentience due to being an object of the "this-ness" (idantā) [of objective perception]. Relying on this, he explains the verse with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). Therein also:

He explains "all this" as "the creation of conceptual construction. By the word "also," the creation of the Lord is included. It belongs to "me"—to the reality denoted by the word "I," which in ultimate truth possesses the aforementioned nature, but which in appearance stands as the subject (pramātṛ) consisting of the body and so forth.

He explains "vibhava" (sovereignty) as "svātantrya" (autonomy). The sense is that sovereignty is indeed autonomy itself, not wealth and such. He explains "of one who thus fully knows" with the word "ityevam.
He explains "even in the proliferation of conceptual constructions" with the word "aparikṣīṇa" (undiminished). By the word "api" (even),...
For them, there should generally be an absence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);

however, it should be understood that even when the flow of occasional conceptual constructions arises due to the nature of the body, they remain as the Great Lord (*maheśatā*) himself. This [state] does not exist for those who are perpetually seized by conceptual construction.

There is no such rule for this reflection, because it is absent there. The word "api" (also/even) is to be applied twice, according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). He explains the term "maheśatā" (the state of being the Great Lord) by saying "liberated even while living. The sense is that liberation is indeed the attainment of the state of the Great Lord (*maheśabhāva*).

And here, the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) is implied precisely by the proliferation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Regarding this, he states the consensus of the former teachers (*pūrvācārya*) with the words "as it has been said. To the question "What was said?", he replies: "Even doubt...
The meaning here is as follows: enough with doubts concerning objective reality (*vastu*), which have been worn away through the power of yoga.

Even for yogins, there may arise a doubt—perhaps a doubt in the form of a conceptual construction arising from the very nature of the body—which must not be doubted; that is, it should not be made an object of suspicion by asking, "For what purpose has this come?"—insofar as such doubt would cause agitation. However, [it should be understood as follows]:
The intended meaning is that one should lead [the senses] precisely to the state of being objects of disregard. As it has been said:
"By means of disregard and detachment alone, the perceptions of the senses do not perceive [the reality].
This is clear—that is, manifest—and freedom from doubt arises.

"Because for one seized by doubt, it is clearly characterized by doubt. Nor should this conceit be maintained at all times by those seized by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it is undermined by impossibility.
[Objection: "In that case, what is the difference between the bound and the liberated regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*)? It is said in reply:
The liberated one perceives this common object of knowledge as non-different from his own self, just like Maheśvara; whereas the bound one, however, perceives it as being absolutely different.
That which consists of the form of "I-consciousness" (ahamiti), presiding over the entire range of subjects from the venerable Lord Sadāśiva down to the level of a worm—
those who, despite being seized by conceptual thought (vikalpa), do not know their own self in that way;
One should offer salutations from afar to those afflicted by the defects of the humors (sannipāta-doṣa); enough with further elaboration.

In place of "sargaḥ" [in the verse], the reading "sargaḥ" is commendable; for the word *sarva* generally implies the inclusion of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) within the creation (sṛṣṭi), and not—

It is precisely from the creation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). However, if the reading is *sargaḥ*, then by the word "this" (*ayam*), there is a reference back to the conceptual construction under discussion; by the word "creation" (*sarga*), there is the naming of the act of creating. The meaning is:
"this creation," that is, the creation of conceptual construction in the form of the creation of individual souls (*jīva*). Furthermore, by the word "also" (*api*)...

The reference is to the creation of Īśa. However, Kashmiri scribes, due to a slight similarity in sound, have written "sarva" (all) in place of "sarga" (creation). Only those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*) can be the authority here. In some manuscripts, the reading "so 'ham" (that I am) also exists, but that is not appropriate.

Because this treatise is devoted solely to determining this very point— namely, that [the world] is established through the delusion produced by the elaboration (prapañca) composed for the purpose of explaining the statement "I am the Self of the universe" (mama viśvātmanaḥ).

Furthermore, this would result in the verse becoming a mere restatement (anuvāda), and a restatement is not appropriate within the Sūtras. Although the commentator has provided a restatement in accordance with his explanation of the term "of the Universal Self" (viśvātmanaḥ), it does not constitute a fault; so, enough of this prolixity.

This applies to those endowed with creative intuition (*pratibhā*), for those devoid of it have no authority here. Alternatively, the word *sarva* alone denotes creation; however, by means of this [word *eka*], its delimitation is effected through the state of being a conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) relevant to the present context. || 12 ||
Now, he provides the introduction to the thirteenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). This is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction, he presents the verse and explains it with the words "meyam" (the object of knowledge).
Here is the commentary:
He provides an introductory commentary (*avataraṇikā*) in order to explain the verse, beginning with the words "Śrīmat": "The Adhiṣṭhātṛ" means the Impeller;

the liberated one identifies with that very [Impeller] as his own Self. Consequently, what is an object of knowledge (*prameya*) for the universe is also mine, and what is an object of knowledge for me is also for the universe; and this is the object of knowledge.

In this manner, even other objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are part of my very own body; thus, through this sequence, the object of knowledge does not exclude itself from other objects of knowledge nor from the class of subjects (*pramātṛ*).
Consequently, everything attains the status of being an object of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), whose essence is a state of rest in the non-duality of a single flavor.
But for the bound soul, all of this is the reverse; thus, he rests solely in the differentiation of the single flavor. || 13 ||

Now, one might object: "The nature of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) has been examined in relation to the levels of Sadāśiva and Īśvara—the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*)—and regarding the bound subject (*paśupramātṛ*) in its fettered form;
but how is this [nature] in the case of Paramaśiva? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In every respect, however, Śiva is filled with the infinite flood of principles merged within him; he is a mass of consciousness and bliss, whose form is the supreme syllable.
Indeed, there is no discourse regarding objects of knowledge whatsoever concerning the Blessed One, the illustrious Supreme Śiva;
rather, he is immersed in—that is, he identifies with—the flood of reality (*tattvaugha*). This explains the meaning of the word "identifies" (*manyate*). Otherwise, [it would not be so].

The sense is that [liberation] is impossible because of being already liberated. Relying on this, he explains the verse with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*). "Of the universe" (*viśvasya*) means of the entire class of subjects (*pramātṛvarga*). By this, the two terms "the object of knowledge" (*meyam*) and "common" (*sādhāraṇam*) are explained. He explains the phrase "by non-difference from one's own self" (*svātmābhedena*).
"Having become my very limb" means: it has become my limb; "unretracted" means undivided. That which is repose within that non-duality which is of a single essence—that is its reality;
such is the state of this liberated one, the object of supreme awareness (*parāmarśa*).

"He approaches" (upaiti)—the sense is that this is because the notion of "I" is grasped everywhere. The phrase "just as Maheśvara" is a word of illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and has not been explained here due to its ease of understanding. He explains the remaining portion of the verse beginning with "baddhaḥ" (the bound one) with the words "of the bound one" (*baddhasya*). This...

The meaning is that the object of cognition (*prameya*) is both one's own and another's. "Contrary" means excluded from being both self-originated and other-originated; such a person is the bound soul (*baddha*). || 13 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fourteenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). This is clear.
Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the words "sarvathā" (in every way).
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

"In every way"— that is, in all its modes, by the very persistence of that which exists exactly as it is, and not by the attainment of a state of being otherwise; "therein"— in that Supreme Śiva— of the internal flood of principles (tattvaugha), beginning with Śiva...

In every respect, because it is dissolved there by resting solely in the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), that state is characterized by a singular wonder of one's own self— consisting of the bliss of resting in one’s own essence through the nature of pure awareness (*saṃvit-svabhāva*) and the essence of innate, unartificial self-reflection (*parāmarśa*).

Dense, uninterrupted, and identical in form with the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*), it is the embodied manifestation of the Blessed One who consists of the universe; it is the unconditioned, unsurpassed abode, eternally pure, and beyond all discourse concerning objects of cognition.
She is designated as having transcended all [worlds]. || 14 ||

[This refers to] the entire collection of principles (tattva) ending with the earth. He explains the second half [of the verse] by means of this causality, saying "that state" (sāvasthā). "That state" refers to the state previously mentioned. He explains the compound word beginning with "consciousness" (cit) by first providing its analysis, saying "awareness" (saṃvit). In that regard as well—

He explains the component "the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpatā*) with the words "by the very essence of awareness" (*saṃvitsvabhāvena*). He explains the component "bliss" (*ānanda*) with the words "one's own self" (*svātma*). Bliss is the form of resting within one's own self;
that is, the bliss of resting in one's own self (*svātmaviśrāntyānanda*), by means of which [is the state described]. This is the essential nature of the bliss of resting in one's own self.
He shows that it is "uncreated" (*akṛtrima*). Uncreated means not constructed because it lacks being established by external objects; for this very reason, it is natural—*svābhāvika*.

Likewise, it consists of reflective awareness (*parāmarśātmaka*), having the form of the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā-parāmarśa-rūpa*), which is the wonder of one's own self (*svātmacamatkāra*).

The "taste" (*āsvāda*) has its own self as its locus and its own self as its object; that which has this as its characteristic—that is, its essential nature—is [the state] by means of which [it is so described]. He explains the component "dense" (*ghana*) with the word "entirely one" (*ekaghana*). Here too, he provides a synonym with the phrase "having that form uninterrupted" (*avicchinnatadrūpā*).

She whose form is uninterrupted is [described as such]. He explains "having the body of the supreme syllable" (*paramākṣaravigraha*) as "possessing a body through the supreme syllable. By the supreme syllable—that is, by that which has a nature transcending all and is imperishable—she is "endowed with a body," meaning she possesses a physical form.
The meaning is "having the nature of the supreme immutable.

To establish the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) stated in the aphorism, he states "of the Lord" to express that this state is connected with Paramaśiva. [He is] "consisting of the universe"—

Of one who is filled with the fullness that overflows the universe, and thus possesses such an unconditioned, unsurpassed abode; of one who is eternally pure, meaning whose nature is eternal, pure light— and yet, it is a marvel, for he consists of the entire universe.
It is the state of the unconditioned, unsurpassed realm (*anavacchinnānuttaradhāmatva*). For there is no modification whatsoever of a whole by its own parts;

this is the resolution. That state in which the discourse regarding objects of knowledge (*prameya*) has dissolved is "the state where the discourse of knowable objects has dissolved" (*galitaprameyakathā*); therefore, it is transcendent to all, meaning it is of a nature that transcends the universe (*viśvottīrṇarūpa*).

"It is designated" [as such]. This is merely a designation; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that very [Self] itself becomes everything in every way, and yet does not become anything, because it is all-enduring. Thus, the point is: what kind of discourse regarding "relatedness," as indicated by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the Sūtra, could there possibly be? || 14 ||
Thus, he states the result of the subject matter described in the fourfold introduction:
"In this way, one who knows his own self as well as its right knowledge and action, and perceives them as they are desired, both knows and acts. (15)

"Thus" means: knowing the Self as having the nature of the Lord (īśvara), and knowing that within Him—though not distinct from Himself—there exist the powers of knowledge and action whose nature is mere sovereignty; such is this Self, and not as shown by the followers of Kaṇāda and others. And thus, knowledge and action do not exist as anything separate from Him.

Reflecting thus, one who is intent on the practice of immersion (samāveśa) knows and accomplishes whatever he desires with this very body; however, one who is not so intent is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) as long as the body exists, and upon its fall, becomes the Supreme Lord himself. || 15 ||
Now he provides the introduction to the fifteenth verse with the words "evam" (thus).
This is clear. Having thus provided the introduction and presented the verse, he explains it with the word "evam.
Here is the commentary (*ṭīkā*):

Thus he explains the word "sound" as "the form of the Lord. The word "self" (*ātman*) is explained by its own verbal root. He explains the word "of this" (*etasya*) as "and of that" (*tasya ca*); the meaning is "of that self. He explains the phrase "knowledge and action" (*jñānakriye*) as "non-distinct from itself" (*svāvyatirikte*), [existing] in the state of powers (*śaktibhāvena*).
The meaning is "because of being established. By this, it is indicated that the word *tathā* functions as a particle denoting conjunction (*samuccaya*).

He provides the explanation of the term *paśyan* as "knowing" (*jānan*). He then briefly restates the explanation already provided for the section ending with *paśyan*, beginning with the words "being thus" (*evaṃbhūtaḥ*), and so forth.

[The commentary] ends with "parāmṛśan". He explains the remaining portion of the verse, beginning with "yathepsitān", with the words "yat" and so forth. "Abhyāsa" (practice) refers to the immersion (*samāveśa*)—which consists in becoming one with the nature of the Supreme Lord; in that regard, it is "supreme."
"Ekaniṣṭhaḥ" means intent upon that [the Supreme Reality]. "Atatparaḥ" means one who, despite being a knower, is attached to external worldly activity.
"Tatpāte" means at the fall of the body. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the entire procedure. And this has been stated in the venerable Spandaśāsana:
Then his dharma is unconditioned, characterized by the nature of knowing and acting;
for he knows and performs everything that he desires.
Thus it is stated in this verse. || 15 ||

Although this meaning is established through one's own realization, the instruction of the lineage of gurus must be stated as its corroborative support; for the vision of the scripture has indeed been shown by means of the section on the traditional authority (āgama).
With the intention that, in this way, this [meaning] becomes firmly established through the guru, through the scripture, and from oneself, [the author speaks].
He demonstrates the lineage of the gurus: "Thus has this new path, easy to practice, been revealed by me; it was taught by the great gurus in the Śivadṛṣṭi treatise."
Therefore, one who places his foot upon this [ground], perceiving his own nature as the creator of the world and constantly entering into that which consists of Śiva-nature, attains perfection.
By our supreme preceptor, the venerable Śrī Somānanda,

in the treatise *Śivadṛṣṭi*, this [system]— being Abhinava, contained within all the secret scriptures, yet unknown due to its being concealed because of the [emphasis on] external and internal ritual conduct and breath-control— [was taught].
Now, he provides the introduction to the sixteenth verse: "of this meaning. Here, the commentary says:
"of this meaning"—that independent Supreme Lord alone am I.

Thus, for such a secret meaning—which, though established by one's own conviction (svapratyayasiddha), that is, established by one's own experience—is a corroborator, meaning it acts as a support. Now, one might object: "Is not the vision of the scriptures (śāstradṛṣṭi) also indeed applicable here? To this he says: "The scripture... [and so on].
He states the conclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*). "Thus"—that is, when the instruction of the lineage of gurus serves as a corroboration for this meaning (or, as the KSTS edition reads:
*when this meaning is corroborated*), the teacher, with this intention—that is, with this underlying purpose—demonstrates the succession of gurus.

He reveals [this]. How so? This is the meaning: it becomes firmly established through the guru, through the scripture, and from oneself. Having thus provided the introduction, he presents and explains the verse.

Regarding this, the commentary explains "by the great teachers" with the words "our [teachers]. In the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise, it is designated by the term *śivadṛṣṭi* because it serves as the cause for the manifestation of the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). This...

He explains [the word] "abhinava" (new/extraordinary) as "all. Regarding the phrase "because of being hidden" (*nighūḍhatvāt*): the meaning is that it is difficult for those devoid of intuition (*pratibhā*) to discern [it], because it is mentioned alongside other means [in those texts].
Now, one might ask: what is the nature of the secret character of those secret scriptures? For it is not...
Those who act in such a way would be seized by partiality. True;

however, in that case, there is no question of partiality at all, for they have merely stated that a certain class of pleasant objects should be cultivated for some specific reason. Indeed, those who have risen above worldly existence are entirely intent upon renunciation from enjoyments.
They do not even enjoy enjoyments that come to them spontaneously;

nor is it easy to maintain [the position] merely by being devoid of the slightest effort toward afflictions such as pride, for that very point has been brought here into clarity by removing the suspicion of the stains of opposing doctrines. Since this is so:
This matter is established through the scriptures, the teacher, and one's own conviction;
thus it is appropriate. For as long as the body persists, the cessation of experience is impossible;
furthermore, the instrument [of experience] must be relinquished from the perspective of ultimate reality.
"Having enjoyed worldly pleasures and abandoned the wandering of existence, I shall attain the supreme state"—
such a hope here would be fitting for one who possesses supreme devotion to Śambhu.

This is because it has been made an object of aspiration by Śīlabhaṭṭa, Nārāyaṇa, and others. Furthermore, the joy arising from that [work] would serve only to kindle supreme bliss for those who are awakened;
however, as for the unawakened, upon hearing it, they fall even more deeply into the abyss of sense-objects.
The statement that these [teachings] "will come to be" indicates their status as a great secret because they will be unsuitable for them to perceive;

it is not, however, intended out of partiality. As for those fools, seized by sense objects, who plunge into those scriptures without any qualification—those intent on deceiving themselves—[in them...]

Compassion must be exercised; however, toward one who does not listen, salutation should be offered from afar. If it is argued that if the path of bliss is easily accessible there, then it is indeed appropriate to show it to everyone, we say no; for while this may be so for those who are awakened, it is not so for those who are unawakened.
Because such a state of affairs does not exist: for example, a man standing at the edge of a chasm sees a jewel situated within the chasm at a short distance;
even though it is nearby, he does not leap and seize it out of fear of falling, but rather descends from there and climbs back up into the interior of the chasm.

Likewise, although the collection of objects described in the secret scriptures (*rahasya-śāstra*) as being worthy of cultivation (*sevyatva*) serves to kindle bliss, it should not be grasped by those who are incapable due to fear of the pitfalls of sense-objects; rather, they should instead be intent on effort for the sake of attaining that [bliss] through means such as tranquility (*śama*).

One's own self alone must be made the witness to one’s own capacity or incapacity, for otherwise the consequence would be self-deception. As for one who, being seized by a swoon, does not even experience his own fall, at that state the Blessed Lord alone is the refuge; enough with further elaboration.
But then, how is it that in those secret scriptures (*rahasya-śāstra*), the state of being worthy of salutation for those substances is explicitly stated without distinction? True.
Insofar as they serve to kindle bliss (*ānanda*), salutation toward them is indeed appropriate; however, as for their consumption...

This is indeed improper; just as a drop of Ganges water within a jar filled with impurities is unfit for drinking despite its inherent worthiness for veneration, so it is here— enough of this digression.
He states the reason to establish that it is easily accomplished (*sughaṭatva*) as taught in the Sūtra, beginning with the words "external and internal" (*bāhyāntara*).
External practice consists of sacrifice and so forth; internal practice consists of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth. "Easily accomplished" means easy to attain.
He explains the phrase "it was said" (*ucyate sma*) by saying "it was stated" (*uktaḥ*). [Objection: In that case, is this not [already] established by those very [Sūtras]?

The path has been described; to the question, "Why have you made this effort in vain? he replies with the words "that very same" (*sa eva*). The intention is that nothing new has been produced. Having explained the first half [of the verse], he explains the second half with the words "since it is thus" (*yata evam*). Therein, he explains the word "that" (*tat*) as follows:
Because of this—

therefore, in this context of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), causing his own awareness (*parāmarśa*) to rest upon that very object, he manifests his sovereignty characterized by universal agency.

When, having contemplated [this] with firmness, one reflects upon it, then by that mere reflection alone, one is indeed liberated while living (jīvanmukta), being none other than the Lord Śiva himself. As it has been said by the venerable Parameṣṭhin: "When the state of Śiva, which resides in all things, is known through a realization of firm nature..."
There is no purpose whatsoever to be served by ritual action or even by meditative cultivation.
"Once gold has been known, what is the use of further cultivation, practice, and so forth?
In every respect, its reality possesses a firmness equal to that of one's father, mother, and other such [dear ones]. (Śivadṛṣṭi).
Having contemplated this, if one enters [that state] incessantly...

He immerses either one or both of the body, the vital breath, and the intellect—along with everything else—into that very state; he attains incessantly various manifestations of power, culminating in the Great Manifestation (or, according to Kṣemarāja’s reading, the Supreme Manifestation). || 16 ||

Thus: he explains "in this way" (*evam*) as meaning "in the manner described"; he explains "here" (*atra*) as meaning "in the domain of the object of knowledge" (*prameyapade*), that is, in the matter to be determined. He explains "placing his foot" (*padaṃ nidadhat*) as meaning "resting his reflective awareness" (*parāmarśaṃ viśramayan*). [He explains] the word "the state of being the agent of becoming" (*bhavanakartṛtām*)...

He explains that sovereignty is characterized by being the creator of all. The phrase "having manifested it from the Self" is explained by its own verbal form (*nigadavyākhyātam*). In this context, he himself states something further for the sake of logical consistency and firmness: "consisting of the nature of Śiva," in order to fulfill the expectancy of the word *tat*.
Thus he explains the remaining fragment of the verse; the ellipsis is "he becomes Śiva himself.
Here he cites the statements from the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, beginning with "as it has been said. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes other statements found therein. And here:

Since the explanation has already been provided at the outset, no further effort is made here. He clarifies the intended meaning of the word *aniśam* with the words "if" (*yadi*). *Aniśam* means by way of a continuous flow;
*anyatamam* means one; *tat* means then; and *tāṃ tāṃ vibhūtim* means that particular collection of supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
As it has been said:
"From that [Supreme] arises the Bindu, from that the Nāda, from that the Rūpa, and from that the Rasa;
these proceed very swiftly as the agitators of embodied beings."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "In that case, would his state not remain merely intermediate? To this he says: "up to the limit of great sovereignty" (*mahāvibhūti-paryantām*). The meaning is that even if inferior supernatural powers (*kṣudrasiddhi*) manifest in the interim, in the end, he will surely attain the Great Accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*), which consists in identity with Supreme Śiva. || 16 ||

Now, if the entity called the self is indeed that very thing, then there would be no distinction between its recognition and non-recognition; for a seed does not fail to produce a sprout when all auxiliary conditions are complete simply because it was not recognized. Therefore, what [is the point]?

What is the insistence on the recognition of the Self? It is said: there are two kinds of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*): the external, such as the sprout and so forth, and that which consists of the essence of the wonder of resting in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), taking the form of joy and the like.
Of these, the former truly does not require recognition, whereas the latter certainly does require it.

Now, he provides the introduction to the seventeenth verse with the words "nanu" (but surely). That very thing—namely, if it is indeed the nature of Śiva—then there would be no distinction between the recognition and non-recognition of that reality whose essence is Śiva; for the seed [of such distinction] lies with the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Even if it is not recognized, why would a seed not produce a sprout when all auxiliary conditions such as water are present?

Indeed, even though it is not recognized by the cognizer—[for it has not been stated that a seed produces a sprout only after being recognized]—the seed certainly produces the sprout. In the same way, so too is the entity called the Self.

Even when not recognized, it is indeed the very form of Śiva. What insistence can there be on the recognition that "the Self is the Lord"? Even in the absence of recognition, the Self is certainly the Lord. He states the rebuttal: "It is said. The causal efficiency (arthakriyā) of external objects, such as seeds which are insentient in nature and consist of sprouts, is external.
