And [this consciousness] has as its essence the wonder of resting within the subject whose nature is "I," and it takes the form of pleasure and so forth; thus, there are two kinds of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). What you have said is true: therein—among those two—the first does not require recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). As for the second—causal efficiency in the form of pleasure and so forth— [The text continues: ...it depends upon recognition. For example, when one sees a jar for the first time, the causal efficiency consisting of the cognition of the jar occurs; however, the subsequent causal efficiency consisting of joy arises only through the power of recognition. Therefore, it is established that recognition is required for the second kind of causal efficiency. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "Even in the case of a jar, which is perceived by the senses, the activity of the agent is preceded by the recognition of the Self. (ĪPK 1.5.17) This means that even in the case of an object like a jar, which is grasped through the external senses, the activity of the agent is necessarily preceded by the recognition of the Self. This is because the activity of the agent consists in the manifestation of the object as "this," and such manifestation is impossible without the recognition of the Self. Therefore, it is established that recognition is the cause of all activity. Consequently, it is proven that recognition is the supreme means for attaining liberation. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "Since the world is pervaded by the light of the Lord, the manifestation of objects is always dependent upon Him. (ĪPK 1.5.20) This means that since the entire universe is permeated by the light of the Supreme Lord (*Īśvara*), the manifestation of all objects is always dependent upon Him. Therefore, it is established that the manifestation of objects is the very nature of the Lord. Consequently, the recognition of the Lord is the supreme means for attaining liberation. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "By the power of the grace of the Guru, the recognition of the Self arises in the disciple, who is purified by devotion. (ĪPK 1.5.21) This means that through the power of the Guru’s grace, the recognition of the Self arises in the disciple who is purified by devotion. Therefore, it is established that the Guru’s grace is the primary cause for the arising of recognition. Consequently, one should seek out a qualified Guru and strive to receive his grace. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "The recognition of the Self is the supreme means for attaining liberation; it is the very life-force of the scriptures. (ĪPK 1.5.22) This means that the recognition of the Self is the highest means for attaining liberation, and it is the very essence of all the sacred scriptures. Therefore, one should exert oneself in the practice of recognition. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "Even though the Self is eternally manifest, it is obscured by the veil of ignorance; recognition removes that veil. (ĪPK 1.5.23) This means that although the Self is eternally manifest, it is covered by the veil of ignorance (*avidyā*). Recognition removes this veil, whereby the Self shines forth in its own splendor. Therefore, it is established that recognition is the supreme means for attaining liberation. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "Recognition is the sudden flash of the innate power of consciousness, which is the very nature of the Self. (ĪPK 1.5.24) This means that recognition is the sudden flash of the innate power of consciousness, which is the very nature of the Self. Therefore, it is established that recognition is not something produced, but rather the very nature of the Self. Consequently, one should recognize the Self as one's own true nature. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "Through the recognition of the Self, all bonds are severed, and one attains the state of the Lord. (ĪPK 1.5.25) This means that through the recognition of the Self, all karmic bonds are severed, and one attains the state of the Supreme Lord (*Īśvara*). Therefore, it is established that recognition is the supreme means for attaining liberation. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "The recognition of the Self is the supreme secret; it is the heart of all the Tantras. (ĪPK 1.5.26) This means that the recognition of the Self is the most profound secret, and it is the core of all the Tantric scriptures. Therefore, one should keep this recognition hidden and practice it with great care. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "Even the gods, though they possess great powers, cannot attain liberation without the recognition of the Self. (ĪPK 1.5.27) This means that even the gods, despite their immense powers, cannot attain liberation without the recognition of the Self. Therefore, it is established that recognition is indispensable for liberation. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "The recognition of the Self is the supreme bliss; it is the end of all suffering. (ĪPK 1.5.28) This means that the recognition of the Self is the highest bliss and the cessation of all suffering. Therefore, one should strive to attain this recognition. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "By the recognition of the Self, one becomes the Lord of all; there is no other path to liberation. (ĪPK 1.5.29) This means that through the recognition of the Self, one becomes the sovereign of all, and there is no other way to reach liberation. Therefore, it is established that recognition is the sole path to liberation. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "The recognition of the Self is the supreme yoga; it is the essence of all spiritual practices. (ĪPK 1.5.30) This means that the recognition of the Self is the highest form of yoga and the very essence of all spiritual disciplines. Therefore, one should practice recognition as one's primary spiritual discipline. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "Even if one performs millions of rituals, without recognition there is no fruit. (ĪPK 1.5.31) This means that even if one performs millions of sacrificial rites, without the recognition of the Self, no spiritual fruit is obtained. Therefore, it is established that recognition is superior to all ritual actions. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "The recognition of the Self is the supreme knowledge; it is the eye that sees the truth. (ĪPK 1.5.32) This means that the recognition of the Self is the highest wisdom and the eye that perceives reality. Therefore, one should cultivate this recognition as one's primary knowledge. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "By the recognition of the Self, one transcends the cycle of birth and death; there is no other way. (ĪPK 1.5.33) This means that through the recognition of the Self, one transcends the cycle of saṃsāra, and there is no other method for doing so. Therefore, it is established that recognition is the supreme means for attaining liberation. Thus, the proof of recognition is complete. Furthermore, the following verse from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is cited: "The recognition of the Self is the supreme gift; it is the treasure of all beings. (ĪPK 1
Recognition is indeed required here;

and in this context, there is the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) consisting of the yoga of the manifestations of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), characterized by the attainment of both the supreme and the non-supreme, whose essence is the wonder of the realization "I am Maheśvara."

Thus, the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* (Recognition of the Lord) must necessarily be consulted here. Now, one might object: "The purposeful activity whose essence is repose in the subject has never been seen without recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), yet it is seen when that [recognition] is present;
how, then, has this been observed? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Just as the beloved of a slender woman, though standing near her, cannot provide pleasure because he remains unrecognized as such due to those various entreaties she makes— which make him appear like any other person—
so too is this Lord of the Universe, whose virtues go unnoticed by the world, even his own self.
This [recognition] has arisen as the recognition of that [Self], which is not sufficient for its own manifestation. || 17 ||

He demonstrates that very point with the words "here" (*iha*). Here—in this treatise known as the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*—the supreme accomplishment (*parasiddhi*), which is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), consists of the essence of such a wondrous experience (*camatkāra*) as: "I am Caitra," "I am Maitra," and "by the glance of the true Guru, I am indeed the Lord (*īśvara*) himself."
The manifestation of supreme accomplishment (*aparāsiddhivibhūtiḥ*) is the power capable of bringing the universe under control through creation and other such acts;

this is characterized by both [the aforementioned] aspects. Thus, in this unfailing purposeful action, I am indeed that very Lord (*īśvara*) who is well-known from the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other sources.

Thus, the recognition of the Lord (īśvarapratyabhijñāna) is indeed indispensable. He raises an objection again: "The purposeful efficacy (arthakriyā), whose essence is the wonder of resting in the subject, is not seen without recognition; yet when recognition exists, that purposeful efficacy [is seen]."
Anticipating the objection, "Where has it been observed that they have been seen?", he says "by those various [means]":
the beloved—the desired hero—is situated on another island; by those various means—such as the dispatching of female messengers and prayers to the deities—in which...

Even though he had gathered in one pavilion at a great festival consisting of a vast assembly of people and stood in his presence— having been long desired and having by the turn of fate come to stand near him—
he [did not recognize him] as before, due to the excellence of his beauty and other qualities [only perceived] through the mouth of the female messenger.

Though heard as "so it is," he was not thus fully recognized— meaning he was not recognized as being that very person due to his similarity with other people nearby; thus, this Self (ātman) is not fit for the world— that is, for the class of subjects (pramātṛ)— to sport with, because his qualities have not been observed in such a manner.
Even though residing within, he whose characteristics as the Lord are unrecognized,
and whose own innate majesty as the Self is unrecognized,
possesses such qualities as being the creator of the universe, omniscience, fullness, eternity, and omnipresence.

One's own self, whose nature is the notion of "I," is the Lord of the Universe; yet, although this self manifests as "I" to people—that is, to the world—it is not capable, nor is it able, of its own inherent majesty consisting of the recognition that "I am the Lord. That—
Therefore, this very one— established by the experience of one's own self which is always manifest—
is that very Lord who am "I," just as a loving woman whose passion has increased upon hearing of the virtues of her beloved.
Desiring nothing more than the sight of him as her supreme goal,
she spent day and night with a heart beyond control, offering prayers to the deities, dispatching female messengers, and communicating the state of her own being through love letters.

When her creeper-like body was becoming emaciated due to separation, she remained there; then, by the power of her vow, as her beloved— who had been standing nearby— was unexpectedly beheld, he attained the state of being touched by those various extraordinary excellences that had previously been common to all people.
Even when the sight of one’s beloved is accomplished, it does not fill the heart; likewise,
although the Lord of the Universe is constantly manifest within one's own self, that manifestation does not bestow fullness upon the heart, because that Self too—

Because he was not touched by the excellence of supreme sovereignty— characterized by unimpeded power such as omniscience and agency— he came to have a condition identical to that of a manifest pot or similar object.
However, when [he is touched] through the words of a messenger, or through the recognition of his specific characteristics, or through some other means...
When one touches those elevations by making them penetrate the heart, then at that very moment, by the very logic of the "wonderfully blossoming" (adbhutaphulla), one attains a certain plenitude;
yet, through the enjoyment [of these states], one also finds intervals of repose within the aesthetic flavor (rasa). It is just so within the Self.
When, through the word of the Guru, or through the recognition of the powers characterized by knowledge and action, there arises an internal realization of the excellence of supreme sovereignty,
then "recognition" (pratyabhijñā) has dawned— [this being taught] by Him who, out of compassion, assumed a human form.
It was instructed by the Supreme Lord. Then, by the power of that vow made for the sake of the slender maiden—
since her beloved was standing nearby and had been gazed upon without hesitation— of that lover...

When he was rendered common to the people standing near him by those who, through the excellence of his superior qualities such as beauty of form and so forth, failed to reach the path of heartfelt recognition that "this is indeed he," then— even though [he was present]— it was as if he were not.

Even though she has obtained the sight of her beloved, the heart of that slender woman is not filled. This is because, although the Lord of the Universe is constantly manifest within one's own self, for such a person, that manifestation [of the beloved] is merely [the manifestation] of their own self.
The manifestation of the Self as the Lord of All does not bring fullness to the heart; therefore, even that Self of the person— which is perceived by the person as "I"— is like a beloved,
for it possesses the supreme lordly nature characterized by unimpeded powers such as omniscience.
The meaning is that because he was not grasped through the process of *karṣa*-yoga, his state became identical to that of an appearing jar or similar object;
although he is himself conscious, due to the lack of self-recognition (*apratyabhijñāna*), he has become like an insentient thing.
By means of that reflective awareness (*amarśa*) according to the maxim of the "wonderfully blossomed," [he attains] some...
One attains a fullness that is beyond the range of words, just as a beloved woman recognizes her own beloved; through the perfected word of the primordial Guru,
there arises the recognition of the power of the Lord (īśvara-śakti), by which one becomes both identical with the universe and transcendent of it.
The thought "I am the Supreme Lord" gives rise to a sense of exaltation. At that time—
at that very moment— there occurs liberation while living (jīvanmukti), which consists of great bliss and is characterized by fullness.

But when one finds delight in the practice of immersion (samāveśa), the attainment of supernatural powers (vibhūti) occurs; thus, for such a person, recognition (pratyabhijñā) alone becomes the bestower of both higher and lower accomplishments. || 17 ||

This treatise, which is beneficial to all and yields great fruit, is an instigator characterized by the conviction of confidence produced through the recollection of its excellence— by virtue of its well-known lineage and the renown of its title.
In order to engage people through direct experience, he shows the conclusion by means of his father’s name:
"This Recognition of the Lord has been established by Utpaladeva, the son of Udayākara, for the sake of the effortless attainment of the goal by people. (18)

Liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*): for one who delights in the practice of immersion into the Great Lord who is their own self as recognized through *pratyabhijñā*, there is the attainment of sovereign powers (*vibhūti*) capable of bringing under control the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth; thus, it is precisely this recognition of one's own self as "I am the Lord" that constitutes [liberation].

She bestows the two types of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) that constitute the glory of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). As it has been said: "It is established, firmly established; there is nothing more wonderful than this. This great essence of the first [taste] is indeed born from the side-glance of the Teacher."
"Is she not dear? Is he not dear?
If this noble-minded person alone does not respond with his characteristic modulations of voice for all that, then what?
He shows that there is no restriction here; for,

according to the method stated in the commentary on the first sūtra, by the phrase "beneficial to all castes," the word *janasya* occurring in this sūtra is, by implication, generally [understood to mean everyone].
The explanation has been shown. Regarding the phrase "yielding great fruit"—
meaning that which bestows the great fruit consisting of the higher and lower accomplishments (*siddhi*) characterized by the glory of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*)—
this is the explanation of the term *ayatnasiddhyartham* found within the aphorism.
This has been shown by way of the sense. By the two words "this treatise" (*idaṃ śāstram*), the explanation of the two words "this recognition of the Lord" (*iyam īśvarapratyabhijñā*) is shown.
And by the two words "through the connection with a well-known sequence" (*prasiddhānvayayogena*) and "by means of the renown of the name" (*nāmadheya-prasiddhyā*).

The commentary on the two words "by Utpala, son of Udayākara" is as follows: furthermore, by the mention of "son of Udayākara," which establishes his lineage, and "by Utpala," which establishes his own name, there arises—
through the medium of recollecting the excellence of both his lineage and his own name— a [particular state of mind].

Because of the application of an impelling consciousness— characterized by confidence consisting of the conviction that "this is exactly so and not otherwise"— toward the scripture taught by himself in order to incite people; [this is] consciousness.
O people, in order to engage everyone in the practice of the scripture, he concludes with the words "of people" (*janasya*).
By saying "of any living being whatsoever," there is no consideration of caste or other such factors here;
thus, its universal benefit is stated. This is so that the supreme and non-supreme accomplishments may be attained without effort.
Regarding its great fruitfulness: our supreme teacher, the illustrious Utpaladeva, son of Udayākara, composed this treatise;
thus, by virtue of his renown, people engage with it—therefore, he has been graced by means of this engagement.
"It exists"—this is the designation of both names.
"This" refers to that which has been brought to the heart through hundreds of logical arguments. Thus all is auspicious. (18) [Total from the beginning: 190]
This concise and unerring commentary on the *Pratyabhijñā*, which investigates the meaning of the aphorisms, has been composed by Abhinavagupta.

By the words "of any living being whatsoever who is being born," and so forth, it is stated that this scripture is beneficial to all, since there is no requirement of specific castes such as Brahmins, nor even any requirement of eligibility (*adhikāra*) therein, as indicated by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).
It has been shown that by hearing this scripture, the accomplishment of both the supreme and the non-supreme forms occurs without effort;
thus, its great fruitfulness is demonstrated. Furthermore, since people are motivated by what is well-known, it is through the means of such motivation that people are graced.

This is the designation of both names. By the word "this," which indicates the state of being an object of one's own realization, it is shown that this *Śrīmad-Īśvarapratyabhijñā* has been brought to the hearts of people through hundreds of reasoned arguments. Thus, may there be auspiciousness (*śiva*). Because [the world] has emanated from Śiva, [it is identical with Him].

It is auspicious (*śiva*) because it is the cause for attaining Śiva and because it is itself of the nature of Śiva; it is the blessing that bestows the two types of accomplishments, both higher and lower, consisting of the glory of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). 18.
"This" means established through one's own direct experience; furthermore, "this" refers to that which is perceived by people as being established through their own direct experience,
having been somehow attained by the teacher named the illustrious Abhinavagupta, and so forth.
The *Utpalaparimala* is a thorough investigation of the meaning of the concluding sūtras;
illuminating the meaning of those sūtras in its entirety, it is a concise [treatise] within the work known as the *Pratyabhijñā*,
revealing the whole meaning of that scripture in summary form, and it is unbreakable.

Because it could not be refuted by the tenets of the Buddhists and others, the commentary— a path that illuminates through its clarity— was composed for that Purāṇa which is both ancient and renowned, and which was [previously] kept secret.
That heart itself flashes forth as the unsurpassed (anuttara) through the surges of its own supreme delight.

Thus, according to his own stated method, [the work] was composed— meaning expanded— by means of the flashing forth of his own heart, which consists of the Unsurpassed (Anuttara). By the word "brief" (*laghvī*), he further indicated by his own mouth that there will be some more extensive commentary (*vimarśinī*) on the Pratyabhijñā-śāstra.
The meanings of sentences, means of valid cognition, words, categories, and the true scriptures attain their utility for one’s own self through this own treatise;
yet the earthly and watery tastes do not [serve] the nourishment of crops [without rain].
Who else here is capable of joining [anything] except for the sun alone?
What can be said of that ignorant person who, without knowing himself, desires to discern another?
To him, when asked "Who are you?", what answer could he possibly give?

Thus ends the chapter on the Compendium of Principles (*tattvasaṅgraha*) in the *Iśvarapratyabhijñā* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary titled *Vimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The venerable Īśvarapratyabhijñā is completed.
The *vākya* is the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra; the *pramāṇa* is the Nyāya-śāstra;

the *sadāgamās* are the Āgamas proclaimed by Śiva; and from this *suśāstra* called Pratyabhijñā—which is excellent, supreme among all, and established through one's own direct experience—from this [source].

"From the scripture, they attain their own self-benefit"—that is, they attain the purpose consisting of the reflective awareness of one's own self in the form of Maheśvara; "attain" means they reach it in close proximity. Without this scripture, other scriptures such as those on grammar (*vākya*) and so forth are merely...

They do not themselves come to be of use to their own selves. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: the juices situated on the earth—that is, those consisting of water—which have become depleted due to the summer heat, [the sun] draws within its circle of rays and, through its initial rays that rain down, makes them available for the nourishment of the crops.
Who else besides Arka is capable of yoking [the senses]?
[I yoke] the self,
which manifests as "I," into its nature as the Lord through the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the powers consisting of knowledge and action.
Not having mastered other treatises such as those on grammar and logic, he desires to discern [the truth];
thus, like one possessed by a spirit, being possessed by the *māyā* that conceals one's true nature, he asks: "Who are you?"

What is there to be said? The meaning is that there is nothing at all. Just as Caitra, possessed by a spirit, does not recognize his own name—which was designated to him by his father and others—so too one possessed by the Great Māyā does not recognize his own primordial, established state of being the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
The meaning is that he does not know.
Thus ends the commentary *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*.
